papers.abstract: Generative Pre-Training (GPT) represents a profound milestone in natural language processing, serving as the foundation for most of today's state-of-the-art large language models. By casting diverse understanding and generation problems into a shared token representation, GPT enables a single architecture and unified optimization loop to master heterogeneous tasks across massive corpora, giving rise to powerful foundation models for natural language. In contrast, 4D spatiotemporal vision lacks a common representational protocol: perception (such as depth and camera estimation) and generation are either handled by separate one-way pipelines or bolted together from unaligned single-modality spaces. In this work, we introduce WorldLatent, a framework that formulates a unified 4D latent space as a common protocol for both world perception and generation. Rather than relying on fragmented, task-specific models or stacked single-modality representations, our framework proposes a multimodal VAE architecture that compresses and fuses complex 4D visual appearance, geometry, and dynamics into a single structured latent representation. Within this formulation, perception and generation operate as complementary denoising processes over the same latent space, enabling one generative model to learn both capabilities simultaneously within a single training loop. Experiments across representative 4D benchmarks verify that our fused latent protocol achieves specialist-level zero-shot 4D perception, coherent 4D generation, and controllable editing from a single model. By demonstrating that diverse 4D tasks can be seamlessly unified under a shared representational protocol, our work provides a scalable foundation for general-purpose 4D spatial intelligence.
authors: Jingxi Chen, Yujia Chen, Cornelia Fermuller, Yiannis Aloimonos, Wen-Sheng Chu, Du Tran
bullets: Addresses the lack of a common representation for 4D spatiotemporal vision.
Uses a multimodal VAE to fuse visual appearance, geometry, and dynamics into one structured latent representation.
Frames perception and generation as complementary denoising processes over the same latent space.
A single model achieves specialist-level zero-shot 4D perception, coherent generation, and controllable editing across representative benchmarks.
Positions the shared latent protocol as a foundation for general-purpose 4D spatial intelligence.

figures.caption: Figure 2. WorldLatent training pipeline. (a) WorldVAE training: Multiple 4D spatiotemporal modalities, including monocular RGB video, depth maps, and camera Plücker coordinates (ray direction d and moment m), are compressed via modality-specific encoders (E1– E4) and fused by a Dense Prediction Transformer (DPT) into a unified latent bottleneck, z4d (WorldLatent). Modality-specific decoders (D1–D4) then reconstruct the original modalities from this shared latent space. (b) Any-to-4D generative modeling: With the WorldVAE frozen, a unified diffusion model is trained within the learned latent space. It takes Gaussian noise, text prompts (Ctext), and partial or empty 4D latents c4d(S) (e.g., S = ∅ for text-to-4D generation, RGB-only for perception, or depth-only for editing) to synthesize the full 4D latent z4d. Finally, the frozen decoders (D1–D4) map z4d back into temporally coherent video, 3D geometry, and camera trajectories.

papers.abstract: World action model (WAM) is a promising paradigm for visuomotor control by jointly modeling world dynamics and actions. Notably, existing WAMs often rely on large generative models and iterative sampling which incur substantial latency for action generation, limiting real-time deployment. In particular, there are two root causes of inefficiency in conventional flow matching or diffusion based action models in WAMs: 1) transporting uninformative Gaussian noise into precise actions necessitating multiple ODE steps, and 2) repeatedly injecting task context through expensive cross-attention modules. Our key insight is that jointly learning and aligning the source and action manifolds streamlines the transport between them, substantially accelerating action generation. Building on this insight, we introduce VITA-WAM, a WAM architecture with manifold-aligned flow-matching (VITA flow matching) that directly transports latent observation representations containing visual, language, and proprioceptive information into latent actions. More specifically, a flow latent alignment (FLA) mechanism is employed to facilitate manifold alignment between latent observation and action representations, enabling accurate generation with few ODE steps. The resulting architecture also eliminates costly attention for observation conditioning during repeated denoising steps. Notably, with a single ODE step, VITA-WAM outperforms 10-step FastWAM by 21.47 pp on LIBERO-Plus and by 1.65 pp on LIBERO, achieving these gains through the FLA objective without distillation, while inferring at 55.67~ms latency, a $2.10\times$ speedup compared to FastWAM.
authors: Boqi Zhao, Dechen Gao, Hanchu Zhou, Hang Wang, Junshan Zhang
bullets: Addresses the latency of conventional diffusion- or flow-matching-based world-action models caused by noise-to-action transport and repeated cross-attention.
Directly transports latent visual, language, and proprioceptive observation representations into latent actions.
Uses flow latent alignment (FLA) to align observation and action manifolds and support accurate generation with few ODE steps.
With one ODE step, it outperforms 10-step FastWAM by 21.47 percentage points on LIBERO-Plus and 1.65 points on LIBERO.
Achieves 55.67 ms inference latency, a 2.10× speedup over FastWAM, without distillation.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Illustration of VITA-WAM architecture. 1) During training (top), a Q-Former fuses visual, language and proprioception into a latent source z0, where the visual signal is the output of the video DiT supervised by video flow matching. The action encoder maps the action chunk into a target latent z1. The source and target representations are jointly learned with VITA flow matching through FM, AE and FLA objectives, with FLA supervising the action chunk decoded from the ODE-generated latent. 2) During inference (bottom), a single video DiT forward pass extracts current-observation features, which are fused with language and proprioception by the Q-Former to construct the source latent z0. The action DiT then performs conditioningfree ODE integration starting from z0 to generate the action latent ẑ1, which is decoded into an action chunk.

Figure 6: Training and inference architecture of VITA-WAM (visual conditioning). The Q-Former constructs the source latent from visual observations, language, and proprioception. During ODE integration, the action DiT additionally uses mixed video–action attention with cached video K/V. The action decoder converts the generated latent into an action chunk.

Figure 1: Comparing conventional flow matching (left) vs. VITA flow matching (right). Conventional flow matching learns to transport Gaussian noise to the target manifold, necessitating multiple ODE steps. VITA flow matching (right) jointly learns and aligns the source and target representation manifolds with the Flow Latent Alignment (FLA) mechanism, thus enabling generation with simplified transport paths and fewer ODE steps. VITA-WAM employs VITA flow matching, significantly improving the efficiency of WAM action generation.

papers.abstract: Robotic manipulation policies can improve action prediction by anticipating how objects move and how their spatial relationships change. World Action Models (WAMs) learn to predict future visual observations, but their training objectives typically leave the underlying 3D geometric transitions implicit. To alleviate this problem, we introduce Foresight Forcing ($\mathcal{F}^{2}$), a WAM that learns a spatial transition representation from changes in a pretrained 3D feature space. During training, a frozen 3D foundation model extracts patch-wise feature differences from aligned current and future observations that provide dense supervision for geometry-aware feature transitions. We distill these targets into spatial transition queries, which are progressively refined from the current observation, language instruction, and proprioceptive state, and use them alongside current visual features to generate actions. At deployment, the policy predicts the queries without future observations or the 3D teacher. Experiments on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, and RoboTwin2.0 demonstrate strong manipulation performance and improved robustness, including 95.01% average success on RoboTwin2.0 Full. On six real-world manipulation tasks, $\mathcal{F}^{2}$ achieves a mean task score of 85.8%.
authors: Mishuo Han, Zhixuan Liang, Zhaoyuan Wan, Wendi Chen, Jiarui Chen, Xinkai Wang, Yue Ma, Yu Zhou, Junting Chen, Yao Mu, Jun Lv, Chuan Wen, Cewu Lu

Uses a frozen pretrained 3D model to extract dense patch-wise feature differences between current and future observations.

At deployment, predicts the transition queries without future observations or the 3D teacher.
Shows strong performance across LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, and RoboTwin2.0, plus a mean task score of 85.8% on six real-world tasks.

papers.abstract: World models facilitate planning and control in robotic manipulation by enabling agents to anticipate the consequences of their actions. However, they typically rely on action-labelled interaction data that is costly to acquire and difficult to scale. These models are also often tied to the specific embodiment they were trained on, limiting transferability to previously unseen robot morphologies. We introduce a 3D latent-action world model that learns continuous action representations directly from point-cloud observations of retargeted human manipulation demonstrations. A contrastive objective is used to encourage consistent representations of motion across embodiments. The resulting unified latent action space serves directly as the search space for model-predictive control, where sampled latent actions condition particle-based future predictions. Executable robot commands are then recovered from the predicted geometric motion without requiring an embodiment-specific action decoder. Through extensive evaluations, we demonstrate that the learned latent actions exhibit controllable and compositional motion, transfer to unseen robot embodiments, and support zero-shot manipulation with unseen gripper geometries. Following task-agnostic adaptation, our model achieves 90%, 92%, and 60% success on reaching, grasping, and placing, respectively, compared with DexWM's reported 72%, 58%, and 28%. Finally, we demonstrate zero-shot real-world manipulation with an unseen dexterous hand, achieving an 86% success rate across 50 trials on five diverse tasks involving pushing, grasping, and lifting everyday objects. These results highlight the potential of geometry-grounded latent actions as a unified, transferable interface for world-model-based robotic manipulation. Project materials, including demonstration videos and source code, are available at https://vinaymohan0409.github.io/DexLatentWorld/.
authors: Vinay Udit Mohan, Xuchuan Huang, Rolandos Alexandros Potamias
bullets: Addresses the high cost of action-labelled data and poor transferability of embodiment-specific world models.

Uses latent actions directly for model-predictive control with particle-based future prediction; executable commands are recovered from predicted geometric motion.
Reports 90%, 92%, and 60% success on reaching, grasping, and placing, respectively, and 86% success across 50 real-world trials on five tasks with an unseen dexterous hand.
Demonstrates controllable, compositional, and transferable motion, including zero-shot manipulation with unseen gripper geometries.

papers.title: DexLatentWorld: 3D Cross-Embodiment Latent Action World Models for Zero-Shot Robotic Manipulation

papers.abstract: Large and diverse video sources, such as egocentric human video and heterogeneous robot recordings, carry rich dynamics but come either without actions or without a shared action space. Latent action models (LAMs) can recover these dynamics, but they train their inverse- and forward-dynamics models (IDM, FDM) from scratch, trading off pixel reconstruction against latent capacity and accuracy. Pretrained video world models natively generate high-fidelity dynamics, yet represent them densely, entangled across all layers. Viewing the world model as a LAM, we show that these dynamics can be extracted with minimal changes to the model. Native LAM operates one pretrained video diffusion transformer as both IDM and FDM, with learnable dynamics registers as the only causal bridge between the two, and trains on counterfactual temporal pairs that differ in motion alone, so that the registers distill a video's dynamics into a compact native latent action. We further propose a pretraining paradigm for vision-language-action (VLA) policies, Pretraining Actions from World models (PAWlicy), in which Native LAM serves as a dynamics teacher on large-scale video; unlike world action models, it never generates video. Native latent actions outperform existing LAMs on the LARY benchmark in both action classification and control regression, and replay the same motion on new robots, in new scenes, and from human hands to robots, although no transfer objective is used in training. With a 3.8B model, PAWlicy reaches a 93.6% average success rate on RoboTwin 2.0 trained with domain-randomized demonstrations, the highest among VLAs. On RoboDojo, it is competitive on every dimension we evaluate, and its Precision, evaluated by us, is on par with the leading leaderboard entries. On real robots, it improves over the pi_0.5 baseline on both tasks. Both stages use only public data and a publicly released world model.
authors: Qinyue Li, Weijie Qiao, Qingyi Tao, Zerui Gong, Zhe Yang, Quanzhou Li, Taolin Zhang, Jinglin He, Zhonghua Wu, Chen Change Loy
bullets: Addresses learning actions from diverse videos that lack actions or share no common action space.
Uses one pretrained video diffusion transformer as both inverse- and forward-dynamics models, connected by learnable dynamics registers.
Trains on counterfactual video pairs differing only in motion to distill compact latent actions without video generation.
Native latent actions outperform existing LAMs on LARY for action classification and control, and transfer motion across robots, scenes, and human-to-robot settings.
The PAWlicy pretraining paradigm achieves a 93.6% average success rate on RoboTwin 2.0 and improves over pi_0.5 on both evaluated real-robot tasks.

(b) In IDM mode, dynamics registers read the clean video through a read-only attention mask and are projected to the latent action â; on AgiBot World and DROID, a kinematic head grounds â in end-effector motion. (c) In FDM mode, the same DiT regenerates the future from v0 and â alone, with â inserted into the token sequence through the adapter MLPin, taking over the conditioning role of text, trained with its original flow-matching loss; both clips of a pair share the noise and diffusion time, so only â can explain their difference.

Sharing attention with the VLM, the latent action DiT reconstructs the past and predicts the future, and the action DiT conditions on it to generate actions. Figure 7 Counterfactual pairs prevent posterior collapse. A latent action is read in IDM mode from a source clip in which the left arm grasps the tissue (top) or from its still counterfactual, which holds the first frame (bottom), and the FDM regenerates the clip from the same start frame with shared prompt, noise, and seed. Circles mark the end pose of the arm. Trained for 2k steps without counterfactual pairs, the FDM reaches for the cup in both cases. This is posterior collapse: the FDM ignores the latent and hallucinates a reach for the cup from the first frame alone. With counterfactual pairs, the same 2k steps already keep the still latent still, although the moving latent still reaches for the cup. At 13k steps the generated end frames match the source in both cases.

papers.title: World Models as Native Latent Action Models
papers.tldr: A pretrained video world model can be minimally adapted into a native latent-action model that extracts transferable dynamics and improves vision-language-action policy training.

papers.abstract: In this paper, we show that visual diffusion models can learn to predict the next best move (NBM) in tasks requiring sequential reasoning and lookahead, without explicitly exploring future steps or exhaustive searching at inference. Previous work demonstrated that these models can generate complete solutions to geometric and reasoning problems. Here, we show that simple fine-tuning on visual state--NBM pairs enables a pretrained model to select actions whose value depends on consequences several steps ahead. Each move is predicted directly in image space from the current state, without an explicit symbolic representation or search procedure. Repeated NBM predictions then construct a solution one decision at a time. We demonstrate this capability on chess puzzles and tile-based pathfinding, and show that it extends to Connect Four, Go and billiards. In chess, the model predicts legal moves and finds the best move far more often than by recalling similar training positions, including piece sacrifices whose benefit emerges only through later tactical continuations. In pathfinding, it constructs shortest paths on uniform-cost maps and cost-optimal routes across terrain tiles with different traversal costs, choosing longer routes when they are cheaper overall. These costs are learned implicitly from examples, without numerical cost supervision. These results show that direct visual move prediction can support globally informed decisions and successful sequential problem solving.

papers.selection_reason: Demonstrates that visual diffusion models can learn to predict the next best move for sequential reasoning tasks, bridging the gap between video generation and decision-making/world modeling.
papers.title: Learning the Next Best Move with Visual Diffusion Models
papers.tldr: Visual diffusion models can learn to predict globally informed next moves directly from images, enabling sequential problem solving without explicit search or symbolic planning.

papers.abstract: Direct visual world models predict the effects of candidate action sequences without recursive latent rollout, yet they leave the temporal structure of action effects unspecified. We introduce Zhengrong (Zhengrong-PoleWM), a world model that decomposes a latent trajectory into an initial-condition anchor, a free response, and delayed responses to action innovations. Nonlinear networks map visual history and causal action prefixes to response coefficients. A shared bank of stable conjugate poles determines how each response evolves with elapsed time. This factorization preserves nonlinear interactions across actions, anchors predictions exactly at the initial state, prevents future actions from affecting earlier predictions, and yields bounded responses to finite control plans. We derive an exact re-anchoring identity that identifies the additional basis direction $\Psi_\kappa(s)$ needed to represent shifted trajectory tails. Across four offline image-goal control benchmarks (Cube, TwoRoom, PushT, and Reacher), Zhengrong-PoleWM achieves $90.83\% \pm 0.47\%$ macro-average success over two training seeds at epoch 20, exceeding the strongest baseline (QQWorld) by 6.08 percentage points. Selecting checkpoints by validation loss yields $91.21\% \pm 1.00\%$. In a controlled first-epoch Cube study without restart regularization, neural and pole response heads outperform a generic direct predictor by 20.67 and 23.34 percentage points, respectively. On an NVIDIA A100 GPU, median latency for a full 30-iteration cross-entropy method search ranges from 74 to 87 ms across the four tasks. The mean of these medians is 77.5 ms, a 15.8% latency reduction relative to Fast-LeWM and a $7.1\times$ speedup over autoregressive LeWM.

papers.title: Zhengrong: World Models with Pole-Based Action-Response Factorization for Direct Visual Planning

papers.abstract: Learning how actions change visual states is essential for prediction and decision-making in embodied tasks. Existing action-conditioned JEPA world models typically predict future representations at discrete observation intervals, leaving the temporal evolution of action effects implicit. We introduce ActField, a continuous-time JEPA world model that explicitly models latent state evolution through an action-conditioned vector field integrated over physical time. ActField separates action-independent evolution from action-induced changes, with the latter modulated by the latent context. A reference-conditioned representation and multi-step dynamics loss further support accurate long-horizon prediction. Together, these components provide a structured and temporally continuous formulation for predicting action-conditioned visual dynamics. Experiments across LIBERO, DROID, and BEHAVIOR demonstrate improved visual prediction fidelity and more accurate action-induced motion prediction over existing world models. Further evaluations on simulated and real-world manipulation tasks demonstrate the utility of ActField in improving downstream policy planning through VLM-guided action selection.

papers.abstract: 4D occupancy forecasting predicts the 3D semantic occupancy of a driving scene seconds ahead. Over a few seconds, the scene changes little while the vehicle moves, so most of the space ahead has already been seen. Sorting the future into unchanged, changed, and unseen space, we find that current camera-based world models fall short on the unchanged part: they fail to hold on to what they have already seen, rather than to forecast what will change. We therefore make what the model has seen its state. PersistWorld streams camera frames into a persistent 3D world state anchored in the scene, writing each frame once instead of rebuilding the state from past frames. The state is learned end to end with the forecast, and an evolver predicts it at any queried time along the ego trajectory. On Occ3D-nuScenes, PersistWorld raises the IoU of the best camera-based world model by 19 points at 1-3 s and by 18 to 24 points up to 8 s, while running more than twice as fast. Code and models: https://github.com/wangzian828/PersistWorld. Project page: https://wangzian828.github.io/PersistWorld
authors: ZiAn Wang, Tianyi Wang, Zhihao Chen, Manni Cui, Junkai Chen, ZhiJin Chen, Ruiqi Liu, Junfei Wu, Huanyu Zhang, Shu Wu

On Occ3D-nuScenes, improves the best camera-based baseline by 19 IoU points at 1–3 seconds and 18–24 points through 8 seconds.

papers.abstract: Scaling visuo-tactile policy learning is constrained by the high cost of real-world data collection and the difficulty of building realistic simulations. Generative models offer a scalable source of training data, yet useful demonstrations require plausible tactile feedback, temporal alignment with visual contact, and accurate actions. To this end, we present VeriTouch, a framework for generating and verifying synthetic visuo-tactile trajectories for policy learning. Conditioned on initial images and task instructions, our world model, VeriGen, jointly generates high-fidelity dual-view videos and realistic tactile sequences over complete manipulation trajectories. By integrating a dedicated tactile expert with a pretrained video model, it captures realistic visual details and tactile deformation dynamics through joint visuo-tactile modeling. Our multimodal verifier VeriEval then checks visual quality while focusing on tactile reliability, assessing tactile realism, contact-force plausibility, and temporal alignment between visible contact and tactile signals, thereby directly filtering out unreliable sequences. Finally, our inverse dynamics model, VeriIDM, combines global scene information from both camera views with fine-grained gripper details and motion across neighboring frames to extract actions from verified videos. Experiments on five real-world tasks show that synthetic data improves all four evaluated policies, with further scaling synthetic trajectories substantially boosting policy performance without additional real-world data collection.
authors: Shuxun Wang, Xiaonan Jiang, Zhaoyu Wang, Ziyuan Chu, Xihang Yue, Pengfei Liu, Haodong Zhu, Shiqi Liu, Mingzhi Zheng, Liang Su, Linchao Zhu
bullets: Addresses the cost of real-world data and limited realism in visuo-tactile simulation.

VeriIDM infers actions from verified videos using scene context, gripper details, and frame-to-frame motion.
Across five real-world tasks, synthetic data improved all four evaluated policies, with more trajectories yielding further gains.

papers.abstract: Automated verification of industrial assembly processes remains a challenging problem due to substantial visual variability, limited availability of labeled defect data, and the fine-grained nature of many assembly errors. Existing approaches often rely on object detection, CAD models, or supervised classification pipelines, which can struggle to generalize across changing products and assembly configurations. In this work, we propose a novel self-supervised assembly verification framework based on Joint Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs). Starting from the JEPA-based world model LeWorldModel, we investigate how the architecture must be adapted to verify the correctness of fine-grained assembly operations. To this end, we formulate assembly verification as a predictive world modeling task operating on before-and-after observations of assembly processes. Experimental results on industrial assembly tasks demonstrate that the proposed approach reliably detects both fine-grained incorrect assembly states and action-state mismatches, achieving an AUROC of 86.9% on a newly introduced assembly verification dataset. These results indicate that JEPA-based predictive representations constitute a promising foundation for robust and data-efficient industrial assembly verification.
bullets: Addresses visual variability, scarce labeled defect data, and subtle assembly errors.
Frames verification as predicting the resulting assembly state from before-and-after process observations.
Adapts the LeWorldModel JEPA architecture for fine-grained assembly verification.
Detects incorrect assembly states and mismatches between actions and resulting states.
Reports 86.9% AUROC, indicating promise for data-efficient industrial verification.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Overview of the LeWorldModel architecture [10], including the encoder, action-conditioned predictor, and SIGReg regularization of the latent representations.

Fig. 3. Overview of the proposed Assembly-JEPA architecture. Images captured before and after an assembly step are encoded into patch-level representations using a shared encoder. A difference map is computed from the pre- and post-action patch embeddings to localize the assembly-relevant region, from which a subset of embeddings is extracted and processed by an action-conditioned predictor. To encourage action-aware representations, an auxiliary inverse action prediction objective is applied to the latent differences between pre- and post-action embeddings. Verification is performed by comparing the predicted postaction representation with the observed representation of the post-action image.

On the modified CLEVR-Change dataset, the model achieves a near-perfect AUROC of 99.5%, with almost complete separation between positive and negative samples. The substantially higher performance on CLEVR-Change can be attributed to the more pronounced visual state changes present in the dataset, whereas the proposed assembly benchmark requires distinguishing highly localized and visually subtle assembly transitions. papers.abstract: Egocentric human manipulation data offer a scalable resource for training dexterous robot policies. However, how effectively robots can learn and benefit from these data remains unclear due to the embodiment gap between humans and robots. We present EgoStudy, a systematic, controlled study of egocentric data for robot learning. Holding the robot dataset fixed, we vary the scale and diversity of egocentric data, data processing strategies, and co-training configurations. We investigate three questions: (1) Which data processing and pretraining choices most effectively exploit egocentric data? (2) Which components of robot action prediction benefit most from scaling these data? (3) How do scaling effects differ between vision-language-action models (VLAs) and world-action models (WAMs)? Our experiments yield three main findings. First, data diversity, alignment between trajectories, and detailed language annotations are key factors in effective transfer. Second, scaling egocentric data yields larger gains in predicting end-effector translation than in predicting fine-grained finger movements. Third, WAMs perform better when egocentric data are limited, whereas VLAs exhibit greater gains as the amount of egocentric data increases. Together, these findings provide practical guidance on processing and using egocentric data to train VLAs and WAMs, while clarifying the benefits and limitations of scaling these data.
authors: Puzhen Yuan, Yanjiang Guo, Yichen Liu, Xiang Zhu, Qingzhou Lu, Chenxin Liu, Tun Ban, Haodong Yan, Zhide Zhong, Jianyu Chen
bullets: Egocentric data transfer improves with greater diversity, trajectory alignment, and detailed language annotations.
Scaling primarily benefits end-effector translation prediction rather than fine-grained finger movement.
WAMs perform better with limited egocentric data, while VLAs gain more as egocentric data scale increases.
The study offers practical guidance for processing and co-training egocentric and robot data.

figures.caption: Figure 5. Which data processing and co-training designs improve transfer? Complete episodes, detailed captions, and the dataset diversity yield lower wrist translation error on both robot holdouts for both model families. This indicates that data diversity and alignment between trajectories and detailed language annotations are key factors in effective transfer. Moreover, fixed-step sampling yields lower error for the VLA, and event-level sampling yields lower error for the WAM.

Figure 7. Which action components benefit most from scaling egocentric data? We measure mean squared error (MSE) separately for wrist translation, wrist rotation, and fingertip pose on high-quality, held-out robot trajectories. Across both robot domains and model families, wrist translation MSE generally decreases as egocentric data scale, while wrist rotation and fingertip pose errors show no consistent decline. We hypothesize that due to human–robot embodiment gap and errors in estimating actions limit transfer primarily to large-scale motions such as wrist translation, with less benefit for the finger movements and wrist rotations.

Figure 4. Does scaling egocentric data improve robot learning? We pretrain the VLA (left) and WAM (right) with 1%, 3%, 10%, 30%, and 100% of the egocentric human data while keeping robot training exposure and the optimization budget fixed. We evaluate wrist translation MSE on held-out trajectories from Bimanual XHand and RoboCasa-GR1. All four model–domain pairs show a consistent downward trend, indicating effective human-to-robot transfer in EgoStudy.

Figure 6. Do pretraining gains carry over to robot control? RoboCasa-GR1 task success increases after posttraining for both model families, consistent with the decrease in pretraining validation loss. Gray dashed lines mark the corresponding baselines without pretraining.

Figure 9. How does backbone choice affect scaling gains between VLA and WAM? The wrist translation error decreases to the same extent across different VLAs, indicating that the 4B backbone is already capable of effectively extracting features shared between the egocentric and robot data. When the backbone of WAM is changed to 5B, its human-to-robot capability declines indicating that WAM relies more heavily on a powerful video backbone to assimilate egocentric data.

Figure 8. How do VLA and WAM visual features change with scale? As egocentric data scale, relative separation R between human and robot features decreases in both robot domains for the VLA but shows no consistent decrease across the WAM layers examined. We hypothesize that human and robot features align more closely in our VLA because it only needs to output actions in a shared action space. Our WAM must also predict future video, which may encourage it to retain visual differences between human and robot hands.

papers.abstract: Navigation systems in colonoscopy are advancing from guiding the endoscopist to steering the scope autonomously. Since an incorrect motion can injure the patient, developing and evaluating these systems calls for a world model of colonoscopy. Such a model must follow a commanded scope motion, keep the colon anatomy consistent, and show lesions and procedural events. Yet camera-controlled generators trained on general scenes lose the colon's structure under motion, and endoscopic generators offer no camera control. We present ColonoWorld, a colonoscopy world model conditioned on a camera trajectory and a coarse 3D tube of the colon, trained on in vivo videos. From a whole-colon tube, it generates a full cecum-to-rectum procedure, even for unseen colon shapes. It also places polyps, instruments, and irrigation at specified locations and times. ColonoWorld outperforms state-of-the-art video generators, reducing camera trajectory error by 32% and FVD by 29%. Our code and annotations will be released at https://aidaslab.github.io/ColonoWorld.

papers.abstract: Distilling localization knowledge into compact detection transformers (DETRs) requires consistent teacher-student query correspondence across decoder layers. However, in DETRs with encoder-based query selection, the teacher and student select top-K proposals independently. Same-rank queries can originate from different spatial locations and correspond to different objects, making rank-based layer-wise supervision unreliable. To address this problem, we propose Trajectory-Aligned Encoder-Decoder Distillation (TAED), a framework for knowledge transfer between DETRs of different capacities. Encoder feature distillation matches normalized multi-scale features to strengthen student representations and increase the number of teacher-student query pairs from the same encoder locations. Source-indexed query alignment pairs native queries from the same encoder locations and retains pairs associated with the same object for which the teacher provides reliable and more accurate final localization than the student. Trajectory-aligned localization distillation maintains these correspondences and uses teacher proposals and corresponding decoder-layer box predictions to guide student refinement, without introducing additional queries. On COCO, TAED improves DINO-R18 and two-stage Deformable DETR-R18 by 2.5 and 1.7 AP, respectively. Further gains on D-FINE and ECDet demonstrate applicability to recent real-time DETRs at no additional inference cost.

Transfers teacher proposal and decoder-layer box trajectories to guide student refinement without adding queries.
Improves DINO-R18 by 2.5 AP and two-stage Deformable DETR-R18 by 1.7 AP on COCO; also applies to D-FINE and ECDet without extra inference cost.

papers.abstract: Multi-robot embodied systems are typically designed to collaborate by coordinating actions, sharing trajectories, or learning joint policies. We ask a complementary question: can collaboration emerge before decision-making, by first building a shared understanding of the environment? We introduce Shared Environmental Understanding, a policy-agnostic representation that aggregates partial egocentric observations from multiple robots into a shared latent world model. This shifts collaboration from the policy space to the representation space, enabling decentralized decision-making with shared environmental context. To this end, we propose Shared Environment Encoding and Retrieval (SEER), a framework that organizes multi-robot observations into a shared memory, retrieves relevant context via spatio-temporal similarity, and encodes it using a predictive latent world model. The resulting representations are injected into downstream navigation agents as tokens. Experimental results demonstrate that SEER captures action-relevant environmental structure and consistently improves navigation performance across both specialized VLN agents and general vision-language model agents, while preserving single-agent capabilities.
authors: Haihong Hao, Lei Chen, Mingfei Han, Chenglong Yan, Dong An, Yuqiang Yang, Changlin Li, Minghao Guo, Salman Khan, Xiaojun Chang
bullets: Addresses the challenge of coordinating robots without requiring shared policies or coordinated actions.
Aggregates partial egocentric observations into a shared environmental understanding for decentralized navigation.
Stores observations in shared memory, retrieves relevant spatio-temporal context, and encodes it with a predictive latent world model.
Injects the resulting shared representations as tokens into downstream navigation agents.

papers.abstract: The physical world is open-ended, dynamic, and partially observable. While foundation models have advanced embodied intelligence, standalone models struggle with long-horizon execution, and simply integrating models with agents may lead to inconsistencies between planning and physical control. To support reliable and adaptive behaviors in the physical world, we introduce Innata-0, a native embodied world system. Innata-0 jointly designs an embodied world-action model and an agent to combine their complementary strengths. The model, Innata-0-WAM, adopts a tri-tower Mixture-of-Transformers architecture that integrates understanding, prediction, and action generation. The agent, Innata-0-Agent, coordinates long-horizon execution through memory, verification, and recovery. A co-design protocol is further proposed to align model training with agent execution and leverage validated experiences to support subsequent adaptation and model improvement. Extensive evaluations demonstrate strong embodied capabilities across understanding, world prediction, and robotic manipulation. Innata-0 represents our first step toward physical intelligence, and we see it as the beginning of a much longer journey.

papers.abstract: World action models guide robots by predicting the effects of actions or generating commands from observations. A model may compare hundreds of candidate futures before acting, repeatedly reading weights that must fit in device memory. Post-training quantization reduces the number of bits used to store pretrained weights, but a smaller model is not necessarily a deployable one: temporary tensors can exceed graphics processing unit (GPU) memory limits, while even small prediction errors can change the selected action. This creates two coupled challenges: identifying bit assignments that preserve task performance and determining which of them meet real execution constraints, without exhausting costly task trials. We present PTQ4WAM, a framework for choosing layer-wise bit assignments and execution routes under memory, latency and task-evaluation budgets. Calibration measurements guide candidate proposals, optionally with a language model agent. We profile full-model routes on the GPU before spending task trials on feasible assignments. Fusing group rescaling and reading visual history in place can make an otherwise infeasible assignment deployable. Across 15 workloads from four model families, the median task score is 99.2% of the corresponding 32-bit floating-point (FP32) score. On fixed GPU replays, the median speedup over FP32 is 2.36 times and the median reduction in peak allocated memory is 71.5%. The code will be released soon.

papers.abstract: Edge cases are not the long tail; they are the norm. An embodied system deployed across changing environments, bodies, objects, and tasks will routinely encounter combinations that were absent from its training data. General-purpose physical intelligence therefore requires world models that reuse prior knowledge, predict consequences, and adapt with little or no additional training. Yet current evaluations of conditional video generation emphasize visual quality, prompt alignment, or isolated physical plausibility, leaving systematic generalization difficult to measure. We introduce AxE Bench, a benchmark that organizes condition changes along eight factors of the acting agent and of its environment, and pairs every original condition with controlled variants that change one side or both. WBench-plus applies the same structure to an existing multi-turn benchmark, pairing each WBench scenario with variants on the environment side, through its world setting or camera behavior, or on the agent side, through its interaction instructions. Additionally, to score generated futures, we develop an evaluation harness that combines vision-language reasoning with targeted computer-vision evidence, converting each video into temporally localized events and comparing generated events with reference events in both time and semantics. We summarize each model with the AxE Score, event Fidelity weighted by its Stability across original-variant pairs. Across twenty models, generated events match reference events far more often in timing than in content: no model exceeds a Fidelity of 13.01, the highest Stability is 0.55, and the highest AxE Score is 7.10. Together, these components turn world-model generalization from an informal aspiration into a falsifiable evaluation program for real and simulated interactions. Our project website can be found at: AxEBench.github.io

papers.abstract: World models support planning by predicting how the environment evolves under candidate actions. However, one-step predictive accuracy alone does not characterize multi-step planning utility, which depends on distinguishing candidate futures. This raises a natural question: How does latent transition geometry shape planning? We investigate this through an action-conditioned transition-field view, using curvature regularization as a controlled intervention. Across four continuous-control tasks, appropriately tuned regularization improves planning, while excessive regularization can be detrimental. By decomposing the transition field into affine and non-affine components, we find that regularization reduces action sensitivity mainly through the non-affine component. To assess its role in planning, we directly manipulate the non-affine action response in frozen models and show that it affects candidate selection and closed-loop success. Further analysis shows that curvature generally brings predicted futures closer together, while preserving more of the differences along the goal direction. This helps explain why the planning effects vary across tasks. We observe broadly consistent planning trends across five sampling- and gradient-based solvers on LeWM and similar rollout-geometry trends on DINO-WM. Qualitative attention visualizations reveal accompanying shifts toward task-relevant visual structure. Together, these findings clarify how latent transition geometry influences multi-step planning.

papers.abstract: Interactive world models generate virtual environments autoregressively from player actions and visual history. However, visual history alone cannot reliably capture the evolving states of independently acting non-player characters (NPCs) in real games, particularly when they are outside the camera view. Recent multi-agent world models address this challenge through joint multi-view generation or persistent shared state, but often rely on external observations, like maps or scene geometry, or predefined state transitions. We present SWAM, a State-aware World Action Model that separates agent-state evolution from autoregressive visual generation in interactive 3D environments. A lightweight state model propagates character dynamics from actions without consuming generated frames, combining motion priors with learned scene-dependent corrections. The predicted states then guide an autoregressive diffusion transformer alongside visual history through a novel conditioning scheme. Rather than requiring an explicit scene geometry map or visibility tests, the conditioning indicates where characters may appear, allowing the diffusion model to learn their appearance and occlusion. This design enables NPCs to evolve independently of visual generation while maintaining consistent observations across visibility changes, interactions, and respawns. Evaluations in a custom Godot-based first-person shooter game demonstrate improvements in visual fidelity, NPC consistency, and long-horizon stability over existing approaches.

Experiments in a custom Godot first-person shooter show improved visual fidelity, NPC consistency, and long-horizon stability over existing approaches.

papers.abstract: World action models (WAMs) predict how the world responds to actions and offer a promising path toward general embodied intelligence, but they are large and run the network many times per plan, so they are hard to deploy on robots. Spiking neural networks (SNNs) compute with sparse binary spikes and use additions instead of multiplications, which saves power. However, existing WAMs use dense videos as the world state, so a spiking version would spend most of its computation on the background. We therefore introduce SpikingWAM, the first spiking WAM, which uses a sparse task skeleton as the world state. Inspired by biological motor control, which attends only to the key positions of a task, the Task Skeleton State (TSS) keeps the keypoints of the arm and the task objects, and a small spiking front end estimates the object keypoints from images. Body Frame Spike Coding (BFSC) and Grid Coincidence Attention (GCA) keep millimetre precision, and the Persistent Single Step Readout (PSR) runs the network once per plan. On the simulated benchmarks LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus and RoboTwin 2.0, SpikingWAM achieves competitive success rates with far less energy than ANN methods and surpasses all compared methods on LIBERO-Plus. Real robot experiments further confirm its effectiveness. These results show that a task skeleton lets spiking networks implement WAMs at very low energy, offering a new solution for low power embodied intelligence. Project page: https://wxqnl.github.io/spikingwam/
authors: Mingquan Liu, Peng Zhou, Shanming Yao, Shuai Wang, Simo Wu, Malu Zhang
bullets: Addresses the high computational and energy costs of large world-action models that repeatedly process dense video observations.
Represents the world with a sparse Task Skeleton State containing arm and object keypoints, estimated from images by a spiking front end.
Introduces Body Frame Spike Coding, Grid Coincidence Attention, and Persistent Single Step Readout for precise, efficient planning.
Achieves competitive simulated-task success with substantially lower energy than ANN methods, surpasses compared methods on LIBERO-Plus, and works in real-robot experiments.

papers.abstract: Residual world models forecast a driving scene through its temporal change, so feature components that stay constant over time vanish from the residual pathway. We ask whether evidence with weak temporal change, such as a waiting pedestrian or a stopped vehicle, can be used more effectively for planning, and introduce MOVER, a complementary event-routing mechanism. A training-time teacher measures how each spatially grounded event query responds when a past frame is removed from shared history and contrasts that sensitivity with the event's pooled temporal residual, prioritizing events that depend on history but receive weak residual evidence. A student predicts the resulting priorities from unperturbed history, so the teacher adds no inference cost. Under fixed total routing mass, one distribution scales a low-rank future bird's-eye-view update and biases trajectory-conditioned event reading. On nuScenes, MOVER reduces ResWorld's UniAD-style average L2 from 0.65 to 0.55 m and its collision rate from 0.23% to 0.12% without direct planner ego status (0.50 m and 0.09% with it), adding 4.1 ms per frame. Matched controls show that the complementary teacher outperforms either signal alone and that the allocation acts mainly during training. Adapted to BridgeDrive-LEAD, MOVER reaches a 96.52 +/- 0.65 driving score over three seeds on the 220-route Bench2Drive closed-loop benchmark, exceeding matched controls in each paired seed by a margin within seed variation.
authors: Xiangyu Li, Yu Jiang, Tianyi Wang, Liang He, Qixing Huang, Zhaomiao Guo
bullets: Residual world models may underrepresent static or slowly changing evidence, such as waiting pedestrians and stopped vehicles.
A training-time teacher identifies events that depend on past frames but receive weak temporal-residual evidence; a student predicts their routing priorities at inference.
The priorities allocate a fixed routing budget between low-rank future bird’s-eye-view updates and trajectory-conditioned event reading, adding no teacher cost at inference.
On nuScenes, MOVER reduces average L2 from 0.65 to 0.55 m and collision rate from 0.23% to 0.12%, with 4.1 ms/frame overhead.
On Bench2Drive, adapted MOVER achieves a 96.52 ± 0.65 driving score across three seeds and exceeds matched controls within paired-seed variation.

papers.abstract: LiDAR world models generate and predict metric 3D observations in the form of LiDAR scans. They typically synthesize scans following the scan pattern of their training sensor or render them from an intermediate 3D surface or field. However, following one scan pattern limits transfer to LiDARs with other patterns, and rendering from intermediate geometry can cause incorrect depths and false returns. In this paper, we propose a scan pattern agnostic 4D LiDAR world model that decouples the scene from sensor observation, so one spatial latent can be observed by heterogeneous LiDARs at the same mounting position without regeneration. Our decoder predicts the hit probability and depth of each ray directly from the latent, combining global scene context with local features retrieved at a preliminary depth. Without an intermediate surface or field, it reduces incorrect depths and false returns, and as each ray is decoded independently from one latent, LiDARs that share a ray receive the same return and observe one consistent scene. Finally, a diffusion transformer generates scenes in this latent and predicts 4D sequences from observed latents warped by the given ego and object motion. On KITTI-360 and nuScenes, our model generates realistic scenes and reduces the registration error between predicted frames by about 70% relative to the best compared world model. Its decoder yields 19 to 28% lower depth error than the rendering used by other world models, and generated scans benefit several downstream tasks. Our code will be open-sourced. More details are available at https://minwoo0611.github.io/OneLatentWorld.
authors: Minwoo Jung, Dongjae Lee, DongGuw Lee, Yeong Sang Park, Maurice Fallon, Ayoung Kim
bullets: Decouples scene representation from sensor scan patterns, enabling multiple LiDARs at the same mounting position to observe one shared latent scene without regeneration.
Directly predicts each ray’s hit probability and depth using global context and locally retrieved preliminary-depth features, avoiding intermediate surfaces or fields.
Uses a diffusion transformer to generate latent scenes and predict 4D sequences under ego and object motion.
On KITTI-360 and nuScenes, reduces predicted-frame registration error by about 70% versus the best compared world model and lowers depth error by 19–28% versus alternative rendering.
Generated scans also improve several downstream tasks; the scope is evaluated on KITTI-360 and nuScenes.

papers.selection_reason: Scan-pattern-agnostic 4D LiDAR world model with direct ray decoding and diffusion transformer; learns and predicts environment dynamics over time.
papers.title: One Latent World for Heterogeneous LiDARs: A Scan Pattern Agnostic 4D World Model via Direct Ray Decoding
papers.tldr: A scan-pattern-agnostic 4D LiDAR world model uses one latent scene representation to generate consistent observations for heterogeneous sensors via direct ray decoding.

papers.abstract: Current AI may have a model of how we use human language, but this does not translate into a reliable representation of physical reality. World models promise to fill this gap by learning how an environment changes over time and predicting the consequences of an action, and they are already used to steer robots and generate explorable worlds. This article asks how AI regulation in three major legal contexts, the European Union, California, and China, copes with the distinctive challenges they raise. I propose a definition and a taxonomy of world models based on who or what acts on their predictions, and identify the risks of misplaced reliance on them. I argue that existing rules tend to cover world models but leave three questions open, i.e., action provenance, trajectory validity, and the weight of simulated evidence, and recommend ways to fill these gaps.
bullets: World models learn environmental dynamics to predict the consequences of actions, supporting robotics and explorable virtual worlds.
The article examines regulation in the European Union, California, and China.
It defines and categorizes world models according to who or what acts on their predictions.
It highlights risks from misplaced reliance on simulated or predicted outcomes.
Three unresolved issues are action provenance, trajectory validity, and the evidentiary weight of simulations.

Figure 2. Roles-based taxonomy

papers.selection_reason: Legal and policy analysis of world models is directly relevant to the world-models topic, though not a technical method.
papers.title: World Models and the Law
papers.tldr: Existing AI laws broadly cover world models but leave important gaps around how their predictions are used and trusted.

papers.abstract: Terraforming Mars is a long-horizon, action-conditioned control problem that requires predicting atmospheric responses to interventions over centuries to identify effective policies. This position paper argues that physics-regularized recurrent state-space world models are the most promising foundation for this setting. Data-driven climate emulators lack action-conditioning, and physics-based general circulation models (GCMs) are too expensive for policy search. Among learned world models, recurrent state-space architectures with physics constraints are better suited than transformer-based alternatives: they provide native uncertainty quantification through their stochastic-deterministic decomposition, remain stable under sparse non-terrestrial training data, and enforce physical consistency at each rollout step. To make this position concrete, we describe a potential architecture combining JEPA-inspired latent encoding, universal differential equation constraints, and a Dreamer-lineage planning head. We also introduce MarsWorld, an open benchmark proposal for intervention-conditioned planetary world models, and discuss broader implications and objections.
authors: Sameera S Kashyap, Akshitha Nagaraj, Razvan Marinescu
bullets: Terraforming requires long-horizon, action-conditioned predictions of atmospheric responses.
Climate emulators often lack intervention conditioning, while physics-based GCMs are too costly for policy search.
The paper favors recurrent state-space models over transformers for uncertainty estimation, sparse-data stability, and stepwise physical consistency.
A proposed design combines JEPA-inspired latent representations, universal differential equation constraints, and a Dreamer-style planning head.
The paper proposes MarsWorld, an open benchmark for intervention-conditioned planetary world models, but presents a position and architecture proposal rather than experimental validation.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Proposed Mars atmospheric world model architecture. S1: A two-stage training strategy separates synthetic pre-training data (MCD v6.1) from observational fine-tuning sources (EMARS, OpenMARS; with TES/MCS as the underlying retrievals); intervention actions at enter the transition model as continuous vectors. S2: A state encoder maps atmospheric fields to a latent z; PINN constraints and UDE residuals regularize the latent and downstream dynamics, merged at the concatenation node. S3: An RSSM propagates stochastic latent zt and recurrent memory ht under action-conditioned transitions ρ(z | h, a) with physics enforced at every step; ht is updated from (ht−1, zt−1, at−1) via the recurrent backbone. S4: An actor-critic head trains within imagined latent rollouts; the actor π(a | z, h) outputs intervention policies, the critic V (z, h) estimates returns from (∆P,∆T,∆O2), and a decoder reconstructs gridded fields against EMARS as an auxiliary signal. S5: Outputs are a learned policy trajectory, a long-horizon atmospheric forecast, and a rollout uncertainty map from stochastic latent samples.

Table 1: Requirements for Mars terraforming simulation vs. existing systems. (i) Mars physical accuracy; (ii) tractable for policy search; (iii) action-conditioned rollouts; (iv) century-scale stability; (v) trainable on sparse non-terrestrial data.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes action-conditioned recurrent state-space world models for long-horizon planetary control, directly fitting interactive and latent-action world-model interests.
papers.title: World Models Are the Right Foundation for Simulating Mars Terraforming
papers.tldr: Physics-regularized recurrent world models are proposed as a practical foundation for learning and planning Mars-terraforming interventions over centuries.

papers.abstract: Causal video world models generate block by block from their own previous outputs. Small errors in early blocks are fed back as history and grow until the scene and the robot fall apart. Teacher forcing trains on clean ground-truth history, so the model never sees the history it will actually condition on, and it also finds a shortcut: copying the previous frame instead of predicting how the scene changes. We present Dynamics Forcing, a training scheme that keeps real video as the only supervision and reshapes how history is presented. History is perturbed in three ways: random noising, self-resampling by the model itself, and joint denoising, in which the most recent blocks are still partly noisy when the next block is predicted. On top of this we move history guidance and first-frame anchor guidance from inference into training, so that the model is pushed to use its history and its reference frame rather than ignore them. Dynamics Forcing needs no teacher model, no distillation, and no additional model at inference. Applied to a 5B video model with LoRA on 77 hours of manipulation video on a single GPU, it better matches unseen real continuations and reduces error accumulation.
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between clean teacher-forced histories and the model-generated histories used at inference.
Perturbs history through random noising, model self-resampling, and joint denoising of recent blocks.
Trains the model to use both temporal history and the first-frame reference via guidance applied during training.
Requires only real-video supervision, with no teacher model, distillation, or additional inference-time model.
Applied to a 5B video model on manipulation video, it better matches unseen real continuations and reduces error accumulation.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Overview of Dynamics Forcing. Top: the block-causal attention pattern over latent blocks, where each block attends to the reference frame, all earlier blocks and itself, and future blocks are masked. Middle: the three history perturbations (random noising, self-resampling, joint denoising) applied to the history blocks while the target block stays real. Bottom: the training-time history guidance (σh=0.5) and first-frame anchor guidance (σa=0.8), which add no forward pass beyond the model’s standard classifier-free-guidance inference.

papers.selection_reason: Training scheme to reduce error accumulation in causal video world models directly fits video world models.
papers.title: Dynamics Forcing: Mitigating Error Accumulation in Causal Video World Models
papers.tldr: Dynamics Forcing trains causal video world models on realistic, perturbed histories to reduce error accumulation during long-horizon generation.

papers.abstract: Safety-critical scenarios are rare in recorded driving and must be generated to test and train motion planners of automated vehicles. In guided diffusion models, each scenario type needs its own weighted objective, separate from the validity check. Optimized together with the attacker, the vehicle under test can cancel the attack or draw it toward itself. We state each scenario as a signal temporal logic specification with clauses typed by role. Every clause names the agent it may change and the agents it may read, and the vehicle under test reads the attacker only from the attack onset. A large language model drafts the specification from a description, and a type checker accepts it. A compiler derives the optimization: it edits a diffusion model's samples by the smallest change that satisfies the specification, each clause moves only its owner, the attacker is solved against the unreacted vehicle under test before its response, and the monitor of the same specification decides acceptance. On nuScenes and CommonRoad, judged independently of the specification, one parameter set produced valid scenarios at a rate 0.14 above a weighted objective tuned per scenario type, and descriptions yielded at least one valid scenario for 11 of the 16 pre-crash types expressible in the public data. Learned planners fail more often on the generated scenarios than on their seeds. Fine-tuning on them lowers a planner's failure rate on critical scenarios, and the time headway one clause of the label requires, not the generator, sets the size of the gain.
authors: Zifan Zeng, Qunli Zhang, Peng Wang, Shiming Liu, Feng Liu, Zheng Hu
bullets: Targets the scarcity of rare, safety-critical driving scenarios for testing and training automated-vehicle motion planners.
Uses role-typed signal temporal logic: clauses specify which agents may be changed or observed, with restricted attacker–vehicle interactions.
An LLM drafts specifications; a type checker validates them, and a compiler derives constrained diffusion optimization and acceptance monitoring.
Across nuScenes and CommonRoad, one parameter set achieved a 0.14 higher valid-scenario rate than objectives tuned per scenario type.
Generated scenarios caused more learned-planner failures than their seeds; fine-tuning reduced failures, with gains limited by the labeled time-headway requirement.

figures.caption: FIGURE 2. Overview of the method for the description of a lead-vehicle braking scenario. Middle: an LLM drafts a role-typed specification, a type check returns errors for repair (contribution 1), and the compiler turns every clause φk into four objects. The exact robustness ρ, a minimum and maximum over time and agents, yields the monitor’s verdict ρ ≥ 0 and, for the observation clause, the onset t⋆. Its smooth lower bound ρ̃ enters a hinge loss whose gradient moves only the clause’s owner. Right: the solver runs in stages derived from the roles (contribution 2): the attacker keeps its seed during its hold time and is then edited against the unreacted seed of the ego, then the ego’s response is edited with the attack fixed, and the ego keeps its seed until the release t⋆ + δ. A specification may name a further guided role, such as a bystander that blocks the ego’s escape lane: it owns its clauses, whose gradients move only that role, and is solved in its own stage after the ego’s. All other agents are context agents and keep their seed trajectories. The monitor of the compiled specification accepts the result or restarts the role from maneuver primitives, and the K seeds of many windows are solved in one batch (contribution 3). Thumbnails (nuScenes, bird’s-eye view, true vehicle sizes): left, a seed scene with every agent’s trajectory (boxes at t = 0); bottom right, the generated scenario at t = 3 s: the lead vehicle brakes into the path of the ego’s unreacted seed (dashed), and the generated ego, identical to its seed until the release (circle), stays behind the lead vehicle.

FIGURE 3. Generated scenarios of six NHTSA pre-crash types, each from an LLM-drafted specification, with the parameter set of all other experiments and no weights: (a), (c)–(e) nuScenes, (b), (f) CommonRoad. The line under each title paraphrases the attack clause of the draft. In every panel the attacker’s seed (dashed red) did something else, the attack is turned against the unreacted seed of the ego vehicle (dashed black), with which it collides, and the generated ego vehicle responds from the release on with the smallest edit that keeps it clear of the attacker, by 0.1 to 0.7m at the closest point: it brakes in (a), (c), (e) and (f) and swerves in (b) and (d). The six pass the independent judges of their types. The drafted road clauses, which confine the attacker to the ego vehicle’s road corridor, are not met at the junctions, which is why the specification’s own monitor accepts only (b), (c) and (f) (Section VI). Footprints every 0.5 s (0.4 s on CommonRoad), light to dark; context agents in grey.

FIGURE 1. A cut-in on US-101 generated from the same seed in three ways; under each panel the speeds of the generated ego vehicle, the attacker and the unreacted seed (dashed), at the top right the monitor’s verdict. (a) Without ownership, the ego vehicle’s clauses also move the attacker and cancel the attack. (b) Without the stage order, the attacker is optimized against the responding ego vehicle: it chases the response, cuts in and brakes to a standstill, the unreacted seed collides with it, and the monitor rejects the output, since the specification asks for an unsafe gap and not a collision. (c) Ours: the attacker cuts in against the unreacted seed and slows down ahead of it, and the ego vehicle keeps its seed until the release t⋆ + δ and then brakes at 2.8m/s2. Footprints every 0.5 s, light to dark; dashed outlines: the seeds.

papers.selection_reason: Generates safety-critical driving scenarios via diffusion models conditioned on specifications, fitting action-conditioned environment generation.
papers.title: Generating Safety-Critical Driving Scenarios from Role-Typed Signal Temporal Logic Specifications Drafted by Large Language Models
papers.tldr: A typed-logic compiler turns LLM-drafted driving specifications into diffusion-generated safety-critical scenarios that expose and help reduce planner failures.

papers.abstract: We introduce MotionPort, which learns low-dimensional latent representations of body motion for accurate dynamics prediction and effective long-horizon planning. Existing world-model planners often search over action representations learned for prediction, yet we show that predictive accuracy alone does not ensure that optimization can discover successful trajectories. MotionPort addresses this mismatch by representing body trajectories rather than action chunks and organizing the search space by motion similarity, helping predicted improvements translate into successful execution. Without fine-tuning state encoders, MotionPort raises average goal-reaching success from 37.9% to 87.8% across three backbones and seven settings in four domains. On the evaluated AntMaze-OGBench tasks, it achieves 72% success, compared with 4% for the strongest baseline.
authors: Renhao Zhang, Abhranil Chandra, Bruno Castro da Silva
bullets: Predictive accuracy alone may not yield an action-search space that supports successful trajectory optimization.
MotionPort represents body trajectories and aligns the latent search space with motion similarity.
It requires no fine-tuning of state encoders.
Across three backbones and seven settings in four domains, average goal-reaching success increases from 37.9% to 87.8%.
On evaluated AntMaze-OGBench tasks, MotionPort achieves 72% success versus 4% for the strongest baseline.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Learning and planning with MotionPort. (a) Representative body trajectories are encoded into geometry-structured motion codes, which condition an action decoder and a dynamics model, while the pretrained state encoder remains frozen. (b) A learned prior initializes motion-code sequences, which are iteratively refined by an optimizer. The diagram shows successive motion segments horizontally and iterative plan refinement vertically. The selected motion is decoded into executable actions and checked before execution.

Figure 5. Effect of learned priors on PushT planning. All methods share the same start and goal. Rows compare planning without (top) and with (bottom) learned priors. Only full MotionPort with the prior successfully reaches the goal in this example.

Figure 3. From imagined optimization to physical execution on Cube. We visualize two-dimensional slices of the planning spaces of HWM-Macro, MP-noGeo, and MotionPort. The top row shows predicted goal costs, while the bottom row shows actual cube-to-goal distances after executing the corresponding actions for 20 environment steps. The same optimization path is shown in both rows, with circles marking the starting points, stars marking the first updates reaching the predicted-cost threshold, and squares marking the final solutions after 30 updates. Solid contours indicate the predicted low-cost region (J/Jref ≤ 0.6), while dashed contours indicate the physical success region (distance ≤ 4 cm). MotionPort exhibits a larger overlap between these regions, allowing optimization to find a solution that succeeds.

Figure 6. Planning efficiency across frozen world models. Goalreaching success versus planning time on long-horizon PushT. Colors distinguish LeWM, HWM, and H-JEPA, while dashed lines with circles represent native planners and solid lines with triangles represent MotionPort. Using their frozen backbones, MotionPort achieves higher success with substantially less planning time.

Results on PushT and Cube show that MotionPort achieves both higher goal-reaching success and smaller gaps between ever and terminal success than most baselines.

Figure 4. A better goal score benefits motion-space planning. Darker regions indicate lower costs, and stars mark the goals. The learned temporal score better captures the maze’s reachable paths. (e) Goal-reaching success on AntMaze-hard with and without ϕ, where MotionPort improves from 38% to 58%, while HWM-Macro decreases from 14% to 12%.

Table 2. Prediction reliability and control performance on PushT and Cube. Validation error (VE) measures prediction accuracy on logged trajectories, while planning error (PE) measures prediction accuracy on planner-selected actions. Error ratio (ER) is defined as PE/VE, and success rate (SR) measures goal-reaching performance (%). Results are reported as mean ± standard error using frozen HWM42. papers.selection_reason: Introduces MotionPort to learn geometry-aligned latent representations of body motion for improved dynamics prediction and long-horizon planning in world models.
papers.title: What Should World Models Plan Over? Learning Geometry-Aligned Representations of Body Motion
papers.tldr: MotionPort improves long-horizon world-model planning by organizing low-dimensional body-motion trajectories around geometric similarity rather than relying solely on predictive action representations.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in physics-based humanoid control enable teams of varying sizes to coordinate their movements and cooperatively transport shared objects. However, adapting learned cooperative behaviors to unseen environmental constraints remains challenging, particularly when obstacles require coordinated detours and changes in team configuration. We propose CarlHOI, a counterfactual predictive imagination framework built upon a counterfactual-anchored relational latent world model (CarlWM) for human-object interaction (HOI), enabling multi-humanoid teams to adapt to unseen environmental constraints without retraining their underlying cooperative control policies. CarlHOI explicitly represents the shared object, individual humanoids, and environmental obstacles as interacting entities. Trained offline using counterfactual simulator rollouts, the model imagines alternative collective futures under different shared waypoint commands, predicting how the coupled humanoid team and object would respond. By evaluating these imagined outcomes through predicted progress, failure, and contact risks, and long-horizon value estimates, CarlHOI selects adaptive guidance commands while preserving the pretrained cooperative controller. We introduce a benchmark comprising three challenging obstacle-constrained transport tasks to evaluate adaptation and generalization. Despite being trained exclusively with four humanoids, our model generalizes without retraining to teams of two to ten humanoids, unseen obstacle geometries and placements, unseen objects, and novel combinations of environmental constraints. Extensive experiments demonstrate improved cooperative transport success over evaluated baselines across diverse configurations. Results highlight the potential of counterfactual predictive imagination to extend pretrained multi-humanoid cooperative skills beyond their original training conditions.
bullets: Targets cooperative transport in environments requiring obstacle detours and changing team configurations.
Models humanoids, shared objects, and obstacles as interacting entities in a relational latent world model.
Imagines outcomes of alternative waypoint commands using offline counterfactual simulator rollouts.
Selects guidance commands using predicted progress, failure, contact risk, and long-horizon value.

Evaluated on three obstacle-constrained transport tasks, with generalization from four-humanoid training to teams of two to ten and unseen configurations; experiments report improved success over evaluated baselines.

papers.selection_reason: Uses a counterfactual latent world model for multi-humanoid cooperative manipulation, fitting robot learning and interactive/latent action world models.
papers.title: CarlHOI: Counterfactual Predictive Imagination for Generalizable Multi-Humanoid Object Interaction under Constrained Environments
papers.tldr: CarlHOI uses counterfactual world-model predictions to adapt pretrained multi-humanoid object-transport skills to unseen obstacles, team sizes, objects, and constraints without retraining.

papers.abstract: Sequence models trained on game moves have been shown to encode world models, with structured linear probes revealing the underlying game states. World models, however, are inherently dynamic: in deterministic board games, a set of rules constrain how states evolve over time. We therefore ask if and how OthelloGPT, a transformer trained only on Othello move sequences, manifests the rules of the game in its activation space. We divide the rules of Othello, and symmetrically their violations, into three classes: placing a disc on an empty square (R1), flanking an opponent's disc (R2), and moving in turn (R3). We find that linear probes accurately separate legal from illegal moves, and also distinguish between the three kinds of rule violations. We introduce an unsupervised rule-violation detector based on the step length of activations between consecutive moves, which identifies illegal moves above chance. We further improve our detection metric by computing step length in the latent space of select sparse autoencoders. Together, we find that OthelloGPT follows game rules of Othello to a large extent, and that we can detect rule violations using structured detectors on model activations.
authors: David L. Cao, Sai Sumedh R. Hindupur, Demba Ba
bullets: Linear probes separate legal from illegal moves in activation space.
Probes distinguish violations involving placement, flanking, and turn order.
An unsupervised detector uses activation step lengths between consecutive moves to identify illegal moves above chance.
Measuring step length in selected sparse-autoencoder latent spaces improves detection.
The study finds that OthelloGPT follows Othello’s rules to a large extent.

Every point is one trained dictionary at expansion factor 16 (8192 latents) on layer-5 activations, scored with Karvonen’s board-game suite [18]; all four panels share the x-axis L0, clipped to [0, 400], and marker shape denotes the architecture. (a) Loss recovered (fidelity) against L0, each point colored by its coverage of the Othello board state. (b) Coverage of the Othello board state against L0. papers.title: From States to Dynamics: Detecting Rule Violations in OthelloGPT
