papers.selection_reason: Directly studies robustness of latent dynamic world models used for embodied AI planning and policy evaluation, fitting the world models topic.
papers.title: Toward Adversarially Robust World Models
papers.tldr: This work exposes two attacks on latent world models and shows that adversarially robust encoders can substantially improve their robustness.

papers.abstract: Food assembly robots pick ingredients from a pan, and every pick must deliver a target weight. We learn a world model of food picking from 61,773 production picks, labeled automatically by a camera and a scale (self-supervised learning). From the pre-pick heightmap of the pan on a 2.5 mm grid, the commanded pick action, the food and the utensil, the model predicts the post-pick heightmap and the picked mass with uncertainty. We evaluate the mass prediction on 12,294 held-out picks of nine foods. The production controller keeps each pick near its commanded target. The model's root-mean-square error (RMSE) of 10.93 g is 9% lower than that of the commanded target or of a per-food mean. This RMSE is 24% lower than that of the controller's internal mass estimate. Gradient-boosted trees on 20 hand-crafted features have a 0.2 g lower RMSE, but they predict only the mass, not the next state that planning and policy learning need. Using the predicted uncertainty, we decline the most uncertain picks and answer 89.4% of picks with an RMSE of 10.28 g. The prediction barely responds to the commanded volume and depth, because they vary little in closed-loop production. The model also fails without warning at target weights not seen in training. Future directions include action-primitive conditioning and a more general model across foods and utensils. We give recommendations for learning world models from production data.
authors: Inkyu Sa, Gaurav Kuppa, Steve Van der Hoeven, Konstantin Stulov, Rajat Bhageria, Luis Rayas
bullets: Learns from 61,773 automatically labeled production picks using pre-pick heightmaps, actions, food, and utensil information.
Predicts post-pick heightmaps and picked mass with uncertainty; mass is evaluated on 12,294 held-out picks across nine foods.
Achieves 10.93 g RMSE, outperforming commanded-target/per-food-mean baselines and the controller’s internal estimate.
Rejecting the most uncertain picks yields 89.4% coverage with 10.28 g RMSE.
Performance is weakly sensitive to commanded volume/depth and can fail without warning on unseen target weights; broader food and utensil coverage is needed.
papers.selection_reason: Learns an action-conditioned food-picking world model from production data for robot planning and mass prediction.
papers.title: Learning a Food World Model That Predicts the Next State from Production Data
papers.tldr: A production-trained food-picking world model predicts both the next pan state and picked mass, enabling uncertainty-aware planning for assembly robots.

papers.abstract: Beckmann Transport Models (BTM) learn one-step generative maps end-to-end from data, without a teacher, a distillation stage, or pretrained features. We introduce Scalable Beckmann Maps (SBM), which bring to BTM the two ingredients behind the quality of modern multistep generators: classifier-free guidance (CFG) and a training recipe that scales, while keeping sampling at a single network evaluation. CFG combines conditional and unconditional velocity or score predictions, which a Beckmann map does not have. Our guidance rests on one observation: the BTM current is a positive multiple of an autonomous denoising field, to which CFG applies as it does to a velocity. With exact denoisers this gives guided BTM. In practice we substitute the map's own conditional and null predictions for the denoisers, which requires no additional network and introduces a bias that we characterize. We show that the guided update is consistent with a guided conservation equation, and that guidance can move the boundaries between basins, sending more noise to the modes a condition favors. Trained from scratch in the latent of a representation autoencoder, SBM reaches a one-step FID of 1.6 on ImageNet 256x256 without a teacher or a feature loss, outperforming the Improved-MeanFlow baseline with 3.2x fewer FLOPs. In text-to-image generation it reaches a GenEval score of 0.86 with one network evaluation. As a world model, where we train without guidance, the recipe alone outperforms DriftWorld on all five metrics of two robot-manipulation benchmarks, with 1.9-2.8x less training compute and no pretrained auxiliary feature encoder.
authors: Ulrik Unneberg, Shiyi Wang, Lee Cheuk-Kit, Felix Berg, Boris Kozinsky, Yilun Du, Michael S. Albergo, Eric Vanden-Eijnden
bullets: Extends Beckmann Transport Models with guidance by applying classifier-free guidance to their autonomous denoising field.
Uses the model’s conditional and null predictions, requiring no additional network, while characterizing the resulting bias.
Provides a guided conservation-equation interpretation in which guidance shifts basin boundaries toward condition-favored modes.
Achieves 1.6 one-step FID on ImageNet 256×256 and a 0.86 GenEval score for text-to-image generation.
Also improves world-model performance across five metrics on two robot-manipulation benchmarks with lower training compute.

Figure 2 Flow matching, BTM and Equilibrium Matching on the same two-dimensional problem: noise is transported to five data points, whose weights are given in the legend. (a) Flow matching learns a time-dependent velocity; arrows show the field at t = 0.5. Because the velocity changes over time, trajectories can bend sharply and even reverse direction, and this curvature makes the ODE hard to integrate in few steps. (b) BTM assumes an autonomous flow. Its flow lines are fixed and never cross, the endpoint map is constant along each of them, and the separatrices of the map (solid) divide the plane into one basin per data point, each receiving source mass equal to that point’s weight. (c) Equilibrium Matching (Wang and Du, 2025) also learns a time-invariant field, whose magnitude is set by a schedule ct, here ct = (1− t)0.8; the shaded bands are a potential reconstructed from the current, ∆ϕ = ∇ · J . A nonconstant schedule ct can bias the endpoint distribution by shifting the basin boundaries: the separatrices of its map (solid) depart from those of BTM (dotted), and the basins of the two lower modes shrink, so these modes receive too little mass. At ct = 1 the autonomous field is identical to that of BTM.

papers.selection_reason: One-step generative map approach demonstrated as a world model for robot manipulation benchmarks, predicting environment dynamics relevant to interactive world modeling.
papers.title: Scalable Beckmann Maps Improve One-step Generation
papers.tldr: Scalable Beckmann Maps add classifier-free guidance and a scalable training recipe to achieve strong one-step generation without teachers or pretrained features.

papers.abstract: Aging is characterized by continuously evolving health states, yet most existing prediction models focus on static health risk at isolated time points rather than explicitly modelling how health trajectories unfold over time. We developed a health world model based on the Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture to represent evolving health states and simulate future trajectories under specified actions. The model combines a state encoder, an action- and context-conditioned predictor, a stop-gradient target encoder, and clinical outcome heads. We trained the model on the US Health and Retirement Study (HRS) and evaluated it without refitting in the English Longitudinal Study of Ageing (ELSA) and the China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study (CHARLS). Open-loop evaluation assessed discrimination and calibration for mortality and worsening of activities of daily living (ADL) and instrumental activities of daily living (IADL). In the held-out HRS test set, the areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROCs) for mortality, ADL worsening, and IADL worsening were 0.89, 0.93, and 0.93 at the first horizon and 0.84, 0.84, and 0.85 at the fifth horizon, respectively. Predicted risks stratified subsequent outcomes across horizons. Across the evaluated horizons, mortality AUROC ranged from 0.867 to 0.881 in ELSA and from 0.796 to 0.801 in CHARLS. Simulated trajectories preserved the expected risk ordering across predefined action regimes. In counterfactual simulations, changes in lifestyle actions shifted predicted risks in directions consistent with observed associations. The model provides a framework for longitudinal risk prediction and action-conditioned simulation in older adults.
authors: Jingyi Wu, Chenghua Guo, Qianlin Zuo, Pengfei Li, Luxia Zhang
bullets: Addresses the limitation of static, single-time-point risk models by representing longitudinal health-state evolution.
Uses a Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture with state encoding, action/context-conditioned prediction, target encoding, and clinical outcome heads.
Trained on the US Health and Retirement Study and evaluated without refitting in English and Chinese aging cohorts.
Showed strong discrimination for mortality and ADL/IADL worsening in HRS, with meaningful risk stratification across future horizons and cross-cohort performance.
Action-conditioned and counterfactual simulations preserved expected risk ordering and produced lifestyle-related risk shifts consistent with observed associations.

papers.title: A world model for longitudinal health-trajectory prediction in older adults across multinational cohorts
papers.tldr: A health world model predicts older adults’ evolving mortality and functional-decline risks across time and simulates how specified actions may alter projected trajectories.

papers.abstract: Camera-conditioned video world models aim to generate 3D-consistent videos from a single image along specified camera trajectories. However, set-union updates in latent spatial memory leave repeated observations unconsolidated, while frontmost-only readout limits simultaneous access to stored evidence at different depths. To address these limitations, we present ENGRAM, a latent spatial memory framework combining reliability-weighted latent fusion and occlusion-aware layered readout. Specifically, recursive fusion integrates geometrically and visually compatible observations in a channel-normalized latent space, consolidating repeated evidence into a shared scene representation. Layered readout exposes multiple depth-ordered latent candidates with their reliability and availability at each target cell. This gives the generator access to information from multiple surfaces as visibility changes. Explicit camera rays provide viewpoint information independently of memory coverage, while geometric consistency constraints guide memory updates. Memory retrieval uses a single projection at latent resolution, avoiding intermediate RGB rendering and VAE re-encoding. We adapt a pretrained video generator using only 256 training scenes. On 100 RealEstate10K test scenes, ENGRAM improves novel-view-synthesis and closed-loop PSNRs over Spatia by 0.82 and 4.48 dB, respectively. On a 200-case WorldScore evaluation subset, it achieves an average score of 67.78, exceeding Spatia by 3.31 points. Project page: https://wchkoutian.github.io/engram-website/.
authors: Chenhao Wu, Zhaolong Su, Yang Liu, Tianrui Su, Yingguang Yang, Shang Luo, Yancheng Chen, Chongyang Zhang, Hao Zheng, Kefu Xu, Congjing Ran, Bin Chong
bullets: Addresses unconsolidated set-union memory updates and frontmost-only readout limitations.
Uses reliability-weighted recursive latent fusion for geometrically and visually compatible observations.
Provides occlusion-aware, depth-ordered latent candidates with reliability and availability information.
Uses explicit camera rays and geometric consistency constraints, with single-projection latent-resolution retrieval.
With 256 training scenes, improves PSNR and WorldScore over Spatia on the reported RealEstate10K and WorldScore evaluations.

papers.abstract: Cities are sensed by many platforms at once: on-board cameras, LiDAR and radar on autonomous vehicles, roadside units at intersections, drones and satellites overhead, and the GNSS traces of millions of trips. Yet most learned representations are built for one platform, one city, and one task. We survey this fragmented landscape through a single lens, the Urban State Representation (USR): a georeferenced, layered, time-varying, uncertainty-aware state that any sensing platform can write to and any downstream task can read from. We (i) formalize USR and five desiderata for it, and relate it to bird's-eye-view (BEV) features, occupancy, vectorized maps, neural fields and 3D Gaussians, scene graphs, road-network graphs, language tokens, and world-model latents; (ii) organize sensing platforms, cross-view (ground-aerial) matching, fusion operators, 3D geometric foundation models, end-to-end and vision-language-action models, and generative world models and data engines in one taxonomy that spans sensors to decisions; (iii) compile 26 urban datasets and simulators across ego, cooperative (V2X), aerial, trajectory, and language settings, with a metric glossary, a cross-benchmark results snapshot, a trend analysis, and a platform-coverage gap analysis; and (iv) review applications and propose, as an outlook, USR-5, a five-test protocol with explicit references and one aggregate score for measuring whether a state is shared, together with a research agenda of six open problems covering cross-city and cross-sensor transfer, uncertainty, efficiency, sim-to-real evaluation, and governance. This survey is an entry point for computer vision, autonomous driving, transportation, and urban computing researchers; the paper list, datasets, and USR-5 code are at https://github.com/binayksingh/Awesome-Urban-State-Representation.
authors: Binay Kumar Singh, Niels Da Vitoria Lobo
bullets: Formalizes USR and five desiderata, relating it to representations including BEV features, occupancy, maps, neural fields, scene graphs, language tokens, and world-model latents.
Provides a sensor-to-decision taxonomy covering sensing platforms, cross-view matching, fusion, geometric foundation models, end-to-end and vision-language-action models, and generative world models.
Compiles 26 urban datasets and simulators spanning ego, V2X, aerial, trajectory, and language settings, alongside metrics, benchmark results, trends, and coverage gaps.
Introduces USR-5, a proposed five-test protocol and aggregate score for evaluating whether representations are genuinely shared across platforms and tasks.
Highlights open problems in cross-city and cross-sensor transfer, uncertainty, efficiency, sim-to-real evaluation, and governance.

papers.abstract: Two centuries ago, an early cinema-like theater called the Diorama could already control its scenes at will. Today's video generation models produce videos of near-cinematic quality, yet they still lack this controllability. This limitation stems from the inherent semantic gap between text and pixels, since a prompt can describe a video only coarsely and leaves its details and relations beyond control. We bring this ability to video generation with Causal Dioramas, modules that decompose a video into a concept graph of variables that can be intervened on individually. Each instruction is translated into an intervention on the concept graph, modifying the specified concepts and their dependents. A connector then conveys this intervention to the video generator, which reuses the original noise to produce a counterfactual video while preserving all other content. Building on Causal Dioramas, we develop a unified framework for controllable generation, counterfactual revision of generated videos and editing of real videos. We outperform both open-source and commercial models in controllability on T2V-CompBench, CoVEBench and OpenVE-Bench.
authors: Yifan Shen, Xinyi Yang, Peiyuan Zhu, Yichang Jian, Jinyuan Hu, Xilin He, Fengming Zhu, Guangyi Chen, Kun Zhang
bullets: Addresses the limited detail and relational control of text-to-video prompts caused by the semantic gap between text and pixels.
Decomposes videos into concept graphs whose variables can be individually intervened on, including their dependents.
Translates instructions into graph interventions and uses a connector to guide the video generator with reused noise for counterfactual outputs.
Supports unified text-to-video generation, revision of generated videos, and editing of real videos.
Reports better controllability than open-source and commercial models on T2V-CompBench, CoVEBench, and OpenVE-Bench.

papers.abstract: Current leading video generation models can synthesize highly realistic videos, while still frequently violating physical and logical constraints in multi-step reasoning and planning, even after training with large-scale reasoning data or existing diffusion RL methods. We attribute these failures to the conventional video training paradigm, which treats a solution as a fixed-length clip rather than a chain of decisions. We present ViDecide, a decision-centric framework that trains video diffusion models to predict state transitions causally and decide when to stop, with a decision-focused training schedule. We further propose Corrective Fine-tuning (CFT), which corrects failed decisions by mapping their noise to the model's own successful continuations, achieving stable improvement without policy-gradient optimization. Across abstract games, planning tasks, and a new benchmark of multi-step robot planning, ViDecide achieves an average strict success rate of 83.8%, far above 23.3% for standard fine-tuning and 67.8% for the strongest prior method, and generalizes to larger puzzles and unseen layouts. Our framework therefore unlocks greater potential for video generation models as reliable reasoners and planners in the visual world. Project page: https://kevin-thu.github.io/ViDecide.
bullets: Targets physical and logical failures in multi-step video reasoning and planning.
Models solutions as causal state transitions with an explicit stopping decision.
Uses decision-focused training and Corrective Fine-tuning to repair failed decisions without policy-gradient optimization.
Reports an 83.8% average strict success rate across games, planning tasks, and robot-planning benchmarks, with generalization to larger puzzles and unseen layouts.

papers.abstract: Weather prediction is undergoing an important shift, with data-driven AI models outperforming leading numerical weather prediction systems on average at a fraction of the computational cost. Yet, whether this success extends to extreme events remains contested. Earlier evaluations have exposed important shortcomings, but have largely focused on deterministic models and metrics, leaving the capabilities of the latest probabilistic models less understood. We conduct an extensive benchmark of tropical cyclone forecasting, comparing GenCast, FourCastNet 3, and FGN with ECMWF's operational physics-based ensemble, IFS-ENS. We develop a suite of probabilistic metrics and diagnostic analyses to assess cyclone tracking, intensity biases, uncertainty, and the wind-pressure relationship that characterizes storm structure. We find that, despite remaining limitations in intensity and ensemble spread, leading AI models substantially outperform IFS-ENS in cyclone tracking: FGN achieves better probabilistic location scores for 90% of evaluated storms in 2025. Further analyses reveal model-specific failure modes and suggest a lingering influence of pretraining data, pointing to opportunities for targeted improvement. Nonetheless, these results suggest that AI models are capable of capturing physical relationships that remain predictive well beyond typical weather conditions, motivating further investigation into how these capabilities emerge and how to strengthen them.
bullets: Benchmarks GenCast, FourCastNet 3, and FGN against ECMWF’s IFS-ENS.
Introduces probabilistic metrics and diagnostics for tracking, intensity bias, uncertainty, and wind–pressure structure.
AI models substantially outperform IFS-ENS on cyclone tracking; FGN has better probabilistic location scores for 90% of evaluated storms in 2025.
Models retain limitations in intensity forecasts and ensemble spread, with distinct failure modes.
Findings suggest AI models capture physical relationships relevant to extreme weather, while pretraining data may influence errors.

papers.abstract: We study a new problem of preventing object penetration in interactive video world models. To understand how existing models handle this, we introduce NoPeBench, a benchmark that evaluates how world models respond to physical obstacles. Our evaluation reveals that none of the open-source models can reliably prevent such failures. Surprisingly, however, these models already encode the information needed to predict such violations. We find that the hidden states of diffusion transformers (DiTs) can predict whether a candidate action will penetrate an obstacle. Building on this, we introduce NoPeWorld, a lightweight framework that detects and prevents penetration. Specifically, we train a small prediction head on top of a frozen DiT's hidden states to read out if a candidate action is safe or not. Unsafe actions are then replaced with safe ones that best preserve the original intent. Despite its simplicity, NoPeWorld substantially reduces the physical violation rate, averaged over six video world models, from 74% to 16%. Remarkably, our method shows zero-shot generalization to open-domain imagery, third-person viewpoints, and moving obstacles. We publicly release our code, the NoPeBench benchmark, and model weights. Project Page: https://nopeworld.github.io .
authors: Yuhang Dai, Yinwei Wu, Ziyue Lin, Han Ji, Xingyi Yang
bullets: Introduces NoPeBench to evaluate obstacle interactions in interactive video world models.
Finds that existing open-source models frequently allow object penetration, despite encoding information predictive of such violations.
Trains a lightweight safety head on frozen DiT hidden states to classify candidate actions as safe or unsafe.
Replaces unsafe actions with safe alternatives that preserve the original intent.
Generalizes zero-shot to open-domain imagery, third-person views, and moving obstacles; code, benchmark, and weights are released.

papers.abstract: When a robot is damaged, it must decide which routes it can still afford, and the amount of risk it may accept can change from one mission to the next. We argue that whether a learned model helps such a robot depends on its decision interface, that is, on what the model hands to the planner. A decision policy tells the planner what to do, whereas an outcome model, a kind of world model, predicts the consequences of each route. We study simulated Unitree Go2 quadrupeds and H1 humanoids with weakened motors, added payloads, or reduced foot friction. We compare four interfaces. The first is a decision policy, and the second is the same policy trained with fixed penalties for infeasible routes. The third is an outcome model that predicts the feasibility and travel time of each route. The fourth, which we call a capability contract, is an outcome model that predicts the chance of success and the travel time of the robot on each terrain and composes them along a route. All share the same collected experience, matched tuning and risk calibration, and an uncertainty guard. Two comparatively low-risk probes let the capability contract rank hazardous terrains about as well as four new trials on every hazard. At a calibrated 5% limit on selecting empirically infeasible routes, outcome models cut declined missions from about 32% to 7-8% on Go2 and from 57% to 35-36% on H1 compared with the plain policy. Fixed penalties narrow this gap, but the best penalty changes with the risk target. Predicting outcomes lets the planner preserve missions by changing routes as risk requirements tighten.
bullets: Robot damage changes which routes are feasible and how much risk is acceptable per mission.
The study compares decision policies, fixed-penalty policies, generic outcome models, and capability contracts that compose terrain-level success and travel-time predictions.
Capability contracts rank hazardous terrains using two low-risk probes, avoiding the need for four new trials per hazard.
At a calibrated 5% infeasibility limit, outcome models reduce declined missions from about 32% to 7–8% on Go2 and 57% to 35–36% on H1.
Fixed penalties help but require retuning as the target risk changes; scope is simulated damaged quadruped and humanoid robots.

papers.abstract: Autonomous racing requires an accurate vehicle dynamics model near the limits of handling, yet a mismatch between the nominal and actual dynamics inevitably remains. To reduce this mismatch, existing methods learn from on-track data, i.e., data collected while the vehicle drives on the track under racing conditions, by adapting the physical parameters of the nominal model or by learning a residual that captures the remaining mismatch. However, these on-track learning methods typically handle either the physical parameters or the residual separately, which restricts their ability to resolve the mismatch. To address this limitation, we propose an interactive semi-parametric learning framework that learns both the physical parameters and the residual under a single shared prediction-error objective. Since updating one changes the learning target of the other, they are recursively updated in turn, each guided by the other's latest update. Each update is then accepted only if it does not increase the shared objective, so that the objective is guaranteed to be non-increasing and convergent over the recursion. Numerical simulations and hardware experiments show that the proposed framework outperforms the baselines. Compared with the nominal model, it reduces the one-step prediction errors of lateral velocity and yaw rate by 90.0% and 81.6% in simulation and by 54.0% and 59.4% on hardware.
authors: Jungbin Kim, Youngim Nam, Cheolhyeon Kwon
bullets: Addresses mismatch between nominal and actual vehicle dynamics during on-track racing.
Jointly learns physical parameters and residuals under one shared prediction-error objective.
Recursively alternates updates, accepting only changes that do not increase the objective.
The objective is guaranteed to be non-increasing and convergent over the recursion.
Simulations and hardware experiments show large reductions in lateral-velocity and yaw-rate one-step prediction errors versus the nominal model.

papers.abstract: Cardiovascular imaging offers several ways to measure blood flow, but each provides an incomplete, resolution-limited, or noisy view of the underlying dynamics. Reconstructing the missing information is inherently ambiguous because several flow fields may be compatible with the same observation. Here, we investigate generative diffusion models as tools for cardiovascular-flow generation and reconstruction using a fully controlled state-of-the-art dataset from a digital twin of a healthy human left heart. First, we show how unconditional samples reproduce the changing anatomy and the highly fluctuating statistical properties of the flow throughout the cardiac cycle. Second, we test the conditional inference of our generative model by reconstructing an entire 2D planar section of geometry and flow configurations from a limited portion. Repeated reconstructions allow us to represent a range of plausible completions, going beyond a single deterministic estimate, while their mean retains the principal features of the reference flow. Comparison with a Gaussian process regression baseline on the same reduced domain highlights the main advantage of diffusion models: their reconstructed ensembles capture a broader range of velocity and gradient fluctuations, better encompassing ground-truth features that the baseline distributions can miss. Our results provide a quantitative proof of concept for probabilistic reconstruction of incomplete cardiovascular-flow measurements and demonstrate the potential for groundbreaking applications to the augmentation of in-vivo cardiovascular imaging data.
authors: Fabio Guglietta, Tianyi Li, Francesco Viola, Luca Biferale
bullets: Cardiovascular imaging provides noisy, incomplete, and resolution-limited observations, making flow reconstruction inherently ambiguous.
Using a controlled digital twin of a healthy human left heart, the study evaluates unconditional generation and conditional reconstruction.
Repeated conditional samples produce plausible completions rather than a single deterministic estimate; their mean preserves key reference-flow features.
Compared with Gaussian process regression, diffusion-model ensembles capture a broader range of velocity and gradient fluctuations and better encompass ground-truth features.
The work is a quantitative proof of concept, with scope demonstrated on simulated healthy-heart data and potential application to in-vivo imaging augmentation.
papers.selection_reason: Diffusion-based probabilistic reconstruction of temporally structured flow; transferable to video and world-model generation.
papers.title: Augmentation of cardiovascular flow measurements with generative diffusion models
papers.tldr: Generative diffusion models can probabilistically reconstruct incomplete cardiovascular flow measurements while capturing diverse, physically plausible flow patterns.

papers.abstract: Visual world models can now generate compelling interactive worlds, but visual realism does not guarantee faithful dynamics. We systematically compare how categorical and continuous prediction shape learned dynamics under both next-token and iterative whole-frame generation. These choices are often bundled in approaches such as autoregressive token models and whole-frame flow matching. We design controlled 2D and 3D environments and evaluate dynamics validity, calibration, and visual quality. In 2D with lossless visual encoding, categorical models achieve higher rollout validity with less training compute, particularly for stochastic entities. Among categorical models, greedy decoding produces the highest rollout validity, while sampling from a next-token model yields the best-calibrated stochastic predictions. Failures in continuous models, such as disappearing game characters, echo those seen in more complex environments. Here, known dynamics let us measure their impact. In 3D, categorical models also achieve stronger long-horizon performance with less training compute. Even models with lossy tokenization remain competitive on semantic accuracy and FVD, despite lower next-frame RGB accuracy. Together, these findings make a strong case for categorical prediction as a compute-efficient route to learning world dynamics.
authors: Sarah Parisot, Melanie Fernandez Pradier, David Bignell, Sergio Valcarcel Macua, Katja Hofmann
bullets: The study separates prediction type—categorical versus continuous—from generation strategy using controlled 2D and 3D environments.
Categorical models achieve higher rollout validity in 2D and stronger long-horizon performance in 3D, particularly for stochastic entities.
Greedy decoding gives categorical models the highest rollout validity, while sampling provides the best-calibrated stochastic predictions.
Continuous models exhibit dynamics failures such as disappearing characters; categorical models remain competitive even with lossy visual tokenization.
Results support categorical prediction as a compute-efficient approach to learning world dynamics, beyond matching next-frame appearance.

papers.abstract: Training a humanoid motion tracker by backpropagating imagined returns through a learned world model is fast, because the model gives a first-order policy gradient. We ask how much of that gradient holds in the simulator. On a tracker for the Unitree G1, the $0.5\%$ of imagined rollouts with the largest gradients carry $22\%$ of the summed gradient norm, yet neither a second rollout from the same state nor the simulator confirms them. When the actions are moved along the model's gradient, the simulator returns 94% of the predicted change in return where the gradient norm is below the batch median, 48% between 3 and 10 times the median, and 1% above 30 times; the part of a gradient that either check confirms stops growing at a few times the median. We therefore cap each rollout's action-gradient norm at 10 times the batch median, draw imagination starts in proportion to their predicted gradient norm so that the cap removes less, and reset episodes where the world model and critic predict the lowest return. Trained on 223 hours of motion and tested on 353 motions that no actor performed in training, the method raises the normalized return of SuperMimic, the baseline it builds on, from 0.953 to 0.967 and the lowest $1\%$ of test clips from 0.65 to 0.76, halves the test clips that fall persistently, from 15--18 to 7--10, and reaches the baseline's final return in 40% of the baseline's iterations and half its training time. On LAFAN1, trained and evaluated on the same clips as prior work, it reaches 0.935 against 0.906.
bullets: Very large imagined gradients are poorly validated: simulator-confirmed return changes fall from 94% at low norms to 1% above 30× the batch median.
The method caps each rollout’s action-gradient norm at 10× the batch median, samples starts by predicted gradient norm, and resets episodes with the lowest predicted returns.
On unseen Unitree G1 motions, normalized return improves from 0.953 to 0.967, while the lowest 1% of clips improve from 0.65 to 0.76.
Persistent-fall clips decrease from 15–18 to 7–10, and baseline final performance is reached in 40% of its iterations and half the training time.
On LAFAN1, the method achieves 0.935 versus 0.906 for prior work.

papers.abstract: Model-based reinforcement learning (MBRL) can improve pretrained vision-language-action (VLA) policies through imagined experiences. However, existing VLA-MBRL methods primarily rely on large-scale image or video generation world models, incurring large computational overhead. Latent world models offer a more efficient alternative but face two challenges: compounding errors during recursive prediction and incompatibility with VLAs' visual input interfaces. In this work, we propose LS-MBPO, a lightweight residual MBRL framework that leverages latent world models to improve upon pretrained VLAs. LS-MBPO introduces two key techniques: (1) Hierarchical Forcing, which combines dense causal supervision with autoregressive feedback to mitigate compounding prediction errors; and (2) Latent Subchunk Rollouts, which leverage action chunks from a frozen VLA policy and a latent residual policy for successive subchunk refinement, bridging the gap between latent imagination and VLA policy execution. We further introduce a Progress-Conditioned Branch-Start Curriculum that progressively shifts rollout starting points from later to earlier task stages, enabling effective policy learning from short imagined rollouts. Extensive experiments on LIBERO, RoboTwin, and a real-world ALOHA robot show that LS-MBPO achieves superior task performance and training efficiency compared to existing methods.
authors: Nan Tang, Han-Tao Zhang, Jing-Cheng Pang, Hao-Nan Wang, Hao-Xiang Ren, Yi-Fei Sheng, Jun-Yin Ye, Tian Xu, Fan-Ming Luo, Hao-Xin Lin, Yang Yu
bullets: Addresses the high computational cost of image/video-based VLA model-based reinforcement learning.
Uses Hierarchical Forcing to mitigate compounding errors in recursive latent predictions.
Introduces Latent Subchunk Rollouts to connect latent imagination with frozen VLA action-chunk execution.
Applies a Progress-Conditioned Branch-Start Curriculum for learning from short imagined rollouts.
Reports strong task performance and training efficiency across LIBERO, RoboTwin, and a real-world ALOHA robot.

papers.abstract: GCM-to-RCM downscaling emulation is dominated by generative diffusion models, but most existing work evaluates skill only per timestep, treating each field as an independent snapshot. This leaves open whether generated sequences are temporally coherent or merely independently plausible, a gap that matters increasingly for sub-daily resolutions since downstream impacts depend on accumulation and persistence, not just on isolated states. This study asks whether autoregressive conditioning can deliver coherent rollouts without error accumulation and ensemble-spread collapse, and whether a single model can expose the resulting coherence-diversity trade-off as a controllable inference choice rather than a fixed design commitment. We introduce a noise-conditioned teacher-forcing training scheme conditioning a diffusion U-Net downscaling model on a noised previous high-resolution state, so the trained model interpolates continuously between autoregressive (AR) and per-timestep independent (PTI) sampling via one noise parameter. We apply the scheme to an hourly, European-domain historical simulation downscaling AWI-CM1 (1$^\circ$) with ICON (0.11$^\circ$, regridded to 0.25$^\circ$) for precipitation and 2-meter temperature. The noise parameter traces a smooth interpolation between ICON's autocorrelation and PTI generation. AR rollouts of up to six months show no progressive degradation, with ensemble spread contracting only slightly within the first 24 hours. In contrast, the same architecture trained on noise-free previous states diverges. For precipitation PTI underestimates maxima by up to 2x in daily aggregations, while AR tracks ICON's maxima closely. For temperature, differences between modes are negligible. These results show that in diffusion downscaling temporal consistency can be achieved architecture-agnostically and offered as a controllable, not fixed, inference choice.
authors: Luca Glawion, Julius Polz, Harald Kunstmann, Benjamin Fersch, Patrick Ludwig, Antonio S\'anchez-Ben\'itez, Christian Chwala
bullets: Targets the gap between snapshot-based skill evaluation and temporal coherence needed for sub-daily climate-impact applications.

Trains a diffusion U-Net with a noised previous high-resolution state, enabling continuous interpolation between autoregressive and per-timestep-independent sampling through one inference-time noise parameter.
On hourly European precipitation and 2-meter temperature downscaling, autoregressive rollouts remain stable for up to six months, with only slight early ensemble-spread contraction.
Autoregressive precipitation better preserves daily maxima, while independent generation underestimates them by up to 2×; temperature differences are negligible.
Noise-free conditioning diverges, indicating that the noise-conditioned scheme is important for stable long rollouts.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of the proposed temporal-noise-conditioned diffusion framework. (a) Training: The conditional diffusion model learns to emulate high-resolution RCM fields from coarse GCM input. The previous-hour RCM state is additionally provided as temporal condition input, corrupted with randomly sampled noise. (b) Inference: The conditioning noise level is controlled by the parameter τ . At its maximum value (τ = 999), the temporal condition consists of pure noise, resulting in per-timestep independent (PTI) samples (dashed lines). This regime also serves to initialize the autoregressive rollout. At a lower noise level (e.g. τ = 50), the previous timestep’s prediction is perturbed with noise and used as the temporal conditioning input. This provides informative temporal context, resulting in temporally consistent autoregressive (AR) sampling (solid lines).

papers.title: Beyond Resolution: Inference-Time Parameterized Temporal Consistency in Generative Regional Climate Downscaling
papers.tldr: A noise-conditioned diffusion downscaling model provides a tunable trade-off between temporally coherent autoregressive rollouts and independent per-timestep generation without progressive degradation.

papers.abstract: Latent world models plan by rolling out hundreds of candidate action sequences through a transformer predictor, so a single decision can take tens of seconds. Existing accelerations prune spatial tokens as in vision-language models, yet a sampling-based planner uses predicted costs only to rank candidates, so a rollout can be compressed freely as long as the ranking survives. We propose SOAR, a training-free method that adapts rollout compression to each planning decision. At every decision, SOAR probes a few candidates under several token budgets and keeps the smallest budget that preserves their ranking, so it compresses as far as the current decision allows, without task labels. A closed-loop study of more than 80,000 episodes fixes the rest of the rollout: the first step, which alone reads a real observation, stays exact, and the context frame is cached rather than recomputed. On seven navigation and manipulation tasks with frozen checkpoints, SOAR matches dense-level planning success at 2.3x speedup and retains 98% at 2.5x. Our code is available at https://github.com/starrywiki/SOAR.
authors: Anqi Li, Kai Liu, Linghe Kong, Yulun Zhang
bullets: Targets the high cost of rolling out hundreds of candidate action sequences for each decision.
Probes a few candidates at multiple token budgets and selects the smallest budget that maintains their ranking.
Requires no training or task labels; the first observation-processing step remains exact and context frames are cached.
Across seven navigation and manipulation tasks, matches dense planning success at 2.3× speedup and retains 98% at 2.5×.
Evaluated in a closed-loop study spanning more than 80,000 episodes with frozen checkpoints.

papers.selection_reason: Latent world model planning acceleration via rollout compression; fits world models and token-level efficiency.
papers.title: SOAR: Training-Free Rank-Consistent Rollout Compression for Latent World Model Planning
papers.tldr: SOAR accelerates latent-world-model planning by adaptively compressing rollouts while preserving candidate-action rankings.

papers.abstract: We present Ego4Gen (Egocentric 4D Future Generation), a world model for 4D future generation in robotic manipu lation. Given a single egocentric image and a text prompt, Ego4Gen jointly generates temporally aligned RGB frames, dense point maps, and dense scene flow, explicitly pre dicting the evolution of scene appearance, spatial struc ture, and motion. Built on Cosmos3-Nano, Ego4Gen ex tends the pretrained generative backbone through modality routed LoRA and asymmetric attention, using geometric pseudo-labels from MotionCrafter to learn to predict future geometry and motion latents. These latents can either be decoded into explicit 3D structure and motion or mapped to robot actions. To this end, we also introduce FlowIn verse, a lightweight inverse dynamics network trained in two stages to translate predicted 4D latents into robot ac tions. Experiments show that these geometry and motion latents outperform the evaluated latent-action and video latent baselines in out-of-distribution settings. Closed loop policy evaluations further demonstrate their utility for translating predicted 4D futures into robot control. To gether, these results support geometry-grounded motion to kens as a world-action interface, connecting 4D future gen eration with robotic manipulation and suggesting a path to ward reduced reliance on action-labeled data.
authors: Yang Liu, Chao Ye, Jiahao Zhang, Zeyuan Hou, Ruijie Fang, Xiyin Ni, Xinyang Ren, Weiyang Lin
bullets: Targets 4D future generation for robotic manipulation while modeling scene appearance, structure, and motion jointly.
Extends Cosmos3-Nano with modality-routed LoRA, asymmetric attention, and MotionCrafter-derived geometric pseudo-labels.
Introduces FlowInverse, a lightweight two-stage inverse-dynamics network that maps predicted 4D latents to robot actions.
Geometry and motion latents outperform evaluated latent-action and video-latent baselines in out-of-distribution settings.
Closed-loop policy evaluations demonstrate that the predicted futures can support robot control and reduce reliance on action-labeled data.

The resulting geometry and motion latents can further support closed-loop action-policy generation.

papers.title: Ego4Gen: Generating Geometry-Grounded Motion Tokens as a World-Action Interface
papers.tldr: Ego4Gen generates future video, geometry, and motion from an egocentric image and text, then converts these predictions into robot actions through geometry-grounded latent representations.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language Navigation(VLN) requires an embodied agent to follow language instructions through unseen 3D environments, where the target spaces often lie beyond the current observation. Navigation world models address this challenge by predicting future views either as pixels or latent representations, providing valuable look-ahead information for action decision. Both paradigms define the future primarily through what the agent may observe, raising a fundamental question: is predicting future views the ultimate form to represent the future for VLN? Cognitive studies show that the human hippocampus prospectively represents both future goals and intervening locations along planned routes. Inspired by this predictive-map view, we organize the navigation-relevant future around goal-directed spatial states and route structure. We instantiate this perspective with two complementary abstractions: a short-horizon waypoint that specifies the next local state to reach, and a mid-horizon corridor that captures the spatial support of the upcoming route. Based on this design, we propose FS-Nav, a future-state world modeling framework that predicts waypoint-corridor states from spatial memory and language instructions, and communicates them to a VLM navigator through top-down and first-person interfaces. Experiments on standard VLN benchmarks demonstrate that FS-Nav achieves state-of-the-art performance. This highlights navigation-relevant future-state modeling as a promising direction for representing the future in VLN.
authors: Kangyi Wu, Pengna Li, Yucheng Wang, Yance Fang, Xihan Ma, Zhizhong Su, Yang Wu, Ye Deng, Jinjun Wang, Jianyi Liu
bullets: VLN agents must plan beyond their current visual observation while following language instructions.
The paper argues that future representation should include goal-directed spatial states and route structure, inspired by predictive-map views of navigation.
FS-Nav predicts short-horizon waypoints and mid-horizon corridors from spatial memory and language instructions.
These future states are communicated to a vision-language navigator through top-down and first-person interfaces.
Experiments on standard VLN benchmarks show state-of-the-art performance, though the abstract provides no further experimental details.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of FS-Nav. The Future State World Model encodes the accumulated spatial memory and navigation instruction, fuses their geometry and language features, and predicts a short-horizon waypoint together with a mid-horizon corridor. The Future State Renderer deterministically renders the same prediction as either a top-down canvas or a first-person overlay. Conditioned on the instruction, observation history, and rendered guidance, the Future-State-Guided Navigator generates an action chunk and interacts with the environment in a closed loop. Flame symbols indicate trainable modules.

Figure 1: Motivation and key properties of future-state world model. (a) FS-Nav represents the upcoming route with a short-horizon waypoint and a mid-horizon corridor. (b) On a single RTX 4090, future-state prediction takes 66.7 ms, over 500× faster than generating a five-frame future observation with Wan2.2-TI2V-5B. (c) The waypoint and corridor each improve navigation performance, with their combination achieving the highest SR on R2R-CE validation unseen.

papers.title: Beyond Future Views: Exploring Future-State World Models for Vision-Language Navigation
papers.tldr: FS-Nav models future navigation states as waypoints and route corridors—not just future views—to improve vision-language navigation in unseen environments.

papers.abstract: World-action models (WAMs) often generate future visual states alongside robot actions, introducing substantial computational overhead during inference. During closed-loop execution, consecutive inference cycles often predict similar action sequences, leading to redundant computation. However, reducing this redundancy requires distinguishing consistent actions from changes that demand fresh computation. To address these challenges, we propose ReActWAM, a training-free framework that combines action-intent-guided prefix skipping with inner-chunk prediction reuse. A coarse-to-fine assessment evaluates motion changes, visual consistency, and action prediction conflicts. For eligible chunks, we draw on first-step differences to adapt the cached latent and network features to the current condition, providing an estimate at a later denoising step that bypasses the redundant prefix. Subsequent inference refines this estimate while reusing stable denoising predictions within the chunk. Experiments across LingBot-VA, FastWAM and the Cosmos family on LIBERO-Long and RoboTwin 2.0 demonstrate $1.41\times$--$5.44\times$ GPU inference speedup, with minimal degradation in task success rates. Real-world experiments on a Franka Research 3 (FR3) robot further achieve $1.46\times$ end-to-end speedup while maintaining success rate.
authors: Zhaochen Guo, Yunke Wang, Siyu Xu, Zijian Wang, Chenghao Xia, Chengbin Du, Shinan Liu, Chang Xu
bullets: Addresses redundant computation in closed-loop WAM inference caused by similar consecutive action-sequence predictions.
Uses training-free action-intent-guided prefix skipping and inner-chunk prediction reuse.
Evaluates motion changes, visual consistency, and action conflicts to determine when cached computation is safe.
Reports 1.41×–5.44× GPU inference speedups with minimal task-success degradation across several WAMs and benchmarks.
Achieves 1.46× end-to-end speedup on a Franka Research 3 robot while maintaining success rate.

Bottom left: recent motion, visual consistency, and predicted upcoming behavior jointly assess action consistency between the current chunk c and reference chunk r. Bottom right: first-step response differences correct cached states at entry i, bypassing redundant early denoising steps. Spatial weights Wz modulate video correction, while within-chunk prediction reuse reduces computation during subsequent refinement.

Red and green indicate ongoing and completed execution. Completion times correspond to the recorded rollout endpoints, and asterisks mark final frames held for temporal alignment.

Mean az and Dir. report the mean normalized vertical command and its direction. Rejected/Accepted denote uncorrected reuse for chunks failing/passing the gate, and Corrected applies correction to the same accepted chunks. papers.selection_reason: Action-consistent caching for world-action models that generate future visual states; fits interactive world models and inference efficiency.
papers.title: ReActWAM: Action-Consistent Caching for Efficient World-Action Models
papers.tldr: ReActWAM accelerates world-action model inference by safely reusing predictions when consecutive robot actions and visual states remain consistent.

papers.abstract: Action-conditioned video world models imagine future observations under candidate robot actions, providing a promising visual tool for robot policy evaluation and interaction simulation. However, existing video world models often optimize global reconstruction errors instead of emphasizing interaction-relevant regions. As a result, they may preserve overall scene appearance but overlook local interaction details, leading to physically implausible outcomes such as hallucinated contact effects and inconsistent robot-object interactions. We introduce MoReWorld, a unified motion-region-guided framework that uses a shared motion region, the part of the environment that moves in response to the robot's actions, to focus dynamics learning and video generation on interaction-relevant regions. The same motion region guides local motion prediction, region-aware supervision, and motion-gated future-feature conditioning. At inference time, the motion region is predicted as a motion probability map from visual history and robot actions, without requiring future observations or ground-truth motion labels. On WorldSimProbe, MoReWorld achieves the highest overall simulator-faithfulness score, with the strongest performance on local consistency, global consistency, and interaction dynamics. These results indicate that motion-region guidance helps the model preserve scene-level consistency while more faithfully predicting action-conditioned interaction dynamics.
authors: Yongkang He, Xiaofen Xing, Xiangmin Xu
bullets: Existing models can preserve global appearance while missing local interaction details, causing implausible contact effects and robot-object behavior.
MoReWorld uses a shared motion region to guide local motion prediction, region-aware supervision, and motion-gated future-feature conditioning.
The motion region is inferred at test time from visual history and robot actions, without future observations or ground-truth motion labels.
On WorldSimProbe, it achieves the highest overall simulator-faithfulness score, with strongest results in local consistency, global consistency, and interaction dynamics.

figures.caption: Figure 2. An overview of MoReWorld. (a) An action-conditioned V-JEPA predictor estimates the future state from history and timealigned actions; a motion head converts its spatial response into a motion probability p̂k and a soft gate gk. (b) During training, WAFT optical flow yields moving/static labels m, s, and URDF rendering yields the environment mask E = 1− ρ that excludes the robot region; their product gives the motion-map labels. (c) The gated future motion Ck and the robot appearance r are injected into the Wan input. (d) A shared Wan denoising transformer jointly processes RGB and VGGT latents and predicts the RGB velocity, clean future VGGT features, and an auxiliary flow velocity, supervised with the motion-region weighted loss.

Figure 3. Qualitative comparison on WorldSimProbe. Each panel shows the initial frame (left) and three later time steps (rows) of one benchmark case. Columns show, from left to right, the ground truth, MoReWorld (Ours), MVA, Ctrl-World, and LingBot-VA. All models receive the same initial frame and action trajectory. Red boxes mark incorrect object responses or robot motion.

Figure 5. Qualitative transfer to in-the-wild images. The four panels show a pear painting (top left), a real tabletop photograph (top right), an illustrated still life (bottom left), and another painted still life (bottom right). Within each panel, columns show input actions as black-background URDF renderings, MoReWorld (Ours), MVA, LingBot-VA, and Ctrl-World, from left to right. The top row shows the supplied initial image; subsequent rows advance in time. Red boxes and the dashed arrow highlight selected object responses. Robotspecific adaptation uses simulated interactions, with no additional training on these external images.

Figure 1. Accurate interaction-dynamics prediction is critical for video world models. (a) Prior models can produce incorrect object responses, yielding false success signals that mislead downstream evaluation. (b) MoReWorld predicts interaction dynamics before generation via a motion-probability intermediate, producing object motion and a final video consistent with the action.
Figure 4. Dynamics score by interaction primitive (%). K.O. denotes knock-over and Rot. rotate. Darker cells indicate higher scores.

Table 2. Component studies on the same 200 WorldSimProbe videos. Visual metrics are computed over both tasks; interaction scores are reported separately. ∆T4 and ∆T5 are relative to the MoReWorld full model, computed as ablation minus full-model score; negative values indicate a decrease. Removing V-JEPA excludes the entire predictive-conditioning branch. Removing the flow head also removes its training loss. The w/o motion-region variant removes motion-region effects from region weighting and motion-gated conditioning while retaining the flow head and VGGT. Bold denotes the best value per column.

papers.selection_reason: Action-conditioned robotic video world model with motion-region guidance for faithful interaction dynamics and robot policy evaluation.
papers.title: Learning Interaction Dynamics via Motion-Region Guidance for Robotic Video World Models
papers.tldr: MoReWorld improves robot video world models by guiding dynamics learning and generation toward regions that move in response to actions.

papers.abstract: We present Zing-1.0, a Playable World System built on Controllable Rendering. An executable engine resolves player actions under the world's rules and produces proxy video from the updated state. A streaming video model synthesizes the player's view from this proxy, and the runtime delivers it to inform subsequent actions. (1) Principle and system. We formulate Controllable Rendering and define the interfaces among world construction, world execution, observation synthesis, and the interaction runtime. To our knowledge, this is the first implementation-independent specification of a Playable World System. (2) AI-native engine. WorldKit provides structured authoring tools and reusable character, camera, and control components for coding agents to construct executable proxy worlds. It supports extensible interactions and precise geometric motion control while separating executable behavior from final visual appearance. (3) Streaming renderer. We adapt MiniMax-H3 for block-causal autoregressive generation and incremental decoding. Proxy video constrains structure and motion, while text and separate scene and subject references specify appearance. We train the generator on diverse tasks and distill it to generate each block in a few denoising steps. The renderer leads the compared streaming editors on OpenVE (3.90) and LongV2VBench (3.44). On StreamEval, Zing-1.0 scores 57.86 on instruction editing and 54.06 on reference editing, exceeding the published baselines on both tracks. (4) Interaction infrastructure. We build an Interaction Runtime that routes player actions to WorldKit while supporting in-play prompt and reference updates. Cross-block joint execution and sparse attention with compressed K/V reduce inference overhead. With the DiT on a single H200 and encoding and decoding on one H100 each, the serving system achieves a steady-state throughput of 23.82 FPS at $832\times480$.
authors: Wenbo Zhang, Guoli Zhang, Xuewen Yu, Xueliang Yang, Jiangqiao Yan, Teng Xia, Xinmiao Wu, Zeyang Tian, Haoze Sun, Jinghui Niu, Hongli Ning, Zhiyuan Liu, Xinna Liu, Weimin Liu, Jialin Liu, Tianpeng Li, Kejun Li, Jun Li, Jiawen Li, Yirong He, Haoyuan Guo, Bosheng Gong, Junhao Gao, Xiaoxiao Fu, Xuezhi Chen, Shengdong Chen, Mingyang Chen, Diying Chen, Yinglun Chai, Yiwen Cai
bullets: Defines interfaces connecting world construction, execution, observation synthesis, and interaction runtime.
WorldKit lets coding agents author executable proxy worlds with reusable characters, cameras, controls, and precise motion.
A block-causal streaming renderer uses proxy video for structure and motion, with text and references controlling appearance.
Reports strong benchmark results, including 3.90 on OpenVE, 3.44 on LongV2VBench, and higher-than-published-baseline scores on both StreamEval tracks.
The runtime supports in-play prompt/reference updates and reaches 23.82 FPS at 832×480 using specified H200/H100 hardware.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Conceptual overview of Zing-1.0 as a Playable World System. World construction produces an executable WorldKit world. Player actions update its state, and proxy frames guide observation synthesis under separate scene and subject references. The interaction runtime links displayed views to their source updates and returns feedback to the player.

Figure 2. Zing-1.0 system architecture, with the control side (the coding agent and WorldKit) and the rendering side (the streaming renderer) connected by proxy frames. Offline construction produces an executable proxy world. Online, player actions update WorldKit state; proxy frames convey its visible consequences to the streaming renderer, while text and references specify appearance. Generated video returns to the browser as feedback for subsequent actions. The runtime coordinates the input-to-display path without feeding generated frames directly into world state.

Figure 4. Architecture of the Zing-1.0 streaming renderer. (a) Frozen Qwen encodes the instruction and references, while the frozen visual VAE encodes the references and live proxy video. (b) The block-causal DiT processes interleaved proxy and target blocks after a static conditioning prefix. Role-specific AdaLN modulates both self-attention and the FFN. Dashed arrows indicate initialization from H3’s video AdaLN branch. (c) The streaming decoder uses cached K/V to decode one latent at a time. Matching labels A and B identify corresponding proxy and rendered frames.

Figure 14. World construction and rule execution in a harvest race. (a–c) Only previously uncut 1 m2 cells whose centers lie within the cutting footprint receive credit. (d–e) World overview and native player view. (f) Schematic score accumulation.

Figure 8. Independent training paths for the DiT and decoder. (a) The DiT starts from H3-Base-Ref2VA and is trained in three successive stages. In autoregressive adaptation, RF changes the history seen by the model without changing the supervised target. Endpoint initialization prepares the student for larger denoising updates, and DMD refines few-step outputs using student rollouts. (b) The decoder is adapted independently on paired latents and RGB frames with reconstruction and temporal losses.

Figure 6. Conceptual examples of the four training data categories. (a) Standalone image and video generation. (b) Paired editing from a source and a text instruction. (c) Subject appearance specified by multi-view reference images. (d) Temporally aligned proxy and target video frames.

Figure 3. WorldKit components. A coding agent authors a world through Creator tools, which retrieve pinned 3C assets from Atlas and build, run, and observe the world in the WorldKit Engine. Each tool returns structured feedback that the agent can read. The sealed package is executed online by the WorldKit CLI on the same engine, which emits proxy frames tagged with their simulation step.

Figure 5. Block-causal attention in training and inference. Rows denote query blocks and columns denote K/V blocks. (a) Parallel teacher forcing evaluates multiple noisy target queries against clean context. Only the two bracketed target rows contribute to the loss in this example. (b) The DiT evaluates one noisy target query per denoising step. After denoising the first target, the DiT caches the K/V of clean X1. The second target reads them alongside the static prefix C and the proxy blocks S1 and S2.

Figure 7. Proxy videos at different granularities: (a) coarse masses, (b) structural blockout, and (c) detailed clay geometry. Consistent proxy colors distinguish the vehicle and the two people across all three inputs, which share the same illustrative rendered target.

Figure 9. Guidance-aware adaptation and DMD gradients. (a) Both branches share the VAE encoding of r, proxy latents s1:K , noisy targets xσ , timesteps t, and target history x1:K−1. Each block k can attend only to x<k in this history. The blank branch replaces only the Qwen context with a blank-prompt embedding, and sg stops gradients through its prediction nθ. (b) DM compares the conditional real and fake scores, whereas CA compares conditional and blank real scores at a separately sampled noise level. The DMD loss uses rollout values, but gradients pass through the packed replay with generated history latents held fixed.

Figure 11. Interactions and locomotion with prebuilt 3C. Rows (a) and (b) show interaction sequences read from left to right. Row (c) presents independent examples of wall contact, vehicle driving, and fixed-wing takeoff. Examples were recorded in separate offline proxy sessions using two WorldKit builds.

Figure 10. Single-latent streaming decoder. (a) A phase embedding and bounded historical K/V support incremental RGB decoding. (b) H3’s inherited phase cycle yields one RGB frame at phase zero and four at each other phase.

Figure 12. Camera control in the engine. (a) Three views of the same paused world. (b) Recorded follow-camera arm length and proxy frames at steps 31, 56, and 385. The arm shortens to 2.50 m when the wall blocks the view. After the camera turns away at step 162, the arm returns to the desired 11.0 m by step 386.

Figure 13. Construction and verification of an agent-authored world. (a) Two tool-reported failures and the corresponding repairs. (b) A Creator preview of the constructed course. (c) The recorded playtest path. Numbers 1–8 indicate the order of first entry into each target region, and grey squares mark pillars.

Figure 15. Composing and selectively cancelling edits in a continuous stream. Recorded outputs from the first three stages of a 60-second StreamEval session, case 009, Instruction Editing, repeat 2 [49]. Requests at 0, 12, and 24 seconds apply a colored-pencil style, add a canyon while retaining the style, and restore the source style while retaining the canyon. The source frame at 11.54 seconds provides scene context. Output samples at 11.53, 14.28, and 32.04 seconds are timed by reception relative to session start.

(b) Corresponding proxy and rendered frames at representative moments of propulsion, camera rotation, airborne motion, and particle effects. Each column uses the same elapsed timestamp across rows.

Figure 17. Continuous scene transitions and persistent interaction state. (a) Broom flight across successive outdoor and interior scenes, including portals into the shop street and back to the stadium. (b) Museum exploration through button and pressure-plate interactions. The barrier remains lowered and the hall light remains on when the cat returns. Each panel contains twelve observations, read left to right and top to bottom.

papers.title: Zing-1.0: A Playable World System Built on Controllable Rendering
papers.tldr: Zing-1.0 combines an executable proxy world with controllable streaming video generation to create an interactive playable-world system.

papers.abstract: Latent action models let a robot policy learn from video by turning the change between two frames into a training target. In egocentric video, a cup can move across the image because a hand pushes it or because the wearer turns. Both changes help predict the next frame, but only the first describes manipulation. During training, EgoLAM supervises the action code with measured wrist motion and supplies camera motion separately to the forward model. Even when the wearer turns while pushing a cup, the training target still describes how the hand pushed it. The action encoder pools object slots around each hand, and wrist translation and rotation can be decoded from the code in a common reference frame. Extracting a code then requires only two RGB frames. Alongside LARYBench classification and regression, we measure how much wrist motion a frozen code retains and how strongly it responds to a synthetic view or lighting change. EgoLAM has the highest hand-motion decoding score among eight evaluated models. Across three LIBERO suites, policies pretrained on its codes and fine-tuned on expert demonstrations achieve 79.38% mean success, 28.73 points above expert behavior cloning and 9.76 points above the strongest other latent action model in each suite on average.

papers.abstract: Interactive video world models aim to predict how visual environments evolve in response to user interventions, including physically consistent state changes induced by applied forces. Existing methods often represent forces as motion trajectories, which may introduce inappropriate motion priors, causing the model to over-rely on encoded displacement patterns. More fundamentally, the model's internal representations do not reliably localize force-induced state changes, making it difficult to associate applied forces with their resulting physical responses. Also, limited force-annotated data make it difficult to produce physically consistent and temporally stable predictions in unseen scenarios. To address these limitations, we propose PhysForce, a two-stage framework that integrates supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning through three complementary components. During supervised fine-tuning, (1) the Latent Force Intervention Encoder maps force location, direction, and magnitude into the video latent space without exposing future motion; and (2) the Physics Attribution Network associates force interventions with localized changes in the latent state, strengthening the learning of physical responses to applied forces. During reinforcement learning, (3) Physics-Aware Reinforcement Learning uses self-supervised rewards on out-of-distribution videos to improve physical consistency and generalization. Extensive experiments show that PhysForce improves force responsiveness, physical consistency, and generalization, demonstrating its effectiveness for interactive video world models.
authors: Xuancheng Xu, Xiaofeng Wang, Yue Ma, Zheng Zhu, Bing-Kun Bao

Experiments report improved force responsiveness, physical consistency, and generalization.

papers.abstract: Predictive world models learn to forecast observations, but accurate short-term predictions do not necessarily produce physically coherent behavior over longer horizons. We investigate how incorporating physical structure can strengthen world models while retaining their underlying predictive objectives. Across token-based models of planetary motion and JEPA-style visual models of mechanical systems, we study conserved-quantity supervision, symmetry-aware representations, temporal consistency, and learned structured dynamics. In planetary motion, angular-momentum supervision improves autonomous next-token forecasting, while the benefits of temporal regularization depend on the accompanying physical objective and representation. In visual models, generating rollouts through supervised energy-based dynamics heads produces more faithful trajectories and phase-space evolution. Together, these findings highlight the importance of how physical structure participates in prediction: improvements in an auxiliary physical readout or a local acceleration estimate do not automatically translate into more reliable long-horizon behavior. Evaluations across initial conditions and physical parameter shifts further reveal where these benefits persist and where generalization remains limited. Our study supports physical structure as a practical means of improving predictive world models and provides a unified framework for understanding its effects on representations, learned transitions, and autonomous rollouts. The central lesson is that effective physical inductive biases should help models both represent physical regularities and use them to generate future states.
authors: Panayiotis Christou, Satyapragnya Kar, Flavjo Xhelollari, Parijat Dube, Rajarshi Das

papers.abstract: Reconstructing the spatiotemporal evolution of landslide runout from limited observations is a central challenge in geohazard assessment: transient flow dynamics are rarely observed directly, and available data are often confined to post-event deposits or brief monitoring windows. We apply LAPIS-SHRED (LAtent Phase Inference from Short time sequence using SHallow REcurrent Decoders) to reconstruct runout events near Mount St. Helens, USA. Trained on physics-based simulation ensembles, the framework supports both backward reconstruction from single frame and forward prediction from short initial window across different runout regimes. Using 32 sensor observations from a single timepoint, LAPIS-SHRED recovers complete runout trajectories with NRMSE below 5.8%, robust across varying observational and training conditions. Validation against observed deposits yields spatial correlation of r = 0.843 against the calibrated simulator's r = 0.853. These results suggest that latent-space temporal inference offers a viable pathway for spatiotemporal landslide reconstruction under extreme observational constraints typical of field settings.
authors: Xingyue Zhang, Yuxuan Bao, Jeffrey Keck, Erkan Istanbulluoglu, J. Nathan Kutz

papers.title: Spatiotemporal Landslide Runout Reconstruction from Sparse Observations with LAPIS-SHRED
papers.tldr: LAPIS-SHRED reconstructs complete landslide runout trajectories from sparse observations, achieving close agreement with physics-based simulations and observed deposits near Mount St. Helens.

papers.abstract: If we optimize an image until a classifier is confident it shows a cat, we may get an adversarial example, not a cat. Planning with a latent world model is a similar search for actions whose predicted future is closest to the goal. Is the result a plan, or an adversarial example of the world model? We show that it can be either. On the released DINO-WM and LeWM, more iterations of the cross-entropy method (CEM) lower the predicted cost but lose up to half of the problems CEM had already solved. The model's own predictions do not reveal these failures. We propose a simple test that executes the plan after every iteration and counts the problems a planner solves and then loses. Unlike an image, a plan comes with its actions, which our round-trip check reads back from the predicted states with a small network, penalizing mismatches. The check reads back the sum of each block of five actions, the part that two consecutive predicted states determine. Without retraining the world model and at only 0.2% to 3.1% more planning time, it improves the widely used planners CEM and MPPI on three released world models, and gains more where planners lose more problems. Without replanning, success rises from 0.39 to 0.76 on Wall with DINO-WM and from 0.56 to 0.94 for MPPI on JEPA-WM. With replanning (MPC), it rises from 0.70 to 0.81 on Cube with LeWM.
authors: Huiyuan Tian, Chih-Yung Wen, Shijian Li
bullets: More CEM iterations can reduce predicted cost while causing planners to lose up to half of previously solved problems.
The world model’s predictions alone fail to reveal these planning failures.
The proposed check executes plans after each iteration and compares predicted actions with actions read back from predicted states.
It improves CEM and MPPI across three released world models with only 0.2%–3.1% additional planning time.
Reported success increases from 0.39 to 0.76 on Wall, 0.56 to 0.94 on JEPA-WM, and 0.70 to 0.81 with MPC on Cube.

(b) Decoded predicted states of the final plan of CEM and of the plan found with the check, with the residual r of each plan at the end of its row. papers.selection_reason: Addresses the reliability of latent world models by proposing a 'round-trip check' that validates plans against actual execution, improving planning robustness.
papers.title: A Plan or an Adversarial Example? A Round-Trip Check for Latent World Models
papers.tldr: A lightweight round-trip check detects adversarial plans in latent world models and substantially improves planning reliability with minimal extra cost.

papers.abstract: We study spatio-temporal forecasting in networked systems under specified actions. The challenge is to capture the action's effects without predicting spurious changes in unaffected regions. However, direct supervision and evaluation of these effects require paired futures with and without the action, whereas observational trajectories reveal only the realized future. We introduce PairST, a benchmark comprising six datasets across traffic, power transmission and water distribution, with paired reference and intervened futures simulated from the same system state. These pairs enable separate evaluation of affected-region forecast accuracy and quiet-region response error. We further propose ActionST, which forecasts the intervened future by writing an explicit response onto an intervention-independent reference forecast. Specifically, node-time addressing constructs a query for each response position, a state-conditioned response writer computes candidate responses, and a graph-aware locality gate controls their strength. Experiments on six datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of ActionST at new action targets, with the lowest mean absolute error on five datasets and the best average rank. Our source code and the PairST benchmark are available at https://github.com/yutong-xia/ActionST.
authors: Yutong Xia, Yangyou Liu, Yuxuan Liang, Yuankai Wu, See-Kiong Ng, Roger Zimmermann
bullets: PairST provides six datasets with paired reference and intervened futures across traffic, power transmission, and water distribution.
The benchmark separately evaluates accuracy in affected regions and response error in quiet regions.
ActionST writes an action response onto an intervention-independent reference forecast using node-time addressing, state-conditioned response generation, and graph-aware locality gating.
It achieves the lowest mean absolute error on five of six datasets and the best average rank, including at new action targets.
