papers.abstract: Motor decoding from electroencephalography (EEG) supports non-invasive brain-computer interfaces, yet existing methods either rely on costly cue-based trials and coarse categorical labels or use pretraining objectives that do not directly capture how movement unfolds, limiting their ability to learn transferable motor representations. To this end, we propose the Mind World Model (MWM), a framework that learns motor EEG representations from scalable naturalistic EEG and egocentric video without action annotations. MWM treats EEG observed up to the current frame as the latent action of a world model: a mind model encodes the EEG, and a world model uses it to predict the representation of a future frame, yielding a movement-grounded pretraining objective. We further introduce the Lateralization-Aware Transformer (LAT), which uses frame averaging to separate shared bilateral from side-specific lateral features, encoding hemispheric correspondence to reduce the burden of learning left-right relationships from data. MWM pretraining produces two models: a mind model for downstream motor decoding and a world model that can be adapted to prediction conditioned on real actions, opening a scalable and flexible path to collect egocentric data for embodied AI. Across 9 classification and 7 regression tasks, the mind model improves task-averaged balanced accuracy by 5.9% and Pearson correlation by 16.2% relative to the strongest baseline in each task family. Compared with an inverse-dynamics latent-action baseline, the world model achieves lower prediction error and benefits 3.3 times more from matched real actions within recordings and 4.7 times more on held-out subjects.
authors: Weikang Qiu, Zheng Huang, Tinglin Huang, Yujun Yan, Rex Ying
bullets: Addresses the limited transferability of EEG motor representations learned from cue-based trials, coarse labels, or movement-agnostic objectives.
Learns from naturalistic EEG and egocentric video without action annotations by treating current EEG as a latent action that predicts future visual representations.
Introduces a Lateralization-Aware Transformer to model shared bilateral and side-specific hemispheric features.
Across 9 classification and 7 regression tasks, improves task-averaged balanced accuracy by 5.9% and Pearson correlation by 16.2% over task-family baselines.
The world model has lower prediction error than an inverse-dynamics latent-action baseline and benefits more from matched real actions, including on held-out subjects.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Existing approaches (top) versus MWM (bottom) on the three challenges of motor EEG representation learning. (1) Cue-based trials are costly to scale, and categorical labels give one class to movements that unfold differently (Tangermann et al., 2012; Schirrmeister et al., 2017; Lawhern et al., 2018). (2) General-purpose EEG foundation models (FMs) pretrain with EEG-only objectives (Kostas et al., 2021; Jiang et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2025a). MWM answers both with one mechanism: it treats the EEG recorded up to the current frame as the latent action of a world model that predicts the next visual state. It therefore learns from naturalistic EEG and egocentric video without action annotations, and its target is the visual consequence of behavior rather than the EEG itself. (3) Existing methods do not explicitly separate bilateral from lateral activity (Schirrmeister et al., 2017; Lawhern et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2025a); MWM does, and pairs each horizontal video mirror with an exchange of only the lateral component Hlat.

Figure 2: The Mind World Model. (a) A frozen encoder g maps the current frame to patch features that a residual predictor advances; the same frozen g builds the target from the next frame. (b) The mind model encodes the EEG window, which ends on the current frame; its LAT encoder is detailed in Figure 3. The EEG reaches the predictor only as AdaLN modulation, never as an input token: it occupies the slot a recorded action would.

Figure 3: The Lateralization-Aware Transformer (LAT) for EEG encoding. (a) Patch embedding, applied within each channel, (b) the learned gate G ∈ [0, 1]C×N×De and the electrode permutation Π ∈ {0, 1}C×C , which act on the embedded tokens before any Transformer block; the mirror acts on the decomposed pair and is an involution, (c) a criss-cross block, (d) a shared Transformer with invariant and equivariant readout heads; under the mirror, Hbi is unchanged and Hlat flips sign after aligning homologous channels, and (e) the paired EEG–video mirror. Only the learned lateral component is exchanged across hemispheres; the raw signal is never permuted.

Figure 4: Lateralization analysis. (a,b) Hand-motion correlations with 95% confidence intervals estimated by bootstrap resampling, using participants as the resampling unit. (c–e) Participantaveraged motor-imagery feature-energy contrasts, normalized by channel-wise mean energy; left– right contrasts share a color scale. Control features h(1) and h(2) are equal-sized halves of h.

papers.tldr: Mind World Models pretrains EEG motor representations by predicting future egocentric-video dynamics, improving motor decoding and enabling action-conditioned world-model adaptation.

papers.abstract: The world evolves through the dynamics of its constituent entities and their interactions, with changes in one entity influencing the behavior of others. To simulate this evolution under different actions, interactive world models need to capture the resulting agent responses as part of the world's own dynamics. In autonomous driving, errors in modeling these responses can misrepresent maneuver safety and undermine the reliability of generated videos used for policy evaluation and learning. To formalize this intrinsic requirement for driving world model, we define self-reactivity as the capability to model agent responses from observed history and a specified ego action, and generate visual futures that reflect those responses without prescribed future agent trajectories. To realize this capability, we introduce ReactDrive, a driving world model that jointly learns agent dynamics and visual generation through a shared agent state representation. Within this framework, dynamics supervision grounds a reactive dynamics prior in observed agent states, while the video objective jointly optimizes the self-reactivity and visual realism. Experiments show improved agent responses, ego controllability, and video quality, a 96.0% preference for agent reactivity in human comparisons across five baselines, and better downstream planning through augmentation with generated videos. We hope this work encourages the community to recognize self-reactivityas a foundational capability for developing and evaluating interactive world models. Project page: https://reactdrive.github.io/ .
authors: Yifan Wang, Xiaoqi Wang, Cho-Ying Wu, Wenbin He, Chenyu You, Liu Ren
bullets: Motivation: Accurate modeling of other agents’ responses is essential for reliable safety evaluation and policy learning in autonomous driving.
Method: Jointly learns agent dynamics and video generation through a shared agent-state representation, using dynamics supervision and a video objective.
Contribution: Formalizes self-reactivity as a core capability for interactive driving world models without requiring future agent trajectories.
Results: Reports improved agent responses, ego controllability, video quality, and downstream planning; human evaluators preferred its agent reactivity in 96.0% of comparisons across five baselines.
Scope: Evaluations focus on generated-video quality, reactive behavior, controllability, and planning augmentation in autonomous driving.

papers.abstract: Video generation models are increasingly important for robot learning, yet most generate each camera view separately or tile all views in a fixed layout. Robot demonstrations, however, are captured by synchronized cameras whose number, placement, and order vary across embodiments. We present ViewDreamer, a single world model that handles variable sets of cameras by disentangling per-view generation from cross-view interaction. Each view follows the generation path of a pretrained single-view model, and views interact only through shared slot tokens. We stabilize multi-view training with a curriculum that gradually increases the number of views. Cross-View Slot Agreement uses visual foundation models to group geometrically and semantically similar regions across views into shared slots. On RoboView-Bench, which covers one to four cameras, ViewDreamer achieves the best generation quality among the models evaluated and improves cross-view consistency over independent per-view generation. These gains carry over to our world-action model (WAM) and action-conditioned world model (AC-WM). Our WAM outperforms the FastWAM-Joint baseline on LIBERO-Plus, RoboTwin 2.0, and RoboDojo, and on a real Franka robot. Both variants improve out-of-domain generalization to various camera settings and scenes.
authors: Ye Mao, Jinhui Xiong, Egor Larionov, Shiyang Lu, Krystian Mikolajczyk, Wei Ye
bullets: Addresses the limitation of models tied to fixed camera counts, placements, or layouts.
Disentangles per-view generation from cross-view interaction using shared slot tokens.
Uses curriculum training and Cross-View Slot Agreement to align geometrically and semantically similar regions.
Achieves the best evaluated generation quality on RoboView-Bench and improves cross-view consistency over independent view generation.
Transfers gains to world-action models, robot benchmarks, and a real Franka robot, including better generalization across camera settings and scenes.

papers.abstract: Video foresight reasoning requires vision-language models to anticipate future events or next actions from currently observed videos. Existing methods fit future captions, rationales, or full visual states, but face two limitations. First, they rely on annotations or external large models for supervision, limiting scalability. We address this with an on-policy self-distillation framework that turns past-future video pairs into a natural self-supervised signal without extra annotations or LLM supervision. Second, they treat the whole future clip as equally valuable, although most of it is irrelevant context information. We address this by defining a foresight score, from which we obtain a contrastive privilege advantage that drives the model to learn the most valuable future information. Since the score is intractable, we optimize a tractable lower-bound surrogate that interpolates this advantage, computed between the true and a random reference future, with a teacher-student distillation advantage; together, they amplify decision-relevant content information and suppress irrelevant context information. We call the resulting framework Future-OPSD. On open-ended prediction and closed-ended planning, Future-OPSD improves base models by up to 14.2 and 15.9 points without compromising general video understanding. Code will be available at https://jingchensun.github.io/future-opsd/
authors: Jingchen Sun, Jiaxing Zhang, Qingqiao Hu, Dingqiang Ye, Yuqi Jia, Yijun Liang, Di Fu, Yunjie Tian, Dongdi Zhao, Changyou Chen
bullets: Addresses the scalability limits of annotated or externally supervised video foresight training.
Uses on-policy self-distillation over past–future video pairs as a natural self-supervised signal.
Introduces a foresight score and contrastive privilege advantage to emphasize informative future content over irrelevant context.
Optimizes a tractable lower-bound surrogate combining true-versus-random future comparison with teacher–student distillation.
Improves base models by up to 14.2 points on open-ended prediction and 15.9 points on closed-ended planning, without harming general video understanding.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of Future-OPSD and comparison with other training paradigms. (a) SFT learns annotated future descriptions y⋆ from past observations x using cross-entropy. (b) Naive OPSD uses a frozen future-aware teacher π0 to score the student’s own response ŷ, converting the teacher–student log-probability gap into token advantages for PPO. (c) Future-OPSD (ours) has a frozen teacher score the same response under the true future z (blue) and a reference future z̃ from another video (orange). The contrastive privilege advantage ℓzt −ℓz̃t compares the two futures, and the teacher–student distillation advantage ℓzt −ℓSt compares the true-future teacher with the past-only student. Their interpolation at down-weights context tokens supported by both futures (next / chop / the) while keeping content tokens specific to the true future (cilantro), helping the student focus on the most valuable future information. The advantages are clipped and centered into At for PPO, and inference uses only the student.

Figure 4. Case study: why Future-OPSD improves video foresight reasoning. On an EgoPlan-IT example with Qwen3-VL-8B, we compare the initial token advantages and trained predictions of Naive OPSD and Future-OPSD. A frozen teacher scores the same initial rollout under the paired future z and a reference future z̃ from another video, giving token log-probabilities ℓzt and ℓz̃t ; ℓSt is the past-only student’s log-probability. The context and content components are Ct = ℓz̃t − ℓSt and It = ℓzt − ℓz̃t . Before clipping and centering, Naive OPSD uses at = It + Ct, while Future-OPSD uses at = It + (1 − λ)Ct with λ = 0.75. Plotted values are initial advantages, with Ct and It below each token. Future-OPSD suppresses context information and amplifies decision-relevant content information, yielding the correct next-action prediction.

Figure 1. Not all of the future is equally important. To answer what will I do next? from what is seen now, only a small part of the future clip carries content information (rinse the knife); most of it is context information (tap, dish rack, sink, sponge) that neither answers the question nor reflects the expected action and trajectory of the ongoing event.

papers.abstract: Learning robotic ultrasound policies requires interactive environments for scalable data generation and repeatable evaluation, while exploration on real patients is limited by acquisition costs and safety constraints. Generative world models offer an alternative, but image history and probe actions alone do not ensure anatomical consistency across wide-range scans and changing acoustic windows. We introduce SonoAtlasWorld, an ultrasound world model built on anatomy as state. A persistent 3D anatomical asset extracted from computed tomography (CT) anchors each scan to a specific anatomy. Probe actions determine anatomical and acoustic visibility conditions for a causal ultrasound generator trained on clinical videos. Our three-stage pipeline combines anatomy-conditioned pretraining, causal conversion and long-rollout alignment. Inference optimizations achieve pose-to-ultrasound throughput of 81.2 FPS. To evaluate anatomical control beyond image similarity, we introduce the Action-Following Index (AFI), which measures normalized reconstruction gain over a static-prefix baseline. On 40 held-out 3D volumes, SonoAtlasWorld achieves liver and macro-organ AFI of 0.428 and 0.262, compared with at most 0.117 and 0.038 for the tested action- and geometry-conditioned methods. Long-rollout alignment reduces brightness drift by 3.46x at the end of 40 repeated scan cycles. SonoAtlasWorld also generates offline policy-training demonstrations and supports anatomically grounded closed-loop evaluation. Scaling the generated training data improves key-plane acquisition success from 48.2% to 81.2% on unseen anatomies in simulation, demonstrating its utility for robotic ultrasound policy learning.
authors: Zheyuan Zhang, Boris Mailhe, Hang Yu, Yikang Liu, Xiao Chen, Ankush Mukherjee, Terrence Chen, Shanhui Sun
bullets: Addresses the need for scalable, safe interactive environments for robotic ultrasound learning.
Conditions a causal ultrasound generator on CT-derived anatomy and probe-controlled anatomical and acoustic visibility.
Combines anatomy-conditioned pretraining, causal conversion, and long-rollout alignment; inference reaches 81.2 FPS.
Introduces the Action-Following Index to evaluate anatomical control beyond image similarity.
On 40 held-out volumes, it improves liver and macro-organ AFI, reduces long-rollout brightness drift, and raises simulated key-plane success from 48.2% to 81.2%.

papers.abstract: World-action models guide robot actions by predicting what happens next, but typically condition on a short observation history. Extending this history increases computation at every decision and can require a separately trained model. We introduce LoCo-WAM, which learns from the outcomes of its actions through test-time training while keeping the same short history length. It uses newly observed frames to update a low-rank adapter in the video expert, whose adapted predictions guide subsequent actions. The updates accumulate within each episode and are reset between episodes, allowing past observations to influence decisions after they leave the input window. LoCo-WAM thus learns from a longer stream of experience without expert action labels, additional data or meta-training. Experiments on two world-action models show improved task success across four simulation benchmarks. On RoboCasa GR-1, a model with 2.4,s of history matches one trained with 9.6,s, while a model with 4.8,s exceeds it by 4.8 percentage points. Our analysis shows that the updates improve prediction of upcoming frames, affect the action mainly through adaptation of the imagined future, and have an increasing effect on actions as the episode unfolds.
bullets: Uses newly observed frames for label-free test-time training while preserving a short input history.
Accumulates updates within an episode and resets them between episodes, retaining information beyond the observation window.
Improves task success across four simulation benchmarks and two world-action models.
On RoboCasa GR-1, 2.4 seconds of history matches a 9.6-second model; 4.8 seconds exceeds it by 4.8 percentage points.
Adaptation improves predicted future frames and increasingly influences actions as episodes progress.

papers.abstract: World models based on Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) learn from pixels to predict the outcome of actions in a latent space. To reach a goal, a planner samples many candidate action sequences, uses the model to predict where each one leads, and executes the best one. However, standard planners draw their candidates from a Gaussian, while the model has only seen the structured, state-dependent actions of its training data. Its predictions for such candidates are unreliable, and planning fails more often as goals move farther away. We propose Skill-JEPA, which learns an action space aligned with the planner. A variational autoencoder conditioned on the current state encodes short action sequences into latent skills with a standard Gaussian prior, and decodes them back into actions. The world model predicts the effect of skills rather than raw actions, and the planner searches over skills starting from that same Gaussian, so its candidates resemble the model's training data. Skill-JEPA adds a single module, trained end-to-end with the world model, and leaves the planner untouched, with no subgoals, hierarchy, or hand-designed skills. Across three JEPA world models and four benchmarks, average success on goals 80 steps away rises from 42% with raw actions to 62%; the gains grow with goal distance and hold across four planners. On AntMaze, a quadruped locomotion task, success on goals two maze cells away rises from 0.4% to 38%. This suggests that part of the difficulty of reaching distant goals lies in the action space, and can be removed without changing the planner.
authors: Tom\'as Couso Coddou, Christ Devia, Rex G. Liu, Rodrigo Toro Icarte
bullets: Standard Gaussian action sampling produces candidates unlike the structured actions seen during training, making distant-goal planning unreliable.
A state-conditioned VAE encodes short action sequences into latent skills with a Gaussian prior and decodes them back into actions.
The world model predicts skill effects, while the unchanged planner searches over skills sampled from the same Gaussian distribution.
Across three JEPA models and four benchmarks, average success for goals 80 steps away increased from 42% to 62%.
AntMaze success for goals two cells away rose from 0.4% to 38%, with improvements growing for more distant goals.

papers.abstract: Planning with learned world models amounts to finding action sequences whose predicted rollouts reach a goal. Sampling-based planners often struggle at longer horizons, while gradient-based methods can become trapped in local minima. Meanwhile, model predictive path integral control (MPPI), a complementary approach, alternates between estimating an expectation under a cost-weighted distribution from samples and updating the plan from this estimate. Its samples, however, are drawn afresh at every iteration from a Gaussian proposal and reach the target distribution only through importance weights. Moreover, a target distribution favoring goal-reaching trajectories can be difficult to define directly, motivating a sequence of intermediate distributions. Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) provides a natural mechanism for evolving such a sequence through importance weighting and resampling. Motivated by this, we formulate latent-space planning as optimization guided by SMC, which moves a population of action sequences while a gradient-based optimizer updates the plan. Inspired by classical planning, we further introduce a PDE-derived cost-to-go that guides the evolution of the sample distribution using the structure of the latent state space. On navigation and manipulation tasks with visual and proprioceptive world models, our formulation outperforms gradient-based planners by $29$ and $50$, sampling-based planners by $35$ and MPPI by $7$ percentage points in average success rate, while succeeding in fewer iterations than gradient-based planners and within 4\% of MPPI.
authors: Hrishikesh Viswanath, Anindita Ghosh, Uttaran Bhattacharya, Aniket Bera
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of long-horizon planning, where sampling methods struggle and gradient methods can get trapped in local minima.
Uses Sequential Monte Carlo to evolve action-sequence populations through intermediate target distributions with importance weighting and resampling.
Combines SMC population updates with gradient-based plan optimization in learned latent world models.
Introduces a PDE-derived cost-to-go to guide sampling using latent-state-space structure.
On visual and proprioceptive navigation/manipulation tasks, improves average success rates over gradient-based, sampling-based, and MPPI planners, with competitive iteration counts.

papers.abstract: In a variety of multi-agent and physical environments, an element's update depends strongly on a few other elements and weakly on many, and both the identity and the number of the elements that matter change with the state of the system. Such graded sparse mechanisms are common, for instance, in flocks, crowds, learned particle simulators and the neighborhood aggregation of graph networks, yet they have received little systematic study as a class of functions with the grading given. In this paper we study the supervised learning of the mechanism when the grading is provided by the environment, as a weight on every element. First, we define the class by axioms, where each element's influence is capped by its weight, the dependence on the weights is regular, and no element is distinguished, and prove a representation theorem: the class is exactly the Lipschitz ball of a transport metric on weighted multisets, and the metric is forced by the axioms. Next, the geometry of the representation gives generalization bounds that depend on the data in two ways. One is via the sparsity profile of the data -- the law of how many elements matter and by how much -- which bounds the rate over all designs with that profile, with an exponent from the profile and no dependence on the number of elements. In a number of natural cases we also show matching lower bounds, up to constants in the exponent. The other is empirical: due to the representation result, classical empirical discrepancy bounds apply to the class as they stand, and the resulting bound is the transport distance between the two halves of the sample in the class's own metric, computed exactly by a matching, with an additional concentration term. Finally, we study a simulated Vicsek flock under four interaction rules at two noise levels, and show that the certificate is non-vacuous, a small fraction of the trivial value on every rule.
bullets: Studies mechanisms where each element’s influence is weighted, state-dependent, and potentially graded sparse.
Proves the class is exactly the Lipschitz ball of a uniquely forced transport metric on weighted multisets.
Derives distributional bounds based on the data’s sparsity profile, with rates independent of the number of elements in relevant cases.
Provides an empirical certificate computed by matching two sample halves, plus concentration, and proves matching lower bounds in natural settings.
In a simulated Vicsek flock across four interaction rules and two noise levels, the certificate is non-vacuous.

papers.abstract: Videos reveal how the world changes, but rarely the actions that cause those changes. Latent action learning recovers such supervision from visual transitions, yet often learns the underlying dynamics largely from scratch. We ask whether a pretrained video generator can instead provide the prior for both inverse and forward dynamics. We introduce O$^{2}$LaF, built on a simple principle: one prior, two dynamics. We initialize both models from the same pretrained video DiT and adapt them to their distinct roles: a feed-forward transition encoder with learnable action queries for inverse dynamics, and a causal, action-conditioned video generator for forward dynamics. By controlling information access and optimizing both dynamics end-to-end through a compact bottleneck, O$^{2}$LaF learns transferable actions from unlabeled videos. Across navigation and robotic manipulation, O$^{2}$LaF sets a new state of the art in few-shot action probing and enables stronger zero-shot action transfer across visual contexts and embodiments. Beyond generative video priors, we further extend our framework to predictive representation priors such as V-JEPA2, achieving competitive performance. Our findings suggest a broader paradigm for latent-action learning: repurposing pretrained video models to discover transferable actions and predict their consequences.
authors: Yuxin Jiang, Wenqiang Sun, Jiaqi Li, Yuchao Gu, Lvmin Zhang, Ivor Tsang, Mike Zheng Shou
bullets: Addresses the challenge of learning action representations and dynamics without action labels, often requiring dynamics to be learned from scratch.
Uses one pretrained video prior for two roles: inverse dynamics via a transition encoder with learnable action queries, and forward dynamics via a causal action-conditioned generator.
Trains both dynamics end-to-end through a compact bottleneck to discover actions transferable across visual contexts and embodiments.
Achieves state-of-the-art few-shot action probing and stronger zero-shot transfer in navigation and robotic manipulation, according to the abstract.
The framework also works with predictive representation priors such as V-JEPA2, suggesting applicability beyond generative video models.

papers.abstract: High-resolution generation enables video world models to render fine-grained scene structures and textures, but directly generating high-resolution video incurs substantial computational and memory costs. We present ScaleWorld, a causal video model that unifies low-resolution world prediction and high-resolution refinement within a single shared backbone. By refining its own predictions, ScaleWorld produces high-resolution world videos without requiring a separate refinement model. For each video chunk, the shared backbone first completes a low-resolution prediction and then performs one-step high-resolution refinement conditioned on that prediction. To support efficient streaming generation, we maintain separate causal states with a long low-resolution history for prediction and a short high-resolution history for refinement. To address task interference during distillation, we separate specialist optimization from capability consolidation and introduce task-asymmetric on-policy distillation (TA-OPD). This procedure transfers prediction and refinement behaviors from specialized teachers into a shared student through local velocity matching under their respective sampling and history policies. {Extensive experiments demonstrate that ScaleWorld achieves high-quality world generation with improved computational and memory efficiency.
authors: Yansong Qu, Wesker Zheng, Quanjian Song, Zhiyuan Zhang, Xiao Cao, Shengchuan Zhang, Liujuan Cao
bullets: Targets the high computational and memory cost of direct high-resolution video generation.
Uses a shared backbone to first predict a low-resolution video chunk, then refine it at high resolution without a separate refinement model.
Maintains long low-resolution and short high-resolution causal histories for efficient streaming generation.
Introduces task-asymmetric on-policy distillation to consolidate prediction and refinement capabilities while reducing task interference.
Experiments show high-quality world generation with improved computational and memory efficiency.

papers.abstract: Most world models for future prediction prioritize aestetic quality of generated videos, but offer only weak physical grounding and limited geometric consistency over time, due to the lack of explicit 4D modeling. In this paper, we introduce plan4d, a possible next milestone towards building a generative plannable 4D world model that predicts future RGB videos together with dense 4D geometry, including depth, cameras, point clouds, and scene flow from an observed scene context and text-specified actions. Since training data with paired actions and dense 4D annotations is inherently scarce, plan4d leverages the complementary priors of foundational video generators and 3D reconstructors. Specifically, we propose a model-stitching architecture that couples Depth Anything 3 with LongCat-Video and augments it with an auxiliary DPT head for scene-flow prediction. The resulting model allows us to plan and generate complex, long-horizon, and fine-grained actions in a dynamic 3D scenes, while substantially improving both visual fidelity and geometric accuracy of the generated future videos. Extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that plan4d achieves state-of-the-art performance in generative 4D modeling of environmental reactions. Project Page: https://fogradio.github.io/plan4d-project
authors: Hangwei Zhang, Rujing Dang, Ruimin Lin, Jiahong Wu, Xiangxiang Chu, Chuanxia Zheng
bullets: Addresses the weak physical grounding and geometric consistency of video-focused world models.
Uses a model-stitching architecture combining Depth Anything 3 and LongCat-Video, with an auxiliary DPT head for scene-flow prediction.
Predicts RGB videos, depth, camera poses, point clouds, and scene flow from observed context and text-specified actions.
Supports complex, long-horizon, fine-grained actions and reports improved visual fidelity and geometric accuracy on synthetic and real-world datasets.
The approach targets settings where paired action and dense 4D supervision is scarce by leveraging pretrained video and 3D reconstruction priors.

papers.abstract: Data assimilation (DA) in partially observed nonlinear systems requires repeated estimation of both hidden states and their uncertainty. Conventional nonlinear filtering can be computationally expensive and often relies on an explicit dynamical model. In this paper, we develop the Neural Conditional Gaussian Model (Neural CGM), a data-driven dynamical model that maps unobserved physical states into a learned latent space, where the dynamics of the latent states follow a conditional Gaussian structure. This structure allows closed-form DA updates in the latent space, while nonlinear encoder-decoder mappings retain the flexibility needed to represent complex dynamics in physical space. A key feature of Neural CGM is its treatment of uncertainty in DA. The latent posterior mean and covariance are mapped to the physical variables through a Gaussian decoder that combines local moment propagation with learned nonlinear corrections. The resulting physical-space posterior statistics depend on the sequentially updated latent distribution rather than on a separate post-processing estimate. The same statistics enter a Gaussian negative log-likelihood during training, so both the posterior mean and uncertainty affect the learned model. Because Neural CGM learns the dynamical model itself, it can also be used for state forecasting and simulation without explicit knowledge of the governing equations. Numerical experiments on benchmark nonlinear dynamical systems show accurate state estimation and forecasting while substantially reducing online assimilation cost relative to conventional nonlinear DA methods. Neural CGM is therefore suited to repeated state estimation, uncertainty quantification, and prediction from partial observations.
bullets: Addresses costly state and uncertainty estimation in partially observed nonlinear systems without requiring explicit governing equations.
Maps physical states to a latent space with conditional Gaussian dynamics, enabling closed-form sequential DA updates.
Uses a Gaussian decoder with local moment propagation and learned nonlinear corrections to produce physical-space posterior means and covariances.
Trains with a Gaussian negative log-likelihood so both state estimates and uncertainty shape the learned model.
Experiments on benchmark nonlinear systems show accurate estimation and forecasting with substantially lower online assimilation cost than conventional nonlinear DA methods.

papers.selection_reason: Develops a Neural Conditional Gaussian Model for nonlinear dynamics that maps states to a latent space with conditional Gaussian structure, enabling efficient data assimilation and prediction.
papers.title: Neural Conditional Gaussian Model: Efficient Data Assimilation with Sequential Uncertainty Quantification for Nonlinear Dynamics
papers.tldr: Neural CGM enables efficient nonlinear data assimilation by combining learned encoder-decoder dynamics with closed-form latent-space uncertainty updates.

papers.abstract: Immersive 3D content allows text and graphical elements, such as subtitles, annotations, and icons, to be placed inside a scene rather than displayed as flat overlays. Placed this way, they respect occlusion and perspective and take on user-assigned materials and lighting while preserving their original shapes. In Gaussian scenes, however, each new glyph or icon requires its own iterative optimization, which limits scalable content creation. We present FFGaussType, which converts extruded glyph and SVG outlines into Gaussian assets in a single forward pass. A point encoder maps anchors sampled on the known surface to a single feature plane, from which a decoder shared by all assets predicts neural Gaussians carrying surface normals. This separates geometric conversion from material and lighting choices, and the feature plane supports image and video coding for compact delivery. We construct a paired dataset of 27,221 glyph and SVG icon assets with anchors and calibrated normal and silhouette renderings, holding out font families for evaluation. Conversion from prepared anchors takes 9.1 ms per asset, at a fraction of the compute and memory of prior baselines. On unseen font families and test icons, FFGaussType achieves $1.62^\circ$ normal error and $0.985$ silhouette IoU, the best among the compared feed-forward converters, matching the fidelity that per-asset fitting needs thousands of steps to reach. The code and dataset will be released after publication.
authors: Haoan Feng, Tianfu Wang, Peimeng Guan, Dae Yeol Lee, Guan-ming Su
bullets: Addresses the scalability problem of iteratively optimizing every glyph or icon for Gaussian scenes.
Encodes sampled surface anchors into a shared feature plane, then decodes neural Gaussians with surface normals.
Separates geometry conversion from material and lighting, while supporting compact image and video delivery.
Uses a paired dataset of 27,221 glyph and SVG icon assets, with font-family holdouts for evaluation.
Achieves 1.62° normal error and 0.985 silhouette IoU on unseen assets; conversion takes 9.1 ms per prepared asset.

papers.title: FFGaussType: Feed-Forward Conversion of Glyph and SVG Geometry into Compact Gaussian Assets
papers.tldr: FFGaussType converts glyph and SVG geometry into compact, renderable Gaussian assets in one fast forward pass instead of per-asset optimization.

papers.abstract: Each fibre-reinforced composite structure has a unique material architecture. The manufacturing methods used and the presence of defects lead to local variations which require material-scale models that can resolve the response in real time at every location in the structure. Concurrent multi-scale schemes provide this capability, but at a prohibitive computational cost for large structures as the number of integration points and time increments scales with size. Surrogates have been studied extensively as replacements for material-scale models to mitigate these computational limitations. A surrogate must represent an arbitrary local architecture including defects, track the irreversible material state over an unknown number of increments, remain stable when driven recursively by its own predictions, and fit within the memory available at every integration point. Here, a Composites World Model based on a Multi-Modal Spiking Transformer architecture is designed to meet these requirements. The proposed architecture combines a material encoder, a Spiking Neural Network memory block that tracks the long-term internal state of the material, and transformer blocks that learn the short-term applied strain state. The system is trained in three stages: material architecture encoding, base training on short time windows, and recursive fine-tuning with scheduled sampling to suppress cumulative error drift. The trained model is disassembled at inference and coupled to a non-linear FE solver, enabling structural scale simulation of composites containing embedded defects. Benchmarks against experimental results for IM7/8552 laminates under tension, compression and transverse shear, for pristine and wrinkled composites, show that the SNN memory block successfully tracks the material internal state and results in prediction errors between 0.4% and 4.8%.
bullets: Motivation: Conventional concurrent multiscale modelling is too costly for large composite structures with many integration points and time increments.
Method: Combines material-architecture encoding, a spiking neural-network memory block for long-term state, and transformer blocks for short-term strain response.
Training uses architecture encoding, short-window base training, and recursive fine-tuning with scheduled sampling to reduce prediction drift.
The model is integrated into a nonlinear finite-element solver for structural simulations with embedded defects.
For IM7/8552 laminates under tension, compression, and transverse shear, including pristine and wrinkled cases, reported errors range from 0.4% to 4.8%.

papers.selection_reason: Integrates a composite World Model with a Spiking Neural Network memory block to simulate material dynamics and defects, demonstrating a computationally efficient approach to predictive modeling.
papers.title: FEA solver integration of a composite World Model with a Spiking Neural Network memory Block for computationally efficient modelling of defects and variabilities
papers.tldr: A spiking-transformer composite world model enables computationally efficient finite-element simulation of defective composites while tracking irreversible material states in real time.

papers.abstract: World models are increasingly used to simulate physical interactions, but training a separate model for each environment limits scalability. Cross-environment prediction requires identifying the current physical rule, which appearance alone may not reveal. We therefore study visual calibration: using object motion and interactions in a short video as direct evidence to infer the current rule and predict motion under that rule from a different initial state. However, differences in data availability across physical conditions can yield a long-tailed training distribution, biasing models toward common rules even when evidence supports rare ones. To study this challenge, we introduce TailWorld, which evaluates the transfer of demonstrated rules across initial states while independently controlling training imbalance and calibration informativeness. The benchmark compares predictions with two reference futures from the same prediction initial state, one following the demonstrated rule and the other a common rule, to measure prediction bias toward common dynamics. We further propose Rule Inference for Transfer (RIFT), which learns how different rules affect object motion, infers the current rule from calibration interactions, and applies it to prediction from a new initial state. RIFT explicitly controls the influence of training frequency on rule inference, allowing sufficiently informative observational evidence to support rare rules. Experiments on TailWorld show that RIFT improves prediction accuracy and physical consistency across varying training imbalances and distribution shifts, with gains in predicting rare dynamics.
authors: Han Xiao, Zhiyong Bao, Xiaotong Liu, Yanhao Chen, Qingqiang Wu
bullets: Studies visual calibration: inferring a scene’s physical rule from object motion and interactions in a short video.
Introduces TailWorld, a benchmark that independently controls training imbalance and the informativeness of calibration evidence.
Proposes RIFT, which separates rule effects on motion from current-rule inference and applies the inferred rule to a new initial state.
Evaluates bias by comparing predictions under the demonstrated rule versus a common alternative rule.
RIFT improves prediction accuracy and physical consistency across training imbalances and distribution shifts, especially for rare dynamics.

papers.selection_reason: Studies world models for predicting physical dynamics from video, introducing a benchmark and method for rule inference, fitting Video World Models.
papers.title: World Models Favor Learned Priors over Visual Evidence
papers.tldr: World models often favor common learned dynamics over visual evidence, while RIFT improves rule inference from brief interactions and transfers rare physical rules to new states.

papers.abstract: Recently, video world models have advanced interactive generation, with large models offering higher quality and smaller models enabling faster inference. Existing speculative methods combine their strengths through fast draft generation and selective target regeneration guided by rewards on decoded frames. However, verification covers only the external scorer's evaluation dimensions and adds decoding and scoring costs. Moreover, these scores provide no correction, requiring costly target regeneration for rejected drafts. To address these limitations, we propose Speculative World Model (SpecWM), a unified, training-free inference framework for streaming world models. It verifies draft chunks using the target's latent velocity field. Verification also yields a reusable correction; two thresholds select Accept, Refine, or Reject. Specifically, one-step refinement reuses it to improve perceptual quality, while three-step refinement strengthens camera following and trajectory consistency. These findings motivate transition-aware refinement. On WBench Navigation, SpecWM improves visual quality at 1.63$\times$ speedup over the target and raises NavScore from the draft's 75.99 to 85.63, achieving the best quality-speed-control trade-off. Additionally, our LongSpecBench shows sustained quality and control over long, multi-turn rollouts, while experiments on Hy-Nomas validate SpecWM across backbones and denoising budgets.
authors: Jiaming Li, Lingzhen Li, Xiaze Yang, Chenyu Zhu, Kaiqi Liu, Xiaotong Zhao, Songlian Li, Toyota Li, Alan Zhao, Haobin Zhong, Yue Ma, Zhiyuan Ma
bullets: Replaces decoded-frame reward verification with checks based on the target model’s latent velocity field.
Uses two thresholds to choose among Accept, one-step Refine, and three-step Refine or Reject.
Reuses verification signals to correct drafts, targeting perceptual quality, camera following, and trajectory consistency.
On WBench Navigation, reports 1.63× speedup and raises NavScore from 75.99 to 85.63.
LongSpecBench and Hy-Nomas experiments support sustained rollout performance and applicability across backbones and denoising budgets.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes a training-free inference framework for streaming video world models with verification and refinement, directly matching video and interactive world model interests.
papers.title: SpecWM: Turning Verification into Refinement for Streaming World Models
papers.tldr: SpecWM turns speculative verification into latent-space refinement, improving streaming world-model quality and control while accelerating inference.

papers.abstract: World models can imagine how a physical scene evolves over the next few seconds, but growers need to know how a crop will develop over weeks to months: will this rice plant have headed a month from now, and how will it look at harvest? We introduce agricultural world modeling, the task of predicting how the same plant will look at a requested horizon of days to months, from one photo of it, its cultivar, and its camera view. In preliminary analysis, even state-of-the-art image generators get this wrong: they often grow the plant too little or give it the color and form of the wrong growth stage. We argue that they do not work out the plant's developmental state, which the photo reveals only indirectly. We therefore propose AgroWM, which reasons about development before it draws growth. Its reasoning module, PhenoClock, works out the current growth stage, predicts the future one, and writes a Growth Script with numeric targets for height, plant area, and color; its generation module, the Rooted Renderer, then edits the photo to follow this script, adding new organs and colors to the photographed plant. Because pixel scores can prefer an unchanged copy of the photo, we instead check each forecast's traits and developmental timing against the plant's own later photos. On rice, 54.6% of the forecasts of AgroWM are matched to the target stage (Stage R@1), against 34.8% for GPT Image 2.5, 24.0% for Qwen Image 2.1, and 47.4% for the strongest domain-specific baseline, the same backbone fine-tuned without Growth Scripts; 9 to 20 weeks ahead, it still reaches 46.4%, against 35.7% for that baseline. On maize, a crop with a different body plan and stage scale, the same design again scores best on all four measures.
authors: Wenkai Ji, Zeteng Li, Yinkun Guo, Jie Zhou, Liang He, Zhenong Jin
bullets: The task is long-horizon crop forecasting from one photo, cultivar, camera view, and requested future horizon.
AgroWM’s PhenoClock estimates current and future growth stages and produces a Growth Script with targets for height, area, and color.
Its Rooted Renderer edits the original plant photo to add future organs and colors according to the script.
On rice, AgroWM achieves 54.6% Stage R@1, outperforming the reported general and domain-specific baselines; it remains strongest 9–20 weeks ahead.
The design also performs best across four measures on maize, suggesting transfer beyond rice, though the work is presented as preliminary.

papers.abstract: Controllable streaming video generation offers a promising route toward interactive game simulation, yet existing methods remain far from practical gameplay. They often fail to jointly achieve high visual fidelity, high frame rates, and low interaction latency, resulting in poor responsiveness and degraded user experience. We present Streaming-AAA, a new paradigm for controllable infinite generation of AAA-quality game videos. Our system generates 1080p gameplay videos at 43 FPS with 198 ms end-to-end latency interaction on merely NVIDIA A800 GPUs, while supporting long-horizon play without severe temporal degradation or collapse. Streaming-AAA is built upon three key designs. First, we redesign the VAE architecture for efficient high-resolution decoding, enabling real-time synthesis at 1080p. Second, we pretrain the diffusion model using diffusion forcing and significantly extend the temporal training horizon, allowing the model to capture long-term dependencies and maintain persistent memory. Third, we perform post-training distillation and memory compression to improve inference efficiency while retaining visual quality and temporal consistency. Experiments show that Streaming-AAA substantially improves visual fidelity, frame rate, latency, and long-term stability over prior controllable video generation approaches, enabling a significantly more playable experience for interactive AAA game video generation.
authors: Zhihao Hu, Jianqi Ma, Jun Zhang, Jiayang Bai, Haifeng Shi, Yanxiang Zhuang, Zhongqian Sun, Weidong Zhang, Wei Yang
bullets: Targets the challenge of jointly achieving high visual fidelity, frame rate, responsiveness, and long-term stability in interactive game video generation.
Redesigns the VAE for efficient 1080p decoding and real-time synthesis.
Uses diffusion forcing with an extended temporal training horizon to capture long-term dependencies and persistent memory.
Applies post-training distillation and memory compression to improve inference efficiency while preserving visual and temporal quality.
Experiments report improved fidelity, frame rate, latency, and long-term stability over prior controllable video generation methods.

papers.abstract: World models aim to predict environment dynamics under actions, enabling the prediction of action consequences without executing them in the real world. Yet despite producing increasingly realistic videos, current world models often fail to capture how small action changes affect future observations. This limits their use in tasks such as robotic policy evaluation and model-based planning, where nearly identical actions can lead to qualitatively different outcomes. To address this, we propose AFFECT, an auxiliary training objective for learning the distribution of visual changes induced by action perturbations. Specifically, we inject temporally correlated noise into the actions of a policy trained on task-agnostic human teleoperation. We then train the world model so that its generated videos respond to this noise as the recorded videos do, without requiring repeated executions from the same initial state. Across OGBench simulation and real-world DROID and ALOHA-2 setups, AFFECT makes world-model rollouts more faithful to real outcomes. On DROID, the Pearson correlation between policy success rates in the world model and on the real robot rises from 0.47 to 0.79, alongside up to 23% lower FVD. These gains carry over to planning, where selecting actions with AFFECT-trained world models improves task success by up to 8.3%.
authors: John Won, Yonghoon Dong, Jinwoo Shin
bullets: Current video-predictive world models may look realistic while misrepresenting the consequences of similar actions.
AFFECT injects temporally correlated action noise during task-agnostic teleoperation and matches the resulting visual-change distributions.
It avoids requiring repeated executions from the same initial state.
Across OGBench, DROID, and ALOHA-2, AFFECT improves correspondence between simulated and real outcomes, lowers FVD, and boosts planning success.
On DROID, success-rate correlation increases from 0.47 to 0.79, with up to 23% lower FVD and 8.3% higher planning success.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of AFFECT. Frozen encoders ϕ, ψ extract video features from both the recorded and generated futures, and perturbation features from the logged action perturbations. Pairing the centered perturbations with each set of video features gives the recorded and predicted action effects (Φ(O),Φ(Ô)), which measure how visual change moves with the perturbation across rollouts. The AFFECT loss optimizes over the distance between the two distributions, so that generated futures respond to perturbations in the same direction and with the same strength as real ones.

Figure 1: Small action perturbations lead to distinct action effects. From the same initial state, actions drawn from a narrow distribution change the gripper’s approach only slightly, yet produce qualitatively different outcomes, where the cube is grasped, missed, or pushed away. A faithful world model must reproduce how these outcomes shift as the action is perturbed, rather than only rendering a plausible video for generic actions.

Figure 3: Planning with action-faithful world models. Success rates (%) of plans selected with each world model on (a) UR5e and (b) ALOHA-2, where one long-horizon task consists of three consecutive subtasks. Candidate action chunks are proposed by an ensemble of five policy checkpoints. Uniform picks one at random, while DreamDojo and DreamDojo + AFFECT imagine each chunk and select the one whose imagined video scores highest under a learned success estimator.
Figure 4: Action-effect localization. Frozen-feature responses on UR5e relative to shuffled pairs, where brighter cells indicate stronger responses.

papers.selection_reason: Action effect matching for dynamics-faithful world models, directly relevant to interactive and video world models.
papers.title: Learning What Actions Change: Action Effect Matching for Dynamics-Faithful World Models
papers.tldr: AFFECT trains world models to faithfully reflect how small action changes alter future observations, improving rollout realism and planning utility.

papers.abstract: Robotic world models predict future video frames from the current observation and a sequence of robot actions. While recent models follow the given actions closely, manipulated objects often collapse or move inconsistently with the action. We attribute this to the conditioning: an action, or a rendering of the robot, specifies where the robot goes but not how the scene responds, leaving a single video model to infer the interaction dynamics implicitly while also rendering appearance. We therefore separate dynamics prediction from visual rendering, with 3D point dynamics as the proxy between them. Specifically, we lift the first frame into 3D points, simulate how they respond to the robot's motion with a learned point dynamics model, and render the simulated points back into pixel-aligned videos that any video model can read. In controlled experiments on the DROID dataset with two video renderers of different architectures, this point dynamics proxy reduces object motion error by 8.6% and 6.2% without degrading image quality, and by 8.1% on a real bimanual robot. Moreover, the video follows the simulation: more accurate dynamics yield more accurate object motion, and editing the points steers the video. This suggests that advances in dynamics modeling can translate into more faithful robotic world models.
authors: Dong An, Tianyu Liu, Haoran Ding, Wen Yang, Anqing Duan, Zhengzhong Liu, Eric P. Xing, Guangyi Liu
bullets: Problem: Video world models often follow robot actions but predict inconsistent or collapsed object motion because scene dynamics and appearance are inferred together.
Method: Lift the initial frame into 3D points, predict their response to robot motion with a learned dynamics model, then render the simulated points into pixel-aligned videos for a video model.
Results: Object-motion error decreases by 8.6% and 6.2% with two DROID video renderers, and by 8.1% on a real bimanual robot, without reducing image quality.
The rendered video tracks the simulated dynamics: better point predictions produce better object motion, while editing points can steer the generated video.
Scope: Results are demonstrated in controlled DROID experiments and on a real bimanual robot.

papers.selection_reason: Separates dynamics prediction from visual rendering in robotic world models by using 3D point dynamics as a proxy, significantly improving object motion accuracy in simulation and real-world manipulation.
papers.title: Point Dynamics as Proxy for Robotic World Models
papers.tldr: A 3D point-dynamics proxy separates robot interaction modeling from video rendering, improving manipulated-object motion while preserving visual quality.

papers.abstract: Latent world models predict the outcomes of action sequences, but comparing candidate plans through recursive rollout remains expensive at test time. We introduce Fast-JEPA, a latent world model planning framework that advances the success-latency Pareto frontier of predictive search. Fast-JEPA reorganizes predictive computation to support effective action-sequence search at low planning cost. It constructs a goal-directed plan to guide search and directly predicts the outcomes of complete candidates for efficient comparison, avoiding recursive state rollout during refinement. Across PushT, Reacher, Cube, and TwoRoom, Fast-JEPA achieves 96.50% average success rate with 2.41x faster planning than INTACT. Search-budget sweeps show that its competitive success and low latency extend across candidate counts and refinement depths. We further introduce DynaGoal, a benchmark for evaluating world-model planning under dynamic out-of-distribution conditions, execution deadlines, and controlled response delays. Fast-JEPA achieves average success rates of 73.83% on DynaGoal-Shift and 87.67% on DynaGoal-Deadline, demonstrating the practical value of low-latency predictive planning under changing control conditions and execution-time constraints. Our code is available at https://github.com/Sofilyzia/Fast-JEPA.
authors: Yao Zhang, Bin Yu, Shijie Lian, Haishan Liu, Changti Wu, Yu Wu, Kai Chen
bullets: Targets the high test-time cost of comparing plans through recursive state prediction.
Builds a goal-directed plan and directly predicts complete candidate outcomes for efficient search refinement.
Achieves 96.50% average success with 2.41× faster planning than INTACT across four tasks.
Maintains competitive success and low latency across different search budgets, candidate counts, and refinement depths.
Introduces DynaGoal to test planning under distribution shifts, deadlines, and response delays; Fast-JEPA reaches 73.83% on Shift and 87.67% on Deadline.

papers.abstract: Interactive game world models separate executable world evolution from visual generation, using video models to render engine-provided scene representations into detailed observations. During sustained gameplay, however, existing generative renderers struggle to follow changing conditions while preserving visual continuity across diverse proxies and target styles. We therefore introduce ContextRenderer, an autoregressive video diffusion framework designed for both dynamic conditioning and cross-proxy generalization. It couples Dynamic-Context Learning (DCL) for chunk-level interaction supervision with Recurrent History Compression (RHC) to follow condition updates while preserving visual continuity within a bounded token budget. Across proxy representations, Cross-Representation Flow Alignment (CRFA) connects proxy reconstruction with appearance and interaction variation through a shared high-fidelity reconstruction. WorldPrism, our interaction-centric dataset constructed from agent-built worlds, AAA gameplay, and open-source videos, supplies the corresponding renderings and chunk-level annotations for these learning tasks. Experiments on GWM-Bench and Solar-Bench show improved reconstruction and visual quality, while qualitative results demonstrate minute-long interactive rendering under changing prompts and subject references. Project page: https://rainzor.github.io/contextrenderer/
authors: Runze Wang, Fei Zha, Bing He, Ke Xu, Zhongyuan Wu, Yuxuan Xie, Wenzheng Wu, Zhongyuan Liu, Youcheng Cai, Ligang Liu
bullets: Targets generative renderers that lose continuity and fail to follow evolving gameplay conditions.
Uses Dynamic-Context Learning for chunk-level interaction supervision and Recurrent History Compression to maintain continuity within a bounded token budget.
Introduces Cross-Representation Flow Alignment to support generalization across diverse scene proxies and target appearances.
Provides WorldPrism, a dataset of agent-built worlds, AAA gameplay, and open-source videos with renderings and chunk-level annotations.
Improves reconstruction and visual quality on GWM-Bench and Solar-Bench; qualitative results show sustained interactive rendering under changing prompts and references.

papers.abstract: World action models (WAMs) predict future videos and actions with one backbone, and their imagined future is often seen as a safety signal. We introduce SteerTrace, a targeted universal attack on WAMs that also traces its effect inside the model. One $\ell_\infty$-bounded (4/255) perturbation per model, shared across frames, tasks, and camera views, pushes the executed action toward an attacker-chosen target. On eight WAMs from four families (FastWAM, Faster-WAM, OpenWAM and LingBot-VA) on LIBERO and RoboTwin, it drives task success close to zero and moves the attacked action toward the target. Same-budget noise and BadWAM produce little action shift in the target direction. We use the signed targeted effect to measure how much of the effect each intervention removes or reproduces. Under the standard attack, restoring future tokens removes 61-94% of the targeted effect in the five models whose action experts attend to them. When the attack is constrained to keep the predicted future close to the clean prediction, the targeted effect can become more dependent on current-frame tokens. In three of these five models, restoring current-frame tokens removes 87-99% of the effect, compared with 9-15% for future tokens. In six models, restoring just 0.36% of the FFN neurons in layers 10-29 of the video expert removes 72-96% of the targeted effect. Residual directions 2-16 hold only 11-18% of the shift energy, yet removing them cancels most of the targeted effect.
authors: Yukun Dai, Tianshi Wang, Fengling Li, Jingjing Li, Xin Li, Lei Zhu
bullets: Targets world action models with one shared ℓ∞-bounded (4/255) perturbation across frames, tasks, and camera views.
Across eight models on LIBERO and RoboTwin, the attack drives task success near zero and shifts actions toward the chosen target; control attacks cause little target-direction shift.
Restoring future tokens removes 61–94% of the targeted effect in five models, while constrained attacks can make current-frame tokens more important.
Restoring only 0.36% of FFN neurons in layers 10–29 removes 72–96% of the effect in six models.
Low-energy residual directions can still be critical: removing directions 2–16 cancels most of the targeted effect despite containing only 11–18% of shift energy.

The action tokens read the K/V of the current-frame tokens C and, if the mask allows (dashed), of the future tokens F . Bottom: three analyses intervene at the sites b–d and measure the remaining targeted effect T ′. (b) For one token group, we restore clean K/V in the attacked run or inject attacked K/V into the clean run. (c) For the top-k FFN neurons ranked by SteerTrace, we restore clean activations in the attacked run or inject attacked activations into the clean run. (d) We remove or keep a band B of the residual shift ∆. State outlines and action-value circles are gray for clean and red for attacked. Green outlines mark replaced states.

papers.selection_reason: Targeted attack and internal tracing for world action models; directly relevant to world-model safety and VLA action prediction.
papers.title: SteerTrace: Tracing How Target Attacks Steer World Action Models
papers.tldr: SteerTrace shows that tiny universal perturbations can reliably steer world action models toward attacker-chosen actions and identifies the internal tokens, neurons, and residual directions responsible.

papers.abstract: Action-conditioned joint-embedding predictive architectures (JEPAs) offer a foundation for predictive decision-making by modeling the consequences of actions in representation space. Yet evaluating local reachability in latent space does not by itself provide a task-level execution interface: intermediate targets must be generated, local inference has finite budgets, and execution requires spatial feedback and persistent interaction state. We introduce LeCompass, a state-indexed execution framework built around a frozen LeWorldModel (LeWM). A proposer supplies intermediate latent targets, while CompassFlow searches the source space of a learned trajectory prior to obtain effective action candidates under limited predictive-evaluation budgets. Patch-token readouts provide spatial feedback, while observation-based memory supports phase transitions and bounded recovery. State-indexed targets support cross-episode context-goal composition. On 1,000 official TEST full-episode Cube trials, the complete LeCompass execution system achieves 86.9% native 4-cm reach. Separate matched analyses show that predictive ranking raises success from 4.7% to 44.9% on TEST PushT and from 33.8% to 77.7% on TEST TwoRoom. These results demonstrate task-level execution with task-dependent roles for latent target proposal, predictive search, and observation-grounded control.
authors: Kai Shi, Shiqi Zhao, Zimo Li, Hairong Qu, Hongyu Ma, Yongsong Yang, Jiahao Ai, Ziran Yin, Peng Yin
bullets: Addresses the gap between local latent reachability and persistent, task-level execution.
Uses a frozen LeWorldModel with a proposer for intermediate targets and CompassFlow to search trajectory-prior actions under limited evaluation budgets.
Adds patch-token spatial feedback and observation-based memory for phase transitions and bounded recovery.
State-indexed targets enable cross-episode context-goal composition.
Achieves 86.9% native 4-cm reach on 1,000 TEST Cube trials; predictive ranking improves matched PushT success from 4.7% to 44.9% and TwoRoom from 33.8% to 77.7%.

papers.abstract: Given past images and known actions, visual continuation generates future frames from one evolving scene state. Keeping this state revisable matters when an object reappears or a later view changes an earlier interpretation. Once past images cannot be replayed, a summary sufficient for current rendering can lose candidates needed after correction. We establish matching sparse and dense bounds on the bits needed for later correction under stable observations and bounded disagreement. For static streams at the stated smoothness and margin scales, correction incurs at least logarithmic overhead in one dimension and polynomial overhead in higher dimensions. Coherent Archive Memory (CAM) stores geometric summaries with exact updates under clipped expansion and coordinate assignments, then uses historical existence constraints to select one state for all requested frames. Exhaustive photographic tests show strict worst-truth image-risk gains from joint witnesses, while controlled neural continuations recover positions hidden in the current view.
authors: Xiyang Zhang, Yuanhe Tian, Hongzhi Wang, Yan Song
bullets: Correction requires extra memory because render-sufficient summaries may discard plausible past explanations.
Theoretical bounds show logarithmic correction overhead in 1D and polynomial overhead in higher dimensions under stated assumptions.
Coherent Archive Memory stores geometric summaries and updates them exactly using clipped expansion and coordinate assignments.
Historical existence constraints select a single state consistently across requested frames.
Photographic and neural continuation tests show improved worst-case image risk and recovery of currently hidden positions.

papers.abstract: Early interactions can reveal physical properties that later observations no longer show. These properties can still gov- ern the effects of future actions. Inspired by the distinction between retention and selective readout in working mem- ory and cognitive science, we introduce LATER, an action- conditioned world model built on CF-JEPA. LATER stores completed real transitions in partitioned memories that remain fixed during candidate rollouts. A response bridge queries these memories using the current state and candidate action, while multi-cut auxiliary supervision trains the memory writ- ers. On distracted Two-Stage PushT, LATER raises terminal success from 15.5% to 25.0% over reconstructed CF-JEPA. In a separate comparison across six models and two scratch- training seeds, LATER achieves the lowest mean physical readout error in both clean and distracted views, reducing along-push mean absolute error (MAE) under distractors by 20.2% relative to CF-JEPA. Controlled history interventions show that later predictions depend on earlier physical evi- dence even when query observations and actions are fixed, with larger effects during pushing than waiting.
authors: Zihan Zhou, Wenxi Xu, Qilin Wang, Hao Tang
bullets: Addresses the problem of physical properties becoming unobservable in later frames while still affecting future actions.
Stores completed transitions in fixed, partitioned memories and uses a response bridge to retrieve evidence based on the current state and candidate action.
Trains memory writers with multi-cut auxiliary supervision within a CF-JEPA-based world model.
On distracted Two-Stage PushT, improves terminal success from 15.5% to 25.0% over reconstructed CF-JEPA.
Achieves the lowest mean physical readout error across six models and two seeds, reducing distractor-induced along-push MAE by 20.2% relative to CF-JEPA.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies must react while visual inference is still running. Overlapping computation and execution reduces waiting, yet leaves perceptual memory stale and successive action chunks disconnected. We present CauSyncVLA, an asynchronous dual-system controller that aligns perceptual-memory prediction and trajectory correction with actual robot execution. Rather than forecasting pixels or physical states, a Causal Latent World Model predicts current perceptual memory from delayed visual anchors and executed state-action history, supervised through action-sensitive distillation to retain the frozen expert's control response. Conditioned on this updated memory, Predictive Flow Warm-Starting (PFWS) aligns the unexecuted action horizon for single-step flow correction without extra training. On LIBERO-10, CauSyncVLA reaches 93.8% success at 5.04$\times$ inference throughput, improving closed-loop robustness and robot motion smoothness.
authors: Xu Pan, Chubin Zhang, Xingrui Yu, Runmin Lan, Zihao Wang, Wenkai Guo, Bofang Jia, Bo An, Ziwei Wang
bullets: Addresses stale visual memory and disconnected action chunks caused by overlapping perception and execution.
Uses a Causal Latent World Model to predict current perceptual memory from delayed visual anchors and executed state-action history.
Applies action-sensitive distillation to preserve the frozen expert’s control behavior.
Uses Predictive Flow Warm-Starting for single-step correction of the remaining action horizon without additional training.
On LIBERO-10, achieves 93.8% success with 5.04× inference throughput, alongside improved robustness and motion smoothness.

papers.abstract: When a storm can head north or south, a forecast down the middle may score better under squared error than either plausible path. The same paradox appears when video generators are tested as world models: fewer denoising steps can raise physics scores even as videos blur or stop moving early. Why? Physics-IQ compares each generated video with one recording, although a scene can have multiple valid futures. An exact decomposition shows its scores can reward reduced variation among generated futures, even when their distribution becomes less accurate. We introduce Kernel Physics-IQ to remove this incentive in expectation, needing only two independent samples per condition. Two-step sampling lowers Kernel Physics-IQ in all five image-to-video models. For CogVideoX, the official score rises by 0.055 while ours falls by 0.131. Changing the sampling schedule reveals further differences official scores miss. In controlled physical systems with known outcome probabilities, our metric favors the true distribution over collapsed predictions. In short, a world model should be judged not only by how closely one video matches what happened, but by how faithfully its predictions represent what could have happened.
bullets: Single-reference squared-error evaluation may favor blurred or prematurely stopped videos that reduce prediction variance.
The authors formally decompose this bias and show that Physics-IQ can improve as generated futures collapse, even when their distribution worsens.
Kernel Physics-IQ removes the incentive in expectation using two independent samples per condition.
Across five image-to-video models, two-step sampling lowered Kernel Physics-IQ; for CogVideoX, the official score rose by 0.055 while the proposed score fell by 0.131.
Controlled physical-system tests show the new metric prefers the true outcome distribution over collapsed predictions.

papers.abstract: Do video world models learn physical laws without a physics loss, or merely imitate motion? Overall motion and appearance scores cannot settle it. We investigate this through nonlinear forced response: an excitation shakes the support of a suspended object. We introduce dual visual-numeric conditioning and adapt six image-to-video backbones to predict this motion using only the flow-matching loss. Wan predicts motion accurately and generalizes to unseen excitations, objects, poses, and scenes. Counterfactual tests suggest capabilities beyond replaying training videos. But what laws have they learned? We design three tiers of tests using Taylor expansions of the dynamics and geometry. All six reproduce the linear response, including resonance; five capture higher-order dynamics, including nonlinear softening. Remarkably, softening is barely present in training: only 0.74% of the swing's squared displacement. Extensions to a double pendulum and a rocking block show sustained dynamics are learned more faithfully than brief impacts. Yet learned dynamics may fail to appear when state estimation or propagation goes wrong. We turn these tests and findings into strategies to improve video training and generation.
authors: Yutao Li, Chen Wang, Wangmeng Zuo, Hui Li
bullets: Tests nonlinear forced responses by shaking the support of suspended objects.
Uses dual visual-numeric conditioning and adapts six image-to-video backbones without a physics loss.
All six models reproduce linear response and resonance; five capture higher-order dynamics such as nonlinear softening.
Wan generalizes to unseen excitations, objects, poses, and scenes, with counterfactual tests indicating more than training-video replay.
Performance is limited when state estimation or temporal propagation fails; sustained dynamics are learned more faithfully than brief impacts.

papers.abstract: World action models (WAMs) predict how a scene will evolve and condition their actions on this predicted future. Deploying them on a robot's onboard computer calls for 4-bit weights, activations and key-value caches (W4A4KV4). Existing 4-bit quantizers for WAMs preserve the generated action, and estimate sensitivity one denoising step at a time. However, they fail to preserve the fidelity of the predicted future: once the action pathway is protected, the remaining action error enters mostly through a degraded future that none of them deliberately protects. We propose LAQ, a latent-aware quantization framework that preserves the predicted future where it is written, stored and read. Specifically, we introduce a reader metric, which measures future error by its effect on the action, and a read count, which weights each rounding error by the number of denoising steps that read it. Together they give the allocation of precision over activations and caches a closed-form solution. We further develop gaze-guided refinement, which gives the tokens the action attends to a second 4-bit pass in the denoising loop and in the cache. All weights stay at 4 bits, with no high-precision branch and no per-task recalibration. On the LIBERO-Plus benchmark, LAQ reaches 76.4% and 83.3% average success on Fast-WAM and Cosmos-Policy, within 1.2 percentage points of the 16-bit models and all above the baselines with 16-bit KV caches. It compresses the model by 3.8x, reduces the peak GPU memory of the whole policy by 2.3x, and runs 1.66x faster than the 16-bit model. On a real AgileX PiPER arm, it reaches 47.0% average success over three tasks, against 52.0% for the 16-bit model and 30.0% higher than QuaRot.
authors: Yichen Guo, Yanlong Chen, Xinyue Zhang, Mohan Liu, Song Zhang, Yawei Li
bullets: Targets W4A4KV4 deployment of world action models on onboard robot computers.
Uses a reader metric to measure future errors by their impact on actions, and read counts to allocate activation/cache precision across denoising steps.
Adds gaze-guided refinement, giving action-relevant tokens a second 4-bit quantization pass in the denoising loop and cache.
On LIBERO-Plus, achieves 76.4% and 83.3% success—within 1.2 points of 16-bit models—while compressing 3.8×, reducing peak memory 2.3×, and running 1.66× faster.
On a real AgileX PiPER arm, reaches 47.0% success versus 52.0% for 16-bit and 30.0% higher than QuaRot.
