papers.abstract: Long-horizon world modeling in partially observable environments requires compact memories that preserve spatial structure despite accumulated localization drift. Inspired by hippocampal episodic and spatial memory and the multi-periodic coding of entorhinal grid cells, we propose HiSTFormer, a hierarchical spatiotemporal world model, which adopts a layer-wise organization of local temporal RoPE and multi-periodic spatial RoPE, together with content-conditioned address offsets, to capture recent temporal context and long-range spatial structure. A fixed-capacity memory keeps KV storage and per-step attention cost bounded as the sequence grows. On MemoryMaze and HM3D, HiSTFormer outperforms strong world-model baselines within the training sequence length and generalizes substantially better to prediction horizons far beyond those seen during training, while using a compact model. The hierarchical spatiotemporal design remains effective across deeper Transformer stacks, with consistent gains as depth increases. These results show that hierarchical spatiotemporal organization and content-adaptive spatial addressing provide effective inductive biases for efficient long-horizon world modeling.
authors: Tiantian Li, Junfeng Lu, Yifei Wang, Zhaoyang Zhang, Lei Wang, Tianyi Qian
bullets: Targets spatial-structure loss caused by localization drift in partially observable, long-horizon environments.
Combines layer-wise local temporal RoPE, multi-periodic spatial RoPE, and content-conditioned address offsets.
Maintains fixed-capacity KV memory, keeping storage and per-step attention cost bounded as sequences grow.
Outperforms strong baselines on MemoryMaze and HM3D, with stronger generalization to horizons beyond training.
The approach remains effective across deeper Transformer stacks, though the abstract does not specify quantitative results.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of HiSTFormer. The temporal Transformer first extracts local context using temporal RoPE. The resulting latent representations are decoded autoregressively into future frames.

papers.abstract: World action models (WAMs) couple generative video modeling with robotic action prediction but typically require large video and action transformers, limiting deployment efficiency. We present LoopedWAM, a compact WAM that recurrently applies a shared six-block core in each expert, executing 30 transformer layers while storing only 12 blocks per expert. To account for their asymmetric inference costs, the video and action experts can operate at different depths: visual features are computed once per query, whereas action computation repeats at every sampling step. We further propose elastic self-distillation, which trains a single elastic checkpoint, LoopedWAM-E, across action-depth and sampling-step budgets. With only 0.58B policy parameters and no robot pretraining, LoopedWAM achieves 96.1% success on LIBERO, 91.9% on RoboTwin 2.0, and 52.2% on RoboCasaGR1, while using $7.4\times$ less peak GPU memory than Fast-WAM under matched inference measurements. On LIBERO, LoopedWAM-E achieves 96.0% success in 27.6 ms or 95.2% in 24.7 ms on an H100, providing multiple accuracy-latency operating points from a single checkpoint; with two sampling steps and four action loops, it stays within 0.5 points of LoopedWAM on all three benchmarks. Ablations demonstrate that weight-shared depth preserves competitive performance, while aggressive action-depth reduction requires explicit budget-aware training. On a real AgileX PiPER arm, LoopedWAM succeeds in 71.3% of 80 trials across four tasks.
authors: Anh Dao, Xinxin Liu, Hang Yu, Jeffrey A Chan Santiago, Yuzhang Shang
bullets: WAMs are costly because they combine video generation with action prediction using large transformers.
A shared six-block core is recurrently applied to execute 30 layers while storing only 12 blocks per expert; video and action experts use different depths.
Elastic self-distillation trains one checkpoint to support varied action-depth and sampling-step budgets.
The 0.58B-parameter model reports 96.1% success on LIBERO, 91.9% on RoboTwin 2.0, and 52.2% on RoboCasaGR1, with 7.4× lower peak GPU memory than Fast-WAM under matched measurements.
On real hardware, it achieved 71.3% success over 80 trials; performance degrades when action depth is aggressively reduced without budget-aware training.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Method overview. (a) Each expert stores a prelude, a shared core, and a coda, and loops the core Kv times in the video expert and Ka times in the action expert (shown for Kv=4, Ka=2). The video expert encodes the current frame once per query and caches its keys and values. At every sampling step, the action expert reads them in a joint attention; late alignment lets action loop r attend to video loop σ(r), so even a single action loop sees the deepest visual features. Both experts also cross-attend to frozen text embeddings of the instruction, and future frames are predicted only during training. (b) One student learns every setting (Ka, N) in S. The target of each macro step is the frozen teacher’s fine Euler map started from the student’s own state (Llocal), and the final chunk is matched to the teacher’s chunk from the same noise (Lend).

Figure 1. LoopedWAM is small, fast, and elastic. (a) Each expert stores 12 blocks and loops its shared 6-block core K times. One checkpoint thus reaches the 30-layer depth of its dense donor with 2.4× fewer parameters, and the depth is chosen at test time. (b) RoboTwin 2.0 success against parameters, as reported by each paper. At 0.58B, LoopedWAM (91.9%) is the best model below 2B and on par with the ∼6B Fast-WAM (91.8%). papers.selection_reason: Compact world action model for robotic manipulation with elastic inference; fits embodied AI, world models, and efficiency.
papers.title: LoopedWAM: Looped World Action Models for Elastic Inference
papers.tldr: LoopedWAM makes world action models more memory- and latency-efficient by reusing transformer blocks and adapting inference depth without substantially sacrificing robotic task success.

papers.abstract: Comparative feedback, in which a judge says which of two candidate outcomes is closer to what happened, is a practical way to train language world models that assign probabilities to an action's outcomes. We show that, fitted with a Bradley-Terry objective, it need not teach the true outcome probabilities and can distort accurate ones. On a simulated robot push with enumerated outcome distributions, this objective takes a model that is accurate on unseen layouts (hazard error 2.4 percentage points, pp) and moves 33 to 43 pp of its probability onto outcomes that none of a condition's enumerated branches produces. The cause is the objective, not the comparisons: its optimum, computed before training, predicts where the model ends up, and a likelihood that knows the judge's rule learns from the same comparisons without the shift. The shift is robust: it recurs on unseen conditions, under five candidate laws and a three-fold denser enumeration, and about 29 pp remain without the physically impossible events. Its cost is conditional: with those events it inflates hazard probabilities, and a threshold inherited from the pre-feedback model costs about 3 pp of utility per decision on trained and 1 to 2 pp on unseen conditions, through false rejects; without them the utility loss averages below 1 pp over six seeds, though a small regret in action choice remains. Audits of readout, response and decision trace the effect from probabilities to actions.
authors: Xinze Shi, Litian Zhang, Zhenjie Su, Zelong Yu, Yuting Zhang, Qihua Feng, Zifeng Kang, Chaozhuo Li, Zhengxuan Hu
bullets: The issue arises from the Bradley-Terry objective itself, not from faulty comparisons; its pre-training optimum predicts the eventual distortion.
In a simulated robot-push task, an initially accurate model shifted 33–43 percentage points of probability to outcomes absent from the enumerated branches.
The effect persisted on unseen conditions, across five candidate laws, and with denser outcome enumeration; about 29 percentage points remained after excluding impossible events.
Distortion inflated hazard probabilities and reduced threshold-based utility by about 3 percentage points on trained and 1–2 points on unseen conditions when impossible events were included.
A likelihood that models the judge’s rule avoided the probability shift, while audits traced the Bradley-Terry effect from probabilities to actions.

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes how Bradley-Terry training distorts outcome probabilities in language world models, directly relevant to world model learning.
papers.title: Bradley-Terry Training Can Distort Outcome Probabilities of Initially Accurate Language World Models
papers.tldr: Bradley-Terry training from comparative feedback can substantially distort accurate outcome probabilities, shifting probability to impossible outcomes and degrading downstream decisions.

papers.abstract: Global medium-range weather forecasting must not only generate ensembles efficiently to characterize uncertainty in future states, but also serve downstream applications such as extreme-event warnings and cross-sphere coupled simulations. We introduce WeatherCraft, a framework that unifies probabilistic generation and reinforcement learning alignment through discrete weather tokens, bringing the GPT-style pretraining--post-training paradigm to global medium-range weather forecasting. A multiscale tokenizer represents atmospheric states as a coarse-to-fine token hierarchy, while a Transformer models causal dependencies across time and scale and predicts tokens within each scale in parallel. Direct sampling generates diverse ensembles, and exact token log-probabilities enable Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) to maximize downstream task rewards without differentiating through evaluators or coupled models. On the ERA5 benchmark, WeatherCraft's eight-member ensemble mean reduces day-15 normalized RMSE by 17.6% relative to the strongest evaluated deterministic baseline and, with KV caching, achieves an approximately $18\times$ inference speedup over GenCast. Direct fair-CRPS adaptation improves ensemble probabilistic skill, while reward-based post-training improves forecasts of persistent land temperature extremes and coupled ocean heat extremes. This work establishes discrete autoregressive modeling as a general foundation for scalable, task-alignable Earth system foundation models.
authors: Jinhan Li, Zhisheng Chen, Yuxuan Li, Yuan Gao, Fan Xu, Hao Wu, Jinlong Du, Kun Wang
bullets: Targets scalable global medium-range ensemble forecasting while supporting warnings and coupled Earth-system simulations.
Uses a multiscale coarse-to-fine tokenizer and a Transformer with parallel prediction within each scale.
Generates diverse ensembles by sampling and applies GRPO using exact token log-probabilities, without differentiating through evaluators or coupled models.
On ERA5, its eight-member ensemble mean lowers day-15 normalized RMSE by 17.6% versus the strongest evaluated deterministic baseline and is approximately 18× faster than GenCast with KV caching.
Fair-CRPS adaptation improves probabilistic skill, while reward-based post-training improves persistent land-temperature and coupled ocean-heat extreme forecasts.

papers.abstract: Action-conditioned video prediction lets robots anticipate the visual consequences of their actions for planning and policy evaluation. Existing predictors denoise each future from noise without using their own estimate of it, which limits the quality of the predicted future, in particular of the manipulated objects, and requires many network calls. We present TwoPass, a self-conditioned training-and-inference framework that keeps the standard flow-matching objective. Self-Generated Draft Training supplies a detached clean-video estimate from the shared network as conditioning at the same noisy state. A Refinement-Only Late Adapter applies a dedicated residual transformation when a draft is present. At inference, Draft-Reuse Iterative Refinement obtains both a solver update and the next draft from each velocity prediction, requiring as few as 4 function evaluations (NFE) per video chunk. Training samples discrete solver-query noise levels and updates the pretrained backbone. Extensive experiments on Bridge and Language Table show that TwoPass achieves state-of-the-art results with 4 NFE, far fewer than the 50-59 calls of existing predictors. Code: https://github.com/PlantPotatoOnMoon/TwoPass.
authors: Yijun Liu, Shijia Ge, Tongtong Feng, Xin Wang, Yuan Meng, Yuwei Liu, Zhi Wang, Wenwu Zhu
bullets: Targets low-quality predictions of manipulated objects and the high inference cost of existing video predictors.
Uses self-generated draft training to condition predictions on a detached clean-video estimate at the same noisy state.
Adds a refinement-only late adapter that applies a residual transformation when a draft is available.
Reuses each velocity prediction to produce both a solver update and the next draft during inference.
Evaluated on Bridge and Language Table, with 4 NFE versus 50–59 calls for existing predictors.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of TWOPASS. (1) Self-Generated Draft Training: on feedback-enabled updates (probability 0.5), two passes share weights and the noisy state. The first runs without gradients and produces a detached draft d = sg(xσ − σṽ) for the supervised second pass. (2) Refinement-Only Late Adapter: a bottleneck with a zero-initialized up-projection sits before the shared prediction head; the role flag r disables it when no draft is available (draft call) and enables it for draft-conditioned (refine) calls. (3) Draft-Reuse Iterative Refinement: inference starts without a draft, then reuses each clean estimate while the solver advances the noisy state, so each solver step costs one network call. Draft training and draft reuse are stages of the same self-conditioning mechanism.

Figure 4. Additional predictions on Bridge. Rows show GT, IRASim, ORV and TwoPass (NFE = 4), at frames 6–15 in the top and bottom examples and at frames 8, 12, 16, 20, 22, 24, 25, 27, 29 and 31 in the middle example. Figure 1. Motivation and concept of TWOPASS. (a) Planning and policy evaluation repeatedly predict the outcomes of candidate actions, so prediction must be accurate and fast. (b) Prediction must capture changing regions and frame-to-frame visual changes; orange contours show simplified outer boundaries of the main regions that change between frames. (c) Self-Generated Draft Training teaches the model to use its own imperfect predictions; a Refinement-Only Late Adapter gives draft-conditioned correction its own pathway; and DraftReuse Iterative Refinement recycles clean estimates without extra network calls. The draft and supervised training passes share a noisy state, whereas inference advances the solver state between calls.

papers.selection_reason: Action-conditioned video prediction for robotic manipulation; directly fits world models and interactive prediction.
papers.title: TwoPass: Draft-Guided Few-Step Video Prediction for Robotic Manipulation
papers.tldr: TwoPass improves action-conditioned robotic video prediction by reusing draft predictions for iterative refinement, achieving state-of-the-art results with as few as 4 network evaluations.

papers.abstract: 3D worlds can now be captured, reconstructed, and generated at scale, yet the objects in them stay still: a pressed pillow does not compress, and a pulled door does not swing. Bringing these objects into interactive 4D world models requires a representation of how they can move, deform, and respond physically to user actions in real time. We present PRIO, a pre-trained representation for interactive objects. Given static geometry, PRIO predicts an object-specific configuration space in a single forward pass. This space provides generalized coordinates for Lagrangian mechanics, allowing physical laws and user actions to govern motion. Configurations are linear in these coordinates, allowing the quantities needed by the dynamics to be precomputed. Dynamics then run at interactive rates without further network inference. Pre-trained on diverse 4D trajectories, PRIO learns priors over object configurations that generalize to unseen shapes. It supports meshes, point clouds, and 3D Gaussians, bringing objects in reconstructed and generated scenes into interaction. We demonstrate its use in real-to-sim workflows and robot manipulation. In addition, compared with existing 4D generation methods, PRIO generates dynamics faster and follows user actions more faithfully.
authors: Shixun Huang, Lifu Wei, Yue Chang, Chen Geng, Heng Zhang, Jinhyung Ahn, Caoliwen Wang, Siyuan Chen, Donglai Xiang, Jiajun Wu, Peter Yichen Chen
bullets: Addresses the challenge of making reconstructed or generated 3D-world objects physically interactive.
Predicts an object-specific configuration space in one forward pass from static geometry.
Uses linear generalized coordinates with Lagrangian mechanics, so dynamics quantities can be precomputed and simulated without further network inference.
Pre-trained on diverse 4D trajectories to generalize configuration priors to unseen shapes and support meshes, point clouds, and 3D Gaussians.
Demonstrated in real-to-sim workflows and robot manipulation; reported faster dynamics and more faithful response to user actions than existing 4D generation methods.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of PRIO. Given a mesh, point cloud or 3D Gaussians, PRIO encodes the geometry into shape tokens and predicts, at any point X , the fields ΦG(X) that span a linear configuration space. The network runs once per object; at inference, user actions drive the dynamics through the Euler–Lagrange equations in real time.

Figure 3. Qualitative inverse kinematics comparison. We evaluate how well each method’s predicted representation captures target configurations. Given an object’s rest shape, we optimize its latent coordinates to fit each target and compare the resulting reconstructions. PRIO reproduces the targets most closely.

Figure 6. Qualitative comparison of interactive 4D dynamics. We evaluate how naturally and plausibly objects move in response to user actions. PRIO deforms each object locally along the action and keeps it intact, whereas the baselines respond weakly or tear it.

Figure 10. Robot interaction. (a) Starting from the pillow’s surface mesh, PRIO models the deformation under a robot grasp at 7.6 ms per step. (b) A humanoid robot grasps eight plush toys in the same scene, all simulated together at 25 ms per step.

Figure 8. Live recordings of real-time interaction across 3D input formats. Screenshots of a user-controlled robot arm interacting with a 3D Gaussian ficus (top) and point-cloud flowers (bottom). The same pre-trained PRIO model simulates both objects’ responses directly in their respective 3D representations, at 125– 292 FPS for the ficus and 155–167 FPS for the flowers.

Figure 5. Interacting with real captured objects. PRIO enables physically driven responses to robot-arm manipulation for objects captured in Deform360 [37]. Ropes bend and plush toys deform naturally without per-object training.

Figure 4. Effect of pre-training scale. Reconstruction error on unseen shapes as the pre-training set grows from 266 to 2,142 objects under the same training budget. The error falls steadily, from 2.19 % to 1.43 %.

Figure 9. Interactive real-world objects. Objects reconstructed from photographs deform under user actions; overlaid frames show the motion. Each responds at interactive rates without perobject training.

Figure 7. Speed and accuracy against VBD. PRIO (left) and VBD [11] run to convergence (right) deform the same apple mesh on the same GPU. PRIO runs 7.1× faster, while their surfaces differ by only 0.1 % of the object size on average.

Table 3. Quantitative comparison on 4D dynamics and generation time. VLM scores (1–5) and end-to-end time to produce the 4D motion. PRIO leads in all metrics with the fastest runtime.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces a pre-trained representation for interactive objects in 4D worlds, enabling real-time physical interaction and dynamics simulation for robot manipulation.
papers.title: PRIO: Pre-trained Representation for Interactive Objects in 4D Worlds
papers.tldr: PRIO predicts a compact, physics-compatible representation of how objects move and deform, enabling fast interactive 4D simulation from static geometry.

papers.abstract: Joint-embedding predictive architecture (JEPA) world models plan from pixels with model predictive control, yet often fail on tasks their model should handle. Test-time adaptation attributes such failures to model error under distribution shift and updates the weights on the current episode, without checking this attribution against the planning loop itself. We follow the executed planning loop on pushing tasks. In most settings, with and without distribution shift, nearly all failures (at least 96%) are stalls, where the object stays in place while the model predicts progress. The warm-started gradient-descent (GD) planner then returns nearly the same plan, a fixed point where the agent mostly idles. We propose Unstick, which pairs on-policy fine-tuning before deployment with a fixed-weight loop breaker: a residual memory of the episode's prediction errors or random re-initialization at every replan. With GD, Unstick recovers most of the adaptation gain on pushing tasks with the memory, and with re-initialization most of it on shape shifts but much less on visual shifts. A large part of what limits these planners under GD is thus a fixed point of the planning loop, present with and without distribution shift, which a planner with fixed weights can break. Code is available at https://github.com/jhlee0619/unstick.
authors: Junhyeok Lee, Dongheon Lee, Kyu Sung Choi
bullets: At least 96% of observed failures are stalls: the object remains stationary while the model predicts progress.
Stalls arise both with and without distribution shift, challenging the attribution of failures solely to model error.
Unstick combines on-policy fine-tuning with a fixed-weight loop breaker: prediction-error memory or random re-initialization at each replan.
Residual memory recovers most adaptation gains on pushing tasks; re-initialization works well for shape shifts but less for visual shifts.
The findings identify planning-loop fixed points as a major limitation of warm-started gradient-descent planners.

papers.selection_reason: Diagnoses and remedies planning-loop failures in JEPA world-model planners for robotic pushing, relevant to world models and embodied planning.
papers.title: Stuck in Place: Stall Diagnosis and Remedies for JEPA Planners
papers.tldr: JEPA planners on pushing tasks often fail because gradient-descent planning gets stuck in fixed-point idle plans, and Unstick mitigates this by breaking the loop with residual memory or re-initialization.

papers.abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) unify world modeling and action generation for robotic control by integrating flow-matching velocities, yet suffer from high multi-step denoising latency. Recent studies have explored speculative inference to accelerate WAMs by drafting and verifying denoising steps in parallel. However, existing methods either require training task-specific draft models or overlook critical WAM denoising dynamics when reusing past velocities as drafts. We revisit the denoising dynamics of WAMs and identify a dual nonuniformity that breaks standard velocity-reuse assumptions: velocity smoothness is nonuniform as adjacent velocity residuals differ sharply at early and final steps, so reuse there yields large residuals, which nonuniform integration time steps further translate into local state errors that accumulate into the final action distribution. Accordingly, we formalize this by theoretically deriving a trajectory error tolerance bound that characterizes how velocity residuals and integration time steps affect the final action distribution. Based on this, we propose WAMotor, the first speculative inference method tailored to the dual nonuniformity in WAMs. It selects reliable anchor velocities by deferring speculation and employs time-step-aware verification that scales acceptance thresholds by integration time step size. WAMotor offers plug-and-play benefits, enabling seamless integration with prior WAMs. Extensive evaluations on LIBERO, RoboTwin 2.0, and LIBERO-Plus show that WAMotor achieves 2.86$\times$--4.28$\times$ end-to-end speedups while maintaining task success rates. Our code is available at: https://github.com/Overdue-Lin/WAMotor

bullets: WAMs incur high latency from multi-step denoising during robotic control.
The method addresses dual nonuniformity: velocity residuals vary sharply across denoising stages, and integration step sizes unevenly amplify state errors.
It derives a trajectory error tolerance bound linking velocity residuals and integration steps to final action-distribution error.
WAMotor selects reliable anchor velocities, delays speculation when needed, and uses integration-step-aware verification thresholds.
Evaluations on LIBERO, RoboTwin 2.0, and LIBERO-Plus show 2.86×–4.28× speedups with maintained success rates.

papers.abstract: Visual world models such as DINO-WM and JEPA-WM plan with an optimizer that searches for actions whose predicted outcome has the lowest cost, its distance to a goal image. A plan can thus fail in two ways: the optimizer never tries a good action that the cost would prefer (a search failure), or the cost, computed on predictions, ranks a bad action first (a scoring failure). The two need different remedies, more search or a better model, but a planner does not record which one occurred. We tell them apart by executing the optimizer's candidates, scoring a known solution with the planner's own cost, and comparing costs on predicted and real outcomes. An error model explains when each arises and so how to use retrieved demonstration windows (DemoProp): start the search from them (a warm start) when prediction errors are small, and average them without the model when large errors make the optimizer pick overrated actions. Across four simulated environments and three world models, on short tasks whose goals the planner can represent, PushT and Wall fail mostly by search, while Metaworld and RoboCasa fail by scoring because the cost, sound on real outcomes (AUROC 0.94 on Metaworld), is at chance on predictions (0.54). The diagnosis tells which remedy pays off: a four times larger search lowers the real-outcome cost only where failures come from search (clearly for DINO-WM), and where they come from scoring, averaging the windows without the model solves 127 of 168 new Metaworld tasks, against at most 87 when the model chooses among them. Within PushT, degrading only the model flips which use is better, and our rule, frozen in advance, follows the flip and solves 678 of 960 new episodes, against 530 for the best fixed use.
authors: Haoxuan Jia, Yang Liu, Shang Luo, Chenhao Wu, Zixiang Ni, Yingguang Yang, Feng Zhang, Chongyang Zhang, Hao Zheng, Kefu Xu, Congjing Ran, Jifeng Zhu, Bin Chong
bullets: Planner failures are separated into search failures—good actions are not tried—and scoring failures—predictions rank bad actions as best.
The diagnosis executes candidate actions, evaluates a known solution, and compares costs on predicted versus real outcomes.
DemoProp warm-starts optimization when prediction errors are small, but averages retrieved demonstrations without the model when errors are large.
Across four environments and three world models, PushT and Wall mainly exhibit search failures, while Metaworld and RoboCasa mainly exhibit scoring failures.
Adaptive remedy selection outperforms fixed demonstration use in the reported PushT evaluation, solving 678 of 960 episodes versus 530 for the best fixed strategy.

papers.abstract: A robotic world model should predict how objects evolve under robot actions and physical dynamics. While recent 3D world models have shown strong predictive capabilities, they still struggle with the heterogeneous dynamics arising from diverse object interactions. To address this in a unified framework, we decompose robotic interactions into distinct physical regimes and assign each to a specialized motion expert. We introduce MoRE, a 3D world model with a mixture of motion experts organized around rigid, deformable, and prehensile dynamics. This design enables a single model to capture diverse physical behaviors while preserving regime-specific priors. Trained on mixed simulation and real-world data, MoRE integrates with Model Predictive Control (MPC) to support diverse manipulation tasks. Experiments show that MoRE improves prediction accuracy across physics regimes, leading to stronger real-world MPC performance. Code, data, and project website are available at https://alwaysleepy.github.io/MoRE-WM-site/.
authors: Ziyu Zhu, Shaowei Liu, Albert J. Zhai, Henry Che, Wei-Chiu Ma, Shenlong Wang
bullets: Addresses the challenge of modeling heterogeneous physical interactions in robotics.
Assigns distinct motion experts to rigid, deformable, and prehensile physical regimes.
Trains on mixed simulation and real-world data and integrates with Model Predictive Control.
Improves prediction accuracy across physics regimes and strengthens real-world MPC performance.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of MoRE. Given the current and historical object states and actions, represented as point clouds, we first encode the scene and actor inputs into point tokens using two encoders. An explicit gating network then selects among specialized motion experts, each tailored to a distinct physical regime, to predict the next object state in 3D. P = prehensile, NP = non-prehensile.

Figure 4: Model Predictive Control (MPC) performance. (a) Box pushing and (b) toy manipulation results. Each section details the prediction error across planning steps (left) and success rate vs. error threshold (right). MoRE achieves lower error and higher success than the baselines.

Figure 3: Qualitative results on DROID evaluation. We compare model predictions with ground truth on challenging DROID scenes with clutter, diverse objects, and partial observations. Even for small, low-resolution manipulated objects, our model produces accurate dynamics, demonstrating robustness to occlusion and noise.

The Vanilla model struggles to treat the box as rigid and the toy sloth as soft. In contrast, our model correctly handles the different cases.

Figure 6: Benchmark tasks visualization: Simulation and real-world benchmarks covering rigid and soft objects under non-prehensile and prehensile interactions, designed to evaluate generalization across diverse physical regimes.

Table 2: Dynamic model comparison across interaction types and physics. We report geometric accuracy (MSE, CD) and material structural metrics (rigidity or Laplacian). Privileged experts (gray) are domain-specific and assume known interaction types at test time, while our Mixture-of-Experts model handles diverse interactions in a unified framework with consistently strong performance.
Table 4: Comparison with Point-World on the DROID dataset. Our method performs better across all three cases, showing strong generalization to real-world object dynamics.

Table 5: Gating Network Accuracy. Expert selection accuracy (%) evaluated over 50 random interactions per task category. The gating network maintains consistently high accuracy across diverse regimes, indicating reliable expert routing for different physical dynamics.

Performance degrades when removing expert specialization, explicit routing, or self-rollout training, highlighting the importance of each component for robust dynamics prediction.

papers.abstract: Neural state-space identification learns dynamical models from measured inputs and outputs. SUBNET combines this task with an encoder that estimates initial states from short measurement histories. Its continuous-time version requires many successive neural-network evaluations during numerical integration, resulting in slow training speed which is a major limitation for practical use cases. We propose deep structured state space models (DS3M), which combine compact nonlinear dynamical components in parallel and in series. Custom GPU kernels implemented with Triton reduce the launch and memory overhead of their sequential evaluation. We explain this construction, describe a port-Hamiltonian variant, and present various benchmark comparisons of accuracy and training time.
bullets: Addresses slow training in continuous-time state-space models caused by repeated neural-network evaluations during numerical integration.
Uses compact nonlinear dynamical components arranged in parallel and series.
Implements custom Triton GPU kernels to reduce launch and memory overhead during sequential evaluation.
Also introduces a port-Hamiltonian variant and evaluates accuracy and training time through benchmark comparisons.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) can improve vision-language-action (VLA) policies beyond imitation, but humanoid exploration is unsafe and simulator RL can exploit residual sim-to-real gaps. We present WEVO, a teleoperation-free framework for post-training a whole-body humanoid VLA in an action-conditioned video world model (WM). Simulated manipulation and locomotion play data improve contact-dynamics and viewpoint-change prediction. A VLA trained on synthetic demonstrations collects 20 autonomous real robot rollouts per task to align the WM with deployment observations. The VLA, whole-body controller (WBC), and video WM then form a closed-loop RL environment with dense progress rewards. Across three real robot tasks, play data improves every evaluated WM metric and downstream policy success; video WM RL raises mean success from 23.3% to 75.0%, compared with 48.3% for real robot RL. We therefore leverage the complementary strengths of both environments: simulation provides policy initialization and broad coverage, while the video WM offers a deployment-aligned environment for policy improvement. Project website: https://qianzhong-chen.github.io/wevo.github.io/.
authors: Qianzhong Chen, Muyuan Lin, Yuyin Sun, Mac Schwager, Cheng-Hao Kuo, Roberto Mart\'in-Mart\'in

Uses simulated play data to improve contact-dynamics and viewpoint-change prediction in an action-conditioned video world model.
Aligns the world model with deployment observations using 20 autonomous real-robot rollouts per task, without teleoperation.
Forms a closed-loop RL environment from the VLA, whole-body controller, and video world model with dense progress rewards.
Across three real-robot tasks, video-world-model RL raises mean success from 23.3% to 75.0%, versus 48.3% for real-robot RL.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) can propose multi-step manipulation plans, but they have no grounded model of how a scene will change, and the pixel-level world models that could check those plans are slow and drift over long horizons. We present Verify2Act, a modular verification framework that separates semantic action proposal from latent physical verification. A VLM proposes candidate plans, a latent world model (V2A-WM) imagines each of them in the DINOv2 feature space, and a dual-head critic checks the imagined rollouts for temporal consistency and goal satisfaction before anything is executed. V2A-WM extends recent flow-matching world models with cross-attention action grounding and a causal temporal history window. We deploy the full system on a low-cost robot arm, training the world model and critic only on data generated in a digital twin. Across six language-conditioned tasks, Verify2Act reaches 83.3\% task success, compared with 61.7\% for a latent world model without our architectural changes, 53.3\% for the VLM alone, and 46.7\% for a pixel-diffusion world model. It verified every plan it executed and incurred no planning-induced failures: all of its failed episodes were caused by low-level grasp or placement slips. In simulation, Verify2Act obtains the highest five-task chain success on CALVIN among the compared baselines with 30$\times$ fewer reflective VLM calls than pixel-diffusion verification, and the highest success on cluttered nut assembly.
bullets: Addresses the lack of grounded scene-change reasoning in VLM-generated multi-step manipulation plans and the inefficiency and drift of pixel-level world models.
Imagines candidate plans in DINOv2 feature space using a flow-matching world model with action cross-attention and causal temporal history.
A dual-head critic evaluates imagined rollouts for temporal consistency and goal satisfaction before robot execution.
On six language-conditioned tasks, it achieved 83.3% success, outperforming the reported latent-world-model, VLM-only, and pixel-diffusion baselines.

All executed plans were verified successfully; remaining failures came from low-level grasp or placement slips, while simulation results showed strong CALVIN and cluttered nut-assembly performance with 30× fewer reflective VLM calls than pixel-diffusion verification.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Verify2Act overview. Stage 1: a VLM proposes candidate multi-step plans from the camera observation and the language instruction. Stage 2: V2A-WM rolls out each candidate in the frozen DINOv2 latent space (St → St+k), conditioned on CLIP action tokens. Stage 3: a goal head scores the terminal latent state against the goal, and a temporal consistency head checks consecutive imagined states; the best verified plan is executed.

Fig. 4. Results on the robot. (a) Task success per task and averaged over tasks. (b) Outcome of the episodes of each method: success, execution failure (the plan was correct but a skill failed), or planning failure (the executed plan could not satisfy the goal).

Fig. 2. V2A-WM training and inference. Training: the delta encoder gives the target latent zgt = fenc(∆St); we interpolate zτ = τzgt + (1− τ)z0 and the flow-matching transformer, conditioned on past frames and CLIP action tokens through cross-attention, predicts the velocity v̂. Inference: a single Euler step integrates from noise z0 to z1 = z0 + v̂, and the delta decoder reconstructs Ŝt+1 = St + fdec(z1).

papers.abstract: Anomaly detection in medical images is a complex task, requiring the development of a robust model using only healthy patient data. Without access to labeled data, modern approaches typically employ self-supervised learning to obtain a model of normality. Since world models promise to build strong internal representations of their environment, we consider them as suitable candidates for the medical anomaly detection environment, namely medical investigations of healthy patients. To this end, we propose MADJEPA, a medical anomaly detector based on an enhanced multi-stage joint-embedding predictive architecture (JEPA). We design a multi-stage training pipeline to produce a robust detector: (1) image-based JEPA (I-JEPA) training aims to learn a strong representation of normal training data; (2) target encoder distillation aims to modulate over-generalization of I-JEPA representations to abnormal data; (3) pseudo-anomaly classification aims to calibrate anomaly predictions by learning a tight boundary around the normal data manifold. To demonstrate our design, we carry out comprehensive experiments on six datasets covering various medical image domains (e.g.~MRI, OCT, X-ray, histopathology), comparing our MADJEPA with numerous state-of-the-art methods. The results show that our carefully designed world model, MADJEPA, attains competitive results, ranking first on three datasets. Our ablation studies further confirm the utility of each training stage, indicating that I-JEPA alone is not sufficient to obtain competitive results in medical anomaly detection. We publicly release our code at https://github.com/Sabina085/madjepa.
authors: Ioana-Sabina Stoian, Florinel-Alin Croitoru, Vlad Hondru, Andreea Iuliana Ionescu, Andrei Paun, Radu Tudor Ionescu
bullets: Addresses unsupervised medical anomaly detection when labeled abnormal data are unavailable.
Combines image-based JEPA representation learning, target-encoder distillation, and pseudo-anomaly classification.
Evaluated across six datasets spanning MRI, OCT, X-ray, and histopathology.
Achieves competitive performance and ranks first on three datasets; ablations support the value of all three stages.
Code is publicly released; the approach is scoped to learning normality from healthy-patient images.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Overview of MADJEPA. Our pipeline is divided into three training stages: 1⃝ self-supervised training via I-JEPA; 2⃝ target encoder distillation to a randomly-initialized student; 3⃝ A: prompt-based pseudo-anomaly generation, and B: normal vs. pseudo-anomaly classification. Together, these training stages build a strong and calibrated representation of normal data. Best viewed in color.

Figure 2. Qualitative visualizations of anomaly maps for the three benchmarks that have ground-truth segmentation maps: BTCV+LiTs, BraTS2021 and RESC. We employ the exact examples selected by Bao et al. [5] from the BMAD original paper. Best viewed in color.

Figure 3. Ablation on the number of sampled target blocks (N ) on BraTS2021 (top) and BTCV+LiTS (bottom). The performance of MADJEPA increases with the number of target blocks. However, on both datasets, beyond 30 sampled blocks, the performance gain is marginal.

Table 1. Anomaly detection performance of our method MADJEPA on the complete BMAD benchmark [5]. We compare our method against a comprehensive set of state-of-the-art anomaly detection techniques from the literature, achieving the best performance on three challenging datasets (BTCV+LiTS, RSNA, CAMELYON16), and second-best on one dataset (BraTS2021). MADJEPA is the only method surpassing the 80% threshold on all datasets and metrics. The best score on each dataset is highlighted in blue bold and the second-best score is highlighted in orange underline. We report mean image-level and pixel-level AUROC scores (where pixel-level annotations are available), along with the corresponding standard deviations, computed across five different seeds. papers.title: MADJEPA: Enhanced Multi-Stage Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture for Medical Anomaly Detection
papers.tldr: MADJEPA uses a three-stage JEPA-based self-supervised pipeline to detect medical-image anomalies from healthy data alone.

papers.abstract: Visual world models enable effective short-horizon goal-conditioned planning, such as reaching nearby targets and pushing objects over short distances, by predicting candidate action outcomes and comparing their representations with a goal representation. However, extending this approach to long-horizon tasks is challenging: prediction errors accumulate over extended rollouts, while latent-space similarity to distant goals provides limited guidance for ranking candidate outcomes. Existing methods address these limitations by introducing intermediate subgoals, either generated by learned models or selected from experience memory. Generated subgoals can contain hallucinations or be inaccurate in aspects such as object positions and timing. Memory-based approaches are constrained by experience coverage and may lack precise guidance for selecting appropriate intermediate states from stored observations. We introduce GEMS, which generates temporally structured subgoals to guide action search and state selection from Latent Experience Memory (LEM). A distance gate determines whether predicted outcomes are evaluated against the generated subgoal or the selected memory state. Experiments across six tasks and task suites spanning manipulation, navigation, and reaching demonstrate the effectiveness of GEMS for long-horizon planning. GEMS outperforms state-of-the-art world-model planning baselines across different manipulation settings, achieving success rates of 92.8% on Cube, 68.4% on Push-T, and 54.1% on Meta-World. It improves over the strongest evaluated baseline on these tasks by 24.0, 7.3, and 22.2 percentage points, respectively. These results demonstrate that generated subgoals and experience memory can jointly strengthen long-horizon planning with a frozen world model.

bullets: Long-horizon planning suffers from compounding prediction errors and weak guidance from distant goal similarity.

papers.abstract: Every move in a robot team changes the world in which its teammates must act. Coordinated manipulation therefore calls for predicting the team's actions together with the physical future they jointly create. We introduce MAWAM, a multi-agent world-action model that jointly generates each robot's future views and executable action chunks in a single sample. Built from a pretrained single-robot world-action backbone, MAWAM jointly denoises all robots' action and future-view tokens through cross-agent attention, while preserving a separate control interface for each robot. MAWAM achieves the highest success on all three real-robot tasks (laundry-bag collection, bath-towel folding, and umbrella handover), with 67.8% mean success, 18.9 percentage points above MA-VLA trained on the same demonstrations and cameras. In simulation, MAWAM reaches 90.3% mean success on eight tasks with teams of up to four arms. Ablations show that cross-agent attention and team-stage future-video supervision both improve coordinated control: without attention, a four-arm relay falls from 95.0% to 39.0%, and without this supervision, Place Food falls from 78.0% to 47.0%.

bullets: Targets coordinated manipulation, where each robot’s move affects teammates’ future actions.
Jointly generates future views and executable action chunks for all robots in one sample.
Uses cross-agent attention to denoise shared action and future-view tokens while retaining separate control interfaces.
Achieves 67.8% mean success across three real-robot tasks and 90.3% across eight simulated tasks with up to four arms.
Ablations show cross-agent attention and team-stage future-video supervision are important for coordination.

papers.abstract: Understanding how stable psychometric traits and time-varying states jointly inform behavior is an important problem in computational behavioral science. Existing personalized agents commonly condition actions directly on a static profile, leaving realized state transitions unused as an explicit source of supervision. We introduce a profile-conditioned state world model that uses observed environment--behavior state transitions to learn transition-informed representations for behavioral prediction. During training, a posterior encoder quantizes realized transitions, while a prior predicts the resulting codes from the psychometric profile and pre-transition context. The prior code and predicted next state then condition macro-level behavior and simulator-grounded execution. Thus, the world model provides structured transition supervision instead of treating personality as a direct action descriptor. We evaluate the framework in VEET, a controlled behavioral simulator with human trajectories, and in AgentSociety as a structurally different synthetic environment. A participant-disjoint split of 240 training, 25 validation, and 48 test participants evaluates generalization to unseen people. On VEET, the model reaches 0.904 Top-1 accuracy (95\% CI: [0.895, 0.913]) and 0.0033 Macro KL. Ablations associate continuous next-state modeling with most of the Top-1 gain, while discrete codes and prior alignment mainly improve Top-3 and distributional alignment. These results establish transition-informed world-model supervision as useful for subject-generalized behavior prediction, without implying causal psychological mechanisms or calibrated long-horizon state dynamics.
authors: Ziyuan Qin, Yang Qiao, Summer B. Frandsen, Michael T. Treadway, Liang Zhao
bullets: Addresses the limitation of conditioning behavior directly on static personality profiles while ignoring realized state transitions.
Uses a profile-conditioned world model: a posterior encoder quantizes observed transitions, and a prior predicts transition codes from the profile and pre-transition context.
Conditions macro-level behavior prediction and simulator-grounded execution on the predicted code and next state.
Evaluated in VEET and AgentSociety with participant-disjoint splits; VEET achieved 0.904 Top-1 accuracy and 0.0033 Macro KL.
Ablations link continuous next-state modeling to Top-1 gains, while discrete codes and prior alignment improve Top-3 and distributional alignment.

papers.abstract: World action models (WAMs) have shown promising generalization and data efficiency in robot manipulation by coupling action generation with predictions of future visual dynamics. Translating these capabilities into reliable task execution, however, remains a challenge for existing post-training methods. Offline supervised fine-tuning provides dense supervision on expert trajectories, but its flow-matching action expert is trained only on noised demonstration actions and never on the intermediate states produced by its own sampler; task-specific adaptation can also compromise pretrained capabilities. On-policy reinforcement learning trains on the policy's own behavior, yet sparse task rewards make exploration and credit assignment difficult, while dense reward shaping still provides scalar evaluations rather than direct action targets. We introduce \textbf{HINT-WAM}, the first on-policy self-distillation framework that supervises the action expert on its own sampling trajectories using hindsight, the future video of the demonstration, as privileged information available to the WAM itself. For each demonstration observation, the student generates its action through its own denoising trajectory, and at the states along this trajectory the same model acts as a teacher conditioned additionally on this hindsight, providing a conditional action distribution as a dense training target, while the student sees only deployment-time inputs and needs no environmental rewards or simulator interaction. To transfer this supervision to a flow-matching action expert, HINT-WAM distills the teacher into the student with an energy score, a distribution-level objective that matches the teacher's action distribution from the student's own samples rather than regressing its velocity field. The project web is available in https://tuandattt.github.io/hintwam/.
bullets: Addresses the gap between offline expert-trajectory training and reliable execution on a model’s self-generated states.
Uses the demonstration’s future video as privileged hindsight for a teacher, while the student receives only deployment-time observations.
Applies on-policy self-distillation along the student’s denoising trajectories to provide dense action targets.
Uses an energy-score, distribution-level objective to transfer the teacher’s action distribution to a flow-matching action expert.
The abstract presents the framework and motivation but reports no quantitative experimental results or explicit limitations.

Stage B (bottom): the student integrates its own ODE without gradients, and its implied actions at selected denoising points are matched to a single sample from the frozen hindsight teacher with the energy score, together with a behavior-cloning anchor. Only the student is deployed.

papers.abstract: We introduce $Z$-sight, a unified robot foundation model that couples vision-language-action (VLA) and generative latent world modeling. Video-based world action models (WAMs) show the value of joint future-and-action generation for control, yet inherit the heavy cost of video generators. Recent latent-space policies avoid pixel generation, yet typically align intermediate features or rely on frozen target encoders, decoupling future prediction from the VLM's native feature space. $Z$-sight instead predicts the future directly in the visual token space in which its VLM perceives the present. Coupling a foresight expert and a continuous action expert with the VLM in a mixture-of-transformers, $Z$-sight jointly denoises future spatial tokens and actions at inference without pixel reconstruction or external encoders. Trained on human video and robot trajectories, $Z$-sight achieves 81.9% success on SIMPLE (+9.6 points over the strongest baseline) and 73.3% across six Unitree G1 tasks (+20.0 points) at 110 ms per chunk, while remaining competitive on tabletop benchmarks.

Uses a mixture-of-transformers that couples the VLM with foresight and continuous action experts.
Predicts future spatial tokens directly in the VLM’s native visual-token space.
Trained on human videos and robot trajectories, it reports 81.9% success on SIMPLE and 73.3% across six Unitree G1 tasks at 110 ms per chunk.
Also remains competitive on tabletop benchmarks.

papers.abstract: World-action models jointly predict future observations and actions, yet reconstruction-oriented visual representations do not explicitly emphasize the spatial relationships and object-state changes needed for manipulation. We introduce Phoenix, which learns representations of scene structure for world-action modeling. Specifically, Phoenix Encoder enriches DINOv3's general visual semantics through dual-teacher distillation of geometric and spatiotemporal semantic knowledge. Next, CS-VAE causally aggregates and compresses Phoenix Encoder features into generative latents while preserving scene information and spatial layout. Finally, Phoenix jointly predicts these latents, complementary appearance latents, and robot actions, linking scene evolution with action generation. To study pretraining data efficiency, we curate approximately 39,000 hours of egocentric and robot manipulation data for representation learning and use the robot demonstration subset for WAM pretraining. Following benchmark-specific post-training, Phoenix achieves state-of-the-art performance across simulation and real-robot benchmarks spanning single-arm, bimanual, and dexterous manipulation. It demonstrates strong robustness to perturbations, achieving success rates of 94.8% on LIBERO-Plus and 72.4% on RoboTwin 2.0 C2R, alongside strong cross-embodiment transfer and real-world manipulation performance on Bench2Dex and RoboDojo-RealWorld, respectively. Pretraining-scale analysis shows larger performance gains from data scaling than a video-VAE-only baseline, indicating stronger scaling benefits and more effective data utilization. Moreover, Phoenix maintains high success rates when adapted with limited downstream demonstrations, demonstrating strong few-shot adaptation. Our code, pretraining data, and models are available on the project page to help the community reproduce our results.
authors: Yupeng Zheng, Chaoyue Li, Linbo Wang, Xiang Li, Yuhang Zheng, Xiaotong Su, Songen Gu, Yichen Zhang, Zebin Xing, Shuai Tian, Jingxiang Guo, Jing Li, Zhiyong Zhao, Zhongpu Xia, Qichao Zhang, Haoran Li, Shuicheng Yan, Dongbin Zhao
bullets: Addresses the gap between reconstruction-focused visual representations and the spatial relationships and object-state changes needed for manipulation.
Uses dual-teacher distillation to enrich DINOv3 features with geometric and spatiotemporal knowledge, then CS-VAE to compress them into generative scene latents.
Jointly predicts scene-structure latents, appearance latents, and robot actions to model scene evolution and action generation.
Pretrained with approximately 39,000 hours of egocentric and robot-manipulation data; achieves strong results across simulated and real-robot, single-arm, bimanual, and dexterous benchmarks.
Shows robustness to perturbations, improved scaling with more data than a video-VAE-only baseline, cross-embodiment transfer, and effective few-shot adaptation.

papers.abstract: Predicting the consequences of an agent's actions requires modeling both the body's motion and the environment's response. Most video world models attempt to learn both from numerical actions, even though geometry and kinematics already specify the intended motion. We introduce Doppel, an embodiment-agnostic video world model conditioned on camera-aligned renderings of future body configurations and numerical action trajectories. By explicitly providing the intended motion, Doppel can focus on predicting object motion and interaction-driven changes in the environment. Rendered motion also provides a common visual interface across different embodiments and action spaces. To train on robot datasets without camera extrinsics, we recover camera poses and align rendered trajectories with recorded observations. We jointly train a single shared video backbone and conditioning adapter on eight datasets spanning eight robot and human embodiments, from single- and bimanual robot arms to a dexterous humanoid and human hands and bodies, using about 600 hours of video without embodiment labels. Across three robot-arm datasets, Doppel improves PSNR over action-only baselines by 1.00 dB on held-out trajectories and 1.20 dB under out-of-distribution evaluation, while predicting more consistent object motion. Training on all eight embodiments (Doppel-8) improves robot predictions over the three-robot model (Doppel-3) on four of six evaluation sets. Project page: https://doppelwm.github.io/.
authors: Yash Jangir, Karan Mirakhor, Renos Zabounidis, Muhammad Zubair Irshad, Sergey Zakharov, Yonatan Bisk, Homanga Bharadhwaj
bullets: Problem: Action-only world models must learn both known body motion and harder-to-predict environmental changes, limiting transfer across embodiments.
Method: Condition video prediction on camera-aligned renderings of future body configurations and numerical action trajectories.
Training: Jointly learns one backbone and conditioning adapter from about 600 hours across eight robot and human embodiments, without embodiment labels.
Results: Improves PSNR over action-only baselines by 1.00 dB on held-out robot-arm trajectories and 1.20 dB under out-of-distribution evaluation.
Scope: Cross-embodiment training improves robot predictions on four of six evaluation sets, while requiring camera-pose recovery when extrinsics are unavailable.

papers.abstract: Rules govern how player actions change interactive worlds. Different rules create distinct gameplay experiences within similar scenes and action spaces. For customizable gameplay, generative world models must follow user-defined rules beyond real-world behaviors. However, realizing user-defined rules presents two challenges: Rule-State Persistence and Rule-to-Visual Realization. The former requires preserving rule definitions, dependencies, and world states across saving and loading, so that restored worlds follow the established rules. The latter requires accurately realizing rule-induced changes on designated objects and attributes, particularly when affected objects are unseen. In this paper, we propose WorldRuler, which organizes rule definitions, dependencies, and object states in an executable 3D rule graph and connects rule execution, video generation, and perceptual feedback in a closed loop. The graph supports joint saving and restoration of rules and world states, while dynamic object binding grounds rule-specified entities in visual instances and uses stored states to constrain generation from their first appearance. We further introduce object attribute state replacement and counterfactual reconstruction training, enabling accurate attribute control and compatible appearance and motion changes while limiting interference with unrelated content. We develop an automated data collection and annotation pipeline using GTA-V and Habitat to construct RuleVerse, a dataset of rule-driven interactions with detailed state and event annotations, including cases where rules take effect before affected objects become visible. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of WorldRuler in preserving rule-state consistency across saving and loading and accurately realizing rule outcomes on designated objects and attributes.
authors: Mingliang Zhai, Chuanhao Li, Jiaming Tan, Zhen Li, Yuwei Wu, Yunde Jia, Zian Meng, Yuanyang Yin, Kaipeng Zhang
bullets: Addresses rule-state persistence across saving and loading and rule-to-visual realization, including unseen affected objects.
Represents rules, dependencies, and object states in an executable 3D rule graph linked to video generation and perceptual feedback.
Uses dynamic object binding, state-constrained generation, attribute state replacement, and counterfactual reconstruction training.
Introduces RuleVerse, a rule-driven interaction dataset built from GTA-V and Habitat with detailed state and event annotations.
Experiments show improved consistency of saved/restored rules and accurate realization of rule outcomes on specified objects and attributes.

papers.abstract: World models are increasingly used in autonomous driving to predict how a scene evolves under the ego vehicle's actions, supporting counterfactual reasoning and model-based planning. However, existing evaluations focus on prediction fidelity and planning performance, and rarely verify that the predictions depend on the conditioning action. In this paper, we study action dependence in action-conditioned semantic forecasting, which predicts future semantic segmentation from past segmentations and the ego action. We compare a forecaster with feature-wise and input-level action conditioning against an identical model without action input, and measure action dependence with test-time action interventions scored by standard segmentation metrics. The evaluation is validated in a synthetic environment with known action-dependent dynamics and applied to Cityscapes and BDD100K, both within each dataset and across the two vehicle platforms. Experiments show that the executed action improves mid-term mIoU by at most 2.5 points on Cityscapes and 0.6 points on BDD100K, whereas a wrong action reduces it by up to 23.2 and 7.0 points, below the model without action input. On real data, feature-wise conditioning depends 1.6 times more on the action than input-level conditioning at similar accuracy, whereas both depend on it equally in the synthetic environment, where the history does not determine the action. These results show that an accuracy gain indicates that a driving world model uses its action, but not how strongly its forecasts depend on it. Code is available at https://github.com/binayksingh/does-action-matter.
authors: Binay Kumar Singh, Niels Da Vitoria Lobo
bullets: The study evaluates whether semantic forecasts change appropriately when the ego action is altered.
It compares feature-wise and input-level action conditioning with an otherwise identical model without action input.
Test-time action interventions are assessed using standard segmentation metrics in a synthetic environment, Cityscapes, and BDD100K.
Correct actions improve mid-term mIoU by up to 2.5 points on Cityscapes and 0.6 points on BDD100K; incorrect actions reduce it by up to 23.2 and 7.0 points, respectively.
On real data, feature-wise conditioning is 1.6× more action-dependent than input-level conditioning at similar accuracy.

papers.abstract: Self-supervised video encoders are commonly trained to either reconstruct pixels or predict latent features, yet it remains unclear how these objectives shape representations for downstream dynamics. We present a capacity-matched study isolating this choice: two identical video encoders with a shared FSQ bottleneck are trained under autoencoding and V-JEPA objectives on a continuous control environment. We introduce a simple asymmetric discretization scheme to apply the same bottleneck to the predictive model. The resulting representations exhibit a clear trade-off: the autoencoder preserves substantially more physical state information and achieves slightly better one-step latent prediction, while the predictive encoder accumulates less error under autoregressive rollout. Structural probes suggest that this advantage is associated with greater robustness to low-level visual perturbations and stronger dependence on temporal context. These results indicate that predictive and reconstructive objectives induce distinct representations of dynamics, trading state fidelity for properties that may benefit long-horizon prediction.
bullets: Studies reconstruction versus latent-prediction objectives using capacity-matched video encoders with a shared FSQ bottleneck.
Introduces asymmetric discretization to apply the same discrete bottleneck to the predictive V-JEPA model.
Autoencoding retains substantially more physical state information and performs slightly better on one-step latent prediction.
Predictive representations accumulate less error during autoregressive rollout, with benefits linked to robustness to visual perturbations and stronger temporal-context dependence.
The objectives create a trade-off between state fidelity and properties useful for long-horizon dynamics prediction.

papers.abstract: World models operate in a world they cannot fully observe. When a hidden disturbance, such as a current pushing a boat, changes the outcome of an action, a counterfactual question follows: what would have happened under a different action, subject to the same disturbance? Its answer separates bad decisions from bad luck. We prove that world models trained on factual transitions cannot answer it on their own, whatever their data or capacity. For many physical systems, the observed outcome and a simple property of the dynamics suffice: natura non facit saltus, nature makes no leaps. When actions and disturbances act as separate forces, their interaction is second-order in time, so the counterfactual outcome is, to first order, the observed outcome plus the difference between the world model's predictions under the alternative and factual actions. This yields a counterfactual world model with no counterfactual data, extra parameters, or retraining. For transitions of duration $h$, we prove an $O(h^2)$ bound on the counterfactual error relative to the disturbance variance, establish a matching minimax lower bound from unpaired factual data, and characterize failures at discontinuities, coordinate folds, and disturbances that scale the command. We validate these predictions from pixels with JEPA world models on frozen DINOv2 and masked autoencoder (MAE) encoders. On four rendered simulators, our approach improves counterfactual $R^2$ from $38$--$46\%$ to $86$--$96\%$ with the same world models; on a fifth, an underwater vehicle, it reaches $90$--$94\%$ with sixteen times more factual data. Four further frozen encoders, DINOv3, SigLIP~2, CLIP and EVA-02, give $81$--$95\%$ on the same simulators. In hindsight planning, it finds the action that would have reached the goal in $35$--$69\%$ of events, against $14$--$23\%$ for an oracle planner that knows the simulator but not the outcome.
authors: Randall Balestriero, Yann LeCun, Kerda Varaku
bullets: Factual transitions alone cannot identify what would have happened under another action when disturbances are hidden.
For smooth systems with separable action and disturbance forces, the counterfactual is approximated by the observed outcome plus the model’s alternative-versus-factual prediction difference.
The method requires no counterfactual data, extra parameters, or retraining, with an $O(h^2)$ error bound and matching minimax lower bound.
Across rendered simulators, counterfactual $R^2$ improves from 38–46% to 86–96%; an underwater-vehicle task reaches 90–94%.

The approach improves hindsight planning, finding goal-reaching actions in 35–69% of events versus 14–23% for the comparison planner, but can fail at discontinuities, coordinate folds, or disturbance-scaled commands.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in world models are opening new possibilities for fine-grained embodied tasks, with hand-object interaction offering a particularly demanding setting. Modeling these interactions involves capturing how hand actions change objects and how the resulting states persist over time. Yet systematic evaluation tailored to these hand-centric capabilities remains underdeveloped. To address this gap, we introduce HandWorldBench, a unified benchmark that systematically evaluates hand-centric world models across human hands, simulated dexterous hands, and real dexterous hands along six dimensions: visual quality, hand fidelity, appearance consistency, instruction following, physical consistency, and temporal coherence. To construct the benchmark, we develop a data curation pipeline that extracts hand-object interaction clips and screens them for quality, yielding 20,500 high-quality egocentric clips from over 600 hours of footage. We then manually select 500 clips covering seven task families for evaluation. Benchmarking eleven models under a unified protocol reveals that stronger hand-pose control does not consistently translate into coherent object-state evolution and persistence or robust cross-embodiment performance, with several specialized hand-control models underperforming general-purpose text/image-to-video generators on dexterous-hand tasks.
authors: Zhaolu Wang, Jiacheng Xu, Lihong Wang, Shuqing Wang, Jianjie Fang, Ziyou Wang, Xvyuan Liu, Rongze Tang, Yiding Ma, Xin Zhang, Jiawei Chen, Wei Wu, Chen Gao, Yong Li, Zhibo Chen
bullets: Evaluates human, simulated dexterous, and real dexterous hand models across six dimensions, including hand fidelity, instruction following, physical consistency, and temporal coherence.
Builds a curated corpus of 20,500 high-quality egocentric hand-object interaction clips from over 600 hours of footage.
Uses 500 manually selected clips spanning seven task families under a unified evaluation protocol.
Benchmarking 11 models finds that stronger hand-pose control does not reliably produce coherent object-state evolution or persistence.
Specialized hand-control models can underperform general-purpose text/image-to-video generators on dexterous-hand tasks.

papers.abstract: Deployed world-action models (WAMs) can keep improving only if they make good use of their own experience. Existing methods supply retrieved rollouts or demonstrations to the policy as context, yet such experience often turns previously solved tasks into failures. What, then, makes good experience for a WAM? We show that experience is valuable only in use: its value depends not on whether the source rollout succeeded but on what is stored, when it is used, and where it enters the policy. We therefore propose F$^3$, which makes these three decisions with Form, Fit, and Fusion. Form compresses successful and failed rollouts alike into short, verified operation records; Fit teaches the policy to read a record and to predict when it helps; Fusion injects the record's images, text and actions into the policy as a prefix and an action prior. Trained once on only 200 examples and deployed with a growing experience library, the model achieves state-of-the-art results on MolmoSpaces and RoboLab without any training on RoboLab: over native Cosmos 3 Nano, it raises success by 12.0 pp and 10.8 pp, reduces steps to success by 12.2% and 11.3%, and cuts regressions by 57%.
authors: Zihe Huang, Sirui Zhou, Haozhi Han, Ruge Zhang, Teng Ma, Tao Ma, Zheng Liu, Ce Zhang, Ting Cao, Yunxin Liu, Yunquan Zhang, Yifeng Chen, Kun Li

Form compresses both successful and failed rollouts into short, verified operation records.
Fit teaches the policy to interpret records and predict when they will help.
Fusion adds records’ images, text, and actions as a prefix and action prior.
Trained on 200 examples, F³ achieves state-of-the-art results on MolmoSpaces and RoboLab, including gains over native Cosmos 3 Nano and 57% fewer regressions.

papers.abstract: Video world models are used as simulators, so when a first frame leaves several physical outcomes open, repeated generations should produce each outcome as often as it occurs in the data. Physics post-training scores every generation against the single recorded future of its history, which makes single videos more faithful, but the expected score is linear in the model distribution and is maximized by always producing the most likely outcome. The log-likelihood of the recorded outcome is maximized by the data distribution, and its gradient weights agreement with the record by the inverse of how often the model produces the generated outcome, a frequency that other generations of the same history with independent noise, its siblings, can estimate. To train with this weight from a finite group, we propose SibPO, which performs Sibling-paired Policy Optimization: siblings estimate a truncated inverse-frequency weight for agreement with the record, and a second term subtracts the same weight times the agreement with the siblings, which makes the expected objective a strictly proper divergence over outcome cells at every group size. On PisaBench, SibPO lowers the KS distance to simulated landing times by 9.1-10.2% relative to the strongest method outside its reward family on three of four video models without degrading single videos, and it lowers the error of estimated robot policy success rates by 13%.
bullets: Single-future scoring can favor always generating the most likely outcome rather than matching the full data distribution.
SibPO estimates inverse outcome frequencies from sibling generations and uses them in a sibling-paired optimization objective.
Its expected objective is a strictly proper divergence over outcome cells for any finite group size.
On PisaBench, it reduced landing-time KS distance by 9.1–10.2% on three of four models and reduced robot-policy success-rate estimation error by 13%, without harming single-video quality.

The matrix pairs the eight generations, grouped by outcome, with each other and with the record (left column): a cell takes the outcome color when the two agree (κ = 1) and stays white when they differ. The reward rg of Eq. (4) weights agreement with the record by ωg , which grows with the white cells of row g, and subtracts the sibling term ρg . The baseline bg recomputes the rewards without xg .

Each block is the readout of one generated video, and five samples per method are only illustrative. Flow-GRPO compares each generation only with the recorded future, so the no-contact outcome loses on average and disappears. SibPO also compares each generation with its siblings, the other generations of the same input. Its reward, in the simplest form, subtracts the mismatch with the record (−) and adds the mismatch with the siblings (+), so the rare outcome is kept.

papers.abstract: Latent Action Models (LAMs) learn control representations from action-free video, but existing pipelines typically train latent policies with behavioral cloning, without an explicit policy improvement objective. Although offline RL offers a natural approach to policy improvement, standard methods do not transfer directly to learned latent action spaces. We find that the structure of learned latent actions makes naive offline RL unreliable: directly maximizing value over latent actions or fitting a unimodal policy can produce latent actions that cannot be realized by physical execution, while the latent representation can merge physical controls that receive different rewards. To understand when latent-space optimization remains valid, we derive conditions under which policy improvement transfers to decoded execution and under which latent and physical optima align. Building on these insights, we propose LAPIS for goal-conditioned latent policy improvement, grounding value-based policy improvement in observed state-latent transitions and using a conditional flow policy to capture their multimodal structure. LAPIS outperforms baselines on most tasks, with the clearest gains in visual manipulation, and remains effective even with only 1% action labels, where competing methods largely collapse.
authors: Donghyeon Ki, Xiaoyu Chen, Jun Ho Seo, Hayeong Lee, Kyungyoon Kim, Byung-Jun Lee, Li Zhao
bullets: Latent Action Models usually use behavioral cloning, lacking an explicit policy-improvement objective.
Naive offline RL can propose unrealizable latent actions or merge physical controls with different rewards.
The paper derives conditions for policy improvement and optimality to transfer from latent actions to physical execution.
LAPIS uses observed state–latent transitions, value-based improvement, and a conditional flow policy for multimodal latent actions.
It outperforms baselines on most tasks, especially visual manipulation, and remains effective with only 1% action labels.

papers.abstract: Planning with a visual world model requires deciding both which actions to execute and how long to search for them. We introduce Selective CEM Refinement (SCR), a learned rule for deciding whether to continue cross-entropy method (CEM) search with a frozen LeWorldModel. After five it- erations, the gate measures how far the mean first action chunk has moved, how much the mean terminal cost of elite plans has fallen, and how widely their first chunks vary. It returns the current plan for execution or continues the same search for ten more iterations. The gate requires no addi- tional world-model rollout. On 16 PushT scenes evaluated with two planning seeds, SCR succeeded in 25 of 32 trials, compared with 28 of 32 for fixed 15-iteration search (Fixed-15). All 25 SCR suc- cesses occurred in trials that Fixed-15 also solved, yield- ing 89.29% paired success retention. Across complete episodes, including replanning, SCR evaluated 23.81% fewer candidate plans and reduced mean controller time per eight-environment batch by 17.22%. Its observed suc- cess rate was 5.36 percentage points above an analytic mix- ture of the two fixed-depth controllers at the same expected candidate workload, although the difference changed sign across planning seeds. Compared with gating only at the initial solve under the same random-draw padding proto- col, gating again at replanning produced nine additional early exits. This reduced total candidate evaluations by 15.79%, while successes fell from 27 to 25.
bullets: SCR decides after five CEM iterations whether to execute the current plan or search for ten more.
Its gate uses first-action movement, elite-plan terminal-cost reduction, and first-chunk diversity, requiring no extra world-model rollout.
On 32 PushT trials, SCR solved 25 versus 28 for fixed 15-iteration search, retaining 89.29% of paired successes.
Across episodes, SCR evaluated 23.81% fewer candidate plans and reduced mean controller time by 17.22% per eight-environment batch.
Replanning-time gating produced more early exits and 15.79% fewer evaluations, but reduced successes from 27 to 25.
