papers.abstract: Occupancy world models struggle to forecast moving objects due to motion uncertainty and shape distortion. A single trajectory can average plausible futures into an implausible path, and repeated re-voxelization can erode or inflate object shape even under correct motion. We introduce ShoWorld to address these challenges through separate motion and shape representations. The motion forecaster predicts probabilistic trajectories conditioned on scene layout, nearby agents and the future ego trajectory. Each hypothesis is rendered into occupancy and fused according to its probability to retain alternative futures. The shape component predicts sub-voxel points with occupancy probabilities and offsets from local geometry. These points move rigidly with the object, and voxel occupancy follows the probability that at least one occupied point falls within it. This representation reduces shape distortion under motion. ShoWorld achieves state-of-the-art results on Occ3D-nuScenes. With ground-truth occupancy and ego trajectory, it improves mIoU and IoU by 6.56 and 9.16 points overall and by 6.06 and 5.53 points on dynamic classes.
authors: Zhiqiang Yan, Guangfa Wang, Yuan Wu, Jian Yang, Gim Hee Lee
bullets: Addresses motion uncertainty and shape distortion in occupancy world models.
Predicts probabilistic trajectories conditioned on scene context, nearby agents, and future ego motion.
Renders and probability-fuses multiple trajectory hypotheses instead of averaging them into one path.
Models shape with moving sub-voxel points, occupancy probabilities, and geometry offsets to reduce voxelization distortion.
On Occ3D-nuScenes with ground-truth occupancy and ego trajectory, improves overall mIoU and IoU by 6.56 and 9.16 points, respectively; dynamic-class gains are 6.06 and 5.53 points.

papers.abstract: Video generation models are increasingly viewed as world simulators, which requires not only plausible motion but dynamics that respond correctly to specified physical parameters. Existing models, datasets and benchmarks, however, largely target physical plausibility, leaving this physical parameter responsiveness insufficiently explored. We introduce PhysResponse, a benchmark that measures it at two levels: scene-conditioned simulator inversion recovers the effective gravity, friction and initial speed of generated motion, and event evaluation tests outcomes near and across critical transitions. Evaluating ten image-to-video models, we find that even the lowest parameter errors exceed those of physically correct videos by over an order of magnitude, that models rarely reproduce both outcomes of a transition pair, and that the two levels expose complementary failures that visual metrics such as PSNR miss. To supply the missing training signal, we construct 72,000 simulated videos of 20 multi-object interaction types with controlled parameters; fine-tuning on them lowers parameter errors, even on held-out interaction types, and transfers to real videos and an external physics benchmark. Continued training with a numerical encoder further lowers all three errors on held-out types. PhysResponse provides a foundation for world simulators that follow physical conditions, not just appearances.
authors: Yuhan Li, Shuran Zhang, Haixin Tian, Baonuo Rao, Weipeng Li, Yujia Hou, Zhenyu Wang, Zijun Wang, Luoyang Lin, Lijing Luo, Jiehui Huang, Kaiyuan Yang, Jingbin Tan, Panwen Hu, Xiaodan Liang
bullets: Measures physical responsiveness through simulator inversion of gravity, friction, and initial speed, plus event outcomes near critical transitions.
Evaluates ten image-to-video models and finds parameter errors far above those in physically correct videos, with frequent failures on paired transition outcomes.
Shows that responsiveness failures are complementary to visual-quality errors, which metrics such as PSNR can miss.
Provides 72,000 simulated videos across 20 multi-object interaction types as training data; fine-tuning improves held-out interactions and transfers to real videos and an external physics benchmark.
A numerical encoder with continued training further reduces errors on held-out interaction types.

papers.abstract: Pre-trained visual world models generate multi-step action plans from current and goal observations, yet terminal-proximity objectives fail to prevent forbidden-zone traversal or rigid-body collision sliding. Purely visual interfaces may lack analytical dynamics, structured states, or explicit collision geometry, requiring internal prediction of action-conditioned process risk. We propose Risk-Triggered Search (RTS) for frozen Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA) world models. Rather than relying on static state features that cannot distinguish candidate plans sharing an observation, RTS unrolls action-conditioned future latent prefixes in the frozen world model and trains a lightweight risk head with process-violation supervision. To intervene selectively while preserving safe nominal behavior, RTS uses the same predicted prefix-risk criterion as both the search trigger gate and hard feasibility gate: safe nominal plans execute directly, whereas alarms trigger local Cross-Entropy Method (CEM) search to minimize nominal deviation within the feasible set. To prevent isotropic Euclidean minimal modification from shrinking obstacle-directed actions into zero-amplitude stalling, we introduce an amplitude-preserving metric $d_{\mathrm{AP}}$ that retains tangential progression while maintaining a unique zero at the nominal plan. Under unified gating and this unique-zero condition, bypassing safe-state search yields closed-loop trajectories strictly identical to every-step same-kernel search. Evaluated under a process-safety benchmark and Safe Arrival Rate (SAR) metric across five tasks, RTS improves SAR over Direct by 12.67--41.67 percentage points on navigation and articulated control and +2.08/+4.17 pp on Cube/PushT boundary cohorts, maintaining 100% action identity with every-step search while cutting controller time by 17.71%--70.41% across 1,968 paired trajectories.
authors: Xinyu Deng, Bohao Lan, Kunpeng Li, Mingkai Yuan, Weihang Pan, Binbin Lin
bullets: Addresses forbidden-zone traversal and collision sliding in visual world-model planning when explicit dynamics or collision geometry are unavailable.
Unrolls future latent action prefixes in a frozen JEPA world model and trains a lightweight risk head using process-violation supervision.
Uses predicted prefix risk for both search triggering and feasibility gating; risky plans invoke local CEM search, while safe plans execute unchanged.
Introduces an amplitude-preserving deviation metric to retain tangential progress instead of collapsing obstacle-directed actions into stalling.
Across five tasks, improves Safe Arrival Rate by 2.08–41.67 percentage points, matches every-step search action-for-action, and reduces controller time by 17.71%–70.41%.

papers.abstract: Interactive video world models turn user commands into the exploration of a generated scene, which requires the scene to keep its 3D structure as the camera moves and each action to keep a stable effect. Existing benchmarks mostly evaluate these properties against references fitted to the video under test, either a scene reconstructed from its own frames or a camera trajectory aligned to the command path with a free scale. Such references can absorb gradual scene deformation and changes in pace and route length, so these errors can pass undetected. We therefore introduce StrideWorld, a benchmark whose references are fixed before the motion they judge. It evaluates scene rigidity against the ground-truth geometry of the start view, and action consistency against the stride of each action, the camera motion of one command. The stride is measured on the model's first steps and then used to test the steps that follow, so each model is judged only against its own steps. Its measurements are validated on rendered videos with known camera motion, and its scores agree with human judgments. Across \nvideos{} videos generated by \nmodels{} open models from $140$ start views, all models but one deform their scenes as the camera moves, with offsets up to $7.3$ times those of a rigid rendering along the same camera path. Most models keep a steady pace when a single action is held. Along composed routes, several models often stall, and most completed routes end away from the positions predicted by each model's own strides. Only the two models that scale commands by the estimated scene depth bring most routes close to these positions. Fine-tuning two models on a few rendered clips removes most of their mid-route stalls. Code, data, and a leaderboard are publicly available at https://github.com/chuangwang123/strideworld.
authors: Chuang Wang, Rui Nie, Jie Song, Junyuan Gao, Jiahe Song, Haitao Zhou, Boyu Zhu, Xing Li, Jiang Wu, Conghui He, Qian Yu, Weijia Li

papers.abstract: Reliable cellular connectivity and collision-free flight are essential for unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) operations in low-altitude urban canyons, where dense 3D buildings obstruct flight clearance, shadow serving base stations, and create strong co-channel interference at street intersections. Existing planners either require prior 3D city meshes and channel knowledge maps unavailable onboard, or rely on model-free reinforcement learning with low sample efficiency and poor cross-city generalization. We propose CommDreamer, a mapless radio-geometric world model that fuses raw onboard 3D LiDAR scans, multicell cellular reports, and shift-invariant relative kinematics to jointly infer local obstacle clearance and directional signal-to-interference-plus-noise ratio (SINR) dynamics. Using a categorical recurrent state-space model, CommDreamer compresses multimodal measurement histories into a coordinate-invariant latent belief, enabling the UAV to foresee deep shadow zones and train a lightweight online policy purely via multi-step latent imagination without prior maps or antenna patterns. Zero-shot evaluations across unseen urban morphologies in our open-source ray-tracing simulator, AeroCity-RT, show that CommDreamer converges within 150 episodes where model-free reinforcement learning fails to complete flights, achieving 100.0% mission success with zero collisions while lifting median route SINR to 8.02 dB and cutting effective SINR outage by over 50% relative to radio-blind world-model and reactive LiDAR baselines.
authors: Yuqi Ping, Tianhao Liang, Tingting Zhang
bullets: Targets safe, cellular-connected flight in dense urban canyons without prior 3D maps or channel knowledge.

papers.selection_reason: Radio-geometric world model for UAV trajectory planning.
papers.title: CommDreamer: Radio-Geometric World Models for Mapless Cellular-Connected UAV Trajectory Planning
papers.tldr: CommDreamer enables mapless UAV trajectory planning by learning a latent world model from onboard LiDAR, cellular reports, and relative motion to jointly anticipate obstacles and radio shadow zones.

papers.abstract: Visual planning with a frozen joint-embedding world model supports robotic reaching and object manipulation by evaluating candidate action sequences against an image goal before execution. Standard cross-entropy method (CEM) planners roll out every candidate independently through a billion-parameter predictor, even when nearby actions induce similar scene changes. This redundant computation grows with population size and search rounds, slowing closed-loop replanning. We observe that candidates within a planning step share an observation history and thus a common action-to-feature map. Based on this insight, we propose ProbeShare, which measures local responses with a few representative probes and reconstructs each candidate's feature grid through scene-conditioned, geometry-aware weighting. When promising candidates move beyond existing probe coverage, ProbeShare evaluates a new probe to rescore nearby candidates. Across four RoboCasa tasks, ProbeShare accelerates episode planning by 43.8--128.9 times over dense RoboJEPA and at least $14.2\times$ over competitive baselines, with greater mean goal progress in a matched-time comparison.
authors: Zejian Kang, Xiantao Lin, Zekai Chen, Boyang Shen, Mingyu Ma, Shengwen Zheng, Chengtai Guo, Xiangru Huang
bullets: Targets redundant computation in CEM planning with frozen, large joint-embedding world models.
Uses a few representative action probes, then reconstructs other candidates’ feature grids with scene-conditioned, geometry-aware weighting.
Adds new probes when promising actions fall outside existing coverage.
Across four RoboCasa tasks, achieves 43.8–128.9× faster episode planning than dense RoboJEPA and at least 14.2× faster than competitive baselines.
Provides greater mean goal progress than dense planning under matched time, with scope limited to the evaluated robotic reaching and manipulation tasks.

papers.selection_reason: Accelerates world-model planning for robot manipulation.
papers.title: ProbeShare: Probing a Few, Sharing Across Many for Fast World-Model Planning
papers.tldr: ProbeShare speeds up visual world-model planning by probing only representative actions and sharing their predicted scene responses across nearby candidates.

papers.abstract: Action-conditioned world models let robots imagine the outcomes of their actions for planning and offline policy evaluation, but these uses need many rollouts, which multi-step diffusion makes expensive. Drifting models move the iteration from inference to training and generate samples in one network pass. DriftWorld brought this paradigm to action-conditioned world models; to strengthen action following, it repels predictions from the current frame, a construction borrowed from classifier-free guidance. We show that this accentuation has a target bias: the push persists even when a prediction matches the recorded future, in kernel, balanced, and unbalanced Wasserstein drifting fields alike. We introduce Mass-Share Accentuation (MSA) to remove this bias. MSA treats the current frame as a counterfactual destination competing with the recorded future in a semi-relaxed optimal transport problem; subtracting the closed-form share of the correct future makes the guidance vanish at the target, and the remainder is shared by all predictions. We prove that the recorded future is the unique fixed point along the motion direction for collapsed predictions, and that the guidance fades with prediction error. On Push-T, Robomimic, and BridgeV2, where trained models under-react rather than overshoot, MSA improves action ranking, response slope, and moving-region error over latent-space baselines at no inference cost, though these benchmarks do not isolate bias removal as the cause.
authors: Md Abtahi Majeed Chowdhury, Md Rifat Ur Rahman, Md Sakib Hossain Shovon, Jaesik Choi, Minhyuk Sung
bullets: Drifting world models reduce the cost of multi-step diffusion rollouts but can weaken action following.
Existing repulsive guidance remains active even when predictions match the recorded future, creating target bias.
MSA uses semi-relaxed optimal transport to subtract the correct future’s closed-form mass share, making guidance vanish at the target.
Theory shows the recorded future is the unique fixed point for collapsed predictions and that guidance decreases with prediction error.
On Push-T, Robomimic, and BridgeV2, MSA improves action ranking, response slope, and moving-region error over latent-space baselines.

papers.selection_reason: Addresses action-conditioned world models for robot planning, directly relevant to interactive world models.
papers.title: Target-Consistent Action Guidance via Semi-Unbalanced Optimal Transport for Drifting World Models
papers.tldr: Mass-Share Accentuation removes target bias from drifting world-model guidance, improving action-conditioned predictions without extra inference cost.

papers.abstract: Video world models keep the world in the context of a generator, so a revisit is synthesized again and earlier edits can drift or disappear. We present WM^MLLM, the first interactive world model built on multimodal large language models (MLLMs), for persistent, editable world generation from a single image. WM^MLLM keeps the world state outside every generator, as a panorama with a revision history, and lets the MLLMs write it: they turn each request into operations on this state, select where a local edit is written, and check every candidate before it becomes the next state. Image generators only propose views, and video only presents them. Users can walk to new places and return, edit objects through text or a box, place subjects, and change lighting, weather or season. By construction, a revisit at the same revision reproduces the earlier view exactly, a local edit leaves every panorama pixel outside its region unchanged, and each request starts from the result of the previous one. Against six world model baselines on MBench-A, WM^MLLM has the highest mean on all four environment-recovery metrics (Epipolar 91.5 versus 0.1 to 74.0) and completes the most camera round trips (85.3% versus at most 50.9%). It has the best value in all 15 CompBench columns against 15 baselines. On 112 local edits judged blind, selecting the region to write after generation raises completion from 34.8% to 83.0%. On 258 WBench and MBench-A items, all 46 revisits recover their earlier views, and all 97 local edits that pass the check leave panorama pixels outside their region unchanged.
authors: Baiang Li, Enze Xie, Jincheng Yu, Jin Wang, Haozhe Liu, Yitong Li, Juanxi Tian, Felix Heide
bullets: Maintains world state outside the generator as a panorama with revision history, preventing revisit drift and preserving prior edits.
Uses MLLMs to translate requests into state operations, select edit regions, and validate generated candidates before updating the world.
Supports navigation, text- or box-based object edits, subject placement, and changes to lighting, weather, and season.
Reports the strongest results across stated environment-recovery and editing benchmarks, including consistent revisits and region-preserving edits.
Scope is single-image initialization with generated views serving presentation rather than state storage.

papers.abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) connect future scene prediction with action planning for autonomous driving. Each driving record pairs an executed ego trajectory with its observed future, providing a factual outcome for learning this connection. We present TrajWAM, a trajectory-conditioned WAM that improves vision-language driving through auxiliary bird's-eye-view (BEV) future learning. An ego-trajectory query conditions DINOv3-aligned BEV predictions from shared planner representations. Training combines factual reconstruction under the executed trajectory with one-sided feature separation under an unlabeled perturbed trajectory. Together, these objectives train the shared planner to generate driving waypoints. Native inference directly generates waypoints and bypasses the auxiliary future-prediction branch. On all 220 Bench2Drive routes, TrajWAM achieves 91.53 Driving Score and 75.45% Success Rate, exceeding a schedule-matched planning-only fine-tuning baseline by 5.31 Driving Score points and eight successful routes.
authors: Xuerui Fang, Gulimila Kezierbieke, Chen Wangxing, Hui Li
bullets: Addresses the challenge of connecting future scene prediction with action planning in autonomous driving.
Uses an ego-trajectory query to condition DINOv3-aligned BEV future predictions from shared planner representations.
Combines factual future reconstruction for executed trajectories with one-sided feature separation for perturbed trajectories.
At inference, directly generates waypoints without running the auxiliary future-prediction branch.
On 220 Bench2Drive routes, achieves 91.53 Driving Score and 75.45% Success Rate, outperforming a schedule-matched planning-only baseline.

papers.abstract: Visual inspection in field robotics and environmental monitoring must localize multiple targets under strict compute and sensing caps. Exhaustive sweeps waste calls on absent classes, while myopic and search-free policies stumble over heterogeneous tariff cliffs or discard viewport edits whose value emerges only after re-querying. We formulate inspection over frozen detectors as neuro-symbolic observation planning under partial observability, decoupling a compact recurrent world model (WM) from exact symbolic feasibility and tariff rules. Receding-horizon beam search with online replanning jointly schedules class queries, crops, enhancements, and termination (stop), paired with slack-aware shadow pricing and legal fallback at larger budgets. Across eight terrestrial, optical, and sonar benchmarks, multi-step lookahead outperforms static schedules and search-free offline RL under tight budgets -- gaining up to 28.4 AP percentage points over static priority on RUOD and 15.1 on ARIS -- while dynamic pricing lifts large-budget performance on all eight domains at 11 ms planning cost. Ultimately, pairing lightweight learned dynamics with exact symbolic constraints turns frozen detectors into adaptive, budget-aware inspection agents without retraining.
authors: Ziyue Kang, Zixi Qi, Yuchen Dai, Nana Lv, Xirong Cheng, Liang Liu, Ying Li, Haoyan Wei, Haiyang Yao
bullets: Targets the challenge of locating multiple classes when exhaustive inspection is too costly and myopic policies miss the value of re-querying edited views.
Combines a compact recurrent world model with exact symbolic feasibility and tariff constraints under partial observability.
Uses receding-horizon beam search to choose class queries, crops, enhancements, and when to stop, with online replanning and slack-aware pricing.
Across eight terrestrial, optical, and sonar benchmarks, multi-step lookahead improves over static schedules and search-free offline RL under tight budgets.
Dynamic pricing improves large-budget performance across all eight domains, with 11 ms planning cost; reported gains reach 28.4 AP points on RUOD and 15.1 on ARIS versus static priority.

papers.abstract: World models support autonomous driving by evaluating candidate trajectories through predicted future scene evolution. However, accurate future prediction does not ensure road-compliant execution; when all candidates violate road boundaries, re-ranking cannot select a feasible trajectory. We propose Physics-Guided Search Distillation (PGSD), a single-view planning framework that combines future representations and execution feedback for verified beyond-pool repair through three components: (1) Execution-Aware Selection checks ego-vehicle road compliance under simulated execution and selects the highest-scoring feasible trajectory; (2) a Clearance-Aware Search Teacher generates beyond-pool corrections and selects demonstrations with larger minimum road-boundary clearance during execution to buffer imitation errors; and (3) a Future-Conditioned Repair Student predicts one correction from rewarder features and execution feedback for single-rollout verification. The pretrained planner and rewarder remain frozen; no future scenes are generated online. On NAVSIM v1, single-view PGSD achieves 90.97 PDMS, exceeding all compared prior single-view planners and retaining 73.2% of the search teacher's PDMS gain over execution-aware selection. On NAVSIM v2 navhard, it reaches 38.96 EPDMS, improving on WorldDrive by 11.24 points (40.5%). The student replaces up to ten search rollouts with a single verification rollout per repair trigger. HUGSIM Hard examples provide qualitative evidence of zero-shot transfer.

Achieves 90.97 PDMS on NAVSIM v1 and 38.96 EPDMS on NAVSIM v2 navhard, with reported gains over prior methods.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon tasks in embodied and web environments involve extended decision sequences and delayed feedback, making accurate planning crucial for success. World models tackle this by learning latent dynamics for imagination-based planning. However, existing approaches merely rely on dense pixel-level observations, which forces the model to absorb redundant information while overlooking relations among task-relevant entities. Consequently, small errors may accumulate over long imagined rollouts and gradually corrupt the predictions. In this paper, we explore world models that imagine over sparse state abstractions, which poses two key challenges: 1) how to remove redundant information and form a compact state abstraction; 2) how to incorporate the relational structure to learn reliable long-horizon dynamics. To address these challenges, we propose Embodied Graph, a relational state abstraction that supports structured dynamics modeling and long-horizon imagination, and the Relational World Model (RWM), which performs imagination directly over graph states. RWM consists of (i) a Task-Aware Embodied Graph Constructor that filters redundant details and maintains graph memory through online updates, and (ii) an Embodied Graph Recurrent State Space Model that learns node-wise latent dynamics while capturing inter-node dependencies. The imagined graph states provide predictions of action consequences to guide decision-making. Experiments on Minecraft and Crafter demonstrate the effectiveness of RWM in embodied environments. Notably, in Minecraft, RWM is the only method that obtains diamonds within the given budget. Experiments on web interaction further illustrate the applicability of relational state prediction to the decision making process of web agents.
authors: Zongyuan Wu, Xin Wang, Tongtong Feng, Yuan Meng, Zeyang Zhang, Ling Feng, Wenwu Zhu

papers.abstract: In human-robot collaboration, natural language lets people direct a humanoid's whole-body movements without programming joint trajectories. A common approach generates a kinematic reference from an instruction and relies on a tracking controller to execute it. However, as the controller maintains balance under contact constraints, the executed motion can depart from the reference in ways that change the action it conveys. Our central insight is that semantic alignment must be evaluated directly on the complete motion the robot physically executes. Building on this insight, we introduce \textbf{SemPhys}, a framework that trains motion generators using semantic feedback from simulated executions. A differentiable world model and a fixed tracking controller predict a short segment of a recorded execution. SemPhys inserts this prediction at its original position, scores the complete trajectory against the instruction, and backpropagates through the predicted segment. A paired anchoring loss stabilizes adaptation by keeping each generated reference close to its counterpart from the initial generator. On BONES-SEED, SemPhys largely preserves instruction retrieval accuracy from reference to execution and achieves the highest retrieval accuracy on executed motions among the evaluated methods.
authors: Zejian Kang, Yeqiang Wang, Zekai Chen, Boyang Shen, Mingyu Ma, Bingqian Wu, Fan Zhou, Jianjie Zhang, Chentao Shen, Wentao Yang, Rui Qian, Xiangru Huang

Adds an anchoring loss to keep adapted references close to those from the initial generator.
On BONES-SEED, it largely preserves reference-to-execution instruction retrieval accuracy and achieves the highest executed-motion retrieval accuracy among evaluated methods.

papers.abstract: Predictive world models for language-guided robot control face a fundamental conditioning challenge: instructions should influence action selection without altering the predicted consequences of fixed actions under identical observations. To address this challenge, we introduce JEPA Dots (Dynamics-Oriented Task Separation), a compact dual-latent framework that jointly learns visual dynamics and language-guided control through separate dynamics and task representations. Language-conditioned task features guide a flow-matching policy, while masked attention restricts world prediction to instruction-independent dynamics history and supplied actions. In closed-loop evaluation on 40 trained LIBERO tasks, JEPA Dots achieves 84.9% overall success with approximately 39.1M parameters, compared with the published 78.7% of NanoVLA-S with 161.0M parameters under a different evaluation protocol. In the reference experiment, JEPA Dots also improves overall success from 76.0% for our task-ID-conditioned adaptation baseline to 84.9%, with LIBERO-Goal success increasing from 67.1% to 88.5%. Instruction-switching experiments further confirm that task representations and policy outputs respond to language changes, while dynamics representations and world predictions remain invariant under fixed observations and supplied actions.

papers.abstract: Arm-free quadrupeds can perform loco-manipulation, walking on three legs while manipulating with a front leg, yet no existing policy for it follows language instructions. World action models (WAMs) have emerged as effective language-conditioned manipulation policies, but are pretrained for robot arms and sample slowly. WAM-Policy turns one WAM into a quadrupedal loco-manipulation policy via two stages. The first, Cross-Morphology Policy Adaptation and Acceleration, adapts the arm-centric WAM to quadrupeds and distills the transferred policy into a student with one video and two action steps by on-policy self-distillation (OPSD). This student, however, is bounded by its teacher, which only imitates demonstrations. The second stage, Task-Specific Improvement and Merging, therefore tunes the teacher by reinforcement learning (RL) and merges the slow specialists into one few-step student by multi-teacher on-policy distillation (M-OPD). On QLM-Bench, ten simulated tasks with 1,000 demonstrations synthesized without teleoperation, the transferred policy reaches 77.0%, and the OPSD student keeps 76.7% while sampling 14 times faster. Task-specific RL and M-OPD lift it to 85.0%. We also deploy the OPSD student on a real Unitree Go2 Air. WAM-Policy thus achieves a stronger quadrupedal policy at a fraction of the inference cost.

papers.abstract: World-Action Models couple action learning with future prediction, enabling robotic policies to capture environmental dynamics for robust control. However, prevailing methods take a reconstruction-oriented approach to model future videos, allocating substantial capacity to appearance details that are incidental to control. In this work, we reformulate world modeling for manipulation as control-centric future prediction in latent space, and present LaST1.0, a unified latent World-Action Model. Rather than modeling an observation-complete video future, LaST1.0 predicts compact, geometry-aware latent targets derived from future wrist views, focusing the supervision on the evolving robot-object interactions required for fine-grained manipulation. To better support this control-centric paradigm, LaST1.0 revisits the visual input interface and attention mechanism of its unified architecture. It adopts a vision-encoder-free design with a lightweight patch embedder, exposing fine-grained visual cues directly to the backbone, and introduces LaST-Attention for structured spatiotemporal interactions across modalities. Evaluations across two robot embodiments, five challenging manipulation tasks, and three simulation benchmarks---RLBench, LIBERO, and LIBERO-Plus---demonstrate that LaST1.0 achieves state-of-the-art success rates and generalizes to novel scenarios. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of control-centric latent world modeling for robust manipulation.
authors: Hao Chen, Xuheng Zhang, Zhuangzhe Wu, Jiaming Liu, Shaobo Zhang, Jialin Gao, Zhonghao Yan, Di Wu, Sixiang Chen, Peng Jia, Chi-Wing Fu, Shanghang Zhang, Pheng-Ann Heng

Evaluated on two robot embodiments, five manipulation tasks, and RLBench, LIBERO, and LIBERO-Plus.

papers.abstract: A cell observed after a gene knockdown has an uncertain future, both in how its appearance will evolve and when it will divide. Existing approaches predict endpoints or population-level changes without jointly modeling individual trajectories and division timing. In this work, we present MitoWorld, a stochastic world model that generates these future appearances as continuous evolution in a Gaussian reference latent, terminated by a division hazard and converted into images by a conditional diffusion renderer. The ordinary transition provably preserves its Gaussian reference, tying its noise to its dynamics; paired observations identify its discrete transition where stationary marginals cannot. The hazard turns division timing into a survival likelihood that can be tested against real cycle lengths. On 325 held-out MitoCheck tracks spanning 17 knockdowns and a control, MitoWorld lowers FID by 34.6\% and the video metric JEDi by 45.6\% relative to the strongest baselines. Its latent-space prediction intervals achieve near-nominal 90\% coverage, are 35\% narrower than those of a model with freely fitted noise. The hazard also yields cell-cycle length distributions with KS distance close to the model-based finite-sample reference. Testable single-cell stochastic dynamics thus offer a generative tool for time-lapse perturbation screens.

On 325 held-out MitoCheck tracks across 17 knockdowns and a control, it improves FID by 34.6% and JEDi by 45.6% versus the strongest baselines.
Produces near-nominal 90% prediction-interval coverage, narrower intervals, and realistic cell-cycle length distributions.

papers.abstract: Driving scenes keep changing during model computation, making both observation freshness and action-delivery time central to world-action planning. To retain rich generative world priors in autonomous driving without stalling real-time control, we present SWIFT (Slow World, Instant Freshness, and Timely action), a deployment-oriented asynchronous world-action system that moves world updates off the observation-to-action critical path. On a background GPU, a slow Video DiT streams surround-view history into read-only predictive world context, trained with a predictive span that covers both the update interval and background world computation. On a foreground GPU, a lightweight freshness carrier encodes current surround-view images into a gated key/value bank at every step, letting a fast Action DiT combine live visual feedback with the latest completed world context without waiting. On open-loop NAVSIM, SWIFT reaches 94.2 PDMS at 198.4 ms per decision with a trajectory scorer; on closed-loop Bench2Drive, it achieves an 80.30 Driving Score at 109.9 ms foreground latency. SWIFT further transfers to the Waymo E2E hidden test (8.0050 Rater Feedback Score) and nuScenes (0.54 m mean endpoint error, 0.03% mean collision rate). Across all four benchmarks, SWIFT achieves the best results among compared world-action methods, establishing a favorable accuracy-latency trade-off.

Reports strong accuracy-latency results across NAVSIM, Bench2Drive, Waymo E2E, and nuScenes benchmarks.

papers.abstract: General robot manipulation requires both semantic competence and physical foresight. World action models (WAMs) acquire an understanding of and predictive capability over the physical world by jointly modeling visual foresight and action distributions. However, existing WAMs still lack semantic competence: they have limited ability to perform open-world scene understanding, semantic reasoning, and long-horizon planning. Although vision-language models (VLMs) provide these capabilities, effectively integrating their semantic priors into WAM prediction and control remains challenging. To address this challenge, we propose CoT-WAM, a jointly trained WAM-VLM framework. CoT-WAM uses a learnable embedding to exchange information between the VLM and the WAM, which is supervised by textual and goal-image signals during training to encode rich intent information. A tailored two-stage training strategy enables joint optimization and more effective collaboration between the VLM and WAM. We evaluate CoT-WAM on six benchmarks covering control performance, zero-shot generalization, and long-horizon planning. CoT-WAM achieves SOTA performance on LIBERO, CALVIN, and RoboCasa-Kitchen, and demonstrates stronger zero-shot generalization on LIBERO-Plus and LIBERO-Pro without fine-tuning. On RoboCasa365, it further improves long-horizon planning over baselines with and without external planners. Real-world experiments further demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in practical deployments.

papers.abstract: When humans learn to manipulate an unfamiliar object, they may already be able to anticipate how its state will change while still being unable to control it skillfully. This gap between prediction and control motivates us to study how the priors acquired by video generation models can be used effectively by an action policy. We present ZERITH V2.5, a video-action model (VAM) in which the action policy reads intermediate features of a video generation model, and use it to study, under fixed demonstrations and a fixed total number of updates, what kind of predictive training improves subsequent action learning. We find that the way video predictive training is supervised affects subsequent action learning. In our experiments, adapting at many noise levels yields a large gain, while adapting only at the noise level used at deployment yields none. Weight-transfer experiments further show that the gain stays with the adapted weights when they remain in the video generation model and disappears when they are used only to initialize the action policy. Initial loss and gradient measurements at the start of joint training indicate that target-domain predictive training gives the video model a better starting state, making subsequent joint learning of prediction and action easier. Under matched data and training budgets, predictive adaptation improves control. We evaluate the complete policy on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, Meta-World MT50, and real-robot tasks.

papers.abstract: Scalable world modeling requires coordinating scene-wide goals with fine-grained objects and dynamic characters under limited time and context budgets. We introduce GTA (Generative Tower of Agents), which represents every unit at every level of an adaptive scene hierarchy as a holon, both a self-contained construction task and a composable scene unit. Parallel agents recursively plan the hierarchy top-down, generate assets, and assemble and refine them bottom-up. Uniform interfaces carry scene-wide requirements down the hierarchy, guiding local construction so that each holon fits into the larger one. GTA accelerates scalable world modeling through high-throughput parallel execution while preserving well-structured layouts and fine-grained asset details. GTA then populates the assembled environments with dynamic human characters whose appearance and motion are guided by the scene, yielding realized 4D worlds. papers.abstract: A latent safety filter decides from the latent of a world model whether a planned action is safe. Conformal calibration sets the threshold of the filter so that it accepts an unsafe action only with a small probability. However, the filter can still be conservative and refuse many safe actions, depending on the latent. To measure the conservatism that a latent forces on the filter, we group similar latents and actions into cells. A filter that gives one decision per cell can refuse the unsafe transitions of a cell only by refusing the safe ones in it as well. We call the share of safe transitions that lie in such cells the overlap. We prove that the overlap is the minimum share of safe transitions that such a filter has to refuse in order to accept no unsafe transition in the data. Both the overlap and the conformal calibration can be applied to any latent. We use this to compare three existing designs, in which the safety labels train a classifier on top of the world model, the world model itself, or a separate encoder beside it. In a visual navigation task, the separate encoder has the lowest overlap, and at the same conformal level its filter refuses the fewest safe actions and lets the planner reach the most goals of the three.
authors: Johannes Mootz, Mani Amani, Reza Akhavian
bullets: Latent safety filters may reject many safe actions even when calibrated to accept unsafe actions only rarely.
The proposed overlap groups similar latents and actions into cells and measures the share of safe transitions in cells containing both safe and unsafe outcomes.
The overlap is proven to be the minimum fraction of safe transitions any cell-level filter must reject to accept no unsafe transitions in the data.
The framework applies to arbitrary latents and compares safety prediction via a classifier, the world model, or a separate encoder.
In visual navigation, the separate encoder has the lowest overlap, rejects the fewest safe actions at the same conformal level, and enables the planner to reach the most goals.

papers.abstract: A frozen latent world model combined with sampling-based model predictive control is a visual planner. At deployment, the executed action can depart from the commanded one, and the frozen model has no way to notice. We show that the model can be run in reverse: for any hypothesized actuation shift, it predicts what it should have observed under that shift, and comparing this prediction with what was actually observed quantifies the shift and lets the planner correct itself. Unlike the residual energy, which mixes the shift with the model's own error, the score keeps only the part of the residual that a shift can produce. This shift score detects the shift with a locally optimal test, estimates it with Cramer-Rao error bars, names the dominant generator, and compensates the planner once an alarm fires. On PushT, TwoRoom and OGBench-Cube with a frozen latent world model, measured detection follows the prediction to within 0.05 AUROC. Self-correction raises success from 0.650 to 0.862 on PushT and from 0.378 to 0.432 on the harder Cube task, levels with an oracle that is told the true shift at the same block, better than five common test-time adaptation methods. On a real robotic arm, the score identifies a base-joint offset that no joint encoder registers and reduces the reach error from 36 mm to 3-5 mm, and under shifts drawn at random and sealed before the session, estimates recover 92-94% of the error reduction achieved with the true shift. The broader implication is that a frozen world model can act as a filter by predicting the future, testing action-interface uncertainty and validity, and finally correcting failures.
authors: Siqing Li, Luming Yang, Yijia Jiao, Junze Deng, Alper Yilmaz
bullets: Addresses the inability of frozen planners to notice when executed actions differ from commands.
Runs the world model in reverse to score hypothesized actuation shifts against actual observations.
The shift-specific score separates actuator shifts from the model’s intrinsic prediction error and supports locally optimal detection, estimation, and source identification.
Self-correction improves success on PushT and Cube tasks and reduces real-robot reach error from 36 mm to 3–5 mm.
Scope: evaluation covers simulated manipulation tasks and a real robotic arm with sealed or unknown action shifts.

papers.abstract: Simulating how physical systems respond to changing conditions is central to control, design, and scenario studies. To our knowledge, prior PDE foundation models have not been trained or evaluated on changes within trajectories. Our counterfactual test measures how far predictions move toward a changed solver branch from the same state. Models trained on fixed conditions follow changes only partly. A PDE foundation model given a condition input after pretraining barely responds. PhysDial adapts a pretrained video diffusion transformer to eight two-dimensional PDE families. Coefficients enter with the noise level, condition fields as reference frames, and equation text as a prompt. In Kolmogorov flow, switches within trajectories account for about 5% of the training samples. At matched compute, they halve the error after a change in forcing wavenumber or amplitude. A few trajectories at new amplitudes more than halve extrapolation error. Without physics pretraining, PhysDial matches or exceeds PDE foundation models under training conditions on two turbulent flows. At step 64 on the Kolmogorov test split, PhysDial has 1.07 times the solver's small-scale energy and Walrus 7.1 times. Our experiments suggest that a learned simulator uses a condition only as far as its training data make that condition necessary for prediction. Learning from trajectories that diverge under intervention can help scientific simulators predict what would happen if a system's forcing or parameters changed.
authors: Yilong Dai, Yiming Sun, Shengyu Chen, Jiaqi Gong, Xiaowei Jia, Runlong Yu
bullets: Fixed-condition PDE models only partially follow within-trajectory changes, while simply adding condition inputs after pretraining has little effect.
PhysDial combines coefficients, condition fields, and equation text as conditioning for a pretrained video diffusion transformer across eight 2D PDE families.
Including intervention samples in Kolmogorov-flow training roughly halves errors after changes in forcing wavenumber or amplitude at matched compute.
A few trajectories at new amplitudes substantially reduce extrapolation error; without physics pretraining, PhysDial matches or exceeds PDE foundation models on two turbulent flows.
The approach suggests simulators learn to use conditions only when training data make them necessary for prediction.

papers.title: PhysDial: Adapting Pretrained Video Models for PDE Simulation under Changing Physical Conditions
papers.tldr: PhysDial adapts pretrained video diffusion models to simulate PDEs under changing physical conditions by training on trajectories that diverge after interventions.

papers.abstract: Recent progress in integrating vision-language-action (VLA) models with world modeling has significantly advanced end-to-end autonomous driving by allowing systems to reason about imagined futures instead of merely reacting to current observations. However, most world VLA models generate future frames at the pixel level with plenty of dense visual tokens. Although such generated futures can be visually plausible, they preserve many driving-irrelevant appearance details, i.e., only a small portion of the tokens directly encode critical planning-relevant factors, such as agent geometry, motion dynamics, and interactions. This introduces a significant performance bottleneck. An important question thus arises: what world state should a world VLA model reason over to support planning beyond pixel-level prediction? We argue that planning-oriented world modeling should focus on a compact and structured agent-centric latent state that captures the interactions between objects in the driving scene over time. As such, we introduce AgentWorld, an agent-centric VLA world model that uses discrete agent tokens jointly for reasoning and trajectory planning. Each token is dynamically grounded to a surrounding agent associated with its object's state, such as semantic identity, 3D geometry, motion, and interaction context. AgentWorld learns these tokens through three key processes: explicit geometric grounding, reasoning-oriented supervised fine-tuning, and agent-oriented reinforcement learning. Extensive open-loop and closed-loop experiments under diverse driving scenarios show that AgentWorld enhances planning capabilities, fully exploits visual evidence and agent dynamics, and yields interpretable agent-centric world states.
bullets: Pixel-level future generation contains many visually plausible but planning-irrelevant details.
The model represents each surrounding agent with discrete tokens encoding identity, 3D geometry, motion, and interaction context.
Agent tokens are learned through geometric grounding, reasoning-oriented supervised fine-tuning, and agent-oriented reinforcement learning.
Open- and closed-loop experiments across diverse driving scenarios show stronger planning, better use of visual and dynamic information, and interpretable world states.

The right panels present the corresponding perception, reasoning, and planning results.

(b) World models learn predictive latent futures, yet their imagined states fail to align with causal reasoning. The rationale explicitly references decision-relevant agent tokens, encouraging the policy to plan based on surrounding-agent interactions rather than shortcut cues.

papers.abstract: We present a global-in-time spectral Duhamel-Picard method with polynomial expansions for post-exposure bake (PEB) simulation. The coupled acid-quencher reaction-diffusion equations are reformulated as nonlinear Volterra integral equations using the Duhamel principle. Full trajectories are represented by finite polynomial expansions, with temporal coefficient fields determined over the bake interval by Anderson-accelerated Picard iteration, thereby avoiding sequential time marching. In 3-D PEB simulations, we employ Chebyshev and Legendre temporal bases while evaluating the Duhamel integrals using the corresponding Gaussian quadrature rules. We demonstrate that the proposed method simulates a large domain of $1200\times1200\times100$ voxels on the order of one minute. The representation is further incorporated into a physics-informed neural operator (PINO) with a mixed-transform variant of a factorized Fourier neural operator, which is trained without precomputed solution trajectories. Together, the integral formulation and its PINO extension enable accelerated, time-marching-free prediction of concentration fields at arbitrary times within the bake interval.
bullets: Reformulates coupled acid–quencher reaction-diffusion equations as nonlinear Volterra integral equations.
Uses Chebyshev or Legendre temporal expansions with Gaussian quadrature and Anderson-accelerated Picard iteration.
Avoids sequential time marching by solving for full bake trajectories over the interval.
Simulates a 1200×1200×100 voxel 3-D domain on the order of one minute.
Extends the formulation to a mixed-transform factorized Fourier PINO trained without precomputed solution trajectories.

papers.abstract: Goal recognition is the task of inferring an agent's intended goal from its observed behavior. Most existing work focuses on high-level symbolic recognition, abstracting away the continuous motion through which agents reach their goal. Methods that do reason over continuous trajectories rely on an explicit dynamics model that is hard to acquire and rarely transfers across settings. Neither approach explicitly learns how agents move toward each candidate goal, limiting accuracy on ambiguous trajectory prefixes where such knowledge is most needed. We present WoRD (Waypoint Recognition with Diffusion), which uses a learned trajectory prior to infer the agent's goal from partial observations. At each step, WoRD runs one warm-started denoising chain per candidate goal, steers each chain toward the observed trajectory through a closed-form log-likelihood gradient, and reweights the resulting samples by Bayes' rule into a calibrated posterior over goals. We evaluate WoRD on simulated robot settings, pedestrian trajectories, and vehicle trajectories using four metrics targeting distinct failure modes. Across all three settings, the same inference procedure preserves calibrated multimodal beliefs through ambiguous prefixes where filter- and classifier-based observers collapse to a single mode or grow overconfident.
bullets: Addresses the limitations of symbolic recognizers and methods requiring hard-to-transfer dynamics models.
Learns a trajectory prior and runs a warm-started denoising process for each candidate goal.
Steers samples toward observed motion using a closed-form likelihood gradient, then applies Bayes’ rule to estimate goal posteriors.
Evaluated on simulated robots, pedestrian trajectories, and vehicle trajectories with four metrics covering distinct failure modes.
Preserves calibrated multimodal beliefs during ambiguous trajectory prefixes, unlike filter- and classifier-based observers that may collapse or become overconfident.

figures.caption: Figure 5: Four metric trade-offs across the five evaluation domains. Each panel scatters one point per (method, domain) for the six methods over the five domains. Colour identifies the method; marker shape identifies the domain (legend below). WORD points carry a thicker outline. The desirable corner is bottom-right in every panel; panel (d) reverses the x-axis so lower Brier still points right.

Figure 2: WORD online inference on a 2-goal synthetic scenario. An agent (green) starts at the bottom of a 10× 10 world and must reach one of two goals separated by a circular obstacle; WORD maintains one denoising chain per candidate goal and updates a posterior as observations arrive. (a) Prior. Before any observation, the score network ϵθ shapes Gaussian noise into two obstacle-aware trajectory clusters, one towards each waypoint, and the goal prior is uniform. (b) Ambiguity. The agent has skirted the lower edge of the obstacle but its heading is still consistent with both goals; both clusters survive and the posterior remains nearly balanced. A filtering baseline would already have collapsed onto one mode here. (c) Observation guidance. Once the agent commits left of the obstacle, the score-guidance term ∇τ log p(Z | τ ) (orange) pins each chain to the observed path; the right cluster must arc awkwardly over the obstacle to remain reachable, and posterior mass shifts toward w1. (d) Commitment. As the agent approaches w1, the surviving chain dominates and the posterior collapses. Pseudocode is in algorithm 1.

At this point, the past path and the current heading remain consistent with two of the exits (green w1, red w2) so a faithful belief over the agent’s goal must keep both alive until later observations rule one out.

papers.abstract: Recent world action models (WAMs) drop future prediction at inference, assuming that representations learned through auxiliary future supervision still benefit action generation. However, our layerwise analysis of Fast-WAM reveals a depth-dependent mismatch: while probes decode future state transitions more accurately from deeper visual layers, the gradients and visual focuses of the future and action objectives increasingly diverge with depth, leaving much of this predictive information unused by the action pathway. To address this issue, we introduce RelayWAM, which adds an explicit transition space between the video and action backbones. Conditioned on the task instruction, robot state, and current action estimate, recurrent transition layers extract step-relevant predictive cues across depth and relay them directly into the action attention, without generating future frames at inference. Experiments show that RelayWAM substantially amplifies the benefit of future supervision, translating into stronger generalization under distribution shifts in both simulation and real-world robot tasks. On LIBERO-Plus, RelayWAM achieves 72.03% mean success, compared to 56.42% without future supervision and 51.50% for Fast-WAM.
authors: Fangchuan Wang, Hao Zhang, Qiyan Zhao, Huanqi Zhao, Guanting Ye, Xu-Yao Zhang, Yuqing Gao
bullets: Future information becomes more decodable in deeper visual layers, but its gradients and visual focus increasingly diverge from the action objective.
RelayWAM inserts instruction-, robot-state-, and action-conditioned recurrent transition layers between video and action backbones.
These layers extract predictive cues across depth and feed them into action attention without predicting future frames at inference.
The method strengthens the practical value of future supervision in simulated and real-world robot tasks.
On LIBERO-Plus, RelayWAM reaches 72.03% mean success, versus 56.42% without future supervision and 51.50% for Fast-WAM.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Overview of RelayWAM and the representation–utilization gap. Left: Training-focus attribution reveals that existing futuresupervised WAMs suffer from an objective mismatch—action relies on local gripper–object regions while future prediction attends to the whole scene—whereas RelayWAM aligns both focuses. Top right: Linear probing shows that future supervision writes rich predictive cues (∆R2) into deeper Video DiT layers. Bottom right: RelayWAM introduces an explicit transition space to relay these cues to the Action DiT without test-time future generation, reaching 72.03% success on LIBERO-Plus.

Figure 4. Architecture of RelayWAM. Attached to selected intermediate and deep layers of the Video DiT, recurrent transition layers extract step-relevant future information from visual representations conditioned on the task instruction, robot state, current action estimate, and flow time. The extracted cues are progressively accumulated across depth into action-aligned transition tokens Tl, projected into transition keys and values (K̂l, V̂l), and injected directly into the native Action DiT attention. This enables action generation to leverage multi-depth predictive representations without generating future observations at inference time.

Figure 3. Action and future supervision diverge across depth in Fast-WAM. Top left: gradient energy projected onto top-k action and future directions shows that the two objectives share subspaces in shallow layers (layer 4) but become nearly orthogonal in deep layers (layer 28). Top right: held-out future R2 decoded from action-sensitive subspaces drops well below random subspaces of equal dimension as depth increases. Bottom: training-focus maps on “open the middle drawer” and top-10% focus concentration averaged over five tasks. Unlike Fast-WAM (solid), RelayWAM (dashed) keeps both objectives focused on task-relevant regions.

Figure 5. Real-world apple picking on a Piper robotic arm. Left: qualitative rollouts under out-of-distribution apple placements with leaf occlusion (top) and colored ambient lighting perturbations (bottom). Right: success rates (%) across 20 trials per setting. Without any large-scale embodied pretraining (unlike DM0.5), RelayWAM outperforms Fast-WAM across all settings and maintains strong robustness under severe illumination shifts (70% vs. 15%).

Figure 6. Controlled 2×2 ablation of future supervision and the transition space. LIBERO-Plus success rate (%) versus layer20 future predictability (R2) across all four controlled variants. Adding future supervision alone (w/o transition space) raises R2 but yields only a +5.2-point success gain over the base model (w/o both), whereas introducing the transition space unlocks the utility of predictive features and amplifies the gain to +15.6 points (72.03% overall).

Figure 2. Causal erasure of future information in Fast-WAM vs. RelayWAM. We erase residual future directions from a sliding window of 4 consecutive Video DiT layers read by the action pathway, leaving the video backbone unchanged. Top: held-out R2 of the residual future decoded after future erasure (solid red) versus variance-matched random erasure of the same rank (dashed blue). Bottom: resulting action shift normalized by noise-resampling variance, plotted at the center of each erased window. While FastWAM (left) is insensitive to future erasure, RelayWAM (right) shows a pronounced action shift across intermediate-to-deep layers (layers 12–20), confirming active utilization of predictive cues. Shaded bands indicate 95% confidence intervals over episodes.

papers.abstract: Goal-conditioned planning with image observations and goals requires predictions that distinguish visual states and action consequences. Spiking neural networks offer sparse computation, but single-step spikes can obscure motion cues and merge actions with different physical outcomes. We propose the Spiking Latent World Model (SpikWM), an end-to-end joint-embedding predictive architecture (JEPA) with one simulation step per image and one neural update per latent position. Spiking Regional Encoding retains spatial cues through regional pooling. Bi-Spike Action Encoding combines positive and negative binary responses, while Causal Membrane Prediction carries subthreshold evidence across the latent history with learned group-wise time constants. The encoder and predictor are trained jointly on reward-free image--action trajectories using next-embedding prediction and SIGReg. With a common planner, SpikWM achieves mean success rates of $88.67\%$, $97.33\%$, $99.33\%$, and $86.67\%$ on Push-T, Two-Room, Reacher, and OGBench-Cube, respectively, outperforming two spiking baselines. Push-T ablations support each module, and controlled replays examine responses to appearance and physical state changes. Under a matched planning budget, SpikWM reduces estimated arithmetic energy by $75.6\%$ relative to LeWM. Code will be released at https://github.com/ShawnYE618/SpikWM.
authors: Shuhan Ye, Hongbin Yu, Chong Wang, Hui Lu, Jiaming He, Yi Yu, Jiangbo Qian, Xudong Jiang
bullets: Addresses the challenge of predicting visually distinct states and differing physical outcomes from image–action sequences.
Uses a joint-embedding predictive architecture with regional spatial encoding, bidirectional spike action encoding, and causal membrane memory.
Trains end-to-end on reward-free image–action trajectories using next-embedding prediction and SIGReg.
With a common planner, reports 86.67%–99.33% mean success across four benchmarks and outperforms two spiking baselines.
Reduces estimated arithmetic energy by 75.6% versus LeWM under a matched planning budget.

figures.caption: Figure 2. SpikWM architecture and planning. Spiking Regional Encoding (SRE) combines spatial spike processing, regional pooling and an output projection. Bi-Spike Action Encoding (BAE) uses learned group thresholds and combines two binary streams through separate maps. Causal Membrane Prediction (CMP) includes conditional causal blocks, final normalization and an output projection. Within each block, LayerNorm precedes action-conditioned scaling and shifting. Shared SRE branches learn from next-latent prediction and SIGReg. The cross-entropy method replans using terminal goal distance.

Figure 3. Open-loop forecasts on four tasks. Frame pairs show steps 15/20 (Push-T), 30/35 (Two-Room), 20/35 (OGBench-Cube), and 25/30 (Reacher). We render state readouts of the latent forecasts under shared actions [6].

papers.abstract: Visual proxies decouple explicit world-state simulation from photorealistic video synthesis, offering a controllable interface for both offline clip creation and real-time interactive streaming. Yet a practical renderer must address two challenges. Upstream proxies vary from coarse layouts to fine articulated geometry depending on the interaction, and streaming inference must operate in a few causal steps without accumulating drift across self-generated history. We present Invoker-Render, pairing a bidirectional creation model with a causal four-step streaming model under a shared conditioning interface over structural proxies, an appearance reference, and language. Trained on an aligned approximately 200-hour multi-granularity corpus, Invoker-Render honors fine geometric constraints when supplied while synthesizing plausible local motion under coarse proxies, enabling runtime selection of input detail. To bridge bidirectional creation and real-time streaming without compounding step compression and rollout drift, we introduce Progressive Forcing (ProForcing). ProForcing first trains a causal predictor and distills it into a four-step renderer using histories derived from training videos. Training then shifts to continuous self-generated rollouts. A pipelined serving stack supports efficient streaming inference. Experiments show versatile control across proxy families, granularities, and camera paths, consistent gains over recent streaming baselines, and stable 30-minute racing rollouts that preserve scene and subject appearance.
authors: Ruoyu Wang, Hao Zhong, Yanming Yang, Jiahao Tian, Lin Liu, Biao Gong, Guoshan Lu, Yiding Tian, Chunhua Shen, Zhenzhong Lan, Chi Zhang
bullets: Addresses varying proxy detail, from coarse layouts to fine articulated geometry, and drift during long self-generated rollouts.
Combines a bidirectional creation model with a causal four-step streaming renderer under a shared conditioning interface.
Introduces Progressive Forcing, transitioning from video-derived histories to continuous self-generated rollouts during training.
Supports adaptive control detail, plausible motion under coarse proxies, diverse camera paths, and efficient pipelined streaming.
Reports consistent gains over recent streaming baselines and stable 30-minute racing rollouts preserving scene and subject appearance.

figures.caption: Figure 4: Comparison of ProForcing with representative causal video training recipes. Rows align five training pipelines across four functional stages from causal adaptation (Stage 1) to long-sequence tuning (Stage 4). Self Forcing initializes from a bidirectional ODE teacher [18], Causal Forcing/++ and Causal-rCM initialize from causal teachers [72, 74, 78], and LongLive appends streaming long tuning [61]. ProForcing adapts block-causal attention via TF and RF (Stage 1), distills four-step RF-DMD with GAN supervision under data-anchored histories (Stage 2), and transfers the student, fake score model, discriminator, optimizer states, and student exponential moving average (EMA) directly into continuous long-rollout SF-DMD (Stages 3–4).

Figure 1: Controllable video rendering with Invoker-Render. Conditioned on multi-granularity structural proxies, an appearance reference, and text, our framework unifies bidirectional video creation and four-step causal streaming.

Figure 3: Capture and multi-granularity proxy construction pipeline. From a shared scene state, the pipeline renders matched coarse and fine structural proxies for each event.

papers.abstract: Language-conditioned traffic simulation enables scalable test scenarios steered by natural language. The goal is to control selected agents while surrounding traffic reacts to their observed behaviour. For example, a vehicle instructed to cut in late should cause the following vehicle to brake only when the manoeuvre becomes observable. Yet simulators can leak private instructions across agents, causing surrounding vehicles to react before the instructed behaviour becomes observable. Such premature reactions defuse desired events and alter the ensuing closed-loop scenario. Existing benchmarks measure what agents do, not what they could have known, leaving this failure unmeasured. We formalise it as intent leakage and address it through evaluation, data and modelling. Our paired intervention test holds an instructed agent's executed trajectory fixed while varying its private instruction, isolating leakage-induced changes in surrounding agents. We also construct WOMD-PACT, an automatically generated, verifiable dataset of 531,099 WOMD scenes with timed behaviour tags with reaction episodes identified through a counterfactual ghost test and grounded private instructions. Finally, we introduce CaFe, a dual-stream diffusion-forcing simulator fine-tuned in closed loop that restricts inter-agent interactions to public beliefs, preserving legitimate anticipation without leaking private intent. Our evaluation reveals that existing conditioning designs displace 23-83% of nearby uninstructed agents through private-intent leakage, even when the instructed agent's executed motion is held fixed. CaFe eliminates measurable leakage while maintaining comparable WOSAC realism (0.763), demonstrating that causal faithfulness can be enforced without sacrificing measured simulation realism.
authors: Steven Yu Tung, Shubham Vaijanath Phoolari, Christoph Lauer, Abhinav Valada, Steven Peters
bullets: Identifies intent leakage: uninstructed agents may react before an instructed maneuver becomes publicly observable.
Introduces a paired intervention test that holds the instructed agent’s trajectory fixed while varying its private instruction.
Provides WOMD-PACT, a verifiable dataset of 531,099 timed traffic scenes with counterfactual reaction episodes and grounded instructions.
Presents CaFe, a dual-stream diffusion-forcing simulator that limits interactions to publicly available beliefs.
Existing designs displace 23–83% of nearby agents through leakage; CaFe eliminates measurable leakage while achieving comparable WOSAC realism (0.763).

figures.caption: Figure 3. CaFe. The private stream conditions each agent on its own instruction, while a language-blind pass of the frozen backbone predicts public beliefs from committed motion. In inter-agent attention, an agent reads its own private features and the public beliefs of others, never their private futures or instructions. After each one-second commit, both streams update from the new observable history. The example on the right shows how public beliefs change as an agent’s motion reveals its intention.

Figure 2. Measuring intent leakage. We replay the instructed agent’s motion without its private instruction, compare surrounding agents across rollouts, and quantify leakage along two dimensions: the fraction of affected agents and their mean displacement.
Table 4. Effect of guidance. WOSAC 2025 realism, collision and off-road rates without and with guidance. Guided CaFe has 0.0% affected agents at 8 s.

Table 1. Instruction datasets for trajectory-level driving. We compare factual verification, private per-agent instructions, symmetric coverage, interaction identification and timing at behaviour onset. ∼ indicates partial support and – denotes single-agent or inapplicable settings.

Table 2. Intent leakage and realism on 1,000 WOMD-PACT validation scenes with 32 rollouts each. Variants reproduce the information routes of the cited works on a shared backbone with identical training data, sampler and leak-free guidance, isolating what each agent can observe. ECoSim [6] is evaluated as published as an external autoregressive baseline. Affected is the percentage of nearby moving uninstructed agents displaced by more than 0.5 m when instructed agents replay identical motion with their instructions removed, evaluated on the 746 eligible scenes (750 for ECoSim). Displacement is the mean displacement among affected agents. Realism and its components follow WOSAC 2025. n/a means that the leakage test is inapplicable (no-text backbone) or that mean displacement is undefined because no agents were affected. Bold indicates the best result among variants sharing our backbone.

papers.title: CaFe: Causally Faithful Conditional Traffic Scenario Generation
papers.tldr: CaFe prevents language-conditioned traffic simulators from leaking an agent’s private instructions to surrounding vehicles while preserving realistic closed-loop behavior.

papers.abstract: Aggregating observations into a limited number of latent tokens and learning physical interactions in the latent space has emerged as an effective approach for Transformer-based neural operators to solve Partial Differential Equation (PDE) problems involving large-scale observations. However, existing methods typically compress observations using a single aggregation pattern, making physical information not retained by that pattern invisible to the latent space and thereby constraining physical interactions within it. To address this limitation, we propose PArallel Latent Space Neural Operator (PANO), a novel neural operator for solving PDEs that formulates physical interactions among observations as an additive combination of interaction results from parallel latent spaces with shared parameters. Specifically, PANO transforms observations into multiple distinct compressed representations through independent mappings, learns physical interactions in parallel based on these representations, and finally fuses the decoded results to predict the target physical field. Within PANO, we further propose Coupled Assignment Projection (CAP) to construct bidirectionally consistent encoding and decoding mappings, and Pairwise Latent Space Attention Layer (PaLA) to jointly update latent representations of each latent space through adaptive cross-space interactions. Extensive experiments on nine benchmarks spanning diverse physical systems, geometries, and observation scales demonstrate that PANO achieves state-of-the-art performance. Notably, PANO reduces equivalent plastic strain prediction errors on Unilateral Stamping by 28.3% (or more) and lift-coefficient prediction errors on AirCraft by 21.4% (or more) compared with existing methods. Code is available at https://github.com/ZijiangY1116/PANO.
authors: Zijiang Yang, Xiaomeng Wu, Chen Kuang, Dongmei Fu
bullets: Single-pattern latent compression can hide physical information and limit learned interactions.
PANO independently maps observations into multiple latent representations, models interactions in parallel with shared parameters, and fuses decoded outputs.
Coupled Assignment Projection (CAP) builds bidirectionally consistent encoding and decoding mappings.
Pairwise Latent Space Attention (PaLA) enables adaptive cross-space interaction when updating latent representations.
Across nine benchmarks, PANO achieves state-of-the-art performance, including at least 28.3% lower error on Unilateral Stamping and 21.4% lower error on AirCraft than existing methods.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Motivation. (a) Existing methods encode input point tokens into a latent space through a single aggregation pattern. (b) PANO additively combines interaction results from parallel latent spaces. (c) Darcy ground truth. (d–e) Assignment maps of a single-latent-space model (Wang & Wang, 2024) and PANO, with points colored by their highest-weight latent token. Compared with (d), the parallel latent spaces in PANO exhibit distinct local preferences, collectively enabling a more comprehensive latent representation of the input. X and Y denote the observation and the target physical field, respectively. B denotes the number of blocks.

Figure 4: Prediction performance and latent-space representations on AirCraft. (a) AirCraft geometry. (b) Prediction error maps. (c) Visualization of latent tokens learned by PANO-P. We plot each latent token at its weighted center in the physical domain and color it according to the effective number of points it covers. (d) Relative L2 errors (↓) for surface physical fields and lift coefficients. PANO outperforms existing methods. Moreover, PANO-P jointly represents physical states over the AirCraft through multiple latent spaces with distinct regional preferences at each stage.

Figure 3: Comparison on standard benchmarks in relative L2 error (↓). PANO-D achieves the best performance. Moreover, compared with LinearNO, PANO exhibits lower prediction errors in regions with sharp variations in the physical fields.

Figure 2: Illustration of PANO. (a) Observations are embedded into point tokens, updated through stacked PANO-Blocks, and projected to the target physical field. (b) CAP constructs shared assignments to obtain bidirectionally consistent encoding and decoding mappings. (c) PaLA learns cross-space token associations. SelfAttn denotes a standard self-attention layer.

Figure 5: Visualization of CAP and PaLA with (a) PANO-P and (b) PANO-D. CAP is visualized through assignment maps for 2D tasks and latent-token spatial centers for 3D tasks. papers.abstract: Video world models should maintain a world that keeps evolving as the viewpoint changes. Yet when the camera turns away and returns, current models often freeze the unobserved scene, lose objects, or change their appearance, because content outside the view has no representation that keeps changing. We present PanoEvo, which uses a Panoramic Evolver to evolve the world state in the latent space of a panoramic video diffusion model, where every viewing direction is present at every time step, so the scene evolves whether or not it is observed. Existing panoramic video models are not trained to evolve a scene from a single image or the objects within it, so we build PanoEvo-Data, an event-centric dataset from real 360{\deg} videos, and train the Panoramic Evolver coarse-to-fine as an image-to-panoramic-video model. Since each view covers only a small part of the low-resolution panorama, directly projected views are blurry and often show low-quality details or structural errors. A Perspective Renderer, built on a perspective video diffusion model, reads this state via latent-space projection and direction-restricted cross-attention to render sharp, high-quality views. PanoEvo achieves the best overall score among 23 publicly evaluated models on WRBench and the highest total score on STEVO-Bench. Code, models, and data will be released.
authors: Longtao Jiang, Mingfei Han, Jianmin Bao, Tingjun Dai, Jinjie Wei, Zhiran Zhang, Xin Tao, Zhihui Li, Salman Khan, Xiaojun Chang
bullets: Addresses the failure of video world models to evolve off-screen content as viewpoints change.
Uses a Panoramic Evolver to update all viewing directions in latent space at every time step.
Introduces PanoEvo-Data, an event-centric dataset from real 360° videos, and trains the evolver coarse-to-fine from images to panoramic video.
Uses a Perspective Renderer with latent projection and direction-restricted cross-attention to generate detailed views from the panoramic state.
Reports the best overall score among 23 publicly evaluated models on WRBench and the highest total score on STEVO-Bench.
