papers.abstract: World models (WMs) generate driving scenarios beyond recorded logs, enabling the training and evaluation of autonomous driving systems in unseen interactions. However, existing WMs struggle to ensure both behavioral realism and visual fidelity, since they overlook the relationship between vehicle interactions and the ego visual observations. We propose a closed-loop interactive WM that couples behavior modeling and visual rendering. First, imitation-learned background-vehicle (BV) policies are fine-tuned with multi-agent reinforcement learning in the closed loop against an end-to-end ego planner that reacts to the rendered images, so that their interaction behaviors match those in real logs. Second, the viewpoints exposed by these interactions guide a per-Gaussian diagnosis of each 3D Gaussian vehicle asset, which attenuates view-dependent colors on under-observed Gaussians and fills never-observed surfaces with generated Gaussians, while preserving the observed appearance. Third, signal lights are rendered according to the driving intentions of the vehicles, by an editor that learns the light states unobserved for a vehicle through counterfactual fine-tuning with a light-state classifier. On long-tail closed-loop scenarios, our method reduces the divergence from real-world interaction behaviors by 85% and improves novel-view vehicle PSNR by 2.0dB over the state-of-the-art WM. The significance of BV light signaling in WMs is shown, as the rendered signal lights conveying BV driving intentions indirectly impact ego driving behaviors in a quarter of the scenarios.
authors: Jia Hu, Yang Chang, Panqu Wang, Zhijun Fu, Chang Liu, Changjian Yu, Jintao Lai
bullets: Existing world models often fail to align realistic vehicle interactions with the ego vehicle’s visual observations.
Background-vehicle policies are fine-tuned via multi-agent reinforcement learning against an ego planner that reacts to rendered images.
Vehicle assets are diagnosed per Gaussian using interaction viewpoints to repair under- and never-observed surfaces while preserving observed appearance.
Signal lights are rendered from inferred vehicle intentions using counterfactual fine-tuning and a light-state classifier.

On long-tail closed-loop scenarios, the method reduces interaction-behavior divergence by 85% and improves novel-view vehicle PSNR by 2.0 dB; signal lights affect ego behavior in about one quarter of scenarios.

papers.abstract: Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) have emerged as a promising paradigm for predictive visual representation learning. However, our analysis of I-JEPA reveals a growing discrepancy between semantic and geometric learning: improved semantic recognition during pretraining is accompanied by degraded 3D geometric representations. We hypothesize that this partly stems from predicting highly abstract latent representations with incomplete spatial context, favoring semantic regularities over fine-grained geometric information. To address this issue, we introduce CascadeJEPA, a spatially coupled cascaded prediction framework that promotes richer patch-level interactions through full-grid context encoding and cross-attention between prediction stages, while largely preserving the original I-JEPA architecture. Extensive experiments demonstrate substantial improvements over I-JEPA across multiple 3D geometric tasks while maintaining strong semantic recognition performance. Furthermore, its advantages extend to future feature forecasting and world model planning, highlighting the potential of enhanced geometric representations to support predictive world modeling.
authors: Kailai Zhou, Ziqi Chen, Xiaoning Xu, Yuefeng Wu, Zixuan Fu, Zijun Lin, Zhihao Li, Youwei Pang, Xiaoqi Zhao, Xun Cao, Bihan Wen
bullets: I-JEPA can improve semantic recognition while degrading 3D geometric representations.
CascadeJEPA addresses this by encoding full-grid spatial context and using cross-attention between cascaded prediction stages.
The approach largely preserves the original I-JEPA architecture while enabling richer patch-level interactions.
Experiments show substantial gains across multiple 3D geometric tasks without sacrificing strong semantic recognition.
Benefits also extend to future feature forecasting and world-model planning.

This unidirectional coupling promotes richer patch-level interactions while largely preserving the original I-JEPA architecture.

papers.abstract: Driving world models forecast what a vehicle's sensors will record next. Most forecast camera video and some add LiDAR, but thermal cameras, which still see in darkness and some adverse weather, are rarely a forecast target, and to our knowledge no world model forecasts all three sensors. We study joint forecasting of RGB, thermal, and LiDAR on real adverse-weather sequences of the DSERT-RoLL dataset. We post-train a pretrained video world model for each sensor and represent LiDAR as a depth video aligned with the RGB camera, with densification and encoding chosen by what the model's video tokenizer can reconstruct. A tri-sensor model sees all three sensors as one video. We score LiDAR in meters against measured returns and compare against persistence baselines passed through the same tokenizer as the model. With this matching, an apparent loss of the thermal model to persistence in fog disappears. On all 58 validation sequences in six weather conditions, post-trained RGB and thermal forecasts beat compression-matched persistence. Joint training lowers the LiDAR error at 2s by 2.1m at a small cost in camera fidelity, and only the tri-sensor model's LiDAR forecasts beat persistence in mean error. Blanking one sensor degrades the forecasts of the others more in snow than in fog.
authors: Faysal Mehrab Chowdhury, Md. Mahfuzur Rahman, Ahmed Rafi Hasan, Kishor Datta Gupta, Mohd Ariful Haque, Savannah Shannon
bullets: Addresses the lack of world models forecasting RGB, thermal, and LiDAR together, especially under darkness and adverse weather.
Post-trains a pretrained video world model for each sensor and represents aligned LiDAR as a depth video; a tri-sensor model processes all modalities jointly.
Evaluated on 58 DSERT-RoLL validation sequences across six weather conditions using compression-matched persistence baselines.
RGB and thermal forecasts outperform matched persistence; joint training reduces LiDAR error at 2 seconds by 2.1 m with a small camera-fidelity cost.
Removing one sensor harms the others more in snow than fog, indicating stronger cross-modal dependence in snow.

papers.abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) jointly generate future video and robot actions through iterative denoising. Few-step distillation reduces the number of model evaluations, but its coarse updates can move the student away from the teacher's trajectory. We propose Anchored Path Matching (APM), which supervises endpoint and short-transition predictions from states reached by the student. From each state, we continue the teacher to zero noise and use its endpoint and first intermediate state as targets. Modality-routed adapters learn to match both targets from the same starting state. When the two gradients conflict, anchor-priority updates preserve the endpoint gradient and remove the opposing component of the local gradient within each modality. One checkpoint supports 1-, 2-, and 4-step joint generation. The sampling budget can be chosen at deployment without retraining or teacher queries. On RoboTwin 2.0, we train only on Clean demonstrations and evaluate directly on the domain-randomized Random setting. At one step, APM improves closed-loop success over continued base distillation at matched inference budgets by 2.0 percentage points on Clean and 1.4 on Random. Video peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) rises from 30.169 to 32.317 dB, with gains in structural similarity (SSIM) and learned perceptual image patch similarity (LPIPS). On two real-robot tasks, APM improves success over the one-step teacher and reduces control-cycle latency by $21.3\times$ relative to the eight-step teacher.Project page: https://jialonglong.github.io/Anchored-Path-Matching/.
authors: Jialong Liu, Junjie He, Yandu Chen, Bin Zhou, Heng Su, Peijun Tang, Jianan Wang, Changhao Chen
bullets: Few-step distillation can cause student rollouts to drift from the teacher’s trajectory.
APM supervises both the teacher’s final denoised prediction and an intermediate transition from student-reached states.
Modality-routed adapters match these targets, while anchor-priority updates resolve conflicting gradients.
A single checkpoint supports deployment-time selection of 1-, 2-, or 4-step generation without retraining or teacher queries.
On RoboTwin 2.0 and two real-robot tasks, APM improves success and substantially lowers control-cycle latency; video quality also improves.

papers.abstract: Action-conditioned world models are increasingly used as world models for planning, yet a world model that makes plausible, realistic-looking videos that are consistent with the training data can produce poor decisions. We address two key questions: (1) when can we trust a world model for planning, and (2) what should we do when we cannot? We introduce CURE (Certify, Upweight, Rollout, Explore), a certificate-guided technique that assesses whether a world model can be trusted for planning and determines what to do next: whether to upweight the training data to debias the model; roll out more samples at test time; or explore by collecting new data where support (how well the training data cover the planner's decisions) is missing. We deploy CURE across multiple domains, spanning simulated physics based on PhyWorld, MuJoCo arm control, and Language-Table pushing in simulation and on real videos. The decisions our certificate trusts have lower regret than those it does not (e.g., 0.06 vs. 0.38 on Language-Table sim and 0.07 vs. 0.38 on MuJoCo contact), whereas video perceptual quality does not identify good decisions. By focusing on decision quality rather than perceptual quality, CURE lowers regret over the best pessimistic decision rule by 10-25% across support levels, and over world-action models, search and policy learning by 41-64%, given the same data.
authors: Raphael C. Kim, Michele Santacatterina, Jingsen Zhu, Ramin Zabih
bullets: Realistic-looking, training-consistent videos do not guarantee good planning decisions.
CURE uses certificates to assess whether the model’s support covers the planner’s decisions.
Depending on the diagnosis, it upweights data, rolls out more samples, or explores unsupported regions.
Across physics, robotic control, and pushing tasks in simulation and real videos, trusted decisions had lower regret than untrusted ones.

papers.selection_reason: Action-conditioned world models for planning with certificate-guided trust and data-support diagnosis.
papers.title: Plausible Videos Can Lead to Poor Decisions: Diagnosing and CURE-ing World Models for Planning
papers.tldr: CURE diagnoses when video world models are reliable for planning and chooses whether to debias training data, sample more rollouts, or collect new data to reduce decision regret.

papers.abstract: Visual world models predict future visual states conditioned on actions, but recursive errors in entity poses and spatial relations limit their long-horizon prediction for robot planning and control. We ask whether a separately predicted relational state can correct this drift without restructuring the visual model. This is challenging because graph nodes and visual states share neither elements nor a feature space. We propose Joint Graph--Visual Dynamics Correction (JointGV), a plug-in based on a cross-granularity dynamics hypothesis: despite their different representations, graph-node and visual-state changes describe the same physical transition. JointGV rolls out a task-conditioned scene graph alongside the visual world model, couples their predicted changes, and combines the resulting graph-motion context with graph-predicted node positions to compute a bounded residual. Graph-learning and correction gradients do not propagate into the original visual dynamics. We attach JointGV to DINO-WM (spatial tokens) and DreamerV3 (a global latent state), evaluating both on DMC Cheetah Run and Walker Walk across three seeds and extending the evaluation to contact-rich manipulation with DMC Finger Turn Hard. Across 32-step rollouts, JointGV improves structural and visual-prediction accuracy, reducing joint-position error by 11--28\%. For spatial tokens, learned graph--visual change coupling gives lower error than broadcasting the same mean graph-motion context to every token, particularly when non-adjacent parts appear close together in the image. On real-robot inverted-pendulum sequences, JointGV reduces DINO-WM's 32-step pole-angle error from $12.56^\circ$ to $6.69^\circ$ and improves DreamerV3 and LeWorldModel as well. In simulated inverted-pendulum control, an actor trained with JointGV-corrected rollouts completes 46 of 50 episodes, compared with none using the original rollouts.
authors: Tian Lyu, Yichen Jiang, Ziyuan Cheng, Yunda Yan, Xiangyu Pan, Junjie Jiang, Jialin Yu, Boyu Ning, Pietro Li\`o, Fan Mo
bullets: Addresses recursive drift in entity poses and spatial relations during long-horizon prediction for robot planning and control.
Rolls out a scene graph alongside the visual model, couples graph and visual changes, and applies a bounded residual using graph-motion context and node positions.
Acts as a plug-in for DINO-WM and DreamerV3 without backpropagating graph-learning or correction gradients into the original visual dynamics.
Across 32-step rollouts, reduces joint-position error by 11–28%; on real inverted-pendulum sequences, lowers DINO-WM pole-angle error from 12.56° to 6.69°.
In simulated inverted-pendulum control, JointGV-corrected rollouts enable 46/50 successful episodes versus none with original rollouts.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of JointGV. Given the current RGB observation and action, the original visual world model (yellow) predicts the uncorrected next visual state Zt+1 and its change ∆Zt. In parallel, JointGV (blue) uses Relation Transformer (RelTR) features to construct a task-conditioned scene graph and predicts the node-feature change ∆N̂t. For the spatial-token case shown here, learned projections map the visual-token and graph-node changes into a shared space, where a change-alignment adapter produces the graph-motion context. The predicted node positions provide a complementary position context. A bounded, gated correction combines these contexts with the original visual prediction to produce Ẑt+1 = Zt+1 + Ct. Setting Ct = 0 recovers the original prediction. Decoded images are shown only for visualization; the global-state adapter is described in Sec. 3.4.

papers.title: JointGV: Structure-Aware Correction of Visual World Models with Parallel Graph Dynamics for Long-Horizon Modeling

papers.abstract: State-of-the-art world models have been used to produce sequences of gameplay that accord with provided user-input actions. However, high quality, consistent gameplay generation often comes at the cost of inference speed, making real-time interactive play and ideation challenging. The substantial quantities of data used to train state-of-the-art models have also made custom training of these models appear impractical, limiting many of their potential uses in creative fields. In this work we demonstrate a major step towards efficient world models: achieving both fast high-quality inference, and improved data efficiency. This is done by replacing the next-token prediction paradigm with a two-stage discrete diffusion-based approach, introducing a lightweight refinement transformer which carries out iterative masked predictions. Building on an autoregressive world model capable of generating highly consistent and complex sequences over minutes (Kanervisto et al., 2025), we achieve substantial model speed-up (79x) with a modest quality trade-off. Additionally, we demonstrate that this model can be trained to reproduce high-quality, consistent gameplay using a dataset containing approximately one day (28 hours) of gameplay data. Our results demonstrate progress towards removing barriers to the use of world models in settings where real-time inference and data efficiency are essential.
authors: Raluca Stevenson, David Bignell, Jennifer C. White, Tabish Rashid, Emanuele Aiello, Mariya Hendriksen, Junha Hyung, Sadegh Aliakbarian, Abdelhak Lemkhenter, Marko Tot, Katja Hofmann, Sarah Parisot
bullets: Targets the slow inference and heavy data requirements that limit interactive and creative uses of world models.
Replaces next-token prediction with two-stage discrete diffusion and iterative masked prediction via a lightweight refinement transformer.
Builds on an autoregressive model designed for consistent, complex gameplay over minutes.
Demonstrates high-quality, consistent gameplay training using approximately one day of gameplay data.
Scope: the speed–quality trade-off and data-efficiency claims are demonstrated for gameplay generation.

papers.abstract: JEPA-style latent world models let embodied agents plan toward new goals with model predictive control, but they are still too slow for real-life embodied control: sampling-based MPC repeats predictor inference tens of thousands of times per plan, and even on high-end GPUs one planning step can take tens of seconds. We observe substantial latent locality in this repeated-inference workload: the predictor maps close actions to close latents, and inside a quantized predictor this closeness takes a form that hardware can exploit, differential bit-level sparsity. Unlike an input stream, whose temporal similarity is given, a planner itself decides which candidates it evaluates together, so the planner can choose its own references and, with reference forest sampling, manufacture more sparsity: it couples the sampled action sequences of each group to a shared root, with competitive planning quality. We build the accelerator on the insights of the rich line of bit-level sparsity accelerators and design it and the planner tightly coupled as a single co-design: the planner increases sparsity and exposes structure for hardware scheduling, and the bit-exact hardware effectively uses the sparsity that the planner creates. On three JEPA world models, our co-design is 1.28-1.80x faster than a dense accelerator and uses 38-52% less energy, and it is 1.22-1.58x faster than prior bit-sparse design and uses 16-36% less energy, with the same area. To our knowledge, our planner is the first planner that manufactures differential bit-level sparsity across its candidates and exposes its structure for hardware scheduling, and our co-design is the first algorithm-hardware co-design for JEPA-style world-model planning.
authors: Wenbo Zhu, Paul Yi-Chia Chen, Yuanhan Li, Zishen Wan, Christopher Torng
bullets: JEPA world-model planning is slow because sampling-based MPC repeatedly runs predictor inference at large scale.
The method groups action sequences around shared reference roots, manufacturing latent similarity and hardware-exploitable differential sparsity.
A tightly coupled accelerator uses this sparsity and planner-exposed structure for efficient scheduling.
Across three JEPA world models, it achieves 1.28–1.80× speedup and 38–52% lower energy than a dense accelerator.
Compared with prior bit-sparse hardware at the same area, it achieves 1.22–1.58× speedup and 16–36% lower energy.

papers.abstract: Latent world models plan towards a goal image by minimising the distance between predicted and goal latents. This distance is not geodesic: it has local minima, latent traps, behind walls, at corners and in dead ends, and memoryless receding-horizon replanning keeps the agent in them, revisiting states far from the goal. We propose Episodic Kernel Repulsion (EKR), a training-free cost term that penalises candidate plans by a top-$k$ Gaussian kernel to a novelty-gated memory of the latents the agent has actually visited, rescaled by the current base cost so that its strength is comparable across models. Across two JEPA world models and four benchmarks, EKR raises average success from 31.8% to 46.7% (LeWM) and from 54.7% to 64.0% (H-JEPA) with the same model, planner and budget. Same-memory counterfactuals show that, in most settings, EKR pushes plans away from visited states, in navigation, often at a higher base cost; stuck episodes and revisits drop accordingly. In seven of eight settings it matches or exceeds $4\times$ samples at $0.8$--$1.5\times$ compute. Without tuning, it transfers to DINO-WM with CEM: $+6.7$ and $+19.3$ points on official and longer-goal Wall tasks, and from 44.7% to 100.0% and from 21.0% to 32.0% on long-horizon PointMaze and Push-T.
authors: Yican Zhao, Bolin Yang, Ruizhe Wang, Haiyang Guo, Fuji Yang, Bingo Wing-Kuen Ling, Zelin Zang
bullets: Latent distance-to-goal objectives can create local minima, especially near walls, corners, and dead ends.
EKR penalizes candidate plans near a novelty-gated memory of visited latents using a top-k Gaussian kernel.
Across two JEPA world models and four benchmarks, EKR improves reported average success while using the same planning budget.
It reduces stuck episodes and revisits, often steering plans away from visited states even at higher base cost.
The method transfers without tuning to DINO-WM with CEM and improves performance on Wall, PointMaze, and Push-T tasks.

papers.abstract: Robot failures are difficult to collect at scale, limiting the range of failure scenarios represented in robot learning datasets. We present FailureGen, a method for generating synthetic videos with temporal event annotations by reusing action trajectories from recorded failures. The method comprises four stages: (1) fine-tuning an action-conditioned Cosmos world model on successful and failed real executions; (2) annotating source recordings to identify failure-associated donor segments and compatible successful hosts; (3) transferring donor motion into host contexts, with optional spatial offsets, to generate continuous video rollouts; and (4) annotating and filtering the generated samples according to observed events and visual quality. We study two implementations with different tasks and robot configurations, with visual failure detection serving as one downstream application. In a preliminary comparison, a detector trained on real and generated data achieves an average precision of 0.51, compared with 0.41 using real data alone, and detects 33 of 36 failure intervals, compared with 28 of 36. By reusing observed failures in additional contexts, FailureGen expands the data available for studying robot failures and developing downstream learning methods.
authors: Akul Santhosh, Chaitra Sathe, Aastha Jhunjhunwala
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of collecting robot failures at scale and broad coverage.
Fine-tunes a world model on successful and failed executions, then transfers failure-associated donor segments into compatible host trajectories.
Generates continuous rollouts with optional spatial offsets, followed by event annotation and visual-quality filtering.
Evaluated in two task and robot configurations, with visual failure detection as a downstream application.
In a preliminary comparison, adding generated data improved average precision from 0.41 to 0.51 and detected 33/36 versus 28/36 failure intervals.

papers.abstract: The physical world has inertia: it evolves from what already exists rather than being recreated at every instant. However, many existing video world models lack an explicit mechanism for inertial state evolution, leaving the continuity of motion and structure implicit in video prediction. During autoregressive rollouts, repeated reconstruction can accumulate errors and destabilize the predicted dynamics. To address this limitation, we introduce InertialWorld, an Inertial Video World Model that makes inertia a structural prior for autoregressive prediction: existing scene evidence is carried across time rather than reconstructed at every step. Central to this formulation is Inertial Memory, which turns memory from passive predictive context into an evolving video state with two complementary views: a dense Eulerian grid preserves scene-aligned evidence, while persistent Lagrangian carriers bind local content to learned canonical coordinates. At each step, the model transports the carrier content according to action-conditioned motion, predicts the complete next video state from the transported carriers and dense grid, and uses a learned gate to combine transported and newly predicted content into the memory for the next step. Extensive experiments across multiple domains, including robot manipulation, 3D game simulation, and open-world navigation, demonstrate that InertialWorld achieves competitive autoregressive prediction performance against strong video world model baselines. Codes link: https://github.com/YuanGao-YG/InertialWorld
authors: Yuan Gao, Fan Xu, Yu Guo, Yuxu Lu, Zhengru Fang, Hao Wu, Xiaomeng Huang
bullets: Addresses error accumulation and unstable dynamics caused by repeatedly reconstructing each video frame.

Performs competitively with strong video world-model baselines across robot manipulation, 3D game simulation, and open-world navigation.

papers.abstract: Physical agents must use what they previously saw or touched after visibility or contact is lost. Their actions change the implications of these remembered facts. We introduce executable perceptual memory (EPM), a world-model framework that advances explicit perceptual state alongside neural latent dynamics during imagination. Its evolving read-out informs reward prediction, value estimation and policy learning. We align reward inputs with the transitions that produced them and supervise the reward head on open-loop rollouts of recorded actions. On Memory Maze $13\times13$, EPM reaches 30.37 return at 1M interactions, compared with 23.37 when the same evolving read-out informs only policy and value on a common perceptual front end: a gain of 7.00 [3.80, 10.21]. The complete method also improves control on $9\times9$ and in MiniWorld. Probes of remembered, out-of-view arrivals show stronger reward anticipation in both visual implementations. Concentration, tactile recovery and real tactile frames demonstrate complementary roles of remembered facts in imagined-policy training, motion-dependent decisions and sensory-content retention. EPM connects persistent perception to the predicted consequences and learning signals of a world model for Physical AI.
authors: Xianyao Li, Ruitong Tian, Rui Min, Fang Xu, Jing Du
bullets: Addresses how physical agents can use visual or tactile information after it is no longer observable.

Additional tests show benefits across maze sizes and MiniWorld, with improved reward anticipation for remembered out-of-view events.

papers.abstract: Accurate seasonal precipitation forecasts help societies prepare for drought, flooding, and crop failure months in advance. While data-driven methods have made rapid progress in weather and subseasonal forecasting, operational seasonal precipitation prediction still relies on numerical ensemble systems. These systems are computationally expensive and exhibit biases and drift that increase with lead time, motivating more efficient data-driven alternatives. Yet this transition faces three linked challenges: comparing data-driven forecasts with operational ones requires (1) a global benchmark that does not exist, scoring them requires (2) metrics that capture operational priorities beyond anomaly correlation (ACC) and RMSE, and training them must (3) rely on a single, short observational record. To address the first two challenges, we introduce \BenchName, the first such benchmark, covering monthly precipitation forecasts 1--5 months ahead. It pairs global $1^\circ$ satellite precipitation with oceanic and atmospheric predictors, includes seven operational centers, and provides 310,944 simulated months from 52 climate models for training. Beyond standard scores, we introduce two operationally motivated metrics for anomaly strength and monthly rain-belt position. To address the third challenge, we develop \MODEL, which learns from simulations what the record lacks and transfers it to Earth through three modules: SimForced aligns the climate background, SimMemory transfers a history encoder pretrained on simulations, and SimAnalog supplements Earth labels with simulated analog outcomes. Extensive experiments show that \MODEL{} improves ACC, CRPS, anomaly strength, and rain-belt position by 12.0\%, 3.6\%, 2.9\%, and 0.3\% over the strongest operational or data-driven model, opening a path from simulated worlds to Earth system prediction.
authors: Qiuyan Sun, Mengxuan Chen, Haoyuan Liang, Guowen Li, Zhen Huang, Jianhao Lin, Juepeng Zheng, Haohuan Fu
bullets: Addresses the lack of a global benchmark, operationally relevant metrics, and sufficient observational history for seasonal precipitation forecasting.
Covers monthly global precipitation forecasts at 1° resolution, includes seven operational centers, and provides simulated training data from 52 climate models.
Introduces metrics for anomaly strength and monthly rain-belt position alongside standard ACC and RMSE-style evaluation.
MODEL uses simulated-data alignment, pretrained history representations, and simulated analog outcomes to transfer knowledge to Earth observations.
Experiments report improvements in ACC, CRPS, anomaly strength, and rain-belt position over the strongest baseline; the approach is evaluated within the benchmark’s global seasonal-forecasting scope.

papers.abstract: Videos provide a rich source of physical interaction for learning robot behavior without action annotations, yet effective latent actions must capture not only local transitions but also how those transitions evolve over time. We introduce ReLAP, a latent-action pretraining framework that couples local transition learning with recurrent multi-step prediction in a frozen JEPA representation space. A shared inverse dynamics model infers compact continuous latent actions from adjacent observations, while a latent world model recurrently predicts the future JEPA features. Because each predicted feature becomes the context for the next transition, errors at later steps backpropagate through the rollout to earlier latent actions, encouraging temporally coherent dynamics beyond pairwise reconstruction. We transfer this representation to a vision-language model using two complementary objectives: latent distillation from the frozen inverse teacher and recurrent future-feature prediction through the frozen latent world model. The resulting policy is then adapted to robot demonstrations with action flow matching. At deployment, the explicit latent-action and world-model branches are removed, and the fine-tuned VLM predicts physical actions directly, reducing inference complexity. With only 11M pretraining samples and 1.06B trainable parameters, ReLAP achieves 97.9% on standard LIBERO and 70.0% over zero-shot LIBERO-Plus perturbations. On the LARY latent-action benchmark, ReLAP ranks second in both mean regression error and mean classification accuracy among the compared methods. These results demonstrate that recurrent action-free latent action pretraining can learn compact, temporally structured, and transferable representations for downstream robot control.
authors: R. Gnana Praveen, Ali Rouzbayani, Zhiying Jiang, Bidhan Roy
bullets: Addresses the limitation of pairwise latent-action learning, which may miss how physical transitions evolve over time.
Uses a shared inverse dynamics model for compact latent actions and a recurrent latent world model for multi-step JEPA feature prediction.
Transfers the learned representation to a vision-language model through latent distillation and recurrent future-feature prediction, then adapts it with action flow matching.
At deployment, removes the auxiliary latent-action and world-model branches so the VLM directly predicts robot actions.
Achieves 97.9% on LIBERO, 70.0% on zero-shot LIBERO-Plus perturbations, and ranks second on both LARY metrics among compared methods.

papers.abstract: World models have shown great potential in serving as a simulator for robot manipulation. However, existing models are either fit to a single environment or lack ability to simulate long-horizon contact-rich events. We present DreamFAR, a world model whose dynamics model is trained from scratch on a large robot-native teleoperation dataset, with no internet-video pretraining. We present an architecture and learning recipe designed for training on robot-native data. DreamFAR is significantly smaller than the high-performance video generation models, yet shows better understanding of contact and causality, and runs 10 FPS on a commercial GPU. Experimentally, DreamFAR significantly outperforms existing models in predicting the long-horizon future. We further demonstrate various applications where DreamFAR can be used, including policy evaluation and mixed-data co-training. Project page: https://www.yimingdou.com/DreamFAR/
authors: Yiming Dou, Botao He, Antonio Loquercio, Andrew Owens, Jitendra Malik, Sumedh Anand Sontakke, Ruoshi Liu
bullets: Addresses the limited environment scope and poor long-horizon contact simulation of existing world models.
Trains from scratch on a large robot-native teleoperation dataset, without internet-video pretraining.
Introduces an architecture and learning recipe tailored to robot-native data.
Runs at 10 FPS on a commercial GPU while outperforming existing models on long-horizon future prediction.
Supports applications including policy evaluation and mixed-data co-training.

figures.caption: Figure 8: Contact-based memory keeps placed objects persistent. Three models with the same architecture but different memory selection. We show one frame from a rollout of each model. Without memory the bin is empty, sparse time-strided memory hallucinates its contents, and contact-based memory matches the real observation.

Figure 2: Overview of DreamFAR: (a) Each view is encoded as per-position latents projected onto the unit sphere and decoded by a flow decoder. (b) When the robot makes or breaks contact with an object, we insert the corresponding keyframe into contact memory, which are index by end effector pose. (c) We use a transformer that has a number of design decisions that make it well suited to streaming and long-horizon generation.

Figure 5: Metric Drift on ABC over one minute. We evaluate the video prediction performance of DreamFAR and the existing baseline models on standard video quality metrics, including PSNR, LPIPS and FID. We run 60-s rollout (600 frames) on 1,000 held-out episodes and average the results into 10-s bins. DreamFAR degrades the slowest on all three metrics and significantly outperforms all baseline models, indicating the stability of its long-horizon prediction.

Figure 4: Visual comparison against baselines on a long-horizon prediction. IWS collapses within seconds, WEAVER hallucinates texture drastically in the wrist view, Cosmos-Predict 2.5 drifts and over-sharpens texture, while DreamFAR manages to keep the scene layout and the manipulated objects consistent over the whole minute, and it even predicts the writings on the whiteboard that is visually similar to the GT.

papers.abstract: We present WM-Quant, to our knowledge, the first post-training quantization (PTQ) framework designed specifically for JEPA-style world models. Although world models typically feature relatively few parameters, action planning algorithms often require thousands of inferences, which can quickly become computationally expensive. PTQ is a natural way to reduce this cost. However, we show that in world models using autoregressive model predictive control (MPC) rollouts, quantization error can compound with each predictor step, resulting in action rankings from the quantized model becoming near-random. WM-Quant addresses this with three components that build on existing PTQ methods: early-encoder precision, control-path preservation, and rollout-aware scaling. Early-encoder precision protects accurate latent state and goal information to mitigate long-term error propagation. Control-path preservation allows the world model predictor to distinguish between fine-grained actions, significantly improving action rankings and execution. Rollout-aware scaling jointly calibrates encoder and per-step predictor activation ranges with respect to an entire rollout rather than a single prediction, reducing the cumulative rollout error. Across multiple world models, environments, and PTQ methods, WM-Quant substantially improves planning success at low bit-widths, approaching full-precision performance at W4A4.
authors: William Hammer, Andrew Heuer, Nikhil Krishna, Matthew Grenier, Ramtin Zand
bullets: Quantization errors can compound across autoregressive rollouts, making action rankings nearly random.
The framework combines early-encoder precision, control-path preservation, and rollout-aware scaling.
Calibration accounts for entire rollouts and jointly handles encoder and per-step predictor activations.
Across multiple models, environments, and PTQ methods, WM-Quant substantially improves low-bit planning success.
At W4A4, performance approaches that of full-precision models.

papers.abstract: Autonomous driving requires anticipating how traffic will evolve while responding quickly to new observations. Video foundation models offer the first ability, but repeated history encoding and iterative video generation make them costly to use for driving. We present AR-WAM, an efficient streaming world-action model that combines autoregressive temporal modeling with single-pass future conditioning. Because its video backbone is causal, AR-WAM updates its visual context incrementally, reusing past computation and conditioning future prediction on observed motion. We further hypothesize that future features computed from recent observations can improve generalization in dynamic traffic without iterative video generation. AR-WAM therefore obtains these features in one forward pass and uses them to condition trajectory generation, and reinforcement learning then improves the policy through direct optimization of driving rewards. With a single front camera, AR-WAM achieves 91.5 PDMS after supervised training and 94.0 after reinforcement learning on NAVSIM-v1, outperforming the compared strong end-to-end world-action models. In a dynamic setting of continuous driving, supervised AR-WAM keeps its visual history across decisions and outperforms strong world-action baselines.
authors: Baiting Luo, Shatadal Mishra, Ahmadreza Moradipari, Nejib Ammar
bullets: Addresses the cost of repeated history encoding and iterative video generation in driving-oriented video foundation models.
Uses causal autoregressive temporal modeling to incrementally update visual context from a single front camera.
Computes future features in one forward pass to condition trajectory generation, avoiding iterative video generation.
Applies reinforcement learning to optimize driving rewards and improve the policy.
Achieves 91.5 PDMS after supervised training and 94.0 after reinforcement learning on NAVSIM-v1; it also performs well in continuous dynamic driving while retaining visual history.

papers.abstract: Deepfake detectors often perform well on the dataset they are trained on, but their performance drops when tested on videos from different datasets. In this paper, we study whether a predictive video model can provide a signal that generalizes better across datasets. Instead of relying only on generator-specific artifacts, as many existing detectors do, we use a model trained to predict natural video and measure the difference between what it predicts and what it observes in a video. Using V-JEPA 2.1, we keep the encoder frozen and adapt the predictor using rank-16 LoRA. We define the difference between the predictor output and the frozen encoder target as the prediction residual. We hypothesize that manipulated clips produce, on average, larger prediction residuals than authentic clips, and use this as our consistency-margin prior. We process these residuals using a lightweight Latent Consistency Head (LCH), which separates residual magnitude from direction for training and classification. To test whether the direction of the consistency margin affects cross-dataset generalization, we compare standard and reversed margin objectives while keeping the remaining training setup fixed. We match the two settings on FF++ validation performance before evaluating them on unseen data. The reversed-margin setting exhibits a larger cross dataset generalization gap on average, providing evidence that the direction of the consistency margin affects cross-dataset transfer. Our complete model adds only 8.25M trainable parameters, which is 2.47% of the total 334M parameters. Trained only on FF++, it achieves an AUC of 90.5 on Celeb-DFv2 and performs well across several other cross-dataset benchmarks. Our ablations show that separating residual magnitude from direction, reducing dataset-specific variation, and using a low-rank projection improve cross-dataset generalization in our experiments.
authors: Pradip Gupta, Shubham Mandloi, Ravi Kumar Satzoda, Sujeeth Bharadwaj, Yassine Benajiba, Dan Roth
bullets: Deepfake detectors often lose accuracy across datasets because they rely on generator-specific artifacts.
The method uses V-JEPA 2.1 with a frozen encoder, a rank-16 LoRA-adapted predictor, and a Latent Consistency Head to analyze prediction residual magnitude and direction.
It tests standard versus reversed consistency-margin objectives; the reversed direction produces a larger cross-dataset generalization gap.
Trained only on FF++, the model reaches 90.5 AUC on Celeb-DFv2 and performs well on other cross-dataset benchmarks.
Ablations support separating residual magnitude from direction, reducing dataset-specific variation, and using low-rank projection; the model adds 8.25M trainable parameters.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of ConsistencyNet. V-JEPA 2.1 constructs prediction residuals for prediction lengths δ ∈ {2, 4}. LCH processes the residual using PASC, ℓ2 normalization, parallel projections, SAP, and temporal aggregation before real/fake classification. Residual magnitude is used separately by the consistency-margin objective.

Real and forged samples largely overlap before LCH, while the learned representations show clearer class separation after LCH.

papers.abstract: Vehicle-in-the-loop (VIL) simulation requires a lateral dynamics model that accurately reproduces vehicle responses and reliably generates horizontal lateral-position and heading commands through recursive integration. This paper presents a probabilistic lateral motion prediction model with improved response fidelity. A two-degree-of-freedom vehicle model provides the physical prior, while a recurrent neural network learns correlated residual corrections to lateral acceleration and yaw rate. To maintain prediction fidelity during recursive motion generation, multistep rollout training feeds corrected responses into subsequent states and histories and directly penalizes accumulated lateral-velocity error. A conditional Gaussian characterizes response uncertainty, which is propagated to lateral-response, position, and heading predictions through augmented-state linearization. Evaluation results demonstrate improved lateral-response and integrated-motion prediction. Compared with the Deep Dynamics lateral adaptation, the proposed model reduces mean lateral-position root-mean-square error (RMSE) from 0.596 m to 0.483 m, an improvement of 19.0%, while reducing mean lateral-velocity RMSE from 0.0469 m/s to 0.0441 m/s. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of combining physical priors, probabilistic residual learning, and multistep rollout training for response-faithful lateral motion prediction.
authors: Xiangyang Ye, Chaosheng Huang, Jinwen Yang, Zhengxian Chen, Jun Li
bullets: Combines a two-degree-of-freedom vehicle model with an RNN that learns correlated residual corrections to lateral acceleration and yaw rate.
Uses multistep rollout training and accumulated lateral-velocity loss to preserve fidelity during recursive prediction.
Models uncertainty with a conditional Gaussian and propagates it to lateral response, position, and heading.
Outperforms Deep Dynamics lateral adaptation, reducing mean lateral-position RMSE by 19.0% and lateral-velocity RMSE from 0.0469 to 0.0441 m/s.

papers.abstract: Interactive video world models serve as simulators for embodied agents: from a starting image and an action trajectory, they generate the views the agent would see. The starting image fixes how high the camera is, for example 0.15 m for a floor robot or 2.2 m for an overhead camera, and a faithful simulator must keep this height as the camera moves. We show that six recent open-weight models fail to do so: as motion replaces the starting view with generated content, they move the camera toward human eye level, a failure we call camera-height regression. Our benchmark, EyeHeight, pairs six rendered elevations (0.15 m to 2.2 m) and four calibrated real-world rig heights with scale-free multi-view height estimation. All six models lose their initial height during a $180^\circ$ turn-and-walk rollout: initialized at 0.15 m, only 0-20% of clips end within $1.3\times$ of the starting height as inferred viewpoints converge to human heights of 1.1 m to 1.5 m, whereas ground-truth renders remain within a few percent. In Matrix-Game models, homography-tracked floor motion stays consistent with constant elevation during rotation even as newly outpainted room geometry yields a higher reconstructed viewpoint. Regression grows with rotation angle, begins while the start frame remains in context, and largely reverses in SANA-WM when a $360^\circ$ turn restores the initial view. We trace this pull to human-centric video priors in which floor-level views are nearly absent: in SANA-WM, textual height cues and dense floor-disparity maps do not prevent it, whereas classifier-free text guidance during the first half of denoising strengthens it. Combining unguided sampling with height-balanced fine-tuning recovers more retention but costs 5 MUSIQ points, a loss fixed during those same early steps. Viewpoint drift alone shifts the paths predicted by visual navigation policies.
authors: Sheng Lu, Guangpin Tao, Tong Lu, Ying Tai
bullets: Six recent open-weight models exhibit camera-height regression during 180° turn-and-walk rollouts, especially from floor-level viewpoints.
The EyeHeight benchmark evaluates six rendered elevations and four calibrated real-world camera heights using scale-free multi-view height estimation.
Height drift increases with rotation, begins while the initial frame remains in context, and can partially reverse when the starting view is revisited.
Human-centric video priors appear to drive the failure; text height cues and floor-disparity maps do not reliably prevent it.

Unguided sampling plus height-balanced fine-tuning improves retention but initially incurs a 5-point MUSIQ cost, which can be recovered during early denoising steps; viewpoint drift also alters navigation-policy paths.

papers.abstract: In Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs), a well-constrained projector output does not by itself prevent representation collapse. We find that, from initialization, the encoder representation is dominated by a component shared by different inputs. A batch-normalized projector removes this component, so regularization after the projector cannot correct it, and the differences between representations shrink until they collapse. We propose SADL (Supply And Demand Loss), which keeps the original training objective and constrains the encoder directly when needed. SADL compares the representation differences that the projector output demands with the differences the encoder can retain and pass on to the projector, and adds a constraint on the encoder only when supply falls short of demand. It works with different Demand Regularizers and introduces no auxiliary networks, additional trainable parameters, or architectural changes. In single-task and jointly trained four-task LeWorldModel (LeWM) and INTACT experiments, SADL lowers the collapse rate over ten random seeds from 50% to 0%. After one epoch of training, encoder effective rank is 3.4-6.4 times that of the corresponding baseline without SADL, and latent prediction error falls to 1/20-1/303 of it. Without additional tuning, SADL stays robust as its loss weight spans orders of magnitude, and with several Demand Regularizers INTACT exceeds 95% mean search-free control success. On four image datasets, SADL also consistently improves accuracy and stability across random seeds. These results show that matching the representation differences a regularizer demands with the differences the encoder can supply leads to faster and more stable representation learning in control and image classification.
bullets: Batch-normalized projectors can remove shared representation components, leaving downstream regularization unable to prevent collapse.
SADL compares representation differences demanded by the projector with those retained by the encoder and intervenes only when supply is insufficient.
It preserves the original objective, works with multiple Demand Regularizers, and requires no auxiliary networks, parameters, or architectural changes.
Across LeWM and INTACT experiments, SADL reduced collapse from 50% to 0% over ten seeds and improved effective rank and latent prediction error.
SADL also improved control success, image-classification accuracy, and stability across random seeds.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of SADL. The Demand Regularizer D(Z) and qexc = Fexc(sg(Z)) jointly determine the demand capacity q; excitation and transmission determine the supply capacity k. Their mismatch is penalized by the one-sided Supply Regularizer S alongside the task loss. The figure displays the scalar dependence on q and k; Section 3.4 gives its gradient-routing arguments.

Figure 3: ImageNet-LT (top) and Galaxy10 (bottom): representative attention maps, shared threedimensional feature geometry, and paired online-validation curves. The baseline remains vulnerable to representation degradation; SADL converges faster and more stably.

Figure 2: Demand–supply mechanism. qreg and qexc, computed from the detached endpoint, determine the demand capacity q, while the weaker of excitation kexc and transmission ktr determines the supply capacity k. The Supply Regularizer acts only for k < q and updates H so that even the smaller supply term meets the demand; ordinary task and Demand Regularizer gradients remain in place.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon manipulation tasks require a robot to perform a sequence of physical interactions with its environment, typically combining several different skills. Planning such behaviors efficiently is challenging: given a library of parameterized skills, solutions lie in a vast hybrid space of skill sequences and their parameters, and evaluating each candidate skill's feasibility and effect with a high-fidelity world model such as a physics simulator is computationally expensive. MOSAIC, a recent skill-centric approach, lets the skills guide a non-sequential search toward the regions of this space where they are likely to succeed; however, it pays the full cost of simulation for every parameterized skill it considers. In this work, we introduce Lazy-MOSAIC, a lazy planning framework that instead searches over hypothesized skill outcomes. A cheap learned skill-effect world model predicts, in a fraction of a millisecond, a skill's feasibility and the world state it produces. Lazy-MOSAIC then uses these predictions to focus expensive simulation on promising candidate skills and, when a hypothesis is invalidated, repairs only the affected part of the search, while ensuring that every skill in a returned plan is validated in simulation. We evaluate Lazy-MOSAIC on cluttered-shelf retrieval tasks of increasing difficulty and demonstrate it on a physical robot, showing that it plans substantially faster than baselines with fewer simulator queries, while matching or exceeding their success rate in every setting. Visit skill-mosaic.github.io.
authors: Itamar Mishani, Mukund Krishnakumar, Oren Salzman, Maxim Likhachev
bullets: Targets the costly search over skill sequences and parameters in multi-skill manipulation tasks.
Uses a fast learned world model to predict skill feasibility and resulting world states.
Repairs only affected search regions when predictions are invalidated, while simulating every skill in the final plan.
Evaluated on increasingly difficult cluttered-shelf retrieval tasks and demonstrated on a physical robot.
Plans faster with fewer simulator queries while matching or exceeding baseline success rates across settings.

An ensemble of M models provides the uncertainty from prediction disagreement.

papers.abstract: Interactive video world models enable exploration through text and camera controls, yet direct object interaction requires finer control. Hands provide a natural interface, but translating continuous hand movements into coherent visual responses remains challenging because of complex hand-object dynamics and demanding real-time computation. To address these challenges, we introduce LynnReal-Hand, a hand-controlled video world model that unifies precise interaction modeling with efficient streaming generation. We curate 100K interaction clips spanning diverse real and synthetic environments and develop hand-aware supervision to improve fine-grained hand motions and object interactions. Building on this foundation, we learn a causal flow map for few-step generation and introduce region-aware score distillation that combines complementary video and image priors to refine interaction dynamics and visual appearance. To further reduce inference latency, we propose Ultra-Fast-VAE, a compact video decoder that preserves high reconstruction fidelity with substantially lower computational cost. Extensive evaluations on HandBench demonstrate superior hand-following accuracy and visual quality compared with existing approaches. Our full-sequence model achieves an FVD of 181.67 and a MANO Dice score of 93.02, while the three-step causal model maintains a MANO Dice score of 92.49. For real-time interaction, 540p streaming on a single H200 reaches 18.03 FPS with 741ms latency and an optimized peak GPU memory footprint of only 34.89GB. We will release the datasets, model weights, and the full training and inference code to support research on hand-controlled video world models.
authors: Shaohao Rui, Chaoyang Zhang, Xiaofeng Mao, Weijie Ma
bullets: Addresses the challenge of translating continuous hand movements into coherent visual responses under complex hand–object dynamics and real-time constraints.
Trains on 100K real and synthetic interaction clips with hand-aware supervision for fine-grained motion and object interaction modeling.
Combines causal flow-map generation, region-aware score distillation, and Ultra-Fast-VAE for few-step generation and lower-latency streaming.
On HandBench, achieves an FVD of 181.67 and MANO Dice scores of 93.02 for the full-sequence model and 92.49 for the three-step model.
At 540p on a single H200, reaches 18.03 FPS with 741 ms latency and 34.89 GB peak GPU memory; datasets, weights, and code will be released.

papers.abstract: Model-based reinforcement learning (MBRL) leverages a model of the environment, used for planning and generating samples without interacting with the real world. Motivated by evidence that informed initialization significantly improves the efficiency of MBRL, we propose TDec-Init, an algorithm to warm-start neural dynamics models using transition Jacobians. Using a decoupling algorithm based on the decomposition of a tensor of stacked Jacobian samples, we recover weights and flexible nonlinearities, and use them to initialize a feedforward neural network. In the low-data regime, we show on several benchmark environments that our approach outperforms random initialization and value training, and either matches or outperforms Sobolev training, while requiring fewer training steps between episodes.
authors: Maxime Rochkoulets, Joppe De Jonghe, Mariya Ishteva
bullets: Addresses inefficient model initialization in model-based reinforcement learning.
Decomposes stacked Jacobian samples to recover neural-network weights and flexible nonlinearities.
Uses the recovered parameters to initialize a feedforward dynamics model.
On several benchmark environments, it outperforms random initialization and value training, and matches or exceeds Sobolev training.
Requires fewer training steps between episodes in the low-data regime.

papers.abstract: World-action models (WAMs) couple action generation with predictions of future states. An initial action chunk may be flawed. A future prediction that is not conditioned on the chunk may fail to reflect the changes that the proposed actions would induce in visual representations, limiting its usefulness for refinement before execution. We introduce ThinkWAM, a latent WAM that establishes bidirectional feedback before execution through a proposal-rethink-refine loop: the policy first proposes a complete action chunk, the proposal corrects multi-horizon future latents through a learned residual, and the corrected latents are injected into a second pass of the same action head, which generates the executable chunk. An affordance-guided observation-action memory and a near-fine, far-coarse multi-horizon prediction scheme, both motivated by predictive coding, support this loop, and all prediction stays in latent space. ThinkWAM achieves 98.70% success on LIBERO, 84.76% on LIBERO-Plus without OOD fine-tuning, 85.75%/65.85% on RoboTwin 2.0 Clean/Random, and 65.17% on RoboCasa24. ThinkWAM achieves 64.4% mean success across three real-world OOD conditions. The mean two-pass inference latency per action chunk is 153.48 ms on LIBERO, 164.61 ms on RoboTwin, and 101.2 ms on the Galaxea A1Z. Ablations show complementary gains from rethinking and affordance guidance. Diagnostics indicate that proposal-conditioned corrections change both predicted futures and action trajectories, showing that the corrected future representations improve the final action.

papers.abstract: While the ability of video generation models to accurately depict scientific phenomena has received growing attention, determining whether these models genuinely understand the underlying principles remains a critical challenge. Existing benchmarks typically evaluate video samples in isolation, making it difficult to expose models that simply fit superficial visual priors. In scientific experiments, a small change in one condition produces a markedly different outcome even when the rest of the setup remains fixed. Capitalizing on this sensitivity, we introduce SciWorldBench, a benchmark comprising paired scientific experiments. Each pair varies a single condition in an otherwise fixed setup, yielding two mutually exclusive expected outcomes. Each generation prompt specifies the condition but omits the expected outcome. We evaluate ten text-and-image-to-video (TI2V) models using an independent vision-language model (VLM) that assesses each video without access to the condition text or the label identifying the correct outcome. A pair is scored as correct only when both videos depict their respective scientifically correct outcomes. Across all ten models, we find that the two videos in an experimental pair frequently depict the same outcome even though the conditions require different results. This recurring failure suggests that current video world models struggle to apply the underlying scientific principles reliably during generation. We will publicly release the benchmark dataset and open-source the evaluation code.
authors: Xue Yang, Haonan Cai, Xinyu Hang, Zhimeng Huang, Xuanyi Liu, Chuanmin Jia, Siwei Ma
bullets: Introduces paired scientific experiments with mutually exclusive expected outcomes and a single changed condition.
Evaluates ten text-and-image-to-video models using an independent vision-language model blinded to prompts and labels.
Scores a pair as correct only when both videos show the scientifically correct outcomes.
Finds that models often generate the same outcome for both conditions, indicating unreliable scientific reasoning.
The benchmark dataset and evaluation code will be publicly released.

papers.abstract: Forecasting the behavior of spatio-temporal systems often requires more than accurate predictions: models should uncover the dynamical modes governing future evolution. Existing temporal graph and latent dynamical models achieve strong forecasting performance, but their latent representations often entangle multiple dynamical patterns, limiting interpretability. Conversely, regime-inference methods explicitly model such modes but typically do not support generative forecasting over graph-structured systems. We introduce HERON, a self-supervised regime-aware generative framework that unifies graph-structured trajectory generation with regime identification. HERON factorizes the latent state into discrete system-level regimes, capturing global dynamical modes, and continuous entity-level dynamics, yielding a modular regime interface compatible with existing spatio-temporal backbones. Crucially, the inferred regime actively conditions system dynamics, enabling regime tracking and controlled simulations under alternative dynamical modes. Without regime annotations, HERON jointly learns forecasts and regime dynamics in a self-supervised manner, recovering meaningful modes across controlled synthetic and real-world datasets while maintaining competitive forecasting performance. These results open a path toward interpretable, controllable generative modeling of spatio-temporal dynamics.
authors: Jeremy Baffou, Pascal Frossard, Dorina Thanou
bullets: Addresses the entanglement of multiple dynamical patterns in latent representations and the lack of graph-based generation in regime-inference methods.
Factorizes latent states into discrete system-level regimes and continuous entity-level dynamics.

Learns forecasts and regimes self-supervised, without regime annotations.
Recovers meaningful modes on controlled synthetic and real-world datasets while maintaining competitive forecasting performance.

B) Encoder: The encoder proceeds hierarchically. A GNN first extracts node- and graph-level embeddings (embit, embGt ), which are used to infer the regime rt via a transition module. papers.abstract: Precipitation nowcasting involves two distinct scales of uncertainty: macroscopic storm evolution and fine-scale local convective variations. Current generative ensemble methods entangle both scales within independent random noise draws. This coupling causes two practical limitations: every ensemble member must execute the full sampling trajectory from scratch, so an N-member ensemble costs N times a single forecast; moreover, divergent trajectories spatially misalign heavy-rain echoes across members, causing standard pixel-wise averaging to blur critical high-intensity extremes. We present ForeSay, a generative nowcasting framework that decouples macroscopic evolution prediction from local stochastic detail generation. Given historical radar frames, a vision-language model first predicts a textual scenario of future storm dynamics to condition a Rectified Flow generator. Guided by this shared macroscopic prior, ensemble members share early trunk sampling steps to establish the storm trajectory and branch with fresh noise only in later steps to explore local convective details. Because members then differ mainly in local details, self-anchored support-consensus decoding replaces pixel averaging with discrete support voting to preserve sharp heavy-rain cores. Across six datasets, ForeSay achieves the best CSI at the highest precipitation thresholds, with relative improvements over the strongest baseline on each dataset ranging from over 10% to 84%. Our 8-member ensemble retains the forecasting skill and diversity of eight independently sampled runs while reducing computational cost from 8x to 5.2x that of a single forecast.
authors: Xudong Ling, Wenjie Luo, Chaorong Li, Tianxi Huang, Tao He, Guiduo Duan
bullets: Addresses the cost and blurring caused by independently sampled generative ensemble forecasts.

Uses support-consensus decoding instead of pixel averaging to preserve sharp heavy-rain cores.
Across six datasets, achieves the best high-threshold CSI, with reported relative gains of over 10%–84%; an 8-member ensemble costs 5.2× rather than 8× a single forecast.

papers.abstract: Urban navigation for Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) requires planning that accounts for environmental geometry, vehicle dynamics, and moving obstacles. This paper presents JEPTERA, a navigation architecture that integrates a Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA), Model Predictive Control (MPC), PID control, and a safety layer. JEPA predicts the UAV's motion response to candidate commands for MPC action selection, while the safety layer checks trajectories against occupied space and predicted obstacle motion. Simulator adapters and platform-specific YAML configurations separate the planning core from simulator interfaces. An ablation study evaluated six configurations across three gym scenarios, totaling 180 runs. The complete architecture achieved the highest aggregate success rate, completing 28 of 30 runs. Additional tests completed one route across three city maps without collisions. Separate integration tests demonstrated operation in Gazebo/ROS 2, MuJoCo, and CARLA without modifying the core planning logic. These results support the feasibility of the integrated architecture for simulated urban UAV navigation and its portability across simulator interfaces.
authors: Gibran Fathoni Belva, Mansur Arief, Ahmad Alfan Alfian Irfan
bullets: Targets urban UAV planning under environmental geometry, vehicle dynamics, and moving obstacles.

papers.abstract: Proposal-conditioned scene predictions can lack a common object-level reference across candidate trajectories. Aggregate planning scores also leave the objects and times associated with violations implicit. We present WTR-Drive (World-Task-Risk Driving), a Drive-JEPA-based planner that separates shared scene estimation from proposal-conditioned reasoning. A proposal-independent World Memory estimates object states, map structure, and future motion by re-reading the original visual features at each refinement round. Proposal feedback updates a residual Task branch without writing back to World Memory. This branch guides refinement through candidate-specific retrieval and gated visual feedback. A final Task readout supplies candidate-conditioned features for scoring. We derive structured risk targets from existing candidate-scoring rollouts without additional simulator calls. For at-fault collision and time-to-collision violations, the targets encode event existence, association with shared object slots, and the first violation time bin. On the NAVSIM navtest split, WTR-Drive achieves 94.66 PDMS on v1 and 88.24 EPDMS on v2 (expert-frame sequential evaluation). These scores are 0.96 and 0.44 points above the published Drive-JEPA values, respectively. Candidate-level analysis shows that higher best-candidate scores can coexist with lower selected-trajectory scores, revealing a gap between candidate quality and selection effectiveness.
authors: Haoyu Xing, Shaobing Ding, Guanglei Zhao, Guanhua Zhao, Nawu Peng, Mingyang Hou
bullets: Addresses missing shared object references and implicit violation details in proposal-conditioned planning.

Adds a residual Task branch with candidate-specific retrieval and gated visual feedback for trajectory scoring.
Supervises collision and time-to-collision risks using event existence, object association, and first-violation timing.
On NAVSIM navtest, reports 94.66 PDMS on v1 and 88.24 EPDMS on v2, above published Drive-JEPA scores; analysis exposes a candidate-selection gap.

papers.abstract: Epidemic forecasting supports public health decisions ranging from capacity planning to intervention timing, for which both point accuracy and calibrated uncertainty are essential. Although neural models have advanced point forecasting, producing reliable probabilistic predictions over multiple future horizons remains challenging. Renewal models encode epidemic propagation, while neural forecasters learn flexible multi-horizon representations; integrating these strengths within a probabilistic future rollout remains underexplored. We propose EPI-SST (Epidemic State Space Transformer), a probabilistic forecaster centered on an evidence-driven renewal transition. At each horizon, neural evidence produces a bounded update to an internal multiplier and advances a finite-memory renewal state that generates the future mean trajectory. A separate heteroscedastic Gaussian head controls predictive scale using a validation-selected log-variance penalty. Across four epidemic surveillance benchmarks, EPI-SST achieves the lowest pooled RMSE on every dataset, reducing RMSE by up to 14.2 percent relative to the strongest baseline. It also achieves the lowest continuous ranked probability score (CRPS) at horizons h = 4, 5, 6 on every dataset, with reductions of up to 43 percent relative to the strongest probabilistic baseline. During the abnormal 2019-2020 influenza season, EPI-SST reduces CRPS by 16.9 percent and calibration error by 78.9 percent; a three-seed replication preserves its distributional lead. Ablation studies and frozen-path interventions show that the renewal transition, attention conditioning, horizon coupling, and uncertainty-scale control make complementary contributions to predictive performance.
authors: Yiyun Chen, Zewen Liu, Shengpu Tang, Max S. Y. Lau, Wei Jin
bullets: Targets reliable multi-horizon epidemic forecasts with both accurate means and calibrated uncertainty.
Uses neural evidence to update a bounded internal multiplier and advance a finite-memory renewal state for future means.
Adds a heteroscedastic Gaussian head with validation-selected log-variance regularization to model predictive uncertainty.
Across four surveillance benchmarks, it achieves the lowest pooled RMSE on every dataset, with reductions up to 14.2% versus the strongest baseline.
It also leads on CRPS at horizons 4–6, including improved performance during the abnormal 2019–2020 influenza season; ablations support complementary roles for its components.

papers.abstract: Tractor-trailer systems are difficult to control, especially unstable during reverse motion, and their dynamics depend on difficult-to-measure factors, including road friction and suspension coefficients. We introduce a learned dynamics model for tractor-trailer control and compare it with a reduced-order dynamics model with Fiala tire forces as an analytic baseline. Specifically, we compare a model predictive path integral (MPPI) controller that uses the learned dynamics model to an MPPI controller that uses the analytic model, as well as to three additional baseline controllers. In the main closed-loop tracking experiments across four simulated environments, MPPI with learned dynamics achieves mean speeds closer to the target magnitudes and lower root-mean-square (RMS) hitch angles than MPPI with the analytic model at every tested setpoint, with higher completion rates in seven of eight reverse configurations.
authors: Aaron Chen, David Shen, Taekyung Kim, Kaleb Ben Naveed, Dimitra Panagou
bullets: Tractor-trailer control is challenging because reverse motion is unstable and key dynamics factors are difficult to measure.
The study compares MPPI using learned dynamics with MPPI using a reduced-order Fiala-tire model and three other controllers.
Across four simulated environments, learned-dynamics MPPI tracked target speeds more closely and reduced RMS hitch angles at every tested setpoint.
It achieved higher completion rates in seven of eight reverse configurations.
Results are limited to simulated closed-loop tracking experiments.

papers.abstract: An autonomous vehicle must foresee the consequences of its actions, especially in the rare, time-critical situations where crashes happen. A world model offers this foresight, but only within the coverage of its training data, which poses an exploration-exploitation dilemma. Within this coverage a planner can hardly improve on the data, and beyond it the model's errors mislead it. Logs of competent driving rarely contain the failures that would widen the coverage, and agents that learn from interaction gain them only by failing themselves, without being shown what to do instead. We propose SAFER, a framework that learns offline from failures that others make, judged by an expert, and keeps learning online from its own driving. Offline, partially trained agents and scripted, recoverable perturbations Stage failures in simulation, and an expert Annotates every visited state with its action and value, so that much of what the planner explores is covered before it drives. In planning, a chunked latent world model Foresees the consequences fast enough for real-time use, and a risk-aware sampling-based planner Evaluates candidate maneuvers by their return minus a bounded collision penalty. Online, a loop continuously Refines the model wherever this driving leaves the coverage of the offline data. In closed-loop evaluation against the compared methods, SAFER reaches the highest route completion and reward per step on the CARLA Leaderboard routes, 0.95 and 0.77 from a privileged bird's-eye view, and the highest episode reward in MetaDrive, 53.4 in regular and 49.0 in safety-critical traffic. Project page: https://ys-qu.github.io/safer-website.
authors: Yansong Qu, Zilin Huang, Zihao Sheng, Sikai Chen, Samuel Labi
bullets: Addresses the exploration–exploitation dilemma caused by limited world-model training coverage and scarce failure examples in driving logs.
Stages recoverable failures in simulation and uses an expert to label visited states with actions and values before deployment.
Uses a chunked latent world model with a risk-aware sampling-based planner that penalizes collisions.
Continuously refines the world model online when driving encounters situations outside offline coverage.
Achieves the best reported route completion and reward per step on CARLA routes, plus the highest episode reward in MetaDrive among compared methods.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Technical overview of SAFER, illustrated with its CARLA instance. The numbered badges link each part to its scene of the analogy in Fig. 2. (a) Stage and Annotate: the expert, weaker Roach checkpoints and scripted hold and late-brake events drive until the first violation, and the expert labels every visited state with its action and value (Section 3.2). (b) Foresee: from the context Mt of the past BEVs, the dynamics imagines the 16 latents of a candidate chunk in one pass, and heads read them as the behavior-cloned prior, the reward and its five factors, survival, value and collision risk (Section 3.3). (c) Evaluate: every 0.1 s, the planner scores 135 candidate chunks on their imagined futures (Eq. (28)), refits its sampling distribution to the 16 best in each of two iterations and executes the first action (Section 3.5). (d) Refine: the planner’s own driving fine-tunes the dynamics, the reward and the risk head online, while the encoder, the prior and the value stay frozen and the planner scores with slowly moving EMA copies (Section 3.6). The crash frame in (a), the context frames in (b) and the candidates and risk curves in (c) are from a recorded collision of the corpus (Fig. 5a); the other two BEV frames are illustrative.

Figure 2: An everyday analogy for SAFER (top) and the corresponding stages of the method (bottom, detailed in Fig. 3); the numbered badges link each stage to its scene. (1) Parents praise what works and point to negative examples, so that the child need not fail first. (a) Likewise, weaker drivers and scripted perturbations stage failures in simulation, and the expert labels every visited state with its action and value. (2) The child learns what each choice leads to. Hard work (action) brings good grades (reward), a far goal is worth pursuing (value), and staying out all night is risky (risk). (b) Likewise, the world model foresees these quantities for each candidate action chunk, and (c) the planner scores the candidates by their return minus a price on risk. (3) Away from home, school and work keep reshaping the beliefs while the core ones stay. (d) Likewise, the planner’s own driving refines the dynamics and the reward and risk heads, while the prior and the value, whose targets only the expert provides, stay fixed.

Figure 1: Learning paradigms for autonomous driving, compared by where the experience beyond competent driving comes from.
