papers.title: SAFER: Navigating the Exploration-Exploitation Dilemma in World-Model-Based Planning for Autonomous Driving
papers.tldr: SAFER combines expert-labeled failure exploration, fast latent world-model planning, and online refinement to improve autonomous driving in rare and safety-critical situations.

papers.abstract: Masked modeling is the dominant self-supervised paradigm for point-cloud videos. However, it leaks the information it is meant to predict, whether it reconstructs masked points as in MAE-style methods or predicts their latent features. Because point-cloud tokens are anchored at points sampled from each frame, querying a target at its own position reveals where its geometry has moved, in reconstruction and latent prediction alike. For latent predictors, random spatio-temporal masks introduce a further shortcut, as visible frames on both sides of each target allow interpolation rather than forecasting. The pretext task thus reduces to completion. Once the target positions are withheld, a masked latent predictor performs only slightly better than copying the last frame. To remove this leakage, we propose PointWM, a latent world model that turns completion into forecasting by predicting the features and geometry of future frames from strictly earlier context. Each target is queried only with its last-seen position and timestamp, while a latent action learned without annotations is meant to capture the part of the future that the past leaves undetermined. On HOI4D action segmentation with a P4Transformer backbone, PointWM improves F1@50 over training from scratch by 24.9 offline and 29.1 under strictly causal inference. These results show the promise of latent world models as a leakage-free pretraining paradigm for point-cloud videos.Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/InitalZ/PointWM.
authors: Zhuoyue Zhang, Jian Liu, Jihua Zhu, Ajmal Saeed Mian
bullets: Masked point-cloud video modeling can leak target motion through target positions and bidirectional temporal context.
PointWM converts completion into forecasting using only earlier frames, last-seen target positions, and timestamps.
An unsupervised latent action models future information not determined by the past.
On HOI4D action segmentation with a P4Transformer, it improves F1@50 by 24.9 offline and 29.1 with strictly causal inference versus training from scratch.
The method is evaluated for point-cloud video pretraining and its broader effectiveness beyond this setting is not established in the abstract.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) and World-Action Models (WAMs) have emerged in autonomous driving with the promise of strong generalization to long-tail scenarios. Although these models achieve state-of-the-art results on autonomous driving benchmarks, most existing benchmarks are dominated by nominal scenarios and therefore cannot test this promise. To test one such long-tail capability that is critical for safety, we introduce ReactBench-AD, a benchmark that measures how driving models react to objects that appear in the ego vehicle's path. Built on real NAVSIM and PhysicalAI-Autonomous-Vehicles scenes, ReactBench-AD composites a crossing pedestrian, a standing pedestrian, or a stationary car consistently across all camera views and history frames. Each edited scene thus forms an exact, pixel-level counterfactual pair with its original, which allows us to isolate the causal effect of the inserted object on the predicted trajectory. Evaluating four VLAs and two WAMs, we find that they react weakly, often barely at all. Finally, we test how easily one of the evaluated VLAs, ReCogDrive, can be taught to brake hard for imminent hazards: a short fine-tuning stage on edited scenes substantially improves its reactions, with the learned behavior generalizing to unseen objects and fully real scenes, at minimal cost to nominal driving. These results call into question the out-of-the-box long-tail capabilities of these models, but suggest that they can be a strong foundation for acquiring them with little additional training, highlighting the value of real or synthetic data that demonstrates the long-tail behaviors nominal datasets rarely contain. Code and data will be made publicly available.
authors: Nikos Theodoridis, Reenu Mohandas, Sushil Sharma, Ciar\'an Hogan, Ganesh Sistu, Anthony Scanlan, Tim Brophy, Ciar\'an Eising
bullets: Addresses the lack of safety-critical, long-tail scenarios in existing autonomous-driving benchmarks.
Introduces counterfactual scenes with crossing or standing pedestrians and stationary cars inserted into the ego vehicle’s path.
Uses pixel-level matched original and edited scenes to isolate the causal effect of hazards on predicted trajectories.
Evaluations of four VLAs and two WAMs find weak, often negligible reactions to inserted hazards.
Fine-tuning ReCogDrive on edited scenes improves braking, generalizes to unseen objects and real scenes, and preserves nominal driving performance.

papers.title: ReactBench-AD: Do Driving VLAs and World-Action Models React to Imminent Hazards in Their Path?

papers.abstract: Autonomous vehicle (AV) decisions at intersections affect the delay, braking, and motion smoothness of surrounding human-driven vehicles (HDVs). Learning socially compatible behavior requires connecting imagined interaction outcomes with feedback from executed actions. We propose a world-model reinforcement learning framework combines imagined policy improvement with direct value and policy calibration from finalized interactions, balancing AV progress with HDV interaction burden. An interaction-aware latent model supports imagination, while off-policy correction and replay updates enable observed rewards and transitions to supervise both the critic and actor. Simulation experiments at an unsignalized intersection achieve a 100% success and reductions in following-HDV acceleration variation of 65.5% and 44.0% relative to PIWM and DreamerV3, respectively. Ablations identify complementary roles for value calibration in reducing HDV burden and policy calibration in improving passage efficiency. Tests under out-of-distribution traffic shifts further show lower ego jerk and HDV acceleration variation than PIWM at comparable passage times.
authors: Sen Shen, Ning Liu, Xiangrui Kong, Yingwei Li, Dongkun Han
bullets: Targets socially compatible AV behavior at unsignalized intersections by balancing passage efficiency with HDV interaction burden.
Uses an interaction-aware latent world model for imagined policy improvement, plus off-policy replay to calibrate both value and policy from finalized interactions.
Simulation achieved 100% intersection success and reduced following-HDV acceleration variation by 65.5% versus PIWM and 44.0% versus DreamerV3.
Ablations associate value calibration with lower HDV burden and policy calibration with improved passage efficiency.
Under out-of-distribution traffic shifts, the method produced lower ego jerk and HDV acceleration variation than PIWM at comparable passage times.

papers.abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) have emerged as an important paradigm in robot learning, jointly predicting future scene states and robot actions from current observations and instructions. However, future states entangle task-related changes with large amounts of task-irrelevant content, such as static backgrounds, which weakens the model's ability to capture changes relevant to task execution. To address this, we propose Difference World Action Model (DiffWAM), a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) framework that enhances world representations by jointly learning future-state prediction and consecutive visual difference prediction. We define consecutive visual differences as differences between the latent representations of consecutive observations, providing an explicit learning signal for temporal variation. The framework comprises a World Expert for future frame prediction, an Action Expert for action generation, and a Diff Expert for predicting these latent differences along the trajectory. A structured unidirectional attention mask conditions the Diff, World, and Action Experts solely on the current-frame representation while blocking attention between experts. This design allows both the World and Diff Experts to be removed during inference, introducing no additional inference overhead. DiffWAM achieves state-of-the-art performance on the LIBERO and RoboTwin 2.0 benchmarks and substantially improves over FastWAM on real-world manipulation tasks. Specifically, it attains average success rates of 98.8%, 92.65%, and 88.3%, outperforming the state-of-the-art baseline (i.e., FastWAM) by 1.75, 1.55, and 15.0 percentage points, respectively.
authors: Xinheng Zhang, Haoyu Xiong, Chao Jing, Xiaohan Zhang, Linshan Li, Hongbang Fan, Xingyu Chen
bullets: WAMs can be distracted by task-irrelevant future-state content, such as static backgrounds.
DiffWAM jointly predicts future frames, robot actions, and latent differences between consecutive observations.
Its Mixture-of-Experts design uses World, Action, and Diff Experts with attention masking to isolate their roles.
The World and Diff Experts are removed at inference, so the method adds no inference overhead.
It reports state-of-the-art results on LIBERO and RoboTwin 2.0 and improves over FastWAM on real-world manipulation tasks.

Structured unidirectional attention separates the expert pathways. At inference, both visual prediction experts are removed, retaining only the Observation Encoder and Action Expert without additional inference overhead.

papers.abstract: Driving world models usually generate videos from six pinhole cameras with separate optical centres and small overlaps, and must learn to keep these views consistent. We present PanDWM, which stitches them into one $360^\circ$ panoramic band. Camera boundaries then fall inside one image, so keeping the views consistent means keeping the image continuous, and each pixel still records its camera ray. Conditioned on layouts, a causal student generates the band window by window in four steps; it is distilled from a causal teacher and trained on its own rollouts. A feed-forward decoder lifts each frame along these rays into 3D Gaussians, and static Gaussians from neighbouring frames complete them into 4D scenes. On nuScenes, scored in one stitched $360^\circ$ view, PanDWM has lower FID and FVD than the multi-camera baselines at $8$-$46\times$ their speed, and keeps its 50-step teacher's FID while lowering FVD by 22-25%.
authors: Jiajun Sun, Zeyu Zhang, Zeyu Ren, Guangfeng Jiang, Yang Zhao, Hao Tang
bullets: Stitches six camera views into one panoramic band, making cross-view consistency an image-continuity problem while preserving camera-ray information.
Generates the panorama window by window with a four-step causal student distilled from a teacher and trained on its own rollouts.
Lifts frames into 3D Gaussians and combines neighboring-frame static Gaussians to form 4D scenes.
On nuScenes, it achieves lower FID and FVD than multi-camera baselines while running 8–46× faster.
Compared with its 50-step teacher, it maintains FID and reduces FVD by 22–25%.

papers.abstract: Video world models promise to predict the future of a scene from its present. Do current models keep this promise? We probe this question counterfactually. When a small change to the present flips the future, such as a box resting a few millimeters before or past a table edge, a model that tracks the state of the world must flip its prediction too. We build FlipTest, a three-level hierarchy of increasingly strict tests over 1,680 initial frames from 10 simulated and 15 real-world tasks. At the base, visual minimal pairs, two nearly identical frames whose true futures differ, test whether predictions change across the boundary; matched controls go further and test whether they change only where the future does; and dense sweeps, the strictest level, locate exactly where they change. All 11 video world models we evaluate fall short. The best averages 18.3% pair accuracy over real and simulated scenes, below the 25% of random guessing. Models flip as often on steps that leave the future unchanged as on steps that change it, and their response stays flat across the sweeps. On the same frames, a vision-language model is selective and traces a near S-shaped curve near the boundary, and a coding agent that measures the image comes close to the true boundary. This implies that the deciding information is in the frame, and video models just miss it. We therefore urge the community to rethink world modeling as pure video prediction. Next-frame prediction must do more than draw plausible pixels; it must also identify the causal states that control future dynamics.
authors: Mi Luo, Lijun Yu, Adams Wei Yu, Ang Cao, Baochen Sun, Ming-Hsuan Yang, Nan Hua, Yuan Hao, Alex Dimakis, Ya Xu, Ed H. Chi, Xuezhi Wang, Yinxiao Liu
bullets: Tests counterfactual boundary cases where nearly identical frames have different true futures.
FlipTest evaluates 11 models across 1,680 frames from 10 simulated and 15 real-world tasks using minimal pairs, matched controls, and dense sweeps.
All models fall short; the best achieves 18.3% pair accuracy, below random guessing, and responds similarly to consequential and inconsequential changes.
A vision-language model and coding agent more accurately detect the relevant boundaries, suggesting the information is visible but missed by video models.
The results challenge pure next-frame prediction and call for models that identify causal world states controlling future dynamics.

papers.abstract: Dynamic spatial reasoning from monocular video enables vision-language models (VLMs) to understand how 3D environments evolve over time, supporting physical world understanding and embodied intelligence. Existing efforts primarily address observed-dynamics understanding, whereas agents in dynamic environments also require future-dynamics prediction beyond the observation boundary. Moreover, external geometric processing and textual descriptions can increase inference complexity or lose information when representing continuous dynamics. These limitations motivate a shared internal state that preserves observed dynamics and remains predictive beyond the input video. Accordingly, we present Pros4D, a framework for modeling evolving 4D worlds in latent space that unifies retrospective understanding of observed-dynamics with prospective reasoning for future-dynamics prediction. Specifically, Pros4D-Engine derives geometry-grounded supervision and constructs paired examples for both tasks, while Pros4D-Bench evaluates them across eight spatial task categories spanning dynamic cameras, objects, and scenes. At the model level, Pros4D compresses observed dynamics into latent observed states and autoregressively rolls them forward into latent future states. 4D Latent Alignment (4DLA) grounds these states through complementary visual-semantic and geometric supervision, while joint language supervision connects them to task reasoning. Experiments across benchmarks show consistent improvements over strong baselines in both capabilities.
authors: Rongxin Gao, Dongxuan Liu, Chu Li, Chengyang Ji, Jialing Huang, Runyu Chen, Kairun Wen, Chenxin Li, Jingrui Ye, Haosong Zhen, Xinghao Ding, Yue Huang, Yuzhi Huang, Xiaodong Tu, Jingyan Jiang
bullets: Addresses the gap between recognizing observed dynamics and forecasting dynamics beyond a video’s observation window.

Experiments report consistent improvements over strong baselines on both observed-dynamics understanding and future-dynamics prediction.

papers.abstract: Latent world models predict the future in an embedding space rather than in pixels. An encoder trained only to predict collapses and maps every observation to the same point, so existing models add a mechanism against collapse, such as a target network, a variance penalty or a distribution penalty. These mechanisms keep the embedding from collapsing, but they leave its distances without meaning, and the model cannot tell a reversible transition from an irreversible one. We propose Sense, a single cross-entropy loss over the directed distance $d(x\to y)=\sum_i \mathrm{ReLU}(y_i-x_i)$ that replaces these mechanisms. The loss avoids collapse on its own, and since the encoder no longer needs the predictor, the predictor is fitted afterwards to fixed embeddings by plain regression. On four pixel environments, the return distance learned by Sense detects irreversible transitions with an AUC between 0.95 and 1.00, where LeWorldModel stays between 0.39 and 0.59. On TwoRoom, the navigation benchmark of LeWorldModel, planning with Sense reaches the goal in 100% of episodes against 91% for LeWorldModel. As the goal moves farther away, the planning failure rate of every baseline grows, while that of Sense stays near zero in Cup, Cliff and Sokoban and is the lowest of all methods in Pendulum.
bullets: Existing latent world models prevent representation collapse but do not give embedding distances clear meaning.
Sense replaces anti-collapse mechanisms with one cross-entropy loss based on directed distance.
The encoder is trained without a predictor; the predictor is later fitted by plain regression to fixed embeddings.
Across four pixel environments, Sense detects irreversible transitions with AUC 0.95–1.00, versus 0.39–0.59 for LeWorldModel.
Sense achieves 100% goal-reaching on TwoRoom and maintains near-zero or lowest failure as goals move farther away, depending on the environment.

papers.abstract: Joint-embedding predictive architecture (JEPA) world models predict future embeddings instead of pixels and plan in latent space. Two challenges remain: 2D images leave the metric geometry that manipulation acts on implicit and entangled with appearance, and what these models imagine stays hidden, as they are mostly judged in simulation by short-horizon latent planning. We present JEPA4R, a JEPA world model that observes single-depth-camera point clouds, predicts and plans in their latent space, and acts through a policy head on its frozen latents; we call this 4D point planning. A decoder on the frozen world model shows what it imagines as 4D point clouds, with a mean point error within 1.1 cm over 200 steps. Under the policy-learning protocols of OGBench and CortexBench, JEPA4R leads pixel JEPA models on OGBench Cube-Single, Cube-Double, Cube-Triple and Scene, and ranks first on MetaWorld and Adroit Relocate with 98.4% and 88.0%, above the runner-up, R3M, at 96.0% and 65.3%. Trained only in a digital twin, JEPA4R and its policy heads run zero-shot on the real arm with both a gripper and a dexterous hand.
authors: Jiarui Dong, Zhiheng Liang, Yanjun Li, Zeyu Zhang, Heejeong Nam, Haoyu Chen, Hao Tang

papers.abstract: Flow-matching robot policies generate each action chunk through repeated network evaluations, one per denoising step. Cross-cycle caches such as C$^3$ache reuse computation from earlier replanning calls, but whether they beat simply taking fewer steps is unclear. We compare the two in Fast-WAM, a 6B-parameter world action model, on LIBERO-Goal. Two uncached steps keep the success of ten: on all 500 initial states they are non-inferior within two percentage points, for one checkpoint and noise seed. Under PyTorch's default compile mode, they also cut a replanning call on an RTX A6000 from 202 to 92 ms. This leaves little room for caching. A cache that keeps two fresh steps cannot be faster than two uncached steps: every call still encodes the images, runs the video expert and computes those two steps. Caching the first of two steps, refreshed every fourth call, saves at most 11--14% of a call by our cost model. Cached policies are also fragile. Their losses tracked the share of the flow path the cached steps cover: under Fast-WAM's current time shift, C$^3$ache's eight cached steps cover 80% of the path instead of 44%, and the cached policy succeeds on 63% of states against 95% uncached. Resampling the noise on every call cost caches covering 60% or more of the path 14--40 points. These results argue for fewer-step baselines and for testing reuse under the deployed sampler and noise settings. We release our evaluation harness, logs and a checklist.
bullets: The study compares computation reuse across replanning calls with simply reducing denoising steps on LIBERO-Goal.

Caching offers limited speedups when fresh steps and image/video processing remain necessary; estimated savings were at most 11–14% in one setup.
Cache performance degraded when cached steps covered more of the flow path or noise was resampled, motivating evaluation under deployed sampler settings.

papers.abstract: World-action models (WAMs) augment vision-language-action policies (VLAs) with future prediction so that the policy can anticipate how its actions will affect the physical world. Existing WAMs supervise complete future observations. However, observations typically change little over an action chunk, so the future loss is dominated by copying static background content rather than learning task-relevant robot and object motion, limiting policy learning. Moreover, existing WAMs rely on large video generation models or separate world models, incurring heavy training and inference compute that hinders closed-loop deployment. To improve policy performance, we propose visual residual learning, supervising only the feature change from the current frame to the future frame in a frozen DINOv3 space. Compared with complete future features, this residual learning target yields a higher feature rank with richer and more diverse representations of scene changes, and spatially concentrates on the robot arm and manipulated objects rather than the background. To further improve computational efficiency, we present ResWAM, a residual world-action model with 2.3B parameters in total, including a lightweight 0.5B dual-branch DiT that jointly trains an action branch and a residual branch via conditional flow matching. Without robot pretraining (i.e., pretraining on external robot action trajectories beyond the benchmark demonstrations), ResWAM achieves top average success rates on LIBERO-Plus (81.1%), RoboTwin 2.0 (93.8%), and RoboDojo (9.40% success, 13.41 score) at the lowest training (2.7-4.0 TFLOPs) and inference compute (1.0-1.4 TFLOPs), and leads real-robot Open, Put, and Stack (80.0% average, +10.0% over $\pi_{0.5}$) at 92.7 ms latency.
authors: Chongyu Fan, Gaowen Liu, Ramana Rao Kompella, Jason Corso, Sijia Liu
bullets: Existing world-action models waste capacity reconstructing mostly static backgrounds instead of modeling robot and object motion.
The method learns residual feature changes between current and future frames in frozen DINOv3 space, emphasizing manipulated regions.
A lightweight 0.5B dual-branch DiT jointly models actions and visual residuals using conditional flow matching.
Without robot pretraining, ResWAM reports strong results across LIBERO-Plus, RoboTwin 2.0, RoboDojo, and real-robot tasks, with 92.7 ms latency.
Scope: results target action-conditioned visual prediction and manipulation; the abstract does not establish broader settings beyond these evaluations.

papers.abstract: World models learned from offline data allow an agent to plan without further interaction with the environment, but the sampling-based planners used with them handle safety constraints only by scoring or rejecting sampled action sequences. We instead pose safe planning in the latent space of a learned world model as a successive convex program (SCP), in which a learned discrete-time control barrier function is imposed as a constraint at every step of the horizon. SCP requires smooth dynamics, so we build the networks from smoothed MaxMin activations and spectrally normalised layers, and bound the resulting linearisation error in terms of the Lipschitz bound and the smoothing width. As SCP is a local method, we start it from a sampled plan. On two Safety-Gymnasium navigation tasks with offline data, this planner has fewer violations than MPPI and CEM drawing 128 times as many samples at equal wall-clock time in our main comparison, though not significantly, and earns greater return at longer horizons, and is much safer than SCP without a sampled start. SCP converged more often on Lipschitz-bounded models. Unlike sampling, it also reports at each step whether its plan is a feasible, first-order optimal KKT point of the planning problem in the model, or that no feasible plan was found nearby. Our implementation is publicly available at https://github.com/youngers2006/scwm.
bullets: Addresses safety constraints that sampling-based planners handle only by scoring or rejecting action sequences.
Uses a successive convex program in latent space, initialized from a sampled plan, with a learned discrete-time control barrier function enforced across the horizon.
Builds smooth, spectrally normalised networks and bounds linearisation error using Lipschitz bounds and smoothing width.
On two Safety-Gymnasium navigation tasks, it had fewer violations than MPPI and CEM under the reported equal-time comparison, with higher return at longer horizons.
Planning converged more often on Lipschitz-bounded models and reports whether a feasible first-order KKT point was found nearby.

papers.abstract: For more than half a century, video games have pursued better graphics, more natural interaction, and more engaging gameplay. Generative video models (VMs) now bear on all three. Neural networks already draw most of the pixels in shipped games, and recent world models let a lightweight game engine keep the world state while a VM turns the engine's coarse proxy video into final frames. These systems, however, treat the VM as a renderer that only restyles motion the engine has already authored, which leaves most of its generative capacity unused and limits the diversity a game can offer. We present GameWM, a design for next-generation games built on a clear division of labor. The GameWM-engine keeps what must be exact: rules, state, camera, and the layout of the world, which also spares the video model from having to remember it. The GameWM-VM generates what is expensive to author by hand: the look of the world and the detail of the player's interactions. One game mechanic can then be realized in many visually and physically distinct ways, while its outcome stays exactly as the engine computed it. To realize this division of labor, we build GameWM as a complete system: a data engine centered on interactions rather than exploration, an interface through which authored character sheets, scene art, and skill descriptions enter the model, and a model family from 5B to 33B parameters with a real-time causal variant for play. Together they give every player a fresh version of the same game: each player's own character, world, and skills turn the same engine mechanics into a new experience, while every event keeps the timing and outcome the GameWM-engine computed.
authors: Bing He, Runze Wang, Fei Zha, Zhongyuan Wu, Ke Xu, Tao Zhuang, Yuxuan Xie, Zhongyuan Liu
bullets: Motivation: Existing video world models mainly render engine-authored motion, underusing their generative capacity and limiting gameplay diversity.
Core design: A GameWM-engine maintains rules, state, camera, and world layout; a GameWM-VM generates appearance and interaction details.
System components include an interaction-centered data engine, interfaces for character sheets, scene art, and skill descriptions, and models ranging from 5B to 33B parameters.
A real-time causal variant supports gameplay while preserving the engine-computed timing and outcomes.
The design aims to give players personalized characters, worlds, and skills without changing the underlying game mechanics.

papers.abstract: JEPA-based world models predict action consequences in latent space, but representative planning approaches rely on candidate-action search, requiring repeated evaluation of action sequences and incurring substantial online computational cost. Direct action generation avoids this search, yet how to leverage latent predictions to guide action generation given task goals remains a key challenge in translating learned physical dynamics into effective decisions. We introduce WA-JEPA, a world-action model that couples action generation, action-conditioned latent prediction, and goal-aware feedback. The model first generates an action proposal and predicts the resulting future scenes and proprioceptive states, then refines the proposal through two complementary feedback paths, using the task goal as a reference. Goal-discrepancy residual feedback (GDRF) uses differences between the latent representations of predicted scenes and the task goal to guide chunk-wise action refinement. Future-scene context feedback (FSCF) preserves fine-grained predicted scene representations to guide subsequent action refinement. Jointly learned from offline demonstrations, this process iteratively updates the same plan before execution, making future predictions directly participate in action generation without candidate-action search. We evaluate short-horizon goal reaching, long-horizon tasks, and full-task execution. The results show that goal-aware predictive feedback supports competitive task performance while maintaining a compact model and low online computational cost. Code is available at https://github.com/Dovisya/WA-JEPA.
authors: Tao An, Weihang Liang, Tianqi Wang, Chuqing Cao, Wenming Tan, Kai Zhang, Haibo Lei, Tao Xie, Lijun Zhao, Ruifeng Li
bullets: Addresses the high online cost of repeatedly evaluating candidate action sequences in JEPA-based world models.
Generates an action proposal, predicts future scenes and proprioceptive states, then iteratively refines the same plan using the task goal.
Combines goal-discrepancy residual feedback with future-scene context feedback for chunk-wise action refinement.
Learns the action generation and predictive feedback process from offline demonstrations.
Evaluated on short-horizon reaching, long-horizon tasks, and full-task execution, achieving competitive performance with a compact model and low online computation.

papers.abstract: Cyber-physical-human systems close a loop around people by sensing human behavior, predict it and act on it. Human teams are a natural target, because collaboration breaks down in ways that a timely prompt could prevent. Collaborative mixed reality makes this loop practical, since each headset senses who speaks, where its wearer looks and who stands together, and it can deliver a light prompt. In this loop, the headsets are sensors, the prompts are actuators and the team is the plant. Closing the loop needs a plant model that is small enough to learn from few teams, safe to iterate and readable by a designer. We propose ANCHOR, which models a team as a ball in an energy bowl. The bottom of the bowl is where the team rests, and it is set by the team's recent behavior, its own history and other teams. Formally, ANCHOR is a switched port-Hamiltonian system with 52 parameters, and each part stands for a testable claim from team psychology. Because of this structure, for any fitted parameters, a forecast moves away from rest only when task progress or a prompt pushes it, and prompts of bounded size that are spaced in time move it a bounded distance. On \nGroups{} four-person teams held out from training, a team that drifts from its usual behavior returns most of the way within half a minute. After 32 s, about 24% of the deviation remains, and ANCHOR predicted 30%. Forecasts are clearly better when the resting point blends its three sources than when it uses one. ANCHOR matches the accuracy of a black-box baseline with about 40,000 parameters. It anticipates conversation collapse with an AUROC of 0.85. In simulation under assumed prompt effects, it removes 2.2 times as much breakdown time per prompt as periodic prompting.
bullets: Models teams as a ball settling in an energy bowl whose resting point reflects recent behavior, team history, and other teams.
Uses 52 psychologically motivated parameters, designed for learning from few teams and supporting safe, interpretable prompting.
On held-out four-person teams, it predicted recovery from behavioral drift and retained 30% of the deviation after 32 seconds, versus about 24% observed.
Matched a roughly 40,000-parameter black-box baseline and detected conversation collapse with AUROC 0.85.
In simulation with assumed prompt effects, it removed 2.2× more breakdown time per prompt than periodic prompting.

papers.abstract: Generative models play a rapidly growing role in the design and simulation of molecules. The most widely used applications of generative models are in large language models (LLMs), owing to the natural flexibility of language for specifying and answering queries. However, generalist LLMs do not effectively handle large sets of 3D coordinates, whereas specialist generative models of 3D molecules cannot reach the controllability afforded by language. To bridge these capabilities, we propose Nahual, a decoder-only autoregressive diffusion model for any sequence of text and 3D molecules. To enable expressive autoregression on continuous coordinates, we propose next-token diffusion, whereby a causal transformer denoises each token while attending to the clean tokens before it, without increasing context size. We train Nahual on a curated set of twelve 3D chemistry tasks ranging from microsolvation to molecular conformer search to adsorption on metal surfaces, with associated evaluation metrics and baselines. The result is a single set of end-to-end-trained weights that simultaneously performs all tasks and surpasses state-of-the-art models specialized for crystal structure prediction and property-conditional molecule generation. Our results demonstrate the viability of scaling generalist decoder-only models for native multimodal understanding and generation across language and chemistry. Code is available at https://github.com/the-matter-lab/nahual.
authors: Austin H. Cheng, Marcel M\"uller, Andreas Burger, Yeonghun Kang, Tsz Wai Ko, Marta Skreta, Luka Mucko, Ella Miray Rajaonson, Cher Tian Ser, J\'er\^ome F. Gonthier, Alex Zook, Varinia Bernales, Al\'an Aspuru-Guzik
bullets: Addresses the gap between language models’ controllability and specialist models’ ability to handle 3D molecular coordinates.
Uses causal-transformer next-token diffusion to autoregressively denoise continuous coordinate tokens without enlarging context.
Trained end-to-end across twelve 3D chemistry tasks, spanning microsolvation, conformer search, and metal-surface adsorption.
A single model performs all tasks and surpasses specialized baselines for crystal structure prediction and property-conditional molecule generation.
Demonstrates the feasibility of generalist multimodal models for language-and-chemistry generation.

papers.abstract: Violation-of-expectation (VOE) benchmarks evaluate intuitive physics in video world models by testing whether physically impossible events produce greater prediction errors than matched possible events. However, conventional VOE evaluations aggregate prediction errors across space and time, making it unclear whether successful discrimination reflects model's understanding of physical violations at the locations and time where they occur. To address this limitation, we introduce localized VOE evaluation, a framework that measures prediction error differences between possible and impossible events within spatial regions and temporal intervals associated with physical violations. We compare global, temporally localized, and spatiotemporally localized evaluations of V-JEPA models pretrained on developmental egocentric videos or large-scale natural video datasets. Our results reveal that global and localized judgments can diverge in both directions: global aggregation can either obscure correct localized discrimination or produce apparent discrimination without corresponding localized evidence. During continued pretraining on developmental egocentric videos, agreement between global and localized judgments changes non-monotonically, while confidence in localized judgments increases despite modest improvements in accuracy. Together, these findings establish localized VOE evaluation as a complementary diagnostic for assessing intuitive physics in video world models and demonstrate that global prediction errors do not necessarily reflect the spatiotemporal evidence of physical violations.
bullets: Conventional VOE benchmarks aggregate prediction errors across space and time, obscuring where and when violations are detected.
The proposed framework compares errors for possible versus impossible events within violation-relevant spatial regions and temporal intervals.
Experiments compare global, temporal, and spatiotemporal evaluations of V-JEPA models pretrained on developmental egocentric or large-scale natural videos.
Global and localized judgments can diverge: aggregation may hide valid localized discrimination or suggest discrimination without localized evidence.
During continued developmental-video pretraining, localized confidence rises despite only modest accuracy gains, with global-local agreement changing non-monotonically.

The scatter plot compares global (x-axis) and localized (y-axis) surprise scores, defined as prediction error for the impossible video minus that for the possible video. Positive scores indicate correct discrimination. The four quadrants distinguish pairs classified correctly by both evaluations, either evaluation alone, or neither. Heatmaps show the surprise score, with red indicating greater error for the impossible video and blue indicating the opposite. Magenta outlines mark annotated violation regions. In Scenario 1, spatial averaging obscures the localized violation signal, yielding correct localized but incorrect global discrimination. In Scenario 2, elevated background error produces a positive global margin despite a negative localized margin. (d) Global and localized accuracy across four V-JEPA models and five physical principles in Physical Concepts. (e) Global, spatiotemporallocal, and spatial-local accuracy across the same models and three physical principles in IntPhys 1. Dashed lines indicate chance performance (50%).

Frame labels follow the same convention as in Figure 1. Each heatmap shows the surprise score map for the corresponding video pair produced by a different model, with patches containing the physical violation outlined in magenta. papers.selection_reason: Introduces localized violation-of-expectation evaluation for video world models, directly targeting intuitive-physics assessment in predictive video models.
papers.title: Probing Where Surprise Happens: Localized Violation-of-Expectation Evaluation of Video World Models

papers.abstract: World models develop internal simulators that can learn the structure and dynamics of an environment. It has been demonstrated that their internal representations are both meaningful and causal, but are these representations faithful to the governing dynamics of the environment they are learning? We introduce Anchored Recovery Certification (ARC), a procedure that utilizes a discrete Fr\'echet distance calculation with ground truth to evaluate dynamical consistency on candidate world models up to an affine gauge. We use the procedure on TD-MPC2 (decoder-free world model) that has learned the pendulum swing on an observation lift under varying hyperparameters at k = 5, 10, 25 steps. The model is then steered within a PCA-derived intervention subspace and compared against a ground-truth simulator using relative error to investigate dynamical faithfulness. ARC sufficiency held for TD-MPC2 most consistently at k = 10, with six of seven constraints statistically significant after Holm-Bonferroni correction, while the relative error between the simulator and the causal latent remained substantial. Further research could be conducted with decoder world models such as DreamerV3 (reconstruction loss) to investigate whether the results differ.
authors: Jerome Francisco, Kyle Deng, George Flint, Kevin Zhu
bullets: Tests dynamical consistency and causal faithfulness in world-model representations.
Introduces Anchored Recovery Certification (ARC), using discrete Fréchet distance to compare latent dynamics with ground truth up to affine gauge.
Evaluates decoder-free TD-MPC2 on a pendulum task across horizons k = 5, 10, and 25, including PCA-subspace interventions.
ARC was most consistently sufficient at k = 10, with six of seven constraints statistically significant after Holm–Bonferroni correction.
Despite this consistency, substantial relative error remained between the simulator and causal latent; decoder-based models remain future scope.

papers.abstract: Single-pass primitive decoders such as LocateAnything and VFlash predict all quantized coordinate tokens of a geometric primitive in one forward pass, enabling fast, System-1 visual planning. We study what matters when such a decoder serves as a System-1 world model: a fast action-conditioned predictor that ranks candidate pushes by their predicted outcome. On ManiSkill3 PushT-v1 (512 held-out test families, 8,192 rollouts) and on human demonstrations from lerobot/pusht (2,384 test windows), we compare decoders, training losses, rigid-body projections and coordinate frames, using matched checkpoints, hierarchical bootstrap confidence intervals and Holm correction. Two factors of similar size dominate. First, expressing inputs and outputs in the SE(2) frame of the object's initial pose lowers decision regret by 1.9-2.2x for each of five decoders, and the object-frame model trained on 128 families matches the world-frame model trained on 512. Second, single-pass decoding outperforms iterative decoding: in the object frame, single-pass heads reach 0.020-0.021 regret at 1.6-1.8 ms per decision, against 0.046 for 10-step DDIM diffusion and 0.059 for KV-cached autoregression at 10.3 and 12.9 ms. The choice among single-pass heads has no measurable effect on regret, and our registered hypothesis that the frame effect exceeds the decoder spread is not supported. Soft-token expectation with an end-to-end 2D Kabsch projection gives the lowest trajectory error (11.35 px on ManiSkill3, 3.78 px on lerobot/pusht), exact rigid-body consistency, and lower regret than diffusion at every budget from 4 to 50 DDIM steps, at 3-29x lower latency.
bullets: Evaluated decoders, losses, geometric projections, and coordinate frames on simulated and human PushT tasks.
Representing inputs and outputs in the object’s initial SE(2) frame reduced decision regret by 1.9–2.2× across five decoders.
Single-pass decoding achieved 0.020–0.021 regret in 1.6–1.8 ms, outperforming 10-step diffusion and cached autoregression in both speed and regret.
Soft-token expectation with end-to-end 2D Kabsch projection produced the lowest trajectory error and exact rigid-body consistency.
Decoder-head choice had no measurable regret effect; the preregistered claim that frame effects exceed decoder differences was not supported.

papers.abstract: A satellite forecast of a typhoon should give a low-error picture of the next two days, together with an ensemble whose members are coherent fields and whose spread responds to the storm at hand. A small direct regression network already gives the lowest squared error on held-out storms, so a generative model has to earn its cost through the part of the future that the regression smooths away. We present TyphoonWorld, a discrete-token world model that generates only that part. Conditioned on tokens of the regression forecast, the latest frames and the best-track state at forecast time, it samples residual fields lead by lead, and members add these residuals to the regression center. We compare it under one protocol with per-pixel Gaussian networks, a diffusion model of the same residuals, residuals from other storms and an unconditional token world model, on 276 forecast windows from 46 held-out storms of Digital Typhoon. TyphoonWorld matches the squared error of the regression, lowers the CRPS of the area colder than 220 K, a direct measure of deep convection, by 14 to 39% against every other ensemble, and ties its spread to forecast error as closely as the Gaussian network, with a correlation of 0.78 across windows. It uses 56% of the parameters of the unconditional world model.
authors: Xiaoyu Chen, Tianyi Li, Xuanyi Zhang
bullets: Targets the fine-scale future details smoothed out by low-error direct regression forecasts.
A discrete-token world model samples residual fields lead by lead, conditioned on the regression forecast, recent imagery, and best-track state.
Evaluated on 276 windows from 46 held-out Digital Typhoon storms against Gaussian, diffusion, cross-storm residual, and unconditional-token ensembles.
Matches regression squared error and reduces CRPS for deep-convection area by 14–39% versus all comparison ensembles.
Its spread–error correlation is 0.78, while using 56% of the unconditional world model’s parameters.

papers.abstract: World models have been widely applied to multi-agent planning and forecasting, but exogenous environmental changes are rarely incorporated as replaceable drivers in a unified state-evolution process. This limits assessment of whether environmental perturbations propagate through physical systems with faithful dynamics. We propose the Earth World Model (EWM), an Earth-centred forecasting framework that compresses heterogeneous multi-source observations into a reusable low-dimensional latent state representing the system's history and current condition. Given explicit exogenous drivers, a shared transition operator recursively updates the latent state, and physics-constrained decoding produces multi-step forecasts. Replacing the drivers enables environmental scenario analysis and evaluation of dynamic-response fidelity. We evaluated EWM for power forecasting and environmental-perturbation response at six photovoltaic sites and one wind-power site. Across four photovoltaic sites and three forecast horizons, three independent training runs yielded mean $R^2$ values of 0.8578-0.9095. In a separate six-site decoder ablation, the mean net per-unit response $\rho$ under the prescribed irradiance intervention increased from 0.180 with a multilayer perceptron decoder to 0.922 with an analytic physical decoder, close to site- and horizon-specific analytic references. The wind model achieved an injection elasticity of $0.9990 \pm 0.0006$, while pre-intervention outputs remained unchanged. These results show that forecast fit and intervention response should be evaluated separately and that the tested EWM configurations preserved response amplitude and temporal boundaries under the prescribed interventions.
authors: Huijun Qiao, Ziqiang Zhang, Jinnong Liao
bullets: Addresses the limited treatment of replaceable exogenous environmental drivers in unified world-model state evolution.
Compresses heterogeneous observations into a reusable low-dimensional latent state, recursively updated by a shared transition operator.
Uses physics-constrained decoding for multi-step forecasts and enables environmental scenario analysis by replacing drivers.
Evaluated on photovoltaic and wind-power sites, achieving strong photovoltaic forecast fit and near-ideal prescribed intervention responses.
Shows that forecast accuracy and intervention fidelity are distinct evaluation objectives; scope is limited to the tested renewable-energy settings and interventions.

papers.abstract: Scaling device-control evaluation requires scaling both the worlds agents interact with and the tasks they must solve. We introduce SynthDCB, a scalable benchmark for environment awareness and device control built through world distillation. World distillation transforms knowledge of device behaviors, interaction constraints, and environmental effects into modular executable components, which are composed into interactive worlds with explicit states, actions, and temporal dynamics. A unified capability representation connects tool discovery, world execution, and task synthesis, allowing new capabilities to enter evaluation through a shared construction pipeline. SynthDCB instantiates Home, Car, and Phone domains with 114 device classes, 1,166 functions, and 95 events, supporting five task families with 32 subtypes. The stateful design enables task validation and agent evaluation through state correctness and tool-call traces. We evaluate seven models on 2,560 test tasks; the best achieves 68.2% Pass@1. Error analysis reveals challenges in answer delivery, feasibility diagnosis, and temporal coordination. Construction experiments demonstrate scalability across domains and token efficiency: world distillation reduces token consumption by 0.9-66.0% and 46.2-92.5% relative to Codex with low and xhigh reasoning effort, respectively, while achieving broader capability coverage. SynthDCB makes executable world construction the basis of scalable device-control benchmarking, connecting an expanding space of capabilities and interactions to verifiable agent evaluation.

papers.abstract: Plan-conditioned driving world models are used to compare candidate plans, so their forecast should change with the plan as the real scene would, yet widely used control metrics check only whether the camera follows the command. Recorded drives already contain real outcomes of plans that were never driven: retiming a log gives pose-matched images and LiDAR for other speeds, and a stereo rig records a laterally shifted view. Against these references, released world models move their camera but barely move the scene: their scene response, the share of the real change in distance that the forecast reproduces, reaches at most about a third of real video's, and the trajectory score cannot tell an executed speed command from an ignored one. Interventions inside the generator trace the failure to the plan's channel. The forecast geometry follows the context frames; once they carry the planned geometry, plan tokens add little. ReTime-Compose therefore delivers the plan as geometry, without training. It transports the frames of one logged-speed rollout to the planned cameras, and the frozen model completes only what no frame covers. Frozen generators then follow a 0.54 m lateral shift nearly as the real scene does on KITTI, nuScenes and Argoverse 2, and respond more than re-sampling to slow-down plans in three generators and to speed-up plans in two.
bullets: Existing control metrics can miss whether a forecast reflects the planned scene dynamics.
Retimed driving logs and laterally shifted stereo views provide pose-matched references for evaluating scene changes.
Released models reproduce at most about one-third of the real video’s scene response, and trajectory scores may not distinguish obeyed from ignored speed commands.
ReTime-Compose transports logged frames to the planned camera geometry and lets a frozen model generate only uncovered content.
It closely matches real responses to a 0.54 m lateral shift across KITTI, nuScenes, and Argoverse 2, and improves speed-plan responses across multiple generators.

papers.abstract: Clinical world models expose language-model agents to predicted patient responses, but simulations can be unreliable for poorly supported treatments or unfamiliar hospitals. We introduce Support-Gated World-Model decision support, a lightweight extension of a propose--simulate--refine agent. A recurrent dynamics ensemble predicts short-horizon physiological responses to documented norepinephrine dose categories, while a behavior model estimates observational action support. The interface withholds predictions with insufficient support or excessive ensemble disagreement and abstains when no candidate qualifies. Evaluation on eICU-CRD includes 70 hospitals and 30,700 decision transitions, with 14 hospitals held out for testing. At 62.0% factual-transition coverage, joint gating yields a MAP mean absolute error of 7.3 mmHg, compared with 9.2 mmHg for random selection at the same coverage. The gated agent achieves 60.0% agreement with recorded actions at 81.0% decision coverage, compared with 55.0% agreement and 99.5% coverage for an ungated ensemble agent. Component ablations show lower factual risk with joint gating than with either gate alone.These results characterize a reliability--coverage trade-off in selective clinical simulation; they do not identify individualized treatment effects or establish improved patient outcomes.
bullets: Targets unreliable simulations for unfamiliar hospitals or poorly supported norepinephrine treatments.
Uses a recurrent dynamics ensemble plus a behavior model to gate predictions by observational support and ensemble disagreement.
Withholds unsupported predictions and abstains when no candidate qualifies.
On eICU-CRD, joint gating reduced MAP mean absolute error to 7.3 mmHg versus 9.2 mmHg for random selection at equal 62.0% coverage.
The approach improved agreement with recorded actions to 60.0% at 81.0% coverage, but does not establish individualized treatment effects or better patient outcomes.

papers.abstract: Direct image-to-video diffusion models entangle pixel synthesis with implicit latent motion, precluding persistent 3D mechanical equilibrium, mid-rollout intervention, and counterfactual force control. Conversely, single-pass programmatic 3D reconstruction from an uncalibrated photograph leaves monocular depth and support clearance underconstrained, causing reconstructed scenes to interpenetrate or collapse under gravity. We present TelePhysica, a closed-loop framework that reconstructs an executable, multi-regime physical world from a single photograph to drive stateful 3D interaction and trajectory-grounded video synthesis. A vision-language coding agent synthesizes separable visual meshes and declarative physical models within a two-stage verification loop that pairs pixel-aligned silhouette critique with a zero-force gravitational equilibrium preflight. The verified world compiles into a unified solver coupling rigid bodies, articulated chains, co-dimensional cloth shells, and 3D tetrahedral elastodynamics, whose simulated rollouts condition pretrained video diffusion models through pixel-aligned structural streams. On a 100-scene single-image benchmark, closed-loop execution raises equilibrium-verified world recovery from $0\%$ in single-pass synthesis to $81\%$. Controlled constitutive ablations show over an order-of-magnitude larger localized corner displacement and out-of-plane pleating in finite-element cloth than in matched rigid-plate proxies. Conditioning video diffusion on simulated trajectories increases dynamic motion-mask overlap by $2{\times}\text{--}5{\times}$ and preserves motion direction under counterfactual force reversals where direct image-to-video models fail.
authors: Ruiqi Shu, Xufeng Zhan, Yuanzhi Liang, Haibin Huang, Chi Zhang, Xuelong Li
bullets: Addresses image-to-video models’ lack of persistent 3D mechanics and single-pass reconstruction failures such as interpenetration or collapse.
Uses a vision-language coding agent with silhouette critique and zero-force gravitational preflight to build verified visual meshes and physical models.
Compiles scenes into a solver supporting rigid bodies, articulated chains, cloth shells, and tetrahedral elastodynamics.
On a 100-scene benchmark, equilibrium-verified recovery improves from 0% with single-pass synthesis to 81% with closed-loop execution.

Simulated trajectory conditioning improves dynamic motion-mask overlap by 2–5× and preserves motion direction under reversed forces; finite-element cloth exhibits stronger deformation than rigid proxies.

papers.abstract: World-model video encoders such as V-JEPA learn how scenes change (direction, speed, order, state) from video alone. To answer questions, they are joined to a language model trained on captions and question-answer pairs. But each caption or question names only a few attributes of a clip, so the model learns to retrieve those attributes rather than to read the clip, and the dynamics the encoder carries go unused: on the same items, a linear probe reads speed from frozen V-JEPA features at 87% while the VLM answers at chance. We show where dynamics lives in a frozen encoder: in a subspace shared across videos for predictive encoders such as V-JEPA, but not as a shared component of frame-wise, text-aligned encoders such as SigLIP. We then build counterfactual supervision that makes the language model read it: pixel transformations turn public videos into answer-balanced variants whose answers are set by the transformation and differ only in the change. Trained in a single stage on 4.53M public samples with 32 visual tokens per frame, where open video LLMs use several stages, 9M to 172M samples and 64 to 256 tokens per frame on average, the resulting V-JEPA-LM models (1B to 8B, Qwen3 and Llama) lead every size class in average score across eleven video benchmarks; our 4B model scores 72.1, against 61.1 for the best open 4B and 64.8 for the best open 8B model. A controlled encoder x supervision study shows that the encoder decides what can be read and the supervision what is read: at a matched budget, counterfactual supervision adds 4.5 points on average and 38 on the speed questions of natural benchmarks. Code and models: https://github.com/kkt94/Llama-V-JEPA-LM.
authors: Keuntae Kim, Dongjun Kim, Yong Suk Choi
bullets: V-JEPA retains shared representations of dynamics such as direction, speed, order, and state, but standard caption-based training largely leaves them unused.

papers.title: V-JEPA-LM: Video-Language Models That Read Dynamics Beyond Static, Text-Aligned Representations

papers.abstract: World models that support planning, control, and interpretable reasoning require latent representations that genuinely encode action. Yet the large-scale video data from which such models are learned overwhelmingly lack action annotations. Latent-action models infer action-like variables from observation sequences, enabling action-aware learning from unlabeled videos or trajectories. A fundamental concern, however, remains: a latent that improves future prediction may simply encode the current state, episode progress, task identity, or other predictive shortcuts. Existing evaluation practices---reconstruction loss, rollout fidelity, action recovery, or downstream performance---cannot isolate this distinction. We introduce the Latent Action Support Ratio (LASR), a dimensionless metric that measures, under offline evaluation on held-out data, whether a learned latent provides predictive support for action-related targets beyond the current state and non-action alternatives. LASR provides two complementary summaries: GeoLASR captures typical support, while WorstLASR identifies the weakest case. We instantiate the LASR benchmark with recorded actions and corresponding physical state changes as targets, episode-held-out splits, one predictor type for all comparisons, and positive and negative controls. Experiments on recorded robot manipulation data and a matched multi-task panel demonstrate that LASR detects known action information, rejects representative non-action shortcuts, and enables graded comparisons among imperfect latent representations. We further use LASR to train and audit a lightweight residual adapter, obtaining descriptively better point estimates whose uncertainty is assessed with paired comparisons. LASR thus provides a principled offline protocol for measuring action-related predictive support in world-model latents.

papers.abstract: Joint world action models (WAMs) generate future actions and states together, modeling world-action trajectories rather than actions alone. However, trajectory imitation does not ensure that these trajectories are task-effective or consistent with dynamics. We present \textbf{world action trajectory optimization (WATO)}, which optimizes generated actions and future states jointly for control. WATO uses both as references in a dynamics-constrained trajectory optimization problem and differentiates the task loss through the optimized trajectory to train the generator. This makes generated trajectories task-aware and dynamics-consistent while using trajectory optimization only during training. At deployment, WATO directly generates candidate trajectories and ranks them with a world model, without iterative trajectory optimization. Across $7$ visual control environments, WATO improves average success from $79.9\%$ for the imitation joint WAM to $91.7\%$, outperforming strong model-based, goal-conditioned RL, and generative control baselines. Compared with cross-entropy method (CEM), WATO is on average $11.5\times$ faster and uses $600.5\times$ fewer world model evaluations at deployment.
bullets: Joint world-action models generate future actions and states, but imitation alone may yield ineffective or dynamically inconsistent trajectories.
WATO jointly optimizes generated actions and states using task loss and dynamics constraints during training.
Gradients through the optimized trajectory make the generator task-aware and dynamics-consistent.
At deployment, it directly generates candidate trajectories and ranks them with a world model, without iterative optimization.
Across 7 visual control environments, WATO raises average success from 79.9% to 91.7% and is faster and more evaluation-efficient than CEM.

papers.abstract: Image-goal planning with a frozen visual world model depends on how predicted observations are scored against the goal. Mean-squared error (MSE) between embeddings from a pretrained visual encoder can provide a useful signal near a goal, yet favor states across an obstacle that are visually similar to the goal and difficult to reach. We fit a small residual adapter on top of frozen I-JEPA embeddings to improve this latent goal cost. Starting near each goal, a planner collects trajectories from progressively wider regions of initial states. The adapter learns from the order of observations along successful trajectories, with additional comparisons inferred from failed rollouts. No task-specific progress labels are used for fitting, so the procedure can be applied to other goal-reaching tasks. DotWall and PointMaze are used in this work. In paired 50-case evaluations with identical starts, goals, world models, and planner settings, success increases from 54% to 98% in DotWall and from 82% to 96% in PointMaze. On 16 unseen DotWall layout-goal cases, the adapter fitted on one fixed layout improves agreement between latent-cost ordering and shortest legal-path ordering from 71.9% to 85.8%. The results indicate that planning experience can improve a frozen visual representation's goal cost without retraining the encoder or the world model.
bullets: MSE in pretrained visual embeddings can favor visually similar but obstructed states.
A residual adapter is trained on trajectory orderings from progressively broader starts, using failed rollouts for extra comparisons and no task-specific progress labels.
In paired evaluations, success rises from 54% to 98% on DotWall and from 82% to 96% on PointMaze.
On unseen DotWall layout-goal cases, agreement with shortest legal-path ordering improves from 71.9% to 85.8%.
The approach is evaluated on DotWall and PointMaze and depends on planning experience to adapt the goal cost.

papers.abstract: This paper presents a multifidelity (MF) formulation of Operator Inference (OpInf) for learning non-intrusive, physics-based reduced-order models (ROMs) of nonlinear dynamical systems. OpInf learns reduced operators from projections of snapshot data by solving a least squares regression problem. However, generating high-fidelity snapshots can be computationally expensive, limiting parameter coverage and the temporal extent of training trajectories for many aerospace applications, which can lead to inaccurate or unstable ROM predictions. This work proposes MF-OpInf, which combines limited high-fidelity snapshots with more plentiful low-fidelity snapshots through a control-variates-inspired MF least squares formulation to learn a single set of reduced operators across multiple trajectories. Low-fidelity trajectories provide additional parameter coverage and extend beyond the high-fidelity training time horizon. The low-fidelity snapshots are also used to construct an improved reduced basis through weighted proper orthogonal decomposition. We demonstrate MF-OpInf on a nonlinear reaction-diffusion problem with parametrized sinusoidal forcing and a two-dimensional incompressible flow past a cylinder with a parametrized inlet pulse. In these experiments, under an equal training simulation budget, MF-OpInf reduces the mean relative prediction error at unseen parameters by up to $87\%$ for the reaction-diffusion problem and $28\%$ for the cylinder flow problem over the test time regime, which extends beyond the high-fidelity training time horizon. These results demonstrate that MF-OpInf can improve temporal extrapolation and prediction at unseen parameters without increasing the training simulation budget.
authors: Vignesh Sella, Anirban Chaudhuri, Karen Willcox
bullets: Addresses the cost of generating high-fidelity snapshots, which limits parameter coverage and training time horizons.
Uses a control-variates-inspired multifidelity least-squares formulation to learn one set of reduced operators across trajectories.
Incorporates low-fidelity data into a weighted POD basis to improve the reduced representation.
Demonstrated on parametrized reaction-diffusion and cylinder-flow problems, improving unseen-parameter prediction errors by up to 87% and 28%, respectively.
Improves temporal extrapolation beyond the high-fidelity training horizon under an equal training simulation budget.

papers.abstract: Imitation policies can perform complex manipulation, yet small execution errors can accumulate and cause failure. Refinement can correct these errors, but existing approaches often require additional on-policy learning or costly online planning. Our key insight is that a pretrained policy already supplies a useful nominal behavior: refinement can focus on predicting how small action corrections change its outcome. We therefore learn this local response in a form that is cheap to optimize. Our \textit{action-affine world model} (A\textsuperscript{2}WM) learns local action sensitivities offline from action-perturbed policy rollouts. Given interaction history and a policy proposal, it predicts task-relevant geometry as a nominal trajectory plus a linear response to corrections. It predicts the full planning horizon directly, avoiding the propagation of intermediate errors through recursive model evaluations. Quadratic penalties on predicted task errors and linear correction constraints then yield a cheap convex quadratic program (QP). Online refinement requires one model evaluation and one QP solve, while both policy and model weights remain frozen. Across four simulated manipulation tasks, our framework achieves the highest success rate among evaluated baselines, adding only 3.8 ms of mean refinement overhead per control step, excluding base-policy sampling.
bullets: Addresses execution errors that accumulate in imitation-based manipulation.
Learns local action sensitivities offline from action-perturbed policy rollouts.
Predicts full-horizon task geometry as nominal behavior plus linear action corrections.
Performs refinement with one model evaluation and one QP solve while keeping policy and model weights frozen.
Achieves the highest success rate among evaluated baselines across four simulated tasks, with 3.8 ms mean overhead per control step excluding policy sampling.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Overview of fast inference-time policy refinement. A frozen base policy generates action proposals every K control steps. At each control step, the action-affine world model uses interaction history and the current proposal to predict a nominal trajectory Z̄ and a causal action-response matrix F , yielding the direct multi-step prediction Ẑ = F∆A+ Z̄. With F and Z̄ fixed, quadratic task costs and linear correction bounds define a convex QP over ∆A. The first optimized correction is applied to the base action, and refinement repeats after the next observation. Both the base policy and world model remain frozen during deployment.

Fig. 1. (a) Success rate comparison across four simulated manipulation tasks. Our method achieves the highest observed success rate on each task among the evaluated refinement methods, tying GPC-OPT on PushT. (b) Success–latency trade-off. Our method achieves the highest taskaveraged success rate with only a modest increase in mean per-control-step inference time over the frozen diffusion policy (DP). Inference time includes both policy sampling and online refinement. GPC-QP is our baseline that linearizes the GPC world model around the action proposal via its Jacobian and solves a quadratic program for refinement.

Fig. 5. Breakdown of online refinement latency. Times are amortized per control step and averaged equally across the four tasks, excluding simulation and each method’s base-policy sampling time. For GPC-RANK, we instead subtract our method’s single-proposal sampling time, retaining excess candidate-sampling cost as Extra DP. Model Computation includes Jacobian evaluation for GPC-QP; Optimization includes scoring, gradientbased refinement, and QP processing; Other covers remaining overhead.

Fig. 3. Offline learning of the action-affine world model. A frozen imitation policy collects rollouts with action perturbations. Each training window contains interaction history H, a recorded proposal Abase, executed action corrections ∆A, and future observables Z. Conditioned on history and proposal, the model outputs F and Z̄, forming the direct multi-step prediction Ẑ = F∆A + Z̄. Prediction errors over the full horizon jointly supervise the nominal forecast and action response.

For each configuration, we fix the initial state, interaction history, and base-policy proposal, and vary the perturbation amplitude α along a fixed action direction. We compare the block’s x-position after eight steps from independent simulator branches (Ground Truth), A2WM, and the baseline MLP world model trained with eight-step supervision. Shaded regions indicate the QP correction bounds.

Fig. 6. Multi-step prediction accuracy across four tasks. (a) A2WM versus recursive nonlinear MLPs trained with one- or eight-step losses. (b) Direct versus recursive action-affine predictors, all compatible with QPbased refinement. Errors are normalized per task by the eighth-step RMSE of A2WM in (a) and Direct in (b), then averaged equally across tasks. In (b), thick curves average two training seeds and faint curves show individualseed results.

papers.abstract: Embodied foundation models hinge on diverse robot interaction data, which are costly to collect. Egocentric human videos offer a complementary source of experience, and latent action models (LAMs) provide a popular means of leveraging these videos for policy supervision. Compared with world-action models (WAMs), LAMs can offer greater training efficiency and potentially lower inference costs by avoiding explicit pixel prediction during policy learning and execution. However, most existing LAMs learn latent actions solely through video reconstruction, which can cause their representations to cluster by visual appearance rather than by the underlying actions. As a result, they struggle to align human actions with their robot counterparts. To bridge the gap, we introduce SALA, which emphasizes establishing the semantic correspondence for latent actions. Without requiring paired data, we use the language descriptions of unpaired human and robot clips to estimate semantic similarities and supervise cross-embodiment correspondence. Specifically, we translate these similarities into soft neighborhood structures that guide human latent actions toward semantically related robot latents, while robot action reconstruction grounds the latent space in control. The resulting shared latent action space provides a unified supervision signal for training an embodied foundation model on both human and robot videos. Notably, latent action supervision enables scaling along two axes: (1) pre-training on increasing amounts of general human video consistently reduces robot action prediction error on downstream tasks, and (2) post-training on increasing amounts of task-specific human video substantially improves real-world robot task success rates.
bullets: Addresses the poor cross-embodiment alignment caused by learning latent actions primarily from video reconstruction.
Uses language descriptions of unpaired human and robot clips to estimate semantic similarities and create soft neighborhood supervision.
Combines cross-embodiment alignment with robot action reconstruction to ground the shared latent space in control.
Enables unified training on human and robot videos without requiring paired data.
Scaling general human video reduces downstream robot action prediction error, while task-specific human video improves real-world task success.

papers.abstract: Recent video world models have witnessed the paradigm shift from single-agent to multi-agent involvements, which can reveal more complicated dynamics and cross-agent interaction in the real world. However, existing approaches commonly adopt implicit inter-agent communications via cross attention, which lack explicit geometry constraints and unified 3D state, thereby leading to poor multi-view consistency and struggling with recovering out-of-sight agents. In addition, most of them assume a static background, failing to represent uncontrolled background dynamics. To address these problems, we propose Artemis: a geometry-grounded multi-agent world model with explicit memory sharing. An explicit 3D world map is reconstructed from multi-agent observations to enforce a unified 3D state across agents, offering high cross-view consistency. Specifically, an action-guided geometric injection module is developed to simultaneously render decomposed foreground-background control maps, which are then injected into a diffusion transformer through a designed GeoAdapter block. Compared to previous methods assuming static-only background, our GeoAdapter can also distinguish uncontrolled non-agent dynamics, which are conditioned on their own multi-frame history positions to provide consistent motion cues. Keyframes selected from progressive video rollouts are used to progressively update the reconstructed 3D world maps. To effectively capture complex dynamic patterns, we curate a novel dataset sampled from the CARLA simulator called MA-CARLA. Extensive experiments demonstrate the superiority of our proposed method in terms of visual fidelity and cross-view consistency in the generated videos. In addition, our Artemis can support simultaneous multi-modal rollouts with both 2D video and 3D point map maintenance, scale to scenarios beyond two agents and multi-camera setting.
bullets: Addresses poor cross-view consistency, out-of-sight agent recovery, and static-background assumptions in prior multi-agent world models.
Reconstructs an explicit 3D world map from multi-agent observations to enforce a unified geometric state.
Uses an action-guided GeoAdapter to inject decomposed foreground–background control maps into a diffusion transformer.
Models uncontrolled background dynamics using their own multi-frame position histories, while keyframes progressively update the 3D map.
Introduces the MA-CARLA dataset; experiments report improved visual fidelity and cross-view consistency, with support for multi-modal 2D video/3D point-map rollouts and more than two agents.

figures.caption: Figure 4: Overall pipeline of Artemis. We initialize the shared 3D map by registering individual observations. Given action inputs, control maps disentangling background static, foreground controlled agent proxy, and uncontrolled environmental dynamics are rendered respectively from the reconstructed global map. Then, these controls are injected into DiT, guiding the generator’s rollouts. After each inference block, keyframes are selected to update the static world map.
