papers.abstract: Diffusion-based world models can generate and predict trajectories in high-dimensional dynamical systems, but predictive accuracy does not imply that their latent coordinates recover the underlying state variables or causal interactions. We ask whether a frozen pretrained diffusion model can be equipped with identifiable coordinates without retraining its generative backbone. We show that auxiliary-variable nonlinear ICA guarantees can be transferred to Contrastive Diffusion Alignment (ConDA), which learns only a lightweight alignment map on top of frozen diffusion latents. Under standard TCL/GCL assumptions, the aligned representation identifies latent dynamical states up to permutation and componentwise invertible transformations, preserves the latent dynamic structural causal model, and reduces lagged graph recovery to transition-Jacobian sparsity. We evaluate TCL-, GCL-, and CEBRA-based ConDA against TDRL, CaRiNG, IDOL, temporal SuaVE, and iVAE across physical and robotic video systems. TCL and GCL achieve near-perfect blockwise state recovery and competitive lagged graph recovery, including exact recovery in a simulated falling-body system. In a simulated bipedal robot, learned dynamics recover the sign and temporal structure of responses to held-out control perturbations. These results show that a frozen generative diffusion model can be equipped with coordinates that are identifiable, structurally interpretable, and useful for analyzing intervention-relevant dynamics.
bullets: Addresses the gap between accurate trajectory prediction and recovery of true latent state variables or causal structure.
Applies auxiliary-variable nonlinear ICA guarantees to Contrastive Diffusion Alignment (ConDA) without retraining the diffusion backbone.
Under TCL/GCL assumptions, states are identified up to permutation and componentwise invertible transformations, while latent structural dynamics are preserved.
Experiments on physical and robotic video systems show near-perfect blockwise state recovery, competitive lagged graph recovery, and exact recovery in a simulated falling-body system.
Control-perturbation tests in a simulated bipedal robot recover the sign and temporal structure of held-out responses.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of the proposed framework. (a) A frozen pretrained diffusion model serves as a generative world model: it embeds video frames yt into diffusion latents xt by inversion (solid arrows) and decodes latents back into frames (dashed arrows). The latents are in turn generated by a lagged dynamic SCM over the latent state st, driven by inputs ut and independent noise, through xt = g(st). (b) TCL- or GCL-based ConDA trains only a lightweight map h, using temporal or auxiliary information, to obtain zt = h(xt). Under nonlinear ICA assumptions, zt identifies st up to permutation and componentwise invertible transformations, and can be lifted back to xt for generation. (c) Lagged causal structure is characterized theoretically by inverse transition-noise Jacobian sparsity and estimated empirically from states aligned from zt. Dynamics learned in these coordinates are validated by predicting responses to held-out control perturbations.

Figure 2: Recovered lag-1 dynamics graphs across datasets and methods. Binary adjacency matrices are shown for IDOL, CaRiNG, TDRL, temporal SuaVE, iVAE, ConDA-CEBRA, ConDATCL, ConDA-GCL, and the true-state reference. Blue entries indicate recovered edges and gray entries indicate absent edges. Rows correspond to the different dynamical systems considered in the study. The ConDA variants more closely reproduce the sparsity structure of the true-state dynamics, with TCL and GCL showing particularly strong agreement across settings.

Figure 5: Dynamic intervention effects under positive and negative control perturbations in Microduck. Mean dynamic intervention effects over a 1s rollout horizon for interventions on the forward command ux and lateral command uy. The top row shows positive interventions, do(ux = 0.25) and do(uy = 0.17), relative to the corresponding zero-control baselines, while the bottom row shows negative interventions, do(ux = −0.25) and do(uy = −0.17). papers.abstract: Model-based planners that roll out imagined futures assume the transition model faithfully propagates task-relevant signals---a property rarely measured directly. In a single-seed case study of a Recurrent State Space Model world model with active-inference planning in the CARLA driving simulator, we identify a \textbf{posterior-prior gap}---posterior (observation-filtered) states retain obstacle information that imagined rollout states progressively lose: a supervised obstacle probe achieves AUC 0.85 on posterior states, but the same probe applied to imagined prior states shows monotonic decay (AUC 0.85$\rightarrow$0.71 over 15 steps; logit separation drops 57\%). Because the probe is identical, the decay isolates the transition model---not the representation---as the information bottleneck. Obstacle avoidance drops to 0\% without privileged runtime coordinates, and the planner's own ensemble-based epistemic term does not flag the loss---ensemble disagreement yields AUC 0.52 as an obstacle classifier (chance level), making the failure an unflagged imagination failure---an unknown unknown at planning time. As a secondary contribution, we show that \textbf{task-conditioned weighting of Effective Free Energy components} over the same world model yields lane keeping ($81.2 \pm 1.8$\% route completion) and obstacle avoidance (28/28 avoided, \emph{using privileged coordinates}) in the CARLA simulator, with runtime weight modulation enabling post-evasion centering.
bullets: Posterior states preserve obstacle signals (probe AUC 0.85), while imagined priors decline from AUC 0.85 to 0.71 over 15 steps.
Using the same probe isolates the transition model—not the state representation—as the information bottleneck.
Obstacle avoidance falls to 0% without privileged runtime coordinates, and ensemble disagreement fails to detect the loss (AUC 0.52).
Task-conditioned Effective Free Energy weighting supports 81.2 ± 1.8% route completion and avoids 28/28 obstacles when privileged coordinates are available.
Findings come from a single-seed CARLA case study and may not generalize beyond this setting.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Posterior-prior epistemic gap across imagination depth. AUC (left axis) and logit separation (right axis) both decay monotonically as the RSSM rolls out imagined states without observations. AUC drops from 0.85 (posterior) to 0.71 (k=15), with logit separation decaying 57% over 15 steps. The sharpest drop occurs at k=1.

Table 4. Preference gap ∆ across modalities and methods. Top rows vary input modality (separate world models); bottom rows vary the preference objective (same 64×64 model). α: contrastive down-weighting factor.

Table 3. Ablation on R1 (518m, 3 obstacles, 3 episodes each). Same 64×64 model throughout. “w/o privileged” removes all six privileged mechanisms simultaneously (not individually isolated); Compl.: route completion.
Table 1. Task-conditioned EFE component weights. Same world model checkpoint; only β weights and horizon differ.

papers.abstract: Endovascular catheter navigation relies on continuous fluoroscopy, exposing patients and clinical staff to ionizing radiation throughout the procedure. We investigate whether a physics-based world model can sustain the navigation task between deliberately sparse X-ray acquisitions, and whether the model can signal when its internal state estimate is no longer reliable. We formulate sparse-fluoroscopy navigation as a partially observable Markov decision process where a Cosserat rod simulator supplies transition dynamics, sparse noisy projections provide observations, and a particle filter maintains a belief over the device state, reduced in this implementation to a tip state with a geometric contact proxy. We evaluate this formulation in a deliberately simplified setting: a synthetic planar vessel phantom with a quasi-static rod model and simulated projections, without clinical or animal data. In this setting, the belief-state model tracks the simulated tip with a root mean square error of 1.30 mm while acquiring observations at one fifteenth of the continuous rate (0.97 mm at every frame, 1.51 mm at one thirtieth), reported 90 percent credible intervals achieve 0.92 empirical coverage, and the belief-derived contact risk estimate discriminates unsafe contact events with an AUROC of 0.68. These results constitute a proof of concept on a simplified simulation rather than a demonstration of clinical readiness; their purpose is to establish that calibrated belief, rather than point-estimate accuracy alone, is the essential property a sparse-imaging world model must deliver.
bullets: Frames sparse-fluoroscopy navigation as a partially observable Markov decision process.
Uses a Cosserat rod simulator for dynamics, simulated projections for observations, and a particle filter over catheter-tip state.
At one-fifteenth of the continuous imaging rate, tip tracking reached 1.30 mm RMSE; 90% credible intervals achieved 0.92 empirical coverage.
Belief-derived contact risk detected unsafe events with AUROC 0.68.
Results are limited to a synthetic planar phantom and do not establish clinical readiness.

Fig. 1. Simulation snapshot on the synthetic planar phantom (seed 0, k = 15, step 194, which is 14 steps after the last acquired frame). Ground-truth rod, particle cloud, and dead-reckoning estimate inside the synthetic vessel. This is a proof-of-concept simulation; no real anatomy or fluoroscopy is involved.

papers.abstract: Within the CG animation production pipeline, the challenges artists tackle in Lighting can be immense. Even minor adjustments require re-rendering massive scenes with slow offline renderers; global illumination has to be sampled and complex shaders have to be evaluated, leading to iteration times of minutes to hours per frame. To accelerate this process, we introduce a novel neural render proxy (NRP) that enables differentiable relighting of static scenes with fixed camera and materials at interactive rates. Our main insight is the decoupling of traditional rendering into path sampling and emission computation. From a single, light-agnostic render pass, we collect light transport data in the form of path samples. This enables rapidly sampling lighting conditions on the fly, and training a scene-specific lightweight neural network that learns how light is transported from any scene location to any image pixel. This approach is compatible with non-differentiable production renderers, induces minimal memory requirements during inference, and scales only with resolution and the number of light sources and parameters, but independently of scene and appearance complexity. Our evaluation demonstrates interactive frame rates for relighting (~30-60 Hz) while closely approximating the visual fidelity of ground-truth path tracing. In addition, the differentiable NRP enables fast, gradient-based inverse workflows, allowing artists to efficiently solve for lighting parameters from intuitive image-space edits or generative targets.
authors: Sergio Sancho, Alexander Rath, Marco Manzi, Pascal Chang, Amit H. Bermano, Derek Nowrouzezahrai, Markus Gross, Marios Papas
bullets: Targets slow lighting iteration caused by global-illumination sampling and complex shader evaluation.
Decouples rendering into path sampling and emission computation using a light-agnostic render pass.
Trains a scene-specific neural network to predict light transport from scene locations to image pixels.
Supports relighting at approximately 30–60 Hz with inference cost tied to resolution and lighting parameters, not scene complexity.
Enables gradient-based inverse lighting workflows from image edits or generative targets.

figures.caption: Figure 12: Controllable relighting using our optimization pipeline. Left two columns (Art-directed edits): Lighting parameters are optimized to adhere to hand-drawn scribbles depicting desired illumination phenomena. Right two columns (Generative edits): We leverage generative image models (Qwen-Image-Edit) to create relighting targets. In both cases, given an initial image and a target, we optimize through our NRP to extract physically plausible lighting parameters that accurately reconstruct the prompted appearance. © Disney

Figure 2: Our Pipeline. Training (left): We collect lighting agnostic paths from path tracing the scene before generating denoised image with random lighting conditions to serve as training data. Our neural render proxy (NRP; middle) is a lightweight MLP with hashgrid positional encoding that predicts light transport to a sensor pixel from an input light. To reduce training time and avoid spectral bias, we condition the NRP on auxiliary features (albedo, depth and normals) at sensor image coordinates. At inference time (top right), we can relight the scene at interactive rates by inserting virtual light sources into the scene. Since the NRP is also differentiable, we can optimize for lighting parameters (bottom right) using gradient descent, driven by any number of image-space guidance approaches.

Figure 5: Qualitative image-based relighting comparison. Our relighting setting matches that of image-based relighting using generative networks. Two leading approaches with similar input settings (image, auxiliary features, and lighting condition) are presented. Generative models do not preserve scene geometry, do not adhere to material appearance behavior, and produce lighting that is plausible, but is not physically reasonable. Our method produces high-quality and high-fidelity appearance in real-time. Note that the aspect ratio is different since the generative models used consider squared images.

Figure 4: Production scenes. Interactive relighting results created by artists using our neural render proxy on large-scale production scenes. Each row shows three different light configurations for the same scene. Our method faithfully captures complex light transport effects including fur (top), translucency (middle), and volumetric lighting (bottom). © Disney

Figure 4: Qualitative comparison of component ablation variants on the Kitchen scene. Top row: tonemapped renderings under the same light position. Bottom row: FLIP error maps (HDR mode) against the ground truth, with shared scale. Our full pipeline (rightmost) produces the lowest perceptual error.

Left: Higher spp improves reconstruction quality and prediction quality. Interestingly, at low spp regimes, the model prediction can perform better than the data it was trained on. Right: Bigger models improve prediction quality. We use 256 neurons with 8 layers by default.
Figure 10: Multi-view lighting edits. By training an NRP for each view, our method enables interactive and consistent lighting edits across multiple views simultaneously.

Figure 6: Path-based training. PSNR (dB) in tonemapped space, averaged across three scenes. Each bar is a network trained on N images at S spp with NEE (N×S). Blue: increasing dataset size at 1 spp. Orange: fixed budget of 1024 total samples per pixel, redistributed across images. Dashed red line: our method, trained on light-agnostic path data from a 64 spp render. Despite 16× fewer sampled paths, our approach outperforms all image-based configurations.

Figure 9: Inverse optimization comparison. A light source is optimized from a random initial position to match a target appearance. Error maps (middle) show the relative squared error of path-traced re-renders against the target. Our NRP approach converges to lower parameter error in less time than traditional (Mitsuba) and neural (ZeroGrads) baselines (right). This comparison serves as validation: Baselines operate at low spp for tractable runtimes, and their accuracy could improve with higher sample counts at proportionally longer optimization times.

Figure 7: Quality metrics vs. samples per pixel. Mean prediction quality for network size 256×8 (blue) and denoised reconstruction from the GATHERLIGHT pass (red), averaged across three scenes. Higher spp improves both reconstruction and prediction quality. Notably, at low spp the learned model can outperform the reconstruction it was trained on. Unless stated otherwise, we use 512 spp for training.

Figure 14: Limitations in narrow regions. When queried in undersampled spaces, our NRP can struggle to accurately model occlusions. As shown here, placing the light source inside the narrow cavity of the lamp results in incorrect light propagation.

papers.abstract: Actions in expert demonstrations exhibit temporal structure. An ordered-versus-shuffled analysis across five environments confirms this dependence. We ask whether action proposals that better reflect expert continuity can improve visual world-model planning. Rather than imposing generic smoothness, we learn continuations from the temporal structure of demonstrated actions. Our locality-gated deep-kernel Gaussian-process prior, LG-DKGP, combines recent and longer-range executed action history, predicts a neural continuation, and learns a temporal Gaussian-process (GP) residual. A training-derived exploration scale initializes search around the corrected mean; a frozen world model evaluates progress toward the goal. Training first fits the neural mean, then jointly optimizes the prior with the GP residual using expert future actions. The resulting planner achieves 87.07\% macro success across five simulated tasks spanning native and fragment-level goal attainment, compared with 71.03\% for INTACT, 61.66\% for PRISM, and 58.66\% for LeWM. Component interventions and expert-relative action-structure comparisons support demonstration-informed continuations and reveal task-dependent effects of visual conditioning, history length, and planning horizon.
authors: Shaobo Yang, Zichen Ai, Ziyang Ma, Qian Yang, Bin Fang
bullets: Expert actions show meaningful temporal dependence: ordered demonstrations outperform shuffled ones.
LG-DKGP combines recent and long-range action history with a neural continuation and temporal Gaussian-process residual.
A training-derived exploration scale initializes planning, while a frozen world model evaluates goal progress.
The planner reaches 87.07% macro success, compared with 71.03% for INTACT, 61.66% for PRISM, and 58.66% for LeWM.
Component studies indicate task-dependent effects from visual conditioning, history length, and planning horizon.

papers.abstract: Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) enable future prediction in latent space without pixel reconstruction. However, latent predictive consistency alone does not establish the relative driving quality of candidate plans. We present ActWorld-JEPA, a joint-embedding formulation for candidate-based driving. Where Plan-Conditioned JEPA (PC-JEPA) uses global and step-wise trajectory intentions to guide recurrent latent prediction, then combines the predicted future with the current scene through gated cross-attention; Relational Residual Reranking ($R^3$) models agreement and discrepancy between plan and future representations under planning supervision, yielding bounded, gated residual corrections to the base planning scores. This formulation connects latent prediction to candidate selection using only observed context and proposed trajectories at inference. Benchmark-specific implementations report 94.1 PDMS on NAVSIM v1 navtest, with the final selector calibrated using aggregate NAVTEST feedback, and 91.6 and 42.7 EPDMS on NAVSIM v2 navtest and navhard, respectively. The nuScenes evaluation reports a mean $L_2$ error of 1.20 m and a predicted collision rate of 0.76% over 1--6 s. This work provides an effective path from JEPA's predictive representations to driving decisions informed by anticipated consequences.
authors: Ziying Song, Shengkai Zhang, Caiyan Jia, Lei Yang, Lin Liu, Yuchen Liu, Ziyang Liu, Zirui Li, Gang Wang, Peiliang Wu, Li Wang, Yadan Luo, Chen Lv
bullets: Addresses the gap between latent future-prediction consistency and the relative quality of candidate driving plans.
Uses Plan-Conditioned JEPA to predict future latent states from scene context and global/step-wise trajectory intentions.
Applies Relational Residual Reranking to model plan–future agreement and discrepancy, producing gated corrections to base planning scores.
Reports 94.1 PDMS on NAVSIM v1, 91.6/42.7 EPDMS on NAVSIM v2 navtest/navhard, and 1.20 m mean L2 error with 0.76% predicted collision rate on nuScenes.
Inference uses only observed context and proposed trajectories; the reported selector is calibrated using aggregate NAVTEST feedback.

figures.caption: Figure 2. The overall architecture of ActWorld-JEPA. The driving encoder extracts the current representation, and the planner produces candidate trajectories. PC-JEPA encodes global and step-wise plan conditions, initializes plan-modulated latents, and rolls out candidatespecific futures. Cross-attention and gated residual interaction fuse predicted future evidence with the current scene. R3 combines plan and fused-future features to rank the original candidates. The rightmost trajectory panel illustrates future-guided selection.
Figure 4. Qualitative comparison of trajectory selection by Drive-JEPA (top) and ActWorld-JEPA (bottom) across five challenging driving scenarios. Selected trajectories are shown in red.

(b) Drive-JEPA [50] combines video-JEPA representations with multimodal trajectory distillation and momentum-aware selection. (c) ActWorld-JEPA conditions latent prediction on candidate plans and relates the predicted futures to trajectory ranking through PC-JEPA and R3. Both observed scene context and candidate intention contribute to the decision. (d) Planning performance. PDMS on NAVSIM v1 navtest [10], comparing ActWorld-JEPA with Epona [65], DiffusionDrive [30], DIVER [43], GraphWorld [45], GoalFlow [57], DriveFuture [16], and Drive-JEPA [50].

(b) Future-consistent candidate ranking gates the bounded correction, adds the baseline score bkt , and selects an original trajectory. papers.title: ActWorld-JEPA: Action-Conditioned JEPA World Models Meet Latent Planning for End-to-End Autonomous Driving

papers.abstract: Physical AI aims to learn transferable physical knowledge from real-world experience to understand, predict, and act in the physical world. Internet videos and embodied demonstrations provide complementary observations of motion, interaction, and state evolution. A foundational data challenge is to measure and preserve this physical information as training supervision. In video-language pretraining, captions express observed processes in language, yet a semantically correct description can omit the interactions and transitions that define those processes. Rich physical experience in video does not automatically translate into sufficient language supervision. This gap calls for a yardstick to assess annotation quality, compare captioning strategies, and guide training-data refinement. Motivated by our data construction for world-model pretraining, we introduce PhysCapBench, to our knowledge the first unified physical-caption benchmark spanning all three domains: third-person scenes, egocentric manipulation, and handheld-gripper demonstrations. It provides human-verified annotations for 1,500 video sequences and evaluates accuracy and coverage through seven physical dimensions. We examine downstream utility through video reconstruction and manipulation-policy fine-tuning. Physical captions reduce reconstruction LPIPS by 8.6-9.5% on third-person videos and 26.9-30.9% on egocentric videos relative to metadata captions. Training-instruction enrichment improves both PhysCapBench scores and policy success, including a 7.5-percentage-point gain for pi0.5 on a RoboTwin 2.0 subtask. PhysCapBench makes the physical content of language supervision inspectable and comparable, providing a cross-domain basis for its evaluation and improvement.

papers.abstract: Accurate forecasting of Earth's dynamic systems is vital in geophysics, where neural operators offer a powerful data-driven paradigm. Standard operators often treat the Earth as a flat Euclidean plane, introducing geometric artifacts. In contrast, Spherical Neural Operators (SNOs) resolve this mismatch by operating within the spherical spectral space, naturally adapting to spherical geometries. However, for computational efficiency, existing SNOs typically rely on the rotation equivariance assumption. This assumption simplifies the transitions of physical states into isolated spectral modal evolutions, thereby over-idealizing the Earth as a homogeneous system. To solve this problem, we no longer rely on the rotation equivariance assumption that isolates spectral modal evolution, but directly derive an explicit modal interaction kernel and propose Diagonal Spherical Neural Operators named DIAGNO. DIAGNO explicitly parameterizes cross-modal interactions through spectral modal decomposition, thereby preserving the inherent heterogeneity of Earth dynamics. Furthermore, leveraging the unique diagonal structure of the spherical spectrum, we design inter- and intra-diagonal interaction mechanisms to natively capture essential zonal and meridional dynamics, respecting intrinsic geophysical regularities. Extensive experiments across simulated fluid dynamics and real-world Earth system reanalysis (including atmosphere and ocean) datasets demonstrate DIAGNO's superior capability, consistently achieving state-of-the-art performance in multi-step forecasting. Beyond this, we validate DIAGNO's practical analytical value in professional geophysical domains by assessing its fidelity in capturing climatological anomalies and maintaining physical consistency.

Also evaluates climatological-anomaly fidelity and physical consistency for practical geophysical analysis.

papers.abstract: Generating diverse robot videos requires control over scene geometry, robot motion, and viewpoints. End-to-end video generation offers limited direct access to these variables, making targeted edits and reuse across tasks difficult. We present BWM-Forge, a code-driven framework for controllable video generation in robotics. Given robot assets and a task description, the framework accepts an initial image, an image with motion data, or a human demonstration video. A coding agent constructs editable Blender scene programs that specify objects, robot motion, and cameras. The resulting proxy videos provide structural and motion references for a video generation model, which adds visual detail. A multi-agent harness coordinates input processing, scene construction, review, and rendering. Automated evaluation and user feedback support iterative refinement, while an experience repository stores and retrieves reusable modeling and rendering rules. This design supports multiple robot embodiments, synchronized viewpoints, and appearance variation from a shared scene program. We evaluate the framework on 15 tasks covering five robot types. Compared with LingBot-World Base Cam on these tasks, BWM-Forge achieves higher aesthetic quality, imaging quality, subject and background consistency, motion smoothness, and RoboJudge-9B physical adherence and instruction alignment scores. The baseline scores higher in dynamic degree. Qualitative cases illustrate viewpoint control, scene variation, feedback-driven edits, and experience reuse across scenes. These results demonstrate a practical approach to generating controllable robot videos through editable, executable scene representations.

papers.abstract: Multimodal coding agents decouple 4D world construction from visual generation, repurposing video models from world generators toward generative renderers. This division of labor raises a fundamental question: if code builds the world, can video models just render it? A reliable generative renderer hinges on two complementary criteria: (i) world preservation, retaining prescribed 4D kinematics and camera paths; and (ii) visual realization, persistently binding text-specified target attributes over time. To evaluate this capability, we introduce WorldDraft, a benchmark of $432$ strictly paired test cases across $48$ executable 4D world families spanning six dynamic challenge categories. Under a $3 \times 3$ factorial design, WorldDraft orthogonally crosses draft granularity (abstract proxy to previs) and appearance alignment (neutral to conflicting) under identical dynamics. Extensive evaluations across $12$ representative models reveal that: (I) world preservation and visual realization remain in stark operational tension; (II) richer draft scaffolding anchors structure but paradoxically impairs appearance fidelity; and (III) conflicting source cues trigger severe source leakage (up to $64\%$), exposing fragile cross-modal disentanglement. To mitigate these bottlenecks, we propose WorldDraft-Primer, a plug-and-play visual prompting strategy that consistently improves both objectives across frozen video renderers. Together, WorldDraft and WorldDraft-Primer lay a foundation for bridging programmatic 4D simulation with video generation, advancing physically grounded generative rendering.

papers.abstract: Particle-based volumetric flow measurement techniques have proven their efficacy in quantitatively assessing the dynamic characteristics of unsteady flows within the realm of fluid mechanics. Despite recent advances in multi-frame particle tracking, an open challenge in this area is maintaining trajectories in temporally under-sampled 3D sequences, where inter-frame displacements are large. In this work, we develop DiffTR-Flow3D, a diffusion-based model that estimates flow motion from spatiotemporal three-dimensional particle recordings via a stochastic diffusion process. DiffTR-Flow3D conditions the diffusion process with both global and local particle dynamics and enhances flow estimation by leveraging historical particle trajectories. Extensive experiments, including numerical simulations and real-world measurements, demonstrate that DiffTR-Flow3D achieves state-of-the-art displacement estimation accuracy compared with learning-based flow estimators, and, when integrated into particle tracking pipelines, substantially improves their long-term tracking performance, while exhibiting robustness and generalization across diverse flow patterns. This work is expected to provide fluid researchers with an effective tool for the consistent and precise analysis of particle trajectories in temporally under-sampled 3D sequences with large inter-frame displacements.

figures.caption: Fig. 1 Overview of DiffTR-Flow3D. a, Overview of the noise perturbation and reverse denoising processes in DiffTR-Flow3D. The forward diffusion process, q(d1:N |d0), progressively perturbs the flow motion structure d0 ∼ q(d) over N steps to approximate a Gaussian noise distribution. Conversely, the reverse process, pθ(dn−1|dn), iteratively eliminates Gaussian noise from the corrupted flow dN , thereby guiding particles toward their target destinations. b, The flow motion estimation pipeline in DiffTR-Flow3D. This module employs a two-stage flow motion estimator designed to handle diverse displacement distributions in particle dynamics. It first performs a coarse flow estimation between two point sets, followed by a refinement stage that eliminates position offsets using soft alignment operations to capture both local and global correlations. c, Illustration of the feature extraction pipeline in DiffTR-Flow3D. d, The workflow of motion estimation/refinement employed by DiffTR-Flow3D. e, Schematic of the multi-frame trajectory prediction scheme in DiffTR-Flow3D. This scheme first establishes particle trajectories via flow estimation over three consecutive timesteps. Subsequently, particle positions for the next timestep are predicted using temporal fitting functions derived from prior trajectory information. Finally, the proposed flow estimator calculates the residual motion, which is used to correct the trajectories.

papers.abstract: Turbulence modeling relies on human choices of closure form, physical inputs, and tunable parameters. Training closures a posteriori is efficient only with gradients through long chaotic rollouts, which few solvers provide. Most a posteriori approaches therefore resort to gradient-free optimization, and nearly all fix the closure form in advance, learning only its parameters. In this work, we introduce a gradient-aware agentic framework that poses closure discovery as a bilevel problem: a multi-agent large language model (LLM) system searches over closure forms, while a GPU-native differentiable computational fluid dynamics (CFD) solver supplies gradients, making differentiable a posteriori learning an action of the autonomous AI agent. For each proposal, the agents construct a differentiable training program by embedding the analytical, neural, or hybrid closure in the solver, implementing a differentiable objective, and validating the gradient path. They then decide whether to evaluate the closure, compute its parameter sensitivities, or train it a posteriori, select the optimization settings, and revise subsequent proposals using the simulation outcomes and returned gradients. Truncated-horizon gradients make this training usable under chaotic dynamics for closures with tens of thousands of parameters. Demonstrations include dissipation-law and subgrid-scale closure discovery in two-dimensional turbulence and wall-model discovery for large-eddy simulation of three-dimensional channel flow. With gradient-based training, the agent recovers reference coefficients that forward evaluation alone does not reach within the same budget, and autonomously discovers and trains analytical and neural closures that improve agreement with the targeted reference statistics. These results demonstrate the feasibility of end-to-end autonomous turbulence model development in time-resolved flows.
authors: Yi Liu, Xiantao Fan, Mingqi Xu, Jian-Xun Wang
bullets: Recasts turbulence-closure discovery as a bilevel search over closure forms and parameters.
Agents generate differentiable CFD training programs, validate gradient paths, choose evaluations or training actions, and revise proposals from simulation feedback.
Truncated-horizon gradients enable a posteriori training under chaotic dynamics, including closures with tens of thousands of parameters.
Demonstrations cover 2D turbulence dissipation and subgrid-scale closures, plus 3D channel-flow wall models.
The approach recovers reference coefficients and discovers analytical and neural closures with improved agreement to target statistics compared with forward evaluation alone under the same budget.

papers.abstract: Satellite constellations now image the Earth daily, capturing the lifecycle of events from deforestation to urban construction. Anticipating these events before completion enables timely intervention, yet existing systems cannot jointly identify where a change occurs, what it will become, and when it will finish across an open vocabulary. Building such a model requires diverse event data, but events are like needles in a haystack, making manual annotation at global scale infeasible. We address this problem by representing change as the vector difference between vision-language model embeddings at distinct time points. This arithmetic approach allows us to search for semantic transformations directly in the latent space, enabling (1) an automated data engine for global event discovery without manual annotation and (2) the largest global satellite event dataset to our knowledge, comprising 21,000+ locations across 64+ event types with ~2M images from PlanetScope and Sentinel-2 spanning six continents, to train (3) a novel global-scale event anticipation model. Our model detects change with a 93.5% max F1 score, outperforms baselines 3.6x on predicted event retrieval, and forecasts completion dates with a 3-day median error, even nine months before completion. Code: https://github.com/ShreelekhaR/predicting-the-needle
authors: Shreelekha Revankar, Mikhail Klassen, Creon Levit, Ash Hoover, Kavita Bala, Bharath Hariharan
bullets: Targets the challenge of identifying where change occurs, what it becomes, and when it finishes across diverse event types.

Introduces a dataset with 21,000+ locations, 64+ event types, and approximately 2 million satellite images across six continents.
The resulting model achieves 93.5% maximum F1, 3.6× stronger predicted-event retrieval than baselines, and 3-day median completion-date error up to nine months ahead.

papers.abstract: Autonomous navigation of mobile robots in crowded environments, while preserving pedestrians' psychological comfort, requires distinguishing pedestrians from other obstacles, predicting their future motion, and accounting for uncertainty in the predicted trajectories of both pedestrians and the robot. This work extends a previous MPC framework by integrating obstacle and pedestrian detection, Koopman-based motion prediction, and online prediction-error estimation directly within the collision-avoidance mechanism. To reduce collision-avoidance complexity in crowded scenarios, nearby obstacles are aggregated, thereby reducing the number of collision-avoidance constraints. Simulation studies evaluate the prediction-error margins and the computational benefits of semantics-aware aggregation. In a paired 300-seed closed-loop comparison with a moving generic obstacle, Markov residual tightening reduces the fraction of runs with physical contact from $10.0\%$ to $1.33\%$, at a mean travel-time cost of $0.68$ s. In a separate crowd-navigation semantic ablation, the offline robot-footprint/personal-space overlap occupies $2.11\%$ of observed time with pedestrian-aware handling versus $22.84\%$ with generic-obstacle handling.

In a 300-seed comparison, Markov residual tightening reduced physical-contact runs from 10.0% to 1.33%, with a mean travel-time cost of 0.68 s.
Pedestrian-aware handling reduced offline robot-footprint/personal-space overlap from 22.84% to 2.11% versus generic-obstacle handling.

papers.abstract: Parameterized-action MDPs (PAMDPs) ask an agent to choose a discrete action together with continuous parameters whose meaning depends on that choice. Model-free PAMDP methods act fast but need many interactions; model-based methods are sample-efficient but plan at every decision, which makes them slow to act. We introduce HyLI (Hybrid Latent Imagination), a model-based agent that learns a hybrid policy entirely in the latent imagination of a world model and acts with a single forward pass. To address learning problems that the PAMDP structure creates, HyLI adds counterfactual mode evaluation, which gives every discrete action a learning signal at every imagined state, and success-window replay, which keeps rare successes in training. On seven standard PAMDP benchmarks, HyLI is within one published standard deviation of, or above, the published score of the strongest model-free baseline in our comparison on all 7 tasks, reaches 90% of that score with 2.4x fewer environment steps than that baseline (5.0x when its reward-free pre-training is counted), and decides 67x faster than the model-based planner DLPA at its published planner settings. It is the only method in our comparison that is both more sample-efficient than that baseline and fast enough for real-time control.
authors: Atahan Cilan, \.Ihsan Mert Muhac{\i}ro\u{g}lu, \"Umit Can Bekar
bullets: Addresses the trade-off between fast but data-hungry model-free methods and slow model-based planners.
Learns a hybrid policy entirely through latent imagination in a learned world model.
Uses counterfactual mode evaluation to train every discrete action and success-window replay to preserve rare successes.
Across seven benchmarks, matches or exceeds the strongest compared model-free baseline’s published score on all tasks.
Reaches 90% of that baseline’s score with 2.4× fewer environment steps and decides 67× faster than the DLPA planner under its published settings.

papers.abstract: In active object search, a robot must decide where to look and when to stop. Imperfect detection complicates both decisions: a non-detection may indicate occlusion, an out-of-view target, or a false negative, while a detection may be a false positive. This raises the question of which representations a world model needs to support reliable search under imperfect detection. We introduce Bayesian Active Miss-aware Object Search (BAMOS) to investigate how target belief, occupancy belief, and detector errors affect search decisions. Through comprehensive ablations in Isaac Sim and HSSD houses, we examine the roles of these representations and their update mechanisms across different detector configurations. Notably, target belief and its update mechanisms are critical to search performance, with their contribution generally increasing as detection errors become more prevalent. These findings highlight the importance of maintaining and updating target beliefs to support reliable active search under uncertain detector observations, providing insights into the design of world models for embodied agents. Code is available in https://github.com/gokyeongryeol/BAMOS.
bullets: Imperfect detections make both search-location and stopping decisions uncertain.
The method models target belief, occupancy belief, and detector errors in a Bayesian active-search framework.
Ablations in Isaac Sim and HSSD houses evaluate these representations and their update mechanisms across detector configurations.
Target belief and its updates are critical, especially as false detections and missed detections become more prevalent.
The work informs world-model design for embodied agents operating under uncertain observations.

papers.abstract: Multiplayer generative world models must produce observations that agree on shared entities despite different camera motions and occlusions. Explicit world representations provide spatial control, but precise modeling of individual game maps limits scene diversity, while shared geometry alone cannot ensure consistent appearance across views. We present CoCode-World, a shared 3D proxy framework that separates structural control from visual synthesis for two-player video generation. Programmable proxies specify scene layout, motion, and occlusion, while RGB references guide character and scene appearance. To coordinate visual details across players, we concatenate paired proxy videos, appearance references, and target views in a consistent spatial layout and generate both views jointly with a pretrained video model. This formulation uses the model's native attention for cross-view communication within a single generation branch, with LoRA adaptation learning proxy adherence and appearance correspondence from paired observations. We construct a two-player GTA~V dataset that pairs synchronized RGB observations with proxy videos derived from shared map geometry and game-engine state. Experiments demonstrate appearance transfer to characters and scene styles unseen during training, with improvements in video quality and cross-view player identity over the evaluated baseline. Ablations further examine how proxy construction and cross-view communication affect generation. Project page: https://iapple233.github.io/CCW/.

bullets: Addresses inconsistent shared entities caused by different camera motions and occlusions in multiplayer world models.
Uses programmable 3D proxies for scene layout, motion, and occlusion, while RGB references control character and scene appearance.
Generates both player views jointly by concatenating proxy videos, references, and target views, enabling native attention-based cross-view communication.
Applies LoRA adaptation to improve proxy adherence and appearance correspondence from paired observations.

On a two-player GTA V dataset, transfers unseen character and scene styles and improves video quality and cross-view player identity over the evaluated baseline; ablations study proxy design and communication.

papers.abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) can improve robot learning by jointly predicting future visual states and actions, but generating a visual future at every replanning step is expensive and sometimes unnecessary. This raises a critical question: when should a robot policy imagine the future? In this paper, we propose Bind-WAM, a binding-uncertainty-guided WAM for selective future imagination. Bind-WAM introduces language-object binding uncertainty, selectively invoking joint future-action generation when the current observation does not support stable task-relevant action generation. An offline labeling pipeline uses complete demonstrations and action context to identify task-relevant objects and detect reference mismatch, invisibility, and identity drift. The resulting pseudo-labels supervise a lightweight router that predicts binding uncertainty from the current observation and language instruction. At inference, a shared WAM policy invokes selective future imagination according to the predicted uncertainty and its change between consecutive replanning steps. Simulation and real-world experiments demonstrate that Bind-WAM can establish binding uncertainty as a strong, interpretable signal for selective future imagination.
authors: Chenhao Qiu, Shuyi Chen, Songen Gu, Shufeng Nan, Tianyu Wang, Siyu Lin, Yifan Li, Bingwen Zhu, Yanwei Fu
bullets: Addresses the high cost and unnecessary use of generating visual futures at every replanning step in World Action Models.
Uses offline demonstrations and action context to label task-relevant objects and detect reference mismatch, invisibility, and identity drift.
Trains a lightweight router to predict binding uncertainty from the current observation and language instruction.
A shared WAM policy triggers future imagination based on predicted uncertainty and its change across replanning steps.
Simulation and real-world experiments support binding uncertainty as an interpretable signal for selective imagination.

papers.title: Bind-WAM: Binding-Uncertainty-Guided Selective Future Imagination in World Action Models

papers.abstract: In robotics and embodied AI, a core challenge for world models is adapting to sudden, persistent, yet initially unknown changes in robot dynamics during interaction. For instance, when a robotic arm grasps an object with an unknown payload, the robot dynamics change suddenly. If the world model fails to adapt, its prediction errors accumulate over the open-loop rollout and ultimately mislead the robot's actions. Existing world models, however, struggle to simultaneously satisfy three critical requirements for dynamics adaptation: responsiveness, reacting promptly to sudden changes to curb prediction error accumulation; stability, distinguishing persistent changes from transient disturbances to prevent incorrect updates; and persistence, retaining the adapted dynamics without new observations so that later predictions do not revert to the old dynamics. Inspired by predictive coding in the human brain with multi-timescale adaptation, we propose AFTER-WM, a world model with Adaptive Fast-slow Timescales for Error-driven Retention, whose prediction errors drive a fast correction that fades and a slow correction that persists, while dynamically adjusting the combination weights of pre-trained experts without altering them, to overcome the trade-offs among responsiveness, stability and persistence. On five simulated robot datasets and real UAV data, AFTER-WM has a lower multi-step mean error than all ten compared models and the highest mean return in a joint-failure control task. In simulation, its multistep mean error is 16%-34% below the strongest compared model's and is also the lowest 1-4 steps after a change and under transient disturbances alone, and its step-40 error is the lowest as well, reflecting responsiveness, stability and persistence. All code (method, baselines, experiments) and datasets will be released online.
authors: Haoyi Zhang, Qi Zhang, Yunfan Ren, Yi Bin, Lei Zhu, Heng Tao Shen
bullets: Targets world-model failures when robot dynamics change unexpectedly, such as after grasping an unknown payload.
Uses a fast correction for prompt adaptation and a slow correction for retained dynamics, with prediction errors driving both.
Dynamically reweights pretrained experts without modifying their parameters.
Evaluated on five simulated robot datasets and real UAV data, achieving lower multi-step mean error than ten compared models and the highest mean return in a joint-failure control task.
Reported gains cover early adaptation, transient disturbances, and long-horizon retention; code and datasets are planned for release.

papers.abstract: Multivariate time series forecasting often improves the prediction of a target by modeling the interactions among variables, and cross-variable modules such as cross-sectional pooling, inter-variable attention, and graph structures are used to construct such interactions. However, by intervening on the cross-variable reading of existing models at inference time, we find that although these models substantially reduce forecasting error through cross-variable interaction, their reading is nearly identical for all targets: the gain appears to come from dependencies among variables but mainly comes from the common component. We term this phenomenon spurious dependency and attribute it to common-component confounding: present in every variable, the common component affects how reading distinguishes sources, so that reading tends to be shared across targets and concentrates on a few similar averages; dependencies thus make up a small share of the read-in content, and a common component composed of several drivers is only partly captured. Theoretical analysis further shows that the common component and dependencies place different requirements on reading and should therefore be handled in different ways. Accordingly, we propose PRELUDE, a separated-reading framework that estimates the common component holistically through cross-sectional pooling and multiple common factors, and reads dependencies for each target via lead-lag relations in the innovation space obtained by prewhitening. Extensive experiments on 16 real-world datasets from four domains show that PRELUDE effectively mitigates spurious dependency and achieves the best overall performance: it attains the best MSE on 23 of the 24 short-horizon and air-quality settings and reduces the average MSE by 6.1% relative to the strongest baseline.
authors: Dongqing Song, Jianyu Xu, Haobin Ding, Xinyi Guo, Jiahao Du, Ruiqi He, Ruiqi Liu, Yuntong Xie, Chao He
bullets: Existing cross-variable models often improve forecasts through common components rather than truly target-specific dependencies, causing spurious dependency.
The framework models the common component holistically with cross-sectional pooling and multiple common factors.
It captures target-specific lead–lag dependencies in a prewhitened innovation space.
Across 16 real-world datasets from four domains, PRELUDE achieves the best MSE in 23 of 24 short-horizon and air-quality settings.
It reduces average MSE by 6.1% versus the strongest baseline.

papers.abstract: Conditional generative modeling with limited target data can benefit from representations learned in a related source population. We develop a transfer learning framework for conditional flow matching that accommodates distinct source and target response distributions and dimensions. Two procedures exploit a representation learned from source data: TFM-Freeze estimates a target velocity head with the representation fixed, whereas TFM-Adapt jointly learns the head and a representation adaptation under a functional anchoring penalty. For explicit neural network classes, we establish bounds on conditional squared Wasserstein risk that account for source estimation, target fitting, representation mismatch, and numerical integration. When the source representation admits a smooth correction, adaptation replaces the frozen mismatch contribution by the cost of learning the correction and a controllable regularization bias. An information lower bound identifies regimes in which adaptation attains a strictly faster conditional squared Wasserstein risk rate than any generator restricted to the frozen context information. We also develop independent validation procedure for selecting among fitted conditional generators. We show that the selection procedure satisfies an oracle inequality, and the switching rule guarantees, with high probability, no increase in conditional energy risk relative to a target-only generator. Simulations and real data applications illustrate the gains from our proposed methods and the effectiveness of target validation in guarding against negative transfer.
bullets: Addresses conditional generative modeling when target data are scarce and source and target response spaces may differ.
TFM-Freeze estimates a target velocity head while keeping the source representation fixed; TFM-Adapt jointly learns the head and a regularized representation correction.
Derives conditional squared Wasserstein risk bounds covering source estimation, target fitting, representation mismatch, and numerical integration.
Shows adaptation can achieve faster risk rates than generators limited to frozen context information when the source representation has a smooth correction.

A target-validation and switching procedure has an oracle guarantee and can avoid increasing conditional energy risk relative to a target-only generator; simulations and real-data applications demonstrate practical gains.

papers.abstract: In this report, we introduce the Reciprocal World Model (RWM) and present Duo v1, a full-duplex world model that continuously perceives audiovisual inputs while responding to users in real time. The RWM treats intelligence and physical reality as equally fundamental to what constitutes a world. Existing world models largely focus on simulating the latter, leaving reasoning and decision-making as external controls rather than intrinsic parts of the world itself. In RWM, we identify two equally fundamental capabilities: Intent, which provides the cognition underlying world interactions, and Realization, which generates coherent audio-visual behavior. To realize this formulation, Duo v1 introduces three key technical designs: (1) Leveraging autoregressive modeling for continuous interaction reasoning and participation decisions, rather than restricting it to instruction understanding for diffusion models. (2) Constructing chunk-specific conditions and synchronize tokens across Intent and Realization on a unified timeline. Module-specific attention masks enforce causal dependencies both within and across chunks, preventing access to future inputs. (3) Mitigating distribution shift in both modules through dual rollout distillation, training on autoregressively generated Intent tokens and synthesized audiovisual histories from Realization. Both modules continuously perceive real-time audio, video, and text, enabling full-duplex interaction with spontaneous conversations and interruptions. Beyond conversation, users can share real objects, reshape virtual scenes, guide assistants, or play audiovisual games without mouse or keyboard controls. The release of Duo v1 makes our first step, with the next version coming soon. We look forward to broader exploration of this emerging field.
authors: Hengyuan Cao, Biao Gong, Guoshan Lu, Qiyuan Zhang, Lin Liu, Yiding Tian, Yilei Jiang, Yuxin Ma, Chengzhang Wu, Kun Chen, Yiqian Xie, Ting Liu, Xin Zheng, Xijun Gu, Tianren Ma, Jiancheng Pan, Chi Zhang, Xuzhe Zheng, Siyi Li, Zhenzhong Lan
bullets: The Reciprocal World Model treats cognition and physical reality as equally fundamental components of an interactive world.
Its Intent module handles interaction reasoning and participation decisions, while Realization produces coherent audio-visual responses.
Chunk-specific conditions, synchronization tokens, and causal attention masks coordinate both modules without access to future inputs.
Dual rollout distillation reduces distribution shift by training on generated intent tokens and synthesized audiovisual histories.
Duo supports spontaneous conversation, interruptions, object sharing, virtual-scene manipulation, and audiovisual games without mouse or keyboard controls.

papers.abstract: Pretrained video world models are compared and chosen as components for robot learning largely by future-prediction scores. On its own, such a score cannot be read as evidence of prediction, because it mixes encoder quality, the near future's resemblance to the recent past, and the predictor's own contribution. We separate the three with a matched control. On 27,000 future-retrieval trials from household egocentric video, a model must pick the true continuation of a clip among eleven candidates from the same video (chance 0.091), ranked zero-shot by its own training criterion. Each model is paired with a persistence control, an identical copy whose predictor is never invoked, so the paired difference isolates the predictor. Score and contribution dissociate within the native-video V-JEPA family alone: the predictor adds +0.291 top-1 for V-JEPA 2.1 but +0.03 to +0.04 for V-JEPA 2 on the identical trials. Across five models the contribution ranges from +0.291 to negative, and it is negative only for the two action-conditioned models, which we evaluate outside their training regime. Persistence alone recovers the encoder ordering expected from pretraining, a sign that the probe tracks real signal. We suggest reporting each future-prediction score together with its persistence baseline. The gap between them, not the score, is what makes the number interpretable: a necessary check costing one forward pass. Establishing downstream usefulness is a separate matter, for a planning or control evaluation.
bullets: A matched control separates encoder quality, persistence of recent visual context, and the predictor’s contribution.
Across 27,000 household-video future-retrieval trials, models select the true continuation among 11 candidates.
Within V-JEPA, predictor gains vary substantially: +0.291 for V-JEPA 2.1 versus +0.03–+0.04 for V-JEPA 2.
Across five models, predictor contributions range from positive to negative; negative results occur for action-conditioned models tested outside their training regime.
The study recommends reporting the score gap from persistence; downstream planning or control usefulness requires separate evaluation.

papers.abstract: Modern machine learning models for global weather forecasting achieve remarkable predictive accuracy, yet they frequently produce states that violate fundamental physical laws, including conservation of mass, hydrostatic balance, or spectral energy scaling. We term these outputs physical hallucinations and propose PhysXAI, a rigorous diagnostic framework that detects, localises, and attributes such inconsistencies. Unlike existing post-hoc metric suites, PhysXAI is a learnable system that explicitly decouples forecast error from physical plausibility. We formalise the problem through a novel joint condition on numerical and physical residuals, and introduce a multi-branch encoder that extracts representations from conservation, dynamical, spectral, cross-variable, and spatiotemporal residuals. A key innovation is a physics-consistency contrastive learning objective, which we theoretically show the latent representation to be approximately isometric to the physical residual space, ensuring that diagnostic decisions remain grounded in physically meaningful deviations. We further derive an adaptive multi-objective loss with gradient-based weighting to balance competing diagnostic objectives. The framework produces spatially resolved hallucination maps, violation-type classifications, and calibrated Bayesian uncertainty, enabling both detection and interpretable attribution of physical inconsistencies. We conduct a comprehensive comparative evaluation of PhysXAI across ERA5, WeatherBench 2, and MERRA-2, using forecasts from GraphCast, Pangu-Weather, and NeuralGCM, with Python-written code and a fully reproducible experimental protocol. Our theoretical analysis and empirical evaluation establish PhysXAI as a principled framework for diagnosing physical hallucinations and advancing trustworthy AI for weather forecasting.
bullets: Targets violations of mass conservation, hydrostatic balance, spectral energy scaling, and other physical constraints.
Decouples forecast-error assessment from physical plausibility using joint numerical–physical residual conditions.
Combines residual representations across conservation, dynamics, spectra, variables, and space–time with contrastive learning and adaptive multi-objective weighting.
Produces spatial hallucination maps, violation-type classifications, and calibrated Bayesian uncertainty for attribution.
Evaluated across ERA5, WeatherBench 2, and MERRA-2 forecasts from GraphCast, Pangu-Weather, and NeuralGCM; the abstract reports theoretical and empirical validation but no specific numerical results.

papers.abstract: Embodied world models (WMs) are implicit learning systems that predict the next future latent state directly from observations and actions. Unique from other end-to-end learning systems, the dynamics predictor of WMs can simulate the environment's response to alternative actions without physical deployment nor pre-specifying states of the dynamical system. Current metrics focus on the quality of model outputs, e.g., clarity of reconstructions or task success, but fail to assess the fidelity of modeling consequences of counterfactual actions. Inspecting the forced response to action perturbations through sensitivity analysis is one way to audit how well WMs can predict the consequences of counterfactual actions. Deploying WMs on hardware will require new evaluation frameworks to analyze the tradeoffs between state error and accurate sensitivity prediction.
authors: Ayush Gaggar, Jared Berry, Todd D. Murphey
bullets: Existing metrics overlook fidelity to counterfactual action consequences.
Sensitivity analysis can audit model responses to perturbed actions.
Evaluation should assess the tradeoff between state-prediction error and sensitivity accuracy.
The framework is motivated by reliable deployment of world models on physical hardware.

figures.caption: Figure 4: Designing world models will often involve a tradeoff between low state error and low error in predicted action sensitivity. For four example scenarios: a) Structured environments, like open-loop pick and place, only require low state error. b) High accuracy in both action sensitivity and state prediction is only possible when robot motion can be modeled and is repeatable. c) Poor performance in both dimensions is acceptable with effectively unlimited time and compute for non-critical tasks. d) Action sensitivity is more relevant than state error in unstructured, unknown environments, where environmental uncertainty dominates error.

papers.abstract: Reference capacitively coupled plasma (CCP) simulations provide spatially resolved plasma fields but are costly to generate across operating conditions. We compare the data efficiency of five surrogate architectures--Coordinate MLP, PCA-Net, U-Net, Fourier neural operator (FNO), and Transolver--for predicting RF-cycle-averaged electron density, ion density, electric potential, and electron temperature in 1D planar and 2D axisymmetric GEC CCP benchmarks. We assess the number of reference simulations needed to achieve 1% and 2% mean relative L2 error for parameter-interior and parameter-boundary test cases, and examine architecture-specific mechanisms. FNO achieves the lowest or joint-lowest reference-case requirement in seven of eight comparisons. In 1D, FNO reaches 1% interior error with 50 training cases, compared with 100 for Transolver and 200 for U-Net. In 2D, FNO and U-Net each reach 1% interior error with 100 cases; FNO and Transolver each reach 2% parameter-boundary error with 200 cases, compared with 400 for U-Net. At the stricter 1% 2D parameter-boundary target, Transolver requires 400 cases versus 800 for FNO. Additional analyses investigate FNO spectral modes and padding, U-Net skip connections, Transolver adaptive slicing, and PCA-Net projection versus prediction error. The results support FNO as a data-efficient baseline for the tested CCP settings, while showing that the preferred architecture depends on the accuracy target and operating-parameter region.
authors: Zhenyu Zou, Junjue Liao, Hao Yang, Luowei Yin, Chenyu Wang, Yufeng Wei, Zhichao Peng, Chun Chen, Daniel Zhengyu Huang, Kangxin Liu, Haoran Guan, Rubing Han, Yipei Chen, Peiting You, Yuwei Fan
bullets: Five architectures are compared for predicting RF-cycle-averaged electron density, ion density, electric potential, and electron temperature in 1D and 2D CCP benchmarks.
Data efficiency is evaluated by the number of reference simulations needed to reach 1% or 2% mean relative L2 error for interior and boundary parameter cases.
FNO requires the fewest or tied-fewest reference cases in seven of eight comparisons.
In 1D, FNO reaches 1% interior error with 50 cases; in 2D, FNO and U-Net reach it with 100 cases.
For the strictest 1% 2D boundary target, Transolver needs 400 cases versus 800 for FNO, highlighting target- and region-dependent trade-offs.

papers.selection_reason: Evaluates data-efficient surrogate models (FNOs) for predicting plasma physics fields, directly relevant to world models (predicting environment dynamics) and efficient AI (data efficiency).
papers.title: AI4Plasma I: Data-Efficient Surrogate Modeling of Capacitively Coupled Plasma Fields

papers.abstract: Autonomous cyber defense is widely studied with deep reinforcement learning, but most work trains policies inside simulators because learning requires many trial-and-error interactions. Simulator-based training carries a fidelity gap: trained policies face authentication delays, partial action failures, service dependencies, and user traffic patterns that the simulator did not represent, and degrade on transfer. Training directly in the network being defended removes the gap but makes every interaction slow and costly, so sample efficiency becomes the binding constraint. Model-based reinforcement learning has reduced sample requirements on games and physical robots by orders of magnitude by planning inside a learned world model, but it has not been applied to defenders trained in operational networks. We present FOE-Dreamer (Factored Opponent-Enhanced Dreamer), a model-based reinforcement learning framework that trains a defender online and directly in a network on cloud infrastructure, without a simulator stage. FOE-Dreamer separates three sources of variation in the latent state: a controllable component driven by defender actions, an exogenous component driven by benign user activity, and an opponent embedding inferred from defender-observable signals alone. Separating the components reduces the variance in policy gradients during planning in imagination. Against two scripted attacker profiles with user activity emulated by the GHOSTS framework on an 8-host OpenStack testbed, FOE-Dreamer trains within a 3-day budget on a single GPU and achieves about 2$\times$ better episode loss than Rainbow and IQN baselines under matched compute. Both the factoring and the opponent model contribute to the gain, and the learned latents are consistent with the intended separation.
bullets: Addresses the simulator-to-network fidelity gap while avoiding the high interaction cost of online training.
Separates latent state variation into defender-controllable, benign-user, and opponent-related components.
Infers the opponent component only from signals observable to the defender and uses the model for imagined planning.
On an 8-host OpenStack testbed with two scripted attackers, it trained within a 3-day single-GPU budget.
Achieved about 2× better episode loss than Rainbow and IQN under matched compute; both factoring and opponent modeling contributed.

papers.abstract: Driving world models aim to simulate how a scene unfolds under different ego actions. This requires plausible motion of surrounding vehicles as well as precise ego-trajectory control. Learning vehicle motion from perspective video alone is challenging because motion is entangled with appearance and vehicles can be occluded. Prior work therefore conditions video generation on layouts that specify vehicle motion, providing control over surrounding vehicles but requiring their future trajectories as inputs. We introduce BirdDreams, an autoregressive driving world model that jointly generates perspective video and a schematic bird's-eye-view (BEV) video, making scene layout part of the predicted future. The BEV, rendered from scene annotations for training, depicts roads and vehicles as simple shapes at a fixed metric scale, providing a top-down view of their positions and motion with reduced occlusion between vehicles. Perspective video, by contrast, retains scene details that the BEV omits, such as traffic signals and object appearance. Joint attention between two video diffusion transformers, one per stream, lets each stream inform the other during generation. The predicted BEV also provides a geometric interface for ego control: we translate and rotate its latest frame along an input ego trajectory and use the resulting frames as a soft condition that shows how the scene would appear to move if only the ego vehicle moved. At inference, BirdDreams generates both videos from a single camera image without requiring an HD map or vehicle-state inputs. On PhysicalAI-AV and nuScenes, BirdDreams follows input ego trajectories more faithfully than prior driving world models and generates more plausible ego motion without ego-action conditioning. Human evaluation shows that BirdDreams outperforms a perspective-only baseline in generating realistic surrounding-vehicle behavior.
authors: Junyoung Seo, Jaewoo Seo, Seungryong Kim, Laura Leal-Taix\'e, Xiuming Zhang, Seung Wook Kim
bullets: Addresses the challenge of modeling surrounding-vehicle motion and precise ego control from perspective video, where appearance and occlusion confound motion learning.
Uses two autoregressive video diffusion transformers with joint attention: one generates detailed perspective video, while the other generates a metric-scale schematic BEV video.
Uses the predicted BEV as a geometric interface for ego control by transforming its latest frame along a requested ego trajectory as a soft condition.
At inference, requires neither an HD map nor vehicle-state inputs.

On PhysicalAI-AV and nuScenes, it follows ego trajectories more faithfully, produces more plausible ego motion without ego-action conditioning, and improves surrounding-vehicle realism in human evaluation versus a perspective-only baseline.

papers.abstract: Regular time-series generation from irregular time series is typically reduced to one-shot imputation: complete each partial sequence once, freeze the completions, and train a generator on the resulting surrogate dataset. We show that this open-loop strategy is structurally flawed. Point imputers collapse ambiguous missing regions to conditional averages, while stochastic imputers become stale as the generator evolves; the binding constraint is therefore iteration, not imputer design. We introduce a co-evolving Monte Carlo EM framework that closes the imputer-generator loop. Each E-step samples missing values from the posterior of the current generator, and each M-step retrains the generator on these completions, preserving unconditional generator training. Since our diffusion prior operates in a lifted 2D representation while observations live in time-series space, we further introduce Posterior Sampling for Lifted Representations (PSLR), which enforces operator-consistent conditioning, uncertainty preservation, and manifold consistency during the E-step. Across ten datasets and four corruption regimes, our method achieves state-of-the-art performance, improving over the strongest baselines by 59% in discriminative score, 15% in predictive score, 73% in Context-FID, and 71% in feature-correlation error. Ablations show that our approach reduces average discriminative score by 73% over single-step baselines, closing most of the remaining gap to the clean-data oracle. Code is available at https://github.com/azencot-group/PSLR.
authors: Idan Arbiv, Gal Fadlon, Omri Azencot
bullets: Open-loop one-shot imputation is flawed because deterministic imputations collapse ambiguity and stochastic imputations become stale as the generator changes.
The method alternates posterior sampling of missing values with generator retraining, preserving unconditional generator training.
Posterior Sampling for Lifted Representations (PSLR) enforces consistent conditioning, uncertainty preservation, and manifold consistency between lifted and time-series spaces.
Across ten datasets and four corruption regimes, it reports substantial improvements over the strongest baselines across discriminative, predictive, Context-FID, and feature-correlation metrics.
Ablations indicate that co-evolution closes most of the gap to a clean-data oracle.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overview of our framework. We initialize a generator from a simple decomposition of irregular time series, then refine it via a co-evolving Monte Carlo EM (MCEM) loop that alternates between posterior sampling (E-step) and generator updates (M-step). Posterior Sampling for Lifted Representations (PSLR) enables conditioning in the lifted space by iteratively denoising and correcting samples to match the observations.

papers.selection_reason: Develops a co-evolving Monte Carlo EM framework for irregular time series generation using a diffusion prior in lifted representations. This learns and generates future temporal dynamics, fitting the video world models category.
papers.title: Closing the Loop: Co-Evolving EM for Irregular Time Series Generation in Lifted Representations
papers.tldr: A co-evolving Monte Carlo EM framework jointly imputes missing values and trains a generator, enabling high-quality regular time-series generation from irregular observations.

papers.abstract: World action models (WAMs) have emerged as a promising paradigm for robotic manipulation. They act by first predicting how a task should be performed and then decoding the actions from that future. However, the remaining actions are invalid once execution drifts from the prediction. Simply replanning from the already out of distribution state rarely restores what the task still requires; existing execution monitors decide when to stop, but not what to restore. We observe that the answer is already in hand: the future the WAM predicted before acting depicts exactly the states it intended to pass through. We introduce FAVOR (Future Anchored Verification and Online Recovery), a lightweight framework that keeps these predicted frames as anchors and uses them for verification and recovery. An Anchor Verifier compares each observation with its anchor, together with the executed actions, to flag deviations that break the task. Anchor-Guided Recovery uses a vision-language model to turn the flagged anchor into a short corrective instruction. Under strengthened instruction guidance, the WAM executes this instruction to return to the intended future. It then resumes the task. FAVOR raises the task success of the base WAM from 97.85% to 98.10% on LIBERO and from 72.60% to 72.98% on LIBERO-Plus without modifying the policy.
bullets: Addresses the problem that execution drift invalidates remaining actions and replanning from the deviated state may not restore task progress.
Stores the WAM’s predicted future frames as anchors for monitoring and recovery.
An Anchor Verifier compares observations and executed actions against anchors to identify task-breaking deviations.
A vision-language model converts flagged anchors into corrective instructions, after which the WAM resumes execution.
Improves success from 97.85% to 98.10% on LIBERO and from 72.60% to 72.98% on LIBERO-Plus without changing the policy.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of FAVOR. (a) The frozen WAM predicts future frames and the IDM decodes an action chunk; the predicted frames are retained as anchors. Every ∆ steps, the verifier compares the observation with its anchor: a pass continues execution, and the failure interrupts the remaining actions and triggers recovery. (b) The Anchor Verifier encodes the prediction–observation pair with DINO, fuses it with action and horizon embeddings, and outputs a failure score through a causal GRU; an alarm is raised when the score exceeds τ . (c) Anchor-Guided Recovery: a VLM reads the alarmed anchor, the current observation, and the task, and issues a corrective instruction.
Figure 3: Effect of the guidance scale on recovery predictions. All branches start from the same trigger state and the corrective instruction “pick up the cup”.

Figure 4: Qualitative examples of Anchor-Guided Recovery on LIBERO. In each case, the top row shows the observed execution and the bottom row the WAM’s retained prediction up to the alarm (orange frame); red circles mark where the observation departs from its anchor. Right of the alarm, native continuation under the original instruction fails (top), while the corrective instruction issued by the VLM (green) restores the anchored condition and the task succeeds (bottom). Both branches start from the same simulator state at the alarm.
