papers.tldr: FAVOR improves world action model reliability by using predicted future states to detect execution drift and guide online recovery.

papers.abstract: Understanding 4D scenes is a core challenge in visual intelligence, requiring models to jointly capture scene geometry, appearance, and dynamics from partial observations. However, existing approaches are subdivided into feedforward models for direct geometric prediction, and generative models for visual synthesis. We introduce UGG, a unified framework for 4D scene understanding that jointly models RGB video and geometric representations such as depth and camera pose. By assigning different noise levels across modalities and time, UGG formulates visual generation and geometric prediction as conditional completion within a single generative model. This flexible formulation enables the model to learn from diverse, heterogeneous datasets with different subsets of geometric and visual annotations. Furthermore, our generative formulation enables inference-time search over multiple plausible scene hypotheses, using geometric evidence extracted from observed RGB frames to improve geometric prediction without ground truth geometry. We demonstrate UGG's effectiveness over non-unified baselines across camera-controlled video generation, depth estimation, and camera pose prediction, including in challenging sparse observation settings. Code and visualizations are available at https://ugg-model.github.io/
authors: Amani Kiruga, Zhiyi Li, Ruojin Cai, Hansen Lillemark, Xiaoshan Wu, Ayush Tewari, Yilun Du
bullets: Addresses the split between feedforward geometry predictors and generative visual models for partial 4D scene observations.
Uses modality- and time-dependent noise levels to jointly model video and geometric representations.
Learns from heterogeneous datasets with varying subsets of visual and geometric annotations.
Supports inference-time search over plausible scene hypotheses, using RGB-derived geometric evidence without ground-truth geometry.
Outperforms non-unified baselines across camera-controlled video generation, depth estimation, and camera pose prediction, including sparse-observation settings.

figures.caption: Figure 4: Qualitative comparison of camera-controlled generation. Figure 3: Conditional completion with noise as masking. We specify each task by the clean/noisy pattern over RGB, depth, camera-ray, and text tokens. Clean tokens provide observed context, while noisy tokens are denoised as missing targets, enabling generation and prediction with the same model architecture.

Figure 2: Generative-predictive transformer. We model RGB, depth, and camera pose as spatially aligned tokens, with camera pose represented as dense ray maps. Partial observations are zero-noise context tokens, while missing modalities are noisy tokens to be denoised. A unified transformer processes all tokens with modality-specific projections and feed-forward layers together with shared multimodal self-attention, enabling information exchange across modalities. The decoded RGB, depth, and ray maps form a complete 4D scene representation for cross-modal generation, geometric prediction, and inference-time consistency search.

papers.abstract: Video world models promise general-purpose interactive simulators, but their training is limited by action supervision: action labels are scarce, fragmented across incompatible specifications, and do not scale with the unlabeled video pretraining corpus. A common workaround jointly trains an action encoder to compress consecutive frames into a latent action and a decoder to reconstruct the next frame from the previous frame and that latent, forcing the latent to capture only new information. This has two limitations: learning the action space from scratch can limit generalization to unseen domains, and the bottleneck trades expressiveness for separation, with tighter settings losing nuance and looser ones risking scene leakage under domain shifts. We argue for a different starting point: rather than learning actions from scratch, we start from a pretrained foundation model (V-JEPA 2), whose embeddings of a frame pair already carry substantial action information after large-scale, diverse video pretraining. The remaining challenge is to extract the action while discarding the scene. We propose a label-free contrastive adaptation framework that pulls together frame pairs sharing the same motion under a different scene and pushes apart pairs from the same scene with different motion, reshaping the geometry of the pretrained space without imposing a reconstruction bottleneck. We introduce a unified evaluation protocol along three axes (action expressiveness, scene invariance, and action-conditioned video generation quality) across robot manipulation, camera navigation, game, and driving benchmarks, most of which are unseen during adaptation. Compared with annotation-free latent-action methods, our representations are substantially more expressive while matching their scene invariance, and they yield world models that transfer demonstrated actions to new scenes more faithfully.
authors: Runjia Li, Minghao Chen, Junyu Xie, Philip Torr, Andrea Vedaldi, Tomas Jakab
bullets: Addresses scarce, fragmented action supervision in video world-model training.
Starts from V-JEPA 2 frame-pair embeddings instead of learning an action space from scratch.
Uses label-free contrastive adaptation: matches similar motion across scenes and separates different motion within a scene.
Evaluates action expressiveness, scene invariance, and action-conditioned generation across robotics, navigation, games, and driving.
Reports more expressive representations with comparable scene invariance and better transfer of actions to new scenes than annotation-free latent-action methods.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of the proposed learning pipeline. Left: Contrastive action adaptation. An anchor frame pair (ot, ot+k) is encoded as a two-frame clip by the OnlyAct encoder ϕθ, a pretrained foundation model with low-rank adapters whose weights are shared across all branches. The positive keeps the action but changes the scene: the moving region of the anchor, found by optical flow, is cut out and pasted at a shifted location onto the background of a different scene (for moving cameras, a different photometric augmentation of the anchor is used instead). The hard negative is drawn from a non-overlapping window (ot′ , ot′+k) of the same video, sharing the scene but corresponding to a different action. In the action space, the anchor is pulled towards its positive and pushed away from its hard negative. Right: Action-conditioned video world model. The frozen OnlyAct encoder ϕθ maps consecutive frame pairs into the learned action space, yielding an action stream α1:t that conditions an autoregressive video world model Gψ. Given past frames o1:t and the action stream, Gψ predicts the next frame ot+1, and is rolled out autoregressively to generate subsequent frames.

Figure 6: Additional action-transfer results. Latent actions extracted from the demonstration frames (top) condition the video world model generations (bottom). OnlyAct reproduces the demonstrated actions across various settings. Best seen as videos in the supplementary material which also includes more examples.

Figure 3: Two control modes. After pretraining the video world model on latent actions from the OnlyAct encoder, the learned action space supports two modes. First, action transfer extracts an action stream from a demonstration video and uses it to condition the world model from a new initial frame, reproducing the demonstrated action with no labels. Second, real-action control learns a lightweight interface from real actions onto the learned latent-action space on a small action-labeled set, so that real actions drive the world model directly.

Figure 5: Action transfer. Latent actions extracted from the demonstration frames (top) condition the video world model generations (bottom). OnlyAct faithfully reproduces the demonstrated action in the new target scene, e.g. in the cross-source example it turns right and then performs the attack action. Best seen as a video in the supplementary material.

Figure 4: Real-action control. Left: OnlyAct learns to generate videos that faithfully respond to different actions, Right: comparison of action representations between OnlyAct and AdaWorld using t-SNE.

Transfer: a source clip’s actions drive a different scene; Dir↑ is the cosine between the optical-flow direction of the generated video and of the source (0: unrelated; 1: same). ◦Seen by our encoder without action labels. †Retrained on our data. ∆: ours minus the best baseline. Bold: best; underline: second best (no-action row excluded).

papers.selection_reason: Addresses the action supervision bottleneck in World Models by extracting action representations from a pretrained foundation model (V-JEPA 2) via label-free contrastive adaptation. This is highly relevant to Latent Action Models and Multimodal Foundation Models.
papers.title: OnlyAct: Extracting Action Representations from Foundation Models for World Models
papers.tldr: OnlyAct adapts pretrained video representations into expressive, scene-invariant latent actions for more transferable video world models without action labels.

papers.abstract: Formal world models can support planning, verification, and safety reasoning, but constructing them from open-ended natural-language situations is difficult, particularly in multi-agent settings where several formalizations may be plausible. We study whether five LLMs can generate such world models as partially observable stochastic games and whether mechanical validity is sufficient to establish that the resulting model faithfully represents the intended decision problem. We introduce a benchmark of 44 scenarios spanning game, situational, and cultural settings and evaluate generated world models along three dimensions: mechanical validity, reference-relative structural agreement, and semantic criteria. Across three empirical tracks, we analyze 410 first-pass generations. In the reference-backed game track, 134/135 generated world models pass a strict mechanical audit, yet mean permutation-invariant structural F1 is only 0.366, with just 28/134 mechanically valid models exactly matching the authored reference. In the cultural track, explicitly naming the country changes the generated structural representation for most LLMs while producing only small changes in automated semantic scores. These results show that executability is a necessary but insufficient criterion for LLM-generated world models: models that are mechanically valid can still differ substantially in the structure used by downstream neuro-symbolic reasoning and planning.
authors: Souhaila Djaffal, Amna Jamal, Gagana Madhugiri Devaraja, Anidipta Pal, Jobst Heitzig
bullets: Evaluates five LLMs generating partially observable stochastic-game models from natural-language scenarios.
Introduces a 44-scenario benchmark covering game, situational, and cultural settings.
Assesses mechanical validity, reference-relative structural agreement, and semantic criteria across 410 generations.

papers.abstract: Pretrained video diffusion models (VDMs) offer a powerful foundation for World Action Models (WAMs), which jointly predict robot actions and future observations. Building such models requires injecting low-dimensional robot signals (e.g. proprioception, actions, and values) into a latent space shaped by natural videos, and a key design choice is the interface through which these signals enter: existing schemes treat it as a formatting detail, spending a separate latent frame on each signal or bolting on dedicated encoders and decoders. We argue that signal injection is instead a distribution-alignment problem: how well a representation matches the prior of the pretrained VDMs during denoising. Using the relative reconstruction error of a frozen VDM denoiser as a probe, we find that conventional spatial encodings sit far off this prior, whereas frequency-domain packing yields latents that the denoiser corrects far less. Motivated by this diagnostic result, we propose MetaWAM, which folds all robot signals into a single unified meta-frame: each signal is assigned to a disjoint frequency-domain channel band and lifted to the spatial latent by an inverse DCT, yielding a decodable interface aligned with the pretrained VDM prior without any added module or architectural change. A fixed band layout together with slot-aware routing lets the same meta-frame support policy, world-model, and value prediction over a shared set of robot variables. On RoboCasa, MetaWAM reaches 68.9% success while collapsing the per-signal frames into one and cutting inference latency by 39%, and attains 85.0% success on three real-world Franka tasks. Code and models are available at https://github.com/showlab/MetaWAM
authors: Guoqiang Liang, Yiqi Lin, Yanzhe Chen, Kevin Yuchen Ma, Mike Zheng Shou
bullets: Frames signal injection as a distribution-alignment problem rather than a formatting choice.
Uses frozen-denoiser reconstruction error to show frequency-domain encodings better match the pretrained video latent prior than conventional spatial encodings.
Packs proprioception, actions, and values into disjoint frequency bands, lifted by inverse DCT without adding modules or changing architecture.
Supports policy, world-model, and value prediction through a fixed band layout and slot-aware routing.
Reports 68.9% success on RoboCasa with 39% lower inference latency, and 85.0% success across three real-world Franka tasks.

papers.abstract: Generative driving planners can represent diverse ego futures, but a downstream scorer can choose only among sampled candidates; it cannot recover an absent maneuver. We present ForeseeDrive, which turns future scene evolution into a deployable interface for shaping candidate generation. Rather than reconstructing dense future states or scoring a fixed menu, ForeseeDrive derives query-indexed tokens from logged actor motion, occupancy evolution, route interactions, and TTC margins, and predicts the same token space from present context at deployment. The tokens condition trajectory geometry before candidates materialize. A zero-token-gated residual path and candidate-preservation loss limit unnecessary drift, while a TTC-margin guard targets brittle safe-to-unsafe boundary crossings. Under their respective benchmark protocols, ForeseeDrive reaches 89.2 PDMS on NAVSIM navtest, 0.41\,m average L2 and 0.05\% collision rate on nuScenes validation, and a 76.50 driving score on Bench2Drive. Controlled DiffusionDrive/NAVSIM diagnostics show an exact zero-token no-op, a small aligned-over-shuffled selected-PDM advantage under preservation, mixed oracle-best quality, and localized TTC-boundary failures. Together, the benchmark results and bounded mechanism tests support future-conditioned generation as a practical interface for anticipation. Code is included in the supplementary materials.
authors: Shaokai Wu, Xunchu Zhou, Pinzhi Wang, Bo Dong, Yuting Hu, Yanbiao Ji, Qiuchang Li, Xiao Cui, Qi Kong, Hongtao Lu, Yue Ding
bullets: Addresses a key limitation of candidate scoring: it cannot recover maneuvers absent from the sampled set.

Reports 89.2 PDMS on NAVSIM navtest, 0.41 m average L2 with 0.05% collisions on nuScenes validation, and a 76.50 driving score on Bench2Drive.
Diagnostics indicate an exact no-op without tokens, modest benefits from aligned token ordering, mixed oracle-best quality, and localized TTC-boundary failures.

papers.abstract: World-Action Models improve robot control by predicting future visual dynamics, but iterative video denoising incurs substantial inference overhead. Recent approaches reduce this cost through partial future denoising, yet typically rely on fixed refinement budgets. Our empirical observations reveal that preferred refinement depths vary across tasks and states, while different future regions exhibit varying relevance to action generation. Motivated by these findings, we propose Elastic-WAM, which adaptively allocates world refinement computation across temporal denoising time and spatial future space. A unified spatiotemporal refinement demand field governs when to stop world refinement, how far to advance each denoising step, and which regions to refresh. We parameterize this field with a shared temporal basis and spatial amplitudes, and learn it through a three-stage action-grounded supervised procedure. At inference, the learned field guides recurrent sparse world refinement to improve task success while reducing inference overhead. Evaluations across diverse simulation benchmarks and real-world long-horizon manipulation demonstrate state-of-the-art control performance with reduced inference latency.
authors: Haitian Li, Tianfu Li, Xuxi Zhao, Zizheng Liu, Yangcheng Yu, Yiwen Hou, Zeyu Xiao, Mutian Xu, Ziqian Yang, Haonan Chen, Lin Shao
bullets: Fixed denoising budgets fail to account for task-, state-, and region-dependent refinement needs.

Three-stage action-grounded supervision trains the refinement policy, which drives recurrent sparse refinement at inference.
Experiments in simulation and real-world long-horizon manipulation report state-of-the-art control with lower inference latency.

papers.abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) have recently emerged as a promising paradigm for robotic manipulation, endowing policies with strong capabilities for modeling temporal and physical dynamics. Existing WAMs, encompassing both video-first action prediction and joint video-action modeling, directly transfer global physical representations from world models to action generation. However, global scene representations may underemphasize local robot-object interactions, creating a mismatch between representations optimized for world evolution and those required for manipulation. To bridge this gap, we propose LaST0.5, a novel WAM that introduces an interaction-centric physical representation between world modeling and action generation. Specifically, LaST0.5 learns a compact interaction-centric latent space under the supervision of visual interaction cues between the robot and the environment. This reasoning space is instantiated as a latent expert that bridges the world expert and the action expert within a Mixture-of-Transformers architecture. Furthermore, LaST0.5 performs adaptive world-to-action transfer by jointly predicting future representations and progress values, using progress consistency to adjust action execution and trigger future resampling. Finally, we pretrain LaST0.5 on a large-scale robotic data corpus comprising over 14k hours of data, establishing interaction-centric physical reasoning as a scalable and effective paradigm. LaST0.5 achieves 99.5% on LIBERO, surpasses the previous state of the art on ten evaluated RLBench tasks, and demonstrates robust long-horizon execution and precise dexterous manipulation in real-world experiments.
authors: Xuheng Zhang, Yiming Zhang, Jialin Gao, Hao Chen, Jiaming Liu, Ji Li, Runzhong Huang, Yinxi Wang, Chenyang Gu, Zihan Yang, Yaowei Liu, Zhonghao Yan, Ziyu Guo, Renrui Zhang, Peng Jia, Pheng-Ann Heng, Shanghang Zhang
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between global world representations and the local robot–object interactions needed for manipulation.
Uses a latent expert within a Mixture-of-Transformers to connect world and action experts through interaction-focused physical reasoning.
Adaptively transfers world predictions to actions by jointly predicting future representations and progress values, enabling execution adjustment and future resampling.

Pretrained on over 14k hours of robotic data; achieves 99.5% on LIBERO, exceeds prior state of the art on ten RLBench tasks, and performs robustly in real-world long-horizon and dexterous manipulation.
Scope: evaluated across benchmark and real-world robotic manipulation tasks, with the abstract not specifying broader domains.

figures.caption: Figure 2: The LaST0.5 Framework. (a) LaST0.5 unifies a World Expert, Latent Expert, and Action Expert within a Mixtureof-Transformers (MoT) architecture. To bridge global scene dynamics and precise local control, the Latent Expert distills future frames into compact, interaction-centric representations. (b) The Adaptive World-to-Action Transfer (AWAT) mechanism predicts progress values to assess task-progress consistency in imagined futures. Action execution is dynamically truncated when progress value drops, adapting the execution horizon to the predicted progress sequence. (c) Attention mask of LaST0.5.

Figure 1: Overview. Existing WAMs directly transfer representations of global scene dynamics to action prediction, potentially overlooking the localized robot–environment interactions required for manipulation. LaST0.5 bridges this gap through Interaction-Centric Latent Reasoning (ICLR), which learns a compact latent space supervised by visual motion and objectaffordance cues, establishing a hierarchical reasoning paradigm that progressively transforms global world representations into interaction-centric abstractions and ultimately into robot actions. LaST0.5 achieves state-of-the-art performance on the LIBERO and RLBench simulation benchmarks and demonstrates robust long-horizon and precise manipulation in real-world tasks.

papers.abstract: Human gameplay supplies paired observations, actions, and visual consequences that can supplement robot-policy training. We study event-and-foresight pretraining for InternVLA-A1.5, combining recorded keyboard/mouse event prediction with history-conditioned visual supervision through a frozen video model. Coverage-preserving anchor selection constructs one-second targets, and an attention mask prevents teacher-forced future actions from entering foresight queries. The selected corpus contains 394 recordings across 20 games, with 223.36 hours of recorded timestamp span and 2,072,084 training anchors. After 12,400 game-pretraining updates, we compare the resulting initialization with the public base under the same suite-specific robot fine-tuning protocol. Across four LIBERO suites, aggregate success increases from 1,718/2,000 (85.90%) to 1,811/2,000 (90.55%), a gain of 4.65 percentage points. Suite gains are 9.2, 6.8, 0.2, and 2.4 points on Spatial, Object, Goal, and Long. The 40-task breakdown shows 24 improvements, 10 declines, and six ties. These results support the practical value of the complete game-pretraining stage in this evaluated setting, while revealing heterogeneous task outcomes. The comparison includes additional optimization and does not isolate the effects of game data, the two objectives, or training variability.

papers.abstract: This work presents the 2nd-place solution (Team IF1001) to the 2026 BEHAVIOR Challenge, which evaluates mobile manipulation across 100 household tasks. Our method is built on a powerful world action model (WAM), Cosmos 3. We improve Cosmos 3 by using richer visual history, task-progress conditioning, and task-group and skill-specific LoRA adapters. During inference, we apply a separate progress estimator to supply task-progress context, and use task- and progress-conditioned routing to select a task-group or skill-specific policy, complemented by action-candidate aggregation, rolling inpainting, and task-specific temporal and gripper control. To meet the minimum inference requirement of 1 FPS, we use neither recursive self-improvement (RSI) nor agentic harness methods and rely on no closed-source models; during official private-test evaluation, our system handled concurrent requests across 100 evaluation ports with limited hardware resources, sustaining an average end-to-end inference rate above 2 FPS per port. Our method achieves a mean Q-score of 0.613 and a full-task success rate of 40.9%, averaged over 3 self-evaluation rounds across all 100 tasks. On the official private test set, with 20 instances per task, our system achieves a mean Q-score of 0.615 and a full-task success rate of 41.2%.

Avoids recursive self-improvement, agentic harnesses, and closed-source models while sustaining over 2 FPS per evaluation port on limited hardware.
Achieves a 0.615 mean Q-score and 41.2% full-task success on the official private test set.

papers.abstract: End-to-end autonomous driving systems increasingly rely on generating multiple trajectory candidates and selecting one for execution. In this setting, a central challenge is no longer only candidate generation, but how to evaluate candidates according to their long-horizon consequences under uncertainty. Existing methods still mainly use deterministic point scores, heuristic subscores, or single-outcome evaluations, which makes it difficult to capture delayed failures, tail risk, and ranking instability under plausible future perturbations. We present RiSE-Drive, a framework for risk-sensitive long-horizon candidate evaluation in end-to-end autonomous driving. RiSE-Drive first performs candidate-conditioned latent future rollout, then estimates long-horizon outcome distributions instead of single scalar scores, and finally ranks candidates using a tail-risk-aware and perturbation-robust decision criterion. This reformulates candidate scoring from deterministic oracle-style evaluation into distributional outcome assessment with explicit risk control. As a result, the evaluator is encouraged to prefer candidates that are not only strong under nominal conditions, but also reliable under long-horizon rollout and safety-critical deviations. Experiments on the NAVSIM-v1 and NAVSIM-v2 benchmarks, as well as the closed-loop HUGSIM benchmark, show that RiSE-Drive achieves state-of-the-art performance and significantly improves the robustness of candidate selection.
authors: Yu Zhao, Hongyi Duan, Ming Yin, Hongyuan Zhang, Fan Yang, Hongzhi Wang, Xiubo Liang
bullets: Addresses delayed failures, tail risk, and unstable candidate rankings in end-to-end autonomous driving.
Uses candidate-conditioned latent future rollouts to estimate distributions of long-horizon outcomes.
Ranks candidates with a tail-risk-aware, perturbation-robust decision criterion rather than deterministic point scores.
Evaluated on NAVSIM-v1, NAVSIM-v2, and closed-loop HUGSIM, where it reports state-of-the-art performance and more robust candidate selection.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of the RiSE-Drive pipeline. Multi-view observations are encoded, and the proposal generator produces 𝐾 ego-trajectory candidates. A future-condition generator predicts 𝐿 branch-specific condition codes that parameterize plausible downstream evolutions. For each candidate–condition pair, RiSE-Drive initializes a latent consequence state, propagates it along the trajectory, and decodes one branch-level long-horizon outcome sample. The resulting branchwise consequence traces are pooled over time and across branches and mapped to ordered outcome quantiles by a distribution head. The final ranking score combines the mean estimate, lower-tail CVaR, and cross-condition instability, thereby favoring candidates that remain reliable under plausible future deviations rather than merely optimal under a single nominal forecast.

Figure 3: Qualitative results of RiSE-Drive on representative NavSafe safety-critical scenarios. From left to right, columns (a)–(d) correspond to UNPL (unprotected left turn), EXR (exit ramp), YLD (yielding), and RDBT (roundabout). Each column shows two temporal snapshots of one representative case. Magenta denotes the RiSE-Drive plan, green the human future trajectory, orange dashed the ego history, and blue the future trajectories of surrounding vehicles. Across all four cases, RiSE-Drive produces smooth, route-consistent, and interaction-aware behaviors while remaining close to safe human driving in conflict-prone regions.

papers.abstract: Learning representations from multimodal observations is difficult in reinforcement learning with limited interaction data. Multimodal Joint Predictive Representation combines multimodal latent prediction with contrastive learning across modalities, but its recursive rollout depends on earlier predictions and its pairwise alignment focuses on correspondence between modalities. We propose Improved Predictive Representation, which combines prediction from action prefixes with alignment at the observed anchor based on Contrastive Multimodal learning. At each horizon, it predicts future representations directly from the observed anchor and the corresponding sequence of actions. We evaluate two crop configurations: IPR-S with a minimum retained crop area of 10%, and IPR-H with 50%. Across five DeepMind Control Suite tasks, IPR-H achieves an average return across tasks that is 10.0% higher than the baseline with visual and depth images and 3.4% higher with visual images and position vectors. The relative performance of the two configurations varies across tasks. In Webots, both IPR configurations achieve higher mean final returns than the baseline without LiDAR, but not when LiDAR is available.
bullets: Addresses recursive prediction errors and limited pairwise modality alignment in multimodal representation learning.
Predicts future representations directly from the observed anchor using action sequences, while aligning modalities at that anchor.
Evaluates two crop configurations: IPR-S (10% minimum retained area) and IPR-H (50%).
Across five DeepMind Control Suite tasks, IPR-H improves average return by 10.0% with visual/depth inputs and 3.4% with visual/position inputs.
In Webots, both variants outperform the baseline without LiDAR, but not when LiDAR is available; performance varies by task and crop configuration.

papers.abstract: Egocentric human video (EHV) records close-range hand-object interaction (HOI) and the temporal structure of everyday activities, offering a potentially scalable source of experience for robot manipulation. Using this experience for robot control requires recovering useful supervision without recorded robot actions and accounting for differences in morphology, viewpoint, and action space. We define Ego2Robot learning as the process of learning or adapting robot manipulation policies from EHV, organized into four learning paradigms: explicit embodiment transfer, explicit action and task supervision, egocentric video representation pretraining, and latent action and dynamics modeling. The four paradigms differ in what they derive from human video: robot-format demonstrations, interpretable supervision, visual representations, or predictive models of actions and dynamics. For each paradigm, we trace what EHV information is extracted, how robot policies use it, and when the additional data is required. Besides, we review the benchmark datasets that cover EHV, robot demonstrations, and synthetic and simulated resources. This paper links EHV data's contribution to the task information preserved and the robot-specific grounding used during training or deployment. Finally, we identify challenges in physical feasibility, agent coordination, in-context adaptation, controlled evaluation, and predictive control.
authors: Yi Wang, Jingqiu Wu, Lei Yao, Zhaoshuo Li, Haoyu Zhu, Yirui Zhou, Huaiyuan Xu, Ying Zheng, Chuang Yang, Lap-Pui Chau
bullets: Organizes Ego2Robot learning into four paradigms: embodiment transfer, action/task supervision, representation pretraining, and latent action/dynamics modeling.
Analyzes what information each paradigm extracts from human video and how robots use it for policy learning.
Reviews benchmarks spanning egocentric videos, robot demonstrations, and synthetic or simulated resources.
Highlights open challenges in physical feasibility, human–robot coordination, in-context adaptation, evaluation, and predictive control.

papers.abstract: Pretrained latent world models can support visual planning and control, but their predictions may fail when physical dynamics change at deployment. We study whether such models can adapt from only a few interactions without modifying their pretrained weights or identifying the changed physical parameters. We introduce a few-shot residual adaptation approach that learns self-supervised corrections from latent prediction errors. The corrections are applied both inside the latent predictor and directly to its predicted latent state, while the pretrained world model remains frozen. We evaluate the approach in simulation and on a real robot under center-of-mass and friction shifts. These changes reduce the success of the frozen model to near zero. Using three interaction episodes for adaptation, our dual-site approach recovers 90\% success under the center-of-mass shift and 100\% under the modified friction on the real robot. Ablations show that correcting both locations outperforms single-site adaptation. Our diagnostics further suggest that much of the learned correction reduces a general prediction mismatch, while successful control also depends on shift-specific information captured during adaptation.
authors: Jakub Suliga, Pankhuri Vanjani, Nisarga Nilavadi, Wolfram Burgard, Rudolf Lioutikov
bullets: Addresses deployment failures caused by shifts in physical dynamics without retraining or identifying changed parameters.
Learns residual corrections from latent prediction errors and applies them both within the latent predictor and to its predicted latent state.
Evaluated in simulation and on a real robot under center-of-mass and friction shifts.
With three adaptation episodes, real-robot success reached 90% for the center-of-mass shift and 100% for the friction shift.
Dual-site correction outperformed single-site adaptation; learned corrections captured both general prediction mismatch and shift-specific information.

papers.abstract: Protein engineering requires navigating rugged fitness landscapes, where small sequence changes can produce large functional differences, but experimental screening can only sample a small fraction of sequence space. Thus, a central challenge is to efficiently traverse the large combinatorial space of mutations in silico. We introduce ProTEUS, a mutation-resolved world model for closed-loop protein evolution. Pretrained on deep mutational scanning assays, ProTEUS learns a joint representation of sequence, evolutionary, and structural information using MutationFormer, a mutation-biased attention architecture. Variants are represented as states in this joint latent space, and mutations define actions whose functional consequences are predicted. To support exploration of many mutants, we developed a fast, physics-constrained all-atom predictor that utilizes explicit geometric constraint enforcement to achieve >10 fold increase in speed than AlphaFold3 with guaranteed physical validity. Lastly, ProTEUS refines its prediction and understanding of protein activity through closed loop experimental feedback to guide evolution toward a desired phenotype. ProTEUS surpasses established models in both zero-shot and supervised fine-tuning mutation prediction tasks. We experimentally demonstrate its utility in two closed-loop multi-objective engineering campaigns on aldehyde dehydrogenase and levansucrase, yielding variants with >10 fold higher activity than wild type. ProTEUS provides a world-model framework that connects virtual evaluation of mutational outcomes with experimental learning for efficient protein evolution.
authors: Yikun Zhang, Minghao Guo, Guangxue Xu, Peter Yichen Chen, Wojciech Matusik, Wengong Jin, Jingjing Chai, Kaiyi Jiang
bullets: Addresses the challenge of exploring vast, rugged protein fitness landscapes when experiments can test only a small fraction of variants.
Uses MutationFormer to jointly represent sequence, evolutionary, and structural information from deep mutational scanning data.
Models variants as latent-space states and mutations as actions with predicted functional consequences.
Includes a physics-constrained all-atom structure predictor reported as over 10× faster than AlphaFold3 while maintaining physical validity.
Outperformed established mutation-prediction models and produced variants with over 10× wild-type activity in two closed-loop campaigns on aldehyde dehydrogenase and levansucrase.
papers.selection_reason: ProTEUS is a mutation-resolved world model for closed-loop protein evolution, using a physics-constrained predictor and feedback loops. This fits World Models (Latent Action Models, Interactive World Models).
papers.title: ProTEUS: A mutation-resolved world model for closed-loop protein evolution
papers.tldr: ProTEUS is a closed-loop protein evolution framework that predicts mutation effects, rapidly evaluates structures, and uses experimental feedback to guide engineering toward desired phenotypes.

papers.abstract: Efficient robotic 3D reconstruction requires selecting views that contribute new surface measurements with few physical captures. Pretrained world models can guide this choice, but a predicted surface may not produce valid depth measurements under the operating conditions of the deployed sensor. We present a deployment adaptation methodology for next-best-view selection that learns a sensor-return adapter from limited local calibration data while keeping the pretrained predictor fixed. The adapter estimates measurement dropout over each predicted surface, allowing the selection method to favor views likely to fill gaps in the measured reconstruction. In a real-robot experiment with a structured-light sensor, the adapted method achieves higher measured surface coverage with 60% fewer captures than nominal selection. The adapted method recovers a surface region that the nominal method repeatedly targets but fails to measure. These results suggest that robots can reuse pretrained predictive models while adapting their decisions to local operating conditions in data-scarce environments.
authors: Nikita Sarawgi, Omey M. Manyar, Satyandra K. Gupta
bullets: Targets efficient robotic 3D reconstruction by selecting views that add new surface measurements.
Keeps a pretrained predictor fixed and learns an adapter from limited local calibration data.
Estimates measurement dropout on predicted surfaces to prioritize views likely to fill reconstruction gaps.
In a real-robot structured-light experiment, the adapted method achieved higher measured surface coverage with 60% fewer captures than nominal selection.
Scope: adapts decisions to local sensor operating conditions in data-scarce deployments.

papers.abstract: In the absence of extrinsic rewards or task supervision, human behavior is guided by intrinsic motivation---neural signals that drive curiosity, creativity, play, and other essential facets of intelligence. Intrinsic motivation plays an important developmental role in building robust world models that enable generalization and adaptation. Yet existing studies leave open how a broad range of intrinsic motivations interacts with world-model representation learning to support downstream control. This limits our understanding of which intrinsically collected experiences build reusable models. To address these gaps, we integrate 24 intrinsic objectives, including established methods and explicit variants spanning curiosity, entropy, and competency, into a common model-based reinforcement learning framework. We evaluate the world models they build through zero-shot, few-shot, and multi-task control in locomotion, manipulation, and open-ended gaming environments, using three representation-learning strategies: observation reconstruction, latent prediction, and redundancy reduction. Curiosity-driven exploration with observation reconstruction yields the strongest aggregate family profile, although the best individual pairing depends on the experiment. In compositional vision-based tasks, intrinsic motivation derived from both episodic and lifelong novelty---providing a complementary memory to the world model's generic recurrent state---achieves the best zero-shot transfer and few-shot adaptation. These findings motivate designing intrinsic motivation and representation learning jointly. Our results demonstrate world models as a powerful tool for measuring the quality of intrinsically motivated experience, and positions intrinsic motivation as a key ingredient for building world models autonomously.
authors: Reece Keller, Declan Kutscher, Xaq Pitkow, Aran Nayebi
bullets: Integrates 24 intrinsic objectives spanning curiosity, entropy, and competency into a common model-based reinforcement-learning framework.
Evaluates learned world models on zero-shot, few-shot, and multi-task control across locomotion, manipulation, and open-ended gaming.
Compares observation reconstruction, latent prediction, and redundancy-reduction representation learning.
Curiosity with observation reconstruction performs best overall, while episodic plus lifelong novelty achieves the strongest transfer and adaptation in compositional vision tasks.
Results suggest intrinsic motivation and representation learning should be designed jointly.

papers.abstract: Synthetic data augmentation promises to scale offline reinforcement learning beyond fixed logged datasets, but leading diffusion-based generators model the transition tuple (state, action, next state, reward, terminal) as a monolith: no single factor can be natively redrawn in isolation. We present FaST (Factored Synthesis of Transitions), which factors transitions via the chain rule into state, action, dynamics, reward, and terminal stages, fitting each with an estimator matched to its statistical properties. Across twelve D4RL locomotion and maze benchmarks, TD3+BC and IQL agents trained on FaST transitions match the SynthER diffusion baseline while generating transitions over 90x faster. The explicit action-given-state conditional can also be re-queried for a fixed state, enabling targeted action synthesis: drawing N candidate actions per generated state and keeping the highest-advantage one under a value function fit to the same data, thereby synthesizing improved behavior during generation rather than filtering for it post-hoc. Best-of-10 synthesis beats training on real data on 11 of 12 medium and medium-replay settings (+8.9 D4RL points on average, up to +28.4), and is competitive with advantage-filtered SynthER at a fraction of its generation cost. On expert mixtures both mechanisms degrade identically, tracing the failure to the advantage estimate itself rather than to either targeting mechanism.
authors: Daniel Campa, Spandan Das, Srinjoy Das
bullets: Addresses the inefficiency and inflexibility of monolithic diffusion models for offline RL transition synthesis.
Uses a chain-rule factorization into state, action, dynamics, reward, and terminal stages, with estimators suited to each factor.
Matches the SynthER baseline across 12 D4RL locomotion and maze benchmarks while substantially reducing generation cost.
Best-of-10 targeted action synthesis improves over real-data training on 11 of 12 medium and medium-replay settings, averaging +8.9 D4RL points.
Performance degrades on expert mixtures because of inaccurate advantage estimates, not the synthesis mechanisms themselves.

papers.abstract: Assisted history matching remains non-unique because many geological realisations can reproduce equivalent production responses with substantial differences between individual well matches. This ambiguity increases when a field comprises several depositional settings and modelling strategies. The paper applied a graph autoencoder approach to history matching of a benchmark Brugge field that comprises different depositional zones. Each stratigraphic zone is modelled with its dedicated generative model that comprises a joint latent space for optimisation history matching loops. Graph-based generators operate directly on the active cells of the corner-point grid, so its irregular geometry is handled without conversion to a regular lattice. The optimisation search in the 160-dimensional joint latent space is done with the Covariance Matrix Adaptation Evolution Strategy. The multi-component objective function includes static well data mismatch, dynamic production mismatch, and a geological realism penalty based on the Decoder induced latent metric. Latent space diagnostics with topological data analysis are applied prior to history matching to test whether one generator is sufficient or whether a multiple generator formulation is required. The results show that the zone-based formulation gives coherent latent spaces, preserves the main porosity and permeability relations that vary from one zone to another, and supports history matching while keeping the solutions within the learned geological manifold. The matched models reproduce field oil and water production within the prior uncertainty range and provide a comparable well-level match to previously published Brugge studies based on Ensemble Kalman Filter, Particle Swarm Optimisation with principal component analysis of parameterisation, and Multiple Kernel Learning with Particle Swarm Optimisation.
authors: Gleb Shishaev, Anton Shirokov, Shadfar Davoodi, Mohammed Al-Shargabi, Vasily Demyanov, Daniel Arnold
bullets: Addresses ambiguity in history matching across multiple depositional settings and well responses.
Uses dedicated graph autoencoders for each stratigraphic zone with a shared 160-dimensional latent optimisation space.
Optimises static, dynamic, and geological-realism objectives using Covariance Matrix Adaptation Evolution Strategy.
Applies topological data analysis to assess whether one or multiple generators are needed.
Produces field-scale oil and water matches within prior uncertainty while preserving zone-specific porosity–permeability relationships and geological realism.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon urban navigation requires sequential local decisions whose errors can compound over time. Imitation learning (IL) rarely learns from failures, while physical trial-and-error reinforcement learning (RL) is costly. Action-conditioned world models can provide imagined feedback by predicting visual consequences for candidate actions. However, a frozen world model may become less reliable as the policy evolves. In this paper, we introduce RIWANAV, a post-training framework that casts the coupled adaptation of a world model and an action model (policy) as task-specific recursive self-improvement (RSI). Each cycle alternates two updates. The world model evaluates policy actions through imagined outcomes, providing comparative feedback for group-relative policy optimization (GRPO). The improved policy then constructs a grounded self-curriculum, selecting expert-consistent action-video pairs by behavioral novelty and prediction error. The refined world model supplies feedback for the next policy update, closing the recursive self-improvement loop. Experiments show that RIWANAV outperforms training baselines and prior methods, validating the proposed recursive self-improvement loop between the policy and world model. Real-world trials further demonstrate its practical applicability.
bullets: Addresses compounding errors in long-horizon navigation and the limitations of failure-insensitive imitation learning and costly physical RL.
Alternates world-model refinement and policy improvement in a recursive self-improvement loop.
Uses imagined action outcomes for group-relative policy optimization and behavioral novelty/prediction error to build a grounded self-curriculum.
Experiments report gains over training baselines and prior methods, with real-world trials supporting practical applicability.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Recursive self-improvement loop in RIWANAV. (1) The current world model imagines action consequences that improve the policy. The flame marks the component optimized in each phase.

All three models receive the same observation, language goal, and action; the aligned recorded future is shown as reference. The rows depict night traffic, a bicycle-lined sidewalk, and a rainy sidewalk. In these cases, the RIWANAV world model after recursive updates better preserves traversable corridors and scene layout, with fewer long-horizon artifacts.

Fig. 1. From imitation learning to recursive world–action models selfimprovement. (a) Imitation learning trains the policy from expert trajectories but provides limited supervision for policy-induced failures. (b) A frozen world model enables learning from imagined outcomes, but its predictions become misaligned with the evolving policy. (c) RIWANAV closes the training loop: imagined outcomes improve the policy, while grounded policyinduced samples refine the world model for subsequent policy learning.

papers.abstract: We introduce CNP-Flow, a flow matching framework for temporal generation that learns conditional source distributions through flow reversal. Whereas standard conditional flow matching (FM) incorporates conditioning through the vector field and draws source samples from a standard Gaussian, CNP-Flow uses a conditional noise predictor (CNP) to produce an isotropic Gaussian source for each temporal condition. The CNP is supervised by source samples obtained through flow reversal, which maps observed targets backward through a pretrained FM model. A three-stage pipeline pretrains the FM model, trains the CNP, and fine-tunes the FM model using the learned source distribution, while preserving the FM backbone architecture. Across video prediction, video interpolation, and 7-DoF Franka robot motion planning, CNP-Flow consistently improves generation quality. It also matches baseline performance with fewer function evaluations. Project page: https://embodiedai-ntu.github.io/cnpflow
bullets: Standard conditional flow matching uses a fixed standard-Gaussian source and encodes conditions only in the vector field.
CNP-Flow trains a conditional noise predictor to generate an isotropic Gaussian source tailored to each temporal condition.
Its three-stage pipeline pretrains flow matching, learns sources from backward-reversed target samples, then fine-tunes the flow model.
The method improves generation quality across video prediction, video interpolation, and 7-DoF Franka motion planning.
It matches baseline performance with fewer function evaluations.

papers.abstract: Urban navigation requires embodied agents to pursue long-horizon goals through local decisions based on egocentric observations. However, existing agentic navigation methods often struggle to translate distant goals into coherent local decisions in large-scale physical environments. Their reliance on linguistic reasoning over transient observations or limited history constrains anticipation of the consequences of actions and future conditions, despite the importance of such foresight for navigating long and complex urban routes. To bridge this gap, we propose PreAct-Nav, an agentic navigation framework that equips frozen policies with anticipatory reasoning for robust urban navigation. Our central idea is to anchor local decisions in persistent medium-horizon subgoals, assess the consequences of predicted actions before execution, and continually update the reasoning context using actual outcomes. At its core, a navigation memory module maintains the active subgoal and relevant experience across decisions, translating distant goals into actionable intermediate objectives. We further introduce a predictive world sandbox that uses an action-conditioned world model (AC-WM) to forecast world dynamics conditioned on candidate movements. A vision-language model (VLM) reasoner interprets these predictions under the current subgoal to retain or revise actions. After execution, real observations are used to assess outcomes, correct inconsistent assumptions, and update memory to continue or reformulate the subgoal. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that the proposed PreAct-Nav improves action selection through memory updates and visual prediction, with more pronounced gains on longer routes and routes with more turns.
bullets: Targets the difficulty of translating distant navigation goals into coherent local decisions in large, complex environments.
Maintains persistent medium-horizon subgoals and relevant experience through a navigation memory module.
Uses an action-conditioned world model to predict candidate movement outcomes in a visual sandbox.
A vision-language reasoner evaluates predictions, while real observations update memory and revise actions or subgoals.
Evaluations report stronger gains on longer routes and routes with more turns.

After execution, real observations are checked against expected cues to update subgoal status and open-question progress.

Compared with reasoning from observed history and language-based future thoughts, PreAct-Nav maintains medium-horizon subgoals to decompose long-horizon navigation tasks and uses action-conditioned future visual cues to preview, review, and revise local actions before execution. Real feedback updates memory for subsequent decisions.

papers.abstract: We introduce DreamFormer, a model-based agent that acquires language-conditioned, multi-task skills by imitating expert demonstrations within the latent imagination of a learned world model. DreamFormer first learns a task-agnostic Transformer world model from unstructured play data, then acquires task-specific behaviors by optimizing an intrinsic reward that aligns agent-generated rollouts with expert demonstrations in latent space. Since the policy is trained on-policy inside imagination, it is exposed to its own errors during training, mitigating the covariate shift inherent to offline behavioral cloning. To make long-horizon imagination affordable, DreamFormer encodes a high-resolution multi-view robotic observation into a single input token, avoiding both spatial downsampling and the multi-token representations used by prior Transformer world models. On the long-horizon CALVIN benchmark, DreamFormer outperforms LUMOS, the comparable model-based agent, on single-environment evaluation (2.52 vs 2.34 average tasks completed per chain of five) while keeping imagination rollouts tractable. Against HULC, the behavior cloning baseline, it nearly doubles performance on zero-shot transfer to an unseen environment (1.30 vs 0.67), indicating that dynamics learned by the world model transfer more readily than a directly cloned policy. This is consistent with the role attributed to internal models in biological agents, where a model of environment dynamics supports behavior in situations not previously encountered.
bullets: Learns a task-agnostic world model from unstructured play data, then optimizes task behavior in imagined rollouts aligned with expert demonstrations.
On-policy training within imagination exposes the policy to its own errors, reducing offline behavioral-cloning covariate shift.
Compresses high-resolution multi-view observations into a single token to keep long-horizon Transformer imagination tractable.
On CALVIN, completes more tasks than LUMOS in single-environment evaluation (2.52 vs. 2.34) and nearly doubles HULC’s zero-shot transfer performance (1.30 vs. 0.67).

papers.abstract: Trained action policies write manipulation skill into network weights, tying what is learned to the distribution it is learned from. In-context learning (ICL) avoids this coupling but has not matched trained policies, because a demonstration recorded in another scene carries no feedback from the world the robot currently faces. We observe that what an agent learns in context is semantic, recording task steps and object roles rather than visual appearance, so experience gathered in one world transfers to another. Based on this insight, we propose World In-Context Learning (WICL), a paradigm in which a frozen model starts from a demonstration, rehearses the task in a world such as a simulator, and writes the feedback into its context rather than its weights. We build RoboScript, a modular infrastructure that implements WICL for agentic manipulation. From a single demonstration, RoboScript learns each task through rehearsal in simulation, freezes the learned knowledge as a Task Memory, and deploys the frozen memory on new scenes with data isolation that ensures every deployment input is available on a real robot. On all 50 tasks of RoboTwin 2.0, RoboScript reaches 83.4% mean success across clean and randomized settings with one demonstration per task and no gradient updates, exceeding the strongest trained action policy by over 20 points. The method generalizes across visual distributions, improves through reflection, scales with the foundation model, and transfers to a physical dual-arm robot through cross-embodiment memory adaptation. With a world in the loop, a robot can learn a manipulation task in its context as well as it learns one in its weights. All code is available at https://github.com/ArcheOne-AI/RoboScript
bullets: Addresses the limitation that demonstrations from other scenes lack feedback about the robot’s current world.
RoboScript implements WICL by combining one demonstration with simulated rehearsal, reflection, and frozen Task Memory.
Achieves 83.4% mean success across all 50 RoboTwin 2.0 tasks using one demonstration per task and no gradient updates.
The approach generalizes across visual distributions, benefits from larger foundation models, and transfers to a physical dual-arm robot through cross-embodiment adaptation.
Scope: performance is demonstrated for agentic manipulation, with deployment inputs isolated to information available on the real robot.

papers.abstract: World action models jointly predict video and actions conditioned on language. Existing studies focus primarily on architectures and training mechanisms, typically treating language-video alignment acquired through video pretraining as an established foundation. However, introducing action learning may impair this alignment. Principled guidance on data and supervision design for maintaining language-video alignment during action learning remains limited. To investigate this, we curate a pool of approximately 47,000 hours of general videos, egocentric videos, UMI demonstrations, and robot demonstrations. Building on this, we systematically study how language-video supervision, language-video-action supervision, and the joint use of these two forms affect WAM performance. In particular, we examine how language annotation quality affects pretrained language-video capabilities, and how action supervision from UMI and robot demonstrations extends these capabilities to language-video-action modeling. To better scale the model, we further conduct detailed studies on joint training recipe and model architecture. Under a fixed training budget, mixing egocentric videos and UMI demonstrations improves control generalization. Model architecture affects how effectively these experiences are used, while scaling pretraining under the selected configuration brings further gains. The resulting recipe, post-trained on RoboTwin Clean demonstrations only, achieves success rates of 88.10% and 61.56% under Easy (Clean-to-Clean) and Hard (Clean-to-Random) conditions, respectively. Our model achieves 40.00% SR across three real-world tasks, compared with 23.33% for the strongest baseline, indicating better generalization under unseen conditions. We release the curated data, training code, and model weights.
bullets: Problem: Action learning can weaken pretrained language–video alignment, but guidance on data and supervision design is limited.
Method: Systematically evaluates language–video, language–video–action, and joint supervision using about 47,000 hours of general, egocentric, UMI, and robot videos.

Key findings: Egocentric video mixed with UMI demonstrations improves control generalization under a fixed training budget; architecture and joint-training choices affect how well these data are used.
Scaling the selected pretraining setup and post-training on RoboTwin Clean demonstrations yields 88.10% success in Easy and 61.56% in Hard conditions.
The model reaches 40.00% success across three real-world tasks, versus 23.33% for the strongest baseline, and the authors release data, code, and weights.

papers.abstract: Soft powered descent landings are becoming evermore important in the field of space exploration and scientific advancement, because of their ability to deliver mission critical payloads, both highly accurately and safely. The high efficiency restriction on planetary landings due to the severely limited fuel supply results in the need for optimal guidance trajectories and control. Model based reinforcement learning is proving to be an important tool in simplifying the highly complex process of generating optimal guidance trajectories and control. In this work, we present DreamLander, a state of the art model based reinforcement learning algorithm based on DreamerV3, to generate optimal guidance and control for a realistic 6 degree of freedom entry descent landing problem. The model based approach creates a sample efficient and highly generalizable model that can be applied to a variety of scenarios whilst maintaining a high degree of accuracy, landing within 2 meters of the designated landing zone, and with velocity norm less than 0.3 meters per second. DreamLander makes use of state sensor observations, making progress toward End-to-End solutions of the Entry Descent Landing problem.
bullets: Targets soft powered descent, where limited fuel demands efficient guidance trajectories and control.
Uses model-based reinforcement learning built on DreamerV3 for the entry-descent-landing problem.
Operates from state sensor observations, advancing toward end-to-end landing solutions.
Reportedly lands within 2 m of the designated zone with velocity norm below 0.3 m/s.
Designed to be sample-efficient and generalizable across landing scenarios.

papers.abstract: World models have increasingly been applied as a model-based control method for robotics tasks such as manipulation and locomotion. While early world model architectures relied on decoders to prevent mode collapse and learn a predictable latent space, recent works on world models, such as Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture or LeWorldModel, increasingly aim to learn embeddings without a grounding decoder, utilising only a latent forward dynamics predictor and a stabilising entropy term. In this paper, we set out to demonstrate that the further introduction of two additional latent losses to LeWorldModel, a backward dynamics predictor and an inverse dynamics action predictor, enforces further structure on the latent embedding, leading to further gains in both performance and planning efficiency. These are critical properties for improving the applicability of such methods to real-time model-based control of real-world robots. We demonstrate these gains on standard world model benchmarks and two simulated robot manipulation tasks.
bullets: Targets more effective, real-time model-based control for robotics.
Extends LeWorldModel with a backward dynamics predictor and an inverse dynamics action predictor.
Uses these auxiliary latent losses to impose additional structure on learned embeddings.
Evaluated on standard world-model benchmarks and two simulated robot manipulation tasks.
The abstract does not report specific quantitative gains or limitations.

papers.selection_reason: Improves latent world models for robot control with backward and inverse dynamics losses, fitting both world-model and embodied-AI interests.
papers.title: $Σ$-LeWM: Learning World Models via S-Information for Robot Control
papers.tldr: Σ-LeWM improves decoder-free world models for robot control by adding backward and inverse-dynamics losses that structure latent representations and enhance performance and planning efficiency.

papers.abstract: A world model predicts how a scene changes after an action, and a planner uses it to search for actions that reach a goal. If the camera moves or the controller changes, the same command moves the robot differently: when its commands are turned by 90 degrees, a frozen planner with the LeWM world model that succeeds in 77.5% of episodes succeeds in only 7.8%. Current fixes retrain the model, need training data, or forget a set-up when it returns. We propose Library of Hands (LoH), a training-free method that keeps the world model frozen and corrects only the map from commands to applied actions, which we call the hand. LoH reads the hand through the frozen model, with no extra sensor: it finds the action that best explains the change between two camera images (a reading). It stores every hand it identifies, so a returning set-up is recognised rather than re-learnt. In closed-loop tests, LoH more than doubles success on three simulated tasks, from 28.6% to 62.3%, and loses only 0.6 percentage points when nothing changes. It also works, unchanged, with two other world models and on two of three models pretrained on real robot data, and its gain grows with the quality of its readings.
bullets: Problem: Camera or controller changes can make a planner’s commands produce different motions, sharply reducing performance.
Method: Infer the current command-to-action mapping—or “hand”—from image changes using the frozen world model, without extra sensors or training data.
LoH stores identified hands so previously seen setups can be recognized instead of relearned.
In closed-loop tests, success increased from 28.6% to 62.3% across three simulated tasks, while unchanged setups lost only 0.6 percentage points.
The method also transferred unchanged to other world models and most tested models pretrained on real-robot data; performance depended on reading quality.

papers.abstract: Likelihood-based methods are widely used to learn the parameters of partially observable Markov decision processes (POMDPs). While finite-sample guarantees for policy suboptimality exist for certain POMDP subclasses, analogous guarantees for parameter recovery remain less well understood. For any candidate POMDP parameter, we bound its parameter recovery error in terms of its likelihood gap to the ground truth, the structural conditioning of the observation and transition kernels, and the behavior policy used to collect data. The bound applies in both the undercomplete and overcomplete regimes, with the latter following naturally from the undercomplete analysis. Because the result applies to any sufficiently good candidate, it yields finite-sample guarantees for the maximum-likelihood estimator and any procedure producing a parameter with controlled likelihood gap. This is particularly useful for near-optimal learning in infinite-horizon POMDPs, where existing approaches largely rely on model-based planning with accurate transition and observation kernel estimates. The bound separates the contributions of the behavior policy and model, showing how data-collection choices, including action coverage, and their effects on mixing can accelerate parameter learning.
bullets: Addresses the gap between likelihood convergence and parameter recovery in POMDPs.
Bounds parameter error using the likelihood gap, observation/transition-kernel conditioning, and the behavior policy.
Covers both undercomplete and overcomplete POMDP regimes.
Applies to maximum-likelihood estimators and any method producing a sufficiently good likelihood candidate.
Separates model and behavior-policy effects, including action coverage and mixing, to guide data collection.

papers.selection_reason: Likelihood-to-parameter convergence bounds for POMDP model learning; relevant to model-based world-model estimation.
papers.title: From Likelihood Convergence to Parameter Convergence in POMDPs
papers.tldr: The paper converts likelihood near-optimality into finite-sample parameter-recovery guarantees for POMDPs, while exposing how model conditioning and data-collection policies affect learning.

papers.abstract: Video world models conditioned on an input video make it possible to explore real, recorded dynamic scenes, enabling re-shooting of footage, free-viewpoint replay, and real-to-sim environments for embodied agents. Such uses require the generated rollout to stay faithful to the recorded world, yet existing benchmarks start from a single image or a text prompt, and video-conditioned generation is evaluated mainly on perceptual quality and camera following. These evaluations do not directly assess whether exploration preserves subject identity, event progression, and scene consistency upon revisiting a location. We introduce WanderBench, a benchmark for exploring dynamic worlds from video. It comprises 745 single-shot source videos of real and AI-generated content in three difficulty tiers (3-25 s), paired with camera routes given as keyboard actions, and evaluates six dimensions with 24 human-validated sub-metrics. Benchmarking eight models, we find that as clips grow longer, models keep the static scene and visual quality but lose camera control and the source dynamics, and that none keeps revisited places consistent. We further propose WanderLand, a training-free framework that conditions each frame of a frozen model on the same-instant source and, on revisits, on its own earlier static content. WanderLand improves five models on every dimension, by up to 8.3 points in source-dynamics fidelity.
bullets: Introduces a benchmark of 745 real and AI-generated single-shot videos across three difficulty tiers, paired with keyboard-action camera routes.
Evaluates six dimensions through 24 human-validated sub-metrics, including identity, event progression, camera control, and consistency when revisiting locations.
Across eight models, longer rollouts preserve static appearance and visual quality but degrade camera control and source dynamics.
No evaluated model maintains consistency when revisiting previously seen places.
Proposes WanderLand, a training-free conditioning framework that improves all dimensions across five models, with up to 8.3 points in source-dynamics fidelity.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of WanderBench. (a) Data collection and curation. (b) Six evaluation dimensions with 24 sub-metrics. (c) Task setting: given a source video and action keys, a model re-renders the scene from novel viewpoints while staying synchronized with the source.

Figure 3: Overview of WanderLand. WanderLand wraps a frozen video world model and leaves its weights, sampler, and seed unchanged. It only rebuilds the camera and source render the model already takes as input, taking evidence for every frame in a fixed order (top): the latent source first, then previous frames, and generation only where neither exists. All geometry comes from the model’s own front-end. The frozen model then generates the output rollout.

Each column shows one frame per second, and the key above it is the camera action held during the preceding second. papers.abstract: A key challenge in action-conditioned world modeling is to construct macro-states from high-dimensional observations that support recursive prediction under actions, while keeping their predicted evolution consistent with visual changes in generated observations. We propose QCC-WM, a visual world model based on Quotient-based Causal Construction. QCC-WM uses action responses to guide macro-variable construction for recursive action-conditioned prediction. A shared reference quotient measurement constrains the consistency between predicted states and observed changes, allowing macro-level predictions to provide structured constraints for future visual generation. Using translational and rotational actions and their predicted responses, the model aggregates local visual features into macro-nodes with spatial correspondence through causal abstraction, and recursively predicts node content and motion under a shared reference measurement. Macro-level predictions guide future observation generation, while predicted motion transports historical appearance information. Node-level errors between generated observations and macro-level targets are then mapped back to the corresponding spatial regions for correction, improving consistency between visual generation and macro-level predictions. On the US-VLA dataset, QCC-WM achieves an ROI-MSE of 0.01861 for four-step prediction. Compared with the best baseline at each prediction horizon, it reduces LPIPS by 48.59%, 41.68%, and 30.23% for four-step prediction and eight- and sixteen-step recursive extrapolation, respectively. Ablation studies and mechanism analyses show that motion-guided reference transport mainly improves pixel reconstruction, while node-level error feedback further improves perceptual quality and consistency between generated observations and macro-level predictions.
bullets: Addresses the challenge of linking high-dimensional visual observations, action-conditioned macro-state prediction, and future image generation.
Uses action responses and causal abstraction to aggregate local visual features into spatially corresponding macro-nodes.
A shared reference quotient measurement and motion-based appearance transport constrain recursive state and visual prediction.
Node-level visual errors are mapped back to spatial regions to correct generated observations and improve consistency.
On US-VLA, it reports 0.01861 ROI-MSE for four-step prediction and reduced LPIPS versus the best horizon-specific baseline for four-, eight-, and sixteen-step prediction.

The model then reads back the current generation under the same quotient measurement and maps the remaining node-level errors to the corresponding spatial locations to obtain future observations. The reference quotient mapping connects node construction, macro-state prediction, and spatial generation.

papers.abstract: World models enable agents to plan and learn from imagined experience, but in an unfamiliar environment they must learn its mechanics from limited interaction. A mechanic is a rule for how an action or an interaction changes part of the environment. Each occurrence of a mechanic that the model observes is one exposure. We ask how many exposures a world model needs to predict the effects of a new environment's mechanics. We address this question on ARC-AGI-3, a benchmark of interactive games defined by their programs. We introduce MechEval, which labels 69 recurring mechanics across 20 games from these programs. It scores each prediction on the cells the mechanic changes at each exposure. As a test bed, we build WARC (World model for ARC-AGI-3), a 35M-parameter vision transformer that is pretrained on other games and updates all of its parameters after each transition. On held-out games, WARC learns to predict four in five mechanics with at least 80% accuracy on the cells they change and keeps that accuracy to the end of the recordings. Half of them reach that accuracy within about 80 exposures, in a single play of the game, and without updates only one in seven does at all. In closed-loop play on the public games, WARC-Agent, which pairs WARC with a fixed graph explorer, triples the explorer's official efficiency score from 0.15 to 0.46, mostly through test-time training. On the hidden games of the Kaggle leaderboard, our entry scores 0.20.
bullets: Studies how many observations are needed to predict mechanics—rules governing how actions alter an environment—in unfamiliar games.
Introduces MechEval, covering 69 recurring mechanics across 20 ARC-AGI-3 games and scoring predictions on changed cells.
Builds WARC, a 35M-parameter vision transformer that updates all parameters after each observed transition.
On held-out games, WARC predicts four in five mechanics with at least 80% accuracy; about half reach that level within roughly 80 exposures.
Pairing WARC with a fixed graph explorer triples the public-game efficiency score from 0.15 to 0.46, while the hidden-game leaderboard score is 0.20.

papers.abstract: World models are widely considered to be a potential key component of model-based reinforcement learning and robot planning, but typically require task-specific training on substantial interaction data. We investigate whether a pretrained tabular foundation model (TabFM) can serve as a training-free dynamics model for world modeling by framing next-state prediction as in-context regression over transition pairs, and where such a model helps and where it breaks. Across synthetic dynamical systems and robot locomotion benchmarks, TabFM is more accurate than LSTM and MLP models trained from scratch on the same limited transitions in almost all settings, and among regressors fitted to the same data it is the most accurate on locomotion, while a Gaussian process is more accurate on smooth low-dimensional systems. However, models trained on the full dataset remain substantially better on most systems. When rolled out autoregressively over multiple steps, TabFM's accuracy depends strongly on how much context it is given. With a short context, its rollouts quickly degrade to the level of a trivial baseline, whereas with a long context they improve substantially and, on one locomotion task, exceed a trained LSTM. Inference is also about three orders of magnitude slower than an LSTM. Overall, in their current state, we find that training-free priors are useful as predictors when data are scarce and enough context is available, but they are not yet a substitute for trained world models in planning.
bullets: Frames next-state prediction as in-context regression over transition pairs using a pretrained TabFM.
Outperforms from-scratch LSTM and MLP models in almost all limited-data settings; performs best among same-data regressors on locomotion.
Gaussian processes are more accurate on smooth, low-dimensional systems, while models trained on full data remain substantially better overall.
Autoregressive rollout quality depends strongly on context length: short contexts degrade quickly, whereas long contexts can outperform a trained LSTM on one locomotion task.
Inference is about three orders of magnitude slower than an LSTM, limiting current use in planning.
