papers.selection_reason: Evaluates training-free tabular foundation models as dynamics models for next-state prediction in world modeling.
papers.title: An Evaluation of Tabular Foundation Models as Training-Free World Models
papers.tldr: A pretrained tabular foundation model can provide useful training-free dynamics predictions from scarce data, but limited context, rollout degradation, and slow inference prevent it from replacing trained world models.

papers.abstract: LiDAR point clouds and 3D semantic occupancy represent two distinct modalities capturing fine-grained metric geometry and dense volumetric semantics, respectively, holding natural potential for mutual complementarity. However, existing world models typically forecast these modalities independently or cascade them heuristically, missing the opportunity for reciprocal cross-modal regularization. To address this, we propose \textbf{LO-World}, a unified 4D world model that forecasts both modalities within a shared BEV latent space. This single-stream formulation enables dense semantics and metric geometry to mutually reinforce each other, while eliminating multi-pipeline redundancy. Specifically, LO-World couples an efficient hybrid range-voxel autoencoder with a flow-matching generator that caches historical context to reduce iterative sampling latency. Extensive experiments demonstrate that LO-World outperforms prior state-of-the-art baselines, improving occupancy forecasting IoU by 10.9% and reducing LiDAR Chamfer Distance by 30.1%. Meanwhile, it sustains a real-time throughput exceeding $25$~FPS on a single RTX 4090. Our code is available at https://github.com/lzzzzzm/LO-World.
bullets: Addresses the missed mutual complementarity between semantic occupancy and metric LiDAR geometry.
Uses a unified single-stream BEV latent model with a hybrid range-voxel autoencoder.
Employs flow matching with cached historical context to reduce iterative sampling latency.
Reports 10.9% higher occupancy forecasting IoU and 30.1% lower LiDAR Chamfer Distance than prior state-of-the-art baselines.
Exceeds 25 FPS on a single RTX 4090, though the abstract does not specify broader limitations or evaluation scope.

papers.selection_reason: Unified BEV latent world model jointly forecasts 4D occupancy and LiDAR, improving environment dynamics prediction.
papers.title: LO-World: Unified BEV Latent Modeling for Joint 4D Occupancy and LiDAR Forecasting
papers.tldr: LO-World jointly forecasts 4D occupancy and LiDAR in a shared BEV latent space, achieving stronger accuracy with real-time performance.

papers.abstract: One-step stochastic world models avoid the mode averaging of deterministic feature predictors without the tens of network evaluations per step that diffusion and flow matching require. The simplest such objective is nearest-of-m matching (conditional implicit maximum likelihood estimation, IMLE): draw m candidate futures and pull only the one closest to the observed outcome. Recent work conjectures that a small m suffices for feature-space world models and that a strictly proper energy score should replace the hard minimum. We test both claims with one-step world models on frozen DINOv2/v3 patch tokens, using benchmarks whose futures can be enumerated. Under mode-like uncertainty, nearest-of-m with m=16 covers the enumerated futures better than 50-step flow matching (at about 1/30 of its latency), one-step flow generators and an energy-score generator at matched parameter counts, and its rollouts stay on the token manifold where flow rollouts drift. One quantity governs the choice of m: the nearest-of-m objective is the expected distortion of a random codebook of m draws from the generator. This view yields three predictions, recorded before the corresponding runs: (i) memorization of the realized outcome in contexts that never repeat, whose strength is governed by the codebook's miss distortion I(m) rather than its miss probability, and which an energy-score generator does not escape by raising m; (ii) a flattening of mode probabilities with m, matching a known optimum within 0.01; and (iii) under-dispersion on continuous high-dimensional outcomes, which bounds the method on real robot video. Per-step matching on self-rollouts cuts long-horizon error by a third on a stochastic Push-T variant; an ablation separates its manifold and coverage benefits. Planning success does not improve despite accurate risk estimates, a negative result we report with its diagnosis.
bullets: Nearest-of-m training selects the closest of m sampled futures, avoiding deterministic mode averaging with one network evaluation.
For frozen DINOv2/v3 patch tokens and enumerable futures, m=16 outperformed 50-step flow matching, one-step flow generators, and energy-score generators at matched parameter counts.
The method keeps rollouts on the token manifold and improves long-horizon stochastic Push-T error by one third with per-step self-rollout matching.
Increasing m flattens mode probabilities and can cause memorization in nonrepeating contexts; the key factor is expected codebook miss distortion, not merely miss probability.
Continuous high-dimensional outcomes remain under-dispersed, and better risk estimates did not improve planning success.

papers.selection_reason: One-step stochastic world models on video tokens with rollouts and planning; directly fits world-model prediction and action-conditioned future generation.
papers.title: How Many Candidates Does a One-Step World Model Need? A Random-Codebook Account of Nearest-of-m Training on Frozen DINO Tokens
papers.tldr: Nearest-of-16 one-step world models offer strong multimodal token coverage at roughly 1/30 the latency of 50-step flow matching, but random-codebook analysis reveals memorization and under-dispersion limits.

papers.abstract: Spatial generalization in robot world models depends on whether action representations capture the physical relationships that remain valid across changing spatial configurations. Yet different coordinates can describe the same interaction, whereas similar motions can produce different outcomes when local physical conditions change. How these distinctions affect learned prediction remains insufficiently understood. This study evaluates matched action representations defined in world, object, and surface coordinate frames using a controlled robotic peeling benchmark. Global pose and contact relocation experiments reveal a cost associated with limited training data when equivalent interactions receive different spatial descriptions. Removing information about peel thickness creates an irreducible ambiguity because identical predictive inputs can correspond to different material removal outcomes. Coordinates defined relative to the surface improve consequence prediction and counterfactual action selection under accurate local observations, but learned predictors remain vulnerable to uncertainty in the coordinate frame. Joint centering of the surface and tool removes sensitivity to translation of their common origin, whereas incorrect contact geometry and actual execution deviations introduce different failure mechanisms. These results show that effective spatial generalization depends on preserving the relationships between actions and states that determine physical consequences, rather than simply minimizing coordinate variation. This perspective provides a principled basis for designing robot world models that reuse physical knowledge across spatial configurations while retaining the distinctions essential to prediction and planning.
bullets: The study compares matched action representations in world, object, and surface coordinate frames using a controlled robotic peeling benchmark.
Equivalent interactions described differently can increase data requirements, while omitting peel thickness creates irreducible ambiguity in material-removal predictions.
Surface-relative coordinates improve consequence prediction and counterfactual action selection when local observations are accurate.

Jointly centering the surface and tool removes sensitivity to their shared translation, but uncertainty in coordinate frames, incorrect contact geometry, and execution deviations cause distinct failures.
The findings support designing representations that preserve outcome-relevant action–state relationships for reuse across spatial configurations.

papers.selection_reason: Action representation for spatial generalization in robot world models; fits interactive world models and robot manipulation.
papers.title: Action Representation for Spatial Generalization in Robot World Models
papers.tldr: Robot world models generalize spatially when action representations preserve the physical relationships that determine outcomes, not merely when they reduce coordinate variation.

papers.abstract: Sampling-based planners such as MPPI and CEM query a learned world model thousands of times per control step, so low-bit world models are an obvious way to make model-based control cheaper on a robot. With round-to-nearest activation quantization and no calibration, we find that planning can collapse, by up to 100 points of success, while the world model's latent one-step prediction error stays no larger than that of a stochastic rounding scheme that plans well. At the same bit width, what decides the outcome is not the size of the rounding error but whether it persists across planner iterations and is shared across candidates. Round-to-nearest leaves an error that persists, and an iterating planner drifts toward the candidates that this error favors; in TD-MPC2, holding the same dither fixed within a step or an episode brings the drift back. Dither shared by all candidates and redrawn at every iteration removes most of the damage at the same bit width and without training: at least half of it in all 19 affected Meta-World cells (task $\times$ bit width) of TD-MPC2 (median 95%), in 4 of 5 DINO-WM cells, and in all 8 affected tasks of a 317M-parameter multi-task TD-MPC2. Captured as CUDA graphs on an Ampere GPU, a W8A4 integer TD-MPC2 world model runs its planning rollouts 1.9-3.3$\times$ and the whole planning step 1.3-1.5$\times$ faster than FP32, though not faster than BF16 with pre-converted weights; shared dither adds at most 2.3% latency. In TD-MPC2, block-scaled NVFP4 removes most of the damage and MXFP4 part of it, which ties the failure to coarse grids with a shared scale. Hypotheses, thresholds and analysis code were fixed before the data that test them, and the hypotheses that failed are reported.
bullets: Round-to-nearest activation quantization can severely degrade planning despite one-step prediction error comparable to stochastic rounding.
The key issue is error persistence and sharing across planner candidates, not simply rounding-error magnitude.
Redrawing common dither each planner iteration removes most of the degradation without retraining across tested TD-MPC2 and DINO-WM settings.
An W8A4 integer TD-MPC2 world model speeds planning rollouts by 1.9–3.3× and full planning steps by 1.3–1.5× versus FP32; dither adds at most 2.3% latency.
Block-scaled NVFP4 largely avoids the problem, while fixed dither within a step or episode restores planner drift.

papers.selection_reason: Low-bit world models for sampling-based planners, directly relevant to world models, robot navigation, and efficient inference.
papers.title: Planners Exploit Deterministic Error: Dithered Low-Bit World Models
papers.tldr: Shared, per-iteration dithering makes aggressively quantized world models substantially safer for sampling-based planning by preventing persistent, candidate-shared rounding errors from steering the planner.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) requires large amounts of interaction data or a reliable simulator, both hard to obtain for nonlinear soft robotic hardware. Recent work shows that a time-scale separation inherent to soft robot dynamics justifies their reduction to low-dimensional invariant manifolds, known as adiabatic spectral submanifolds (aSSMs). We demonstrate that an aSSM-reduced model, a simple polynomial ordinary differential equation learned purely from pre-collected data, can serve as an RL training environment. On a pneumatically actuated soft arm, we train a trajectory-tracking policy in 3 hours on a six-dimensional aSSM-reduced model and deploy it without fine-tuning, whereas reproducing this policy training extrapolates to 3 years of hardware interaction. Our policy tracks dynamic targets with 40% lower error than otherwise identical policies trained on a 4.8-million-parameter recurrent neural network (RNN) or a 1.7-million-parameter transformer, which take 13 and 100 hours to identify, against 5 minutes for our mathematically justified 6,924-parameter model.
bullets: Soft-robot RL is hindered by costly hardware interactions and unreliable or unavailable simulators.
A time-scale separation reduces the robot dynamics to a low-dimensional adiabatic spectral submanifold (aSSM).
A 6,924-parameter polynomial ODE learned from pre-collected data provides the RL training environment.
On a pneumatically actuated soft arm, the policy trained in 3 hours deployed without fine-tuning and achieved 40% lower tracking error than comparable RNN- and transformer-based approaches.
The approach remains demonstrated on one soft-arm trajectory-tracking task and depends on the validity of the aSSM reduction.

papers.abstract: A purely data-driven method grounded in the theory of adiabatic spectral submanifolds (aSSMs) was recently used to model and control nonlinear soft robotic simulators. Here, we extend the methodology to learn aSSM-reduced models from data collected from hardware soft robotic platforms. Specifically, we learn a five dimensional (5D) aSSM-reduced nonlinear ordinary differential equation (ODE) that accurately models the dynamics of a soft-helicoid trunk robot. We then use this ODE in a model predictive control scheme to demonstrate real-time precision control across various challenging closed-loop trajectory-tracking tasks, ranging from 2D to 3D trajectories with static and dynamic constraints. We find that our methodology enhances accuracy and precision across all control tasks compared to available data-driven linear methods and model-free reinforcement learning. While we focus here on a soft-helicoid trunk robot, our methodology relies solely on hardware data and is therefore applicable to a broader class of soft robotic systems.
bullets: Learns a nonlinear reduced-order ODE directly from hardware data.
Integrates the learned model into a model predictive control scheme.
Demonstrates closed-loop tracking with static and dynamic constraints.
Reports improved accuracy and precision over data-driven linear methods and model-free reinforcement learning.
The hardware-data-based approach is intended to generalize to other soft robotic systems.

papers.abstract: Understanding 3D scene dynamics in minimally invasive surgery (MIS) is a fundamental step toward physically intelligent and autonomous surgical systems. However, existing public datasets offer limited scalability and diversity in real-world clinical scenarios. Moreover, annotations typically focus on either tissue or instruments alone, overlooking tool-tissue interactions. This gap limits applications such as augmented reality guidance and autonomous surgery driven by vision-language-action (VLA) models or world models, which demand large-scale, high-quality 3D supervision. In this work, we construct SurgTAP-3D, a large-scale in-vivo pseudo-3D surgical motion tracking dataset and benchmark, comprising 520K frames, 4,549 action clips, and 1.4M 2D/3D point trajectories from diverse robotic and manual procedures under unified action categories. To make annotation scalable, we design a unified framework for surgical 3D point tracking that converts uncalibrated monocular surgical videos into structured 4D annotations through contact-region prompting, active-tool segmentation, dynamic bundle adjustment, and global 4D refinement. This pipeline adapts foundation priors to surgical videos and produces temporally consistent trajectories, pseudo-scale geometry, camera poses, and instrument masks. The dataset captures realistic challenges inherent to surgical environments, including occlusions, smoke, bleeding, and rapid instrument motion. We establish a comprehensive benchmark on SurgPose, SurgT, and STIR, covering both instrument and tissue tracking. We demonstrate instrument displacement estimation, deformable surface reconstruction, and foundation-model fine-tuning. Extensive experiments and analysis demonstrate the effectiveness of our dataset and annotation framework for 3D surgical point tracking, reconstruction, and surgical action understanding. Homepage: https://wrld.github.io/surgtap-3d/
bullets: Addresses limited scale, diversity, and interaction-aware 3D supervision in existing surgical datasets.
Provides 520K frames, 4,549 action clips, and 1.4M 2D/3D point trajectories from robotic and manual surgeries.
Uses contact-region prompting, tool segmentation, dynamic bundle adjustment, and global 4D refinement to convert monocular videos into structured annotations.
Includes temporally consistent trajectories, pseudo-scale geometry, camera poses, and instrument masks despite occlusions, smoke, bleeding, and fast motion.
Benchmarks instrument and tissue tracking, displacement estimation, deformable reconstruction, and surgical action understanding.

papers.abstract: Robot policies increasingly act through a small vocabulary of discrete latent actions learned from unlabeled video, yet training leaves open which motion receives which code. We find this choice highly unstable: two independently trained runs of Moto's latent motion tokenizer assign the same robot clips to nearly unrelated codes (adjusted Rand index 0.001), and evaluating one tokenizer in bf16 instead of fp32 reassigns 74% of its tokens. We use this freedom to impose the representational geometry of macaque ventral premotor cortex (PMv), recorded while a monkey drew shapes, on the tokenizer's code assignment, with a straight-through similarity loss trained alongside its reconstruction objective on robot video. In one training run per target, on five shape categories the loss never saw, the PMv-trained tokenizer reaches a representational similarity of 0.52 with PMv, against 0.20-0.26 for released and no-prior tokenizers and 0.42 for the 95th percentile of random kinematic encoders. Kinematic, language, and random targets do not transfer (-0.17 to -0.03). Two results limit the claim: a hand-picked kinematic descriptor, the stroke's initial direction, matches PMv better (0.65), and a label-shuffled PMv control scores 0.41. We specify the downstream manipulation test, on a CALVIN pipeline that reproduces Moto's published results, before running it.
bullets: Latent-action assignments vary drastically across training runs and numerical precision, despite similar robot motion inputs.
The method adds a straight-through similarity loss to align a video-trained tokenizer’s code geometry with macaque ventral premotor cortex (PMv) activity.
On held-out shape categories, PMv alignment reaches 0.52 versus 0.20–0.26 for released or no-prior tokenizers and 0.42 for random kinematic encoders.
Kinematic, language, and random targets do not transfer, but a hand-designed initial-stroke-direction descriptor scores higher (0.65).
A shuffled-PMv control still scores 0.41, and downstream manipulation effects are specified for future testing rather than reported.

papers.abstract: Quadrotors inspecting buildings and tunnels must navigate unknown clutter with a forward-facing depth camera whose limited field of view constrains scene understanding and collision-avoiding navigation. Recent world-model agents learn navigation through imagined experience (e.g., AirDreamer), but remain data-intensive and often lack explicit geometric memory and awareness of what the camera can observe. We propose ScanDreamer, a map-grounded world model that constructs an online 2D scan-memory map from depth images and vehicle pose. Our world model, actor, and critic are conditioned on this map, which also defines a geodesic progress reward. Moreover, a forward-cone penalty discourages horizontal motion outside the camera's viewing direction. During imagination, ScanDreamer propagates the quadrotor pose over a frozen map and derives progress and wall-contact signals from the mapped geometry. We train ScanDreamer for 0.8 million environment steps (5.5 h on one GPU) and evaluate it in NVIDIA Isaac Sim over 1560 episodes spanning unseen layouts and parameter ranges. Across three seeds (mean $\pm$ SD), ScanDreamer achieves 96.3 $\pm$ 0.3% success with 3.6 $\pm$ 0.3% collision, compared with 59.6 $\pm$ 3.0% success and 28.8 $\pm$ 2.8% collision for AirDreamer at the same online-interaction budget. Removing the forward-cone penalty increases collisions to 9.9 $\pm$ 3.1%. These results show that combining explicit map memory, map-grounded imagination, and perception-aware motion substantially improves navigation performance and data efficiency. The source code is available at https://github.com/WANGSHUAIzzzz/ScanDreamer.
bullets: Builds an online 2D scan-memory map from depth images and vehicle pose to provide explicit geometric memory.
Conditions the world model, actor, and critic on the map and uses mapped geometry for geodesic progress and wall-contact signals.
Adds a forward-cone penalty to discourage motion outside the forward-facing camera’s view.
In Isaac Sim, it achieves 96.3% success and 3.6% collision across 1,560 episodes, outperforming AirDreamer under the same interaction budget.
Removing the forward-cone penalty raises collisions to 9.9%, highlighting its role in perception-aware navigation.

papers.abstract: A driving foundation model must learn reusable decision knowledge from rare critical events and apply it under strict runtime constraints. We introduce DriveFoundry, a closed-loop framework improving iteration efficiency under data and computation budgets by coupling structured causal data refinement with adaptive inference. The Data Engine builds traceable scene-candidate records linking scene evidence and factor-decision relations to candidate trajectories and outcome assessments. Candidate comparisons and counterfactual annotations clarify how scene factors affect behavioral feasibility and preference. Verified model failures guide VLM-assisted annotation and expert correction, refining training data and annotation systems. The model engine, Xiaomi-Drive-o1, unifies Perception, Causation, Action, World, and Value within a shared vision-language backbone to enable cross-task knowledge transfer. Block-wise latent refill passes candidate-specific evidence and predicted visual consequences between task blocks, connecting scene understanding, planning, and evaluation. A learned value-of-computation head selects tasks and allocates latent tokens based on expected benefit and cost, adapting inference to each decision. On PhysicalAI, the 9B model achieves the lowest ADE@1 across evaluated splits and horizons among tested models. In AlpaSim, it outperforms Alpamayo 1.5 across all metrics and achieves lower close-encounter and off-road rates than the 34B Alpamayo 2 Super, while trailing in progress and AlpaSim scores. For the 0.8B variant, joint training reduces 5 s minADE@6 by about 54% without altering the inference path or token budget. Adaptive inference matches full reasoning performance using only 28% of tokens. Real-vehicle tests confirm runtime feasibility, supporting a unified paradigm for learning from critical experience and dynamically allocating computation.
bullets: Builds traceable scene–factor–decision records with candidate comparisons and counterfactual annotations to refine training data from critical events and verified failures.
Uses Xiaomi-Drive-o1, a shared vision-language model integrating perception, causation, action, world modeling, and value estimation.
Connects task blocks through candidate-specific latent evidence and predicted visual consequences, while a value-of-computation head allocates inference effort adaptively.
Reports strong benchmark results, including the lowest ADE@1 among tested models on PhysicalAI and broad metric improvements over Alpamayo 1.5 in AlpaSim.
Joint training improves 5 s minADE@6 for the 0.8B model by about 54%, and adaptive inference reaches full-reasoning performance with 28% of the tokens; real-vehicle tests support runtime feasibility.

papers.abstract: High-resolution weather prediction is important for resolving local atmospheric patterns missed by coarse global forecasts. Large pretrained weather backbones have improved global forecasting, but adapting them to produce future high-resolution fields from recent coarse states remains challenging and costly. We formulate this setting as Predictive Spatiotemporal Weather Downscaling (PSWD), a task that jointly refines spatial and temporal resolution while predicting future high-resolution trajectories. To this end, we propose a framework that decomposes prediction into spatial and temporal stages using a shared pretrained backbone, fixed numerical scaffolds, and lightweight residual heads. For backbone adaptation, we introduce PROLA (PRincipal-Orthogonal Low-rank Adaptation), which allocates a fixed low-rank budget between pretrained weights' principal directions and their orthogonal complement. PROLA further rescales rank-1 optimizer updates using gradient signals, improving adaptation without increasing trainable rank. Experiments in the PSWD setting show that PROLA outperforms representative low-rank adaptation baselines. Further experiments across diverse datasets and tasks support the broader applicability of PROLA, showing that its benefits extend beyond the primary weather downscaling setting.
bullets: Addresses predictive spatiotemporal weather downscaling: forecasting future high-resolution fields from recent coarse states.
Uses a shared pretrained backbone with separate spatial and temporal stages, fixed numerical scaffolds, and lightweight residual heads.
Introduces PROLA, which splits a fixed low-rank budget between principal weight directions and their orthogonal complement.
Rescales rank-1 optimizer updates according to gradient signals without increasing trainable rank.
Experiments report improvements over representative low-rank adaptation baselines, with benefits also observed across diverse datasets and tasks.

papers.abstract: Dexterous manipulation requires rich spatial foresight over both the surrounding scene and the robot hand. Existing world-action models often acquire such predictive knowledge through explicit future prediction. We introduce DexForesight, a framework that learns spatial foresight implicitly by injecting dynamics-aware world representations into the latent space of a dexterous policy. During training, DexForesight learns an action-conditioned spatial world model from offline scene depth, kinematic hand geometry, and demonstration trajectories. The world model predicts 3D hand-point motion and visual feature changes, capturing both articulated hand dynamics and scene changes under demonstrated actions, including the motion of fingers occluded from the cameras. We then freeze the world model and align policy queries with its predictive world queries, transferring the learned spatial dynamics into policy latents and using them to condition action generation. At deployment, only the policy is retained, operating on RGB observations, language, and robot state without depth input or explicit future prediction. On 11 DexJoCo simulation tasks, DexForesight improves the overall success rate of the base policy from 49.4% to 60.5%. On three real-robot dexterous manipulation tasks, DexForesight achieves 58.3% success, compared with 50.0% for the strongest baseline. Project page https://dexforesight.github.io/
bullets: Learns an action-conditioned spatial world model from depth, hand geometry, and demonstrations.
Predicts 3D hand-point motion and visual feature changes, including occluded finger dynamics and scene changes.
Aligns policy queries with world-model predictions, then freezes the world model and transfers its dynamics into policy latents.
At deployment, the policy uses only RGB observations, language, and robot state.
Improves success from 49.4% to 60.5% on 11 DexJoCo tasks and achieves 58.3% versus 50.0% for the strongest baseline on three real-robot tasks.

DexForesight outperforms prior world-action models in both simulation and real-robot evaluations.

papers.abstract: Surgical procedures are inherently partially observable, requiring surgeons to continuously infer evolving anatomical dynamics and future surgical states beyond the current observation. However, existing self-supervised learning methods primarily learn from observed surgical videos through masked reconstruction or predicting representations within the camera's current field of view, lacking the capability to explicitly model the out-of-sight surgical dynamics. Inspired by latent predictive world models, we introduce SurgWorld, a video-native, self-supervised framework for surgical representation learning, which treats a specified spatial or temporal shift as a pseudo-action and learns to predict the target latent representation from a partial observation. Specifically, we propose Out-of-Sight Dynamics Modeling (OSDM) as the pretraining objective for predicting representations conditioned on relative spatio-temporal shifts. We further regularize the learned latent dynamics from OSDM with a Geometric Visual Similarity (GVS) objective by aligning patch-level relational structures between predicted and target representations, preserving spatial geometry and local visual coherence for dense perception. These two objectives are integrated through an agglomerative training framework that consolidates complementary supervisory signals from multiple teachers to learn a unified latent representation of surgical dynamics and visual geometry. Extensive transfer learning experiments on 17 surgical benchmarks show that SurgWorld consistently outperforms existing vision foundation models across surgical workflow recognition, fine-grained action understanding, and dense visual perception. We further conduct tailored qualitative and quantitative analyses, demonstrating that SurgWorld effectively captures surgical dynamics beyond the directly observed context through latent prediction.
bullets: Addresses the partial observability of surgery, which limits methods focused only on visible content.
Uses spatial or temporal shifts as pseudo-actions and introduces Out-of-Sight Dynamics Modeling to predict target latent representations.
Adds Geometric Visual Similarity regularization to preserve patch-level spatial relationships and local visual coherence.
Combines complementary supervisory signals through an agglomerative training framework for unified dynamics and geometry representations.
Transfers effectively across 17 surgical benchmarks spanning workflow recognition, fine-grained action understanding, and dense perception.

papers.abstract: High-fidelity LiDAR simulation remains a bottleneck for scalable development and validation of autonomous systems. Existing generators can synthesize realistic scans, but they are typically constrained to a single sensor configuration, offer limited control over structure and geometry, and drift in long-horizon 4D generation. We present CrossLiDAR, a unified transformer-based framework capable of generating controllable and spatio-temporally consistent multi-sensor LiDAR sequences. Our approach leverages a rectified flow objective with a Multi-Modal Diffusion Transformer (MM-DiT) backbone, within a compact latent space of range images. To support multiple LiDAR sensors, an Inter-sensor Module enables interaction across sensors, while a ControlNet-style branch provides structural conditioning (e.g., BEV priors or 3D bounding boxes). For modeling the temporal consistency, CrossLiDAR generates short $N$-frame sequences and extends them autoregressively to improve long-horizon coherence. Our model significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, achieving an average improvement of 29.56\% in JSD and 15.36\% in MMD evaluated on nuScenes and the Waymo Dataset. CrossLiDAR bridges the gap to modern autonomous-driving simulation by enabling calibration-consistent multi-sensor LiDAR rollouts over long horizons for controllable, scenario-based testing.
bullets: Addresses single-sensor limitations, weak structural control, and long-horizon drift in LiDAR generation.
Uses a rectified-flow objective with an MM-DiT transformer operating in a compact range-image latent space.
Models cross-sensor interactions and supports conditioning from BEV priors or 3D bounding boxes.
Generates short sequences and extends them autoregressively for longer temporal consistency.
Improves JSD by 29.56% and MMD by 15.36% over state-of-the-art baselines on nuScenes and Waymo.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of CrossLiDAR Framework. Our framework utilizes a latent rectified-flow [26] formulation to generate synchronized multi-sensor LiDAR sequences. (Left) A frozen VAE encoder first maps range images into a compact latent space zt. (Right) These latents are processed by an MM-DiT [9] backbone, which incorporates two different attention mechanisms: an Inter-sensor Module for crosssensor alignment and a LiDAR Sequence Module for temporal consistency. The generation is guided by a dedicated ControlNet [70] branch for BEV and 3D layout control. Finally, a frozen VAE decoder transforms the denoised latents back into high-fidelity temporal point clouds.

papers.abstract: Generative world modeling from large-scale visual data offers a promising path toward scalable robot manipulation. This calls for an intermediate representation that can be supervised at scale and remains actionable for downstream control. We propose 3D full-object flow, an object-centric motion representation that assigns dense 3D trajectories to points across the complete surface of a target object, including its occluded regions. By extending visible-surface object flow to the full object geometry, this representation makes complete object motion explicit and applies uniformly to both rigid and deformable objects. To realize the potential of this representation at scale, we introduce a 1210-hour full-object flow dataset that addresses the scarcity of large-scale supervision for complete 3D object motion. The dataset integrates diverse real-world videos and physical simulations, with a scalable annotation pipeline for recovering full-object motion from real-world observations and quality metrics for systematically assessing annotation quality. We then train a world model that takes an image and a task description as input and predicts dense full-object flow over the reconstructed object geometry. Experiments show reliable annotation quality, data-scalable flow prediction, and effective downstream manipulation across novel scenes and robot embodiments. Project website with additional results and videos: https://nus-lins-lab.github.io/ObjectWorld/.
bullets: Introduces 3D full-object flow: dense trajectories over an object’s complete surface, including occluded regions, for rigid and deformable objects.
Provides a 1210-hour dataset combining real-world videos and physical simulations to supervise complete 3D object motion.
Develops a scalable annotation pipeline and quality metrics for recovering and evaluating full-object flow from observations.
Trains a world model that predicts full-object flow from an image and task description over reconstructed object geometry.
Reports reliable annotations, scalable flow prediction, and effective manipulation across novel scenes and robot embodiments.

figures.caption: Fig. 3: Object-centric full-object flow prediction framework. Given an initial RGB-D observation and task instruction, Qwen2.5-VL [39] extracts task-conditioned visual-language features, while a joint PointTransformer V3 [40] (PTv3) encodes reconstructed object and scene geometry. These features are fused into object tokens and refined by self-attention. The object queries attend to scene and language context through a cross-attention decoder, conditioned on noisy flow and time t, before a flow head predicts dense trajectories over the complete object surface.

papers.title: ObjectWorld: Scaling Object-Centric World Models with A Large-Scale 3D Full-Object Flow Dataset

papers.abstract: In offline reinforcement learning, diffusion models fill two roles with complementary strengths. Typically guided by a critic, a diffusion policy is value-aware and favors high-return, behavior-supported actions, but it is short-sighted: it never lays out the states it intends to visit. A diffusion planner is far-sighted, synthesizing such a long-horizon trajectory, but it is only behavior-driven at execution, realizing each planned transition using only offline behavior.Each is strong exactly where the other is weak. We introduce DPDP to bring them together at the planner's execution step, where a planned transition becomes an action. Reading the planner's inverse-dynamics executor as a posterior over actions: the environment's transition likelihood relates an action to the planned next state, while the behavioral prior determines its weight under the offline data. Replacing this prior with a value-optimized diffusion policy preserves the planned transition likelihood and favors valuable actions that can serve the plan. We target the resulting clean-action distribution in two ways. A training-free sampler composes policy and inverse-dynamics scores at matched action noise levels and applies Langevin correction; this route uses a shared action noise schedule and an approximately common terminal prior. A preference objective instead amortizes the transfer into a single diffusion executor. Across D4RL, DPDP improves the planner it builds on, staying competitive with reactive diffusion policies on locomotion and leading on long-horizon navigation.
bullets: Addresses the short-horizon nature of critic-guided diffusion policies and the behavior-only execution of diffusion planners.
Reinterprets the planner’s inverse-dynamics executor as an action posterior and replaces its behavioral prior with a value-optimized diffusion policy.
Provides a training-free score-composition sampler with Langevin correction and a preference-based objective for a single amortized executor.
Across D4RL, improves its underlying planner, remains competitive with reactive diffusion policies on locomotion, and leads on long-horizon navigation.

On both suites, the policy and the planner are individually comparable, and unifying them exceeds both on the suite average.

Table 2: Gym-MuJoCo locomotion on D4RL. Normalized return averaged over five seeds; columns as in Table 1. The blue DQL+ (value policy) and DV+ (planner) are our reimplemented schedulematched base models. These are dense-reward, reactive tasks with no goal to reach: every step is scored on the spot, so they reward immediate control rather than foresight. The value policy DQL+ therefore leads and planning is unnecessary, yet the transfer still improves the base planner DV+ on nearly every task, narrowing the gap to the reactive frontier.

papers.abstract: Dexterous manipulation with world action models (WAMs) relies on hand configuration and contact information, yet joint-state and whole-hand tactile observations may be partially or entirely missing. RGB images provide scene context and hand-object geometry but are insufficient to reliably recover these missing modalities. We further observe a correlation between hand state and tactile information. Motivated by this observation, we introduce BAT-WAM, a framework that bridges visual, joint-state, and tactile representations for WAMs. BAT-WAM learns separate codebooks and decoders for the tactile and action streams. An RGB-conditioned continuous latent bridge connects the two streams for bidirectional learning, while visual information serves as continuous context. Under the HTBench evaluation protocol, BAT-WAM reduces the root mean squared error (RMSE) of tactile reconstruction by 34.73% under fully masked conditions and 38.84% under partially masked conditions, relative to an image-conditioned HandTouch checkpoint. For future tactile prediction conditioned on target-time RGB and historical actions, it reduces mean RMSE by 85.56% relative to OpenWAM with HandTouch. Real-robot experiments further show that BAT-WAM consistently outperforms related WAM baselines in dexterous manipulation. Generalization experiments on unseen objects and scenes also demonstrate substantial improvements over baseline models. These findings support joint modeling of visual context, hand state, and touch as a representation approach for multimodal WAMs.
bullets: Addresses missing or incomplete hand-state and whole-hand tactile observations, which RGB alone cannot reliably reconstruct.
Uses separate tactile and action codebooks/decoders connected by an RGB-conditioned continuous latent bridge for bidirectional learning.
Reduces tactile reconstruction RMSE by 34.73% under fully masked and 38.84% under partially masked conditions versus an image-conditioned HandTouch checkpoint.
Improves future tactile prediction mean RMSE by 85.56% versus OpenWAM with HandTouch.
Outperforms related baselines in real-robot manipulation and generalizes better to unseen objects and scenes.

papers.abstract: Learning predictive models for dynamics is difficult because observations are often sparse and noisy, while the underlying dynamics evolve on nonlinear configuration manifolds and are affected by environmental dissipation and stochastic disturbances. Standard neural dynamics models can fit short-term trajectories but often violate physical structure, accumulate error over long horizons, or rely on parameterizations that introduce singularities such as gimbal lock. We introduce LieSPHGP, a stochastic Gaussian-process framework for learning rigid body dynamics with port-Hamiltonian structure and stability-aware robustness. LieSPHGP represents motion on Lie groups and Lie algebras, enabling coordinate-consistent optimization without singular parameterizations. Learned mass, potential energy, dissipation, and control components retain physical roles and a separate diffusion term represents stochastic forcing. Each component is modeled by Matérn kernel Gaussian processes which capture uncertainty induced by noisy observations. To improve physical validity, Lie group exponential map updates preserve rotational constraints, while positive-definite damping ensures nonnegative deterministic energy dissipation. The implicit-explicit integrator additionally provides unconditional stability for the frozen linear damping subsystem. The resulting model learns predictive dynamics that are robust to noise, respect rigid body geometry, and capture both intrinsic motion and environmental dissipation. Experiments on various noisy rigid body benchmarks show improved prediction accuracy, stronger long-horizon stability, and better satisfaction of manifold constraints compared with neural dynamics baselines. Code, data and interactive results are available on the project website: https://thribhuvanrapolu.github.io/liesphgp/
bullets: Targets sparse, noisy dynamics on nonlinear configuration manifolds, where standard neural models may violate physics or become unstable over long horizons.
Uses Matérn-kernel Gaussian processes for mass, potential energy, dissipation, control, and stochastic forcing components.
Represents motion through Lie groups and Lie algebras to avoid singular parameterizations and preserve rotational geometry.
Combines positive-definite damping with an implicit-explicit integrator for nonnegative dissipation and unconditional stability of frozen linear damping.
Noisy rigid-body benchmarks report improved prediction accuracy, long-horizon stability, and manifold-constraint satisfaction versus neural dynamics baselines.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of the proposed framework. Given noisy observations of a dynamical system, we learn a physics-structured model that captures both the underlying dynamics and their uncertainty while preserving the geometric structure of the state space. The learned model is then used to design a controller that drives the true system toward a desired state or trajectory without additional training. We demonstrate the framework on a 3D pendulum evolving on SO(3) and a quadrotor evolving on SE(3).

Figure 2: LieSPHGP framework. Five GP subnetworks (M−1, V , D, G and the diffusion ξ), each a level (constant, or linear for V ) plus a Matérn-kernel random-feature Gaussian process (Section 3.2, Algorithm 5), define a stochastic port-Hamiltonian system on SO(3) or SE(3) (Section 3.1), integrated with the Lie-IMEX solver (Section 3.3, Algorithm 4). At each training step one GP weight sample W ∼ q(W ) is drawn and held fixed throughout each rollout; starting from y0, the solver gives the prediction x̂−k and its Jacobians Ak, Bk, and a Lie-group EKF propagates the covariance P− k = AkPk−1A ⊤ k +BkB ⊤ k , so the diffusion enters only through the process covariance BkB ⊤ k , while the noisy observations yk and the learned measurement-noise scales σobs enter the measurement update. Training minimizes L = Eq(W )[EKF NLL]+βKL ( q(W ) ∥ p(W ) ) , the EKF negative log-likelihood of the noisy windows plus a KL term on the GP weights (Section 3.4, Eq. 21). Each parameter group has its own Prodigy optimizer, so its learning rate ηk(t) is adapted separately during training (Algorithm 1).

Figure 13: Physics Identification in Quadrotor System (Control Matrix): Actuated rows of the learned control map M−1G along a 10-s ground-truth tracking flight (training seed 0). The top row shows body-z thrust (vz), and the next three show body torques (ωx, ωy, ωz), with one column per rotor. The torque rows contain the rotor mixing matrix Bmix. Each row is divided by the magnitude of its nonzero ground-truth entries (37.0, 1658, 1658, and 777, from top to bottom). The normalized ground truth (dashed black) is therefore −1, 0, or 1, and all panels share the same vertical scale. PH-NODE (Duong et al., 2024) is shown in purple and LieSPHGP in orange. The body-x and body-y force rows are omitted because they are zero in the true model and the controller does not use them.

Figure 14: Physics Identification in Quadrotor System (Dissipation): Comparison of the learned diagonals of M−1 1 Dv for translational damping (top row) and M−1 2 Dω for rotational damping (bottom row) along a 10-s ground-truth tracking flight (training seed 0). The models compared are the ground truth (black, dashed), PH-NODE (Duong et al., 2024) (purple), and LieSPHGP (orange). LieSPHGP is closer to the ground truth for both translational and rotational damping, while PH-NODE over-estimates both (Table 16).

Figure 11: Physics Identification in Windy Pendulum System: Comparison of the learned diagonals of the matrices M−1G for control (top row) and M−1D for damping (bottom row) along the ground-truth swing-up flight (training seed 0). The models compared are the ground truth (black, dashed), PH-NODE (Duong et al., 2024) (purple), Lie-PH-NN-SDE (blue), and LieSPHGP (orange). LieSPHGP follows the ground truth for both products; PH-NODE over-estimates the damping about six times, and Lie-PH-NNSDE has the wrong sign of the y control gain near the upright.

Figure 6: Closed-loop SE(3) quadrotor tracking using learned dynamics. Three-dimensional trajectories for two of the ten held-out 10-s flights (A and B). Thin lines show individual Brownian motion samples, thick lines show the mean over those five samples, and dashed lines show the reference. Each model supplies the dynamics to the same geometric tracking controller with an IDA-PBC attitude loop. The controller’s commands are allocated to the four rotors of the contact-free PyBullet CF2P plant (Panerati et al., 2021). LieSPHGP (orange) tracks close to the controller using the true dynamics (green), while PH-NODE (purple) deviates during turns. Across all flights and seeds, the position RMSE is 0.133m for LieSPHGP and 0.251m for PH-NODE (Table 5).

Figure 4: Closed-loop IDA-PBC control of the stochastic SO(3) pendulum using learned dynamics. Each model supplies its learned dynamical subnetworks to the same IDA-PBC controller acting in the windy pendulum environment, with the objective of stabilizing the pendulum at the upright configuration. LieSPHGP (orange) closely follows the controller constructed from the true model, which uses ground truth components (green), and reaches the target, whereas PH-NODE (purple) does not reach the upright. The experiment demonstrates that differences in learned physical structure that are modest in open-loop prediction can become consequential for downstream control.

Figure 3: Open-loop prediction on the windy pendulum. Roll, pitch, and yaw (Euler xyz angles of R, as in Figure 4) predicted over 10 s from the true initial state using recorded inputs. Roll = ±π corresponds to the hanging position. Black shows ground truth. Lines show the mean of 32 sampled paths, except for PH-NODE’s single deterministic path. Shading shows ±1σ and ±2σ. The true SDE uses independently sampled wind. We show the held-out trajectory with the largest difference in mean rotation error between Lie-PH-NN-SDE and LieSPHGP (43.1◦ versus 7.0◦). Over all 10 held-out trajectories, Lie-PH-NN-SDE has the larger error on 9. On the shown trajectory, 2σ coverage is 0.97 for both the true SDE and LieSPHGP, and 0.47 for Lie-PH-NN-SDE.

Figure 7: Open-loop prediction on a held-out BlueROV2 test segment. Predicted positions x, y, and z (positive downward), and position error, using recorded thruster commands and the measured initial state. Vertical dotted lines mark the first time position error exceeds 0.1m (valid prediction time). LieSPHGP shows the mean of 32 sampled paths with a ±2σ band (training seed 0). The physics model uses published vehicle parameters. LieSPHGP learns M−1, V , D, and G from training data alone. The shown segment has the median LieSPHGP valid prediction time among the 15 test segments.

Figure 5: Control using the learned dynamics. The learned subnetworks M−1, V , D, and G define the IDA-PBC control law. Energy shaping replaces the learned potential with a desired potential whose minimum is at the target, while damping injection adds damping Kω. The errors are Lie-group differences, xe = x ⊖ x∗ (Section 3.4), whose attitude part is eR = Log(R∗⊤R)∨ with R∗ the target attitude. For the quadrotor, IDA-PBC forms the inner attitude loop of an outer position-tracking controller (Appendix A.4).

papers.title: Stochastic Port-Hamiltonian Gaussian Processes for Learning from Noisy Dynamics on Lie Groups

papers.abstract: Hierarchical Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (H-JEPA) enable long-horizon visual control but rely on costly test-time gradient descent for planning. Our analysis reveals that iterative optimization consumes up to 97.7% of episode runtime and that low predicted rollout costs do not necessarily translate into successful control. We further identify a planning-horizon asymmetry between long-horizon top-level composition and short two-step subordinate planning. To address these challenges, we propose WARP-JEPA, a hierarchical amortized planning framework that replaces online gradient optimization with learned multi-candidate trajectory proposers while keeping the world models frozen. WARP-JEPA combines a lightweight world-model-in-the-loop causal Transformer at the top level with parallel residual MLPs at subordinate levels. The proposers are trained using model-based rollout costs and best-of-K behavior cloning, enabling efficient candidate selection without test-time gradient optimization. Across 30 frozen H-JEPA models on four benchmarks, WARP-JEPA achieves 9.6-18.8x faster episode inference on long-horizon tasks (2.9-3.0x on Cube) and improves task success by up to 33.3 percentage points. These results demonstrate that amortized planning can substantially improve both inference efficiency and control performance without retraining the world models. Code is available at https://github.com/hideinsewer/WARP-JEPA.
bullets: H-JEPA planning can spend up to 97.7% of episode runtime on iterative optimization, and low predicted rollout costs may not ensure successful control.
The method uses a hierarchical planner: a causal Transformer for top-level composition and parallel residual MLPs for short-horizon subordinate planning.
Proposers are trained with model-based rollout costs and best-of-K behavior cloning, while the underlying world models remain frozen.
Across 30 frozen H-JEPA models and four benchmarks, inference is 9.6–18.8× faster on long-horizon tasks and 2.9–3.0× faster on Cube.
Task success improves by up to 33.3 percentage points, demonstrating gains in both efficiency and control without world-model retraining.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Architecture of WARP-JEPA (asymmetric TM shown). Blue: frozen H-JEPA modules; orange: learned proposers. (a) A standard 1-layer causal Transformer decoder TϕL [33] cross-attends to the context tokens M (Eq. (4)); each query joins the previous macro-action with the state imagined by the frozen PL, which also scores the KL plans with zero extra rollouts. (b) Proposers are trained with relaxed WTA rollout cost plus best-of-K behavior cloning (Eq. (3)) through frozen Pl. papers.selection_reason: Proposes WARP-JEPA, a framework for amortized rollout planning in frozen H-JEPA models, directly addressing planning efficiency and control in embodied AI and interactive world models.
papers.title: WARP-JEPA: World-Model-in-the-Loop Amortized Rollout Planning for Frozen Hierarchical Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures
papers.tldr: WARP-JEPA replaces costly test-time gradient planning in frozen hierarchical world models with learned amortized trajectory proposal, making long-horizon control faster and more successful.

papers.abstract: Visual generative models increasingly blur the line between synthesizing observations and simulating environments. Yet visual plausibility alone does not constitute successful world modeling: compelling outputs may lack persistent state, physical dynamics, or causally consistent responses to interactions. We define a generative world model as a predictive dynamical system that maintains a persistent, history-conditioned representation of an environment, updates that representation in response to actions or interventions, and generates temporally coherent trajectories that reflect outcomes under observed and counterfactual interventions. From this definition, we derive an intelligence-oriented framework spanning perceptual grounding, persistent state modeling, controllable transformation, dynamics-aware prediction, and closed-loop interaction. We present WorldFoundry, open-source infrastructure for reproducible inference and evaluation across video, 3D and 4D, embodied action, and interactive world systems. WorldFoundry unifies model and benchmark discovery, runtime and asset preparation, execution orchestration, artifact management, and interactive visualization, while modality-specific adapters preserve native inputs, execution semantics, output representations, and evaluation protocols. Explicit manifests, durable artifact contracts, and evidence-aware scorecards separate execution readiness from evaluative claims, making each claim traceable to its supporting artifacts. The catalog contains 270 model entries, 74 benchmarks, and 62 registered metric entries, with readiness and execution evidence recorded separately. WorldFoundry enables reproducible comparison of persistent, controllable dynamics across heterogeneous systems, advancing the field from perceptual synthesis toward measurable world intelligence.
bullets: Defines world models as history-conditioned dynamical systems that update with actions or interventions and generate coherent observed or counterfactual trajectories.
Organizes evaluation around perceptual grounding, persistent state, controllable transformation, dynamics-aware prediction, and closed-loop interaction.
Supports video, 3D/4D, embodied-action, and interactive systems through modality-specific adapters that preserve native execution and evaluation protocols.
Provides discovery, runtime preparation, orchestration, artifact management, visualization, manifests, and evidence-aware scorecards.
Catalogs 270 model entries, 74 benchmarks, and 62 metric entries, while separating execution readiness from evaluative claims.

papers.abstract: Latent world models enable visual control by planning action sequences in compact representation spaces, but a gap remains between how latent dynamics are learned and how they are used for planning. First, teacher-forced training does not expose the dynamics model to the recursively predicted latent states encountered during planning. Second, sampling-based planners typically initialize action search from goal-agnostic proposals, without exploiting the action-conditioned dynamics learned by the world model. We introduce Dynamics-Informed Action Learning (DIAL) to bridge these two gaps. During training, rollout alignment exposes the forward model to its own autoregressive latent predictions, while multi-step inverse supervision trains a lightweight inverse dynamics head to infer actions from latent-state transitions. We further apply the inverse head to model-generated transitions with its parameters held fixed, encouraging predicted rollouts to retain action-relevant information. At test time, DIAL autoregressively couples the inverse and forward dynamics to construct a dynamics-informed action sequence toward the goal, which initializes the mean of the Cross-Entropy Method (CEM) proposal distribution. The subsequent CEM search then refines this initialization using the standard sampling and updating procedure. Experiments across four visual control benchmarks demonstrate that DIAL outperforms existing latent world models and planning baselines in both standard and long-horizon scenarios.
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between teacher-forced latent dynamics training and recursive planning, plus goal-agnostic action proposals.
Uses rollout alignment to train on the model’s own predicted latent states.
Adds multi-step inverse dynamics supervision and applies the fixed inverse head to model-generated transitions to preserve action-relevant information.
At test time, couples inverse and forward dynamics to initialize Cross-Entropy Method (CEM) planning, which then refines the action sequence.
Outperforms existing latent world models and planning baselines across four visual-control benchmarks, including long-horizon settings.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of DIAL. (2) Multi-step inverse supervision trains the inverse-dynamics head Gψ on observed latent state pairs and uses a frozen inverse head Gψ̄ to encourage model-generated states to preserve action-relevant information. (3) Dynamics-informed planning autoregressively couples Gψ and Fθ to generate a goal-directed action sequence, which initializes only the mean of the CEM proposal.

papers.abstract: We introduce Latent-WAM++, a representation-centered World Action Model (WAM) for end-to-end autonomous driving. Existing WAMs are primarily trained to predict future states or final actions, leaving the intermediate world and action representations that connect prediction to planning only indirectly constrained. Latent-WAM++ matches the supervision of each representation to its role in planning. World Representation Construction combines scene-ego future prediction, SIGReg-based distribution stabilization, and frozen geometric priors to learn a temporally predictive, non-degenerate, and geometry-aware world representation without an EMA target encoder. Trajectory MeanFlow Planner directly predicts multimodal trajectory proposals while being optimized with an Improved MeanFlow velocity-space objective, enabling one-step sampling. Visual-Action Representation Alignment further aligns the resulting pre-output action features with a stop-gradient target derived from current visual semantics. Latent-WAM++ achieves state-of-the-art performance on NAVSIM v2 and under zero-shot evaluation on HUGSIM, reaching 90.1 EPDMS on NAVSIM v2 and 47.0 average RC and 30.1 average HD-Score on HUGSIM. Training the planner end to end costs 190 GPU-hours for Latent-WAM++ versus 1,600 for Latent-WAM, a reduction of 88.1%.
bullets: Addresses weak supervision of intermediate world and action representations in existing World Action Models.
Learns a temporally predictive, geometry-aware world representation using future prediction, SIGReg stabilization, and frozen geometric priors.
Uses a MeanFlow-based planner for multimodal trajectory proposals with one-step sampling.
Aligns pre-output action features with current visual semantics through visual-action representation alignment.
Reports 90.1 EPDMS on NAVSIM v2, zero-shot results on HUGSIM, and 88.1% lower planner training cost than Latent-WAM.

papers.abstract: Latent-action world models learn actions from video without labels, and recent methods aim to share these actions across bodies. Transfer between 2D characters with different body structures remains underexplored. In this paper, we study whether an action learned from one character can make a character with a different body perform the same action. A cat, a blob and a human can all jump, but each moves its body in its own way. The usual transfer gain mixes body motion with screen movement and can assign a perfect score to a model that ignores its action. To address this, we introduce a transfer score that compares the correct action with wrong ones from the same source. We test five training objectives on a new synthetic benchmark of 2D cartoon characters with six body plans, the standard Sprites benchmark, and 431 selected animal and human animations from DeformingThings4D. With a fixed camera, a baseline that only copies the source's screen movement scores 0.71, as high as most learned models. In contrast, with a camera that follows the body, the best model reaches only 0.46 for an unseen animal family and 0.20 for humans. With this camera, a linear probe identifies the action class of unseen animal families with 66% to 86% balanced accuracy (chance 17%). The learned actions therefore retain information about which action is performed, but the correct action closes only part of the prediction error gap for a new character.
bullets: Cross-body-plan transfer is studied for 2D characters such as cats, blobs, and humans performing shared actions.
The paper introduces a transfer score that contrasts the correct source action with incorrect actions from the same source to avoid rewarding screen-motion copying.
Five training objectives are evaluated on a new six-body-plan cartoon benchmark, Sprites, and selected DeformingThings4D animations.
With a fixed camera, screen-motion copying reaches 0.71, revealing that standard transfer gains can be misleading.
Body-following-camera results are lower: the best model scores 0.46 on an unseen animal family and 0.20 on humans, while action classes remain linearly decodable at 66–86% balanced accuracy.

papers.selection_reason: Directly studies latent-action world models and action transfer across body plans, fitting the latent-action-models subtopic.
papers.title: Action Transfer Across Character Body Plans in Latent-Action World Models: An Empirical Study of Animated Characters
papers.tldr: The study shows that latent actions retain transferable action information across differently shaped animated characters, but current models achieve only partial zero-shot action transfer when screen-motion shortcuts are removed.

papers.abstract: Autonomous robot teams deployed in remote, unstructured environments may face changes in the environment, hardware, and team composition that degrade previously effective policies. Shifting mission objectives can be handled by selecting a different solution from an existing Pareto set, but shifting deployment conditions can reorder the set itself, making previously dominated policies competitive or new policies necessary. However, evaluating these policies in new contexts while minimizing risk to the hardware remains an open problem. We argue that, although largely untested in this domain, world models merit investigation for post-deployment multi-objective adaptation. By predicting policy outcomes under updated estimates of current conditions, world models could enable teams to re-evaluate existing policies without physically executing each candidate, provided predicted performance changes reflect those realized on deployed systems. We identify research priorities for model-based policy re-evaluation, validation of predicted against realized performance, and incorporating shared information into world models to support coordinated team adaptation.
bullets: Environmental, hardware, or team changes can reorder the Pareto set, making previously dominated or new policies viable.
Selecting among existing Pareto-optimal policies may address objective shifts but not changing deployment conditions.
World models could predict policy outcomes under updated conditions, reducing the need to physically test every candidate.
Safe adoption requires validating predicted performance against outcomes on deployed systems.
Shared information should be incorporated to support coordinated adaptation across robot teams.

figures.caption: Figure 1: This is a proposed pipeline for maintaining a shared, current representation of the world using world models after deployment. Distributed agents collect local observations, model predictions are tracked against realized performance, and if the context is out of distribution, the model can be updated. The model is used to evaluate policies when objectives change, or possibly even learn new policies with the updated world models.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes using world models for post-deployment multi-objective adaptation in remote robot teams, directly addressing world models for robotics.
papers.title: Multi-Objective Adaptation After Deployment: A Position on World Models for Remote Robot Teams
papers.tldr: World models could help remote robot teams safely reassess and adapt policies after deployment as conditions and objectives change.

papers.abstract: World models enable planning through internal simulation, while natural language provides intuitive task specification. Yet, language-conditioned world modeling remains fragmented across domains with disparate action spaces, datasets, and evaluation protocols. We introduce LCWM, a shared task that maps an initial agent-view observation and a language instruction to an action sequence that fulfills the instruction. Its accompanying benchmark, LCWM-Bench, integrates 15 datasets across navigation, robotics, 3D gaming, and driving under a shared action interface and evaluation protocol, pairing 142,987 episodes with 428,961 instructions in three styles. We further propose Tiresias, an agent that plans via selective imagination: a language-conditioned diffusion policy generates candidate trajectories, a trajectory ranker shortlists them, and a video-pretrained world model imagines their visual consequences. A visual ranker evaluates these rollouts, complementing trajectory scores to select the final plan. Tiresias achieves competitive planning and imagination performance on LCWM-Bench. Ablations demonstrate the complementary benefits of trajectory ranking and visual verification, while experiments with alternative proposal methods show that the trained rankers remain effective beyond our diffusion policy. Together, LCWM-Bench and Tiresias provide a unified evaluation setting and an effective starting point for studying language-guided planning through world models.
bullets: LCWM-Bench unifies 15 datasets spanning navigation, robotics, 3D gaming, and driving under shared actions and evaluation.
The benchmark contains 142,987 episodes and 428,961 instructions in three language styles.
Tiresias uses a language-conditioned diffusion policy to propose trajectories, then combines trajectory ranking with video-based visual verification.
A video-pretrained world model imagines the visual outcomes of shortlisted plans before final selection.
Ablations support the complementary value of trajectory ranking and visual verification; performance is reported as competitive on LCWM-Bench.

papers.title: Tiresias: Towards Language-Conditioned World Models
papers.tldr: Tiresias enables language-guided planning by ranking imagined action trajectories in a unified cross-domain world-model benchmark.

papers.abstract: Embedded AI is moving from perception to prediction. Robots now use world models$\unicode{x2014}$learned simulators that predict the outcome of candidate actions in a compressed latent space before any is executed. Every predicted step must be computed on board within a tight power and thermal budget, yet the energy these steps fundamentally require, and how far real hardware sits from it, have not been characterized. We derive lower bounds on the arithmetic operations and the CMOS dynamic energy of a latent state transition from information theory and Boolean circuit complexity. Profiling a DreamerV3-style Recurrent State Space Model (RSSM) shows that every rollout operation is memory-bandwidth bound and that a GPU consumes at least $5.9\times10^{10}$ times the CMOS energy floor. Transient 3D thermal simulations show that this inefficiency is also a thermal one, since sustained back-to-back planning heats a millimeter-scale silicon tile to 556 K even behind an ideal copper heat spreader. Guided by this chain from bound to bottleneck, we propose the World Model Planning Accelerator (WMPA), a chip architecture for embedded world model planning that combines near-memory computation, real-time entropy estimation, variable-precision rollout units, and copy-on-write latent scratchpads. With a design target of 40x lower power, the same tile stays near ambient at 306 K in simulation, pointing toward practical planning on thermally constrained robots.
bullets: Derives information-theoretic and Boolean-circuit lower bounds for latent state-transition operations and their CMOS dynamic energy.
Finds that DreamerV3-style RSSM rollouts are memory-bandwidth bound, while GPU energy is reported as far above the CMOS energy floor.
Thermal simulations show sustained planning can overheat a millimeter-scale silicon tile, even with ideal copper heat spreading.
Proposes WMPA with near-memory computation, entropy-aware precision, variable-precision rollout units, and copy-on-write latent scratchpads.
A 40× lower-power design target is simulated to keep the tile near ambient temperature, suggesting feasibility for thermally constrained robots.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have continuous deficiency in spatial reasoning tasks that require \emph{mental spatial transformation}, such as reasoning under hypothetical changes in viewpoint or position, known as perspective-taking tasks. Existing approaches either scale linguistic reasoning or augment VLMs with static geometric representations, but neither directly enables active transformation of the represented scene. World models offer this capability, yet existing systems typically communicate through synthesized RGB images, introducing a latent-to-pixel-to-latent bottleneck. We introduce \emph{WorldMind}, a framework for test-time scaling of spatial reasoning through latent world simulation. Given a query and observation, the VLM selects useful spatial transformations, while a world model executes them and exposes aligned intermediate latent features directly to the VLM. The resulting latent evidence is incorporated into subsequent reasoning steps, enabling iterative spatial simulation without repeatedly decoding imagined states into pixels. To optimize this interaction, WorldMind further employs process-verifiable reinforcement learning that rewards reasoning progress only when the associated action and latent transition are valid. WorldMind thus scales spatial reasoning by allocating additional inference-time computation to active world simulation rather than generating more language or pixels. Across VSI-Bench, MMSI-Bench, and MindCube-Tiny, WorldMind achieves an average improvement of 16.0% over the base VLM and 8.3% over the strongest RGB-based world simulation.
bullets: Targets VLM deficiencies in mental spatial transformations, including hypothetical viewpoint and position changes.
The VLM selects useful transformations, while a world model executes them and returns aligned latent features directly for iterative reasoning.
Uses process-verifiable reinforcement learning to reward only valid actions and latent transitions that make reasoning progress.
Achieves average gains of 16.0% over the base VLM and 8.3% over the strongest RGB-based world simulation across three benchmarks.
Scope: focused on visual spatial reasoning and perspective-taking tasks evaluated on VSI-Bench, MMSI-Bench, and MindCube-Tiny.

figures.caption: Figure 4: Overview of WorldMind design. Given the currently observed RGB frames and a spatial query, WorldMind augments standard VLM visual tokens with the selected latent features from a pre-trained world model, and performs iterative reasoning through camera actions and latent world simulation. Then, it fine-tunes the VLM in two stages: (1) supervised fine-tuning with simulated reasoning trajectories; and (2) process-verifiable reinforcement learning, which further optimizes action selection and reasoning using intermediate and final rewards.

papers.abstract: Advection-diffusion plays an essential role in transport phenomena such as atmospheric and cloud dynamics. Improved forecasting of cloud motion, in turn, enhances solar power production forecasts and facilitates the integration of additional photovoltaic (PV) sources into the power grid. However, both classical numerical models and emerging deep learning approaches face challenges when applied to spatially irregular sensor networks such as those formed by weather stations. In this work, we adopt a graph signal processing perspective and model advection-diffusion particles as signals on a graph to capture the dynamics of these processes. We introduce a Physics-Informed Graph Neural Network (PING) for forecasting future advection-diffusion particle concentrations on irregular grids. The model incorporates a discretized advection-diffusion equation as a soft constraint in the loss function to guide learning toward physically consistent solutions. This model is on par with state of the art models on synthetic and real transport phenomena datasets, including sea surface temperature and cloud index datasets. Furthermore, the PING model is successfully coupled with models for forecasting PV power production. This hybrid approach leverages data fusion from ground-based sensors at PV stations and satellite images with cloud concentration to improve the accuracy of intra-day PV power production.
bullets: Targets cloud and other transport dynamics relevant to solar power prediction.
Represents advection-diffusion concentrations as graph signals on irregular grids.
Uses a discretized advection-diffusion equation as a soft loss constraint for physical consistency.
Performs comparably to state-of-the-art models on synthetic, sea-surface-temperature, and cloud-index datasets.
Couples with PV forecasting models using ground sensors and satellite cloud imagery to improve intraday power forecasts.

papers.abstract: Learning control from action-free recordings is challenging because intervention effects are unobserved and policies may exploit errors in reconstructed dynamics. We present a hierarchical model-based reinforcement learning framework that uses shared structure across related systems to learn system-specific control policies from action-free recordings. A hierarchical dynamical system reconstruction model captures shared dynamics and individual variation through low-dimensional embeddings. These embeddings are then reused to parameterize shared policy and value networks, linking differences in reconstructed dynamics to differences in control. Policies are trained entirely via simulation under an explicit intervention model with additive latent perturbations. Piecewise-linear recurrent neural networks enable mechanistic analyses of the controlled dynamics, while decoder-based constraints make the immediate effects of interventions interpretable in observation space and permit interventions on one modality while protecting another from direct manipulation. On Lorenz-63 and double-pendulum systems, hierarchical policies improve transfer over independently trained policies. On Lorenz-63, they also achieve a higher mean reward than repeated planning with the same reconstructed models, perform comparably to methods trained with controlled interactions, and generalize to systems absent from policy training after embedding inference alone. Applications to neural-behavioral recordings demonstrate suppression of predicted movement under constrained neural perturbations. Together, these findings show how shared dynamical representations support transferable control and mechanistic hypothesis generation from action-free recordings.
bullets: Addresses the challenge of learning intervention effects when recordings contain no observed actions.
Reconstructs related dynamical systems with low-dimensional embeddings capturing shared structure and individual variation.
Reuses embeddings to parameterize shared policy and value networks, connecting inferred dynamics to control.
Uses simulated interventions, interpretable decoder constraints, and piecewise-linear recurrent networks for mechanistic analysis.
Improves transfer on Lorenz-63 and double-pendulum systems, and can generalize to unseen systems after embedding inference.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Framework overview. a: A hierarchical DSR model is trained on multiple related dynamical systems (“subjects”) and used as world model for MBRL. Subject-specific parameters φ(j) are obtained by projecting shared parameters Pφ onto low-dimensional subject embeddings S(j). These embeddings are reused to condition the policy πψ and value networks Qθ by modulating group-level parameters Pψ and Pθ. b: For unseen subjects, learning only a new embedding via DSR fine-tuning enables insertion into the control model. c: The high-dimensional dynamics are controlled only in the directions that are decoded (z̃t). To underactuate the problem and for application-specific constraints, actions are constrained to be orthogonal to the target modalities and target dimensions. d: In the Lorenz-63 benchmark, the actions only affect the y− and z−directions.
