papers.abstract: Low latent prediction error does not establish that a world model distinguishes the consequences of its actions. We introduce an evaluation protocol that traces the same intervention through simulator state, raster observations, target embeddings, and predictor outputs. Exact simulator-state forks in a controlled deformable-physics testbed reveal distinct bottlenecks. Changed commands alter particle motion, yet 41.5% of one-step raster pairs are identical. Observation loss is not the whole explanation: among 579 high-visibility counterfactuals, median predictor-to-target response is 0.0051 and 0.0217 across two seeds, falling to 0.0027 and 0.0116 after variance normalization. An isotropic state perturbation matched to the target counterfactual embedding shift produces 190x and 53x larger predictor changes on the same visible pairs, isolating action-path under-use rather than a dead or globally shrunk predictor. MSE-only training gives 8.36x lower 10-step latent error in matched seeds, but in spectrally concentrated spaces; one VICReg target encoder is also strongly concentrated, so neither error nor rank alone certifies physical state. Finally, stiffness remains near chance even from full-resolution rasters and mechanical state while privileged material parameters decode perfectly, indicating weak identifiability under this excitation rather than encoder discard. These results motivate auditing physical effect, observation visibility, representation geometry, and action dependence separately.
bullets: A counterfactual protocol traces interventions from simulator state through raster observations, target embeddings, and predictor outputs.
In the testbed, 41.5% of one-step raster counterfactual pairs are identical despite changed particle motion, revealing an observation bottleneck.

Among visible counterfactuals, predictor responses are very small; matched isotropic embedding perturbations cause 53–190× larger changes, indicating action-path under-use rather than a globally inactive predictor.
MSE-only training achieves lower 10-step latent error, but concentrated representations show that prediction error and rank do not guarantee physical-state encoding.
Material stiffness remains near chance from images and mechanical state while privileged parameters decode perfectly, indicating weak identifiability under the tested excitation.

papers.abstract: Model-based reinforcement learning (MBRL) approaches have demonstrated strong performance across diverse domains in recent years, learning accurate world models from agent trajectories. However, despite this progress, current approaches still struggle to surpass human performance on tasks that require long-term memory and planning. In this work, we address the problem of long-term memory in MBRL by moving beyond the commonly studied paradigm of architecture design. We introduce Test-Time Model-Based Reinforcement Learning (TT-MBRL), using gradient descent at test time to encode the memory of episode observations into world model parameters. This enables the agent to learn a distinct world model for each episode, improving memory capabilities compared to traditional approaches that solely rely on contextual memory. We first establish a proof of concept on a simplified two-dimensional variant of the Memory Maze environment, which we refer to as Memory Maze 2D, showing consistent improvements across different world model architectures. We then demonstrate the effectiveness of TT-MBRL in the 3D domain, achieving new state-of-the-art results on the Memory Maze benchmark. Finally, we show that TT-MBRL maintains strong performance on non-memory benchmarks such as DeepMind Control and Atari 100k.
authors: Maxime Burchi, Fayaz Ali Dharejo, Radu Timofte
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of surpassing human performance on tasks requiring long-term memory and planning.
Learns a distinct world model for each episode by updating model parameters at test time, rather than relying only on contextual memory.
Validated across multiple world-model architectures in a simplified 2D Memory Maze setting.
Achieves state-of-the-art results on the 3D Memory Maze benchmark while retaining strong performance on DeepMind Control and Atari 100k.

Without test-time optimization, the model accumulates prediction errors and struggles to make accurate long-term predictions. This makes it difficult to learn an optimal policy for the actor-critic.

Figure 3: During training, the world model learns to predict the common patterns shared among multiple episode trajectories collected during exploration. The agent can solely rely on contextual memory to identify patterns that are unique to each new episode, which can lead to incoherent future predictions. At test time, the agent can leverage both contextual and neural memory. This allows the world model to make more accurate predictions and learn an improved policy for each new episode.

papers.title: Encoding Memory in World Models with Test-Time Model-Based Reinforcement Learning

papers.abstract: AI weather prediction models are released with 32-bit (fp32) weights and run in fp32 by default, although current GPUs compute much faster in 16-bit formats. We run five publicly available models -- Aurora, Pangu-Weather, FourCastNet, SFNO and FastNet -- on a single 16 GB GPU from 52 initial dates in 2024, in fp32 and with their networks in half precision (fp16), and verify the forecasts against ERA5. The physical state must stay in fp32: converting the whole model rounds it in physical units, which in fp16 overflows and in bf16 discards meaningful information. With the state, its normalisation and denormalisation in fp32, running the network in fp16 changes the global RMSE by at most 1.4%, and by about 0.5% or less for four of the five models, equivalent to less than one hour of lead time up to day 8 and at most two hours at day 10. The differences show no systematic pattern by region, scale or for tropical and extratropical storms, apart from a small tropical penalty in FourCastNet, and fp16 leaves the CRPS, spread and calibration of Aurora's ensemble almost unchanged. No value overflowed fp16's numeric range (+/-65,504); the largest stay 38 to 544 times below it. A 10-day forecast in fp16 is 1.3-3.5 times faster than in fp32 and uses 1.4-3.7 times less energy. Sensitivity experiments show that rules of thumb from other applications of reduced precision carry over only partly: the first and last layers dominate for some models but not for others, and no type of layer is sensitive on its own. For running AI weather models on a single GPU, fp16 with the state in fp32 is practically lossless at a fraction of the cost. bf16, often preferred for its wider range, is as fast but less accurate than fp16 for every model, and simple 8-bit quantisation costs far more skill.
bullets: Evaluates five public models across 52 initial dates against ERA5 using fp32 and mixed-precision fp16 inference.
Keeping the state, normalization, and denormalization in fp32 avoids overflow and loss of meaningful physical information.
Global RMSE changes by at most 1.4%—about 0.5% or less for four models—with minimal effects on regional, storm, ensemble, and calibration behavior.
fp16 inference is 1.3–3.5× faster and uses 1.4–3.7× less energy on a single 16 GB GPU.
bf16 is less accurate than fp16 in these tests, while simple 8-bit quantization causes substantially greater skill loss.

papers.selection_reason: Half-precision inference of AI weather models reduces compute and energy cost, fitting efficient AI, while the models themselves are environment-dynamics predictors.
papers.title: Half-precision inference of AI weather prediction models: negligible loss of skill at a fraction of the cost
papers.tldr: Running AI weather models with fp16 networks while keeping physical states in fp32 preserves forecast skill almost entirely while substantially reducing inference cost.

papers.abstract: Machine-learning surrogates are increasingly used to accelerate computational fluid dynamics, yet progress is limited by the lack of benchmarks capturing realistic, time-dependent turbulent flows. We introduce TurtLES, a 14 TB dataset of 3D turbulent cylinder wakes in the shear-layer transition regime, computed via high-fidelity implicit large-eddy simulations. The dataset contains 400 trajectories of 400 time steps each, with 3-11 million points per frame, spanning variations in geometry, Reynolds number, and angle of attack. Unlike existing datasets, TurtLES combines (i) physically realistic turbulence with an active energy cascade driven by vortex stretching, (ii) dense irregular meshes, and (iii) long-horizon temporal dynamics. We benchmark state-of-the-art neural operators on autoregressive rollouts and identify key failure modes, including temporal instability, loss of small-scale energy, and challenges in learning on large irregular domains. TurtLES provides a new benchmark for evaluating surrogate models on 3D turbulent wakes at industrially relevant mesh resolution.
authors: Jarno Platenburg, Armand Kassa\"i Koupa\"i, Paola Cinnella, Patrick Gallinari
bullets: Provides a 14 TB dataset with 400 trajectories of 400 time steps each and 3–11 million points per frame.
Covers variations in geometry, Reynolds number, and angle of attack using high-fidelity implicit large-eddy simulations.
Combines active vortex-stretching turbulence, dense irregular meshes, and long-horizon temporal dynamics.
Benchmarks neural operators with autoregressive rollouts and exposes temporal instability, small-scale energy loss, and irregular-domain learning challenges.
Targets surrogate evaluation at industrially relevant 3D turbulent-wake resolutions.

papers.selection_reason: Neural PDE surrogate benchmark for long-horizon 3D turbulent dynamics is directly relevant to learned predictors of environment dynamics.
papers.title: TurtLES: A Large-Scale Benchmark for Turbulent 3D Neural PDE Surrogates
papers.tldr: TurtLES is a large-scale benchmark for testing neural PDE surrogates on realistic, long-horizon 3D turbulent cylinder wakes.

papers.abstract: Predicting the long-term behavior of partially observed dynamical systems such as the coupled atmosphere-ocean system is central to societal decision-making. Motivated by the success of deep learning emulators in weather forecasting, data-driven climate models represent a promising approach. However, climate emulation poses distinct challenges: models must account for unresolved fast variables introduced by unavoidable coarse-graining, reproduce long-term statistics, and remain stable over arbitrarily long rollouts and under external perturbations. These requirements motivate stochastic data-driven emulators, but modern generative models lack stability guarantees. We introduce forced-dissipative stochastic interpolants, a generative framework for learning stochastic reduced dynamics. Its architecture uses structural constraints inspired by turbulent dynamics, which provide stability by design while retaining the flexibility of stochastic interpolants to represent complex probabilistic dynamics. Building on the theory of Markov-chain stability, we establish a Foster--Lyapunov drift condition and prove geometric ergodicity for our emulator, together with stability under steady external forcing. We evaluate the framework on the two-timescale Lorenz-96 system, a prototype of partially observed multiscale turbulence. The resulting emulator remains stable over long integrations and under finite-amplitude forcing, with accurate prediction of forced responses of both the mean and variance.
authors: Mario Massy, Sara Shamekh, Fabrizio Falasca, Matthieu Blanke
bullets: Targets climate-like systems where coarse-graining creates unresolved fast variables and long rollouts must remain statistically realistic and stable.
Introduces forced-dissipative stochastic interpolants for learning probabilistic reduced dynamics.
Uses turbulence-inspired structural constraints to ensure stability by design.
Proves a Foster–Lyapunov drift condition, geometric ergodicity, and stability under steady external forcing.
On the two-timescale Lorenz-96 system, maintains stable long integrations and accurately predicts forced mean and variance responses.

papers.abstract: Recently, world-action models (WAMs) have emerged as a powerful framework for robot manipulation. By jointly modeling action generation and future observation prediction, WAMs can act and anticipate the outcomes of the actions. However, existing WAMs typically rely on frozen pretrained encoders trained with reconstruction, which may not produce representations well suited for robot control. In this paper, we tackle the problem of learning physicallygrounded, control-relevant representations for WAMs. We propose MDF++, a visuo-tactile world-action model that learns latent representations of multisensory observations end-to-end with a diffusion backbone. While naive joint training can lead to feature collapse, MDF++ introduces a multi-task learning strategy that leverages cross-modal correlations to learn task-relevant representations. We evaluate MDF++ on a suite of contact-rich manipulation tasks, including realworld bolt screwing and nut mating, and show that it outperforms WAMs built on frozen pretrained representations by up to 50%. Additional videos are available on our website: jointmdf.github.io.
authors: Zixuan Huang, Jinhao Yu, Zachary Charlick, Dmitry Berenson
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between reconstruction-trained frozen representations and representations needed for robot control.
Uses a diffusion-based visuo-tactile world-action model to jointly generate actions and predict future observations.
Introduces multi-task learning with cross-modal correlations to prevent feature collapse during end-to-end training.
Evaluated on contact-rich tasks, including real-world bolt screwing and nut mating.
Reports up to 50% improvement over WAMs using frozen pretrained representations.

figures.caption: Figure 2: MDF++ training overview. MDF++ jointly trains observation encoders with a latent diffusion world-action model. During training, it samples structured 2D noise patterns for control-relevant tasks, including policy learning, world-action modeling, forward/inverse dynamics, and random masking, to capture temporal and cross-modal dependencies. To avoid collapsed representations that are easy to denoise but weak for control, MDF++ blocks each modality’s denoising loss from updating its own encoder. Instead, each encoder is trained through cross-modal prediction losses, encouraging task-relevant cues for predicting other sensory modalities and actions.

Figure 4: Detailed architecture of MDF++. The model jointly tokenizes vision, tactile, force, proprioception, and action streams, and a diffusion transformer operates over the resulting latent tokens to predict actions and future multimodal observations.

papers.abstract: A joint-embedding predictive architecture (JEPA) that applies prediction supervision only at masked positions struggles to clearly capture object shapes and boundaries in its latent representations. We further observe that some existing methods improve spatial structure while also retaining rich variations in texture and color. However, preserving more low-level visual information does not necessarily make representations better suited to prediction and action. This raises a key question: how can we strengthen the spatial structure in latent representations that supports prediction and action without over-encoding these details? We introduce LEF-JEPA, which learns spatial structure through target-guided latent recovery and transfers this supervision to the visual encoder through a relative-energy constraint; the energy module is used only during pretraining and adds no inference overhead. To reduce the cost of energy optimization during pretraining, we further construct a conditional Ising Hamiltonian that allows low-energy-state search to be performed by specialized Ising solvers. On physical hardware, we validate the feasibility of achieving lower forward latency with fewer local updates. Under a unified CIFAR-10 pretraining and frozen-encoder evaluation protocol, both realizations outperform V-JEPA2.1 in image classification, foreground segmentation, and visual planning.
authors: Zhiyuan Liu, Zhihao Xu, Sicheng Liu, Huanhuan Huang
bullets: Addresses JEPA’s difficulty capturing object shapes and boundaries when prediction supervision is applied only to masked positions.
Uses target-guided latent recovery and a relative-energy constraint to transfer spatial-structure supervision to the visual encoder.
Introduces a conditional Ising Hamiltonian to reduce the cost of energy optimization via specialized Ising solvers.
The energy module is used only during pretraining, so it adds no inference overhead.
Under a unified CIFAR-10 pretraining and frozen-encoder evaluation, both implementations outperform V-JEPA2.1 in classification, foreground segmentation, and visual planning.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of LEF-JEPA. (a) Visible tokens from the online encoder are partitioned into disjoint candidate and anchor sets. The anchors condition the latent energy landscape over perturbed candidate representations. Multi-level target representations both supervise the displacement induced by K energy-gradient updates (Lfield) and provide the target-energy reference for visual-encoder supervision (Lenc), together with the masked-prediction objective (Lpred). (b) The neural energy realization contextualizes candidate representations with multi-level anchors and aggregates the energy contribution of each token. (c) The conditional Ising realization predicts Hamiltonian coefficients (h, J), invokes a physical photonic CIM to search for low-energy spin states, and differentiably rescores them to form a smooth scalar energy.

Figure 3. Patch-token PCA on CIFAR-10 samples. LEF-JEPA produces coherent regions aligned with object extent and boundaries. PCA is fitted independently per image, so colors are not comparable across methods.

Figure 4. Spatial representations and foreground segmentation on PartImageNet. Each method is shown with patch-token PCA and foreground predictions. Green, red, and blue denote true positives, false positives, and false negatives. LEF-JEPA yields more complete masks and sharper boundaries.
Figure 5. Two-Room planning trajectories. Each column fixes the same task across methods. Yellow, green, cyan, and red denote the start, goal, executed path, and final state.

Figure 6. Effect of the number of energy-gradient updates K on pretraining latency and downstream transfer. Each CIM trajectory uses one physical solve and reuses its low-energy state pool across all K updates. CIM latency excludes cloud communication and queueing; bars report means over three independently pretrained encoders.

papers.abstract: Video generation models can produce highly realistic videos while generating physically inconsistent object motion. This limitation suggests that visual modeling alone may not provide a transferable representation of physical dynamics. We introduce MotionCore, a framework for learning physical dynamics via a learnable partial differential equation solver and focuses on rigid-body motion. We introduce a latent neural simulator learning to predict the evolution of object-level physical states from observed motion. Its predictions are then converted into spatially aligned latent controls for a controllable video diffusion model. The generator serves as a visual interface: it provides appearance and scene detail, while the learned dynamics model specifies the physical trajectory. To preserve this trajectory through the interface, MotionCore combines a diffusion-matching objective with a low-capacity decodability constraint on object identity and position. We evaluate MotionCore on public physical-consistency benchmarks and on paired data with known trajectories. Results indicate that MotionCore improves physical consistency and trajectory obedience in the evaluated rigid-body settings, while maintaining comparable visual quality. A controlled ablation protocol compares learned dynamics with an analytic prior and studies the choice of latent evolution processor.

bullets: Targets physically inconsistent object motion in otherwise realistic video generation.
Learns object-level state evolution with a neural PDE solver focused on rigid-body dynamics.

Uses diffusion matching plus a low-capacity decodability constraint to preserve object identity and position.
Improves physical consistency and trajectory obedience on evaluated benchmarks while maintaining comparable visual quality; scope is limited to rigid-body settings.

papers.abstract: Reliable relative tracking is fundamental to cooperative autonomous underwater vehicles (AUVs), yet remains challenging under nonlinear vehicle dynamics and degraded underwater visual conditions. Active light markers improve robustness to appearance variation, but provide deliberately sparse observations that can become incomplete or corrupted by occlusion, reflections, and detection noise during dynamic motion. To address the resulting partial-observation control problem, this paper proposes FATHOM, a world-model-guided diffusion action-trajectory selection framework for sparse-marker AUV tracking. FATHOM first integrates structured marker observations, inertial measurements, action history, and temporal dynamics into a predictive tracking belief using a multimodal task-supervised recurrent state-space model. A diffusion action prior then generates multiple expert-like multi-thruster trajectories, whose future tracking consequences are predicted through the learned latent dynamics. Rather than directly executing a generated trajectory, FATHOM selects the most favorable candidate under an explicit receding-horizon objective and continually updates the decision from onboard observations. Extensive offline analyses verify the learned predictive belief, multi-step world-model prediction, diffusion trajectory generation, and predictive selection. More importantly, comprehensive real-AUV experiments, including strong pose-based comparisons and component ablations, demonstrate robust autonomous tracking across nominal and challenging motions with naturally occurring partial marker visibility, while maintaining real-time onboard operation without motion-capture feedback.
authors: Xiaorui Wang, Zeyu Sha, Mingyang Yang, David Chen Wang, Feitian Zhang
bullets: Addresses partial-observation tracking caused by occlusion, reflections, detection noise, nonlinear dynamics, and degraded underwater vision.
Builds a predictive tracking belief from marker observations, inertial measurements, action history, and temporal dynamics using a multimodal recurrent state-space model.
Generates multiple multi-thruster action trajectories with a diffusion prior, predicts their consequences in latent dynamics, and chooses among them using a receding-horizon objective.
Offline analyses validate belief modeling, world-model prediction, trajectory generation, and predictive selection.

Real-AUV experiments and component ablations show robust autonomous tracking under nominal and challenging motions with partial marker visibility and real-time onboard execution without motion-capture feedback.

papers.abstract: We fine-tune a pre-trained V-JEPA1 predictor from bidirectional latent inpainting to action-free causal forecasting while keeping the encoder frozen. Using contiguous past observations, horizon-aligned targets, and group-level causal attention, the model forecasts eight future token groups, corresponding to sixteen frames, in one forward pass. On CARLA Town12, it retrieves the correct future among 591 candidates in 69.0% of cases, compared with 55.3% for persistence, with greater gains at longer horizons and on tokens exhibiting greater change. It also outperforms a compact predictor trained from scratch with six times fewer parameters. Semantic analysis indicates driving-relevant information in predicted features: a fixed linear probe trained on real encoder tokens achieves 0.16 mIoU on patches undergoing semantic-class changes, versus 0.13 for persistence. Vehicle-conditioned retrieval improves over persistence by 15 percentage points at the longest horizon. Pixel-space evaluation shows modest L1 gains but little improvement under LPIPS, motivating direct evaluation through latent and semantic measures alongside an oracle reconstruction reference. These findings support further investigation of latent forecasting for driving perception, while downstream utility remains unverified.

papers.abstract: Personalized health coaching requires moving beyond retrospective wearable summaries toward quantitative, actionable behavioral prescriptions. We introduce Coachable Health Age (CHA), an interpretable health-age metric built from modifiable physiological and behavioral signals passively captured by consumer wearables. Across the WEAR-ME (N=2,780), All of Us (N=22,748), and longitudinal Fitbit (N=1,464) cohorts, CHA aligns with established cardiometabolic health constructs and improves prognostic discrimination for incident cardiovascular and metabolic disease beyond age, sex, and body mass index. To enable prospective behavioral optimization, we developed Sensor World Model (SensorWM), an action-conditioned wearable world model pretrained on over 2.2 million person-weeks of longitudinal sensor data from approximately 100,000 participants. SensorWM accurately forecasts multi-week physiological responses to candidate lifestyle changes ($R^2=0.664$), outperforming generic time-series foundation models while preserving downstream clinical signal for diabetes, hypertension, and other health outcomes. Finally, we integrate CHA and SensorWM into an agentic counterfactual coaching system to synthesize personalized 12-week coaching plans. In blinded paired reviews, certified lifestyle coaches preferred counterfactual-grounded plans over plans grounded in wearable history alone for overall quality (71.4%, P < 0.001) and anticipated adherence (71.0%, P < 0.001), and board-certified clinicians judged 99.2% of counterfactual-grounded plans to meet clinical safety criteria (vs. 97.6% of comparison plans). Automated evaluations across the full cohort (N=2,780) also favored counterfactual-grounded plans. By closing the loop between longitudinal tracking, trajectory prediction, and counterfactual coaching, our framework provides a scalable path to systematically improve cardiometabolic health.
authors: Simon A. Lee, Zeinab Esmaeilpour, Menglian Zhou, Marius Guerard, Sohrab Sidhu, Alexandru Solot, Hamid Palangi, Pramod Rudrapatna, Ming-Zher Poh, Max A. Xu, Daniel McDuff, Dimitrios Antos, Yuzhe Yang, Jeffrey N. Chiang, Anthony Z. Faranesh, Lindsey Sunden, Mark Malhotra, Shwetak Patel, A. Ali Heydari, Ahmed A. Metwally

papers.abstract: We introduce GPWM, a Generative Particle World Model that predicts how 3D scenes evolve by generating the motion of particles and rigid bodies over time. Unlike video world models that generate scene appearance, GPWM operates directly in 3D physical space. A single representation and architecture cover rigid, deformable, cloth, and granular materials, in both passive physics and robotic interaction. GPWM is an object-aware multi-resolution transformer that combines flow matching with diffusion forcing to generate coherent physical trajectories far beyond its training horizon. We train and evaluate GPWM on ParticleWorlds, a 25.5-million-frame corpus spanning diverse geometries, materials, interactions, and robot embodiments. GPWM outperforms the best prior learned-dynamics baseline in each of six physical domains, reducing prediction error by 31% on average. Breaking from the domain-specific setting of prior methods, a single Unified GPWM models these heterogeneous regimes with one set of weights, largely outperforming per-domain baselines and even surpassing our own specialist models in two domains. GPWM further generalizes to unseen geometries, physical properties, object counts, and rollout horizons. Beyond prediction, GPWM enables contact-rich planning by learning a generative prior over joint actuator-object motion. Instead of searching over unconstrained actions, planning searches the model's latent noise for interactions that achieve a desired object-space goal. With the same world model, noise-space planning substantially outperforms action-space search on pushing and picking, where complex contact sequences are hard to discover. Executed open-loop in simulation, the resulting plans achieve goal-directed manipulation without reference action trajectories or goal-specific policies.
bullets: Models rigid, deformable, cloth, and granular materials in passive and robotic-interaction settings with one representation and architecture.
Uses an object-aware multi-resolution transformer with flow matching and diffusion forcing to generate coherent long-horizon trajectories.
Trained and evaluated on the 25.5-million-frame ParticleWorlds corpus spanning varied geometries, materials, interactions, and robot embodiments.
Reduces prediction error by 31% on average across six physical domains versus the strongest prior learned-dynamics baseline, while generalizing beyond training conditions.
Enables noise-space planning for pushing and picking, outperforming action-space search without reference trajectories or goal-specific policies.

Each block (right) applies temporal attention, 3D relative spatial attention, and pointwise feed-forward layers, modulated by AdaLN-Zero from the per-frame noise level τ , and the network outputs clean future displacements.

papers.abstract: Visual interaction models that support users during ongoing physical tasks require evaluation in closed loop, where assistant responses can change subsequent user behavior and task outcomes. Existing benchmarks largely rely on offline replay and therefore cannot capture these effects. We introduce Interactive Visual Gym, a framework for closed-loop evaluation and training of visual interaction models through joint simulation of executable task environments and human users. We contribute three simulators that recreate everyday tasks and human-aligned action spaces across cooking, household manipulation, and mobile-interface domains, together with a persona-conditioned user simulation harness that collaborates with the assistant while incorporating controlled execution errors and other out-of-plan behaviors. We instantiate the framework as IVG-Bench, a benchmark with 315 interaction scenarios. Evaluating state-of-the-art VLMs as visual interaction models reveals substantial limitations: the best-performing model, Claude Opus 5.5, completes only 53.5% of tasks within the time limit, exhibits significant weaknesses in factual grounding and actionable guidance, and is often too slow to prevent errors when response latency is considered. We verify our evaluation protocol with a human study which finds 78.5% agreement between our interaction-quality metric and participant preferences. We further show that the environments provide useful learning signals: in a proof-of-concept GRPO experiment, closed-loop training improves both task success and interaction quality for Qwen3.5-4B model in our cooking environment.
bullets: Addresses the gap between offline replay benchmarks and real-world interaction, where assistant responses affect user behavior and task outcomes.
Provides simulators for cooking, household manipulation, and mobile-interface tasks, plus persona-conditioned users with execution errors and out-of-plan behavior.
Introduces IVG-Bench with 315 interaction scenarios for evaluating visual grounding, actionable guidance, latency, and task completion.
The best evaluated model completed 53.5% of tasks within the time limit; the interaction-quality metric achieved 78.5% agreement with human preferences.
A proof-of-concept GRPO experiment improved task success and interaction quality for Qwen3.5-4B in the cooking environment.

papers.abstract: How would we know whether a machine truly understands the world? We argue that one key capability is observational theory learning: acquiring reusable theories from pure observations and applying them to new situations. Current visual reasoning benchmarks focus primarily on the latter, presenting each task as a few-shot puzzle grouped by a common rule. We introduce BabyTheorist, a benchmark for controlled training and evaluation of observational theory learning. BabyTheorist generates continual streams of before-after visual observations from hidden compositional programs; during training, learners see only the resulting transitions, with no program labels, task identities, or support sets. To support theory learning and evaluation, BabyTheorist controls the program language, a curriculum over program complexity, recurring frequent subprograms, and a continual train-test protocol with level skipping. Seven representative baselines plateau well below ceiling, with the gap widening as the curriculum advances---evidence that BabyTheorist isolates a capability current program-learning approaches do not yet address.
bullets: Generates continual streams of before-after visual observations from hidden compositional programs.
Learners receive only observed transitions—without program labels, task identities, or support examples.
Controls program complexity, curriculum progression, recurring subprograms, and continual evaluation with level skipping.
Seven representative baselines plateau below ceiling, with larger gaps at higher curriculum levels.
Targets observational theory learning, beyond solving isolated few-shot visual reasoning puzzles.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of continual observational theory learning. A useful theory system should continually evolve as a learner receives a stream of observations. Theory application combines them to explain new observations.

papers.abstract: World-action models adapt pretrained video generators, and vision-language-action models build on vision-language backbones, tying policy architecture and inference cost to large transformers designed for generation rather than control. While recent world-action models mostly scale the video backbone and its data, we argue that the choice of latent space is just as critical, and that the policy should be trained natively in that space. We introduce Latent Action JEPA (La-JEPA), a compact world-action model whose policy transformer is trained from scratch in the feature space of a pretrained V-JEPA 2.1 encoder; it predicts future features with actions during training and generates only actions at inference. Among policies without embodied pretraining, La-JEPA achieves state-of-the-art average RoboTwin 2.0 success under both clean-only and full training, and state-of-the-art LIBERO-Plus success with corrected instructions, while using far fewer parameters than the strongest competitors; with full training, its success scales with model size up to 2.1B. Its S and B policies run two to five times faster than Fast-WAM and Faster-WAM while outperforming both on LIBERO-Plus and RoboTwin 2.0, and La-JEPA outperforms the closest JEPA-based methods, LeapBot-WA and JEPA-WAM, without their pretrained policy backbones. On four real-robot tasks, its average success is comparable to $π_{0.5}$. A design study shows that JEPA features outperform video VAE latents, most clearly out of distribution, and that training-time future prediction improves the policy even when skipped at inference. Tailoring the policy's design, including its latent space, to control can thus matter more than the knowledge transferred from a pretrained generative backbone, suggesting that robot foundation models may benefit from architectures designed for control rather than inherited from generation.
bullets: Motivation: Existing world-action and vision-language-action policies inherit costly architectures designed for video or language generation rather than control.
Method: Train a policy transformer from scratch in pretrained V-JEPA 2.1 feature space; use action-conditioned future-feature prediction during training, but generate only actions at inference.
Results: La-JEPA attains state-of-the-art average performance among policies without embodied pretraining on RoboTwin 2.0 and corrected-instruction LIBERO-Plus benchmarks.
Efficiency: Its S and B variants run 2–5× faster than Fast-WAM and Faster-WAM while outperforming them on the reported benchmarks.
Design insight: JEPA features outperform video-VAE latents, and training-time future prediction helps even when omitted during inference; real-robot performance is comparable to π0.5 on four tasks.

papers.abstract: Current 4D occupancy world models use heavy cross-attention or deep recurrence to disentangle ego-motion from scene dynamics. This requires significant computational capacity. However, this effort is largely redundant since the ego-vehicle's intended future motion is provided by the downstream motion planner. We present FreeOcc, a lightweight continuous-time world model that introduces explicit $SE(2)$ geometric decoupling into a conditional flow-matching framework. By mathematically factoring out self-motion, we create a purely dynamic feature space. This space supports attention-free temporal fusion and allows physics-constrained ODEs to operate strictly on residual agent kinematics. To maximize deployment efficiency, FreeOcc introduces an uncertainty-aware blending mechanism. This routes well-observed voxels to a single-pass decoder, reserving the ODE solver exclusively for ambiguous, high-uncertainty regions. Requiring only 28.3M parameters-roughly 40% of comparable models-our optimal ensemble mode (FreeOcc-E) runs at 27 FPS. On nuScenes, FreeOcc achieves state-of-the-art forecasting performance with a 0.47 m Near Field Chamfer Distance (NFCD) and 32.1% mIoU. Furthermore, the model transfers zero-shot to SemanticKITTI. It also proves highly robust, retaining 92.8% of its ideal mIoU under significant sensor packet loss and timestamp jitter.
bullets: Addresses the computational cost of disentangling ego-motion from scene dynamics in 4D occupancy world models.
Uses explicit SE(2) geometric decoupling to create a purely dynamic feature space with attention-free temporal fusion.
Applies physics-constrained ODEs only to residual agent motion and ambiguous, high-uncertainty voxels.
The 28.3M-parameter FreeOcc-E runs at 27 FPS and reports 0.47 m NFCD and 32.1% mIoU on nuScenes.
Transfers zero-shot to SemanticKITTI and retains 92.8% of ideal mIoU under sensor packet loss and timestamp jitter.

figures.caption: Figure 16: Rain scene overview (nuScenes scene-0441). Left: front camera image showing wet road, reflections, and rain droplets. Right: LiDAR BEV coloured by height; the intersection geometry and parked vehicles are clearly visible despite rain-induced noise in the point cloud.

Figure 1: Overview of FreeOcc. Previous sweeps are encoded into BEV, fused by a continuoustime temporal aggregator, propagated to future ego frames by SE(2) warping, and decoded by the Discriminative Occupancy Decoder plus the Physics-Aware Continuous Flow Matching. The final prediction blends both paths using decoder uncertainty.

Figure 3: 4D occupancy forecasting on nuScenes(sample 1720) in BEV and 3D views across six horizons. FreeOcc-E is compared against OccWorld and ViDAR; more qualitative examples are given in Section D.

Figure 2: Ego-aware future propagator. At each horizon, the warped BEV—obtained via SE(2) ego-motion alignment—is explicitly added to the residual scene dynamics predicted by a ConvGRU and a residual projector.

Figure 10: Zero-shot SemanticKITTI predictions (sample 2070). BEV and 3D occupancy predictions from a nuScenes-trained model evaluated on SemanticKITTI, comparing FreeOcc-E against OccWorld and ViDAR. Despite domain differences (64-beam LiDAR, different driving context, no fine-tuning), FreeOcc-E preserves road-level structure and major obstacles. The denser 64-beam input provides richer geometric detail than nuScenes’s 32-beam data, and FreeOcc adapts without retraining, an advantage of operating on raw 3D geometry rather than appearance-dependent features.

At 3.0 s, OccWorld exhibits boundary blur and noise around moving objects. FreeOcc-D slightly over-predicts occupancy, whereas FreeOcc-E preserves sharper boundaries and cleaner free space.

Agreement is strongest at short horizons. By τ=6, the main discrepancies appear in the far field and around dynamic actors, while large static structures remain well preserved.

Top: 3D occupancy predictions at the maximum forecasting horizon (τ = 6, 3.0s), comparing our model variants (FreeOcc-D, -G, -E) against Ground Truth. Bottom: BEV temporal evolution at τ = 3 and τ = 6. Road geometry, vegetation boundaries, and building walls are consistently captured, reinforcing the cross-domain robustness reported in Table 4.

Each panel renders occupied voxels coloured by the decoder’s predicted aleatoric uncertainty ŝv; cool tones indicate low uncertainty and warm tones indicate high. At short horizons, uncertainty is concentrated near dynamic actors and occupancy boundaries. As the horizon increases, uncertainty expands into the far field and intensifies around moving objects. By τ=6 (3.0 s), most remaining structures are assigned substantially higher uncertainty. This behaviour is consistent with the ensemble design in Section 3.7, which assigns more weight to the ODE path where decoder confidence weakens.

Columns span τ=1 to τ=6, comparing FreeOcc against OccWorld and ViDAR on a dense urban scene with multiple interacting vehicles. Figure 12: Robustness on nuScenes (τ = 4, 2.0s, sample 2500). Occupancy predictions under ideal and imperfect sensor conditions. FreeOcc-E retains its predictions under severe temporal perturbations, while OccWorld and ViDAR break into fragments and hallucinated clusters when temporal input is degraded.

Figure 13: Cross-domain robustness on SemanticKITTI (τ = 4, 2.0s, sample 2090). Zero-shot predictions under ideal (top two rows) and imperfect (bottom two rows) sensor conditions. The cross-domain robustness gap compounds both the sensor-domain shift (nuScenes→SemanticKITTI) and the temporal perturbation, yet FreeOcc-E retains recognisable road and object geometry in both cases, while OccWorld and ViDAR suffer severe structural collapse.

Figure 14: Robustness on nuScenes at τ=6 (3.0 s, sample 1600). Long-horizon predictions under ideal (top) and imperfect (bottom) sensor conditions. At the maximum forecasting horizon, OccWorld and ViDAR dissolve into discontiguous fragments, whereas FreeOcc-E preserves the road layout and principal object silhouettes. The gap between ideal and imperfect rows is noticeably smaller for FreeOcc-E than for OccWorld or ViDAR, consistent with the quantitative retention rate in Table 5.

Figure 15: Cross-domain robustness on SemanticKITTI at τ=6 (3.0 s, sample 2090). The most challenging evaluation setting: simultaneous cross-domain transfer, long-horizon prediction, and degraded sensor input. FreeOcc-E still recovers the overall road layout and major object boundaries, whereas OccWorld and ViDAR suffer near-complete structural collapse.

Cool colours (cyan/green) indicate low uncertainty; warm colours (orange/red) indicate high uncertainty. Uncertainty increases with horizon and concentrates on dynamic objects and far-field voxels. papers.abstract: State-space models (SSMs) recover low-dimensional latent dynamics from high-dimensional observations, but latents are generally not identifiable from observational data alone. Interventional state-space models (iSSMs) use perturbations to break observational symmetries and identify parameters up to permutation, scaling, and shift. However, prior work restricts identifiability to linear latent dynamics and piecewise-linear emissions, excluding many behaviors characteristic of neural circuits. We extend iSSMs to a substantially broader model class: we prove that (i) affine identifiability holds under general injective emission functions and Gaussian latent transitions, and (ii) with interventions, identifiability up to permutation, scaling, and shift is preserved under general nonlinear latent dynamics. We validate our theory on simulated FitzHugh-Nagumo dynamics, and then demonstrate two applications: adjudicating between competing models of decision-making; and predicting responses to unseen micro-stimulation in macaque and human neural recordings, with proof-of-concept generalization to a held-out stimulation site in the latter. Finally, simulations yield practical guidance for designing stimulation protocols that improve identifiability.
bullets: Addresses the non-identifiability of latent states from observational data alone.
Proves affine identifiability with general injective emissions and Gaussian transitions.
Shows intervention-based identifiability up to permutation, scaling, and shift for general nonlinear latent dynamics.
Validates the theory on FitzHugh–Nagumo simulations and applies it to decision-making models and neural stimulation responses.
Provides simulation-based guidance for designing stimulation protocols that improve identifiability.

papers.abstract: Autoregressive driving world models systematically suffer from structural drift, identity drift, and quality decay over long rollout horizons due to transient conditioning signals that lack persistent state. We present WAM-Sim, a driving world model anchored by a persistent hierarchical memory and optimized via online flow-matching RL. WAM-Sim structures persistent context across three temporal and semantic scales: pose-aligned structural tokens encoding persistent road topology, read-only scene tokens supplying geolocated background appearance, and write-once instance tokens preserving individual traffic participant identities across occlusions and chunk boundaries. To restore visual sharpness and physical plausibility degraded by multi-scale conditioning, we introduce an online post-training framework that optimizes self-generated rollouts via flow-matching RL guided by hierarchy-aligned visual rewards and a vision-language model physical judge. The invariant memory empirically confines policy optimization within the anchored context, helping suppress semantic collapse and reward hacking, while online RL systematically enforces physical commonsense and fine-grained visual fidelity. On the nuScenes benchmark, WAM-Sim achieves a superior generation fidelity (FID=3.47, FVD=25.72) and strong downstream perception performance (24.16 mAP, 71.23 road mIoU). On minute-scale rollouts of self-collected data, WAM-Sim substantially mitigates structural and identity drift, preserving high scene similarity and subject identity coherence across extended horizons. Project page: https://fudan-generative-vision.github.io/WAM-Sim.
bullets: Targets structural drift, identity drift, and visual quality decay in autoregressive driving world models.
Uses pose-aligned structural tokens, read-only scene tokens, and write-once instance tokens to preserve roads, appearance, and traffic-participant identities.
Applies online RL to self-generated rollouts using visual rewards and a vision-language physical judge.
Reports FID 3.47, FVD 25.72, 24.16 mAP, and 71.23 road mIoU on nuScenes.
Minute-scale self-collected-data rollouts show improved scene similarity and identity coherence.

papers.abstract: World action models (WAMs) for autonomous driving couple the driving policy and the visual world model in a single generative network whose objectives are fixed post-training. Conditioning on a new driving objective requires retraining. We study energy guidance as a general mechanism and present GuidedWAM, a model-agnostic framework for injecting driving objectives into frozen WAMs at sampling time. Our framework constructs each objective as differentiable energies on the sampler's intermediate clean-action estimate, which needs only forward access to the frozen model, and is stabilized by sampling-time guidance scheduling, per-energy normalization, and velocity-bounded correction. On the NAVSIM v2 hard-split, guidance improves all three frozen, publicly released WAMs by 1.8 to 3.6 EPDMS, averaged over three sampler seeds, and adds less than 10% to the sampling time per step. These results position energy guidance as a practical post-training control channel for WAMs.
bullets: Addresses the need to condition fixed-objective WAMs on new driving goals without retraining.
Applies model-agnostic energy guidance to intermediate clean-action estimates using only forward access to the frozen model.
Stabilizes guidance with scheduling, per-energy normalization, and velocity-bounded corrections.
Improves three frozen WAMs by 1.8–3.6 EPDMS on NAVSIM v2 hard-split across three sampler seeds.
Adds less than 10% sampling time per step, supporting practical post-training control.

papers.abstract: Building a playable world requires more than generating plausible video: it demands responsive control, persistent spatial structure, and coherent interactions with dynamic entities. Using generated frames as the sole recurrent world representation ties these requirements to view-dependent appearance synthesis, making it difficult to maintain long-term spatial and temporal consistency in generation and interaction. We present PlayGen2, a real-time interactive world model that separates learned 3D state evolution from neural rendering. PlayGen2 maintains a persistent world memory comprising static geometry represented by a volumetric occupancy grid and identity-indexed 3D states for the player and other entities. Within a fixed-size local region, its world-state model jointly learns action-conditioned entity dynamics, geometry completion, and entity discovery, committing updates to a persistent world memory. A separate neural renderer synthesizes first-person observations from depth and semantic projections of the world state, without feeding generated images back into state prediction. Using Doom as a testbed, we demonstrate that the model successfully learns world dynamics including geometry-aware player motion and player--NPC interactions. The framework is computationally efficient, enabling the complete simulation and rendering pipeline to achieve approximately 160ms backend latency on a MacBook Pro with an M4 Pro chip. Beyond single-player interaction, we demonstrate zero-shot deployment on unseen Doom maps, multiplayer interaction through the composition of single-player models, and programmable gameplay through rule-based state interventions. These capabilities demonstrate the transferability and extensibility of the learned game-world model. Code and pretrained model weights are publicly available.
bullets: Targets the challenge of combining responsive control, persistent spatial structure, and coherent interactions in generated playable worlds.
Uses a persistent memory with a volumetric occupancy grid for static geometry and identity-indexed 3D states for players and other entities.
Jointly learns action-conditioned dynamics, geometry completion, and entity discovery within a local region, while a separate renderer generates first-person views.
In Doom, it models geometry-aware movement and player–NPC interactions, with an end-to-end backend latency of about 160 ms on an M4 Pro MacBook Pro.
Demonstrates zero-shot use on unseen maps, multiplayer via composition of single-player models, and programmable gameplay through rule-based state interventions.

papers.abstract: Robot world models predict action-conditioned future visual states to support robotic planning and decision making. However, visual reconstruction does not fully capture task progress, semantic evaluation alone provides limited constraints on fine-grained visual errors, and homogeneous predictions limit comparative feedback. We present RoboImagine, a framework for post-training autoregressive robotic world models through candidate-future comparisons with semantic and visual feedback. Diverse search promotes diversity among candidate trajectories under shared visual observations, action sequences, and task instructions. A frozen multimodal evaluator provides task-relevant semantic preferences through pairwise video comparisons in both presentation orders, complemented by pixel- and perceptual-level visual consistency feedback that constrains local structural and appearance errors. These signals drive policy optimization through group-relative advantages. Fixed initial context and branch-specific rolling histories support long-sequence generation with bounded context and consistent conditioning between candidate generation and policy optimization. Experiments with separately trained models on RT-1, BridgeV2, and RoboCasa cover real-world and simulated manipulation. On RT-1, under matched initialization, update counts, and evaluation protocols, RoboImagine improves PSNR by 1.26 dB and reduces LPIPS by 11.93% relative to continued supervised fine-tuning. Ablations show that diverse search improves prediction quality and that combined semantic and visual feedback yields higher external multimodal evaluation scores than visual feedback alone while maintaining comparable visual fidelity. Rolling histories further improve long-horizon prediction. These results support improving visual fidelity, task relevance, and long-horizon prediction through candidate comparison and complementary feedback.
bullets: Addresses the limits of relying on visual reconstruction or semantic feedback alone for evaluating robotic futures.
Uses diverse candidate trajectory search, pairwise multimodal semantic comparisons, and pixel/perceptual consistency signals.

papers.abstract: Selecting a next motion in a populated scene is not just a matter of avoiding what is currently in the way: an action can be locally feasible yet drift onto the road instead of the crosswalk, cut into a stream of crossing pedestrians, or bottleneck a narrow passage. These failure modes are invisible from the current state alone, and acting on them requires reasoning about what each candidate action will cause. World models offer exactly this, namely action-conditioned predictions of the future, but rolling them out at every decision step is a cost deployable navigation systems cannot pay, and the field has largely traded foresight for speed. We argue this is a false dichotomy. The natural place for a world model in human-aware navigation is at training time, as a preference oracle that distills foresight into a fast policy, rather than at inference time, as an online planner. We pair a discrete visual action prior with two task-aligned world models, one for nearby social dynamics and one for future scene semantics, that score candidate actions by their predicted consequences and refine the policy through group-relative preference distillation. At deployment, both world models are removed and the policy acts in a single forward pass. Across five held-out evaluation scenarios, this yields navigation that is simultaneously safer, more socially and group-coherent, and more goal-directed than strong reactive and learned baselines, with naive observers rating the resulting motion as more human-like. Taken together, our findings point to a different approach for bringing world-model foresight into deployable agents: not accelerating rollouts, but amortizing them into the policy so that the cost of looking ahead is confined to training. Project page: https://seoneun.github.io/-NeurIPS-2026-Seeing-Beyond-the-Next-Step/
bullets: Reactive navigation may choose locally feasible actions that cause unsafe, socially disruptive, or semantically inappropriate futures.
The method uses a discrete visual action prior and two task-aligned world models: one predicts nearby social dynamics, while the other predicts future scene semantics.
World models score candidate actions during training and guide group-relative preference distillation; they are removed at deployment for single-pass inference.
Across five held-out scenarios, the resulting policy is reported as safer, more socially and group-coherent, more goal-directed, and more human-like than reactive and learned baselines.
The approach confines the computational cost of foresight to training rather than performing online world-model rollouts.

papers.abstract: Replay attacks are difficult to detect in vision-based control systems because previously recorded observations can remain plausible while the physical system follows a different trajectory. This paper develops an adaptive dynamic-watermarking framework for detecting replay attacks against vision-based controllers. A private Gaussian watermark is added to the nominal control input, and a control input-conditioned latent dynamics network (LDN) predicts the corresponding evolution in a compact latent space learned from image observations. Attack evidence is obtained from the discrepancy between the predicted latent response and the latent representation of the received image observation. A reinforcement learning policy adjusts the watermark covariance using the latent state and detector confidence, thereby balancing attack detectability, watermark energy, and control distortion. A Lagrangian penalty on task-specific safety costs is included during training to limit the adverse effect of the excitation. The framework is evaluated on a vision-guided UR5 manipulation task in which the robot reaches a target while avoiding a moving human arm under nominal and replay-attacked observations.
bullets: Addresses replay attacks where recorded camera observations remain plausible despite changed physical trajectories.
Adds private Gaussian noise to control inputs and predicts image-derived latent dynamics conditioned on those inputs.
Detects attacks through discrepancies between predicted latent responses and received-image latent representations.
Uses reinforcement learning to adapt watermark covariance based on latent state and detector confidence.
Evaluated on a vision-guided UR5 reaching-and-avoidance task under nominal and replay-attacked observations.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Overview of the proposed framework. (a) The live observation xt−H is provided to the vision-based controller policy F , which predicts the control input ut−H . In parallel, an encoder maps xt−H to the latent state zt−H . The latent state, together with the detector confidence cj , is provided to the DWM policy to select the covariance Σt−H , from which the private watermark ϕt−H is sampled. The watermark and control input are combined to form the watermarked control input ūt−H , which is applied to the plant. (b) When a replay attack occurs, the encoder maps the received replayed observations to latent states [z′t−H+1, . . . , z ′ t]. These are compared with the predicted latent states [z̃t−H+1|t−H , . . . , z̃t|t−H ] to obtain the residual window rj , defined in (8). The MCUSUM detector processes this window, and the resulting evidence updates the attack confidence cj through (18). When attack evidence persists, the supervisor switches to the damped-stop controller and applies uds t as specified in (7).

papers.abstract: We study whether \emph{long-horizon model-based value expansion} can serve as an effective framework in pixel-based offline reinforcement learning (RL). Long-horizon model-based value expansion from pixels is substantially harder than state-based environments, as the agent must learn both the representation and its dynamics, and errors from either can accumulate recursively over imagined trajectories. We introduce MAC-v2, which enables long-horizon model-based expansion from pixels by training a reconstruction-free latent world model with action chunking. By learning representations from prediction and control objectives, MAC-v2 does not need to encode control-irrelevant visual details that can hinder the dynamics prediction. Action chunking further mitigates the prediction error by reducing the number of recursive model predictions required for value expansion. Across diverse visual benchmarks including visual OGBench, MMBench2, Robomimic, and LIBERO-10, MAC-v2 achieves strong performance against model-free and model-based offline RL baselines. Our analyses show that long-horizon model-based value expansion is critical for the performance of MAC-v2, and that both action chunking and latent learning objectives are essential for reliable long-horizon latent imagination.
bullets: Addresses compounding representation and dynamics-prediction errors in imagined pixel-based trajectories.
Learns latent representations through prediction and control objectives rather than visual reconstruction.
Uses action chunking to reduce the number of recursive model predictions during value expansion.
Performs strongly across visual OGBench, MMBench2, Robomimic, and LIBERO-10 against model-free and model-based offline RL baselines.
Analyses indicate that long-horizon expansion, action chunking, and latent learning objectives are all important for reliable performance.

papers.abstract: The Universal Manipulation Interface (UMI) enables scalable demonstration collection independently of a specific robot. However, its moving, close-range gripper cameras entangle camera and object motion without a stable external view, leaving the metric geometry needed for precise manipulation implicit in RGB. We introduce Spatial-UMI-Dream, a 5B spatial World Action Model (WAM) pretrained on 605 hours of RGB-D UMI data through two-stage training -- world-only adaptation followed by joint world-action learning -- to jointly predict future RGB, fisheye-aligned metric depth, and actions. Stereo-derived depth makes scene scale and spatial relationships explicit within a unified dual-gripper RGB-D representation. Furthermore, evaluating UMI policies requires testing whether UMI's robot-independent demonstration collection translates into policy generalization across robot embodiments, alongside robustness to environmental changes. We introduce RoboTwin-UMI, a twenty-task simulation benchmark built on RoboTwin with UMI wrist-mounted fisheye observations, enabling controlled, repeatable evaluation of UMI policies under environment and embodiment changes separately and jointly without additional fine-tuning. On RoboTwin-UMI, Spatial-UMI-Dream achieves 79.10% in-domain success and 72.15% under combined embodiment and environment shifts, exceeding the strongest evaluated baseline in each setting by 4.65 and 10.30 percentage points, respectively. It also exhibits the smallest success-rate drop under embodiment transfer among the evaluated policies. In a matched pretraining ablation, RGB-only pretraining leads to a 5.75-percentage-point decrease in in-domain success compared with RGB-D pretraining. Across six real-world tasks, Spatial-UMI-Dream achieves 85.0% average success, exceeding the strongest baseline by 24.2 percentage points. Project page: https://weiduoyuan.com/spatial-umi-dream/
bullets: Addresses the lack of explicit metric geometry in UMI’s close-range, moving-camera observations.
Pretrains a 5B model on 605 hours of RGB-D UMI data, first for world modeling and then jointly for world-action prediction.
Introduces RoboTwin-UMI, a 20-task benchmark for separately and jointly evaluating environment and embodiment shifts without fine-tuning.
Achieves 79.10% in-domain and 72.15% under combined shifts, with the smallest embodiment-transfer drop among evaluated policies.
Across six real-world tasks, reaches 85.0% average success; RGB-only pretraining reduces in-domain success by 5.75 percentage points versus RGB-D.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: Model architecture and two-stage training of Spatial-UMI-Dream. In both stages, dual-gripper RGB and metric depth (Fig. 3) form a unified RGB-D canvas. The shared world-action transformer uses block-causal attention to condition prediction on preceding visual history. Stage 1: world-only adaptation predicts future RGB-D observations, decoded through the Wan VAE and supervised by Lworld. Stage 2: the transformer backbone is initialized from the Stage 1 world-only adaptation checkpoint. Joint world-action training additionally encodes UMI state and noisy actions, and jointly predicts future RGB-D observations and actions through the Wan VAE and action decoder, optimized with Lworld + λaLaction.

papers.abstract: Accurate modeling of the daily evolution of sea ice concentration (SIC) is central to improving the credibility and operational forecasting capability of deep learning-based sea ice prediction. However, existing deep learning methods often couple the underlying sea ice evolution relationships and data errors within high-dimensional nonlinear mappings, making it difficult to construct a stable and verifiable evolution core and apply it reliably to practical forecasting. To address this issue, this study proposes a reanalysis-forecast dual-domain decoupled framework for learning sea ice evolution operators. The framework builds upon a lightweight physical baseline to generate daily evolution trajectories, employs a temporally constrained joint multi-lead compensation network to com?pensate for unresolved processes, and introduces an ice-mass?aware transport mechanism to suppress numerical dissipation. In the forecasting stage, the parameters of the base evolution core are fixed, while a lightweight variable-semantic adaptation mechanism calibrates inter-domain distributions and evolution responses, thereby separating forecast-domain errors from base evolution errors. Experiments show that the constructed base evolution core can accurately and stably simulate daily sea ice evolution at both short-term and annual scales under reanal?ysis forcing, and can be effectively transferred to the forecast domain through lightweight adaptation, achieving stable prac?tical forecasting capability while preserving the base evolution structure. The source code will be made publicly available at https://github.com/zhangmaqun65535/SNM upon acceptance of this manuscript.
bullets: Addresses the entanglement of sea-ice dynamics and data errors in existing deep-learning forecasting methods.
Uses a lightweight physical baseline, a temporally constrained multi-lead compensation network, and ice-mass-aware transport to model unresolved processes and reduce numerical dissipation.
Freezes the base evolution core during forecasting and applies lightweight variable-semantic adaptation to correct domain shifts.
Experiments indicate stable evolution simulation from short-term to annual scales under reanalysis forcing and effective transfer to the forecast domain.
The approach is scoped to Arctic sea-ice concentration evolution and forecast-domain adaptation; specific quantitative results are not reported in the abstract.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Overall architecture of the proposed network. In the reanalysis domain, the model takes the initial SIC and multi-lead forcings as inputs, generates the daily state trajectory through the Lightweight Physical Trajectory Module (Pθ), and jointly estimates residuals in a single forward pass using the Temporally Prefix-Constrained Multi-Lead Compensation Module (Cϕ), thereby producing the evolution-core output. During forecasting, the evolution core remains frozen. Variable-Specific Input Adaptation (VSIA) calibrates the observed initial condition and forecast forcings, while Response-Domain Semantic Correction (RDSC) further refines the output. The model thereby establishes a structured separation among physical propagation, multi-lead residual learning, and forecast-domain adaptation.

papers.abstract: Masked discrete diffusion models offer a promising alternative to autoregressive generation, but iterative sampling can be costly, and intractable sequence likelihoods complicate reward fine-tuning. We introduce IDRF, a framework for reward fine-tuning of few-step masked discrete diffusion generators. Starting from a standard reverse-KL-regularized objective, IDRF replaces the intractable sequence-level KL penalty with inverse-distillation regularization. With an optimal auxiliary denoiser, we prove that the population inverse-distillation loss upper-bounds the sequence-level KL divergence to the reference distribution. IDRF optimizes a trajectory-based surrogate of this loss without reference-model rollouts, so the student keeps its own few-step sampler. We view few-step generation as a finite-horizon Markov decision process and optimize reward with a clipped policy-gradient objective over the student's trajectories. Across DNA, image, and text generation, IDRF achieves high reward with up to $32\times$ fewer denoising steps than the reference while mitigating reward hacking and preserving sample quality.
bullets: Targets expensive iterative sampling and intractable sequence-level KL regularization in masked discrete diffusion.
Replaces the sequence-level KL penalty with inverse-distillation regularization and proves an upper bound under an optimal auxiliary denoiser.
Optimizes a trajectory-based, clipped policy-gradient objective over the student’s own few-step sampler.
Across DNA, image, and text generation, achieves high reward with up to 32× fewer denoising steps than the reference while mitigating reward hacking and preserving sample quality.

papers.abstract: Video generation models (VGMs) offer strong spatiotemporal priors for embodied observation--action modeling. However, joint-space action vectors lack explicit image-space structure and vary in dimensionality and semantics across embodiments, making it challenging to directly leverage the rich spatiotemporal priors of VGMs. End-effector visualizations provide an alternative but do not specify the full articulated configuration needed for robot execution. We present Dream4ACT, a world model built for joint video-action modeling across embodiments. To unify action representations across embodiments, we introduce a shared visual action interface, called action views, which render target joint configurations from four prescribed virtual cameras using URDF-based forward kinematics. This shared visual representation preserves embodiment-specific articulated geometry while allowing observation and action sequences to share a video autoencoder and diffusion transformer. Through masked flow-matching, our model supports forward dynamics, inverse dynamics, and joint observation--action generation within a single jointly trained model by varying which future sequences are corrupted. To recover executable action sequences from predicted action views, we propose a training-free, URDF-constrained multiview recovery mechanism, without a learned embodiment-specific decoder. Dream4ACT achieves an average success rate of 88.98\% on RoboTwin~2.0 and an overall score of 65.66 on TriWorldBench, supporting effective closed-loop manipulation and competitive action-conditioned multiview prediction through the visual action interface.
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between embodiment-specific joint-space actions and video models’ image-space representations.
Renders target joint configurations from four virtual cameras using URDF-based forward kinematics as shared “action views.”
Uses masked flow matching in one jointly trained model for forward dynamics, inverse dynamics, and observation–action generation.
Recovers executable actions with a training-free, URDF-constrained multiview procedure.
Reports an 88.98% average success rate on RoboTwin 2.0 and a 65.66 overall score on TriWorldBench.

papers.abstract: JEPA-style world models learn action-conditioned latent dynamics without reconstructing observations, but distributional regularization alone does not ensure that their representations preserve information needed for control. We identify static collapse, a failure mode in which the encoder preserves episode-specific static content while suppressing manipulation-relevant state changes. Because static content is temporally predictable yet diverse across episodes, this failure can persist despite regularizers such as SIGReg. A controlled study on OGBench-Cube shows that introducing randomized backgrounds substantially degrades planning performance while leaving the underlying manipulation task unchanged. To address this problem, we propose motion-guided contrastive regularization. Our approach compares predicted latent transitions with transitions to candidate observations from the same episode, reducing the usefulness of static background identity for distinguishing action outcomes. Optical-flow similarities provide soft contrastive targets, allowing candidates with similar motion to receive similar supervision. Combined with latent prediction and SIGReg, our objective encourages representations to preserve within-episode state distinctions and similarities between related transitions. Our method improves planning success over LeWorldModel (LeWM) from 52% to 78% on OGBench-Cube with randomized backgrounds and from 14% to 54% on LIBERO-Object, while maintaining comparable performance on four other visual-control benchmarks.
authors: Yiwen Chen, Qiqi Hou, Jisoo Jeong, Yinhao Zhu, Huaizu Jiang, Amir Said
bullets: JEPA-style latent dynamics can preserve episode-specific static content while discarding manipulation-relevant state changes, harming control.
Randomized backgrounds expose this failure: planning degrades even when the underlying manipulation task is unchanged.
The method contrasts predicted latent transitions with same-episode candidate observations, using optical-flow similarity as soft supervision.
Combined with latent prediction and SIGReg, it promotes within-episode state distinctions and motion-related similarities.
Planning success improves from 52% to 78% on OGBench-Cube and from 14% to 54% on LIBERO-Object, with comparable performance on four other benchmarks.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Static collapse and our solution. (A) We train JEPA world models end-to-end on OGBench-Cube (Cube) and a variant with randomized backgrounds (Cube-RB). Only distant pixels (depth ≥ 1.0m) are replaced, so the robot, cube, and dynamics are unchanged and only task-irrelevant background variation is added. On Cube-RB, LeWorldModel (LeWM; Maes et al., 2026) maps distinct states within each episode to tightly clustered latents, whereas our motionguided contrastive regularization preserves within-episode state variation. (C) Planning success of LeWM, Planning with Latent Dynamics Models (PLDM; Sobal et al., 2026), and our method. LeWM and our method perform similarly on Cube, but LeWM’s success drops on Cube-RB and is low on LIBERO-Object. Our method achieves the highest success of the three in all settings.

Figure 2: Motion-guided contrastive learning. The world model encodes the current observation xt and predicts ẑt+1. The true next observation xpos = xt+1 provides the positive sample, while other frames from the same episode provide negative candidates xm and xn. All observations share the same encoder. Image-space: Optical flow is computed from xt to each candidate. Comparing these fields with the positive flow assigns higher target similarity to candidates with similar motion (xm) than to those with different motion (xn). Latent-space: Angles illustrate cosine similarities between the predicted transition ẑt+1 − zt and candidate transitions zj − zt. Our motion-guided contrastive loss matches the resulting latent similarity distribution to the motion-derived target distribution through cross-entropy. The prediction loss aligns ẑt+1 with zpos. papers.abstract: Generative video models are increasingly used as visual world simulators, yet their primary strength lies in rendering plausible pixels rather than reasoning about how a world should evolve. Coherent world evolution requires more than visual fidelity: when an event occurs, a model must infer its consequences for the entities in the world and then render the resulting state. For example, after a wild beast appears, the model should not only depict the wild beast, but also infer whether a nearby person should flee, take cover, or fight back based on the realized scene. Existing diffusion-based video models lack an explicit mechanism for maintaining world state and reasoning over such event-conditioned consequences, often producing visually plausible but behaviorally static or causally inconsistent outputs. To make this reasoning gap concrete and measurable, we propose a new problem, Out-of-Sight Causal Evolution, which requires a model to render an event, reason about its consequences for the evolving world state, and reveal a causally plausible outcome as the world continues to evolve, even out of sight. As a baseline reference solution, we introduce EvoWorld, a brain-renderer collaboration framework in which a vision-language model serves as the world brain: it observes generated segments, maintains an evolving account of the world, and reasons about plausible state transitions, while a segment-autoregressive video renderer realizes them visually. We further introduce EvoWorld-Data and EvoWorld-Bench for training and evaluating event realization, causal reactions, and revisit consistency. Experiments show that EvoWorld substantially improves event-conditioned causal evolution over recent models while preserving visual quality and consistency, establishing a reference point for reasoning-guided, autonomous world evolution beyond the current field of view.
authors: Yequan Bie, Dengyang Jiang, Zhixuan Chen, Xiaozhuan Liang, Haoxuan Che, Quande Liu, Xi Chen, Hao Chen
bullets: Introduces Out-of-Sight Causal Evolution, requiring models to render events, infer their consequences, and reveal plausible outcomes later—even off-screen.
Uses a vision-language “world brain” to track evolving state and reason about transitions, paired with a segment-autoregressive video renderer.
Provides EvoWorld-Data and EvoWorld-Bench for evaluating event realization, causal reactions, and revisit consistency.
Experiments report improved event-conditioned causal evolution while preserving visual quality and consistency.
Targets limitations of existing diffusion video models, which often produce visually plausible but behaviorally static or causally inconsistent scenes.
