papers.abstract: A robot action can satisfy shape and range constraints yet carry the wrong semantics: axes may be permuted, signs inverted, rotations rescaled, or gripper polarity reversed. We study learned state-action-effect relations as offline contracts for detecting these mismatches and ranking their likely fields. Clean held-out transitions calibrate alarms; a fixed inverse vocabulary supports closed-set localization. On ten LIBERO Spatial tasks comprising 432 source episodes, a capacity-controlled comparison at 2.5% empirical clean false-positive rate gives 46.1% recall for a ridge forward residual, 61.0% for a four-component joint Gaussian mixture, and 65.7% for the exact conditional of that same mixture. The joint score retains a 14.9 percentage-point advantage over ridge, while conditioning improves recall by a further 4.7 points. Joint scoring instead has higher localization: 95.8% versus 94.6%. These matched-rate comparisons are retrospective diagnostics, not deployment calibration guarantees. Earlier Object/Goal results broaden tasks within the LIBERO convention; DROID, all three HYDRA tasks, short temporal faults, small offsets, exact repair, and simulated mitigation fail their respective gates, while xArm contributes one task only. The evidence supports a bounded offline diagnostic and a detection-localization tradeoff, rather than joint-density superiority or cross-robot safety.
authors: Rui Zhu, Xurui Li, Haixu Tang
bullets: Targets semantic mismatches such as permuted axes, inverted signs, rescaled rotations, and reversed gripper polarity that can satisfy basic action constraints.
Uses learned state-action-effect relations as offline contracts, calibrates alarms on clean held-out transitions, and localizes faults with a fixed inverse vocabulary.
On ten LIBERO Spatial tasks at a 2.5% empirical clean false-positive rate, exact conditional scoring reached 65.7% recall versus 61.0% for a joint Gaussian mixture and 46.1% for ridge residuals.
Joint scoring achieved 95.8% localization versus 94.6% for ridge, indicating a detection–localization tradeoff.
Findings support a bounded offline diagnostic, not deployment-calibration guarantees, cross-robot safety, or broad robustness beyond the tested scope.

papers.abstract: Diffusion models for temporal prediction typically corrupt each future frame with independent noise, leaving temporal dependence entirely to the denoiser. We propose Dynamical State-Space Diffusion (DSSD), which learns the temporal structure of the corruption process itself. DSSD builds a temporal kernel from the damped oscillatory modes of a stable diagonal state-space model, whose learned decay rates and frequencies let the corruption capture multiple timescales and oscillatory correlations, while the denoiser architecture remains unchanged. Running this model on a finite clip, however, requires the state before the first frame, which is unobserved; starting from a zero state leaves the early frames with less noise than the diffusion schedule prescribes. We avoid this by using the Cholesky factor of the model's stationary covariance as the temporal operator. We prove that this operator is causal, exactly invertible, keeps each frame's noise variance equal to that of standard diffusion, and reduces to the identity at the clean end of the process, and that it is exactly the Kalman innovations form of the state-space model. The denoiser is trained to predict the temporally correlated noise, and sampling removes and reapplies the temporal mixing at each step. On scientific-field and robot-video datasets, DSSD outperforms diffusion baselines that share its denoiser, and the evolution of its learned modes during training shows that the temporal operator adapts to each dataset.
authors: Woojun Lee, Hankyeol Kim, Pilsung Kang
bullets: Addresses the loss of temporal structure in standard frame-independent diffusion corruption.
Uses learned damped oscillatory state-space modes to model multiple timescales and temporal correlations while keeping the denoiser unchanged.
Applies a stationary-covariance Cholesky operator to handle unobserved pre-clip states while preserving per-frame noise variance and exact invertibility.
Provides theoretical links to causal diffusion operators and the Kalman innovations form.
Outperforms matched-denoiser diffusion baselines on scientific-field and robot-video datasets; learned modes adapt during training.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes a diffusion-based world model for spatiotemporal prediction, fitting video world models.
papers.title: Dynamical State-Space Diffusion for Spatiotemporal Prediction
papers.tldr: DSSD improves spatiotemporal diffusion by learning temporally correlated corruption through a stable state-space model rather than adding independent noise to each frame.

papers.abstract: We present a shared framework that adapts Cosmos world foundation models for real-time interactive world simulation in Physical AI. By streaming visual observations in response to actions and scene controls, the framework enables users and embodied agents to interact with evolving virtual environments. It supports both predicting the visual consequences of actions and generating observations from physical state maintained by an external simulator. We demonstrate this approach across camera navigation and robot manipulation, controllable video transfer, and multi-view autonomous vehicle (AV) simulation. These examples provide a shared foundation for developing interactive virtual environments for Physical AI training and evaluation. Our code and model checkpoints are available at https://github.com/nvidia/cosmos and https://huggingface.co/collections/nvidia/cosmos3-examples. The project website is available at https://research.nvidia.com/labs/cosmos-lab/cosmos-simulation.

figures.caption: Figure 17: Multi-view RGB–LiDAR generation. Each column represents a camera or LiDAR stream. Colors denote language tokens (lavender), clean controls (green), and noisy target latents (light orange), as in Fig. 2. Each camera reads its own prompt and WSM control, while LiDAR reads all camera prompts and its HD-map control. Learned identity embeddings distinguish cameras 0, . . . , 𝑁 − 1 and LiDAR 𝑁 , retaining their identities when selecting camera subsets. Arrows connect conditioning inputs to their consumers, and the lower bidirectional links show cross-sensor attention under the temporal visibility rules. Representative views are shown, with tokenizers and optional initial observations omitted. See Sec. 7.1 to 7.3 for the model architecture, caption preparation, and training recipe.

Figure 1: From Cosmos 3 to interactive world simulation. A shared post-training recipe adapts Cosmos3Nano from the Cosmos 3 family (NVIDIA, 2026a) into three example models for camera navigation and robot manipulation, single-view video transfer, and multi-view autonomous vehicle (AV) simulation. Each specialized model incorporates domain-specific controls tailored to its application and trained on datasets reflecting the types of interactions and physical dynamics relevant to that domain.

Figure 4: Shared post-training stages for interactive world simulation. Stages follow Causal-rCM (Zheng et al., 2026c) from top to bottom, with context and purpose alongside. Solid arrows initialize the next stage. Dashed paths supply the frozen stage-1 causal teacher for TF-dCM and the frozen stage-0 bidirectional teacher for SF-DMD. SF-DMD also uses a trainable auxiliary score model to evaluate student rollouts.

Figure 2: Autoregressive video generation with streaming controls. (a) Each generator chunk groups clean controls 𝒰𝑘 with the corresponding visual tokens. The history ℋ𝑗 comprises previously denoised chunks ̂︀𝒱𝑘 and the retained controls. The current chunk ̃︀𝒱𝜏𝑗 is progressively denoised with clean controls held constant. (b) The action-based example shows 4 individual clean action tokens per latent interval. For video transfer, aligned source latent frames form the clean control group 𝒰𝑗 for the target chunk’s interval. Source tokens entering the cache keep their conditioning role for future predictions.

Figure 5: Packed and replay-based teacher forcing. (a) The action-conditioned schematic shows 1 latent time step per chunk, with the same clean controls in both branches. Color identifies the clean-reference or noisy-target branch, while controls remain clean in both. The mask permits clean-to-clean attention, strictly earlier clean history for noisy queries, and joint reads within each noisy chunk. For larger single-view chunks, clean queries can read only their own latent interval and earlier clean intervals. (b) The replay noisy pass reads language 𝒯 , an available prefix ℋprefix from earlier segments, and strictly earlier clean chunks. (c) The clean pass supplies layerwise K/V for parallel noisy-target evaluation, with shared parameters and a single optimizer update. The dashed arrow marks the retained or recomputed gradient path through the cache.

Figure 3: Temporal-causal attention for action-conditioned video generation. Rows represent queries and columns stand for keys/values. Each generator chunk contains clean controls 𝒰𝑘 and visual tokens ̃︀𝒱𝑘, with chunk indices starting at 𝑘 = 0. When conditioning on actions, 𝒰0 is a null group and the first vision group is the clean frame 𝒱0. Language uses causal self-attention, while generator queries access reasoner keys/values, but not vice versa. Token counts are schematic only. (a) In Cosmos 3, every generator chunk can read from every other. (b) After causal conversion, reads are allowed only within the current block and to earlier ones. Video-transfer and multi-view layouts can further restrict token-role visibility.

Figure D.4: Cosmos3-Nano-Sim-Auto chunk wall time by GPU count and layout on GB200. Shipped flags, from the same-allocation ladders of Tab. D.7; bars give the median of the run medians of a configuration and whiskers their range where the configuration was repeated. Labels give the GPU layout as model ranks plus map GPUs, where map GPUs draw and encode controls on separate GPUs, so the GPU count of a configuration is their sum; blue bars are RGB and orange bars RGB + LiDAR.

Figure 6: State and dependencies in one streaming generation step. Initial context supplies language and any available observed history, while streaming inputs provide the current conditions 𝒰𝑗 . Denoising reads these inputs without modifying retained K/V. Completed latents feed the cache update and stateful decoding, which can overlap on separate GPUs. The generator refreshes clean K/V for the completed chunk and appends the retained entries before the next prediction (Eqs. (20) and (21)). For single-view action conditioning, this refresh processes latent frames in temporal order within the chunk.

Figure C.9: Object-motion errors under depth and segmentation conditioning. The depth example at 4.00 s and the segmentation example at 3.00 s show the simulator holding the target above an empty table. The prompts describe the shoe and turtle on the counter, and the generated observations place them there despite the lifted target in the source. Both examples come from 600-frame, 30-FPS VisDex rollouts using the iteration-1,500 SF-DMD checkpoint, a 30-latent-frame K/V window, and 3 sink frames.

Figure D.7: LiDAR range views under different weather prompts. The front ±90∘ of sweep 15 is shown for the same scene controls and random seed (2025). Brighter pixels indicate greater range on a shared 0–100m scale, and black pixels denote missing returns. Compared with sunny conditions, rain produces gaps in road-surface returns, while fog suppresses distant returns and preserves much of the nearby road.

Figure 23: Multi-view RGB–LiDAR generation with Cosmos3-Nano-Transfer-Auto. This urban intersection under strong sun glare illustrates joint generation across eleven cameras and LiDAR. The white van retains its appearance in the rear-right and rear-fisheye views, while the forward and right-facing cameras agree on the direction of sunlight. Overlaid WSM controls align with the generated road markings and vehicle positions. The views follow the rig’s spatial layout around a central LiDAR sweep, whose height coloring distinguishes the road surface, nearby vehicles, and surrounding buildings.

Figure 24: Multi-view RGB–LiDAR generation with Cosmos3-Nano-Sim-Auto. Camera views are arranged by their viewing directions around the vehicle, with generated LiDAR shown centrally. WSM controls are overlaid on the RGB frames to highlight adherence to the supplied scene structure. Buildings, vehicles, and cyclists retain consistent geometry and appearance across overlapping views. The LiDAR point cloud is color-coded by height and captures corresponding scene geometry.

Matched crops show inconsistent body proportions and front–rear interpretation of the generated red vehicle during a passing maneuver. The vehicle is visible in all three illustrated frames. The 121-frame, 30-FPS generation uses a 31-latent-frame K/V window and 3 sink frames.

Figure 8: Initial-state caption rewriting on an AgiBot-GEAR example. The initial frame shows the patterned slippers on the floor beside the right cabinet wall. Figure 10: Cosmos3-Nano-Sim-Bimanual camera navigation from a shared initial image. The first column shows the shared initial image. Each row then shows frames at 2.5, 5, 7.5, and 10 s from one rollout conditioned on a different camera trajectory (follow behind, crane up follow, truck left, and truck right). Figure 14: Attention in Cosmos3-Nano-Sim-Transfer. Rows are queries and columns are keys/values, using the visual conventions of Fig. 3. 𝒰𝑖, 𝒱𝑖, and ̃︀𝒱𝑖 denote spatial controls, clean RGB, and noisy RGB for latent-frame chunk 𝑖. (a) The clean pass preserves causal language attention and gives control and RGB queries access to all language tokens. Control queries read controls through the current chunk and strictly earlier clean RGB, while clean RGB queries also read their own clean chunk. (b) The noisy pass reuses the clean pass’s language, control, and RGB keys and values. Each noisy RGB query reads controls through its current chunk, strictly earlier clean RGB, and noisy RGB within its own chunk. Neither controls nor noisy RGB can read the current clean RGB target. Three chunks are shown, with the optional conditioning prefix omitted.

Figure 19: Camera and LiDAR sampling on a shared physical timeline. The illustrative grids share a temporal origin. Camera frames (𝑅𝑖) are sampled at 30 FPS, and the Wan2.2 tokenizer applies 4× temporal compression to produce camera latent steps (𝐶𝑗) spaced by 4/30 seconds (7.5 Hz). LiDAR sweeps and their latent steps (𝐿𝑘) retain the same 1/10-second spacing. Dashed guides and rings mark coincident camera-latent and LiDAR timestamps every 0.4 seconds, spanning three RGB latent intervals and four LiDAR intervals. Variable-length attention processes each segment, and the results are scattered back to the original query order. Each attention call returns a normalized output and log-sum-exp (LSE) statistics. LSE-weighted merging recovers joint normalization when key subsets are disjoint and attention scores match, as in Eq. (D.10). papers.abstract: Graphical user interface (GUI) agents can improve decision-making with world-model foresight, provided that predicted states accurately reflect post-action interfaces. Existing state representations fail to jointly capture interface layout, UI semantics, and explicit locations. We introduce Typed Spatial Markdown (TSM), a Markdown-style textual state representation for desktop web interfaces. TSM serializes block-level and atomic-level UI elements according to their spatial relationships, jointly encoding their types, visual semantics, explicit locations, optional control states, and hierarchical membership. To train a screenshot-to-TSM renderer, we construct AtomBlock-WebUI, a dataset with precise annotations at both granularities. By injecting element-type labels into HTML and directly extracting bounding boxes after rendering, we avoid annotation errors caused by post-hoc inference from webpage structures. Building on TSM, we propose MKD2World, a desktop web world model trained in two stages for current-state description and action-conditioned next-state prediction. During inference, the web agent queries MKD2World as needed and performs a ``digest'' step, in which it interprets each predicted state and extracts task-relevant evidence for selecting the best action. Experiments show that MKD2World-9B achieves an EleF1 score of 26.50 on the out-of-domain test set, outperforming GPT-5.6-Sol(14.98) by 11.52 points. Across Online-Mind2Web tasks, MKD2World-9B improves the success rate of the Qwen3.5-35B web agent from 22.94% to 37.61%, achieving competitive performance among leading open-source GUI world models. Code is available at https://github.com/OmniAI-Lab-CUHKSZ/MKD2World.
authors: Zhihao Nan, Sifan Zhou, Yiming Cheng, Jinkai Zheng, Zheng Zhu, Si Shi, Ming Li, Fei Yu

MKD2World-9B achieves 26.50 EleF1 out of domain and raises Qwen3.5-35B agent success from 22.94% to 37.61% on Online-Mind2Web.

papers.abstract: Embodied video world models predict scene changes caused by robot actions, yet generated object responses may remain inconsistent with task intent and contact dynamics. Critical responses in embodied scenes often concentrate in local regions and specific time intervals. Inspired by chain-of-thought reasoning, we introduce ReactWorld, an embodied video generation model guided by structured interaction anticipation. In the generation backbone's feature space, an interaction response field predictor anticipates how the interaction will unfold, explicitly describing participant roles, future motion response intensity, and local motion changes. A response feedback adapter forms increments to object features from the difference between the object branch's outputs with predicted and zeroed local dynamics inputs. It also converts predicted displacements into positional biases for temporal attention. These two mechanisms guide object feature updates and information retrieval across frames, respectively. Through interaction anticipation and generative feedback, ReactWorld achieves an average score of 77.51 on RBench, outperforming PhysisForcing by 3.29 points with improvements in all nine categories. On EZS-Bench, it achieves a Domain score of 86.98 and an average score of 81.87.
authors: Hanwei Liu, Huijia Zhang, Hanzhang Wang, Guangyu Liu, Hanbei Zhan, Linjie Hu, Bin Xiao, Xuan Zhou, Dong Zhang

papers.abstract: Recent video world models allow users to explore generated environments through camera navigation. Continuous hand motion provides a fine-grained action channel for interacting with the people and objects encountered during exploration. We present Touch\'{e}World, a framework that integrates gesture-driven interaction into a camera-controlled video world model. Given an initial image and a scene-description prompt, the model generates video conditioned on temporally aligned camera and hand controls. We construct joint camera--hand training data from heterogeneous egocentric videos through annotation completion, consistency-based filtering, and temporal alignment. Building on a pretrained camera-controlled world model, we combine spatial hand-skeleton conditioning with numerical hand-motion features through parameter-efficient adaptation. Causal adaptation and few-step distillation support chunk-level online generation, allowing users to update their controls based on generated visual feedback. We further introduce Touch\'{e}Bench to evaluate hand-motion following, camera--hand coordination, online interaction, and object response. Together, these components establish a framework for studying continuous exploration and hand-driven interaction within generative worlds.
authors: Jiaao Yu, Yanjian Zhang, Haoyang Jiang, Guillaume Wisniewski, Nadi Tomeh, Shijie Jia
bullets: Addresses the need for fine-grained hand interaction beyond camera-only navigation in video world models.

Builds joint training data from heterogeneous egocentric videos using annotation completion, consistency filtering, and temporal alignment.
Adapts a pretrained camera-controlled world model with hand-skeleton and numerical motion features using parameter-efficient methods.
Introduces chunk-level online generation and TouchéBench for evaluating hand following, camera–hand coordination, online interaction, and object response.

papers.abstract: Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) support planning by comparing predicted latent states with an encoded goal. For this comparison to guide temporal progress, states closer in time to the goal should receive lower costs. However, training representations for prediction and distribution regularization does not directly enforce this ordering. We examine this mismatch in flat LeWorldModel (LeWM) by analyzing how its Euclidean goal cost changes with temporal separation. Our analysis identifies conditions under which states at different long offsets receive similar average costs, weakening their temporal distinction. To learn the missing ordering explicitly, we introduce Time-to-Goal (T2G), a lightweight metric trained on latent triples from offline trajectories. A margin ranking loss encourages smaller distances for temporally nearer states, requiring no rewards or policy labels. The learned metric then replaces the Euclidean planning cost while the JEPA encoder and predictor remain frozen. Diagnostics on AntMaze and FourRoom show that T2G preserves stronger temporal contrast and improves near--far ranking at long offsets. Across four navigation and manipulation benchmarks, T2G improves the average planning success rate from 32.7\% (flat LeWM) to 63.0\% and approaches or even surpasses the performance of the hierarchical H-JEPA baselines. These results show that learning temporal ordering for the goal cost can substantially improve latent planning even with a flat world model.
bullets: Flat JEPA Euclidean goal costs may fail to distinguish states by temporal proximity, especially at long offsets.
T2G trains a lightweight metric on offline trajectory latent triples using a margin-ranking loss, without rewards or policy labels.
The metric replaces Euclidean planning costs while keeping the JEPA encoder and predictor frozen.
Diagnostics show stronger temporal contrast and improved near–far ranking on AntMaze and FourRoom.
Across four benchmarks, average success rises from 32.7% to 63.0%, matching or surpassing hierarchical H-JEPA baselines.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overview of T2G metric training. A latent triple (zt, zt+k, zt+k+∆) is sampled from an offline trajectory, where the near and far states are separated from the anchor by k and k+∆ steps, respectively. The three encoder blocks denote the same frozen JEPA encoder applied to the corresponding observations. T2G evaluates the learned temporal distances from the anchor to the near and far latents and optimizes the metric with a margin ranking objective, so that the near state is closer to the anchor than the far state by at least a margin m. Only the metric network and its scale are updated, and the world model remains frozen.

Figure 6: Temporal guidance of Euclidean squared and T2G costs on recorded AntMaze (top) and FourRoom (bottom) executions. Left: mean cost to the same sampled future goals, normalized by each cost’s mean over the tested offsets. Middle: normalized temporal contrast between offsets separated by one model step (five environment steps). Right: the fraction of comparisons in which the temporally nearer state receives a lower cost, with ties receiving half credit; the dashed line marks 50%. Horizontal axes report temporal separation in environment steps. At long offsets, T2G maintains a larger positive contrast and higher ranking accuracy in both environments.

Figure 2: Changes in the components of Euclidean temporal contrast on AntMaze (left) and FourRoom (right), using 50 recorded planner executions per environment. The horizontal axis is the separation k from a sampled future goal in model steps, with a fixed comparison gap of ∆ = 1 model step (five environment steps). Curves show |δ∆B(k)| and |δ∆q(k)|, each divided by the environment’s mean Euclidean squared distance DE over the tested offsets. In both environments, the B term varies little, while changes in the q term become smaller at longer offsets.

Figure 4: Overview of T2G planning. The current observation o1 and goal observation og are encoded into latents z1 and zg by the frozen JEPA encoder. A solver optimizes an action sequence a1:H , and the frozen predictor rolls out the resulting latent trajectory z1→z2→· · ·→zH . Each predicted latent is scored by its learned temporal distance to the goal, dθ(zt, zg), and the solver updates the actions to minimize the aggregated cost. The updated actions are executed and planning is repeated from new observations in a receding-horizon loop, while the encoder, predictor, and solver remain unchanged.

papers.abstract: Adaptive sampling can substantially improve the value of sparse ocean observations by directing mobile robots toward measurements that are most informative for an evolving environment. Recent learned generative ocean models can produce high-resolution forecasts and ensembles at substantially lower computational cost than traditional numerical models, creating an opportunity to use rich predictive forecasts directly in closed-loop robotic sampling. However, these models do not natively provide the explicit uncertainty representations assumed by classical informative-planning methods, and their forecasts often evolve in learned latent spaces rather than directly in physical ocean variables. We develop a multi-robot closed-loop adaptive sampling framework that uses a single learned generative model for forecasting, uncertainty estimation, planning, and measurement assimilation. The model forecasts an ensemble in latent space, decodes it to physical ocean states, and uses ensemble statistics to construct A- or D-optimal sampling objectives. We select sampling locations subject to robot reachability under predicted currents. The collected measurements are assimilated back into the latent state using observation-conditioned diffusion sampling. Across 120 test scenarios A- and D-optimal sampling generally outperforms static, random, and systematic-coverage baselines while adding little planning overhead. Our experiments uncover several scenarios in which model uncertainty diverges from forecast error, motivating future work in uncertainty quantification.
bullets: Addresses sparse ocean observations and the lack of explicit uncertainty estimates in generative forecasting models.
Generates latent-space ensembles, decodes them to physical states, and derives A- and D-optimal sampling objectives from ensemble statistics.
Plans reachable robot locations under predicted currents and assimilates measurements through observation-conditioned diffusion sampling.
A- and D-optimal strategies generally outperform static, random, and systematic-coverage baselines with little additional planning overhead.
Some scenarios show divergence between model uncertainty and forecast error, highlighting a limitation in uncertainty quantification.

papers.abstract: Self-supervised world models are often said to organize their latents around physical quantities. We test this on 2D decaying Navier-Stokes flow in three pre-registered studies, each tested once on held-out data. In Study 1, a joint-embedding predictive architecture (JEPA) trained to predict the flow fails the pre-registered criteria for organizing its latent around fluid quantities better than an untrained network of the same architecture (not supported); a JEPA trained on non-physical linear dynamics and a static invariance model that never sees time do as well or better. In Study 2, plain autoencoders that render the field make enstrophy prominent in their slowest unsupervised latent directions (best r 0.80-0.86 vs 0.38 untrained; fresh seeds, sealed data). Adding VICReg lowers this prominence in every comparison, though not by the pre-registered margin for vorticity, while raising the autoencoders' linear decodability (partially supported). In Study 3, we build steerable directions ("dials") by routing: the decoder gets overall scale only through a small conditioning code, while its other pathway carries a degraded copy of spectral shape. Label-free rules find a loudness dial in all 8 trained models and a shape dial in 3 of 5 fresh seeds on sealed data, against a pre-registered bar of 4; neither control shows a shape dial (partially supported). Across the studies, what a latent contains and what can be controlled through it come apart. In exploration, a supervised direction reading spectral shape almost perfectly moved nothing when steered. During the build, the loudness dial had to be found by its effect on the output (closest to a pure rescaling), not by data variance; for shape, a variance rule and an effect-constrained rule each worked in 3 of 5 seeds. The program used about 70 logged hours on one consumer GPU; all pre-registrations, deviations, code and outputs are public.
bullets: Three pre-registered studies test physical organization and steerability in 2D decaying Navier–Stokes representations.
A predictive JEPA did not organize latents around fluid quantities better than an untrained counterpart; non-physical and static controls matched or exceeded it.
Plain autoencoders made enstrophy prominent in slow latent directions, while VICReg reduced this prominence but improved linear decodability.
Decoder-routing produced a reliable loudness dial and an inconsistent shape dial; neither control produced a shape dial.
A direction that read spectral shape almost perfectly failed to change shape when steered, showing a gap between representation and control.

papers.abstract: Robot imitation learning is limited by the scarcity of action-labeled data, while action-free demonstrations such as videos are abundant. Recent latent-action methods learn action-relevant representations from observation transitions, but they do not optimize latent actions for downstream control, leading to latent representations that are difficult for policies to model and difficult to accurately decode into continuous robot actions. This paper introduces ELA, an end-to-end framework for learning from video demonstrations via latent actions jointly optimized for policy learning and action decoding. ELA jointly trains a latent action model, latent action policy, and action decoder, enabling policies to leverage abundant video data with only a handful of action-labeled robot demonstrations. Experiments on simulated and real-world manipulation tasks show that ELA consistently outperforms prior latent action baselines. Moreover, it integrates seamlessly with existing imitation learning methods through lightweight 4M-parameter action decoders, requiring no changes to policy architectures or training objectives. Additional materials can be found on: https://end2end-latent-action.github.io/
bullets: Addresses the scarcity of action-labeled robot data by leveraging action-free video demonstrations.
Jointly trains a latent action model, latent action policy, and action decoder for downstream control.
Uses lightweight 4M-parameter action decoders without changing existing policy architectures or training objectives.
Outperforms prior latent-action baselines on simulated and real-world manipulation tasks.
Scope: applies to imitation learning with video demonstrations and limited robot action labels.

figures.caption: Figure 1: ELA Overview. In the Policy-update pass, the LAM is frozen and the alignment and policy losses are used to update the policy network.

papers.abstract: Large language models understand passengers' driving commands, but as driving agents they reason in generated text for seconds and must infer each action's consequences implicitly from the scene. We present Jev-AD, which pairs Jev, a typed decision model that answers predefined questions with probabilities, not generated text, with a language world model that predicts for every candidate action how nearby vehicles move over the next two seconds. Code turns these predictions into foreseen consequences, which Jev compares instead of inferring them from coordinates. In simulated highway merging (500 car-episodes), this foresight lowers the same decision model's collision rate from 26.0% to 2.4% at 0.25 seconds per decision, and Jev-AD achieves the passenger's intent in 93% of free-form command trials. In 500 replayed real-world NGSIM episodes, foresight lowers the collision rate from 48.2% to 2.8%, and the world model, learned from this traffic, foresees 93% of dangerous actions. Project page: https://ys-qu.github.io/jev-ad-website.
authors: Yansong Qu, Jiancong Chen, Samuel Labi
bullets: Addresses the risk that language-based driving agents reason too slowly and infer action consequences implicitly.
Combines Jev, a typed probabilistic decision model, with a language world model forecasting two seconds of surrounding-vehicle motion.
Uses code to convert forecasts into explicit consequences that Jev compares across candidate actions.
In simulated highway merging, foresight reduced collision rate from 26.0% to 2.4% while maintaining 0.25-second decision latency.
Across free-form commands and replayed NGSIM episodes, the system achieved 93% intent fulfillment and reduced replay collision rate from 48.2% to 2.8%.

papers.abstract: Surgical world models have the potential to provide intra-operative guidance, accelerate risk-free training and facilitate transfer of expert surgical maneuvers. However, the use of world models for transferring surgical expertise has been largely unexplored. Moreover, recent approaches in this domain have mainly relied on ground truth kinematics actions or expert annotations for specific tasks, limiting their applicability beyond the narrow range of tasks with ground-truth annotations. In contrast, existing works in the natural domain have shown promising results in learning latent actions solely from unlabeled videos and transferring the learned actions across contexts. We observe that this paradigm is short-sighted for the surgical domain, failing to capture the hierarchical and goal-directed structure of surgical procedures. Thus, we propose a novel multi-step action learning framework to learn context-invariant latent actions that are easily transferable across various surgical contexts. We perform extensive experiments on the publicly available datasets, SurgToolLoc-2022 and PitVis-2023, verifying our approach with both quantitative metrics and qualitative evaluation by surgical experts. We have published our code and the implementation details at https://github.com/bhattarailab/Surgical-Vision-World-Model.
authors: Saurabh Koju, Love Panta, Deepak Thapa, Rudra P. K. Poudel, Prajwal Ghimire, Angus Watson, Yash Raj Shrestha, Prashnna Kumar Gyawali, Binod Bhattarai
bullets: Addresses limited surgical world-model transfer methods that depend on ground-truth kinematics or task-specific expert annotations.
Introduces a multi-step action learning framework designed to capture the hierarchical and goal-directed structure of surgical procedures.
Learns latent actions intended to transfer across diverse surgical contexts without requiring task-specific annotations.
Evaluated quantitatively and through surgical-expert qualitative assessment on SurgToolLoc-2022 and PitVis-2023.
Code and implementation details are publicly available.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon consistency is essential for video world models, yet it becomes difficult to maintain once observed content falls outside the context window. Existing memory mechanisms either retrieve history as implicit context, which remains constrained by context capacity and entangles static and dynamic information or consolidate history into explicit global representations, which struggle to model evolving dynamics and accumulate geometric errors. To overcome these limitations, we introduce GROME, a novel factorized memory framework that augments video world models for long-horizon coherence across both static scenes and dynamic entities. GROME operates via three synergistic components: 1) Static-Dynamic Factorization decouples historical evidence into static and dynamic components, preserving static scene geometry and dynamic entity states separately; 2) Local Memory Retrieval selects spatially aligned static history to eliminate geometric drift alongside the latest dynamic entity states to ensure temporal continuity; 3) Training-Free Memory Injection seamlessly grounds the factorized memory into video world models via their native conditioning pathways. Experiments on long-horizon revisit scenarios demonstrate that GROME substantially enhances scene persistence and dynamic entity fidelity over existing methods, all while preserving the visual quality and controllability of the frozen backbone without additional training. Beyond self-rollouts, GROME readily accommodates external observations as plug-and-play memory, unlocking flexible and controllable video continuation and scene exploration.
bullets: Addresses context-window limitations and errors from mixing static and evolving information in video-model memory.
Factorizes history into static scene components and dynamic entity states.
Retrieves spatially aligned static memories and the latest dynamic states to reduce geometric drift and preserve temporal continuity.
Uses training-free injection through the world model’s native conditioning pathways.

Long-horizon revisit experiments show improved scene persistence and dynamic-entity fidelity while preserving visual quality and controllability; it also supports external observations for video continuation and exploration.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overview of GROME. GROME factorizes historical evidence into static scene and dynamic entity components. Both are retained over extended rollouts as local spatial memories, with the dynamic component further organized by explicit temporal indexing. Given a target camera trajectory, relevant historical evidence is separately retrieved from the static and dynamic components to render references. These static-dynamic references are then injected into the model’s native history-conditioning pathway through a set of training-free injection strategies, conditioning generation together with the local context and user actions. This allows GROME to better preserve consistency over long rollouts while maintaining generation quality and controllability.
Figure 4: Qualitative comparison. GROME better preserves revisit scene structure and entity consistency simultaneously across diverse revisit trajectories compared with existing world models.

Figure 12: Static complex-memory revisit-case 2. The L-shaped explore–return trajectory distributes pose and scene evidence across several views, causing context-based methods to drift or omit content. GROME retrieves complementary static scene evidence through max-coverage retrieval, preserving the revisit scene structure. Red boxes mark representative failures.

Figure 11: Static complex-memory revisit-case 1. When exploring both sides of the kitchen, the visual evidence required for the return view is distributed across multiple historical frames, exceeding the model’s finite context window. GROME retrieves and consolidates local memories to reconstruct comprehensive, high-fidelity static scene references. Red boxes highlight representative inconsistencies in the baselines.

Figure 20: Robustness to imperfect geometric projection. Although rendered historical memories often exhibit geometric artifacts such as disocclusion holes and blur, GROME leverages them as soft spatial guidance rather than rigid pixel-level targets via timestep-aware memory routing. Guided by pretrained world priors, the frozen model corrects moderate rendered distortions and plausibly synthesizes unobserved regions during finer denoising steps while maintaining scene consistency.
Figure 6: Local retrieval vs. Global consolidation.
Figure 7: Applications of GROME.

Figure 8: Evaluation set and trajectory design. The top panels show representative static and dynamic scene categories and their proportions. The bottom panels illustrate exploration-and-revisit camera trajectories; dashed arrows mark returns to previously observed regions.

Figure 13: Static complex-memory revisit-case 3. Complex camera trajectories create multi-view spatial configurations where different parts of the target view are scattered across disparate historical references, exposing the limits of single-frame retrieval. While maintaining a monolithic global cache often suffers from accumulated drift and high overhead, GROME retains historical evidence as local point clouds and selectively retrieves them under target poses. This strategy synthesizes complementary scene evidence to generate the target view with high-fidelity revisit consistency. Red boxes mark representative baseline failures.
Figure 15: Dynamic complex-memory revisit-case 2.

Figure 14: Dynamic complex-memory revisit-case 1. Explicit-memory baselines overlook dynamic entities during memory construction, freezing them at outdated historical states, whereas context-only generation inevitably loses long-range environmental evidence. By factorizing static structure from dynamic entities, GROME simultaneously preserves background consistency and enables dynamic states to evolve. Red boxes mark representative failures.
Figure 16: Dynamic complex-memory revisit-case 3.

Figure 19: Spatially Grounded Exploration. Additional spatially grounded exploration cases. Each row shows the source evidence, the memory transformation or composition, and the resulting rollout under a novel camera trajectory. This arrangement exposes which visual content originates from each memory region.

Figure 21: Representative failure cases of GROME. (a) At long rollout horizons, appearance and color drift inherited from the frozen backbone can still accumulate despite Reference Value Adaptation. (b) Severe local geometry errors can produce sparse or corrupted warped evidence. Although the pretrained VWM usually tolerates moderate projection imperfections, extreme artifacts may be interpreted as plausible scene content and propagate into the generated frame.

Figure 2: Comparison of memory paradigms. Implicit memory suffers from substantial scenecontent overlap and ambiguous in dynamic states, while explicit memory consolidates historical frames into a global 3D scene but struggles with evolving dynamic entities and accumulated geometric drift. GROME instead factorizes historical frames into static-dynamic memory, preserving both persistent static scene structure and evolving dynamic entities over long-horizon generation.
Figure 5: Qualitative ablation of GROME. Static-dynamic factorization and three injection strategies demonstrate their complementary roles in maintaining static scene and evolving entity states.

Figure 17: Long-horizon qualitative comparison. When historical views leave the finite context, implicit memory and explicit memory-based baselines drift from the scene, while GROME preserves static structure beyond 1,400 frames. On dynamic scenes, factorized memory retains evolving dynamic entities without forcing them to remain in a stale state.

Figure 18: Video-to-Memory Continuation. Additional real-world video-continuation cases. Each row pairs an observed video with a GROME rollout generated along a new camera trajectory. Revisit frames assess retention of previously observed scene content, while novel-view frames show the continuation beyond the input.

Implicit memory methods rely on temporally indexed 2D frames, whereas explicit memory methods maintain global 3D reconstructions. In contrast, GROME introduces a unified, factorized memory: both static and dynamic components are grounded as local pointmaps, with the dynamic stream retaining source timestamps for temporal indexing.

papers.title: GROME: GROunding Factorized MEmory into Video World Models
papers.tldr: GROME improves long-horizon video world-model consistency by separately remembering static scene geometry and dynamic entities, then injecting retrieved memories without retraining the backbone.

papers.abstract: Cascade world-action models (WAMs) use predicted visual futures to condition robot actions, but inherit costly iterative inference from diffusion-pretrained experts. We ask what a single-step predicted future must preserve to support accurate single-step action prediction. In the evaluated WAM, resampling video noise has little effect on downstream actions, yet naively truncating both streams to one step substantially reduces task success. Video-space supervision only partially closes this gap, and a local sensitivity analysis shows that vision prediction errors have highly unequal consequences for action accuracy. These findings motivate DirectWAM, which converts pretrained video and action experts into single-step predictors without stochastic sampling through action-sufficient distillation, while retaining the explicit future-to-action cascade. After learning a one-step action model, we train the future predictor by decoding actions from its own predicted futures and backpropagating demonstration action error through the expert, with an optional future-latent reconstruction loss. The resulting objective evaluates the student-generated future through its downstream control consequences rather than relying on representation matching alone. DirectWAM achieves 97.1% average success across four LIBERO suites and 85.4% on RoboTwin 2.0, outperforming Flash-WAM at the same one-evaluation-per-stream budget. This advantage has also extended to three real-world tasks that we designed. Compared with the full iterative teacher, it reduces inference latency by $28.0\times$.
bullets: WAMs can lose task success when diffusion inference is naively reduced to one step, even though video-noise resampling has little effect on actions.
Vision prediction errors have unequal impacts on action accuracy, motivating action-sufficient rather than purely representation-matching distillation.
DirectWAM retains the future-to-action cascade and trains the future predictor through downstream demonstration-action error, with optional future-latent reconstruction.
It achieves 97.1% average success on four LIBERO suites and 85.4% on RoboTwin 2.0, outperforming Flash-WAM at the same inference budget.
The method also extends to three designed real-world tasks and reduces latency 28.0× versus the full iterative teacher.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of DirectWAM. (a) Video randomness produces similar downstream actions. (b) Naive step truncation and visual supervision induce a noticeable performance gap. (c) DirectWAM is a deterministic one-step cascade WAM trained through action-sufficient distillation.

papers.tldr: DirectWAM distills cascade world-action models into fast, single-step predictors by training future representations for their downstream control value, achieving strong simulated and real-world performance with 28× lower latency than iterative inference.

papers.abstract: Learning a universal action representation from video requires modeling dynamics that are consistent across different executions of the same action yet invariant to changes in embodiment and appearance. Existing latent action models infer actions from visual transitions, but their representations often entangle the underlying action with irrelevant visual variations, limiting transfer across embodiments. We introduce DreamX, which repurposes a pretrained video diffusion model as a universal latent action learner. Our approach extracts compact latent actions from the video model's rich spatiotemporal features, compressing each latent video frame by $\boldsymbol{300\times}$ ($\boldsymbol{1{,}200 \rightarrow 4}$ tokens). In addition, by leveraging the video model's generative prior, these latent actions capture action-relevant dynamics disentangled from visual appearance. The resulting latent space serves as a shared action interface across embodiments (human and robot), environments, and action parameterizations. On LARY-Bench, DreamX achieves state-of-the-art performance among latent action models. Moreover, actions encoded in one setting remain effective in another: the latent space supports any-to-any video transfer and zero-shot action transfer across diverse embodiments and environments. Furthermore, this shared interface also enables policy learning in a compact latent action space, reducing the computational cost of video-diffusion-based policies.
authors: Jisoo Kim, Chaehyun Kim, Junsu Kim, Jiho Park, Seongchan Kim, Eunbeen Hong, Soowon Son, Fu-En Yang, Seungryong Kim
bullets: Addresses the challenge of disentangling action dynamics from embodiment- and appearance-specific visual variation.
Extracts latent actions from rich spatiotemporal video features and compresses each frame 300×, from 1,200 to 4 tokens.
Uses the diffusion model’s generative prior to create a shared action interface for humans and robots.
Supports any-to-any video transfer, zero-shot action transfer, and policy learning in a compact latent action space.
Achieves state-of-the-art performance among latent action models on LARY-Bench, according to the abstract.

papers.abstract: Although existing candidate trajectory evaluators have substantially improved end-to-end planning accuracy, their underlying mechanism remains suboptimal. Model-based evaluators typically make scoring future-aware by explicitly predicting candidate-conditioned future states over the planning horizon, which we term rollout. However, rollout incurs high inference cost and accumulates prediction errors. We argue that planning does not require reconstructing a full future scene for each candidate, but only future-relevant information for reliable comparison. We therefore propose RFWorld, a Rollout-Free World model for end-to-end trajectory evaluation. RFWorld constructs a shared scene memory and shapes it into a future-readable representation via lightweight training-time temporal readout with semantic supervision, keeping training overhead low. At inference time, candidate trajectories directly query the shared memory via sparse spatial readout for scoring, reducing computation by roughly the planning horizon times the number of candidate trajectories, while avoiding recursive rollout errors. Experiments on NAVSIM and Bench2Drive show that RFWorld learns a more planning-aligned world representation and achieves state-of-the-art performance.
authors: Junzhe Wang, Jinqing Zhang, Qingjie Liu
bullets: Existing rollout-based evaluators are costly and accumulate prediction errors over the planning horizon.
RFWorld builds a shared scene memory and trains it with lightweight temporally supervised readout to encode future-relevant information.
At inference, candidate trajectories sparsely query the shared memory instead of generating candidate-specific future states.
This reduces computation by roughly the planning horizon multiplied by the number of candidates.
Experiments on NAVSIM and Bench2Drive report state-of-the-art performance and more planning-aligned representations.

papers.abstract: Pretrained video generation models distill internet-scale motion priors into robot policies, but full video is a redundant signal for action prediction. We argue that dense 3D motion is the medium through which video pretraining best transfers to robot actions, and that predicting motion rather than video affords better sample-efficiency for action prediction. FloMo is a 5B video-generation model fine-tuned to predict 3D scene-flow and action tokens. Rendering scene flow as RGB and encoding it into the same latent space as video enables a pretrained video generation backbone to efficiently adapt to predict 3D scene flow. Co-trained on action-free human video and action-labeled robot teleoperation data, our model benefits from human-video pretraining and generalizes to unseen objects, motion primitives, and tasks. Replacing motion prediction with a video prediction objective degrades out-of-distribution generalization, while adding a video prediction target alongside motion lowers policy success rather than improving it. When motion, video, and action are predicted jointly, action tokens attend far more to motion than to video, suggesting that predicting video wastes model capacity. Together, these results indicate that motion effectively mediates the transfer from video pretraining to action. More information can be found at flomo-wam.github.io.
authors: Jeremy Collins, Namra Patel, Ayush Agarwal, Shitij Govil, Animesh Garg
bullets: Motivation: Full video is redundant for action prediction; dense 3D motion may transfer video-learned priors more effectively.
Method: A 5B video-generation model is fine-tuned to predict 3D scene flow and action tokens, using rendered flow encoded in the video model’s latent space.
Training: The model combines action-free human video with action-labeled robot teleoperation data.

Findings: Motion prediction supports generalization to unseen objects, motion primitives, and tasks; replacing or augmenting it with video prediction harms policy success and out-of-distribution generalization.
Interpretation: Action tokens attend substantially more to motion than video, indicating that video prediction can waste model capacity.

papers.abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) improve robotic manipulation by jointly modeling visual dynamics and robot actions. However, most existing WAMs model dense short-horizon visual dynamics, capturing local interactions but providing limited long-range task context. Extending prediction horizons increases uncertainty and computation while entangling task-level evolution with fine-grained local dynamics, obscuring their dependencies and distinct roles in action generation. We propose HiLo-WAM, which decouples long-horizon task evolution from local visual dynamics while jointly modeling their interaction with robot actions. A sparse long-horizon visual stream captures historical task context and future evolution, while a dense local dynamics visual stream models short-horizon robot-object interactions. The two streams operate at different temporal scales within a unified dual-DiT architecture and guide actions through structured cross-stream attention. Progressive inference further reduces unnecessary computation through stream-wise partial denoising, joint denoising, and dynamic skipping. Experiments demonstrate strong long-horizon manipulation performance: HiLo-WAM achieves a 93.70% average success rate on RoboTwin 2.0 and a 17.43 progress score on RoboDojo long-horizon tasks, with robust in-domain and OOD performance on the Fourier GR-3 robot. Ablations confirm the complementary contributions of long-horizon task evolution and local interaction dynamics, while temporal-scale analyses highlight the importance of balancing temporal coverage and resolution. Progressive inference further achieves a 2.93x speedup while improving performance.
authors: Xingyu Wang, Yanjiang Guo, Zhijing Ding, Jiaxin Fang, Zeyu Lai, Jiayu Dong, Weikang Wan, Jianyu Chen, Yuxiang Gao, Mengdi Xu
bullets: Addresses the limited long-range context and high computational cost of dense short-horizon WAM prediction.
Uses sparse long-horizon and dense local-dynamics visual streams at different temporal scales.
A unified dual-DiT architecture connects the streams with structured cross-stream attention to guide actions.
Progressive inference with partial, joint, and dynamically skipped denoising achieves a reported 2.93× speedup.
Reports 93.70% average success on RoboTwin 2.0 and a 17.43 progress score on RoboDojo long-horizon tasks, with in-domain and OOD performance on Fourier GR-3.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Architecture of HiLo-WAM. HiLo-WAM builds on a dual-DiT World Action Model consisting of a shared Video DiT and an Action DiT. The visual world is modeled at two complementary temporal scales: a sparse long-horizon visual stream captures historical context and coarse future evolution, while a dense local visual dynamics stream captures fine-grained local interactions. Both visual streams are jointly modeled with robot actions. During inference, the visual streams progressively terminate and are cached, while the action stream continues denoising to completion.

papers.abstract: A robot world model that serves as a simulator must do more than generate plausible videos: it must faithfully follow commanded actions, maintain consistency across camera views, and sustain coherent long-horizon rollouts. We present PrimeSim, an action-conditioned, multiview world model simulator that addresses these challenges through progressive midtraining and posttraining. Starting from a pretrained video generator, we midtrain on 30,110 hours of robot demonstrations spanning 22 platforms. To improve action following, we introduce a unified cross-embodiment action representation and frame-aligned dual-path conditioning to strengthen action-frame correspondence. To maintain multiview consistency, we develop view-aware interleaved attention with explicit camera identities, enabling cross-view information exchange while preserving view-specific representations. We further introduce a fast-video, slow-memory posttraining framework that transforms the bidirectional video generator into an efficient autoregressive simulator. By combining fast causal generation, self-rollout training, and hierarchical temporal memory, PrimeSim mitigates error accumulation from self-generated histories and supports coherent long-horizon simulation. PrimeSim runs at 10.1 FPS, remains stable over long-horizon rollouts on rigid and deformable manipulation tasks, and transfers to held-out platforms within 100 to 200 gradient steps where the pretrained backbone does not. Against five open-source action-conditioned world models it leads four of the five WorldSimProbe suites and posts the best overall EWMBench score, while fine-grained local calibration still trails the field; its rollouts are faithful enough to support GRPO-based policy optimization. We release the model weights, inference code, and training code.
authors: Travis Davies, Wentao Ma, Lihao Guo, Tengfei Ma, Xiaowen Chang, Jiafeng Xu, Shilong Wang, Yiqi Deng, Shaowen He, Xiaoqi Li, Qian Zhu, Ran Cheng, Hao Dong
bullets: Targets faithful action following, multiview consistency, and stable long-horizon rollouts beyond merely plausible video generation.
Midtrains a pretrained video generator on 30,110 hours of demonstrations across 22 robot platforms using unified actions and frame-aligned conditioning.
Uses view-aware interleaved attention plus camera identities to preserve consistency across views.
Converts the bidirectional generator into a 10.1-FPS autoregressive simulator with fast-video, slow-memory posttraining, self-rollouts, and hierarchical temporal memory.
Leads four of five WorldSimProbe suites and achieves the best overall EWMBench score, while fine-grained local calibration remains weaker; released with model weights and code.

(b) The model is conditioned on a language prompt, a unified action representation over head, torso, waist, end-effector, gripper and chassis, and three camera views, and predicts future frames; post-training makes generation autoregressive with a selected KV-cache memory at four denoising steps. (c) Capabilities: fidelity against prior systems, action following measured against simulation ground truth, few-shot adaptation to an unseen embodiment, and use as a simulator: success rate in PrimeSim predicts success rate in the LIBERO [51] physics simulator with r = 0.99, so policies can be trained in the model and the result carried back to the robot.

Left: the task-category and embodiment distributions. Right: example frames from each of the five embodiment classes.

Figure 2 Overview of the data pipeline. Raw demonstrations from teleoperation, UMI, and simulation are converted through four stages: video quality filtering, action quality filtering, action preprocessing, and data alignment. Each stage lists the operations applied to the incoming data. The pipeline produces a unified corpus of 30,110 hours across 20 dataset families and 22 robot platforms (Table 12).

Figure 8 Zero-shot and few-shot generation on an unseen setting and camera pose. Both subfigures show the AgileX Piper bimanual arm on XVLA [100], held out of pre-training entirely: the embodiment is in the corpus, but the scene, the garments and the camera placements are not. Rows are cameras (head, left wrist, right wrist) and columns are seven frames sampled uniformly from a single rollout. (a) Without adaptation the model controls the arms and renders the cloth, but the generated cloth state drifts from the commanded action once the motion becomes contact-rich. (b) After 200 gradient steps the arm trajectories and the cloth deformation track the commanded actions much more closely and the three views stay mutually consistent, so most of the cost of the transfer is recovered.

Figure 7 Few-shot adaptation to unseen embodiments. Each pair shows the midtrained model above the pretrained backbone for one platform held out from training: a single 7-DoF arm (xArm 7) drawn from Open X-Embodiment [17], a bimanual platform (ViperX 300, as used by ALOHA [98]) and the original Stanford UMI gripper [14]. Similar embodiments do occur in the corpus, and they are what make transfer possible at all, since a wholly alien platform would leave nothing to build on. They are still new embodiments, however, and adaptation between embodiments does not happen for free: each brings its own kinematics, camera mounting and data distribution, which have to be acquired rather than inherited. All initialisations are finetuned under an identical recipe with single-trajectory batches at a batch size of 1, and none receives an embodiment identifier or any embodiment-specific parameters. The midtrained model reaches an action-following rollout within 100 to 200 gradient steps on all three platforms. The pretrained backbone, which must initialise the action-conditioning and multiview modules from scratch, does not reach the same regime even at ten to twenty times that budget.

Figure 10 Counterfactual action following on LIBERO. Our evaluation is built on counterfactual commands, meaning action trajectories that do not correspond to the demonstrated behaviour. Faithful generation therefore requires the model to respond to the commanded motion rather than replay the recorded one. Static scene elements remain stable across the rollout while the commanded motion is carried out, indicating that the generated future is driven by the action rather than by visual plausibility alone.

papers.abstract: Humanoid loco-manipulation requires coordinated body motion and hand interaction over time, and a plausible-looking command sequence can still drop a held object or leave an interaction incomplete. We present action-conditioned latent foresight, a latent world-action model (WAM) that evaluates proposed command sequences before execution. An action generator proposes joint motion-hand command sequences from vision, language, and the robot state. An action-conditioned endpoint predictor estimates the visual features each sequence prefix reaches and measures progress toward a demonstration-derived subgoal, while a joint temporal prior scores temporal consistency given the robot state and preceding commands. The robot executes the first commands of the best-scoring sequence and replans from the next observation. During training, action consistency regularization reconstructs the first demonstrated command from observed and predicted feature changes, encouraging the predictor to retain action-relevant information. On ten tasks in the humanoid loco-manipulation simulation benchmark SIMPLE, our method achieves 89.7% average success, compared with 73.7% for Psi-Zero and 82.0% for DiT4DiT. On seven real-robot tasks, it achieves 85.7% under standard conditions and 65.7% under unseen object configurations, while GR00T N1.7 achieves 70.0% and 48.6%, respectively. Project page: https://ju6276.github.io/Action-Grounded-Foresight/
authors: Ju Dong, Xinyu Xiao, Yiming Zhou, Tianshuo Yang, Xuerong Liu, Lei Zhang, Jian Chen, Haocheng Zhao, Yu Fu, Yujie Wei, Diwen Zheng, Alois Christian Knoll, Angela P. Schoellig, Ping Luo, Jianwei Zhang
bullets: Targets failures where plausible motions drop objects or leave interactions incomplete.
Uses a latent world-action model combining visual-language-state-conditioned action generation, endpoint prediction, and temporal consistency scoring.
Executes only the best sequence prefix, then replans from the next observation; training adds action-consistency regularization.
Achieves 89.7% average success in ten SIMPLE simulation tasks and 85.7% on seven real-robot tasks under standard conditions.
Performance drops to 65.7% on unseen object configurations, indicating reduced robustness to novel arrangements.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in video modeling have driven substantial progress in world action models (WAMs). Existing approaches exploit pretrained video priors by decoding actions from latent representations or inferring them from generated videos. The underlying link is causal: robot actions produce changes in the scene, and video observations of these changes provide evidence for inferring the actions that produced them. However, existing training formulations do not by themselves ensure that actions and their predicted visual consequences are consistent, potentially limiting the use of pretrained capabilities. We treat video and action as paired modalities linked by this causal relationship and learn their correspondence through a unified training framework designed to better exploit pretrained video priors. Cycle WAM first augments video-action co-training with bidirectional conversion to reinforce cross-modal correspondence and recover forward and inverse dynamics. It then introduces a differentiable cycle-reconstruction objective to further couple the two mappings. The resulting model supports both forward and inverse dynamics, with the potential to improve performance through more effective use of pretrained video priors. Cycle WAM achieves state-of-the-art performance among comparable methods on LIBERO-Pro and substantially improves DreamZero on DROID. Comparisons with UWM characterize its inverse-dynamics performance and show sharper visual detail in the displayed forward-dynamics predictions.
authors: Qinglin Yang, Jiepeng Wang, Yuxing Huang, Haibin Huang, Kai Xu, Chi Zhang, Ruizhen Hu, Xuelong Li
bullets: Addresses inconsistency between predicted actions and their visual consequences in existing world action models.
Uses bidirectional video–action conversion to learn both forward and inverse dynamics.
Adds a differentiable cycle-reconstruction objective to strengthen cross-modal correspondence.
Achieves state-of-the-art performance among comparable methods on LIBERO-Pro and substantially improves DreamZero on DROID.
Comparisons with UWM indicate stronger inverse-dynamics performance and sharper forward-dynamics visual predictions.

papers.abstract: Phase-field models resolve microstructural evolution during rapid alloy solidification, but their computational cost limits long trajectories, stochastic ensembles, and studies across process conditions. We present a variance-preserving denoising diffusion bridge model (VP-DDBM) for state-conditioned prediction of two-dimensional Al-Cu solidification. Given the current phase, concentration, and prescribed temperature fields, the model predicts the subsequent state and is applied autoregressively. Across two held-out thermal gradients, VP-DDBM produces lower long-horizon errors than deterministic U-Net and SI-ConvNeXt baselines in domain-mean phase, domain-mean Cu concentration, and leading-tip position. It also retains fine dendritic structure over long rollouts, whereas the deterministic U-Net progressively smooths the morphology. VP-DDBM predicts the phase and concentration evolution approximately $73\times$ faster than the phase-field solver, showing potential for faster process-condition screening and ensemble-based microstructure studies.
bullets: Addresses the high computational cost of phase-field simulation for long trajectories, ensembles, and process-condition studies.
Uses a state-conditioned VP-DDBM to autoregressively predict future phase and concentration from current fields and temperature conditions.
Outperforms deterministic U-Net and SI-ConvNeXt baselines on long-horizon phase, Cu-concentration, and tip-position errors across two held-out thermal gradients.
Preserves fine dendritic morphology better than the deterministic U-Net during long rollouts.
Runs approximately 73× faster than the phase-field solver, supporting faster screening and ensemble studies.

papers.abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) use the predictive knowledge of pretrained video diffusion models for robot control through future video prediction. However, iterative video denoising is costly, and inaccurate visual predictions can compromise action prediction. Our key idea is to make this predictive knowledge available through visual representations computed from the current observation, enabling action prediction without generating future videos. We introduce DreamFree, a WAM that repurposes a pretrained video diffusion model as a predictive visual encoder through representation distillation. The visual encoder learns to predict a frozen video diffusion model's representation using only the current observation. An action module is then trained to predict actions by extracting action-relevant information from the visual encoder. Across real-world and simulated tasks, DreamFree achieves higher success rates than state-of-the-art VLAs and WAMs, while performing real-time closed-loop control at 11Hz with a 14B video diffusion backbone. Experiments show that DreamFree can translate stronger video priors and additional video data into better robot control and enable learning new robot tasks from video demonstrations, including videos from a different embodiment, without action annotation for the new tasks.
authors: Jaehyeong Jo, Sangwon Jang, Sihyun Yu, Seonghyeon Ye, Yekyung Nah, Hojung Jung, Kimin Lee, Sung Ju Hwang
bullets: Avoids costly iterative future-video generation and reduces errors from inaccurate visual predictions.
Uses representation distillation to train a visual encoder that predicts frozen video-diffusion representations from the current observation.
An action module extracts action-relevant information to produce robot actions.
Achieves higher success rates than state-of-the-art VLAs and WAMs across real-world and simulated tasks, with 11Hz closed-loop control using a 14B backbone.
Supports leveraging stronger video priors, extra video data, and unannotated demonstrations—including videos from different embodiments—for learning new tasks.

papers.abstract: Predicting how the world evolves in response to robot actions is central to policy learning, evaluation, and planning. However, many action-conditioned world models predict future observations in 2D image or video space without explicitly modeling the underlying 3D scene, making spatial consistency across viewpoints and over long-horizon interactions challenging. We introduce 3D World Simulator, an action-conditioned multimodal world modeling framework that jointly predicts appearance, geometry, and tactile observations from a unified 3D representation. Our approach combines a hybrid particle-voxel autoencoder that compresses point clouds into compact 3D voxel latents with an action-conditioned latent dynamics model that predicts their evolution. The shared 3D representation supports geometrically consistent rendering from arbitrary viewpoints and flexible integration of spatially aligned tactile signals. Our experiments demonstrate interactive, long-horizon, multimodal prediction at 50 Hz. We then show how our model enables scalable data generation for policy training and evaluation using tactile and multi-view visual observations, including wrist-mounted and novel camera views. Furthermore, we scale our method to large datasets containing diverse objects and demonstrate model-based planning with unseen objects and robot configurations. Together, these results highlight the potential of hybrid particle-voxel dynamics as a foundation for multimodal 3D world simulation.
authors: Jimmy Wang, Yifan Chou, Kaifeng Zhang, Yixuan Wang, Binghao Huang, Tao Yu, Saleh Nabi, Yunzhu Li
bullets: Addresses the challenge of maintaining 3D spatial consistency across viewpoints and extended interactions.
Combines a particle-voxel autoencoder for compact point-cloud representations with action-conditioned latent dynamics.
Jointly models appearance, geometry, and spatially aligned tactile observations from a shared 3D representation.
Supports interactive multimodal prediction at 50 Hz, including wrist-mounted and novel camera views.
Enables scalable policy data generation, evaluation, and planning with unseen objects and robot configurations.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of Model Architecture. (a) We introduce a hybrid particle-voxel autoencoder that compresses an input point cloud into a compact 3D voxel latent. This voxel latent is progressively upsampled into finer voxels, which are then upsampled into dense visual particles and optional tactile particles. Each visual particle is attached to Gaussian parameters that can be rendered at novel viewpoints. (b) Our 3D latent dynamics model then directly operates on voxel latents produced by the autoencoder. Given robot actions, history latents, and a current latent observation, the dynamics model uses 3D convolutions and spatiotemporal attention to autoregressively predict future voxel latents during open-loop rollouts. These latents can then be decoded into point clouds, multi-view renders, and tactile observations.

papers.abstract: Scientific agents can find interventions that work without understanding why they do. We study this failure mode in controlled synthetic regulatory systems, where agents must experimentally identify a hidden fault and rescue the resulting phenotype. Across seven LLMs, every model restores the healthy phenotypes more often than it identifies the fault. Claude Opus 4.6 and Sonnet 4.6 rescue every organism while diagnosing only 55% and 35% of them. This failure is not simply due to insufficient exploration or unavailable evidence. In most cases, the cause is experimentally identifiable, and agents encounter evidence that distinguishes competing causes in 91% of relevant sessions, and still frequently misdiagnose the system. Targeted probes reveal where experimental reasoning breaks down. Models reliably interpret decisive evidence and revise hypotheses when the causal comparison is explicit, and can locate that evidence within a full experimental record. However, they struggle to predict the outcome of the experiment under each competing cause, a necessary step in using the observed result to distinguish between them. Agents can therefore gather the right evidence and still infer the wrong cause. As AI systems take on a growing role in synthesising scientific evidence, these findings highlight the need to evaluate how they use evidence to reach causal conclusions, alongside whether their interventions succeed.
authors: Anna Gogleva, Thomas Charman, Martin Balla, Karl Gemayel
bullets: In controlled synthetic regulatory systems, all seven evaluated LLMs restored healthy phenotypes more often than they diagnosed the hidden fault.
The strongest agents rescued every organism but diagnosed only 55% and 35% of cases, respectively.
Misdiagnosis persisted despite agents encountering evidence distinguishing competing causes in 91% of relevant sessions.
Models could interpret decisive evidence and revise hypotheses when causal comparisons were explicit, but struggled to predict outcomes under each competing cause.
Evaluations of scientific AI should assess causal inference and evidence use, not only intervention success.

figures.caption: Figure 8: Tracing the diagnosis–rescue gap through the investigation. Successive analyses rule out insufficient exploration and, for most systems, missing evidence, while bidirectional testing (dashed box) marks a correlate of successful diagnosis. Probes localise the remaining failure: models interpret and revise on isolated evidence, and still locate it inside a full record, but cannot derive what each competing cause predicts.

Figure 1: Controlled experimental environment. (a) A synthetic organism maps environmental inputs through an unknown gene regulatory network to three observable phenotypes; one example hidden fault is highlighted. Agents cannot observe the network directly and must learn about the system through perturbations. (b) Each session proceeds under a fixed experimental budget. All sessions include exploration and prediction; disease sessions additionally require diagnosis of a hidden fault followed by an intervention to rescue the phenotypes.

Figure 7: Evidence use breaks in context. (a) Each probe shows more of the investigation and gives less help with it: the two competing causes, the readout each one predicts, both, or neither. (b) Accuracy on decisive evidence, each gray line represents a model; per-model values are in Tables 5 and 6. Accuracy stays close to 1.00 for as long as the predicted readouts are given (Probes 1–2 and 3a), falls once the models must work them out (3b–c), and falls further in live sessions.

Figure 3: Exploration does not simply explain diagnostic success. (a) Models differ substantially in both the number of experiments they run and the ratio of genes they probe. (b) Within each model, sessions above versus below its median experiment count show no consistent advantage from greater exploration.

Figure 4: Alternative hypotheses and discriminating experiments. (a) Two different faults can produce the same abnormal readout, leaving both as plausible causes. (b) An experiment is discriminating if its outcome differs depending on which fault is present. Values in (a) and (b) are illustrative. (c) We classify the 60 organisms by whether an alternative fault fits the initial observation and, if so, whether an available experiment can distinguish it from the true fault.

Figure 2: The diagnosis–rescue gap. (a) A downstream gene can provide a plausible diagnosis and rescue target, restoring the phenotype without correcting the true fault.
