papers.abstract: Standard spatiotemporal graph convolutional networks need a fixed-size adjacency matrix, coupling model weights to a specific sensor count N; they cannot produce any output at a sensor absent from training. We present OmniST, a topology-invariant forecaster whose computation has zero structural dependency on the number of nodes, and which, composed with inductive split-conformal calibration, gives distribution-free, coverage-guaranteed prediction intervals at arbitrary (including never-seen) sensor locations, preserving that guarantee as sensors are added or removed. Topology invariance follows from coordinate-based tokenization, k-nearest-neighbor attention from geographic coordinates at each forward pass, and per-node temporal processing via a bidirectional GRU. On real Delhi air-quality data (37 stations, 2019-2023), OmniST attains a 30-day PM2.5 MAE of 31.0 ug/m3 and degrades at most 1.1 percent when 40 percent of stations are removed. Its inductive forecasts at unseen stations beat nearest-neighbor interpolation (about 12 percent) and a learned kriging GNN (IGNNK, about 21 percent), and, unlike either, carry a finite-sample coverage guarantee. The guarantee holds at 90 percent or above under 30-50 percent node dropout across four real datasets over three domains (Delhi and Beijing air quality, NOAA GHCN weather, Caltrans PeMSD7-M traffic), and still holds at 325 real sensors (full PeMS-BAY). We also fix a temporal-drift failure: static conformal under-covers over time (about 0.50 late), but a rolling adaptive-conformal estimator restores target coverage (0.89 overall, 0.96 late) at the cost of wider intervals.
bullets: Addresses fixed-node graph models that cannot predict at unseen sensor locations.
Uses coordinate-based tokenization, dynamic geographic k-nearest-neighbor attention, and per-node bidirectional GRUs.
On Delhi PM2.5 data, reports 31.0 µg/m³ 30-day MAE and at most 1.1% degradation after removing 40% of stations.
Unseen-location forecasts outperform nearest-neighbor interpolation and IGNNK, while uniquely providing coverage guarantees.
Rolling adaptive conformal calibration mitigates temporal-drift undercoverage, producing wider but better-calibrated intervals.

papers.abstract: Dynamic driving scene reconstruction has made remarkable strides in recent years by leveraging generative priors, particularly in the quality of novel trajectory rendering. Nevertheless, a significant gap remains between the generated data and real-world sensor observations, severely hindering further improvements in reconstruction fidelity. In this paper, we present ReconDreamer#, a self-evolving framework that synergizes reconstruction and generation for dynamic driving scenes, which substantially bridges the gap between synthesized novel trajectory data and recorded real-world observations. Within this self-evolving closed-loop framework, the generative and reconstruction models mutually reinforce each other through iterative refinement, ultimately yielding a significant enhancement in the 3D representation capability of the reconstruction model. Additionally, we introduce a geometry-prior-based adaptive ground model to further enhance the rendering quality of the reconstruction model. To validate the effectiveness of the proposed method, we conduct comprehensive evaluations on Waymo, nuScenes, PandaSet, and EUVS benchmarks. Specifically on Waymo, at a 6-m lateral shift, ReconDreamer# improves NTA-IoU and NTL-IoU by 8.8% and 3.0%, respectively, and reduces FID by 15.1% relative to ReconDreamer++.

Evaluated on Waymo, nuScenes, PandaSet, and EUVS benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Recent work has improved computer-use agents (CUAs) by combining retrieved task-relevant tutorials and look-ahead planning using world models with MLLM judges. However, the contribution of each component -- tutorials, the judge, and the world model -- to overall improvement has not been evaluated in isolation. To fill this gap, we first construct OSWorld-Tutorial and ScienceBoard-Tutorial: two datasets for CUAs with curated multimodal tutorials, covering everyday and scientific domains. We then propose RAG-PolicyJudge (RAG-PJ), a policy-judge framework for CUAs conditioned on task-specific tutorials: the policy proposes candidate actions, and the judge selects among them. To isolate the effect of world models given tutorials, we compare RAG-PJ with and without common world models: using either zero-shot text-based descriptions of next states or an oracle that returns ground-truth visual observations. We find that RAG-PJ gains little benefit from these rollouts when tutorials are present, even with perfect visual futures. This suggests prior world-model gains in tutorial-conditioned methods come mainly from tutorial understanding and the judge's ability to select the proposed actions, rather than from predicted rollouts. Error analysis reveals that the bottleneck is not rollout fidelity, but the judge's ability to reason over future states and recognize task completion. This highlights the need to improve not just next-state prediction in world models, but also reasoning over their predicted rollouts. Datasets and code are available at https://github.com/realjoenguyen/RAGPJ-official.

Error analysis identifies future-state reasoning and task-completion recognition as key bottlenecks.

papers.abstract: Intracardiac flow is driven by complex, and time-varying cardiac motion and interaction with the heart valves, producing complex flow features that may provide valuable information for disease diagnosis and treatment planning. 4D Flow MRI enables non-invasive, time-resolved measurement of three-dimensional cardiovascular velocity fields. However, substantial noise and limited spatial and temporal resolution limit its ability to accurately resolve flow features. We propose 4D-MRAR (4D Magnetic Resonance Augmented Reconstruction), a deep learning (DL) method to super-resolve and denoise 4D Flow MRI data. Unlike prior DL methods that train and infer on static vascular regions, our method predicts intracardiac flow within hearts undergoing large deformation. Moreover, it uniquely allows for simultaneous super-resolution in 3D space and time. The method combines a residual convolutional neural network, a recurrent neural network, and an implicit neural field to predict high-resolution velocity and pressure fields while efficiently enforcing the governing equations of fluid flow during training. Trained on a synthetic dataset obtained from computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulations of left ventricle (LV) flow, our method generalizes to synthetic whole-heart 4D flow MRI data, and demonstrated promising performance on real 4D Flow MRI. The produced super-resolved flow fields exhibit significantly improved accuracy and greater consistency with the governing equations of blood flow compared with prior methods.
authors: Yusuf A. Ozturk, Jie Zheng, Fanwei Kong

Produces more accurate, physically consistent flow fields than prior methods, though training relies on synthetic CFD data.

papers.abstract: Effective world modeling requires compressing salient history information that facilitates future prediction. However, most existing approaches inherit tokenization and conditioning mechanisms from video generation, where objectives are centered around perceptual realism rather than predictive utility. This discrepancy limits the world model's effectiveness, especially in environments dominated by visual nuisances or task-irrelevant background details. To this end, we introduce Compression Forcing (CF), a general framework that aligns history compression with the predictive objective of world modeling. Compression Forcing features Dynamics-Aware Tokenization (DAT), a novel tokenization method that compresses history observations into a sequence ordered by decreasing dynamics saliency. Built on a diffusion backbone, this structure enables Hierarchical History Guidance (HG-H), allowing selective amplification of dynamics-salient information during inference. Extensive experiments across various environments demonstrate improved prediction fidelity, physical realism, and downstream decision-making performance, establishing Compression Forcing as a highly flexible and effective approach for world modeling.
authors: Siqiao Huang, Partha Kaushik, Michael Chen, Hengkai Pan, Kaiwen Geng, Omar Chehab, Fernando Moreno-Pino, Max Simchowitz
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between video-generation tokenization and world-modeling objectives, particularly under visual nuisances.
Introduces Dynamics-Aware Tokenization, which orders compressed history tokens by decreasing dynamics saliency.
Uses Hierarchical History Guidance with a diffusion backbone to selectively amplify salient information during inference.
Experiments across varied environments report better prediction fidelity, physical realism, and downstream decision-making.
Scope: designed for environments where task-irrelevant visual details can hinder predictive modeling.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overview of the Compression Forcing Framework. (a) DAT encodes history context into a hierarchical token sequence, with leading tokens capturing dynamics and trailing tokens capturing static details. (b) The Diffusion Backbone predicts the next frame conditioned on arbitrary-length prefixes of DATencoded latents and the agent’s action. (c) HG-H composes score estimates from varying-length prefixes, enabling inference-time amplification of dynamically salient history information.

As the slot index increases, cross-attention shifts from regions with dynamic motion (the athlete in motion) to static objects in the background.

papers.abstract: World models are increasingly used to support prediction and planning in embodied agents, but the knowledge is usually established before deployment and then carried into later encounters. Continual operation faces a different problem. A familiar environment may change, and the agent must use previous experience without allowing old expectations to override current physical evidence. This study asks what repeated physical experience must contribute for a spatial world model to become progressively more useful rather than simply more persistent. A physics-grounded dynamic maze separates recurring spatial change from the continuous consequences of action. Cross-episode Spatial Change Memory learns relations among environmental transformations, while state-action-outcome experience refines predictions of motion. Structured experience progressively reduces the need for future route correction and transfers to spatial transitions not encountered during learning. The advantage disappears when past changes contain no information about future ones. Continuous navigation further shows that predictive memory changes behavior when a previous decision becomes invalid but leaves behavior unchanged when the decision remains correct. Physical tests expose a complementary limit: correct topology does not guarantee correct action prediction, and accumulated physical experience reduces this mismatch within the modeled dynamics. The results characterize continual world knowledge as experience that improves future prediction and action beyond stored episodes while remaining revisable by the physical outcomes it is intended to predict.
bullets: Continual operation requires using past experience while remaining responsive to current physical evidence.
Cross-episode Spatial Change Memory captures recurring environmental transformations, while state-action-outcome experience improves motion prediction.
Structured experience reduces future route corrections and transfers to unseen spatial transitions when past changes predict future ones.
Navigation behavior changes when prior decisions become invalid but remains stable when they are still correct.
Physical experience reduces mismatches between correct environmental topology and inaccurate action predictions within the modeled dynamics.

papers.abstract: Humans imagine scene changes under hypothetical motions, an ability central to spatial reasoning and robotic planning. However, this capability remains underexplored in vision-language models and world models. We formalize this capability as Counterfactual Spatial Imagination (CSI) and introduce FlowBench, a resource for training and evaluating both, with 428K training examples spanning simulated and real-world scenes, household environments and tabletop manipulation, and diverse question types. A scalable, fully automatic pipeline pairs each hypothetical motion with spatial questions and, in simulation, exact outcome frames and optical flow. For VLMs, proprietary models exhibit an imagination gap, performing worse when motion outcomes must be inferred than when observed, and open-source models perform near chance; fine-tuning Qwen3-VL-8B on FlowBench-Sim-Train raises its accuracy by 29.5 percentage points in simulation and 16.9 on real images, a strong sim-to-real transfer. For world models, training on FlowBench-Sim improves text-to-flow prediction for all four model families we test, raising the accuracy of Psi-0.6 from 52.1% to 61.7%. FlowBench thus serves as a training and evaluation resource for both. Code and datasets are released at https://github.com/liuyifan22/FlowBench.
authors: Yifan Liu, Baihan Zhang, Khai Loong Aw, Klemen Kotar, Daniel L. K. Yamins
bullets: Introduces Counterfactual Spatial Imagination (CSI) as a benchmarkable capability for spatial reasoning and robotic planning.

Fine-tuning Qwen3-VL-8B improves accuracy by 29.5 percentage points in simulation and 16.9 on real images, indicating sim-to-real transfer.
FlowBench training improves text-to-flow prediction across four tested world-model families, including Psi-0.6.

papers.abstract: Koopman representations describe nonlinear dynamics through linear evolution in a transformed space, offering an attractive framework for their linear simplicity and generality. Yet these advantages do not necessarily translate into improved performance in deep latent data assimilation (LDA). We systematically compare seven representative methods and structural baselines across five systems spanning approximately periodic to strongly chaotic dynamics and a broad range of state dimensions. We evaluate forecast and assimilation accuracy, physical state recovery, latent-trajectory behavior, and dynamical consistency, and assess Gaussian error assumptions, objective convexity, and uniqueness of analysis solutions. Our results reveal a trade-off between representational flexibility and optimization tractability. Linear evolution of the latent state can stabilize short-term forecasts but restrict expressiveness in strongly chaotic and high-dimensional systems, without consistently improving assimilation accuracy. Parameterized linear operators offer greater flexibility, yet their joint optimization with the encoder--decoder remains nonconvex. Methods with closed-form analysis updates generally perform better and exhibit greater robustness in our experiments, although matrix inversion remains a computational bottleneck. These findings show that the practical benefits of Koopman structure depend on both sufficient observational information and the choice of assimilation procedure.
authors: Zhiwei Zhang, Wenxuan Yuan, Xiaoyuan Cheng, Pouria Behnoudfar, Chuanqi Chen, Charlotte Moser, Yuta Tarumi, Jin-Long Wu, Rossella Arcucci, Takemasa Miyoshi, Nan Chen, Marc Bocquet, Sibo Cheng
bullets: Compares seven representative methods and structural baselines across five systems, from near-periodic to strongly chaotic dynamics.

Parameterized linear operators are more flexible but require nonconvex joint optimization with the encoder–decoder.
Closed-form analysis updates are generally more robust, while matrix inversion remains a computational bottleneck.

papers.abstract: Neural controlled differential equations (Neural CDEs) evolve hidden states along continuous paths constructed by interpolating discrete observations. Sparse measurements leave the input between observation times undetermined, and admissible continuous paths consistent with the same data can produce different terminal states. We characterize this ambiguity for planar drivers with bounded speed. The set of compatible terminal states admits a leading-order zonotopic approximation determined by feasible signed areas and transported Lie brackets. Its projection onto a scalar prediction yields a computable, target-specific ambiguity certificate. We also study the number of measurements needed to reduce the remaining uncertainty. For nondegenerate planar CDEs, the optimal worst-case radius over deterministic adaptive sampling policies scales as $N^{-1}$ when speed is bounded and $N^{-2}$ when both speed and acceleration are bounded, where $N$ is the number of observation intervals. Synthetic experiments assess the certificate using admissible continuous completions and examine the role of path regularity.
authors: Rostislav Gusev, Evgenia Romanenkova, Alexey Zaytsev
bullets: Characterizes how different continuous paths consistent with the same sparse observations can yield different terminal states in planar Neural CDEs.
Approximates compatible terminal states with a zonotope based on feasible signed areas and transported Lie brackets.
Provides a computable, target-specific ambiguity certificate by projecting terminal-state uncertainty onto a scalar prediction.
Shows optimal worst-case uncertainty scales as N⁻¹ with bounded speed and N⁻² when acceleration is also bounded.
Synthetic experiments evaluate the certificate under admissible path completions and varying path regularity.

papers.abstract: Automatic rigging is a fundamental task for both static 3D and dynamic 4D mesh animation, yet existing methods do not provide a unified feedforward solution for these two settings. While static 3D riggers achieve strong quality, they often provide limited control over bone count and become temporally unstable when applied frame by frame to dynamic meshes. Existing 4D methods, in contrast, typically rely on expensive per-sequence optimization. We propose MoTWorld, a template-free, data-efficient framework for unified 3D and 4D skeleton generation. Built on flow matching, MoTWorld generates temporally aligned skeletons for an entire sequence in a single feedforward pass, while naturally handling single-mesh 3D rigging. The model further supports explicit skeleton-count control, uncertainty estimation for candidate selection, and masking-based interpolation, forecasting, and backcasting. To address limited paired 4D rigging data, we adopt a curriculum that initializes from large-scale 3D rigging data and adapts to mid-scale 4D mesh-skeleton data. Experiments show that MoTWorld achieves strong static 3D rigging performance with controllable bone complexity, as well as high-quality and temporally consistent 4D reconstruction and prediction results.

papers.abstract: Learned temporal models are moving beyond offline forecasting toward interactive environments for decision making, yet logged-trajectory accuracy need not predict closed-loop behavior under policies optimized in the learned model. This forecasting-control gap matters in tokamak magnetic control, where coupled plasma-circuit dynamics and actuator constraints can amplify errors through feedback. Using a calibrated free-boundary Grad-Shafranov solver, we collect four datasets in a 2x2 design over physics-parameter and current-reference coverage. At matched budgets of 500, 1k, 3k, and 5k rollouts, we train 16 action-conditioned Transformers; PPO policies optimized in the 5k surrogates are then evaluated without adaptation on six reference-solver conditions. Only joint-coverage D4 shows monotonically decreasing cross-condition mean error, whereas D1 improves in distribution but degrades out of distribution. Binary completion masks substantial closed-loop differences: D2-D4 each complete 83.3% of conditions, but reach on average 99.0%, 94.7%, and 90.5% of the evaluation horizon, while their worst conditions reach 94.2%, 68.2%, and 43.2%. Policies trained with action noise complete 5/24 matched conditions, compared with 19/24 under nominal training, and have a lower mean horizon-capped episode length. Based on one trained policy per configuration and one evaluation realization per condition, the results support combining prediction error, episode completion, condition-level duration, and tracking quality.
authors: Guoyang Shi, Siqi Ding, Xuanhe Wang, Pei Guo, Changquan Yu, Jiale Hu, Jiayi Zhi, Zhengyuan Chen, Jianguo Chen, Tianyuan Liu
bullets: Forecasting accuracy on logged trajectories does not necessarily predict feedback-control performance.
Researchers train action-conditioned Transformers on four physics/reference coverage datasets using matched rollout budgets.
Policies optimized in learned models are evaluated without adaptation in a calibrated free-boundary Grad–Shafranov solver.
Only the jointly covered dataset improves monotonically across cross-condition mean error; other datasets can degrade out of distribution.
Binary completion rates hide differences in episode duration and tracking quality, motivating multiple closed-loop metrics.

papers.abstract: Evaluating end-to-end autonomous driving under rare, safety-critical vehicle-pedestrian interactions requires photorealistic, sensor-level scenarios. However, trajectory-based scenario generators cannot synthesize raw visual observations, whereas video-based approaches lack controllability. To bridge this gap, we present ControlPed, a novel framework that combines trajectory-level conflict synthesis with 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) to generate photorealistic, motion-controllable safety-critical scenarios. Built upon HazardPed, a dataset derived from 10,352 traffic videos comprising 422 conflict trajectories, HD maps, and 857 annotated 3D human motions, ControlPed first generates conflict trajectories, lifts them into 3D human motion sequences via text-conditioned motion diffusion, and finally renders multi-view sensor observations using animatable 3DGS avatars. Safety evaluation in 88 rendered photorealistic scenarios reveals that seven leading end-to-end driving models suffer a severe performance drop, with their mean HDScore plunging from 88.8 to 47.4, exposing major failure modes under dangerous pedestrian behaviors. The dataset and testing benchmarks will be released to facilitate safety assessment of vehicle-pedestrian interactions.
bullets: Addresses the gap between controllable trajectory generators and video-based methods that cannot synthesize raw sensor observations.

The dataset and evaluation benchmarks are planned for release to support vehicle–pedestrian safety assessment.

papers.abstract: We present Isekai3D Synthetic Data Generation (SDG), a platform for simulating and capturing synthetic 3D gameplay for research in vision and world models, neural graphics, gameplay agents, and other applications. The platform combines reusable environment and character assets with Unreal Engine plugins in a two-stage workflow. First, world simulation generates gameplay while recording the world state, character movements, actions, and camera tracks needed for replay. Second, the recorded simulation is replayed to capture selected outputs, such as rendered video, images, and depth maps, at a specified resolution and frame rate under selected rendering and camera configurations. Separating simulation from capture allows the same recorded gameplay to produce multiple output variants without repeating the original simulation. Visual outputs are accompanied by frame-aligned camera, character, and action metadata. The platform uploads generated data directly in a training-friendly format, reducing intermediate storage, preparation time, and manual processing. This report describes the design of our overall system, including the platform's assets, plugins, and their functionality, explaining how they work together to generate diverse synthetic gameplay data.

papers.abstract: Neural operators provide efficient surrogates for computational fluid dynamics (CFD), but most are designed for static geometries and are not equipped to model unsteady flows induced by continuously moving boundaries. We study dynamic-boundary 4D CFD prediction for articulated moving geometries and introduce RoboCFD-4D, a temporally resolved robotic CFD benchmark spanning diverse morphologies and flow conditions. To address the computational and autoregressive challenges of this setting, we propose DynaSolver, a neural operator that explicitly conditions on boundary evolution and causal flow history. DynaSolver employs an efficient physical-token formulation that amortizes point-to-token projection across the operator stack, substantially reducing repeated point-space spatio-temporal computation while retaining accurate point-level reconstruction. We further introduce Replay-Augmented Parallel Training, which exposes the model to autoregressively generated histories while preserving parallel dense supervision, narrowing the gap between ground-truth-conditioned training and autoregressive rollout. Experiments on RoboCFD-4D show that DynaSolver achieves the best full-rollout accuracy among a broad range of learned CFD surrogates, with its advantage increasing as rollout proceeds, indicating substantially reduced autoregressive error accumulation. Project page: https://made-gpt.github.io/DynaSolver-ProjectPage.
bullets: Addresses CFD surrogate modeling for articulated geometries with unsteady, continuously changing boundaries.
Introduces RoboCFD-4D, a temporally resolved benchmark covering varied morphologies and flow conditions.
Uses physical tokens to reduce repeated point-space spatio-temporal computation while retaining point-level reconstruction.
Replay-Augmented Parallel Training exposes the model to its own autoregressive histories during training.
Experiments report the best full-rollout accuracy among evaluated learned CFD surrogates, with growing benefits over longer rollouts.

figures.caption: Figure 7 | Overview of the RoboCFD-4D data generation pipeline. Public robot assets are standardized and repaired at the link level, followed by prescribed motion synthesis and reusable link-local SDF construction. The transformed link-local fields define the prescribed moving immersed boundary for multi-condition CFD simulations. Aligned volumetric fields and tracked near-surface observations are then extracted and subjected to geometric, numerical, and dataset-level validation before inclusion in the final published dataset.

Figure 2 | Overview of DynaSolver. Given the spatial condition, boundary evolution, and previous CFD states over a causal window, DynaSolver lifts and fuses the point-wise inputs before mapping them into separate surface and volume physical tokens. A single Fast Slice/Deslice pair encloses the spatio-temporal operator stack, where self-attention, cross-attention, and causal attention jointly model spatial and temporal flow interactions. The reconstructed point features are decoded into a residual flow field and added to the previous CFD state to predict the current velocity and pressure.

Figure 3 | Comparison of training strategies for autoregressive flow prediction. Dense Unrolled Training (a) and Dense Pushforward Training (b) construct autoregressive histories sequentially, whereas Parallel Teacher-Forcing Training (c) predicts all transitions in a clip simultaneously from ground-truth histories. Our Replay-Augmented Parallel Training (d) decouples autoregressive history generation from student optimization: a frozen model first rolls out replay inputs (d.1), which are then used for parallel dense supervision of the current model (d.2). Red solid arrows→ denote feedforward computation, while green dashed arrows d denote backpropagation.

In contrast, RoboCFD-4D requires joint modeling of articulated three-dimensional boundary motion and the resulting time-evolving flow field across diverse robot morphologies.

papers.abstract: World action models (WAMs) jointly generate actions and imagined futures, but a plausible prediction need not be realized by its co-generated action. We introduce WISE (\emph{World Action Inference Scaling through Evaluation}), a pre-execution selector that scores each sampled rollout on action validity and temporal regularity, inverse-dynamics consistency between the proposed action and the imagined motion, and instruction-conditioned task progress, and executes the highest-scoring candidate while keeping the WAM frozen. With four candidates per decision, WISE raises closed-loop success from 6.0\% to 24.0\% on RoboLab with Cosmos~3 Edge and from 75.1\% to 78.3\% mean success on LIBERO with DreamZero, and exceeds the best existing selector in aggregate by 4.0 and 0.9 points. Component ablations and agreement analyses show that the three scores rank candidates differently and that task progress carries the largest weight in the fused decision.
bullets: Addresses the gap between plausible imagined futures and actions that actually succeed.
Scores sampled rollouts using action validity and temporal regularity, inverse-dynamics consistency, and instruction-conditioned task progress.
Executes the highest-scoring candidate without updating the underlying world action model.
With four candidates, success increases from 6.0% to 24.0% on RoboLab and from 75.1% to 78.3% on LIBERO.
Task progress contributes the largest weight, while the three scoring components rank candidates differently.

Figure 2: WISE at each control decision. A frozen WAM samples B paired action–future candidates (B = 4 in our evaluations). Each candidate receives three scores in [0, 1]. The IDM maps imagined frames back to actions for comparison with the candidate’s proposed controls; the task evaluator scores progress at the final imagined frame. WISE sums the scores, executes the selected action chunk, and observes the resulting state before replanning.

papers.abstract: A robot that acts around people needs a world model of the human: a belief over the person's body state and a dynamics model that predicts where that state goes next. This abstract argues that two published components form exactly these two halves, and specifies how to couple them. KNOWN [1] reconstructs the 3D human body while estimating both aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty in real time (11.6 ms per frame); its aleatoric term identifies unreliable observations, its epistemic term identifies inputs from low-density regions of the training data, and refinement driven by the epistemic term reduces the error on such inputs from 81.3 to 70.3 mm. PhysMoP [2] predicts future body configuration by solving the Euler-Lagrange equations of the body with learned dynamics terms, reducing the 80 ms prediction error from 9.6 to 2.1 mm on Human3.6M and from 12.1 to 0.7 mm on 3DPW. We define the interface between the two, propose three mechanisms by which KNOWN's uncertainty enters PhysMoP, and specify an evaluation protocol on in-the-wild video. No new experimental results are reported here.
bullets: KNOWN estimates 3D body state plus aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty in real time.
PhysMoP predicts future body configurations using Euler–Lagrange physics with learned dynamics.
The work defines an interface and three mechanisms for incorporating KNOWN’s uncertainty into PhysMoP.
It proposes evaluating the coupled system on in-the-wild video; no new experiments are reported.
Prior results cited in the abstract show improved performance for both reconstruction and prediction, but are not results of this work.

figures.caption: Figure 1: The two halves of the human world model. (a) KNOWN [1]: a regression network outputs a distribution over SMPL pose θ, shape β and camera C; forward kinematics and projection give the observation model p(p2D | X), from which aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty are read off; the uncertainties enter training through the NLL and uncertainty-guided refinement. (b) PhysMoP [2]: a physics branch predicts the Euler–Lagrange terms M , C, G and integrates them, a data branch predicts the whole future, and a fusion network combines the two. The arrow is the coupling proposed in Sec. 4: KNOWN’s per-frame belief becomes the history q1:T that PhysMoP integrates forward.

Figure 3: Qualitative results of PhysMoP on two Human3.6M test sequences [2]: ground truth in grey, prediction in blue, from the last history frame to 1 s ahead. Larger overlap means smaller prediction error.

Figure 2: Qualitative results of KNOWN on two Human3.6M images [1]. Left to right: input; per-joint aleatoric uncertainty (radius of the red circles); per-joint epistemic uncertainty (yellow); reconstruction colored by per-vertex epistemic uncertainty, before (left) and after (right) uncertainty-guided refinement. Dashed circles mark the occluded or ambiguous parts the uncertainties single out.

papers.abstract: In the prediction and control of physical systems, combining records from different experiments and operations is expected to supply information that no single experiment provides on its own. Time-series foundation models, which learn a shared predictor from diverse time series, offer a framework for treating such records as a common training resource. Moreover, query-based prediction models, which switch between known and target signals within the same time series, make it possible to handle response prediction and control-input generation in a unified manner. However, in control-experiment data, the connections between signals change with the experimental stage, such as system identification, filtering, and feedback control, which calls for a formulation that handles signal values and connection structures dynamically and in a unified way. We formulate a control foundation model that defines a data space of dynamic graphs containing connections, signal values, and missing values, together with an operation on this space that specifies the known signals and the prediction targets. This allows response prediction and control-input generation to be described as a common masked prediction problem, even for experimental data with different connections and recorded signals. The Block Diagram Transformer (BDT), which implements this formulation, combines attention along the time axis with a graph neural network that follows the block-diagram connections, and can be initialized with the pretrained parameters of existing time-series foundation models. Trained on control-experiment data that mix multiple experimental settings, the proposed model stabilized an unstable system through feedback control, which is difficult to achieve by fine-tuning existing time-series foundation models. Ongoing work applying this approach to a wide range of target systems is also yielding promising results.
bullets: Addresses control data whose signal connections change across stages such as identification, filtering, and feedback.
Formulates response prediction and control-input generation as one masked prediction problem over dynamic graphs with missing values.
Introduces the Block Diagram Transformer (BDT), combining temporal attention with a graph neural network guided by block-diagram connections.
BDT can be initialized from pretrained time-series foundation models and trained on mixed control-experiment settings.
The model stabilized an unstable system through feedback control, an outcome reported as difficult for fine-tuned existing time-series foundation models.

papers.title: Control Foundation Models across Changing Block Diagrams: Generalizing Time-Series Prediction to Dynamic Graphs
papers.tldr: A control foundation model represents changing block-diagram connections and signal values as dynamic graphs, enabling unified prediction and control across experiments.

papers.abstract: Accurate long-horizon probabilistic predictions of dynamical systems are a prerequisite for model-based decision-making. Variational Bayesian last layers (VBLLs) are an attractive model class for this setting, offering tractable uncertainty at near-deterministic cost, yet they are trained exclusively with single-step likelihood objectives that may be insufficient for reliable multi-step rollouts. We revisit VBLLs through the lens of Gibbs variational inference, which decouples posterior inference from the choice of training loss. Building on this perspective, we introduce a family of multi-step training losses that progressively incorporate long-horizon structure, robustness via continuous ranked probability scores (CRPS), and training on full autoregressive rollouts. Our approach retains the simplicity of VBLLs while directly optimizing for multi-step predictive quality. Across illustrative synthetic environments, a diverse suite of chaotic dynamical systems, and real-world data, we show that multi-step, CRPS-based objectives substantially improve long-horizon accuracy and distributional fit, consistently outperforming single-step likelihood training.
bullets: Targets unreliable multi-step rollouts from variational Bayesian last layers (VBLLs).
Uses Gibbs variational inference to decouple posterior inference from the training loss.
Introduces losses that progressively capture long-horizon structure, CRPS robustness, and full autoregressive rollouts.
Evaluations span synthetic environments, chaotic systems, and real-world data.
Multi-step CRPS objectives improve long-horizon accuracy and distributional fit over single-step likelihood training.

papers.abstract: End-to-end autonomous driving policies require effective visual representations that capture both spatial scene structure and temporal dynamics. Video latent prediction has emerged as an effective paradigm for learning spatiotemporal visual representations, yet it remains unclear whether scaling this objective with action-free driving videos can yield representations that benefit end-to-end planning. We study action-free video latent prediction as a scalable pretraining objective and introduce ScaleDrive, a driving-oriented framework pretrained exclusively on large-scale internet open-world driving videos, without action annotations or benchmark-specific data. We keep the pretrained video encoder frozen during downstream end-to-end planning training to isolate the transferability of representations learned from internet driving videos. Ego-motion and depth probes show that scaling action-free video pretraining progressively strengthens the temporal and geometric information encoded in the frozen representation. We systematically study the visual representation transfer across different end-to-end driving policies and closed-loop benchmarks, where ScaleDrive consistently improves downstream performance and demonstrates that scaling action-free video latent prediction yields representations that generalize across both planning policy architectures and evaluation scenarios and protocols.
bullets: Addresses whether action-free video pretraining can learn representations useful for downstream driving.
Pretrains a video encoder exclusively on large-scale internet open-world driving videos, without action labels or benchmark-specific data.
Freezes the encoder during downstream planning training to isolate representation transferability.
Probes indicate that scaling strengthens encoded temporal and geometric information, including ego-motion and depth cues.
Improves performance consistently across driving policy architectures, closed-loop benchmarks, and evaluation protocols.

papers.abstract: Few-step autoregressive video diffusion enables efficient generation, yet maintaining consistency over long rollouts remains challenging, especially when subjects or scenes reappear after going out of sight. Despite progress in fidelity and rollout robustness, existing distillation methods do not fully exploit richer historical information to constrain the student's current prediction. To address this gap, we introduce \textbf{History Forcing}, a unified on-policy distillation framework that strengthens historical supervision for few-step autoregressive video generators. The framework uses the residual between teacher predictions with and without informative historical context to decouple this supervision. Such a historical context can be obtained using earlier generated chunks with less accumulated drift or a fixed-view teacher rollout that keeps the scene visible while the student looks away. The residual is then weighted and added to the score or velocity prediction used for distillation, forming a corrected target. By aligning the student with this corrected target through distillation, History Forcing incorporates long-range historical constraints into autoregressive generation. Our method achieves state-of-the-art performance among 1.3B models, with a VBench quality score of 85.07 for 15s video generation and a VBench-Long aggregate score of 79.82 for 60s generation. For out-of-sight world modeling, evaluations further demonstrate more plausible scene evolution and more consistent states when the camera returns, with Evolution Quality improving from 2.35 to 2.70 on PlayWorld and Object Consistency from 58.43 to 62.18 on MemoBench.
bullets: Addresses scene and subject inconsistency when content reappears after going out of view.
Uses teacher-prediction residuals between context-rich and context-poor rollouts as corrected distillation targets.
Historical context comes from earlier, less-drifted chunks or fixed-view teacher rollouts that preserve scene visibility.
Reports strong results for 15–60-second generation and improved out-of-sight scene evolution and object consistency. The abstract does not state limitations.

papers.abstract: We reimplement the dynamics model of the Robotic World Model (RWM) and test the uncertainty estimate that its follow-up, RWM-U, uses to penalize reward in offline policy optimization. Our implementation matches the released model's gradients. On held-out data, training on the model's own rollouts beats one-step training at the preregistered long horizon for all ten episodes, but loses on short one-step windows. RWM-U's ensemble disagreement ranks rollout errors better than forecast step (Spearman rho = 0.90 at 100 steps), yet its spread substantially understates error: one-sigma coverage on the released checkpoint is 4.6% at 100 steps, versus 68% for a calibrated Gaussian. Rolling ensemble members on their own predictions raises coverage to 33%. The implemented squared-error loss on sampled predictions drives each member's variance toward zero. A horizon-specific rescaling restores one-sigma coverage under leave-one-episode-out evaluation, but not two-sigma coverage. We also identify two defects in the released evaluation pipeline. The study covers one robot, one gait and one dataset; it trains no policy.
bullets: The reimplementation matches the released model’s gradients.
Training on model-generated rollouts outperforms one-step training at the preregistered long horizon, but not on short windows, across all ten episodes.
RWM-U ensemble disagreement strongly ranks rollout errors (Spearman ρ = 0.90 at 100 steps) while substantially understating their magnitude.

Released-checkpoint one-sigma coverage is 4.6% at 100 steps; rolling members on their own predictions raises it to 33%, and rescaling restores one-sigma coverage under leave-one-episode-out evaluation.
The study finds a variance-collapse issue in the squared-error loss and two defects in the released evaluation pipeline; it trains no policy and covers one robot, gait, and dataset.

papers.selection_reason: Reproduces and evaluates the uncertainty estimation of a robotic world model's dynamics, directly relevant to world-model reliability.
papers.title: Right Ranking, Wrong Scale: Reproducing the Robotic World Model's Dynamics Model and Testing the Uncertainty of Its Follow-up

papers.abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) have recently shown great promise in robotic control, benefiting from the future imagination capability of large-scale pretrained video models. However, most existing WAMs require explicitly imagining future states at test time, incurring substantial computational overhead and latency that make them unsuitable for real-time robotic control. In this paper, we propose W2A, a two-stage distillation framework for real-time robotic manipulation that distills intermediate denoising representations from a video diffusion model into an action model during training, while entirely discarding the video model at test time. We hypothesize that although video latent representations are high-dimensional, a compressed low-dimensional subspace is sufficient to provide effective supervision for action generation. This makes it possible to transfer such information effectively into an action model. Extensive experiments in both simulation and real-world settings demonstrate competitive success rates while significantly improving inference efficiency. On LIBERO, W2A achieves a 95.9% average success rate. More importantly, W2A achieves about 21x faster inference than the representative WAM baseline.
bullets: Existing world action models often imagine future states at test time, creating prohibitive computational overhead for real-time control.
W2A uses two-stage training to transfer intermediate denoising representations from a pretrained video diffusion model into an action model.
The approach assumes effective supervision can be compressed into a low-dimensional subspace of the video latent space.
The video model is discarded at deployment, reducing inference cost while retaining useful world priors.
W2A reports a 95.9% average success rate on LIBERO and approximately 21× faster inference than a representative WAM baseline.

papers.abstract: Safe autonomous driving requires more than recognizing the current scene: the ego vehicle must anticipate how surrounding traffic participants will evolve under its own motion. However, existing end-to-end driving models typically encode scenes into dense visual or BEV features, leaving object-level interactions implicit. We propose (INTERACT INTERaction-aware Action-Conditioned Trajectory learning), a three-stage framework that learns a slot-based object-centric world model from unlabeled driving videos and transfers it to trajectory planning. INTERACT first learns recurrent slots that group dense visual features into temporally structured scene-entity representations without object annotations. It then infers latent ego actions from slot context and video transitions, and uses them to condition future slot prediction, capturing how ego motion and surrounding entities co-evolve. Finally, the learned slots, latent actions, and future slot predictions are distilled into a trajectory planner to guide trajectory generation and selection. Extensive experiments on NAVSIM and nuScenes validate the effectiveness of INTERACT. In particular, it achieves state-of-the-art performance on NAVSIM, with improvements in safety-critical collision metrics.
bullets: Addresses the challenge of predicting how surrounding traffic evolves in response to the ego vehicle’s motion.
Uses recurrent slots to discover temporally structured scene entities without object annotations.
Infers latent ego actions and conditions future slot prediction on those actions to model interaction dynamics.
Distills learned slots, actions, and future predictions into a trajectory planner.
Validated on NAVSIM and nuScenes, achieving state-of-the-art NAVSIM performance with improved collision-related metrics.

papers.abstract: World-action models (WAMs) predict scene changes to guide robot actions, yet their RGB futures entangle state changes with appearance and lack 3D geometry. Recent WAMs add geometry as a training signal or a control interface, or build native 3D models, but decide what geometry to model rather than how the action should read it. Intuitively, control-relevant cues lie at embodiment--object interactions and their transitions, yet probing existing WAMs reveals that their action attention underweights these interactions in favor of the rest of the embodiment. To focus the action on these interactions, we present Gnomon4D, a WAM that jointly generates future video, robot actions, and GeoDelta, a video-aligned 4D geometric motion field recording the image-plane displacement and depth change of embodiment and object points. With the embodiment and objects in one field, their relative motion, which marks an interaction, can be read off. Guided by this motion and the task, Interaction-Salient Attention (InSAttn) selects where the action reads, and Transition-Anchored Aggregation (TransAgg) selects when, around grasp and release. As GeoDelta encodes surface motion rather than embodiment-specific controls, it serves as a human--robot quasi-action that links action-free pretraining on EgoManip-5000H, which we curate, to robot mid-training on Robot-30H. Gnomon4D leads on RoboTwin~2.0, VLABench, and RoboDojo, and outperforms real-robot baselines, especially under visual shifts. Project page: https://droliven.github.io/Gnomon4D.
bullets: Addresses the problem that RGB-based world-action models entangle appearance and state changes, while action attention often overlooks control-relevant interactions.
Jointly predicts future video, robot actions, and GeoDelta, a video-aligned 4D field of image-plane displacement and depth changes for embodiment and object points.
Uses Interaction-Salient Attention to select where to attend and Transition-Anchored Aggregation to focus around grasp and release transitions.
GeoDelta enables action-free pretraining on EgoManip-5000H and robot mid-training on Robot-30H by acting as a human–robot quasi-action.
Leads on RoboTwin 2.0, VLABench, and RoboDojo, and outperforms real-robot baselines, particularly under visual shifts.

papers.abstract: Cooperative perception (CP) requires substantial communication bandwidth to exchange sensing information among connected agents. A variety of compression techniques have been proposed to reduce transmission costs while retaining task-relevant information. However, most existing methods follow a frame-wise compression paradigm, overlooking temporal predictability and repeatedly transmitting information that could be inferred from historical context. To address these limitations, we propose MirrorComm, the first world model-based communication-efficient CP framework. Specifically, mirrored world models at the transmitter and receiver predict the transmitter's current observation from a shared history of its reconstructed observations. The transmitter compares this prediction with its current observation and selectively transmits observation updates to correct prediction errors, reducing repeated transmission of predictable information. Experiments on the OPV2V dataset across two downstream tasks including object detection and semantic segmentation show that MirrorComm reduces communication bandwidth requirements by up to approximately 66-fold while maintaining comparable performance to a state-of-the-art (SOTA) method. Ablation studies further demonstrate the effectiveness of the individual components.
bullets: Targets the bandwidth burden of exchanging sensing information among connected agents.
Predicts current observations from shared histories at both transmitter and receiver, exploiting temporal predictability.
Sends only updates that correct prediction errors instead of repeatedly transmitting predictable content.
On OPV2V object detection and semantic segmentation, reduces bandwidth by up to approximately 66-fold with comparable performance to a SOTA method.
Ablation studies support the effectiveness of its individual components.

papers.abstract: Recent interactive video world models generate visually compelling videos from a single image, following user-provided camera motion and text prompts. However, such low-level control demands substantial user effort to realize a high-level intent, and the generated world struggles to remain persistent as the exploration proceeds. In this work, we present AgiWorld, an agentic video world model that explores and builds a persistent world from a single image and a free-form instruction. For high-level planning, our agent AgiWorld-Agent designs the world and the journey through it in a world state and directs the exploration. For low-level realization, our video world model AgiWorld-WM generates the video chunk by chunk and stores it with its geometry in a spatial memory, from which the agent updates its world state. This closed loop keeps the world faithful to the user's intent and keeps the agent's world state consistent with the generated content throughout the exploration. We co-design the two levels around the shared spatial memory and an interface of metric camera trajectories and structured prompts. In AgiWorld-WM, to handle occlusion and accumulated geometric errors in the spatial memory over long rollouts, we propose occlusion-aware history selection, which retrieves past views by surface visibility, and reliability-based memory maintenance, which prefers reliable geometry and earlier observations. AgiWorld-WM achieves state-of-the-art overall performance on world revisiting and exploration benchmarks, and qualitative results and ablations show that AgiWorld builds persistent worlds from free-form instructions over minute-long journeys. Persistence thus arises not from the video model alone but from its closed loop with the agent.
bullets: Addresses the user effort required by low-level camera control and the loss of world consistency during extended exploration.
AgiWorld-Agent plans the world and journey from a free-form instruction, while AgiWorld-WM realizes exploration as video chunks.
A shared spatial memory stores generated views and geometry, enabling the agent to update its world state and maintain consistency.
Occlusion-aware history selection and reliability-based memory maintenance mitigate visibility and accumulated geometric errors.
Reports state-of-the-art overall performance on revisiting and exploration benchmarks, with qualitative results and ablations supporting persistence over minute-long journeys.

papers.abstract: Repeated satellite imagery permits understanding of how our planet changes over time, letting us predict its future and plan mitigating actions. Most existing studies that rely on a time series of satellite observations forecast the spectral values at each pixel for a future target date. However, clouds, shadows, and sensor noise often corrupt these observations, so that spectral forecasters waste much of their capacity on low-level features or noise rather than real change. With the advent of Earth foundation models, we argue that forecasting in embedding space is a feasible and more effective alternative. To this end, we design a token space that handles irregular histories from different sensors and foundation models and supports forecasts at any query date. Tokens from this space are inputs to our proposed forecaster, E$^2$Forecast, which is a transformer with two branches: a Gaussian branch that directly predicts a mean point forecast and per-dimension standard deviations, and a rectified-flow branch that generates forecast ensembles. On Sentinel-1 and Sentinel-2 benchmarks, forecasting embeddings instead of spectral values halves the cosine distance (from 0.20 to 0.10) and greatly reduces overconfidence, lowering the z-score standard deviation from 2.63 to 1.22. By comparing new observations with its forecasts, E$^2$Forecast can also detect anomalous changes without labels or retraining, raising F$_1$ from 41.58 to 48.70 on a global benchmark. This consistent superiority is validated on nine remote sensing foundation models. Beyond change detection, we believe our approach advances the field by permitting effective reuse of diverse pretrained task heads. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/ucam-eo/e2forecast.
bullets: Pixel-level spectral forecasting is easily disrupted by clouds, shadows, sensor noise, and irregular observations from different sensors.
The method uses a token space for irregular histories and arbitrary query dates, with a two-branch transformer: Gaussian forecasts and rectified-flow ensembles.
On Sentinel-1 and Sentinel-2 benchmarks, embedding forecasts reduce cosine distance from 0.20 to 0.10 and improve uncertainty calibration.
Forecast-versus-observation comparisons enable anomaly detection without labels or retraining, increasing F₁ from 41.58 to 48.70 on a global benchmark.
The approach supports reuse of diverse pretrained remote-sensing task heads; scope is demonstrated across nine foundation models.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of E2Forecast. (a) Each image in an irregular time series is converted into an Earth embedding ei by an Earth foundation model si, which may differ across observations. (b) The historical embeddings with their dates, the location and the query date τ∗ form a token sequence for a masked transformer fθ . In one pass, the probability-estimation branch predicts the per-dimension Gaussian (µ,σ) of the future embedding, and the embedding-generation branch denoises a noisy target zt = t z1 + (1 − t) ϵ by flow matching. (c) For forecasting, the probability branch gives a point forecast ê∗ pt = µ/∥µ∥2 with uncertainty σ without sampling, and the generation branch turns J noise draws into ensemble forecasts with S Euler steps. (d) For anomaly change detection, a new observed embedding is compared with both the Gaussian forecast and the closest ensemble forecast in units of σ, giving an anomaly change map without change labels or a detection head.

papers.abstract: Retrieving objects from densely packed storage requires anticipating how contact disturbs surrounding objects when limited clearance prevents lifting the target over clutter. However, contact can propagate beyond the target's immediate neighbors, while accumulated prediction errors make learned dynamics unreliable over long planning horizons. We introduce DARE (Disturbance-Aware REtrieval), a geometry-aware relational dynamics framework that uses retrospective correction to improve long-horizon prediction for disturbance-aware retrieval. DARE encodes compact object descriptors and predicts action-conditioned disturbance propagation through object-level message passing. When a sparse observation becomes available, a learned corrector uses the prediction discrepancy to amend an earlier predicted state and reruns the intervening dynamics, propagating the correction through the predicted contact chain. These predictions guide a receding-horizon planner that balances retrieval progress against displacement and rotation of surrounding objects, permitting necessary contact while discouraging harmful disturbance. Experiments in planar and RoboCasa environments evaluate long-horizon prediction, generalization, and robustness for disturbance-aware retrieval in dense clutter. See our project website: https://the-back-to-the-future.github.io
bullets: Targets retrieval when limited clearance requires contacting surrounding objects.
Uses geometry-aware object descriptors and relational message passing to predict action-conditioned disturbance propagation.
Applies a learned corrector to sparse observations, amending earlier states and rerunning dynamics through predicted contact chains.
Guides receding-horizon planning that balances retrieval progress with surrounding-object displacement and rotation.
Evaluated in planar and RoboCasa environments for prediction, generalization, and robustness in dense clutter.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: Pipeline Overview: Given object geometry and the current scene state, DARE propagates action-conditioned interactions over an object graph to predict scene evolution under candidate target motions. The resulting rollouts capture direct and indirect disturbances to surrounding objects, enabling the planner to select a retrieval trajectory that balances goal progress against collateral disturbance.

Fig. 1: Disturbance-aware retrieval. (a) Collision avoidance leaves the target blocked. (b) Direct retrieval topples a neighboring object. (c) Our method predicts contact-induced disturbance to plan retrieval through controlled contact, preserving stability of surrounding objects.
Fig. 6: Dynamics prediction. Terminal translation (left) and rotation (right) errors normalized by the no-motion error at each horizon. Rotation is omitted for symmetric pucks.

Fig. 8: Retrospective correction under noise. Translation (top) and rotation (bottom) RMSE over 40-step rollouts versus observation noise σ, fixed within each rollout. Shading indicates noise levels beyond the noise training range.

Fig. 4: Tabletop dynamics prediction under noise. Outlines in purple, light blue and dark blue, indicate predicted object poses in a held-out scene as the target (yellow) pushes through clutter. Uncorrected predictions drift (top), direct observation updates inherit noise (middle), and noise-trained correction maintains alignment with the objects (bottom).
Fig. 7: Effect of joint training. Terminal translation (top) and rotation (bottom) errors with shared pretrained initialization and matched additional optimization steps.

Fig. 3: Retrospective correction for long-horizon prediction. The corrector combines prior predictions with the observation mismatch at t15 (yellow) to estimate a corrected state t̃11, the first step after the last observation t10. Rerolling from it propagates the correction through the learned dynamics and initializes the next cycle, mitigating error drift.

papers.title: Back to the Future: Predicting Long-Horizon Dynamics with Retrospective Correction for Disturbance-Aware Retrieval
papers.tldr: DARE improves long-horizon disturbance prediction for retrieving objects from dense clutter by retrospectively correcting predicted contact dynamics and guiding disturbance-aware planning.

papers.abstract: Robust 4D reconstruction of deformable endoscopic scenes from monocular videos remains challenging due to non-rigid tissue deformation, illumination changes, occlusions, and unknown camera trajectories. Reliable dynamic reconstruction of endoscopies could significantly enhance visualization, diagnostic accuracy and intraoperative guidance of minimally invasive procedures. We propose SurgicalTS, a self-supervised triangle-splatting framework for dynamic endoscopic scene reconstruction from static monocular cameras. The scene is represented by a canonical set of triangles jointly optimized with a deformation network. We introduce a quaternion-based deformation model, an improved color parametrization, spatio-temporal priors, and a redefined initialization strategy that improves completeness under occlusions. Extensive evaluation on challenging in-vivo endoscopy videos from diverse procedures shows that SurgicalTS successfully models soft-tissue deformations and tool-tissue interactions over time, while consistently outperforming state-of-the-art methods. Our method also reduces training times while maintaining competitive geometric and photometric accuracy results, highlighting the effectiveness of quaternion-based deformation modelling with physical consistency for robust and efficient 4D reconstruction of endoscopic scenes.
bullets: Targets non-rigid tissue motion, illumination changes, occlusions, and unknown camera trajectories in endoscopic videos.
Represents scenes with canonical triangles jointly optimized with a deformation network.
Introduces quaternion-based deformation, improved color modeling, spatio-temporal priors, and occlusion-aware initialization.
Evaluated on diverse in-vivo procedures, where it models tissue deformation and tool-tissue interactions over time.
Reports consistent outperformance of prior methods, reduced training time, and competitive geometric and photometric accuracy.

papers.abstract: The transition of information-centric artificial intelligence to safety-critical applications is impeded by the limitations of conventional offline-training paradigms in open-world environments. This paper presents Control AI, an architecture for Online Active Learning (OAL) inspired by the continuous Prediction-Evaluation-Correction process of biological intelligence. The framework combines the hierarchical representation capacity of deep neural networks with the real-time error-feedback adaptation of adaptive control. A prediction model maps sensory input into a latent manifold, an optional latent model represents transitions in that space, and a reconstruction model maps the latent state back to observable signals. Residuals between predictions and measurements provide the internal learning signal. Spatial and temporal cross-reconstruction architectures prevent OAL from collapsing to a trivial identity mapping, while coupled, dual, and localized variants shorten error-transmission paths. Localized predictive coding style OAL is implemented through guidance-backpropagation and target-backpropagation architectures, and hybrid and scaled variants support high-dimensional deployment. The paper focuses on the architectural rationale and the progression from a conceptual feedback loop to practical large-scale configurations.
bullets: Addresses the limitations of offline training when safety-critical systems encounter changing, unanticipated conditions.
Combines deep hierarchical representations with real-time adaptive-control feedback.
Uses prediction, optional latent transition modeling, reconstruction, and residual errors as the learning signal.
Introduces spatial and temporal cross-reconstruction plus localized, dual, coupled, hybrid, and scaled variants to avoid trivial identity mappings and support larger deployments.
The abstract emphasizes architectural rationale and configuration progression rather than reporting quantitative experimental results.

papers.abstract: Zhuangzi dreamt he was a butterfly and, on waking, could not tell which was the dream. We ask a version of his question of a model of the fly brain: placed inside a world generated by a world model, can a fixed brain tell that the world is a dream? We treat it as a question about what a connectome-constrained model trained on one task makes available beyond that task: do its responses make the defects of a dream linearly decodable? The observer is a published model of the fly visual system trained only for optic-flow estimation; reality is the MPI-Sintel movie on the model's 721-column retina; dreams are continuations of five real frames by three small world models (a persistence random walk, an MDN-RNN and an RSSM) at three temperatures. The judge is a classifier two-sample test on temporal statistics of cell-type responses, with sequence-level cross-validation. In the trained observer's responses all nine dreams are separable from reality (AUC 0.85-0.99, mean over 50 trained models), in those of the same network before training much less so (0.58-0.75 for the learned world models; paired difference 0.20-0.37), equally on sequences the observer never saw, and in an order unrelated to pixel error. Because these AUCs are near ceiling, we add graded probes made of each window's own real frames with only their order broken. Swapping one adjacent pair of the 14 generated frames gives 0.73 on the trained responses against 0.54 before training and 0.56 for pixel statistics; the trained curve reaches 0.75 at 1.1 swapped pairs of seven, the pixel statistics at 4.7, and the untrained network not at all. A detection horizon, the test on the first k generated frames, orders the world models where the full-length AUC saturates.
bullets: The study asks whether a fixed, biologically constrained visual model exposes detectable defects in generated worlds beyond its optic-flow task.
It compares responses to MPI-Sintel reality with continuations produced by three small world models under three temperatures.
A classifier two-sample test on temporal statistics of cell-type responses evaluates dream–reality separability with sequence-level cross-validation.
All nine dreams were separable in trained-model responses (AUC 0.85–0.99), substantially more than in the untrained network; separability was unrelated to pixel error.
Breaking temporal order in generated frames was detectable earlier from trained neural responses than from pixel statistics, and detection horizons differentiated the world models.

papers.title: The (Butter)fly Dream: Linear Separability of World-Model Rollouts in a Connectome-Constrained Visual Model
papers.tldr: A connectome-constrained fly-vision model can linearly distinguish several world-model-generated “dreams” from real visual sequences, especially after task training.

papers.abstract: Navigation world models predict future observations conditioned on navigation actions to support planning, but their generalization across real-world environments remains constrained by the limited coverage of action-labeled data. Action-free navigation videos provide diverse visual experience, yet lack the recorded actions required for action-conditioned training. We introduce OpenNWM, a generalist navigation world model with latent action pretraining. It learns universal latent actions from large-scale action-free videos through visual prediction pretraining, and further aligns them with physical motions via action-conditioned post-training. To support video pretraining, we curate NavAnywhere, a large-scale action-free navigation video dataset comprising 17.5 million visual observations from 15 heterogeneous sources. It captures navigation by ground robots, humans, and drones, with diverse viewpoints and motion patterns across five broad scene types: residential areas, public and commercial spaces, urban settings, parks, and natural landscapes. Experiments demonstrate improved visual prediction on in-domain and out-of-domain benchmarks, together with improved navigation performance. These results show that latent-action pretraining enables diverse, action-free videos to improve dynamics learning and generalization for open-world navigation.
bullets: Addresses limited action-labeled data and poor cross-environment generalization in navigation world models.
Pretrains universal latent actions through visual prediction on action-free navigation videos.
Post-trains the latent actions with action-conditioned data to align them with physical motion.
Introduces NavAnywhere, a dataset of 17.5 million observations from 15 sources spanning varied agents, viewpoints, motions, and environments.
Reports improved visual prediction on in-domain and out-of-domain benchmarks, as well as better navigation performance.

papers.abstract: We present Xiaomi Auto World Model 2.0, a unified streaming causal world model for Physical AI. It models and generates causal physical evolution in the real world, and unifies heterogeneous conditioning inputs for view-consistent generation. The architecture integrates View-Temporal Attention (VTA) to capture cross-view spatial dependencies and temporal dynamics, together with Multi-view Rotary Position Encoding (RoPE) to encode positional relationships across views and time. WorldRec 2.0 reconstructs static and dynamic 3D Gaussians from multi-view, multi-temporal observations in a single forward pass and uses their renderings as explicit scene context to preserve geometry and appearance during long-horizon generation. Conditioning inputs are fused through VAE latent concatenation in a shared representation space. We incorporate Gated Linear Attention (GLA) into the temporal layers of VTA for efficient streaming inference, reducing computation and KV-cache memory during multi-view rollouts. A physical-interaction data pipeline covers diverse interactions and long-tailed events. From Pre-train onward, these data are combined with large-scale videos and heterogeneous visual modalities to learn visual, geometric, and dynamic priors. During Mid-train, training across diverse view configurations further improves the model's ability to capture how actions and object states shape subsequent scene evolution. After distillation-based Post-train, we apply the model to closed-loop simulation, closed-loop training, and World Action Model (WAM) applications. These applications generate physically consistent future states and support world-state prediction, policy learning, and action generation for Physical AI.
bullets: Addresses the need to model real-world physical evolution and long-horizon, view-consistent scene generation.
Combines View-Temporal Attention, multi-view RoPE, and Gated Linear Attention for spatial-temporal modeling and efficient streaming inference.
WorldRec 2.0 reconstructs static and dynamic 3D Gaussians from multi-view observations and uses rendered geometry and appearance as scene context.
Fuses heterogeneous conditioning through shared VAE latent representations and trains on interaction data, videos, and diverse view configurations.
Supports closed-loop simulation and training, world-state prediction, policy learning, and action generation through World Action Model applications.

figures.caption: Figure 4 Architecture and training pipeline overview. The Causal World Model uses VTA and GLA to retain an efficient DiT backbone under multi-view settings. To handle diverse conditions, we adopt a unified condition injection design, enabling training across multiple tasks and datasets. During post-training, we introduce long-video rollout to improve long-horizon generation stability and Random Gradient Sampling to reduce memory usage. Overall, the model is trained in three stages to achieve efficient and controllable streaming generation.

Figure 2 Overview of our data pipeline. We integrate three data categories: general data, physical world driving and robotics data, and physical causal data. The collected videos undergo basic filtering, scoring, and captioning. We further prepare world-control conditions for the corresponding data subsets, including layouts, and scene contexts, to support causal world model training.

Figure 3 Overview of the dataset distribution. We report the sample count distribution, caption token count distribution, and scene composition of the general and physical-world autonomous-driving data. Robotics data are omitted because they are predominantly collected in a small number of indoor settings.

Figure 13 Architecture of the closed-loop training strategy based on the causal reasoning world model simulator. The strategy comprises three core components: an end-to-end driving model, a reinforcement learning (RL) post-training module, and a causal reasoning world model simulator. Solid lines denote data flow; dashed lines denote gradient propagation. The proposed strategy fine-tunes the action generation model via post-training.

Figure 1 Xiaomi Auto World Model 2.0 supports unified, streaming causal world modeling across general video generation, autonomous driving, and embodied robotics. Examples include text-to-video and image-to-video generation, controllable prediction across varying views, and action-conditioned rollouts for embodied manipulation. papers.tldr: Xiaomi Auto World Model 2.0 is a causal, streaming multi-view world model that generates physically consistent future scenes for driving and embodied-AI applications.

papers.abstract: Whether an action-conditioned world model responds to actions is usually checked by replacing or removing the actions and measuring the loss in accuracy. Taking biological experiments as the guiding case, we show that such diagnostics report action effects where there are none: under autocorrelated designs, future actions stand in for history the model does not see. When the design law is known, a conditional randomization test written as an e-value is valid in finite samples whatever the model. A second failure arises whenever many sites share one action sequence, as in world models: the pooled score turns small model errors along the action contrast into an e-value near zero, so a valid test loses its power although the effect is real. Tempering the score changes the bet, not the validity. The log e-value is concave in the tempering factor and zero at zero, so too small a factor costs little and too large a one can cost everything; every single factor we tried, estimated or tuned, failed in some setting, and mixtures over a fixed grid never did. Our own preregistered analysis of optogenetic ERK experiments failed by pooling; a tempered statistic, registered before the data were obtained, then rejected the null on a never-opened field (E = 1.1e10). In three registered tests on models trained by others, the pooled test rejected in 0 of 96 units of a diffusion model, and reached the power bar in 10 of 26 Atari games under IRIS's token likelihood and 1 of 6 control tasks under TD-MPC2; mixtures fixed in advance reached it in 96 units, 24 games and 6 tasks. On recorded robot video with iVideoGPT the mixture rejected in 155 of 159 trajectories; the pooled test did not collapse there (143). Under exact nulls the statistics made 14 rejections in 26,664 tests.
bullets: Autocorrelated action designs let future actions stand in for unobserved history, producing apparent action effects where none exist.
Pooling many sites that share one action sequence can drive e-values near zero from small model errors, masking real effects.
Conditional randomization e-values remain valid in finite samples when the design law is known, regardless of the model.
Tempering changes test power rather than validity; fixed-grid mixtures were robust across tested settings, unlike individual tempering factors.
In registered evaluations, mixtures outperformed pooled tests across diffusion, Atari, control, and robot-video tasks, while exact-null testing produced 14 rejections in 26,664 tests.
