papers.selection_reason: Statistical testing of action-conditioned world models; directly relevant to interactive world model evaluation.
papers.title: Stand-In Effects and Pooling Amplification: Lessons from Biological World Models for Testing Action Effects
papers.tldr: Standard action-effect tests can falsely detect effects or lose power when actions are autocorrelated or pooled across many sites; finite-sample-valid e-value mixtures address both issues.

papers.abstract: Robots manipulating in cluttered spaces must often plan from partial views where foreground objects occlude the target, surrounding geometry, and usable free space. Reactive policies often miss these hidden constraints, while exhaustive search becomes computationally prohibitive in dense clutter. We present SCOUT, an occlusion-aware planning framework that bridges high-level deliberation with grounded physical rollouts. SCOUT leverages an object-centric scene representation to reconstruct hidden geometry and derive a relational planning state capturing blocker hierarchies and accessibility corridors. To navigate the vast action space in clutter, an LLM proposes structured action candidates which are then rigorously evaluated via Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) using a learned action-conditioned world model. Evaluations on 'Reveal' and 'Placement' tasks show that SCOUT outperforms Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies, embodied agents, and 3D world models, with significant gains in long-horizon tasks requiring reasoning over occluded geometry. We further validate the framework's robustness through real-world robotic manipulation in a cluttered shelf environment.
bullets: Addresses hidden geometry, blockers, and free-space constraints in cluttered, partially observed environments.
Reconstructs occluded structure into a relational planning state with blocker hierarchies and accessibility corridors.
Uses an LLM to propose structured actions, then evaluates them through MCTS with a learned action-conditioned world model.
Outperforms several policy and world-model baselines on Reveal and Placement tasks, especially for long-horizon occlusion reasoning.
Validated in real-world manipulation within a cluttered shelf environment.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of SCOUT. From partial RGB-D observations, GHOST reconstructs an objectcentric hidden scene representation, which is converted into a relational planning state. An LLM generates structured action proposals, and MCTS with a learned world model evaluates simulated rollouts to guide selection of a multi-step plan.
Figure 2: GHOST scene representation pipeline. Multi-view RGB-D observations are fused into object-centric slots, refined via slot interactions, and rendered into a unified 3D scene representation.

Figure 7: Failure analysis of SCOUT. (a) Failure decomposition as percentages of all rollouts. Most failures stem from hidden-scene reconstruction errors, followed by transition-prediction and geometric-validity errors. (b) Transition-prediction failure: the selected action does not create enough free space to retrieve the target. (c) Hidden-scene failure: a small back-row target remains too occluded to be reconstructed from partial observations. (d) Geometric-validity failure: dense clutter leaves no feasible retrieval corridor under the current primitive set.

papers.abstract: Interactive world generation requires both accurate local control and stable scene consistency over long rollouts. Existing methods improve local generation through camera or geometry conditioning and extend historical context with memory mechanisms. However, long-horizon exploration remains challenging due to incomplete target-view guidance and inconsistencies accumulated during scene updates. We present \textbf{GSExplorer}, a generation--reconstruction framework built around a persistent 3D Gaussian world state. At each step, the current 3DGS scene provides multimodal rendering conditions for a video generator, while camera geometry is injected through a separate Relative Ray Encoding branch. Generated videos are then fed back to a SLAM-based reconstruction backend, where appearance and geometric consistency checks produce a shared support mask for selective scene updates and cross-chunk pose refinement. We further design a data-construction pipeline that reproduces realistic 3DGS degradation during scene extrapolation, yielding 293K training pairs of degraded multimodal renderings and real target videos. GSExplorer achieves the best overall performance among the compared methods on both single-step and three-step WorldScore evaluation, including a Camera Control score of 99.07 in single-step extrapolation. On 481-frame leave-and-return rollouts, it also shows strong revisit consistency.
bullets: Addresses incomplete target-view guidance and accumulated inconsistencies during long-range scene exploration.
Conditions a video generator on multimodal renderings from the current 3DGS state plus camera geometry via Relative Ray Encoding.
Uses SLAM reconstruction with appearance and geometry checks for masked scene updates and cross-chunk pose refinement.
Trains on 293K pairs designed to mimic 3DGS degradation during scene extrapolation.
Reports best overall performance among compared methods on single- and three-step WorldScore evaluations, with strong 481-frame revisit consistency.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Overview of GSExplorer. Starting from a 3DGS scene initialized from a single image, we render multimodal scene conditions along the planned camera trajectory at each step. These conditions, together with camera geometry and text prompts, guide the conditiondriven generator to produce a completed video. The generated video is then fed back to the SLAM-based world update, where content and geometric masks are combined into a support mask for selective scene updates. The support mask also filters correspondences for cross-chunk alignment, as indicated by the dashed arrow. The updated 3DGS world state then provides reliable conditions for the next step, forming a generation–reconstruction loop.

Figure 2. Architecture of the condition-driven video generator. Multimodal 3DGS renderings are encoded as scene conditions and injected into the diffusion backbone through one input projection and five residual projections. Camera intrinsics and poses define tokenwise ray geometry, which is incorporated through a separate RRE attention branch in every DiT block using geometry-aware Q/K/V and output transforms. Text prompts follow the original Wan cross-attention pathway.

Figure 3. Training-pair construction pipeline. First, long sequences are filtered and sampled into 57-frame clips containing 8 context frames and 49 target frames. Next, we reconstruct the full sequence with 3DGS-SLAM while forcing Gaussian insertion at the first target frame. Together, these steps improve target-view alignment while preserving the desired context-limited degradation. We then retain only Gaussians born within the context frames, recovering the desired context-limited degradation. Finally, the retained 3DGS is rendered at the target poses to produce multimodal degraded conditions paired with the real target frames.

Figure 4. Qualitative WorldScore results across one-, two-, and three-step extrapolation. P and C denote the text prompt and camera instruction. GSExplorer accurately follows both controls while maintaining high visual quality and coherent spatial structure.

Figure 8. Additional qualitative comparison of long-horizon revisit results. After extended leave-and-return exploration, GSExplorer better preserves the scene content and spatial layout of the initial view.
Figure 7. Additional qualitative results on WorldScore. GSExplorer follows the specified text and camera controls while maintaining coherent scene appearance and geometry during extrapolation.
Figure 5. Qualitative comparison of long-horizon revisit results. GSExplorer better preserves the content and details of the starting view after long-range exploration.

Figure 6. Cost across generation steps on WorldScore. Step time, peak GPU memory, and scene storage over three extrapolation steps for outdoor (top) and indoor (bottom) scenes. Each additional step increases runtime by only a few seconds and scene storage by a few hundred MiB, keeping incremental costs modest.

Table 7. Conditioning architectures and added parameters of geometry-conditioned video models. Ratios are computed from unrounded parameter counts relative to the nominal backbone sizes. papers.abstract: Selecting a reinforcement-learning (RL) policy usually requires additional environment interaction, while learned world models offer cheap but potentially biased evaluations. This raises two distinct questions: can shared model errors preserve pairwise rankings despite poor absolute values, and do they make a small number of real audits more informative? We derive an exact pairwise simulation identity and a relative bound separating common-mode Bellman residuals from policy-specific error. The analysis motivates RAVEL (Relative Auditing of Value Errors in Learned models), a selective policy tournament whose eliminations use held-out real outcomes. We test 45 SAC, TD3, and PPO policies per task in DMC cheetah-run and walker-walk. At rollout horizon 500, model rankings remain strong (Kendall tau = 0.962 and 0.800), and same-run differential-error ratios are 0.674 and 0.106. Yet mean paired audit-error correlations are only 0.007 and 0.090, and pairing changes standard deviation by -2.5 percent and +1.9 percent. Simultaneous intervals attain 99.98 percent and 99.75 percent coverage, but certify only 13.2 percent and 0 percent of decisions at eight audits. RAVEL improves low-budget walker-walk regret, whereas real-only successive halving is better at the largest budget, rejecting the precommitted twofold efficiency target. Frozen-model optimization lowers real return without increasing predicted return on average. Thus ranking fidelity, useful audit covariance, and upward model exploitation are distinct properties, separated in part by closed-loop trajectory divergence.
bullets: The study separates ranking fidelity, audit informativeness, and susceptibility to model exploitation as distinct properties.
It derives an exact pairwise simulation identity and a relative bound distinguishing shared Bellman errors from policy-specific errors.
RAVEL uses held-out real outcomes in a selective policy tournament to eliminate candidates with limited audits.
Model rankings were strong on DMC cheetah-run and walker-walk, but paired audit-error correlations were near zero and simultaneous intervals certified few decisions at eight audits.

RAVEL reduced low-budget walker-walk regret, while real-only successive halving performed better at the largest budget; frozen-model optimization reduced real return without improving predicted return on average.

papers.abstract: When a World Action Model fails at control, is the bottleneck proposal generation or trajectory scoring? We introduce pico-WAM, a compact model with supplied physical state for tracing policy-dynamics interactions. Using 206 Push-T demonstrations and 15 training seeds, we compare data regimes and search configurations. Counterfactual branch training improves short-horizon cost ranking and enlarges the coverage advantage of policy-restarted over warm-started search by 4.8 percentage points; restart wins under both data regimes. Replacing learned trajectory scores with simulator costs improves coverage by 12.2 points while retaining learned proposals. Substituting simulator states in proposal generation alone shows no detected gain. Component diagnostics and a separate door-opening study show why better ranking need not yield better control or outperform imitation. These controlled interventions identify scoring as an effective improvement target in the tested setting and provide a reproducible protocol for diagnosing compact world models.
bullets: Studies proposal generation versus trajectory scoring using supplied physical state, 206 Push-T demonstrations, 15 training seeds, and controlled search interventions.
Counterfactual branch training improves short-horizon cost ranking and increases policy-restarted search’s coverage advantage over warm starts by 4.8 percentage points.
Simulator trajectory costs improve coverage by 12.2 points while retaining learned proposals; simulator states alone do not show a detected proposal-generation gain.
A separate door-opening study shows that better ranking may not translate into better control or outperform imitation.
Findings are scoped to the tested settings and support a reproducible diagnostic protocol for compact world models.

papers.title: pico-WAM: Evaluating Counterfactual Prediction and Planning Error in a Compact World Action Model

papers.abstract: An AI can find a safe action faster than any human, but it must never decide what counts as safe. We present GURU, a hierarchical neuro-symbolic multi-agent system for mission-critical digital engineering and operations, built on one partition of authority: learned models propose, rank, and accelerate; a symbolic rules engine checks every consequential action against hard limits before it executes; and validated physics confirms and decides. GURU runs a workflow as a closed control loop, with Navigation, Action, and Planning agents sharing one Common Internal Language and one training factory. Nuclear, aviation, and national-security guidance now requires this pattern; a harnessed language model keeps the model at the center, GURU puts a validated reference there. In computational fluid dynamics, the workflow raised the converged-simulation rate on unseen aircraft geometries from under 1 percent to 74 percent over 100 single-attempt cases, ran 54 live cases to Mach 6 on three facilities, and an ablation put the symbolic layer at 13 points of boundary-layer capture. Knowledge-graph retrieval and role adapters raised ParaView control success from 55 to 75 percent. In space domain awareness, where a language model cannot be trusted to decide, a frozen self-supervised world model under validated propagation scored highest of five methods at conjunction risk, including fully fine-tuned language models, with several-times-lower seed variance: the trustworthy design gives up nothing in accuracy, and the recipe transferred to reactor anomaly detection. A radar-to-avoidance debris pipeline was demonstrated in stages on a 2026 reentry; the hierarchy coordinates simulated teams of 200 aircraft. Training scaled near-linearly past 1,000 Aurora nodes and ran at 8,000. The approach extends to a control-grade microreactor digital twin with validated physics, not a learned model, as the safety basis.
bullets: Uses Navigation, Action, and Planning agents connected by a shared internal language and training factory in a closed-loop workflow.
Applies symbolic verification before consequential actions execute, with validated physics serving as the safety basis rather than learned models.
Improved unseen-aircraft CFD convergence from under 1% to 74% across 100 single-attempt cases; also demonstrated live Mach 6 cases on three facilities.
Knowledge-graph retrieval and role adapters increased ParaView control success from 55% to 75%; validated world modeling achieved the best conjunction-risk score among five methods.
Demonstrations span space-domain awareness, reactor anomaly detection, debris avoidance, large simulated aircraft teams, and a control-grade microreactor digital twin.

figures.caption: Figure 5: Data Factory outputs feed multiple automated-machine-learning frameworks trained in parallel. Candidate models are evaluated, compared, and ranked under Monte Carlo cross-validation, and the best predictor for each target is registered for downstream use in the workflow.

Figure 1: The GURU hierarchy. The Planning layer performs long-horizon forecasting and planning with JEPA world models and model predictive control. The Action layer turns plans into bounded decisions through optimization, parameter prediction, and anomaly detection. The Navigation layer executes and monitors operations across software and physical systems. Feedback flows bidirectionally, so plans constrain low-level action while observations update the planner. The middle layer, labeled Discrete actions in the figure, is the Action layer.

Figure 8: Knowledge-graph construction pipeline. Heterogeneous software sources are converted into a common, provenance-preserving observation representation, using vision-language models and automatic speech recognition (ASR) for video and deterministic or vision-language extraction for PDF documents, before being transformed into candidate claims and merged into a canonical knowledge graph. The shared intermediate schema allows document and video evidence to contribute to the same reusable representation.

Figure 21: The horizon-aware forecaster that produces the forward tracks. The extended model takes a look-ahead interval, up to 72 hours (at most 7 days), from as much as 28 days of history, and predicts the embedding of the whole future trajectory rather than a single point. Sweeping the look-ahead forward and backward turns the same model into a scanner across the historical archive for behavior staggered in time to avoid notice. The forecaster is a joint-embedding predictive architecture (LeCun, 2022; Assran et al., 2023).

Figure 17: Software-control architecture and knowledge-learning loop for ParaView. The Planning agent decomposes a user goal into structured actions; the Grounding agent maps each action and the current application state to executable code or GUI operations; and the Execution agent applies the selected operation and returns the resulting state. Tutorials, documents, and interaction trajectories provide knowledge for retrieval and role-specific training.

Figure 2: The GURU platform. The Learning Engine trains Navigation, Action, and Planning agents. The rules engine validates schemas, ontologies, constraints, and execution state. The agent society coordinates specialized agents through message pools and a shared workspace for auditable execution. Inputs span sensor streams, simulation outputs, documents, and direct user interaction, and the same platform drives applications in digital engineering, space operations, and reactor operations.

Figure 4: The Common Internal Language unifies agents through a shared semantic substrate for concepts, values, rules, and procedures, a uniform message format for the global workspace, and hierarchical task structures ready for planning and execution. Inset: a natural-language and geometry request is translated into typed, unit-aware attribute records with explicit provenance and uncertainty fields.

Figure 3: Lightweight clients capture multimodal input and workflow intent. Structured representations and high-dimensional embeddings are routed to backend services for reasoning, orchestration, and execution across local, cloud, and high-performance computing environments. Remote applications can be driven and viewed through a streamed display.

Figure 45: CFD simulation outcomes by grid generator and parameter selection. Stacked outcome shares for the earlier Pentagrow pipeline with predicted parameters, the extrusion-based generator with random parameters, and the extrusion-based generator with learned parameter selection. Outcomes are failed grid generation, failed initial solve, failed during adaptation, not finished, not converged, and converged. The rightmost configuration is the headline result in the text: 100 cases, one attempt each, of which 92 completed and 74 converged.

Figure 6: Current and target states are encoded into latent embeddings. The predictor learns action-conditioned transitions in that latent space, which lets agents forecast the behavior of an interface or environment without reconstructing raw observations.

Figure 7: Multimodal sources for software-knowledge acquisition. Document and video tutorials provide procedural demonstrations and application knowledge, while autonomous ParaView exploration produces state-action-outcome trajectories. The exploration examples show before-and-after application states; several attempts did not achieve the requested goal, which is why execution without an error is never treated as achievement. Both sources are transformed into reusable observations for knowledge extraction and agent training.

Figure 49: Quantitative comparison of anomaly-detection methods and JEPA scoring rules. (Top left) Balanced accuracy at the warning threshold by method. (Top right) Correct-classification rate per fault group. (Bottom left) Temporal anomaly scores for four JEPA scoring variants. (Bottom right) Balanced accuracy and average precision for each scoring rule. Embedding kNN gives the best and most consistent balance across fault families.

Figure 46: Frozen JEPA matches or exceeds configuration-matched baselines on conjunction risk, with seed-stable performance. Mean binary F1-score over 10 seeds on the shared test split, with every method trained under the same budget (batch size 96, 1,000 training steps); labels show mean ± standard deviation. The frozen JEPA encoder with a small MLP head scores highest, and its low seed-to-seed variance shows the result does not depend on a lucky seed, even though none of its backbone weights are trained.

Figure 11: GURU CFD Suite workflow for high-speed aerial vehicles. The figure shows one representative airframe from the live run described above, the Fury: from a natural-language prompt, GURU configured an aerodynamic sweep at Mach 2 to 4, 40 to 50 km, plus or minus 5 degrees angle of attack, about 1M cells, and autonomously submitted it to HPC. Post-processed output for the Fury airframe shows Mach contours and surface pressure-coefficient distribution, the computational mesh, converged residual histories, and axial surface pressure and heat-flux profiles. Video: https://youtu.be/GQIJjjVolNY

Figure 13: The generation model maps image embeddings and augmented renderings into meshable vehicle geometries. Representative outputs span 11 aerial vehicle classes, from fixed-wing subsonic and transonic to supersonic and hypersonic, eVTOL, flying-wing and blended-wing-body, delta-wing and canard, high-lift, rotorcraft, lighter-than-air, and unconventional configurations, with 673 geometries reaching successful volume-grid generation.

Figure 36: Historical traffic replay with modeled hazard bands and candidate reroutes. The dashboard combines recorded aircraft tracks, event evidence, illustrative debris bands, and proposed route alternatives. The evidence panel distinguishes published predictions, event confirmation, and traffic records; the decision panel summarizes modeled intersections and rerouting costs. The displayed alternatives are simulation outputs, not aircraft actions that occurred during the event. Also identified in the dashboard - limits on route completion, cost estimation, and multi-aircraft conflict assessment. Video: https://youtu.be/Jtyf78QsXlE

Figure 20: Two-phase design. In pre-training, the world model learns from context and target windows split from up to 28 days of state-vector history, with a slow exponential-moving-average target encoder and a Gaussian anti-collapse regularizer optimized under an MSE objective in embedding space. In the conjunction stage, the frozen encoder produces embeddings for the history of two objects, which are combined into a symmetric pair representation and read by a conjunction head trained on public conjunction-message labels to output a collision risk score.

Figure 43: OpenMC drum-angle runs are fit to a smooth reactivity model used by the point-kinetics controller. The MPC then chooses drum rotations to track a scheduled power target or to maximize power while holding a fuel-temperature cap.

Figure 18: Ablation of context, retrieval, and learned adaptation for ParaView software control (successful attempts out of 150 per configuration). Explicit program state, API information, and capability catalogs improve base-model performance, while graph retrieval is most valuable when supplied context is limited. Under full context (state, API inventory, and catalogs), the role-specific Planning and Grounding adapters provide additional gains, with retrieval and adaptation showing complementary effects in some configurations.

Figure 9: Knowledge-graph snapshot for ParaView by semantic family. The graph contains 105,125 nodes and 106,202 edges from 64 source packages (42 PDF, 19 video, two API, and one exploration package), including 1,552 exact API definitions, of which 1,478 carry nonempty signatures. The panels count nodes in the ten semantic families; the remaining nodes include procedure steps and transitions, which are stored as supporting control-flow records. These are corpus-wide counts, not counts of facts relevant to any single goal. Automatic semantic matching between documentation and exploration was disabled in this release, so shared storage should not be read as complete automatic linkage.

Figure 19: 2D projection of JEPA world-model embeddings for orbital time-series windows. Non-maneuver windows and maneuver windows separate cleanly, and a simple linear boundary achieves an area under the curve near 0.98 with no labeled supervision during pre-training and no deep downstream classifier fit to the embedding.

Figure 41: Learned models predict dose rate and the effective multiplication factor for each candidate shielding layout, while the optimizer searches material configurations that keep the multiplication factor near target and reduce external dose. Later iterations reach lower-dose designs while keeping the reactor viable.

Figure 48: JEPA anomaly score tracks each injected reactor disturbance. Response of unsupervised anomaly detectors to controlled perturbations in heat-pipe microreactor data. (Top) The injected thermal and heat-removal deviations over time. (Bottom) Normalized anomaly scores from the JEPA embedding-kNN detector, classical detectors, language-model baselines, and Chronos-2, with shaded bands marking injected-disturbance windows. The JEPA score rises during each disturbance and falls back toward nominal between events.

Figure 32: HRRR wind field near a candidate. The map shows interpolated horizontal wind at approximately 2.51 km above sea level at 07:01:47 UTC on January 24, 2026. Colors encode wind speed and arrows indicate the direction of air motion. The vertical profile compares the interpolated field with the adjacent 07:00 and 08:00 analyses and the earlier constant-wind assumption. At the candidate location and height, the interpolated wind is approximately 6.4 m/s toward 141 degrees true. These are atmospheric-model fields, not debris velocities.

Figure 50: Scalability demonstrations across space, fusion, and engineering workflows. (a) Orbital JEPA world-model training on Aurora, run as 16 models in parallel to 8,000 nodes, shown with the maneuver embeddings and classification metrics of Figures 19 and 23c. (b) GPU-native reinforcement-learning environments with vectorized anomaly detection for fusion-facility operations, with near-linear distributed training on Frontier. (c) Geometry-synthesis model training on Aurora (512 nodes). (d) ParaView interface exploration (about 2,000 nodes) and LoRA fine-tuning for software control (512 nodes) on Aurora. (e) Scalable OpenMC, configuration-driven automated workflows, and large-scale AutoML optimization with mesh success-rate improvements on Frontier (1,000 to 4,000 nodes). Inset drawings are illustrative icons of each workload.

Figure 37: Flagged anomalies are organized within a four-class taxonomy of data quality, operational, safety-relevant, and routing, with associated confidence values and evidence trails supporting interpretation and response selection. The example record is shown with its data-integrity flag; taxonomy alignments are candidates for source review, not findings of a violation, conflict, or loss of separation.

Figure 29: Radar measurements surrounding a candidate detection. Columns show reflectivity, radial Doppler velocity, and dual-polarization correlation coefficient before and after the selected detection.

Figure 30: Conditional motion estimates for four regional echo sequences. Blue markers show selected radar echo centers, and yellow arrows indicate fitted movement over their observation intervals. N1, N2, and S3 exhibit slow southeastward motion; the earlier S4 sequence exhibits faster eastward motion. Gray paths in N1 show competing associations. The orange square in S4 marks the later seven-cell detection, which has not been linked to that sequence.

Figure 38: Interactive multi-aircraft evaluation interface. The dashboard combines synchronized map and altitude views with scenario controls, timeline playback, mission outcomes, communication and navigation-denial status, and per-aircraft diagnostics. Operators can inspect each agent’s local observation, assigned course and goal, received messages, physical characteristics, policy or MPC output, and predicted trajectory, while selecting separate policies and checkpoints for each force and rerunning configurable Torch-based evaluation scenarios. https://youtu.be/9kXCKju5cyA

Figure 47: JEPA embeddings expose a conjunction-risk direction fit on the training split (labeled train-fitted in the panels). A class-balanced logistic probe was fit using only the training-set embeddings and then applied unchanged to validation and test pairs. (Top) Risk-score distributions for Baseline risk and Elevated risk pairs across train, validation, and test splits. (Bottom) Two-dimensional projection of the same pairs using the risk axis fit on the training split and the leading residual embedding direction after subtracting the risk-axis component. The held-out validation and test panels show that the learned risk ordering also appears for conjunctions not used to fit the probe.

Figure 15: Candidate solver-parameter configurations evaluated across representative cases under 2 competing objectives, both minimized, with the estimated trade-off front for each case. Successful simulation without errors is treated as an explicit optimization target.

Figure 34: Simulated debris trajectories, uncertainty regions, and radar observations. The map overlays alternative fragment paths and smoothed coverage bands with timestamped radar echoes and candidate motion estimates. The bands summarize the simulated spread with added spatial margins. Radar overlays support comparison with observations.
Figure 14: Generated geometries are rotated into a standardized aerodynamic frame so that inlet direction, lift and drag axes, and solver boundary conditions stay consistent across cases.

Figure 27: OrbitGuard Analysis Console for a synthetic exercise, showing track tables, relative encounter geometry, orbital-element histories, conjunction metrics, classifier outputs, maneuver plans, and an event timeline. Avoidance maneuvers are deterministic trade studies that require operator approval. The console supports detailed policy evaluation and trains operators to interpret evidence, identify threat-like behavior, and select a response. Video: https://youtu.be/aAnbW2aGpN8

Figure 25: OrbitGuard Globe View from a synthetic exercise. The view displays the protected satellite, candidate tracks, projected orbits, threat classifications, and proposed avoidance trajectories in an interactive three-dimensional view, and supports operator training and visual analysis of how synthetic adversarial behavior evolves into observable orbital behavior.

Figure 44: Interactive interface for the reactor-control simulation. The dashboard shows reactor power, the effective multiplication factor, the control-drum angle, and the fuel temperature alongside the core visualizations, and lets a user drive the controller live. Video: https://youtu.be/w5S9YC7DB_c

Figure 24b: The maneuver-family blind-spot analysis. All 607 validated maneuvers are grouped by maneuver family and orbital regime, and color encodes the median reconstruction error against the bracketing-TLE truth on a log scale. Single-burn families in low-Earth orbit reproduce well, while multi-burn and large transfers land thousands of kilometers off: multi-burn maneuvers fail validation about 33% of the time against about 5% for single burns. The analysis also exposes a coverage gap, since roughly 60% of recorded maneuvers fall outside the available tracking window and cannot be validated, a data limitation rather than a model deficiency.

Figure 26: Synthetic intercept generation and refinement performance. The table compares a 100-generation evolutionary search, a 300-generation search, and a 100-generation search with local refinement, and shows that refinement produces the strongest sub-kilometer and sub-100-meter results. The delta-v versus minimum-distance scatter plot shows the tradeoff between maneuver effort and intercept quality, with refined candidates reaching lower miss distances without a proportional rise in total delta-v. The trajectory panels show target, no-burn baseline, and optimized chaser paths with burn locations, illustrating how timed maneuvers turn natural misses into close intercepts.

Figure 39: Multi-aircraft training and evaluation results. (Top left) Moving averages of Blue target arrival, world success, and episode return during late-stage training. (Bottom left) Fixed-checkpoint evaluation on 256 unseen worlds. (Top right) Paired held-out comparison of multistage training iterations I1 and I2. (Bottom right) Single-GPU throughput as the number of parallel 200-aircraft scenarios grows, with the observed range across repeats.

Figure 31: Checking displacement-based motion against radial Doppler measurements. Each row shows a selected observation pair: measured displacement on the left, projection of the inferred velocity toward the radar in the center, and comparison with Doppler measurements on the right. Gray points are individual Doppler gates, orange diamonds are bulk estimates, and blue crosses are predicted radial speeds. The displayed differences are approximately 0.46 to 0.73 m/s. This agreement supports local kinematic consistency under the selected association.

Figure 23a: Simulation-based virtual range training data. 200,396 GMAT simulation records across three maneuver classes (no maneuver, orbit raise or lower, high delta-v) with broad orbital-element coverage.

Figure 23b: A t-SNE projection of the simulation dataset, showing clear separable structure across all three maneuver classes, with low-Earth and geostationary markers appearing across all class regions, confirming the embedding captures both maneuver type and orbital-regime context rather than random synthetic variation.

Figure 23c: PatchTST plus Transformer plus JEPA classifier trained entirely on simulation-based virtual-range data, with per-class precision, recall, and F1 between 0.95 and 1.00 across all maneuver types. The result is not driven by the dominant baseline class.

Figure 33: Alternative Minnesota reentry scenarios compared with radar observations. The full-region map shows simulated trajectories extending from northern Minnesota toward Iowa; the inset resolves their relationship to the N1 to S4 radar regions. Orange, purple, and teal distinguish dense, intermediate, and lightweight component families, while gray paths show the earlier steep-entry case. The lower panel shows altitude histories against time after the assumed 06:31 UTC epoch, with blue bars indicating

Right: self-organizing maps derived from large-scale OpenMC simulations, illustrating interactions among key design variables and identifying regions that satisfy criticality and compactness objectives.

(a) HTR-10 initial criticality: the OpenMC keff of 1.01369 plus or minus 0.00014 is +59 pcm from the IRPhEP benchmark and remains within the plus or minus 500 pcm acceptance band. (b) Baikal-1 reactor skyshine: OpenMC reproduces the measured dose-rate trend from 50 m to 1 km, spanning more than four orders of magnitude and consistent with the COG result of Heinrichs et al. (2022). (c) KRUSTY radial-reflector-height benchmark: OpenMC follows the published Poston et al. MCNP keff trend and captures the approach to criticality as reflector height increases.

Figure 35: Aircraft avoidance in a constructed synthetic encounter. The left panel compares a straight flight path, reactive DAIDALUS guidance, and an additional forecast-based maneuver screen followed by DAIDALUS monitoring. The right panel shows minimum normalized separation from airborne fragments at one-second evaluation intervals; values below one violate the configured protection thresholds. Reactive guidance turns the aircraft but still produces sampled violations, whereas the forecast-assisted maneuver avoids them in this example. The experiment uses perfect simulated states and access to future fragment trajectories and is separate from the uncertainty ensembles.

Figure 24a: A single validated case, a small station-keeping burn on Sentinel-3A on 25 February 2024. papers.selection_reason: Presents GURU, a hierarchical neuro-symbolic multi-agent system for mission-critical operations, combining learned models with symbolic rules and validated physics, relevant to embodied agents and interactive world models.
papers.title: GURU: A Hierarchical Neuro-Symbolic Multi-Agent System for Verification-Aware Automation of Mission-Critical Digital Engineering and Operations
papers.tldr: GURU is a hierarchical neuro-symbolic multi-agent system in which learned models propose actions, symbolic rules enforce hard safety limits, and validated physics makes final decisions for mission-critical operations.

papers.abstract: We test whether Koopman structure helps a differentiable world model used to train a simulated Unitree G1 whole-body tracking policy by backpropagation through imagined rollouts, replacing the MLP world model of an otherwise unchanged pipeline. It does not: return is at best equal (0.823 versus 0.830), one-step error on identical data is 1.3 to 1.6 times the MLP's, and training is about 15% slower. Lifted rollouts diverge or fail to train policies; of the schemes tested, re-lifting at every imagined step trains best. Re-lifting never uses the lifted linear dynamics and leaves a model affine in the action, with state-dependent offset and slope; an action-affine MLP also predicts worse, so the accuracy cost belongs to this class. At a fixed state, the dynamics' curvature in the action explains only part of it. Across states, the policy's actions span a curved region, so an affine model fits policy data only as the tangent at the policy's action, the operating point: on G1, the MLP's tangent there is as accurate as the MLP; at the mean action, 31 times worse. The offset must encode, from the state alone, where the policy acts, whereas an MLP reads the action. Supplying the policy's action removes most of the remaining gap on G1, Ant and Humanoid. The only tested online repair approaching the MLP feeds the action into the nonlinear lift, abandoning the structure. For this use, the MLP world model remains the better choice.
bullets: Replacing the MLP with Koopman-based models yields comparable-or-worse return, higher one-step error, and roughly 15% slower training.
Lifted rollouts diverge or fail to train policies; re-lifting each imagined step performs best but does not use lifted linear dynamics.
The resulting action-affine structure poorly represents the curved state-dependent action regions visited by the policy.
Providing the policy action to the model recovers most of the accuracy gap across G1, Ant, and Humanoid; nonlinear action lifting largely abandons the intended structure.
For this setting, the standard MLP world model remains preferable.

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes differentiable action-conditioned world models for humanoid whole-body tracking policy training, relevant to interactive world models and robot learning.
papers.title: Why Koopman Structure Does Not Help Differentiable World Models for Humanoid Whole-Body Tracking
papers.tldr: For differentiable world models guiding humanoid whole-body tracking, Koopman structure offers no benefit over an MLP and can reduce accuracy and training speed.

papers.abstract: Interactive video world models draw each frame from a memory bank of earlier frames stamped with their capture times. With frames, weights and noise fixed, reversing the timestamps of two views flips the state that generators of two families draw: they take the newest timestamp as the truth. That reading is right as long as states never return. After an agent undoes an action, the newest view of a region is outdated and the only view of the present is older; memories for changing worlds delete that older view, and memories that keep it hand the generator the past. Temporal databases separate when a record is stored from when its content holds, its valid time. ReDate keeps every frame and dates each retrieved token by its valid time, read from the agent's action log. The frozen generator then reads a reverted region as one that has just reached a new state, so ReDate needs no training. We prove that trusting the newest timestamp is right exactly when every current view is dated after every outdated one, that without a view taken after the return only the action log tells a reverted region from an up-to-date one, and that a generator able to draw from its own prediction gains more from re-dating than from deletion when the moved tokens keep little weight. After an undo, ReDate raises the share of FAR's steps showing the current state from 0.36 to 0.62 and HY-WorldPlay's from 0.003 to 0.19. We also propose a calibrated state metric to test any memory after undos.
bullets: Problem: Using the newest capture timestamp as truth fails when an agent reverses an action and the current state is represented by an older frame.
Method: Retain all frames and re-date retrieved tokens using valid times inferred from the agent’s action log.
Theory: Newest-timestamp selection is correct only when all current views are newer than all outdated views; after a return, the action log may be essential.
Results: After undo, current-state coverage rises from 0.36 to 0.62 for FAR and from 0.003 to 0.19 for HY-WorldPlay.
Scope: Re-dating is especially beneficial when moved tokens receive little weight, and the paper introduces a calibrated metric for evaluating memory after undos.

papers.selection_reason: Valid-time memory mechanism for interactive video world models after action undos; directly targets action-conditioned world generation and embodied memory.
papers.title: Old Is Not False: Valid-Time Memory for Interactive Video World Models
papers.tldr: ReDate improves interactive video world models after undo actions by assigning memory tokens their valid state time rather than their capture time, requiring no retraining.

papers.abstract: Many systems are observed only through unpaired snapshots, with population samples available at each time point but no correspondence between samples at different times. These snapshots determine the one-time distributions but leave the temporal coupling unspecified, requiring a modeling prior to connect successive times. We propose the lift-project stochastic differential equation (SDE), an autonomous SDE on the observed coordinate and a few hidden coordinates, trained only to match the snapshots. Most existing methods, including time-dependent SDEs, Schrödinger bridges and optimal transport, evolve the observed coordinate alone. For a scalar observation, the classical comparison theorem implies that all such models have non-negative lagged covariance, so on data whose lagged covariance turns negative, their error has a computable floor. The lift-project SDE is not bound by this floor. On two representative partially observed systems, the Duffing and pendulum oscillators, at comparable fit to the snapshots, the proposed method reduces the lagged-covariance error by factors of 2.4 and 6.6 relative to the strongest baseline and is the only model below the error floor; one hidden coordinate is already enough for such improvement. Furthermore, if a second experiment changes only the initial state of the hidden coordinate, no single model that evolves the observed coordinate alone can fit both experiments, whereas a single lift-project SDE can.
bullets: Unpaired snapshots identify one-time distributions but not how observations are coupled across time.
The method trains an autonomous SDE jointly over observed and hidden coordinates using only snapshot matching.
For scalar observations, observed-only models have a non-negative lagged-covariance constraint and an associated error floor.
On Duffing and pendulum oscillators, the method reduces lagged-covariance error by factors of 2.4 and 6.6 versus the strongest baseline.
One hidden coordinate suffices for improvement, and a single lift-project SDE can fit experiments differing only in hidden initial state.

papers.selection_reason: Learns hidden-state dynamics of partially observed systems from unpaired snapshots; technically transferable to environment-dynamics prediction in world models.
papers.title: Learning hidden-state dynamics from unpaired snapshots with lift-project SDEs
papers.tldr: Lift-project SDEs use a few hidden coordinates to learn temporal dynamics from unpaired snapshots, capturing negative lagged correlations that observed-only models cannot.

papers.abstract: Generative view synthesis aims to synthesize novel-view videos from reference observations along user-defined camera trajectories. Maintaining global scene consistency throughout this process remains challenging for camera-conditioned interactive video generators. Existing approaches typically select reference frames based solely on camera poses, overlooking whether the content remains semantically relevant or even visible. To address these limitations, we draw inspiration from semantic and episodic memory in human cognition, in which semantic memory captures generalized knowledge across experiences, whereas episodic memory preserves information tied to specific past events and contexts. Motivated by the complementary roles of semantic and episodic memory, we introduce SE-Mem, a Semantic-Episodic Memory framework that organizes historical observations in a structured 3D representation and augments its elements with semantic importance scores. A two-stage memory retrieval strategy is designed to identify the most informative frames to provide contextual guidance. Taking into account both semantic significance and geometric visibility, SE-Mem preserves semantic coherence and fine-grained visual details during novel view synthesis. Extensive evaluations show that our approach improves visual quality and achieves competitive geometric consistency across multiple benchmarks.
bullets: Addresses reference-frame selection methods that rely mainly on camera poses and may retrieve irrelevant or invisible content.
Structures historical observations in a 3D representation and assigns semantic importance scores inspired by semantic and episodic memory.
Uses a two-stage retrieval strategy to select informative frames for contextual guidance.
Combines semantic significance with geometric visibility to maintain coherent semantics and fine-grained visual details.
Evaluations report improved visual quality and competitive geometric consistency across multiple benchmarks.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of SE-Mem. Given a sequence of target camera poses {ctgt}, SE-Mem maintains a Semantic-Episodic Memory that combines 3D episodic observations with semantic importance scores. Historical frames are processed to obtain 3D point representations and importance maps, which are integrated into a voxelized memory representation. During synthesis, a two-stage retrieval strategy selects reference frames by considering target-view visibility and voxel importance. The retrieved frames and their corresponding camera conditions are then provided to a camera-conditioned video generator to synthesize novel views, while newly generated observations are incrementally incorporated into the memory.

Figure 4. Qualitative results on the Viewpoint Revisiting task. Our method maintains scene consistency when returning to previously observed viewpoints, successfully recovering the original environment with reduced perceptual drift and improved visual fidelity.

Figure 5. Qualitative results on DL3DV under the Viewpoint Revisiting setting. Representative examples show that SE-Mem preserves scene structure and previously observed content when the camera returns to earlier viewpoints across diverse indoor and outdoor scenes.

Figure 1. Scene-consistent generative view synthesis with SE-Mem. Given a single reference image and a user-defined camera trajectory, SE-Mem synthesizes a sequence of novel views while preserving previously observed scene content. Its Semantic-Episodic Memory combines structured 3D observations with semantic importance to retrieve relevant historical views, helping maintain scene consistency when the camera revisits earlier viewpoints in both indoor and outdoor environments.
Figure 6. Qualitative synthesis results on in-the-wild images from internet sources. SE-Mem preserves scene structure across the illustrated camera trajectories without domain-specific fine-tuning.

Figure 3. Visualization of importance maps. Given an input scene (left), our hierarchical importance scoring module (Eq. papers.abstract: State of the art latent dynamics world models achieve impressive performance for robot planning. But do they actually encode the physics of the world? In this paper, we show that popular world models today achieve strong results on tasks that reduce to image similarity but forget key details about objects in the scene like mass, deformation, friction, and bounciness. We achieve this by defining precisely what ought to be encoded in such a world model and introducing two new evaluation methods that can directly tease physical properties and easily scale to new ones. Our evaluation, which we call Roz, includes 10 contrastive tasks and 3 continuous tasks, totaling 1734 individual scenarios. We validate our eval on control tasks. On our own model, AnonWM, we find that performance roughly improves with training steps, while not necessarily being correlated with reconstruction MSE. We argue current model failures are a symptom of evaluation strategies (probes and planners) that are opaque, model-specific, and high-compute. Roz requires only a model that can ingest still frames or video, a way to extract latents, and a distance function between them, and it can be run in one pass. We hope future evaluations will adopt Roz's evaluation techniques. More broadly, we hope Roz can be a case study for a future where benchmarks allow rapid iteration and comparison across models.
bullets: Current world models can perform well on image-similarity tasks while missing properties such as mass, deformation, friction, and bounciness.
Roz introduces two evaluation methods covering 10 contrastive and 3 continuous tasks across 1,734 scenarios.
The evaluation requires only frame/video input, latent extraction, and a latent distance function, avoiding opaque, model-specific, high-compute probes and planners.
On AnonWM, performance generally improves with training steps but is not necessarily correlated with reconstruction MSE.
Roz is validated on control tasks and aims to support rapid, model-agnostic comparison of world models.

papers.abstract: Deploying generative world models for end-to-end closed-loop evaluation and policy learning requires precise scenario control, consistent observations, and sustained generation quality during extended interactions. This report presents X-World 1.6, advancing X-World 1.0 toward a more reliable and versatile driving simulator. The upgraded base model offers finer-grained control over traffic semantics, including traffic lights and road markings, together with improved spatial consistency across cameras. Virtual City capabilities broaden scenario construction through a family of models conditioned on diverse 2D and 3D references, including support for generating multi-camera future videos from a single image. An enhanced post-training framework enables efficient causal, few-step generation with stronger temporal coherence, better quality retention over longer rollouts, and improved alignment with human preferences. We also introduce a dedicated evaluation suite to support systematic assessment and guide model iteration. Together, these upgrades expand the scenarios X-World can simulate and improve the efficiency and reliability of its generated observations, supporting broader use in autonomous-driving development.
bullets: Adds fine-grained control over traffic lights, road markings, and other traffic semantics.
Improves spatial consistency across cameras and supports multi-camera future-video generation from a single image.
Broadens virtual-city construction using diverse 2D and 3D references.
Introduces post-training for efficient few-step causal generation, stronger temporal coherence, and improved long-rollout quality.
Provides a dedicated evaluation suite for systematic assessment and model iteration.

papers.abstract: Most agentic robotic systems use vision-language models (VLMs) either to orchestrate predefined skills or to directly generate actions, constraints, and control programs. The former is limited by the available skill library, while the latter requires VLMs to reason about precise geometry and contact. In this paper, we propose WorldSketch, a new paradigm for agentic robotics in which a VLM constructs a world model rather than generating robot actions. The VLM acts as an agent that actively queries perception tools to build and visually validate a minimal kinematic world model, capturing only task-relevant objects, their interaction geometry, and possible motions. A geometric planner then jointly optimizes contact and whole-body motion on the resulting model. Moreover, the world model is self-improving: execution feedback verifies outcomes, updates uncertain hypotheses, and enables the agent to revise the model when its predictions are contradicted. We demonstrate the generality of this paradigm across RoboCasa, LIBERO-PRO, and R2R-CE navigation, achieving zero-shot success rates of 91%, 97%, and 76%, respectively. On RoboCasa, WorldSketch outperforms the next-best zero-shot agent baseline by 58 percentage points while using 10 times fewer VLM input tokens; on LIBERO-PRO, it exceeds CaP-X by 82 percentage points. In navigation, it matches the success rate of step-by-step VLM agents while using 6 times fewer input tokens.
bullets: Addresses the limits of skill-library orchestration and the difficulty of precise geometric reasoning by VLMs.
The VLM actively queries perception tools to construct and visually validate minimal kinematic models of relevant objects, interactions, and motions.
A geometric planner jointly optimizes contact and whole-body motion using the constructed model.
Execution feedback verifies results, updates uncertain hypotheses, and supports model revision when predictions fail.
Demonstrated across RoboCasa, LIBERO-PRO, and R2R-CE navigation, with success rates of 91%, 97%, and 76%, respectively, while using substantially fewer VLM input tokens than comparable approaches.

papers.abstract: Tactile sensing provides robots with direct observations of contact physics, local geometry, and interaction dynamics, making it a vital source of feedback for contact-rich manipulation. However, existing tactile manipulation studies are often developed and evaluated within specific task settings, making it difficult to systematically compare how tactile information contributes under different interaction conditions. In this work, we develop a benchmark in simulation comprising 128 tasks organized around three complementary evaluation regimes: Precise, Recognition, and Dynamic. The benchmark further includes controlled static and dynamic task variants and 12 perturbation settings for evaluating robustness under changes in visual and physical conditions. These settings motivate studying tactile information as a temporally evolving interaction representation rather than only as an instantaneous observation. We therefore propose an action-conditioned latent predictive world model that integrates tactile history and learns a tactile state through prediction of future tactile latents. Building on this representation, we design a model that conditions action generation on the learned tactile state and uses predicted future tactile information to refine candidate actions through predictive tactile reflection. Experiments on the proposed benchmark show consistent gains from incorporating tactile information across the evaluated regimes. Project Page: https://tacmind-bench.github.io/
bullets: Covers Precise, Recognition, and Dynamic evaluation regimes with static and dynamic variants.
Includes 12 perturbation settings to test robustness to visual and physical changes.
Learns a temporally evolving tactile state by predicting future tactile latents from tactile history and actions.
Uses predicted tactile information to refine candidate actions through predictive tactile reflection.
Experiments show consistent gains from incorporating tactile information across the benchmark regimes.

papers.abstract: Learning the continuous-time evolution of nonlinear dynamical systems relies on trajectory-based objectives, which require simulating the learned dynamics during training and backpropagating through the numerical scheme, at a cost that grows with the rollout horizon. We show that trajectory-based objectives degenerate as the rollout horizon increases, hindering gradient-based optimization, and that the numerical scheme biases the learned dynamics by constraining the spectrum of the learned Jacobian to its absolute stability region. To overcome these limitations, we introduce Velocity Matching (VM), a simulation-free objective that relies on piecewise-linear interpolation and stochastic collocation, and approximates the velocity population risk to second order in the sampling step. We develop a theoretical framework for velocity-based learning, introducing stability estimates that control trajectory errors in terms of velocity errors, which enable us to establish universal and continuous-time approximation results when the learned velocity field is parameterized by deep neural networks. Building on a bias-variance decomposition of the VM objective, we show that its higher-order approximation of the velocity population risk yields a consistent minimizer; that it relates to the residual of an A-stable continuous-stage Runge-Kutta scheme, thus connecting VM to implicit integration without requiring any implicit solve; and that it implicitly matches the action of the learned Jacobian to that of the true one along the observed trajectories, without requiring access to the underlying velocity field or its Jacobian. Numerical experiments on nonlinear ordinary differential equations and semi-discretized time-dependent partial differential equations show that VM improves accuracy over trajectory-based objectives, while avoiding both the cost of simulation and the instabilities of long rollouts.
bullets: Trajectory-based training becomes harder over long horizons and can bias learned Jacobians through the numerical scheme’s stability constraints.
Velocity Matching uses piecewise-linear interpolation and stochastic collocation to estimate velocity risk without simulating learned trajectories.
The method provides theoretical stability and approximation guarantees, including for deep-neural-network velocity fields.
Its higher-order objective has a consistent minimizer and implicitly aligns learned and true Jacobian actions along observed trajectories.
Experiments on nonlinear ODEs and semi-discretized time-dependent PDEs show improved accuracy over trajectory-based objectives.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Learning paradigms for dynamical systems. Rows separate trajectory-based (top) from velocity-based objectives (bottom). (a) Rollout training simulates the learned dynamics via numerical integration, and minimizes the discrepancy between the predicted x̂k and ground truth x(tk) states, with gradients backpropagated through the entire unrolled trajectory. (b) Teacher forcing spans both rows, as it admits either reading: it replaces multi-step rollouts with one-step predictions, avoiding backpropagation through time. As discussed in Section 2, its loss can equivalently be read as a regression of the learned increment onto finite difference estimates vk ≈ ∂tx(tk), at the observed states; the bottom panel shows the explicit Euler case, where the increment is f̂ itself. (c) Velocity Matching instead evaluates the learned velocity field f̂ along the piecewise-linear interpolant x̃(t) of the observations, at times t sampled uniformly over the observation window, and regresses it onto the derivative ∂tx̃(t) of the interpolant.

Figure 5: Validation and test errors - ODEs. (Left) Validation trajectory, velocity and Jacobian errors as functions of wall-clock training time, for Euler, Stuart–Landau and active Müller–Brown systems. Solid lines denote the mean, and shaded areas the standard deviation, over three independent runs. (Right) Test trajectory error against the total training time, for each independent run. Trajectory-based strategies saturate at a common error level, whereas VM attains errors up to one order of magnitude lower, at a training cost comparable with that of TF.

papers.abstract: Joint-embedding predictive architectures (JEPAs) have recently emerged as general-purpose visual world models for control. A prominent example is LeWorldModel (LeWM), which trains end-to-end from pixels using an isotropic Gaussian anti-collapse regularizer (SIGReg) and plans by minimizing the squared Euclidean distance between predicted and goal embeddings. In this work, we investigate the test-time robustness of this latent planning interface. Analyzing the learned metric on Push-T, we first find that task-relevant object state heavily dominates latent distance: shifting the block by a single pixel displaces the embedding $3\times$ further than an equivalent agent shift, and swapping the block pose alone accounts for $99\%$ of the distance between scene pairs. However, because this pose information is distributed across a curved, high-dimensional manifold rather than a fixed linear subspace, the encoder cannot be trivially edited post-hoc to isolate or redirect it. We next demonstrate that this geometry is highly vulnerable at test time. A white-box $\ell_\infty$ perturbation of just $ε{=}4/255$ applied to a single input frame causes the encoder to register the block at an arbitrary, attacker-chosen pose in $73$--$95\%$ of scenes without disturbing the encoded agent state. Perturbing either the goal image or the live camera observation drops Push-T planning success from $87\%$ to $32\%$, whereas uniform random noise at twice the magnitude has negligible impact. This vulnerability persists across all four standard LeWM benchmarks (Push-T, Two-Room, Reacher, and OGBench-Cube). At $ε{=}8/255$, the attack bridges $82$--$97\%$ of the squared latent distance to the target embedding in every environment, inducing planning degradation proportional to each task's reliance on the spoofed entity.
bullets: LeWM’s latent distance is dominated by task-relevant object pose: changing block pose explains 99% of scene-pair distance, while a one-pixel block shift has much greater effect than an equivalent agent shift.
A white-box ℓ∞ attack with ε=4/255 can make the encoder perceive an attacker-chosen block pose in 73–95% of scenes without altering the encoded agent state.
Perturbing either the goal image or live observation reduces Push-T planning success from 87% to 32%; random noise at twice the magnitude has negligible impact.
The vulnerability transfers across Push-T, Two-Room, Reacher, and OGBench-Cube, with larger attacks bridging most of the latent distance to the target embedding.
The attack’s planning impact scales with how strongly each task relies on the spoofed entity.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview. Top: LeWM encodes the camera frame ot and the goal image og with a frozen ViT-Tiny encoder Eθ , forecasts the latent ẑH under candidate actions with an action-conditioned transformer predictor Pψ , and a CEM planner searches for the actions that minimize the latent cost C. Bottom: our attacker (orange) leaves all of this untouched. It (1) renders a counterfactual scene õ in which the task object is displaced, (2) encodes it with the public encoder to a target z⋆, (3) optimizes an L∞-bounded perturbation δ with Eθ(o+δ) ≈ z⋆ by gradient steps through the encoder, and (4) adds δ to the goal image (i) or to the camera frames (ii). papers.title: Spoofing the Latent State: Imperceptible Goal-Image Attacks Derail Planning in LeWorldModel

papers.abstract: Tracking points that leave the camera's field of view (FoV) requires reasoning about unobserved scene dynamics, a fundamentally different problem from tracking visible correspondences. We present TAP-Out, an offline method that makes this out-of-view (OOV) reasoning explicit by leveraging generative video outpainting as a world-model prior. Given a narrow-FoV input video, TAP-Out outpaints a complete 360° equirectangular video, locates target objects within the panoramic scene via video object segmentation, and synthesises object-centred perspective crops on which standard in-frame trackers operate. This decoupled design composes off-the-shelf foundation models without requiring task-specific architectural modifications. On the TAPVid360 benchmark, TAP-Out achieves state-of-the-art performance, improving OOV tracking accuracy by approximately 3x over the best prior method. We demonstrate its flexibility on out-of-frame object segmentation and detection and we provide detailed diagnostic analyses across motion regimes, static versus dynamic content, and hallucination quality, characterising when and why the approach succeeds or fails. Code is publicly available at https://github.com/finlay-hudson/TAP-Out
bullets: Addresses out-of-view tracking, which requires inferring unobserved scene dynamics rather than matching visible correspondences.
Outpaints a complete 360° equirectangular video, segments target objects panoramically, and generates perspective crops for conventional tracking.
Combines off-the-shelf foundation models without task-specific architectural changes.
Achieves approximately 3× higher out-of-view tracking accuracy than the prior best method on TAPVid360.
Also supports out-of-frame segmentation and detection, with analyses of motion, scene dynamics, and hallucination quality.

papers.abstract: Future dynamic novel-view synthesis requires extrapolating multiple motion regimes within the same scene. A single dynamics model may not simultaneously represent stationary regions, coordinated motion, local interactions, and articulated trajectories. We introduce Motion Regime Expert Routing for Gaussian Splatting (MoRE-GS), a causal, render-aware framework for forecasting dynamic 3D Gaussian scenes. MoRE-GS freezes a Gaussian representation reconstructed exclusively from the observed temporal prefix and forecasts its control-keypoint motion using four complementary experts: persistence, a coefficient-space Transformer, a graph convolutional network, and a structured Transformer with rigid and non-rigid motion constraints. A compact routing table assigns expert mixtures across soft motion groups and forecast-horizon bins, while a persistence gate suppresses unreliable extrapolation. Across D-NeRF and HyperNeRF scenes, MoRE-GS achieves improved performance against other methods, and these results demonstrate that renderer-calibrated composition of complementary motion predictors improves causal dynamic Gaussian forecasting across heterogeneous motion regimes. Project page: https://advanced-vision-and-learning-lab.github.io/MoRE-GS-website/
bullets: Addresses the challenge of extrapolating stationary, coordinated, interactive, and articulated motion within one scene.
Freezes a Gaussian representation from the observed temporal prefix and predicts control-keypoint motion causally.
Combines persistence, coefficient-space Transformer, graph convolutional, and rigid/non-rigid structured Transformer experts.
Uses a compact routing table and persistence gate to select expert mixtures and suppress unreliable forecasts.
Improves performance over other methods on D-NeRF and HyperNeRF scenes, according to the abstract.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in video generation have achieved impressive visual quality, yet they often fail to produce physically consistent dynamics due to the lack of explicit modeling of underlying physical processes. Existing approaches either rely on simulators with strong assumptions or use coarse semantic guidance, and further struggle to effectively inject physical priors into generation models. In this work, we propose Seeing the Unseen, a unified framework for physics-grounded video generation. Our approach decomposes the problem into two stages: learning physical dynamics and injecting them into video synthesis. First, we introduce a lightweight Particle-based Graph Dynamics Simulator (PGDS) that learns generalizable physical interactions from data and predicts plausible 3D motion trajectories. Second, we propose a Visible--Invisible Motion Field (VIMF) that captures both motion observable in the input frame and motion that emerges over time due to object dynamics. This representation enables more complete and structured motion guidance compared to conventional physical signals. By integrating these trajectories into a diffusion-based generator, our method produces videos that are both visually coherent and physically consistent. Extensive experiments demonstrate improved motion accuracy, interaction consistency, and reduced physical artifacts compared to strong baselines.
bullets: Addresses physically implausible dynamics in video generation caused by weak or coarse physical modeling.
Uses a lightweight Particle-based Graph Dynamics Simulator to learn interactions and predict plausible 3D trajectories.
Introduces a Visible–Invisible Motion Field that represents observed motion and motion emerging over time.
Injects the learned motion guidance into a diffusion-based video generator.
Experiments report improved motion accuracy, interaction consistency, and fewer physical artifacts than strong baselines.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of our proposed framework. Given an input image, we first lift it into a 3D scene particle representation. A particle-based graph dynamics simulator then predicts physically plausible 3D motion trajectories, which are rendered into reference-visible and future- merg nt motions to guide physically consistent video generation.

Figure 3: Architecture of the physics-guided video generation model. The visible and future visible motion fields are encoded by a frozen 3D VAE and concatenated with the noisy video latent along the channel dimension. A zero-initialized injection strategy preserves the pretrained model behavior while progressively incorporating motion guidance.

Figure 4: Qualitative comparison with existing methods. Our method produces physically plausible dynamics with accurate object interactions (e.g., correct collision responses and domino chain propagation), while baseline models frequently exhibit artifacts such as object interpenetration, implausible motion trajectories, or failure to trigger expected physical events.

Figure 8: Unified motion encoding and injection pipeline. The visible tracking video Vvis and future-visible tracking video Vfv are encoded using a frozen 3D VAE to obtain two latent sequences. These are concatenated with the noisy video latent to form a multi-channel input to the diffusion transformer. To preserve pretrained behavior, the patch embedding weights corresponding to tracking channels are zero-initialized, while the original weights are copied from the pretrained model. The first frame is injected via noise replacement to provide appearance conditioning.

Figure 7: Architecture of the Particle-based Graph Dynamics Simulator (PGDS). The simulator follows an Encode–Process–Decode pipeline. Given particle states, a graph is first constructed based on spatial proximity. Node and edge features are encoded to capture material properties and geometric relations. A message-passing processor then iteratively propagates interaction effects across the graph. Finally, a decoder predicts particle velocities, which are used to update positions and roll out future dynamics.

For each comparison, human annotators judge which method produces better results across three criteria: (a) instruction-following, measuring how faithfully the generated video adheres to the given text prompt; (b) video quality, assessing visual fidelity, temporal coherence, and artifact severity; and (c) overall preference. papers.abstract: Planning with world models enables test-time adaptation for embodied agents, offering superior generalization over direct policy learning. However, long-horizon tasks remain hindered by cumulative errors and search complexity. Existing hierarchical methods often use rigid macro-actions or latent skills, leading to brittle representations and limited fine-grained control. We introduce ID-WM (Implicit Dynamics World Models), a hierarchical world model that decouples state-space reachability from local control. Our framework utilizes a high-level model to sample feasible transitions across the state manifold and a low-level world model as an inverse dynamics solver to ground these transitions into precise actions. This allows the planner to identify reachable subgoals without being constrained by low-level execution details. By prioritizing local physical feasibility over global behavioral patterns, ID-WM synthesizes novel long-horizon plans from short segments, transcending the specific behavioral modes seen during training. We demonstrate its effectiveness across three navigation and manipulation suites, achieving a 38.5% improvement over state-of-the-art policy and diffusion-based planners. Crucially, by leveraging this hierarchical structure to mitigate compounding errors, our approach yields a 135% performance gain over single-level world model MPC, particularly in complex, unseen configurations for long-horizon tasks. Videos can be viewed at https://id-wm.github.io
authors: Gaoyue Zhou, Yvonne Wu, Zichen Jeff Cui, Nicolas Ballas, Mido Assran, Lerrel Pinto, Yann LeCun
bullets: Addresses compounding prediction errors and search complexity in long-horizon planning.
Uses a high-level model to sample feasible state transitions and a low-level inverse-dynamics model to realize them.
Enables fine-grained control without rigid macro-actions or fixed latent skills.
Synthesizes novel long-horizon plans from short segments, including in unseen configurations.
Improves performance by 38.5% over state-of-the-art policy and diffusion planners and by 135% over single-level world-model MPC across three navigation and manipulation suites.

papers.abstract: World action models (WAMs) learn latent variables from observations and use these to both predict the evolution of the scene and to generate actions. The prediction has to be of the whole scene, whereas only a portion of the scene causes actions. WAMs fitted to demonstrations do not, in general, guarantee that they will generate actions solely from the latent causes of the demonstrated actions (the action-relevant latent variables), as the model could just as well learn to imitate in this way whilst entangling the action-relevant latent variables with the nuisance variables. We therefore separate out what causes action from what prediction depends on. We prove that under a sparsity constraint the latent variables used to generate actions are an invertible function of the action-relevant latent variables alone and the true structure is identified up to a permutation of the latent variables. This requires neither sufficient temporal dependence nor any assumptions on how the unobserved regimes evolve and holds even when the action-relevant latent variables are statistically dependent on the rest. We therefore propose CWAM (Causal WAM), which incorporates the constraint into a pretrained WAM by adding a sparse routing path to its action head, with the world modeling objective remaining unchanged. Experiments on both synthetic data and real-world robots validate the theory as well as showcase the improved efficiency in closed-loop success.
authors: Juntao Cheng, Jinzhou Tang, Fan Feng, Henrik I. Christensen, Yujia Zheng
bullets: WAMs may entangle action-relevant factors with nuisance variables when learning from demonstrations.
A sparsity constraint separates variables needed for action generation from those needed for full-scene prediction.
Under this constraint, action latents are identifiable up to permutation, without requiring sufficient temporal dependence or independent latent factors.
CWAM adds a sparse routing path to a pretrained WAM’s action head while leaving world modeling unchanged.
Synthetic and real-robot experiments support the theory and show improved closed-loop success efficiency.
