papers.selection_reason: Causal separation of action-relevant latents in world action models with robot validation; directly fits latent action and interactive world model interests.
papers.title: CausalWAM: Learning the Causes of Actions in World Action Models
papers.tldr: CausalWAM identifies and uses only the latent factors that cause demonstrated actions, improving closed-loop action efficiency without changing the world-modeling objective.

papers.abstract: Neural emulators of chaotic PDEs are trained on one-step prediction but deployed autoregressively, where their errors compound. Jacobian-based regularisers aim to curb this growth, but in a chaotic system part of the growth is physical and cannot be trained away. We separate the two sources of this error with a first-order decomposition. We compare the emulator's error with a counterfactual that propagates the same one-step mistakes through the solver's Jacobian, giving an amplification ratio: the factor by which the model's own dynamics amplify its errors. We study 21 configurations across four PDEs, five architectures and two model sizes (8-10k and 33k parameters), with errors measured at one Lyapunov time. Jacobian fine-tuning reduced the error by more than 10% for 1 of 34 seeds whose amplification ratio was at most 1.25, and for all 20 seeds whose ratio was at least four; for the latter, the error fell by a factor of 8 (small models) and 55 (33k models) in geometric mean over seeds. The gain approximately equals the one-step accuracy cost of fine-tuning divided by the amplification ratio. Matching the solver's Jacobian along the model's own error direction (EDJM) outperformed random directions at the same cost on 28 of 35 seeds; input-noise injection performed comparably to EDJM.
bullets: Chaotic PDE forecast error combines unavoidable physical growth with amplification caused by the emulator’s dynamics.
The study introduces an amplification ratio by comparing model errors with a counterfactual propagated through the solver’s Jacobian.
Across 21 configurations spanning four PDEs, five architectures, and two model sizes, fine-tuning helped all seeds with amplification ratios of at least four, but few with ratios at most 1.25.
For strongly amplifying models, geometric-mean error decreased by factors of 8 for small models and 55 for larger models at one Lyapunov time.
Error-direction Jacobian matching generally beat random-direction matching, while input-noise injection performed comparably to error-direction matching.

papers.selection_reason: Jacobian-based regularization for stable autoregressive dynamics emulation; transferable to learned world models.
papers.title: When Does Jacobian Fine-Tuning Stabilize Neural PDE Emulators?
papers.tldr: Jacobian fine-tuning stabilizes neural PDE emulators mainly when their own dynamics strongly amplify prediction errors, while offering little benefit when amplification is weak.

papers.abstract: World-action models increasingly apply test-time scaling, spending extra inference computation on candidate selection and adaptive allocation to improve control. Such gains are credible only when candidates carry exploitable signal, nominal compute savings become real speedup, and evaluation stays reliable. We audit all three on Cosmos Policy and RoboCasa with a premise-first, pre-registered methodology. On clean data, a learned value selector is 1.66 pp worse than random; a hindsight oracle gains only 1.40 pp, with an episode-level interval spanning zero; and 82% of states show identical candidate outcomes, leaving little selection headroom. Token pruning cuts per-forward FLOPs by up to 47% but yields at most a measured 1.15$\times$ end-to-end speedup on the deployed path (1.25$\times$ on a decode-excluded path), short of a 1.5$\times$ target, and our adaptive-allocation experiment is inconclusive under a power gate. We further identify and fix a silent rendering corruption whose rate rises sharply along compute-heavy planning paths while leaving the official direct-policy result unaffected, and release a detector, fix, and scripts. These findings show why test-time scaling should be audited as a chain of premises (decision signal, realized efficiency, evaluationintegrity) rather than by success rate alone. Conclusions are scoped to the tested configuration.
authors: Jun Liu, Dajie Sun, Zhenglun Kong, Zhenjiang Fan, Peiyan Dong, Fan Yang, Wenbin Zhangg, Geng Yuan, Xue Lin, Yanzhi Wang, Dong Huang
bullets: On clean Cosmos Policy and RoboCasa data, a learned value selector underperforms random selection, while a hindsight oracle offers only limited, statistically uncertain gains.
Most states (82%) have identical candidate outcomes, leaving little headroom for candidate selection.
Token pruning reduces per-forward FLOPs by up to 47%, but achieves at most 1.15× measured end-to-end speedup on the deployed path; adaptive allocation remains inconclusive.
A silent rendering corruption increases on compute-heavy planning paths without affecting the official direct-policy result.
The authors release a corruption detector, fix, and scripts, and recommend auditing decision signal, realized efficiency, and evaluation integrity separately.

figures.caption: Figure 2. A premise-first audit of test-time scaling in Cosmos Policy on RoboCasa. (1) Planning selection. Limited variation in candidate outcomes constrains the headroom for selection, and the deployable value selector underperforms random selection, while the hindsight oracle provides only modest evidence of improvement. (2) Adaptive allocati n. Substantial nominal FLOPs reductions translate into modest end-to-end latency gains, while the joint allocation effect remains unresolved at the available noise and statistical power. (3) Evaluation reliability. Rendering corruption becomes much more frequent in the compute-intensive planning path than under directpolicy or best-of-N evaluation, while the official direct-policy result remains essentially unaffected. All findings are scoped to the tested Cosmos Policy–RoboCasa configuration.

Figure 5. The premise-first methodology as a chain of gates. Each candidate test-time-scaling gain passes three checks in order before it is credited: verify that the decision signal exists (causal ablation and oracle ceiling); a statistical power gate that halts a run which cannot resolve the pre-registered outcome; and closed-loop measurement under framebuffer-sentinel render-integrity checking. A “no” at the first gate reports a negative result and at the second an inconclusive one, separating a genuine negative from an underpowered or invalid measurement.

Figure 3. Auditing best-of-N planning selection. (a) Success-rate difference against the random baseline for the deployable value selector and the hindsight oracle, under state-level and episode-level bootstrap, with 95% CIs. The value selector is below zero under both schemes; the oracle estimate crosses zero under episodelevel resampling and is an upper bound, not a deployable selector. (b) Only a minority of query states show any outcome variation across candidates and repeated executions, leaving little for a selector to recover in the rest; a stricter decomposition (Supplement Section 13) further separates stable between-candidate differences from variation that is not stable across repeats.

Table 1. Measured per-forward FLOPs (a), measured end-to-end query speedup under whole-frame token pruning (b), and the measured dense-query component breakdown (c), on Cosmos Policy (RoboCasa, batch 1, 5 denoising steps, 11 latent frames × 196 tokens = 2156; NVIDIA RTX A6000, bf16, eager, N = 30). Panel (b) directly times the complete query, dense against pruned, not a composition of component times: the deployed path is the query as the eval calls it (future-image decode and value extraction included); the decodeexcluded path removes future-image decode on both sides and is most favorable to pruning. This is a latency-only measurement (dropped frames receive zero output), so action quality is not assessed; no pruning level on either path reaches the pre-registered 1.5× target. Setup, environment and result-file paths are in Supplement Section 9.

Table 3. Full end-to-end query latency under whole-frame token pruning, both paths, all levels (Cosmos Policy, RoboCasa, batch 1, 5 denoising steps; NVIDIA RTX A6000, bf16, eager). Every value is directly measured over N = 30 timed queries per cell; median with the 10th and 90th percentiles. The deployed path is the query as the eval calls it (future-image decode and value extraction included); the decode-excluded path removes future-image decode on both sides. Speedup is dense median divided by pruned median. No pruning level on either path reaches the pre-registered 1.5× target. This expands the medians and speedups of main-body Table 1(b).

Table 4. Of 48 varying states, only 20 (7.6%) have a stable between-candidate outcome difference; the other 28 exhibit variation without satisfying the stable-separation criterion. All 28 are graded (0.5 vs 0 or 0.5 vs 1); none is a full-repeat flip. Repeat disagreement concentrates in TurnOnStove (per-candidate repeat agreement 0.83 vs 0.97–1.00 elsewhere).

papers.selection_reason: Empirical audit of test-time search for world action models; relevant to interactive world models and test-time learning.
papers.title: When Does Test-Time Search Help World Action Models? An Empirical Audit of Candidate Selection and Simulator Integrity
papers.tldr: An audit finds that test-time search provides little reliable benefit for the tested world-action-model setup because candidate selection has weak signal, compute savings translate poorly to end-to-end speedups, and simulator corruption can undermine evaluation.

papers.abstract: Accurate forecasting with uncertainty quantification is critical in a variety of scientific applications ranging from epidemiology and economics to energy systems and earth sciences. Yet most forecasting models still need to be developed and trained separately for each domain-specific dataset. Time series foundation models (TSFMs) aim to remove this limitation and enable the application of the same model across domains through large-scale pretraining. However, most existing TSFMs treat each time series independently and therefore cannot model interactions among time series and external drivers. Here, we introduce Chronos-2, a foundation model for zero-shot forecasting that models the interactions between multivariate time series and heterogeneous covariates, which commonly arise in scientific applications. The model infers relationships among time series directly from historical context and generates probabilistic forecasts without task-specific treatment. Across various benchmarks, Chronos-2 achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on average by improving skill scores by 5.2 percentage points relative to the strongest baselines and increasing win rates by 10 percentage points. Chronos-2 is also computationally efficient, generating forecasts for 100 time series in under one second on a single mid-range GPU, 50x and 1000x faster end-to-end than the best task-specific point and probabilistic forecasters, respectively. In addition, we demonstrate its effectiveness in diverse scientific settings -- including infectious-disease forecasting, macroeconomic modeling, carbon-flux prediction, and runoff simulation -- where the model matches or surpasses specialized methods developed for each domain. These results show that a single pretrained model can capture structure shared across temporal systems.
authors: Abdul Fatir Ansari, Oleksandr Shchur, Jaris K\"uken, Andreas Auer, Boran Han, Pedro Mercado, Syama Sundar Rangapuram, Huibin Shen, Lorenzo Stella, Xiyuan Zhang, Mononito Goswami, Shubham Kapoor, Danielle C. Maddix, Pablo Guerron, Florian Saupe, Markus Reichstein, Tony Hu, Junming Yin, Nick Erickson, Prateek Mutalik Desai, Hao Wang, Huzefa Rangwala, George Karypis, Yuyang Wang, Michael Bohlke-Schneider
bullets: Addresses the limitation of existing time-series foundation models that forecast each series independently.
Infers relationships among multivariate series directly from historical context without task-specific treatment.
Achieves strong average benchmark performance, improving skill scores by 5.2 percentage points and win rates by 10 percentage points over the strongest baselines.
Produces forecasts for 100 time series in under one second on a single mid-range GPU and is substantially faster than task-specific forecasters.
Performs competitively with specialized methods in infectious-disease, macroeconomic, carbon-flux, and runoff forecasting.

figures.caption: Figure 1: The complete Chronos-2 pipeline. (a) Architecture overview: Input time series (targets and covariates) are first normalized (scaling) and then tokenized for downstream processing. The Transformer stack alternates between time and group attention layers. The output from the Transformer stack is mapped to quantile predictions through a neural network. The figure illustrates two time series tasks, the first (in cyan) with two targets and one known (future) covariate, and the second (in pink) with one target and two known covariates. (b) Tokenization: Meta features are appended to the time series which indicate the position of an observation (time index) and whether it is missing (mask). Time series and meta features are split into non-overlapping patches and mapped to high-dimensional embeddings via a neural network. (c) Attention layers: Each Transformer block alternates between time and group attention layers: the time attention layer aggregates information across patches within a single time series, and the group attention layer aggregates information across all series within a group at each patch index. The groups corresponding to the two time series tasks are highlighted in cyan and pink. A group is a flexible notion of relatedness and may correspond to a single time series, multiple series sharing a source or metadata, variates of a multivariate series, or targets along with associated covariates. The group attention layer enables the model to infer relationships between different time series in the group based on the available context at inference time (in-context learning).

Figure 5: Zero-shot forecasting of complex human-centric systems. (a) Forecasting incidence of Acute Respiratory Infection (ARI) and Influenza-Like Illness (ILI) across 31 European countries. Performance is evaluated using the Weighted Interval Score (WIS) relative to a simple quantile baseline provided by RespiCast (European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control, 2026), calculated as log2(WISbaseline/WISmodel); values greater than 0 indicate improvement over the baseline. Plots show the median relative WIS (solid lines) and 95% confidence intervals (shaded bands) over 67 rolling evaluation windows (Oct 2024–Jan 2026). In univariate mode (U), Chronos-2 is competitive at short horizons (1 week) against the operational RespiCast Hub-Ensemble (a consensus of mechanistic and statistical models). At longer horizons (> 1 week), Chronos-2 significantly outperforms the ensemble, with in-context learning yielding further gains by exploiting cross-country correlations (Wilcoxon signed-rank test p < 0.001). (b) Joint forecasting of German Consumer Price Index (CPI) components (2021–2025). Performance is measured by the Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE) relative to a Seasonal Naive baseline, log2(RMSEbaseline/RMSEmodel). While univariate inference (U) performs comparably to robust statistical baselines, enabling in-context learning significantly improves accuracy by leveraging shared structural patterns within CPI groups. Pairwise comparisons (right) confirm that Chronos-2 outperforms the strongest baseline (AutoETS) on the majority of item-window pairs (Wilcoxon signed-rank test p < 0.001 for both 3-month and 12-month horizons).

Figure 3: Evaluation of Chronos-2 on time series forecasting benchmarks (best viewed in color on a screen). Performance is evaluated using the Mean Absolute Scaled Error (MASE) and Scaled/Weighted Quantile Loss (SQL/WQL) for point and probabilistic forecasts, respectively. The Win Rate measures the proportion of pairwise comparisons where a model outperforms competitors, while the Skill Score reflects the average percentage improvement over a Seasonal Naive baseline. Dark purple bars denote Chronos-2 in univariate mode (group attention disabled); light purple segments highlight the performance gain attributed to in-context learning (ICL) via group attention. Error bars indicate 95% confidence intervals obtained through bootstrapping. (a) Results on fev-bench (n = 100 tasks), a rigorous benchmark where 68 tasks involve multivariate dependencies. Chronos-2 outperforms all baselines, including statistical ensembles, tree-based methods, task-specific deep learning models, and existing foundation models, while maintaining fast inference speed; Wilcoxon signed-rank test p < 10−6 against all baselines (see Tables S4 and S5 in the Appendix for results in tabular format and Table S6 for the p-values). (b) Results on Chronos-Bench-II (n = 27 tasks) and GIFT-Eval (n = 97 tasks), which focus primarily on univariate forecasting. Chronos-2 outperforms or ties state-of-the-art methods; notably, enabling ICL yields performance improvements even in these univariate settings by retrieving patterns across related series. n.s. indicates that the performance difference relative to Chronos-2 is not statistically significant (p ≥ 0.05) based on the Wilcoxon signed-rank test; see Tables S7, S8, S10 and S11 in the Appendix for results in tabular format and Tables S9 and S12 for the p-values.

Figure 6: Ecosystem carbon and energy flux prediction with Chronos-2. We evaluate the performance of Chronos-2 on daily eddy-covariance targets from the FLUXNET collection (Pastorello et al., 2020). (a) Comparison of the distribution of site-level RMSE across 65 sites for net ecosystem exchange (NEE), latent heat flux (LE), and sensible heat flux (H) over the June–August 2020 evaluation window between supervised regression baselines (XGBoost, trained either as a single pooled model across sites or as site-specific models) and Chronos-2 in zero-shot mode. Box plots show the median (center line), interquartile range (box limits), and 1.5× interquartile range (whiskers); points denote outliers. (b) Representative summer time series at the Monte Bondone site in Italy (IT-MBo), showing observed fluxes (black) and Chronos-2 predictions from the meteorological covariates with 10–90% prediction intervals (red shaded); the corresponding covariates (TA, SW_IN and VPD) are shown below. (c) Rolling one-month-ahead forecasting over the full year 2020. For each evaluation month, models condition on the preceding 12 months of context and predict the subsequent month (step size: 1 month). Bars report normalized RMSE (RMSE divided by the target standard deviation) stratified by prediction month for Chronos-2 and XGBoost, highlighting seasonal variations in predictability across NEE, LE, and H.

Figure 8: Hierarchical forecasting with Chronos-2. (a) Mean and maximum coherence error on the Tourism-Q and Tourism-M datasets for Chronos-2 (U) and Chronos-2 (ICL). Enabling ICL reduces the coherence error on both datasets. (b) Root-level forecasts on Tourism-Q. Solid red line shows the direct forecast generated by the respective models for the root level, while the dashed blue line shows the bottom-up aggregated forecasts. The shaded region shows the coherence gap. Chronos-2 (ICL) produces a narrower gap than Chronos-2 (U) indicating that group attention implicitly learns the aggregation structure. (c) Distribution of per-series scaled quantile loss (SQL) with bottom-up reconciliation on Tourism-Q (left) and Tourism-M (right). Chronos-2 (ICL) achieves the lowest median SQL on both datasets (0.56 and 0.60, respectively), outperforming the end-to-end HierE2E model trained specifically for hierarchical coherence as well as ETS and ARIMA statistical baselines. Methods are ordered by median SQL.

Figure 4: Qualitative analysis of in-context learning (best viewed in color on a screen). Probabilistic forecasts show the 10% to 90% quantile interval; bar charts show SQL forecast errors per time step. (a) Retail sales forecasting: univariate inference versus in-context learning with covariates including promotions, customer traffic, and holiday indicators. Covariates are shown in the lower panels. (b) Regime change: store closure at different positions relative to the forecast horizon. The top and bottom rows show the same series with different forecast origins, so that the closure falls within the forecast horizon (top) or entirely within the historical context (bottom). (c) Scenario analysis with simulated future covariates: promotion intensity (top four panels) and customer count trajectories (bottom panel) varied across hypothetical trajectories. (d) Energy load forecasting: univariate, past-only covariates, and full covariates (air temperature, dew temperature, sea-level pressure). The three rows show progressively more covariate information available to the model.

Figure 2: Generation of multivariate synthetic training data. We generate multivariate synthetic time series by applying random transformation functions to time series sampled from univariate generators. Univariate generators produce diverse temporal patterns to serve as the building blocks for multivariate data. These include: (a.1) KernelSynth (Ansari et al., 2024a), which draws samples from Gaussian processes defined by the random composition of basic kernels (e.g., linear, periodic); (a.2) Trend-Seasonality-Irregularity (TSI), which stochastically combines structural components; and parametric simulations using random (a.3) Autoregressive (AR) and (a.4) Exponential Smoothing (ETS) processes. (b.1) Instantaneous transformations impose coupling between variables without time delays. A mixing function transforms univariate samples at each time step. We employ (b.2) random linear operators (e.g., random dense, sparse, sign or aggregation matrices) and (b.3) non-linear mappings via random Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs) to simulate complex static dependencies. (c.1) Sequential transformations introduce time-delayed relationships between time series. A random function maps a look-back window of univariate series to multivariate outputs. We generate (c.2) linear lead-lag relationships via a Temporal Causal Model, which samples sparse directed edges across time and variates (simulating Vector Autoregression), while (c.3) non-linear dynamic correlations are introduced via random Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs).

Figure 7: Rainfall-runoff simulation using Chronos-2. Performance is evaluated using the Nash–Sutcliffe Efficiency (NSE), where a score of 1.0 represents perfect correspondence between simulated and observed discharge. (a) Top: Distribution of NSE scores across 1,582 catchments in the CAMELS-DE dataset. The zero-shot Chronos-2 (ICL) model achieves a median NSE of 0.68, significantly outperforming univariate inference (Chronos-2 (U), NSE=0.15) by leveraging meteorological covariates. While the domain-specific LSTM ensemble achieves higher performance (NSE=0.90), fine-tuning Chronos-2 (FT) bridges this gap, matching state-of-the-art performance without ensembling, access to static attributes, or training on the NSE metric. Box plots show the median (center line), interquartile range (box limits), and 1.5× interquartile range (whiskers). Bottom: Exceedance probability curves showing the cumulative proportion of basins (y-axis) achieving an NSE score greater than or equal to a specific threshold (x-axis). The fine-tuned model closely tracks the reliability profile of the LSTM ensemble. (b) Hydrograph for a single catchment (DE110180) over one year. The zero-shot prediction (top) captures the relationship between rainfall and runoff but exhibits high uncertainty (shaded region denotes 10-90% prediction interval). Fine-tuning (bottom) tightens the predictive distribution, accurately modeling the discharge.

Table 1: Ablation study on training data composition, group attention, and long-context training. All metrics are reported as skill scores (higher is better). For each ablation group, the reference model is shown in bold. Training data ablations and the group attention ablation use the first stage (Stage-1) training protocol. †Equivalent to the Stage-1 checkpoint.

papers.selection_reason: Multivariate time-series foundation model predicting temporal dynamics with covariates; transferable to world-model learning.
papers.title: Chronos-2: A foundation model for multivariate time series forecasting
papers.tldr: Chronos-2 is a pretrained model for zero-shot probabilistic forecasting that captures interactions among multiple time series and heterogeneous external covariates across domains.

papers.abstract: Historically rare ''one-in-a-generation'' storms are occurring with unprecedented frequency, causing catastrophic damage and mounting casualties, and exposing the vulnerability of infrastructure designed around short observational records. To overcome the limitations of sparse data, we present StormGen, a generative machine-learning model that transforms an observed storm's initial hours into complete, physically plausible hourly rainfall lifecycles in minutes. Evaluated on a decade of southeast Texas rainfall, StormGen produced close counterparts for 4\5% of the most severe 2\% of storms--compared to just 3\% for stochastic storm transposition--and maintained spatial coherence over full 24-hour sequences. Crucially, from a single hour of initial rainfall, the model successfully reconstructed the specific lifecycle, spatial pattern, and extreme catchment totals of Hurricane Harvey itself, despite the event being entirely absent in training. Because storm timing alone can more than double peak flows, these complete generated scenarios provide a vital mechanism to stress-test flood protections against unprecedented extremes.
authors: Valerie Tsao, Nathaniel W. Chaney, Manolis Veveakis, Marta Zaniolo
bullets: Addresses infrastructure vulnerability caused by short rainfall records and increasingly frequent rare storms.
Uses generative machine learning to complete observed storm beginnings into full hourly rainfall sequences.
On a decade of southeast Texas data, closely matched 45% of the most severe 2% of storms, versus 3% for stochastic storm transposition.
Reconstructed Hurricane Harvey’s lifecycle, spatial pattern, and extreme catchment totals from only its first hour, despite its absence from training.
Generated scenarios can stress-test flood protections because storm timing strongly affects peak flows.

figures.caption: Figure 2: StormGen generates realistic, nonduplicate storms and improves coverage of the extreme tail. (a) Continuous ranked probability score (CRPS) of StormGen and SST ensemble against HRRR by lead time; lower is better. Lines show means and shading shows the spread across events. (b) Spatial power spectra of rainfall fields. Higher spatial frequencies correspond to finer-scale features, such as localized area of heavy rain. (c) Distance of each event to its nearest training event against its similarity to an independent held-out reference set, with marginal densities. The shaded region marks events that resemble observations without duplicating training events. These quantities measure duplication and resemblance, not the probability of physical realism. (d) Percentage of reference events in each severity class that have a close counterpart in each catalog, at a fixed tolerance in storm-property space. Error bars show pointwise 95% percentile bootstrap confidence intervals from 2,000 resamples of reference events within each severity class, with candidate catalogs and matching criteria held fixed. papers.abstract: Motion planning in clutter is embodiment-specific: the feasible free space and reachable commands depend on each robot's geometry and dynamics. Existing cross-embodiment policies output normalized commands that disregard these differences, or compensate through per-robot training and distillation. World models can in principle pool cross-embodiment data, yet command-conditioned models bind their latent dynamics to a single action space, while pose-conditioned models omit the mapping from commands to body-specific motion. On flat ground, however, embodiment affects the planner's observations only through the camera ego-motion. This letter proposes Hourglass, an hourglass-shaped architecture that factorizes cross-embodiment motion planning at this interface: a body-agnostic world model and each robot's differentiable ego-dynamics, which map commands to that ego-motion, are coupled only through it. The world model is trained on data pooled across embodiments and camera mounts; each robot's ego-dynamics is a reduced-order template with identified physical parameters. A generalist parameter-conditioned policy is learned once at this junction: each imagined step rolls out the template and then the world model, and imagination training through each robot's template makes the policy body-aware. On seven simulated robots of five locomotion types, the generalist policy outperforms imitation-learning and diffusion-policy baselines on the same world model by 3.8--10.6 percentage points in success rate and matches per-robot specialists without dedicated training, while approaching its parameter-conditioned MPPI teacher within 1.4--2.8 points without an online map. After three minutes of teleoperated driving for identification, the synthetic-data-trained model transfers zero-shot to a real skid-steer robot unseen in training, navigating unseen indoor scenes.
authors: Zhidong Wang, Zirui Li, Haoran Xu, Yujie Yan, Zitong Shan, Jingsong Liang, Han Yu, Chen Lv
bullets: Addresses embodiment-specific feasibility caused by differences in robot geometry and dynamics.
Factors planning through camera ego-motion: a shared world model is coupled to robot-specific command-to-motion dynamics.
Trains a single parameter-conditioned generalist policy using imagined rollouts through each robot’s dynamics template.
Across seven simulated robots spanning five locomotion types, it outperforms comparable baselines and matches per-robot specialists without dedicated training.
Transfers zero-shot to an unseen real skid-steer robot after three minutes of teleoperated identification, navigating unseen indoor scenes.

papers.abstract: Continuous-time world models generate a latent trajectory through a single ODE integration, but adding stochastic conditioning does not ensure that the model uses it. In our teacher-forced baseline, posterior means vary by only about 1% of the prior scale, and matched and swapped latents yield indistinguishable reconstruction PSNR at the reported precision. We study a supervision-shortcut hypothesis: ground-truth intermediate states can reduce the need for trajectory-associated latent information. We introduce SPT-Flow, which samples one latent per trajectory and matches a free-running ODE rollout to demonstration states at multiple readout times. Re-anchoring experiments support the proposed mechanism. On LIBERO, with both models trained for 30k optimizer steps, SPT-Flow improves best-of-10 PSNR over our retrained ODEWorld baseline by 2.0 and 2.4 dB at the mid-trajectory and final frames and reduces mean LPIPS by 23%, with comparable per-sample inference cost. The rollout control recovers most of the accuracy gain; learned latent conditioning adds diversity and best-of-K gains while reducing mean sample accuracy relative to this control. The diagnostics support trajectory-associated latent utilization; semantic mode coverage under matched conditions in the robotic setting remains unverified.
authors: Mingyang Lyu, Yinqian Sun, Gongce Cao, Yuhao Zhang, Lu Jia, Qian Zhang, Bo Wang, Pin Lyu
bullets: Teacher-forced training can make stochastic latents nearly unused because ground-truth intermediate states provide a shortcut.
SPT-Flow samples one latent per trajectory and matches a free-running ODE rollout to demonstration states at multiple readout times.
On LIBERO, it improves best-of-10 PSNR by 2.0 dB mid-trajectory and 2.4 dB at the final frame, while reducing mean LPIPS by 23% versus the retrained ODEWorld baseline.
A rollout-control variant recovers most accuracy gains; learned latent conditioning adds diversity and best-of-K gains but lowers mean per-sample accuracy.
Semantic mode coverage under matched robotic conditions remains unverified.

papers.title: SPT-Flow: One Integration, Many Futures in Continuous-Time World Models
papers.tldr: SPT-Flow improves continuous-time world models by training trajectory-level latents against free-running rollouts, encouraging latent use and producing more accurate, diverse futures.

papers.abstract: Learned world models ship as software components whose model versions, preprocessing, and test harnesses change between releases. Work on model updates already counts per-sample regressions, or negative flips, that an accuracy check hides. Two problems remain: a test can pass under one configuration and fail under another, and a harness fault can produce erroneous scores and wrong verdicts without a crash. We present TetraState, a regression-testing protocol for paired possible/impossible video tests. Each test runs under four fixed model-native configurations; its number of correct verdicts assigns one of four outcome classes. Inconclusive tests and failed executions are reported separately alongside the verdict rate. Revisions are compared by per-test outcome transitions, and the harness is versioned as part of the system under test. On all 506 IntPhys 2 Main tests and two heterogeneous systems, Cosmos 3 Nano and V-JEPA 2, two V-JEPA 2 harness revisions move modal accuracy by only 0.2 and 2.6 points yet change 11 and 214 test labels; in the second, accuracy rises although fewer tests are judged correctly, and 43 regressions keep the modal verdict, so a modal-verdict flip check misses them. These results outline a research agenda on configuration-level regression oracles for learned components.
authors: Junyu Huo, Zihao Wan, Ziqi Mao, Gouri Ginde
bullets: World-model releases can change model configurations, preprocessing, and test harnesses, causing inconsistent verdicts or faulty scores without crashes.
TetraState evaluates each paired possible/impossible video test under four fixed model-native configurations.
Tests are assigned one of four outcome classes based on correct verdict counts; inconclusive tests and failed executions are reported separately.
Per-test outcome transitions expose regressions that modal accuracy can hide: harness revisions changed 11 and 214 labels despite only 0.2- and 2.6-point modal-accuracy shifts.
The study motivates configuration-level regression oracles for learned components.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces TetraState, a regression-testing protocol specifically designed for learned video world models (Cosmos, V-JEPA), addressing the challenge of verifying model updates and harness configurations.
papers.title: One Verdict Is Not Enough: Regression Testing Learned World Models and Their Test Harnesses
papers.tldr: TetraState reveals configuration- and harness-level regressions in learned world models that aggregate accuracy and verdict-flip checks can miss.

papers.abstract: Latent dynamics learning has emerged as a prominent approach for Model Order Reduction (MOR) of time-dependent, parameterized Partial Differential Equations (PDEs). Traditional autoencoder-based approaches are intrinsically tied to fixed spatial discretizations during both training and inference, motivating the development of meshless methodologies. In this context, conditioning provides a natural mechanism for representing temporal evolution through spatially continuous functions, enabling mesh-agnostic Latent Dynamics Models (LDMs). In this work, we introduce a unified mathematical framework for mesh-agnostic LDMs based on conditioning in Neural Fields (NeFs). Leveraging a taxonomy of conditioning mechanisms (weak, strong, and pure), we formulate meshless LDMs as NeFs conditioned on a latent state. We establish a Universal Approximation Theorem (UAT) for this class of models and analyze their stability by deriving Lipschitz bounds for different conditioning mechanisms. Our analysis reveals an expressivity--stability trade-off, providing insight into why more expressive conditioning, despite its higher representational capacity, can potentially degrade performance during temporal extrapolation. Finally, we provide a comprehensive comparison of meshless and mesh-based architectures in the continuous limit of the spatial discretization, showing that meshless models guarantee grid-independent Lipschitz bounds, unlike mesh-based counterparts. Our experiments across Burgers' equation, Navier--Stokes flow past a cylinder, and linear advection show that meshless LDMs can achieve predictive accuracy comparable to or better than their mesh-based counterparts while using only 2% of the trainable parameters and exhibiting nearly constant error across spatial discretizations.
authors: Lorenzo Tomada, Federico Pichi, Gianluigi Rozza
bullets: Recasts meshless latent dynamics models as neural fields conditioned on a latent state, enabling inference across spatial discretizations.
Introduces a unified framework covering weak, strong, and pure conditioning mechanisms.
Proves a universal approximation theorem and derives Lipschitz stability bounds for each conditioning type.
Identifies an expressivity–stability trade-off: more expressive conditioning can impair temporal extrapolation.

Experiments on Burgers’ equation, cylinder-flow Navier–Stokes, and linear advection show comparable or better accuracy than mesh-based models, with 2% of their trainable parameters and nearly discretization-independent error.

papers.selection_reason: Meshless latent dynamics models conditioned on latent states are transferable to learned environment dynamics and world-model prediction.

papers.tldr: This paper develops mesh-agnostic latent dynamics models for PDE model reduction, with theory and experiments showing grid-independent stability and competitive accuracy using far fewer parameters.

papers.abstract: Continual reinforcement learning (CRL) requires agents to operate under environmental changes while reusing prior knowledge whenever possible. We argue that model-based reinforcement learning provides a promising framework for this setting because learned world models (WMs) can, in principle, support change detection, knowledge reuse, adaptation, and acquisition of new knowledge. However, such benefits depend heavily on whether the learned model can generalize beyond the contexts in which it was trained. In this work, we propose to formulate this problem with a contextual Markov decision process in which context is decomposed into behavioral and physical components. This view organizes continual WM learning into reuse, adaptation, and acquisition of new knowledge. As a first step, we study direct reuse when behavioral rules remain unchanged. Using Dyna-Q and TD-MPC in controlled FourRooms tasks, we find that zero-shot reuse can degrade substantially under physical-context changes and that this behavior depends strongly on the observation representation used by the WM. Additional ablation studies and latent-space diagnostics suggest that learned representations do not automatically provide the invariances needed for reuse. These results identify representation generalization as an important bottleneck for reliable world-model reuse in CRL.
bullets: Frames continual world-model learning as a contextual MDP with behavioral and physical context components.
Organizes continual learning into knowledge reuse, adaptation, and acquisition.
Studies direct reuse when behavioral rules stay fixed using Dyna-Q and TD-MPC in controlled FourRooms tasks.
Finds that physical-context changes can substantially degrade zero-shot reuse, depending strongly on observation representation.
Latent diagnostics and ablations indicate that learned representations do not automatically provide the invariances needed for reliable reuse.

papers.abstract: Latent world models allow reinforcement learning agents to learn policies from imagined trajectories, yet determining the optimal depth of model reliance remains a fundamental challenge. Fixed imagination horizons apply uniform prediction depths regardless of trajectory reliability, exposing target values to compounding model error or over-relying on critic approximations. We introduce density-guided bootstrap boundaries, a trajectory-dependent mechanism that adapts the depth of imagined returns using a score-informed relative density proxy. The proxy accumulates the estimated divergence of a score-corrected auxiliary field formed by a feature displacement network and a noise-conditioned score estimator along imagined paths. We propose two gating mechanisms: a hard boundary that halts return expansion at a discrete state, and a soft boundary that continuously shifts the return recursion toward critic bootstrapping. Both variants preserve boundary value estimates and apply corresponding survival weights to actor and critic losses. Formulated independently of specific dynamics models and instantiated within Dreamer V3, we prove that the resulting gated Bellman operator is a strict contraction mapping and that early bootstrapping monotonically reduces conditional target variance. We clarify the theoretical assumptions distinguishing our expansion proxy from exact path likelihoods. Across continuous-control tasks and Atari Pong, empirical evaluations show that dynamic boundary selection enhances sample efficiency and late-training performance over fixed-horizon and auxiliary-enabled baselines.
bullets: Addresses the challenge of choosing a fixed imagination horizon when model predictions become unreliable.
Uses a score-informed relative-density proxy to estimate trajectory reliability and determine bootstrap depth.
Introduces hard boundaries that stop return expansion and soft boundaries that gradually shift toward critic bootstrapping.
Preserves boundary value estimates and applies survival weights to actor and critic losses.
Theory establishes contraction of the gated Bellman operator and reduced conditional target variance from earlier bootstrapping; experiments cover continuous control and Atari Pong.

papers.selection_reason: Improves latent world-model RL by adaptively bounding imagined rollout depth, directly relevant to interactive world models.
papers.title: Density-Guided Bootstrap Boundaries for Latent World-Model Reinforcement Learning

papers.abstract: A nonlinear dynamical system can be characterized by the autonomous evolution of its state in time and its dependence on system parameters. As a parameter varies, the dynamics can change quantitatively and, at bifurcation points, qualitatively. When the governing equations are unknown, a data-driven model should therefore capture both elements from observational data, rather than reproduce the dynamics at a single operating condition only. Parameter-aware reservoir computing (PARC) is a model-free framework for this purpose, where the parameter is supplied to a reservoir computer through an additional input channel. PARC is trained on time series recorded at several parameter values, and the trained reservoir, run in closed loop as an autonomous dynamical system, generates trajectories at parameter values that were never observed. rc_prediction is an open-source Python package that implements this workflow. It provides multi-parameter training of a reservoir, autonomous closed-loop prediction at user-specified parameter values, parameter scans, and a standard echo state network for forecasting at a fixed parameter. Hyperparameter optimization and optional GPU acceleration through PyTorch are also provided. We use three benchmark dynamical systems as examples to demonstrate its usage. As one of the featured applications, here we illustrate the prediction of critical transitions and system collapse: trained only on pre-critical data, the model is queried beyond the training range to predict whether the system collapses, to estimate the critical parameter $p_c^{*}$, and to characterize transient lifetimes.
authors: Jin-Cheng Rao, Zheng-Meng Zhai, Ying-Cheng Lai
bullets: Trains parameter-aware reservoir computers on time series collected across multiple parameter values.
Generates autonomous closed-loop trajectories at user-specified parameters not present in the training data.
Supports multi-parameter training, parameter scans, fixed-parameter echo state network forecasting, hyperparameter optimization, and optional PyTorch GPU acceleration.
Demonstrates applications on three benchmark dynamical systems, including predicting collapse and estimating critical transitions from pre-critical data.
Scope is data-driven prediction when governing equations are unknown; performance is illustrated through benchmark examples rather than a universal guarantee.

papers.abstract: Test-time scaling (TTS) improves large language model agents by sampling and selecting among multiple candidate trajectories, but common realizations assume that these trajectories can be executed in parallel. This assumption breaks in realistic deployments, where enterprise workspaces and cloud services are shared and persistent, costly or infeasible to replicate, and actions may introduce irreversible side effects or cross-trajectory interference. Existing generative world models avoid direct execution, but typically compress environment state into a single prompt, limiting their ability to reliably simulate transitions under partial observability. Instead, we introduce Agentic World Modeling (AWM), which reformulates next-observation prediction as a multi-turn evidence-acquisition task. For each hypothetical action, an agentic simulator adaptively queries the real environment through safe read-only interfaces, reasons over the returned evidence, and uses executable computation to construct the resulting observation without mutating shared state. Integrated with trajectory-level TTS, AWM enables parallel exploration over a single shared environment. Across $\tau$-bench, AppWorld, and OfficeBench, AWM outperforms a single-shot simulation baseline by 40.07% on average, and surpasses a trained world-model baseline by 12.36% on average. These results establish interactive, read-grounded simulation as a practical foundation for safe and scalable agentic test-time scaling in shared, non-resettable environments.
authors: Wendi Li, Huseyin A. Inan, Wei-Ning Chen, Yanzhi Chen, Chetan Bansal, Saravan Rajmohan, Sharon Li
bullets: Addresses the impracticality of executing many agent trajectories in shared, persistent, or irreversible environments.
Uses multi-turn evidence acquisition: an agentic simulator queries safe read-only interfaces, reasons over evidence, and computes hypothetical observations without mutations.
Integrates the simulator with trajectory-level test-time scaling to explore multiple trajectories on one non-resettable environment.
Outperforms single-shot simulation by 40.07% on average and a trained world-model baseline by 12.36% across τ-bench, AppWorld, and OfficeBench.
Scope: relies on environments that provide sufficiently informative safe, read-only interfaces.

papers.abstract: Web world models increasingly predict the consequences of candidate actions before agents act, yet a plausible predicted future does not necessarily support the correct safety decision. In a matched human evaluation of 3,000 predictions from ten frozen open models, 86.1% are judged semantically plausible. However, several models exhibit highly asymmetric authorisation behaviour, combining low false-safe execution with poor recall of clarifiable ASK cases and a strong preference for BLOCK. This motivates safety sufficiency: whether a predictive interface preserves and exposes the policy-decisive information required to distinguish actions that may be EXECUTED, require clarification through ASK, or should be BLOCKED. We introduce SafeWebWorld, a benchmark for evaluating safety sufficiency across five web-safety domains through action-conditioned futures, policy-decisive evidence, and policy-conditioned decisions. Under a controlled Security-Aligned Supervised Fine-Tuning protocol, evidence preservation can improve substantially while authorisation-sensitive decisions deteriorate. To determine whether this deterioration reflects loss of authorisation-sensitive score structure or a failure of the decision readout, we introduce Latent Authorisation Recovery (LAR). Frozen-score recalibration reveals substantial but backbone-dependent recovery, while paired recovery provides only a modest additional gain. Yet within-family and matched-authorisation evaluations remain poor, showing that aggregate recoverability does not imply robust fine-grained authorisation behaviour. Overall, plausible prediction, evidence preservation, and aggregate recovery are each insufficient on their own to establish robust authorisation.
authors: Zhifei Hu, Alexandra I. Cristea, Adel Bibi, Jialin Yu
bullets: A human evaluation of 3,000 predictions from ten frozen open models found 86.1% semantically plausible, but several models overused BLOCK and missed clarifiable ASK cases.

Security-Aligned Supervised Fine-Tuning improved evidence preservation but could worsen authorisation-sensitive decisions.
Latent Authorisation Recovery recovered some performance through score recalibration, but fine-grained and matched-authorisation behaviour remained poor.

papers.abstract: Achieving the broad task generalization of embodied models in physical environments remains a central challenge in robot learning. We study this challenge in World Action Models (WAMs) through two complementary capabilities: video generalization, which predicts the visual evolution of new tasks, and action generalization, which translates these predictions into executable behavior through a video-to-action bridge. By varying video and action supervision for tasks outside an initial training set, we examine their respective contributions to task transfer. On RoboTwin 2.0, using only in-distribution video-action supervision yields a 25.07% success rate on out-of-distribution tasks. Introducing videos of these tasks without their action labels raises success to 55.90%, while adding just one action-labeled demonstration per task further improves it to 70.70%. These findings suggest that broader video coverage enables task transfer by leveraging existing inverse-dynamics capabilities, while even sparse action supervision further strengthens those capabilities. Guided by this perspective, we introduce WorldBridge, a WAM with separate video and action experts connected through structured attention and trained with joint flow matching. WorldBridge incorporates visual memory at two temporal scales and action forcing, alongside a unified data processing pipeline that standardizes and filters heterogeneous robot trajectories and egocentric hand-derived supervision. Across multiple manipulation benchmarks, WorldBridge achieves state-of-the-art performance among the compared methods, including 96.23% on RoboTwin 2.0 full data setting and 80.9% on clean to random setting, 82.8% on RoboCasa GR1 TableTop, and 57.6% on DOMINO Level-1. Our study highlights the complementary roles of video prediction and action grounding in developing robots that generalize across tasks.
authors: Jun Cen, Yubo Guo, Hao Li, Liangkai Li, Yaoxu Lyu, Meng Wei, Zeqi Xiao, Sizhe Yang, Yuqiang Yang, Yifan Ye, Shanghang Zhang, Duo Zheng
bullets: Task transfer benefits from both video and action generalization: video-only supervision raises out-of-distribution success from 25.07% to 55.90%, while one action-labeled demonstration reaches 70.70% on RoboTwin 2.0.

The model uses two-scale visual memory, action forcing, and a unified pipeline for heterogeneous robot and egocentric supervision.
It reports strong performance across manipulation benchmarks, including 96.23% on RoboTwin 2.0, 82.8% on RoboCasa GR1 TableTop, and 57.6% on DOMINO Level-1.
The study emphasizes complementary roles for visual prediction and action grounding in task generalization.

papers.abstract: Vehicle-infrastructure cooperation can complement onboard sensing with broader and more informative observations of the traffic environment, providing valuable support for end-to-end autonomous driving. However, existing cooperative driving methods mainly exploit roadside information to enhance the representation of the current scene, while the future consequences of prospective driving actions are rarely modeled explicitly. This limits the ability of the planner to anticipate how its decisions may interact with the evolving traffic environment. To address this issue, we propose V2X-WAM, a cooperative world action model that tightly couples cooperative scene understanding, action generation, and future-world reasoning. V2X-WAM constructs a reliability-aware spatiotemporal representation from vehicle- and infrastructure-side observations, while compressing infrastructure information into a compact quantized message for efficient communication. Based on the resulting cooperative representation, a multimodal planner generates prospective trajectories, which explicitly condition future occupancy and dynamic-flow prediction. The predicted world consequences are then fed back to refine the planned trajectory, forming a closed interaction between action and future-world evolution. Experiments on a large-scale real-world cooperative driving dataset demonstrate that V2X-WAM consistently improves planning accuracy and safety over representative end-to-end cooperative driving methods, while achieving stronger future-world prediction and substantially lower communication overhead. Ablation studies further validate the effectiveness of the proposed design.
bullets: Addresses the limitation that existing V2X methods mainly represent the current scene without explicitly modeling action consequences.

Experiments show improved planning accuracy and safety, stronger future-world prediction, and substantially lower communication overhead; ablations support the design.

papers.abstract: Video world models generate future visual observations from camera or action inputs, with the goal of synthesizing persistent 3D worlds that can be explored across time and space. Existing benchmarks typically evaluate short interactions or rely on camera trajectories fixed before generation. The performance of video world models under long-horizon exploration with extensive camera motion remains under-explored. We introduce WorldProbe, a diagnostic benchmark that uses a goal-conditioned multimodal agent to adapt camera actions online during generation. WorldProbe comprises 164 test cases across four probing families. Across 10 state-of-the-art models, we generate more than 1,600 rollouts totaling approximately 800 minutes, with horizons up to 180 seconds. Our evaluation across four dimensions reveals both the degradation of local measures and the emergence of long-range inconsistencies. We find that recent models sustain visual and content quality for longer, while long-range memory and evolution remain weak. These results expose a gap between locally stable generation and persistent world consistency that is largely missed by existing benchmarks. Code and benchmark resources are available at https://github.com/Untitled-W/WorldProbe.
bullets: Existing benchmarks largely miss failures under long-horizon exploration with online camera motion.
WorldProbe uses a goal-conditioned multimodal agent to adapt camera actions during generation across 164 test cases and four probing families.
Evaluation of 10 state-of-the-art models covers over 1,600 rollouts, approximately 800 minutes, and horizons up to 180 seconds.
Models increasingly preserve local visual and content quality, but long-range memory and world evolution remain weak.
The benchmark reveals a gap between locally stable videos and persistent, consistent 3D worlds.

papers.abstract: We introduce Weighted Adjoint Matching, a method to finetune a pretrained diffusion or flow matching model given a differentiable reward. We derive it from Adjoint Matching, which reformulates finetuning as a stochastic optimal control problem with a quadratic control cost. Building on the observation that these models generate coarse features before fine details, we place a time-dependent weight on the control cost. A high cost early in the generative process preserves balance and diversity in the coarse features, which carry most of the semantics, while a low cost at the end lets the model increase the reward by refining details. We prove that our method is equivalent to maximizing the reward under time-varying Kullback--Leibler regularization on the generative paths. Experiments on Gaussian mixtures and on MNIST show a better tradeoff between reward and mode balance than Adjoint Matching.
bullets: Targets finetuning with a differentiable reward while maintaining diversity and mode balance.
Uses a time-dependent quadratic control cost: high early to preserve coarse features, low late to refine details.
Is equivalent to reward maximization with time-varying KL regularization over generative paths.
Experiments on Gaussian mixtures and MNIST show a better reward–mode-balance tradeoff than Adjoint Matching.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces a method for finetuning flow matching models with time-dependent control costs, relevant to generative world models and reward-based optimization.
papers.title: Weighted Adjoint Matching: Finetuning Flow Matching Models with Time-Dependent Control Cost
papers.tldr: Weighted Adjoint Matching finetunes diffusion or flow-matching models by protecting early semantic structure while rewarding late-stage detail refinement.

papers.abstract: World-Action Models (WAMs) offer visual foresight for robotic manipulation, but pixel-space models repeatedly reconstruct entire future scenes, incurring high computational cost and spatio-temporal redundancy. In physical manipulation, consecutive frames often share most of their visual context; the changes between them are what an action policy needs to anticipate. We introduce DeltaWAM, a change-centric WAM that makes a compact delta token the unit of future prediction. Each token is a single vector encoding changes between consecutive dense DINO feature maps. DeltaWAM builds on DeltaWorld, a latent world model pretrained on large-scale videos, to autoregressively predict one delta token per future frame. A flow-matching action expert then conditions on the predicted transitions and current DINO features, which serve as spatial anchors, to generate action chunks. Trained for 256 GPU hours on two H100 GPUs, DeltaWAM has 0.725B parameters and achieves 92.8% average success on LIBERO. It also shows robust generalization under procedural perturbations on LIBERO-Pro. Inference takes 142.1 ms per action chunk with 3.86 GB peak memory.
bullets: Addresses the redundancy and computational expense of reconstructing entire future scenes in visual foresight.
Represents each frame transition as a single delta token derived from consecutive dense DINO feature maps.
Uses DeltaWorld for autoregressive delta prediction and a flow-matching action expert conditioned on predicted changes and current visual anchors.
Achieves 92.8% average success on LIBERO and robust generalization to procedural perturbations on LIBERO-Pro.
Runs at 142.1 ms per action chunk with 3.86 GB peak memory; scope is demonstrated on robotic manipulation benchmarks.

papers.selection_reason: Change-centric world-action model for robotic manipulation that predicts compact delta tokens for visual foresight and generates action chunks; directly relevant to embodied manipulation and visual world models.
papers.title: DeltaWAM: Change-Centric Visual Foresight via Delta Tokens for an Efficient World-Action Model
papers.tldr: DeltaWAM predicts compact visual changes rather than full future frames, enabling efficient robotic action generation with strong LIBERO performance and low inference cost.

papers.abstract: Time series forecasting is typically framed as learning a direct mapping from historical to future observations in the observation space. However, sequences of observations generally provide only a partial view of the dynamics of the underlying system, with future observations being shaped by latent dynamics. Recent latent-space forecasting methods thus achieve improved performance by predicting future observations from latent-space representations of historical observations rather than directly forecasting future observations in the observation space. Next, while future observations are also shaped by external factors, how to incorporate external, often multimodal, information into forecasting, so that it can shape latent-state formation and evolution directly, remains underexplored. We propose WorldTS, a world-modeling based forecasting framework that integrates multimodal covariates directly into the forecasting to further improve forecasting performance. Specifically, WorldTS employs a two-stage training strategy. First, it learns forecasting-relevant latent state dynamics conditioned on multimodal covariates, yielding encoded future states. Next, the learned state dynamics are frozen, and an observation decoder is trained to map the predicted future states back to future observations. Extensive experiments on 21 real-world datasets offer insight into WorldTS and its effectiveness.
bullets: Addresses the limitation that historical observations only partially reveal the system’s underlying dynamics.
Uses a two-stage world-modeling framework to learn covariate-conditioned latent state dynamics and decode them into future observations.
First learns forecasting-relevant future latent states using multimodal covariates.
Then freezes the learned dynamics and trains an observation decoder to reconstruct future observations.
Experiments on 21 real-world datasets demonstrate the framework’s effectiveness; the abstract does not specify numerical gains or scope limitations.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of WorldTS. TS Encoder/Decoder denote the time-series encoder/decoder; Predictor denotes the covariate-conditioned state predictor. Cov Encoder and Modal Adapter are the numerical-covariate encoder and modality-specific MLP projector. Stage 2 (Observation Decoding) freezes the encoders and predictor and trains the decoder to recover future observations.

papers.selection_reason: Latent world-modeling approach for time-series forecasting with multimodal covariates; fits environment-dynamics prediction.
papers.title: WorldTS: World Modeling for Multimodal Covariate-aware Time Series Forecasting
papers.tldr: WorldTS improves time-series forecasting by modeling latent dynamics conditioned directly on multimodal external covariates.

papers.abstract: Recent empirical and theoretical advances suggest that joint-embedding predictive architectures (JEPAs) may learn meaningful representations for action-conditioned prediction of future outcomes, thus becoming one of the foundational structures for world models. However, accurate prediction does not, in general, necessarily imply recovery of underlying causal states that give rise to the observed dynamics. This work investigates when and how JEPAs can recover the underlying causal states from observations. We first introduce a latent variable model, in which high-dimensional observations are generated from latent causal states whose dynamics are governed by action-conditioned transition mechanisms. Based on this formulation, we develop a general information-theoretic objective that combines conditional likelihood maximization for learning transition dynamics with entropy maximization for preserving latent state information. We then establish identifiability conditions under which representations learned by this general objective recover the underlying latent causal states up to component-wise invertible transformations and permutation. One key condition for such identifiability is sufficient action-induced variation in the transition mechanisms. Guided by this finding, we instantiate the general objective with an action-modulated Gaussian additive-noise model, yielding action-modulated JEPA (A-JEPA). Experiments on synthetic environments verify the theoretical findings under the identifiability conditions and robustness to moderate violations, while visual benchmarks demonstrate improved state recovery and transfer to unseen transition mechanisms.
bullets: Motivation: Accurate action-conditioned prediction does not necessarily reveal the causal states underlying observed dynamics.
Method: Formulates a latent causal-state model and combines conditional transition-likelihood maximization with entropy maximization to preserve state information.
Theory: Derives identifiability conditions allowing recovery of latent causal states up to component-wise invertible transformations and permutation.
Key condition: Actions must induce sufficient variation in the transition mechanisms.
Results: A-JEPA validates the theory in synthetic environments and improves state recovery and transfer to unseen transition mechanisms on visual benchmarks.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Assumption and model-specification analysis. Left: latent-state recovery degrades as the observation mapping becomes increasingly non-invertible. Middle: reducing action-induced variation in either the conditional mean or variance degrades recovery. Right: the proposed method remains robust to Laplace and Student-t noise, while uniform noise leads to a larger degradation.

Figure 4: Representation and transition recovery across four visual control environments.Columns correspond to TWOROOM, OGB, REACHER, and PUSHT, while rows report component-wise state recovery (MCC), joint-state information preservation (nonlinear state R2), and multi-step actionconditioned prediction (rollout R2), respectively. Figure 1: Analysis of latent-state recovery. Left: effect of the trade-off between transition likelihood and information preservation. Middle: effect of increasing action-induced mechanism variation. Right: component-wise recovery across latent dimensions compared with JEPA-style baselines.

papers.selection_reason: Identifiability analysis of action-conditioned JEPA representations for causal state recovery; directly advances latent-action world models.
papers.title: I Act Therefore I Am: When Is JEPA's Action-Conditioning Enough to Learn Causal Mechanisms?
papers.tldr: The paper characterizes when action-conditioned JEPAs can recover causal latent states rather than merely predict future observations, and proposes A-JEPA to do so.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models excel at instruction following, yet most remain feed-forward: they condition actions only on the current observation and discard both long-horizon temporal context and the hierarchical structure of VLM representations. We present PRIME W0, a hierarchical conditional flow-matching framework that closes this gap through three synergistic designs: (1)per-layer KV injection from a pretrained VLM into an Adaptive MoE action expert; (2)dynamics-aware conditioning via asynchronous world-model subgoal-image prediction and a DINOv2 historical-frame semantic bridge; and (3)Action Dynamic Manifold (ADM) flow matching with covariance-structured noise that respects robot kinematic coupling. PRIME W0 is trained in four stages---VLM pre-training, DAT/NTP visuomotor pre-training, DiT flow-matching decoder assembly with WM injection, and end-to-end SFT---and achieves state-of-the-art results on LIBERO and real-robot benchmarks, with systematic ablations validating each architectural component.
bullets: Addresses the limitations of feed-forward VLA models, which ignore long-horizon context and hierarchical visual-language representations.
Injects pretrained VLM key-value features into an adaptive mixture-of-experts action module.
Uses asynchronous world-model subgoal-image prediction and DINOv2 historical-frame features for dynamics-aware temporal conditioning.
Applies covariance-structured flow matching on an Action Dynamic Manifold to model coupled robot actions.
Reports state-of-the-art performance on LIBERO and real-robot benchmarks, with ablations supporting the proposed components.

figures.caption: Figure 1: PRIME W0 architecture.

Figure 2: Four-stage training pipeline. (1) VLM Pretrain: the vision–language backbone is trained on general multimodal supervision (e.g. captioning / VQA). (2) NTP / task-specific pre-training: with DAT action tokens, the VLM learns visuomotor next-token prediction over instruction–observation–action sequences. (3) DiT Pretrain: the VLM is frozen while the MoT / Adaptive MoE flow-matching action expert is trained with world-model conditioning to denoise continuous actions (and associated state tokens). (4) SFT: both the VLM and the action expert are jointly fine-tuned end-to-end, optionally with action-prefix tokens that shorten the denoising trajectory at inference. Flame / snowflake icons indicate trainable vs. frozen modules.

Figure 5: Scaling with world-model capacity. LIBERO-Long success scales monotonically with WM size; the largest gain is between 5M and 50M parameters (+5.9%). Better subgoal-image prediction directly benefits the asynchronous WM→VLM→ADM pipeline.

Figure 3: Training data mixture. Robot demonstration data used by PRIME W0 totals approximately 10,000 hours, comprising Teleop (60%, ∼6,000 h; laboratory setups, data-collection factories, and public datasets), UMI (30%, ∼3,000 h; portable UMI fisheye egocentric collection), and Simulation (10%, ∼1,000 h; reconstructed scenes with procedural objects and physics randomisation).

Figure 4: ADM cross-attention to WM subgoal-image tokens across manipulation phases. Attention to WMpredicted subgoal tokens peaks at contact-establishment and placement phases, confirming that forward scene predictions actively condition manifold-constrained action generation during critical moments.

Table 4: Component ablation. Each row adds one module on top of the previous variant. Metrics: LIBERO-Long success (%) and real-robot average success (%).

papers.selection_reason: Hierarchical VLA with world-model subgoal prediction for manipulation; fits embodied AI, world models, and spatial intelligence.
papers.title: PRIME W0: Physical Priors from World Models for Embodied Manipulation
papers.tldr: PRIME W0 enhances vision-language-action models for embodied manipulation by combining hierarchical VLM features, world-model dynamics, temporal context, and kinematics-aware action generation.

papers.abstract: Deep learning has shown remarkable success in the data-driven modeling of dynamical systems. Much of its success is attributed not to the flexibility of neural networks but to inductive biases based on physical prior knowledge, such as energy conservation and symplecticity. However, existing methods do not fully exploit the fact that real-world physical systems are interconnections of components. Some methods require the interconnection to be known a priori, while others assume the system to be reducible to an ordinary differential equation (ODE) and learn only the reduced ODE, discarding the algebraic constraints imposed by the interconnection. Here, we propose Dirac-interconnected neural elements (DINEs), a neural network model that represents a physical system as a differential-algebraic equation (DAE), whose algebraic constraints are given by a Dirac structure in kernel representation. With DINEs, we simultaneously identify from data the interconnection among the components as a Dirac structure and learn the characteristics of the components as neural networks. This allows us to keep the learned subsystems in unreduced form and isolate or compose them to make a new system without retraining. Moreover, DINEs can handle partially observable systems. Experimental results demonstrate these capabilities on physical systems beyond the reach of existing methods.
bullets: Targets a limitation of existing physics-informed models: known interconnections or ODE reduction can discard algebraic constraints.
Represents physical systems as differential-algebraic equations with Dirac structures in kernel form.
Jointly identifies subsystem interconnections and learns subsystem characteristics with neural networks.
Supports partially observable systems and enables subsystem isolation or recombination without retraining.
Experiments demonstrate these capabilities on physical systems beyond the reach of existing methods.

papers.abstract: World models can achieve strong control performance without faithfully capturing the dynamics of their environment, limiting their potential for mechanistic interpretability and scientific discovery. Here, we introduce world2vec to learn mechanistic world models without reward information directly from observations and actions. World2vec learns latent dynamics that faithfully reproduce the true system over long prediction horizons, with at least one order of magnitude fewer parameters than DreamerV3, TD-MPC2 and LeWM. This enables state of the art performance in controlling continuous environments from pixels and accurate system identification across a benchmark of 71 attractors, demonstrating how world models are amenable to scientific discovery.
authors: Tobias Schmidt, Rodrigo Gonzalez Laiz, Kriszti\'an Szuppinger, Steffen Schneider
bullets: Targets world models that control effectively but may not faithfully represent environment dynamics.
Learns latent dynamics without reward information and maintains accurate predictions over long horizons.
Uses at least an order of magnitude fewer parameters than DreamerV3, TD-MPC2, and LeWM.
Achieves state-of-the-art pixel-based control in continuous environments.
Accurately identifies systems across a benchmark of 71 attractors, illustrating potential for scientific discovery.

papers.selection_reason: Learns action-conditioned latent dynamics world models from observations and actions for control and long-horizon prediction.
papers.title: world2vec: Mechanistic world models through latent dynamics learning
papers.tldr: world2vec learns compact, mechanistically faithful world models from observations and actions alone, supporting both control and scientific system identification.

papers.abstract: Interactive world models generate visual content conditioned on user actions, yet maintaining spatial consistency over long-horizon exploration in real time remains challenging. Existing approaches rely on either temporal context or explicit 3D memory, both of which scale poorly because memory grows with the length of the generated stream. Moreover, explicit 3D memories condition latent video generators by re-encoding RGB renderings, which precludes real-time generation. In this paper, we introduce a Latent 3D Gaussian Memory (L3G) that combines the efficiency of feed-forward reconstruction with a compact, rapidly renderable scene representation. Building on this memory, we propose L3G-World, in which a memory updater and a video diffusion transformer (DiT) alternate autoregressively to generate spatially consistent worlds. The memory updater spawns Gaussians in newly observed regions and refines existing ones, so that the memory grows with scene extent rather than stream length. Each Gaussian further stores a VAE latent feature, allowing the memory to be rendered directly into the DiT's latent space without VAE re-encoding. Experiments show that L3G-World achieves state-of-the-art generation quality and long-horizon spatial consistency, with up to $38.6\times$ fewer 3D primitives, $3.2\times$ faster memory updates, and $359\times$ faster memory rendering relative to the most efficient prior 3D-memory baseline for each metric, enabling real-time world generation at 9 FPS.
authors: Jinhyeok Choi, JoungBin Lee, Jongmin Lee, Minkyeong Jeon, Jiyoung Kim, Kaeun Han, Yoonjin Yoon, Seungryong Kim
bullets: Addresses the poor scalability and slow rendering of temporal-context and explicit-3D-memory world models during long-horizon exploration.
Alternates a memory updater with a video diffusion transformer to autoregressively generate observations and maintain scene consistency.
Stores VAE latent features in Gaussians, avoiding RGB rendering and VAE re-encoding during conditioning.
Grows memory with newly explored scene extent rather than generated stream length, while refining previously observed regions.

papers.abstract: A playable, programmable game world must maintain persistent state, enforce executable rules, and support extensible gameplay mechanics. Existing video world models can generate plausible combat, yet struggle to keep hit reactions and health updates consistent with game rules. We introduce Fight World Model (FWM), which separates rule-governed combat execution from video rendering. An executable engine maintains state and resolves interactions. A deterministic compiler encodes these outcomes and attempted actions in a spatially and temporally aligned interaction proxy. The proxy aligns action and skill windows, brief hit reactions, and persistent health by fighter identity and timing. These cues can be controlled separately to render interactions under modified rules. Identity-bound references preserve character appearance across side switches. We train FWM on FightWorld Corpus, spanning 52 skill effects, 187 character-appearance variants, and 15 arenas. Without retraining the renderer, FWM supports damage scaling, limited-hit immunity, lifesteal, and multi-stage skill mechanisms beyond the native game. It also allows character and arena customization. Experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of FWM, which outperforms existing game world models in action fidelity, hit reactions, health-state consistency, and character appearance preservation. Our project is available at https://fight-world-model.github.io.
authors: Jiahua Li, Zixu John, Tom Zhong, Fuping Wu, Tianhao Xu, Ruicheng Zhang, Jun Zhou, Zunnan Xu

Supports modified combat rules—including damage scaling, limited-hit immunity, lifesteal, and multi-stage skills—without retraining the renderer.
Experiments report stronger action fidelity, hit-reaction quality, health consistency, and appearance preservation than existing game world models.
