papers.abstract: Mobile robots must open doors and drawers, yet their scene maps record what each object is and whether it has moved, not how it will respond to a pull. This paper proposes PhysVLMM, a method that maintains a physical belief for every articulated part of a Vision-Language-Motion Map and answers a planner's queries about it, with two algorithms: a map update and a query. Watching a part move provably cannot identify its dynamics, and a measured pull identifies only the pulled part, up to one direction. PhysVLMM therefore (i) keeps that direction as a posterior instead of a point estimate, (ii) passes the evidence of each pull in closed form to the untouched look-alike parts of the map, and (iii) answers whether an action will succeed at a stated risk, or abstains. On real doors and drawers in 18 homes, it identifies the joint type in 86% of held-out pulls (48% for a learned single-view method) and predicts the response to a pull with 41% lower error than differentiable simulation (CRPS 0.323 vs. 0.544), four orders of magnitude faster (13 ms vs. 230 s per case). The posterior lowers the final-position error from 0.460 to 0.270, sharing lowers the force error of untouched parts from 56% to 42%, and at every stated risk from 0.02 to 0.30 the false-safe answers stay within it. Pooling all measured parts of a home does as well as the look-alike groups, and simpler variants predict where a pulled part stops at least as well.
bullets: Addresses the gap between scene maps and the physical response of doors, drawers, and other articulated parts.
Maintains posterior beliefs over motion direction, propagates evidence to untouched look-alike parts, and can answer or abstain based on stated risk.
On real doors and drawers across 18 homes, identified joint types in 86% of held-out pulls.
Reduced pull-response error by 41% versus differentiable simulation and ran four orders of magnitude faster.
Risk-controlled answers remained within the specified false-safe rate from 0.02 to 0.30.

papers.abstract: AI has made remarkable progress in mathematics, solving challenging problems with machine-checkable proofs in Lean, yet typically relying on predefined mathematical definitions and formal specifications. This raises a natural question: can it reason rigorously about an unknown world? We introduce the Algebraic World Model (AWM), a framework that turns interaction with unfamiliar environments into explicit mathematical models supporting formal reasoning. AWM explores the environment and develops executable Python hypotheses, continually testing and revising them against observations. It then structures these hypotheses into typed objects and shared rules, simplifies their structure through category-theory-guided transformations, and formalizes the resulting model in Lean 4 to prove reachability and impossibility. AWM can formally prove that a goal is unreachable, even beyond explored trajectories. On two impossible game levels, it constructs closed, kernel-checked Lean proofs excluding every legal winning sequence in all six runs, while Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra, equipped with coding tools, produce none in twelve baseline runs. Four of AWM's six initial bounds are correct, compared with one for Opus 5.5 and none for GPT-6 Astra; given only feedback that a cheaper win exists, AWM revises its rules and constructs new proofs, reaching six of six correct bounds. Moreover, AWM produces interpretable mathematical models whose rules can be inspected and tested step by step. Across all 25 public ARC-AGI-3 games, these models enable Lean to replay the winning trajectories of all 183 levels and generalize beyond observed play, predicting unseen transitions and detecting changes in game mechanics. With Claude Opus 5, AWM clears all levels with a score of 99.9, while its certified winning trajectories use only 43% of the human baseline's actions.
authors: Guancheng Pan, Qixin Tan, Yang Yuan, Andrew Chi-Chih Yao
bullets: Addresses the challenge of rigorous reasoning when mathematical definitions and specifications are initially unknown.
Explores environments, proposes and tests executable Python hypotheses, then organizes them into typed objects and shared rules.
Uses category-theory-guided simplification and Lean 4 formalization to certify reachability, impossibility, and generalization beyond observed trajectories.
On two impossible game levels, it produced kernel-checked proofs excluding every legal winning sequence, while baseline models produced none.

Across 25 ARC-AGI-3 games, its models replayed all 183 winning trajectories, predicted unseen transitions, and detected changing mechanics; with Claude Opus 5, it achieved a 99.9 score using 43% of human-baseline actions.

papers.abstract: We introduce Continuous-Action World Models (CoAWM), a framework for learning cross-embodiment spatiotemporal dynamics priors that support robot action generation across embodiments and execution frequencies. At its core is a shared latent function space that captures the spatial and temporal structure of robot actions. We learn this space through two stages. First, function pretraining brings trajectories from different embodiments and sampling frequencies into a common representation, learning shared dynamics priors through action reconstruction and consistency across temporal sampling views. By accommodating heterogeneous robot trajectories, this stage broadens the range of data sources available for pretraining and facilitates scaling to larger and more diverse datasets. Second, we connect the pretrained function space to a world-model backbone, enabling observations, language instructions, and the current robot state to condition the prediction of a latent action function. A single decoder takes any query time and returns the corresponding end-effector action. By separating shared dynamics priors from task-conditioned action selection and temporal sampling, our approach provides a unified foundation for transferring robot experience across embodiments and control frequencies.
bullets: Addresses the challenge of transferring robot experience across heterogeneous embodiments and execution frequencies.
Pretrains a shared latent function space using action reconstruction and consistency across different temporal sampling views.
Connects this space to a world model conditioned on observations, language instructions, and the robot’s current state.
A single decoder produces end-effector actions for any queried time, separating shared dynamics from task-specific action selection and temporal sampling.
The abstract describes a unified transfer framework but reports no quantitative experimental results or explicit limitations.

Training Stage A learns shared spatiotemporal priors from typed trajectories across embodiments and temporal sampling grids. Training Stage B connects observation-conditioned latent prediction to the learned function space using latent and physical reconstruction supervision. At inference, current multimodal observations and visual features condition latent prediction; the function decoder combines the predicted latent with physical query times and observed context to produce embodiment-specific control commands.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in video world models have enabled the generation of increasingly realistic and interactive virtual environments, opening new possibilities for player-customizable gameplay. Agentic frameworks further advance this direction by decoupling explicit game logic and controllable world representations from visual generation. However, existing approaches support only simple game settings and predefined motion patterns, generalize poorly to unseen environments and characters, and offer limited real-time interactivity. In this paper, we introduce Wizard, an agentic game world model that enables real-time, precise control over character motions while generalizing zero-shot across novel scenes, characters, and actions. To achieve this, we construct a diverse dataset spanning 750 scenes and 178 characters, incorporating skeleton and geometry information as structured representations. We leverage these representations as intermediate proxies to condition a video generation model, together with an adaptive masking mechanism that improves alignment between the conditioning signals and generated video rollouts. Furthermore, we introduce an agentic framework that explicitly maintains and updates game states, allowing players to freely configure their virtual worlds and exercise fine-grained control over character motions while preserving visual quality and gameplay consistency. By combining agentic control with structured proxy-based generation, our framework unlocks new possibilities for player-driven game creation with real-time, generalizable, and mechanically consistent world simulation.
authors: Yuzhe Wu, Zijun Lin, Yeying Jin
bullets: Addresses limited generalization, motion control, and interactivity in existing video world models.
Uses skeleton and geometry representations as structured proxies to condition video generation.
Introduces adaptive masking to better align control signals with generated video rollouts.
Maintains and updates game states through an agentic framework for consistent, configurable gameplay.
Targets real-time, visually coherent world simulation with player-driven character control.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Overview of Wizard. Our method supports diverse gameplay experiences, including world exploration, character summoning, character transformation, and scene manipulation. By combining agentic control with geometric scene proxies and articulated character skeletons, Wizard achieves fine-grained control, zero-shot generalization, and mechanics-consistent gameplay with real-time interaction at 24 FPS.

Figure 2. Dataset Overview and Processing Pipeline. We construct 50.3 hours of data spanning 750 scenes and 178 characters from four complementary sources. Scene geometry and character skeletons are jointly encoded into unified visual proxies, followed by filtering and captioning to produce aligned proxy–video training pairs.

Figure 3. Inference Pipeline of Wizard. (a) Character animation is driven by motions retrieved from a high-quality library and retargeted from compatible source skeletons to the target character’s skeleton. (b) Scene manipulation is performed by a world agent that edits 3D scene geometry and renders visual proxies using OpenGL. (c) State-aware combat control adapts boss behavior to the current game state and enforces rule-based combat mechanics. (d) Real-time video generation is conditioned on visual proxies, reference images, and previously generated frames.

Figure 4. Video Generator Architecture and Character-Aware Adaptive Masking. (a) Visual proxy latents are concatenated with noisy video latents along channels, then combined with first-frame and character-reference tokens along the sequence dimension for DiT processing. (b) Skeleton-derived spatial masks restrict reference attention to the corresponding character regions, binding appearance guidance to character locations.

Figure 5. Visualization of Zero-Shot Generalization and Mechanics-Consistent Gameplay Enabled by Wizard. For each example, reference images are shown on the left, with visual proxies in the top row and the corresponding video rollouts in the bottom row.

Figure 6. Visualization of Open-Ended Creative Gameplay Enabled by Wizard. For each example, reference images are shown on the left, with visual proxies in the top row and the corresponding video rollouts in the bottom row.

papers.abstract: Video generation is shifting from end-to-end synthesis toward agentic generation, where planning, tool use, and feedback enable coherent, controllable multi-shot videos. In parallel, video world models provide action-conditioned observations and predicted futures, serving as interactive environments for agents. We study their intersection through the agent harness: an executable runtime that constructs context, exposes tools, maintains state, routes feedback, and manages budgets around video models. This report examines three directions. First, agentic video generation, where harnesses coordinate scripting, shot planning, asset management, production, and editing, alongside the evaluation challenges of these systems. Second, agentic world modeling, where harnesses mediate observation, control, execution, and state. We discuss hybrid designs in which game engines or agent-written programs maintain world state while video models render observations, and how agents and world models can mutually evaluate and improve one another. Third, recursive self-improvement (RSI) in video model development, distinguishing output revisions, updates to harness state, generator parameters, and evaluators, and changes to the improvement procedure itself. We identify how these improvements feed back into subsequent development. Across these directions, we analyze essential agent capabilities, including audiovisual perception, long-horizon planning, memory, code-based interaction, feedback-guided control, skill reuse, and multi-agent coordination. We conclude with challenges in autonomous video production, lifelong memory, programmable hybrid control, autonomous model development, provenance, cost accounting, and evaluation linking video quality and task performance to sustained improvements in models and harnesses.
authors: Liaoyuan Fan, Yuhao Zheng, Dongxing Mao, Hangyu Ran, Siyuan Hu, Weijia Mao, Rui Zhao, Weijia Wu, Guian Fang, Yanzhe Chen, Zeyu Zhu, Yuxin Jiang, Yiren Song, Yuchao Gu, Junchao Yi, Qi Hu, Dan Kong, Alex Jinpeng Wang, Kevin Qinghong Lin, Mike Zheng Shou, Wei Liu
bullets: Agent harnesses manage context, tools, state, feedback, and budgets around video models.
Agentic video generation coordinates scripting, shot planning, asset management, production, and editing for coherent multi-shot videos.
Agentic world models combine action-conditioned video predictions with interactive control, potentially using game engines or programs to maintain world state.
Recursive self-improvement can revise outputs, harness state, model parameters, evaluators, or the improvement process itself.
Key open challenges include long-horizon planning, memory, provenance, cost accounting, hybrid control, and evaluation tied to sustained improvement.

papers.abstract: Memory in reinforcement learning raises two problems. Attention finds the relevant item by scoring the whole store, which is costly for robots under latency and energy limits. When a retrieved memory pays off, credit for acquiring it must cross the whole sequence. We argue that both are governed by one quantity, the value of information, and propose to estimate it from archived rollouts with a learned world model. We obtain that, when read at the observation, it yields a provable lower bound on the optimal value of the acquiring action, which floors its TD target and attributes this floor to the observation that earned it. Read at the decision, it defines the optimal retrieval set. A pilot retrieval system, to be trained and improved with this signal, solves a memory task with reduced context.
authors: Daniel Strauss, Nikolaos Sotirakis, Zhenshan Bing, Alois Knoll
bullets: Targets costly attention over entire memory stores in latency- and energy-constrained reinforcement learning.
Estimates information value from archived rollouts using a learned world model.
At observation time, provides a provable lower bound on the acquiring action’s optimal value and credits the observation.
At decision time, defines the optimal retrieval set.
A pilot system solves a memory task with reduced context, though further training and improvement are needed.

papers.abstract: Choosing a robot action model requires evidence about task capability, adaptation cost, deployment requirements, and the reliability of reported conclusions. Success rates alone offer limited guidance to researchers with different computing budgets and goals. We propose RoboSeed, a multidimensional evaluation framework for vision-language-action (VLA) and world-action models (WAM), within a continuing program to train, evaluate, and openly release robot models with verifiable evidence for model selection. The framework defines five dimensions: capability, downstream training affordability, deployment affordability, locally verified research value, and reproduction evidence. It maps empirical measurements and audit criteria to 0-100 profiles using fixed normalization anchors, with balanced, training-constrained, and deployment-constrained preference settings. Interface and protocol checks establish when comparisons are appropriate. Missing measurements remain explicit, incomplete aggregate scores are withheld, and weighted input coverage identifies evidence gaps. We apply the framework to representative VLA and WAM models, drawing on local training, released-weight evaluation, task-level audits, and an evaluation-system study. The results reveal budget-dependent backbone choices, sensitivity to adaptation recipes, and differences between language and visual task interfaces. Reproducible scoring code and machine-readable evidence support extension to additional models. The study provides dimension-level assessments and priorities for further measurement, while incomplete serving traces and heterogeneous protocols preclude overall numerical rankings.
authors: Xin Ma, Furong Chen, Xinlong Man, Bo Zhang, Yalong Guo, Haolan Lei, Chaochen Cui, Hongyuan Zhang, Mulin Chen, Yi Wang, Lap-pui Chau, Chuang Yang
bullets: Assesses five dimensions: capability, downstream training affordability, deployment affordability, locally verified research value, and reproduction evidence.
Uses fixed normalization anchors, multiple budget preferences, and interface/protocol checks to make comparisons more reliable.
Applies the framework to representative vision-language-action and world-action models using local evaluations, audits, and released weights.
Finds budget-dependent backbone choices, sensitivity to adaptation recipes, and differences between language- and visual-task interfaces.
Provides reproducible scoring code and machine-readable evidence, but does not produce overall rankings because serving traces and protocols are incomplete or heterogeneous.

papers.abstract: Vulnerable road user (VRU) prediction must operate under partial observability and distribution shift, so reliable uncertainty matters alongside accuracy. Masked pretraining is attractive in this setting because it naturally exposes the model to missing content during self-supervision, but existing time-series masked autoencoding methods are typically deterministic and do not constrain how confidence should change with observability. We introduce eCoMAE, an evidential masked pretraining method for multivariate time series that explicitly aligns predictive evidence with what is observed. eCoMAE combines block-wise time-step masking with a Normal-Inverse-Gamma decoder and three observability-aware mechanisms: uncertainty-weighted mean consistency on positions visible in both a masked view and a reference pass, evidence suppression on masked positions, and representation consistency across stochastic masks. On IMPTC benchmark for VRU intention prediction under leave-one-environment-out weather shift, eCoMAE improves the strongest baseline from 0.7971 to 0.8068 in OOD accuracy and from 0.0718 to 0.0648 in OOD AURC. Additional evaluation on pedestrian trajectory forecasting across IMPTC, Waymo, nuScenes, and inD further yields the best fine-tuning MSE on all four datasets. These results show that observability-aligned evidential pretraining improves reliability under shift and remains effective beyond the primary benchmark.
authors: Shang Gao, Franz G\"otz-Hahn, Konrad Doll, Bernhard Sick
bullets: Addresses the need for calibrated uncertainty when VRU prediction faces missing observations and weather-related distribution shift.
Uses block-wise time-step masking with a Normal-Inverse-Gamma evidential decoder.
Enforces observability-aware mean consistency, suppresses evidence at masked positions, and promotes representation consistency across masks.
Improves OOD intention-prediction accuracy and AURC on IMPTC, and achieves the best fine-tuning MSE across four trajectory-forecasting datasets.
The method is evaluated on VRU intention and pedestrian trajectory forecasting, with scope focused on these benchmarks and tasks.

papers.abstract: Diffusion transformers (DiTs) have become the dominant architecture for high-fidelity image synthesis, yet they suffer from slow training convergence and high computational cost. Two recent lines of work address this from complementary angles: Representation Alignment (REPA) accelerates DiT training by aligning intermediate features with a pretrained external representation model (e.g., DINOv2), while Representation Auto-Encoders (RAE) replace the pixel-space VAE with a compact representation-space tokenizer learned from self-supervised features. However, these approaches are developed and applied in isolation: REPA still relies on a pixel-space VAE for latent diffusion, and RAE does not exploit the alignment signal that accelerates the diffusion backbone. We present \textbf{UniRA}, a unified framework that couples representation alignment and representation auto-encoding into a single objective. UniRA learns a representation-space tokenizer whose output serves simultaneously as the diffusion target and the alignment anchor, so the tokenizer, the diffusion backbone, and the external representation model are co-optimized. We give a theoretical result showing that this joint optimization preserves the representation quality of the external model while accelerating diffusion convergence, and we derive a principled weighting that balances the reconstruction, alignment, and generation objectives. On ImageNet class-conditional generation at 256*256 and 512*512, UniRA matches or surpasses state-of-the-art DiTs (SD3, REPA, RAE) in FID while reducing training steps by up to 5*. We further show that the unified representation space supports improved zero-shot classification and linear probing, confirming that generation and understanding benefit from a shared, aligned latent space.

bullets: Addresses slow convergence and high computational cost in diffusion transformers, which existing alignment and auto-encoding approaches tackle separately.
Jointly learns a representation-space tokenizer used as both the diffusion target and alignment anchor, co-optimizing it with the diffusion backbone and external representation model.
Provides a theoretical guarantee for preserving external representation quality and derives weighting across reconstruction, alignment, and generation objectives.
On ImageNet class-conditional generation at 256×256 and 512×512, matches or surpasses reported DiT baselines in FID while reducing training steps by up to 5×.

The shared latent space also improves zero-shot classification and linear probing, though the abstract reports results only for ImageNet class-conditional generation and related representation evaluation.

papers.abstract: Learning continuous-time dynamical systems from data is an active area of research. The Koopman formalism is often used here, because it is a flexible approach that is informative about the system's fundamental properties. The formalism represents dynamical systems through linear operators acting on a suitable function space. A practical difficulty arising in the numerical approximation of Koopman operators is the choice of a ``dictionary'', meaning an effective finite-dimensional representation of the function space. In this paper, we focus on learning dynamical systems in continuous-time, and so we consider numerical approximations of the Koopman generator instead of the Koopman operator. Our main contribution is a data-driven random-feature method to obtain a parsimonious and effective function representation for Galerkin approximation methods such as gEDMD. The representation we construct is data-informed, which allows us to improve upon data-agnostic methods. We empirically demonstrate the suitability of our method for forecasting tasks and system analysis. The numerical experiments show that our approach is accurate, and faster than iterative optimization. Further, we prove convergence of our approximation of the vector field and the resulting trajectories. In addition to the numerical results, we also make theoretical contributions, including a general convergence criterion for the semigroup generated by the gEDMD approximation and a counterexample showing that gEDMD does not generally preserve exponential boundedness. With our contribution, we advance the frontier of efficiently learning continuous-time dynamics from data, towards interpretable and mathematically robust modelling based on the Koopman framework.
authors: Ana \v{C}ukarska, Maximilian Gollwitzer, Viola Muning Li, Vladyslav Fediukov, Zahra Monfared, Felix Dietrich
bullets: Addresses the challenge of choosing a finite-dimensional dictionary for Koopman-generator approximations.
Uses data-driven random features within Galerkin methods such as gEDMD to produce a parsimonious representation.
Experiments demonstrate accurate forecasting and system analysis, with faster computation than iterative optimization.
Proves convergence of the approximated vector field and resulting trajectories.
Provides semigroup convergence criteria and shows that gEDMD does not generally preserve exponential boundedness.

papers.abstract: Distribution Matching Distillation (DMD) distills multi-step diffusion models into few-step generators by minimizing reverse KL divergence. Despite its strong performance, DMD guides samples by local density alone, which introduces two limitations: teacher scores can be unreliable in regions of low teacher density, and the mode-seeking behavior of reverse KL can collapse the student onto a subset of the teacher modes. We first connect DMD to Wasserstein gradient flow, showing that its gradient follows from a fixed-point formulation with integral KL (IKL) as the energy functional. This perspective motivates augmenting IKL with an optimal transport term that addresses these limitations by guiding outlier samples toward the target and promoting mode coverage. We realize this term using Sinkhorn divergence estimated from finite batches. In practice, however, errors in the estimated Sinkhorn velocity can perturb in-domain samples for which IKL guidance is already accurate. To this end, we introduce sDMD, which adaptively activates the Sinkhorn correction based on discriminator outputs, focusing on outlier samples where IKL may be unreliable. With 2--4 sampling steps on FLUX.1-dev, Qwen-Image-20B, and Wan2.1-14B, sDMD outperforms distillation baselines on GenEval, DPG, WISE, and VBench while improving sample diversity over DMD2.
authors: Jaihoon Kim, Lingxiao Li, Soshi Shimada, Roshni Cooper, Minhyuk Sung, Yiwei Zhao
bullets: DMD can suffer from unreliable teacher scores in low-density regions and reverse-KL mode collapse.
The method interprets DMD through Wasserstein gradient flow with integral KL as its energy.
It adds a finite-batch Sinkhorn divergence term to guide outliers toward the target distribution and improve mode coverage.
An adaptive discriminator-based gate limits Sinkhorn corrections on in-domain samples where standard IKL guidance is reliable.
With 2–4 sampling steps, sDMD outperforms distillation baselines across reported quality benchmarks and improves diversity over DMD2.

papers.abstract: World action models (WAMs) increasingly couple internal visual or world representations with action generation, making their world-to-action pathways a critical yet poorly understood source of robustness. We investigate when perturbations to these internal representations actually become behaviorally consequential, and uncover a pronounced mismatch between representation perturbability and closed-loop vulnerability: attack effectiveness varies sharply across visual K/V routes, while larger representation displacement does not reliably imply stronger control failure. Our analysis attributes this mismatch to the action-conditioned readout, where keys determine where action queries read and values determine what content they receive. This motivates an action-facing view of vulnerability, in which the effect of a perturbation depends on how it is routed into action generation rather than on representation-space magnitude alone. We instantiate this view with Tail-AV, a short-probe signal for identifying vulnerable routes, and operationalize it in PASA-KV, which selects action-facing K/V targets before training a fresh task-shared attack. Experiments across multiple WAM systems and a physical robot validate readout-informed target selection, demonstrate strong closed-loop attacks, and reveal substantial system-level differences in resistance.
authors: Zhongbo Wu, Jiakai Huang, Zheng Zhang, Siyu Xu, Kaixiang Chen, Xiaohong Liu, Shan You, Chang Xu, Tao Huang
bullets: WAM robustness can differ sharply across visual K/V routes, even when representation perturbations are similarly large.
Keys control where action queries read, while values control the content delivered to action generation.
Tail-AV provides a short probe for identifying vulnerable action-facing routes.
PASA-KV selects these targets before training a fresh task-shared attack.
Experiments on multiple WAMs and a physical robot show strong closed-loop attacks and substantial differences in system resistance.

papers.title: PASA-KV: Attacking Action-Facing Visual Routes in World Action Models
papers.tldr: PASA-KV finds and attacks the visual key/value routes that most directly influence action generation, showing that perturbation impact depends on action-facing readout rather than representation displacement alone.

papers.abstract: Interactive video world models aim to follow user actions while maintaining scene consistency over extended interactions. History-based methods reuse generated latents to preserve scene content, but three limitations of this reuse contribute to error recirculation. 1) The latent generated at each interaction is retained as history, potentially containing blurred details, geometric distortions, or semantic drift. 2) Although retrieved historical content matches the current scene, it can still contain errors that are carried into the next chunk. 3) New outputs then become history for later interactions, potentially reinforcing the same errors through repeated reuse. To limit this cycle, we aim to predict the future scene state from the current generated latent and the next action before generating the next interaction's video chunk. This future-state prior provides guidance for the next chunk, with the aim of reducing the errors carried forward from history. To this end, we propose a plug-and-play Causal Next-Chunk Predictor (C-NCP) with cross-model adaptability and prediction-guided modulation. We integrate C-NCP into four base generators and evaluate the augmented models across three benchmarks for interactive long-video generation and action-conditioned world modeling. Extensive experiments demonstrate reduced error accumulation and improved long-horizon consistency across diverse generation settings. The project page is at https://GuangYuanKK.github.io/futureworld.
authors: Guangyuan Li, Kelu Yao, Shuolin Xu, Xinlei Yu, Wei Xing, Lei Zhao, Peng-Tao Jiang, Xiaogang Xu, Xiaobin Hu
bullets: History-based interactive video models can recycle blur, distortions, semantic drift, and prior errors across interactions.
The proposed plug-and-play Causal Next-Chunk Predictor forecasts a future scene state from the current latent and next action.
This prediction guides generation of the next video chunk through prediction-guided modulation.
C-NCP adapts across models and is integrated into four base generators.
Experiments on three interactive video and action-conditioned world-modeling benchmarks report reduced error accumulation and improved long-horizon consistency.

papers.abstract: For a time-homogeneous Markov process, the fixed-lag solution operator \( (T_\tau f)(x)=\mathbb E[f(X_{t+\tau})\mid X_t=x] \) of the Kolmogorov backward equation evolves observables linearly and deterministically, even when the dynamics are stochastic. We approximate this operator using a two-stage method where we first approximate this operator directly from data, without knowledge of the governing equation (e.g., Fourier Neural Operator), and then compress the Galerkin projection onto a finite-dimensional observable space that is fixed in advance or selected variationally. The error analysis traces the learning error of the estimator, the sampling error of the Galerkin inner products, and the invariance and reconstruction properties of the observable space to the computed spectra and forecasts. The sampling error enters only through a multiplicative factor. Near an isolated spectral cluster, the invariance defect of a subspace controls its distance from the target invariant subspace. The forecast error is controlled by the one-step error of the reduced model and the projection error of the observable; when the measure is invariant and the reduced model preserves constants and is stable on mean-zero observables, the bound is uniform in the horizon. For deterministic dynamics, a learning rate for Fourier neural operators (FNOs) gives one explicit bound for the learning error. Numerical experiments illustrate spectral approximation and forecasting, including long-rollout stability and a comparison with extended dynamic mode decomposition (EDMD) when fewer transition pairs than basis functions are observed.
authors: Yuanchao Xu, Claire Valva, Ben Gao, Isao Ishikawa
bullets: Approximates the fixed-lag Markov transition operator directly from data, potentially using Fourier Neural Operators.
Compresses the learned operator into a finite-dimensional observable space chosen in advance or variationally.
Provides error analysis linking learning, sampling, subspace invariance, and reconstruction errors to spectral and forecast accuracy.
Under invariant-measure and stability conditions, forecast-error bounds remain uniform over the forecasting horizon.
Numerical experiments demonstrate spectral approximation, long-rollout stability, and performance when transition pairs are fewer than basis functions, compared with EDMD.

papers.abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) can condition robot actions on generated visual futures, but this additional context is neither cost-free nor uniformly beneficial. We examine what a predicted future actually changes: the action delta $\Delta a$ between the future-conditioned and future-free execution paths of the same model. Under a shared WAM checkpoint, this delta barely shifts average benchmark success ($+0.8$ points on LIBERO, $-0.8$ on RoboTwin~2.0), while generating visual futures increases inference latency by 1.7--1.9$\times$. These aggregate metrics conceal a concentrated failure mode that we term \emph{future-induced negative transfer}: while predictive deltas benefit long-horizon tasks ($+2.4$ points on LIBERO-Long) and remain negligible on most routine manipulations, they induce severe degradation on precision tasks---with \emph{Press Stapler} and \emph{Place Can Basket} losing 54.0 and 34.0 points, recurring as top failure modes across independently trained WAM variants. We introduce \textbf{Utility-WAM} for in-place correction of future-conditioned control. Its primary learning component is a residual adapter that repairs future-induced velocity deltas under a frozen shared WAM by aligning them with ground-truth dynamic guidance and penalizing excess error beyond the future-free baseline. The adapter selectively eliminates the majority of severe task drops (reducing losses to 6.0 and 14.0 points) while preserving long-horizon foresight. To eliminate superfluous video computation, a lightweight pre-generation gate reuses counterfactual action outcomes to selectively bypass video generation on 75.5\% of RoboTwin queries, cutting latency by 38\% while improving average success to 93.3\% on RoboTwin~2.0 and 98.9\% on LIBERO. On physical bimanual manipulation across three real-world tasks, Utility-WAM succeeds in 53 of 60 trials, compared to 43 for FAST-WAM.
authors: Feihong Zhang, Xi Lin, Yulong Shi, Zuxing Lu, Yanghong Mei, Zhaopeng Gu, Tingyu Yuan, Zihao Liang, Yinuo Wang, Zhaowen Li

Utility-WAM reduces major task losses, reaches 93.3% success on RoboTwin 2.0 and 98.9% on LIBERO, and succeeds in 53/60 real-world trials versus 43/60 for FAST-WAM.

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes and corrects future-conditioned world-action control, with a selective video-generation gate for efficiency; spans world models, efficiency, and manipulation policy learning.
papers.title: Utility-WAM: Correcting Future-Induced Action Changes
papers.tldr: Utility-WAM corrects harmful future-conditioned actions and skips unnecessary video generation, improving efficiency and robustness in robot manipulation.

papers.abstract: Predicting future physical states stands as a central challenge in embodied intelligence. Existing video world models leave 3D dynamics implicit, action-based formulations remain tied to specific robot configurations, and 3D motion prediction models use flow-only supervision, providing a limited learning signal for physical dynamics. To circumvent these limitations, we introduce \method{}, a generative world model that jointly predicts future video and query-based 3D trajectories. By parameterizing 3D motion as continuous displacement tokens aligned with the video grid, a unified Mixture-of-Transformers (MoT) backbone jointly denoises both modalities under a rectified-flow objective. This formulation couples explicit geometric dynamics with visual evolution, effectively unlocking the physical commonsense embedded within pretrained video models. To empirically scale and validate this unified architecture, we train \method{} on a heterogeneous mixture of 1.44 million object-level samples spanning simulated and real-world domains. We further introduce WorldFlowBench, comprising 1,678 evaluation samples from 11 data sources across simulated and real-world interactions, including spatial reasoning tasks. Across all three evaluation sets, WorldFlow achieves the lowest average displacement error (ADE) and final displacement error (FDE) among the evaluated learning-based methods. Notably, on the challenging SpatialCog set, WorldFlow achieves an ADE of 0.060 m, a 54.2\% reduction compared with the strongest external baseline. It also reduces ADE and FDE by 55.9\% and 68.5\%, respectively, compared with its flow-only variant. Project page: https://worldflow-rbs.github.io/.
authors: Yuhao Lu, Jiongxu Chen, Hexiang Wei, Jiajin Wu, Juelin Li, Mingjian Liang, Fan Yang, Zhuowei Liang, Zihao Liu, Zhennan Wang, Sheng Wang, Lin Shao

Represents 3D motion as continuous displacement tokens aligned with the video grid.
Uses a unified Mixture-of-Transformers backbone to jointly denoise video and 3D trajectories with a rectified-flow objective.
Pretrained on 1.44 million object-level samples and evaluated with WorldFlowBench across 1,678 samples from 11 sources.
Achieves the lowest average and final displacement errors among evaluated learning-based methods, including a 54.2% ADE reduction over the strongest external baseline on SpatialCog.

papers.abstract: Embodied world models should not only imagine plausible futures, but also perceive the geometric, semantic, and motion structure of the evolving world. We present GenSight, a unified embodied world model that brings future video generation and dense perception into a single pretrained video diffusion transformer. GenSight uses a unified spatiotemporal representation for video, depth, embodiment segmentation, and first-frame-relative 2D flow. Built on a shared DiT backbone, GenSight uses lightweight task modulation to predict all modalities within the same architecture. All tasks are jointly optimized within a unified velocity prediction space. At inference, GenSight supports two complementary modes: multi-step future video generation with aligned dense predictions and single-step dense perception from an observed video. By unifying modality representation, model architecture, and prediction space, GenSight avoids separate modality-specific pipelines and couples appearance, geometry, semantics, and motion in a shared representation. It promotes cross-modal consistency and allows dense perception to benefit from the spatiotemporal priors learned through video generation. Trained on embodied manipulation data spanning multiple robot embodiments and human-hand interactions, GenSight demonstrates strong performance in both video generation and dense 4D perception, highlighting the effectiveness of unifying seeing and imagining for embodied world modeling.
authors: Haitang Feng, Zhuoman Liu, Zhennan Wang, Sheng Wang, Juelin Li, Chengzhi Zhao, Hexiang Wei, Lin Shao

Trained on embodied manipulation data across robot embodiments and human-hand interactions, it shows strong performance in generation and dense 4D perception.

papers.abstract: Learning from offline datasets is limited in scalability, as collecting new experience is often costly or unsafe in the real world. World models offer an alternative way to generate new experience through a learned dynamics model, yet learning policies in latent space is limited due to compounding errors in imagined rollouts. To this end, we propose using the world model as a local transition generator, leveraging critic guidance to choose actions inside that model to generate synthetic experiences. We study action refinement methodologies, introducing Critic-Guided Synthetic Experience (CGSE) generation in world models. Specifically, CGSE augments an existing offline dataset by sampling candidate actions using an offline policy and refining each to maximize a first-order approximation of the $Q$-function within a trust region. We then use a frozen latent world model to imagine the future state given each updated action, and use the critic to choose the best one, appending this synthetic transition to the replay buffer. Our method requires no additional real-environment interaction or test-time planner, as it generates synthetic experience offline using the world model. On three OGBench manipulation tasks, CGSE improves an offline policy by a relative improvement of $7.1\%$ on the average success rate.
authors: Jorge de Freitas, Christos Ziakas, Alessandra Russo
bullets: Addresses limited scalability and safety of collecting new offline experience, while reducing errors from long imagined rollouts.

papers.abstract: Test-time compute mechanisms, such as retries, confidence-based escalation and non-local routing, are conventionally deployed as black-box additions to trained models. They typically add forward passes or halting heads, but give no structural account of what the extra compute buys or what it costs against the model's stability guarantees. We therefore propose a theoretical and empirical framework for test-time compute on a Latent Dynamics Model used as the memory. When an encoder's latent state $(q,p)$ is advanced by a damped symplectic (velocity-Verlet) step of a learned Hamiltonian, every mechanism that expands access has an exact phase-volume Jacobian, a bounded energy change and an exact latch-transport law. We split reachability failures into escape failures and reach failures. A Lorentz squeeze resolves escape failures by injecting bounded, re-absorbable energy. A gated canonical translation (a one-step channel across $C_T$) resolves reach failures at $\detJ=1$ exactly. We verify this certificate stack on a designed analytic testbed. Reaching just beyond $C_T$ with the squeeze requires energy that grows quadratically in the excess distance. The gated channel's energy cost equals the potential difference between its endpoints, which is zero on the matched channel measured here, and so does not grow with distance in this testbed. An untrained state-replacing map annihilates phase volume and erases stored charge, while the gated channel transports it. On a learned physics-structured memory, we show calibrated compute rationing and evaluate the scaling limits of non-local routing against a physics-free baseline. The main contribution is the formalization and verification of the certificate stack, not benchmark performance.
authors: Pratik Jawahar, Riccardo Maggioni, Jonas Petersen, Matteo Cozzi, Gian-Alessandro Lombardi, Marek Gajewski, Camilla Mazzoleni, Federico Martelli
bullets: Identifies two access failures: escape failures and reach failures.
Uses a Lorentz squeeze for bounded, re-absorbable energy injection in escape failures.
Uses a gated canonical translation that preserves phase volume exactly for reach failures.
Analytic tests show squeeze cost grows quadratically beyond the access boundary, while matched-channel translation has zero measured potential cost.
Demonstrates compute rationing and non-local routing limits on learned physics-structured memory; benchmark superiority is not the focus.

papers.abstract: In variable-step operator learning, agreement at observed step sizes does not by itself determine predictions at other temporal resolutions. We propose an operator whose step-size dependence is prescribed by a first-order Duhamel approximation of semilinear dynamics. It combines exact linear propagation with a local nonlinear function of the field and its derivatives, allowing evaluation below the observation interval without supervision densely sampled across step sizes. Under suitable conditions and at fixed spatial resolution, we prove that agreement between models at two step sizes controls their prediction differences throughout a prescribed range. We also give conditions for local identifiability of both components from two step sizes, supporting interpretation of the learned structure. A latent extension applies the same construction to learned fields. We evaluate the base model on two synthetic problems and the extension on two real datasets against several baselines.
bullets: Targets the ambiguity of predicting at unseen step sizes when models only agree at observed resolutions.
Uses a first-order Duhamel approximation: exact linear propagation plus a local nonlinear function of the field and its derivatives.
Proves that agreement at two step sizes bounds prediction differences across a prescribed range at fixed spatial resolution.
Provides conditions for locally identifying the linear and nonlinear components from two step sizes.
Evaluates the base and latent variants on synthetic and real datasets against several baselines.

papers.abstract: World models let observers explore and interact with generated worlds. Recent work shows that when observers revisit a region, current models often fail to regenerate it consistently. We view this as a context retrieval problem. LLM agents manage context retrieval at two layers of their stack. At the model layer, the KV cache design determines how much context fits in memory. At the agent harness layer, harnesses such as Claude Code pick the context sent to the LLM. Prior work on world models has mostly focused only on the model layer. In this paper, we make three contributions. First, we build a benchmark to measure world model context retrieval. It generates new worlds for every episode, preventing a model from recalling rooms using training data. It also separates context retrieval from guesses based on nearby frames. Second, we build an agent harness that performs context compaction for world models, which to our knowledge no prior work has studied. Third, we use our benchmark to study four world model designs. Context compaction lets our world models retrieve rooms up to 4 times beyond their context window without retraining. However, world models with sliding-window attention lose most of their context retrieval when dreaming. Therefore, a dreaming world agent benefits more from extending the reach of its world model using context compaction than switching to sliding window attention at the model layer.
bullets: Frames inconsistent regeneration of revisited regions as a context-retrieval problem spanning model and agent-harness layers.
Introduces a benchmark with newly generated worlds that separates true context retrieval from memorization and nearby-frame cues.
Presents an agent harness for compacting context, an approach not previously studied for world models.
Shows context compaction enables retrieval of rooms up to 4× beyond the context window without retraining.
Finds dreaming agents benefit more from harness-level context compaction than from switching to sliding-window attention.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces context compaction for world models to address context retrieval failures, a key challenge for video world models.
papers.title: Context Compaction for World Models
papers.tldr: Context compaction helps world models consistently retrieve revisited regions beyond their native context window, while sliding-window attention performs poorly during dreaming.

papers.abstract: Predictive world-model objectives need not organize latent histories according to distinctions required for later control. With privileged simulator access during training, should response-derived structural information be predicted, decoded, or imposed directly on latent geometry--and how do these choices compare with structured belief distillation? We define posterior-marginalized structural tests whose response distributions induce a pseudometric over histories, then train quotient-preserving (QP) world models by aligning shared latent Euclidean distances to that metric. Across a fixed six-task diagnostic suite, the largest differences appear under held-out structural variation: QP improves planning success by 26.1 points $[21.5,30.7]$ over metric decoding and 6.4 points $[3.8,9.0]$ over structured belief distillation. On GridWorld, metric decoding accurately recovers held-out structural distances ($\rho=.91$) while its native latent geometry remains more distorted than QP's (paired IQD difference $.22$ $[.20,.24]$), showing that relational recoverability and direct geometric alignment can diverge.
bullets: The work addresses a mismatch between predictive latent histories and distinctions needed for downstream control in partially observable environments.
Posterior-marginalized structural tests define a pseudometric over histories.
Quotient-preserving (QP) models align shared latent Euclidean distances directly with this structural metric.
Across six diagnostic tasks, QP improves planning success by 26.1 points over metric decoding and 6.4 points over structured belief distillation.
On GridWorld, metric decoding recovers structural distances well ($\rho=.91$), but its latent geometry is more distorted than QP's, indicating recoverability and geometric alignment can diverge.

papers.abstract: In reinforcement learning (RL), temporal reasoning is essential for estimating the density of future outcomes under a policy's occupancy measure. While self-predictive representations have been a dominant paradigm for occupancy density estimation, we find that they yield surprisingly poor estimates. On the other hand, generative occupancy models can produce remarkably accurate samples from the occupancy measure. Yet, they cannot easily recover occupancy densities, limiting their use for control despite their expressivity. In this paper, we propose Geometric Time Score Estimators (GTSE), a framework that bridges the two paradigms by learning occupancy density estimators along probability paths. We analyze how GTSE implicitly induces better occupancy estimators through improved representation learning and show how to directly extract self-predictive representations from this framework. Through experiments across several locomotion and manipulation tasks, we show that GTSE improves performance over state-of-the-art methods by $2\times$ to $6\times$ in goal-conditioned RL settings, and that the representations learned using our framework transfer effectively to downstream RL tasks. Website: https://aravindvenu7.github.io/website/gtse/
authors: Aravind Venugopal, Grace Liu, Jeff Schneider, Benjamin Eysenbach
bullets: Self-predictive representations can estimate future occupancy densities poorly, while generative models produce accurate samples but do not readily provide densities for control.
GTSE learns occupancy density estimators along probability paths, connecting the strengths of both paradigms.
The framework improves representation learning and enables direct extraction of self-predictive representations.
Experiments on locomotion and manipulation tasks report 2×–6× better performance than state-of-the-art methods in goal-conditioned RL.
Learned representations transfer effectively to downstream RL tasks.

papers.abstract: Accurate precipitation forecasting remains elusive as physics-based models struggle to resolve mesoscale convection and machine learning often yields physically inconsistent, blurred results that consistently underestimate extreme events. We present FitzRoy, the first system that simultaneously achieves state-of-the-art predictive skill and physical realism over the continental United States. Through a reinforced diffusion framework, where a conditional discrete diffusion model is refined via reinforcement learning, FitzRoy effectively resolves the long-standing trade-off between pointwise accuracy and structural fidelity. Across lead times up to 24 hours, FitzRoy consistently matches or exceeds state-of-the-art models while preserving structural realism and capturing extreme events. Its low-latency inference further enables deployment in real-time operational settings. In case studies such as the 2025 Texas Hill Country floods and the 2026 Missouri floods, FitzRoy signals record-breaking accumulations that existing models largely missed. By bridging the gap between realism and skill, FitzRoy establishes a new frontier for high-fidelity precipitation forecasting.
authors: Ozan Sener, Anand Avati, David Hafner, Jierui Lin, Laura Manduchi, Xiaoying Pang, Langwen Huang, Torsten Hoefler, Russ Schumacher, Vladlen Koltun
bullets: Addresses blurred, physically inconsistent forecasts and systematic underestimation of precipitation extremes.
Uses a conditional discrete diffusion model refined through reinforcement learning.
Across lead times up to 24 hours in the continental United States, it matches or exceeds state-of-the-art predictive skill while preserving realistic structures.
Low-latency inference supports real-time operational deployment.
Case studies of major Texas and Missouri floods show signals of record-breaking accumulations that existing models largely missed.

papers.selection_reason: Reinforced conditional diffusion for high-fidelity spatiotemporal forecasting; transferable to predictive world models.
papers.title: Skillful and realistic precipitation forecasting with reinforced diffusion
papers.tldr: FitzRoy combines diffusion modeling and reinforcement learning to produce accurate, physically realistic precipitation forecasts that better capture extreme events.

papers.abstract: Search-based machine-learning (ML) agents improve a solution by writing candidate programs, executing them, and keeping the best. Execution gives the search reliable feedback, but a single run can take hours, and most runs end in programs the agent discards. Recent agents try to save these runs by letting a large language model act as a world model that predicts how each program would perform. However, a wrong prediction feeds the search false information. We argue that an agent does not need to predict the outcome of execution, only the decision that execution would support. We propose World Reward Models (WRMs), which learn from real execution results to choose directly which candidate will perform better, without predicting any intermediate outcome. We prove that a selector which predicts execution from the same inputs cannot outperform the best direct selector, that predicted outcomes add an error which can make a likelihood-trained world model prefer the worse program on every instance, and that cross-entropy on executed winners drives a WRM toward the optimum. Our WRM, ForeCritic, adapts a 9B typed decision model to 5k executed program pairs. On 12,438 held-out pairs from 26 ML tasks, it picks the better program 79.4% of the time, while general-purpose LLM judges reach 53--62%, and its probabilities are calibrated. Inside AIDE, ML-Master, and ForeAgent, it cuts mean task time by 4.4--7.5 times while keeping their mean scores within 0.01 or raising them.
authors: Yuxiao Lee, Zherui Yang, Fan Liu, Hao Liu
bullets: Search-based agents waste substantial time executing programs that are ultimately discarded.
WRMs learn from executed comparisons to select the better candidate directly, avoiding error-prone intermediate outcome prediction.
Theoretical results show direct selection can outperform outcome-based world modeling, while winner-based cross-entropy training approaches the optimal selector.
ForeCritic selects the better program 79.4% of the time on 12,438 held-out pairs across 26 ML tasks, versus 53–62% for general-purpose LLM judges.
Integrated into three agents, it reduces mean task time by 4.4–7.5× while maintaining or slightly improving mean scores.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes predicting reward/decision instead of full world outcomes, a world-model idea transferable to model-based agents.
papers.title: Predict the Reward, Not the World: World Reward Models for ML Agents
papers.tldr: World Reward Models skip predicting program outcomes and directly predict which candidate will perform better, making search-based ML agents much faster without sacrificing solution quality.

papers.abstract: Pneumonia changes across respiration, inflammation, and organ function, while the measurements that describe it arrive at different times and are often incomplete. We introduce PULMOWORLD, a world model for longitudinal pneumonia dynamics that connects asynchronous state estimation, recursive simulation, and evidence-constrained planning. History-aware filtering separates state propagation from observation-driven correction, so a measurement updates the shared belief only when it is observed. That belief supports recursive forecasts of clinical values and modality representations, and summaries of future prognosis. Cap-MBRL searches imagined continuations inside an authorized action set and replaces a frozen fallback only when a candidate meets the risk budget and a predicted-cost margin. On the pneumonia cohort MASS, recursive forecasts are competitive with task-trained sequence models, and simulated future states retain prognostic information. Trained separately on public MIMIC-IV-CXR chest radiographs and clinical trajectories, this model improves prognostic discrimination over latest-value fusion in development and is competitive on long-horizon error on the locked pneumonia panel. In five known-mechanism MASS-Syn environments, Cap-MBRL lowers selection regret relative to direct fallback execution.

papers.abstract: Embodied systems can update policies, world models, skills, and executable programs from deployment experience, allowing one interaction to benefit later tasks. When a system also revises and reuses its data-acquisition, feedback, or learning procedures, experience changes the process that produces capability, introducing recursive self-improvement. This paper surveys research in physical AI through the connection between persistent capability and its improvement process. We first explain the functional distinction between learner updates and improvers, then compare policy learning, imagined experience, memory and skill accumulation, and executable harnesses. These approaches connect to revisions of curricula, rewards, and research programs in different ways. Contact validity, recovery, retention, and resource costs determine whether the resulting gains accumulate during continued deployment. An L0-L3 rubric distinguishes task-local adaptation, persistent capability gain, inherited process revision, and verified improver gain. Representative benchmarks and within-study contrasts relate these distinctions to existing results. We further propose common-data and interactive comparisons that evaluate reference and revised improvers from shared learner starts, separating the use of experience from its acquisition. This perspective connects the diverse methods, physical operating conditions, and evaluation evidence, underpinning embodied RSI. A comprehensive list of studies in this survey is available at https://github.com/nkd-lkz/physical-ai-rsi-survey.
authors: Xiaofeng Han, Kaize Luo, Zenghuang Fu, Zichong Zhu, Zhe Feng, Changwei Wang, Rongtao Xu, Weiliang Meng, Xiaopeng Zhang
bullets: Distinguishes ordinary learner updates from improvers that revise data collection, feedback, or learning procedures.
Reviews policy learning, imagined experience, memory and skill accumulation, and executable learning harnesses.
Identifies contact validity, recovery, retention, and resource costs as factors governing whether gains persist during deployment.
Introduces an L0–L3 rubric spanning task-local adaptation to verified improvement of the improver itself.
Proposes common-data and interactive comparisons to separate learning from experience from improving how experience is acquired.

figures.caption: FIGURE 1. Overview of the review framework for recursive self-improvement in physical AI. (a) Conceptual distinctions among programmed robots, learned policies, persistent self-improvement, and recursive improvement. (b) Physical experience and feedback support capability updates, while system-generated process revisions are retained and reused to govern later learning. (c) Persistent artifacts can modify the learner, the improver, or both. (d) The evidence rubric distinguishes task-local adaptation (L0), persistent capability gain (L1), inherited process revision (L2), and verified improver gain (L3). L3 requires greater subsequent gains from shared learner starts under matched resource budgets and independent tests. The levels specify evidence requirements for individual claims. Comparisons are schematic, and robot scenes are illustrative renderings.

FIGURE 3. Evidence requirements across a declared reset boundary. Episode context c, retained learner state x, and improvement procedure ϕ have different persistence roles. L0 describes task-local changes that reset; L1 concerns retained capability gains in later independent attempts. L2 requires a system-generated process revision to be inherited and used in a later learner update. L3 requires greater subsequent gains under shared learner starts, matched resource budgets, and independent tests. The diagrams illustrate the criteria and corresponding evaluation conditions.

FIGURE 5. Four carriers of persistent physical experience. Policy and value updates change parameters and action selection; world models retain predictive structure learned from observed transitions; indexed memory and skill libraries support retrieval and composition; programs and harnesses retain changes to execution logic, illustrated by a recovery branch. Each panel exposes the retained representation and its later use. A program change is classified by its functional role in execution or in producing later updates.

FIGURE 6. Fixed-model planning and model–policy co-improvement. The fixed-model planner evaluates imagined action alternatives and executes a selected action while retaining model parameters. In the coupled loop, real transitions train the model, the updated model generates imagined trajectories for policy learning, and the updated policy collects further physical experience. Solid and dashed paths distinguish physical and model-generated experience. The observed–predicted offset is schematic; coupling alone does not establish inherited revision of the improvement procedure.

FIGURE 2. Information boundaries between physical interaction, learner updates, and improver revision. Observations supply experience for learner updates; system-generated procedure changes are retained and used in later update rounds. Development screening can inform these revisions. A concealed reporting audit evaluates frozen candidates on independent held-out outcomes and supplies no feedback to the updates being assessed. Grids, contact geometry, records, and program differences are schematic representations.

FIGURE 7. Four locations for inherited improver revision. Changes to acquisition alter the selected experience; changes to feedback alter the training signal; changes to learning or search alter the update routine; changes to a development gate alter which candidates are retained. Highlighted differences are accepted, inherited, and used in a later cycle. The rows describe alternative intervention locations. Development-gate revisions remain subject to declared external constraints, while independent reporting tests stay fixed for the comparison.

FIGURE 8. Physical continuity and learning-state retention are separate, coordinated processes. Contact changes or calibration drift can require physical recovery before redeployment. Candidate changes to retained state are checked on earlier and new tasks, then accepted or rolled back to the previous checkpoint. Recovery is not itself a learning update. The resource ledger spans collection, recovery, updating, and verification, including robot time, computation, human effort, and wear or repair.

FIGURE 4. Developmental trajectories of self-improvement in Physical AI. The 46 selected works are grouped by mechanism, with a separate column for recent work. Branches indicate thematic grouping, not causal inheritance or increasing RSI maturity. Intervals have unequal duration; within-period placement follows mechanism. R, S, and D denote reported real-robot, simulated/virtual, and non-embodied settings, not evidence strength. P denotes a project report without an assigned experimental-setting tag. Persistent updates and task gains alone do not establish improver gain.

FIGURE 9. Conceptual physical failure modes. (a) A plausible pose can yield unstable contact, illustrated by contact-normal and tangential-slip directions. (b) Partial observations can produce a false-positive judgment despite an unsuccessful physical outcome. (c) A new-task update can disrupt an earlier skill. (d) Sensor calibration or actuator offsets can change the observation–action mapping. The scenes, state changes, and offsets are illustrative rather than experimental measurements.

FIGURE 11. Common-data and interactive conditions for improver comparison. In the common-data condition, cloned learner starts and identical permitted evidence enter the reference and revised improvers. In the interactive condition, each improver acquires its own evidence under matched starts and resource ceilings. Branch-specific successor learners are assessed by independent held-out tests that provide no update feedback. The two conditions assess evidence use and acquisition plus updating, respectively; report subsequent gain, retention, transfer, and actual costs.

FIGURE 12. Crossed evaluation of learner starts and improvement procedures. Each row clones a learner start and applies the reference and revised improvers; the horizontal contrast uses G and ∆G as defined in Eq. (3), with common budgets and test conditions omitted from the displayed notation. Diagonal comparisons change both learner state and improver. Estimate uncertainty over independent replicates and report absolute gains alongside relative contrasts. Match resource ceilings and record realized consumption, including construction, collection, computation, human assistance, energy, and resets. The diagram contains no measured results.

FIGURE 10. Evaluation objects in representative robot-learning protocols. Cells name the task structure, split, or metric targeted by each scoped protocol. Dashes denote objectives not encoded as direct targets in that protocol, rather than capabilities absent from the environment. CALVIN instruction chains differ from a learning history; LIBERO and Continual World explicitly evaluate sequential retention and transfer. The RoboCasa365 row denotes its public multi-task leaderboard. Sources: RLBench, Meta-World, ManiSkill2, CALVIN, LIBERO, Continual World, RoboCasa, and RoboCasa365. papers.selection_reason: Survey connecting persistent capability, world-model updates, memory, and recursive self-improvement in embodied physical AI.
papers.title: Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI: Mechanisms, Evidence, and Evaluation
papers.tldr: This survey frames embodied recursive self-improvement as systems that improve both their capabilities and the processes used to acquire those capabilities, and proposes ways to evaluate it.

papers.abstract: Controllable human motion generation has largely focused on specifying what action should occur or where the body should move. We study a complementary question: can full-body motion be controlled by specifying only when each foot contacts the ground? We introduce StepControl, an autoregressive diffusion model conditioned on a future binary left/right foot-contact schedule, without requiring target root and body poses, or semantic prompts. StepControl represents contact as explicit temporal events and injects them through dedicated cross-attention with classifier-free guidance. We further introduce a stochastic mixture noise schedule and warmup strategy for stable long-horizon autoregressive generation. Experiments show that StepControl follows prescribed contact timing more accurately than adapting existing spatially guided motion generators to contact constraints. It maintains effective contact control over long continuous rollouts and responds to edited schedules such as cadence changes, stop-and-go pauses, limping gaits, and bilateral jumping. Our results show that minimal foot-contact schedules provide an effective and intuitive temporal interface for controllable motion generation.
authors: Hojun Jang, Jinseok Bae, Donggeun Lim, Taesun Kim, Seungbin Jeong, Younghwan Lee, Yong Seok Kim, Young Min Kim
bullets: Addresses motion control without target poses, root trajectories, or semantic action prompts.

Introduces stochastic mixture noise scheduling and warmup for stable long-horizon rollouts.

Scope: control is specified temporally through foot contacts rather than detailed spatial or semantic constraints.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of StepControl. (a) Motion tokens with per-frame diffusion levels and frame embeddings attend to event condition tokens via dedicated per-layer cross-attention, predicting clean motion X̂(0) for continuous long-horizon generation. (b) Within each sliding window, 2D foot-contact signals C are expanded into 9D event-aware representations E. Conditioned on E, the denoiser steps down noisy future latents via per-frame DDIM updates (ki → k′ i), commits the earliest finalized frame x̂ (0) t to clean history, and appends a new terminal noise state (k = 99) as the window slides forward.

ARDY is rendered with its native body model.

papers.abstract: Benchmarks such as WildfireSpreadTS (WSTS) have enabled data-driven forecasting of wildfire spread from multimodal satellite time series, but they suffer from limitations: size restricts them to large fires that burn for weeks, and they are from similar environments. We introduce AFSeq, a multimodal dataset of 1,194 recent fire events (2023 to 2026) from 8 different countries across three regions, dominated by the short, small fires that existing benchmarks underrepresent. Our dataset is the largest and most diverse to date for time-series-based wildfire spread prediction. We also introduce UTAE-AR, an extension of a classical U-Net with Temporal Auto Encoder, enhanced with recurrent modules before the decoder. This allows the model to not only predict the next day but the whole sequence in an autoregressive way. Moreover, our model can feed its own predicted fire mask back one day at a time, producing the day-by-day forecasts that single-step models cannot. Our results show that UTAE-AR surpasses state-of-the-art on both WSTS, WSTS+ and AFSeq for next-day accuracy while having 21.5% of their parameters, and being able to predict confidently at a longer horizon.
authors: Jose Guillen, Renzo Zanca, Valentin Barriere
bullets: Introduces AFSeq, a multimodal dataset of 1,194 fire events across 8 countries and 3 regions, emphasizing small and short-lived fires.
Addresses the limited size and environmental diversity of existing benchmarks such as WildfireSpreadTS.
Presents UTAE-AR, a U-Net with temporal encoding and recurrent decoder-side modules for day-by-day sequence forecasting.
The model feeds predicted fire masks back autoregressively to produce multi-day forecasts rather than only next-day predictions.
Reports state-of-the-art next-day accuracy on WSTS, WSTS+, and AFSeq with 21.5% of their parameter count, plus confident longer-horizon forecasts.

papers.abstract: Time-series data play an important role in various tasks, such as weather forecasting, web traffic analysis, and speech recognition. Recently, pioneering studies have increasingly adopted Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA) based encoders to learn time-series representations through latent-space prediction. However, they often overlook the underlying factors governing transitions between time-series observations. In this work, we hypothesize that explicitly modeling the information behind changes in time series can facilitate time-series modeling. Building on this hypothesis, we propose ACTS-WM, a self-supervised latent action-conditioned world model framework for time-series analysis. First, we introduce a latent action modeling approach that infers the underlying information behind time-series transitions as latent actions, without requiring explicit action annotations. We then develop a JEPA-based encoder and an action-conditioned world model to predict target time-series representations conditioned on the learned latent actions and task information. We evaluate ACTS-WM across 4 representative tasks on 22 datasets from diverse domains, covering univariate and multivariate forecasting and classification. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate that ACTS-WM can improve downstream performance over pretrained JEPA-based encoders by learning complementary representations.

papers.abstract: On PushT, our fixed action updater (1,505 parameters) solves 8 of 16 scenes reserved from our configuration selection. The comparison planners perform as follows: Selected Adam (7 tasks solved, total planning and encoding time 218.440s), adapted iCEM (2 tasks solved, total planning and encoding time 49.309s), released LePlanner (16 tasks solved, total planning and encoding time 5.652s). The total planning and encoding time for our action updater is 59.079s. Note that our action updater does not satisfy the task-cost criterion we fixed before evaluation. We also conduct another matched experiment where we only replay the first ten commands in each context and then allow the next solve 4, 8 or 12 updates (subsequent solves all get 8 updates). Among all 16 contexts (8 scene clusters), the 3 budgets get 9, 8 and 7 successes, respectively. Interestingly, the extra updates did not rescue any failing task in this experiment. All the changes in success/failure happen in one scene cluster, where we observe that the extra updates decrease the costs of the selected latent world-model trajectories for our updater, while the tasks that used to be successes become failures. The code, weights, evaluators, execution traces and cost accounting accompany the paper.
bullets: The study evaluates learned and optimization-based planners across 16 held-out PushT scenes.
The fixed 1,505-parameter action updater solves 8/16 scenes in 59.079s of planning and encoding.
The released LePlanner solves all 16 scenes in 5.652s, outperforming the other reported planners on success and time.
In a matched replay experiment, allowing 4, 8, or 12 updates yields 9, 8, and 7 successes, respectively.
Extra updates lowered selected latent-trajectory costs in one scene cluster but turned prior successes into failures; the updater also did not meet the preregistered task-cost criterion.

papers.abstract: Embodied world models predict the visual consequences of candidate actions before execution. However, existing action-conditioned world models often adopt uniformly weighted visual generation objectives that can be misaligned with embodied prediction needs. Even with explicit motion conditioning, these objectives can underemphasize spatially sparse changes that are critical to interaction. We propose KineWorld, a transport-aware world-modeling framework that extends robot kinematics from motion conditioning to the spatial allocation of generative supervision. Kinematic Transport Lifting (KTL) constructs renderer-derived, camera-aligned transport fields from commanded robot motion. Transport-Aware World Diffusion (TAWD) calibrates their motion support on the video-latent grid and reweights future-RGB flow matching through a normalized mixture of uniform and transport-focused distributions. We train KineWorld using ALOHA-AgileX bimanual manipulation data from RoboTwin 2.0. KineWorld achieves an EWMScore-P of 68.95 in single-view evaluation and a TWB-Score of 54.82 in multi-view evaluation. These results support a shift from appearance fitting toward action-consequence modeling for embodied decision-making.
bullets: Existing action-conditioned world models may underemphasize sparse but important interaction changes under uniform visual-generation objectives.
Kinematic Transport Lifting builds camera-aligned transport fields from commanded robot motion.
Transport-Aware World Diffusion calibrates these fields on the video-latent grid and mixes uniform with transport-focused supervision.
Trained on ALOHA-AgileX bimanual manipulation data from RoboTwin 2.0, KineWorld reports an EWMScore-P of 68.95 for single-view and a TWB-Score of 54.82 for multi-view evaluation.
The framework targets action-consequence modeling, with scope demonstrated on bimanual manipulation data.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of KineWorld. Kinematic Transport Lifting (KTL) converts the commanded robot rollout into camera-aligned transport and injects its latent representation as a clean structural condition. Transport-Aware World Diffusion (TAWD) calibrates the transport support and derives mean-one token weights for the flow-matching objective, emphasizing action-responsive regions under a fixed weight budget. The weighting branch is used only during training, while the inherited action expert remains unchanged.
