Figure 1: (a) Token-conditioned WAMs use numerical trajectories or learned action embeddings for video generation (Zhu et al., 2024; Guo et al., 2025; Liao et al., 2025), but typically apply uniform RGB supervision, potentially underemphasizing interaction-critical local changes. (b) Auxiliary-cue WAMs incorporate motion-focused auxiliary cues, such as masks (Chen et al., 2026c), action images (Zhen et al., 2026), optical flow (Chen et al., 2026b), or projected kinematic fields (Yang et al., 2026), to improve motion localization. These cues alone do not directly change the spatial weighting of the primary RGB objective, potentially leaving motion localization and supervision priorities misaligned. (c) KineWorld introduces action-guided RGB supervision by lifting camera-aligned kinematic transport onto the video latent grid and reweighting flow matching, enabling actionconsequence-oriented supervision while preserving the total token weight.

papers.abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) are becoming increasingly important and useful for embodied intelligence, as they enable robots to anticipate the consequences of candidate actions before interacting with the physical environment. However, underwater robots are usually subject to passive dynamics, such as inertia, buoyancy, hydrodynamic drag, and persistent drift, which can continue to affect the vehicle even after an action is completed. Existing WAMs, which primarily predict action-conditioned visual observations, are not explicitly designed to capture such passive motion dynamics. In this paper, we present AquaWAM, the first World Action Model designed for underwater embodied agents. Instead of predicting future images, AquaWAM models both action-conditioned and passive physical dynamics, including the thruster dead band, the inertial glide that outlasts each command, and ambient currents. Specifically, it senses through the DVL, IMU, pressure sensor and joint encoders, while cameras supply only semantics for understanding goals and target pose. By modeling compact navigation states rather than high-dimensional visual observations, AquaWAM substantially reduces the model size and computational cost compared with conventional WAMs. Experimentally, AquaWAM achieves a 72.6% task success rate across 20 underwater tasks on the USIM benchmark, outperforming existing methods while making action decisions 2.7x faster than U0 on an NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin. Our model also remains effective when some onboard sensor measurements are unavailable. For example, without DVL velocity measurements, our method still achieves a 61.6% success rate, compared with 39.4% for U0.
bullets: Addresses inertia, buoyancy, drag, thruster dead bands, drift, and currents that conventional visual WAMs do not explicitly capture.
Uses DVL, IMU, pressure, and joint-encoder data for compact navigation-state prediction, while cameras provide semantic and target-pose information.
Achieves 72.6% success across 20 USIM underwater tasks and makes decisions 2.7× faster than U0 on a Jetson AGX Orin.
Maintains robustness under missing DVL velocity measurements, achieving 61.6% success versus 39.4% for U0.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) leverage large-scale vision-language pretraining for semantic robot control, but often lack explicit foresight into how robot actions change the scene. World-Action Models (WAMs) address this limitation by conditioning policies on predicted futures, yet existing approaches typically rely on computationally expensive video generation with substantial pixel-level redundancy. We present LaWAM, a Latent World Action Model that exposes predictive dynamics to robot policies through compact latent visual subgoals instead of reconstructed future video. At the core of LaWAM is a latent-action-conditioned Latent World Model (LaWM). We obtain LaWM by training a latent action model in the latent space of a pretrained vision foundation model and repurposing its forward decoder to predict future observation features for scene evolution. LaWAM then conditions action generation on these predicted latent visual subgoals to enable dynamics-aware robot control. LaWAM achieves state-of-the-art or competitive success rates (SRs) across LIBERO (98.6% SR), RoboTwin (91.22% SR), and real-world manipulation tasks while retaining low-latency inference. LaWAM runs in 187 ms per action-chunk prediction and achieves up to 24x lower wall-clock latency than pixel-space WAMs.
authors: Jialei Chen, Kai Wang, Kang Chen, Shuaihang Chen, Feng Gao, Wenhao Tang, Zhiyuan Li, Weilin Liu, Zhuyu Yao, Boxun Li, Yuanbo Xu, Chao Yu
bullets: Addresses the limited action foresight of vision-language-action models and the computational cost of pixel-space world-action models.
Learns a latent action-conditioned world model in the latent space of a pretrained vision foundation model.
Uses predicted future observation features as compact visual subgoals for action generation.
Achieves strong performance on LIBERO, RoboTwin, and real-world manipulation tasks, including 98.6% and 91.22% success rates on LIBERO and RoboTwin.
Provides low-latency inference at 187 ms per action chunk, with up to 24× lower wall-clock latency than pixel-space WAMs.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of LaWAM. Stage 1 learns a latent-action-conditioned world model from visual transitions: an inverse-dynamics encoder infers latent actions, and the decoder is retained as LaWM to predict future observation features. Stage 2 integrates LaWM into a VLA policy: latent-action distillation teaches the policy to drive LaWM, whose predicted latent visual subgoal is passed to an Alternate-DiT action expert for subgoal-conditioned action generation.

(b)–(e) Given only one initial observation in each environment or embodiment, LaWM applies the same extracted latent actions to generate context-specific latent rollouts. Panels (d) and (e) use unseen screenshots from pi.website.

Curves show feature cosine similarity for rollout vs. ground-truth future states (blue), ground-truth future vs. initial states (gray), and rollout vs. initial states (green). papers.abstract: Multimodal intelligence can be viewed as human-guided co-evolution between worlds and agents through interaction. However, scaling this process faces two bottlenecks: constructing heterogeneous, verifiable environments is costly, and manual Harness iteration cannot keep pace with growing task diversity and complexity. A key insight is that tasks with different modalities and surface forms can share the same underlying capability requirements. We therefore introduce The Trinity, a recursive self-improvement framework coupling world generation with Harness evolution through three roles: Creator, Explorer, and Evolver. Drawing on verified execution trajectories, Evolver shifts the basis of task organization from surface categories to shared requirements, reorganizing the original task tree into a hierarchical capability tree. We introduce Capability-Driven Real2Sim2Real: for heterogeneous tasks at the same node, Creator abstracts their common requirements into simplified, verifiable simulated worlds for capability learning, while evaluation on original tasks measures transfer. Along this capability tree, Explorer progressively evolves reusable capability modules through selective inheritance, forming a Harness tree whose validated updates accumulate across iterations within a fixed topology. The resulting Harnesses specialize in different capabilities, motivating a Capability-Aware Harness Router that uses public task information to select compatible module configurations from the tree. Our evolved Harnesses improve mean performance by 34 points across 28 training benchmarks and 26 points across 18 unseen benchmarks, including two real-world embodied tasks.

papers.abstract: Action-conditioned world models offer a scalable alternative to costly real-world interaction for improving robot policies. However, existing world-model-based methods largely treat world models as forward-only surrogates of the physical environment, leaving untapped a capability no physical environment affords: rewinding to past decision points to explore counterfactual futures. We introduce Rollback, a policy improvement paradigm that turns world models from passive simulators into counterfactual engines: it rolls back to critical decision points, branches into alternative actions, and contrasts their outcomes to attribute success to individual decisions. This concentrates imagination where it matters most and distills counterfactual outcomes into fine-grained, action-level supervision without a separately learned value model. We build a scalable training system that unifies distributed world-model search with asynchronous real-robot execution, forming a self-reinforcing cycle: real-world experience continually sharpens the world model, and a sharper world model in turn drives further policy improvement. We term the world-model side of this cycle test-time physics grounding, a capability that hand-built physics simulators lack: while the world model serves as the training environment, real transitions from the policy it trains correct its dynamics through a lightweight LoRA pipeline. Experiments on three challenging real-world tasks show that Rollback improves success rates over the strongest baseline by an absolute 10.67%, 11.11%, and 11.85% on block extraction, ball tossing, and tabletop curling, respectively, while achieving more stable improvement throughout training. Although initialized from teleoperated demonstrations far below human level, Rollback surpasses the average success rate of human players on both ball tossing and tabletop curling within 8 hours of training.
authors: Jiayi Luo, Yang Zhang, Liliang Chen, Nan Wang, Chen Gao, Boxiang Qiu, Zhuoxuan Li, Baorui Peng, Chuankang Li, Yuxiang Yan, Si Liu, Qingyun Sun, Shuicheng Yan, Maoqing Yao, Jianxin Li, Guanghui Ren
bullets: Addresses the limitation of forward-only world models, which cannot identify which decisions caused success or failure.

Combines distributed world-model search with asynchronous real-robot execution in a self-reinforcing training cycle.
On three real-world tasks, it improves success rates over the strongest baseline by 10.67%, 11.11%, and 11.85% absolute.
Surpasses average human success on ball tossing and tabletop curling within 8 hours, despite starting from below-human teleoperated demonstrations.

The world model predicts both multi-view observations and the robot’s proprioceptive state. (c) World model–policy co-evolution continually incorporates real trajectories to refine the world model through test-time physics grounding (LoRA SFT followed by DMD) while the policy keeps improving.

Policy snapshots are sent to search workers and edge sites; world-model snapshots are sent only to search workers.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have made substantial progress in robotic manipulation, but their generalization remains constrained by the diversity and coverage of action-labeled robot demonstrations. Human videos provide much broader behavioral and environmental experience, while learning from them faces a fundamental trade-off between scalable data and explicit action grounding. We introduce ThinkWorld, a VLA learning framework that grounds action reasoning in world dynamics and strengthens it through reinforcement learning with world imagination. ThinkWorld represents each action thought as a Chain-of-Dynamics (CoD), a sequence of discrete motion tokens that captures the intermediate dynamics connecting the current world to a future state and serves as a common action representation across embodiments. We first initialize CoD with action-labeled demonstrations, then predict the future induced by each CoD and reinforce those whose predictions better match the observed outcome. This enables videos without action annotations to provide direct supervision from observed state transitions, allowing human and robot experience to refine the same reasoning space. Experiments in simulation and on real robots demonstrate effective human-to-robot transfer and strong generalization to unseen tasks and environments.
authors: Chaehyun Kim, Chi-Pin Huang, Jisoo Kim, Min-Hung Chen, Yu-Chiang Frank Wang, Seungryong Kim, Fu-En Yang
bullets: Addresses limited diversity and coverage of action-labeled robot demonstrations.

Uses unlabeled human videos as supervision through observed state transitions, aligning human and robot experience in one reasoning space.
Simulation and real-robot experiments show human-to-robot transfer and generalization to unseen tasks and environments.

In stage (b), reinforcement learning (RL) uses the alignment between imagined and observed futures as a scalable reward for CoD reasoning over human and robot videos, strengthening action reasoning without motion annotations and improving guidance for continuous control.

papers.abstract: Scientific discovery often begins with an unexpected observation that prompts a new research question. In a world with altered physical laws, can large language models (LLMs) notice unexpected behavior, such as heavier objects falling more slowly, and discover the law through experiments without being told what to investigate? To evaluate this ability, we introduce LongChang, an automated framework that creates simulated worlds with altered physics, where one or more laws differ from ordinary physics. The evaluated LLMs act as explorers, manipulating objects and building tools to investigate their own questions without research tasks or hints about these laws. Separate LLM agents generate and review scenes, review tool designs, and evaluate reports for correctness and experimental support using the altered physical laws and exploration records. These records guide scene evolution for further exploration, allowing the full cycle to run without human intervention. Among 12 LLMs, GPT-6-Astra achieves a discovery rate of 16.7%, while the other 11 score 0%. The exploration records reveal uninvestigated anomalies and only partial identification of the altered physical laws.

papers.abstract: World models are widely proposed as core components for enabling agents to reason over long temporal and spatial horizons. Yet current evaluations often emphasize task performance while providing limited insight into whether learned world models acquire predictive latent dynamics that reflect the underlying structure of the environment. Here we introduce the concept of faithful latent world models as an equivariance condition between the environment's transition map and the learned latent dynamics. We propose latent rollout consistency (LRC) as a metric to evaluate action-conditioned latent prediction. Strikingly, we find that across the studied state of the art latent world models, none solves the task by actually faithfully modeling the dynamics of the environment.
bullets: Motivates evaluating latent dynamics beyond task performance, especially for long-horizon reasoning.
Defines faithful latent world models through an equivariance condition linking environmental transitions to learned latent dynamics.
Introduces latent rollout consistency (LRC) to measure action-conditioned latent prediction.
Finds that none of the studied state-of-the-art latent world models faithfully models the environment’s dynamics.

papers.abstract: Vision--Language--Action (VLA) models generate robot actions from visual observations and language instructions, but their understanding of physical dynamics remains limited. Video world models can capture scene dynamics, yet generating future videos introduces high latency into the control loop. We introduce PDRVLA, whose lightweight Physical Dynamics Module extracts physical tokens from vision--language features to condition action generation without online video generation. The module learns through direct prediction of future RGB, depth, and optical-flow features, with auxiliary supervision through a frozen pretrained video world model. Training relies entirely on publicly available data, expanded through human-to-robot synthesis, subtask annotation, and embodied chain-of-thought (ECoT) annotation. Across four simulation benchmarks, PDRVLA achieves success rates of 99.3% on LIBERO, 89.9% on LIBERO-Plus, 93.6% on RoboTwin~2.0, and 81.5% on SimplerEnv. Ablations show improved future prediction with world-model supervision and evaluate how subtask conditioning, future object-pose supervision, and ECoT training affect action success.

papers.abstract: We present a survey of approaches to Bayesian inference with simulator forward models, focusing on settings with prohibitively expensive simulators. In this domain, Bayesian optimization-based methods have emerged as the most promising approach. We unify existing methods into a general framework, enabling consistent reasoning about shared algorithmic structure across the fragmented literature. Within this framework, we identify the primary design choices and perform a systematic empirical comparison of their effects on inference efficiency in terms of required simulation budget. A key result of our study is that inference efficiency is often dominated by the choice of surrogate-model response variable, as it directly governs the complexity of the modeled function. Specifically, we demonstrate that the prevalent scalar log-likelihood is a poor response variable, as it discards crucial information. Based on this insight, we introduce the concept of custom \emph{proxy variables}: transformations of simulator outputs engineered to retain more information and provide smoother response surfaces, substantially improving inference efficiency over standard response variables. We provide actionable guidance and a numerically robust Julia package to facilitate practical adoption of Bayesian optimization for simulator inverse problems.
bullets: Bayesian optimization is identified as a promising approach for simulator-based Bayesian inference under tight simulation budgets.
The paper unifies fragmented methods into a common framework and systematically compares their design choices.
Surrogate-model response variables often dominate inference efficiency because they determine the modeled function’s complexity.
Scalar log-likelihoods are criticized for discarding information; custom proxy variables can preserve information and yield smoother response surfaces.
The work offers practical guidance and a numerically robust Julia package for simulator inverse problems.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in interactive world models have made it possible to generate controllable, dynamic environments from action inputs. Yet current models struggle to maintain coherence beyond roughly one minute of rollout, a limitation rooted not in model capacity but in the scarcity of long-horizon training data. Existing gameplay video datasets typically consist of clips under ten seconds, with captions that describe whole clips in coarse and undifferentiated text, which is insufficient for controllable long-horizon generation. We address this with GameVerse, a minute-scale gameplay video dataset purpose-built for long-horizon interactive world modeling. GameVerse contains 69.7K clips spanning 1,655 hours and 349.6 million frames across diverse first- and third-person gameplay, including 1,358 hours of continuous two-minute sequences, an order of magnitude longer than prior datasets. Clips pass through a unified pipeline of scene-consistent segmentation, quality filtering, camera pose estimation, and event-based caption annotation. Each clip is paired with a temporally stable camera trajectory that remains coherent across minutes, together with captions that separate static scene context from dynamic foreground events and align to event boundaries rather than fixed time windows. Comprehensive analysis shows that GameVerse surpasses existing public datasets in scale, diversity, and annotation quality. Experiments further demonstrate that training on GameVerse substantially extends the temporal horizon of interactive world models.

Experiments show that training on GameVerse substantially extends the temporal horizon of interactive world models.

papers.abstract: World action models (WAMs) predict the visual consequences of the actions they generate, which makes test-time selection a natural way to improve a fixed policy: imagine the futures of candidate actions and execute the best one. The benefit of selection is bounded by the selectable headroom, how much better the best candidate truly is, but the standard estimate, which executes each candidate once and keeps the best outcome, conflates candidate quality with the randomness of everything that follows. We introduce a denoised counterfactual protocol, based on bitwise-reproducible branching, repeated continuations, held-out oracles, and common random numbers, that measures the headroom a selector can realize, and use its measurements to build a fail-gated selector. Across four WAMs, two benchmarks, over 100,000 branched rollouts, and pre-registered tests, we find that (i) the standard estimate overstates the selectable headroom of native samples: bounds from 17 continuations per candidate place its selectable share between 24% and 66% for three WAMs; (ii) structured action perturbations create up to 16 points of selectable headroom; and (iii) in both WAMs with action-conditioned imagination, imagined futures carry candidate-outcome information with no detectable loss relative to real futures, information that the value head of Cosmos Policy leaves unused. Deviating from the policy chunk only when a readout of the WAM predicts failure, the selector raises closed-loop task success from 76.9% to 81.6% on held-out episodes of training tasks, with the largest gain where the policy fails most often, and from 62.6% to 69.8% on unseen tasks.
authors: Haojia Gao, Yue Cao, Yumin Liu, Haohua Que, Mingkai Liu, Guanqiu Guo, Zhuo Zou, Bokui Chen, Xueqian Wang
bullets: Standard one-shot estimates overstate selectable headroom because they mix candidate quality with downstream randomness.
A counterfactual protocol uses reproducible branching, repeated continuations, held-out oracles, and common random numbers to measure realizable headroom.
Structured action perturbations add up to 16 points of selectable headroom; native-sample selectable share is estimated at 24–66% for three WAMs.
Action-conditioned imagined futures retain candidate-outcome information comparable to real futures, but Cosmos Policy’s value head does not exploit it.
A fail-gated selector improves success from 76.9% to 81.6% on held-out training tasks and from 62.6% to 69.8% on unseen tasks.

papers.abstract: Accurate forecasting of global total electron content (TEC) is important for space weather monitoring and the reliable operation of satellite communication and navigation systems. We propose a physics-guided generative artificial intelligence (AI) framework for day-ahead global TEC forecasting. The framework builds on flow matching, which learns to gradually transform samples from an initial distribution into new samples that share the statistical characteristics of the target data. The proposed model incorporates ionospheric dynamics described by a partial differential equation (PDE) into this transformation process, guiding the changes between initial and target samples using physical knowledge. The model further combines the physical dynamics with statistical patterns captured from data to learn this transformation, adaptively adjusting their relative contributions at each location. The model is trained and evaluated using one year of global TEC data generated by the Thermosphere Ionosphere Electrodynamics General Circulation Model (TIEGCM). The results demonstrate that our model improves both spatial and temporal forecasting accuracy over representative benchmarks, including statistical, deep learning, and generative AI methods at all lead times and across latitudes. The average root mean square error (RMSE) is 39.2% lower than that of ConvLSTM and 23.8% lower than that of the same framework without physical guidance. The learned contribution weights vary systematically with latitude and across geographic locations, showing how the physical contribution changes across the forecast domain. These findings demonstrate that explicit physical guidance improves generative forecasts of global TEC and highlight the value of incorporating physical dynamics into generative AI modeling.

papers.abstract: We present a variational control framework that connects sampling-time guidance and reward-based model adaptation through a shared Jacobian pullback. Starting from terminal reward maximization with a path-space KL penalty, the Gibbs variational principle and Doob transform yield a correction to the generative dynamics. A local denoising approximation exposes the pullback that transports output preferences to the controlled variable. This construction gives Variational Optimal Guidance (VOG) in state space and extends to Distilled Variational Optimal Control (DVOC) by amortizing locally improved endpoints into model parameters. The resulting controls share a local variational rule: VOG acts through the denoising Jacobian, while DVOC realizes the parameter pullback by endpoint distillation. Under a linear MMSE model, VOG's exact correction lies in the data subspace. On ImageNet, VOG reduces DiT-XL/2 FID from 2.27 to 2.04 at 250 sampling steps and from 7.58 to 4.44 at 25 steps. After 20 updates on Z-Image-Turbo, DVOC improves HPSv3++ and four held-out evaluator scores over the untrained model, with the highest corresponding means among the trained methods compared. These results connect inference-time control and reward adaptation through a common geometric principle.
authors: Ruoyu Wang, Xinyi Ye, Yunshuo Shi, Liangyu Yuan, Beier Zhu, Chi Zhang

papers.abstract: World-action models (WAMs) incorporate the prediction of future observations into robot policy learning. However, most WAMs build on billion-parameter vision-language or video-generation backbones, which incur high training cost and inference latency. In this letter, we present GAWM (Geometry-Aware World Model), a compact multi-task WAM that predicts future observations in the latent space of a frozen DINOv3 encoder. GAWM compresses the features of each camera view into a small set of tokens. A lightweight predictor, conditioned on the task rather than on actions, forecasts these tokens at two future horizons. The forecast is supervised with the dense patch features of future frames, which requires it to encode the spatial layout of the future scene. An action decoder directly regresses a chunk of future actions from the current and predicted tokens. With fewer than 100M parameters and no robot or video pretraining, GAWM outperforms billion-parameter WAMs on RoboTwin 2.0 and performs comparably to billion-parameter VLAs on LIBERO. On a dual-arm robot, it achieves lower action-prediction error on held-out demonstrations than a fine-tuned billion-parameter VLA, with substantially lower inference latency. Ablation studies show that the latent world model substantially improves performance when training data or training time is limited. Code is available at https://github.com/gaoxiang12/ga-wm.
authors: Yang Liu, Xiaoli Liu, Liuzhao Li, Yuduo Song, Muyuan Liu, Xiang Gao

Uses fewer than 100M parameters, requires no robot or video pretraining, and performs strongly across RoboTwin 2.0, LIBERO, and a dual-arm robot; benefits are especially pronounced with limited data or training time.

papers.abstract: Learning from experience is essential for building the next generation of agents that continually expand their capabilities. Pretrained vision-language models (VLMs) already internalize rich world knowledge, yet this knowledge is rarely leveraged to drive policy improvement through online interaction. Realizing this potential efficiently remains challenging, as policy updates shift the agent's interaction distribution, requiring the world model to adapt accordingly, while continually updating large pretrained models is computationally expensive. To address this challenge, we introduce Dwell, a model-based reinforcement learning (RL) framework that reframes a VLM as a recurrent latent transition operator, endowing it with the ability to predict, adjust, and act in latent space. Leveraging the VLM's own representations and its dual role as both world model and policy, the agent continually learns from real interactions to anticipate and evaluate action outcomes, and from latent imagination to improve its behavior. Across five interactive visual environments, Dwell achieves the strongest overall performance among trainable methods while substantially reducing the compute required for imagination, showing that effective world models for VLM agents need not reconstruct the future; they need to predict futures that are useful for action. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/Tom111-lhx/Dwell
authors: Haoxi Li, Sikai Bai, Jianfei Ma, Qinglin Hou, Xiaocheng Lu, Tao Han, Jie Zhang, Song Guo

papers.abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) learn representations for robot control by coupling future visual prediction with action generation. Successful manipulation depends primarily on how the robot and task-relevant objects evolve, whereas future-video prediction must also reconstruct the appearance and background of the entire scene. We therefore propose Trace-WAM, which augments video-action learning with future 3D motion prediction as an auxiliary objective. This objective supervises temporal point correspondence together with image-plane displacement and depth change, directly describing the interaction dynamics and spatial changes involved in manipulation. To this end, we adopt a three-branch Mixture-of-Transformer (Tri-MoT) architecture to jointly learn video prediction, motion prediction, and action generation. The motion expert predicts future trajectories from current visual features, allowing motion supervision to shape the representations used for action generation. Because the action expert does not consume predicted trajectories, inference retains the current-observation policy path: a single visual forward pass followed by action denoising. Experiments on RoboCasa-GR1, LIBERO, and LIBERO-Plus demonstrate strong in-distribution performance and out-of-distribution generalization, with particularly clear gains over Fast-WAM under limited demonstrations and distribution shifts.

Experiments on RoboCasa-GR1, LIBERO, and LIBERO-Plus show strong in-distribution performance and improved generalization, especially with limited demonstrations and distribution shifts.

papers.abstract: Learning controllable world dynamics from heterogeneous interaction videos is challenging because robot embodiments use incompatible action spaces, while human videos lack native control labels. We present RynnWorld-Latent, a cross-embodiment video world model that uses the 3D-grounded latent actions introduced by RynnLAM as a shared conditioning interface. This representation enables joint pretraining on human interaction videos, robot demonstrations, and simulation rollouts without requiring a common native action space. Built on a pretrained video transformer, RynnWorld-Latent combines global action tokens with an identity-initialized local pathway that aligns actions with future video latents. We pretrain on 23 datasets comprising approximately 553.5M frames and adapt the model to target robots through post-training. The framework supports two data-generation routes: digital teleoperation uses target robot commands to generate action-video demonstrations, while latent-action synthesis transfers source motion to an edited initial frame and pairs the resulting rollout with retargeted pseudo robot actions. Experiments show improved video prediction metrics on public benchmarks and two real-robot platforms, alongside qualitative action following when different action sequences share the same initial observation. Synthetic mid-training improves policy success rates on LIBERO and LIBERO-Plus, and both generation routes improve real-world policy success rates over real-demonstration-only training in the evaluated settings. These results support universal latent actions as a scalable interface for learning controllable visual dynamics across heterogeneous embodiments.
authors: Haoyu Zhao, Yinzhou Tang, Zixuan Wang, Minghao Zhu, Dongchi Huang, Xingyue Zhao, Qin Zhao, Kehan Li, Siteng Huang, Xin Li, Zhenyu Zeng, Mingxiu Chen, Deli Zhao, Zhongyu Li
bullets: Addresses incompatible robot action spaces and missing control labels in human videos.
Uses RynnLAM latent actions as a universal interface for joint cross-embodiment pretraining.
Combines global action tokens with an identity-initialized local pathway to align actions with future video latents.
Supports digital teleoperation and latent-action synthesis for generating robot-targeted training data.
Reports improved video prediction and policy success across benchmarks and evaluated real-robot settings; scope is limited to the described platforms and tasks.

figures.caption: Figure 2 Overview of theworld-model data engine. Top: Scalable data editing. RynnLAM extracts latent actions from a source human video, while its first frame is edited to depict the target robot. Conditioned on the edited frame and the original latent actions, RynnWorld-Latent generates robot video rollouts. The generated observations are paired with pseudo-actions obtained through motion retargeting and inverse kinematics. Bottom: Digital teleoperation. Human control signals are retargeted to robot actions, which condition RynnWorld-Latent together with a reference scene. Generated frames provide visual feedback to the operator, while the recorded actions and generated observations form synthetic demonstrations without physical robot execution.

papers.abstract: Computationally expensive simulations and real-world observations often provide data at a lower temporal resolution than downstream tasks require. Averaging observations at fixed grid points can introduce errors, and motion estimates alone do not determine how the physical field values change. In this work, we study whether learning to correct a simple numerical interpolation improves the reconstruction of intermediate scientific fields. Our model, interpolative FLow EXpert (iFLEX), first estimates the missing field by taking a weighted average of the two observations at each grid point, giving more weight to the observation closer to the requested time. During training, subtracting this estimate from an observed intermediate field gives the residual that a conditional diffusion model learns to generate. Both observations condition the model, together with the target time, the interval between observations, and available physical parameters. To reconstruct an unobserved intermediate field, the generated residual is added to the weighted average. We evaluate iFLEX on Navier-Stokes Kraichnan turbulence, Shanghai radar precipitation, and sea surface temperature. Across these datasets, iFLEX achieves lower reconstruction error than the evaluated baselines, including optical-flow and diffusion models developed for video frame interpolation in computer vision. In a controlled turbulence comparison at a Reynolds number of 36,000, learning the residual reduces relative Frobenius norm error from about 13.7 for direct field generation to 10.5, with the diffusion backbone and training setup held fixed. Code is available at https://github.com/paulpuren/iflex.
authors: Pu Ren, Michael W. Mahoney, N. Benjamin Erichson
bullets: Targets missing temporal resolution in simulations and observations, where averaging and motion estimates alone may poorly capture field evolution.
Builds a time-weighted average of two observed fields, then generates a correction residual conditioned on both observations, target time, interval length, and physical parameters.
Evaluated on turbulence, radar precipitation, and sea-surface temperature data.
Achieves lower reconstruction error than evaluated optical-flow and video-interpolation diffusion baselines.
In controlled turbulence experiments, residual learning reduced relative Frobenius error from about 13.7 to 10.5 versus direct field generation.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overview of iFLEX for temporal interpolation between two observed physical fields. Linear interpolation provides an initial estimate of the intermediate state, while a conditional diffusion model generates the correction needed to reconstruct the missing field. The two endpoint observations are processed by a shared spatial encoder, and their features are combined and supplied to the denoising network through learned gates. The requested interpolation time, observation interval, available physical parameters, and diffusion noise level are incorporated through feature-wise linear modulation (FiLM). After the final denoising step, the generated residual is added to the linear estimate to obtain the reconstructed intermediate field.

Figure 5: Reconstruction accuracy depends on both spatial structure and computational cost. (a) Comparison of the ground-truth and reconstructed spatial spectra for NSKT at Re = 12000. The intended diagnostic is the windowed vorticity power spectrum; the underlying figure export requires the verification noted in the text. (b) RFNE versus inference time for the evaluated methods at the same Reynolds number. iFLEX achieves 4.11% RFNE but requires 35.39ms per generated field, compared with 13.20% and 3.54ms for Super SloMo. Bubble size represents model parameter count.

Figure 1: Interpolation using two observed states achieves lower reconstruction error than the tested one-endpoint predictor on NSKT. (a) Observations are separated by a time interval ∆t, and intermediate fields are reconstructed at a finer temporal spacing δt. Unlike prediction from an initial state, interpolation uses observations from both ends of the interval. (b) At Re = 36000, iFLEX achieves lower relative Frobenius norm error (RFNE) than the one-endpoint predictor (Model A) across the tested intermediate times. Over the full evaluation set, the RFNE is 10.5% for iFLEX and 20.4% for Model A. Reconstruction errors are generally larger near the midpoint, where the requested state is farthest in time from both observations.

Figure 7: Learning the interpolation residual gives the lowest reconstruction error in the NSKT ablation study at Re = 36000. (a) The full model achieves 10.48% RFNE, compared with 20.44% for the one-endpoint predictor (Model A), 12.71% without interval duration conditioning (Model B), 10.75% with fixed-gap training (Model C), and 13.73% for direct generation of the full intermediate field (Model D). (b) Model A uses only the first observation and has larger errors toward the end of the interval, whereas iFLEX uses both endpoints. (c) The full model is compared with Model C, which is trained at a fixed gap of T = 20. The curves show the error at each intermediate time.

Figure 4: iFLEX achieves lower reconstruction error across the observation interval on NSKT, Shanghai radar, and SST. The panels report RFNE at each requested intermediate step, using 20 intermediate states for NSKT at Re = 12000, eight for radar, and ten for SST. Errors are generally largest near the middle of the interval, where the requested field is farthest in time from both observations. The curves display RFNE as a fraction rather than a percentage.

Figure 10: The SST example shows similar broad temperature patterns across the methods, with differences in local gradients and finer spatial variations. The rows compare the ground truth with U-Net, EDEN, Super SloMo, and iFLEX at intermediate indices k = 2, 4, 6, 10. The panel labels t denote target indices. On the held-out South Pacific test set, iFLEX achieves 1.81% RFNE and 0.87 SSIM (Table 2). These scores summarize the full evaluation set rather than the displayed examples.

Figure 6: iFLEX achieves lower reconstruction error than Super SloMo and EDEN across three temporal gaps on NSKT at Re = 36000. The panels show RFNE at each intermediate step for T = 12, 16, and 24. During training, iFLEX samples T ∈ {5, . . . , 20}; therefore, the first two gaps lie within its training range, while T = 24 exceeds it. Errors generally increase toward the midpoint of the observation interval, particularly for the longer gap. RFNE is plotted as a fraction.

Figure 2: In these examples, iFLEX more closely reproduces the vortex structures in the ground-truth NSKT fields than Super SloMo. The panels compare the ground truth with reconstructions from Super SloMo and iFLEX at t = 0.005 s and t = 0.02 s, using the same two endpoint observations. Red boxes highlight differences in vortex shape and fine-scale structures. Each intermediate field is reconstructed independently.

Figure 9: The illustrated radar reconstructions show differences in the location and intensity of localized precipitation. The rows compare ground-truth fields with reconstructions from U-Net, EDEN, Super SloMo, and iFLEX at intermediate indices k = 2, 4, 6, 8. The panel labels t denote these indices. In this example, iFLEX more closely retains localized precipitation structures at the middle target times than EDEN or Super SloMo. Aggregate RFNE is 32.69% for iFLEX, 56.54% for EDEN, and 36.77% for Super SloMo (Table 2).

Figure 8: iFLEX more closely reproduces the vortex structures in the illustrated NSKT fields at Re = 36000. The rows show the ground truth and reconstructions from U-Net, EDEN, Super SloMo, and iFLEX, evaluated at intermediate indices k = 5, 10, 15, 20. The panel labels t indicate target indices, rather than physical time in seconds. Differences are visible in the location and shape of vortices and in smaller vorticity structures. Over the corresponding test set, iFLEX achieves 10.48% RFNE compared with 22.87% for Super SloMo (Table 1); these aggregate values are not errors for the individual displayed fields.

Table 13: iFLEX achieves the lowest RFNE for all three evaluated Reynolds numbers outside the training range. Its errors are 0.50% at Re = 600, 0.73% at Re = 1000, and 10.48% at Re = 36000. The larger error in the upper-range case reflects the greater reconstruction difficulty of the tested flow, rather than parameter extrapolation distance alone. All methods use 256 × 256 crops and T = 20.

Table 12: iFLEX achieves the lowest reconstruction error at both unseen Reynolds numbers within the training range. At Re = 12000 and 24000, its RFNE is 4.11% and 7.10%, compared with 7.81% and 12.23% for PIT-UNet. All methods use 256× 256 crops and T = 20. Bold denotes the best value at the reported precision.

Table 11: iFLEX achieves the lowest RFNE and highest SSIM at every Reynolds number used during training, when evaluated on independent held-out trajectories. RFNE ranges from 1.21% at Re = 2000 to 9.35% at Re = 32000. All methods use 256× 256 crops and T = 20. Bold denotes the best value at the reported precision.

Table 10: Explicit mean and difference features improve reconstruction at the three evaluated Reynolds numbers outside the training range, while endpoint-only fusion performs comparably at the two unseen values within it. Both models are trained at Re ∈ {2000, 4000, 8000, 16000, 32000} and evaluated with T = 20. At Re = 36000, complete fusion achieves 10.48% RFNE, compared with 11.26% for endpoint-only fusion. Bold indicates the best value at the reported precision.

Table 1: iFLEX achieves the lowest reconstruction error at all three unseen Reynolds numbers. All methods are trained using Re ∈ {2000, 4000, 8000, 16000, 32000} and evaluated with 20 intermediate states between the endpoint observations. The values Re = 12000 and 24000 are unseen but lie within the training range, while Re = 36000 tests extrapolation beyond that range. At Re = 36000, iFLEX achieves 10.48% RFNE, compared with 22.87% for Super SloMo and 25.52% for EDEN. RFNE denotes relative Frobenius norm error, PC denotes Pearson correlation, and SSIM denotes structural similarity. Inference time (IT) is reported in milliseconds per generated intermediate field. Bold values indicate the best reconstruction scores.

Table 8: iFLEX reduces reconstruction error relative to linear interpolation at all three tested radar observation gaps. Both methods become less accurate as the gap increases. At T = 12, residual refinement reduces RFNE from 55.02% to 40.42%. Bold indicates the better result within each gap.
Table 7: Training settings for iFLEX. All three datasets use Adam with a learning rate of 10−4. The denoising architecture is shared, while training duration and batch size vary by dataset.

Table 2: iFLEX achieves the lowest reconstruction error on Shanghai radar precipitation and sea surface temperature. The evaluations use eight intermediate states for radar and ten for sea surface temperature. Radar precipitation shows substantially larger reconstruction errors, while linear interpolation is already accurate for the more slowly varying temperature fields. On SST, iFLEX reduces RFNE from 1.94% for linear interpolation to 1.81%. Inference time (IT) is reported in milliseconds per generated intermediate field. Bold values indicate the best reconstruction scores.

Table 15: Reconstruction error varies more between the two evaluated trajectories at Re = 32000 than at Re = 8000 or 12000. Values report the mean and sample standard deviation of trajectorylevel RFNE for a fixed trained checkpoint. Each trajectory contributes 256 spatiotemporal samples with 20 intermediate targets. Table 14: iFLEX retains the lowest RFNE when EDEN and Super SloMo are additionally conditioned on Reynolds number. Conditioning improves EDEN under the tested implementation, while the constant-channel condition increases Super SloMo’s error. At Re = 36000, the conditioned baselines achieve 23.67% and 24.26% RFNE, respectively, compared with 10.48% for iFLEX. Bold indicates the lowest error at each Reynolds number.

Table 3: Dataset characteristics and evaluation configurations. NSKT contains simulated vorticity fields, while Shanghai radar and SST contain observed precipitation and temperature fields. papers.selection_reason: Develops iFLEX, a generative refinement learning method for temporal interpolation in scientific machine learning (e.g., Navier-Stokes). This fits the 'Video World Models' subtopic as it learns to predict and reconstruct intermediate physical field states over time.
papers.title: Generative Refinement Learning for Temporal Interpolation in Scientific Machine Learning
papers.tldr: iFLEX improves intermediate scientific-field reconstruction by learning a conditional diffusion residual on top of time-weighted linear interpolation.

papers.abstract: Interactive world generation requires models to follow successive commands while preserving relevant history and action consequences. We present Hy-Nomas, a video world model with an 8B diffusion backbone that supports free-form text instructions and continuous camera control across multiple interaction turns. It generates variable-length segments conditioned on current inputs and cached history. Our central design aligns structured video captions with action-aware causal attention: descriptive context remains accessible across segments, while action instructions are restricted to their intended temporal windows. A vision-language Prompt Enhancer (PE) translates user requests and multimodal interaction histories into structured conditions for the next segment. A multi-stage curriculum progressively introduces causal generation, text interaction, camera control, and training on model-generated histories, followed by diffusion distillation. In human evaluation, Hy-Nomas shows superior performance over existing world models. We release model weights, code and benchmarks, together with a lightweight adaptation workflow, to support reproducible research on interactive world generation.
authors: Qiaoling Chen, Jiaxiang Cheng, Xueqing Deng, Tiankai Hang, Ji Hou, Jiaqi Li, Yifan Liu, Tao Lu, Junshu Tang, Yu Tang, Yao Teng, Yu Tian, Heng Wang, Weizhi Wang, Xiyao Wang, Xilun Wu, Mingyu Yang, Yangbin Yu, Rui Zhao, Longjun Cao, Linghao Chen, Haoyi Duan, Jiaming Han, Mingji Han, Enhua Jiang, Shunkai Li, Yanzhe Liang, Qinwei Ma, Cong Wang, Lei Wang, Bing Wu, Ke Xing, Ray Ying, Zhentao Yu, Key Zhang, Yuan Zhou, Zhengguang Zhou, Kai Zou
bullets: Supports successive text instructions and continuous camera control across multiple interaction turns.
Generates variable-length video segments conditioned on current inputs and cached interaction history.
Uses action-aware causal attention to preserve descriptive context while limiting actions to their intended time windows.
A vision-language Prompt Enhancer converts user requests and multimodal histories into structured next-segment conditions.
Human evaluations report better performance than existing world models; weights, code, benchmarks, and an adaptation workflow are released.

figures.caption: Figure 5: Overview of the model architecture. A structured multi-segment prompt, a video clip, and a camera trajectory are encoded into text, video, and camera tokens, respectively. Text and video tokens are processed by N = 54 dual-stream MMDiT blocks. Within each block, segmentwise causal attention with 3D RoPE allows tokens to attend to the current and preceding segments, while diffusion timestep embeddings modulate both streams. The two streams pass through separate MLPs, and camera cross-attention further conditions the video stream on camera tokens. During autoregressive generation, keys and values associated with both text and video tokens are stored in the KV cache as context for subsequent segments. The 3D VAE decoder maps denoised video latents to RGB frames. Purple, blue, and green denote the text, video, and camera streams, respectively.

Figure 10: Overview of Hy-Nomas-Bench. Top: Model outputs for an example case from Bench-3 (interleaved text–camera control). Bottom: (a) World settings span diverse scenes, visual styles, subjects, and viewpoints. (b) 280 cases cover multi-turn text interaction, camera navigation, interleaved control, and spatial memory. (c) Unified control maps instructions to text, binary key states [T, 8] (W/A/S/D and four arrow keys), or per-frame 4 × 4 camera-to-world matrices [T, 4, 4], where T is the frame count. Generation continues across turns without world resets. (d) Three annotators evaluate prompt following, physical plausibility, camera control, and memory consistency through pairwise comparisons. Results are summarized by win/tie/loss rates and net win rate (win minus loss, in percentage points).

Figure 2: Data pipeline. Raw videos are split, transcoded, and filtered by basic video properties and visual quality. Hierarchical clustering supports within-cluster deduplication, and a VLM assigns labels to each video from a predefined taxonomy. Video tagging adds captions and, for selected clips, camera-trajectory annotations. Across each training stage, adaptive sampling adjusts the training distribution in response to weaknesses identified from evaluations of earlier stages.

Figure 1: Interactive world generation with Hy-Nomas. Free-form text instructions and continuous camera control can be interleaved across successive interaction turns. At each turn, a vision-language Prompt Enhancer converts the user request and observed world history into a structured text prompt and a duration for the next video segment. Conditioned on these inputs and cached context, Hy-Nomas autoregressively generates the next segment, allowing the world to unfold through continued interaction.

Figure 6: Comparison of segment-wise and action-aware causal attention. (a) Tokens attend to all video and text tokens in the current and preceding segments. (b) Action-aware masking further restricts access to action-specific text tokens. Colors indicate query-to-key modality pairs; gray cells are masked. head denotes the environment description for the current segment, and a0, . . . , an denote actions within that segment.

Figure 3: Structured video captioning. The VLM annotates segments sequentially, maintains subject identities, interleaves scene and camera descriptions chronologically, and records subject actions separately with timestamps. A final text-only turn reviews, translates, and validates the annotations to produce aligned English and Chinese captions. During training, camera-motion sentences and their tags are removed when camera trajectories are available and retained otherwise.

Figure 4: Structured caption format. Video-level fields define perspective, style, and shared subject profiles. Segment descriptions interleave scene information and camera-tagged motion chronologically, excluding main-subject references. The first segment provides a full description; later segments describe changes. Subject actions and their visible outcomes are recorded separately in action-tagged entries using subject tokens. Action intervals are non-overlapping and remain within segment boundaries.

Figure 7: Segment Forcing with streaming backward. Each current segment receives a flowmatching loss; a one-step low-noise estimation supplies cached context for later segments. Streaming backward retains only one segment’s computation graph at a time, accumulating gradients for a single optimizer step after the full sequence. The cache update of the final segment is skipped.

Figure 19: Qualitative results of LoRA-SFT. We compare the distilled model with domain-specific LoRA-SFT variants. The upper examples show improved cinematic aesthetics after cinematic LoRA-SFT, while the lower examples show more physically plausible robotic manipulation, with cup deformation more faithfully reflecting the gripper’s applied pressure. LoRA-SFT denotes the distilled model with the trained LoRA weights merged into it.

Figure 9: Prompt Enhancer (PE) workflow. PE generates an initial dense caption in the first turn. In subsequent turns, users can choose text prompts or camera control, and PE combines the selected input with the full interaction history to generate a dense caption that AR-DiT uses to produce the next video segment. Each turn’s dialogue and generated video are appended to the history.

Figure 11: Illustration of the design of Bench-4: Spatial memory. Each uses a static anchor object and four outbound–return pairs. Bench-4 evaluates object permanence under different camera movements, and appearance/layout consistency. Left: Different trajectory types. Center: Scene, camera frustum, and trajectory. Right: Inference results by Hy-Nomas.

Figure 8: Downstream LoRA adaptation workflow. Train LoRA adapters on the base autoregressive model (before distillation), then merge the learned weights into the distilled model for efficient deployment, without full-model fine-tuning or repeating distillation.

Figure 15: Pairwise human evaluation of camera control. We compare Hy-Nomas with Genie 3, HappyOyster-Wandering, and LingBot-World v2 on 100 shared trajectories. We measure how accurately the model responds to navigation commands.

Figure 17: Pairwise human evaluation of spatial memory. We compare Hy-Nomas with Genie 3, HappyOyster, and LingBot-World v2 on 60 shared scenarios involving reversible or revisiting camera trajectories. We measure how well the model remembers the anchor object and its surrounding environments.

Figure 13: Pairwise human evaluation of multi-turn text control. We compare Hy-Nomas with HappyOysterDirecting and LingBot-World v2 on prompt following and physical plausibility. Within each evaluation dimension, the two 100% stacked bars show wins (green), ties (gray), and losses (pink) from the perspective of Hy-Nomas.

Figure 16: Pairwise human evaluation of interleaved text and camera control. We compare Hy-Nomas with the adapted LingBot-World v2 baseline on 60 scenarios with alternating text and camera inputs. We consider prompt following, physical plausibility, and camera control during the evaluation.

Figure 21: Rank-gap-weighted human evaluation of Hy-Nomas-PE (ours). Bench-1 and bench-3 are reported separately; each pair compares Hy-Nomas-PE with Qwen3.8-27B and Kimi-K3. Bench-1 evaluates prompt following and physical plausibility; bench-3 also evaluates camera control. Category labels are shared within each benchmark. Each 100% stacked bar shows win (green), tie (gray), and loss (pink) votes from the perspective of Hy-Nomas-PE.

Figure 20: Pairwise human evaluation of cinematic LoRA-SFT against the distilled model. We evaluate prompt following and physical plausibility on Bench-1, and camera control on Bench-2. The three 100% stacked bars show wins (green), ties (gray), and losses (pink) from the perspective of LoRA-SFT relative to the base model. LoRA-SFT denotes the distilled model with the trained LoRA weights merged into it.

Figure 12: Qualitative comparison of multi-turn text interaction. In the first example, Hy-Nomas clearly shows the apple being grasped, lifted, and brought to the plate. LingBot-World v2 changes the apple’s color and gripper structure, while HappyOyster-Directing shows discontinuous views without a clear grasp-and-lift progression. In the second example, Hy-Nomas visualizes the requested spatula, cutting on the board, and strawberries in the glass bowl. LingBot-World v2 only shows cutting strawberries and a knife without spatula, while HappyOyster-Directing does not move strawberries into the bowl.

Table 2: Multi-stage training of Hy-Nomas. Stage 2 progresses from segment-causal to actionaware and camera-conditioned CPT. Segment-causal CPT includes a continuation on higher-quality data. Downstream LoRA adaptation is performed separately after the listed training stages.
Table 1: Summary of primary architectural settings.

Table 3: Models evaluated on each benchmark. Checkmarks indicate the model is evaluated on the benchmark; dashes indicate that the benchmark settings is not applicable to the model’s provided interaction interface. For LingBot-World v2, we adapt their open-source model for Bench-3.

papers.abstract: Joint-embedding predictive architectures (JEPAs) enable world models to plan from images by predicting future embeddings. However, their visual prediction objectives do not explicitly incorporate task-relevant state information, so the physical state that determines task progress may not be reliably captured in the latent space. Supervising world models with simulator state can make planning more informative, but it requires deciding which state features matter. Features are typically selected by hand or weighted uniformly, and a uniform weighting gives every standardized state feature equal influence, so redundant coordinates can overcount the same variation, while irrelevant ones can obscure task-relevant differences. To address this limitation, we propose SWIM (State Weighting with Inverse-Dynamics Model), which learns state weights from offline trajectories by predicting recorded actions from current states and observed future displacements. The learned weights quantify each feature's contribution to action prediction and define a weighted state metric for state-supervised training, which we demonstrate by aligning latent and state distances. The inverse-dynamics model is used only during training, so the resulting world model plans from images with no additional planning-time computation. Across five simulated robotic manipulation tasks, SWIM consistently improves planning success over uniform state weighting.
authors: Jiaming Hu, Shi Bo, Yan Zheng, Tian Wang, Florian Dubost, Alejandro Mottini, Junze Liu, Arvind Srinivasan, Kai Zhong, Kun Qian, Sharon Gao, Vianne Gao, Houyu Zhang, Qingjun Cui
bullets: Addresses the problem that visual JEPA objectives may miss physical state information important for task progress.
Learns feature weights by predicting recorded actions from current states and future observed displacements.
Uses the weights to define a state metric for aligning latent and state distances during training.
The inverse-dynamics model is training-only, adding no planning-time computation.
Improves planning success over uniform state weighting across five simulated robotic manipulation tasks.

papers.abstract: System identification, namely the inference of mathematical representations of dynamical systems from measured data, is fundamental to engineering diagnostics, prognostics, and decision-making. Bayesian filtering offers a principled framework for probabilistic state estimation but traditionally relies on prescribed transition and observation models. Recent advances in deep Bayesian filtering address this limitation by embedding learnable representations within probabilistic state-space formulations, enabling data-driven identification of unknown dynamics while retaining physical structure and uncertainty-aware inference. This tutorial provides a systematic introduction to deep Bayesian filtering for nonlinear structural system identification, focusing on the interplay between learned dynamics, physical inductive biases, and posterior inference. The Deep Markov Model serves as a data-driven reference, while the Physics-guided Deep Markov Model (PgDMM) and Neural Extended Kalman Filter (Neural EKF) illustrate complementary approaches based on amortized variational inference and differentiable Kalman filtering, respectively. Their capabilities are examined through dynamic state estimation and joint dynamic state and parameter estimation on a three-dimensional shear-frame benchmark with hysteretic Bouc-Wen connections and sparse acceleration measurements. The results highlight important distinctions between measurement-conditioned reconstruction and open-loop forecasting, demonstrate how physical structure can improve latent-state interpretability without necessarily ensuring predictive fidelity, and reveal differences in the robustness of response and parameter estimation. Practical guidelines for model construction, training, evaluation, and deployment are provided, together with an outlook on remaining challenges in uncertainty calibration, identifiability, and real-world validation.
authors: Wei Liu, Konstantinos Vlachas, Eleni Chatzi
bullets: Addresses data-driven identification of unknown nonlinear structural dynamics from measured data while retaining probabilistic state estimation.
Introduces Deep Markov Models, Physics-guided Deep Markov Models, and Neural Extended Kalman Filters as complementary approaches.
Evaluates dynamic state estimation and joint state–parameter estimation on a three-dimensional shear-frame system with hysteretic connections and sparse acceleration data.
Distinguishes measurement-conditioned reconstruction from open-loop forecasting and compares robustness of response and parameter estimation.
Highlights unresolved challenges in uncertainty calibration, identifiability, and validation on real-world systems.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Common probabilistic state-space skeleton and method-specific realizations of the three deep Bayesian filtering frameworks considered in this work. The top panel shows the latent state zk evolving under the transition model fν and generating observations xk through the emission model hϕ, with the dynamics driven by inputs uk. Inference recovers the latent state from the observation sequence through an approximate posterior q. The bottom panels arrange the three frameworks according to increasing physics-based inductive bias. The DMM constitutes the fully data-driven baseline, with learned transition, emission, and amortized inference models and no prescribed physical organization of the latent state. The Neural EKF introduces an intermediate level of structure by replacing the amortized encoder with the EKF predict-update recursion and, in its structural specialization, by organizing the latent state into displacement- and velocity-like coordinates, while retaining learnable transition and emission models. The PgDMM introduces stronger physics-based bias by embedding a parameter-dependent ROM within the transition and emission models, while retaining the amortized inference architecture of the DMM.

Figure 5: Recovery of unmeasured structural displacement (left) and velocity (right) from the inferred latent states in the dynamic state estimation setting. Results are shown for channel 9, corresponding to the longitudinal (x) direction of the fifth sensor in Figure 2a, selected because its estimation errors are closest to the average errors of each framework. Neither displacement nor velocity is directly observed by either model. The inferred states are projected at their original scale and processed consistently with the reference signals. For displacement, frequencies below 1 Hz are removed, eliminating the integration-related linear trend that cannot be determined from acceleration measurements and accounting for no more than approximately 3% of the reference displacement energy. For velocity, the mean is removed.

papers.selection_reason: Deep Bayesian filtering and Deep Markov Models for learned dynamics are transferable to world-model learning, though the application is structural system identification.
papers.title: Deep Bayesian Approaches for Interpretable Nonlinear Structural System Identification
papers.tldr: A tutorial compares deep Bayesian filtering methods for interpretable, uncertainty-aware identification of nonlinear structural dynamics, emphasizing trade-offs between physical structure, latent interpretability, and predictive reliability.

papers.abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) leverage pretrained video generative models for robotic control by jointly predicting future visual observations and actions. The visual prediction objective plays a key role in adapting pretrained video representations to the target robot domain. Yet standard visual prediction inherited from video pretraining treats all visual regions uniformly, despite their differing relevance to robotic control. We therefore investigate the spatial allocation of visual supervision in WAMs and show that focusing supervision on dynamic regions can substantially improve policy performance. Building on this finding, we introduce Motion-Guided Asymmetric Prediction (MoGAP), which augments WAM training with motion-focused visual prediction. MoGAP allocates noise asymmetrically across regions, training the model to reconstruct more heavily corrupted dynamic regions using less corrupted static regions as context. MoGAP is trained alongside standard video-action prediction through a training-only auxiliary prediction path within the shared video diffusion backbone. It uses motion cues derived directly from training videos, requiring neither an external teacher nor additional modalities. Across robot manipulation benchmarks and WAM architectures, MoGAP consistently improves policy performance, increasing success rates on the GR-1 tabletop benchmark from 38.8% to 47.5% for Fast-WAM (Wan2.2-5B) and from 52.3% to 62.3% for Cosmos3-Nano.
authors: Taeyoung Kim, Junyoung Sung, Heeseung Kwon, Minseop Kim, Jinwoo Shin
bullets: WAMs benefit from allocating more visual supervision to regions that move and matter for control.
MoGAP applies asymmetric noise: dynamic regions are more corrupted, while static regions provide context for reconstruction.
It adds a training-only auxiliary prediction path alongside standard video-action prediction, using motion cues from training videos without extra modalities or teachers.
Across manipulation benchmarks and WAM architectures, MoGAP improves success rates, including GR-1 gains from 38.8% to 47.5% and 52.3% to 62.3%.

papers.abstract: Traditional multiple sclerosis (MS) image analysis has primarily focused on retrospectively detecting and segmenting lesions. This study investigates whether baseline FLAIR MRI can identify regions at risk for future lesion formation beyond population-level spatial patterns. We introduce FORESEE-MS, an evaluation protocol that uses a fold-specific population-prior atlas as a baseline and assesses predictions using pooled voxel-level discrimination (AUROC and AUPRC) and within-patient lesion localization (Recall@Top-K%), with patient-level bootstrap confidence intervals. We evaluated five deep learning models (3D U-Net, Attn+ResBlock+VAE, ViT, and two SwinUNETR variants) using 5-fold cross-validation on 39 subjects from the MSSEG-2 dataset. The atlas achieved the highest pooled voxel-level AUROC and AUPRC, with no deep learning model reliably outperforming it on either metric. However, the 3D U-Net and Attn+ResBlock+VAE achieved higher mean voxel-level within-patient Recall@Top-K% than the atlas at all evaluated thresholds, although most paired confidence intervals for the differences included zero. These findings suggest that baseline FLAIR may contain patient-specific predictive information, but in this small cohort, it remains uncertain whether this information improves lesion forecasting beyond a population-prior atlas.
authors: Maryam Akhavan Aghdam, Sudip Mittal, Noorbakhsh Amiri Golilarz, Shahram Rahimi
bullets: Tests prospective lesion forecasting rather than retrospective lesion detection or segmentation.
Compares five deep learning models with a fold-specific population-prior atlas using voxel-level discrimination and within-patient localization metrics.
Evaluates models with 5-fold cross-validation on 39 subjects from the MSSEG-2 dataset.
The atlas performed best on pooled voxel-level AUROC and AUPRC, while 3D U-Net and Attn+ResBlock+VAE had higher mean within-patient Recall@Top-K%.
Most paired confidence intervals included zero, so improvement over the atlas remains uncertain in this small cohort.

figures.caption: Fig. 1: Overview of the FORESEE-MS workflow. (a) Training-subject follow-up new-lesion masks are used to construct the fold-specific population-prior atlas and supervise the deep learning models. (b) At inference, the models receive only baseline FLAIR and the distance-to-brain-boundary map. (c,d) The atlas and each deep learning model independently produce voxelwise risk maps for future lesion formation. (e) Risk maps are evaluated using pooled voxel-level AUROC and AUPRC and within-patient Recall@Top-K%. (f) Held-out follow-up lesion masks are used only for evaluation.

Fig. 3: Qualitative comparison of predicted risk maps for three MSSEG-2 subjects. (a) Subject 057 (hit): deep learning models assign high risk around a ring-shaped FLAIR hyperintensity adjacent to new lesions, while the atlas produces smaller periventricular hotspots. (b) Subject 021 (partial hit): most methods highlight the smaller lesion but miss the larger lesion above it. (c) Subject 094 (miss): no method places a hotspot directly on the lesion in the displayed slice, although some models assign high risk to nearby regions. In each map, blue to red indicates low to high relative risk within the brain.

Fig. 2: Recall@Top-K% across methods: (a) voxel-level recall averaged over 28 lesion-positive subjects and (b) lesionlevel recall pooled over 147 lesions. Error bars indicate 95% patient-level bootstrap CIs for each method.

Table 1: Pooled voxel-level AUROC/AUPRC from 5-fold cross-validation across 39 subjects, with 95% CIs estimated from 1,000 patient-level bootstrap resamples. Best values in each column are shown in bold.

papers.selection_reason: Predicts future 3D states (lesions) from baseline MRI using deep learning, aligning with the concept of environment dynamics forecasting in world models.
papers.title: FORESEE-MS: Toward Prospective Spatial Forecasting of Future Multiple Sclerosis Lesions from Baseline FLAIR MRI
papers.tldr: FORESEE-MS evaluates whether baseline FLAIR MRI can predict future MS lesion locations beyond a population-prior atlas, finding suggestive but inconclusive patient-specific predictive information.

papers.abstract: We tackle the challenge of building real-time interactive video worlds with user-defined behaviors. Such worlds must track object states, apply interaction rules, and render the resulting consequences as users act. Yet existing end-to-end video world models typically learn interaction dynamics within the generator, making it difficult to specify object-level rules and reason about their consequences. In this work, we introduce BoxWorld, which separates interaction reasoning from generative rendering. Given user-specified rules, a coding agent creates a Box World Engine that determines interaction outcomes and exposes the resulting object states through a lightweight interface of layout boxes, persistent object attributes, and dynamic status variables, leaving appearance and physical effects to generative rendering. A Box-State Generative Renderer then renders this evolving state stream into video autoregressively, enabling online control over object motion, state switches, and conditional events. Rendering this state stream is non-trivial: the renderer must respond to object-level state updates in real time while remaining coherent with the generated history. To this end, we introduce a three-stage training strategy that learns object grounding from open-domain videos and state transitions from gameplay videos, both annotated automatically, and finally performs rollout distillation on self-generated histories. We further propose PairedStateBench, a paired benchmark for fine-grained interaction control. BoxWorld substantially outperforms end-to-end world models and remains competitive across multiple public benchmarks. Project page: https://boxworld-web.github.io.
authors: Zike Wu, Ahmed Hatem, Chintan Trivedi, Wallace Michel Pinto Lira, Xuebin Qin, Lele Wang, Renjie Liao
bullets: A coding agent converts user-defined rules into a Box World Engine that tracks object states and determines interaction outcomes.
A Box-State Generative Renderer turns state updates into coherent autoregressive video while supporting online control of motion, switches, and conditional events.
The system uses a three-stage training strategy covering object grounding, state transitions, and rollout distillation.
PairedStateBench is introduced to evaluate fine-grained interaction control.
BoxWorld substantially outperforms end-to-end world models and remains competitive on multiple public benchmarks.

papers.abstract: World-action models (WAMs) offer a promising framework for embodied intelligence, yet mainstream approaches remain centered on video foundation models or vision-language models. Even when geometric features extracted by 3D models such as VGGT are incorporated, they are typically passed into a video model or VLM that serves as the primary backbone, leaving 3D geometry as an auxiliary input or prediction target rather than the native foundation for world modeling. We present E0.5, a geometry-native world-action model built directly on 3D foundation models. E0.5 introduces two key innovations. First, it adopts a 3D foundation model as the primary backbone, making 3D geometry the native representation for both world modeling and action prediction. Second, it explicitly predicts future 3D states together with actions, enabling the model to capture geometric world dynamics beyond action-only modeling or future video prediction. Experiments on RoboTwin 2.0 first demonstrate the effectiveness of E0.5 without embodied-data pretraining, achieving success rates of 89.90\% and 50.09\% under clean and randomized settings, respectively. Building on these results, we further pretrain E0.5 on more than 160k robot trajectories from AgiBotWorld-Beta, jointly learning robot actions and future geometry within the pretrained 3D foundation. This embodied pretraining improves mean real-world manipulation success rates by approximately 15 and 7 percentage points on AgileX Piper and Zerith H1, respectively. Together, these results demonstrate the potential of geometry-native foundations to acquire robot interaction knowledge and transfer it to physical manipulation. E0.5 embodies this geometry-native approach as a member of the VWA family of world-action models.
authors: Era AI Lab Team, Jianhao Lai, Zhihao Zhan, Zhiquan Liao, Qichang Li, Shubin Chen, Zhiyuan Liu, Hongsen Lei, Jianman Lin, Xiaoxin Lin, Ke Gong, Baiyue Gu, Shiming Chen, Junlin He, Longqi Yang, Junrong Xiao, Haolin Luo, Xiaojuan Su, Jianfeng Li, Yu Luo, Xu Sun, Likui Zhang, Jusheng Zhang, Qinhan Lyu, Tianshui Chen, Liang Lin, Guangrun Wang

Uses a 3D foundation model as the primary backbone for both world modeling and action prediction.
Predicts future 3D states alongside actions to model geometric world dynamics.
On RoboTwin 2.0, achieves 89.90% success in clean settings and 50.09% in randomized settings without embodied-data pretraining.
Pretraining on over 160k robot trajectories improves real-world manipulation success by approximately 15 and 7 percentage points on AgileX Piper and Zerith H1, respectively.

papers.title: E0.5: From Reconstructive to Future-Predictive 3D Foundations for Robotic World-Action Modeling
papers.tldr: E0.5 makes 3D geometry the native foundation for world-action modeling and jointly predicts robot actions with future 3D states, improving simulated and real-world manipulation performance.

papers.abstract: Changing a deployment policy can invalidate a world model's uncertainty while leaving the physical transition mechanism and predictor unchanged. For one-step prediction, if source and target laws share the conditional mechanism $P(Y|X)=Q(Y|X)$, then the intervention is identified by the pre-outcome change of measure $w(X)=dQ_X/dP_X$. For policy-controlled dynamics this ratio factors into state-occupancy and action-propensity terms. Weighted conformal calibration transports marginal coverage to the target law; with an estimated ratio $\hat w$, $P_Q\{Y \in C_{\hat w}(X)\} \ge 1-\alpha-TV(Q,\hat Q) \ge 1-\alpha-E_P|w-\hat w|$. Population log-loss regret for a source-versus-target domain classifier bounds the same ratio error. If $h$ is its clipped target posterior, $\rho$ is the target-domain prior, and $\Delta(h)$ is population log-loss regret, then $E_P|w-\hat w_h| \le (1/(\rho\gamma))\sqrt{\Delta(h)/2}$. An exact cancellation improves the dependence from a generic odds-map bound of order $\gamma^{-2}$ to $(\rho\gamma)^{-1}$. Our experiments use a released DINO-feature world model and physical Franka trajectories. Under the strongest controlled state-action shift, ordinary 90% conformal sets cover 55.0%, whereas oracle and learned-ratio calibration cover 91.0% and 90.9%. The learned surrogate remains within 0.9% total variation of the target law. Calibration is relative to the deployment law: the model can remain fixed while calibration follows the intervention. We machine-check in Lean 4 the finite-support algebraic and causal identities used in the classifier-regret argument, including its coverage-composition step.
bullets: Under shared transition mechanisms, policy changes affect calibration through a pre-outcome density ratio over states and actions.
Theoretical bounds relate target coverage loss to ratio-estimation error, which can be controlled using domain-classifier log-loss regret.
An exact cancellation improves the classifier-based error dependence from order γ⁻² to (ργ)⁻¹.
In experiments, ordinary 90% sets covered 55.0%, versus 91.0% with oracle and 90.9% with learned-ratio calibration under strong shift.
The approach is validated on DINO-feature world-model predictions and physical Franka trajectories; key finite-support identities are machine-checked in Lean 4.
