papers.selection_reason: Conformal uncertainty calibration for fixed world models under policy intervention directly fits world models and learned environment dynamics.
papers.title: Calibrated for Which Policy? Conformal Uncertainty for Fixed World Models Under Intervention
papers.tldr: Weighted conformal calibration can preserve uncertainty coverage after policy interventions by reweighting fixed world-model predictions toward the deployment distribution.

papers.abstract: Direct-policy World Action Models (WAM) have demonstrated the benefits of decoupling action generation from explicit future visual prediction for efficient inference in autonomous driving and embodied control. However, they still require tens of denoising steps to achieve competitive action quality, incurring substantial latency and hindering real-time deployment. Simply reducing the number of denoising steps will collapse the nonlinear multi-step denoising trajectory into coarse updates, substantially degrading action quality. To reduce the denoising steps while enabling real-time action generation, we present an effective world action model with one-step action generation, namely OSWAM, for autonomous driving and embodied control. We argue that it is the absence of structured action priors in random noise initialization that forces direct-policy WAMs to recover coherent action sequences through iterative denoising. Hence, we construct imagination tokens to initialize the diffusion process, providing physical priors and action-conditioned representations. We further introduce privileged information distillation with future conditioning to enhance future-aware action generation. As a result, OSWAM can efficiently and effectively generate high quality actions in just one diffusion step. Our experiments demonstrate that OSWAM achieves comparable or even better results in both autonomous driving and embodied control than direct-policy WAM and Joint-WAM that require tens of steps. It obtains approximately $3\times$ speedup over direct-policy WAM baselines and supports real-time compiled inference with latency as low as 40ms on an NVIDIA RTX 5090 GPU. The project page is available at https://gwenzhang.github.io/OSWAM/
bullets: Direct-policy world action models typically need tens of denoising steps, limiting real-time deployment.
OSWAM uses imagination tokens to provide physical priors and action-conditioned representations at diffusion initialization.
Privileged information distillation with future conditioning improves future-aware action generation.
Experiments report comparable or better performance than multi-step direct-policy and Joint-WAM baselines, with about 3× speedup and latency as low as 40 ms on an NVIDIA RTX 5090.
The abstract evaluates autonomous driving and embodied control, without specifying broader domains or limitations.

papers.selection_reason: OSWAM reduces world action model inference to a single diffusion step using imagination tokens, enabling real-time autonomous driving and embodied control.
papers.title: OSWAM: An Effective World Action Model with One-Step Action Generation
papers.tldr: OSWAM enables high-quality one-step action generation for autonomous driving and embodied control by initializing diffusion with structured action priors and distilling future-aware information.

papers.abstract: Latent world models are typically pre-trained offline and kept frozen at test time, so planning with them can degrade under distribution shift. Test-time adaptation (TTA) can mitigate this degradation by updating the model during deployment. Unlike pre-training on fixed data, TTA for planning is closed-loop: the planner uses model rollouts to select actions, and the resulting transitions drive the next update. This raises the question: which objective should guide TTA for planning? Under a prediction-only objective, the model is fit only to the outcomes of its own actions, so it can remain wrong about the actions that would reach the goal, and low prediction error need not translate into better planning. Inspired by reward-biased maximum likelihood from adaptive control, we introduce Optimistic Test-Time Adaptation (OpTTA). Its objective has two terms, the prediction loss on observed transitions and the planner's goal-reaching cost on its candidate rollouts, both minimized over the model parameters. The planning term biases adaptation toward models that are optimistic about reaching the goal, without any additional environment interaction. Across visual and environment shifts on manipulation, reaching and navigation tasks, OpTTA raises final planning success over the frozen model by 13.5 percentage points on average, compared with 6.9 for the prediction-only objective (AdaJEPA), when only the predictor is adapted. When the encoder is adapted as well, the gains are 13.5 and 7.5 points. These experiments span three JEPA world models with different encoders and training objectives and, for temporal straightening, both CEM and gradient-based planners. Our results suggest that test-time adaptation of world models for planning benefits from an optimistic, task-aware term in addition to the prediction loss.
bullets: Frozen latent world models can plan poorly when deployment conditions differ from training.
Prediction-only adaptation fits observed transitions but may remain inaccurate about goal-reaching actions.
OpTTA jointly minimizes observed-transition prediction loss and the planner’s goal-reaching cost on candidate rollouts.
Across manipulation, reaching, and navigation shifts, OpTTA improved final planning success by 13.5 percentage points on average, versus 6.9–7.5 for prediction-only adaptation.
The approach was evaluated with three JEPA world models and both CEM and gradient-based planners, without additional environment interaction.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces Optimistic Test-Time Adaptation (OpTTA) for world models, adding a planning term to prediction loss to improve goal-reaching under distribution shift.
papers.title: Adapt for Planning, Not just Prediction: Optimistic Test-Time World Model Adaptation
papers.tldr: Optimistic, goal-aware test-time adaptation improves world-model planning under distribution shift more than prediction-only adaptation.

papers.abstract: Feed-forward 3D foundation models have recently reshaped multi-view reconstruction, yet dynamic 4D understanding still often relies on large-scale motion supervision or hand-crafted, architecture-specific heuristics. We ask whether frozen 3D foundation model tokens already encode motion-relevant information that can be exposed by lightweight readout functions, rather than re-learning motion-specific features with high-capacity decoders. Through probing on three representative backbones, we find that static--dynamic separation is decodable from frozen token representations. Our rank-restricted and spectral analyses on $π^3$X reveal that the recovered motion cues are concentrated in a low-dimensional subspace. Building on this, we propose Probing-based Motion Distillation (PMD), which converts pairwise motion-state compatibility scores against a fixed anchor token into dense motion masks. Trained on only 160 YouTube-VOS videos using a single 16 GB GPU, PMD transfers zero-shot to DAVIS, SegTrackv2, and FBMS-59 without target-benchmark fine-tuning. With multi-view pretrained geometric backbones, PMD outperforms training-free heuristics and approaches substantially heavier supervised and self-supervised methods, suggesting that motion decoding from frozen 3D foundation models can be lightweight and data-efficient.
bullets: Motion information can be separated from static content using simple readouts over frozen tokens.
Rank-restricted and spectral analyses on π³X indicate that motion cues lie in a low-dimensional subspace.
ProMo3D introduces Probing-based Motion Distillation, using anchor-token compatibility scores to produce dense motion masks.
Trained on 160 YouTube-VOS videos, PMD transfers zero-shot to DAVIS, SegTrackv2, and FBMS-59.
With multi-view pretrained geometric backbones, PMD outperforms training-free heuristics and approaches heavier supervised and self-supervised methods.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of Probing-based Motion Distillation (PMD). Given an input frame group, a frozen feed-forward 3D foundation model such as π3X [36], VGGT [34], or Depth Anything 3 (DA3) [21] produces token representations. A lightweight probe trained on only 160 videos maps these features into a probe-induced static–dynamic discriminative representation. PMD then converts anchor-based pairwise probe scores into dense dynamic score maps, which are thresholded into coarse masks and optionally refined with SAM2 [29]. It transfers zero-shot to DAVIS [26, 27], SegTrackv2 [17], and FBMS-59 [14], while requiring substantially less training data and trainable capacity than high-capacity motion decoders such as GeoMotion [8].

Figure 3: Qualitative comparison on DAVIS [26] and SegTrackv2 [17] against training-free methods based on feed-forward 3D foundation models. The semantic classes shown here are absent from the 160-video training subset of π3X-PMD. All binary masks shown here are generated without SAM2 [29] refinement. PMD produces cleaner dynamic score maps and more coherent coarse masks.

Figure 5: Scene-diversity starvation analysis. (a) Low-rank probing (k = 8) matches or exceeds full-rank probing under reduced training data, indicating a compact static–dynamic discriminative structure. (b) Downstream mask quality degrades gradually rather than collapsing.

Figure 2: Layer-wise motion decodability on DAVIS-all [27]. Low-rank quadratic probes expose static–dynamic discriminative cues across the multi-view geometric modules of all three backbones, outperforming linear and diagonal probes.

Figure 6: Semantic leakage in π3X-PMD. The two static background flamingos receive elevated dynamic scores alongside the moving foreground instance, illustrating imperfect separation of motion and semantic cues.

Figure 7: Stress test of the fixed anchor token a = 0 convention on a DAVIS-all [27] evaluation example for the two non-padded backbones in the main analysis. The upper-left reference patch is marked in green in the input frame. For each backbone, we compare a standard case where the fixed a = 0 patch is static with a rare violation where the same patch is fully dynamic according to the ground-truth mask. For both DA3-PMD and DUSt3R-PMD, the violation moderately increases the background response, but it does not invert the prediction: the moving foreground remains separable and is recovered by both the coarse and refined masks.

Figure 4: Low-rank structure of the probe-induced static–dynamic discriminative representation on π3X-PMD, illustrated for DAVIS-all [27]. (a) Principal Component Analysis (PCA) illustrates clear separation between static and dynamic tokens. (b) The singular spectrum decays steeply in the leading components, especially in earlier layers, revealing strong rank concentration. (c) Performance saturates at a very low effective rank, indicating that the probe-induced motion cues are compact.
Figure 8: Additional layer-wise motion decodability on DAVIS-all [27]: VGGT [34], π3 [36], and MapAnything [13].

Figure 11: Limitation: Fine-grained Motion vs. Binary Detection. PMD highlights the breakdancer with the most prominent motion and assigns moderately elevated scores to nearby people with subtler in-place motion relative to the static background. However, the pipeline ultimately produces a binary static–dynamic mask rather than distinguishing different motion types or motion magnitudes.

Figure 10: Scene-diversity starvation and layer-wise semantic leakage on π3X [36]. Visualization of PMD dynamic score maps across network depth under varying amounts of training data. While deeper representations entangle motion with semantics, reducing the training subset to only 10 videos exacerbates this leakage across all layers. The starved probe incorrectly highlights static foreground objects, whereas the 160-video model maintains a focus on actual motion, particularly in its shallow and intermediate layers.

Figure 9: Additional scene-diversity starvation analysis on DAVIS-all [27]. We report token-level Normalized Gain for the default low-rank quadratic probe (k = 8) across π3X [36], DA3 [21], and DUSt3R [35] while reducing the number of YouTube-VOS training videos. Solid lines denote the mean over available random subset seeds, and shaded bands denote one standard deviation when multiple seeds are available. Performance degrades gradually as training diversity is reduced, while the uncertainty bands remain moderate overall and widen mainly in the most data-starved regimes.

papers.selection_reason: Probes frozen 3D foundation models to decode motion cues, contributing to the understanding of environment dynamics in video data.
papers.title: ProMo3D: Probing Motion Cues in Frozen 3D Foundation Models
papers.tldr: ProMo3D shows that frozen 3D foundation-model tokens contain low-dimensional, decodable motion cues that enable lightweight, data-efficient motion-mask prediction.

papers.abstract: Force-sensitive manipulation requires contact and load information that is not provided explicitly by visual observations. We present CW-WAM, a world action model that jointly predicts video, motion, and contact wrench. Inspired by hybrid motion-force control, it contains a unified interaction module that treats both motion and contact wrench as modeling targets and predicts time-aligned motion-wrench chunks as control references. A pair-causal attention mechanism structures the motion-wrench dependencies, while a long fixed-length wrench memory retains past interaction information. The predicted wrench chunk acts as a force reference for a 20-Hz outer-loop admittance controller within a slow-fast control system that maintains force feedback and smooth motion between model queries. CW-WAM improves contact prediction and increases the insertion success rate from 25% to 70% for square pegs with 1-mm clearance per side and from 40% to 95% for power adapters, compared with WAM without wrench input. It also improves lifting-height accuracy across different loads. Our framework with an admittance controller reduces force-reference RMSE from 4.8 to 2.7 N for peg insertion and from 2.0 to 1.3 N for wiping, respectively, with smaller force fluctuations during successful execution. Project website: https://cw-wam-project.github.io/
bullets: Addresses the lack of explicit contact and load information in visual observations.
Jointly predicts video, motion, and time-aligned contact-wrench chunks using pair-causal attention and long wrench memory.
Uses predicted wrench as a force reference for a 20-Hz outer-loop admittance controller in a slow-fast control system.
Compared with WAM without wrench input, insertion success rises from 25% to 70% for square pegs and from 40% to 95% for power adapters.
Reduces force-reference RMSE from 4.8 to 2.7 N for peg insertion and from 2.0 to 1.3 N for wiping, while improving lifting-height accuracy across loads.

papers.abstract: The microphysics of dark matter (DM) is imprinted on cosmological structure across an enormous dynamic range. Nonlinear cosmological observables are most reliably modeled with N-body and hydrodynamic simulations. However, systematic N-body scans over DM theory space are prohibitively expensive. Machine learning emulators provide a possible solution, but are currently limited by either low resolution or only the ability to emulate specific observables. We introduce Astrolabe, a flow-matching-based generative emulator designed to be free of both constraints. Astrolabe acts directly on the 6N phase-space coordinates of N individual particles. With no voxel grid in the output, there is no voxel-resolution ceiling, and in principle any observable can be measured from inference. Astrolabe is computationally tractable via a field-particle hybrid transformer in which every particle cross-attends to multiscale field tokens, so compute and memory are linear in N. Astrolabe incorporates physical flow matching by taking the prior distribution for the flow to be approximate COmoving Lagrangian Acceleration (COLA)-based coordinates rather than unphysical noise, with momentum and mass conservation enforced at all points along flow time. In the Lambda-CDM cases we test, Astrolabe produces realistic fields with accurate power spectra, halo mass functions, velocity profiles, and halo density profiles. We also observe out-of-distribution generalization, with accurate emulation of dark-acoustic oscillation initial conditions. Astrolabe is also capable of being fine-tuned to simulate very large N and we demonstrate this by emulating a TNG50-3-dark simulation at a fraction of the cost. This method represents a first step toward a general and powerful cosmology simulation surrogate, which may eventually permit the inclusion of baryonic physics and a systematic exploration of richer dark sector interactions.
authors: Ibrahim Elsharkawy, David Curtin, Yonatan Kahn, Neal Weiner
bullets: Addresses the high computational cost of scanning dark-matter theory space with N-body and hydrodynamic simulations.
Generates all 6N particle phase-space coordinates directly, avoiding voxel-resolution limits and restricting inference to predefined observables.
Uses a field-particle hybrid transformer with linear-in-particle compute and memory, plus COLA-based priors and enforced momentum and mass conservation.
Produces realistic power spectra, halo mass functions, velocity profiles, and density profiles in tested ΛCDM cases, and generalizes to dark-acoustic oscillation initial conditions.
Can be fine-tuned for very large particle counts, demonstrated on a TNG50-3-dark simulation at lower cost; broader baryonic and dark-sector applications remain future scope.

papers.selection_reason: A generative emulator for cosmology simulations using flow matching, which predicts future environments and acts as a world model for physical dynamics.
papers.title: ASTROLABE: A 3D Particle-Level Surrogate for Cosmology Simulation with Physical Flow Matching
papers.tldr: Astrolabe is a particle-level flow-matching emulator that efficiently generates cosmological simulations while preserving physical constraints and supporting flexible observable measurements.

papers.abstract: Deterministic dynamics modeling of tendon-driven continuum robots remains challenging owing to uncertainties in material behavior, tendon transmission, friction, and contact. Measured joint configurations and nominal tendon commands do not fully characterize these internal mechanical factors, leaving uncertainty in the subsequent motion. We therefore develop a history-conditioned, physics-informed flow-matching framework for probabilistic dynamics prediction, using motion and actuation histories to predict the distribution of the next complete joint configuration. By recursively sampling next-step configurations under prescribed commands, the model predicts distributions of future whole-body motions. In simulation, scenario-specific models achieve five-second trajectory Energy Scores (lower is better) of 12.05 mm under internal friction variation and 9.29 mm under unobserved actuation disturbances. Relative to the conditional variational autoencoder and diffusion baselines, Flow attains lower Energy Scores and coverage closer to the nominal level in both scenarios. Ablations support history and structural conditioning in both scenarios. On the physical robot, predictions under two tendon-command profiles excluded from training capture the principal motion sequences, with five-second Energy Scores of 11.91 and 11.42 mm, lower than the compared baselines. The predicted-to-measured spread ratios are 1.65 and 1.22 (closer to 1 is better). These results support history-conditioned probabilistic dynamics prediction under incomplete mechanical observations.
bullets: Addresses uncertainty from material behavior, tendon transmission, friction, and contact that is not captured by current configurations and nominal commands.
Uses motion and actuation histories with structural conditioning to predict distributions of the next complete joint configuration.
Recursive sampling produces distributions of future trajectories under prescribed tendon commands.
In simulation and physical-robot tests, the method achieved lower Energy Scores than variational and diffusion baselines, while capturing principal motion sequences.
Results support probabilistic dynamics prediction under incomplete mechanical observations, with evaluation focused on tested friction, actuation-disturbance, and command-profile scenarios.

papers.abstract: Interactive world models keep the KV of past chunks as retrieval memory so that revisited places stay consistent. On a single consumer machine (one RTX 4090, 32 GiB of host memory, one NVMe SSD), long sessions with such memory hit two walls. The first is capacity: the KV of Matrix-Game 2.0 exhausts host memory after 45 seconds of video in bf16 and after 2.8 minutes in int4. The second is the model's positional horizon of 4.3 minutes. We show that this memory is capacity-bound rather than bandwidth-bound and that its access set is known before compute, because the camera pose is an input. An analytical model built on these observations predicts spill points to within one chunk and classifies zero versus non-zero stalls correctly on held-out configurations. Guided by it, WorldPager stores int4 KV in a GPU/DRAM/NVMe hierarchy instead of recomputing it, prefetches each chunk's memory from the extrapolated pose, never waits on a miss, and writes back in the background; to our knowledge, it is the first to place the KV memory of an interactive world model on an NVMe tier with zero-stall prefetching. With training-free position handling, it generates 37.5 minutes of video continuously with zero stalls and constant host memory, at about 9.5 frames per second. On a sealed test set, int4 storage shows no measurable quality loss; on long-gap revisits it lowers image quality by about one MUSIQ point.
bullets: Addresses host-memory exhaustion and the model’s limited positional horizon during long interactive sessions.
Uses an analytical access model based on known camera poses to predict spill points and classify potential stalls.
Stores KV memory in a GPU/DRAM/NVMe hierarchy, prefetches before computation, avoids waiting on misses, and writes back asynchronously.
Generates 37.5 minutes of continuous video at about 9.5 FPS with zero stalls and constant host memory on a single RTX 4090 system.
Reports no measurable quality loss with int4 storage on a sealed test set, but about a one-point MUSIQ drop for long-gap revisits.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. WorldPager overview. KV of past chunks is stored as int4 blocks (one block per layer and chunk) in a pinned DRAM pool and spills to NVMe. A miss reuses the previous retrieval set instead of waiting. Cold dirty blocks are written to NVMe by a background thread.

papers.title: WorldPager: Zero-Stall Tiered Memory for Long-Horizon World Models on a Single Consumer GPU

papers.abstract: We present GaussianSpline, a dynamic 4D Gaussian Splatting method that models per-Gaussian motion using adaptive, non-uniform piecewise cubic B\'ezier splines. Unlike approaches based on global deformations, fixed-order polynomials, or uniformly parameterized splines, GaussianSpline jointly learns the B\'ezier control points and the temporal partition of each Gaussian's trajectory. This adaptive representation allocates greater temporal capacity to highly dynamic regions while maintaining compact trajectories for near-static regions, enabling high-fidelity reconstruction of complex and rapidly changing motion. To jointly achieve globally smooth motion and local adaptivity, we enforce $G^1$ continuity between consecutive B\'ezier segments using a reflection-based constraint on their control points. This produces smooth, fully differentiable trajectories while preserving the flexibility of non-uniform temporal parameterization. Experiments on the Neural 3D Video benchmark, the Google Immersive dataset, as well as on synthetic scenes demonstrate that GaussianSpline substantially improves reconstruction quality in scenes with highly non-uniform and challenging dynamics, while maintaining competitive performance on general dynamic scenes compared with state-of-the-art 4D Gaussian Splatting methods.
bullets: Models each Gaussians motion with adaptive, non-uniform piecewise cubic B�e9zier splines.
Jointly learns spline control points and per-Gaussian temporal partitions.
Uses a reflection-based constraint to enforce G�b9 continuity between spline segments.
Targets complex, highly non-uniform motion while keeping near-static trajectories compact.
Demonstrates improved reconstruction on Neural 3D Video, Google Immersive, and synthetic scenes, with competitive general-scene performance.

papers.abstract: Neural synchrony is hypothesized to help the brain organize visual scenes into structured multi-object representations. In machine learning, synchrony-based models analogously learn object-centric representations by storing binding in the phase of complex-valued features. Rotating Features (RF) instantiate this idea with vector-valued activations, encoding object presence in magnitudes and affiliation in orientations. We propose Orthogonal Rotating Features (OrthoRF), which enforces orthogonality in RF's orientation space via an inner-product loss and architectural modifications. This yields sharper phase alignment and more reliable grouping. In evaluations of unsupervised object discovery, including settings with overlapping objects, noise, and out-of-distribution tests, OrthoRF matches or outperforms current models while producing more interpretable representations, and it eliminates the post-hoc clustering required by many synchrony-based approaches. Unlike current models, OrthoRF also recovers occluded object parts, indicating stronger grouping under occlusion. Overall, orthogonality emerges as a simple, effective inductive bias for synchrony-based object-centric learning.

papers.abstract: World models are emerging as a fundamental component of policy learning for real-world agents, enabling agents to predict future world states and plan actions within a learned representation of the dynamic environment. Existing approaches, however, often model appearance, metric geometry represented by projected LiDAR depth, and ego motion either partially or independently, overlooking the fact that these modalities are different projections of a shared underlying world state. This separation can lead to information loss and cross-modal inconsistency, ultimately limiting downstream performance. Motivated by this unified view of the world, we propose DriveUniTok, a unified multimodal tokenizer for driving world-action models (WAMs) that encodes these modalities in a single decodable continuous latent. We freeze DriveUniTok and adapt a pretrained diffusion model, DriveUniWAM, to predict future unified latents; the tokenizer then decodes them into future appearance, projected LiDAR depth, and ego trajectories. Experiments on NAVSIM demonstrate that our unified design achieves better future prediction and planning performance at lower downstream computational cost than separate-stream alternatives. With reinforcement learning post-training, DriveUniWAM achieves a PDMS of 91.54, reaching state-of-the-art performance among the evaluated WAM-based planners.

papers.abstract: Cities must coordinate domains like infrastructure, mobility, environmental management, emergency response, and public services as conditions evolve. An urban Spatio-Temporal Intelligence (STI) system helps the city monitor citywide states, analyze problems, plan and execute interventions, and adapt through feedback, making urban governance more timely, effective, and transparent. Recent urban twinning and agentic AI techniques provide foundations for such systems. From a twin-agent perspective, this survey takes a system-level view of how these disparate techniques can be coherently integrated into an urban STI system. Specifically, we review how the twin reconstructs and represents a persistent, information-enriched urban environment, and how the agent understands the twin via interfaces, reasons over it, acts reliably, and continuously evolves with the city. Built upon this synthesis, we summarize a two-loop blueprint, where an inner agent loop for grounding, reasoning, and verification, and an outer system loop linking data, twin, agentic action, feedback, and update. We then use this to structure an STI research agenda and show how a shared prototype supports diverse urban domains.
authors: Zhen Dong, Haiping Wang, Wei Tu, Yuan Liu, Bing Wang, Xuan Sun, Jinzhou Cao, Ronald Clark, Zhiheng Fu, Mohammed Bennamoun, Danfeng Hong, Yuanzheng Cui, Gemine Vivone, Pedram Ghamisi, Bisheng Yang, Qingquan Li, Deren Li
bullets: Motivates STI systems that coordinate infrastructure, mobility, environment, emergencies, and public services as conditions change.

Introduces a two-loop blueprint: an inner loop for grounding, reasoning, and verification, and an outer loop connecting data, twin, action, feedback, and updates.
Uses the framework to organize a research agenda and describe a shared prototype spanning diverse urban domains.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Detailed technical organization of this review. Urban twinning reconstructs, completes, represents, and enriches city states; urban agents access these states through textual and feature interfaces, reason over them, and operate through governed agentic architectures; the future vision couples both subsystems through a two-loop blueprint and adapts it across urban domains. Leaf labels summarize closely related technical topics.

Fig. 8. The four-layer organization of urban agent. General language models are grounded in city evidence, strengthened with spatio-temporal reasoning, embedded in agentic architectures, and constrained for reliable operations.

Fig. 3. The four-stage urban twinning framework. Recovery and completion determine the physical state contained in the twin, while physical representation and information embedding organize and enrich that state for subsequent operation.

Fig. 7. Strategies for embedding information in an urban twin. Inside-out methods lift or learn semantic features from reconstruction signals, whereas outside-in methods ground external fields, attributes, and relations on twin carriers.

Fig. 9. Urban agent systems organized by task. Analysis and planning transform urban evidence into analytical results and plans; interaction and control apply decisions to environments; mobility prediction and urban simulation model individual futures and collective dynamics.

Fig. 5. Inferring unobserved scene states. Generation synthesizes new 3D scenes or 4D evolution from weak conditions, whereas completion extends partial scene observations while preserving consistency with the measured spatial and temporal evidence.
Fig. 4. Recovering observable urban states. Analytical and feed-forward paradigms process images, 3D data, or multimodal observations to recover static or dynamic scenes.

Fig. 6. Three forms of physical representation. Explicit representations enumerate directly addressable primitives, implicit representations encode continuous scene functions, and hybrid representations attach learned features or attributes to explicit spatial anchors.

Fig. 10. The proposed system blueprint. The inner loop grounds, reasons, and acts, then replans before action. The outer loop updates the twin, executes an approved decision, observes the outcome, and starts the next full cycle.

papers.abstract: Video world models trained on large-scale robot data promise a safe and scalable approach for learning and evaluating policies that act in the physical world. However, they still struggle with long-horizon rollouts and out-of-distribution generalization, and they remain computationally demanding at inference time. Typically, video world models make predictions in the latent space of a reconstruction-trained autoencoder, which however is not directly optimized for dynamics modeling. On the other hand, world models designed for latent planning usually optimize latents to be predictable, but they forgo accurate prediction of observations in pixel space. In this paper, we show that it is possible to achieve the best of both worlds: a latent geometry optimized to make future prediction as simple as possible without sacrificing accurate prediction of future observations. More precisely, we find that temporal objectives for representation learning, paired with a past-conditioned decoder architecture, lead to consistent improvements in generative video world models at the same training budget. The gains include up to 5x cheaper inference, over 7x faster training, and 15-24% lower pixel and perceptual errors out of distribution and over long horizons. Our world models also agree more closely with real-world policy evaluation when using a vision-language model to judge task success from their pixel-space predictions. Overall, our study indicates that temporal predictability is an important design criterion for the latent space of video world models, and provides concrete guidance on how to incorporate it into the training of autoencoders.
bullets: Reconstruction-trained autoencoder latents are not optimized for dynamics, limiting rollout quality and generalization.
The approach combines temporal representation-learning objectives with a past-conditioned decoder.
This yields up to 5× cheaper inference and over 7× faster training at the same training budget.
Pixel and perceptual errors decrease by 15–24% on long-horizon and out-of-distribution predictions.
Generated-video task evaluations align more closely with real-world policy evaluations.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Method overview. (1) An autoencoder is fine-tuned on pairs of nearby video frames xt, xt+1, with a reconstruction loss and a temporal objective on the latents zt, zt+1 and the action at; the decoder D conditions on the past frame xt to reconstruct xt+1 from its latent. (2) An actionconditioned diffusion world model is trained on the latents from the frozen encoder E. (3) From a context frame x1 and a sequence of actions a1:T , the world model generates latents, which D decodes conditioning on x1 as the past frame. We highlight in orange and green the two components that distinguish our recipe from a standard video world model: the temporal objective, and the past-conditioned decoder.

Latent prediction gives the largest perceptual gains with few sampling steps, and the lowest LPIPS from the fourth prediction step on and throughout training.

Figure 2: Latents can be predictable and informative in a synthetic setting. Left: Synthetic observations have a predictable component (signal, the dot) and an unpredictable noise component (the static). An encoder E is trained with reconstruction, temporal contrastive learning or both, and three readouts are then trained on its frozen latents: a world model predicts the next latent from the current latent and action, a probe predicts the signal, and a decoder D reconstructs the observation. Right: the error of each readout at latent size 100, divided by the error of the same readout trained on the raw observation; geometric mean and standard error over 3 seeds, lower is better. Reconstruction alone leaves the next latent as hard to predict as the raw observation and reads the signal far less accurately; contrastive learning alone loses the observation; their combination avoids both failures.

The pipelines of Table 2 against the number of DDIM sampling steps (top), along the long rollouts (middle) and over world-model training (bottom). papers.abstract: Assistive agents in shared-control settings face a dual challenge: acting proactively to align with the human's intentions while remaining legible enough for the human to comprehend and fluently respond in real time. We present Dream2Assist, a model-based reinforcement learning framework for tightly-coupled shared decision making that addresses both sides of this challenge. Our approach extends a recurrent state-space world model with intent inference, enabling an assistive policy trained via fictitious co-play to anticipate and support discrete human objectives without overriding human agency. Beyond the computational framework, we describe the full deployment pipeline needed to translate a world-model-based policy into a safe, human-centered system in a resource-efficient way. Crucially, we address the sim-to-real-human gap via policy down-selection and reward restructuring within an iterative human-machine interface design. We validate the framework through three human-subjects studies and a preliminary on-vehicle deployment spanning two qualitatively distinct domains: high-speed racing (N=30) and urban driving with richer intent structure (N=10). Our results demonstrate that intent conditioning yields measurable improvements in torque alignment and collision rate. We surface key design insights and practices for deploying learning-based assistive agents in safety-critical, real-time human-robot teaming.
authors: Jonathan DeCastro, Thomas Balch, Emily Sumner, Deepak Gopinath, Laporsha Dees, Patricio Reyes Gomez, Elliot Weiss, Megan Applegate-Kenton, Todd Rowell, John Leonard, Avinash Balachandran, Guy Rosman
bullets: Targets the challenge of proactive yet understandable assistance in tightly coupled human–vehicle control.
Extends a recurrent state-space world model with human-intent inference and trains the assistive policy through fictitious co-play.
Includes a deployment pipeline with policy down-selection, reward restructuring, and iterative human–machine interface design to address the sim-to-real-human gap.
Validated in three human-subject studies and a preliminary on-vehicle deployment covering high-speed racing and urban driving.
Intent conditioning improved torque alignment and collision rate; the work also reports deployment insights for safety-critical human–robot teaming.

papers.abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) combine future-video prediction with robot action learning, yet improvements in task success alone do not reveal how predictive supervision manifests in execution behavior or whether its benefits persist under task and environmental shifts. We conduct controlled future-video prediction loss ablations within FastWAM and OpenWAM, keeping model architecture, initialization, robot training data, and training steps fixed within each model family. Under clean conditions on seen tasks, predictive supervision increases success rates by 24.38 and 72.91 percentage points, respectively. Trajectory clustering further reveals higher success rates within several coarse trajectory clusters, including cases where cluster frequencies change little, indicating that the gains are not solely reflected in changes in the prevalence of trajectory patterns. However, these benefits do not consistently persist under distribution shifts: improvements on unseen tasks vary across models and tasks, while both models exhibit low success rates under the evaluated environmental randomizations, without a consistent advantage from predictive supervision. We further introduce future-video prediction as an auxiliary training objective for $\pi_{0.5}$, where a lightweight Transformer predictor used only during training increases success from 82.94% to 89.19%. These findings support future-video prediction as effective auxiliary supervision for action learning, while distinguishing improved execution on familiar tasks from reliable transfer and showing that such gains need not rely on a large pretrained video diffusion transformer (DiT) in the evaluated setting.
authors: Hanwen Cui, Yuanyuan Li, Qing Guo, Zhida Zhang, Chao Chen, Xi Chen, Jie Cao
bullets: Controlled ablations in FastWAM and OpenWAM isolate future-video prediction while holding architecture, initialization, data, and training steps fixed within each family.
Predictive supervision substantially improves success on clean, seen tasks: +24.38 and +72.91 percentage points in FastWAM and OpenWAM, respectively.
Trajectory analysis suggests gains reflect better execution within existing trajectory patterns, not only shifts in which patterns occur.
Under unseen tasks and environmental randomizations, improvements are inconsistent or absent, with both models performing poorly in the evaluated shifts.
Adding a lightweight training-only Transformer predictor to π₀.₅ raises success from 82.94% to 89.19%, showing that large pretrained video diffusion models are not required in this setting.

papers.abstract: Most action-conditioned video world models remain limited to a single player, while existing multiplayer models support only small, fixed groups of agents. We introduce FlockWorld, an artificial-life environment built on Reynolds's Boids algorithm for studying population-scale multi-agent video world models. Specifically, FlockWorld renders synchronized egocentric crops, assigns distinct colors to preserve camera-agent identity across views, exposes rule-derived accelerations as actions, and lets the number of camera agents be configured independently of the size of the surrounding population. We further introduce FlockDiT, an action-conditioned latent diffusion transformer trained with flow matching on FlockWorld data to jointly generate synchronized egocentric videos for multiple agents. Our results suggest that joint generation benefits agent detection at density-matched settings and that diffusion forcing improves rollout fidelity. Together, FlockWorld and FlockDiT provide a controlled testbed for multi-agent video generation.
authors: Meryem Koksal, Yunzhe Wang, Volkan Ustun
bullets: Addresses the limitation of existing action-conditioned video world models, which typically support one agent or small fixed groups.
Builds an environment from Reynolds’s Boids algorithm with synchronized egocentric views, color-based agent identities, and configurable camera-agent and population sizes.
Introduces FlockDiT, an action-conditioned latent diffusion transformer trained with flow matching for joint multi-agent video generation.
The abstract reports improved agent detection in density-matched settings and better rollout fidelity with diffusion forcing.
Provides a controlled testbed rather than a claim of broad real-world performance; its scope is artificial-life simulation.

papers.abstract: World action models have demonstrated promising performance in robot policy learning, yet their high inference latency remains a critical bottleneck for real-world deployment. Recent approaches have sought to improve inference efficiency by reducing test-time future-frame imagination or accelerating action prediction. However, these methods often leverage representations from all video world model layers without explicitly considering their varying relevance to action prediction, leading to redundant computation and suboptimal representation utilization. In this work, we propose TurboWAM, a fast world action model that efficiently aggregates structured world representations conditioned on action predictions. Specifically, TurboWAM introduces a structured world representation aggregation module that adaptively fuses representations from different world model layers according to their relevance to the evolving action denoising state. Furthermore, TurboWAM employs a structured action supervision mechanism that adaptively modulates gradients from action supervision across different world model layers during backward propagation, facilitating world representation learning. During inference, by reducing the number of world model layers executed and caching relevant representations across action denoising steps, TurboWAM substantially reduces computational overhead. Extensive experiments on multiple robot manipulation benchmarks demonstrate that TurboWAM achieves low inference latency while maintaining competitive task success rates compared with state-of-the-art methods.
authors: Guile Wu, Shuangzhi Li, Xingxin Chen, Chengjie Huang, Sam Hosseini, Tongtong Cao, Yingxue Zhang, Dongfeng Bai
bullets: Addresses high inference latency that limits real-world deployment of world action models.

Reduces inference cost by executing fewer world-model layers and caching relevant representations across denoising steps.
Experiments on multiple robot manipulation benchmarks show low latency with competitive task success rates.

papers.abstract: Interactive world models hold immense potential for high-stakes applications in robotics, game engines, and immersive digital twins, yet existing benchmarks primarily focus on perceptual similarity rather than the physical-causal coherence essential for real-world utility. We introduce WMEval, a comprehensive benchmark that evaluates interactive world models against Unity-based physical simulations. By leveraging Unity as a high-fidelity ground-truth oracle, we shift evaluation beyond perceptual visual assessment toward the objective state-based verification required for downstream applications. Spanning 9 diverse scenes, WMEval assesses action controllability, scene and character consistency, prompt adherence, kinematics, fluid mechanics, physical causality, and lighting. By executing matched action sequences in both the simulator and the world model, WMEval enables evaluation at both the perceptual level and the physical-causal level, using simulator-derived states as reference. Experiments on state-of-the-art models reveal significant room for improvement in dimensions that remain hidden by standard perceptual metrics but are vital for real-world deployments. Our code is available at: https://github.com/hao-ai-lab/WMEval.
authors: Lanxiang Hu, Yixin Huang, Abhilash Shankarampeta, Zilin Dai, Yuyuan Wu, Kun Qian, Junze Liu, Arvind Srinivasan, Mingjia Huo, Will Lin, Kai Zhong, Weiqi Zhang, Tian Wang, Qingjun Cui, Tajana Rosing, Hao Zhang
bullets: Evaluates world models across 9 diverse scenes using Unity as a high-fidelity ground-truth oracle.
Tests controllability, scene and character consistency, prompt adherence, kinematics, fluid mechanics, physical causality, and lighting.
Runs matched action sequences in both the simulator and world model, comparing perceptual and simulator-derived states.
Finds substantial weaknesses in state-of-the-art models that standard perceptual metrics fail to reveal.
Code is publicly available on GitHub.

(f–h) Specialized Continuum & Environmental Physics: LiquidContainer (fluid mechanics), RacingCar (non-linear vehicle kinematics), and SunRisesAndSets (temporal lighting/shadow kinematics) isolate complex physical phenomena.

papers.abstract: Video world models (VWMs) are rapidly emerging as scalable neural simulators for robotic manipulation. However, most benchmarks only evaluate them as open-world video generators, using Vision-Language Models (VLMs) that lack strict 3D spatial and kinematic reasoning. To bridge this gap, we introduce RoboWorM, a comprehensive, deployment-aware benchmark that leverages known hardware priors such as robot kinematic trees and fixed camera configurations, to systematically examine structural and spatiotemporal fidelity. RoboWorM curates 1,605 episodes across single-arm, bimanual, and humanoid morphologies, spanning both Markovian and long-horizon non-Markovian tasks under single- and multi-view setups. To explicitly measure physical consistency, we propose two deterministic, VLM-free metrics: KIVA for intra-view kinematic stability, and RIGIS for multi-view geometric consistency. By exploiting intrinsic robotic invariants, KIVA improves hallucination detection alignment with human annotations by 25.8% relative to the strongest frontier VLMs, while RIGIS achieves a 130% higher Spearman correlation with human preferences. Furthermore, since real-world deployment requires low inference latency, we utilize RoboWorM to conduct the first large-scale audit of the quality-efficiency trade-off. Evaluating 9 state-of-the-art acceleration techniques across 3 leading world models (over 29,000 generated rollouts), we demonstrate how these acceleration methods can retain superficial visual quality while silently compromising deployment-critical physical constraints. Using our metrics, we achieve 2.3$\times$ maximum inference speed-up with minimal quality loss.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models are bottlenecked by the scarcity of robot data. Egocentric human manipulation videos offer an abundant, diverse, and semantically-rich alternative that inherently captures manipulation intent. However, the embodiment gap makes it difficult to extract action-relevant representations from these videos. From the perspective of action execution, human hands and robots share analogous manipulation primitives---reaching, grasping, placing---yet exhibit distinct kinematics tied to their embodiments. This might motivate our key approach: egocentric video pretraining can yield shared action representations capturing transferable manipulation skills, while human-specific motion patterns should be disentangled to avoid interfering with robot policy learning. To this end, we propose EXE, an Egocentric Cross(X)-Embodiment pretraining framework that learns a factorized latent action representation from egocentric human videos, separating shared manipulation priors from embodiment-specific signals. By leveraging the shared action space, the robot policy acquires generalizable manipulation semantics from diverse human demonstrations without being biased by human-specific kinematics. This shared knowledge transfers across embodiments with different kinematic structures, enabling the same pretraining to benefit both parallel grippers and dexterous hands. EXE yields consistent gains over baseline without pretraining on RoboTwin 2.0, RoboCasa GR1, and real-world manipulation tasks.

papers.abstract: While interactive video world models require autoregressive generation, directly adapting pretrained bidirectional video diffusion models into autoregressive ones with teacher forcing can disrupt their visual priors and degrade autoregressive generation quality. In this paper, we introduce Mix Forcing, a causal pre-training paradigm for interactive video world models, implemented with the Mixture-of-Bidirectional-and-Autoregressive (MoBA) attention. Mix Forcing jointly trains a video diffusion model with both teacher forcing and bidirectional training, yielding a strong causal initialization for few-step post-training. In self-attention, Mix Forcing leverages teacher forcing to learn causal next-chunk prediction for autoregressive rollout, while using bidirectional attention to preserve pretrained visual priors. To support online text interaction, Mix Forcing further adopts a chunk-wise cross-attention design that conditions each video chunk on a shared environment prompt and its own local prompt, without exposing future instructions to the current chunk. Following causal pre-training on a 14B image-to-video model, we apply consistency and distribution matching distillation to obtain a four-step autoregressive generator. Experiments on our internal benchmark and public benchmarks, including WBench and SANA-WM-Bench, show that our model achieves state-of-the-art visual quality and timely event following with precise camera control. Notably, our model supports high-fidelity long-horizon generation without quality degradation even over one-hour rollouts. Project page is here: https://zelingao98.github.io/mixforcing

Applies consistency and distribution-matching distillation to produce a four-step autoregressive generator.
Reports state-of-the-art visual quality, event following, and camera control, with high-fidelity rollouts lasting up to one hour on reported benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Video world models are expected to generate videos that accurately follow specified camera trajectories while maintaining consistent 3D structures. However, existing models are predominantly trained on densely sampled videos with small inter-frame camera motions. When applied to sparse, large step trajectories, they often produce frozen frames, inaccurate camera motion, and severe geometric drift. We attribute this degradation to a mismatch between the gradual viewpoint transitions seen during training and the large viewpoint changes required at inference time. To address this problem, we propose Dense Trajectory Teacher Distillation (DTTD), a post-training framework that transfers a model's generation capability from dense trajectories to large camera motions. Given a sparse trajectory, DTTD interpolates additional camera poses to construct a dense trajectory covering the same path. The frozen base model then generates reliable teacher videos along this familiar dense trajectory, and pose aligned teacher observations are used to evaluate candidate videos generated under the original sparse trajectory. In this way, the model serves as its own generation teacher, requiring neither additional video data nor a stronger external video generator. We further combine dense teacher supervision with geometry aware rewards that assess cross frame consistency and camera trajectory following, and use the resulting preferences for offline preference optimization. To stably expand the model's motion range, we introduce a cumulative curriculum that progressively incorporates larger motion steps while retaining simpler trajectories to reduce capability forgetting.

A cumulative curriculum progressively increases motion difficulty while retaining simpler trajectories to limit capability forgetting.

papers.abstract: Robot policy evaluation informs deployment decisions and policy improvement, but physical testing and simulator preparation require substantial effort. World models offer a complementary route through closed-loop interaction in generated environments. Recent benchmarks have demonstrated their potential as policy evaluators through outcome-based evaluation (i.e., assessing task success or failure). However, such evaluation does not establish whether world models faithfully simulate how policies fail. Misrepresenting failures can lead to incorrect diagnoses of policy weaknesses and make policies appear ready for deployment even when small scene changes cause them to fail. We therefore ask: do world models faithfully simulate how and at which stages policies fail, and under what conditions they transition from success to failure? To answer this question, we introduce WorldFailBench with three evaluation tasks. Failure reason tests whether models reproduce the observable errors policies make. Failure stage assesses whether failures concentrate at the same stages of full-task execution. Failure boundary examines whether models reproduce the conditions under which policies transition from success to failure under controlled scene changes in simulation. The benchmark covers manipulation tasks in the LIBERO and RoboTwin simulation environments and real-world manipulation tasks performed by the G1 humanoid robot. Experiments across seven world models reveal substantial gaps in their understanding of policy failures, providing guidance for developing more reliable world models for policy evaluation.

papers.abstract: Interactive video world models require coordinated control over viewing perspectives, character actions, and camera motion. Existing methods typically leave view modes implicit in text captions, conflate action with camera motion, and inject controls through fragmented architectural pathways that capture interdependencies only indirectly. In this work, we present World-in-Context, an interactive world modeling framework powered by In-Context Conditioning (ICC). Rather than relying on specialized conditioning pathways, World-in-Context unifies view, action, and camera controls into explicit tokens contextualized directly within a shared self-attention space. Our formulation reveals that (i) explicit view tokens disentangle conflicting dynamics and unlock emergent view switching from single-view data, while (ii) action and camera inputs play complementary roles in governing local responsiveness and global stability. To preserve temporal continuity across execution intervals, we further introduce Interaction-Transport RoPE (IT-RoPE), parameterizing temporal attention with accumulated control transitions. On WBench, World-in-Context-5B achieves navigation performance on par with 22B EchoWM ($81.5$ vs. $81.6$) and attains a $93.8\%$ perspective-switching success rate, substantially outperforming existing 5B baselines ($18.8\%$). Controlled analyses further demonstrate compounding advantages of World-in-Context under richer conditioning mixtures, favorable data efficiency, and natural applicability to causal rollouts.
authors: Harold Haodong Chen, Rui Peng, Rongjin Guo, Lingteng Qiu, Kejie Qiu, Chao Xu, Zilong Dong
bullets: Addresses implicit view control, entangled action–camera effects, and fragmented conditioning in existing world models.
Uses In-Context Conditioning to unify view, action, and camera inputs within shared self-attention.
Introduces Interaction-Transport RoPE to maintain temporal continuity across control execution intervals.
On WBench, the 5B model matches the navigation performance of 22B EchoWM and achieves 93.8% perspective-switching success.
Analyses indicate benefits from richer conditioning, improved data efficiency, and compatibility with causal rollouts.

papers.abstract: Unrecognized anomalies in critical infrastructure can rapidly cascade into catastrophic physical or operational failures. Current anomaly detection approaches often rely on direct access to the monitored system by utilizing onboard sensors, such as motor encoders, to detect anomalous states. However, legacy hardware often lacks these sensors, or strict security protocols may prohibit access altogether. We therefore present AWARE, a world model framework that is capable of anomaly detection using only external camera monitoring via system dynamics estimation and state prediction. Evaluated across 240 real-world robotic crane trajectories, including payload collisions and motor degradations, AWARE demonstrates a 26% improvement in anomaly classification over our strongest baseline under noisy, camera-only state estimation. Furthermore, the inferred dynamics parameter can be decoded to identify the source of faults, localizing the degrading motor with 88% accuracy.
authors: Luke Beddow, George Mavroghenis, Rodrigo Chacon Quesada, Kamil Dreczkowski, Cong Sun, Jiankai Wang, Oscar Kwong-Fai Pang, Antoine Cully
bullets: Addresses anomaly detection when onboard sensors are unavailable or access is restricted.
Uses a world model for camera-only dynamics estimation, state prediction, and introspection.
Evaluated on 240 real-world robotic crane trajectories involving payload collisions and motor degradation.
Improves anomaly classification by 26% over the strongest baseline under noisy visual state estimation.
Localizes the degrading motor with 88% accuracy from inferred dynamics parameters.

figures.caption: Figure 1: System and model overview, showing human-operated robotic crane used for anomaly detection experiments. Figure 2: AWARE framework. Our model consists of two key components. First, a Latent Dynamics Estimator (green) reconstructs a latent encoding of system dynamics (ẑt) using a history of state-action pairs. Second, a World Model (blue) predicts the next state, given this encoding, the same history, and the current action. This integrated framework enables introspection (yellow) and anomaly detection (red) by comparing dynamics estimations and state prediction errors (et) against their expected distributions under normal operation.

The remaining states (q3–q7) are estimated by a boom-mounted ZED 2i camera utilizing a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN). (3) Operator Interface: A multi-color indicator lamp provides real-time visual feedback, signaling nominal operation (green light) or system alerts (red light).

papers.abstract: Decision Transformer (DT) has demonstrated strong performance in various offline reinforcement learning (RL) tasks by conditioning action generation on expected future returns and historical trajectories. However, treating expected future returns as the condition provides an incomplete description of the future, as trajectories with different state transitions and behaviors may share similar returns. Moreover, expected future returns inherently depend on task-specific reward functions, which makes policy learning reliant on reward-labeled datasets and restricts its scalability to tasks with similar but unseen rewards. Recently, Joint Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPA) have emerged as a promising paradigm of self-supervised learning-based world models, which learn predictive representations of future dynamics in latent space rather than reconstructing future states in the original space. Inspired by JEPA, we propose DT-JEPA, an offline pretraining and online fine-tuning framework that learns general knowledge from reward-free offline trajectories and achieves excellent adaptation to unseen tasks. Instead of predicting a single deterministic future embedding, we design a novel probabilistic predictor to model the conditional distribution of future representations in the latent space, thereby capturing both predictive information and uncertainty about future dynamics. Theoretically, we show that 1) the JEPA objective seeks to maximize a variational lower bound on the mutual information between historical representations and future trajectories; and 2) predictive future-conditioned policy learning admits a finite-sample performance bound with an O(N-1/4) estimation term. Experiments on D4RL benchmarks demonstrate that DT-JEPA achieves efficient adaptation across varying offline RL tasks, outperforming traditional DT-based and other offline RL methods.
authors: Changxu Ni, Yiyang Ni, Jun Li, Feiran You, Hongyang Du, Haitao Zhao, Shi Jin
bullets: Decision Transformer return-conditioning can miss distinct future dynamics and depends on task-specific reward labels.
DT-JEPA learns general predictive knowledge from reward-free offline trajectories before online task adaptation.
A probabilistic latent-space predictor models both future dynamics and their uncertainty instead of reconstructing future states.
Theoretical analysis connects the JEPA objective to mutual information and establishes a finite-sample performance bound.
On D4RL benchmarks, DT-JEPA adapts efficiently across tasks and outperforms DT-based and other offline RL methods.

papers.abstract: Latent world models are routinely selected, checkpointed and ablated on one-step prediction loss, on the assumption that a model which predicts the next latent better is a better model. In model-based RL this assumption is known to be unreliable; we ask whether it also fails for latent world models, where the training target is the model's own embedding and the loss is not expressed in interpretable units. We introduce a frozen-decoder protocol reporting one-step error in physical units, decomposed into the part already present in the encoder's representation and the part the predictor adds. Applying it to a recent end-to-end JEPA world model across three continuous-control environments, we move the metric by fine-tuning and measure goal-conditioned planning on the same checkpoints, with three training seeds and paired planning seeds throughout. Within one environment, a per-epoch ladder shows the relationship saturating after a single epoch: the first epoch improves fidelity by 32% and planning by 4.4 pp, but across the fifteen checkpoints that follow -- a further 15% fidelity improvement, monotone in every training seed -- the correlation between one-step error and planning success is r = -0.010. This is not a task-ceiling artifact: stratifying by a model-independent measure of training-data support, planning in the lowest-support stratum starts at 80%, leaving ample headroom, and is nonetheless flat from epoch 1 onward. Across environments the exchange rate is equally unstable: a 93% fidelity reduction on TwoRoom yields -0.7 pp of planning, while a 40% reduction on PushT yields +4.9 pp [+1.1, +8.9]. All results replicate under a decoder-free measure, latent drift. We also show that a matched continued-training control absorbs the entire fidelity gain we had attributed to an auxiliary objective.
bullets: The study tests whether lower one-step latent prediction error reliably indicates better goal-conditioned planning.
A frozen-decoder protocol measures prediction error in physical units and separates encoder representation error from predictor-added error.
Across three continuous-control environments, fidelity improvements often produced little, no, or inconsistent planning improvement.
Within one environment, later checkpoints improved fidelity by 15% while planning-error correlation was effectively zero (r = -0.010).
The findings replicated with a decoder-free latent-drift metric, and a continued-training control explained away gains attributed to an auxiliary objective.

papers.abstract: Accurate neural world models are central to model-based robotics, where they enable robots to predict future states from previously observed trajectories. Multi-step autoregressive training improves long-horizon prediction, but fixed rollout horizons also increase computational cost and can amplify early training errors when the model is still inaccurate. Existing training schemes typically use the same rollout length throughout optimization, independent of the model's current predictive reliability. We propose an epistemic uncertainty-driven adaptive rollout strategy for offline world model training following an auto-curriculum training scheme. Instead of always unrolling to a fixed horizon, the model terminates autoregressive rollouts once epistemic uncertainty exceeds a threshold calibrated from a warm-up phase. We study two uncertainty estimators: a five-head ensemble with a shared recurrent backbone and Monte Carlo Dropout. A two-stage warm-up procedure stabilizes uncertainty estimates before we enable adaptive truncation. Experiments on ANYmal-D and ANT show that ensemble-based adaptive truncation matches or improves the prediction accuracy of fixed-horizon training and the RWM-U baseline while requiring substantially fewer cumulative rollout steps. Training a world model on ANYmal-D following the presented approach reaches comparable final performance with the baselines with roughly 72% less rollout computation. These results indicate that epistemic uncertainty is useful not only for downstream policy regularization, but also for making world model training itself more compute-efficient.
bullets: Fixed rollout horizons can waste computation and amplify early autoregressive prediction errors.
The method adaptively stops rollouts when epistemic uncertainty exceeds a warm-up-calibrated threshold.
It evaluates a five-head ensemble and Monte Carlo Dropout as uncertainty estimators within an auto-curriculum.
On ANYmal-D and ANT, ensemble-based truncation matches or improves fixed-horizon and RWM-U prediction accuracy.
ANYmal-D training achieves comparable final performance with roughly 72% fewer cumulative rollout steps.

Thus, they show faster convergence and a lower RMSE error compared to the adaptive model with p = 0.8, which is trained on the transition from short to long rollouts.

Fig. 7: Validation error across the 32-step prediction horizon for different MC Dropout rates. For p = 0.1 and p = 0.4, adaptive truncation does not engage. Thus, the model trains only with the minimal rollout length, and its forecast error increases dramatically. The model with p = 0.8 is trained on both short and long rollouts, but its accuracy over the 32 forecast steps is higher than that of its fixed and adaptive ensemble counterparts.

papers.abstract: Actions that condition world models are highly heterogeneous, and thus existing action-conditioned world models are typically built for individual action types, fragmenting already limited action-annotated data across separate models. We introduce UniAction, a unified action-conditioning framework that represents any action as a sparse set of action elements, each with a discrete semantic identity and a continuous spatiotemporal grounding coordinate. By mapping these coordinates directly into the pretrained video model's native positional space, UniAction allows heterogeneous actions to condition a shared world model within the same spatiotemporal structure. We further introduce cardinality-calibrated attention to address the bias from differing action representation granularities. We evaluate UniAction on four representative action forms: force, camera control, hand pose, and robot pose. UniAction outperforms conditioning alternatives in action following, and a single jointly trained model surpasses the action-specific experts, showing that heterogeneous action data benefit from unified model and joint training.
authors: Bowen Xue, Zizhang Li, Hong-Xing Yu, Jiajun Wu
bullets: Addresses fragmented action-labeled data caused by action-specific world models.
Maps discrete action identities and continuous spatiotemporal coordinates into a pretrained video model’s positional space.
Uses cardinality-calibrated attention to reduce bias from different action representation granularities.
Evaluated on force, camera control, hand pose, and robot pose conditioning.
The jointly trained unified model improves action following and surpasses action-specific experts.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of UniAction. Diverse action forms are represented as sparse action elements: semantic identities index tokens in a shared codebook (Sec. 3.1), spatiotemporal positions use the backbone’s native positional encoding (Sec. 3.2), and action and video tokens interact via cardinality-calibrated attention (Sec. 3.3).
Figure 3: Qualitative comparison across four action forms. UniAction follows the input actions more faithfully than other conditioning mechanisms. Overlays indicate the input action.

papers.abstract: We introduce RynnUnify, a 16B unified embodied model that combines strong embodied understanding with long-horizon visual planning through interleaved video--language reasoning. With capabilities spanning spatial reasoning, physical prediction, and grounding, RynnUnify connects an understanding of the physical world with visual anticipation of how it evolves across successive subtasks. Building on these capabilities, we further develop an agentic extension through reinforcement learning to selectively use video predictions for reasoning about unobserved states and interaction outcomes. We also develop a world-action extension of the full RynnUnify model, translating its understanding and prediction capabilities into robot control. To evaluate these capabilities, we introduce Rynn-VP and Rynn-GEU for long-horizon visual planning and anticipatory reasoning. Experiments show that RynnUnify achieves the highest average embodied understanding score among the evaluated unified multimodal models and improves the Rynn-VP overall score by 9.75 points over Cosmos 3 Nano. Its agentic extension improves the Rynn-GEU average by 6.0 points over direct reasoning, while the world-action extension achieves 51.5\% success on 20 selected composite RoboCasa365 tasks and 46.7\% average success across three real-robot tasks. Together, these results establish RynnUnify as a shared foundation for embodied understanding, visual planning, and robot control, taking a step toward a unified embodied brain.

papers.abstract: Environments with randomized dynamics are widely used to ask whether world models need explicit context inference. However, randomization can leave little predictive information for a context encoder to add, because distinct latent parameters may produce similar transitions at visited states, or those states may already reveal the active context. We formalize the remaining one-step information as predictive headroom and compare kernels under fixed and visited state--action distributions to distinguish changes in query coverage from changes in context weights. We analyze discrete and continuous environments and find low headroom both when kernels differ little and when visitation reduces an otherwise large discrepancy. At the same time, resetting state components increases headroom, showing that context evidence accumulates in state. We propose reporting this headroom alongside the randomized parameters, so that gains from explicit context inference can be interpreted relative to the information missing from the current state and action.
authors: Oleg Smirnov, Sofiane Ennadir, John Pertoft, Bjartur Hjaltason, Sara Karimi
bullets: Introduces predictive headroom: the remaining one-step information a context encoder could provide beyond the current state and action.
Separates changes in kernel differences from changes caused by which states and actions are visited.
Finds low headroom when randomized kernels are similar or when visitation already reveals the active context.
Shows that resetting state components increases headroom, indicating that context evidence accumulates in state.
Recommends reporting predictive headroom alongside randomized parameters to interpret context-inference gains.

papers.abstract: Continuous visual world simulation requires coupling evolving scene geometry with temporally persistent appearance. We present UniWorld, a unified framework that integrates depth trajectories and reference appearance within a shared video generation model. The central design maintains visual and geometric histories on a common timeline. Noise-aligned overlapping continuation places generated history at the prescribed sampling noise level and commits only newly generated latents. Rolling depth latent state preserves the corresponding geometric controls, incrementally reads newly available geometry, and keeps the conditioning fixed within each sampling window. Together, these mechanisms ensure exact preservation of latent history while bounding the active depth state by the window size. We evaluate continuous generation, paired history interventions, and long-horizon behavior across diverse scene categories. The same generator supports estimated, native, and on-demand simulator depth, while cached and incremental execution paths produce bitwise-identical outputs. Appearance changes and geometric control branches operate through the same interface without modifying committed history. The measured steady-state DiT execution path achieves real-time generation throughput, demonstrating the efficiency of UniWorld for continuous visual world simulation.
authors: Xin Zhang, Yabo Chen, Shuaiwei Wang, Zixuan Duan, Haibin Huang, Feng Xu, Xuelong Li
bullets: Addresses the challenge of coupling temporally persistent visual appearance with changing scene geometry.
Uses noise-aligned overlapping continuation to preserve generated latent history while committing only new content.
Maintains rolling depth latents and fixed per-window conditioning to control geometry with bounded active state.
Supports estimated, native, and on-demand simulator depth, with cached and incremental execution producing identical outputs.
Evaluations cover continuous generation, history interventions, and long-horizon behavior across diverse scenes; the steady-state DiT path achieves real-time throughput.

papers.abstract: Robot manipulation involves localized changes: picking up a cup moves the cup while leaving the surrounding scene largely unchanged. Yet existing 3D visual pretraining methods, including recent dynamics-aware variants, model state transitions at the scene level, compressing the motion of everything in a scene into a single global latent action. This conflates semantically distinct transitions in scenes with multiple moving parts, obscures dependencies between changing regions, and leaves the learned representation vulnerable to task-irrelevant scene content. We introduce DynaSlots, an action-free, label-free pretraining framework that decomposes each point cloud frame into a small set of temporally consistent slots and models dynamics at this per-slot level rather than the scene level. A temporal slot propagation module promotes consistent slot assignments across frames; an inverse dynamics model then extracts one latent action per slot from feature differences, and a diffusion-based forward dynamics model, paired with a self-supervised interaction head, predicts each slot's future state while learning pairwise proximity-and-motion relations. Experiments on Meta-World, Adroit, and a RealMan RM65-B robot demonstrate that DynaSlots outperforms prior scene-level baselines. It achieves superior success rates in simulation and exhibits strong robustness to scene clutter and unseen objects in real-world manipulation. Code is available at \href{https://zhucezhanghao12345-source.github.io/DynaSlots-Anonymous/}{https://zhucezhanghao12345-source.github.io/DynaSlots-Anonymous/}.
authors: Meng Li, Lijiang Chen, Qi Zhao, Jun Jiang, Longhao Zou, Shuchang Lyu, Guangliang Cheng
bullets: Addresses scene-level dynamics modeling, which conflates multiple moving parts and incorporates task-irrelevant content.
Decomposes point-cloud frames into a small set of temporally consistent slots without actions or labels.
Learns per-slot latent actions through inverse dynamics and predicts future slot states with diffusion-based forward dynamics.
Uses a self-supervised interaction head to capture pairwise proximity-and-motion relationships.
Outperforms scene-level baselines in Meta-World and Adroit, with robust performance amid clutter and unseen objects on a RealMan RM65-B robot.

The displayed losses are noise prediction, slot VICReg, relation BCE, and assignment entropy.
