papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning has gained attention for improving action-conditioned world models (ACWMs), as it enables reward-driven optimization of visual quality (VQ) and action-following fidelity (AF) beyond flow-matching optimization. Realizing this potential requires reward signals that reliably rank videos by both VQ and AF. However, existing rewards capture only one dimension: metric-based rewards assess VQ but require ground-truth videos and do not directly assess AF, while inverse dynamics model (IDM) rewards assess AF without references but do not guarantee VQ. Moreover, IDMs, typically trained on real videos, may provide unreliable rewards for generated videos containing visual artifacts and physical inconsistencies. In this work, we introduce the Action and Video Mismatch Benchmark (AVM-Eval), comprising 67.2k pairs that evaluate how reliably IDMs assess AF on real and generated videos. We then propose ACWM-RM, a reward model that jointly assesses VQ and AF without ground-truth videos during reward computation. To train it, we first construct the Action and Video Mismatch Preference Dataset (AVM-Pref) with 506.3k pairs providing complementary supervision: action-mismatch pairs supervise AF, while video-mismatch pairs supervise VQ and expose the model to generated videos. We then pretrain an action-conditioned predictor on real videos to learn forward dynamics before jointly training it with a patch-weighted score head on AVM-Pref to transfer these dynamics to AF assessment on generated videos. Evaluation on AVM-Eval reveals the limited reliability of IDMs on generated videos, while downstream RL experiments show that ACWM-RM outperforms reward baselines in both criteria.
authors: Shibo Hong, Siyu Ren, FengJiao Chen, Zhongyuan Peng, Wei Shi, Yixin Cao
bullets: Existing rewards assess either visual quality with ground-truth videos or action fidelity without reliably handling visual artifacts.

Experiments show IDMs are unreliable on generated videos, while ACWM-RM outperforms reward baselines on both criteria in downstream reinforcement learning.

papers.abstract: Humans reason about the physical world by flexibly combining different forms of inference as a problem unfolds. Achieving this flexibility is a major open challenge in AI: capabilities often remain separated across specialized models, limiting how they can be composed and jointly adapted to a task. We introduce $\Psi$-0.6, a unified vision-language world model that adaptively composes perception, language, geometry, and simulation within a shared reasoning process we call streams of thought. These streams interleave images, text, and explicit representations of geometry and motion, all of which the model can generate and interpret through a shared token interface. $\Psi$-0.6 surpasses leading open-weight models zero-shot on multi-view spatial reasoning, with further gains from reasoning through geometric intermediates. It also supports counterfactual simulation: generating and interpreting imagined scenes to determine, for example, whether moving an object would obstruct a pathway. Reinforcement learning from task feedback jointly optimizes the selection, generation, and use of intermediate representations, improving visual question-answering accuracy with gains that transfer to unseen benchmarks. $\Psi$-0.6 offers a path toward adaptive physical reasoning -- not only predicting the physical world but also choosing the representations through which to reason.
authors: Khai Loong Aw, Klemen Kotar, Baihan Zhang, Yifan Liu, Lilian Chen, Atlas Kazemian, Rahul Venkatesh, Daniel Yamins
bullets: Interleaves images, text, geometry, and motion representations as composable “streams of thought” through a shared token interface.
Performs zero-shot multi-view spatial reasoning and benefits from explicit geometric intermediate reasoning.
Supports counterfactual simulation, such as predicting whether moving an object would block a path.
Reinforcement learning from task feedback improves intermediate-representation selection and visual question answering, with gains transferring to unseen benchmarks.
The abstract focuses on adaptive physical reasoning; specific limitations and quantitative results are not reported.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Architecture, training recipe, and prompting interface. (A) Ψ-0.6 is a unified model across diverse modalities. Pretraining, mid-training, and post-training sample different sequence families; hollow tokens denote stochastically included sequence elements. Generic prompting interface: prompts specify the available information and requested inference pathway. Ψ-0.6 is interactive: it can generate a view based on a user-specified camera pose, then use that generated view as context for subsequent reasoning. (B) Fine-grained control: each patch is represented by a pointer token and content tokens. Pointers specify modality and spatial and temporal locations, enabling targeted conditioning and scene edits. Probabilistic prediction: Ψ-0.6 represents a distribution over compatible continuations, allowing the same prompt to yield alternative predictions through sampling.

papers.title: $\Psi$-0.6: Adaptive Streams of Thought in a Unified Vision-Language World Model
papers.tldr: Ψ-0.6 is a unified vision-language world model that adaptively combines visual, linguistic, geometric, and simulated reasoning for flexible physical-world inference.

papers.abstract: Video encoder models are increasingly used as world models for physical AI, where a policy plans by rolling out the latent, so what physics the latent holds bounds what the agent can plan over. Moreover, existing interpretability work probes quantities belonging to a single object; the quantities that make physics relational, such as momentum transfer, restitution, and friction, are defined between bodies and have not been examined. We probe relational physics attributes in two frozen self-supervised video encoders (V-JEPA2 and VideoMAE) under two-body settings and test if they transfer across environments. Our early findings are mixed. Both encoders separate elastic from inelastic collisions reliably. V-JEPA2's own predictor is less likely to predict a collision that creates kinetic energy compared to one that loses it. Momentum-violation detection appears in only one of the two encoders, a kinetic-energy readout survives a change of environment for V-JEPA2 but not for VideoMAE, and neither model holds a friction coefficient that survives a change of geometry.
bullets: Examines relational quantities between objects, including momentum transfer, restitution, kinetic energy, and friction.
Tests frozen V-JEPA2 and VideoMAE encoders in two-body interaction videos and evaluates cross-environment transfer.
Both encoders reliably distinguish elastic from inelastic collisions.
V-JEPA2 is less likely to predict collisions that create kinetic energy, while momentum-violation detection appears in only one encoder.
Kinetic-energy representations transfer across environments for V-JEPA2 but not VideoMAE; friction representations transfer across geometry for neither.

figures.caption: Figure 5: Whether attribute emergence is visible depends on the pooling, not on the model. Out-of-fold R2 across depth on the 150 momentum-conserving clips, mean over 12 fold seeds with ±1 sd bands. Solid: object-local pooling, object A’s own tokens. Dashed: frame-wide pooling, the protocol of the single-object literature. Under object-local pooling the quantities are already available at the patch embedding and nothing emerges; under frame-wide pooling every curve starts at zero and rises through the first third. Mask-only floors at A.pre, computed under the identical protocol, are negligible (−0.37 to +0.05 for VideoMAE-base, −0.15 to +0.22 for V-JEPA2-ViT-L).

Figure 6: A frame-wide pool carries the sum of the two objects and not their difference. Out-offold R2 across depth, pool all.pre, 12 fold seeds with ±1 sd bands. The symmetric combination vA + vB reaches 0.955 and 0.938, well above either individual velocity, while the antisymmetric combination vA − vB peaks at 0.011 and 0.023—those are maxima over all 13 and 25 layers, so there is no depth at which the difference is recoverable.

Figure 7: The five two-body regimes. One clip per regime, cropped to the action; contact falls at frame 20 in every scene. Rows one and two are the same seed with and without the momentum edit, and share a crop, as do rows three and four: the members of a pair are identical up to the contact frame and diverge only afterwards, so nothing before contact distinguishes them. Green borders mark momentum-conserving clips, red momentum-violating ones, purple the physically impossible arm. The ratio at the right of each row is KEpost/KEpre. Reading that column shows why the energy experiment needs its own stimuli: the momentum edit moves kinetic energy as a side effect (the elastic violating twin lands at 2.15), so energy creation cannot be attributed to anything on the momentum axis. Only the last row creates energy while conserving momentum exactly.

Figure 3: Energy created against energy conserved, read two ways. Left: out-of-fold AUC of a linear probe separating the clips that create energy (e = k) from those that conserve it (e = 1) across depth, pooled all.pre; momentum is conserved in both sets. Both encoders peak far below an observer given the contact geometry, which reads the same label at 1.000. Right: the models’ own surprise, with nothing fitted. Each is shown only the pre-contact segment, which the three endings share exactly, and emits one forecast. Note the differing y scales.

Figure 4: The ingredients of friction decode; the coefficient does not follow. Out-of-fold R2 for incline angle θ, down-slope acceleration a and friction coefficient µ across depth on 150 incline scenes, mean over 12 fold seeds with ±1 sd bands. Each encoder is shown at its own best pool. The dotted line is the oracle ceiling: µ recovered from (a, θ) on ground-truth labels through the identical protocol, R2 = 0.997. θ is already at 0.957 and 1.000 at the patch embedding.

Figure 1: Momentum-violation detection across depth, by elasticity. Out-of-fold AUC of the norm route—regress the ∆p vector, take | · | outside the probem, pooled all.pre. The grey line is chance. Legend values give the best layer with its p corrected by a grid-max permutation null over all layers. VideoMAE clears the corrected null in both regimes; V-JEPA2 clears it marginally in the elastic regime and not at all in the inelastic one.

Figure 2: Elastic versus inelastic collisions across depth. AUC from the all.post pool on the 150 momentum-conserving clips (75 per class), mean over 12 fold seeds with ±1 sd bands. The distinction is built through the network, rising from 0.581 and 0.536 at the patch embedding. Both peaks lie below an observer given the contact geometry, which reads the same label at AUC 1.000 from restitution alone.

Table 2: A friction coefficient decoded within one floor geometry does not survive a change of geometry, while cube size does. Probes are trained on one dataset and applied unchanged to the other, restricted to the overlapping µ range [0.151, 0.399] (164 slide / 148 incline scenes), pool all.all, each domain standardised by its own moments so only the direction has to transfer. The two sets make µ a different function of the visible kinematics — flat: µ = a/g with corr(µ, a) = +0.9998; tilted: µ = (sin θ − a/g)/ cos θ with corr(µ, a) = −0.645 — so a readout that is really tracking acceleration cannot cross. SIZE is the control: it faces the identical domain gap (camera 14 vs 18, flat vs tilted, different band pattern). The third row of each block is the diagnostic: the same µ probe scored against the target set’s acceleration.

Table 3: The same four quantities, read from four pools. Out-of-fold R2 at the best layer. Objectlocal pools read their own object well and the other poorly; the frame-wide pools reverse this, reading each object worse than its own pool does while reading the sum better than any object-local pool reads anything.

Table 1: Reading µ directly and composing it from decoded (a, θ) give the same answer, because on this set they are the same function. Out-of-fold R2 on the incline set (n = 150), grouped folds with nested ridge penalty, mean ± sd over 12 fold seeds; each encoder at its own best pool. DIRECT regresses µ from activations. COMPOSED decodes a and θ separately and learns a second-stage linear map from the out-of-fold (â, θ̂) to µ. Every stage is out-of-fold, so no scene’s own â or θ̂ is used to fit the map that scores it. Over the sampled range µ is 0.997 linear in (a, θ), so the two routes are the same function and the tie is uninformative rather than positive.

papers.selection_reason: Probes relational physics in video encoders used as world models, directly relevant to world model evaluation.
papers.title: Interpreting Physics in Video Encoders using Multi-Object Interaction Videos
papers.tldr: This study probes whether frozen video encoders represent relational physics, finding reliable collision-type distinctions but limited, encoder-dependent transfer across environments and geometries.

papers.abstract: PDE foundation models enable data-efficient adaptation but are deployed autoregressively, so short-horizon accuracy need not imply reliable simulation. We ask whether the short-horizon advantage of a foundation-model recipe persists when its predictions are repeatedly fed back as inputs for a long horizon. We define error amplification as G=E(H_f)/E(H_s), which measures full-horizon error relative to short-horizon error. We evaluate seven models on seven two-dimensional time-dependent PDE datasets: scratch-trained FNO and DeepONet; fine-tuned DPOT, GPhyT, Poseidon, and Walrus; and frozen in-context VICON. We report VRMSE, relative L_2, and relative MAE. Six datasets provide paired short- and full-horizon scores, while CE-RM contributes short-rollout sweeps only. At least one fine-tuned foundation model outperforms both scratch baselines in 26 of 30 short-rollout dataset--budget cells under every metric. Nevertheless, full-horizon VRMSE exceeds short-horizon VRMSE in 140 of 144 paired trained configurations, with a median error amplification of $2.04$. The count below VRMSE one falls from 104 to 53, and 12 full rollouts exceed ten although none does at the short horizon. Walrus achieves the lowest full-horizon VRMSE in 16 of 24 cells, yet its median error amplification is $2.70$. Relative L_2 and relative MAE show the same qualitative pattern. These results show that favorable short-horizon rankings can coexist with substantial error amplification. PDE foundation-model benchmarks should therefore report horizon-resolved absolute errors, amplification statistics, and failure incidence rather than a single local forecast score.
authors: Jaewan Park, Seid Koric, Giri Krishnan, Sudhakar Pamidighantam, Surresh Marru
bullets: Evaluates seven models across seven two-dimensional, time-dependent PDE datasets using VRMSE, relative L2, and relative MAE.
Fine-tuned foundation models beat both scratch baselines in 26 of 30 short-rollout dataset–budget cells.
Full-horizon VRMSE exceeds short-horizon VRMSE in 140 of 144 paired configurations, with median error amplification of 2.04.
Walrus has the lowest full-horizon VRMSE in 16 of 24 cells, but its median amplification is 2.70.
Results motivate reporting horizon-resolved errors, amplification, and failure incidence—not only local forecast accuracy.

papers.selection_reason: Benchmarks autoregressive rollout reliability and error amplification of PDE foundation models; transferable to world-model evaluation.
papers.title: Beyond Local Accuracy: Benchmarking the Rollout Reliability of PDE Foundation Models
papers.tldr: PDE foundation models can excel at short-horizon forecasts yet become substantially less reliable during long autoregressive rollouts.

papers.abstract: Covariate-aware time series foundation models (TSFMs) accept a future path for a control variable and return a forecast, inviting what-if queries. The query is interventional; the models are trained on observational data. We determine whether their answers are the conditional slope $\partial E[Y|X]$ or the interventional effect $\partial E[Y|do(X)]$, at three levels. Theory: a Bayes-optimal observational predictor answers interventional queries associationally unless the adjustment set is available and used; for in-context least squares we derive the resulting confounding gap -- a model's effect estimate under an observational minus under a randomized context -- in closed form, a parameter-free reference line. Behaviour: on a preregistered grid with exact counterfactual ground truth, Chronos-2, TiRex-2, TabPFN-TS and TimesFM-2.5 all track this line ($R^2$ 0.90-1.00) and respond more confounded than regression itself (slopes 1.3-1.8), on linear and nonlinear structural models. Pairs of models with identical observational laws prove this is not an identifiability limit: when the effect is identifiable, least squares recovers 100% of the true effect difference, Chronos-2 75%, TiRex-2 34%. Representation: linear probes decode the data-generating regime (94-96%) and the true effect ($R^2$ 0.7-0.9) from embeddings that the forecasts ignore. On two physical systems with randomized actuators, pretrained models under-respond by 2-5x and ignore in-window confounding. Minutes of interventional post-training on 3,000 synthetic series cut the gap by up to 83% and transfer outside the training prior. Its forecasting cost is a replay-distribution effect: replaying the model's own pretraining prior cuts it from +47% to +10% MASE, and with low-rank adaptation yields a recipe meeting the preregistered criterion over three seeds (52-61% gap reduction at +1-3% cost) while improving the DoTime benchmark.
bullets: Theory predicts that observationally trained predictors answer what-if queries associationally unless they use an appropriate adjustment set.
Chronos-2, TiRex-2, TabPFN-TS, and TimesFM-2.5 closely follow the predicted confounding pattern across linear and nonlinear systems.
The models’ embeddings contain information about the causal regime and true effects that their forecasts fail to use; randomized physical-system tests show 2–5× under-response.
Minutes of interventional post-training reduce the causal gap by up to 83%; low-rank adaptation achieves 52–61% reduction at 1–3% extra cost and improves DoTime.
Scope: findings concern covariate-aware TSFMs evaluated on synthetic structural models and two physical systems with randomized actuators.

figures.caption: Figure 7. Causal Chambers. (a) Wind tunnel: horizon-average effect of do(load in + δ) on downwind pressure versus the in-window confounding bias predicted from context (septile bins). An associational predictor has slope 1 (least squares, V1), an adjusting one slope 0 (least squares, V2). Pretrained models have slope ≈ 0 at every visibility and a response one third to one half of the identified effect: they ignore the covariate rather than adjust for it. (b) Response scale on both systems: on the light tunnel the post-trained model overshoots by 1.6–2.1×.

Figure 2. Measured confounding gap against the Proposition 1 prediction, one point per (α, γ) cell (slopes and R2 in Table 1). The identity line is in-context least squares; the horizontal line is a causal predictor. All four TSFMs lie on or above the line with the confounder hidden (V0) or past-only (V1); supplying the confounder’s future (V2, theory 0) removes only part of the gap and, for TiRex-2 and TimesFM-2.5, little or none of it. Right: the least-squares control validates the harness (R2 = 1.000).

Figure 6. Nonlinear structural model (E11). X responds to tanh(Z), Y to 1.5 tanh(X) and a convex function of Z; the reference is an in-context kernel ridge regression with the same three visibility rules, and its own observational-minus-randomized gap is the x-axis. Chronos-2 and TiRex-2 again sit above the reference under V0 (slopes 1.35 and 1.53, R2 0.82 and 0.92); post-training on the linear family transfers (gap 0.57→0.15 under V0, 0.58→0.02 under V1); the linear least-squares control is itself close to the nonparametric reference (slope 0.92, R2 0.90).

Figure 1. Foundation models forecast associations, not interventions. (a) One what-if query is posed under two contexts from the same structural model: observational (Z drives both X and Y ) and randomized (the edge is cut). A model that estimates the effect answers the same number in both. (b) Chronos-2 does not: under observational context its response to do(X+δ) is inflated by the confounding. The difference at the first intervened step is the confounding gap, derived in closed form for in-context least squares (Proposition 1). (c) Supplying the confounder’s future should close the gap (star: least squares does); three models fail in three ways.

Figure 4. Matched observational distributions (E7). Pairs of structural models with identical (X,Y ) law but effects βA = 1 and βB ∈ {0.5, 0.25, 0} (mean ± s.d. over pairs). Where the effect is not identifiable every model, including least squares, answers the same number: not a failure. Where it is (V2), least squares recovers the full difference, Chronos-2 three quarters, TiRex-2 one third: information present, not used.

Figure 8. The repair trade-off. Gap reduction against forecasting cost for every variant of Table 2 (filled diamonds: median cost; open circles: mean; ICR = in-context randomization). (a) Variants without pretraining-prior replay form a curve on which reductions above 50% cost at least 10% median MASE. (b) KernelSynth replay (green) removes the mean-cost tail at full-parameter learning rates (v11) and, with low-rank adaptation, moves the curve into the preregistered region (v18, v19).

Figure 3. Causal compass. Each point is a confounded cell. A causal predictor sits at the origin, an associational one on the vertical axis; covariate dominance pushes left. Chronos-2 (V2) moves toward the origin but stops; TabPFN-TS does not move; TiRex-2 (V2) moves left: supplying Z’s future collapses its response to X .

Figure 5. Linear probes on Chronos-2 encoder embeddings ([REG] token + patch mean; 600 episodes; held-out 5-fold). The pretrained encoder separates randomized from confounded contexts (96%) and encodes the true effect (R2 0.80/0.71) but not the confounding bias (R2 ≈ 0). After post-training all four rise: the encoder begins to represent the bias it must subtract.

Figure 9. Gap path over the horizon CGt = Eobs[∆ŷt]/δ − Eint[∆ŷt]/δ, averaged over the 16 confounded cells. In-context least squares answers with the contemporaneous coefficient at t = 1 (0.40 under V0, 0.33 under V1) and then accumulates through the autoregressive carry (to 0.15 and 0.65). Chronos-2 and TiRex-2 answer with the long-run association from the first step: their gap is 0.6–0.8 at t = 1 and 0.85–0.9 thereafter. This is why the impact slope exceeds 1 while the cumulative slope is close to 1.

Figure 10. Sensitivity versus context length. Under randomized context S rises monotonically toward 1 with L (Proposition 2); under observational context it stays at 1.3–1.4 at every L: the confounding does not wash out. TiRex-2 under V2 moves the other way as the known-future covariate increasingly dominates.
Figure 11. Left: E2 spurious effects. Right: E8 out-of-prior transfer of post-training (confounding gap before and after IPT).

Table 2. Repairs (Chronos-2 unless stated; 3× 3 confounded grid; KS = KernelSynth). Gap reduction relative to the pretrained model; b̂int under V1; spurious effect at β = 0 under observational V1 context (pretrained 0.47; least squares 0.42); change in M4-hourly MASE (mean / median over 200 series); DoTime effect-direction accuracy (pretrained 0.684). papers.selection_reason: Audits time series foundation models for causal intervention vs association, providing a transferable technical contribution regarding the reliability of predictive models for environment dynamics.
papers.title: Forecasting Associations, Not Interventions: A Preregistered Causal Audit of Covariate-Aware Time Series Foundation Models
papers.tldr: Covariate-aware TSFMs generally forecast observational associations rather than causal interventions, but brief interventional fine-tuning substantially reduces this gap.

papers.abstract: Existing approaches for robot learning in simulation often require substantial manual effort to construct scenes and specify tasks, limiting training scalability and data diversity. Meanwhile, in-the-wild robot demonstrations naturally provide diverse and realistic observations of real-world interactions. Leveraging these demonstrations for simulation requires both high-fidelity visual reconstruction and physically consistent interactions. General-purpose agents offer flexible adaptation to diverse scenarios and strong reasoning about 3D spatial relationships, while specialized generative models provide high-fidelity reconstruction of scene appearance and geometry. We introduce WorldMirror, an agentic real-to-sim framework that constructs interactive digital twins from in-the-wild robot demonstrations. Our central idea is to formulate real-to-sim construction as the iterative refinement of an executable world program. A coding agent decomposes the observed scene, plans reconstruction steps, and orchestrates specialized image and 3D generation tools, refining the program through verification feedback. A camera-pose-anchored scene representation organizes the world into static visual context, support geometry, and editable interactive assets while preserving spatial relationships among the scene, objects, and robot. The agent uses this representation to diagnose and correct reconstruction errors, enabling physically consistent interaction and trajectory replay. Experiments on DROID demonstrate that WorldMirror can reconstruct visually faithful and geometrically consistent interactive worlds while preserving the physical validity of recorded robot trajectories.
authors: Tianling Xu, Weijie Wan, Honghao Su, Kailun Su, Junyuan Tang, Huichi Zhou, Haozheng Zhang, Qi Xiong, Ping Luo, Wenbo Ding, Tianxing Chen, Yue Chen
bullets: Addresses the manual effort and limited scalability of constructing robot-learning scenes and tasks in simulation.
Uses a coding agent to decompose demonstrations, orchestrate specialized image and 3D generation tools, and refine an executable world program with verification feedback.
Employs a camera-pose-anchored representation separating static context, support geometry, and editable interactive assets while preserving spatial relationships.
Supports error diagnosis, correction, physically consistent interactions, and replay of recorded robot trajectories.
Experiments on DROID show visually faithful and geometrically consistent reconstructed worlds that preserve trajectory validity.

papers.abstract: We examine how closely pretrained LeWorldModel (LeWM) reproduces the effects of small action changes. Using matched simulator and model responses, we measure action sensitivity with Gram matrices at three perturbation scales. Across nearly a thousand states from Reacher and OGBench Cube, the most sensitive action directions differ by median angles of about $36^\circ$ and $42^\circ$, respectively, at the smallest scale. Increasing the perturbation tenfold reduces median normalized Gram discrepancy by roughly 70\% on Reacher and 47\% on Cube. Geometry measured in pixels and embeddings varies more across scales than the chosen physical-state geometry. On held-out directions, environment Grams achieve median embedding response errors of 17\% and 28\%, compared with 26\% and 38\% for an isotropic reference with the same trace. LeWM's errors are higher at this scale. These findings support scale-specific evaluation of action sensitivity; its effect on control remains an open question.
bullets: Action-sensitive directions differ from the simulator by median angles of about 36° on Reacher and 42° on OGBench Cube at the smallest scale.
Larger perturbations reduce normalized Gram discrepancies by roughly 70% on Reacher and 47% on Cube.
Pixel- and embedding-based geometries vary more across scales than physical-state geometry.
Environment-derived Grams yield lower held-out embedding-response errors than an equal-trace isotropic reference, while LeWM errors are higher at this scale.
Whether these geometric mismatches affect control performance remains open.

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes the action sensitivity and geometry preservation of the LeWorldModel, a latent action model, providing insights into the fidelity of world models to physical dynamics.
papers.title: Does LeWorldModel Preserve Local Action Geometry?
papers.tldr: LeWorldModel only partially preserves the local geometry of action effects, with fidelity varying substantially by perturbation scale and representation.

papers.abstract: We present a surrogate-accelerated Bayesian history-matching framework, demonstrated on a realistic synthetic model ($N=100{,}188$ cells). The forward map $\mathcal{G}$ is replaced by a Fourier neural operator $\mathcal{G}_\theta$ trained in a closed loop, $\hat{x}_{n+1}=\mathcal{G}_\theta(u,\hat{x}_n)$, with the discrete black-oil residual $R(x_{n+1},x_n)$ as a physics-informed neural operator (PINO) penalty, truncated backpropagation and noise injection. We assimilate production data and 4-D seismic using adaptive regularised ensemble Kalman inversion (aREKI), and synthesise $\Delta V_p$ inside the rollout via a closed-form Gassmann transform of the surrogate, under a two-stage schedule (aREKI on production, then an ensemble smoother with multiple data assimilation, ES-MDA, on both). To temper the ill-posedness, we invert $(\log K,\phi)$ not in $\mathbb{R}^{2N}$, where $N_e\ll 2N$ leaves a rank-deficient covariance and a null space the data never inform, but on a chart $u=\Psi(\tilde m)$, $\tilde m\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$, $d\ll 2N$, given by a Parseval-exact truncated cosine transform or a variational auto-encoder decoder. The ensemble then spans its own search space; the directions the data cannot constrain are cut to those the chart can express, and every member decodes to a geologically plausible field. For the rollout we prove an exposure bound $W_1\le\sum_j L^{\,n-1-j}\mathbb{E}e_j$, a physics-penalty contraction $\|D_x\mathcal{G}_\theta\|\le\alpha 0.999$ on pressure and saturation and rolls out in $0.579$ s, a $\sim2500\times$ speed-up, bringing an $N_e=190$-member, $N_a=10$-iteration joint inversion within one GPU-hour.
authors: Clement Etienam, David Blom, Hari Pattathil, Tsubasa Onishi, Harpreet Sethi, Lalson Vincent, Suraj Pawar, Kishan Ramesh Kumar, Pandu Devarakota, Faruk O. Alpak
bullets: Replaces the reservoir forward simulator with an autoregressive Fourier neural operator trained using black-oil residual penalties, truncated backpropagation, and noise injection.
Assimilates production and 4-D seismic data through a two-stage aREKI and ES-MDA workflow, with seismic changes synthesized using a Gassmann transform.
Restricts inversion of permeability and porosity to low-dimensional cosine-transform or variational-autoencoder charts to reduce unidentifiable directions and promote plausible fields.
Provides an exposure-bound analysis and reports stable rollouts, a roughly 2500× speed-up, and completion of the stated ensemble inversion within one GPU-hour on the synthetic model.
Demonstration is limited to a realistic synthetic model with 100,188 cells.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Cartoon of the end-to-end workflow. A synthetic, fault-dissected reservoir model with unknown petrophysical properties (logK,φ) (left) is sampled by an ensemble of full-physics finite-volume runs; these train an autoregressive PINO–FNO surrogate that rolls out the black-oil state in closed loop; the surrogate’s own state is pushed through a closed-form Gassmann map to a 4-D seismic observable and through the Peaceman heads to production observables; and a two-stage ensemble Bayesian inversion (aREKI→ES-MDA) assimilates both to return a posterior reservoir model (dashed feedback). Each block corresponds to a stage of the pipeline and a subsection of this paper.

Figure 9: End-to-end orchestration of the pipeline. Each box is a distributed stage logged to a timestamped directory; the forward stage runs data-parallel over R GB200 GPUs, the inverse stage drives the two-stage aREKI→ES-MDA joint inversion.

Each panel shows the surrogate-derived Vp (left), the finite-volume reference (centre) and their absolute difference (right), with Inj1, Tau_1, Tau_2 marked. The velocity slow-down in the water-swept region between baseline and monitor is precisely the time-lapse signature ∆Vp (3.20) that the joint inversion assimilates to resolve the inter-well connectivity invisible to production data.

Figure 3: MLflow training/validation curves for all 13 PhyNeMo loss components over 700 epochs. All converge within ≈ 200 epochs; oscillations reflect the K=10 TBPTT window schedule and the AdamW learning-rate decay γ = 0.99999.

Figure 5: Time-resolved R2/L2 for production fields (left) and the Gassmann-derived 4-D seismic observable (right). Pressure/saturation R2 > 0.999; the seismic delta is reproduced with high fidelity, validating the petro-elastic forward channel of §3.2.
Figure 4: Surrogate (FNO Peaceman head) vs. FV reference well responses for Tau_1/Tau_2: WOPR R2>0.9999, WBHP_PROD R2=0.98 (reported to finite precision; we avoid the “100%” shorthand).

Figure 4 compares surrogate and FV well responses on a member of the 5-realisation held-out test set (§4.2); Figure 5 reports time-resolved field and seismic accuracy; Figure 6 shows 3-D field snapshots spanning the full production history. Across the 20-step rollout the field errors stay small (pressure differences <2500 kPa, <4% of range; saturation errors localised at the injector front), consistent with Proposition 2.7.

Figure 10: MAP permeability vs. truth (each panel: MAP, best, prior, true model; log-mD). Production-only (left) leaves the inter-well connectivity under-determined; the joint inversion (right) recovers the high-K corridor and fault block matching the true model, the visual case for “why joint is better”.

Figure 6: Three-dimensional field comparison at four report steps spanning the ≈2200-day reservoir production history (extracted from the rollout animation). Within each panel the rows are pressure, water saturation and oil saturation, and the columns are the autoregressive PINO surrogate (left), the finite-volume reference (centre) and their absolute difference (right); the injector Inj1 and producers Tau_1, Tau_2 are marked. Pressure differences stay <2500 kPa and the saturation error remains localised at the advancing injector front, growing only mildly over the rollout: the signature of the bounded Lipschitz amplification of Proposition 2.7 under the K=10 TBPTT/PINO contraction (Theorem 2.4).

Figure 7: The autoregressive surrogate’s stand-alone forward rollout of the full three-dimensional reservoir-model state, pressure, water saturation and oil saturation (top to bottom in each panel), predicted in closed loop in gradient-free mode with zero teacher forcing, at four report steps. Injected water advances from Inj1 and sweeps oil toward the producers Tau_1, Tau_2; the pressure field relaxes globally (elliptic) while the saturation front advects locally (hyperbolic), exactly the diffusivity hierarchy κP≫κS of Theorem 2.4. This is the state cube that the Peaceman heads and the Gassmann petro-elastic map read to form the observables assimilated in §3.4.
Figure 15: Posterior RMSE histograms (joint inversion). MAP/best markers lie at the low-RMSE tail across all four responses.
Figure 13: Joint posterior permeability percentiles (true, prior, P10/P50/P90, best, mean; log-mD). The posterior concentrates on the true high-K corridor and fault structure.

Figure 2: Autoregressive rollout with K=10 truncated BPTT. State is fed back every step; the backward graph is detached at the window boundary (red), so gradients propagate at most K steps and memory is bounded.

Figure 12: Producer bottom-hole pressure (WBHP_PROD) ensembles across the Ne=190 members (blue: individual realisations; red: observed/true history). The dashed vertical line is the assimilation/forecast boundary (first 15 steps assimilated, final 5 forecast). Left: the prior ensemble, forward rollouts of the unconditioned prior realisations, shows a wide, biased predictive spread. Right: the posterior ensemble after the joint aREKI→ES-MDA update tracks the observed history, including across the forecast window. We caution that the posterior P10–P90 band narrows to within the 25% production-noise envelope of Γp; a predictive band tighter than the observation noise on assimilated data is a symptom of over-collapse rather than an unqualified success, and should be read together with the spread diagnostics called for in §5.1.

The dashed vertical line marks the assimilation/forecast boundary: the first 15 report steps (left) are assimilated, the final 5 (right) are forecast blind. The joint posterior (right sub-panel) concentrates markedly more tightly than the production-only posterior (left), including over the forecast window, quantifying the seismic information gain (sP2=0.876 vs. sP1=2.556, Tab. 5).

papers.selection_reason: Uses autoregressive Physics-Informed Neural Operators as surrogates for reservoir dynamics, acting as a fast predictor of environment states (world model) and improving computational efficiency.
papers.title: Autoregressive Physics-Informed Neural Operator Surrogates and Joint 4-D Seismic-Production Bayesian History Matching
papers.tldr: A physics-informed Fourier neural operator surrogate enables fast joint production–4-D seismic Bayesian history matching in a low-dimensional geological parameter space.

papers.abstract: We introduce TWIG (Time-Causal Wavelet Operator for Irregular Graphs), a graph-native neural operator for autoregressive surrogate modeling on static irregular graphs. TWIG transforms each node history into causal multiscale temporal features that separate recent variation from progressively slower memory components, then propagates these features through graph-wavelet operator blocks with gated pointwise channel mixing. The architecture is causal by construction and designed for closed-loop forecasting, where predictions are recursively reused as future inputs. We evaluate TWIG on three irregular-domain forecasting problems spanning regional diffusion, three-dimensional subsurface hydrology, and aerodynamic flow, with graphs ranging from 400 to 5,233 nodes and model capacities from approximately 70k to 10M parameters. TWIG achieves the lowest aggregate rollout errors on the subsurface-hydrology and regional-diffusion benchmarks and ranks second on the 10M-parameter aerodynamic-flow benchmark, behind the GPS Transformer. Across all three settings, TWIG consistently outperforms the corresponding non-time-causal Graph WNO baseline. These results demonstrate that TWIG provides an effective and scalable approach to stable autoregressive forecasting of dynamical fields on irregular graphs.
bullets: Targets closed-loop forecasting of dynamical fields on static, irregular graphs, where predictions are recursively reused.
Transforms node histories into causal multiscale features separating recent changes from slower memory components.
Processes these features with graph-wavelet operator blocks and gated pointwise channel mixing.
Evaluated on regional diffusion, subsurface hydrology, and aerodynamic flow across graphs with 400–5,233 nodes.
Achieves the lowest aggregate rollout errors on two benchmarks, ranks second on aerodynamic flow, and consistently outperforms a non-time-causal Graph WNO baseline.

papers.selection_reason: Autoregressive graph-native surrogate prediction of physical dynamics is a learned environment-dynamics predictor with transferable value for world-model research.
papers.title: TWIG: A Time-Causal Wavelet Operator for Autoregressive Forecasting on Irregular Graphs
papers.tldr: TWIG is a causal graph neural operator that combines multiscale temporal wavelets with graph-wavelet propagation for stable autoregressive forecasting on irregular graphs.

papers.abstract: Understanding and controlling how systems evolve is central to science and engineering, where many problems require reasoning about complete trajectories. Existing approaches typically learn local dynamics or generate trajectories, but objectives constructed from individual transitions can miss dependencies across time, while generative models do not necessarily provide a tractable objective for evaluating and optimizing arbitrary paths. We study $\textit{action learning}$, the problem of recovering a stochastic action from trajectory observations, yielding a common objective for reasoning about dynamical systems. We introduce $\textbf{LEAP}$ ($\textbf{L}$earned $\textbf{E}$nergy on $\textbf{A}$ction $\textbf{P}$aths), which anchors the unknown action to a tractable reference process and learns the remaining correction by comparing observed trajectories with reference trajectories. This construction yields a differentiable objective on path space that can capture both local dynamical structure and nonadditive dependencies across time. Once learned, the same action can be flexibly reused for path ranking and inference, mechanism steering, constrained optimization and sampling. Across stochastic physical systems, many-body orbital dynamics and molecular simulations, LEAP recovers underlying dynamics, captures dependencies across time and enables transfer across inference objectives and physical conditions. We show that $\textit{action learning}$ is a promising framework for turning trajectory observations into reusable objectives for scientific inference and control.
bullets: Addresses the limits of transition-based objectives and trajectory generators for reasoning about complete paths.
Anchors an unknown stochastic action to a tractable reference process and learns a correction from trajectory comparisons.
Produces a differentiable path-space objective that captures local dynamics and nonadditive temporal dependencies.
Supports path ranking, mechanism steering, constrained optimization, and sampling using the same learned action.
Demonstrated across stochastic physical systems, orbital dynamics, and molecular simulations, including transfer across objectives and physical conditions.
papers.selection_reason: Recovering action and energy from trajectories is a latent-action world-model learning approach with transfer to dynamics modeling.
papers.title: Action Learning for Scientific Simulations
papers.tldr: LEAP learns a reusable trajectory-level action from observed and reference paths, enabling inference, control, optimization, and sampling of dynamical systems.

papers.abstract: Video foundation models have advanced rapidly in understanding and generating visual sequences, while video world models seek to capture the underlying dynamics of the world they depict. Despite their different objectives, both concern the relationship between video observations and an evolving world. This survey adopts world modeling as a unifying lens for examining these developments. Viewing an observed video as a partial, lossy, and temporally ordered projection of a latent temporal world, we organize the literature around four complementary operations: reading infers world properties from observed video; writing synthesizes video from specified or learned world conditions; sharing integrates understanding and generation through common modeling mechanisms; and interacting predicts and updates world states under actions and evolving observations. This perspective distinguishes temporal coherence in observed or generated sequences from consistency in the underlying world state. Across tasks, representations, models, datasets, and benchmarks, we trace a shift in emphasis from clip-level recognition and perceptual fidelity toward persistent state, controllable evolution, physical and causal validity, and evaluation grounded in interaction and downstream decisions, and we distill the open challenges that follow.
authors: Shengqiong Wu, Meng Luo, Bobo Li, Ziwei Liu, Shuicheng Yan, Ming-Hsuan Yang, Philip Torr, Hao Fei
bullets: Frames video as a partial, lossy, time-ordered projection of a latent temporal world.
Organizes research into reading world properties, writing videos, sharing understanding and generation, and interacting through actions and observations.
Distinguishes sequence-level temporal coherence from consistency of the underlying world state.
Highlights a shift from clip recognition and perceptual fidelity toward persistent state, controllable evolution, physical and causal validity, and decision-oriented evaluation.
Identifies open challenges in representations, models, datasets, benchmarks, and interaction-based assessment.
papers.selection_reason: Survey unifying video foundation models and world models directly fits world modeling and video understanding.
papers.title: Reading, Writing, Sharing, and Interacting with the World through Video
papers.tldr: This survey unifies video foundation and world models through four operations—reading, writing, sharing, and interacting—to study how videos represent and support reasoning about evolving worlds.

papers.abstract: Tasks such as quadrotor dynamic-gate racing require agents to anticipate external motion while maintaining precise high-frequency control. World-model-based reinforcement learning provides a natural solution by learning latent dynamics for future imagination, yet it often entangles environmental evolution and the robot's own dynamics in a single learned rollout, where model bias can affect policy optimization efficiency. We propose DiffDreamer, a differentiable reinforcement learning framework that tightly couples a learned world model with differentiable simulation for actor optimization. In one optimization step, the learned world model propagates latent states that capture external dynamics and history-dependent features, while the differentiable simulator propagates the robot's explicit physical state. We further decompose the actor objective into a critic-driven pathway for non-differentiable task rewards and a simulator-driven pathway for differentiable motion rewards. Experiments on aggressive tracking and dynamic-gate racing show that DiffDreamer improves training convergence over the model-free, model-based, and differentiable-RL baselines, and final performance over these baselines and classical planning and control methods. Additional experiments assess reward decomposition and the odometry-conditioned relative-state representation through ablations. We also provide proof-of-concept real-world flight experiments for validation.
authors: Fanxing Li, Yuxiang Huang, Shengyang Wang, Fangyu Sun, Shuyu Wu, Tianbao Zhang, Dexin Zuo, Yan Yufei, Danping Zou, Wenxian Yu
bullets: Targets aggressive tracking and dynamic-gate racing, where agents must anticipate moving obstacles while controlling quadrotors at high frequency.
Uses a world model for external dynamics and history-dependent latent features, while a differentiable simulator handles the robot’s explicit physical state.
Splits actor optimization between critic-based non-differentiable task rewards and simulator-based differentiable motion rewards.
Experiments report faster training convergence and better final performance than multiple learning, planning, and control baselines.
Ablations and proof-of-concept real-world flights evaluate reward decomposition and odometry-conditioned relative-state representations.
papers.selection_reason: Couples a learned world model with differentiable simulation for agile quadrotor RL control, directly relevant to embodied robot learning and world-model-based policy optimization.
papers.title: DiffDreamer: Coupling World Models with Differentiable Simulation for Agile Quadrotor Control
papers.tldr: DiffDreamer combines learned world-model predictions with differentiable quadrotor simulation to improve agile control in dynamic environments.

papers.abstract: Robot world models simulate how environments evolve in response to robot actions. Latent action models enable learning dynamics from videos by encoding visual transitions as proxy actions. However, reconstruction-driven latent actions mix robot motion with object responses and other scene changes, complicating their correspondence with robot controls. We propose SkeLAM, a skeleton-guided latent action model for controllable robot world modeling. SkeLAM decomposes latent actions into a kinematic component grounded by robot skeleton supervision and a residual component retaining complementary visual dynamics. Cross-modal swap reconstruction encourages RGB-derived and skeleton-derived kinematic representations to be interchangeable during video reconstruction. The world model incorporates both components through separate conditioning pathways, while branch dropout reduces its dependence on future-derived residual information. A lightweight adapter maps robot actions to the kinematic space, and subsequent world-model fine-tuning adapts generation to these predicted conditions. At inference, the model generates future observations from the current observation and robot actions. On DROID, SkeLAM reduces end-effector ADE by 19.5% and LPIPS by 11.1% compared with DreamDojo. Motion probing supports kinematic specialization, while qualitative results demonstrate zero-shot human-to-robot motion transfer in generated rollouts. Policy evaluation shows agreement between predicted success rates and those measured in real robot executions.
authors: Qi Lv, Jiayi Lin, Yuxin Jiang, Jianzong Wang, Xiang Deng, Mike Shou Zheng
bullets: Addresses the entanglement of robot motion, object responses, and scene changes in reconstruction-based latent actions.
Decomposes latent actions into a skeleton-grounded kinematic component and a complementary visual residual.
Uses cross-modal swap reconstruction, separate conditioning pathways, and branch dropout to improve controllability.
A lightweight adapter maps robot actions into the kinematic latent space for future-observation generation.
On DROID, it reduces end-effector ADE by 19.5% and LPIPS by 11.1% versus DreamDojo; results also support motion specialization and zero-shot human-to-robot transfer.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes SkeLAM, a skeleton-guided latent action model that decomposes latent actions into kinematic and residual components for better controllable robot world modeling.
papers.title: Skeleton-Grounded Latent Action Model for Robot World Models
papers.tldr: SkeLAM makes robot world models more controllable by separating robot kinematics from other visual dynamics in latent actions.

papers.abstract: World action models increasingly rely on pretrained video models assumed to capture physical dynamics for prediction, planning, and action generation. Existing evaluations assess plausibility, probe representations, or measure predictive surprise, but rarely identify which history-conditioned physical expectations conflict with observations. We introduce PhysTrace, a training-free framework aligning MLLM-generated, history-conditioned expectations with observed video windows to temporally localize physical violations and provide interpretable descriptions without task-specific probes or classifiers. We also introduce IntPhys2-Timing, adding violation intervals to IntPhys2. PhysTrace achieves a Hit Rate of up to 70.7% across physical principles on IntPhys2-Timing and outperforms the compared methods in overall possible-impossible discrimination accuracy on IntPhys2. Applied to reconstructed videos along the trajectories of pretrained diffusion/flow-based video models, PhysTrace reveals attribute- and noise-dependent patterns in physical violation localization, enabling interpretable physical consistency analysis across timesteps.
authors: Taekoan Yoo, Wonkyung Jung, Kyunghun Kim, Kyeongbo Kong
bullets: Addresses the lack of evaluations that identify which physical expectations conflict with video observations.
Uses MLLM-generated, history-conditioned expectations aligned with video windows to detect and describe violations without task-specific probes or classifiers.
Introduces IntPhys2-Timing, an extension of IntPhys2 with annotated violation intervals.
Achieves up to 70.7% hit rate across physical principles on IntPhys2-Timing and improves overall possible–impossible discrimination accuracy over compared methods on IntPhys2.
Reveals attribute- and noise-dependent violation-localization patterns across timesteps in reconstructed diffusion- and flow-based video trajectories.
papers.selection_reason: Training-free temporal localization and interpretable evaluation of physical consistency in video generative models.
papers.title: PhysTrace: Interpretable Temporal Evaluation of Physical Consistency in Video Generative Models
papers.tldr: PhysTrace is a training-free framework that temporally localizes and explains physical inconsistencies in generated videos by comparing history-conditioned expectations with observed events.

papers.abstract: Synthesizing physically grounded dexterous hand-object interactions is important for VR/AR, gaming, and robotics, yet remains challenging because subtle contact dynamics, diverse object geometries, and target trajectories must be jointly respected while maintaining natural grasps. Existing methods either track mocap trajectories with limited transfer to novel objects, or rely on hand-only generative priors that fail to capture coupled hand-object motion, sacrificing contact fidelity and sample efficiency. To tackle these challenges, we introduce PiHand, a Physically grounded Interaction-aware Hand motion synthesis framework. PiHand first trains expert policies that track mocap demonstrations in simulation, distills them into a unified hand-object interaction prior using a goal-conditioned VAE, and finally solve diverse dexterous manipulation tasks through bounded residual exploration in its latent space. With only a single reward and no complex curriculum training, this yields general tabletop manipulation policies that generalize to unseen objects and trajectories on GRAB and DexYCB. The same prior transfers to object catching and bimanual handover, two tasks that are rarely seen in its training data. Across all tasks, PiHand consistently outperforms baselines in all metrics. We will release the processed data and model checkpoints.
authors: Niklas Berndt, Xianghui Xie, Enes Duran, Yixiao Wang, Gerard Pons-Moll
bullets: Addresses the challenge of jointly modeling contact dynamics, diverse object geometries, target trajectories, and natural grasps.
Trains simulation expert policies from mocap, distills them into a goal-conditioned VAE prior, and performs bounded residual exploration in latent space.
Uses a single reward without complex curriculum training.
Generalizes to unseen objects and trajectories on GRAB and DexYCB, and transfers to object catching and bimanual handover.
Reports consistent improvement over baselines across all evaluated metrics; data and checkpoints are planned for release.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces latent hand-object interaction priors for physics-based dexterous manipulation policy learning, fitting robot learning and latent action modeling.
papers.title: PiHand: Latent Hand-Object Interaction Priors for Physics-Based Policy Learning
papers.tldr: PiHand learns a latent, physics-grounded hand–object interaction prior that enables dexterous manipulation policies to generalize across unseen objects, trajectories, and tasks.

papers.abstract: Joint-embedding predictive architectures (JEPAs) learn world models in latent space, enabling efficient planning but leaving their states opaque. We introduce Inside-JEPA, which places relational channels for ordered entity pairs inside the JEPA latent state and shows that an inverse-dynamics loss can ground these channels without relation labels when its head reads them, either alone or as part of the full state. On Something-Something V2, latent prediction alone performs no better than a random relation head, while inverse-dynamics supervision that recovers actions from channel changes improves relational AUROC by .065-.103 across ten settings with annotated boxes, by .081 on RH20T robot episodes with held-out tasks, and by .050-.061 across five relations using off-the-shelf detection and tracking. An inverse head on entity latents decodes actions more accurately but barely improves relational grounding; shuffled labels, two label-free objectives, and action labels on only 5% of the pairs also fail to ground the channels. Given an action, predicted relational changes approach the quality of observed future relations (AUROC .599 vs .621). For one-step relational goals, a supervised readout of the 16 channels ranks the correct action among the top five of 65 in 43% of cases, compared with 24% for prediction-only latents and 17% for a frequency prior.
bullets: Latent prediction alone does not ground relational channels beyond random performance.
An inverse-dynamics head that reads relational-channel changes improves relational AUROC across video, robot, and tracked-object settings.
Using entity latents alone decodes actions better but provides little relational grounding, highlighting the importance of channel-specific supervision.
Grounded channels can predict future relational changes nearly as well as observed relations and support one-step action selection.
The approach relies on entity detections or tracking and evaluates a fixed set of relational channels and tasks.
papers.selection_reason: Latent world-model grounding with relational channels and inverse dynamics, directly contributing to world-model research.
papers.title: Inside-JEPA: From Prediction to Relational Grounding in Latent World Models
papers.tldr: Inside-JEPA shows that inverse-dynamics supervision can ground interpretable relational channels within JEPA latent world models without relation labels.

papers.abstract: World Models (WMs) can support Multimodal Agents (MAs) through simulated experience, while Agent trajectories can inform World Model refinement. Evaluating this interaction requires separate evidence about action selection and state evolution. We introduce Dual Exam, which tests Agents under fixed environment response mechanisms and World Models under fixed action interventions across physical, digital, social, and scientific domains. The Agent track compares 10 configurations on 1,088 items in 15 reporting categories. The World Model track contains 400 cases across eight scenarios; 15 configurations have full coverage and one covers six scenarios. GPT 6 Astra leads the case-weighted Agent Index at 31.3, and GPT-Image-2 leads the full-coverage WM Overall at 21.7. These scores use different tasks and metrics and are not directly comparable. A 150-case pilot of one coupled pairing records zero task successes and motivates component-level diagnosis. Results reveal uneven task performance and failures to preserve task-relevant state. Their value for predicting coupled success or sustained reciprocal learning remains to be established.
authors: Zhefan Rao, Meng Chu, Xuan Zhang, Jingfan Chen, Guohao Cai, Runyi Li, Shiyi Du, Ning Lu, Xu Huang, Zhixuan Chen, Feng Nie, Harold Haodong Chen, Hanwen Wang, Wen-Jie Shu, Yajing Bai, Xianfeng Wu, Xuanhua He, Shuhan Guo, Ziyue Ma, Ruichuan An, Long Bai, Miaosen Chai, Wenhao Chai, Jingye Chen, Qi Chen, Xuhang Chen, Wei Chow, Minghao Fu, Yunhao Gou, Haokun Gui, Dong Huang, Wei Huang, Zi Cheng Huang, Haibo Jin, Lingdong Kong, Leung Chun Ho, Tianqin Li, Yanheng Li, Jiayuan Liu, Jiyang Liu, Mingyu Liu, Shaoteng Liu, Xiaocheng Lu, Yawen Luo, Zeyu Qin, Tiancheng Shen, Yueqi Song, Zhaolong Su, Hengkai Tan, Tianhao Tang, Yiran Tao, Juncheng Wang, Qinghe Wang, Shangshang Wang, Yingying Wang, Fang Wu, Tiange Xiang, Qiushi Yang, Weicai Ye, Weichen Yu, Jiarui Zhang, Jize Zhang, Liuzhou Zhang, Renrui Zhang, Sheng Zhang, Wenhu Zhang, Junru Zhao, Lingting Zhu, Yuxin Zuo, Yutong Bai, Long Chen, Yang Deng, Ziqi Huang, Yeying Jin, Weijia Li, Kevin Qinghong Lin, Quande Liu, See-Kiong Ng, Hongliang Ren, Hongru Wang, Shujun Wang, Qifeng Chen, Haoxuan Che

papers.selection_reason: Evaluates world models under fixed action interventions, fitting interactive world models.
papers.title: Dual Exam: Controlled Evaluation of Multimodal Agents and World Models
papers.tldr: Dual Exam separately evaluates multimodal agents’ action selection and world models’ state evolution, revealing uneven performance and limited evidence that either predicts successful agent–world-model coupling.

papers.abstract: Robot demonstrations record what the robot saw and what it did. They do not specify how the 3D world changed in between. Scene-level 3D flow describes it by tracking 3D scene points, providing the world representation with 4D geometry. Prior work has used flow to improve robot policies. Flow served as an intermediate prediction that a separate model converts into actions, as a prior injected at inference time, or as an extra output learned together with the action. In all of these designs, flow stays outside the policy, as a separate module or as an extra prediction head. We introduce UniFlowWAM, a Unified World-Action Model that makes 3D scene flow a third modality on par with vision and action. Its world representation therefore covers both visual semantics, through future visual features, and 4D geometry, through 3D flow, and flow receives its own supervision. UniFlowWAM is a diffusion transformer with one expert per modality, and the three experts exchange information through joint attention. We train UniFlowWAM under a ten-objective role grid, where each objective assigns every modality exactly one of three roles, namely target, condition, or absent. The same model thus serves as a policy, as forward and inverse dynamics, and as a predictor of future visual features or 3D flow. We evaluate UniFlowWAM on RoboCasa-GR1, LIBERO, and LIBERO-Plus in simulation, and on four real-world bimanual manipulation tasks. On RoboCasa-GR1, UniFlowWAM raises the success rate of its base model without flow from 52.1% to 56.4%. It preserves in-distribution success on LIBERO at 98.1% and reaches 87.7% zero-shot on LIBERO-Plus. On the real robot, it achieves 87.0% average success, compared with 68.5% for the strongest baseline.
authors: Jialin Tian, Zhuofan Li, Xinkai Wang, Bokai Lin, Chenyi Wang, Xinyu Zhan, Cewu Lu, Lixin Yang
bullets: Addresses the limitation that 3D flow is typically handled outside the robot policy as a separate module or output.
Uses a diffusion transformer with one expert each for vision, action, and 3D flow, connected through joint attention.
Trains across ten objectives that assign each modality as a target, condition, or absent, enabling policy, dynamics, and future-feature prediction tasks.
Improves RoboCasa-GR1 success from 52.1% to 56.4%, while achieving 98.1% on LIBERO and 87.7% zero-shot on LIBERO-Plus.
Reaches 87.0% average success on four real-world bimanual tasks, compared with 68.5% for the strongest baseline.
papers.selection_reason: Unified action-world model treating 3D flow as a co-equal modality for manipulation policies and dynamics prediction.
papers.title: UniFlowWAM: A Unified World-Action Model with Visual Semantics and 4D Geometry
papers.tldr: UniFlowWAM unifies vision, actions, and 3D scene flow in one multimodal model, improving simulated and real-world robot manipulation performance.

papers.abstract: Robust manipulation of soft objects, such as garments, is a critical skill for service and household robots to adopt, but remains challenging due to its high-dimensional state space, and material-dependent deformations. Humans address this challenge by using mental world models that "imagine" the shape and material properties from partial observations, which enables them to predict how actions affect future states. As such, embedding such world models in robots allows for better generalization in manipulating a wide variety of garments in the real world. However, learned world models typically require large amounts of real world data that is strenuous to collect, and a mechanism to infer latent properties that govern dynamics. We present a Soft-Object World Model that performs generative full-state estimation and action-conditioned dynamics prediction using a transformer backbone trained on large-scale simulated soft object interactions, with measures to mitigate the sim-to-real gap. By learning to infer latent shape and material cues through in-context learning over a variable-length partial point-cloud history, the model generalizes across robot embodiments, material parameters, garment types and shapes, and manipulation coordination modes without weight updates. The world model is then integrated with a Goal-Conditioned action planner for motion synthesis. We validate the approach in simulation and real world for bimanual garment folding, reporting improvements in reconstruction fidelity, prediction accuracy, and task success.
authors: Hengyi Sim, Quentin Rouxel, Dennis Hong, Darwin Caldwell, Fei Chen
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of garment manipulation under high-dimensional, material-dependent dynamics and partial observations.
Uses a transformer trained on large-scale simulated soft-object interactions for generative full-state estimation and action-conditioned prediction.
Infers latent garment shape and material properties from variable-length partial point-cloud histories through in-context learning.
Integrates the world model with a goal-conditioned planner for bimanual motion synthesis.
Simulation and real-world folding experiments show improved reconstruction fidelity, prediction accuracy, and task success.
papers.selection_reason: In-context world model for action-conditioned soft-garment dynamics prediction and bimanual manipulation.
papers.title: In-Context Learning World Models for Robot Dual-Arm Manipulation of Soft Garment with Partial Observations
papers.tldr: An in-context transformer world model enables dual-arm robots to infer and manipulate partially observed garments across varied materials, shapes, and embodiments without model updates.

papers.abstract: Active inference casts perception, learning and planning as variational inference, where the Expected Free Energy (EFE) defines the planning objective. Recent work showed that EFE minimization can be written as Variational Free Energy (VFE) minimization on a generative model augmented with epistemic priors, and that the resulting entropy-corrected objective is minimized by sum-product message passing (SP-MP) on modified factor functions. These formulations treat model uncertainty as inference over a finite set of known models. We extend them to planning during learning, where beliefs over the observation and transition parameters $\theta_A$, $\theta_B$ are Dirichlet priors. Closed-form Dirichlet updates are usually obtained by a structured mean-field factorization between parameters and states, but under exactly that factorization the information-gain corrections vanish. We resolve this by giving every factor its own parameter prior, frozen during a rollout. Conjugacy then makes each factor belief a product of a marginal over the categorical variables and a one-step Bayes posterior of the parameters. This reintroduces the datum-dependent parameter posteriors that mean-field factorization destroys. We show that evaluating the epistemic priors under the resulting Bethe joint recovers the information gains. Stationarity of this single closed-form objective yields SP-MP whose factor functions are augmented by the information-gain weight. Experiments on two grid POMDPs, in which only a planner that learns the model finds the safe route, show that the method plans to efficiently learn $\theta_A$ and $\theta_B$. It reaches the goal on every episode, whereas SP-MP planners with the same inference update plateau or take the risky route.
bullets: Addresses the loss of information-gain corrections when parameter and state beliefs use structured mean-field factorization.
Uses factor-specific, rollout-frozen Dirichlet parameter priors to recover datum-dependent parameter posteriors.
Derives a single closed-form Bethe objective whose stationarity yields sum-product message passing with information-gain-weighted factors.
In two grid POMDPs, the learning planner found the safe route and reached the goal on every episode, unlike comparison planners that plateaued or chose the risky route.
papers.selection_reason: Active inference with parameter learning in generative models of environment dynamics is relevant to world models.
papers.title: Parameter Learning in Active Inference via Variational Message Passing
papers.tldr: A variational message-passing method enables active-inference planners to learn observation and transition models while planning, preserving information-gain incentives under mean-field factorization.

papers.abstract: World models are increasingly used to reduce environment interaction when post-training vision-language-action (VLA) policies with reinforcement learning. Yet they are typically trained to predict pixels one step ahead, even though their role here is not merely to render visually faithful videos but to produce learning signals from imagined rollouts that improve the policy. We show that this mismatch is substantial: lower pixel MSE can produce worse policy gradients, and a world model trained for policy utility can yield better downstream policies despite 17% higher pixel MSE on the next frame. We propose the Downstream-Return Imagination Learning Loop (DRILL), a bilevel framework that updates the world model to maximize the policy's return after an inner GRPO update on imagined rollouts. DRILL has two instantiations. DRILL-VWI is a closed-form surrogate, requiring no additional simulator rollouts, that reweights prediction errors by policy visitation, the group-relative GRPO advantage, and model confidence. DRILL-IMG is a full meta-gradient method that differentiates through the inner update using truncated Hessian-vector products. We show that DRILL-VWI recovers the local one-step component of the DRILL-IMG meta-gradient under score-compatibility and small-residual assumptions. Across five manipulation simulators and two VLA backbones, DRILL-IMG raises mean success rate by 13.1 points over WMPO and 7.9 points over RLVR-World, and complements RLVR pretraining rather than competing with it. More broadly, we believe video world models for VLA reinforcement learning can be productively trained by the policy gradients they produce, not only by pixel-level prediction.
authors: Zhaolu Kang, Tailong Luo, Lei Wei, Guangyuan Dong, Sihan Liu, Yingjie He, Siheng Wang, Shuaibo Li, Rongchao Zhang, Zhen Tian, Richeng Xuan, Zhichao Hu
bullets: Pixel prediction quality can misalign with policy utility: lower next-frame MSE may yield worse policy gradients.
DRILL uses bilevel optimization to update the world model based on returns after an inner GRPO update from imagined rollouts.
DRILL-VWI is a rollout-free surrogate that weights errors by policy visitation, GRPO advantage, and model confidence.
DRILL-IMG differentiates through the inner update with truncated Hessian-vector products; DRILL-VWI approximates its local one-step gradient under stated assumptions.
Across five manipulation simulators and two VLA backbones, DRILL-IMG improves mean success rate by 13.1 points over WMPO and 7.9 points over RLVR-World.
papers.selection_reason: Trains action-conditioned world models to improve VLA policies via imagined rollouts, directly relevant to world models and embodied policy learning.
papers.title: DRILL: Training World Models to Improve Policies, Not Predict Pixels
papers.tldr: DRILL trains world models to produce useful policy-learning signals rather than merely predict pixels, improving downstream VLA policy performance.

papers.abstract: World models have recently emerged as a promising direction toward developing generalist agents capable of understanding, predicting, and interacting with diverse environments. However, despite growing interest, the concept of a world model remains loosely defined, encompassing approaches ranging from predictive dynamics models and learned simulators to models that jointly generate future observations and actions. This introductory paper aims to clarify the concept of world models and provide a unified perspective on their role in developing generalist agents. Starting from the partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP) framework, we connect world modeling to classical control, dynamical systems, signal processing, and reinforcement learning. We introduce different approaches to world modeling, emphasizing the knowledge they capture, their learning objectives, and how they support decision-making. We further explore the relationship between world modeling and policy learning, highlighting how these capabilities can be unified through conditional prediction without requiring separate models. Rather than offering an exhaustive survey of existing methods, this paper focuses on fundamental concepts, modeling principles, and connections, with the goal of providing an accessible and unified introduction to world models for generalist agents.
bullets: Frames world modeling within the partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP) setting.
Connects world models to control, dynamical systems, signal processing, and reinforcement learning.
Organizes approaches by the knowledge they capture, their learning objectives, and how they support decision-making.
Explains how world modeling and policy learning can be unified through conditional prediction rather than separate models.
Focuses on foundational concepts and connections, not an exhaustive survey of existing methods.
papers.selection_reason: Provides a unified introduction to world models for generalist agents, directly aligned with the world-models topic.
papers.title: An Introduction to World Models for Generalist Agents
papers.tldr: This paper offers a unified introduction to world models, clarifying their definitions, principles, and role in building generalist agents.

papers.abstract: Before acting on an object, a robot needs to anticipate how its hand motion will change the physical world and what the resulting scene will look like. Existing approaches typically entangle action-conditioned dynamics, camera motion, and visual synthesis within a video generation model, or represent dynamics as point trajectories without explicit object structure. We introduce DeXplicit, a dexterous manipulation world model that instead predicts how the world evolves explicitly in metric 3D before rendering its visual consequences. Given an initial scene and a future hand trajectory, a lightweight 3D dynamics network predicts object-centric motion and deformation, providing structured and geometrically grounded future world states. These predictions then serve as a strong scaffold for video generation: appearance is transported through the predicted 3D motion and projected into future views, allowing the renderer to focus on completing uncertain and newly visible content rather than implicitly learning world dynamics from pixels. This explicit-3D-first decomposition also enables efficient causal generation, requiring only two denoising steps per block while conditioning on generated history. Across HOT3D, OakInk2, and PhysTwin, DeXplicit reduces moved-point error by 27-40% relative to PointWorld and improves object fidelity IoU+ by 47% on HOT3D under a shared renderer. Our design with two-step causal generation achieves a 57x speedup from our 14B bi-directional configuration in video synthesis.
authors: Adam Lee, Mutian Xu, Yukang Cao, Shulin Tian, Ziwei Liu
bullets: Addresses the entanglement of dynamics, camera motion, and visual synthesis in existing video-based world models.
Uses a lightweight 3D dynamics network to predict object-centric motion and deformation from an initial scene and future hand trajectory.
Transports appearance through predicted 3D motion, letting video generation focus on uncertain or newly visible content.
Reports 27–40% lower moved-point error than PointWorld across HOT3D, OakInk2, and PhysTwin, plus 47% higher object-fidelity IoU+ on HOT3D under a shared renderer.
Two-step causal generation provides a reported 57× speedup relative to the authors’ 14B bidirectional configuration.
papers.selection_reason: Action-conditioned dexterous manipulation world model with explicit 3D dynamics, fitting interactive world models and robot manipulation.
papers.title: DeXplicit: Making Physical State Explicit in Dexterous Manipulation World Models
papers.tldr: DeXplicit improves dexterous-manipulation world modeling by predicting explicit metric-3D object motion before rendering future video.

papers.abstract: Video provides a natural source of supervision: what happens next serves as a learning signal for visual world modeling. Yet masked video pretraining focuses on recovering missing content from surrounding context rather than predicting the future from the past. Autoregressive methods instead predict forward one token at a time, but have yet to match joint-embedding methods in representation quality. This gap motivates us to revisit the granularity and space of future prediction. In this work, we introduce VANE, a self-supervised visual pretraining framework built on next-frame prediction in embedding space. A causal encoder summarizes past observations for a state predictor that infers the representation of the entire next frame, making temporal evolution the primary learning signal. This prediction is carried out in a fixed embedding space provided by a frozen semantic tokenizer, emphasizing scene content and structure. To retain fine-grained spatial detail alongside semantic content, a lightweight auxiliary generative decoder reconstructs future-frame patches conditioned on the predicted representations. To unify visual modeling across images and videos, we construct a local-to-global crop sequence for still images, allowing the same encoder to predict newly revealed regions from earlier crops under the same objective. Experiments show that VANE improves with model and data scaling, achieving SOTA on most anticipation, recognition, and dense perception benchmarks among unified encoders. Especially on EPIC-KITCHENS-100 action anticipation, it surpasses V-JEPA 2.1 by 7.1 points in mean-class recall@5. These results demonstrate that next-frame prediction in embedding space is effective and scalable for visual world modeling.
authors: Yifeng Yao, Jinghan Li, Zhihao Zhang, Yajiao Xiong, Yang Jin, Kun Xu, Huishuai Zhang, Dongyan Zhao
bullets: Motivation: Existing masked and autoregressive video methods do not fully capture future dynamics or match joint-embedding representation quality.
Method: A causal encoder summarizes past observations, while a state predictor infers the next frame in a fixed space from a frozen semantic tokenizer.
Detail: An auxiliary lightweight decoder reconstructs future-frame patches to preserve spatial detail alongside semantic content.
Unification: Still images are converted into local-to-global crop sequences so the same prediction objective applies to images and videos.
