Results: VANE improves with model and data scaling, reaches state-of-the-art on most evaluated unified-encoder benchmarks, and exceeds V-JEPA 2.1 by 7.1 mean-class recall@5 points on EPIC-KITCHENS-100 action anticipation.
papers.selection_reason: Next-frame prediction in embedding space for scalable visual world modeling and video representation learning.
papers.title: Learning from Next-Frame Prediction: Towards Unified and Scalable Visual Representation Learning
papers.tldr: VANE learns scalable visual representations by predicting entire future-frame embeddings, combining semantic next-frame prediction with fine-grained spatial reconstruction across images and videos.

papers.abstract: We propose AgentDreamer, an agent-guided optimization framework that aligns text instructions with simulated motion through explicit 3D motion planning. Given a text instruction and scene geometry, an off-the-shelf agent translates the instruction into a structured semantic motion prior, specifying what should move, in which direction, and in what temporal order. The agent represents this prior using parametric functions over a series of temporal chunks, yielding dense 3D trajectories. We then optimize the parameters of a differentiable MPM simulator such that its rollout best matches the prior while remaining constrained by the scene dynamics. This allows the agent to provide semantic guidance from language, while the simulator grounds it in physically feasible motion. We further introduce Motion-IG, an information-theoretic metric for text-motion alignment based on masked text recovery. By comparing the likelihood of recovering masked motion-related content with and without the simulated motion, Motion-IG measures the information contributed by the motion beyond that available from the remaining text and scene context. Experiments show that AgentDreamer improves text alignment over video-based guidance, producing simulations that more closely follow the requested physical behavior.
authors: Mijeong Kim, Suho Park, Junha Park, Bohyung Han
bullets: Converts language into structured semantic motion priors describing objects, directions, and temporal order.
Represents priors as parametric dense 3D trajectories across temporal chunks.
Optimizes a differentiable MPM simulator to match the priors while respecting scene dynamics.
Introduces Motion-IG, an information-theoretic metric for measuring text–motion alignment.
Improves text alignment over video-based guidance in experiments.
papers.selection_reason: Text-controllable physics simulation via agentic 3D motion planning fits interactive world models.
papers.title: AgentDreamer: Agentic 3D Motion Reasoning for Text-Controllable Physics Simulation
papers.tldr: AgentDreamer uses an agent-generated 3D motion plan to optimize differentiable physics simulations that better follow text instructions.

papers.abstract: Social world models predict how interactions develop after an action, helping agents negotiate, cooperate and mediate. In these situations, one action can lead to several plausible futures, hence predicting only one future can overlook consequential alternatives, while exploring them through repeated simulations increases inference cost. We propose DSWM, a Distributional Social World Model that predicts alternative responses, their probabilities and immediate and final outcome values in one output per candidate action. We train a 4B model on repeated simulations using supervised fine-tuning and GRPO. At inference time, the actor uses these possible consequences to choose an action. Across three seen and two unseen environments, with interaction backbones absent from training collection, DSWM achieves the best average performance on 13 of 15 metrics. Ablations show that retaining multiple futures and their predicted probabilities improves outcomes in all five environments.
authors: Viet-Thanh Pham, Thuy-Trang Vu, Zhuang Li, Lizhen Qu, Gholamreza Haffari
bullets: Models alternative responses, their probabilities, and immediate and final outcome values for each candidate action.
Trained on repeated simulations using supervised fine-tuning and GRPO.
Evaluated across three seen and two unseen environments, including interaction backbones absent from training data.
Achieves the best average performance on 13 of 15 metrics.
Ablations indicate that preserving multiple futures and their probabilities improves outcomes across all five environments.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes a Distributional Social World Model that predicts alternative responses and probabilities for social interactions, fitting the definition of interactive world models.
papers.title: Anticipating Social Consequences with Distributional World Models
papers.tldr: DSWM predicts multiple likely social consequences and their values in one pass, helping agents choose better actions without costly repeated simulations.

papers.abstract: Forecasting future human motion requires jointly reasoning about an agent's global trajectory and 3D body pose, which are tightly coupled, particularly in team sports where multiple interacting players introduce complex social dynamics. We exploit a socio-temporal encoder that fuses trajectory and pose at the input level and models them jointly through shared factorized attention. The model is further enhanced by a per-joint loss reweighting scheme that emphasizes dynamic joints and prevents degenerate solutions, and a frequency-domain trajectory smoothing term that improves trajectory prediction while indirectly benefiting pose forecasting. To ensure fair comparison with prior joint forecasting methods, we identify and correct evaluation biases arising from overlapping sequence construction, adopting instead a non-overlapping protocol and a deterministic, oracle-free strategy for multi-future prediction. Our approach improves over prior joint forecasting methods on both WorldPose and 3DPW, with the largest gains on pose accuracy, demonstrating that the proposed joint formulation generalizes beyond the densely interactive scenarios that motivate it.
authors: Marc Peral, Guillem Capellera, Luis Ferraz, Antonio Rubio, Stella Gra{\ss}hof, Dan Witzner Hansen, Antonio Agudo
bullets: Targets tightly coupled global motion and 3D body-pose forecasting in socially interacting sports agents.
Uses socio-temporal encoding with input-level trajectory–pose fusion and shared factorized attention.
Adds dynamic-joint loss reweighting and frequency-domain trajectory smoothing.
Corrects evaluation bias from overlapping sequences using non-overlapping data and deterministic, oracle-free multi-future prediction.
Outperforms prior joint forecasting methods on WorldPose and 3DPW, with the largest gains in pose accuracy.
papers.selection_reason: Joint trajectory and 3D pose forecasting with socio-temporal attention; transferable as a learned predictor of multi-agent dynamics.
papers.title: Unified Trajectory and 3D Pose Forecasting for Multi-Agent Sports Analysis
papers.tldr: A unified model jointly forecasts multi-agent trajectories and 3D poses, improving pose and trajectory prediction under a fairer evaluation protocol.

papers.abstract: World models help agents assess the consequences of their actions before acting. Many real systems, however, involve multiple actors who make their own decisions, can evolve even when the agent takes no action, and are only partially observed through event logs. We formalize these systems as event worlds and ask whether large language models can predict future observations from the log and the agent's proposed actions. We build complementary benchmarks from human Diplomacy games and real Polymarket trades. Our hierarchical framework compares prediction with and without other actors' actions, then tests multi-step rollouts, predictions for actions never taken, and usefulness to agents. Fine-tuning and more data improve prediction when all actors' recorded actions are given. With only the agent's action, models struggle when other actors strongly affect the outcome, and larger models and longer histories help little. This gap also limits multi-step prediction and agent decisions, with models overestimating plan success. Yet imagined experience and initialization from world models can still improve policy learning. Anticipating other actors' actions remains a central challenge for event world modeling.
authors: Juntong Ni, Zewen Liu, Bohan Wang, Lige Zhang, Wei Jin
bullets: The study extends world modeling from single-actor settings to partially observed event worlds with autonomous actors and ongoing dynamics.
It evaluates LLMs on human Diplomacy games and real Polymarket trading logs.
A hierarchical framework tests prediction with or without other actors’ actions, multi-step rollouts, counterfactual actions, and agent usefulness.
Fine-tuning and more data improve prediction when all actors’ recorded actions are available, while larger models and longer histories help little when they are hidden.

Hidden-actor uncertainty harms multi-step prediction and decision quality, with models tending to overestimate plan success; imagined experience and world-model initialization can still aid policy learning.
papers.selection_reason: Investigates LLMs as event world models predicting future observations conditioned on agent actions in multi-actor environments.
papers.title: From Single-Actor Environments to Multi-Actor Event Worlds: Can LLMs Be Event World Models?
papers.tldr: LLMs can model multi-actor event worlds when other actors’ actions are visible, but struggle to anticipate unseen actors and reliably support planning.

papers.abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) have emerged as a promising approach to learning generalist robot policies using rich spatiotemporal priors from pre-trained video diffusion models. A recent line of WAMs improves inference efficiency by conditioning a separate action decoder on intermediate future video representations extracted from a single denoising step, avoiding costly iterative denoising required for video generation. This design makes action prediction depend directly on the quality of these future representations. In this paper, we introduce Future REpresentation learning via self-Distillation with temporal context (FRED), a framework that trains WAMs to improve the quality of future video representations from noise in a single denoising step. Specifically, FRED uses self-distillation to predict future representations from noise, using representations extracted from ground-truth future observations as targets. We further condition the video model on historical observations, providing temporal context for predicting future representations better. Across diverse real-world manipulation scenarios, FRED consistently outperforms competing WAMs. It achieves particularly large gains on long-horizon and out-of-domain tasks under zero-shot environment generalization, and substantially improves human-to-robot skill transfer, reaching 50.0% task success on tasks absent from robot training data and demonstrated only in human videos, compared with 19.4% for the best competing WAM.
authors: Huiwon Jang, Suhyeok Jang, Hyeonmo Kang, Seungku Kim, Jinwoo Shin, Sihyun Yu
bullets: WAMs use future video representations to guide action prediction without costly iterative video denoising.
FRED self-distills representations predicted from noise using representations from ground-truth future observations as targets.
Historical observations provide temporal context for more accurate future representation prediction.
Across real-world manipulation tasks, FRED outperforms competing WAMs, especially on long-horizon and out-of-domain tasks.
For skills shown only in human videos, FRED reaches 50.0% task success versus 19.4% for the best competing WAM.
papers.selection_reason: Improving future video representations for world action models directly fits world models and embodied robot learning.
papers.title: Self-Distilling Future Video Representations for World Action Models
papers.tldr: FRED improves efficient World Action Models by self-distilling better single-step future video representations with temporal context, substantially boosting long-horizon, zero-shot, and human-to-robot generalization.

papers.abstract: Canada's increasing wildfire activity requires frequent national hazard mapping to guide proactive mitigation, including fuel management, land-use planning, infrastructure protection, and evacuation routing. However, process-based wildfire simulation frameworks (e.g., BurnP3 and BurnP3+) rely on computationally intensive Monte Carlo simulations to model burn probability, fire intensity, and rate of spread. These workflows can take days to weeks to process a single regional modelling unit. To overcome these computational bottlenecks, we present three contributions developed through collaboration between AI researchers and wildfire modelling experts: (a) a standardized framework for training, fine-tuning, and evaluating AI surrogate models against process-based wildfire simulators; (b) a multi-task deep learning surrogate trained on national-scale data to emulate burn probability, mean fire intensity, and mean rate of spread at a fraction of the computational cost (seconds); and (c) domain-specific metrics and counterfactual evaluation protocols to probe out-of-distribution generalization. Integrating geospatial data (fuel, terrain, ignition likelihood) and regional weather, our model approximates BurnP3+ simulation outputs, achieving strong performance across agreement, rank-correlation, error, and spatial-overlap metrics. It preserves downstream hazard classifications and produces physically plausible responses to expert-informed counterfactual interventions. On a representative region, the surrogate achieves 806-fold end-to-end CPU acceleration and uses 13% of BurnP3+'s host memory, facilitating rapid scenario analysis.
authors: Hager Radi Abdelwahed, Toluwaleke Olutayo, Chirag Goel, Jana Osea, Aldo Zaimi, Tom Swystun, Sandy Erni, Francisco Emiliano Lopez Saavedra, Yan Boulanger, Ga\'etan Marceau Caron
bullets: Addresses the high computational cost of Monte Carlo process-based wildfire simulations for national hazard mapping.
Introduces a framework for training, fine-tuning, and evaluating AI surrogates against wildfire simulators.
Uses geospatial and regional weather inputs to predict burn probability, mean fire intensity, and mean rate of spread.
Achieves strong agreement and spatial performance, with 806-fold end-to-end CPU acceleration and 13% of BurnP3+ host memory on a representative region.
Evaluates out-of-distribution behavior using domain-specific metrics and expert-informed counterfactual interventions.
papers.selection_reason: Develops an AI surrogate modeling framework to emulate the dynamics of wildfire spread, acting as a learned predictor of environment dynamics with significant acceleration.
papers.title: Accelerating Wildfire Hazard Mapping Across Canada with an AI Surrogate Modelling Framework
papers.tldr: A multi-task AI surrogate reproduces key BurnP3+ wildfire hazard outputs across Canada in seconds, enabling substantially faster scenario analysis while preserving hazard classifications and physical plausibility.

papers.abstract: Recent world action models provide visual foresight and future prediction for robot manipulation, but lack explicit mechanisms for compositional skill reuse. Agentic robotics combines code-based planning and reasoning with reusable skills, but often lacks predictive grounding in physical dynamics. We introduce AW-0, an agentic world action model framework that integrates code-based planning with joint video and action prediction. We jointly model code, future video, and robot actions as three coupled generative streams within a unified mixture-of-transformers architecture. Within this architecture a code expert generates parameterized skill routines and control logic while video and action experts generate future visual states and low-level motor commands. Code serves two complementary roles: it structures multi-step prediction and control within the world model and represents skills as reusable programs for subsequent agentic execution. We further introduce an automated curation pipeline that labels robot and human video trajectories with aligned programs and consolidates recurring routines into reusable skill libraries. Evaluations on RoboTwin 2.0 and physical bimanual manipulation tasks show improved task performance over VLA and WAM baselines, alongside gains in language following, semantic reasoning and robustness, demonstrating that agentic code enables connection between planning, prediction and execution within WAMs.
authors: Zhuoyang Liu, Dantong Niu, Botong Zhang, Boning Shao, Jing Wang, Ruijie Zheng, Yuvan Sharma, Runyu Lu, Jiaming Liu, Renrui Zhang, Roei Herzig, Yutong Bai, Ken Goldberg, Danfei Xu, Yuke Zhu, Guanzhi Wang, Linxi "Jim" Fan, Trevor Darrell
bullets: Addresses the gap between predictive world action models and agentic systems with reusable, code-based skills.
Uses a unified mixture-of-transformers architecture with coupled code, video, and action generation streams.
Represents skills as parameterized programs while using code to structure multi-step prediction and control.
Introduces automated trajectory curation that aligns robot and human videos with programs and builds reusable skill libraries.
Evaluations on RoboTwin 2.0 and physical bimanual tasks report improved task performance, language following, semantic reasoning, and robustness over VLA and WAM baselines.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces an agentic world action model coupling code-based planning with joint video and action prediction for robot manipulation, directly fitting embodied AI and world models.
papers.title: Agentic World Action Models
papers.tldr: AW-0 unifies code-based planning, future video prediction, and robot action generation to make world action models more compositional, reusable, and grounded in physical dynamics.

papers.abstract: Video world models predict future frames from past frames and actions. They serve as simulators in which agents train, plan or are evaluated, and that humans can control interactively. They generate in the latent space of a video autoencoder, whose compression sets their cost per frame and how long each action waits to take effect. Yet world models often reuse the autoencoders of text-to-video generators, built for offline generation with no agent waiting and, without their training data and code, not retrainable at another compression. We therefore ask how, where and how much a world model should compress. We build CADRE, an open family of causal diffusion representation autoencoders spanning multiple spatio-temporal compressions. Its members differ only in a small bottleneck on frozen features and share a diffusion decoder self-distilled to one or a few steps. We train the same world model on each autoencoder in two domains, manipulation and navigation, with two environments each. CADRE forms most of the latency-quality frontier, especially with a moving camera. Our study also leads to four findings. At strong compression, a diffusion decoder is sharper than perceptual regression. In robot manipulation, temporal compression is more effective in the autoencoder than in the world model. Manipulation and navigation call for opposite compressions: temporal compression costs little when the camera is still, and spatial compression when it moves. Surprisingly, with a still camera, coarser spatial tokens hurt motion far more than image quality. Code, models and a live demo are at https://kyutai.org/blog/2026-10-21-cadre
authors: Adrien Ramanana Rahary, Yutong Bai, Nicolas Dufour, Patrick P\'erez, David Picard
bullets: World-model autoencoders determine both per-frame computation and how quickly actions affect predictions.
CADRE is a family of causal diffusion representation autoencoders covering multiple spatial and temporal compression levels.
The same world model was evaluated across manipulation and navigation domains with multiple environments per domain.
CADRE achieves most of the latency–quality frontier, particularly in moving-camera settings.
Findings include sharper reconstruction from diffusion decoding under strong compression and different optimal compression choices for manipulation versus navigation.
papers.selection_reason: Rethinks video autoencoders for interactive world models with causal diffusion representation autoencoders; directly relevant to video and interactive world models.
papers.title: Rethinking Video Autoencoders for Interactive World Models
papers.tldr: CADRE shows that video-autoencoder compression should be tailored to interactive world-model latency and environment dynamics, rather than inherited from offline video generators.

papers.abstract: Existing world models typically perceive a scene through current visual frame or a narrow history window. However, these observations may not reveal the physics properties that determine transition dynamics, such as an object's mass distribution, joint damping, or surface friction. Without calibrating these physics factors for world models, predictions tend to regress toward an empirical prior and induce severe drift in novel test scenes. To this end, we propose PhysiCalWorld, which calibrates action-conditioned world models to the instance-specific dynamics via in-context prompting, without fine-tuning or analytical physics modeling. Our method encodes an exploratory interaction clip collected within the test scene into a compact physics descriptor token, which grounds subsequent predictions in the scene's actual physical behavior. PhysiCalWorld is trained end-to-end with the latent prediction loss alone, without physics labels. At inference time, the descriptor token is extracted once and can be reused across rollouts with negligible compute overhead. We evaluate PhysiCalWorld across four environments covering diverse physics variations and show that it substantially improves rollout prediction accuracy and visual planning success rate. The learned descriptors also form a physically structured latent space and generalize beyond the physics ranges seen during training.
authors: Yunhao Luo, Wentao He, Yinpei Dai, Hyelin Nam, Hongze Fu, Joyce Chai, Nima Fazeli, Jeong Joon Park
bullets: Addresses physics ambiguity—such as mass distribution, damping, and friction—that causes prediction drift in novel scenes.
Encodes an exploratory interaction clip into a compact physics descriptor token for in-context conditioning.
Trains end-to-end using only latent prediction loss, without analytical physics modeling or physics annotations.
Reuses the descriptor across rollouts with negligible inference overhead.
Across four environments, improves rollout accuracy and visual planning success; descriptors generalize beyond training physics ranges.
papers.selection_reason: In-context physics calibration for action-conditioned world models via compact descriptor tokens.
papers.title: PhysiCalWorld: In-Context Physics Calibration for World Models
papers.tldr: PhysiCalWorld calibrates world models to scene-specific physics from a brief exploratory interaction, improving predictions and visual planning without fine-tuning or explicit physics labels.

papers.abstract: World models turn visual representations into predictions and actions. We argue that their visual foundation should combine physical-state information, native language alignment, and pixel reconstruction, so that a single representation can support prediction, instruction, and inspection. However, existing encoders typically specialize in only one or two of these capabilities; we therefore introduce ALPS, a pretrained visual state encoder that unifies all three in a single set of patch tokens. Using only still images and text, we pretrain a ViT-B/16 from scratch with language, reconstruction, and spatial correspondence objectives, and then refine it via cross-view self-distillation. In a unified evaluation across fifteen public encoders, ALPS achieves the lowest aggregate LIBERO state-probe error among ViT-B models (matching the 3.5x larger V-JEPA 2-L) while maintaining strong language alignment and accurate pixel reconstruction. Downstream, frozen ALPS tokens reach the highest mean policy success on LIBERO (85.5%) when paired with our native text tower, match or exceed leading encoders on world-model planning across PushT, Wall, and Granular, and allow predicted future tokens to be decoded directly into pixels for visual inspection. We hope this work helps establish visual pretraining as a shared foundation for understanding, prediction, and action in world models.
authors: Yanqing Liu, Letian Zhang, Chengzhi Liu, Zijun Wang, Jieru Mei, Hongliang Fei, Yuyin Zhou, Cihang Xie
bullets: Addresses the limitation that existing visual encoders typically support only one or two of these capabilities.
Pretrains a ViT-B/16 from scratch using language, reconstruction, and spatial-correspondence objectives on still images and text, followed by cross-view self-distillation.
Uses a single set of patch tokens for prediction, instruction following, and visual inspection.
Across 15 public encoders, ALPS has the lowest aggregate LIBERO state-probe error among ViT-B models while retaining strong language and reconstruction performance.
Frozen ALPS tokens achieve 85.5% mean policy success on LIBERO with its text tower and support competitive world-model planning and pixel decoding of predicted future states.
papers.selection_reason: Pretrained visual state encoder unifying physical-state, language, and reconstruction for world models; evaluated on robot policy learning and world-model planning.
papers.title: ALPS: Visual State Encoders for World Models
papers.tldr: ALPS is a visual state encoder that unifies physical-state representation, language alignment, and pixel reconstruction for world models.

papers.abstract: Financial crime detection requires identifying illicit activity within large transaction networks, where suspicious behaviour is rare and unfolds over time. Existing graph-based methods capture relationships among accounts but typically underuse the temporal behaviour encoded in account transaction histories. We introduce Temporal-Context Edge Enrichment (TCEE), a framework that addresses this gap by summarising each account's transaction history with a frozen time-series foundation model (TSFM), and enriching each transaction's representation with the relevant temporal context from these summaries. These enriched representations can be scored directly for edge classification, or fed into a graph neural network (GNN) as edge features to capture broader structural information. Across six AMLWorld datasets, TCEE improves PR-AUC over the strongest evaluated baseline on five by a relative 10.8% on average, while training 6.0x faster end-to-end. Feeding TCEE's representations into a GNN raises PR-AUC a further 4.8% on the four smaller datasets. On an Ethereum phishing dataset, we show that TSFM-generated account representations fed into a GNN are also effective for node classification, improving PR-AUC by 14.5% over the strongest baseline. As TSFMs continue to advance, our results suggest they can strengthen financial crime detection by capturing temporal signals that complement graph-based approaches.
authors: Danae Natalie Savvidi, H. \c{C}a\u{g}r{\i} Bilgi, Kubilay Atasu, Arie van Deursen
bullets: Addresses the underuse of temporal account behaviour in graph-based illicit-activity detection.
Summarises each account’s transaction history with a frozen TSFM and enriches transaction-edge representations with relevant temporal context.
Representations support direct edge classification or integration as edge features in a GNN; TSFM account representations also support node classification.
Across six AMLWorld datasets, TCEE improves PR-AUC on five and trains 6.0× faster end-to-end; GNN integration provides further gains on four smaller datasets.
On Ethereum phishing detection, TSFM-based account representations improve node-classification PR-AUC over the strongest baseline.
papers.selection_reason: Utilizes frozen time-series foundation models to summarize transaction history for financial crime detection, leveraging temporal world modeling.
papers.title: Leveraging Time-Series Foundation Models for Financial Crime Detection
papers.tldr: TCEE uses frozen time-series foundation models to add account transaction-history context to graph-based financial crime detection, improving PR-AUC and training speed across multiple datasets.

papers.abstract: Accurate short-term forecasting of atmospheric seeing is of significant interest for astronomical observations and free-space optical communication systems, where rapid variations in optical turbulence can affect system performance and operational planning. In this work, we benchmark machine learning models for predicting atmospheric seeing up to two hours in advance, with a particular focus on probabilistic forecasting and uncertainty quantification. We compare two probabilistic approaches, Gaussian Processes (GPs) and a normalizing-flow- based model (FloTS), against deterministic recurrent neural network (RNN) and long short-term memory (LSTM) baselines. All models are trained and evaluated on seeing measurements from the Maunakea summit. We assess the models using both deterministic metrics, including the root mean square error and the Pearson correlation coefficient, and probabilistic metrics that evaluate the quality and calibration of predictive uncertainty estimates. The results show that deep learning approaches outperform standard recurrent networks for short-term forecasting, with LSTM and FloTS achieving the best overall predictive accuracy. While Gaussian Processes provide a useful probabilistic baseline, their predictive distributions are limited by the Gaussian assumption. FloTS combines competitive forecasting accuracy with flexible uncertainty quantification and produces the most informative probabilistic forecasts.
authors: Mary-Joe Medlej, Rahul Srinivasan, Simon Prunet, Aziz Ziad, Christophe Giordano
bullets: Targets short-term atmospheric seeing prediction for astronomy and free-space optical communications.
Benchmarks Gaussian Processes and FloTS against deterministic RNN and LSTM baselines using Maunakea summit measurements.
Evaluates both forecast accuracy and the quality and calibration of predictive uncertainties.
LSTM and FloTS achieve the best overall predictive accuracy, while FloTS produces the most informative probabilistic forecasts.
Gaussian Processes offer a useful baseline but are constrained by their Gaussian predictive assumption.
papers.selection_reason: Develops probabilistic models for short-term atmospheric seeing forecasting, which involves predicting temporal environment dynamics.
papers.title: Probabilistic Machine Learning for Short-Term Atmospheric Seeing Forecasting
papers.tldr: Probabilistic deep-learning models, especially FloTS, provide accurate and informative uncertainty-aware forecasts of atmospheric seeing up to two hours ahead.

papers.abstract: World models are increasingly used for planning, where a planner ranks candidate actions by returns imagined by the model. However, these models are judged mainly by how well they render frames, even though a visually faithful rollout can still assign the wrong return. To identify where this mismatch arises, we introduce a transition-level diagnostic that replaces imagined transitions with real ones and measures the reduction in return error against a budget-matched random control. Our analysis yields two findings. (1) Event transitions, the few steps where a reward is earned or an episode ends, are rendered as well as other steps (median pixel-error ratio 0.85), yet restoring them removes a median of 70% of the return error. In contrast, restoring transitions with the largest MSE, SSIM or LPIPS error removes less than a random choice. Across the 44 Atari-100k model--collection pairs that pass our reliability checks, including three released families, event patches outperform random patches in 39 (sign test p=1.4 x 10^{-7}), with a median gain of +44 percentage points. (2) The remaining error is structured: a complementary patch separates errors at true events from those elsewhere, while an eight-step timing tolerance recovers few events missed by our deterministic models. This structure also guides repair: a rule recorded before four repair outcomes were known predicts when a diffusion model repairs these failures. Event patches improve plan ranking, and the same concentration appears on control tasks with rare reward events.
bullets: The study introduces a transition-level diagnostic that replaces imagined transitions with real ones and measures the resulting reduction in return error against random patches.
Event transitions have similar visual error to other steps, but restoring them removes a median 70% of return error.
Patching the highest-MSE, SSIM, or LPIPS transitions performs worse than random selection, while event patches outperform random patches in 39 of 44 reliable Atari-100k model–collection pairs.
Remaining return error is structured around true events and timing; an eight-step tolerance recovers few missed events.
Event patches improve plan ranking, and similar error concentration appears in control tasks with rare reward events.
papers.selection_reason: Diagnoses why world models misassign returns despite visually faithful rollouts; directly relevant to interactive world models for planning.
papers.title: Events, Not Pixels: Where World Models Get the Return Wrong
papers.tldr: World models can render frames accurately yet misestimate returns because a small number of reward and termination events dominate planning errors.

papers.abstract: Interactive video world models predict how an environment evolves under user actions, but most existing systems assume one controlled agent and one task-specific action interface. We study multi-agent video world modeling, where one model generates a joint visual future for multiple controlled agents while interpreting heterogeneous controls ranging from binary game buttons to continuous robot commands. This task presents two complementary challenges. First, every agent-indexed action stream must control its intended visual entity independently. Second, the model must adapt the meaning of each control variable across different tasks, where the same tensor dimension may denote an attack, steering command, or robot command. We introduce LiveAct, centered on a Heterogeneous Action Interface (HAI) whose two components mirror this decomposition. To support independent control, Agent-Aware Spatial Modulation uses language-driven spatial gates and agent-specific attention to bind each action stream to its intended visual agent. To accommodate heterogeneous controls, Schema-Guided Action Adaptation describes each control variable in language and modulates its semantic token with the synchronized numerical value. We further transfer the complete interface to a blockwise causal generator through teacher forcing and rollout-aware distribution matching, enabling efficient streaming generation while retaining agent-specific control and action semantics. We instantiate the formulation on six multi-agent sources spanning games and multi-robot manipulation, and evaluate visual quality, action following, agent attribution, and latency. Across games and robot manipulation, LiveAct reaches 0.898 and 0.942 agent-attribution accuracy without agent locations or identity crops, and the causal generator attains 17.70 FPS at $512\times 448$.
authors: Xinyu Wang, Huafeng Shi, Yue Ma, Zijie Meng, Teng Xi, Yuzhuo Chen, Yucheng Wang, Ruicheng Zhang, Guoxin Zhang, Pengfei Wan, Xiu Li, Fangneng Zhan
bullets: Addresses multi-agent world models that must bind each action stream to the correct visual agent and interpret task-dependent controls.
Introduces a Heterogeneous Action Interface combining Agent-Aware Spatial Modulation with Schema-Guided Action Adaptation.
Transfers the interface to a blockwise causal generator using teacher forcing and rollout-aware distribution matching for streaming generation.
Evaluated across six game and multi-robot manipulation sources on visual quality, action following, attribution, and latency.
Achieves 0.898 and 0.942 agent-attribution accuracy and 17.70 FPS generation at 512×448, without agent locations or identity crops.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces LiveAct, a multi-agent interactive video world model with a Heterogeneous Action Interface, directly fitting the World Models taxonomy.
papers.title: LiveAct: Towards Real-Time Multi-Agent World Models with Heterogeneous Action Interfaces
papers.tldr: LiveAct enables real-time multi-agent video world modeling with independent control of multiple agents and heterogeneous action interfaces across games and robot tasks.

papers.abstract: Dynamic scheduling requires dispatching online arrivals while anticipating future jobs, as poor decisions can compound downstream costs under nonlinear tardiness objectives. We show that a pretrained large language model (LLM) can serve as the exogenous component of a structured world model, forecasting uncertain future job arrivals. Specifically, we exploit an afterstate decomposition, which separates known deterministic shop transitions from uncertain exogenous job arrivals, enabling the LLM to forecast only the latter through a compact belief representation. Building on this, we develop Afterstate World-Model Planning (AWMP), which combines an evolved, belief-conditioned dispatching strategy with short scenario-based rollouts. A surprise-triggered refresh mechanism queries the LLM only when newly observed arrivals deviate sufficiently from previous forecast, and online residual self-calibration further conditions the LLM on its recent forecast errors to handle nonstationary arrivals. Across diverse arrival distributions, AWMP reduces weighted tardiness by 6-21% on dynamic job-shop and 22-46% on flexible job-shop benchmarks, relative to the best of eight classical priority-dispatching rules.
authors: Ni Zhang, Haofeng Yuan, Jianan Zhou, Shiji Song, Zhiguang Cao
bullets: Targets dynamic job-shop scheduling, where poor dispatch decisions can compound downstream tardiness.
Uses afterstate decomposition to let the LLM model only uncertain exogenous arrivals via a compact belief representation.
Combines belief-conditioned dispatching with short scenario-based rollouts in Afterstate World-Model Planning (AWMP).
Reduces LLM queries through surprise-triggered refreshes and adapts to nonstationary arrivals using online residual self-calibration.
Across diverse arrival distributions, weighted tardiness decreases by 6–21% on dynamic job-shop and 22–46% on flexible job-shop benchmarks versus the best of eight classical rules.
papers.selection_reason: LLM-based exogenous world model for forecasting job arrivals in dynamic scheduling; fits world models broadly.
papers.title: LLM-Based Exogenous World Modeling for Dynamic Scheduling
papers.tldr: AWMP uses an LLM to forecast uncertain future job arrivals and improve online scheduling under dynamic, nonlinear tardiness costs.

papers.abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) have shown strong potential for robot manipulation by jointly learning visual dynamics and executable actions. However, their video and action objectives do not explicitly constrain the 3D geometry that is crucial for precise manipulation. Recently, geometry-aware WAMs introduce depth or 4D prediction branches, whereas representation alignment methods supervise intermediate WAM features with pretrained 3D foundation models. Yet we find that such pointwise alignment benefits the video features but degrades action learning, since dense geometric feature targets overly restrict compact action features. To address this limitation, we propose Relational Geometry Forcing (RGF), which transfers geometric priors from a frozen 3D foundation model by aligning pairwise feature relations instead of pointwise features. Specifically, RGF applies three complementary relational objectives, where intra-frame and cross-view relations transfer scene geometry and multi-view correspondence to the video features, while action-temporal relations couple action dynamics to geometric scene evolution. Applied only during training, RGF requires no explicit geometry branch or extra inference module. Extensive experiments in simulation and the real world demonstrate the effectiveness of Relational Geometry Forcing, showing consistent gains across diverse manipulation scenarios and WAM paradigms.
authors: Yuan Xu, Yixiang Chen, Qisen Ma, Jiabing Yang, Peiyan Li, Kai Wang, Jianhua Yang, Jianlou Si, Jun Huang, Jing Liu, Nianfeng Liu, Yan Huang, Liang Wang
bullets: WAMs lack explicit constraints on the 3D geometry needed for precise manipulation.
Pointwise alignment with 3D foundation-model features can help video representations but hurt compact action representations.
RGF aligns intra-frame, cross-view, and action-temporal feature relations to transfer geometry, correspondences, and scene-action dynamics.
The method is training-only and adds no explicit geometry branch or inference module.
Experiments in simulation and the real world show consistent gains across diverse manipulation settings and WAM paradigms.
papers.selection_reason: Relational geometry forcing for world action models targets manipulation, action-conditioned world dynamics, and geometry-aware multimodal reasoning.
papers.title: Relational Geometry Forcing for World Action Models
papers.tldr: Relational Geometry Forcing improves world action models for precise robot manipulation by transferring 3D geometric structure through relational rather than pointwise feature alignment.

papers.abstract: Predictive representations for robot manipulation should connect scene geometry with the state changes induced by actions. Our intuition is that understanding what an action will change starts with understanding where things are: complementary RGB and depth observations ground a common scene representation from which to infer those changes. Guided by this intuition, we introduce \textbf{DepState-JEPA}, a dual-stream RGB--Depth joint-embedding predictive architecture that connects spatial understanding with action-conditioned prediction through a shared latent state, \textbf{DepState}. Built on V-JEPA~2.1, the framework uses depth both as a complementary observation stream and to ground both modalities in metric 3D space, aggregating shared information into DepState while retaining modality-private features for decoding. Ray-conditioned readouts predict local features without target depth; after an action-conditioned transition, the same decoders predict future RGB and depth features using the predicted state and fixed initial private features. Robot-state readouts provide recursive proprioceptive inputs; object-trajectory supervision and calibrated forward kinematics shape state learning through motion targets and joint--TCP consistency. Comparisons show stronger RGB-encoder transfer after RGB-D adaptation, feature completion, conditioned visual forecasting, and manipulation success. Within-model ablations identify contributions from depth content, metric coordinates, and future-state matching, with additional control gains from FK regularization.
authors: Xiujian Liang, Liuyuan Na, Zehao Du, Jiacheng Xu, Weixi Song, Mingyang Sun, Xingjun Ma, Cewu Lu, Jianhua Sun
bullets: Addresses the need to predict action-induced scene changes from complementary RGB and depth observations.
Uses a dual-stream RGB–Depth JEPA architecture with shared DepState features and modality-private information.
Grounds both modalities in metric 3D space and predicts local, future RGB/depth features after actions.
Adds robot-state readouts, object-trajectory supervision, and forward-kinematics consistency to shape state learning.
Reports gains in RGB-encoder transfer, feature completion, visual forecasting, and manipulation success; ablations support depth, metric coordinates, future-state matching, and FK regularization.
papers.selection_reason: Depth-grounded action-conditioned predictive state representation directly targets robot manipulation and interactive world modeling.
papers.title: DepState-JEPA: Learning Depth-Grounded State Representation for Visual Perception and Manipulation
papers.tldr: DepState-JEPA learns a shared, depth-grounded latent state that links 3D scene understanding to action-conditioned visual and robot-state prediction for manipulation.

papers.abstract: World action models (WAMs) are shown to substantially diverge under generalization performance based on their generative backbones. We investigate this gap through the representational geometry that WAMs inherit from their backbones and how policy training reorganizes it. Our central hypothesis is that a useful representational prior would structure geometry that separates nuisance information from the in-distribution manifold in advance of training as a policy. We quantify this with nuisance orthogonality; orthogonality of the feature under visual variation outside the empirical in-distribution manifold. Across various image and video backbones, we show that a higher orthogonality from the representational prior is associated with stronger robustness to visual variations after WAM training, enabling policy generalization measurable prospectively for world models. In addition, analyzing the resulting robust WAMs reveals nuisance suppression; relative suppression of feature displacement caused by such variations and robust action generation of the policy. Together, these findings provide a geometric perspective on how the representational prior of the world model shapes the generalization performance of WAMs.
authors: Junha Chun, Youngjoon Jeong, Taesup Kim
bullets: WAM generalization varies substantially with the choice of generative backbone.
The study introduces nuisance orthogonality to measure whether representations separate out-of-distribution visual variation from the in-distribution manifold.
Across image and video backbones, greater prior orthogonality predicts stronger robustness after policy training.
Robust WAMs exhibit nuisance suppression and more stable action generation under visual variations.
The work offers a geometric perspective on how backbone representations shape policy generalization.
papers.selection_reason: Directly studies representational priors and generalization in world action models for policy learning, relevant to world models and embodied robot learning.
papers.title: How Representational Priors Shape Generalization in World Action Models
papers.tldr: Representational priors that geometrically separate nuisance visual variation from the in-distribution manifold lead to more robust, better-generalizing world action models.

papers.abstract: Frontier black-box Large Language Model (LLM) agents are proficient at long-horizon reasoning and precise action generation. However, when it comes to a specific agentic task, they have no internalized knowledge of how that particular environment unfolds. A world model offers a natural remedy, providing the agent with environment specific knowledge by foreseeing how the environment will respond to the action it is about to take. Prior world models for LLM agents mainly predict next observations at each step, which is costly and often uninformative because individual observations provide limited task-relevant guidance and not every step requires call for foresight. This raises a key question: what a world model should predict and when should it be invoked for agentic tasks? Our pilot study suggests that world model guidance is most useful when it anticipates pitfalls within a bounded multi-step future. Motivated by this, we introduce Pitfall Anticipation World Model (PAWM), which selectively intervenes when a potential pitfall arises and predicts the impending failure to steer the agent away from it. PAWM is trained in two stages: Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) on synthetic data labeled with agent pitfalls, followed by GRPO co-training with a black-box LLM to further optimize it in the target environment. PAWM improves Claude Sonnet 4.5 performance by 24.3% on ScienceWorld and 7.7% on WebArena-Lite, outperforming a range of baselines. These results demonstrate that PAWM provides an effective form of world model guidance for black-box LLM agents.
authors: Jiongxiao Wang, Han Ding, Youzhi Luo, Yawei Wang, Yun Zhou, Linbo Liu, Panpan Xu
bullets: Addresses the limited environment-specific knowledge of black-box LLM agents in long-horizon tasks.
Argues that predicting every next observation is costly and often provides little task-relevant guidance.
Uses selective intervention to anticipate potential pitfalls within a bounded future and predict impending failures.
Trains in two stages: pitfall-labeled synthetic-data SFT, followed by GRPO co-training with a black-box LLM in the target environment.
Improves Claude Sonnet 4.5 performance by 24.3% on ScienceWorld and 7.7% on WebArena-Lite, outperforming reported baselines.
papers.selection_reason: World model that anticipates pitfalls and steers LLM agents by predicting environment responses to actions; fits interactive world models.
papers.title: Steering Black-Box Large Language Model Agents with Pitfall Anticipation World Model
papers.tldr: PAWM steers black-box LLM agents by predicting imminent multi-step pitfalls and intervening only when needed, improving performance on ScienceWorld and WebArena-Lite.

papers.abstract: Recovering dynamic 3D scene geometry, appearance, and the physical motion states that govern scene evolution from multi-view videos is important yet challenging. A key difficulty is that appearance can be deceptive. Under rendering supervision alone, a model may fit the observed images by changing color or opacity to compensate for inaccurate deformation, rather than recovering the true evolving geometry and motion. This issue is especially severe in scenes with fast or locally complex motion, where inaccurate trajectories can still produce plausible images over the observed frames, but lead to unreliable reconstruction and discontinuous future prediction. In this paper, we propose PhyMo, a framework for learning evolving dynamics from multi-view videos. We introduce a Motion-Aware Trajectory Representation that drives the model to recover accurate motion from deformation, rather than relying on appearance shortcuts to explain observed motion. On top of this, we propose a Continuous Motion Evolution module with bidirectional kinematic continuity constraint to promote temporally consistent evolution of displacement, velocity, and acceleration. Together, these designs yield geometrically faithful interpolation and continuous motion extrapolation. Experiments on four dynamic scene benchmarks demonstrate state-of-the-art performance.
authors: Shangjia Liu, Jinxi Li, Siyuan Zhou, Bo Yang, Bing Wang
bullets: Addresses inaccurate geometry and motion recovery when rendering supervision lets appearance compensate for deformation errors.
Uses a Motion-Aware Trajectory Representation to learn motion directly from deformation.
Adds Continuous Motion Evolution with bidirectional continuity constraints on displacement, velocity, and acceleration.
Produces geometrically faithful interpolation and continuous motion extrapolation.
Achieves state-of-the-art performance across four dynamic-scene benchmarks.
papers.selection_reason: Learns physical dynamics and continuous future motion from multi-view video, fitting video world models and 3D dynamic scene recovery.
papers.title: PhyMo: Learning Physical Dynamics with Accurate and Continuous Motion from Multi-View Videos
papers.tldr: PhyMo learns physically faithful, continuous 3D motion from multi-view videos by preventing appearance-based shortcuts and enforcing kinematic consistency.

papers.abstract: World models predict how embodied systems evolve under actions, but their accuracy can degrade when physical conditions move outside the training distribution. We study two components of causal modeling: which inputs a predictor may use, and how its mechanism computes their effects. In a synthetic benchmark with shortcut features, a frozen dependency mask derived from paired interventions reduces mean out-of-distribution (OOD) RMSE from 1.769 for a fully connected predictor to 0.697, close to the generator-oracle mask (0.694). For robot link-mass extrapolation in CausalWorld, with disjoint training and test mass ranges, we develop finger-local world models in which link masses enter inertia and dynamics-bias terms through explicit affine coefficients, actions act through either a learned torque network or the known PD controller, and learned residuals capture contact-related effects. Compared with a separately trained control whose mass inputs are fixed at training means, the known-PD model turns out-of-range masses into a consistent predictive gain: median time-averaged joint R2 over 150-step rollouts rises from 0.609 to 0.727, with improvement in all ten task-seed runs (exact two-sided sign test, p = 0.002). In a shared 100-step forecast, the learned-torque model is competitive with the strongest recurrent robotic world model (RWM) configuration (median joint R2 of 0.755 - 0.768 versus 0.752), whereas supplying out-of-range masses sharply degrades the MLP and recurrent predictors. These results indicate that how a physical parameter enters the dynamics mechanism determines whether its out-of-range value helps or harms prediction.
bullets: A frozen dependency mask from paired interventions reduces synthetic OOD RMSE from 1.769 to 0.697, nearly matching the oracle mask at 0.694.
For robot link-mass extrapolation, finger-local models explicitly incorporate masses into inertia and dynamics-bias terms, with learned residuals for contact effects.
Using the known PD controller for action effects raises median 150-step joint R² from 0.609 to 0.727 across out-of-range mass tests.
A learned-torque model is competitive with the strongest recurrent robotic world-model configuration in 100-step forecasts.
Out-of-range physical inputs can help or harm prediction depending on how the model embeds them in the dynamics mechanism.
papers.selection_reason: Directly addresses world models for embodied systems (CausalWorld) and handles physical parameter shifts using causal modeling, a key challenge in robotics.
papers.title: Causal world models under physical parameter shifts
papers.tldr: Causal structure and physically explicit parameterization substantially improve world-model prediction under out-of-distribution physical changes.

papers.abstract: Amodal video segmentation asks for the complete mask of an object in every frame, including the parts hidden behind other objects. The best current methods generate these masks with fine-tuned video diffusion models, which need many denoising steps and an extra depth network, and give a different answer for every sample. Self-supervised video world models of the JEPA family are trained on a closely related task: predicting the representation of masked space-time regions from the visible ones. We therefore treat occlusion as masking. The tokens that the object's visible mask does not cover are dropped, the pre-trained V-JEPA 2.1 predictor fills them in, and a light head decodes the observed and predicted features into amodal masks. The resulting model, OccJEPA (Occlusion-as-masking JEPA), is deterministic and 33.5x faster than the diffusion-based state of the art, and more accurate on SAIL-VOS, on TAO-Amodal, including a held-out test split (+4.00 AP50) and visible masks tracked by SAM2, and on Kubric. Controlled experiments trace the gain to the predictor's pre-trained weights rather than to its capacity, for world models from 87M to 1.85B parameters. Code is available at https://github.com/zgp110/occjepa.
bullets: Amodal video segmentation must infer object regions hidden behind occluders in every frame.
Visible-mask tokens are retained while uncovered space-time tokens are masked and predicted by a pretrained V-JEPA 2.1 predictor.
A lightweight decoder converts observed and predicted features into complete object masks.
OccJEPA is deterministic, 33.5× faster than diffusion-based methods, and more accurate across SAIL-VOS, TAO-Amodal, and Kubric.
Controlled experiments attribute improvements to pretrained predictor weights rather than model capacity across 87M–1.85B-parameter world models.
papers.selection_reason: Applies a pretrained V-JEPA world model by treating occlusion as masking for amodal video segmentation, directly relevant to video world models and video understanding.
papers.title: OccJEPA: Occlusion as Masking for Amodal Video Segmentation
papers.tldr: OccJEPA reframes object occlusion as masked-token prediction, using V-JEPA 2.1 to produce fast, deterministic amodal video masks.

papers.abstract: We study a jump-modified Wasserstein gradient flow of the squared maximum mean discrepancy generated by the energy kernels $K(z)=-|z|^q$, $0<q<2$, in every dimension $d\ge2$ as well as the one-dimensional range $1\le q<2$. Under subcritical density and finite-moment assumptions, we prove global well-posedness. The added jumps transfer mass toward smaller values of the first variation and dissipate the same MMD energy as the transport term. Under our hypotheses on the target and jump rates, every Borel probability measure with finite MMD energy and zero jump dissipation is equal to the target. Combining this rigidity with compactness and a second-moment identity yields convergence to the target from finite-second-moment data, without additional uniform-in-time density or moment assumptions. We also construct a global collision-free particle process whose energy is nonincreasing along each path. A quantitative mean-field estimate applies to general initial empirical approximations, including deterministic configurations; propagation of chaos for exchangeable data and long-time target approximation follow as consequences.
authors: Ansh Desai, Jason Liu, Srujan Roplekar, Matthew Rosenzweig
bullets: Addresses convergence of MMD gradient flows with energy kernels in dimensions d≥2 and for 1≤q<2 in one dimension.
Adds jumps that move mass toward lower first variation while dissipating the same MMD energy as transport.
Proves global well-posedness under subcritical-density and finite-moment assumptions.
Establishes convergence to the target using rigidity, compactness, and a second-moment identity, without uniform-in-time density or moment bounds.
Constructs a collision-free particle process and proves mean-field estimates for general empirical initializations; propagation of chaos and long-time approximation follow.
papers.selection_reason: Studies a jump-modified Wasserstein gradient flow for Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD) with energy kernels. This theoretical work on generative processes and particle dynamics is relevant to world models and generative modeling.
papers.title: A Jump-Modified Wasserstein Gradient Flow for Maximum Mean Discrepancy with Energy Kernels
papers.tldr: A jump-augmented Wasserstein flow for energy-kernel MMD is shown to be globally well posed, converge to the target, and admit a collision-free particle approximation with quantitative mean-field guarantees.

papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly expected to interact with environments and improve their decisions during deployment. However, how anticipating future outcomes and drawing on accumulated interaction experience can jointly support decision-making remains underexplored. We propose a test-time framework, inspired by Model Predictive Path Integral (MPPI) control, that combines multi-branch predictive analysis with experience-based adaptation. At each step, the agent proposes multiple candidate actions and imagines their outcomes with a world model, so that alternatives can be compared without being executed in the environment. Since language environments provide neither explicit dynamics nor costs, the predicted outcomes are evaluated for task progress and risk, and MPPI-style weights over the resulting costs guide the final decision. A dual-branch experience memory enables self-improvement: the planner branch refines candidate generation and action selection, while the world model branch improves next-observation prediction. Experiments on ALFWorld and ScienceWorld across three backbones demonstrate the strong overall performance of our method and the effectiveness of experience-guided predictive control. Our code will be made publicly available.
authors: Haori Lu, Tianyu Gao, Yaoyao Liu, Yingying Li
bullets: Addresses the challenge of combining future-outcome anticipation with accumulated interaction experience in deployed LLM agents.
Uses a world model to imagine outcomes for multiple candidate actions without executing them in the environment.
Applies MPPI-style cost weighting based on predicted task progress and risk to select actions.
Employs dual-branch experience memory to improve both candidate planning and next-observation prediction.
Shows strong overall performance on ALFWorld and ScienceWorld across three LLM backbones.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes test-time framework combining world-model predictive paths with experience-based adaptation, directly fitting interactive world models and test-time learning.
papers.title: Self-Improving Agents with World Model Predictive Paths
papers.tldr: A test-time framework helps LLM agents make better decisions by simulating multiple action paths, weighting them by predicted progress and risk, and learning from experience.

papers.abstract: We present WorldStream, an open-ended 3D world model with three simultaneous capabilities: it extends playable terrain beyond any pre-specified map, acts on open-ended language in the running world, and restores visited places with their edits. A hierarchical planner over a typed decision model emits structured decision state: Macro fixes settlement, ecology, transport, and hydrological structure across a group of tiles; Micro specializes that contract into tile semantics under measured terrain and accepted neighbor commitments. Deterministic local code compiles accepted plans into terrain, roads, settlements, vegetation, and entities. Streaming separates their reach: plans run ahead along the predicted corridor, compilation only where movement will soon need it, geometry behind the user released. One world record retains plans, seeds, object identities and mutable state, boundary commitments, and edits by attribute, revised as the user advances and edits; returning tiles recompile from it. The same record grounds interaction: the model acts on existing entities, including stateful NPCs that update as they act, edits the present region, or attaches intent to unplanned regions. Together they yield a world expanding under bounded budgets, connected across independently planned tiles, and interactive.
authors: Xiaoxiao Ma, Weiyang Jin, Yanwen Ma, Haoran Li, Zhixiang Wei, Songchun Zhang, Yaowei Li, Junhao Zhuang, Zeyue Xue, Yuming Li, Zheming Fu, Haoyang Huang, Nan Duan, Feng Zhao
bullets: Hierarchical Macro/Micro planning coordinates settlements, ecology, transport, hydrology, and tile-level semantics across expanding terrain.
Deterministic local compilation turns accepted plans into terrain, roads, settlements, vegetation, and entities.
Streaming prioritizes planning ahead, compiling near the user, and releasing geometry behind them to manage bounded budgets.
A persistent world record stores plans, seeds, object identities, mutable state, boundary commitments, and edits for consistent revisitation.
The system supports interaction with existing entities, stateful NPCs, current-region edits, and intent attached to unplanned regions.
papers.selection_reason: Streaming interactive 3D world generation with persistent state and language-driven actions fits interactive world models.
papers.title: WorldStream: Streaming Interactive 3D Worlds with Hierarchical Planning and Persistent State
papers.tldr: WorldStream creates an open-ended, interactive 3D world that streams new terrain, responds to language, and persistently preserves edits and state.

papers.abstract: World models let agents compare imagined outcomes before acting, but an agent must still decide which alternatives to explore and when a proposed plan should replace its learned policy. We introduce SDI (Sibling Disagreement in Imagination), which connects these decisions through a shared actor-based reference. SDI compares action sequences imagined from the same model state, using repeated rollouts of the actor's own sequence to measure variation under fixed behavior. This reference scales both the spread across candidate returns, which provides an exploration signal, and a proposed plan's predicted advantage, which governs action acceptance. The agent executes a planned action when its advantage exceeds the reference variability by a fixed factor; otherwise, it follows the actor. SDI reuses the base agent's world model, actor, and critic without requiring an additional disagreement ensemble. Exploration and planning guide training data collection, while evaluation uses the learned actor alone. Across Meta-World, Adroit, and DM-Control, SDI achieves a higher observed task-average score than every compared baseline in each suite and matches or exceeds the strongest baseline's performance on 15 of 18 tasks. Component ablations and robustness analyses further examine the roles of exploration, planning exposure, and action acceptance. Paired evaluations from identical simulator states show that the gate improves both recovery from actor failures and preservation of successful behavior relative to ungated planning, while substantially reducing return degradation. Together, these results support comparing imagined alternatives against a shared actor reference as a unified approach to exploring and planning with world models.
bullets: Addresses the challenge of selecting alternatives to explore and safely accepting plans in world-model agents.
Compares imagined action sequences from the same model state and measures variability in repeated rollouts of the actor’s sequence.
Uses this reference to scale exploration signals and accept a plan only when its predicted advantage exceeds reference variability by a fixed factor.
Reuses the base world model, actor, and critic without an additional disagreement ensemble; evaluation runs the learned actor alone.
Across Meta-World, Adroit, and DM-Control, SDI has the highest task-average score among compared baselines in each suite and matches or exceeds the strongest baseline on 15 of 18 tasks.
papers.selection_reason: Unified exploration and planning through imagined rollouts in world models for control; directly relevant to world models and robot learning.
papers.title: Second Thoughts: Exploring and Planning through Comparative Imagination in World Models
papers.tldr: SDI uses variation in repeated actor rollouts as a shared reference to decide both what to explore and when imagined plans should override the learned policy.

papers.abstract: Objects move, cameras pan, and weather drifts with the wind: much of what changes in sequential data is motion. Motion changes where things are, not what they are, and is therefore a symmetry of the data. Yet standard recurrent networks are not equivariant to it: their memory stays put while the input moves on. Flow equivariant recurrent networks first brought this symmetry into sequence models, for motions of constant velocity, or flows, by enumerating a bank of velocities. We extend this idea in three directions: from simple recurrent networks to convolutional LSTMs, from flows to motions whose velocity changes in time, and from enumerating velocities to estimating them. Treating a sequence as a field over time, we show that motion becomes a gauge symmetry: a global symmetry made local in time. Built on this view, our motion equivariant convolutional LSTM (MELSTM) uses its velocity model as the gauge field and is provably equivariant to every motion. Across future-frame prediction, classification of digits visible only through their motion, and action recognition under camera shake, MELSTM outperforms a convolutional LSTM and its flow equivariant counterpart with the same number of parameters: it is more accurate, generalizes to longer horizons and to unseen motions, and carries a fraction of the flow equivariant model's state.
authors: Vahid Hosseinzadeh, T. Anderson Keller, Michael Puthawala
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between moving inputs and stationary recurrent memory.
Extends motion-equivariant recurrence from simple RNNs to convolutional LSTMs and from constant-velocity flows to time-varying motion.
Estimates motion rather than enumerating a bank of velocities.
Demonstrates gains in future-frame prediction, motion-based digit classification, and action recognition under camera shake.
Outperforms parameter-matched convolutional LSTMs and flow-equivariant models while using substantially less state, according to the abstract.
papers.selection_reason: Motion-equivariant convolutional LSTM for future-frame prediction and action recognition; relevant to predictive video models and video understanding.
papers.title: Motion Equivariant Convolutional LSTM: When Motion Becomes a Gauge Symmetry
papers.tldr: MELSTM makes convolutional LSTMs equivariant to time-varying motion by estimating motion as a local gauge field, improving robustness to unseen and longer-horizon motions.

papers.abstract: Universal Manipulation Interface (UMI) pairs wrist-camera videos with camera trajectories and gripper openings, providing scalable, robot-free data for learning how bimanual actions change a shared scene. Existing interactive world models, however, typically rely on text or single-camera control and struggle to follow each arm's actions while maintaining consistency between the two wrist views. We introduce UMI-WM, an action-conditioned bimanual world model that jointly generates both wrist views from observation history, per-arm relative camera poses, and gripper widths, with cross-view consistency, action following, and visual fidelity. UMI-WM injects each arm's actions into its own wrist stream, while sparse hub tokens exchange scene information between the two streams. Camera-aware geometry conditioning and camera-guided noise further support per-view motion control and cross-view geometric exchange. We adapt the model for block-causal generation and distill the 30-step Teacher into a Student with four denoising steps. We train UMI-WM on self-collected open-world and in-studio UMI recordings combined with public manipulation data. To evaluate action following, we use an inverse dynamics model (IDM) to recover relative camera poses and gripper widths from generated videos, and introduce Bimanual Action Fidelity (BAF) to measure how closely these recovered actions match the conditioning actions. UMI-WM achieves the best results on all five reference-video fidelity metrics and the best or competitive performance on VBench and WorldArena. The Teacher and Student outperform all compared baselines in action following, while the four-step Student generates paired wrist videos 6.9 times faster than the Teacher.
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of modeling two-arm actions while preserving consistency between separate wrist-camera views.
Jointly conditions generation on observation history, per-arm camera poses, and gripper widths.
Uses per-stream action injection, sparse cross-view hub tokens, camera-aware geometry, and camera-guided noise.
Introduces Bimanual Action Fidelity (BAF) to evaluate whether generated videos follow the specified actions.
Outperforms baselines in action following and fidelity; its four-step Student runs 6.9× faster than the Teacher.
papers.selection_reason: Action-conditioned bimanual world model that generates paired wrist-camera videos, fitting interactive world modeling.
papers.title: UMI-WM: Interactive World Modeling for Bimanual Manipulation from Wrist Cameras
papers.tldr: UMI-WM generates action-conditioned, synchronized videos from both wrist cameras to model and control bimanual manipulation efficiently.

papers.abstract: Dexterous in-hand manipulation requires policies that coordinate high-DoF hand joints through intermittent, contact-rich interaction. Beyond target-orientation tracking, such policies must discover finger gaits that preserve object stability while adapting to geometry, anisotropy, pose, contact, and sensing changes. We propose \method, a tactile-conditioned behavior prior model for dexterous reorientation. \method distills multi-scale sphere specialists into a latent controller and lets downstream policies reuse the fixed tactile prior through residual latent actions, reducing renewed exploration from raw joint commands. The prior conditions on tactile-proprioceptive history so latent behavior reflects the current hand-object interaction. We evaluate arbitrary-pose transfer across anisotropic objects, commanded-axis rotation, and an arm-hand Grasp-to-AnyPose task in which the robot must grasp, lift, transport, and reach goal poses for novel tool geometries and generalized placements. Extensive experiments demonstrate that the proposed method accelerates training and enables stable policies where matched raw-action PPO remains near failure, with successful sim-to-real transfer in in-hand and arm-hand tasks.
bullets: Targets contact-rich, high-DoF manipulation requiring finger gaits that maintain object stability under changing geometry, pose, and sensing.
Distills multi-scale sphere specialists into a latent controller conditioned on tactile-proprioceptive history.
Downstream policies reuse the fixed prior through residual latent actions instead of exploring directly from raw joint commands.
Evaluated on arbitrary-pose transfer, commanded-axis rotation, and arm-hand Grasp-to-AnyPose tasks involving novel tool geometries and placements.
Experiments report faster training, stable policies where matched raw-action PPO nearly fails, and successful sim-to-real transfer.
papers.selection_reason: Tactile-conditioned behavior prior for dexterous manipulation using residual latent actions; fits robot learning and latent-action modeling.
papers.title: TacBPM: A Tactile-conditioned Behavior Prior Model for Dexterous Reorientation
papers.tldr: TacBPM uses a tactile-conditioned behavior prior to help dexterous hands learn stable in-hand reorientation with less exploration than raw joint-control policies.

papers.abstract: Current world models for explicit world simulation typically follow two distinct pathways: (1) video generative models (e.g., Sora), which simulate realistic appearances but fail to preserve 3D consistency; and (2) 3D generative models (e.g., Marble), which generate geometrically consistent scenes but often yield static, less realistic observations. We present AEON, a unified framework that bridges video-based and 3D-based world models and combines the benefits of both. The key insight of AEON lies in a generative model that operates within the text- or image-conditioned video latent space while producing renderable 4D graphics primitives---specifically, 4D Gaussian Splatting (4DGS)---as the explicit world representation. We train a 4D reconstruction model to predict both 4DGS and camera poses from monocular videos, serving as our initialized 4D decoder. Furthermore, we design a domain adapter that translates generative video latents into reconstructive 4D latents through a distillation process on the video VAE. AEON naturally supports video-based world modeling by rendering 4DGS at predicted camera trajectories, and constructs a persistent 4D environment with scene dynamics for realistic world simulation. Consequently, AEON empowers a diverse range of world modeling applications and achieves state-of-the-art performance on standard benchmarks. Project Page: https://weiqi-zhang.github.io/AEON
authors: Weiqi Zhang, Wenyuan Zhang, Yu-Shen Liu, Junsheng Zhou
bullets: Addresses the gap between video models’ visual realism and 3D models’ geometric consistency and persistence.
Operates in text- or image-conditioned video latent space while producing explicit, renderable 4D Gaussian Splatting (4DGS).
Trains a monocular-video 4D reconstruction model to predict 4DGS and camera poses, then adapts generative video latents through VAE distillation.
Supports video-based simulation by rendering 4DGS along predicted camera trajectories and enables persistent dynamic environments.
Reports state-of-the-art performance on standard benchmarks, according to the abstract.
papers.selection_reason: Unified video and 3D world model generating 4D Gaussian splatting for persistent simulation.
papers.title: AEON: Unifying Video and 3D World Models
papers.tldr: AEON unifies realistic video generation with persistent, geometrically consistent 4D world modeling by generating renderable 4D Gaussian Splatting representations.

papers.abstract: Motivated by the human ability to integrate experience across language, perception, and action, we introduce UniWALM, a unified world-action-language model that learns video, action, and language in a single shared representation, where each modality is both a conditioning signal and a supervision target. We ask: can jointly generating language enrich this shared representation, improving manipulation and supporting memory-dependent behavior? Unlike prior approaches that attach a reasoning or vision-language model to a video-action backbone and run them as distinct stages, UniWALM unifies all three modalities inside a single mixture-of-transformers backbone whose per-modality diffusion heads co-denoise synchronously, decoding subtask and textual memory in the same pass as action with no separate planning stage; the generated language is re-consumed on the next step, closing a language-as-memory loop without an external planner or memory bank. To keep the action stream reliable under this richer objective, we further introduce Flow Matching with Correction (FMC), a training objective that teaches recovery from perturbed action trajectories at no inference-time cost. UniWALM consistently improves over same-backbone baselines (e.g., FastWAM) on compositional pick-and-place (MolmoSpaces) and across the memory-dependent subset of RMBench, where it reaches 34.5% without any pretrained language or reasoning model and exceeds Mem-0's keyframe-equipped setup (28.5%) using only a single anchor frame. On a real-world Find-the-Item task, generating textual memory lifts success from 11.1% to 61.1%, while state-of-the-art VLAs stay at or below chance (<=33.3%).
authors: Rahul Sajnani, Diego Romeres, Mingyuan Zhang, Kai Gao, Carl Qi, Baichuan Huang, Srinath Sridhar, Dylan Randle, Lillian J. Ratliff, Jose Barreiros, Manikantan Nambi, Jeroen Vanbaar
bullets: Learns shared representations across video, actions, and language, with each modality serving as both input and training target.
Uses a mixture-of-transformers backbone with synchronized modality-specific diffusion heads to generate actions and textual memory in one pass.
Re-consumes generated language on subsequent steps, creating a language-as-memory loop without an external memory bank or planner.
Introduces Flow Matching with Correction to improve recovery from perturbed action trajectories without inference-time overhead.
