Reports gains on compositional manipulation, memory-dependent benchmarks, and a real-world Find-the-Item task; scope is demonstrated on these tasks and settings.
papers.selection_reason: A unified VLA model that integrates video, action, and language with a language-as-memory loop, directly relevant to embodied control and world modeling.
papers.title: UniWALM: Unified World Action Language Model for Embodied Robot Control
papers.tldr: UniWALM unifies video, action, and language generation in one model, using language as memory to improve memory-dependent robot manipulation without a separate planner.

papers.abstract: Planning under uncertain control execution noise requires reliable feedback policies across diverse environments. We introduce Planning Under Noise (PUN), a neural operator that learns noise-aware value fields for planning in unseen geometries. Building on an established screened-Poisson formulation of stochastic optimal control, we address two challenges: specifying boundary conditions that support navigation across varying geometries and efficiently computing fields with reliable gradients. Zero-Dirichlet obstacle boundaries terminate sampled paths at walls, weakening the goal signal along long routes and making it harder to estimate reliably. We instead impose reflecting Neumann conditions on obstacles and a Dirichlet condition at the goal, allowing sampled paths to continue exploring free space until they reach the target. To solve the resulting PDE without a configuration-space mesh, we extend a Monte Carlo (MC) solver, Walk on Stars (WoSt), to higher dimensions. However, local MC fluctuations can reverse estimated gradient directions and cause planning failures, making direct planning require costly sampling. PUN amortizes this computation by learning geometry-to-field mappings from noisy, partially converged Monte Carlo labels, avoiding expensive convergence for every training example. At inference, test-time scaling uses bounded local search guided by the predicted global field. We evaluate PUN on planning tasks across dimensions. Across four noise levels, PUN matches or outperforms all compared planners, achieving 95-100% success on the 4D replanning benchmark while maintaining the lowest runtime. At the highest tested noise level in 4D, PUN achieves 10.7-60.6% relative gains in success rate over other methods while running 3.29-32.15 times faster.
authors: Michael Chen, Hong Chul Nam, Xi Deng, Anima Anandkumar
bullets: Uses reflecting obstacle boundaries and a goal Dirichlet condition to preserve navigation signals along long routes.
Extends the Walk on Stars Monte Carlo solver to higher-dimensional, mesh-free PDE computation.
Amortizes noisy, partially converged field estimation by learning geometry-to-field mappings.
Combines predicted global fields with bounded local search at inference time.
Across four noise levels, achieves 95–100% success on a 4D replanning benchmark with the lowest runtime; at the highest noise, it is 3.29–32.15× faster than alternatives.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces a neural operator for planning under noise, using a screened-Poisson formulation and Walk on Stars solver for efficient value field computation.
papers.title: Planning under Noise with Neural Operators
papers.tldr: PUN learns noise-aware value fields for fast, reliable planning across unseen geometries under uncertain control execution.

papers.abstract: Evaluating and post-training robot policies through physical interaction is costly and difficult to scale, motivating action-conditioned world models as interactive simulators. However, visually plausible predictions can misrepresent contact dynamics, providing unreliable feedback for policy evaluation and learning. We introduce PhysCanvas, a state-consistent visuo-tactile world model for contact-rich robot manipulation. PhysCanvas unifies multi-view RGB, tactile images, marker displacement, task state, and actions within a unified vision space. All modalities share a video VAE and pretrained generative backbone, allowing optical touch to reuse visual and temporal priors. Motion images derived through forward kinematics and camera projection provide spatially aligned action conditioning, while an initial RGB anchor and updated reference observations guide sequential generation. Our consistency-aware post-training uses the frozen Scene Reward Model, Modality Reward Model, and State Reward Model to supervise scene preservation, visual-tactile compatibility, and agreement with real task outcomes. The resulting world model supports closed-loop policy rollouts for evaluation and provides imagined interactions and rewards for GRPO policy updates. Across four real-world manipulation tasks, when policies are rolled out in the world model, State Reward Model supervision increases the arithmetic mean of task-wise Pearson correlations between world-model and real-world success rates from 0.602 to 0.885. Policy post-training in the reward-guided world model further increases $\pi_{0.5}$'s mean real-world success rate from a 59.1% SFT baseline to 70.8%. These results demonstrate the value of unified multimodal modeling and consistency-aware post-training for robot policy evaluation and learning. Project page: https://zebinx.github.io/PhysCanvas_HomePage/.
authors: Zebin Xing, Yuhang Zheng, Yupeng Zheng, Yichen Zhang, Zichen Li, Shangqing Zhou, Yujie Zang, Yuchen Liu, Zhongpu Xia, Haoran Li, Qichao Zhang
bullets: Addresses the unreliability of visually plausible world-model predictions for contact dynamics in robot manipulation.
Unifies multi-view RGB, tactile images, marker displacement, task state, and actions in a shared vision-based generative model.
Uses kinematics- and projection-derived motion images for action conditioning, plus RGB anchors and reference observations for sequential generation.
Consistency-aware reward models supervise scene preservation, visual–tactile compatibility, and agreement with real task outcomes.
Across four real-world tasks, correlation with real-world success rates improved from 0.602 to 0.885; reward-guided post-training raised mean success from 59.1% to 70.8%.
papers.selection_reason: A state-consistent visuo-tactile world model for contact-rich manipulation, enabling policy evaluation and learning through consistency-aware post-training.
papers.title: Physical Canvas: A Vision Tactile World Model For Robot Policy Evaluation And Learning
papers.tldr: PhysCanvas is a consistency-aware visuo-tactile world model that enables more reliable robot policy evaluation and post-training through imagined contact-rich interactions.

papers.abstract: Reliable multi-view forecasting requires videos from different cameras to describe the same evolving 3D scene. To this end, we introduce Video-Point Model (VPM), a world model that conditions on multi-view video histories and a language instruction to jointly forecast future videos from arbitrary viewpoints and the 3D trajectories of persistent scene points. We extend a pretrained world model with camera-conditioned multi-view processing that integrates complementary observations across cameras, and add a trajectory head that predicts how physical points move through time. Each trajectory tracks a single point across all views, and supervising these trajectories alongside video generation therefore anchors appearance changes in every camera to a shared description of 3D motion. To support training and evaluation, we build VPM-Data, a simulation corpus pairing synchronized multi-view videos with persistent point trajectories, and VP-WorldBench, a forecasting benchmark spanning simulated and real environments. We further extend VPM to robot control by adding robot actions as a token modality in the generator. Action tokens share the point-supervised backbone and are denoised jointly with future videos, thereby grounding the policy in the same 3D-aware representation. On VP-WorldBench and existing 4D generation benchmarks, point supervision improves both video fidelity and 3D motion accuracy over a video-only counterpart, and in simulated and real-robot experiments, it also raises the manipulation success of the action-enabled model.
authors: Byungwoo Jeon, Sunghwan Hong, Dohyeon Kim, Jonghoon Lee, Jungwoo Park, Inhee Lee, Doosan Baek, Jinil Kim, Taehyun Lim, Hanbyul Joo, Marc Pollefeys, Saining Xie, Jinwoo Shin
bullets: Addresses inconsistent multi-view predictions by anchoring camera observations to shared 3D point motion.
Extends a pretrained world model with camera-conditioned multi-view processing and a trajectory-prediction head.
Introduces VPM-Data and VP-WorldBench for training and evaluating multi-view 4D forecasting.
Adds robot actions as a jointly denoised token modality, enabling 3D-aware manipulation policies.
Point supervision improves video fidelity, 3D motion accuracy, and manipulation success across simulated and real settings.
papers.selection_reason: Multi-view video and point-trajectory forecasting world model with action-conditioned robot control.
papers.title: Learning the 4D World through Point Trajectory Forecasting
papers.tldr: VPM learns a shared 3D-aware world model by forecasting multi-view videos and persistent point trajectories, improving visual, motion, and robot-control forecasting.

papers.abstract: Robots exploring unknown indoor environments must decide where to move while much of the environment remains unseen. Predicting the occupancy of unseen space beyond the current sensor range can improve these decisions, but recent approaches commonly rely on learned models that require offline training and repeated inference during exploration. We introduce the Mondrian-Anchored Prior for Learning-free Indoor Exploration (MAPLE), a training-free predictive approach that adapts the Mondrian process into an online generative prior conditioned on observed geometric cues in the current partial map. MAPLE generates multiple plausible map hypotheses and evaluates visibility separately within each to estimate frontier gain, preserving differences in predicted visibility across hypotheses. Across KTH floor-plans and real-SLAM environments at multiple sensor ranges, MAPLE consistently improves over non-predictive exploration and remains competitive with learned predictive approaches. Its lightweight procedural construction enables predictive exploration with limited computational resources. Experimental results further show that more accurate map prediction does not necessarily produce better exploration, highlighting the importance of how predictions are represented and used in exploration decisions.
bullets: Addresses exploration decisions when large parts of an indoor environment are beyond the sensor range.
Adapts the Mondrian process into an online generative prior conditioned on geometric cues from the partial map.
Evaluates visibility separately for each map hypothesis, preserving uncertainty in predicted frontier gains.
Improves over non-predictive exploration and remains competitive with learned predictive methods across floor-plan and real-SLAM settings.
Shows that better map prediction alone does not guarantee better exploration; prediction representation and decision use are crucial.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces a training-free predictive prior (MAPLE) for indoor exploration, improving over non-predictive methods using geometric cues.
papers.title: MAPLE: Mondrian-Anchored Prior for Learning-free Indoor Exploration
papers.tldr: MAPLE enables training-free indoor exploration by generating multiple plausible unseen-map hypotheses and using them to estimate frontier visibility.

papers.abstract: Statistical learning in high dimensions suffers from the curse of dimensionality. Fortunately, many functions of practical interest are compositionally sparse, meaning they admit a composition of local functions, each depending on only a few variables, allowing sample complexity to depend on local arity rather than ambient dimension. Yet realizing this benefit requires exploiting hidden compositional structure, which theory does not establish for practical gradient-based training. We study this gap with CSFRBench, a controlled benchmark that hides the target's compositional computation during training but retains it for diagnosis, and find that dense networks and sparsity-based baselines leave much of that benefit unrealized. Inspired by the spatial organization of biological neural circuits, we introduce Learned Wiring (LeWi): each neuron has a learned low-dimensional embedding, only nearby neurons connect, and embeddings and weights are trained jointly. LeWi improves sample efficiency on targets with hierarchical structure, intermediate reuse, or independent modules. Across 32 additional targets generated by independently sampled computation graphs, LeWi is the most sample-efficient method not given the target graph, with 27% lower mean learning-curve area than dense networks. Dense networks perform better on targets with a single high-arity function. LeWi's representations and connectivity align with the target computation. On 17 world-model prediction tasks spanning control, navigation, and manipulation, LeWi beats the dense baseline on 16 and wins 99/119 baseline comparisons. These results show that jointly learning connectivity and weights can exploit computational structure to improve sample efficiency.
authors: Hangyu Zhou, Constantine Dovrolis, Stephen Mussmann
bullets: High-dimensional learning is sample-inefficient when models fail to exploit compositionally sparse functions.
CSFRBench evaluates whether methods can discover hidden computational structure without access to the target graph.
LeWi embeds neurons in a low-dimensional space and connects nearby neurons while jointly training embeddings and weights.
LeWi is strongest on hierarchical, reusable, or modular targets; dense networks do better for single high-arity functions.
Across benchmarks, LeWi reduces mean learning-curve area by 27% versus dense networks and wins 99 of 119 comparisons on world-model tasks.
papers.selection_reason: Learned wiring improves sample efficiency on world-model prediction tasks across control, navigation, and manipulation; transferable to learned environment dynamics.
papers.title: Learning Computational Structure for Sample-Efficient Prediction
papers.tldr: Learned Wiring improves sample-efficient prediction by jointly learning sparse connectivity and weights that recover hidden compositional structure.

papers.abstract: Despite the success of video world models, extending them to multiple agents is difficult because it requires generating several agent-specific video streams that are consistent in time and between agents. To address this gap, we introduce OverSeer, a multi-agent world model that augments egocentric agent views with auxiliary camera views. We suggest that, by fixing the auxiliary views in space, they act as a proxy for a world-centric representation: Unlike the agents' views, which can change entirely due to a simple change in agent position, changes in the auxiliary views directly map to localized changes in the world state. We show that these fixed views substantially help the model to maintain consistency. We also show that, due to their redundant and semi-static nature, the auxiliary views can be efficiently compressed with a delta-VAE that encodes only the changes relative to a static reference image, reducing the number of tokens required to process them. Experiments in Minecraft and Doom demonstrate improved world and agent consistency, with qualitative results on real-world multi-camera captures indicating that the approach is not tied to game engines. Our compression analysis further shows that delta-VAE substantially reduces the computational overhead of auxiliary-view generation. We conclude that these fixed views provide a simple and efficient way to improve multi-agent world models.
authors: Runjia Li, Kam Woh Ng, Minghao Chen, Junlin Han, Jianyuan Wang, Zhaochong An, Juan-Manuel Perez-Rua, Andrea Vedaldi, Shikun Liu
bullets: Addresses the challenge of generating multiple temporally and cross-agent-consistent video streams.
Augments egocentric agent views with spatially fixed auxiliary cameras as a proxy for world-centric state.
Uses a delta-VAE to encode only changes from static reference images, reducing auxiliary-view token and computation costs.
Experiments in Minecraft and Doom show improved world and agent consistency; qualitative real-world multi-camera results suggest broader applicability.
Scope: demonstrated primarily in game environments, with real-world evidence limited to qualitative results.
papers.selection_reason: Multi-agent video world model with fixed auxiliary views and delta-VAE compression; fits video world models and efficient auxiliary-view processing.
papers.title: OverSeer: Multi-Agent World Models Beyond What Agents See
papers.tldr: OverSeer improves multi-agent world models by adding compressed fixed-camera views that help maintain consistency across agents and time.

papers.abstract: Learning latent dynamics is fundamental to building action-conditioned world models for planning. Among existing families, Joint Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) offer a natural framework by modeling transitions directly in latent space rather than at the pixel level. However, two issues remain in JEPA-based world models: (i) physical grounding lacks explicit aggregation of temporal context and (ii) action planning always overly relies on generic sampling distributions. To this end, we propose $\mathcal{G}$-JEPA, which incorporates temporal context into physical grounding for latent world models and couples the learned models with prior-guided action planning. Specifically, during learning, we incorporate a shared causal temporal module that aggregates temporal context within observation and prediction sequences under physical state supervision, grounding both in task-relevant physical states. When planning, we further introduce action inference through stepwise conditioning of a generative action distribution on the current and goal latent representations together with their evolving discrepancy, yielding anchored proposals that guide model-based online refinement. Together, physical state supervision guides temporal representation learning, while the action prior guides search through the learned world model. Experiments demonstrate improved planning performance on manipulation tasks, including tasks with increasing temporal separation between initial and goal observations. Code is publicly available at https://github.com/myl11045/G-JEPA.
authors: Yilei Man, Yang Chen, Jingcai Guo
bullets: Addresses missing temporal context in JEPA-based physical grounding and the reliance on generic action sampling.
Uses a shared causal temporal module to aggregate observation and prediction histories under physical-state supervision.
Infers actions by conditioning a generative action distribution on current and goal latents plus their evolving discrepancy.
Combines temporally grounded representations with prior-guided online model-based refinement.
Reports improved manipulation-task planning, including tasks with larger temporal gaps between initial and goal observations.
papers.selection_reason: JEPA-based latent world model with temporal physical grounding and action-conditioned planning fits latent action and interactive world models.
papers.title: Exploring Temporal Context-Aware Physical Grounding in Latent World Models
papers.tldr: $$-JEPA improves latent world-model planning by grounding temporally aggregated representations in physical states and guiding action search with goal-aware priors.

papers.abstract: Tracking large human-motion datasets has become the dominant route to general, expressive humanoid whole-body control, but scaling across many motions is expensive. Current pipelines use model-free reinforcement learning, either merging per-motion specialists through lossy distillation, or brute-forcing a single policy with cluster-scale compute. SuperMimic amortizes learning across all motions with one differentiable world model of their shared dynamics, fit from logged transitions of a standard rigid-body simulator. The world model and the tracking policy train together in one loop, and backpropagation-through-time over short imagined rollouts gives the policy analytic gradients. Fast imagined rollouts and analytic gradients make policy learning efficient. In 3 hours on a single GPU, SuperMimic surpasses the return of a state-of-the-art motion tracker baseline trained for 7 days on 128 GPUs. It reduces GPU-hours by more than $1000\times$ and fails on only 25 of 129,514 benchmark motions, versus 179 failures for the baseline. After 9.8 hours on two GPUs, SuperMimic achieves zero failures. From 1 to 264 hours of motion, the world model's prediction error stays stable, and GPU-hours to a target return grow slowly. Our policy transfers to a physical Unitree G1 across diverse and acrobatic motions. SuperMimic removes compute as the bottleneck to scaling humanoid whole-body control, making it practical to measure motion-tracking scaling laws.
authors: Qiayuan Liao, Yiyang Shao, Junfeng Long, Kevin Zakka, Roberto Horowitz, Pieter Abbeel, Koushil Sreenath
bullets: Addresses the high computational cost of learning across large human-motion datasets.
Fits a shared differentiable dynamics model from simulator transitions and trains it jointly with the tracking policy.
Uses short imagined rollouts and backpropagation-through-time to provide analytic policy gradients.
On the reported benchmark, it exceeds a 7-day, 128-GPU baseline after 3 hours on one GPU, with 25 versus 179 failures; zero failures are reached after 9.8 hours on two GPUs.
Transfers to a physical Unitree G1 across diverse and acrobatic motions, while maintaining stable prediction error as motion data scales from 1 to 264 hours.
papers.selection_reason: Uses a differentiable world model to amortize learning across many motions, significantly reducing compute requirements for humanoid whole-body control.
papers.title: SuperMimic: Scaling Humanoid Whole-Body Control with One Differentiable World Model
papers.tldr: SuperMimic efficiently scales humanoid whole-body motion tracking by jointly training a policy with one differentiable world model, achieving strong simulation results and physical transfer with far less compute.

papers.abstract: World-Action Models (WAMs) have emerged as a promising paradigm for embodied generalist policies by jointly modeling future world evolution and robot actions across diverse manipulation tasks. However, representing diverse futures is only the first step: a capable WAM must also generate futures that match the requirements of the current task and execution progress. In long-horizon manipulation where similar observation-action segments occur across different tasks and stages, existing approaches may generate locally plausible yet misdirected rollouts to drift toward wrong task stage, i.e., a phenomenon we term Stage Confusion. To address this problem, we propose TaskWAM, a closed-loop, stage-aware framework that represents fine-grained task requirements with Mode Tokens and tracks execution progress with State Tokens, forming a structured task state to steer world--action generation toward intended future. We further introduce StageBench, a controlled multi-stage manipulation benchmark with parameterized stage variations and automated evaluation.Extensive experiments on both simulation benchmarks and real-world tasks demonstrate that TaskWAM effectively reduces confusion and achieves competitive performance with state-of-the-art methods. Moreover, TaskWAM provides strong plug-and-play transfer across heterogeneous WAM architectures and robot embodiments, including single-arm robots, dual-arm grippers, dexterous hands, and humanoid robots.
authors: Zhuohao Li, Jiawei He, Yuxuan Yan, Lang Zhou, Yinghao Li, Yanrui Li, Tianyu Zhang, Yi-Yang Song, Xirui Wu andYi-Lin Wei, Fating Hong, Qing Zhang, Zhilin Zhao, Jingdong Wang, Wei-Shi Zheng
bullets: World-action models can produce locally plausible rollouts that drift into the wrong task stage, termed Stage Confusion.
TaskWAM uses Mode Tokens for fine-grained task requirements and State Tokens for execution progress in a closed-loop framework.
StageBench provides controlled multi-stage manipulation tasks with parameterized stage variations and automated evaluation.
Experiments in simulation and real-world tasks show reduced stage confusion and competitive performance.
The approach transfers across WAM architectures and diverse robot embodiments, including single-arm, dual-arm, dexterous, and humanoid robots.
papers.selection_reason: World-action models with stage-aware future steering for long-horizon manipulation; directly relevant to embodied robot learning and interactive world modeling.
papers.title: Plausible Future, Wrong Choice: Steering World-Action Models toward Intended Future
papers.tldr: TaskWAM steers world-action models toward task-appropriate futures by explicitly modeling task stage and execution progress.

papers.abstract: As streaming video generation advances, enabling real-time interaction with generated video is becoming increasingly important. We introduce StreamEval, a unified benchmark for interactive streaming video generation spanning five tasks: avatar dialogue, avatar performance, world generation, instruction editing, and reference editing. StreamEval comprises 300 scripted test cases lasting 15-300s, each specifying initial assets, incrementally arriving multimodal requests, and explicit requirements for state changes and content preservation. Performance is assessed along four evaluation dimensions: task execution, state consistency, visual fidelity, and audiovisual coordination, instantiated through ten task-specific metrics on a 0-100 scale. Evaluating 37 distinct models across 300 test cases, we find that high visual quality and identity retention do not necessarily coincide with reliable request execution or sustained state consistency. In particular, request execution remains challenging: the highest task-specific scores are 36.90 for Following among seven avatar-performance models, 25.93 for Following in text-conditioned world generation, and 15.00 for Edit Success among three reported reference-editing models. These findings identify reliable request execution under timing and preservation constraints as a central challenge for advancing omni-modal real-time interactive systems. The leaderboard is available at https://streameval.ai
bullets: Covers five tasks: avatar dialogue, avatar performance, world generation, instruction editing, and reference editing.
Uses 300 scripted 15–300-second test cases with incremental multimodal requests, initial assets, and explicit preservation requirements.
Evaluates task execution, state consistency, visual fidelity, and audiovisual coordination through ten task-specific metrics.
Results from 37 models show that visual quality and identity retention do not guarantee reliable request execution or sustained consistency.
Request execution scores remain low across evaluated tasks, highlighting a key bottleneck for real-time interactive systems.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmark for interactive streaming video generation, including action/request-conditioned world generation and editing, relevant to interactive world models and video generation.
papers.title: StreamEval: Evaluating Interactive Streaming Video Generation Models
papers.tldr: StreamEval benchmarks interactive streaming video generation and finds that reliably executing evolving requests while preserving state remains a major challenge.

papers.abstract: As a prototypical latent world model, Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) provide strong semantic representations. However, dense patch representations expose a redundant interface to downstream predictors, which must implicitly infer spatial organization and temporal correspondence, presenting three challenges. First, object information is distributed across patches, forcing each downstream predictor to redundantly recover object structure that could otherwise be reused across tasks before modeling interactions. Second, the lack of explicit entity correspondence across time makes historical transitions expensive, restricting the predictor's flexibility in utilizing context. Third, without explicit transport structure, existing JEPA models typically use pointwise l1/l2 distances, which are insensitive to spatial displacement when predicted and goal supports are largely disjoint. We propose the Slot-based Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (Slot-JEPA), which decomposes dense representations into stable semantic slots and time-varying spatial masks. Pretrained once and frozen downstream, this decomposition exposes a reusable object-structured interface. Building on it, our Transition Memory Predictor (TMP) stores visual transitions as compact masks and retrieves useful context using statistics of corresponding slots. Its two branches separate slot-specific dynamics from shared cross-slot dynamics. We further use Unbalanced Optimal Transport (UOT) to supervise mask prediction and evaluate candidate plans by transporting mass between aligned predicted and goal masks, providing a signal better aligned with spatial progress. Across seven visual-understanding benchmarks, the slot-reconstructed features remain transferable. Slot-JEPA also improves goal-conditioned planning across six planar environments and four robotic arm planning tasks on the REALM-JEPA benchmark.
authors: Peisong Wen, Qianqian Xu, Minye Lei, Siran Dai, Yang Liu, Qingming Huang
bullets: Addresses redundant object-structure recovery, missing temporal correspondence, and displacement-insensitive pointwise losses in dense JEPA interfaces.
Decomposes representations into stable semantic slots and time-varying spatial masks, then freezes this pretrained interface for downstream use.
Introduces a Transition Memory Predictor with slot-specific and shared cross-slot dynamics, retrieving transitions through corresponding-slot statistics.
Uses Unbalanced Optimal Transport to supervise mask prediction and compare predicted and goal masks based on spatial progress.
Features transfer across seven visual-understanding benchmarks and improves goal-conditioned planning across six planar and four robotic-arm tasks on REALM-JEPA.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes Slot-JEPA, a latent world model architecture that decomposes dense representations into semantic slots and spatial masks. It introduces a Transition Memory Predictor and uses Unbalanced Optimal Transport for supervision, directly applicable to goal-conditioned planning in robotic environments.
papers.title: Slot-JEPA: Object-Structured Prediction Interfaces for Latent World Models
papers.tldr: Slot-JEPA turns dense JEPA representations into reusable object-centric slots and masks, improving context-aware prediction and goal-conditioned planning.

papers.abstract: Moving from controllable videos to genuinely playable worlds requires persistent world state, executable game rules, and low-latency interaction. We outline a roadmap for the next generation of Matrix-Game that separates game execution from visual generation through an executable game harness, and introduce Matrix-Game 4.0 as the first system built on this design. A lightweight game engine maintains world state and executes interaction rules, a multimodal coding agent translates player ideas into game code and dynamic scene captions, and a renderer based on autoregressive video model transforms engine-rendered low-poly proxies into detailed visuals, conditioned on dynamic captions and memory references. This framework provides continuous guidance for visual generation and enables natural-language creation and modification of scenes and gameplay. Our renderer is trained on aligned low-poly and high-fidelity video pairs and distilled into a causal generator that generates in four-frame chunks with one or two denoising steps. Together with targeted inference optimizations, Matrix-Game 4.0 enables 480p, 60 FPS gameplay on a single NVIDIA RTX5090 with a key-press-to-display latency of 112ms. Single-step generation achieves 83FPS steady-state throughput with 18.2GiB of peak GPU memory usage. With fixed prompts, steady-state throughput also reaches 67FPS on an RTX5080 and 58FPS on an RTX5070Ti. We demonstrate customizable shooter and driving games with engine-enforced mechanics, and release code, model weights, and low-poly game assets to support research and creation of playable game worlds.
authors: Jihai Zhang, Runjia Qian, Kaiqin Kong, Biao Jiang, Puyi Wang, Siru Chen, Tianle Li, Guanjie Chen, Junyi Wu, Chubin Chen, Yuanhang Li, Kaichen Huang, Haobo Zhang, Yangguang Li, Wei Yu, Guibin Chen, Yu Cheng, Yahui Zhou
bullets: Addresses the gap between controllable video generation and playable worlds requiring persistent state, executable rules, and low-latency interaction.

Separates game execution from visual generation: an engine manages state and mechanics, while an autoregressive video model renders detailed visuals from low-poly proxies, captions, and memory references.
A multimodal coding agent converts player ideas into game code and dynamic scene descriptions.
Demonstrates customizable shooter and driving games with engine-enforced mechanics.
Achieves 480p, 60 FPS gameplay on an RTX5090 with 112 ms key-press-to-display latency; code, weights, and assets are released.
papers.selection_reason: Real-time playable game worlds using an autoregressive video renderer and game harness; fits interactive world models and autoregressive video models.
papers.title: Matrix-Game 4.0: Harnessing Video Models for Real-Time Playable Game Worlds
papers.tldr: Matrix-Game 4.0 combines an executable game engine with a real-time video renderer and coding agent to create and modify playable game worlds from natural language.

papers.abstract: Egocentric action transfer aims to decouple the semantic action from egocentric observations and reproduce them in new visual contexts, enabling scalable world simulation, embodied policy learning, and robotic data generation. Existing approaches to transferring actions rely on condition-guided video generation, which converts the observation video into explicit geometric controls (e.g., hand poses or meshes) to drive synthesis. However, these methods introduce geometric estimation errors, making it difficult to preserve physically plausible interactions when transferred to new scenes. Alternatively, motion transfer methods directly extract motion patterns from the observation video, yet motion-level features alone cannot encode rich contact dynamics, frequently leading to severe hand structural collapse and implausible contact layout. To address both limitations, we present EgoACT, a test-time framework for egocentric action transfer that operates directly on the denoising process of video diffusion models without requiring additional geometric estimators. EgoACT uses Velocity-guided Structure Anchoring to stabilize reference-consistent hand-object structure in the early denoising stage, and Sparse Correspondence Calibration to refine reliable local correspondences in the mid-to-late denoising stages. Together, these two components preserve transferable action semantics while improving temporal coherence and interaction realism. We further establish EgoActionBench, a benchmark for evaluating action preservation, visual quality, and hand-object plausibility across diverse egocentric manipulation scenarios. Experiments show that EgoACT generates more coherent and physically plausible interaction videos than strong baselines.
authors: Yue Ma, Pengjie Song, Xinyu Wang, Yi He, Zeqian Long, Fangneng Zhan, Kaichen Zhou, Hongyu Liu, Hongfa Wang, Peihao Li, Haoyang Huang, Nan Duan, Qifeng Chen
bullets: Existing condition-guided methods suffer from geometric estimation errors, while motion-only transfer often loses contact dynamics and causes hand collapse.
EgoACT is a test-time framework that operates directly during video-diffusion denoising.
Velocity-guided Structure Anchoring stabilizes hand–object structure early in denoising.
Sparse Correspondence Calibration refines reliable local correspondences in later denoising stages.
EgoActionBench evaluates action preservation, visual quality, and hand–object plausibility; experiments report more coherent and physically plausible videos than strong baselines.
papers.selection_reason: Egocentric action transfer via video diffusion for world simulation and embodied data generation; fits interactive world models, video diffusion, and learning from human video.
papers.title: Decoupling Action from Egocentric Observation for World Simulation
papers.tldr: EgoACT transfers egocentric actions to new visual contexts by guiding video diffusion directly, preserving realistic hand–object interactions without geometric estimators.

papers.abstract: A single observation can admit several plausible futures, making uncertainty an essential part of world modelling. However, quantum generative models remain underexplored for this task. We introduce Quantum-JEPA, a latent-action JEPA framework that learns distributions of future representations using a conditional quantum Born prior. Circuit measurements generate binary latent actions, which a shared predictor maps to alternative future representations. We train the quantum prior through the quality and diversity of these predictions using a sampled energy objective. Our model learns distinct continuations on constructed multimodal tasks and captures latent-action correlations that support coordinated multi-agent futures. On D3IL, a benchmark of diverse human demonstrations, our trained models generate multiple obstacle-crossing routes from a common starting point without observed motion. On the controlled tasks, our classical and quantum prior implementations improve prediction validity and distributional fidelity over the evaluated variational baselines. Our quantum priors combine competitive predictive quality with a parameter-efficient sampling structure: they avoid an exponentially sized categorical output layer while supporting correlated latent actions. We further validate finite-shot parameter-shift training, including training with readout noise. Unlike most prior work, which focuses on simulation, we also verify the feasibility of inference with trained priors on a real QPU. These results establish a trainable quantum component for JEPA future prediction and a basis for exploring quantum-enhanced world models at larger scales.
authors: Zhiyuan Liu, Sicheng Liu, Haiyu Wu
bullets: Addresses multimodal futures, where one observation can lead to several valid continuations.
Measures quantum circuits to produce binary latent actions, which a shared predictor converts into future representations.
Trains the prior with a sampled energy objective encouraging prediction quality and diversity.
Generates distinct coordinated futures on multimodal controlled tasks and multiple obstacle-crossing routes on D3IL.
Demonstrates finite-shot, noisy-readout training and inference on a real QPU, while avoiding an exponentially sized categorical output layer.
papers.selection_reason: Latent-action JEPA world model using quantum Born priors to learn distributions over alternative future representations.
papers.title: Quantum-JEPA: Quantum Born Priors for Latent-Action JEPA World Models
papers.tldr: Quantum-JEPA uses a conditional quantum Born prior to sample diverse latent actions and generate multiple plausible futures in JEPA world models.

papers.abstract: Real-world observations are noisy and often contain excessive task-irrelevant information. Effective world modeling and planning need to abstract observations into world state representations while filtering out irrelevant information. However, encoders in existing world models are typically non-adaptive, leading to state representations that are easily distracted by task-irrelevant information. As a result, the model may not selectively filter observations to cater to different task demands. To address this problem, we introduce ConfigWM, which realizes configurable perception through task-conditioned state extraction. Given a language description of the task at hand, ConfigWM uses it as a configuration signal to steer how visual embeddings are mapped into a task-specific state space, selectively preserving information relevant to the current task while suppressing task-irrelevant variations. Action-conditioned dynamics are then learned in this task-specific state space for planning. We evaluate ConfigWM in environments with increasing levels of distraction. While existing methods exhibit substantial declines in planning success rate as the environments become increasingly noisy, ConfigWM remains comparatively stable and outperforms the strongest competing method by 22.3% on average across diverse environments. Consistent gains in physical-quantity probing (+0.365 Pearson r) and distracted-to-clean retrieval (+75.5%) further indicate that ConfigWM learns states that preserve task-relevant information while remaining robust to distractors, supporting reliable world modeling and planning in noisy worlds. Project Page: https://configwm.github.io
authors: Yijun Shen, Delong Chen, Xianming Hu, Kai Zhang, Pascale Fung
bullets: Existing world-model encoders are non-adaptive and may retain task-irrelevant information.
ConfigWM conditions visual state extraction on a natural-language task description.
It learns action-conditioned dynamics in the resulting task-specific state space for planning.
Across increasingly distracting environments, ConfigWM remains comparatively stable and outperforms the strongest competitor by 22.3% on average.
Probing and retrieval results indicate stronger preservation of task-relevant information and robustness to distractors.
papers.selection_reason: Task-conditioned configurable perception for action-conditioned world modeling and planning directly fits interactive world models.
papers.title: World Models with Configurable Perception
papers.tldr: ConfigWM uses task descriptions to extract task-specific world states, enabling more robust planning amid noisy, distracting observations.

papers.abstract: Endoscopic video contains state transitions induced by camera displacement, deformable tissue, and instrument interaction, yet existing pre-training methods treat dynamics implicitly. Inspired by action-conditioned joint-embedding predictive world models and by the observation that endoscopic optical flow contains both shared image-plane displacement and localized residual motion, we reformulate passive endoscopic video pre-training as causal motion-guided latent-state prediction. We present EndoWorld-JEPA, to our knowledge the first latent world-model pre-training framework designed for general-purpose endoscopic video representation learning. In place of recorded actions, calibrated poses, or robot kinematics, the model conditions prediction of the next latent state on motion observed up to the current state. Its Optical Motion-guided module separates dominant displacement from residual motion and converts the resulting evidence into an ordered temporal motion condition and spatial local-motion weights. Complementary global and motion-local predictors use these outputs: the temporal condition modulates both latent transitions, whereas the local weights define an auxiliary motion-local state that extends prediction from scene-level evolution to spatially selective dynamics. Patch-wise motion weighting emphasizes localized change while retaining anatomical context, and past-motion-window dropout randomly withholds the complete motion condition to reduce dependence on unreliable motion. This global--local formulation learns predictable visual--motion dynamics in representation space without reconstructing stochastic appearance artifacts. Evaluation shows that a common pre-trained checkpoint achieves strong transfer across four downstream benchmarks, supporting motion-guided global--local latent prediction as an effective pre-training paradigm for endoscopic video.
authors: Jie Wang, Shilong Yang, Tao Zhou, Juan Yu, Rong Qu, Jianfeng Ren, Zhicheng Zhang, Linlin Shen
bullets: Addresses the implicit treatment of camera, tissue, and instrument-induced dynamics in existing endoscopic pre-training methods.
Uses observed motion instead of recorded actions, calibrated poses, or robot kinematics to condition next-state latent prediction.
Separates dominant image-plane displacement from localized residual motion to form temporal motion conditions and spatial motion weights.
Combines global and motion-local predictors, with motion-window dropout to reduce reliance on unreliable motion cues.
A shared pre-trained checkpoint transfers effectively across four downstream benchmarks, supporting the proposed paradigm.
papers.selection_reason: Latent world-model pre-training for endoscopic video with motion-guided prediction fits world-model and video representation learning interests.
papers.title: EndoWorld-JEPA: Motion-Guided Global-Local Latent World Modeling for Endoscopic Video Representation Learning
papers.tldr: EndoWorld-JEPA learns endoscopic video representations by predicting global and localized latent-state dynamics guided by observed optical motion.

papers.abstract: This paper shows that JEPA-style latent world models (LWMs) can learn across diverse domains and data sources by adopting the language-conditioned interface of video generation models. We establish this approach as an effective and efficient basis for planning with imagination and downstream policy fine-tuning. To this end, we introduce LaLa-World, a Language-conditioned Latent World model that learns from simulation and robot trajectories together with broader image and video data. Two designs make this work. First, we describe both numerical actions and visual changes in language, enabling joint training of a single future predictor across heterogeneous datasets. Second, we build the predictor on a language model, allowing it to interpret language conditions while predicting future latent states. The resulting predictor achieves higher average MPC planning performance than existing LWMs trained separately for each domain or task. Adding image and video data further improves average planning performance and robustness to action phrasing. In a matched comparison with an RAEv2-based video generation model baseline, LaLa-World reaches comparable planning performance with $6\times$ less training cost and $13.9\times$ faster planning. Beyond planning, the pretrained LaLa-World serves as an initialization for LaLa-Policy, which jointly predicts actions and future visual representations. LaLa-Policy performs competitively with Cosmos Policy on LIBERO and RoboCasa, with up to $5.5\times$ faster inference.
authors: Junha Song, Geonmo Gu, Jeongeun Park, Heejeong Nam, Lucas Maes, Byeongho Heo, Dongyoon Han, Sangdoo Yun
bullets: Trains one language-conditioned future predictor on simulation, robot trajectories, images, and videos.
Uses language to unify numerical actions and visual changes across heterogeneous data.
Achieves higher average MPC planning performance than domain- or task-specific latent world models.
With additional image/video data, planning robustness to action phrasing improves.
Matches an RAEv2 video-generation baseline with 6× lower training cost and 13.9× faster planning; its policy initialization enables competitive performance with up to 5.5× faster inference.
papers.selection_reason: Language-conditioned latent world model for planning and policy learning, directly fitting world models and embodied vision-language-action research.
papers.title: LaLa-World: Scaling Latent World Models with Natural Language Actions
papers.tldr: LaLa-World scales latent world models across domains by expressing actions and visual changes in language, enabling efficient planning and policy learning.

papers.abstract: Action-free videos are an appealing substitute for costly teleoperated data. Latent action models (LAMs) turn videos into a supervision signal by inferring abstract actions between frames. Existing LAMs observe a single camera view, which resolves 6D robot actions only ambiguously missing out-of-plane movements and potential occlusions. We propose a LAM that ingests synchronized multi-camera views using cross-attention to resolve depth and occlusions before compressing them into latent actions. The latent actions are fed into a policy in which a latent expert and an action expert are coupled by sequential flow matching around a frozen VLM backbone. We further evaluate in strict cross-embodiment settings where task-specific demonstrations come from other embodiments. We show that dual-view LAM pretraining improves the decodability of ground-truth 6D actions by 17% compared to single-view, while scaling single-view data by two orders of magnitude is not sufficient to fully recover out-of-plane motions. The downstream policy improves success rate by +13.5% compared to +6.2% for single-view LAM. A single cross-embodiment is sufficient for skill transfer, and adding a second viewpoint outperforms adding up to four further embodiments. The results transfer to hardware where demonstrations come from a human hand improving success rate by +20% over action-only policies in 850 rollouts. We show that video and robot data are complementary, and that benefits of learning from video are task-dependent. Website: https://learnsyslab.github.io/multiview_latent_action_pretraining/
authors: Oliver Hausd\"orfer, Felix Minzenmay, Mani Majd, Maximilian P. Christof, Shiyuan Zhang, Angela P. Schoellig
bullets: Single-view latent action models ambiguously infer 6D movements, especially out-of-plane actions and occluded interactions.
The proposed model combines cross-attention over multiple views with sequential flow matching between latent and action experts around a frozen VLM.
Dual-view pretraining improves 6D-action decodability by 17% over single-view and yields a +13.5% downstream success-rate gain versus +6.2% for single-view.
One cross-embodiment source is sufficient for skill transfer; adding a second viewpoint is more beneficial than adding up to four additional embodiments.
Hardware experiments using human-hand demonstrations improve success by 20% over action-only policies across 850 rollouts, with benefits varying by task.
papers.selection_reason: Multi-view latent action pretraining from videos for cross-embodiment robot learning; fits latent-action world models and learning from human/video demonstrations.
papers.title: Multi-View Latent Action Pretraining for Cross-Embodiment Robot Learning from Videos
papers.tldr: Multi-view latent-action pretraining uses synchronized cameras to improve cross-embodiment robot learning from action-free videos by resolving depth and occlusions.

papers.abstract: Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) achieve high-quality novel-view synthesis by representing a scene as a continuous volumetric radiance field. However, the geometry encoded by the density field of vanilla NeRF can be noisy and inaccurate, since different combinations of shape and radiance may explain the same input images. To reduce this ambiguity, we augment vanilla NeRF with a geometry-optimization branch based on self-supervised cross-ray consistency. Specifically, this branch samples candidate surface points from the density field, generates virtual rays that intersect at each point from different directions, and renders their appearance using the NeRF network. Based on the visibility-weighted color consistency across these rays, we constrain the implicit geometry. We further regularize the implicit geometry by penalizing opacity at candidates with inconsistent appearance predictions and encouraging local normal smoothness. These geometric constraints are derived from the NeRF predictions and require no ground-truth depth or surface-normal supervision. Experiments on eight Replica scenes show that the proposed method reduces the mean Chamfer distance by 30.8% compared with vanilla NeRF.
bullets: Vanilla NeRF geometry can be noisy because shape and radiance ambiguities explain the same images.
The method samples candidate surfaces from density and evaluates appearance consistency along virtual rays from multiple directions.
Visibility-weighted color consistency constrains geometry without ground-truth depth or normal labels.
Additional regularization penalizes opacity for inconsistent predictions and promotes local normal smoothness.
On eight Replica scenes, mean Chamfer distance decreases by 30.8% versus vanilla NeRF.
papers.selection_reason: Improves NeRF geometry via self-supervised cross-ray consistency, contributing to 3D scene reconstruction and world model representations.
papers.title: Geometry Regularization for Vanilla NeRF via Self-Supervised Cross-Ray Consistency
papers.tldr: A self-supervised cross-ray consistency branch regularizes vanilla NeRF geometry, reducing reconstruction ambiguity and mean Chamfer distance on eight Replica scenes.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon human-object-scene interaction (HOSI) is central to embodied AI, animation, and game development. Existing human-object interaction (HOI) and human-scene interaction (HSI) models excel in their respective domains, but none alone covers tasks requiring multiple interaction skills. Training unified HOSI models is hindered by scarce and costly data. We introduce World2HOSI, a multi-expert orchestration harness that generates continuous HOSI data from 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) scenes and natural language instructions. Our key insight is that long-horizon HOSI hinges not on a stronger single model but on orchestration. Given a shared, structured scene state and an orchestration harness grounded in it, existing experts can jointly accomplish tasks beyond the reach of any of them alone. World2HOSI realizes this insight as a closed loop around a persistent scene state built from decoupled background and object assets. A harness plans action stages over this state, invokes experts via their native conditioning interfaces, and writes each action's effects back, so that every invocation is grounded in the evolving world. To reduce physical artifacts, bounded residual optimization and contact-driven physics simulation further ensure the physical plausibility of human motion and object manipulation, respectively, while preserving interaction intent. Experiments and a perceptual user study show that World2HOSI achieves the best task completion and interaction quality on the evaluated HOSI tasks, while generating more diverse data.
authors: Jiushu Li, Haoran Wang, Yumeng Liu, Zhiyang Dou, Yuan Liu, Yuexin Ma, Cheng Lin
bullets: Addresses the lack of unified models and scarce, costly data for multi-skill long-horizon HOSI generation.
Uses 3D Gaussian Splatting scenes, natural-language instructions, and a shared structured scene state.
A harness plans action stages, invokes experts through their native interfaces, and updates the evolving world after each action.
Bounded residual optimization and contact-driven physics simulation reduce motion and manipulation artifacts.
Experiments and a perceptual user study report the best task completion and interaction quality among evaluated methods, with greater data diversity.
papers.selection_reason: Addresses long-horizon Human-Object-Scene Interaction (HOSI) using a multi-expert harness and a persistent scene state. This fits Robot Learning (manipulation) and Interactive World Models (closed-loop state management).
papers.title: World2HOSI: A Multi-Expert Harness for Long-Horizon Human-Object-Scene Interaction Generation
papers.tldr: World2HOSI orchestrates specialized interaction experts through a persistent 3D scene state to generate physically plausible, long-horizon human-object-scene interactions.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models generate robot actions from visual observations and language instructions, but effective manipulation also requires anticipating how the environment will change. Existing world-action models explore future image prediction and latent dynamics modeling. However, generating complete future images can be computationally expensive, while highly compressed latent representations may obscure local changes. To address these challenges, we propose PLaCA, a world-to-action framework built around future latent change. PLaCA directly predicts spatially structured patch-level future latent change from the current multimodal input, preserving local information about expected environmental changes. We introduce patch-level change-aware supervision to emphasize regions undergoing larger changes and a future-to-action interface that explicitly incorporates predicted future latent change into action generation. Experiments on LIBERO-Long show that PLaCA achieves a 79.0% success rate, improving upon the Action-only baseline by 5.0 percentage points. On CALVIN, PLaCA improves the average sequence length from 2.784 to 3.564. These improvements are achieved while updating only 2.95% of the model parameters during the second training stage, demonstrating the effectiveness of future latent change modeling for downstream robotic manipulation.
authors: Zhan Yi, Yuchen Wang, Chao Li, Lei Hong, Boyuan Yang
bullets: Addresses the cost of full future-image prediction and the loss of local detail in heavily compressed latent dynamics.
Predicts spatially structured future latent changes from visual and language inputs.
Uses change-aware supervision to emphasize regions expected to change most.
Feeds predicted future changes into action generation through a future-to-action interface.
Achieves 79.0% success on LIBERO-Long and raises CALVIN average sequence length from 2.784 to 3.564, while updating 2.95% of parameters in the second training stage.
papers.selection_reason: VLA model predicting patch-level future latent change for robot manipulation directly fits embodied AI and world-model prediction.
papers.title: PLaCA: Learning Patch-Level Future Latent Change for Action Generation
papers.tldr: PLaCA improves robot manipulation by predicting patch-level future latent changes and using them to generate actions.

papers.abstract: Action-conditioned video generative models trained on successful, goal-directed demonstrations tend to ignore the commanded action, rendering a plausible expert-like future regardless of what is asked of them. We trace this failure to training data that lack sufficient action influence. We analyze this metric and prove that it upper bounds the action influence that any model trained on that data can express. Expert demonstrations, whose narrow action distributions let next states be predicted without attending to the action, set a low ceiling that no amount of model capacity alone can raise. Raising it requires collecting different data. We introduce Action Influence Maximization (AIM), an algorithm for actively collecting training data for improving dataset action influence. We compare the performance and data-efficiency of AIM against exploration heuristics and intrinsic-motivation methods on simulated navigation and manipulation tasks. In pixel-based manipulation, AIM is the only method that consistently improves controllability: 500 actively collected episodes added to 3k demonstrations match a world model trained on 300k expert episodes on end-effector controllability, an $85\times$ reduction in data.
authors: Samuel M. Bateman, Tenny Yin, Chongyi Zheng, Lei Huang, Brian Wang, Benjamin Eysenbach, Jaime Fern\'andez Fisac, Dhruv Shah
bullets: Expert demonstrations often have narrow action distributions, allowing models to predict plausible futures without using the commanded action.
The proposed action-influence metric upper-bounds the influence a trained model can express, so model capacity cannot overcome insufficiently influential data.
AIM actively collects training episodes to maximize dataset action influence.
Across simulated navigation and manipulation tasks, AIM is compared with exploration and intrinsic-motivation methods.
In pixel-based manipulation, 500 AIM episodes added to 3,000 demonstrations match the controllability of 300,000 expert episodes, an 85× data reduction.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes action influence maximization to improve controllability of action-conditioned video world models, directly targeting interactive world-model training.
papers.title: Training Controllable World Models via Action Influence Maximization
papers.tldr: Action Influence Maximization collects data that makes world models more responsive to commanded actions, substantially improving controllability with far less data than expert demonstrations alone.

papers.abstract: In joint-embedding predictive architectures (JEPA), an encoder and a predictor are trained together to produce a representation that minimizes the error in predicting the representation of the next observation. Because the representations of both the current and the next observation are learned, it is unclear which features they will include. Earlier characterizations describe the features JEPA selects in terms of their individual predictability, raising the concern that unpredictable features, like a traffic light, will not be encoded into the representation. However, the prediction error is also affected by the relationships between features, e.g., the light's color helps predict whether the traffic will stop. We propose the predictive closure characterization, which accounts for these relationships. Based on a reformulation of the JEPA training objective, we show that selection depends on properties of feature sets. This view agrees with earlier works when features evolve independently, but makes new predictions when they do not, for instance that a feature like the traffic light can still be retained. We test this characterization in controlled experiments, which show that unpredictable features can become better represented when they help predict other features, and that changing one feature's predictive relationships can affect how well others are represented. We also demonstrate implications for steering feature selection: targeting one feature with an auxiliary objective, or supplying it to the predictor as side information, can strengthen the representation of another feature whose future values it helps predict, so steering can be indirect.
authors: Mosh Levy, Aly Lidayan, Yoav Goldberg
bullets: Earlier analyses based on individual predictability may incorrectly suggest that features such as traffic lights are omitted.
The proposed predictive-closure characterization reformulates JEPA’s objective to account for dependencies among features.
Controlled experiments show that unpredictable features are better represented when they improve prediction of other features.
Changing one feature’s predictive relationships can alter the representation quality of others.
Feature selection can be steered indirectly through auxiliary objectives or predictor side information.
papers.selection_reason: Characterizes feature selection in JEPA, a predictive world-model objective, with implications for learned environment dynamics.
papers.title: Predictive Closure: A Set-Level Characterization of JEPA's Feature Selection
papers.tldr: JEPA feature selection depends on predictive relationships among feature sets, allowing individually unpredictable features to be retained when they help predict others.

papers.abstract: Latent world models let an agent plan in latent space. The planner searches for an action sequence that minimizes a cost, and that cost is often the $\ell_2$ distance between the predicted terminal latent and the goal latent. The latent, however, is partly noise: the regularizer that prevents collapse during world model training promotes variance in the directions carrying no signal. We show that the same regularizer also supplies the structure to prune that noise in the latent. SIGReg drives the latent marginal to a standard Gaussian at every step, and assuming further that the latent sequence is a Gauss-Markov process, the transition is linear with its covariance pinned by the map itself, $z' \mid z \sim \mathcal{N}(Az,\, I - AA^\top)$. Fitting the state dynamics $A$ therefore yields the covariance at no additional cost, and in its eigenbasis each latent direction carries its own uncertainty. Furthermore, constraining $A$ to be a normal matrix fixes that basis across timesteps, so one eigenbasis measures the uncertainty over an arbitrary number of steps and serves as a stable basis to compute the planning cost on. We then restrict the $\ell_2$ cost to the $k$-dimensional subspace the state dynamics carry forward with the least uncertainty. The correction is post hoc: the encoder, the predictor, the rollout, and the planner are all left untouched, and only a single constrained matrix, $A$, is fit. We evaluate across six environments and show large gains on the 2D navigation tasks, TwoRoom and PointMaze, raising success rate over the plain $\ell_2$ cost by up to $+54.7$ points under a harder planning setting. Code is available at https://github.com/yjang43/lp2.
bullets: Latent world-model planning often uses terminal ℓ2 distance, but learned latents contain noise in directions unrelated to task signal.
The method fits a constrained normal transition matrix under a Gauss-Markov assumption to derive a stable uncertainty basis across timesteps.
Planning cost is restricted to the k-dimensional subspace propagated with the least uncertainty; the encoder, predictor, rollout, and planner remain unchanged.
Across six environments, the approach shows its largest gains on TwoRoom and PointMaze, improving success by up to 54.7 percentage points in a harder setting.
Scope: effectiveness is especially demonstrated on 2D navigation tasks and depends on the stated Gaussian and Gauss-Markov assumptions.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces a method to prune noise in latent world models for better planning in 2D navigation tasks, improving success rates significantly.
papers.title: Latent Projection for Latent Planning
papers.tldr: A post-hoc latent-space projection filters noisy directions from planning costs, substantially improving performance in challenging 2D navigation tasks.

papers.abstract: Treatment planning is intrinsically counterfactual: clinicians must compare how a patient's tumor and survival would evolve under competing regimens, whereas a retrospective cohort records only the regimen received and one follow-up scan. A treatment-conditioned generator trained on such data can therefore reproduce historical treatment allocation rather than simulate the interventional disease dynamics needed to rank regimens. We introduce \textbf{CaMeWM}, a causal medical world model for supported post-TACE tumor evolution and treatment planning. CaMeWM implements one intervention-to-decision loop rather than three independent prediction tasks: it first admits a queried regimen only for clinically comparable histories with empirical treatment support; it then generates a distribution of lesion-local follow-up worlds through an action-conditioned response descriptor, deterministic anchor, and residual 3D diffusion transition; and it finally maps sampled worlds to restricted mean survival time (RMST) with a response-Cox utility model. Under pre-treatment adjustment and positivity, this loop estimates a prespecified, support-restricted g-formula target; all selection and nuisance estimation are fold-local, and the induced policy is evaluated by cross-fitted, censoring-adjusted doubly robust estimation. Across 79 paired out-of-fold episodes, CaMeWM achieves 0.618 SSIM and 0.528 change-map SSIM for follow-up CT transition, while its generated-world survival pathway attains a 0.615 C-index; factual-only AIPW estimates a 9.60-week RMST gain (95\% CI 0.61--18.13) for the frozen policy. CaMeWM provides an inspectable basis for retrospective, support-restricted treatment planning.
authors: Huanlong Gao, Xuelei He, Fengjun Zhao, Xiaowei He
bullets: Addresses the counterfactual gap in retrospective data, where only the observed treatment and follow-up scan are available.
Uses an intervention-to-decision loop: clinically supported regimen selection, action-conditioned 3D diffusion of lesion-local follow-up worlds, and RMST-based survival utility modeling.
Targets a support-restricted g-formula under pre-treatment adjustment and positivity, with fold-local nuisance estimation and cross-fitted doubly robust policy evaluation.
Across 79 paired out-of-fold episodes, follow-up CT transition achieved 0.618 SSIM and change-map transition 0.528 SSIM; the generated-world survival pathway achieved a 0.615 C-index.
The reported policy showed a 9.60-week RMST gain using factual-only AIPW estimates, with a 95% CI of 0.61–18.13 weeks.
papers.selection_reason: Action-conditioned causal world model for tumor evolution and treatment planning.
papers.title: CaMeWM: A Causal Medical World Model for Generative Tumor Evolution and Treatment Planning
papers.tldr: CaMeWM is a support-restricted causal world model that simulates post-TACE tumor evolution under candidate regimens and uses generated outcomes to inform treatment planning.

papers.abstract: Temperature-field reconstruction and prediction are important for condition monitoring, process analysis, and state assessment in industrial and dynamic environments. This work aims to recover a four-dimensional spatio-temporal thermal state field directly from two-dimensional observations, without requiring a predefined 3D model, prescribed thermodynamic equation, or predefined heating/cooling trajectory. To this end, we propose the Gaussian Thermal State-Space Model (GTSM), which represents thermal evolution through a shared scene-level latent process and Gaussian-specific local thermal states. The resulting continuous dynamics are propagated using differentiable RK2 integration, allowing thermal evolution to be inferred from multi-view and multi-temporal observations and continuously extrapolated beyond the observed interval. GTSM is designed as a backbone-agnostic thermal dynamics module for Gaussian representations and can be integrated with both static 3D Gaussian Splatting and dynamic 4D Gaussian Splatting, supporting thermal reconstruction and prediction under both static and time-varying target geometry. The reconstructed representation further enables novel-view thermal rendering and future-time thermal-state prediction. Experiments on real infrared sequences and synthetic dynamic thermal data demonstrate improved reconstruction accuracy and substantially stronger temporal extrapolation than representative baselines, while also validating the applicability of GTSM to deforming targets.
authors: Yunpeng Zhao, Haoxiang Zhang, Chao Liu
bullets: Models thermal evolution using shared scene-level and Gaussian-specific local latent states.
Uses differentiable RK2 integration to infer continuous dynamics and extrapolate beyond observed times.
Works with both static 3D and dynamic 4D Gaussian Splatting, including deforming targets.
Supports novel-view thermal rendering and future-time thermal-state prediction.
Experiments on real infrared and synthetic dynamic data show improved reconstruction and stronger temporal extrapolation than representative baselines.
papers.selection_reason: Gaussian splatting with state-space dynamics for spatio-temporal thermal field reconstruction and prediction.
papers.title: GTSM: Gaussian Splatting with Thermal State-Space Dynamics for Spatio-Temporal Thermal Field Reconstruction and Prediction
papers.tldr: GTSM reconstructs and predicts continuous 4D thermal fields from 2D observations by combining Gaussian splatting with state-space thermal dynamics, without predefined geometry or thermal trajectories.

papers.abstract: Action-conditioned world models support planning and policy evaluation by predicting future states. However, learning an accurate one-step predictor can require substantial training computation. We introduce Beckmann World Models (BWM), which learn a direct map from noise, visual history, and actions to future frames without a pretrained generative teacher. We adapt the terminal-map conservation law of Beckmann Transport Models to action-conditioned video prediction, training directly from noise-data pairs without conditional populations of generated samples required by DriftWorld. However, transport consistency on interpolated inputs does not ensure accurate prediction from the pure noise used at inference. We address this gap with endpoint-aligned training that directly supervises the source prediction, emphasizes motion and spatial structure, and teaches recovery from generated histories. All components train the same map and retain one network call per future chunk. On PushT and Robomimic Can, the final model reduces 64-frame prediction MSE by 68% and 57%, respectively, relative to same-backbone regression baseline. For policy evaluation, BWM achieves the lowest mean IoU error among the evaluated models, 0.0100, at 24.8 ms per four-frame PushT prediction. On Robomimic Can, the BWM stage trained with motion supervision and generated histories achieves 3.3 times higher throughput and 78% lower peak memory than local one-step DriftWorld. In a latent-space extension to RT-1 and Bridge-V2, equal-update controls show that feature supervision under generated histories improves perceptual prediction. These findings show how terminal-map learning can combine efficient training with accurate one-step visual prediction.
authors: Adam Lee, Shobhit Agarwal, June Pyo Suh
bullets: Addresses the high training cost of accurate one-step visual world models.
Maps noise, visual history, and actions directly to future frames without a pretrained generative teacher or conditional generated-sample populations.
Uses endpoint-aligned supervision, motion and spatial emphasis, and generated-history recovery while retaining one network call per future chunk.
Reduces 64-frame prediction MSE by 68% on PushT and 57% on Robomimic Can versus same-backbone regression baselines.

Achieves 0.0100 mean IoU error at 24.8 ms per four-frame PushT prediction; on Robomimic Can, motion-plus-generated-history training provides 3.3× throughput and 78% lower peak memory than local one-step DriftWorld.
papers.selection_reason: Action-conditioned one-step world model with terminal-map learning for efficient future-frame prediction.
papers.title: Beckmann World Models: Direct Terminal-Map Learning for One-Step Action-Conditioned Prediction
papers.tldr: Beckmann World Models enable efficient one-step action-conditioned video prediction by directly learning terminal maps from noise, with endpoint-aligned training improving accuracy from inference-time noise and generated histories.

papers.abstract: World models are increasingly judged by how well they rank plausible futures, yet plausibility alone is the wrong target. The same scene can evolve under many latent rules, and a future that is smooth and physically valid under one rule can be incoherent under the rule actually in force. We formalize the resulting failure, operator-blindness, and show that it is systematically hidden by standard evaluation: a scorer can attain near-perfect generic ranking while separating current-world from other-world futures no better than chance. We introduce Operator-Mismatch Contrastive (OMC) learning, whose semantic hard negatives are valid-but-wrong-operator trajectories, and a matching protocol that measures world-relative coherence directly. On a controlled synthetic benchmark with in- and out-of-distribution operator parameters, across two trajectory-scoring backbones, and on feature-level external validation with CoPhy ballsCF, OMC raises operator-sensitive scoring far above a chance baseline that nonetheless achieves 0.99 generic top-1. We prove that the wrong-operator negative is necessary both for the protocol to detect the failure and for the objective to fix it, and position OMC as an auxiliary coherence signal (a trajectory-coherence scorer, not a generative model, planner, or control agent) that can be attached to existing world-model representations.
authors: One Octadion, Firmansyah Sundana, Novanto Yudistira
bullets: Standard plausibility ranking can miss operator-blindness: generic ranking may be near-perfect while world-relative discrimination remains at chance.
OMC uses valid-but-wrong-operator trajectories as semantic hard negatives.
A matching protocol directly measures coherence with the operator governing the current world.
Across synthetic in- and out-of-distribution settings, two scoring backbones, and CoPhy ballsCF validation, OMC substantially improves operator-sensitive scoring.
The analysis proves wrong-operator negatives are necessary both to expose and correct the failure; OMC is an auxiliary scorer, not a generator, planner, or controller.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces operator-sensitive trajectory coherence scoring with wrong-operator hard negatives, directly targeting world-model evaluation and representations.
papers.title: Operator-Mismatch Contrastive Learning for World-Relative Trajectory Coherence
papers.tldr: OMC learning trains world-model scorers to distinguish futures that are valid under the current world dynamics from those valid under a different operator.

papers.abstract: Video world models have emerged as promising candidates for high-fidelity world models, offering the potential to synthesize high-quality videos capturing fine-grained interactions between agents and their environments conditioned on multi-modal user inputs. Their impressive capabilities address many of the long-standing challenges faced by physics-based simulators, driving broad adoption in many problem domains, e.g., robotics. For example, video models can generate photorealistic, physically consistent deformable-body simulation without making prohibitive simplifying assumptions, which is a major bottleneck in physics-based simulation. Moreover, video models can serve as foundation world models that capture the dynamics of the world in a fine-grained and expressive way. They thus overcome the limited expressiveness of language-only abstractions in describing intricate physical interactions. However, despite their potential, video models still generate physics-violating future predictions, often manifesting as hallucinations. In this survey, we provide a review of video models and their applications as embodied world models in robotics, including efficient data generation and policy learning, dynamics and rewards modeling in reinforcement learning, policy evaluation, and visual planning. Further, we highlight important challenges hindering the trustworthy integration of video models, such as poor instruction following, hallucinations like violations of physics, unsafe content generation, in addition to significant data and compute overhead. We present potential future directions to address these open research challenges to motivate research and ultimately facilitate broader applications, especially in safety-critical settings. We provide a curated bibliography at https://github.com/irom-princeton/awesome-robotics-video-world-model-papers .
authors: Zhiting Mei, Tenny Yin, Ola Shorinwa, Apurva Badithela, Zhonghe Zheng, Joseph Bruno, Madison Bland, Lihan Zha, Asher Hancock, Jaime Fern\'andez Fisac, Philip Dames, Anirudha Majumdar
