bullets: Covers applications in data generation, policy learning, reinforcement-learning dynamics and reward modeling, policy evaluation, and visual planning.
Video models can represent fine-grained world dynamics and photorealistic interactions, including deformable-body simulation beyond simplified physics models.
Key limitations include physics-violating predictions, poor instruction following, unsafe content generation, and substantial data and compute requirements.
Highlights future research directions for improving reliability and enabling broader use, particularly in safety-critical robotic settings.
Provides a curated bibliography of robotics video world-model research.
papers.selection_reason: Survey of video world models for robotics covering dynamics, policy learning, and planning.
papers.title: Robotic Video World Models: A Survey of Applications, Research Challenges, Future Directions
papers.tldr: This survey reviews how video world models are used in robotics, their promise for expressive physical simulation and decision-making, and the challenges preventing trustworthy deployment.

papers.abstract: World models enable embodied agents to anticipate action consequences, yet jointly modeling locomotion and manipulation across diverse embodiments remains challenging due to heterogeneous action spaces and limited multimodal supervision. We present Ropedia W0, the first egocentric loco-manipulation world foundation model spanning humans and robots with diverse embodiments. We curate Xp-Data, comprising 10k hours of egocentric human data and 3k hours of robot data with unified multimodal annotations and systematic quality control. A unified kinematic representation encodes locomotion through camera poses and manipulation through projected skeletons, with robot skeletons combining embodiment-specific forward kinematics with extensive manual keypoint annotation and correction. We also introduce Xp-Teleop, a long-horizon loco-manipulation benchmark based on high-quality dexterous humanoid teleoperation data. Evaluations demonstrate state-of-the-art performance across five cross-embodiment benchmarks (DreamDojo, $\Psi_0$, $\omega$-HOME, Xp-Teleop, and AgiBot) and on held-out human egocentric video, from zero-shot inference to few-shot and full-data post-training. Scaling human pre-training data improves performance on both human and robot evaluations. After distillation, our model supports real-time, minute-long rollouts, enabling live VR interaction. Applications in policy evaluation, model-based planning, and world-action modeling further demonstrate the model's utility for embodied decision-making.
authors: Tianqi Liu, Hanfei Zhao, Qifeng Liang, Hui En Pang, Jiarui Xu, Sayang Mu, Penghao Qiu, YingSheng Zhang, Jun Wang, Ziang Cao, Mingze Sun, Yukang Cao, Fangzhou Hong, Zhaoxi Chen, Ziwei Liu
bullets: Addresses heterogeneous action spaces and limited multimodal supervision in joint loco-manipulation modeling.
Introduces Xp-Data with 10k hours of human and 3k hours of robot egocentric data, plus unified multimodal annotations and quality control.
Uses a unified kinematic representation combining camera poses for locomotion with projected skeletons for manipulation.
Introduces Xp-Teleop, a long-horizon dexterous humanoid teleoperation benchmark.
Reports strong performance across five cross-embodiment benchmarks and held-out human video; distilled models support real-time, minute-long rollouts and VR interaction.
papers.selection_reason: Egocentric loco-manipulation world foundation model trained on human and robot data, directly relevant to embodied AI and world models.
papers.title: Ropedia W0: Scaling Loco-Manipulation World Models across Embodiments with Human Experience
papers.tldr: Ropedia W0 is a cross-embodiment egocentric world model that learns locomotion and manipulation from large-scale human and robot experience, enabling long-horizon prediction and real-time interaction.

papers.abstract: A seemingly reasonable push in Sokoban can make the puzzle unsolvable. To avoid such mistakes, an agent has to anticipate the consequences of its actions before execution, especially when feedback from the real environment is sparse or actions are irreversible. We introduce Agentic Imagination (Agima), a training framework that trains an agent to imagine before acting, i.e. to be imaginative. Agima trains a single omni model to propose actions, generate images of their outcomes, and then reason over these imagined futures to decide what to execute in the real environment. Rather than committing to a single plan, the agent can simulate a sequence of actions, explore alternatives, and compare possible futures. We first use supervised fine-tuning (SFT) to unify policy and world modeling within a single omni model. This enables the agent to predict future outcomes and perform basic forms of imagination, such as forward thinking and counterfactual branching. We then use agentic reinforcement learning (RL) to teach the agent to reason with its imagined futures and use them effectively for planning. Across four environments spanning Maze2D, Sokoban, Pacman, and PushT, Agima generalizes to harder settings unseen during training. Trained with SFT alone on two-box Sokoban, Agima solves 40% of four-box puzzles while seeing the real board only once every five moves, compared with an action-only planner that only solves 2%. After RL, new behaviors emerge in how Agima uses its imagination: it learns a new unified format that was unseen during the SFT stage, learns to conduct forward thinking only when necessary, and branches more frequently at critical decision points. An agent that can picture where its actions lead can learn when and where to look ahead, that is, to plan. Project page: https://agima.net/.
authors: Jiaxin Ge, Junyi Zhang, Tianning Chai, Hanjun Yoo, Chenyang Wang, Xiuyu Li, Weijia Shi, XuDong Wang, Sewon Min, Luke Zettlemoyer, Trevor Darrell, Haiwen Feng
bullets: Addresses planning failures such as irreversible Sokoban pushes that can make tasks unsolvable.
Uses supervised fine-tuning to unify action policy and visual world modeling in one omni model.
Applies agentic reinforcement learning to teach the agent when and how to reason over imagined futures.
Supports sequential simulation, counterfactual branching, and selective forward thinking rather than committing to one plan.
In four environments, it generalizes to harder unseen settings; in four-box Sokoban, SFT-only Agima solves 40% of puzzles versus 2% for an action-only planner under sparse observation.
papers.selection_reason: Trains agents to imagine action outcomes and plan over generated futures; directly advances action-conditioned world modeling and future prediction.
papers.title: Train An Imaginative Agent
papers.tldr: Agima trains a single multimodal agent to imagine action outcomes, compare possible futures, and plan before acting in environments with sparse feedback or irreversible actions.

papers.abstract: The goal of a world model is to capture the dynamics of an environment. This has the great appeal that it allows agents to plan and simulate a course of actions with the help of a world model. For these uses to be reliable, however, the learned dynamics must behave well beyond the specific state-action combinations observed in expert rollouts. Despite this, the relationship between data coverage, dynamics generalization, and downstream planning performance remains underexplored. We study this relationship through the lens of compositional generalization: can a world model recombine familiar state and action factors into valid dynamics? To answer this, we introduce AnyGoal, a benchmark of goal-shifted task variants built from widely used world-model environments, together with an open-source library. Each task is designed to be within reach of a world model that has learned the underlying dynamics: individual state factors and actions remain within their training support, but their combinations are underrepresented in expert trajectories. Across multiple environments and world model families, we find that current models consistently exhibit failures under these recombinations. By examining dynamics and representation failures across model families, interaction regimes, and evaluation metrics, we study where current world models generalize and where challenges remain for goal-shifted prediction and planning. Together, this framework, benchmark, and analysis provide a basis for evaluating progress toward world models that generalize to new planning tasks.
authors: Heejeong Nam, Divyat Mahajan, Quentin Le Lidec, Randall Balestriero, David Klindt
bullets: Problem: Expert-rollout data may not cover the state-action combinations required by new planning tasks.
Method: Introduces AnyGoal, a benchmark and open-source library of goal-shifted variants across established world-model environments.
Scope: Each task recombines state factors and actions that individually appear in training data but are underrepresented together.
Finding: Multiple world-model families consistently fail on these recombinations across environments and evaluation settings.
Contribution: Analyzes dynamics and representation failures to clarify current generalization limits and support future evaluation.
papers.selection_reason: Directly targets world-model generalization and planning under compositional goal shifts, with a benchmark and analysis across model families.
papers.title: AnyGoal: On World Model Generalization Beyond Expert Rollouts
papers.tldr: AnyGoal benchmarks whether world models can generalize dynamics to new combinations of familiar states and actions needed for goal-shifted planning.

papers.abstract: Agent learning is shifting from learning from human data toward learning through interaction with the world. However, scaling such learning directly in real-world computer systems is challenging and can introduce substantial security risks. We therefore propose Agent World Model in the Wild (WildAWM), a scalable pipeline for synthesizing controllable environments and tasks for training general computer-use agents (CUAs). Whereas existing approaches typically specialize in a single agent interaction interface, we construct executable environments that jointly support graphical user interfaces, model context protocol services, and command-line interfaces, allowing agents to flexibly combine visual interaction, tool use, and code execution. WildAWM is entirely powered by open-source models, demonstrating that high-quality computer-use environments can be generated without proprietary frontier models. Beyond environments, we address three recurring challenges in task synthesis: ensuring solvability, maintaining sufficient difficulty, and producing reliable verifiers, by introducing execution-based quality gates that combine heterogeneous agent rollouts, cross-judge consistency checks, and counterfactual probes of judgment robustness. The resulting pipeline synthesizes 341 long-horizon environment-task pairs that can require over 100 agent steps to solve and remain challenging even for frontier models, with GPT-6-Astra solving only 60% of them. We train two Qwen models of different sizes exclusively in these synthetic worlds. Both models achieve substantial gains across 8 out-of-distribution benchmarks spanning web, claw, and computer-use agents, demonstrating that learning in WildAWM's synthesized worlds generalizes broadly to unseen computer-use tasks. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/MSR-Orchard/WildAWM.
authors: Zhaoyang Wang, Qianhui Wu, Haorui Wang, Simon Yu, Baolin Peng, Canwen Xu, Hao Cheng, Wenlin Yao, Boyi Liu, Yite Wang, Jianfeng Gao, Huaxiu Yao
bullets: Motivation: Training agents through real-world computer interaction is difficult to scale and poses security risks.

Method: Generates executable environments supporting graphical interfaces, MCP services, and command-line interaction, with execution-based gates for solvability, difficulty, and verifier reliability.
Scope: Produces 341 long-horizon environment–task pairs, some requiring more than 100 steps and remaining difficult for frontier models.
Results: Qwen models trained only in WildAWM worlds show substantial gains across eight out-of-distribution web, claw, and computer-use benchmarks.
Availability: The pipeline uses open-source models and its code is publicly released.
papers.selection_reason: Synthesizes controllable interactive computer-use environments for agent training, with execution-based quality gates; relevant to interactive world/environment modeling for agents.
papers.title: Agent World Model in the Wild: Computer-Use Agent Environment Synthesis
papers.tldr: WildAWM synthesizes challenging, verifiable computer-use environments across GUIs, tool services, and command lines, enabling open-source-model training that generalizes to unseen tasks.

papers.abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) jointly predict future video and generate actions, yet remain sensitive to task-irrelevant visual perturbations, i.e., changes in visual appearance that should not affect robot behavior. We identify a gap in conventional WAM training: video prediction encourages representations to preserve appearance information, while action generation does not explicitly enforce invariance to task-irrelevant appearance. Data augmentation exposes WAMs to such perturbations but does not require perturbed and nominal observations to produce consistent action representations, and alignment with external pretrained features does not guarantee the desired invariance. To address this gap, we propose PICA-WAM, a self-supervised training framework that casts perturbation invariance as an auxiliary cross-appearance self-alignment task for WAMs. An exponential-moving-average (EMA) teacher processes the nominal observation to provide a deeper-layer target, while the online WAM processes a perturbed observation and aligns its shallower-layer action representation to this target through a lightweight projection head. Across four strong WAMs evaluated on RoboTwin 2.0, LIBERO-Plus, EBench, and a real robot, PICA-WAM consistently improves robustness under visual perturbations, preserves nominal performance in simulation, and raises the real robot success rate. PICA-WAM further reduces the sensitivity of video features to task-irrelevant appearance and its propagation into actions, as shown by paired layer-wise diagnostics. Code: https://github.com/YudeZou/PICA-WAM-release
authors: Yude Zou, Yifei Yao, Guanbo Jiao, Jianming Ma, Guanjie Zheng, Xing Gao
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between appearance-sensitive video prediction and invariance-required action generation in WAMs.
Uses an EMA teacher on nominal observations and aligns perturbed-observation action features through a lightweight projection head.
Evaluated across four WAMs, RoboTwin 2.0, LIBERO-Plus, EBench, and a real robot.
Consistently improves robustness to visual perturbations, preserves simulated nominal performance, and increases real-robot success.
Layer-wise diagnostics show reduced appearance sensitivity in video features and its propagation into actions.
papers.selection_reason: Improves visual perturbation invariance in world action models for robot behavior, relevant to world models and robot learning.
papers.title: PICA-WAM: Visual Perturbation Invariance via Cross-Appearance Self-Alignment in World Action Models
papers.tldr: PICA-WAM improves WAM robustness to task-irrelevant visual changes by self-aligning action representations across nominal and perturbed observations.

papers.abstract: Existing world models can generate action-conditioned video from a single image. Many focus on camera movement, allowing users to explore the generated scene. However, navigation alone does not ensure that an action follows persistent rules when its outcome depends on state that is invisible in the current frame. We present Stateful Harness, a framework that separates world evolution from video rendering to support stateful and rule-governed interaction. It maintains an evolving world state under specified rules, renders each resulting event with a frozen video model, and uses the generated clip to update the world state for the next turn. At each turn, the harness resolves the action selected by the user and compiles the resulting event into an instruction, while a preview clip from an editable 3D scene provides spatial and camera guidance. To evaluate rule compliance, we build WorldState-Bench, a benchmark of 50 counterfactual twin pairs that share an initial frame and action but differ in hidden state and required outcome. Under rule-only prompting, the best of the 11 evaluated video backends produces the required endings for both cases in 32% of pairs. For MiniMax-H3, specifying the required endings raises this rate from 32% to 64%, while the full harness reaches 92% with the same frozen model. These results support separating rule execution from video rendering for world interactions with hidden state.
authors: Chan Yan Ki, Yanran Zhang, Wenzhao Zheng, Xiaofeng Wang, Zheng Zhu, Lei Chen, Jie Zhou, Jiwen Lu
bullets: Existing action-conditioned video models support navigation but may violate persistent rules when key state is invisible in the frame.
The framework tracks evolving world state, resolves user actions under specified rules, and uses a frozen video model to render each event and inform the next turn.
WorldState-Bench evaluates rule compliance using 50 counterfactual twin pairs with identical initial frames and actions but different hidden states.
Across 11 video backends, the best model succeeds on both required endings in 32% of pairs with rule-only prompting; the full harness reaches 92% with the same frozen model.
The approach targets interactive worlds where correct outcomes depend on hidden state, rather than visual appearance alone.
papers.selection_reason: Stateful rule-governed world interaction framework with hidden-state benchmark, directly relevant to interactive world models.
papers.title: State World Models: Execute the Rules, Generate the Pixels
papers.tldr: Stateful Harness separates rule-based world evolution from video rendering to make generated interactions obey hidden-state-dependent outcomes.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning enables learning high-performance control policies, but its reliance on extensive interaction limits deployment on physical systems where data collection is costly, and failures are unsafe. We introduce Prior-Informed Adaptation (PIA), an offline-to-online model-based RL framework that uses structured simulation priors for rapid adaptation. PIA pretrains a world model on heterogeneous low- and high-fidelity simulated trajectories, then adapts it with limited target-domain interaction using uncertainty-regularized planning. Rather than requiring an accurate simulator for policy transfer, PIA treats simulated trajectories as biased priors whose residual mismatch is corrected during online adaptation. We evaluate PIA in autonomous racing using high-fidelity simulation and on a real full-size autonomous race car. In simulation, PIA adapts faster across track and surface shifts than strong baselines, achieving lower lap times and fewer failures. On hardware, PIA achieves reliable few-shot adaptation with less than one hour of on-vehicle interaction.
authors: Adrian Remonda, Jiajun Xi, Nicklas Hansen, Marcus Greiff, Thomas Lew, John Talbot, John Subosits, Xiaolong Wang
bullets: Addresses the high cost and safety risks of collecting extensive real-world RL data.
Pretrains a world model on heterogeneous low- and high-fidelity simulation trajectories.
Uses uncertainty-regularized planning to correct simulation-to-reality mismatch during online adaptation.
Adapts faster across track and surface changes in simulation, with lower lap times and fewer failures than baselines.
Demonstrates reliable few-shot adaptation on a full-size autonomous race car with less than one hour of on-vehicle interaction.
papers.selection_reason: Model-based RL with simulation priors and online adaptation for autonomous racing; fits world models, embodied navigation, and test-time adaptation.
papers.title: Simulation Priors for Rapid Adaptation in Model-Based RL for Autonomous Racing
papers.tldr: PIA uses biased simulation experience plus limited real-world interaction to rapidly adapt model-based RL controllers for autonomous racing.

papers.abstract: Recent video generation models produce visually compelling outputs, yet their physical plausibility remains poorly measured. Physical plausibility asks whether generated objects obey geometry, kinematics, dynamics, and conservation laws. Existing benchmarks rely on coarse visual-language model judgments or target embodied world models rather than video generation itself. We introduce PVBench, a physical video benchmark that quantitatively measures the plausibility of generated videos across 46 dimensions organized into seven domains, spanning: i) instruction and semantic fidelity, ii) behavioral and causal consistency, iii) perceptual and temporal quality, iv) geometric and spatial consistency, v) material properties and field states, vi) kinematic and spatiotemporal persistence, vii) and mechanical plausibility with conservation laws. PVBench comprises 600 carefully crafted prompts, of which 30% involve physical embodied agents such as robot arms, humanoids, quadrupeds, and multi-agent systems. For challenging physically tractable dimensions, it pairs each with specialized vision models that derive verifiable, physically grounded measurements, such as object-level 6D pose, metric scale, surface normals, kinematics, and numerical conservation-law residuals. It thus avoids relying solely on subjective scoring, while supporting both text-to-video and image-to-video generation. Finally, we validate the agreement between automatic metrics and human judgments through human evaluation. Meanwhile, we evaluate mainstream open-source and closed-source models and present several insights. By releasing the benchmark, prompts, and calibration protocol, we aim to foster physically grounded video generation.
authors: Kaiwei Chen, Moran Li, Zhenye Gan, Yabiao Wang, Chengjie Wang, Kexin Zhang, Yong Liu, Jiangning Zhang
bullets: Covers seven domains, including semantic fidelity, causal consistency, geometry, materials, kinematics, and mechanical plausibility.
Includes 600 prompts, with 30% featuring embodied agents such as robot arms, humanoids, quadrupeds, and multi-agent systems.
Uses specialized vision models to measure 6D pose, metric scale, surface normals, kinematics, and conservation-law residuals.
Supports both text-to-video and image-to-video evaluation and compares metrics with human judgments.
Releases benchmark prompts and a calibration protocol to encourage physically grounded video generation.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmark for physical plausibility of generated videos with object-level measurements; directly relevant to video generation and world-model evaluation.
papers.title: PVBench: Quantifying Physical Plausibility in Video Generation with Object-Level Physical Measurements
papers.tldr: PVBench is a benchmark that quantitatively evaluates the physical plausibility of generated videos using object-level measurements across 46 dimensions.

papers.abstract: Generating reusable driving environments requires both controllable future observations and an explicit representation that supports rendering from different viewpoints, yet existing methods still recover explicit scenes from generated RGB videos through optimization for each sequence. To overcome these limitations, we present Drive2Gauss, a feedforward framework that converts jointly generated RGB, metric depth, and dynamic flow into dynamic 4D Gaussian scenes. A Multimodal Video Generator predicts the three modalities from reference multiview images and future control signals. Furthermore, we introduce a Gaussian Query Decoder that uses depth to initialize sparse 3D queries and flow to associate the queries across time, and integrates appearance information through spatiotemporal feature aggregation and iterative query refinement. The reconstruction stage operates in a single feedforward pass without optimization for each scene. Extensive results on nuScenes demonstrate that our approach attains an FID of 6.38 and an FVD of 12.43 for future RGB generation, a PSNR of 29.91 dB when reconstructing its generated observations, and supports both direct rendering under lateral camera shifts and downstream video fixing. Code and more visualizations are available at https://zttt04. github.io/Drive2Gauss_page/.
authors: Tong Zhao, Zhiyuan Han, Lin Chen, Bowen Xie, Yunxi Qiao, Bohan Li, Weiqing Xiao, Gen Li, Shu Han, Xuyang Dai, Cheng Bi, Hao Zhao, Chaojian Li
bullets: Addresses the need for reusable, controllable driving environments with explicit novel-view rendering.
A multimodal video generator predicts future RGB, metric depth, and dynamic flow from multiview references and control signals.
A Gaussian Query Decoder initializes 3D queries from depth, links them over time using flow, and refines them with spatiotemporal appearance features.
On nuScenes, it reports FID 6.38, FVD 12.43, and 29.91 dB PSNR for reconstructing generated observations.
Supports rendering under lateral camera shifts and downstream video fixing; evaluation is demonstrated on nuScenes and generated observations.
papers.selection_reason: Feedforward 4D Gaussian reconstruction from multimodal generative driving videos conditioned on control signals; action-conditioned world generation and 3D scene recovery.
papers.title: Drive2Gauss: FeedForward 4D Gaussian Reconstruction from Multimodal Generative Driving Videos
papers.tldr: Drive2Gauss feedforwardly reconstructs controllable dynamic 4D Gaussian driving scenes from multimodal generated videos without per-scene optimization.

papers.abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) typically represent the world through latent embeddings from pretrained video models, which entangle heterogeneous aspects of the world, from how it looks (e.g., texture and color) to how it is physically configured (e.g., occupancy and pose). This raises an underexplored question: $\textbf{what should constitute the state of a WAM?}$ We argue that the world state should separate how the world appears from how the world evolves under action: the former captures semantic context, while the latter is governed by physical state. To this end, we propose $\textbf{PrismWAM}$, which decouples physics from semantics while jointly modeling state and action. PrismWAM factorizes an embodied task into a $\mathrm{Semantic\ Planning}\rightarrow\mathrm{Physical\ Rollout}\rightarrow\mathrm{Executable\ Action}$ pipeline: given only the initial RGB observation, semantic planning learns to predict the final goal image, while physical rollout predicts the fine-grained evolution toward this goal in depth space; executable actions are then generated from the depth rollout. Without any embodied action pretraining or additional data augmentation, PrismWAM achieves strong manipulation performance in both simulation and the real world. Notably, PrismWAM even surpasses a broad range of models with large-scale embodied action pretraining (e.g., OpenWAM-$\alpha$). More broadly, we reframe World Action Models from modeling how the world looks to how it responds to action, paving the way for action-centric world models grounded in occupancy, flow, tactile sensing, proprioception, and beyond.
authors: Tianyu Xin, Wanqi Zhong, Bowen Hu, Zhangchi Guo, Lijie Wang, Yiming Wang, Haoran Liao, Heyang Yu, Xiaoyu Tian, Zhiding Yu, Yiming Li
bullets: Identifies entangled visual and physical representations as a key challenge in World Action Models.
Factorizes tasks into semantic planning, physical rollout, and executable action generation.
Predicts the goal image from the initial RGB observation, then models fine-grained evolution in depth space.
Achieves strong manipulation performance in simulation and the real world without embodied action pretraining or extra data augmentation.
Advocates action-centric world models grounded in physical state rather than appearance alone.
papers.selection_reason: Decouples physics and semantics in world action models, predicting goal images and depth rollouts to generate executable actions for manipulation.
papers.title: PrismWAM: Decoupling State Representations in World Action Models
papers.tldr: PrismWAM separates semantic appearance from physical dynamics to plan and execute embodied actions more effectively.

papers.abstract: Generative models for precipitation nowcasting are trained and evaluated predominantly on wet-biased datasets, which over-represent precipitation events to emphasize rare extremes. Selecting test cases based on target observations is known to favor forecasts that match the selected distribution rather than the intended deployment distribution. We show analytically how this target-dependent sampling also shifts the conditional distribution learned by generative models. When training and test sampling match, even an ideal model learns precisely the distribution favored by evaluation, allowing the evaluation bias to conceal the training bias. Using a fixed satellite-to-radar diffusion model, we demonstrate that target-dependent test sampling can reverse the calibration assessment. The model appears under-predictive on a wet-biased test set but over-predictive on a deployment-representative test set. This result is replicated outside the model's training domain after a seven-year gap. Utilizing classifier-free guidance as an example, we demonstrate how the contradictory calibration assessment can misdirect downstream model development.
authors: Christoph Metzl, Stefan Kapsreiter, Kianusch Vahid Yousefnia, Virginia Poli, Richard M\"uller, Frank Kr\"uger, Tobias B\"olle
bullets: Precipitation datasets often over-represent wet events to emphasize rare extremes, creating a mismatch with deployment conditions.
Analytical results show that target-dependent sampling shifts the conditional distribution learned by generative models.
When training and test sampling align, evaluation may conceal the resulting training bias.
For a satellite-to-radar diffusion model, the model appears under-predictive on a wet-biased test set but over-predictive on a deployment-representative set.
The issue persists outside the training domain after a seven-year gap and can misdirect development choices such as classifier-free guidance.
papers.selection_reason: Generative precipitation nowcasting is a predictive video/world-model task, and the paper's sampling-bias analysis is transferable to video world model evaluation.
papers.title: Wet-Biased Data Pipelines Mislead the Training and Evaluation of Generative Precipitation Nowcasting
papers.tldr: Wet-biased, target-dependent sampling can distort both generative precipitation-nowcasting training and evaluation, even reversing conclusions about forecast calibration.

papers.abstract: Hierarchical world models plan over long horizons by passing predicted states from a coarse model to a lower-level controller. Choosing these states can be expensive: the upper-level planner repeatedly differentiates through candidate macro-action trajectories. We replace this search with a lightweight goal-conditioned network trained through the frozen high-level predictor. The network supplies a conditioning vector, while the predictor generates the next latent waypoint. Training uses hindsight goals and state-prediction losses on offline trajectories, without search-solution targets or macro-action labels. Inference retains an autoregressive high-level rollout, but requires no high-level candidate optimization. We evaluate this approach on the shared-latent HWM checkpoints distributed with H-JEPA, using three backbone seeds and three head initializations per backbone. With a common evaluation protocol, mean success is 70.4% on Cube, 48.7% on Push-T, 100.0% on FourRoom, and 71.1% on Visual AntMaze. The method improves over the corresponding HWM search baseline on three environments and has the same mean on Push-T. Dedicated measurements on an NVIDIA L40S give 1.28-4.39x end-to-end speedups for batched evaluation. Ablations identify state-adaptive conditioning as a consistent contributor, while predictor-mediated subgoals and unrestricted conditions have environment-dependent benefits.
bullets: Uses a frozen high-level predictor to generate latent subgoals from learned conditioning vectors.
Trains on offline trajectories with hindsight goals and state-prediction losses, without search targets or macro-action labels.
Maintains autoregressive high-level rollouts while eliminating candidate optimization at inference.
Achieves mean success of 70.4% on Cube, 48.7% on Push-T, 100.0% on FourRoom, and 71.1% on Visual AntMaze.
Delivers 1.28–4.39× end-to-end speedups; state-adaptive conditioning consistently helps, while other components vary by environment.
papers.selection_reason: Uses frozen hierarchical world models for goal-conditioned subgoal learning and planning.
papers.title: Learning Goal-Conditioned Subgoals through Frozen Hierarchical World Models
papers.tldr: A lightweight goal-conditioned network replaces costly high-level trajectory search in hierarchical world models while preserving strong performance and improving inference speed.

papers.abstract: Despite achieving high visual fidelity, video models still suffer from physical hallucinations, limiting their reliability as world simulators. Existing methods leverage model-internal or external signals to improve physical plausibility, but their roles and limitations require a unified explanation. We propose a two-dimensional physical-hallucination risk framework that defines low-density sampling risk and high-density drifting risk. The first risk captures generations assigned low likelihood by the video model, for example, a ball suddenly teleporting despite the model favoring continuous motion, while the second risk captures physical inconsistencies in high-likelihood generations, for example, a ball bouncing progressively higher without additional energy. Our analysis explains how model-internal signals steer sampling toward higher-density regions of the learned distribution to address low-density sampling risk. However, higher model likelihood does not guarantee physical plausibility, motivating external guidance to address high-density drifting risk. Based on this framework, we develop Hallucination-Aware Sampler (HA-Sampler), which applies external physical guidance within latent refinement to generate physically plausible videos, and HA-Scorer, which derives a likelihood-based signal from the generator itself for evaluating generated videos using continuous normalizing flow (CNF), with coarse ODE integration and finite-difference divergence estimates. Experiments on Physics-IQ and VideoPhy benchmarks support our theoretical analysis and demonstrate that our methods outperform the compared sampling and scoring SOTA baselines.
authors: Chenyan Zheng, Fan Wu, Ruibo Li, Jiaxing Li, Minghao Yang, Bang Zhang, Guosheng Lin
bullets: Defines low-density sampling risk as unlikely events and high-density drifting risk as physically inconsistent but likely generations.
Explains that model-internal likelihood signals can reduce low-density errors but cannot ensure physical plausibility.
Introduces HA-Sampler, which applies external physical guidance during latent refinement.
Introduces HA-Scorer, a generator-based likelihood signal using continuous normalizing flows for video evaluation.
Experiments on Physics-IQ and VideoPhy support the analysis and report better performance than compared SOTA baselines.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes Hallucination-Aware Sampler (HA-Sampler) to address physical hallucinations in video generation. Relevant to video world models and video diffusion.
papers.title: Risk Decomposition for Hallucination-Aware Video Sampling
papers.tldr: The paper decomposes physical hallucinations in video generation into low-density sampling errors and high-density physical drift, then introduces tools to mitigate and evaluate both.

papers.abstract: Generalizing real-time physics-based animation across diverse 3D shapes and spatial discretizations remains challenging. In this paper, we introduce PhysSkin++, a physics-informed framework that learns continuous neural skinning fields from static geometries to construct compact deformation subspaces. Specifically, we propose a Neural Skinning Fields Autoencoder that predicts shape-dependent deformation subspaces without per-object network training. To learn these subspaces without simulation trajectories, we develop a Physics-Informed Self-Supervised Learning strategy that combines skinning-field normalization with conflict-aware gradient correction, stabilizing joint optimization under physical and orthogonality constraints. The learned representation supports efficient reduced dynamics with user control and contact interactions, together with direct animation binding to meshes, point clouds, and 3D Gaussians. For prescribed rig animation, we further introduce a self-supervised complementarity objective to learn complementary elastic responses without enforcing complementarity constraints at runtime. Experiments demonstrate cross-shape generalization of the learned skinning fields, real-time reduced simulation, and applications to controllable, collision-aware, and rig-complementary animation.
authors: Yuanhang Lei, Baofei Liu, Xingxuan Li, Tao Cheng, Zixuan Wang, Boming Zhao, Yujun Shen, Siyuan Huang, Ruizhen Hu, Peter Yichen Chen, Hujun Bao, Zhaopeng Cui
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of generalizing real-time physics-based animation across shapes and spatial discretizations.
Uses a Neural Skinning Fields Autoencoder to predict shape-dependent deformation subspaces without per-object training.
Introduces self-supervised physics-informed learning with normalization and conflict-aware gradient correction, avoiding simulation trajectories.
Supports reduced dynamics with user control, contact interactions, and direct binding to meshes, point clouds, and 3D Gaussians.
Also learns complementary elastic responses for prescribed rig animation; experiments show cross-shape generalization and real-time simulation.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces PhysSkin++, a framework for physics-based animation via self-supervised neural skinning. Relevant to world models (physics simulation) and 3D vision.
papers.title: PhysSkin++: Real-Time and Generalizable Physics-Based Animation via Self-Supervised Neural Skinning
papers.tldr: PhysSkin++ learns compact, physics-aware deformation subspaces from static shapes, enabling real-time, generalizable animation across diverse 3D representations and interactions.

papers.abstract: Automated treatment planning (ATP) aims to reduce the unwarranted inter-planner variability of manual planning, while improving treatment quality and efficiency. Most ATP pipelines rely on the prediction of the achievable three-dimensional dose distribution for a given anatomy and the subsequent optimization of machine parameters to reproduce it. Diffusion-based methods are largely slice-wise due to the high dimensionality of radiotherapy data, and assume a one-to-one mapping between anatomy and optimal dose despite the multi-objective nature of treatment planning. They are evaluated on their ability to match reference doses and rarely on their integration in ATP frameworks. We present LaDose, a latent diffusion framework for fully volumetric dose prediction. An autoencoder learned on dose distributions, trained so that perturbed latents decode to plausible doses, compresses dose maps 128-fold and enables 3D diffusion on a single GPU. Prescription values are represented as exact scalar vectors that bypass the image encoder, avoiding resampling and latent compression. Multiscale classifier-free guidance allows for the modulation of clinical trade-offs at inference, without retraining or additional labeled data. On 900 clinically delivered head-and-neck volumetric modulated arc therapy plans from five centers, LaDose reached a median absolute error of 1.18 Gy (1.4--1.8\% of the prescription) and was the only one of six frameworks free of systematic bias with respect to the reference distribution. Guidance scales acted predictably on target coverage and organ-at-risk sparing. Integrated with direct aperture optimization, the pipeline generated plans in 15.2 minutes; in a blinded review, senior clinicians rated 14 of 15 plans acceptable without editing.
authors: J. Boyer-Chammard, R. Vauclin, M. C. Biston, P. Maury, M. Gau, S. Stathakis, V. Gr\'egoire, N. Paragios, E. Deutsch, N. Komodakis
bullets: Addresses slice-wise prediction, one-to-one anatomy–dose assumptions, and limited evaluation within complete ATP workflows.
Compresses volumetric dose maps with an autoencoder, enabling 3D diffusion on a single GPU while preserving prescription values as exact scalar inputs.
Uses multiscale classifier-free guidance to adjust target coverage and organ-at-risk sparing without retraining or additional labeled data.
Evaluated on 900 head-and-neck VMAT plans from five centers, achieving a median absolute error of 1.18 Gy and no systematic reference-dose bias among six frameworks.
With direct aperture optimization, plans were generated in 15.2 minutes and 14 of 15 were judged acceptable without editing by senior clinicians.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes LaDose, a latent diffusion framework for volumetric dose prediction in radiotherapy. Relevant to world models (predicting physical manifolds) and 3D vision.
papers.title: Learning the Dose Manifold: A Latent Diffusion Framework for Volumetric Dose Prediction in Automated Radiotherapy Treatment Planning
papers.tldr: LaDose uses latent 3D diffusion to predict clinically controllable radiotherapy dose distributions and integrate them into automated treatment planning.

papers.abstract: Joint 4D reconstruction of a human and object from a monocular video is essential for understanding how people interact with their environment. While recent methods have made noticeable progress, capturing such human-object interactions remains difficult due to two main challenges. First, a video typically contains composite semantic context spanning multiple interaction phases, making it difficult to track the temporal changes of the interaction in the reconstruction. Second, under human-object occlusion, a single-view observation contains incomplete visual information about the interaction, resulting in geometrically inconsistent reconstructions. To address these challenges, we introduce HORIA, built upon two core designs. First, we decompose the entire input video into temporally grounded and semantically distinct interaction phases with motion-aware captioning, obtaining a specific text description for each phase. Second, conditioned on these text descriptions of the interaction, we propose an interaction-aware re-rendering that compensates for the limited single-view observation. Specifically, we render the initially reconstructed 4D human and object from novel viewpoints and refine the renderings with a text-to-video diffusion prior, which provides auxiliary novel-view supervision beyond single-view cues. As a result, our framework produces temporally coherent and accurate 4D reconstructions under diverse interaction scenarios, achieving state-of-the-art performance.
authors: Hyeongjin Nam, Taeryung Lee, Daniel Sungho Jung, Kyoung Mu Lee
bullets: Addresses interaction-phase changes and incomplete geometry caused by human-object occlusion in single-view video.
Decomposes videos into semantically distinct, temporally grounded phases using motion-aware captioning.
Uses phase descriptions to guide text-to-video diffusion refinement of novel-view renderings.
Provides auxiliary supervision beyond the original monocular observations.
Reports accurate, temporally coherent reconstructions across diverse interactions with state-of-the-art performance.
papers.selection_reason: Reconstructs 4D human and object scenes from monocular video using interaction-aware re-rendering. This advances 3D reconstruction and world modeling for embodied interactions.
papers.title: HORIA: 4D Human and Object Reconstruction from a Monocular Video with Interaction-Aware Re-Rendering
papers.tldr: HORIA reconstructs temporally coherent 4D humans and objects from monocular interaction videos by combining phase-aware text descriptions with diffusion-guided novel-view re-rendering.

papers.abstract: Building embodied agents that can perceive, reason, and act across diverse 3D worlds is a central research direction toward artificial general intelligence. Yet most existing work remains confined to specific tasks in a single scene and transfers poorly to new environments, leaving general embodied agents for open-world settings under-explored. We refer to such agents as Embodied World Agents (EWAs), whose defining property is the ability to understand diverse visual environments and execute general actions in open-world conditions. To advance EWA research, we study open-world embodied navigation-planning and release EmbodiedWorld-200K, a large-scale dataset of over 200K samples spanning diverse scenes. Each example is equipped with multi-level annotations, ranging from low-level camera-motion trajectories to high-level semantic instructions. The dataset also provides unified evaluation splits and task-specific metrics, supporting offline pretraining and fair evaluation of EWAs. Beyond offline supervision, a defining characteristic of an EWA is its interaction with the environment; training solely on offline data is therefore insufficient, especially for generalizing to scenes not covered in the training distribution. Building dedicated real interactive environments, however, is often prohibitively expensive. To address this, we propose a novel training scheme that employs a video world model as a low-cost environment proxy and performs interactive reinforcement-learning (RL) post-training of the EWA within it. Empirically, pretraining on EmbodiedWorld-200K substantially improves the open-world embodied planning ability of the EWA, and further RL post-training inside a world model yields clear gains on out-of-distribution scenes. The dataset, baseline checkpoints, and training and evaluation code are available at https://xiaokunfeng.github.io/EmbodiedWorld-200K/.
authors: X. Feng, J. Tang, Z. Lin, L. Chen, S. Shao, Q. Lu, K. Huang
bullets: Targets embodied agents that can understand diverse 3D environments and perform general actions beyond single-scene tasks.
Provides over 200K navigation-planning samples across diverse scenes with low-level motion and high-level semantic annotations.
Introduces unified evaluation splits and task-specific metrics for offline pretraining and fair assessment.
Uses a video world model as a low-cost proxy environment for interactive RL post-training.
Pretraining improves open-world planning, while world-model RL further improves performance on out-of-distribution scenes.
papers.selection_reason: Embodied navigation-planning dataset with interactive video world models for RL post-training directly fits embodied AI and world models.
papers.title: EmbodiedWorld-200K: Toward Embodied World Agents via Embodied-Planning Dataset and Interactive World Models
papers.tldr: EmbodiedWorld-200K advances open-world embodied agents with a 200K-sample planning dataset and video-world-model-based interactive RL.

papers.abstract: Robotic manipulation is not merely observation-to-action generation, but the realization of task-specified state changes in the physical world. Existing vision-language-action (VLA) methods directly learn observation-to-action mappings, imposing a substantial learning burden due to the gap between semantic understanding and action execution. Although world-action models (WAMs) improve control through future prediction, modeling complete future states wastes capacity on static appearance and action-irrelevant changes. We propose Vision-Language-Delta-Action (VLDA), a paradigm that reformulates full future prediction as compact actionable transition modeling. Its core is a compact Delta variable that captures latent world-state changes, serving as an interface between vision-language understanding and action generation. VLDA learns Delta through a unified objective composed of the Local Transition Filter (LT-Filter) and Global Transition Anchor (GT-Anchor). LT-Filter captures task-relevant manipulation-centric changes while suppressing static reconstruction biases. GT-Anchor provides coarse future-level regularization to preserve the overall direction of state changes. Delta-Driven Action Refinement (DDAR) further grounds Delta in the action manifold and injects it as a structured seed to guide action denoising. We implement VLDA within LoongForge, an open-source training framework for large-scale foundation and embodied models, using its modular and distributed infrastructure for unified two-stage optimization. Experiments show that VLDA improves long-horizon consistency, robustness, and generalization, validating actionable Delta as an alternative to direct action prediction and full future-state modeling.
authors: Lingsen Zhang, Wei Li, Jie He, Henghua Zhang, Kai Mo, Shiyong Li, Yanpeng Wang, Rui Shao
bullets: Targets the learning burden and semantic-to-action gap in direct vision-language-action policies.
Models actionable state changes instead of reconstructing complete future states, reducing focus on static or irrelevant details.
Combines LT-Filter for local manipulation changes with GT-Anchor for coarse future-direction regularization.
Uses DDAR to inject the learned Delta into action denoising as a structured action-space seed.
Experiments report improved long-horizon consistency, robustness, and generalization.],
papers.selection_reason: Compact latent delta as actionable transition for VLA robotic manipulation; fits embodied VLA, robot learning, and latent-action world modeling.
papers.title: Vision-Language-Delta-Action: Learning Compact Deltas as Actionable Transition Interfaces for Robotic Manipulation
papers.tldr: VLDA learns compact, task-relevant state-change representations to bridge vision-language understanding and reliable robotic manipulation actions.

papers.abstract: Game world models have made rapid progress toward real-time interactive generation. Yet action control is still predominantly implemented as feature conditioning, leaving the model to learn from training data how each action should move the visual world. This formulation is poorly matched to a broad class of planar-camera worlds, such as top-down and isometric games. In these worlds, player motion induces a geometrically well-defined planar camera displacement. We observe that the key to spatially consistent control in such worlds is to represent the effect of each action directly in world coordinates. To this end, we introduce ActionRoPE, a parameter-free action interface that converts action-driven camera displacement into world-coordinate rotary positions. As a result, tokens corresponding to the same world location retain the same positional address across time. These world coordinates further expose a spatial asymmetry in generation: regions covered by the initial observation are geometrically known, while newly revealed regions remain to be synthesized. We therefore propose Coordinate-Conditioned Noise Scheduling (CNS), which assigns token-wise denoising schedules according to this known-new structure. It allows observed regions to stabilize earlier, while new content is generated with reference to them. Compared with four representative action-conditioning mechanisms, our approach follows the commanded motion more faithfully and reduces the revisit drift by 66% over the strongest baseline. The same interface transfers across video backbones from 1.3B to 33B parameters and to out-of-distribution scenes. Project Page: https://teawhite.cn/ActionRoPE/
authors: Zhiyang Deng, Yuzhe Wu, Zijun Lin, Yeying Jin
bullets: Addresses the limitations of feature-based action conditioning, which requires models to learn action-to-motion geometry from data.
Uses a parameter-free interface that converts action-induced camera displacement into world-coordinate rotary positions, preserving consistent token locations across time.
Introduces Coordinate-Conditioned Noise Scheduling to stabilize observed regions earlier while synthesizing newly revealed content using them as reference.
More faithfully follows commanded motion and reduces revisit drift by 66% versus the strongest of four representative baselines.
Transfers across video backbones from 1.3B to 33B parameters and to out-of-distribution scenes.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces ActionRoPE, a method for spatially consistent control in game world models by representing actions as world coordinates. This directly addresses action-conditioned generation and controllable world models.
papers.title: ActionRoPE: action as coordinates for spatially consistent control in planar-camera game world models
papers.tldr: ActionRoPE improves spatially consistent control in planar-camera game world models by encoding actions as world-coordinate positional shifts and scheduling denoising based on observed versus newly revealed regions.

papers.abstract: Time-series models increasingly condition on known future inputs. In controlled systems, some of these inputs are actions that can be changed, compared, and optimized before execution. A model must therefore do more than predict the realized future: it must predict how outcomes change under different actions from the same observed history and support reliable comparison of candidate plans. We introduce ActTime, an action-conditioned world model for time series. Over the observed history, ActTime updates variable-specific latent states through an action-conditioned transition and corrects them using observations. It then rolls the same transition forward under candidate actions to generate future trajectories. Training uses only factual trajectories, without paired alternative-action outcomes or planning supervision. We construct a simulator-grounded evaluation suite across building energy, traffic, greenhouse climate, and inventory management, covering factual prediction, intervention-effect prediction, offline decision making, and closed-loop planning. ActTime ranks first in 12 of 16 domain-task settings. Across eight methods, the mean pairwise model-ranking reversal rate is 17.8% between factual prediction and intervention fidelity, and rises to 28.4% between intervention fidelity and decision ranking. These results show that factual accuracy, intervention fidelity, and decision quality are related but not interchangeable.
authors: Xinxing Zhou, Xiaojie Yuan, Yanlong Wen, Ming Jin
bullets: Targets controlled time series where future actions can be compared and optimized before execution.
Maintains variable-specific latent states, updates them with an action-conditioned transition and observations, then rolls them forward under candidate actions.
Trains without paired counterfactual outcomes or planning supervision.
Evaluated on building energy, traffic, greenhouse climate, and inventory-management simulators across prediction, intervention, decision, and planning tasks.
Ranks first in 12 of 16 domain-task settings; model rankings often change across factual prediction, intervention fidelity, and decision quality.
papers.selection_reason: Action-conditioned world modeling for time series directly fits interactive world models.
papers.title: ActTime: Action-Conditioned World Modeling for Time Series
papers.tldr: ActTime learns to simulate how different actions change future time-series outcomes, using only observed factual trajectories, and shows that prediction accuracy does not guarantee reliable intervention or decision quality.

papers.abstract: We study language-conditioned local navigation, where a robot must navigate to a text-specified target visible in its initial observation and stop at the described location. End-to-end navigation policies require diverse training data to generalize across scenes, yet real-robot data is costly to collect and simulated data leaves a sim-to-real gap. Internet egocentric videos offer a scalable source of real-world navigation experience. Our key insight is to learn goal-directed visual dynamics from Internet egocentric videos, and use these dynamics to support robot action generation. To this end, we propose ScaleNav, a unified world-action framework with three-stage training. We first perform instruction-conditioned video pretraining on these videos to learn how observations evolve as the camera approaches instructed targets across diverse real-world scenes. Action alignment then uses action-labeled simulated data to train the model to predict executable action chunks. Joint fine-tuning subsequently optimizes all trainable components together for navigation. ScaleNav achieves success rates of 86.5% on a single-view adaptation of Short-Horizon OVON and 94.9% on our HabitatGS-LN benchmark, outperforming the evaluated baselines on both benchmarks. We further deploy and evaluate ScaleNav on a real quadruped robot, with results supporting the model's ability to generalize to real-world navigation. Code and videos are available at https://zju3dv.github.io/ScaleNav/
authors: Yihui Yang, Yuanhong Yu, Jiawei Wang, Zhongrui Yu, Jia Shi, Kun Zhan, Ruizhen Hu, Xiaowei Zhou, Yu Liu, Sida Peng
bullets: Addresses the high cost of real-robot data and the sim-to-real gap in local navigation.
Pretrains on instruction-conditioned Internet videos to learn goal-directed visual dynamics.
Aligns learned dynamics with executable action chunks using action-labeled simulation data, then jointly fine-tunes the navigation system.
Reports 86.5% success on a single-view Short-Horizon OVON adaptation and 94.9% on HabitatGS-LN, outperforming evaluated baselines.
Real-quadruped deployment results support generalization to physical-world navigation.
papers.selection_reason: Pretrains on internet egocentric videos to learn visual dynamics for language-conditioned local navigation, spanning VLN, human-video learning, and video world models.
papers.title: ScaleNav: Scalable Internet Video Pretraining for Language-Conditioned Local Navigation
papers.tldr: ScaleNav uses large-scale Internet egocentric videos plus simulated action data to train language-conditioned navigation policies that transfer from simulation to real robots.

papers.abstract: Streaming video world models generate the future chunk by chunk, conditioned on their own past and a stream of actions. Trained on short clips, they drift once a rollout exceeds the training horizon, as prediction errors re-enter the context and compound. A common remedy is to train the model on its own rollouts via distribution matching distillation (DMD). For action-conditioned world models, the teacher becomes a bottleneck: an external video model is agnostic to the actions, whereas the model's own pretrained network drifts in the same manner as the student. We observe that a long rollout need not match a teacher, provided it remains a realistic continuation of its own scene that follows the commanded actions. Realism and scene fidelity can be measured against real-data statistics, which remain valid at any horizon, while action following is preserved by the model's conditional generation loss. We propose Fr\'echet Forcing, which fine-tunes a world model together with its deployed multi-step sampler under three constraints. Generative anchoring applies the flow-matching loss after a self-generated history ending on real data. Context fidelity, a Fr\'echet distance (FD) on latent statistics of the free rollout centred on each clip's own ground truth, keeps every rollout faithful to its scene. Reality matching, an FD to real frames in a frozen perceptual space, keeps the generated frames realistic. Because all three targets are derived from short real clips without comparing a rollout against a long recorded future, training requires no teacher, no online critic and no long videos. Fine-tuning MiniWorld-1B, pretrained on 253-frame clips, for at most 36 GPU-hours on 381-frame clips yields rollouts that remain stable beyond 4,000 frames and continue to follow their actions in both robot manipulation and camera-controlled exploration.
authors: Yian Zhao, Yu Yan, Hongcan Guo, Ruochong Zheng, Jian Zhang, Jie Chen
bullets: Addresses compounding errors and drift in long-horizon autoregressive video rollouts.
Fine-tunes the deployed multi-step sampler using generative anchoring, context-fidelity Fréchet distance, and reality-matching Fréchet distance.
Uses statistics from short real clips, avoiding external teachers, online critics, and recorded long futures.
Applied to MiniWorld-1B, the method produced stable rollouts beyond 4,000 frames while continuing to follow actions in manipulation and camera-controlled exploration.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes Fréchet Forcing to train long-horizon streaming world models from short clips by enforcing realism and context fidelity without requiring a teacher model or long videos.
papers.title: Frechet Forcing: Training Long-Horizon Streaming World Models from Short Clips
papers.tldr: Fréchet Forcing trains action-conditioned streaming world models to remain realistic, scene-consistent, and action-following far beyond their short-clip training horizon without requiring a teacher or long videos.

papers.abstract: Visual world models have shown strong potential for robot planning, yet long-horizon manipulation remains challenging due to compounding prediction errors, large search complexity, and latent plans that the low-level controller cannot reliably reach. In this work, we introduce Vector-Quantized World Model (VQ-WM), a latent feedback motion planning framework that integrates discrete long-horizon search with continuous visual feedback control: a discrete latent predictor models transitions between vector-quantized latent states, allowing the planner to look far ahead and find a shortest path to the goal through discrete search and a continuous learned controller sequentially reaches the planned states through visual feedback, correcting deviations to mitigate compounding errors. Whereas most vector quantization uses Euclidean distance, we use a novel estimator of the first-passage-time as a quasi-metric, which aligns the planning abstraction with the controller's capabilities. We evaluate on the physical robot manipulation of the Tower of Hanoi puzzle: whereas existing state-of-the-art foundation models (VLAs, WAMs) only succeed when the solution trace in their training dataset, our method achieves 100\% success rate with only short-play data, demonstrate its ability to compose long-horizon solutions beyond the short demonstrated trajectories and execute them reliably. Our solution also outperforms strongest world-models by 13.3--85.3 percentage points on simulation benchmarks spanning manipulation and locomotion, demonstrating consistent progress and new capabilities.
authors: Xuezhou Xu, Chung-Pang Wang, Zhenzhen Li, Benjamin Riviere
bullets: Addresses compounding prediction errors, large search spaces, and the difficulty of executing latent plans in long-horizon manipulation.
Uses vector-quantized latent states for discrete search and a learned visual-feedback controller to sequentially reach planned states and correct deviations.
Introduces a first-passage-time quasi-metric for quantization that better aligns the planning abstraction with controller capabilities.
Achieves 100% success on physical Tower of Hanoi using only short-play data and outperforms competing world models by 13.3–85.3 percentage points on simulation benchmarks.
Scope: evaluated on manipulation and locomotion benchmarks, with physical-robot validation on Tower of Hanoi.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes a vector-quantized world model for latent feedback motion planning in robot manipulation, directly relevant to world models and learned control.
papers.title: Vector-Quantized World Model: Latent Feedback Motion Planning for Robot Manipulation
papers.tldr: VQ-WM combines discrete latent long-horizon planning with continuous visual-feedback control to reliably solve manipulation tasks beyond the length of its demonstrations.

papers.abstract: World models offer increasingly rich environments for exploration, yet intervening in a world while observing the consequences from freely chosen viewpoints remains challenging. We tackle these challenges by introducing UniState, a framework for controllable world simulation built on a unified world-state representation. This representation unifies spatial memory and user interventions. Users specify object motion directly within spatial memory, while independently choosing the camera trajectory from which the resulting world state is observed. This unification makes the relationship between the scene and the requested changes explicit, removing ambiguity between object motion and viewpoint change from the control specification. Crucially, specifying an intervention does not require prescribing every resulting movement: the video model can synthesize additional motion within controlled objects and plausible interactions with their surroundings. We develop training and sampling strategies that help generated videos follow the specified object motion and camera trajectory while preserving this capacity to generate responses beyond the prescribed transformations. Experiments demonstrate more accurate joint object and camera control than the existing methods, alongside qualitative evidence that intervention-induced scene changes persist across rollouts.
authors: Jaeseok Jeong, Kyungmook Choi, Sohyun Chung, Youngsik Yun, Youngjung Uh
bullets: Addresses ambiguity between object motion and viewpoint changes in interactive world models.
Represents spatial memory and user interventions together, while allowing camera trajectories to be chosen independently.
Uses training and sampling strategies to follow specified object and camera motion while synthesizing plausible additional interactions.
Experiments show more accurate joint object-camera control than existing methods.
Qualitative results indicate that intervention-induced scene changes persist across rollouts.
papers.selection_reason: Controllable world simulation with unified spatial memory and interventions; directly fits interactive world models.
papers.title: UniState: Unifying Memory and Intervention for Controllable World Simulation
papers.tldr: UniState enables controllable world simulation by jointly specifying object interventions and camera viewpoints in a unified world-state representation.

papers.abstract: Emerging Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) are moving beyond representation learning towards latent world models that support prediction, planning, and control. Yet their latent worlds naturally lack a human-interpretable interface. In this Perspective, we argue that as JEPA latents become internal states for prediction and action, interpretability must move beyond what they encode to how latent variables interact, evolve, and causally drive prediction. To this end, we envision a four-stage research agenda, involving Ground, Structure, Verify, and Act, to guide this shift toward actionable latent-world understanding. Within our framework, existing JEPA interpretability efforts provide early evidence for Ground, while systematic analysis of latent structure, causal verification, and intervention remains largely unexplored. Overall, this Perspective aims to call for a broader latent-world interpretability agenda that shifts attention from decoding representations toward understanding, validating, and acting on latent worlds.
authors: Jize Wang, Yongcheng Jing, Xinyi Le, Cailian Chen, Xinping Guan, Dacheng Tao
bullets: JEPAs are evolving into latent world models for prediction, planning, and control, but their internal states lack human-interpretable interfaces.
Interpretability should examine how latent variables interact, evolve, and causally influence predictions—not only what they encode.
The proposed four-stage agenda is Ground, Structure, Verify, and Act.
Existing work offers initial evidence for Ground, while latent structure, causal verification, and intervention remain largely unexplored.
The scope is a research agenda and perspective rather than a reported empirical evaluation.
papers.selection_reason: Perspective on interpretability of latent world models, directly aligned with world model research.
papers.title: World Model Interpretability: From Decoding Representations to Understanding Latent Worlds
papers.tldr: This Perspective proposes shifting JEPA interpretability from decoding representations to understanding, validating, and acting on the latent worlds that drive prediction and control.

papers.abstract: In this letter, we present GOFusion, a real-time visual mapping system for autonomous robot navigation that anchors Gaussian primitives to local occupancy maps, providing both spatial awareness for path planning and high-fidelity appearance that enables information-driven robot navigation. GOFusion builds 3D Gaussian maps from pose estimates and local occupancy maps obtained via visual-inertial SLAM and enables pose corrections to maintain both geometric and visual consistency. Furthermore, it restricts the 3D Gaussian Splatting optimization to active submaps to bound GPU memory usage. Building on the appearance-rich Gaussian map, we introduce a rasterizer-integrated Fisher approximation that quantifies per-primitive sensitivity online, serving as an information-driven heuristic for Gaussian pruning and next-best-view planning. We evaluate GOFusion on public datasets and in real-world drone flights. It not only outperforms several baselines in mapping quality, but also achieves real-time, high-fidelity and uncertainty-aware mapping at scale. Finally, we demonstrate fully autonomous drone exploration for Gaussian map refinement using the proposed Fisher-informed heuristic. Code is available at https://github.com/Bennnoo/GOFusion. We provide a supplementary video demonstration at https://youtu.be/pLQKbxQvb6I.
authors: Boxin Bu, Simon Boche, Haoming Zhang, Jaehyung Jung, Jiaxin Wei, Hannah Schieber, Daniel Roth, Angela P. Schoellig, Stefan Leutenegger
bullets: Targets scalable visual mapping for autonomous navigation with both geometric awareness and high-fidelity appearance.
Anchors 3D Gaussian primitives to occupancy submaps, applies pose corrections, and optimizes only active submaps to limit GPU memory use.
Introduces a rasterizer-integrated Fisher approximation for online primitive sensitivity estimation, Gaussian pruning, and next-best-view planning.
Demonstrates high-quality real-time mapping on public datasets and real-world drone flights, including autonomous exploration for map refinement.
Scope: evaluated for visual-inertial SLAM-based mapping and drone exploration; quantitative performance details are not provided in the abstract.
papers.selection_reason: Presents GOFusion, a real-time system fusing Gaussian Splatting with occupancy maps for navigation. Introduces Fisher-informed heuristics for pruning and next-best-view planning, representing a significant technical contribution to video world models and autonomous navigation.
papers.title: GOFusion: Real-Time Gaussian-Occupancy Submap Fusion for Fisher-Informed Autonomous Robot Navigation
papers.tldr: GOFusion enables real-time, uncertainty-aware Gaussian mapping and autonomous exploration by fusing Gaussian primitives with local occupancy submaps and Fisher-informed planning.

papers.abstract: Controllable video generation has recently achieved impressive visual quality, yet existing control paradigms remain poorly suited to embodied navigation. Text prompts are spatially ambiguous, while camera-trajectory control relies on low-level motion specifications that are unintuitive for human users and difficult to manipulate. In this work, we introduce Map2Vid, a novel task that reformulates embodied navigation video generation as a BEV-map-to-video synthesis problem, together with a large-scale benchmark for systematic evaluation. By using BEV maps, which provide a visual representation of global scene layout and intended navigation routes, Map2Vid enables human-friendly navigation video generation. To support this task, we construct a dedicated dataset with over 100K navigation sequences across 61 indoor scenes, each paired with egocentric videos, BEV maps, camera trajectories and language instructions. We further develop a unified framework that integrates multiple control signals, together with a curriculum training strategy that progressively weakens non-map inputs, enabling flexible inference under both full conditioning and map-only input. Extensive experiments across multiple foundation generation models demonstrate that controllable navigation video generation via BEV map is a viable and promising direction.
authors: Yulin Dai, Yuqian Fu, Tianwen Qian, Zhen Xing, Bojia Zi, Xiaoling Wang
bullets: Reframes embodied navigation video generation as bird’s-eye-view (BEV) map-to-video synthesis.
Provides a benchmark and dataset with over 100K navigation sequences across 61 indoor scenes.
Pairs egocentric videos with BEV maps, camera trajectories, and language instructions.
Uses a unified multi-signal control framework with curriculum training that supports full conditioning or map-only inference.
Experiments across multiple foundation video-generation models show BEV-map control is viable for navigation video generation.
papers.selection_reason: BEV-map-conditioned egocentric navigation video generation; relevant to interactive world models and video generation.
papers.title: Map2Vid: Embodied Navigation Video Generation with Human-Friendly Motion Control
papers.tldr: Map2Vid introduces BEV-map-controlled video generation to make embodied navigation videos more intuitive to specify and evaluate.

papers.abstract: Latent world models such as LeWM plan by searching for an action sequence whose predicted terminal latent is closest to the goal latent under an ambient norm, such as the Euclidean distance. Planning with such a cost assumes that proximity in the ambient latent space reflects proximity to the goal in the environment. Studying LeWM, we find that this assumption holds only in a small neighborhood around the goal, whereas farther away the L2 cost forms spurious low-cost basins that trap the planner. Yet neighborhood-based embeddings show that the latents retain the underlying physical state. We therefore hypothesize that the latents lie near a curved, low-dimensional manifold, and that the terminal cost should measure the distance along this latent manifold rather than through the ambient space. To estimate this manifold distance, we propose the Neighborhood Graph Cost (NGC), which computes shortest-path distances on a mutual nearest-neighbor graph constructed over training latents. NGC changes only the terminal cost and requires no retraining. This single change improves the planning success rate of LeWM across all four benchmark tasks and nearly solves TwoRoom and Reacher: even at the farthest goal offsets tested, NGC reaches 95% and 100% success, whereas the L2 cost falls to 27% and 81%. These results support the manifold hypothesis and our argument that latent world models should plan with distances along the latent manifold.
authors: Zunzhi You, Linwei Tao, Siyu Xu, Yunke Wang, Chang Xu
bullets: Ambient L2 terminal costs work near the goal but create misleading low-cost basins farther away.
Latent representations retain physical state while apparently lying near a curved, low-dimensional manifold.
Neighborhood Graph Cost (NGC) estimates manifold distance using shortest paths on a mutual nearest-neighbor graph of training latents.
NGC changes only the terminal cost and improves success across all four benchmark tasks, nearly solving TwoRoom and Reacher.
Scope: evidence is reported for LeWM and four benchmark tasks; NGC relies on the training-latent neighborhood graph.
papers.selection_reason: Improves latent world model planning by using manifold distances instead of ambient norms, directly relevant to latent-action world models.
papers.title: Latent World Models Should Plan with Distances Along the Latent Manifold
papers.tldr: Replacing ambient L2 distance with latent-manifold shortest-path distance makes LeWM planning substantially more reliable without retraining.

papers.abstract: Learning a single perceptive policy for diverse humanoid loco-manipulation requires unifying high-level task decisions without losing the state-dependent physical responses that make each interaction succeed. This makes the representation between high-level planning and whole-body control critical: kinematic or contact targets provide compact abstractions but do not directly encode interaction-specific control responses, while directly predicting low-level actions requires the planner to model high-frequency closed-loop feedback. We propose FIBER, a framework that uses the executable latent space of a frozen behavioral foundation model (BFM) as a shared planning representation for heterogeneous interaction skills. Our latent policy projection (LPP) maps independently acquired task-specific policies into this representation by identifying latent commands whose induced actions match their local control responses, enabling lower-rate planning while retaining the BFM's high-frequency state feedback. After projection, we aggregate closed-loop latent rollouts from all skills and train a single perceptive flow planner entirely offline. We further introduce AH-BFM, an adaptive-horizon BFM trained with multi-gamma forward-backward (FB) learning to support both precise control and temporally extended whole-body behavior. We evaluate FIBER on box pickup, door opening, and object grasping in simulation and on a real Unitree G1 humanoid. Across 128 diverse variations per task in simulation, FIBER achieves 42.0% mean success, more than tripling projected latent replay (11.6%) and substantially outperforming kinematic planning (3.5%). Real-world experiments further demonstrate sim-to-real transfer, skill chaining, and conditional steering through the same unified planner.
authors: Yutang Lin, Guanya Shi, C. Karen Liu
bullets: Addresses the challenge of unifying task-level planning with interaction-specific, state-dependent whole-body control.
Projects independently learned skill policies into the latent space of a frozen behavioral foundation model (BFM).
Trains a single offline perceptive flow planner on aggregated closed-loop latent rollouts from multiple skills.
Introduces AH-BFM with adaptive horizons for both precise control and extended whole-body behavior.
Across three simulated tasks, achieves 42.0% mean success versus 11.6% for latent replay and 3.5% for kinematic planning; real-robot tests show transfer, skill chaining, and conditional steering.
papers.selection_reason: Latent action-aligned planning for humanoid loco-manipulation using a behavioral foundation model; relevant to latent actions and robot learning.
papers.title: Action-Aligned Latent Planning for Versatile Humanoid Loco-Manipulation
