Generates manipulation videos with stronger instruction adherence and action progression than video-generation baselines, according to the abstract.
papers.selection_reason: Unified world action model for egocentric dexterous manipulation; fits embodied VLA/robot learning and interactive world models.
papers.title: Perceive, Predict, and Plan: a Unified World Action Model for Egocentric Dexterous Manipulation
papers.tldr: P³-WAM unifies 3D perception, action-conditioned video prediction, and goal-directed planning for egocentric dexterous manipulation.

papers.abstract: Recent 3D world models increasingly use features from geometry foundation models (GFMs) as predictive world states, benefiting from their rich geometric priors. However, the view dependence of these features entangles scene dynamics with camera-induced variation, making the resulting state evolution harder to predict. We propose GeoState, a view-decoupled geometry representation for predictive 3D world modeling that separates scene-state evolution from camera-dependent observation. Specifically, a scene tokenizer aggregates multi-view GFM features into a view-decoupled scene state, which a geometry decoder queries using camera rays. An autoregressive world model then predicts future scene states, while camera motion is modeled separately. The predicted states can therefore be decoded under either predicted or externally specified cameras, while retaining a single context-derived scale throughout the rollout without per-frame scale alignment. Experiments show that GeoState outperforms prior 3D world models on Waymo, supports geometrically consistent cross-view querying, and generalizes zero-shot to KITTI and nuScenes. Project page: https://hongchang-liu.github.io/GeoState-project-page/
authors: Hongchang Liu, Jian Liu, Yujuan Ding, Liang Peng, Xun Jiang, Fei Ma, Xing Xu, Yi Bin
bullets: Addresses camera-dependent variation in geometry foundation model features, which complicates future-state prediction.
Aggregates multi-view GFM features into a view-decoupled scene state and decodes geometry through camera rays.
Autoregressively predicts scene states while modeling camera motion separately, enabling decoding from predicted or external cameras.
Maintains a single context-derived scale throughout rollouts without per-frame scale alignment.
Outperforms prior 3D world models on Waymo and generalizes zero-shot to KITTI and nuScenes, with consistent cross-view querying.
papers.selection_reason: View-decoupled geometry states for predictive 3D world modeling.
papers.title: GeoState: Learning View-Decoupled Geometry States for 3D World Modeling
papers.tldr: GeoState learns view-independent geometric scene states so 3D world models can predict scene evolution separately from camera motion.

papers.abstract: Video world models turn actions and camera motion into long visual rollouts, making video a natural interface for interactive simulation. Such interaction requires responsive generation, yet coherent rollouts must retain visual memory of what has already been generated. Chunked video diffusion models usually keep this context in growing KV caches, so later chunks become progressively slower. To address this bottleneck, we introduce Velox, a training-free attention router for region-level context selection using frustum slab correspondences from streaming geometry. Velox represents historical blocks as camera frustum slabs with depth intervals and obtains current-block depth through recency-priority multiwarp. For well-covered regions, frustum slab overlap softly modulates each layer's model-derived block importance. Uncovered regions retain the model-derived route without geometric bias. The fixed token-block granularity matches FlashAttention-style tiled execution and reduces the attention term that grows with rollout length. Frustum slab construction runs asynchronously with denoising on the same H200. At chunk 48, Velox accelerates attention by $4.36\times$ and denoising by $2.43\times$. On the full 158-case WBench navigation split, it remains within 0.15 API-free average points of dense LingBot-Fast-Cam. Please see our project page at https://velox-world.com/velox/ for more details.
authors: Qiuhong Shen, Shizun Wang, Xinchao Wang
bullets: Addresses the slowdown of chunked video diffusion models whose growing KV caches make later rollout chunks increasingly expensive.
Introduces a training-free, region-level attention router based on camera-frustum slab correspondences and depth-aware multiwarp.
Uses geometric overlap to adjust model-derived block importance for covered regions, while leaving uncovered regions unchanged.
At chunk 48, reports 4.36× faster attention and 2.43× faster denoising.
On the 158-case WBench navigation split, stays within 0.15 API-free average points of dense LingBot-Fast-Cam.
papers.selection_reason: Geometry-guided attention routing for efficient long-rollout video world models, with spatial memory via frustum slabs.
papers.title: Velox: Spatial Memory Makes World Models Efficient
papers.tldr: Velox uses streaming camera geometry to route attention to relevant spatial memory, making long-horizon video world-model rollouts faster while preserving navigation quality.

papers.abstract: Physical understanding is crucial for decision making, yet vision models struggle to infer properties such as damping that govern how materials behave. Audio encodes such properties directly, because an object's acoustic response to impact reveals its damping through measurable decay. We probe frozen encoders for the quality factor $Q$, a dimensionless measure of how many oscillations an object completes before its ring dies away, and report how well each embedding orders impacts by $Q$ using the Spearman rank correlation $\rho$, for which $\rho=1$ is a perfect ordering and $\rho=0$ an unrelated one. Audio embeddings reach $\rho=0.73$ and retain most of that advantage on materials withheld from training, while a single video frame taken at the moment of impact, encoded by CLIP, supports only $\rho=0.28$. Having established where the signal lives, we ask how much of that gap vision can recover. We distill a frozen audio teacher into a frozen CLIP backbone through a trained projection head and find that this recovers a useful fraction of the audio advantage. Because pooled correlations on this task are dominated in practice by category identity, we also evaluate under a leave-one-material-out protocol in which the held-out material is withheld from the projection head as well as the probe. Distillation with a four-frame input improves the correlation there from 0.234 to 0.338 (+0.053 over the matched four-frame baseline, 14 of 17 materials), a gain that no category-level strategy can produce. Widening the visual input to four frames spanning the impact supplies half of that improvement at no acoustic cost, which indicates that part of what a single frame misses is visible dynamics.
authors: Zainab Afolabi, Vadim Selyutin, Zhao Gao, Babs Khalidson, Mohamed Ghoneim
bullets: Audio encoders rank impacts by quality factor with Spearman ρ=0.73, retaining most of their advantage on unseen materials.
A single impact-frame encoded by CLIP reaches only ρ=0.28, showing limited visual access to damping cues.
Distilling a frozen audio teacher into a frozen CLIP backbone recovers a useful portion of the audio advantage.
Under leave-one-material-out evaluation, four-frame distillation improves correlation from 0.234 to 0.338 across 14 of 17 materials.
Four frames alone provide half the improvement, indicating that visible impact dynamics—not just category identity—carry relevant information.
papers.selection_reason: Cross-modal distillation of physical damping structure from audio into vision; transferable to learned physical dynamics and multimodal representations.
papers.title: How Much Physics Can Vision Learn from Audio? Probing and Distilling Damping Structure
papers.tldr: Audio embeddings capture damping structure far better than single-frame vision, while distilling audio knowledge and using short video clips helps vision recover part of the gap.

papers.abstract: Accurate motion prediction is critical for safe autonomous driving, yet even strong forecasters leave residual errors in their multimodal proposals. Existing refiners compress complete proposals or update their segments sequentially, preventing the full proposed future from serving as explicit relational context for correction. We introduce FutureLift, a backbone-agnostic refiner that represents each multimodal proposal as a heterogeneous future graph, with spatially grounded temporal nodes connected to agent histories, map elements, alternative modes, and, for joint prediction, other agents future trajectories. Bidirectional temporal edges allow later evidence to revise earlier segments in a single pass, and the updated nodes predict residual coordinate and confidence corrections. Requiring only proposals, scores, and scene context, FutureLift provides a common refinement interface for structurally different forecasting backbones. On Argoverse2 and the Waymo Open Motion Dataset, it consistently improves frozen proposals and outperforms native and specialized refiners across marginal and joint forecasting. On the WOMD motion-prediction leaderboard, FutureLift ranks first in minADE (0.5049m) and minFDE (0.9942m) among the compared standard-input methods, without LiDAR or ensembling, while achieving a competitive 0.4874 Soft mAP.
bullets: Addresses residual errors in complete multimodal trajectory proposals that existing sequential or compressed refiners cannot fully contextualize.
Builds heterogeneous graphs linking future trajectory nodes with agent histories, map elements, alternative modes, and other agents’ futures.
Uses bidirectional temporal edges so later predicted segments can revise earlier ones in a single refinement pass.
Backbone-agnostic interface requires only proposals, confidence scores, and scene context, and improves frozen proposals on Argoverse2 and WOMD.
Ranks first among compared standard-input methods on WOMD for minADE and minFDE, while achieving competitive Soft mAP without LiDAR or ensembling.
papers.selection_reason: Refines multimodal trajectory proposals by modeling future interactions as a graph; contributes to predicting environment and agent dynamics.
papers.title: FutureLift: Lifting Trajectory Proposals into Bidirectional Future Graphs for Motion Forecasting
papers.tldr: FutureLift refines multimodal motion forecasts by modeling each proposal as a bidirectional future graph, improving both marginal and joint prediction across major driving datasets.

papers.abstract: World-model planners evaluate candidate trajectories by predicting their future consequences, implicitly relying on the plan-to-motion relationship learned during training. At deployment, a different downstream controller may execute the same planned trajectory differently, creating a planning-execution gap between the frozen model's imagined future and actual execution. A natural remedy is to replace the planned trajectory with its predicted or observed execution. However, we find that better execution fidelity does not necessarily yield better decisions: directly substituting predicted execution trajectories yields only a 0.048 PDMS improvement across 10 unseen controller configurations, far smaller than the gain from our proposed adaptation. This suggests a semantic mismatch between a planned trajectory, which serves as a reference for downstream control, and an executed trajectory, which already describes the resulting post-controller motion. We introduce ExecutionBridge, which infers controller-specific execution characteristics from planned-executed trajectory pairs and uses them to adapt the native ego latent rollout while keeping the original planned trajectory unchanged. The planner, world model, and reward head remain frozen. On NAVSIM, ExecutionBridge consistently improves planning across unseen controller configurations and multiple frozen world-model planners, with substantially larger gains in challenging driving scenes where execution mismatch more strongly affects candidate evaluation.
authors: Danqi Zhao, Keyu Chen, Wenchao Sun, Minglei Huang, Jianhe Zhang, Yan Zhu, Hao Cheng, Zifan Cao, Sifa Zheng
bullets: Problem: Different downstream controllers can execute the same plan differently, causing a gap between imagined and actual outcomes.
Naively substituting predicted or observed execution trajectories improves fidelity but does not reliably improve planning decisions.
Method: Infer controller-specific execution characteristics from planned–executed trajectory pairs and adapt the planner’s native ego latent rollout.
The world model, planner, and reward head remain frozen; the original planned trajectory is preserved.
On NAVSIM, the method consistently improves planning across unseen controllers and multiple frozen planners, especially in challenging driving scenes.
papers.selection_reason: Adapts frozen world-model planners to controller-induced execution shift for navigation, directly relevant to robot planning and world models.
papers.title: Plans Are Not Executions: Adapting Frozen World-Model Planners to Controller-Induced Execution Shift
papers.tldr: ExecutionBridge adapts frozen world-model planners to controller-specific motion without replacing the original plan, improving decisions under unseen execution behaviors.

papers.abstract: Flow-based Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies are inherently stochastic: different noise seeds can produce action chunks of varying quality from the same observation. At test time, however, the policy typically commits to a single sample without an explicit estimate of its quality. In fine-grained manipulation, executing a suboptimal action can irreversibly disrupt task progress and lead to failure. To exploit policy stochasticity, we introduce a training-free two-axis trigger that uses two initial samples to measure within-chunk temporal variation and cross-sample variance, detecting the critical states. Once triggered, a JEPA-based latent world model ranks candidate action chunks by predicting action-conditioned future latent states and the corresponding changes in task progress. By operating in latent space, the verifier avoids pixel reconstruction and enables efficient and more accurate ranking. Across three real-world tasks, $\textit{i.e.,}$ pen insertion, pipetting, and apple placement), our method raises the average completion score from 50.8% to 65.5%, while adding 326 ms for sampling and verification per triggered decision on a single RTX 4090. Consistent gains are also observed in simulation, where the average success rate rises from 66.4% to 73.6% in the clean setting of RoboTwin 2.0, from 62.8% to 69.6% in its randomized setting, and from 96.9% to 97.6% on LIBERO.
authors: Xueli Sun, Yuxiang Lu, Yantong Liu, Xianzhe Fan, Xi Chen, Zhe Liu, Hengshuang Zhao
bullets: Addresses failures caused by committing to a poor action sample during fine-grained manipulation.
Uses two initial samples to detect critical states from within-chunk temporal variation and cross-sample variance.
When triggered, a JEPA-based latent world model ranks candidate action chunks by predicted future latent states and task-progress changes.
Improves average real-world completion from 50.8% to 65.5% across pen insertion, pipetting, and apple placement, with 326 ms added per triggered decision.
Also reports consistent simulation gains across RoboTwin 2.0 and LIBERO; verification is applied selectively rather than at every decision.
papers.selection_reason: Test-time verification of flow-based VLA policies using a latent world model to rank action chunks.
papers.title: VeriVLA: Adaptive Test-Time Verification for Flow-Based VLAs with Latent World Models
papers.tldr: VeriVLA improves stochastic flow-based VLA decisions by triggering test-time verification and selecting action chunks with a latent world model.

papers.abstract: Many vision-language-action policies rely on action-labeled robot demonstrations and lack an explicit mechanism for predicting future visual states. These limitations hinder learning from action-free videos and can encourage overfitting to demonstration conditions, weakening generalization and robustness. We present TS-WAM, a lightweight Teacher-Student World-Action Model that addresses these challenges through self-supervised temporal learning and explicit future prediction. Its vlm-jepa framework learns from heterogeneous data, including robot demonstrations and action-free human videos, using an EMA target branch without requiring a separately trained external teacher. By coupling vlm-jepa with delta-lwm, TS-WAM learns to predict latent actions from the current observation and instruction and uses them to predict future visual features that guide action generation at inference. A unified end-to-end training architecture jointly optimizes temporal representation learning, visual dynamics, and robot control without a separate latent-action or world-model pretraining stage. The EMA target branch is removed at inference, keeping the deployed policy lightweight. Experiments on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, and SimplerEnv, together with real-world manipulation experiments on Franka Research 3 and RevoTron, demonstrate that TS-WAM achieves strong manipulation performance, generalization, and robustness.
authors: Menghao Yin, Jiaju Yin, Xiyue Dong, Lixin Xu, Zhenhui Zhang, Ke Zhang, Yating Feng, Renjing Xu
bullets: Addresses reliance on action-labeled demonstrations and limited future-state modeling in vision-language-action policies.
Uses self-supervised temporal learning with an EMA target branch to train on heterogeneous robot and human-video data without an external teacher.
Couples latent-action prediction with future visual-feature prediction to guide action generation at inference.
Jointly trains temporal representations, visual dynamics, and robot control end to end, without separate latent-action or world-model pretraining.
Shows strong manipulation performance, generalization, and robustness in simulated benchmarks and real-world experiments.
papers.selection_reason: Jointly learns temporal latent actions, future visual prediction, and robot control from demonstrations and human videos.
papers.title: TS-WAM: Temporal Latent Actions and World-Action Coupling for Vision-Language Robot Control
papers.tldr: TS-WAM is a lightweight vision-language-action policy that learns from both robot demonstrations and action-free videos by predicting latent actions and future visual states for more robust control.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies are typically trained with action prediction as the primary supervision signal, since robots ultimately execute actions. Auxiliary objectives such as latent-action (LA) and future-vision (FV) prediction are often added to improve policy learning, yet they compete with action prediction for the same training budget. We ask whether, under a fixed budget, allocating a substantial share of training samples to such objectives, rather than to further action prediction, can improve policy learning. We build a unified VLA framework that couples a two-stream multimodal diffusion transformer (MMDiT) with a sample-level router, which assigns each training sample to either action prediction or an auxiliary objective and thus makes supervision allocation explicit. Within this framework, we instantiate three LA targets based on LAPA and its DINO-feature variants, and three FV targets based on DINOv3, V-JEPA 2, and Wan2.2 representations. Across LIBERO, CALVIN, and four real-robot tasks, suitable LA and FV supervision outperforms action-only training under the same budget, even when action prediction receives no more than half of the training samples. FV generally outperforms LA, although the strongest LA target remains competitive on CALVIN. Diagnostic analyses suggest that DINO-based LA targets emphasize relative motion, whereas FV targets emphasize absolute position and task identity. We therefore argue that what robot policies learn to predict, and how training is allocated among these targets, should be treated as explicit design choices rather than defaulting to action-dominant training.
authors: Haitao Shen, Hanyu Liu, Yihan Lin, Huiping Liu, Junbo Cui, Daoheng Li, Yang Li, Jing Zhang, Wenxin Li, Yuan Yao
bullets: The study questions the default assumption that robot policies should primarily predict actions.
A unified framework uses a two-stream multimodal diffusion transformer and a sample-level router to allocate examples between action and auxiliary objectives.
It evaluates three latent-action targets and three future-vision targets across LIBERO, CALVIN, and four real-robot tasks.
Suitable auxiliary supervision outperforms action-only training, even when action prediction receives at most half the samples; future-vision generally performs best.
DINO-based latent-action targets emphasize relative motion, while future-vision targets emphasize absolute position and task identity.
papers.selection_reason: Rethinks VLA supervision by trading action prediction against latent-action and future-vision world-model objectives.
papers.title: What Should Robot Policies Learn to Predict? Rethinking Supervision Targets in Vision-Language-Action Learning
papers.tldr: Under a fixed training budget, explicitly allocating samples to auxiliary latent-action or future-vision prediction can improve vision-language-action robot policies over action-only supervision.

papers.abstract: Understanding the objectives that drive agents' behavior is crucial in strategic environments, where multiple agents interact and adapt to one another. This challenge arises in domains such as cybersecurity, autonomous driving, and online markets, where agents' underlying incentives are typically unknown and must be inferred from their observed behavior. Inverse reinforcement learning (IRL) provides a natural framework for this problem, but extending IRL to strategic multi-agent settings introduces a fundamental challenge: a reward that explains observed behavior does not necessarily induce optimal strategies when used for decision-making. In this work, we study this problem through the lens of \emph{strategic identifiability}, and show that learning from a fixed policy pair can be insufficient to strategically identify rewards, independent of the number of expert samples $K$. Motivated by this, we introduce an active IRL algorithm for two-player repeated Stackelberg games, in which the leader adaptively selects policies to elicit informative responses about the follower's reward. Combining maximum-likelihood estimation with experimental design, we derive finite-sample guarantees on the Stackelberg sub-optimality induced by the learned reward, matching up to polylogarithmic factors a new minimax learning rate of $K^{-1/2}$. Finally, we evaluate our approach in a realistic anti-poaching setting, demonstrating the benefits of active exploration for reward recovery and downstream strategic performance.
authors: Antoine Bergerault, Cyrille Kone, Giorgia Ramponi
bullets: Strategic multi-agent IRL is challenging because rewards that explain observed behavior may not produce optimal decisions.
The paper formalizes this issue through strategic identifiability and shows that observing a fixed policy pair may be insufficient, regardless of the number of expert samples.
It introduces an active IRL algorithm for repeated two-player Stackelberg games, combining maximum-likelihood estimation with experimental design.
Finite-sample guarantees achieve a Stackelberg sub-optimality rate matching the minimax rate up to polylogarithmic factors.
Experiments in an anti-poaching setting show benefits from active exploration for reward recovery and strategic performance.
papers.selection_reason: Addresses strategic identifiability in multi-agent settings using active IRL, contributing to the understanding of reward learning and latent action models.
papers.title: Learning Rewards in Strategic Games
papers.tldr: Active inverse reinforcement learning can recover strategically useful rewards in two-player Stackelberg games by adaptively probing an opponent’s responses.

papers.abstract: As Vision-Language Models (VLMs) advance, they are increasingly expected to perform spatiotemporal reasoning over motion, actions, and view changes beyond what the input images show. Video World Models (VWMs) provide a natural unified engine for visual imagination by generating task-relevant visual content as additional evidence. However, existing approaches typically invoke a VWM through fixed pipelines centered on a predefined form of visual imagination, such as novel-view synthesis. To support flexible visual imagination for diverse reasoning tasks, we introduce CoWorld Reasoner, an agentic framework that uses a VWM as a unified visual reasoning engine. Its Video World Model-Driven Harness exposes multiple visual operations through tools and uses skills to guide the VLM in deciding whether to imagine, selecting an operation, constructing a generation request, and interpreting the resulting visual evidence. We further introduce VLM-VWM Harness Co-Evolution, which jointly revises tools, skills, and execution code based on execution feedback while keeping both model weights fixed. Across seven benchmarks spanning spatial intelligence, temporal and causal reasoning, and perceptual reasoning, CoWorld Reasoner outperforms direct reasoning with the same VLM. The strongest variant improves on all seven benchmarks, including relative accuracy gains of 11.8% on MMSI and 13.0% on ERQA, and outperforms all five evolving baselines using the same backbone across five benchmarks.
authors: Dongjie Cheng, Ruifeng Yuan, Ran Wei, Ning Song, Yongqi Li, Wenjie Li
bullets: Addresses the limits of fixed visual-imagination pipelines, such as novel-view synthesis, for diverse reasoning tasks.
Uses tools and skills to help the VLM decide whether and how to imagine, formulate generation requests, and interpret visual evidence.
Introduces co-evolution of tools, skills, and execution code from feedback while keeping model weights fixed.
Improves over direct reasoning with the same VLM across seven spatial, temporal, causal, and perceptual benchmarks.
Reports relative accuracy gains of 11.8% on MMSI and 13.0% on ERQA; the strongest variant outperforms five evolving baselines across five benchmarks.
papers.selection_reason: VWM-driven agentic reasoning for spatiotemporal and spatial tasks fits world models, video understanding, and spatial intelligence.
papers.title: CoWorld Reasoner: Agentic Multimodal Reasoning with the Evolving Video World Model-Driven Harness
papers.tldr: CoWorld Reasoner equips a VLM with an evolving, tool-based video world-model harness for flexible visual imagination and stronger spatiotemporal reasoning.

papers.abstract: Risk-sensitive reinforcement learning (RL) addresses decision-making under uncertainty and adverse outcomes. Learning risk-sensitive policies from fixed datasets is important when additional interaction with the environment is costly. Existing work on risk-sensitive RL focuses on online settings or specific risk measures, leaving a general theoretical understanding of its offline setting underdeveloped. In this work, we investigate efficient offline risk-sensitive RL using the optimized certainty equivalent (OCE), a general class of risk measures. We consider two formulations: dynamic-OCE RL, which applies OCE recursively at each step, and static-OCE RL, which applies a single OCE to the cumulative rewards. Under the tabular setting, we develop pessimistic value-iteration algorithms for both formulations and establish tight sublinear suboptimality bounds, explicitly capturing how risk sensitivity, encoded by utility functions, affects learning difficulty. Moreover, we establish minimax suboptimality lower bounds to characterize the problem's fundamental limits. To handle large state spaces, we further develop pessimistic least-squares value-iteration algorithms that incorporate the general OCE risk criterion into linear function approximation. We establish utility-dependent sublinear guarantees with explicit dependence on the feature dimension $d$. To our knowledge, we provide the first offline algorithms along with the first upper and lower suboptimality bounds for both dynamic- and static-OCE RL.
authors: Hanzhen Wang, Boxiang Lyu, Zhongxiang Dai, Siyang Gao, Dake Zhang, Shuang Qiu
bullets: Addresses offline risk-sensitive RL, where further environment interaction is costly and existing theory is limited beyond specific risk measures.
Studies both dynamic-OCE RL, applying risk recursively, and static-OCE RL, applying one OCE to cumulative rewards.
Proposes pessimistic value-iteration algorithms for tabular problems and pessimistic least-squares value iteration for large state spaces with linear function approximation.
Provides utility-dependent sublinear upper bounds and minimax lower bounds, including explicit effects of risk sensitivity and feature dimension.
Claims the first offline algorithms and upper/lower suboptimality bounds for both dynamic- and static-OCE RL.
papers.selection_reason: Develops offline risk-sensitive RL algorithms using Optimized Certainty Equivalents, contributing to the theory of latent action models and policy learning.
papers.title: Provably Efficient Risk-Sensitive Offline Reinforcement Learning via Optimized Certainty Equivalents
papers.tldr: This work develops provably efficient offline RL methods for general OCE-based risk-sensitive objectives, with matching-style guarantees in tabular and linear-function-approximation settings.

papers.abstract: Sky-image irradiance forecasting is dominated by a two-stage design: a video-prediction model forecasts future sky frames, and a separately trained regressor maps those frames to irradiance. We propose a single-stage alternative that co-denoises the future sky-image and clear-sky-index sequences in one diffusion process, with an irradiance head that reads a denoised preview of the future sky rather than the noised diffusion state. The forecaster needs no regression stage and runs from sky images and deterministic covariates alone, with no measured irradiance at its input --- the situation at a site with a camera but no pyranometer. On 2023 SIRTA data the model reaches a pooled RMSE of $104.1$~W\,m$^{-2}$ and a skill score of $+0.34$ on the continuous ranked probability score (CRPS) against smart persistence, higher than any of twelve baseline configurations, and retains that skill when retrained on 2021--2022. On the model's own generated frames, a separately trained regressor reaches $150.6$~W\,m$^{-2}$ against the joint head's $104.1$: roughly $46$~W\,m$^{-2}$ that joint training recovers and a cascade discards. Point accuracy is competitive but not best: a deterministic network that also reads measured irradiance attains $97.6$~W\,m$^{-2}$. The model's CRPS skill leads that network's in every sky-condition tertile, by $0.26$ to $0.30$.
bullets: Addresses the limitations of two-stage systems that first generate sky frames and then regress irradiance from them.
Jointly co-denoises future sky-image and clear-sky-index sequences, while an irradiance head uses a denoised future-sky preview.
Requires only sky images and deterministic covariates, enabling deployment at camera-only sites without a pyranometer.
On 2023 SIRTA data, achieves 104.1 W m⁻² RMSE and +0.34 CRPS skill versus smart persistence, outperforming twelve baselines; skill transfers when trained on 2021–2022.

A separately trained regressor on the model’s frames obtains 150.6 W m⁻² versus 104.1 W m⁻² for the joint head, indicating roughly 46 W m⁻² of recovered accuracy; deterministic irradiance-informed forecasting remains better for point RMSE.
papers.selection_reason: Joint diffusion of future sky images and irradiance; directly fits video world models and future video prediction.
papers.title: Single-stage joint diffusion of sky images and clear-sky index for ultra-short-term irradiance forecasting: what the frame-to-irradiance stage discards
papers.tldr: A single-stage diffusion model jointly forecasts future sky images and irradiance, recovering information that cascaded frame-to-irradiance pipelines discard and achieving strong probabilistic forecasting without measured irradiance inputs.

papers.abstract: Reliable contact-rich manipulation requires detecting execution deviations early enough for corrective action. Yet most monitoring methods are reactive, identifying anomalies only after they become observable. Anticipating such anomalies is challenging because visual observations only partially reveal physical interaction, while planned actions describe intended motion rather than their actual physical consequences. We address this problem with MAIA, a multimodal framework for anomaly anticipation. Its vision-action-force world model learns nominal interaction dynamics and predicts the visual and force responses of planned actions, while a lightweight anomaly head predicts impending interaction anomalies. To enable systematic evaluation, we introduce CRIA, a real-world multimodal dataset of 2,852 trajectories spanning 18 contact-rich manipulation tasks, with frame-level annotations of anomaly onset and evolution. Experiments on both seen and novel tasks show that MAIA achieves more accurate anomaly discrimination than representative baselines while providing earlier warnings, with bACC scores of 0.765 and 0.710 and median anticipation lead times of 28.0 and 25.1 steps, respectively. Moreover, using these predictions for anomaly-aware action selection improves end-to-end task success from 52.6% to 61.5% without retraining the underlying manipulation policy. These results highlight the value of modeling future physical consequences for proactive anomaly anticipation.
authors: Yi Qiao, Maolin Zheng, Haoran Sun, Lujia Dong, Wenzhao Lian
bullets: Reactive monitors detect anomalies too late, while vision alone cannot fully reveal physical interactions.
MAIA uses a vision-action-force world model to predict planned-action outcomes and a lightweight head to anticipate anomalies.
CRIA provides 2,852 real-world trajectories across 18 contact-rich tasks with frame-level anomaly annotations.
On seen and novel tasks, MAIA achieves bACC scores of 0.765 and 0.710 with median warnings 28.0 and 25.1 steps early.
Anomaly-aware action selection raises end-to-end success from 52.6% to 61.5% without policy retraining.
papers.selection_reason: Action-conditioned multimodal world model for anticipating anomalies in contact-rich manipulation.
papers.title: MAIA: Anticipating Interaction Anomalies in Contact-Rich Manipulation via Multimodal World Models
papers.tldr: MAIA anticipates contact-rich manipulation anomalies by modeling future visual and force consequences, enabling earlier warnings and improving task success without retraining the manipulation policy.

papers.abstract: Learning intrinsic dynamics---the relationship between actions and their consequences---is essential for world models. However, visual variations unrelated to the underlying control process can obscure this relationship in learned representations. We investigate the connection between action predictability, defined as the ability to reconstruct an action from consecutive latent states, and the preservation of intrinsic dynamics. Our central hypothesis is that encouraging action predictability discourages representations from discarding the distinctions between different actions and their consequences. We provide two complementary forms of evidence for this connection. Theoretically, we derive a positive lower bound on squared inverse prediction error when the encoder merges distinguishable outcomes of different actions from the same state and appearance, and show that forward prediction can still be exact on those transitions. Empirically, controlled appearance-diversity comparisons, supervision interventions, and latent probes support the role of action prediction in preserving control-relevant transition information. We instantiate action predictability with Concat IDM, which predicts actions from concatenated latent states and updates the shared encoder using action labels already available in offline trajectories, without changing the test-time planner. Across three independent training runs on Push-T with 24 appearances, Concat IDM increases planning success from 9.1% to 77.2%; its paired improvement is 52.9 percentage points larger than that observed with a single appearance. Together, these findings support action predictability as an inductive bias toward intrinsic dynamics and demonstrate the practical benefits of Concat IDM for latent planning under visual diversity.
authors: Jiamin Shi, Yuanhong Zhang, Zhiyang Liu, Jiawei Sun, Jingwen Fu
bullets: Visual changes unrelated to control can cause representations to discard distinctions between actions and their consequences.
The paper links reconstructing actions from consecutive latent states to preserving intrinsic dynamics, with theoretical and empirical support.
Concat IDM predicts actions from concatenated latent states and trains the shared encoder using action labels from offline trajectories.
On Push-T with 24 appearances, Concat IDM raises planning success from 9.1% to 77.2%; the reported gain is larger than with a single appearance.
Scope: evidence focuses on latent planning under visual diversity and the Push-T evaluation setting.
papers.selection_reason: Directly studies latent world models, action predictability, and control-relevant latent dynamics for planning.
papers.title: Learning Intrinsic Dynamics in Latent World Models
papers.tldr: Action-predictability training helps latent world models preserve control-relevant dynamics despite distracting visual variation, substantially improving planning under visual diversity.

papers.abstract: Neural PDE solvers commonly generate multi-step predictions through autoregressive rollout, recursively applying a learned evolution operator and feeding each prediction back as input for the next step. Approximation errors can therefore propagate through the rollout, causing predictions at a shared target time to depend on their temporal origins and rollout depths. For a well-posed deterministic PDE flow, however, states at different times along the same physical trajectory should, under exact evolution, reach the same target state. To this end, we propose Align Latent Rollout (ALR), a regularization approach that promotes consistency across rollout origins through the neural PDE solver's internal representations. A second-order Taylor analysis of latent discrepancy propagation motivates two objectives: zeroth-order latent state consistency, which aligns representations at a shared target time, and first-order latent dynamics consistency, which aligns local evolution responses to shared perturbations. ALR can be integrated into different neural PDE solvers by regularizing suitable internal representations, without modifying their backbone architectures. Experiments across multiple PDE benchmarks and neural-operator backbones show that ALR improves prediction accuracy while reducing shared-target discrepancies across rollout origins.
authors: Xinying Li, Jing Xu, Wenjun Wang, Limei Han, Fenglei Cao, Ruoxi Jiang, Yuan Qi
bullets: Autoregressive rollout errors can make predictions at one target time depend on their starting time and rollout depth.
ALR aligns internal representations across rollout origins without changing the solver backbone.
It uses zeroth-order latent-state consistency and first-order latent-dynamics consistency objectives.
Experiments across multiple PDE benchmarks and neural-operator backbones report improved accuracy and reduced shared-target discrepancies.
papers.selection_reason: Latent rollout consistency for autoregressive dynamics emulation is transferable to world-model training.
papers.title: Same Target, Different Origins: Aligning Latent Rollout for Consistent PDE Emulation
papers.tldr: ALR regularizes latent representations so PDE rollouts from different temporal origins agree at the same target time, improving accuracy and consistency.

papers.abstract: Predicting cost in a multi-agent world model moves most constrained policy updates into imagination: the stronger model-free baseline needs $10$ to $20$ times CA-MAMBA's interactions on the median SMAC configuration, and CA-MAMBA earns $2.8$ to $12$ times the baselines' MAMuJoCo reward at equal budget. In controlled tests on one task per benchmark, pricing the model's cost advantages at parity more than halves a cost-blind learner's cost and meets a tight continuous-control limit the learned multiplier misses, suggesting the model's cost estimates are not the bottleneck.
bullets: Moves most constrained policy updates into imagination using a multi-agent world model.
Requires 10–20× fewer interactions than a stronger model-free baseline on median SMAC configurations.
Achieves 2.8–12× the baselines’ MAMuJoCo reward at equal interaction budgets.
Cost-aware pricing more than halves a cost-blind learner’s cost in controlled benchmark tests.
On one task per benchmark, learned cost estimates meet a tight continuous-control limit, indicating cost prediction is not the main bottleneck.
papers.selection_reason: Multi-agent RL with a world model for constrained policy updates; relevant to world models and robot learning.
papers.title: Constrained Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning in Imagination
papers.tldr: CA-MAMBA uses imagined cost predictions to make constrained multi-agent policy learning far more interaction-efficient and achieve stronger reward under equal budgets.

papers.abstract: Dynamic Gaussian representations have made high-quality, real-time volumetric video increasingly practical, yet challenging motion can still break their reconstruction: small fast-moving objects may disappear, and fine textures in highly dynamic regions are often lost. In particular, simply training longer or using more Gaussians may still fail to recover small, fast-moving objects. We argue that the key bottleneck is not representational capacity itself, but where and when Gaussian primitives are allocated. Existing allocation strategies rely on current Gaussian locations and often overlook the spatiotemporal destinations of relocated Gaussians. To address these limitations, we introduce two complementary strategies. First, Seed Injection identifies under-reconstructed dynamic regions using temporal appearance changes and reconstruction errors, and initializes new Gaussians at geometrically plausible 3D locations through multi-view observations, independent of existing Gaussian locations. Second, Temporal Biased Relocation uses time-resolved optimization signals to guide the spatiotemporal placement of relocated Gaussians. Both strategies maintain a fixed Gaussian budget without modifying the underlying representation. Experiments across multiple dynamic-scene datasets demonstrate improved reconstruction quality, particularly in highly dynamic regions, recovering small, rapidly moving objects and fine-grained appearance details.
authors: Minhyeok Roh, Minseo Lee, Jun Young Jeong, Byeonghyeon Lee, Lucas Yunkyu Lee, Jaesik Park, Eunbyung Park
bullets: Small, fast-moving objects and fine textures can remain unreconstructed despite longer training or more Gaussians.
The work identifies Gaussian placement across space and time—not capacity—as the key bottleneck.
Seed Injection adds Gaussians to under-reconstructed dynamic regions using temporal changes, errors, and multi-view geometry.
Temporal Biased Relocation guides moved Gaussians using time-resolved optimization signals and their spatiotemporal destinations.
Experiments on multiple dynamic-scene datasets show better reconstruction, especially for rapidly moving objects and fine details.
papers.selection_reason: Addresses the representation of dynamic content in volumetric video using Gaussian primitives. This work on dynamic scene representation and allocation is directly relevant to learning and predicting environment dynamics in video world models.
papers.title: Dusting the Phantom: Gaussian Allocation for Fading Dynamic Content
papers.tldr: A fixed-budget Gaussian allocation strategy improves dynamic volumetric video reconstruction by placing primitives where challenging motion and fine detail require them.

papers.abstract: Code world models represent world dynamics through explicit state and executable rules. We investigate how to coordinate object representations, behavioral revisions, and visual memory within this formulation. We present Mallea, a system for building, steering, and memorizing worlds from text. A coding agent infers object interaction requirements from the prompt and jointly plans object structure, properties, and rules, favoring compact representations that support those requirements. The world evolves under the planned rules; optional user actions steer it, while text requests can edit properties or extend capabilities with unaffected state preserved. Object texture memory retains reusable appearance only for whitebox-defined objects and adapts it as those objects change. The program advances world state, while a generative renderer combines current structure with remembered appearance. By organizing construction, intervention, and memory around the same objects, Mallea conditions subsequent observations on the latest state and compatible appearance. Project page: https://lxycopper.github.io/Mallea.
authors: Xuanyi Liu, Ruiqi Li, Siwei Ma
bullets: Represents world dynamics with explicit object states and executable interaction rules.
Infers object requirements from prompts and jointly plans compact structures, properties, and behaviors.
Supports user interventions and text-based edits while preserving unaffected world state.
Maintains reusable texture memory for whitebox-defined objects and updates it as they change.
Renders each evolving world by combining its current structure with remembered appearance.
papers.selection_reason: Code world models with user steering and object memory fit interactive world model interests.
papers.title: Mallea: Building, Steering, and Memorizing Worlds with Coding Agent
papers.tldr: Mallea uses a coding agent to construct, steer, revise, and visually remember executable code-based worlds from text.

papers.abstract: World and action modeling are closely related, yet their reciprocal benefits under unified causal training remain unclear. We introduce OneWM, a simple framework for unified causal training that treats actions as both conditions for world prediction and targets for policy learning within a shared video-action architecture. Using this framework, we investigate whether learning forward dynamics conditioned on specified actions improves action learning, and whether learning to generate actions in turn improves action-conditioned world modeling. We use LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, and RoboCasa365 as embodied testbeds to evaluate both policy learning and world modeling, complemented by real-world policy experiments. Learning the visual consequences of specified actions improves policy performance and generalization across changing scenes. In turn, action learning improves multi-view world-prediction fidelity under the same architecture. Together, these results answer both questions positively, supporting reciprocal benefits between world modeling and action generation under unified causal training.
authors: Yue Su, Bokai Lin, Xinkai Wang, Chubin Zhang, Xiangnan Wu, Kuan Zhang, Weiyang Jin, Jiwen Yu, Yiming Li, Cewu Lu, Lixin Yang, Xihui Liu
bullets: Unifies world modeling and policy learning in a shared video-action architecture.
Treats actions as conditions for predicting future worlds and as targets for learning policies.
Evaluates policy learning and world modeling on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, RoboCasa365, and real-world experiments.
Action-conditioned dynamics improve policy performance and generalization across changing scenes.
Action learning improves multi-view world-prediction fidelity, indicating reciprocal benefits.
papers.selection_reason: Unified causal training of action-conditioned world prediction and policy learning; directly bridges world models and embodied robot learning.
papers.title: Can World and Action Modeling Benefit Each Other under Unified Causal Training?
papers.tldr: OneWM shows that jointly learning action-conditioned world dynamics and action generation benefits both policy learning and world modeling.

papers.abstract: Learned dynamical models can accurately predict trajectories while producing unreliable sensitivities when differentiated or transposed, limiting their use in inverse problems and scientific decision-making. Classical adjoints provide exact local derivatives, but a single adjoint cannot represent the nonlinear response of a system to a family of finite-amplitude perturbations. We introduce SALTO (Solver-Anchored Lifted Transfer Operators), a Koopman-based framework for inferring finite-amplitude sources. In the lifted space, the nonlinear dynamics are approximated by a linear propagator, and its transpose carries each sensor backward in a single solve. The result is a reusable lifted adjoint that predicts the measurement produced by any candidate localized event with one encoder pass and an inner product. To give the model the simulator's exact local behavior, SALTO imposes three structural constraints: it anchors the physical-state dynamics to the simulator's linearized propagator, centers the learned observables so that they vanish to second order at the reference state, and uses a block-triangular lifted propagator. These constraints guarantee that the model reduces to the simulator's tangent dynamics and classical adjoint as the amplitude vanishes, while the learned observables carry only the finite-amplitude correction. On three nonlinear PDE systems, SALTO predicts the measurements of finite-amplitude sources to within 2-8% where the classical adjoint is in error by 41-165%, recovers source position and intensity from sparse sensors nearly as accurately as inversion through the solver, and samples the joint posterior of two interacting sources, matching the solver's posterior on reaction-diffusion at a twentieth of its cost. One trained model serves new sensor layouts and measurement times with a single backward solve.
bullets: Addresses unreliable sensitivities from learned dynamical models and the limited nonlinear coverage of classical adjoints.
Uses a lifted linear propagator whose transpose enables reusable backward sensor propagation for candidate events.
Anchors physical-state dynamics to the simulator linearization, centers observables to second order, and enforces block-triangular structure.
On three nonlinear PDE systems, finite-amplitude measurement errors were 2–8% versus 41–165% for classical adjoints.
Recovers sparse-sensor source properties and joint posteriors at substantially lower cost, with one model supporting new sensors and measurement times.
papers.selection_reason: Learned Koopman dynamics model for nonlinear systems; relevant to world models as predictors of environment dynamics.
papers.title: SALTO: Solver-Anchored Lifted Transfer Operators for Nonlinear Event Inference
papers.tldr: SALTO combines solver-anchored local dynamics with learned Koopman observables to efficiently infer finite-amplitude events while retaining exact small-perturbation behavior.

papers.abstract: Generative gameplay requires more than immediate responses to player actions.Actions should have persistent consequences, while the generated world should act according to its own state and rules, shaping the player's situation and subsequent choices. Video generation captures local dynamics, but limited history, partially observed game state, and the need for contextual behavior decisions make such interactions difficult to sustain through audiovisual prediction alone. We introduce \rig (Reciprocally Interactive Generation), a framework for reciprocal interaction in generative gameplay. \rig combines persistent state and configurable rules, contextual interaction reasoning, and action-conditioned audiovisual generation. Together, these components make interaction consequences and actor behavior jointly determine generated content while maintaining consistency between game state and visible outcomes. We construct a Xonotic gameplay dataset to train an audiovisual generator for learning dynamics and interactions. Further post-training enables \rigarena, an interactive generative first-person shooter (FPS) prototype. Experiments demonstrate more reliable combat outcomes and reciprocal interaction between the player and the generated world. Project page: https://murphylmf.github.io/RIGen/.
authors: Mengfei Li, Yi Zhang, Xingtong Ge, Lunjie Zhu, Fangyu Lin, Peng Li, Guanglu Song, Yu Liu, Wei Xue, Wenhan Luo, Yike Guo
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of sustaining reciprocal, context-aware interactions through audiovisual prediction alone.
Combines persistent state and configurable rules with contextual reasoning and action-conditioned audiovisual generation.
Uses a Xonotic gameplay dataset to train an audiovisual generator for learning game dynamics and interactions.
Introduces RIGArena, an interactive generative FPS prototype created through further post-training.
Experiments report more reliable combat outcomes and stronger reciprocal interaction between the player and generated world.
papers.selection_reason: Action-conditioned generative gameplay with persistent state and reciprocal interaction directly fits interactive world models and video world models.
papers.title: RIGen: Beyond Action Following with Reciprocal Interaction in Generative Gameplay
papers.tldr: RIGen enables generative gameplay where player actions have persistent consequences and the generated world responds according to its own state and rules.

papers.abstract: Humans interpret multimodal observations of the world and forecast how it will evolve. Recent multimodal generative systems have demonstrated similar capabilities: they can integrate multimodal context and synthesize visual outputs that depict changes in the world. To characterize this emerging trajectory, we organize model capabilities into a four-level hierarchy and discover that higher-level tasks remain relatively underexplored despite model progress. To bridge this gap, we explore model performance on multi-step world state prediction, a high-level task that requires models to forecast successive future world states from multimodal observations and diverse references. Such a task requires models to possess entangled understanding and generation capabilities, as well as extensive world knowledge to translate human action sequences, physical transformations, and abstract visual reasoning into coherent visual outputs. We introduce WorldCast, a benchmark comprising 320 manually designed cases across eight categories, and evaluate 12 representative models. The conducted experiments yield three key insights: (a) advances in frontier models are rapidly pushing the boundaries of intelligent world modeling, with the GPT-Image-2.5 System scoring 72.8 and demonstrating early-stage visual state prediction capabilities on real-world tasks; (b) WorldCast reveals substantial gaps between models: even Nano Banana Pro reaches only 42.8 and the best open-source model scores 20.1, with deficits in handling complex context, entangled references, and reasoning-heavy tasks; (c) strong generative models effectively draw on the capabilities of their underlying language models. These findings highlight the need for multimodal generative models that are capable of dynamic planning and reasoning while also being deeply unified to faithfully simulate real-world states.
authors: Wenhao Yan, Haodong Li, Xiaotong Li, Yaxin Luo, Zhengrong Yue, Jialv Zou, Xu Huang, Haojin Yang, Nan Jia, Yan Feng, Peng Pei, Xunliang Cai
bullets: Organizes visual world-modeling capabilities into a four-level hierarchy and identifies high-level prediction as underexplored.
Introduces 320 manually designed cases across eight categories to evaluate multi-step world state prediction.
Evaluates 12 representative models, finding large performance differences and weaknesses in complex-context, reference-entangled, and reasoning-heavy tasks.
Reports early promising capabilities from frontier models, while open-source systems remain substantially behind.
Finds that strong visual generators benefit from the capabilities of their underlying language models.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmark and evaluation of multimodal generative models for multi-step world state prediction, directly relevant to world modeling.
papers.title: WorldCast: Exploring Intelligent Visual Generation in World State Prediction
papers.tldr: WorldCast benchmarks how well multimodal generative models can predict successive future world states from complex observations and references, revealing strong progress but major reasoning and planning gaps.

papers.abstract: Video generators serve as interactive worlds for exploration and simulation, yet realistic and visually appealing frames do not necessarily depict a consistent 3D world. Existing benchmarks assess selected geometric properties or use vision-language models to judge memory and consistency, leaving systematic 3D evaluation underexplored. We introduce Orbia, the first benchmark dedicated to a systematic and comprehensive evaluation of 3D consistency in interactive world models. Through controlled exploration and revisit, we organize the evaluation into three dimensions: input preservation, generated-content persistence, and 3D self-consistency. For input preservation, registered RGB-D references and annotated anchors support appearance, geometry, and spatial stability measurements. For generated-content persistence, we compare revisits to regions absent from the input image with their first generated observations to test whether models preserve what they create. For 3D self-consistency, cross-view depth and feature correspondence, regional scale agreement, and held-out Gaussian rendering test whether generated views describe the same 3D scene. Minute-long exploration and revisits further test long-term consistency. Our construction and annotation pipeline brings together public datasets, self-captured scenes, and simulation, yielding 720 instances across indoor and outdoor environments and six exploration-and-revisit protocols. Evaluation spans 27 text-, action-, and camera-conditioned models through native-interface adapters. Our Orbia benchmark provides a systematic basis for diagnosing 3D inconsistency and developing more persistent video world models.
authors: Dongyue Lu, Guian Fang, Hur Lim, Yonggang Wu, Yanrong Wang, Hongshan Chen, Shengju Qian, Yue Liao, Wei Chow, Lingdong Kong, Tianxin Huang, Yu Yang, Hongji Yang, Junchao Huang, Ao Liang, Yihao Wang, Zihan Wang, Rong Li, Hanlin Chen, Xin Wang, Wei Tsang Ooi, Mike Zheng Shou, Shuicheng Yan
bullets: Evaluates three dimensions: input preservation, generated-content persistence, and 3D self-consistency.
Uses RGB-D references, annotated anchors, cross-view geometry and features, regional scale agreement, and held-out Gaussian rendering.
Tests both short-term and minute-long consistency through controlled exploration and revisits.
Includes 720 indoor and outdoor instances, six protocols, and evaluations of 27 text-, action-, and camera-conditioned models.
Designed to diagnose 3D inconsistency and support development of more persistent video world models.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmark for 3D consistency of interactive video world models, directly relevant to world models and video-based environment simulation.
papers.title: Orbia: Do Generated Videos Form a Consistent 3D World?
papers.tldr: Orbia is a benchmark for systematically measuring whether interactive video generators maintain a consistent 3D world during exploration and revisits.

papers.abstract: Latent Action Models (LAMs) can capture manipulation priors from action-free videos, but discrete latents usually impose a granularity bottleneck, limiting their ability to represent fine-grained action. Recent continuous alternatives mitigate this, but they are typically used as proxies for world modeling and require a further planning step to produce executable actions. We thus introduce UniLAP, a unified continuous latent-action policy that models the latent space via flow matching and bypasses reliance on future frames during inference. By distilling a LAM teacher with a flow-adaptive objective, UniLAP inherits the teacher's action representation while retaining the multimodal distribution of feasible behaviors. To decouple latent representations from task-irrelevant appearance, we extract a label-free motion target to isolate relevant kinematic cues from spurious visual dynamics. With the established embodiment-agnostic latent manifold, UniLAP can be easily adapted to novel platforms. Pretrained on multi-source videos at a compact 1.1B parameter scale, UniLAP outperforms state-of-the-art latent-action and Vision-Language-Action (VLA) baselines across hand pose forecasting, single-arm and humanoid manipulation, and real-world deployment.
bullets: Addresses the granularity limits of discrete latent actions and the extra planning required by continuous world-modeling approaches.
Uses flow matching to model continuous latent actions and distills a latent action model teacher with a flow-adaptive objective.
Extracts label-free motion targets to separate task-relevant kinematics from task-irrelevant appearance.
Builds an embodiment-agnostic latent manifold that adapts to new robotic platforms.
At 1.1B parameters, outperforms latent-action and VLA baselines across pose forecasting, single-arm and humanoid manipulation, and real-world deployment.
papers.selection_reason: Continuous latent-action policy for cross-embodiment manipulation, distilling a latent action model; robot learning and latent action modeling.
papers.title: UniLAP: A Unified Latent Action Policy for Cross-Embodiment Manipulation
papers.tldr: UniLAP learns a continuous, embodiment-agnostic latent-action policy from action-free videos to generate fine-grained manipulation actions without future-frame planning.

papers.abstract: World models, which learn how environments respond to actions, are emerging as a powerful paradigm for planning through imagined futures, transforming decision-making across games, robotics and autonomous driving. Bringing this capability to manufacturing could enable process decisions on timescales inaccessible to high-fidelity simulation. Here we introduce a generative world model for localized highly dynamic laser melt pool that predicts evolution from histories of temperature and phase morphology under candidate actions. Its generative latent dynamics capture the effects of unresolved melt flow, enabling more accurate recursive rollouts than deterministic regressors under transient laser inputs. Because the learned dynamics are differentiable, the model can serve directly as a predictive control plant. Gradients through imagined futures optimize laser schedules that regulate melt-pool depth over previously unseen geometry, path, initialization. We further distil this optimization into an amortized policy that produces control actions in a single forward pass, providing a proof of concept for real deployment on machines.
bullets: Addresses the need for manufacturing process decisions faster than high-fidelity simulation allows.
Learns generative latent dynamics from temperature and phase-morphology histories under candidate laser actions.
Models unresolved melt-flow effects and supports more accurate recursive rollouts than deterministic regressors during transient inputs.
Uses differentiable imagined futures to optimize laser schedules for unseen geometries, paths, and initializations.
Distils optimization into a single-pass policy, offering a proof of concept for real-time machine deployment.
papers.selection_reason: Action-conditioned generative world model for laser melt-pool dynamics used as predictive control plant.
papers.title: Generative World Models Enable Predictive Control of Laser Melt Pool Dynamics
papers.tldr: A generative world model predicts laser melt-pool dynamics and enables fast, gradient-based control of melt-pool depth under new conditions.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models are gaining attention in autonomous driving, inheriting commonsense priors from large language models (LLMs) and widening the navigation interface from a fixed command set to free-form natural-language instructions. However, this open-ended interface exposes a new vulnerability surface: an inattentive driver may issue instructions that are unsafe given the current scene, and a malicious user may issue dangerous ones on purpose. We present the first benchmark suite that evaluates navigation following and conflict awareness together, along with adversarial robustness. Existing VLAs fall short on both: SimLingo completes no language-instructed lane change in closed loop, and all models degrade sharply under conflicting signals. We propose SafeDriveVLA, the first driving VLA that (1) explicitly predicts a three-level navigation-compliance mode to decouple conflict reasoning from action generation, and (2) uses navigation-conditioned world model dreaming to inform this prediction. Unlike prior world models that roll out expert or planned actions, ours dreams of strictly following the navigation signal, showing when following is safe. SafeDriveVLA reaches 88.16 Driving Score (DS) and 68.64% Success Rate (SR) on Bench2Drive, lifts closed-loop language following by 49.3% and reduces collisions under unsafe instructions from 60 to 38 compared to the best SimLingo variant. Video demonstrations are available on our project page.
authors: Shaoyuan Xie, Zihan Zhang, Jingxuan Wang, Jiashu Qu, Xiaoqing Liang, Lingdong Kong, Junchi Lu, Henrik I. Christensen, Qi Alfred Chen
bullets: Introduces a benchmark jointly evaluating navigation following, conflict awareness, and adversarial robustness.
Predicts three navigation-compliance modes to separate conflict reasoning from action generation.
Uses navigation-conditioned world-model rollouts that simulate strictly following instructions to assess their safety.
Achieves 88.16 Driving Score and 68.64% Success Rate on Bench2Drive.
Improves closed-loop language following by 49.3% and reduces collisions under unsafe instructions from 60 to 38 versus the best SimLingo variant.
papers.selection_reason: VLA for autonomous driving with navigation-conditioned world model dreaming; directly fits vision-language-action and interactive world models.
papers.title: SafeDriveVLA: Navigation-Conditioned World Model Dreaming for Conflict-Aware End-to-End Autonomous Driving
papers.tldr: SafeDriveVLA improves autonomous driving safety by reasoning about whether natural-language navigation instructions are safe to follow before generating actions.

papers.abstract: World-action models aim to turn visual anticipation into driving decisions, yet typically train action experts on trajectory representations defined independently of visual dynamics. This motivates deriving action targets directly from visual motion. We first examine a simpler setting in which trajectories are reconstructed from recorded future images. Even without the need for future prediction, reconstruction captures the dominant maneuver but leaves centimeter-scale errors. We therefore introduce VITAL (Vision-Induced Tokens for Action Learning), an action tokenizer that couples a visually derived motion scaffold with a compact residual encoding the trajectory error left by that scaffold. This representation makes visual motion the principal prediction target and gives small metric corrections a separate, normalized learning scale. Using flow matching, the action expert jointly predicts both components from the current image, ego state, and navigation command, without generating future images at inference. The same residual coordinates support bounded reinforcement post-training that refines execution while keeping the predicted visual scaffold fixed. With only one action denoising step, VITAL achieves 90.8 PDMS on NAVSIM v1 navtest, within 0.13 points of its ten-step score at 3.29x the end-to-end inference speed. Without retraining, it achieves 91.1 EPDMS on NAVSIM v2 navtest and 38.6 on navhard. Project page: https://worldbench.github.io/vital
authors: Ao Liang, Youquan Liu, Mingxiao Li, Wei Chow, Lingdong Kong, Yue Liao, Dongyue Lu, Yu Yang, Wei Yin, Runnan Chen
bullets: Addresses trajectory errors caused by action representations that are disconnected from visual dynamics.
Uses a visually derived motion scaffold plus a compact residual encoding for centimeter-scale corrections.
A flow-matching action expert predicts both components from the current image, ego state, and navigation command.
Supports bounded reinforcement post-training that refines execution while keeping the visual scaffold fixed.
Reaches 90.8 PDMS on NAVSIM v1 with one denoising step, near its ten-step score at 3.29× higher end-to-end speed; also reports 91.1 EPDMS on NAVSIM v2 and 38.6 on navhard.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces VITAL, an action tokenizer that couples visual motion scaffolds with residual trajectory error encodings. This bridges visual dynamics and action planning, offering a novel approach to world-action models and latent action representations.
papers.title: VITAL: From Visual Motion to Precise Action
papers.tldr: VITAL derives action representations from visual motion and adds normalized residual corrections, enabling fast, precise driving decisions without predicting future images.

papers.abstract: Existing geometry-aware Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) increasingly rely on external 3D encoders to provide structural priors, but executing these additional encoder paths at inference introduces substantial latency and computational overhead. We propose GeoThinker-$F$, an efficient framework that internalizes spatiotemporal perception by transforming causal MLLM hidden states into predictive latent world representations. Our key insight is that intermediate semantic representations contain sufficient information to predict useful representations of current geometry and future semantics, without requiring an exact reproduction of features from a dedicated 3D encoder. To realize this idea, GeoThinker-$F$ adopts a decoupled two-stage training strategy. In the first stage, the MLLM backbone is frozen while lightweight Latent Frame Prediction (LFP) heads learn from an offline 3D geometry expert and next-frame semantic targets. In the second stage, the external expert is removed, and the model is jointly optimized to generate and selectively integrate its self-predicted priors through a specialized Spatial-Grounded Temporal (SGT) Fusion module. Extensive evaluations show that GeoThinker-$F$ eliminates runtime dependence on external 3D geometry encoders while maintaining competitive performance across diverse spatial intelligence benchmarks. It achieves up to a $3.6\times$ inference speedup, reducing latency from $1.45\,\mathrm{s}$ to $0.40\,\mathrm{s}$ while retaining strong spatial reasoning performance.
authors: Haoyuan Li, Qihang Cao, Huanyuan Zhou, Xin Hu, Sijia Chen, Zihan Guo, Kun Xiang, Yunshuang Nie, Tao Tang, Xinlong Zheng, Jia-Wang Bian, Xianming Liu, Xiaodan Liang
bullets: Addresses the latency and computational overhead caused by external 3D geometry encoders in geometry-aware MLLMs.
Transforms intermediate MLLM hidden states into predictive representations of current geometry and future semantics.
Uses two-stage training: lightweight latent frame prediction heads first learn from geometry and next-frame semantic targets, then the external expert is removed during joint optimization.
Introduces Spatial-Grounded Temporal Fusion to selectively integrate self-predicted spatial-temporal priors.
Reports latency reduction from 1.45 s to 0.40 s while retaining competitive performance across diverse spatial intelligence benchmarks.
papers.selection_reason: Geometry-aware MLLM with predictive world representations and faster spatial intelligence inference.
papers.title: GeoThinker-$F$: Endogenous Predictive World Representations for Fast Spatial Intelligence
papers.tldr: GeoThinker-F internalizes spatial and temporal world representations in an MLLM, removing external 3D encoders and achieving up to 3.6× faster inference while maintaining strong spatial reasoning.

papers.abstract: Long-form agentic video generation must turn a screenplay into shots that remain spatially and temporally consistent across nonconsecutive requests. Passing prompts or recent frames between shots does not provide a shared spatial frame for revisiting a scene or a time-indexed record for replaying an earlier event. We present Any Time, Any Space (ATAS), which compiles a screenplay into shot requests with explicit location, camera, and event-time references. Before generation, it retrieves relevant evidence from a scene memory of registered static geometry and an event memory of dynamic observations indexed by scene, event, and time. After generation, ATAS reconstructs and registers the clip. It updates memory only when review and state checks accept the observation, while film delivery remains independent of memory admission. Across four video generators, ATAS improves all reported cross-shot consistency measures and achieves the highest aggregate benchmark score for each backbone. It also outperforms the compared agents and 3D-guided methods on target-image spatial revisit, leads three event-recapture criteria, and receives the highest human ratings on all six criteria. The video results and code are available on our project page: https://lhmd.top/atas/.
authors: Weijie Wang, Haomin Zhang, Ye Li, Akide Liu, Zeyu Zhang, Haoyu Zhao, Yefei He, Donny Y. Chen, Feng Chen, Bohan Zhuang
bullets: Addresses the lack of shared spatial and time-indexed state when generating nonconsecutive shots.
Compiles screenplays into shot requests with explicit location, camera, and event-time references.
Retrieves evidence from static scene memory and dynamic event memory before generation, then reconstructs and registers generated clips.
Admits new memory only after review and state checks, while keeping film delivery independent of memory updates.
Improves reported cross-shot consistency across four video generators and receives the highest human ratings on all six criteria.
papers.selection_reason: World-state-centric memory framework for long-form agentic video generation.
papers.title: Any Time, Any Space: A World-State-Centric Framework for Agentic Video Generation
papers.tldr: ATAS enables long-form agentic video generation with consistent spatial revisits and temporal event recapture by maintaining structured scene and event memories.

papers.abstract: Foundation models are driving a paradigm shift in robotic intelligence, moving beyond low-level action prediction to goal-directed orchestration of data collection, model training, task planning, and real-world execution. We characterize this emerging paradigm as an agentic robots, in which agents reason over human instructions, interact with robotic environments, rectify execution errors autonomously, and dynamically adjust operational strategies. Although this field develops fast, current studies are not well connected. Researchers have no consistent view of how to combine different agentic functions into a complete robot system. This paper provides a unified overview of existing research on agentic robots. We first trace the development from robot policies to agentic systems, covering vision-language-action models, world models, and world-action models. We then clarify the definition and scope of agentic robots and organize existing research into seventeen categories across four functional domains: Model, Data, Environment, and Harness. Across these domains, we examine how agents shape model learning and robot decisions, collect and curate robot data, construct worlds, tasks, and tests for learning and evaluation, and organize capabilities for robot use. Finally, we discuss open challenges and outline directions for future research. Looking forward, we hope this work contributes to a clearer understanding of agentic robots and supports new approaches to making them more capable, reliable, and adaptive.
authors: Chonghan Qin, Dongming Wu, Kaituo Feng, Jiaxu Wang, Xinlei Yu, Peiwen Sun, Yijia Fan, Xilin He, Bingao Chen, Weitong Lian, Ryan Ji, Wenqi Ren, Xiaobin Hu, Dahua Lin, Yu-Gang Jiang, Xiangyu Yue
bullets: Motivation: Existing studies are rapidly expanding but lack a consistent framework for integrating agentic functions into complete robot systems.
The paper traces the evolution from robot policies to vision-language-action, world, and world-action models.
It organizes research into 17 categories across four domains: Model, Data, Environment, and Harness.
The survey covers agent-driven learning, data collection, world and task construction, evaluation, and capability orchestration.
It identifies open challenges and future directions toward more capable, reliable, and adaptive robots.
papers.selection_reason: Unified overview of agentic robots covering VLA, world models, and world-action models.
papers.title: Towards Agentic Robots: Model, Data, Environment, and Harness
papers.tldr: This paper unifies emerging research on agentic robots—systems that reason, learn, plan, act, and autonomously adapt in real-world environments.

papers.abstract: Agents for mixed-degradation image restoration typically learn what a tool does to an image only after running it: failed calls waste computation and harmful outputs go unnoticed until too late. We propose PreActIR, an agentic restoration framework that predicts tool consequences before execution. For each candidate tool, a tool-conditioned world model forecasts changes in residual degradation, image quality, and fidelity, together with the risk of harm and the uncertainty of the prediction. The agent executes the top-ranked candidate, and an independent verifier commits or rolls back its output before the agent replans from the observed state. PreActIR also audits whether performance is limited by the selector or by the candidate space, and studies targeted tool adaptation as a controlled way to expand that space. In a controlled evaluation that fixes the candidate pool, verifier, and budget and employs reference-annotated degradation states, PreActIR uses 42.5% fewer real tool calls and 63.4% fewer rejected calls than reactive, execute-then-evaluate trial and error, while improving Y-PSNR by 0.92 dB.
authors: Xu Zhang, Jun Wan, Lefei Zhang, Liangpei Zhang
bullets: Addresses inefficient mixed-degradation restoration agents that discover tool behavior only after acting.
Uses a tool-conditioned world model to predict degradation changes, quality, fidelity, harm risk, and uncertainty.
Ranks candidate tools, then uses an independent verifier to commit or roll back results before replanning.
Audits whether limits come from tool selection or the candidate space and studies targeted tool adaptation.
In controlled evaluation, reduces real tool calls by 42.5% and rejected calls by 63.4%, while improving Y-PSNR by 0.92 dB versus reactive trial and error.
