papers.selection_reason: Proposes a tool-conditioned world model for agentic image restoration that predicts tool consequences before execution, enabling safer and more efficient action planning.
papers.title: Look Before You Restore: Learning to Predict Before Acting for Agentic Image Restoration
papers.tldr: PreActIR predicts each restoration tool’s effects and risks before execution, reducing wasted or harmful calls while improving image quality.

papers.abstract: A multiplayer world model must predict how the independent actions of several players change a shared environment, including changes outside a player's current field of view. A point-of-view (POV) video captures such changes only after they enter its field of view, whereas panoramic video records the surroundings in every viewing direction and has served as an intermediate representation of the world state in recent world models. Learning this task therefore requires synchronized POV and panoramic videos of interacting players together with their actions, yet no existing dataset provides this combination in Minecraft, an established testbed in which players act independently in a shared, modifiable 3D world. We present PAWA, a dataset and framework for action-conditioned panoramic multiplayer world modeling. The dataset pairs each player's POV video with world-stabilized panoramic video and aligned actions. Its distributed pipeline decouples CPU gameplay capture from GPU rendering, scales beyond 64 simultaneous players, and re-renders each recorded session under new observation configurations without replaying the gameplay. On this dataset, we develop a dual-tower model that jointly predicts POV and panoramic video and couples the two streams through cross-attention that aligns tokens observing the same direction in a shared world frame. We further introduce a quadratic-phase player encoding that provides many more player codes than existing rotary codes at the same embedding dimension. Experiments show that PAWA outperforms state-of-the-art multiplayer world models in POV prediction quality while also producing high-fidelity panoramic predictions. The dataset and collection pipeline are open source to support further research on multiplayer world models.
authors: Siqi Yang, Yimu Wang, Ziqi Cai, Chengxuan Zhu, Shuchen Weng, Erwin Wu, Zhaofei Yu, Kaipeng Zhang, Boxin Shi
bullets: Addresses the lack of synchronized multi-player POV, panoramic video, and action data for shared-world modeling.
Pairs each player’s POV video with world-stabilized panoramic video and aligned actions; supports scalable capture and re-rendering under new observation configurations.
Uses a dual-tower predictor with cross-attention to align POV and panoramic tokens viewing the same world direction.
Introduces quadratic-phase player encodings to support more player identities at the same embedding dimension.
Outperforms prior multiplayer world models on POV prediction while generating high-fidelity panoramic predictions; the dataset and pipeline are open source.
papers.selection_reason: Action-conditioned panoramic world modeling for multiple agents, predicting POV and panoramic video from independent actions.
papers.title: PAWA: Panoramic Action-conditioned World Modeling for Multiple Agents
papers.tldr: PAWA introduces a Minecraft dataset and dual-stream world model that predicts both player POVs and panoramic shared-world views from multiple players’ actions.

papers.abstract: Learning world models across diverse domains calls for a unified control space, yet ac- tion interfaces vary across domains and action annotations are often scarce. Latent ac- tions learned directly from videos offer a promising way to establish such a space without explicit action supervision. However, learning shared latent actions across domains re- mains challenging, as variations in appearance, embodiment, and dynamics can entangle domain-specific visual cues with transferable transition structure. To this end, we intro- duce OneLA, a simple framework that learns continuous latent actions through a shared orthogonal dictionary and a common predictive objective, without task-specific designs or cross-domain alignment losses during latent action pretraining. These latent actions pro- vide a shared conditioning interface for world models, with lightweight adapters mapping native control commands into the same space. Conditioned on latent actions and the cur- rent visual state, the world model predicts context-dependent transitions for controllable rollout. OneLA improves action readout across domains and reduces action cycle-transfer rotation error by 24.8% over the strongest evaluated baseline. A joint-training comparison further shows a 20.5% improvement in Human Preference Score v3 (HPSv3) for real- scene generation. These results suggest a path toward general-purpose world models that learn from diverse videos and support flexible control through latent action space.
authors: Ziyu Zhu, Zhaoxu Sun, Fan Jiang, Chiyu Wang, Junfeng Ni, Mu Xu
bullets: Addresses scarce action annotations and domain differences in appearance, embodiment, and dynamics.
Learns continuous latent actions using a shared orthogonal dictionary and common predictive objective, without task-specific designs or cross-domain alignment losses during pretraining.
Uses lightweight adapters to map native controls into the shared latent space for world-model conditioning and controllable rollout.
Improves action readout and reduces action cycle-transfer rotation error by 24.8% over the strongest evaluated baseline.
Joint training improves HPSv3 by 20.5% for real-scene generation.
papers.selection_reason: Learns shared latent actions for world models across domains, enabling action-conditioned rollout and controllable generation.
papers.title: OneLA: Learning Many Worlds from Latent Actions
papers.tldr: OneLA learns a shared latent action space from videos, enabling controllable world models across domains with varied control interfaces.

papers.abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) typically adapt video foundation models to robotic control through joint video and action prediction. However, task-level instructions may leave the next physical interaction underspecified, requiring semantic grounding and state-dependent motion selection. To this end, we introduce Atomic-WAM, an understand-then-execute framework that connects task reasoning to action generation through atomic-motion descriptions. Specifically, a vision-language reasoner describes the next local motion from the task instruction and visual context, guiding a WAM to predict future video and an action chunk. Furthermore, an automatic annotation pipeline curates temporally aligned, contact-enriched supervision from multi-view DROID demonstrations. To make atomic-motion predictions executable by the WAM, we post-train the reasoner with Execution-Grounded GRPO (EG-GRPO). With the WAM fixed, EG-GRPO adapts the reasoner through rewards for motion appropriateness and execution success. Finally, Atomic-WAM achieves 39.6% task success under default instructions and 31.6% under vague instructions in a real-to-sim evaluation on RoboLab. Project page: https://ssj9596.github.io/Atomic-WAM-project
authors: Shijun Shi, Zhe Liu, Zhi Hou, Yinan Chen, Tao Zhang, Kai Hu, Yong Liu, Jiangning Zhang
bullets: Addresses underspecified task instructions that do not clearly specify the next physical interaction.
Uses a vision-language reasoner to infer the next local motion from instructions and visual context, guiding a WAM to predict video and action chunks.
Builds temporally aligned, contact-enriched supervision from multi-view DROID demonstrations.
Introduces Execution-Grounded GRPO to train motion descriptions for appropriateness and execution success while keeping the WAM fixed.
Achieves 39.6% task success with default instructions and 31.6% with vague instructions in RoboLab real-to-sim evaluation.
papers.selection_reason: Execution-grounded atomic-motion reasoning for world action models; directly fits VLA, robot learning, and action-conditioned world/video prediction.
papers.title: Atomic-WAM: Execution-Grounded Atomic-Motion Reasoning for World Action Models
papers.tldr: Atomic-WAM improves robotic action generation by grounding task reasoning in executable atomic-motion descriptions.

papers.abstract: World action models (WAMs) jointly predict future visual states and robot actions, but processing dense future-frame tokens incurs substantial inference latency. We propose CF-Prune, a training-free framework for pruning future-frame tokens in pretrained WAMs. Our key insight is that future visual predictions support action generation and therefore need not preserve every visual detail required for high-fidelity video synthesis. CF-Prune combines instruction and action attention to identify task-relevant tokens during the initial denoising forward pass, even when future-frame and action representations remain highly noisy. An entropy-based phase identification mechanism further retains dense computation during precision phases to mitigate pruning-induced performance degradation. Experiments on RoboLab, RoboCasa, and real-world manipulation tasks demonstrate consistent inference speedups. At a 35% pruning ratio, CF-Prune achieves average speedups of 1.19-1.27x while improving task success rates. At a 50% pruning ratio, it achieves 1.29-1.33x average speedups on both simulation benchmarks, with overall success rates within 1.0 percentage point of the baseline.
authors: Baekseung Kim, Junhoo Lee, Sohyeon Hong, Suhyun Jeon, Minkyu Kim, Seungyeon Kim, Donghoon Han, Nojun Kwak
bullets: Addresses high inference latency from dense future-frame token processing in world action models.
Uses instruction and action attention to identify task-relevant tokens during early denoising, without training.
An entropy-based phase mechanism keeps dense computation during precision-sensitive phases.
At 35% pruning, it delivers 1.19–1.27× speedups while improving task success rates.
At 50% pruning, it reaches 1.29–1.33× speedups on simulation benchmarks with success within 1.0 percentage point of baseline.
papers.selection_reason: Training-free future-frame token pruning for world action models, improving inference efficiency on manipulation tasks.
papers.title: Complementary Future Token Pruning for World Action Models
papers.tldr: CF-Prune accelerates pretrained world action models by pruning less task-relevant future-visual tokens while preserving robot-action performance.

papers.abstract: Integrating world models into Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) has emerged as a promising direction, enabling policies to anticipate future dynamics beyond reactive observation-to-action mapping. However, existing approaches vary simultaneously in their world representations, integration paradigms, and policy backbones, making it difficult to determine what truly matters for effective world model integration. To disentangle these factors, we categorize existing efforts into four representative paradigms, namely Implicit Future Alignment, Explicit Future Query, MoT Future Expert, and External World Predictor. We instantiate each within a unified framework and systematically evaluate these paradigms with diverse world representations and policy backbones across in-domain, out-of-domain, long-horizon, dynamic, few-shot, and real-world settings. Our study yields four main findings: 1) world representation effectiveness is paradigm-dependent, whereas 2D semantic representations offer robust, cross-paradigm gains; 2) no single paradigm is universally optimal, yet the decoupled MoT Future Expert offers competitive overall performance, particularly in OOD robustness; 3) world modeling consistently benefits policies built on standard VLMs, while decoupled designs exhibit greater compatibility with pretrained VLAs; and 4) world modeling improves performance over action-only baselines across multiple settings, with notable gains on long-horizon and dynamic tasks. Project page and video demonstrations are available at https://dylanmqs.github.io/WM-in-VLAs/.
authors: Qisen Ma, Yixiang Chen, Yuan Xu, Peiyan Li, Jiabing Yang, Kai Wang, Jianhua Yang, Jianlou Si, Jun Huang, Jing Liu, Nianfeng Liu, Yan Huang, Liang Wang
bullets: The study compares four integration paradigms: Implicit Future Alignment, Explicit Future Query, MoT Future Expert, and External World Predictor.
World-representation effectiveness is paradigm-dependent, while 2D semantic representations provide robust gains across paradigms.
No paradigm is universally best; the decoupled MoT Future Expert performs competitively overall and is particularly robust out of distribution.
World modeling consistently helps standard VLM-based policies and improves action-only baselines, especially on long-horizon and dynamic tasks.
Decoupled designs are more compatible with pretrained VLAs, with evaluation spanning in-domain, OOD, few-shot, long-horizon, dynamic, and real-world settings.
papers.selection_reason: Systematically studies world model integration in Vision-Language-Action models, directly relevant to embodied AI and interactive world models.
papers.title: What Matters for World Modeling in Vision-Language-Action Models?
papers.tldr: A systematic study finds that world modeling improves vision-language-action policies, but its effectiveness depends on the representation, integration paradigm, and policy backbone.

papers.abstract: Video world models aim to simulate complex environments with realistic appearance and dynamics. Maintaining consistency over long interactions requires tracking past actions and understanding how those actions affect the environment. Video world models can only generate partial observations of the entire world at a time. Remembering past observations alone may not be sufficient in every scenario, as they may no longer reflect the world after a sequence of actions. We introduce a paradigm that decouples a persistent, updatable abstract state from the visual state. The abstract state keeps track of the entities' changes as the world evolves, and is used to condition the visual state, which represents the current view. We propose StateCraft, a novel architecture that pairs a language model with a video diffusion model to evolve the dynamic world. We evaluate our approach on generative interfaces, which pose a substantial challenge because a single action may change parts of the state that are not currently visible. To support training and evaluation, we develop a data collection pipeline that produces informative, densely annotated trajectories at scale without human or agent supervision, together with a benchmark measuring generation quality, memory, and controllability. On this benchmark, our approach improves surpasses the state-of-the-art baselines. We demonstrate that StateCraft maintains high self-consistency and strong generation quality over long trajectories. Because the abstract state is explicit, it can be edited directly, and generation follows edits to states never observed in the data. Finally, a proof-of-concept 3D experiment, in which actions change the illumination of an unobserved room, shows that the paradigm can also be applied to spatial environments. Project page: https://insait-institute.github.io/StateCraft/.
authors: Lorenzo Venturoli, Nedko Savov, Xi Wang, Marc Pollefeys, Luc Van Gool
bullets: Addresses the limits of visual memory when actions affect currently unseen parts of an environment.
Pairs a language model for abstract-state evolution with a video diffusion model for visual generation.
Introduces a scalable, automatically generated trajectory pipeline and a benchmark for quality, memory, and controllability.
Outperforms stated baselines on the benchmark and maintains self-consistency and generation quality over long trajectories.
Abstract states can be directly edited, enabling generation from states not observed during training; a proof-of-concept extends the approach to 3D environments.
papers.selection_reason: Augments video world models with persistent abstract-state reasoning for long-horizon interactive simulation.
papers.title: StateCraft: Augmenting Video World Models with Abstract-State Reasoning
papers.tldr: StateCraft improves long-horizon video world modeling by maintaining an editable abstract state alongside visual observations to track hidden world changes.

papers.abstract: We present a Generative World Simulation framework that couples persistent shared world state with continuous first-person audiovisual generation. The framework integrates DAO, a computable world engine, and JING, an Egocentric Interactive Experience Model, to support sustained interaction for humans and agents. DAO maintains the states of characters, objects, and spaces and their relationships, advancing the world according to interaction rules and world time while preserving the consequences of past actions. From this evolving state, DAO derives observer-specific conditions for JING, which combines these conditions with character, object, and scene references, observation history, and current actions to generate each observer's audiovisual experience. Users can explore environments, manipulate objects, and communicate with characters through viewpoint control and text instructions, with their actions shaping both the shared state and subsequent experiences. By connecting world-state evolution with experience generation in a continuous interaction loop, the framework offers an approach to building interactive worlds that retain their history, evolve through action, and persist beyond any individual observer.
authors: XGEN Team, Guohao Cai, Haoxuan Che, Frank Fan, Chenran Huang, Junjia Huang, Jiayi Jiang, Yanheng Li, Leon Liu, Shaoteng Liu, Xi Liu, Feng Nie, Zhefan Rao, An Wang, Hanwen Wang, Pengxiang Yan, Jieming Yu, Qian Zha, Wentao Zheng
bullets: Targets interactive worlds that retain history and persist beyond any individual observer.
DAO tracks characters, objects, spaces, relationships, interaction rules, and world time.
JING generates observer-specific audiovisual experiences from world state, references, history, and actions.
Users interact through viewpoint control and text instructions, with actions updating the shared world.
The abstract presents a framework and interaction loop but reports no quantitative evaluation or specific limitations.
papers.selection_reason: Presents a framework for generative world simulation with persistent shared state and egocentric audiovisual generation, a direct fit for Interactive World Models.
papers.title: Generative World Simulation with DAO and JING
papers.tldr: A framework combines a persistent, shared world engine with continuous first-person audiovisual generation to create interactive worlds that evolve and remember past actions.

papers.abstract: Recent video world models have increasingly adopted 3D memory mechanisms to integrate historical observations into a lightweight and persistent scene representation. This naturally raises a complementary question: if 3D representations can serve as an effective mechanism for memorizing observed scenes, can they also be directly used as the latent space for reconstructing and generating scenes? Motivated by this idea, we represent a scene as a compact and unstructured 3D-anchored latent space (\textbf{SceneAE}). Each latent combines an explicit 3D position with an implicit content feature and is spatially grounded to describe its local scene region, forming a sparse latent point cloud. Unlike conventional video-VAE latents that describe how a scene appears from particular viewpoints, our representation directly describes the scene itself, making it naturally applicable to both reconstruction and generation. For reconstruction, once the scene has been generated, our persistent 3D representation can be projected and decoded into RGB-D observations by different target cameras, without the need to regenerate a video for each new camera trajectory. For generation, we leverage the geometry-content separation to first generate camera-controlled 3D geometry and then synthesize content conditioned on it, reducing camera-appearance entanglement and improving camera controllability. Experiments show that this 3D latent achieves superior generation quality, computational cost, and camera controllability.
authors: Shuofeng Sun, Wenzhao Zheng, Yunpeng Zhang, Yi Wu, Linqing Zhao, Haibin Yan
bullets: Addresses whether 3D memory representations can serve directly as latent spaces for scene reconstruction and generation.
Represents each scene with spatially grounded 3D positions plus implicit content features, forming a sparse latent point cloud.
Projects the persistent representation into RGB-D views from new cameras without regenerating videos for each trajectory.
Separates geometry generation from content synthesis to reduce camera–appearance entanglement and improve camera control.
Experiments report improved generation quality, computational cost, and camera controllability.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces a 3D-anchored latent space for scene generation and reconstruction, fitting World Models (interactive generation) and 3D Vision.
papers.title: SceneAE: Scene Generation and Reconstruction in Queryable 3D-Anchored Latent Space
papers.tldr: SceneAE represents scenes as sparse, queryable 3D-anchored latents that support both camera-flexible reconstruction and controllable generation.

papers.abstract: World models trained via latent dynamics offer a scalable path for embodied planning, yet existing methods suffer from representational collapse, computational overhead, and limited long-horizon capability. We introduce a memory-enhanced latent world model that augments JEPA-style prediction with a content-addressable memory bank. Our approach learns high-level representations directly from observations, operating at multiple temporal scales within a shared latent space, and conditions predictions via adaptive layer normalization. To prevent collapse and ensure effective memory usage, we design two complementary losses that encourage slot diversity and balanced temporal utilization. Experiments on PushT, Tworoom, Reacher, and OGBCube demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance with a lightweight architecture, outperforming conventional latent world models on long-horizon planning tasks.
bullets: Targets representational collapse, computational overhead, and weak long-horizon performance in latent world models.
Uses a content-addressable memory bank with multi-timescale representations in a shared latent space.
Conditions predictions through adaptive layer normalization.
Introduces losses promoting memory-slot diversity and balanced temporal utilization.
Evaluated on PushT, Tworoom, Reacher, and OGBCube, achieving state-of-the-art performance with a lightweight architecture.
papers.selection_reason: Memory-augmented latent world model for long-horizon embodied planning.
papers.title: Enhancing Latent World Models with Associative Memory
papers.tldr: A memory-augmented JEPA-style latent world model improves long-horizon embodied planning while addressing representation collapse and computational cost.

papers.abstract: Geometry foundation models estimate camera poses and 3D scene structure from video sequences, but maintaining consistent reconstructions over long horizons remains challenging. Feed-forward models process long sequences as independent, fixed-length frame windows and align their predictions, causing pose and reconstruction errors to accumulate across windows. Streaming models retain information from past frames to inform future predictions, but cannot revise earlier estimates when later observations reveal errors. To address this, we introduce Scaffold MemOry for Revision (SMORE), a framework equipping frozen geometry foundation models with a revisable external memory for long-horizon inference. Inspired by hippocampal associative memory in biological brains, which links spatial context with sensory experience, SMORE associates where an observer is with what it observes, enabling past observations to be stored, retrieved, verified against new evidence, and revised when inconsistencies are detected. We evaluate SMORE with eight competitive geometry models on five datasets spanning camera pose estimation, multi-view depth estimation, 3D point-cloud reconstruction, simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM), and novel view synthesis. Across all evaluated models, SMORE consistently improves long-sequence pose estimation, reduces multi-view depth error by up to 58%, reduces Chamfer distance for 3D point-cloud reconstruction by up to 43%, and achieves average trajectory error as low as 2.9 cm in long-horizon SLAM. By retaining corrected poses and observations, SMORE further improves the fidelity and spatial consistency of large-scale 3D scene reconstruction. These results establish revisable external memory as a flexible interface for extending pretrained geometry models beyond fixed-context prediction toward iterative, error-correcting inference over long visual sequences.
bullets: Addresses error accumulation from fixed-window and non-revisable streaming inference on long video sequences.
Associates spatial context with observations so past geometry can be stored, retrieved, checked against new evidence, and revised.
Evaluated with eight geometry models across five tasks, including pose, depth, point-cloud reconstruction, SLAM, and novel view synthesis.
Consistently improves long-sequence pose estimation, with reported reductions of up to 58% in depth error and 43% in Chamfer distance.
Achieves trajectory error as low as 2.9 cm in long-horizon SLAM and improves large-scale scene consistency.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes a revisable external memory (SMORE) for long-horizon 3D geometry, fitting World Models (long-horizon prediction) and Adaptation and Memory.
papers.title: Remember, Revisit, Revise: Scaffold Memory for Long-Horizon 3D Geometry
papers.tldr: SMORE adds revisable external memory to frozen 3D geometry models, enabling long-horizon predictions to retrieve, verify, and correct past estimates for more consistent reconstructions.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning provides a direct mechanism for optimizing task objectives in large language model-driven agents, but task rewards are typically sparse trajectory-level signals that only evaluate task success, without directly supervising action-conditioned environment transitions, leaving the model with limited explicit understanding of action consequences and environment dynamics. Recent work introduces auxiliary supervision through policy and world modeling co-training, yet typically treats complete environmental observations uniformly as world modeling targets, overlooking the varying decision relevance of observation content. We propose DGS-WM (Decision-Guided Selective World Modeling), a decision-guided policy-world modeling co-training approach for language agents. DGS-WM employs a Decision-Guided Observation Selection component that filters observation units with decision value as world modeling targets based on their support for subsequent policy responses, and a Confidence-Adaptive Weighting component that adaptively adjusts supervision strength according to the model's prediction confidence on selected targets. Together, these components form a decision-aware auxiliary world modeling loss, jointly optimized with the RL loss on the same policy model. Across multiple benchmarks covering single-hop/multi-hop question answering and interactive web tasks, DGS-WM achieves consistent improvements under different model scales and RL algorithms, demonstrating more stable and effective performance compared to full-observation world modeling methods.
authors: Maolin Ran, Minda Chen, Di Huang, Wei Xiong, Fei Huang, Weiwen Liu
bullets: RL agents receive sparse task-level rewards, which provide limited supervision about action consequences and environment dynamics.
DGS-WM selects observation units for world-model training based on their value for subsequent policy decisions.
It adaptively weights selected targets according to the model’s prediction confidence.
The decision-aware world-modeling loss is jointly optimized with the RL objective on the same policy model.
Experiments across question-answering and interactive web tasks show consistent, more stable improvements across model scales and RL algorithms versus full-observation modeling.
papers.selection_reason: Decision-guided selective world modeling for language agents; directly relevant to world models.
papers.title: Model What Matters: Decision-Guided Selective World Modeling for Language Agents
papers.tldr: DGS-WM improves language-agent reinforcement learning by selectively modeling only observation details that inform future decisions and weighting them by prediction confidence.

papers.abstract: State-of-the-art visuomotor policies are increasingly capable of executing complex tasks, yet can fail during deployment in ways they cannot predict or recover from on their own. Improving their performance and robustness typically requires collecting more data, retraining, or modifying the policy architecture, all of which are time- and resource-intensive in practice. We instead propose an offline-trained monitoring-and-intervention framework that improves a policy during deployment using only black-box query access. From a limited set of labeled on-policy rollouts, we learn a policy-conditioned liveness value that measures the nominal policy's progress toward task completion; we additionally train a compact latent world model using these rollouts together with play data. At deployment, the liveness value continuously monitors execution. When it detects a loss of progress, a short-horizon planner searches the world model for corrective actions using the same value as its planning objective, after which control returns to the nominal policy. We evaluate our method on the LIBERO-Goal task suite and on a Franka Panda manipulator, using the vision-language-action model $\pi_{0.5}$ and a diffusion policy as nominal policies, and demonstrate significant improvements in task success rates, while supporting real-time control. Additional results and videos are available on the project website (https://policy-improvement-wm.pages.dev/).
authors: Colton Crosby, Hao Wang, Mac Schwager, Somil Bansal
bullets: Addresses deployment-time failures that nominal policies cannot predict or recover from without retraining or new data collection.
Learns a policy-conditioned liveness value from labeled on-policy rollouts to measure progress toward task completion.
Trains a compact latent world model from on-policy rollouts and play data, then plans short corrective interventions when progress is lost.
Evaluated on LIBERO-Goal and a Franka Panda using π₀.₅ and a diffusion policy, with reported task-success improvements and real-time control.
Scope: interventions rely on offline training data and black-box query access to the nominal policy.
papers.selection_reason: Deployment-time policy improvement via latent world model planning and liveness monitoring.
papers.title: Back on Track: Deployment-time Policy Improvement via World Model Planning
papers.tldr: An offline-trained monitor and world-model planner can improve black-box visuomotor policies during deployment by detecting stalled progress and intervening with corrective actions.

papers.abstract: Foundation models for dynamical systems can forecast unseen partial differential equations (PDEs), ordinary differential equations (ODEs), and time series during inference. However, it remains an open question whether these foundation models truly learn generalizable in-context forecasting strategies. We show that looped transformers are capable of emulating propagators for dynamical systems in-context by first establishing a link between linear attention and (extended) dynamic mode decomposition. We then generalize this insight into the $\textit{Test-Time Forecasting}$ (TTF) framework in which a one-step forecaster leverages iterations of gradient descent as recurrent depth. We demonstrate that lightweight TTF models trained on ODEs and PDEs generalize to out-of-distribution system dynamics during autoregressive rollout after being trained for one-step prediction. Our results reinforce TTF as a theoretically motivated framework for designing recurrent depth models capable of forecasting unseen dynamical systems at test-time.
authors: Jeffrey B. Lai, John Quinn, Anthony Bao, William Gilpin
bullets: Addresses whether foundation models learn generalizable in-context forecasting strategies for unseen ODEs, PDEs, and time series.
Links looped transformers and linear attention to dynamic mode decomposition, motivating their ability to emulate dynamical propagators.
Introduces TTF, where repeated gradient-descent iterations provide recurrent depth at test time.
Shows models trained only for one-step prediction on ODEs and PDEs can generalize to out-of-distribution dynamics during autoregressive rollout.
Scope: the abstract does not report specific datasets, numerical gains, or limitations beyond the demonstrated ODE/PDE setting.
papers.selection_reason: Foundation model for forecasting unseen dynamical systems; fits learned predictors of environment dynamics.
papers.title: Test-Time Forecasting: Recurrent Depth Enables In-Context Dynamics Prediction
papers.tldr: Test-Time Forecasting uses recurrent gradient-descent iterations to help lightweight one-step forecasters predict unseen dynamical systems during inference.

papers.abstract: Robotic ultrasound can standardize image acquisition and reduce operator workload and variability, but policy learning remains limited by the lack of realistic, controllable simulation environments. While controllable world models have advanced rapidly in natural-image domains, ultrasound world modeling remains challenging because each frame captures only a cross-section of unobserved 3D anatomy, causing small probe motions to induce large appearance changes. Existing approaches rely on robot-tracked poses and latent-space prediction, but do not directly generate the observations required for interactive control. We propose SonoWorld, a causal ultrasound world model that learns video dynamics from unlabeled clinical videos and grounds them to 6-DoF control using a small set of freehand clinical scans tracked with an EM sensor. SonoWorld is trained in three stages: pretraining a latent-action-conditioned video diffusion model on around 6.9 million unlabeled multi-organ ultrasound frames; grounding the learned video dynamics to metric probe poses with a small EM-tracked thyroid dataset; and applying distribution matching distillation to enable causal, long-horizon autoregressive generation with selectively caching eviction tokens at inference time. We evaluate controllability through pose-following fidelity, round-trip consistency, and axis-specific control under synthetic actions on held-out tracked scans, and further validate it with a user study. In model-based action discrimination, SonoWorld correctly ranks the target-directed probe motion over an equal-magnitude opposite motion in up to 74.8% of trials. To our knowledge, SonoWorld is the first causal, pose-controllable ultrasound world model learned primarily from freehand clinical videos, providing a data-driven interactive environment for robotic ultrasound data acquisition and policy evaluation.
authors: Zefan Yang, Zheyuan Zhang, Boris Maihe, Yikang Liu, Hang Yu, Ankush Mukherjee, Xiao Chen, Pingkun Yan, Terrence Chen, Shanhui Sun
bullets: Addresses the lack of realistic, controllable simulation environments for robotic ultrasound, where small probe motions can cause large image changes.
Learns video dynamics from about 6.9 million unlabeled multi-organ ultrasound frames and grounds them to 6-DoF probe poses using a small EM-tracked thyroid dataset.
Uses staged training with latent-action-conditioned video diffusion, pose grounding, and distribution-matching distillation for causal long-horizon generation.
Evaluated pose-following, round-trip consistency, axis-specific control, and user-study performance on held-out tracked scans.
Correctly ranked target-directed motion over equal-magnitude opposite motion in up to 74.8% of trials.
papers.selection_reason: Pose-controllable ultrasound world model with latent actions and token eviction, directly relevant to interactive world models.
papers.title: SonoWorld: Towards Interactive Pose-Controllable Ultrasound World Models
papers.tldr: SonoWorld is a causal ultrasound world model that generates pose-controllable video for interactive robotic ultrasound simulation and policy evaluation.

papers.abstract: Memory for long-horizon video generation must satisfy two competing requirements: it must remain bounded so generation can continue indefinitely, while still recovering what was observed at a place when the camera returns, regardless of how long ago it was seen. Reconstruction-based memories provide spatial recall by caching and reprojecting explicit geometry, but require growing storage and depend on estimated 3D structure. Recurrent memories keep a constant-size state, but retention is governed by temporal recurrence, causing old observations to fade with time. We introduce SMART, a slot memory addressed by region tokens, which combines bounded storage with spatially addressed recall. SMART stores content in a constant-size slot recurrence whose writes are addressed by the observing camera and whose reads are queried by the rendering camera, without constructing an explicit 3D representation or maintaining a growing cache. Consequently, recall is conditioned on inter-view geometry rather than on recency. Each read additionally provides a confidence estimate that conditions a chunk-causal diffusion transformer, allowing it to selectively trust retrieved content while relying on its generative prior elsewhere. On long trajectories in Memory Maze and Minecraft, SMART maintains high-fidelity recall far beyond its training horizon while using constant memory and per-step cost.
authors: Eren Cetin, Julius Erbach, Vukasin Bozic, Hyojun Go, Zixiang Zhao, Nikolai Kalischek, Federico Tombari, Konrad Schindler, Dominik Narnhofer
bullets: Addresses the trade-off between bounded memory and recalling observations when the camera revisits a location.
Uses a constant-size slot recurrence with writes keyed by the observing camera and reads queried by the rendering camera.
Avoids explicit 3D reconstruction and growing caches by conditioning recall on inter-view geometry.
Provides confidence estimates to a chunk-causal diffusion transformer, which balances retrieved content with its generative prior.
On Memory Maze and Minecraft trajectories, maintains high-fidelity recall beyond the training horizon with constant memory and per-step cost.
papers.selection_reason: Bounded spatially addressed memory for long-horizon video generation, relevant to video world models and embodied memory.
papers.title: Long-horizon Video Generation with Slot Memory Addressed By Region Tokens
papers.tldr: SMART enables long-horizon video generation with constant memory by retrieving past visual content based on spatial camera regions rather than recency.

papers.abstract: World models of visual information predict future image frames conditioned on given action sequences. This predicted scene evolution is driven by deterministic changes such as controlled motion on a robot platform, as well as stochastic changes such as rendering of manipulated objects or previously occluded regions. Our key insight is that the spatial location of these stochastic changes is itself learnable. We leverage this insight by jointly regressing both the deterministic next-state prediction and the spatial uncertainty map, then using the uncertainty map to guide a conditional diffusion process. We propose Decoupled Drift-Diffusion World Model (D3WM), which uses a transformer trained with a Gaussian negative-log-likelihood objective to produce both the deterministic next-state prediction and a spatial map of heteroscedastic aleatoric uncertainty. The learned uncertainty map then provides a structured spatial gate for a conditional diffusion model: deterministic regions are anchored to the predicted state, while uncertain regions, such as disocclusions or dynamic textures, are sampled by the diffusion process. We frame this decomposition under a variance-gated stochastic differential equation that separates deterministic drift from stochastic diffusion. D3WM shows improved results over competitive baselines in two distinct types of action spaces: robotic tabletop manipulation and camera motion.
authors: Anton Arapin, Aditya Singh, Yixin Wang, Jun Gao, Bernadette Bucher
bullets: Targets world-model predictions containing both deterministic motion and stochastic changes such as disocclusions or dynamic textures.
A transformer jointly predicts the deterministic next state and a spatial heteroscedastic uncertainty map using Gaussian negative log-likelihood.
The uncertainty map gates a conditional diffusion process, anchoring predictable regions while sampling uncertain ones.
The method is formulated as a variance-gated stochastic differential equation separating drift from diffusion.
Improves over competitive baselines across robotic tabletop manipulation and camera-motion action spaces.
papers.selection_reason: Action-conditioned future frame prediction with uncertainty-gated diffusion, directly a world model.
papers.title: Decoupled Drift-Diffusion World Models for Consistent Future Frame Prediction
papers.tldr: D3WM separates predictable motion from spatially localized uncertainty to generate more consistent future video frames.

papers.abstract: We present LidarVerse, a real-time unified LiDAR world model for sensor simulation across tasks and sensors. Existing LiDAR simulators largely follow one of two complementary paradigms: reconstruction-based methods preserve the geometry of a captured scene but require lengthy per-scene optimization, whereas generative methods amortize learning across data but lack the consistency needed for long-horizon rollouts. LidarVerse brings both paradigms into a single, unified conditional generative framework. A universal tokenizer maps LiDAR range sequences into a shared latent space, where a bidirectional teacher learns a common interface for conditioning on a LiDAR prefix, an HD-Map, a persistent spatial cache, and optionally, text. Varying the available scene evidence turns the same model into a generator of new worlds, a point-cloud forecaster, or a generalizable resimulator of observed scenes without per-scene optimization. We distill the teacher into a four-step autoregressive causal student and maintain both a rolling temporal K/V cache and a world-aligned spatial cache, enabling persistent long-horizon rollouts with real-time inference at 11 FPS on a single H100 GPU. LidarVerse achieves state-of-the-art performance on most reported metrics across all three evaluation protocols, while its tokenizer supports 32-, 64-, and 128-beam LiDAR and generalizes to an unseen scanning pattern. These results demonstrate that generative and reconstruction-grounded LiDAR simulation can be realized within one model, providing the core capabilities for future closed-loop sensor simulation.
authors: Henry Che, Xuanchi Ren, Sanja Fidler, Shenlong Wang, Laura Leal-Taix\'e, Shengyu Huang
bullets: Combines reconstruction-based scene consistency with the scalability of generative modeling in one conditional framework.
Uses a universal tokenizer and a shared latent interface conditioned on LiDAR prefixes, HD maps, spatial memory, and optionally text.
A single model supports new-world generation, point-cloud forecasting, and resimulation without per-scene optimization.
A distilled four-step causal student with temporal and spatial caches enables persistent long-horizon rollouts at 11 FPS on one H100 GPU.
Reports state-of-the-art performance on most metrics across three evaluation protocols and generalizes across LiDAR beam counts and an unseen scanning pattern.
papers.selection_reason: Unified LiDAR world model for sensor simulation and forecasting, fitting world models and 3D perception.
papers.title: Into the LidarVerse: A Real-Time Unified LiDAR World Model Across Tasks and Sensors
papers.tldr: LidarVerse is a unified, real-time LiDAR world model that supports world generation, forecasting, and scene resimulation across sensors and tasks.

papers.abstract: Full waveform inversion (FWI) is a powerful tool for high-resolution subsurface model reconstruction, but it remains highly nonlinear and ill-posed, especially when the initial model is inaccurate or the acquired data are noisy and incomplete. Annealed Stein variational gradient descent (ASVGD) provides a particle-based Bayesian framework for FWI by approximating the posterior distribution with an ensemble of velocity models, thereby enabling uncertainty quantification beyond a single deterministic solution. However, conventional ASVGD-FWI commonly relies on simple handcrafted priors, such as Gaussian or smoothing assumptions, which are often insufficient to represent complex geological structures. To address this limitation, we introduce a learned diffusion model (DM) as an implicit regularization mechanism within the ASVGD-FWI framework. Instead of explicitly evaluating the diffusion prior density, the trained diffusion model acts as a learned geological projection operator that guides updated particles toward the distribution of plausible velocity models. In this way, the proposed method combines data consistency from FWI, posterior diversity from ASVGD, and structural realism from the diffusion prior. Numerical experiments demonstrate that the diffusion-regularized ASVGD-FWI produces more geologically consistent mean models, suppresses nonphysical artifacts, and yields uncertainty estimates that are more concentrated around structurally complex and poorly constrained regions. These results suggest that learned diffusion priors can effectively enhance Bayesian FWI by improving both inversion stability and the interpretability of posterior uncertainty.
authors: Chao Li, Mrinal K. Sen, Sergey Fomel, Yangkang Chen
bullets: Addresses the nonlinearity and ill-posedness of FWI under inaccurate initial models and noisy or incomplete data.
Integrates a learned diffusion model into annealed Stein variational gradient descent as an implicit geological prior.
Combines FWI data consistency, ASVGD posterior diversity, and diffusion-based structural realism.
Produces more geologically consistent mean models, fewer nonphysical artifacts, and more focused uncertainty in complex, poorly constrained regions.
The evidence is based on numerical experiments; the approach depends on a trained diffusion prior to represent plausible velocity models.
papers.selection_reason: Uses a learned diffusion model as a prior/projection operator for Bayesian inversion, a transferable generative-model idea.
papers.title: Structure-aware Bayesian full waveform inversion via diffusion-regularized Stein variational gradient descent
papers.tldr: A diffusion model improves Bayesian full waveform inversion by guiding particle-based solutions toward realistic geological structures while preserving uncertainty estimates.

papers.abstract: Training from offline data has allowed for substantial progress in domains such as robotics, leading to general-purpose policies that can be easily applied zero-shot or efficiently finetuned for downstream tasks. However, these policies can still have poor generalization, both due to the choice of modeling objective and from learning from a static dataset. In this work, we focus on the challenging task of zero-shot goal generalization, where a policy is evaluated on unseen tasks that require combining its existing knowledge (compositional generalization). An avenue for improving a policy's generalization is by generating new experience with world models; however, such generation has proven difficult for longer horizons. Thus, to alleviate this issue, we propose TD-Aug, which samples from a geometric horizon model and allows for directly imagining novel outcomes that can be achieved by composing existing knowledge. We demonstrate that training on these future outcomes as goals for goal-conditioned BC policies significantly improves generalization in stitching-based OGBench tasks.
authors: Daniel Lawson, Dhruv Sreenivas, Adriana Hugessen, Khimya Khetarpal, Glen Berseth
bullets: Addresses poor generalization from static offline datasets, especially on unseen tasks requiring composition of known skills.
Proposes TD-Aug, which samples from a geometric horizon model to generate achievable future outcomes.
Uses imagined outcomes as goals for goal-conditioned behavioral cloning policies.
Demonstrates significant generalization gains on stitching-based OGBench tasks.
Scope: focuses on zero-shot goal generalization and avoids the difficulty of long-horizon world-model generation.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes geometric horizon models to generate future experiences for policy generalization, bridging world models and embodied policy learning.
papers.title: Imagining Goals with Geometric Horizon Models for Policy Generalization
papers.tldr: TD-Aug improves zero-shot compositional goal generalization by imagining novel outcomes with a geometric-horizon world model and using them to train goal-conditioned policies.

papers.abstract: As video models enable longer and more realistic interactive experiences, maintaining a world consistent with its history becomes essential. This requires both preserving previously observed content and ensuring coherent world evolution over time. World memory is a critical capability to evaluate alongside visual fidelity and video duration. We introduce WorldMemBench, a benchmark for systematically evaluating world memory in video world models. Across 260 test cases, it assesses static memory through the retention of human identity and appearance, object appearance and geometry, and environmental content and geometry, and dynamic memory through event progression and state persistence. Using controlled camera departures and multi-revisit trajectories, the benchmark evaluates static content against fixed initial references and dynamic events against expected state transitions. It combines appearance and geometry metrics with event-specific assessments, and reports video quality and camera-following accuracy as complementary diagnostics. Evaluation of nine representative models shows that strong static retention does not imply reliable dynamic state evolution, while repeated revisits reveal memory degradation beyond the first return. Human studies support the alignment between our automatic evaluations and human judgments. WorldMemBench provides a systematic testbed for diagnosing memory failures and guiding the development of persistent, temporally coherent video worlds.
authors: Nan Zhou, Jianxiong Gao, Qiuyu Wang, Wen Wang, Jiahao Wang, Yufeng Yuan, Shuaiting Li, Hao Ouyang, Yujun Shen, Weiming Lu, Jun Xiao, Yueting Zhuang, Yongliang Shen
bullets: Benchmarks static memory for human, object, and environmental appearance and geometry.
Tests dynamic memory through event progression and state persistence.
Uses 260 test cases with controlled camera departures and multi-revisit trajectories.
Combines appearance, geometry, event-specific, video-quality, and camera-following metrics.
Evaluation of nine models finds that static retention does not guarantee dynamic consistency, with memory degrading after repeated revisits; human studies support the automatic metrics.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmark for memory in video world models, directly evaluating world-model capabilities.
papers.title: WorldMemBench: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Memory of Video World Models
papers.tldr: WorldMemBench systematically evaluates whether video world models preserve past content and evolve world states coherently over repeated revisits.

papers.abstract: World models are a powerful means of reasoning and planning, but many of these action-conditioned predictive models are high dimensional and computationally expensive. These challenges limit the number of action candidates that can be evaluated by a planner. We show that this cost is avoidable for planners over short horizons, which only require local information with respect to the current state. For a fixed state, the frames reachable by varying a low-dimensional action (a camera movement or an end-effector command) lie on a low-dimensional manifold. We estimate the local shape of that manifold directly via a network trained to estimate how each image region moves per unit of each action axis supervised by data collected from samples by the generator. A correction head fit to trajectory data estimates the shape of this manifold region up to a third-order Taylor polynomial. We call this network estimating the Taylor polynomial describing the manifold shape an Action Jet and compute its radius of validity in closed form. By traversing this approximation of the local manifold shape, we only have to perform inference once per state for any number of candidate actions. Scoring sixteen candidates from a single extraction is over 300x faster than with either source generator, and this gap widens with the number of candidates a planner evaluates. We measure against state-of-the-art action-conditioned generators, IRASim and WorldGym on BridgeData V2, a real 7-DoF manipulation benchmark, and FrameCrafter on DL3DV scenes, where we chart from the novel-view generators DepthSplat and LagerNVS. Because only the tangent comes from the generator and every other term from the data, the Action Jet also predicts held-out frames more accurately than IRASim, the generator that supplied its tangent, at short horizons and at over 100x less compute.
authors: Anton Arapin, Chahyon Ku, Bernadette Bucher
bullets: Problem: High-dimensional world models make evaluating many action candidates computationally expensive.
Method: Learn image-region motion per action dimension and fit a correction head that approximates the local manifold with a third-order Taylor polynomial.
The approximation’s closed-form validity radius defines where the local prediction can be trusted.
Result: Sixteen candidate actions are scored from one extraction at over 300× lower cost than the source generators, with larger gains for more candidates.
Scope: Evaluated on BridgeData V2 manipulation data and DL3DV novel-view scenes against several action-conditioned or view-synthesis generators.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes efficient local action-conditioned world-model approximation for planning.
papers.title: Action Jets: Learning the Local Shape of the Action-conditioned Data Manifold
papers.tldr: Action Jets approximate the local action-conditioned image manifold so planners can evaluate many short-horizon action candidates with one model inference, achieving over 300× faster scoring and improved short-horizon prediction accuracy.

papers.abstract: Humanoid policies trained in simulation can transfer qualitatively to hardware while failing to transfer the force interactions learned during training, compromising torque efficiency, load regulation, and robustness to impacts. This failure can arise from actuator sim-to-real gaps because forces depend on actuator torques. We introduce Contact-UAN, a residual world model that preserves a simulator's physics priors while correcting actuator dynamics to align simulated rollouts with recorded hardware rollouts. For humanoid motion with contact, this requires contact-consistent replay: if hardware playback in simulation begins with misaligned contact wrenches, the residual model learns to correct reset artifacts rather than actuator discrepancies. Using only onboard proprioception, Contact-UAN infers the simulator-side stance-foot pose needed to initialize replay with consistent contact forces. We show that a UAN trained on 6.5 minutes of real-world walking data generalizes to tasks that benefit from accurate force and impulse regulation and produces policies that transfer seamlessly to the real world, yielding 20% lower running torque, 43% lower force-tracking error, extreme compliance, accurate impedance control, and dynamic, robust jumps.
authors: Nolan Fey, Khai Nguyen, Yash Prabhu, Gabriel B. Margolis, Pulkit Agrawal
bullets: Addresses actuator sim-to-real gaps that degrade torque efficiency, load regulation, and impact robustness.
Uses a residual world model that preserves simulator physics while aligning simulated rollouts with hardware behavior.
Infers simulator-side stance-foot pose from proprioception to initialize contact-consistent replay and avoid reset artifacts.
Trained on 6.5 minutes of real-world walking data, it supports force and impulse regulation, impedance control, compliance, and dynamic jumps.
Reports 20% lower running torque and 43% lower force-tracking error during real-world transfer.
papers.selection_reason: Residual actuator world model for sim-to-real humanoid control; fits world models and robot learning.
papers.title: Contact-UAN: Unsupervised Actuator Networks as a Residual World Model for Humanoid Control
papers.tldr: Contact-UAN learns actuator corrections from limited onboard hardware data, enabling contact-aware humanoid policies to transfer with more accurate force control and robust motion.

papers.abstract: This paper studies Wong--Zakai convergence and Fourier neural operator learning for stochastic Volterra integral equations (SVIEs) describing random systems with memory. A Wong--Zakai theorem establishes convergence of pathwise solutions driven by piecewise linear approximations of Brownian motion to the corresponding SVIE solution. This convergence provides a foundation for using mirror-padded Fourier neural operators to learn the solution operator mapping initial conditions and driving noise to entire solution trajectories. Numerical experiments demonstrate competitive prediction accuracy and generalization to temporal grids finer than those used for training, while assessing the influence of padding and computational cost. As a follow-up to \citet{LKP:26}, this study extends their operator-learning framework to SVIEs through separate convergence and approximation analyses tailored to convolutional memory.
authors: Wonjae Lee, Jiuk Jang, Hyungbin Park
bullets: Addresses stochastic Volterra integral equations, which model random systems with memory.
Proves convergence from piecewise linear Brownian-motion approximations to pathwise SVIE solutions.
Trains Fourier neural operators to map inputs and noise to entire solution trajectories.
Numerical experiments show competitive accuracy and generalization to finer temporal grids than those used in training.
Evaluates padding choices and computational cost; the framework is tailored to convolutional memory.
papers.selection_reason: Learns solution operators for stochastic dynamical systems with memory; transferable to world-model prediction.
papers.title: Wong--Zakai Convergence and FNO Learning for Stochastic Volterra Equations
papers.tldr: The paper establishes Wong–Zakai convergence for SVIEs and uses it to support mirror-padded Fourier neural operators that learn solution trajectories from initial conditions and driving noise.

papers.abstract: Time-series language models typically align numerical signals with language using labels, captions, or question-answer pairs. Although such supervision encourages linguistic representations, it does not explicitly require them to preserve information about how the underlying time-series signal evolves. We introduce forecast grounding, a pretraining principle that requires language-aligned time-series representations to remain predictive of the future evolution before they are adapted to downstream tasks. We instantiate this principle in LOTUS, which divides each time-series channel into non-overlapping patches and maps them into the LLM embedding space. It then predicts the next patch from the LLM hidden states of the time-series tokens, encouraging the learned representation to retain temporal information. To capture both temporal changes and periodic patterns, we also propose a temporal-spectral patch representation that combines each raw time-series patch with its spectral representation before mapping it into the LLM embedding space. Across three language model backbones and six downstream evaluation datasets, LOTUS achieves the best average performance with minimal trainable parameters, reaching 59.91% accuracy and outperforming the strongest matched baseline by 3.36%. Our representation analyses further show that LOTUS uses the numerical input and preserves temporal structure in its learned patch representations. These results establish forecast grounding as a promising pretraining principle, enabling compact time-series language models to outperform models 25 to 50 times their size on TSRBench.
authors: Van Dai Do, Huu Hiep Nguyen, Minh Hoang Nguyen, Manh Nguyen, Hung Le
bullets: Addresses the lack of explicit temporal-information preservation in label- or language-supervised time-series models.
Uses non-overlapping channel patches mapped into LLM embedding space and predicts the next patch from hidden states.
Combines raw patch values with spectral representations to capture temporal changes and periodic patterns.
Evaluated across three LLM backbones and six downstream datasets, LOTUS achieves 59.91% accuracy and improves over the strongest matched baseline by 3.36%.
Representation analyses indicate that LOTUS uses numerical inputs and retains temporal structure; it also outperforms models 25–50× larger on TSRBench.
papers.selection_reason: Forecast grounding for time-series representations is transferable to world-model pretraining.
papers.title: Lotus: Learning to Understand Time-series by Learning to Forecast
papers.tldr: LOTUS improves time-series language models by grounding language-aligned representations in future forecasting, helping them preserve temporal structure with few trainable parameters.

papers.abstract: Video prediction requires models to capture complex spatiotemporal dependencies and to retain relevant information over long sequences. PredRNN and its successor PredRNN-V2 address this challenge with spatiotemporal Long Short-Term Memory (ST-LSTM) units that maintain two separate memory states, at the cost of a relatively complex recurrent building block. In this work, we investigate whether the simpler gating of Gated Recurrent Units (GRUs) can be transferred to spatiotemporal predictive learning. To this end, we develop a spatiotemporal GRU (ST-GRU) unit as a GRU-based alternative to the ST-LSTM. The ST-GRU replaces the ST-LSTM's three gates per memory state with two GRU-style gates (update and reset), and merges the temporal memory state into the hidden state, which reduces the number of parameters by about 5%. We incorporate the ST-GRU into PredRNN-V2 and evaluate the resulting model on the Moving MNIST video prediction benchmark, following the original experimental protocol. Averaged over ten predicted frames, the ST-GRU-based PredRNN-V2 achieves an MSE of 55.1, an SSIM of 0.883, an LPIPS of 0.065 and a PSNR of 19.53dB. It does not surpass the original ST-LSTM-based PredRNN-V2 on MSE, SSIM or PSNR, but it achieves a lower LPIPS and performs on par with the earlier ST-LSTM-based PredRNN, while using a simpler recurrent cell. These results suggest that ST-GRUs are a promising building block for spatiotemporal predictive learning and motivate further work on their design and integration.
authors: Augusta van Haren, Hanna Hoogen, Luca Pattavina, Quincy Rommen
bullets: Targets the complexity of PredRNN-V2’s dual-memory ST-LSTM recurrent unit.
Introduces an ST-GRU with update and reset gates, merging temporal memory into the hidden state.
Evaluated on Moving MNIST using the original experimental protocol over ten predicted frames.
Reports MSE 55.1, SSIM 0.883, LPIPS 0.065, and PSNR 19.53 dB.
Does not outperform PredRNN-V2 on MSE, SSIM, or PSNR, but achieves lower LPIPS and matches earlier PredRNN performance with a simpler cell.
papers.selection_reason: GRU-based reformulation of PredRNN-V2 for video prediction; fits video world models.
papers.title: ST-GRU PredRNN-V2: A GRU-Based Reformulation of PredRNN-V2 for Video Prediction
papers.tldr: ST-GRU PredRNN-V2 replaces the complex ST-LSTM with a simpler GRU-based cell, reducing parameters by about 5% while maintaining competitive video-prediction quality.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon agents often struggle to recover from failures whose causes lie several steps earlier, beyond what local reflection or backtracking can resolve. We introduce BELIEFWEAVER, a framework that combines persistent evidence across attempts with prospective reasoning over repair directions. It maintains a relational belief state over frontiers, attempts, observations, and checkpoints. Execution evidence updates related frontier priorities across attempts and rollback, while diagnostic evidence gates execution. An implicit world model (IWM) evaluates repair hypotheses, predicts progress, and identifies relations among frontiers to guide exploration. We further distill these recurring IWM reasoning components into a 9B student through supervised fine-tuning and on-policy distillation (OPD). Across three terminal-based benchmarks, BELIEFWEAVER improves aggregate final score by 5.1 percentage points over native Terminus-2 continuation, with positive trends in exploration efficiency. The distilled 9B student improves final score by 9.8 percentage points over the reported native baseline while reducing estimated teacher API cost by 54.8% relative to the matched teacher. These results show that persistent evidence and prospective reasoning can improve recovery in long-horizon agent tasks while substantially reducing reliance on teacher-model inference.
bullets: Addresses failures whose causes occur several steps before the observed error, beyond local reflection or backtracking.
Maintains relational beliefs over frontiers, attempts, observations, and checkpoints; execution and diagnostic evidence guide priorities and actions.
Uses an implicit world model to evaluate repair hypotheses, predict progress, and identify relationships among exploration frontiers.
Across three terminal-based benchmarks, it raises aggregate final score by 5.1 percentage points over native Terminus-2 continuation, with positive exploration-efficiency trends.
A distilled 9B student gains 9.8 percentage points over the reported native baseline and reduces matched teacher API cost by 54.8%.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces an implicit world model and persistent belief updates for failure recovery in long-horizon agents, directly relevant to world modeling and test-time adaptation.
papers.title: Failure Recovery via Belief Updates and World Modeling for Long-Horizon Agents
papers.tldr: BELIEFWEAVER improves long-horizon agent failure recovery by combining persistent belief updates with prospective world-model reasoning, achieving higher scores while reducing teacher-inference costs.

papers.abstract: Flow matching is a common generative recipe for robot foundation models. Vision-language-action models (VLAs) generate action chunks, while world-action models (WAMs) additionally generate future visual states. Both start generation from a fixed Gaussian prior, despite temporal continuity between past and future states and actions. This requires costly training and iterative sampling, especially for WAMs with an additional visual branch. We introduce $Δ$-flow, which constructs the source from recent history with mild noise rather than from a fixed Gaussian prior. This moves the source closer to the target, reducing transport to a small residual $Δ$ that can be learned efficiently and enables single-step inference. We integrate $Δ$-flow into the VLA policy $π_{0.5}$ and the WAM policies ImageWAM and Fast-WAM. On LIBERO, ImageWAM reaches 90% success in one epoch rather than six, and Fast-WAM reaches 95% in two epochs rather than eight. With LoRA fine-tuning, $π_{0.5}$ exceeds its baseline's five-epoch performance after one epoch. Single-step inference gives $1.54\times$, $2.49\times$, and $4.45\times$ speedups on $π_{0.5}$, ImageWAM, and Fast-WAM, respectively. It preserves action smoothness, achieving a $4.5\times$ reduction in action jerk compared with one-step Gaussian sampling. $Δ$-flow reaches state-of-the-art generalization performance on LIBERO-Plus. Action-history sources can be applied to pretrained WAM policies without retraining. Replacing the Gaussian action source at inference largely preserves task success with a single sampling step and can slightly improve it. We further study how action representation and visual information in action learning affect history-to-future prediction in $Δ$-flow. These results show that $Δ$-flow is simple yet effective, improving the efficiency and generalization of robot foundation models.
bullets: Targets costly iterative sampling and training in vision-language-action and world-action robot models.
Builds the flow source from recent action and visual history, learning only the residual transition to future actions and states.
Integrated into π₀.₅, ImageWAM, and Fast-WAM, it achieves faster training and 1.54×–4.45× inference speedups on LIBERO.
Maintains smooth actions, reducing action jerk 4.5× versus one-step Gaussian sampling, and reaches state-of-the-art generalization on LIBERO-Plus.
History-based action sources can be applied to pretrained world-action models without retraining, though visual and action representations affect prediction quality.
papers.selection_reason: Flow-matching efficiency improvement for robot foundation models including VLAs and world-action models.
papers.title: $Δ$ Flow Matching for Robot Foundation Models
papers.tldr: Δ-flow replaces the fixed Gaussian starting point in robot flow matching with a lightly noised recent history, enabling efficient single-step generation while preserving or improving performance.

papers.abstract: Visual world models predict the consequences of actions from images, but planning with them is typically done by optimizers such as CEM and MPPI. However, these optimizers stall on long-horizon tasks where progress requires motion the objective does not reward, such as moving around a block before pushing it. This paper revisits kinodynamic sampling-based motion planning for world models, using the learned model as the propagator of a tree search in latent space. Our key insight is that the sampling strategies devised for high-dimensional search in configuration space apply directly to the latent space of a world model, where they rapidly expand through intermediate states that myopic optimizers never sample. We present two exploration strategies for the high-dimensional latent space, nearest-neighbor-guided RRT and projection-based KPIECE, with GPU-native batched expansion for efficient device utilization. We evaluate with an off-the-shelf DINO-WM on four simulated domains and a real-world block-pushing task. Our approaches match or exceed the success rate of CEM and MPPI at up to 13.8x lower planning time in simulation, and improve the success rate by 20% on the real robot.
bullets: Addresses optimizer failures when successful actions require temporarily unrewarded intermediate motion.
Uses the world model as a latent-space propagator for kinodynamic tree search.
Introduces nearest-neighbor-guided RRT and projection-based KPIECE with GPU-batched expansion.
Evaluated in four simulated domains and a real-world block-pushing task.
Matches or exceeds CEM/MPPI success rates with up to 13.8× lower simulation planning time and 20% higher real-robot success.
papers.selection_reason: Sampling-based planning with learned world models for robot manipulation.
papers.title: Sampling-based Kinodynamic Planning with World Models
papers.tldr: Sampling-based tree search in learned visual world-model latent spaces enables faster and more effective long-horizon planning than conventional optimizers.

papers.abstract: Scaling expert demonstrations alone does not enable generalist robot policies to improve from deployment. Real-world rollouts contain successes, suboptimal behavior, and failures: imitating every recorded action can reinforce poor behavior, while filtering out failures discards evidence of physical interactions and their consequences. We introduce \textbf{LoopWAM}, a closed-loop world-action model that learns directly from this full quality spectrum, using rollouts from both itself and other deployed policies. Source-dependent noise sampling unifies behavior learning and action-conditioned world modeling, while quality steering and quality-weighted supervision retain full video supervision across qualities and regulate action imitation. Video and action tokens interact throughout parallel denoising, allowing learned consequences to inform action generation directly. On RoboChallenge Table30-V2, three deployment-and-training rounds raise success from 23.67\% to 43.33\%, a 19.7-percentage-point gain, with a final score of 56.80. LoopWAM also achieves 94.5\% average success on RoboTwin~2.0 and 49.5\% overall success on RoboCasa365 without additional embodied pretraining, obtaining the best overall results among the compared methods across all three benchmarks. On challenging shirt folding task, two rounds of deployment-driven improvement after single-task post-training raise success from 13.20\% to 55.56\%. These results demonstrate closed-loop improvement from mixed-quality experience under both multi-task learning and single-task post-training. \href{https://loop-wam.github.io/}{\textcolor{orange}{Project Page}}
authors: Wenxuan Guo, Yingping Liang, Zhaoguo Wang, Ziyuan Li, Angyuan Ma, Zhenyu Wu, Chengkun Wang, Bingyao Yu, Ze Chen, Borui Zhang, Xiuwei Xu, Meng Zhang, Erjin Zhou, Jiwen Lu
bullets: Addresses the problem that imitating all deployment actions can reinforce failures, while discarding failures loses information about physical interactions and their consequences.
Uses a closed-loop world-action model trained on rollouts from its own and other policies across successes, suboptimal behavior, and failures.
Combines source-dependent noise sampling, quality steering, and quality-weighted supervision to learn from full video data while regulating action imitation.
Video and action tokens interact during parallel denoising, enabling predicted consequences to directly inform action generation.
Across three deployment-and-training rounds, success on RoboChallenge Table30-V2 rose from 23.67% to 43.33%; gains were also reported on RoboTwin 2.0, RoboCasa365, and shirt folding.
papers.selection_reason: Closed-loop policy improvement from deployment rollouts with action-conditioned world modeling, relevant to robot learning/manipulation, interactive world models, and continual/online learning.
papers.title: LoopWAM: Closed-Loop Generalist Policy Improvement from Deployment Rollouts
papers.tldr: LoopWAM improves generalist robot policies by learning from mixed-quality deployment rollouts in a closed loop, substantially increasing task success without additional embodied pretraining.

papers.abstract: Expert demonstrations show how to complete contact-rich tasks, but provide limited coverage of how interaction forces respond to different actions. Task-agnostic play provides broader experience of contact dynamics without specifying task goals. To fully leverage these two types of data, we introduce ForceWAM, a force world action model that decouples knowledge of task-compatible interaction outcomes from knowledge of how local actions change contact. A world model learns from successful demonstrations to jointly predict future video and six-axis force/torque trajectories. Together, these futures describe the expected evolution of motion and contact during the task. A separate inverse dynamics model (IDM) learns from both task and play, mapping current observations and recorded visual-wrench futures to their associated robot actions. Play data thus provide knowledge of force responses for goal-directed execution. At deployment, the IDM reactively translates generated futures into actions, reusing them with fresh wrench feedback between world-model updates. Across real-robot force-regulated sliding, box flipping with and without disturbances, and ring placement, ForceWAM achieves $85$-$95\%$ mean success, surpassing world-modeling and reactive baselines. Our experiments further show that adding task-agnostic play data improves success by $15$-$45$ percentage points, demonstrating its value for learning contact-rich execution. Project page and code are available at https://force-wam.github.io/.
authors: Zijun Xu, Wendi Chen, Xinkai Wang, Jiachen Zou, Hongjin Chen, Hairuo Liu, Bokai Lin, Shihao Ma, Ke Ma, Zhiwei Zhang, Zhuohao Yan, Ke Wu, Haoming Song, Xueqi Li, Chuan Wen, Jieru Zhao, Wenchao Ding, Cewu Lu, Lixin Yang
bullets: Addresses limited force-response coverage in expert demonstrations for contact-rich tasks.
A world model trained on demonstrations predicts future video and six-axis force/torque trajectories.
An inverse dynamics model trained on demonstrations and play maps visual-wrench futures to actions.
On real-robot sliding, box flipping, and ring placement, it achieves 85–95% mean success.
Adding play data improves success by 15–45 percentage points across experiments.
papers.selection_reason: Force world action model for contact-rich manipulation from demo and play data; fits robot learning and video world models.
papers.title: ForceWAM: Decoupling Future and Response Learning from Demo and Play Data for Contact-Rich Manipulation
papers.tldr: ForceWAM combines task demonstrations with task-agnostic play to learn contact-aware world futures and convert them into robust manipulation actions.

papers.abstract: We introduce WorldOracle, a benchmark specifically designed to evaluate action-conditioned world models (ACWMs) against paired real-world executions. Given the same initial observation and low-level action sequence, WorldOracle asks whether a predicted rollout reproduces what happens in the real world, including physical consequences and task-state transitions. We evaluate models along four complementary dimensions: physical state correctness, interaction spatial alignment, key interaction area fidelity, and multi-view action coherence. To support this evaluation, we curate real-world training and evaluation suites that cover different interaction dynamics and embodiments. The evaluation suite contains long, multi-segment episodes with both successful and failed executions, enabling evaluation across varied action outcomes and behavior distributions. Experiments on seven representative ACWMs reveal distinct model strengths and failure modes. WorldOracle provides a systematic foundation for measuring and advancing action-conditioned world modeling for manipulation. We will release the datasets, evaluation code, and leaderboard.
authors: Haoyi Duan, Liliang Chen, Nan Wang, Yang Zhang, Yuhang Lu, Xiaotong Chen, Wei-Cheng Tseng, Shenyuan Gao, Zhaoshuo Li, Jingyi Jin, Pooya Jannaty, Dhruv Shah, Yuke Zhu, Ming-Yu Liu, Maoqing Yao, Guanghui Ren
bullets: Evaluates predicted rollouts against paired real executions, including physical consequences and task-state transitions.
