The resulting representation supports observed-frame rendering and action-conditioned simulation, extending SLAM maps to describe how deformable objects respond to manipulation. On the PhysTwin benchmark, our method improves reconstruction and prediction PSNR over PhysTwin by 10.4\% and 11.0\%, respectively. On the TUM RGB-D benchmark, it reduces average camera tracking error by 20.6\%, improves SSIM by 3.6\%, and reduces LPIPS by 8.3\% compared with 4DGS-SLAM.
authors: Guangming Wang, Zhishuo Liu, Haibing Wu, Wanli Ma, Yixiong Jing, Olaf Wysocki, Brian Sheil
bullets: Addresses predictive 4D mapping of dynamic, deformable scenes from moving-camera RGB-D video.
Separates static background and dynamic object Gaussian fields, using the former for localization and a spring–mass model for deformation, inertia, and damping.
Uses virtual observation forces to smoothly align simulated surface nodes with depth observations and updates physical parameters over the observation window.
Transforms dynamic Gaussians along the simulated deforming surface while enforcing surface alignment during rendering optimization.
Improves reconstruction and prediction PSNR on PhysTwin, and tracking, SSIM, and LPIPS on TUM RGB-D, relative to the cited baselines.
papers.selection_reason: Builds physics-aware 4D Gaussian scene representations that support action-conditioned future simulation, fitting interactive world-model interests.
papers.title: Physical SLAM: Physics-aware Simultaneous Localisation and Mapping
papers.tldr: Physical SLAM reconstructs deformable objects’ 4D Gaussian representations while learning their physics, enabling camera tracking, rendering, and action-conditioned future-state prediction.

papers.abstract: Multi-player interactive world models aim to simulate shared environments from multiple players' perspectives, but achieving robust generation while scaling to more players remains challenging. Existing approaches that rely on fully-connected communication (e.g., Solaris) incur quadratic attention costs as the number of players grows, while centralized approaches (e.g., $\gamma$-World) suffer from interference between unrelated events in a shared global representation. To address these challenges, we present Multics, a multi-player video generation framework with hierarchical communication that structures information exchange across player, group, and global levels. This hierarchy introduces group tokens into self-attention as intermediate group-level representations that aggregate locally relevant player information. These tokens connect to global tokens for cross-group communication, while the hierarchical topology limits direct mixing between unrelated local events. Group-token parameters are shared across group slots, allowing the same communication module to accommodate varying numbers of players without introducing new group-specific parameters. We further propose budget-constrained dynamic grouping based on recent camera trajectories, which adaptively groups relevant players while limiting unnecessary communication. Experiments demonstrate that Multics achieves state-of-the-art performance in 4- and 6-player settings, with improved cross-player consistency, player-specific action and camera controllability, and interference robustness. Moreover, Multics generalizes from 4-player training to 6-, 8-, and 10-player inference without retraining, while reducing self-attention computation compared with fully-connected communication.
authors: Kaiyi Huang, Wangbo Yu, Yukun Huang, Jiwen Yu, Kunhao Liu, Donglin Yang, Wenbo Hu, Ying Shan, Xihui Liu
bullets: Addresses quadratic communication costs and interference from unrelated events as player count grows.
Uses player-, group-, and global-level communication, with shared group tokens linking local information to global context.
Dynamically groups relevant players from recent camera trajectories under a communication budget.
Achieves state-of-the-art results in 4- and 6-player settings with stronger consistency, controllability, and interference robustness.
Generalizes from 4-player training to 6-, 8-, and 10-player inference without retraining while reducing self-attention computation.
papers.selection_reason: Presents Multics, a multi-player world model with hierarchical communication, addressing scalability and interference in interactive world simulations.
papers.title: Multics: Generative Multi-Player World Model with Hierarchical Communication
papers.tldr: Multics generates scalable multi-player worlds by using hierarchical, dynamically formed communication groups instead of fully connecting all players.

papers.abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) have emerged as a promising alternative for embodied intelligence by jointly predicting future world states and robot actions. However, their heavy visual encoding and iterative generative inference incur substantial latency, limiting their applicability to high-frequency closed-loop control. Existing training-free acceleration methods typically optimize a single stage, yielding limited speedups or degraded control under aggressive reuse. In this work, we systematically profile the inference overhead of WAMs and observe abundant redundancy across Transformer computation, diffusion denoising, and consecutive policy queries. However, the safe removal of such redundancy depends strongly on its impact on action prediction and control sensitivity. Based on these observations, we introduce \textbf{MARS}, a training-free and plug-and-play framework for multi-level WAM acceleration. MARS selectively removes low-impact attention computation, adaptively accelerates diffusion inference according to motion granularity, and speculatively reuses predicted future visual representations across consecutive queries with online verification. Together, these complementary mechanisms provide remarkable acceleration while limiting approximation error. Extensive experiments across LIBERO, LIBERO-PRO, and RoboCasa show that MARS achieves up to $4.00\times$, $3.94\times$, and $2.10\times$ end-to-end speedups, respectively, while maintaining task success rate close to the original policy. Moreover, MARS generalizes across different model backbones and across simulation and real-robot experiments, substantially improving the efficiency--performance trade-off of WAM inference. Our code is available at https://github.com/PKU-VaLuE-Lab/MARS.
authors: Zengyuan Zuo, Yongchang Zhang, Guangyu Zhao, Tianze Zhang, Biao Wu, Meng Fang, Yiwu Zhong
bullets: WAMs are slowed by heavy visual encoding, iterative diffusion inference, and repeated policy queries, limiting high-frequency control.
MARS is training-free and plug-and-play, targeting redundancy in Transformer attention, diffusion denoising, and consecutive queries.
It removes low-impact attention computation, adapts diffusion effort to motion granularity, and reuses future visual features with online verification.
Experiments on LIBERO, LIBERO-PRO, and RoboCasa report up to 4.00×, 3.94×, and 2.10× speedups, respectively.
The approach transfers across model backbones and simulation-to-real-robot settings, though its scope is demonstrated on the evaluated WAM tasks and systems.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes MARS, a training-free framework for accelerating World Action Models (WAMs) through multi-level optimization, directly contributing to efficient interactive world models.
papers.title: MARS: Systematic Multi-Level Acceleration for World Action Models
papers.tldr: MARS accelerates World Action Model inference at multiple levels, achieving up to 4× end-to-end speedup while keeping task success close to the original policy.

papers.abstract: Frontier large language models (LLMs) now reason about space well enough to program robots, yet the world models behind robot policies are implicit, held in network weights or predicted video, and cannot be inspected or corrected directly. We present D-World, an explicit world-language-action model built on the Sense, Plan and Act decomposition. A perception agent writes the scene as an executable digital twin using generated vision and geometry code. A planning agent searches for actions in simulation and, after each executed action chunk, revises the twin's object states and named physical parameters against what the robot measured. A parameter revision is accepted only if replaying the latest chunk does not increase any measured residual beyond its tolerance, and every chunk is checked in the updated twin before it runs. Structural mismatches return to perception for reconstruction. We call this measurement-grounded cycle of correction and revision recursive self-improvement (RSI), in which the LLM stays frozen while the world it acts in improves. We model the choice of actions that both advance the task and expose model error as a dual control problem and show that the cost of incorporating evidence into the twin sets the threshold at which probing pays, so cheap local revision counteracts the turn-off of cautious controllers. Each episode runs a real-to-sim-to-real loop, and its recorded twins can be refitted and re-rendered offline into higher-fidelity environments for post-training. Because perception and planning communicate only through the twin and language, either can be replaced by a learned model, and since inference dominates the loop, the loop speeds up with faster models. On a dual-arm robot, towel and toaster tasks show local revisions, such as one reducing the bread's rendered-depth residual from 22.4 to 1.5 mm, that let execution continue without reconstruction.
bullets: Addresses the opacity and lack of direct correction in implicit robot world models.
Uses a Sense–Plan–Act architecture where perception builds an executable scene twin and planning searches for actions in simulation.
Revises object states and physical parameters after each action chunk, accepting updates only when replayed measurements remain within residual tolerances.
Frames information-seeking actions as dual control, balancing task progress with exposing and correcting model errors.
Demonstrates real-to-sim-to-real operation on dual-arm towel and toaster tasks, including local corrections that avoid full scene reconstruction.
papers.selection_reason: Explicit world-language-action model with digital-twin self-improvement for robot manipulation and planning.
papers.title: D-World: An Explicit World-Language-Action Model with Recursive Self-Improvement under Dual Control
papers.tldr: D-World enables robots to improve an explicit, inspectable digital twin through measurement-grounded planning and execution, without updating the underlying LLM.

papers.abstract: Clinical decisions depend on anticipating how a patient's condition will evolve as treatment is adjusted and new evidence becomes available. Existing medical world models capture patient-state evolution, but often define the evolving state around a particular modality or task, limiting reuse as inputs or prediction targets change. These models also retain history through observation sequences or recurrent or latent summaries rather than exposing preceding patient states and clinical actions as an ordered transition context. This distinction matters because similar current measurements may follow different recent changes, treatment exposures, and observed responses. To tackle these limitations, we propose PatientWM, a clinical world-model framework built around a unified patient state and sequential latent history. Availability-aware encoders integrate observations available at each decision time into the patient state, while typed decoders produce task-specific clinical readouts without defining the state around any single target. PatientWM further conditions each next-state prediction on the current state and supplied action together with a bounded, ordered history of preceding latent patient states and clinical actions, preserving recent treatment and response context. Experiments across MIMIC-III, MIMIC-IV, and three external clinical datasets show superior performance in clinical prediction, multi-step forecasting, and action-planning evaluation. Transfer experiments further demonstrate the generalizability of PatientWM's patient state. Together, these results establish its ability to forecast clinical evolution and support planning.
authors: Ziwen Kan, Jie Peng, Bo Yan, Davis Hobley, Zheng Zhang, Yu Tian, Tianlong Chen, Song Wang
bullets: Addresses the limited reuse of modality- or task-specific clinical world models.
Builds unified patient states from observations available at each decision time.
Uses typed decoders for task-specific clinical readouts without defining the state around one target.
Predicts next states from the current state, clinical action, and bounded history of prior states and actions.
Shows strong performance across clinical prediction, multi-step forecasting, action planning, and transfer evaluations.
papers.selection_reason: Clinical world model that predicts patient-state evolution conditioned on current state and clinical actions, fitting interactive world models.
papers.title: PatientWM: Towards Generalizable Clinical World Models via Unified Patient States
papers.tldr: PatientWM models clinical evolution with a reusable patient state and ordered latent history to improve prediction, forecasting, and treatment planning across datasets.

papers.abstract: Neural operator splitting composes a library of neural operators, one per physical mechanism, into zero-shot simulators of new equations. Existing approaches, however, require these mechanisms and their labels to be specified in advance. We ask whether a pretrained library can instead be adapted and grown from unlabeled trajectories in which multiple mechanisms act simultaneously. We introduce SPLICE, a framework that discovers operators without mechanism labels on mixture data. The contributions of the candidate operators to each trajectory are inferred by solving a convex optimization problem. A calibrated test then assigns each discovered operator the mechanism it implements. Failure cases are also detectable, when the library lacks the required physics or when mechanisms are insufficiently separable. Across one and two dimensional systems, the discovered operators recover mechanisms from unlabeled mixtures and compose into zero-shot simulators of unseen equations; a frozen library can also grow an operator for physics absent from pretraining, without labels and without forgetting. On Navier-Stokes, the discovered operators compose about as accurately as their supervised counterparts.
authors: Lucas Thil, Jesse Read, Guillaume Doquet, Rim Kaddah
bullets: Removes the need to predefine mechanisms and labels when adapting neural operator libraries.
Infers each candidate operator’s contribution using convex optimization, then assigns mechanisms with a calibrated test.
Detects failures when required physics is missing or mechanisms cannot be sufficiently separated.
Recovers mechanisms from unlabeled mixtures and composes them into zero-shot simulators of unseen equations.
Can add previously unseen physics without labels or forgetting; on Navier–Stokes, performance is about as accurate as supervised counterparts.
papers.selection_reason: Learned neural-operator simulators of physical dynamics are directly relevant to environment-dynamics prediction in world models.
papers.title: SPLICE: Sparse Physics Library Identification and Compositional Expansion
papers.tldr: SPLICE discovers and expands libraries of physics-specific neural operators from unlabeled trajectories containing multiple interacting mechanisms.

papers.abstract: Relational learning typically predicts from a database state, but decision making asks a different question: how will that state change under an action? In operational systems, the answer depends on system-specific dynamics that may not be visible in the database itself. We view each such system as a relational "world" and ask whether a model can infer how it behaves from observed executions. We introduce TabWM (Tabular World Model) and WorldRel, a generator of executable relational worlds for pretraining. Given executions from an unseen world, TabWM uses them as context to predict the sparse structured edits caused by a new action without parameter updates. Across 512 held-out worlds, complete-edit F1 rises from 0.016 with no observed executions to 0.685 with 64, where a correct edit must match its operation, relational location, and value. Because these predictions are explicit relational edits, they can be applied recursively to imagine candidate futures and compare actions before they are taken. Broader search over these predicted futures improves the realized return of selected action sequences. Together, these results suggest that relational dynamics can be learned in context, broadening relational learning from modeling system state to modeling how that state changes under action.
bullets: Motivation: Relational models usually predict states, but decision making requires predicting state changes under actions whose dynamics may be system-specific.
Method: TabWM uses executions from an unseen world as context, without parameter updates, to predict sparse structured edits for new actions.
WorldRel is introduced as a generator of executable relational worlds for pretraining.
Across 512 held-out worlds, complete-edit F1 increases from 0.016 with no executions to 0.685 with 64 observed executions.
Predicted edits can be recursively composed to imagine futures; broader search over them improves the realized return of selected action sequences.
papers.selection_reason: Learns relational world dynamics from executions and predicts action-induced edits; fits interactive world models.
papers.title: Relational Learning as World Modeling
papers.tldr: TabWM learns unseen relational-world dynamics from observed executions and predicts how actions will change database state, enabling better action planning.

papers.abstract: Cross-task generalization remains difficult for world action models (WAMs), even when their predicted futures depict plausible manipulation. This gap can be attributed directly: we make this gap directly testable by decoupling a WAM into a world model and an inverse-dynamics model (IDM), then holding the IDM fixed while replacing the source of future images. We introduce Align Once, Evaluate Everywhere (AoE), a camera-space inverse-dynamics model pretrained on large-scale robot data, which provides this recovery interface for different future sources across tasks and environments. Through it, we find that actions recovered from recorded futures of unseen tasks execute almost as well as replayed demonstrations, whereas futures predicted by world models collapse across benchmarks. The failures are not generic: they concentrate on the gripper and interaction geometry while generation capacity is spent on task-irrelevant background. This diagnosis suggests that supervision should target exactly these regions. We therefore introduce the vision-to-action (VITA) loss, which passes generated futures through the frozen AoE and penalizes discrepancies in the recovered actions, redirecting generation toward action-relevant detail. Across two world models and three manipulation benchmarks, this simple change raises the execution success of generated futures from near zero to 47.0%. The same loss also transfers to WAMs and yields consistent gains in native control.
authors: Chen Zhao, Zipeng Ye, Yihan Lin, Yuchen Xie, Jing Zhang
bullets: AoE decouples world models from inverse-dynamics models by holding the IDM fixed while swapping future-image sources.
Actions recovered from recorded futures of unseen tasks nearly match replayed demonstrations, but actions from predicted futures fail across benchmarks.
World-model errors concentrate on gripper and interaction geometry, while generation focuses on task-irrelevant backgrounds.
The VITA loss uses frozen AoE-recovered actions to emphasize action-relevant visual details.
Across two world models and three manipulation benchmarks, VITA raises generated-future execution success from near zero to 47.0% and improves native control.
papers.selection_reason: Diagnoses and improves cross-task generalization in world action models using a VITA loss, central to world model research.
papers.title: What Limits Cross-Task Generalization in World Action Models?
papers.tldr: Cross-task failure in world action models stems mainly from poor prediction of gripper interaction geometry, and action-based supervision substantially improves control from generated futures.

papers.abstract: Physics-informed generative models augment a data-fitting objective with residual penalties that encourage physical constraints to hold in generated samples. However, improving constraint satisfaction need not improve fidelity to the data distribution. We study this conflict in residual-regularized diffusion models and identify two possible consequences. First, the same prediction error can incur different residual costs near different feasible states, preferring states with lower residual sensitivity (avoidance). Second, this preference can extend to feasible states outside the data support, where the residual also vanishes (leakage). Motivated by this analysis, we propose a data-anchored penalty that weights prediction errors by the residual Jacobian at the clean training sample and normalizes the resulting magnitude. This removes the incentive to relocate to less sensitive states without changing the model architecture or sampling procedure. Experiments on a controlled synthetic system, three PDE systems, and molecular transition-state generation with flow matching demonstrate the benefits of anchoring. Code is available at https://github.com/TanjaBien/anchored_diffusion.
authors: Tanja Bien, Samir Darouich, Llu\'is Pastor-P\'erez, Vinh Tong, Loay Mualem, Mathias Niepert
bullets: Physics constraints may improve residual satisfaction while reducing fidelity to the data distribution.
Residual sensitivity varies across feasible states, creating incentives for avoidance and leakage.
The proposed penalty weights prediction errors using the residual Jacobian at clean training samples and normalizes the magnitude.
Experiments cover a synthetic system, three PDEs, and molecular transition-state generation with flow matching.
The method improves anchoring without architectural or sampling-procedure changes.
papers.selection_reason: Addresses distributional bias in physics-informed generative models. The proposed 'data-anchored penalty' is a transferable technical contribution for learning physical dynamics.
papers.title: Characterizing and Mitigating Distributional Bias in Physics-Informed Generative Models
papers.tldr: Residual penalties can make physics-informed generative models avoid data-supported states or leak into unsupported feasible states; a data-anchored penalty mitigates both without changing architecture or sampling.

papers.abstract: World models capture environment dynamics and support counterfactual reasoning for planning. In image-goal navigation, where the target often lies beyond the current field of view, the agent must not only model environmental dynamics but also maintain a persistent spatial memory of the scene. Existing approaches either introduce spatial context by fine-tuning pretrained models on the target task, which underexploits their spatial priors, or rely on external 3D reconstruction, which is computationally expensive for real-world deployment. In this paper, we propose the Geometry Grounded World Action Model (G$^2$WAM) for image-goal navigation. G$^2$WAM encodes spatial cues through a learned scene-coordinate localization module that anchors the current, goal, and history frames in a common reference frame, yielding a stable and consistent spatial context that enables efficient navigation without explicit 3D reconstruction. Following the world-action-model paradigm, G$^2$WAM jointly predicts future states and actions, eliminating the need for costly cross-entropy method (CEM) style planning. In addition, G$^2$WAM operates entirely in latent space, avoiding the computational burden of pixel-level reconstruction and substantially reducing inference cost. Across four trajectory prediction benchmarks, G$^2$WAM reduces average ATE and RPE by 40.1% and 35.2%, respectively. In closed-loop navigation experiments, it improves the success rate from 54.0% to 63.0% and the success weighted by path length (SPL) from 36.4% to 59.2%, while maintaining high efficiency.
authors: Ke Gui, Chenghao Shi, Ziyue Wang, Longwen Chen, Xieyuanli Chen, Huimin Lu
bullets: Addresses image-goal navigation when targets are outside the current view and persistent spatial memory is required.
Uses learned scene-coordinate localization to anchor current, goal, and history frames in a shared reference frame.
Jointly predicts future states and actions in latent space, avoiding pixel reconstruction and CEM-style planning.
Reduces average ATE and RPE by 40.1% and 35.2% across four trajectory prediction benchmarks.
Improves closed-loop success rate from 54.0% to 63.0% and SPL from 36.4% to 59.2%, while maintaining efficiency.
papers.selection_reason: Geometry-grounded world action model for image-goal navigation with latent state-action prediction and persistent spatial memory.
papers.title: G$^2$WAM: World Action Models for Efficient and Geometry Grounded Image-Goal Navigation
papers.tldr: G$^2$WAM enables efficient image-goal navigation by combining geometry-grounded spatial memory with latent world-action modeling, improving trajectory prediction and navigation success without explicit 3D reconstruction or costly planning.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models are often pretrained via imitation learning, making reinforcement learning (RL) post-training important when deployment moves beyond demonstration coverage. Existing refinement paradigms expose a reliability--efficiency tension: model-free refinement avoids simulator bias but is interaction-intensive, whereas model-based refinement can exploit unreliable imagination even as its simulator adapts. We propose Model-Evolving Reinforcement Learning (MERL), a trust-calibrated framework that couples policy optimization with an online-updated simulator comprising a world model and a reward proxy head. Across stages, simulator reliability controls the imagined-data ratio and rollout horizon; within rollouts, chunk-level trust controls replay selection and optimization weight. For recursive imagination without exact grounded continuations, a residual predictor estimates trust without querying future ground truth. On perturbed LIBERO-PRO tasks, MERL reaches 79.7% average success, improves high-threshold learning speed by 10.9% over the matched model-free control, and outperforms same-protocol external baselines across three training seeds. Fixed-data adaptation from 50 demonstrations per task achieves 80.0% average success on two physical-robot tasks.
authors: Wenzhan Li, Yiran Qin, Heng Zhou, Huirui Wang, Yulan Guo, Ruimao Zhang
bullets: Addresses the efficiency–reliability trade-off between interaction-heavy model-free refinement and potentially biased model-based refinement.
Couples policy optimization with an online-updated world model and reward proxy, using simulator reliability to adjust imagined-data ratios and rollout horizons.
Uses chunk-level trust for replay selection and optimization weighting, with a residual predictor for recursive imagination without future ground-truth queries.
On perturbed LIBERO-PRO tasks, achieves 79.7% average success and 10.9% faster high-threshold learning than matched model-free control.
With 50 demonstrations per task, reaches 80.0% average success on two physical-robot tasks.
papers.selection_reason: VLA RL post-training with a trust-calibrated evolving world-model simulator directly fits embodied robot learning and interactive world models.
papers.title: Trust-Calibrated VLA Policy Post-Training with Evolving Imagination
papers.tldr: MERL improves VLA reinforcement-learning post-training by dynamically trusting and weighting imagined experience as its learned simulator evolves.

papers.abstract: The growing use of language models for forecasting motivates a broader evaluation of their world-model capabilities. Such evaluation must go beyond predictive accuracy to assess hidden-state inference and intervention prediction. Real-world forecasting benchmarks offer limited access to hidden-state ground truth and controlled experiments. We introduce CivWorldBench, a benchmark built on a multi-agent strategy game engine with recorded internal states, controlled observations, and paired intervention rollouts. Its 1,900 decision points from 475 worlds support three task levels: association forecasting, belief inference, and intervention prediction. Reference predictors support attributable evaluation of capability gaps, with an expert harness and empirical ceiling estimates contextualizing scores. Stored trajectories make intermediate predictions verifiable, while agent-play experiments test whether world-model capabilities support decision-making. The main panel comprises eleven frontier language models. Composite benchmark scores correlate with real-world forecasting leaderboards on matched model panels, more closely than with a general-capability index, supporting its use as a proxy for real-world forecasting capability. Strong association forecasts do not consistently extend to belief inference or intervention prediction, and effect magnitudes remain poorly calibrated despite informative direction predictions. Process verification reveals errors missed by final-answer evaluation, and structured reasoning improves intervention prediction for the strongest model in the process study. Agent-play experiments identify useful assisted plans and motivate evaluating decision-relevant capabilities beyond association forecasting. These findings identify hidden-state inference, intermediate-state prediction, and effect calibration as priorities for world-model training.
authors: Ang Li, Haofei Yu, Zhengwei Tao, Liang Chen, Kuan Li, Miaomiao Li, Chenran Cai, Bin Liang, Jiaxuan You, Kam-Fai Wong
bullets: Benchmark uses a strategy-game engine with recorded states, controlled observations, and paired intervention rollouts across 1,900 decision points from 475 worlds.
It evaluates association forecasting, belief inference, and intervention prediction, with reference predictors, expert harnesses, and estimated performance ceilings.
Scores correlate with real-world forecasting leaderboards, while strong association forecasting does not reliably transfer to hidden-state or intervention tasks.
Models often predict intervention directions correctly but poorly calibrate effect magnitudes; process verification uncovers errors missed by final answers.
Agent-play studies find useful assisted plans and highlight the need to evaluate decision-relevant world-model capabilities.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces CivWorldBench, a benchmark for evaluating language world models in multi-agent sandbox worlds, focusing on belief inference and intervention prediction. Relevant to world model evaluation and dynamics.
papers.title: CivWorldBench: Evaluating Language World Models in Structured Multi-Agent Sandbox Worlds
papers.tldr: CivWorldBench evaluates language-model world models beyond forecasting accuracy by testing hidden-state inference and intervention prediction in controlled multi-agent worlds.

papers.abstract: Recent world action models draw on video generation priors to jointly predict future observations and robot actions. Adapting these priors to control requires determining how future predictions should guide policy learning. RAP-WAM combines predictive Rehearsal and Action Perturbations (RAP) with future-supervised queries and Coupled Action Projection for policy learning. Predictive rehearsal trains on model-generated inputs while retaining recorded targets, and accumulates recurring errors into a spatial prior. We perturb actions and measure changes in video predictions. Action-response-based spatiotemporal credit assignment combines these responses, prediction error, and the rehearsal prior to allocate visual supervision; spatially aggregating the responses determines supervision intensity across future action steps. No separate scoring network or deployment-time probe is required. The base learns from a video-pretrained backbone without intermediate pretraining on external embodied data. We evaluate the fixed base and its agent-refined, task-conditioned system. On 42 RoboDojo tasks, their average success rates are 12.85% and 15.62%, with Scores of 17.86 and 20.59. Across 15 real-robot tasks, the complete system achieves 89.00% task-macro-average success, exceeding the strongest of five baselines by 37.67 percentage points. Across 315 fixed-output simulation windows, 45.21% of response-top20 positions fall outside error-top20, revealing information beyond prediction error.
authors: Yuanpeng He, Ceyao Zhang, Fangjing Li, Kefei Zhu, Lijian Li, Yueheng Li, Tianjia He, Wenpin Jiao, Zhi Jin, Yaodong Yang, Yuanpei Chen
bullets: Addresses how future video predictions should guide policy learning in world-action models.
Uses predictive rehearsal, action-response perturbations, future-supervised queries, and Coupled Action Projection.
Allocates visual supervision using prediction error, action responses, and a spatial rehearsal prior without a separate scoring network or deployment-time probe.
On 42 RoboDojo tasks, average success was 12.85% for the fixed base and 15.62% after agent refinement.
On 15 real-robot tasks, the complete system achieved 89.00% task-macro-average success, 37.67 percentage points above the strongest of five baselines.
papers.selection_reason: Learns world-action models from video prediction and uses action perturbations to guide robot policies, directly relevant to world models and embodied learning.
papers.title: RAP-WAM: Learning World-Action Models through Predictive Rehearsal and Action Perturbations
papers.tldr: RAP-WAM learns robot control from video-pretrained world-action models by combining predictive rehearsal with action perturbations for targeted future supervision.

papers.abstract: Video world models must generate physically plausible futures, not just realistic frames. Existing approaches typically use semantic, physical, or predictive information to guide the visual generation stream, leaving a fundamental question: where inside the generator should predictions of scene evolution live? Standard video tokens jointly encode appearance and dynamics, but provide no distinct state for learning and reading predictive dynamics. We answer this question with the Physical Registry: temporally grounded registry slots inside a video DiT that are initialized from an observation-conditioned forecast, co-evolve with video tokens, and receive future-representation supervision, making predictive dynamics an explicit, readable state of the generator. In a controlled comparison of predictive-state interfaces on Physics-IQ Verified, Physical Registry improves vanilla fine-tuning by 9.9/8.7 points on I2V/V2V, the largest gain among the interfaces we compare. Across all Cosmos and WAN backbones, Physical Registry improves Physics-IQ Verified scores. With only 0.45% additional parameters, it enables Cosmos 3 Nano 16B to surpass the published I2V score of Cosmos 3 Super 64B (43.56 vs. 42.7). On WorldModelBench, it also improves physical adherence and the total score for all four evaluated backbones. Because the registry becomes candidate-specific while remaining readable, the Physical Registry Selector (PRS) ranks emerging futures by how far their intermediate registry readouts depart from the shared forecast before full denoising is complete. Across four backbones, this selection improves I2V scores by 5.6-15.9% without completed-video external scoring. Together, these results support a broader principle: dynamics prediction should live as an explicit model state that co-evolves with the video representation. Project page: https://grainsack.github.io/physical-registry/
authors: Shinseong Kim, Jaeseok Jeong, Jianlong Fu, Youngjung Uh
bullets: Video tokens normally mix appearance and dynamics without a distinct, readable state for scene evolution.
The method inserts temporally grounded registry slots into a video DiT, initialized from an observation-conditioned forecast and supervised with future representations.
Across Cosmos and WAN backbones, it improves Physics-IQ Verified and WorldModelBench performance; the abstract reports gains of 9.9/8.7 points for I2V/V2V in controlled comparisons.
With 0.45% extra parameters, Cosmos 3 Nano 16B exceeds the published I2V score of Cosmos 3 Super 64B.
The Physical Registry Selector ranks futures from intermediate registry readouts, improving I2V scores by 5.6–15.9% without completed-video external scoring.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces explicit predictive-state registry slots inside video diffusion world models, directly advancing physically plausible video prediction.
papers.title: World Models Need a Physical Registry: Learning Internal Predictive States for Physically Plausible World Models
papers.tldr: Physical Registry adds explicit predictive-state slots to video world models, improving physical plausibility and enabling early ranking of candidate futures.

papers.abstract: Generalist robot manipulation can benefit from pretrained vision-language models (VLMs) for semantic reasoning and video generation models (VGMs) for world modeling. However, existing unified models that directly fuse them through shared attention at multiple layers can make it harder to draw on their specialized capabilities. We introduce PINT, a unified model that coordinates semantic reasoning, world modeling, and action generation through a shared chunk-level Predictive Intent while preserving expert-specific pathways. PINT inserts learnable Intent Tokens into the VLM sequence to form this representation, conditioning both the VGM and an Action Expert (AE). It replaces only the VGM's prompt conditioning and retains the VGM at inference, where the AE reads its representations through one-way attention. Rather than prescribing what Predictive Intent should encode, PINT learns it jointly from the native prediction objectives of the VLM, VGM, and AE, which provide complementary views of the same upcoming task execution. Training uses two stages: Stage 1 freezes the VGM so that future video prediction shapes Predictive Intent with task-relevant future dynamics, while Stage 2 fixes the learned Intent and adapts the VGM and AE. Without embodied pretraining, PINT achieves strong in-distribution (ID) performance and substantially improves out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization, reaching 15.5% on RoboTwin 2.0-Hard compared with 1.8% for Fast-WAM and 3.2% for StarVLA, and 79.5% on LIBERO-Plus compared with 51.5% and 75.0%, respectively. Across five real-world bimanual tasks, PINT reaches 68% ID and 24% OOD success, compared with 35%/9% for pretrained Motus and 67%/35% for pretrained $\pi_{0.5}$.
authors: Xinyu Guo, Chao Jing, Li Yi, Xingyu Chen, Zhengxing Wu
bullets: Addresses the challenge that tightly fusing VLMs and VGMs can weaken their specialized capabilities.
Uses learnable Intent Tokens from the VLM to condition a video generation model and an Action Expert through one-way information flow.
Learns Predictive Intent jointly from VLM, VGM, and action-prediction objectives, using a two-stage training strategy.
Reports strong in-distribution performance and improved out-of-distribution generalization, including 15.5% on RoboTwin 2.0-Hard and 79.5% on LIBERO-Plus.
In real-world bimanual tasks, achieves 68% in-distribution and 24% out-of-distribution success without embodied pretraining.
papers.selection_reason: Unified model combining VLM, video world model, and action expert for manipulation.
papers.title: PINT: A Unified Model with Shared Predictive Intent for Robot Manipulation
papers.tldr: PINT improves generalist robot manipulation by coordinating vision-language reasoning, video world modeling, and action generation through a shared learned Predictive Intent while preserving expert-specific pathways.

papers.abstract: Bubbly flows involve strongly coupled bubble motion, deformation, and hydrodynamic interactions, making high-fidelity simulation computationally expensive. We propose a neural surrogate that jointly predicts bubble trajectories and interface deformation in a compact, shared representation, replacing costly mesh-resolved simulation with fast generative inference. Because two-phase flow dynamics is nonlinear and chaotic, we treat forecasting as a conditional generative problem rather than deterministic regression, predicting entire future windows in a single pass. We train and evaluate the surrogate on BubbleSH, a Front-Tracking dataset of rising deformable bubble swarms, assessing performance using trajectory, shape, and distributional metrics over kinematic, morphological, and interaction-based properties. The surrogate reproduces key flow statistics while running several orders of magnitude faster than the underlying DNS solver.
authors: Kiet Bennema ten Brinke, Rachna Ramesh, Douwe Orij, Ivo Roghair, Vlado Menkovski
bullets: Targets the costly simulation of coupled bubble trajectories, deformation, and hydrodynamic interactions.
Represents bubble state compactly with shared spherical-harmonic features.
Uses coupled flow matching to generate entire future windows probabilistically, accounting for nonlinear and chaotic dynamics.
Evaluated on the BubbleSH front-tracking dataset with trajectory, shape, and distributional metrics.
Matches key flow statistics and runs several orders of magnitude faster than the underlying DNS solver.
papers.selection_reason: Generative neural surrogate for bubbly flow dynamics, a learned predictor of physical environment dynamics.
papers.title: Probabilistic Simulation of Gas-Liquid Interfaces with Coupled Flow Matching on Spherical Harmonics
papers.tldr: A conditional generative neural surrogate rapidly predicts bubble motion and deformation while preserving key bubbly-flow statistics.

papers.abstract: Video-based interactive world models aim to enable real-time, user-controllable environments. Yet most existing systems are trained and rolled out at a fixed temporal rate, limiting both runtime-rate adaptation and physical-horizon coverage -- a limitation we term temporal-rate coupling. Specifically, when runtime generation throughput differs from the learned temporal rate, the generated world evolves unintentionally more slowly or quickly. Moreover, using a single temporal rate imposes an inherent trade-off between temporal granularity and physical horizon: higher rates capture finer motion but cover a shorter duration under a fixed context window. To address both limitations, we introduce Rate-Adaptive Rollout (RAR), a framework that enables interactive world models to roll out at controllable temporal rates. At its core, Stride-RoPE aligns latent frames sampled at different rates on a shared physical-time coordinate, enabling consistent multi-rate rollout, unseen-rate generalization, and online rate switching without discarding history. Meanwhile, RAR uses multi-stride video sampling to enable joint learning of fine-grained dynamics and long-horizon evolution. Across action- and camera-controlled environments, RAR achieves temporally consistent multi-rate rollout and online rate switching while preserving high-rate generation quality and extending physical horizons under matched training budgets. RAR also transfers to pretrained world models while preserving perceptual quality.
authors: Yaoyang Liu, Dongyu Yan, Yihua Du, Shengju Qian, Zeke Xie, Xin Wang, Ying-Cong Chen, Long Chen
bullets: Addresses temporal-rate coupling: fixed training and rollout rates can cause unintended slowdowns or speedups and limit horizon coverage.
Uses Stride-RoPE to align latent frames across sampling rates on a shared physical-time coordinate.
Supports unseen-rate generalization and online rate switching without discarding prior history.
Multi-stride video sampling jointly learns fine-grained dynamics and long-horizon evolution.
Demonstrates consistent multi-rate rollout, preserved high-rate quality, longer horizons, and transfer to pretrained models across action- and camera-controlled environments.
papers.selection_reason: Rate-adaptive rollout for interactive world models; directly targets controllable multi-rate world simulation.
papers.title: RAR: Rate-Adaptive Rollout for Time-Consistent Interactive World Models
papers.tldr: RAR enables interactive world models to generate temporally consistent video at controllable rates while supporting both fine motion and longer physical horizons.

papers.abstract: Morphogenesis is driven by the interplay of genetic regulation and tissue mechanics. In vivo video data is limited, particularly under genetic mutations and environmental perturbations, making generalization beyond the most representative conditions in the dataset challenging. However, at tissue scales, the dynamics of Drosophila can be described as a continuum flow, motivating the usage of representations learned across other physical systems as priors for developmental dynamics. We investigate finetuning Walrus, a Continuum Dynamics Foundation Model pretrained across a broad set of simulated continuous systems, on tissue velocity fields from only 12 wild-type Drosophila blastoderm videos. We evaluate autoregressive prediction both in-distribution and zero-shot under unseen temperature and genetic perturbations. Zero-shot refers to evaluation on perturbation conditions never seen during wild-type finetuning, without any additional training. In-distribution, a Fourier Neural Operator model trained from scratch achieves best performance on VRMSE. However, Walrus (CRPS) is the strongest model under the most severe distribution shift of unseen samples of mutated embryos and temperature conditions. Interestingly, predictions capture the shape of the mean surface tissue velocity trajectory and its separation between 17{\deg}C and 27{\deg}C, including the timing of the peak at Germ Band Extension onset, a biologically meaningful milestone of embryo development. Our results provide preliminary support that representations learned from different dynamical systems can transfer to experimental morphogenesis in developmental regimes, provided they admit a continuum description. More broadly, our results motivate further study of physics foundation models as a new complementary tool for the simulation of morphogenesis in low-data regimes.
authors: Louisa Cornelis, Haewon Jeong, Irina Espejo, Payel Mukhopadhyay
bullets: Uses only 12 wild-type blastoderm videos to fine-tune Walrus on tissue velocity fields.
Evaluates autoregressive prediction both in-distribution and zero-shot on unseen temperature and genetic perturbations.
A Fourier Neural Operator trained from scratch performs best in-distribution on VRMSE.
Walrus achieves the strongest CRPS performance under the most severe shifts involving mutated embryos and temperature conditions.
Predictions recover biologically meaningful temperature-dependent trajectories, including peak timing at Germ Band Extension onset.
papers.selection_reason: Transfers a continuum dynamics foundation model to predict tissue velocity fields, fitting learned environment dynamics.
papers.title: From Simulated Fluids to Living Tissue: Zero-Shot Foundation Model Transfer to Perturbed Embryos
papers.tldr: A continuum-dynamics foundation model pretrained on simulated physical systems can transfer zero-shot to perturbed Drosophila embryo dynamics, especially under severe distribution shifts.

papers.abstract: We propose the task of Interactive 4D Volumetric Liquid Forecasting: predicting the spatiotemporal evolution of a future dense 3D liquid velocity field conditioned on how a solid object moves through it. This task provides an upstream physical forecasting primitive for systems that need to reason about motion-conditioned liquid response, including robotic liquid manipulation, digital twins, and rigid-fluid video generation. Existing works have made efforts in predicting flow around static or prescribed solid geometries and synthesizing visually plausible fluid motion. Yet these approaches provide limited coverage for interactive liquid dynamics, as they are not capable of forecasting how a moving solid induces a future full-domain liquid response. In this forecasting scenario, the hydrodynamic effect is condensed near an evolving liquid-solid interface, but the prediction target is a global spatiotemporal rollout. To address this challenge, we propose a two-level recurrent forecasting framework, TIDE/TIDES: TIDE isolates localized interface-driven forecasting, while TIDES adds transport-aware coupling and explicit stabilization to reduce accumulated rollout error. Across adapted neighboring baselines, controlled component ablations, motion/size OOD tests, and long-horizon evaluation, TIDES achieves the best forecasting performance and the ablations identify localized interaction, transport coupling, and stabilization as the key contributors. Together, our task formulation, benchmark, and TIDE/TIDES study establish a controlled foundation for moving-solid-conditioned dense liquid forecasting. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/jongwonryu/TIDE-TIDES.
authors: Jongwon Ryu, Sunjae Yoon, Junyeong Kim
bullets: Targets global, spatiotemporal liquid-flow rollouts conditioned on solid-object motion, addressing a gap in interactive fluid forecasting.
TIDE models localized, interface-driven effects, while TIDES adds transport-aware coupling and explicit stabilization for rollout robustness.
Experiments include baseline comparisons, component ablations, motion/size out-of-distribution tests, and long-horizon evaluation.
TIDES achieves the best reported forecasting performance, with localized interaction, transport coupling, and stabilization identified as key contributors.
The task, benchmark, and code provide a foundation for robotics, digital twins, and rigid-fluid video generation.
papers.selection_reason: Action-conditioned spatiotemporal liquid forecasting is an interactive world model.
papers.title: Interactive 4D Volumetric Liquid Forecasting under Moving-Solid Interaction
papers.tldr: Introduces a benchmark and recurrent framework for forecasting dense 4D liquid velocity fields under moving-solid interactions.

papers.abstract: Interactive world models must capture how multiple participants jointly change a shared environment while observing different parts of it. Competitive games make this challenge concrete: players cooperate and compete, while fog of war, team vision and camera placement determine what each can see. Modeling these interactions requires data that connect individual observations and actions to shared state and events. We introduce the Esports World Model Dataset (EWM), a collection of human gameplay spanning StarCraft II, Dota 2 and Counter-Strike 2, with 3,053 games and maps and approximately 4,880 player-view hours, including estimated hours for the ongoing CS2 extension. It includes 4,628 completed StarCraft II views, all ten perspectives for 303 Dota 2 matches, and up to ten views per round in CS2. Across these views, replay-clock alignment connects rendered video with game-native actions, structured state and events from the same match. The three games expose complementary observation conditions: private fog of war, shared team vision and first-person viewpoints. In StarCraft II, player-specific entity records further distinguish live observations from remembered snapshots and link co-observed entities across opposing views. Together with temporal alignment, these records allow researchers to distinguish legitimate information differences from disagreement about shared state. By connecting human decisions, shared dynamics and player-specific information, EWM supports research toward jointly controlled multiplayer world models and interactive environments populated by teammates and opponents learned from human play.
authors: Weiyu Ma, Zeyuan Gong, Xuhui Liu, Wenxuan Zhang, Jian Ding, Xinyu Cui, Jian Zhao, Mohamed Elhoseiny
bullets: Covers human gameplay from StarCraft II, Dota 2, and Counter-Strike 2 across 3,053 games and maps and approximately 4,880 player-view hours.
Aligns rendered video with game-native actions, structured state, and events using replay clocks.
Captures complementary information settings: private fog of war, shared team vision, and first-person views.
Includes StarCraft II records that distinguish live observations from remembered snapshots and link entities across opposing views.
Supports studying how teammates and opponents jointly affect shared environments despite differing observations.
papers.selection_reason: Dataset specifically designed for interactive world models with multi-agent observations, actions, and shared state.
papers.title: Esports World Model Dataset
papers.tldr: EWM is a multimodal esports dataset linking multiple players’ views, actions, and shared game state to support multiplayer world-model research.

papers.abstract: Learned world models for autonomous driving operate in unconstrained latent spaces, yet the physical systems they represent are governed by strict non-holonomic constraints: ground vehicles cannot realize instantaneous pure lateral motion. We study long-horizon latent rollout modeling for autonomous driving and ask whether rollout quality can be improved by assigning a motion-aware geometry to latent transitions, rather than by redesigning the predictor architecture. Starting from an unconstrained latent rollout baseline, we introduce Directional Pullback Regularization (DPR), a training time method that defines a kinematics-aware anisotropic Riemannian metric in decoded state space and pulls it back through the decoder Jacobian to the latent manifold. The resulting latent-space metric assigns higher cost to latent directions that decode to lateral vehicle motion, while preserving the original encoder-dynamics-decoder backbone. This yields a clean three-way comparison among an Unconstrained Latent Rollout model (ULR), an Euclidean Pullback Regularization ablation (EPR), and the full directional method (DPR). We evaluate all models on open-loop ego-motion rollout over a common 10-second test horizon, using training rollout lengths of 1, 3, 5, and 10 steps. Across all four training regimes, DPR achieves lower 10-second final displacement error than both ULR and EPR. The strongest relative accuracy gain appears for models trained with 3-step rollout supervision, where DPR reduces the 10-second final displacement error by approximately 44 percent relative to ULR. The strongest overall control-relevant tradeoff is obtained for longer rollout-trained models, especially at 10 steps, where DPR simultaneously improves displacement error, lateral motion consistency, and forward motion preservation relative to both ULR and EPR.
authors: Shatadal Mishra, Ahmadreza Moradipari, Nejib Ammar
bullets: Addresses non-holonomic motion constraints in unconstrained latent rollouts without changing the predictor architecture.
Pulls a kinematics-aware anisotropic metric from decoded state space back onto the latent manifold.
Compared with unconstrained and Euclidean pullback baselines across 1-, 3-, 5-, and 10-step training rollouts.
DPR achieves lower 10-second final displacement error in every training regime; the largest relative gain is about 44% after 3-step training.
With longer rollout supervision, especially 10 steps, DPR also improves lateral-motion consistency and forward-motion preservation.
papers.selection_reason: Improves latent world model rollouts for autonomous driving with kinematics-aware regularization; fits world models.
papers.title: Directional Pullback Regularization for Long-Horizon Rollout of Latent World Models in Autonomous Driving
papers.tldr: Directional Pullback Regularization improves long-horizon latent world-model rollouts by penalizing latent directions that decode to physically implausible lateral vehicle motion.

papers.abstract: Behavioral foundation models (BFMs) provide humanoids with reusable repertoires of whole-body behaviors; in real-world humanoid control, the same behavioral intent may require fundamentally different motions under different terrain constraints. Covering such variation with terrain-matched demonstrations requires enumerating a combinatorial space of behaviors and terrain geometries. We introduce P-BFM, a perceptive behavioral foundation model that factorizes humanoid control into terrain-invariant intent and terrain-conditioned realization. A forward-backward representation maps motion references, target states, and reward functions into a shared intent space without terrain information, while a perceptive policy learns how to realize each intent under the surrounding terrain geometry. We further identify a complementary limitation of purely latent control: behavioral latents can preserve local motion patterns while losing precise global progress. We therefore introduce Explicit Root Instructions (ERI), which separates global transport (e.g., heading and planar velocity) from behavioral intent, while leaving local whole-body adaptation to the perceptive policy. This decomposition leads to a characteristic capability absent from conventional BFMs: one fixed intent induces different, terrain-appropriate behaviors, including changes in step height, stride, posture, foothold placement, and contacts, without terrain-specific demonstrations. Across challenging terrains, P-BFM improves motion fidelity, root-control precision, and perturbation recovery over strong baselines. A single frozen policy further supports motion tracking, goal reaching, reward inference, teleoperation, and terrain-aware recovery, and transfers zero-shot to a Unitree G1 using onboard depth sensing.
authors: Xue Wang, Yitang Li, Yiming Zhang, Siqin Wang, Junhan Sun, Zhihao Liu, Yaojie Shen, Jingbo Yuan, Hao Zhao, Qingdu Li
bullets: Factorizes control into terrain-invariant behavioral intent and terrain-conditioned motion realization.
Uses a forward-backward representation to map motion references, target states, and rewards into a shared intent space.
Adds Explicit Root Instructions to preserve precise global transport while the policy handles local whole-body adaptation.
Adapts step height, stride, posture, footholds, and contacts across challenging terrains, improving fidelity, root control, and perturbation recovery.
A single frozen policy supports tracking, goal reaching, reward inference, teleoperation, and recovery, with zero-shot transfer to a Unitree G1 using depth sensing.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces P-BFM, a perceptive behavioral foundation model for humanoid control that factors intent and terrain-conditioned realization, enabling zero-shot transfer to new terrains.
papers.title: P-BFM: Perceptive Behavioral Foundation Models for Humanoid Control via Unsupervised Reinforcement Learning
papers.tldr: P-BFM enables humanoids to execute the same behavioral intent with terrain-appropriate whole-body motions, without terrain-specific demonstrations.

papers.abstract: Generating coherent videos grounded in a unified underlying world remains a major challenge, particularly under large viewpoint changes, where existing methods often struggle to maintain stable representations of individual objects. To this end, we introduce Totem, an object-centric 3D memory framework for world-consistent video generation. Totem first represents each selected object as a persistent 3D memory aligned to a shared world frame, assigning it a dedicated state. Based on these memories, we design a dual-stream 3D conditioning architecture that combines object memories with scene geometry for target-view synthesis. Moreover, these object memories constrain the model's attention with 3D structural information, thereby preserving object surfaces and relative spatial layouts. Extensive experiments on world-generation and object-centric benchmarks demonstrate that Totem generates videos depicting a more object-consistent 3D world under challenging camera trajectories, while supporting versatile applications.
authors: Zichen Wan, Tianyu Huang, Fan Li, Kai Wang, Hongzhi Zhang, Wangmeng Zuo
bullets: Addresses unstable object representations and incoherent scenes during viewpoint-changing video generation.
Represents selected objects as persistent 3D memories in a shared world frame, with dedicated object states.
Uses dual-stream 3D conditioning to combine object memories with scene geometry for target-view synthesis.
Injects 3D structural information into attention to preserve object surfaces and relative spatial layouts.
Experiments on world-generation and object-centric benchmarks show improved object-consistent 3D worlds under challenging camera trajectories.
papers.selection_reason: Object-centric 3D memory for world-consistent video generation; fits world-model video prediction and generation.
papers.title: Totem: Object-Centric 3D Memory for World-Consistent Video Generation
papers.tldr: Totem enables world-consistent video generation under large viewpoint changes by maintaining persistent, object-centric 3D memories.

papers.abstract: Surgical world models must turn prospective robot actions into visually faithful, structurally consistent instrument motion. We introduce SurgCast, which predicts future instrument skeletons from current structure, robot state, and future actions, then uses the forecast to control video generation. Dual-path injection combines skeleton geometry with derived, instrument-specific motion descriptors through geometric residuals and conditioning modulation. Both paths complement native action conditioning and are retained in a four-step causal student. On SutureBot and SRTH-Porcine-Cholei, the teacher and student improve all seven reported quality and instrument-consistency metrics over their respective direct-action baselines; teacher FVD decreases by 37.6% and 67.3%. Ablations show that future actions improve skeleton prediction and that combining both injection paths performs best across all six metrics under predicted skeletons. These results support using predicted articulated structure and its motion semantics as a control interface for surgical video prediction. Project videos and examples are available at https://surgcast.netlify.app/.
authors: Wanhao Liu, Rulin Zhou, Liangjing Shao, Zhaocheng Lin, Dongyue Li, Jinsong Lin, Guoheng Ma, Hangheng Yang, Zhiqing Tang, Jing Chen, Panshuo Li, Hongliang Ren
bullets: Predicts future instrument skeletons from current structure, robot state, and planned actions.
Injects skeleton geometry and instrument-specific motion descriptors through complementary conditioning paths.
Uses a four-step causal student to retain both injection paths alongside native action conditioning.
Improves all reported quality and instrument-consistency metrics over direct-action baselines on SutureBot and SRTH-Porcine-Cholei.
Teacher FVD decreases by 37.6% and 67.3% on the two evaluated datasets; ablations favor combining both paths.
papers.selection_reason: Action-conditioned future skeleton prediction and controllable surgical video generation directly fit interactive world models.
papers.title: SurgCast: Action-Conditioned Future Skeletons for Controllable Surgical World Models
papers.tldr: SurgCast forecasts action-conditioned instrument skeletons to make surgical video generation more controllable and structurally consistent.

papers.abstract: World Action Models (WAMs), often built upon pretrained video-generation world models, have emerged as a promising framework for general-purpose and open-ended robot control. However, their real-world deployment often suffers from discontinuous and jerky execution. Existing methods typically address this issue by either improving inference efficiency or enhancing action continuity across prediction chunks, without jointly addressing both challenges. To bridge this gap, we propose StreamingWAM, a streaming-diffusion framework for WAM-based robot control. StreamingWAM combines a noise ladder for chunk-wise action prediction, a prefix rollout module for cross-chunk continuity, and dense video-history memory for temporally consistent conditioning. Experiments on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, RoboTwin 2.0, and real-world robotic tasks demonstrate that StreamingWAM improves action continuity across static and dynamic settings, achieving competitive performance while reducing steady-state replanning latency to 72.9 ms in simulation and 57.3 ms on the real robot. The method also produces smoother action transitions, while the streaming staircase reduces sensitivity to the execution horizon K.
authors: Shaojie Ren, Jingwen Sun, Zezhi Liu, Hongjin Chen, Xin Jin, Wei Zou, Zhibo Chen
bullets: Addresses jerky, discontinuous execution in World Action Model-based robot control.
Uses chunk-wise staircase flow matching with a noise ladder for streaming action prediction.
Combines prefix rollouts and dense video-history memory for cross-chunk temporal consistency.
Evaluated in simulation and real-world tasks, with steady-state replanning latency of 72.9 ms and 57.3 ms, respectively.
Produces smoother transitions and reduces sensitivity to the execution horizon K.
papers.selection_reason: Streaming world action model for robot control.
papers.title: StreamingWAM: Streaming World Action Modeling via Chunk-Wise Staircase Flow Matching
papers.tldr: StreamingWAM enables smoother, lower-latency robot control by jointly improving streaming inference and continuity between action chunks.

papers.abstract: Large-scale video generation models are increasingly viewed as a promising path toward world models, yet their ability to capture causally coherent physical dynamics remains poorly understood. Existing evaluations largely emphasize visual quality, prompt adherence, or broad physical plausibility, leaving open whether a model can faithfully realize a complete causal cascade, in which an initiating event propagates through causally dependent interactions to a terminal outcome. We introduce CausalCascade, a simulator-grounded benchmark centered on 50 event-rich Blender scenes with structured event graphs, graph-grounded diagnostic VQA, three levels of future-event specification, and 2,832 controlled counterfactual variants, and use it to evaluate nine image-to-video models with complementary motion-, event-, and counterfactual-level diagnostics. Across the evaluated models, generated motion is more reliably localized spatially than realized with correct spatiotemporal evolution, while richer future-event specification improves event recovery but leaves physical realization limited. Counterfactual evaluation further reveals weak selective responsiveness to physical interventions, while most audited failures are foundational, arising at scene consistency or event occurrence. Together, these results position causal cascade generation as a process-level test of world modeling and highlight the need to jointly recover the intended future, faithfully realize its physical evolution, selectively respond to physical interventions, and maintain a coherent physical world over time. Code and dataset are available at https://github.com/SJTU-DeepDeltaLab/CausalCascade .
authors: Jialiang Li, Zhengning Xu, Zongyang Ma, Shaobo Cui
bullets: Introduces a simulator-grounded benchmark with 50 Blender scenes, structured event graphs, diagnostic VQA, three future-specification levels, and 2,832 counterfactual variants.
Evaluates nine image-to-video models using motion-, event-, and counterfactual-level diagnostics.
Models localize motion more reliably than they realize correct spatiotemporal evolution.
More detailed future-event specifications improve event recovery but do not overcome limitations in physical realization.
Many failures originate in scene consistency and event occurrence, while counterfactual tests reveal weak selective responses to interventions.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmark and evaluation of video models as causal world models; directly relevant to video world models.
papers.title: A Plausible Future Is Not a Causal Future: Can Video Models Generate How the World Unfolds?
papers.tldr: CausalCascade shows that current video models can suggest plausible futures but struggle to generate causally coherent physical event cascades, especially under counterfactual interventions.

papers.abstract: How do we tell a world model what information to preserve? We study this question through the lens of spectral representation learning. We introduce SpecWM, a JEPA framework that explicitly specifies desired relationships between observations through a target similarity kernel and trains the encoder to reproduce those relationships in its embedding geometry. Different kernels provide different supervision, ranging from physical state information to a fully self-supervised temporal kernel requiring only the ordering of observations within trajectories. We characterize the global optima of the objective, establish conditions for linear recoverability and invariance to nuisance information, and connect temporal-kernel similarity to the behavioral successor measure under an idealized setting. Empirically, the choice of kernel strongly controls which physical quantities are recoverable from the representation. More importantly, temporal spectral alignment improves CEM planning success over LeWorldModel from 52% to 68% on OGBench Cube, 49% to 77% on OGBench Scene, and 29% to 51% on CALVIN. These results suggest that explicitly specifying representation geometry provides a simple way to steer what latent world models preserve for control.
authors: Holger Molin, William Peng, Marco Bagatella, Randall Balestriero
bullets: Addresses how to specify what information a world model should retain for downstream control.
Introduces a JEPA framework that trains representations to match target similarity kernels, including physical-state and temporal self-supervised kernels.
Provides theoretical analysis of global optima, linear recoverability, nuisance invariance, and links between temporal similarity and behavioral successor measures under idealized conditions.
Shows that kernel choice determines which physical quantities are recoverable from the learned representation.
Temporal spectral alignment improves CEM planning success over LeWorldModel across OGBench Cube, OGBench Scene, and CALVIN.
papers.selection_reason: Spectral alignment framework for latent world models, improving planning in control tasks.
papers.title: World Modeling through Spectral Alignment
papers.tldr: SpecWM steers world-model representations by aligning embedding geometry with chosen similarity kernels, improving planning performance and controlling which physical information is preserved.

papers.abstract: Rapid advances in large language models have made software engineering agents capable of tackling complex coding tasks. Within a containerized environment, a coding agent receives tool responses or execution results, and determines its later actions by those earlier results. However, most existing coding agents never look ahead: their policies do not anticipate the consequences of actions, and the terminal reward barely attributes a failure to certain earlier steps, so an ill-judged edit can corrupt the repository state irreversibly before any signal arrives. Recent code world models aim to address these challenges, but they are either trained and then frozen before reinforcement learning (RL), or reduced to an auxiliary next-token loss on the environment's outputs. We present ANTE (Anticipate, Then Execute), an agentic RL framework that verifies the policy's pre-action predictions by real execution and turns them into per-step credit for its actions and trust-or-abstain decisions. With an internal belief stated before each action, Belief-Anchored Policy Optimization (BAPO) turns the settled predictions into per-step advantages by anchoring credit on the policy's own forecasts. To turn the trained forecasts into better actions at inference, thereby facilitating effective test-time scaling, ANTE-TTO (test-time optimization) selects among candidate actions without an external scorer. ANTE raises Qwen3-32B from 25.0% to 57.2% pass@1 on SWE-bench Verified, 6.2% above a matched GRPO baseline trained without the belief state; its world model's accuracy climbs from 44% to 69% during RL, and the learned foresight capability transfers across harnesses and out-of-distribution domains. In summary, we aim to build a code world model that knows what has happened, what holds now, and what the next action will achieve.
authors: Yi Ge, Kangrui Ruan, Jifan Chen, Manish Prajapat, Christian Bock, Xiaoyang Wang, Rein Houthooft, Aritra Sengupta, Varun Kumar
bullets: Coding agents often act reactively, making early mistakes that can irreversibly damage repository state before terminal feedback arrives.
ANTE has agents state an internal belief before each action, then verifies it through execution to provide per-step credit and support trust-or-abstain decisions.
Belief-Anchored Policy Optimization (BAPO) converts verified forecasts into action advantages during reinforcement learning.
ANTE-TTO uses the learned forecasts to select among candidate actions at inference without an external scorer.
On SWE-bench Verified, ANTE improves Qwen3-32B pass@1 from 25.0% to 57.2%; its world-model accuracy rises from 44% to 69% and transfers across harnesses and out-of-distribution domains.
papers.selection_reason: Learns verified internal world models for coding agents and uses them for per-step credit and test-time optimization.
papers.title: ANTE: Anticipate, Then Execute -- Learning Internal World Models for Coding Agents from Verified Beliefs
papers.tldr: ANTE trains coding agents to predict the consequences of actions before execution, using verified beliefs for finer-grained learning and improved decision-making.

papers.abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) improve robotic manipulation by jointly predicting future visual states and actions, yet most existing methods make decisions primarily from the current observation. This limits their reliability in long-horizon tasks, where visually similar states may correspond to different interaction histories and task stages. Moreover, directly incorporating historical observations can introduce stale, stage-mismatched, or error-contaminated information, leading to inaccurate world prediction and accumulated closed-loop errors. We propose RM-WAM, a reliable memory-augmented World Action Model that treats memory as a context-dependent predictive resource rather than universally useful historical context. RM-WAM represents history using complementary short-term visual state memory and latent event memory, which respectively capture recent interaction dynamics and longer-term state transitions. A counterfactual memory learning scheme varies the accessible history while keeping the current inputs and prediction targets fixed, enabling the model to learn a context-dependent utility estimate for historical memory. Based on this estimate, a utility-aware gating mechanism adaptively controls memory injection into the world-action backbone. Experiments demonstrate that RM-WAM highlights the importance of reliable and selective memory utilization in long-horizon tasks.
authors: Cui Miao, Junhao Yu, Ping Liu, Ning Yang, Xuhua Chen, He Zheng, Xiaodong Wang, Tao Zhang
bullets: Long-horizon manipulation is challenging because similar observations can reflect different histories or task stages.
Naively using history may introduce stale, mismatched, or error-contaminated information.
RM-WAM combines short-term visual-state memory with longer-term latent event memory.
Counterfactual memory learning estimates when historical context is useful, while utility-aware gating controls its injection.
Experiments demonstrate the importance of reliable, selective memory use in long-horizon tasks.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces RM-WAM, a memory-augmented World Action Model that uses counterfactual learning and utility-aware gating to handle long-horizon tasks and stale information.
papers.title: RM-WAM: Reliable Memory-Augmented World Action Models for Long-Horizon Robot Manipulation
papers.tldr: RM-WAM improves long-horizon robot manipulation by selectively using reliable historical visual and event memories to make better world-action predictions.

papers.abstract: Evaluating robot manipulation policies through repeated physical trials is costly. We study whether an action-conditioned world model can serve as a closed-loop test environment whose policy success rates track those on real robots. Beyond realistic video, the model must return the camera views and proprioceptive state needed for the policy's next action and preserve failed-action outcomes to avoid overestimating policy capability. We introduce ProWorld, a world model that jointly predicts multi-view video and robot state, then feeds both back to a frozen policy for repeated interaction. ProWorld comprises a shared transformer for joint video-state flow prediction and Shared-Time View Encoding to distinguish cameras while preserving temporal synchronization. To reduce interaction hallucinations that turn missed grasps into successful lifts, we augment training with failed interactions collected in high-fidelity simulation, reducing inflated success rates in the generated environment. ProWorld achieves the highest overall TriWorldBench score among the compared methods. Across three policies and four local manipulation tasks, it attains a Pearson correlation of 0.95 and a Spearman correlation of 0.94 between generated and real success rates. These results support joint visual-proprioceptive feedback and failure-aware training as a basis for world-model-based policy evaluation.
authors: Zijun Wang, Tianyi Yan, Haokun Lin, Panwen Hu, Bohang He, Siyu Ren, Xiaoyu Guo, Weijia Liufu, Shuoshuo Xue, Fengjiao Chen, Zipeng Ye, Xuezhi Cao, Zutao Jiang, Hanhui Li, Xiaodan Liang
bullets: Targets the high cost of evaluating manipulation policies through repeated real-robot trials.
Jointly predicts synchronized multi-view video and robot proprioceptive state for feedback to a frozen policy.
Uses a shared transformer and Shared-Time View Encoding to model multiple cameras and temporal alignment.
Trains on failed interactions to reduce hallucinated recoveries that inflate simulated policy success.
Across three policies and four local manipulation tasks, generated and real success rates correlate strongly (Pearson 0.95; Spearman 0.94).
papers.selection_reason: Develops ProWorld, an action-conditioned world model that predicts multi-view video and proprioceptive state for closed-loop policy evaluation, incorporating failure-aware training to reduce hallucinations.
papers.title: ProWorld: Multi-View World Model with Proprioceptive Feedback for Closed-Loop Policy Evaluation
papers.tldr: ProWorld is a multi-view, proprioceptive world model that enables closed-loop robot policy evaluation while preserving realistic failure outcomes.

papers.abstract: Joint-embedding predictive architectures (JEPAs) learn world models directly in latent space, but unconstrained autoregressive predictors may contract the latent distribution over long rollouts.
