We introduce Symplectic Hamiltonian JEPA (LeHami), which replaces the standard predictor with an action-conditioned Hamiltonian flow over a structured latent state (q, p) integrated using an exactly symplectic leapfrog step. This construction preserves phase-space volume at every rollout step and rules out uniform contraction, asymptotically stable fixed points, and merging of distinct latent states, independently of the learned parameters or action sequence. We obtain the momentum-like component from temporal derivatives of the learned position-like representation, providing an explicit second-order state for prediction and control. On conservative and actuated visual pendulum environments, LeHami substantially improves long-horizon velocity prediction over an unconstrained JEPA world model and empirically maintains constant latent volume where the baseline contracts. The learned flow also supports accurate integration at unseen sub-frame step sizes and numerical time reversal. These results show how geometric structure can provide inference-time guarantees that are complementary to representation regularization in latent world models.
authors: Romina Yalovetzky, Randall Balestriero, Yann LeCun
bullets: Addresses latent-space contraction in unconstrained autoregressive JEPAs during long rollouts.
Uses an action-conditioned Hamiltonian flow over position–momentum latents, integrated with an exactly symplectic leapfrog step.
Guarantees phase-space volume preservation and prevents uniform contraction, asymptotically stable fixed points, and state merging.
Improves long-horizon velocity prediction over an unconstrained JEPA on conservative and actuated visual pendulums.
Supports unseen sub-frame integration and numerical time reversal, though the reported scope is limited to pendulum environments.
papers.selection_reason: Action-conditioned latent world model with symplectic structure fits interactive world-model interests.
papers.title: LeHami: Symplectic Latent Dynamics for World Models
papers.tldr: LeHami improves long-horizon latent world-model rollouts by enforcing Hamiltonian, volume-preserving dynamics in a structured latent space.

papers.abstract: Tool-using agents alternate between model generation and tool execution, waiting for each tool call to complete before starting the next generation. This sequential execution is costly during agentic reinforcement learning (RL), which requires large batches of multi-turn rollouts. We introduce ObsSpec, an observation speculation pipeline for agentic RL that uses a small world model to predict tool outputs while the environment executes, allowing the policy to begin its next generation early. ObsSpec retains speculative work only when the predicted and actual observations match exactly, making rollout collection lossless, while co-training keeps the world model up to date as the policy learns. On terminal-use tasks, predictions from a 0.6B world model exactly match actual observations in 66.4% of attempts and arrive roughly 16 times faster. Using these predictions, ObsSpec reduces agent latency by 9.3% and 14.2% for 8B and 32B policies. Across controlled experiments, we characterize the regimes in which ObsSpec reduces agent latency under shared policy resources. Finally, because ObsSpec overlaps policy generation with tool execution, it is architecturally compatible with existing techniques for accelerating RL. Code is available at https://github.com/kylemontgomery1/verl-recipe/tree/obsspec/obsspec.
authors: Kyle Montgomery, Wang Zhang, Chenguang Wang
bullets: Targets the latency caused by sequential policy generation and tool execution in multi-turn agentic RL.
Uses a small co-trained world model to predict tool outputs, letting the policy start generating before execution finishes.
Keeps speculative generations only when predictions exactly match actual observations, avoiding rollout changes.
A 0.6B world model matches terminal-use observations in 66.4% of attempts and predicts them about 16× faster.
Reduces agent latency by 9.3% for 8B policies and 14.2% for 32B policies in reported experiments.
papers.selection_reason: Uses a co-trained world model to speculate tool observations and accelerate agentic RL rollouts.
papers.title: ObsSpec: Accelerating Agentic Reinforcement Learning with Observation Speculation
papers.tldr: ObsSpec speeds up agentic RL rollouts by speculating tool observations in parallel with tool execution while preserving lossless training.

papers.abstract: We investigate whether a physics foundation model (PFM) pretrained for PDE forecasting can be repurposed for closed-loop fluid-flow control. We construct a PFM-based controller by attaching lightweight Gaussian actor and critic heads to frozen pretrained representations and train the policy using proximal policy optimization (PPO). We evaluate the approach on HydroGym's two-dimensional Kolmogorov-flow environment using vorticity observations at \(64\times64\) and \(128\times128\) resolutions and Reynolds numbers \(\mathrm{Re}=100\) and \(200\). Across these settings, we compare the frozen PFM controller against a baseline MLP policy trained with the same PPO framework. The PFM controller achieves consistently higher reward while requiring smaller executed action magnitudes over training, indicating improved control performance with reduced control effort. These results provide initial evidence that representations learned through self-supervised next-frame prediction can be transferred directly to closed-loop fluid flow control. Project page: https://mahindrautela.github.io/morph.
authors: Mahindra Rautela, Shaifalee Saxena, Alexander Scheinker
bullets: Motivation: Repurpose PDE-forecasting representations for fluid-flow control without fully retraining the model.
Method: Attach Gaussian actor–critic heads to frozen PFM representations and train them with PPO.
Evaluation: Test on 2D Kolmogorov flow across two spatial resolutions and Reynolds numbers, comparing against an MLP PPO policy.
Result: The PFM controller consistently obtains higher reward while using smaller executed action magnitudes.
Scope: Results provide initial evidence for transferring self-supervised next-frame prediction features to control.
papers.selection_reason: Physics foundation model for PDE forecasting used for closed-loop control; directly relevant to learned environment dynamics.
papers.title: Physics Foundation Models for Efficient Control of Fluid Flows
papers.tldr: A frozen physics foundation model can be adapted with lightweight policy heads for more effective and less forceful closed-loop control of simulated fluid flows.

papers.abstract: Coding agents are increasingly evolving beyond reproducing what a world looks like toward constructing executable worlds that capture how a world works. This shift calls for executable world modeling, which integrates two core capabilities: world understanding, reasoning about the underlying structural, mechanical, and causal principles of a world, and executable realization, translating that understanding into a code-based system whose behavior emerges from physical interactions. However, existing benchmarks provide only fragmented evaluations centered on physical reasoning, visual fidelity, or behavioral correctness, leaving the integration of these capabilities insufficiently assessed. To bridge this gap, we introduce ExeWorldBench, to our knowledge the first benchmark to comprehensively evaluate world understanding and executable realization through code-based 3D world construction. ExeWorldBench comprises three progressively challenging tasks: Mechanism Executability, which evaluates the realization of individual mechanisms from visual observations; Compositional Executability, which extends to multi-stage systems with spatial, mechanical, and causal dependencies; and Intent-Driven Executable World Synthesis, which requires constructing executable worlds from high-level goals and physical requirements. Extensive experiments on frontier models reveal substantial limitations in executable world modeling, offering insights into the development of more physically grounded and causally coherent world construction systems.
authors: Xinge Peng, Zhen Fang, Ruibing Wang, Yongxuan Lv, Haodong Li, Guohui Zhang, Xiaoxiao Ma, Yiting Lu, Lin Chen, Zehui Che, Feng Zhao
bullets: Targets the gap between visual reproduction and executable, physically grounded world construction.
Evaluates both world understanding and executable realization in an integrated framework.
Includes three tasks: mechanism realization, compositional multi-stage systems, and intent-driven world synthesis.
Experiments on frontier models reveal substantial limitations in physically grounded and causally coherent world modeling.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmark for code-based executable 3D world modeling, directly relevant to world models.
papers.title: ExeWorldBench: Benchmarking Code-Based Executable 3D World Modeling
papers.tldr: ExeWorldBench benchmarks how well AI systems understand and construct code-based 3D worlds whose behavior emerges from physical and causal interactions.

papers.abstract: By predicting future states, latent world models provide rich self-supervision for end-to-end driving, but often inherit dense features from pretrained visual encoders as their world-state interface. This creates a mismatch: visual pretraining produces information-rich, spatially dense features, but their adaptation for motion-conditioned world modeling and planning is deferred to downstream training. The dense grid also makes future prediction more computationally expensive as visual resolution increases. We therefore argue that video pretraining should directly learn state representations suited to downstream world modeling and planning, rather than relying on downstream training to adapt inherited visual features. We propose ***MORE***, a V-JEPA framework that learns **M**otion-**O**riented **RE**gisters during video pretraining as a shared state interface for driving world models and planning. MORE injects temporally aligned ego motion into a small set of registers and uses them as the sole context for masked patch prediction, channeling dense patch-level supervision through a compact state bottleneck. A complementary blockwise register-masking objective further shapes predictive structure in the register space. During downstream training, the same register space defines the future states predicted by the world model and provides shared scene memory for trajectory generation and scoring. On NAVSIM-v2, MORE outperforms the state of the art by 1.6 in EPDMS, while achieving superior efficiency with only 1/10 the inference latency of DriveLaW. These results support learning the state interface for world modeling and planning directly during video pretraining.
authors: Yingdong Gu, Haoyu Wang, Shaocheng Yan, Zhenjun Zhao, Hao Han, Pengcheng Shi, Xianfei Li, Qinghua Tan, Wenlong Liao, Tao He, Jiayuan Li, Pai Peng
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between dense visual features and the compact, motion-conditioned states needed for driving prediction and planning.
Uses a V-JEPA framework that injects temporally aligned ego motion into a small set of registers and predicts masked patches from only those registers.
Adds blockwise register masking to structure predictive information within the register space.
Reuses the registers as future world-model states and shared scene memory for trajectory generation and scoring.
On NAVSIM-v2, reports a 1.6 EPDMS improvement over the state of the art and 1/10 DriveLaW’s inference latency.
papers.selection_reason: Learns motion-oriented registers as a shared state interface for driving world models and planning, conditioned on ego motion.
papers.title: MORE: Learning Motion-Oriented Registers for Driving World Models and Planning
papers.tldr: MORE pretrains compact, motion-aware registers as a shared state interface for efficient driving world modeling and planning.

papers.abstract: Data-driven weather forecasting models are commonly trained on ERA5, yet operational deployment must use timely initial states from physics-based numerical weather prediction (NWP) systems whose distributions differ substantially from ERA5. Direct initialization with these states can degrade autoregressive forecasts, motivating input adaptation that keeps the pretrained forecasting model unchanged. Here, we introduce WeatherBridge, a unified, source-conditioned adapter that maps heterogeneous operational NWP initial states to ERA5 reference states without updating the pretrained forecasting model. WeatherBridge predicts the structured residual corrections with a Swin-UNet and injects source embeddings across multiple spatial scales, allowing the model to capture shared atmospheric structure and source-specific discrepancies. Its training objective combines latitude-weighted ERA5 reconstruction with One-step Rollout Alignment (ORA), which backpropagates one-step forecast error through a frozen FuXi model to optimize the adapted states for both initial state fidelity and downstream forecast compatibility. We evaluate WeatherBridge using daily GFS, HRES, and CMA initializations from 1 January to 22 November 2025 across six variables and lead times up to 240 hours. Relative to raw source initialization of FuXi, WeatherBridge reduces the mean RMSE of FuXi over the 6- 240-hour rollout for 17 of 18 source-variable combinations, with a median reduction of 10.2% and a maximum reduction of 46.3%. The adapter trained with frozen FuXi also improves FengWu forecasts on GFS inputs without retraining either the adapter or FengWu. These results demonstrate that forecast-aware input adaptation can improve forecasts from heterogeneous operational NWP inputs and transfer across pretrained ERA5-based forecasting models.
authors: Mutian Xi, Xinyu Su, Xiaohui Zhong, Hao Li
bullets: Operational NWP states differ from ERA5, causing forecast degradation when directly fed into ERA5-trained models.
A source-conditioned Swin-UNet predicts multiscale residual corrections while keeping the forecasting model unchanged.
Its objective combines latitude-weighted ERA5 reconstruction with one-step rollout alignment through a frozen FuXi model.
Across GFS, HRES, and CMA inputs, it reduces FuXi rollout RMSE for 17 of 18 source-variable combinations, with median and maximum reductions of 10.2% and 46.3%.
The adapter also improves FengWu forecasts on GFS inputs without retraining either model, supporting cross-model transfer.
papers.selection_reason: Input adaptation for pretrained weather forecasting models; relevant to world models as environment-dynamics predictors.
papers.title: WeatherBridge: Forecast-Aware Multi-Source Input Adaptation for Pretrained Weather Forecasting Models
papers.tldr: WeatherBridge adapts heterogeneous operational NWP inputs to the ERA5 distribution for frozen pretrained forecasting models, improving downstream forecasts across sources and models.

papers.abstract: Autoregressive world models have emerged as a powerful paradigm for sample efficient decision making, yet their open loop rollouts often exhibit increasing drift that leads to error accumulation even within a relatively small planning horizon. Hierarchical temporal abstraction is a natural candidate to mitigate such drift by reducing the effective prediction horizon; however, existing hierarchical designs can introduce added structural and conceptual complexity, sometimes making them difficult to control and limiting gains over flat baselines. To this end, we introduce MHWA (Multi-timescale Hierarchical World-Action model), which employs a strided high level context channel to reduce global context update frequency, effectively curbing the propagation of compounding drift. Crucially, via context aware routing, the gating network dynamically reconfigures a low level mixture of experts by using both global context and current observations, thereby enabling flexible high-low coordination, helping alleviate interference commonly observed in static hierarchies. Empirically, using RLiable's seed-by-game aggregation, MHWA (77M parameters) achieves an IQM human normalized score (HNS) of 0.884 across three training seeds on a 14-game Atari subset using 10% subsampled offline data, outperforming a matched JOWA-70M baseline (0.529) and achieving numerically comparable performance to JOWA-150M while using nearly half the parameters and 70.88% fewer training FLOPs per sequence.
authors: Pengcheng Pan, Guoqing Ma, Yuhan Zhang, Yang Chen, Yichen Liu, Ziheng Li, Shan Yu
bullets: Addresses error accumulation and rollout drift that limit open-loop planning in autoregressive world models.
Uses a strided high-level context channel to reduce global context update frequency and shorten the effective prediction horizon.
Dynamically routes a low-level mixture of experts using global context and current observations for flexible high-low coordination.
On a 14-game Atari subset with 10% offline data, achieves 0.884 IQM HNS across three seeds, versus 0.529 for matched JOWA-70M.
Matches JOWA-150M numerically while using 77M parameters and 70.88% fewer training FLOPs per sequence.
papers.selection_reason: Autoregressive world-action model for decision making with hierarchical temporal abstraction fits interactive world models.
papers.title: MHWA: Multi-timescale Hierarchical World-Action Model
papers.tldr: MHWA reduces drift in autoregressive world-model rollouts through multi-timescale hierarchical context and dynamic expert routing, achieving strong Atari performance with substantially lower compute than a larger baseline.

papers.abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) combine action generation with future prediction, allowing predicted futures to support action evaluation and robot decision making. However, the future associated with a candidate action may contain action-induced and environment-driven changes. Directly evaluating the predicted future may not fully characterize the future change associated with the candidate action. For example, a candidate action that worsens a favorable environmental future may still yield a favorable outcome, while one that improves an unfavorable environmental future may still yield an unfavorable outcome. To analyze this issue, we formulate a Structural Causal Model (SCM) for action evaluation in WAMs. The SCM formalizes how action-induced and environment-driven changes jointly shape future evaluation, and reveals a backdoor path through which environmental evolution can also affect the future evaluation associated with a candidate action. Intervention and backdoor adjustment account for this path, providing a causal basis for characterizing the future change associated with each candidate action. Based on this analysis, we propose Causal Action-Gain World Action Model (CAG-WAM). For each candidate action, CAG-WAM predicts an action-conditioned future and an environmental future under the same current observation, and defines their evaluation difference as causal action gain (CAG) for characterizing the future change associated with the candidate action. During training, we incorporate CAG into Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) to guide robot policy learning. During inference, we evaluate the initial action with CAG and, when needed, revise it using predicted future information. Experiments on multiple benchmarks support the effectiveness of CAG-WAM.
authors: Peizheng Guo, Cheng Zhang, Xingyu Zhang, Changwen Zheng, Wenwen Qiang
bullets: WAMs can misjudge actions when predicted futures mix action-induced and environment-driven changes.
An SCM uses intervention and backdoor adjustment to isolate each candidate action’s future change.
CAG-WAM compares action-conditioned and environment-only futures to compute causal action gain (CAG).
CAG guides GRPO-based policy learning and supports inference-time action revision.
Experiments across multiple benchmarks support its effectiveness.
papers.selection_reason: Causal action-gain world action model for robot manipulation; fits robot learning and interactive world models.
papers.title: CAG-WAM: Causal Action-Gain World Action Models for Robot Manipulation
papers.tldr: CAG-WAM uses causal modeling to separate action-driven effects from environmental changes, improving action evaluation and policy learning for robot manipulation.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in video diffusion enable novel-view video synthesis from a single input video, supporting world modeling, embodied intelligence, and robotic simulation. However, existing methods process camera trajectories independently, lacking the cross-trajectory consistency needed for coherent, navigable 4D worlds. We introduce Demiurge, an autoregressive video rerendering pipeline built on a dynamic 4D point-cloud memory cache. It promotes cross-trajectory consistency through four components: (1) an appearance video diffusion model that synthesizes photorealistic novel-view videos conditioned on the 4D memory; (2) a memory-consistent video depth completion model that aligns known-region depths with cached geometry and completes missing regions, mitigating scale ambiguity and discontinuities during memory updates; (3) memory-aware dual-stream warping that provides high-fidelity visual guidance and occlusion cues for novel-view synthesis; and (4) geometry-aware video refinement that enhances perceptual quality. Extensive experiments demonstrate state-of-the-art performance and three key capabilities: coherent spatiotemporal lattice construction over dense multi-view trajectories; large-parallax video rerendering under challenging camera motions, including 180-degree rotations with no input-view overlap; and geometry-faithful outputs that can be directly optimized into high-quality 3D Gaussian Splatting representations with minimal artifacts. Project page: https://hanxinzhu-lab.github.io/demiurge_project_page/.
authors: Hanxin Zhu, Jianqi Ma, Cong Wang, Zhihao Hu, Junyao Gao, Tianyu He, Junyan Lin, Jiayin Xiao, Jiateng Shou, Sen Liang, Weidong Zhang, Zhibo Chen, Jun Zhang
bullets: Addresses cross-trajectory inconsistency in existing novel-view video synthesis methods.
Combines appearance diffusion, memory-consistent depth completion, dual-stream warping, and geometry-aware refinement.
Supports coherent spatiotemporal reconstruction across dense multi-view camera trajectories.
Handles large-parallax motion, including 180° rotations without input-view overlap.
Produces geometry-faithful videos that can be optimized into high-quality 3D Gaussian Splatting representations with minimal artifacts.

papers.title: Demiurge: Forging Navigable 4D Worlds via Autoregressive Video Rerendering
papers.tldr: Demiurge builds coherent, navigable 4D worlds from a single video by autoregressively rerendering novel views with a dynamic 4D point-cloud memory.

papers.abstract: Autoregressive robot video world models based on discrete visual tokens remain unreliable over long rollout horizons. Retaining the entire generated history does not necessarily improve prediction quality. We investigate a possible memory-role conflict in Full Context decoding: persistent scene information, recent visual-action states, and stale generated history compete for attention despite their different predictive roles. This perspective motivates ReCAP (Receding Context with Anchor Preservation), a training-free context-scheduling method for long-horizon robot video world models. ReCAP keeps the pretrained tokenizer, world model, and visual decoder frozen. It preserves the initial scene anchor and a contiguous window of recent complete visual-action blocks while evicting older generated history. The schedule preserves within-block structure and temporal order, requires no additional modules or parameter updates, and bounds active-context growth independently of rollout length. We evaluate ReCAP on RT-1, BridgeV2, LIBERO-90, and CALVIN using frozen autoregressive world models. Across evaluated environments and horizons, ReCAP improves visual fidelity, action-conditioned consistency, and robot structure preservation relative to Full Context. On BridgeV2, it reduces LPIPS by 63.3%. In the system benchmark at H=64, it reduces the logical KV footprint by 73.3% and p50 latency by 6.51%. Attention analyses show increased attention to retained recent states, while history interventions associate larger amounts of stale context with higher prediction error. These observations are consistent with the memory-role-conflict hypothesis, although they do not isolate it from context-length and position-handling effects. Our results support inference-time context scheduling as a practical approach to improving long-horizon robot video prediction and computational efficiency without retraining.
authors: Hao Wu, Tianyu Shao, Shengju Qian, Yizhou Zhao, Fan Zhang, Penghao Zhao, Weiyan Wang, Yufei Huang, Fan Xu, Kun Wang, Xin Wang, Ming-Hsuan Yang, Yuxuan Liang
bullets: Full-context decoding can make persistent scene information, recent states, and stale generated history compete for attention.
ReCAP is a training-free context schedule that freezes the tokenizer, world model, and decoder.
It preserves temporal order and complete recent visual-action blocks while bounding active context growth independently of rollout length.
Across RT-1, BridgeV2, LIBERO-90, and CALVIN, it improves visual fidelity, action consistency, and robot-structure preservation over Full Context.
On BridgeV2, LPIPS falls 63.3%; at H=64, logical KV footprint falls 73.3% and p50 latency falls 6.51%. The memory-conflict explanation remains confounded by context-length and positional effects.
papers.selection_reason: Context scheduling for long-horizon robot video world models; fits video world models and inference memory efficiency.
papers.title: Remembering What Matters for Long-Horizon Robotic World Models
papers.tldr: ReCAP improves long-horizon robot video prediction by retaining the initial scene and recent visual-action context while evicting stale history, without retraining.

papers.abstract: Roadside 4D occupancy forecasting predicts future semantic occupancy in a fixed infrastructure coordinate system. Roadside scenes are globally structured yet locally evolving, requiring comprehensive scene-level context while precisely modeling sparse localized motion. However, existing forecasting paradigms struggle to tackle both requirements. To address this limitation, we propose InfraWorld, a world model formulating roadside occupancy forecasting as selective state evolution. InfraWorld maintains a dense BEV state for the complete scene and persistent motion queries for moving regions, assigning complementary states to global context and local dynamics. Specifically, we propose Dynamic Query Initiation (DQI) to initialize queries in regions supported by motion in the observed history. During rollout, the dense state is updated through Long--Short Temporal Fusion (LST), which combines short-term adjacent-frame continuity with long-term motion trends to preserve stable context while capturing scene evolution. Motion-Aware Query Injection (MAQI) then refines the queries and injects confidence-weighted query information into corresponding BEV tokens, enabling targeted dynamic updates without perturbing global context. Together, InfraWorld concentrates predictive capacity on evolving traffic regions. Extensive experiments on the InfraOcc and Occ3D--nus datasets demonstrate that InfraWorld achieves state-of-the-art performance for roadside 4D occupancy forecasting while retaining its effectiveness under ego-centric settings. Code will be released.
authors: Songkai Wang, Xiaokai Bai, Lei Yang, Hui-liang Shen
bullets: Addresses the challenge of modeling stable global context alongside sparse, localized motion in roadside scenes.
Uses Dynamic Query Initiation to place motion queries where movement is observed in past frames.
Applies Long–Short Temporal Fusion to combine adjacent-frame continuity with longer-term motion trends.
Uses Motion-Aware Query Injection to refine dynamic regions and update corresponding BEV tokens without disrupting static context.
Reports state-of-the-art performance on InfraOcc and Occ3D-nus, with effectiveness also retained in ego-centric settings.
papers.selection_reason: Roadside 4D occupancy forecasting as a world model.
papers.title: InfraWorld: Motion-Aware World Modeling for Roadside 4D Occupancy Forecasting
papers.tldr: InfraWorld forecasts roadside 4D occupancy by combining a dense scene-wide BEV state with persistent motion queries that focus updates on moving regions.

papers.abstract: World-action models inherit broad visual and physical priors from video pre-training. However, standard within-video next-frame prediction allows them to rely on appearance shared between the context and future, rather than learning interactions that transfer across scenes and embodiments. We introduce WATCH, a cross-video pre-training that learns from task-paired human demonstrations collected across diverse environments. Conditioned on the video and actions of one demonstration, the model jointly predicts another demonstration's actions and future frames from its current observation. Predicting one demonstration from another encourages the model to learn task-relevant interactions that transfer across scenes and demonstrators. Our pre-training shows that these capabilities can be learned from readily scalable human-human pairs alone, without requiring matched human-robot demonstrations. Analyses before robot post-training show improved motion alignment across embodiments and better action and video prediction on unseen robots, with representations closer to those learned from robot pairs. After robot post-training, WATCH improves MimicDroid in-context success from 40.9% to 68.3% with Cosmos Policy and from 59.8% to 77.7% with Cosmos3, with the largest gains on the unseen levels. Gains persist under context-free post-training across robot embodiments. WATCH outperforms within-video pre-training and co-training baselines, supporting cross-video prediction as a scalable approach to learning transferable world-action representations.
authors: Jeongeun Park, Taekyung Kim, Dongyoon Han, Sangdoo Yun
bullets: Addresses the limitation of within-video prediction, which can rely on appearance overlap rather than transferable task interactions.
Uses cross-video pre-training on task-paired human-human demonstrations across diverse environments, without requiring human-robot pairs.
Jointly predicts the paired demonstration’s actions and future frames conditioned on the source video, actions, and target observation.
Improves motion alignment and action/video prediction on unseen robots before robot post-training.
Raises MimicDroid in-context success from 40.9% to 68.3% with Cosmos Policy and from 59.8% to 77.7% with Cosmos3; gains are largest on unseen levels and persist across embodiments.
papers.selection_reason: Cross-video human-demonstration pretraining for transferable world-action models directly fits learning from human video and video world models.
papers.title: Learning Transferable World-Action Models from Task-Paired Human Videos
papers.tldr: WATCH learns transferable world-action representations by predicting one human demonstration’s actions and future frames from another, improving robot imitation across unseen environments and embodiments.

papers.abstract: We present ContinuousCloth, a continuous-time, physics-informed neural solver for deformable cloth dynamics that enforces a spring--mass ODE within a neural trajectory model. Unlike classical time-stepping simulators that return trajectories only on a discrete integration grid, ContinuousCloth supports querying at arbitrary timestamps and computing displacement, velocity, and acceleration via automatic differentiation. We evaluate ContinuousCloth along two dimensions. In a physics-only setting, ContinuousCloth achieves trajectory accuracy comparable to high-precision solvers across six diverse boundary-condition scenarios while reducing runtime by up to 17.4 times. When fused with sparse and noisy observations, the spring--mass ODE acts as a strong inductive bias for downstream tasks: interpolation and parameter estimation. That is, ContinuousCloth reduces interpolation error by 7.3 times over a data-only neural baseline in simulation and 2.4 times on real-world cloth sequences, and achieves 2.6 times lower parameter error than a differentiable-solver baseline under high-noise conditions, demonstrating consistent robustness under realistic measurement imperfections.
authors: Yingdong Ru, Lipeng Zhuang, Zhuo He, Gerardo Aragon Camarasa
bullets: Targets limitations of discrete-grid cloth simulators and data-only models.
Embeds a spring–mass ODE in a neural trajectory model.
Supports arbitrary-time queries of displacement, velocity, and acceleration via automatic differentiation.
Matches high-precision solver accuracy while reducing runtime by up to 17.4× across six boundary-condition scenarios.
Improves interpolation and parameter estimation under sparse or noisy observations, including real-world cloth sequences.
papers.selection_reason: Physics-informed neural ODE for continuous-time cloth dynamics is a learned predictor of physical environment dynamics, plausibly transferable to world-model research.
papers.title: Continuous-Time Cloth Dynamics with Physics-Informed Neural ODEs
papers.tldr: ContinuousCloth models cloth dynamics with a physics-informed neural ODE, enabling accurate continuous-time queries and robust learning from sparse, noisy observations.

papers.abstract: Latent world-model planning has shown promising results in goal-conditioned robotic manipulation, but remains challenging for long-horizon planning due to limited temporal guidance and inefficient action search. A distant visual goal provides little guidance for preparatory actions, while uninformed action sampling makes local optimization inefficient. We propose PILOT (Policy-Initialized Local Optimization with Temporal subgoals), which uses a video model to generate intermediate visual subgoals and a learned policy to initialize the cross-entropy method (CEM). CEM refines candidate action sequences toward each subgoal using an action-conditioned world model in a receding-horizon control loop. In our primary real-robot evaluation across four UR5e manipulation tasks, PILOT achieves 68.8% success, compared with 55.0% without policy initialization, 13.8% for policy-only execution, and 0.0% for direct final-goal planning. Simulation results show that these gains persist over longer horizons: PILOT exceeds direct execution of the same policy by 30 percentage points on long Push-T tasks and by 22 percentage points on LIBERO-10. Policy initialization also accelerates local optimization: on Push-T, CEM matches the cost reached by generic initialization after 10 iterations in only 4 iterations and reduces the final planning cost by 24.1% under the same sampling budget. These results show that combining temporal subgoals with policy-guided action search improves both long-horizon task execution and local planning efficiency. Videos are available on the webpage: https://pilot-planner.github.io/.
authors: Yang Liu, Hanchen Cui, Karthik Desingh
bullets: Addresses weak temporal guidance and inefficient action search in latent world-model planning.
Uses a video model to generate intermediate visual subgoals and a learned policy to initialize CEM action-sequence optimization.
Refines actions with an action-conditioned world model in a receding-horizon control loop.
Achieves 68.8% success across four real-robot UR5e tasks, outperforming ablated alternatives reported in the abstract.
Simulation results indicate improved long-horizon execution and faster, lower-cost local optimization.
papers.selection_reason: Combines video-generated visual subgoals and policy-initialized CEM with an action-conditioned world model for long-horizon robot manipulation.
papers.title: PILOT: Guiding Long-Horizon World-Model Planning for Robot Manipulation with Visual Subgoals and Policy Priors
papers.tldr: PILOT improves long-horizon robot manipulation by combining video-generated visual subgoals with policy-initialized action planning.

papers.abstract: Humans and animals do not learn vision from a fixed set of data: they move, interact, and learn from the visual consequences of their actions. Motivated by this developmental view, we study whether robots can improve visual learning by actively collecting experience through curiosity-driven interaction. We introduce DySCOVER, a self-supervised framework for active robot visual learning. A robot observes RGB frames, learns a visual autoencoder that encodes and reconstructs them, and trains a recurrent world model to predict the next visual latent state conditioned on the current state and action. The agent's policy is trained only with intrinsic rewards: reconstruction error encourages visually novel observations, while the world model's error encourages transitions whose consequences are not yet predictable. This prediction error biases the policy toward more intricate trajectories that enrich the agent's set of experiences with observations beyond those encouraged by visual novelty alone. Our experiments conducted with robotic arms as the embodied agents show that adding predictive curiosity improves the vision model over using visual curiosity alone. Across variations in initial conditions, experience capacity, embodiment, and scene content, adding predictive curiosity consistently improved visual learning. These results show that predictive curiosity can improve active visual learning beyond reconstruction-based curiosity alone.
authors: Stelios Zarifis, Panagiotis Filntisis, George Retsinas, Petros Maragos
bullets: Robots actively gather visual experience instead of learning from a fixed dataset.
A visual autoencoder reconstructs RGB observations, while a recurrent world model predicts future visual latents from states and actions.
Intrinsic rewards combine reconstruction error with prediction error to drive curiosity-based exploration.
Robot-arm experiments show predictive curiosity consistently improves visual learning over reconstruction-based curiosity alone.
The study evaluates varied initial conditions, experience capacities, embodiments, and scene contents.
papers.selection_reason: Curiosity-driven robot visual learning uses an action-conditioned recurrent world model and intrinsic rewards, fitting robot learning and interactive world models.
papers.title: Learning to See through Action: Predictive Curiosity for Robots
papers.tldr: DySCOVER helps robots learn better visual representations by seeking both visually novel observations and unpredictable action consequences.

papers.abstract: Pixel-space world models have recently emerged as a promising approach for GUI agents, predicting future screens prior to execution and subsequently re-perceiving them for action selection. However, this two-stage paradigm faces two key challenges in GUI environments: (L1) the high computational cost of pixel reconstruction and (L2) the need to reconstruct large and diverse appearance-level details beyond what is required for action selection. In practice, this screen-generation objective can induce an identity shortcut problem, where future-state prediction largely preserves the current state rather than capturing action-induced changes. In this work, we reformulate GUI world modeling by shifting the prediction target from full-screen reconstruction to action-induced future information in latent space. Concretely, we leverage a large multimodal model as the latent world model, whose shared representations support two dedicated heads for both action selection and predictive transition modeling. The action head directly translates these latent representations into action selection, while the transition head captures action-conditioned future information. To mitigate the identity shortcut, we further introduce an action-aware contrastive objective that encourages the transition representations to capture discriminative action-induced changes. Extensive experiments across offline and online GUI settings show that our method achieves up to 31.9% and 40.6% relative gains in success rate over pixel-space world models, respectively, while substantially reducing inference latency by up to 98.9%. Our code is available at https://github.com/sjyu001/latent2world.
authors: Seungjun Yu, Hojun Choi, Seojeong Park, Jaeyo Shin, Hyunjung Shim
bullets: Addresses the high computational cost and unnecessary visual detail of pixel-space GUI world models.
Uses a large multimodal model with shared latent representations and separate action-selection and transition-prediction heads.
Introduces an action-aware contrastive objective to avoid identity shortcuts and emphasize action-induced changes.
Reports up to 31.9% relative gains offline and 40.6% online over pixel-space world models, with up to 98.9% lower inference latency.
Evaluated in both offline and online GUI settings; the abstract does not specify task or dataset scope.
papers.selection_reason: Latent action-conditioned world model for GUI agents, directly fits interactive world models.
papers.title: Latent World Action Model for GUI Agents
papers.tldr: A latent-space world model for GUI agents predicts action-induced changes instead of reconstructing full screens, improving success rates while greatly reducing inference latency.

papers.abstract: We introduce ClothCode, a unified generative framework for garment state estimation and action-conditioned dynamics prediction in a shared discrete configuration space. A material-aligned tokenizer encodes garment configuration as residual vector-quantized patch tokens, while task-specific Masked Generative Transformers predict these tokens through parallel confidence-guided refinement. Across three garment templates, ClothCode reduces mean displacement error by 26.6% for state estimation and 37.0% for dynamics prediction relative to the strongest baselines. Dynamics prediction requires only 16.7 ms per window, compared with 556.2 ms for diffusion. Integrated into the same model-predictive controller, ClothCode improves real-world folding and flattening success from 56.7% to 78.9%. Further results and videos are available at: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/ClothCode-DE32
authors: Yingdong Ru, Lipeng Zhuang, Shiyu Fan, Zhuo He, Florent P. Audonnet, Gerardo Aragon Camarasa
bullets: Uses a material-aligned tokenizer with residual vector-quantized patch tokens to represent garment configurations in a shared discrete space.
Applies task-specific Masked Generative Transformers with parallel confidence-guided refinement for state estimation and dynamics prediction.
Across three garment templates, reduces mean displacement error by 26.6% for state estimation and 37.0% for dynamics prediction versus the strongest baselines.
Predicts dynamics in 16.7 ms per window, compared with 556.2 ms for diffusion.
With the same model-predictive controller, raises real-world folding and flattening success from 56.7% to 78.9%.
papers.selection_reason: Action-conditioned garment dynamics prediction for robotic manipulation; fits robot learning and interactive world models.
papers.title: ClothCode: Generative Modeling for Garment State Estimation and Dynamics Prediction
papers.tldr: ClothCode is a unified generative model that estimates garment states and predicts action-conditioned dynamics efficiently, improving prediction accuracy and real-world folding and flattening success.

papers.abstract: Forecasting tissue deformation from future instrument motion could support predictive planning and increasingly autonomous surgical systems. We study this problem using a scene-specific differentiable surface model fitted to an observed tool-tissue interaction window. Rather than forecasting absolute simulated positions, we introduce an \textit{observation-referenced} formulation that anchors each tissue point to its last valid observation and adds only the deformation induced by the known, preplanned future tool trajectory. This reduces sensitivity to reconstruction, initialization, and persistent simulation offsets while preserving the predicted deformation response. The physical model uses differentiable, mesh-free position-based dynamics with scene-specific rigidity, attachment, region scale, and grasp coupling. We further introduce an optional \textit{observation-referenced residual model} combining graph-spectral spatial modes with periodic harmonic dynamics for structured motion not explained by the tool input. We evaluate the framework retrospectively on 12 surgical manipulation clips from three datasets. Observation referencing provides the largest gain, with a median within-clip error ratio of $0.598$ relative to the corresponding absolute simulation forecast. The optional periodic residual further improves forecasting when the remaining motion exhibits periodic structure. These results support observation-referenced deformation prediction as a practical building block for future surgical world models, digital twins, and generative simulators that must predict how tissue evolves under instrument actions.
authors: Tom Olesch, Nan Xiao, Xiongye Xiao, Jonathan C. DeLong, Fei Liu
bullets: Addresses tissue deformation forecasting from known future instrument motion for predictive and autonomous surgery.
Fits a scene-specific differentiable, mesh-free position-based dynamics model to an observed tool–tissue interaction window.
Anchors each tissue point to its last valid observation, reducing sensitivity to reconstruction, initialization, and persistent simulation offsets.
Optionally adds graph-spectral spatial modes and periodic harmonic dynamics to capture motion not explained by tool input.
Evaluated on 12 clips from three datasets; observation referencing achieved a median within-clip error ratio of 0.598 versus absolute simulation, while periodic residuals helped for periodic motion.
papers.selection_reason: Action-conditioned tissue deformation forecasting is directly relevant to surgical world models.
papers.title: Observation-Referenced Tissue Deformation Forecasting with Tool-Driven and Residual Dynamics
papers.tldr: An observation-referenced deformation forecasting framework improves surgical tissue-motion prediction by anchoring forecasts to recent observations and modeling tool-induced changes.

papers.abstract: Could model-free reinforcement learning algorithms actually be learning a model of the environment? In this work, we apply counterfactual interventions which hold everything about a state fixed, besides a targeted change, to explore if the value function of a Proximal Policy Optimization agent forms a world model of the Crafter environment. Despite only being trained to optimize reward, we discover that the value function learns concepts such as the rules governing when a diamond is collectible, water and food having an impact on health, heuristics regarding inventory, and more. Finally, we discuss the safety implications of our visualizations and some shortcomings of current reinforcement learning agents that will prevent us from building truly advanced machine intelligence.
authors: Shawheen Naderi, Fatemeh Akherati, Yubei Chen
bullets: Investigates whether model-free RL implicitly learns an environment model.
Uses counterfactual interventions that change one targeted state feature while holding others fixed.
Finds representations of diamond collectibility, health effects of water and food, inventory-related heuristics, and other concepts.
Discusses safety implications of interpreting value-function visualizations.
Highlights limitations of current RL agents for achieving advanced machine intelligence.
papers.selection_reason: Investigates whether a value function learns an environment model; directly relevant to learned representations of environment dynamics.
papers.title: Visualizing the World Model in an Agent's Value Function
papers.tldr: Counterfactual visualizations show that a PPO agent’s value function encodes meaningful aspects of Crafter’s world dynamics despite being trained without an explicit model.

papers.abstract: Accurate artery extraction from X-ray coronary angiography (XCA) is essential for coronary artery disease diagnosis and intervention. However, low vessel visibility, respiratory and cardiac motion, and limited annotations challenge existing methods. Moreover, most deep learning approaches produce binary vessel masks without preserving clinically relevant intra-arterial contrast information. We propose a Temporal Diffusion Bridge Model (TDBM) that formulates vessel extraction as image translation and learns from physics-informed synthetic data without manual vessel annotations. A physics-based XCA synthesis engine generates diverse, perfectly aligned pairs of contrast-enhanced and contrast-free images. Using these pairs, TDBM learns cross-domain mappings to recover high-fidelity vessel information. Temporal conditioning incorporates adjacent frames to improve consistency, while a vessel-aware contrastive loss exploits background-invariant synthetic pairs to enhance vascular discrimination. We evaluate TDBM on two XCA vessel segmentation datasets and conduct a reader study using two real-patient XCA sequence datasets. Zero-shot segmentation is further assessed on retinal imaging and fluorescence microscopy datasets. Results demonstrate that TDBM consistently outperforms existing methods and generalizes effectively across imaging modalities. Code and trained weights will be available at: https://github.com/Advanced-AI-in-Medicine-and-Physics-Lab/TDBM
authors: Jinkui Hao, Donald R. Cantrell, Ramez Abdalla, Sameer A. Ansari, Bo Zhou
bullets: Addresses poor vessel visibility, cardiac and respiratory motion, and limited annotated XCA data.
Generates aligned contrast-enhanced/contrast-free image pairs with a physics-based synthesis engine.
Uses temporal conditioning and vessel-aware contrastive learning to improve consistency and vascular discrimination.
Evaluated on XCA segmentation, real-patient sequence reader studies, and zero-shot retinal and fluorescence microscopy tasks.
Reports consistent improvements over existing methods and effective cross-modality generalization, without specifying numeric results.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces a Temporal Diffusion Bridge Model for vessel extraction that uses physics-informed synthetic data and temporal conditioning, bridging video generation and understanding.
papers.title: Temporal Diffusion Bridge Model for Vessel Extraction Using Physics-informed Synthetic Data
papers.tldr: TDBM uses physics-informed synthetic XCA pairs and temporal diffusion modeling to extract vessels while preserving intra-arterial contrast information without manual annotations.

papers.abstract: Sparse-view cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) is severely under-constrained by limited X-ray projections. Learned reconstruction can provide complementary anatomical information, but using it as a prior in patient-specific Gaussian reconstruction introduces two challenges. First, the discrepancy between the learned prior and current reconstruction is spatially non-uniform: some local differences contain useful missing 3D information, whereas others reflect prior bias. Second, even a volumetrically beneficial correction can conflict with the observed X-ray measurements. Since X-ray measurements are line integrals, spatially separated corrections may affect overlapping rays, with their signed projection responses reinforcing or partially canceling in the measurement residual, so their feasibility cannot always be assessed independently. In this paper, we introduce RePrior, a multi-stage progressive prior-correction framework that addresses correction actionability, measurement feasibility, and representation expressivity. Selective Correction Proposal (SCP) first identifies actionable signed local corrections from prior--reconstruction discrepancies. Measurement-Constrained Reconciliation (MCR) then jointly enforces their consistency with patient-specific X-ray measurements, while Hybrid Residual Enhancement (HRE) recovers additional correction capacity through complementary voxel- and Gaussian-domain degrees of freedom around the reconciled anchor. RePrior requires neither test-time ground truth nor case-specific network fine-tuning. RePrior gains approximately 2.6~dB in 3D PSNR over R$^2$-Gaussian across LUNA16, PANORAMA, and PENGWIN. Beyond prior-assisted reconstruction, it delivers additional gains in volumetric quality and observed-view projection fidelity, with consistent gains in held-out-view fidelity in the backbone-matched evaluation.
authors: Mengrui Yin, Tianxingjian Ding, Wufan Zhao, Ziyang Yan, Yu Tian
bullets: Addresses spatially varying prior bias and conflicts between volumetric corrections and overlapping-ray measurements.
Uses three stages: Selective Correction Proposal, Measurement-Constrained Reconciliation, and Hybrid Residual Enhancement.
Requires neither test-time ground truth nor case-specific network fine-tuning.
Reports approximately 2.6 dB higher 3D PSNR than R²-Gaussian across LUNA16, PANORAMA, and PENGWIN.
Also improves volumetric quality, observed-view projection fidelity, and—under backbone-matched evaluation—held-out-view fidelity.
papers.selection_reason: Addresses sparse-view CBCT reconstruction using a learned prior correction framework (RePrior) that reconciles measurement constraints with volumetric reconstruction, applicable to general 3D reconstruction.
papers.title: RePrior: Measurement-Reconciled Prior Correction for Sparse-View CBCT Reconstruction
papers.tldr: RePrior improves sparse-view CBCT reconstruction by selectively correcting learned-prior errors while enforcing consistency with patient-specific X-ray measurements.

papers.abstract: Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) learn world models by predicting future representations rather than reconstructing observations. Variational JEPA (VJEPA) gives this prediction probabilistic semantics and permits flexible conditional predictive families. We propose MDN-VJEPA, a multimodal probabilistic JEPA that instantiates the latent predictor as a mixture density network (MDN), representing future states with a Gaussian mixture whose components encode alternative futures, their probabilities, and within-mode uncertainty. For sequential prediction, we address two additional structural requirements: multi-modal futures should remain temporally coherent across a trajectory, and predictive beliefs should remain consistent when propagated to the same horizon through different temporal path compositions, as motivated by the Chapman--Kolmogorov equation. Together, these considerations define a three-level hierarchy of multimodal prediction, coherent multimodal trajectories, and compositionally consistent multimodal dynamics. Controlled experiments show that MDN-VJEPA closely recovers known branching predictive laws, that retaining the complete multimodal belief rather than its conditional mean can lead to materially different and substantially better planning decisions under branching futures, and that trajectory-level coupling and distributional consistency improve temporal coherence and multi-horizon agreement. These results support a simple principle: a probabilistic JEPA should preserve not only how uncertain the future is, but which distinct futures constitute that uncertainty, how they form coherent trajectories, and how those beliefs compose through time.
bullets: Addresses the limitation of representing future uncertainty only through averages in sequential world models.
Uses a mixture density network to model future latent states as Gaussian mixtures with alternative modes, probabilities, and within-mode uncertainty.
Introduces a three-level structure: multimodal predictions, coherent multimodal trajectories, and Chapman–Kolmogorov-inspired compositional consistency.
Controlled experiments recover branching predictive laws and show that retaining full multimodal beliefs can improve planning under branching futures.
Trajectory coupling and distributional consistency improve temporal coherence and agreement across prediction horizons.
papers.selection_reason: Probabilistic joint-embedding world model for multimodal future prediction and planning, directly relevant to world models.
papers.title: MDN-VJEPA: Multimodal Probabilistic Joint-Embedding World Models
papers.tldr: MDN-VJEPA extends probabilistic JEPAs with Gaussian-mixture predictions that preserve distinct possible futures, their coherence over time, and consistency across temporal compositions.

papers.abstract: We introduce the Long-Short-Range Neural Network (LSR-Net), a novel neural operator architecture designed for data-driven forward evolution modeling, and extends it to the prediction of nonlinear fluid dynamics. LSR-Net learns the evolution operator of a dynamical system solely from pairs of initial and future state snapshots, which splits the learnable integral kernel into long-range (LR) and short-range (SR) components within stacked network blocks. While the SR component uses standard convolutions to capture local dynamics, the LR component employs a sum-of-exponentials (SOE) representation. This allows for the efficient computation of global interactions as a trainable Fourier multiplier, reducing computational complexity to $O(n \log n)$ where $n$ is the number of pixels in an input snapshot and requiring only a few parameters per channel. LSR-Net is evaluated on three challenging 2D benchmarks: the coupled Burgers equation, the wave equation with a spatially varying coefficient, and the nonlinear shallow water equation {(SWE)}. Results demonstrate that LSR-Net significantly outperforms the baseline short-range network (SR-Net) as well as FNO and DeepONets in predictive accuracy, achieving substantially lower relative errors by effectively capturing both local fine-scale structures and crucial global pattern interactions.
bullets: Learns a dynamical system’s forward evolution operator directly from initial and future state snapshots.
Splits the kernel into short-range components modeled with convolutions and long-range components represented by sum-of-exponentials.
Computes global interactions via a trainable Fourier multiplier with O(n log n) complexity and few parameters per channel.
Evaluated on coupled Burgers, variable-coefficient wave, and nonlinear shallow water equations.
Outperforms SR-Net, FNO, and DeepONets in relative predictive error by capturing both fine-scale local structure and global patterns.
papers.selection_reason: Neural operator learning forward evolution of nonlinear dynamics is a world-model-style predictor of environment dynamics.
papers.title: LSR-Net: Learning the Forward Evolution Operator for Nonlinear Fluid Dynamics
papers.tldr: LSR-Net learns nonlinear fluid dynamics by combining efficient long-range and local short-range interactions, yielding lower prediction errors than several baselines on three 2D benchmarks.

papers.abstract: A robot's learned model of its own dynamics is only valid until those dynamics change: actuators wear, payloads shift, and joints stiffen. A model-based agent that keeps training as if nothing happened adapts slowly, dragged back by a replay buffer full of stale experience. We present Changepoint-Aware World Models (CAWM), a DreamerV3 agent that detects an abrupt dynamics shift from its own internal prediction error, using an online CUSUM test against a rolling baseline that fires only on abrupt change rather than on slow learning drift. It then forgets stale replay, keeping the learned representation while flushing obsolete data. On simulated locomotion under two robot-relevant shifts, doubled gravity and halved actuator gain, CAWM recovers substantially faster than passive retraining. It also beats a strong baseline that respawns a fresh dynamics model on detection, the deep-world-model analogue of model-bank methods. With the response triggered at the shift, CAWM gains +95 to +153 return in the first 30k post-shift frames over three seeds, while matching that respawn at asymptote. Running the detector in closed loop reproduces this gain on the gravity shift. The benefit holds across both shift types, and is largest when the shift is severe enough that old data is genuinely obsolete.
bullets: Targets slow adaptation after actuator wear, payload changes, or joint stiffening make stored experience obsolete.
Uses DreamerV3 with an online CUSUM test on internal prediction error to detect abrupt shifts without reacting to gradual learning drift.
Flushes obsolete replay data instead of retraining from stale experience or replacing the entire dynamics model.
On simulated locomotion with doubled gravity or halved actuator gain, it recovers faster than passive retraining and fresh-model respawning.
With shift-triggered detection, it gains 95–153 return in the first 30k post-shift frames over three seeds and matches respawning at asymptote; benefits are largest for severe shifts.
papers.selection_reason: Detects dynamics shifts in model-based RL and forgets stale replay, directly relevant to world models, online adaptation, and robot learning.
papers.title: Changepoint-Aware World Models: Detecting Dynamics Shifts and Recovering by Forgetting Stale Replay in Model-Based RL
papers.tldr: CAWM detects abrupt robot-dynamics changes and rapidly adapts by discarding stale replay while preserving its learned representation.

papers.abstract: In physics-informed machine learning, a target function $u^*$ is learned from noisy value observations $y_i=u^*(x_i)+ \varepsilon_i$, together with differential information, given either by noisy observations $d_j=(Du^*)(z_j)+ξ_j$ or by a known physical constraint $Du^*=v$. We consider the setting where $D$ is a linear differential operator and analyze a physics-informed kernel estimator $\hat u$ combining $n$ value observations and $m$ differential observations. In this context, we ask how much can differential information improve predictions, and how does this improvement depend quantitatively on $n$, $m$, and $D$. We prove finite-sample bounds, supported by numerical simulations, revealing a two-regime structure for the prediction error. When $m$ is limited, the rate depends jointly on $n$ and $m$; when $m$ exceeds a problem-dependent threshold, the rate saturates and matches the oracle rate obtained when the perfect constraint $D \hat u = Du^*$ is imposed. Examples are discussed for Sobolev spaces which are reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces and include partial Laplacian constraints on the torus and gradient observations on bounded domains. These examples illustrate the range of possible learning rate improvements --- from the standard nonparametric $n^{-1/4}$ to the parametric rate $n^{-1/2}$. Finally, we derive physically consistent rates in a stronger norm that jointly controls the errors in $\hat u$ and $D\hat u$.
bullets: Analyzes kernel estimators combining n noisy function values with m noisy or exact differential constraints.
Provides finite-sample prediction-error bounds with two regimes: joint dependence on n and m when m is limited, and oracle-rate saturation beyond a problem-dependent threshold.
Shows examples where improvements range from n^{-1/4} to n^{-1/2}, including partial Laplacian and gradient information.
Also derives stronger-norm rates controlling both the estimation error and the error after applying the differential operator.
Numerical simulations support the theoretical two-regime behavior.
papers.selection_reason: Analyzes learning rates for physics-informed kernel methods, which are used to model and predict environment dynamics, fitting the World Models category.
papers.title: Fast Learning Rates for Physics-Informed Kernel Methods
papers.tldr: Physics-informed differential data can improve kernel-estimation rates from nonparametric to parametric scales, with gains saturating once enough differential information is available.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon autonomous research has shown promise in accelerating scientific progress through sustained cycles of hypothesis generation, implementation, and validation. However, this Generate-Execute-Feedback paradigm relies on reactive trial-and-error, where costly and time-consuming executions introduce severe feedback delays, throttling evolutionary progress under explosively expanding search space. To address this challenge, we propose JANUS, a framework that unifies future outcomes forecasting and past experience reflection through a Predict-Verify-Evolve loop driven by a co-evolving world model. Within an evolving graph, the research agent proposes candidates while world model scores them by forecasting value improvement, information gain, and exploration utility, then accordingly selects, refines, or prunes branches prior to execution. After receiving ground-truth feedback, JANUS distills experience into evolving skills: hierarchical skills for research agent, exploration-strategy skills for world model, and their coordination protocols. This mechanism enables continual co-evolution: the research agent sharpens candidate generation while the world model refines its predictive judgment over extended horizons. Extensive evaluations on MLS-Bench-Lite and real research tasks demonstrate that JANUS significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, achieving both higher evolving efficiency and ceiling.
bullets: Targets feedback delays and inefficient trial-and-error in Generate–Execute–Feedback research loops.
Uses a Predict–Verify–Evolve loop within an evolving graph to forecast value improvement, information gain, and exploration utility.
Selects, refines, or prunes candidate branches before execution, then incorporates ground-truth feedback.
Co-evolves hierarchical research skills, exploration strategies, and coordination protocols for the agent and world model.
Evaluations on MLS-Bench-Lite and real research tasks report higher evolving efficiency and ceiling than state-of-the-art baselines.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes co-evolving world models that forecast action-conditioned outcomes for long-horizon research agents.
papers.title: JANUS: Enhancing Long-Horizon Autonomous Research with Co-Evolving World Models
papers.tldr: JANUS accelerates long-horizon autonomous research by using a co-evolving world model to predict, filter, and improve research candidates before costly execution.

papers.abstract: Ultrasound (US) acquisition depends on the operator's ability to interpret anatomy and anticipate how the view will change with probe motion. Many robotic US navigation methods select actions without explicitly predicting these anatomical changes. We propose SonoGraph-WM, an action- and goal-conditioned world model for anticipatory probe navigation. The model represents anatomy as scene graphs (SGs), capturing visible structures, their geometry, and spatial relationships without synthesizing US images. Given a history of SGs and probe poses, a unified Transformer jointly predicts future SGs and poses. A receding-horizon planner recursively imagines candidate trajectories, selects the shortest predicted path reaching a goal graph, and follows it over a short execution horizon before replanning from new observations. To reduce reliance on tracked and anatomically annotated US sequences, we generate aligned SG--pose training data from computed tomography (CT) label maps along surface-constrained probe trajectories. On four held-out CT cases, spatial relation F1 remains above 93% over 20 prediction steps, and closed-loop navigation achieves 77.50% and 75.00% success for the gallbladder and pancreas, respectively, using annotation-derived SGs. In robot--phantom navigation experiments with label-map-derived SGs, the planner reached the target view in 73.7% of trials. These findings support CT-supervised anatomical world modeling for probe planning and highlight the importance of frequent observation updates for reliable navigation. Project Page: https://noseefood.github.io/us-sonograph-wm/
bullets: Represents ultrasound anatomy as scene graphs of visible structures, geometry, and spatial relationships instead of synthesizing images.
A unified Transformer predicts future scene graphs and probe poses from observation histories; receding-horizon planning selects and repeatedly updates trajectories toward a goal graph.
CT label maps generate aligned scene-graph/pose training data, reducing dependence on tracked and anatomically annotated ultrasound sequences.
On held-out CT cases, spatial-relation F1 stayed above 93% for 20 prediction steps; navigation success was 77.50% for the gallbladder and 75.00% for the pancreas.
Robot–phantom trials reached target views in 73.7% of cases, with results emphasizing frequent observation updates for reliable navigation.
papers.selection_reason: Action-conditioned scene-graph world model for anticipatory robotic ultrasound navigation; aligns with interactive world models and robot navigation.
papers.title: Scanning While Imagining: A Scene-Graph World Model for Robotic Ultrasound Navigation
papers.tldr: SonoGraph-WM enables anticipatory robotic ultrasound navigation by predicting future anatomical scene graphs and probe poses, then planning through imagined trajectories.

papers.abstract: Active exploration and semantic navigation require an embodied agent to build memory from partial observations, predict how the evolution of observed spatial memory may support future motion, and convert that prediction into actionable plans. We present GLAM, a goal-conditioned latent world model trained over global spatiotemporal memory, and GLAM NAV, the complete navigation system built around it. Given historical map tokens, a navigation goal, and the current robot pose, GLAM jointly predicts future map representations and robot-centric waypoint latents, allowing future spatial context and navigation intent to be inferred in a shared representation space. The model follows a JEPA-like latent prediction paradigm, operates directly on map-level latent tokens rather than RGB reconstruction, and uses a pretrained waypoint encoder-decoder to supervise and decode navigation plans within GLAM NAV. Training data are collected by replaying ObjectNav expert trajectories in Habitat over HM3D v0.2 scene assets and slicing them into multi-timescale prediction samples. On a controlled HM3D-ObjectNav subset reproduction setting, GLAM NAV improves over a reproduced BSC-Nav baseline in both success rate and success weighted by path length.
bullets: Uses historical map tokens, the navigation goal, and robot pose to jointly predict future map representations and robot-centric waypoint latents.
Applies JEPA-like latent prediction directly to map-level tokens instead of reconstructing RGB observations.
GLAM NAV combines the world model with a pretrained waypoint encoder-decoder to generate actionable navigation plans.
Trained on replayed ObjectNav expert trajectories in Habitat using HM3D v0.2 scenes and multi-timescale prediction samples.
On a controlled HM3D-ObjectNav reproduction subset, it improves success rate and success weighted by path length over a reproduced BSC-Nav baseline.
papers.selection_reason: Latent world model over global spatiotemporal memory for active exploration and navigation.
papers.title: GLAM: Training a latent world model over global spatiotemporal memory for active exploration and navigation
papers.tldr: GLAM learns a goal-conditioned latent world model that predicts future spatial memory and navigation waypoints for active exploration and semantic navigation.

papers.abstract: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) aims to transform interaction experience into persistent improvements, yet external feedback is costly and world-model predictions may become unreliable as policies evolve. We introduce RSI-Anything, a domain-general framework built on JEPA-Anything that uses predictive world models to guide action and learning-data selection. Observed feedback drives policy or workflow improvement and conditional world-model adaptation, while component and compatibility checks govern the retention of updated policy-model pairs. Across diverse computational and scientific domains, RSI-Anything demonstrates substantial gains. In code repair, with the coder fixed, success increases from 26.3% with a static verifier to 29.2% through predictive selection and 31.2% after world-model adaptation, at comparable test usage. Graphical user interface (GUI) evaluations showed higher task completion, while average actions decrease by 39.4%. Across five successive policy versions, laboratory-planning scores more than double from 21.80% to 46.01%. In reaction optimization, RSI-Anything achieves 96.15% mean best observed yield versus 82.16% for Bayesian optimization under the same 40-experiment budget. An end-to-end immune-science application further connects workflow evolution and predictive modeling with therapeutic hypothesis generation. These results demonstrate how predictive world models and retained system updates enable recursive improvement across diverse environments.
authors: Taoyong Cui, Pinxian Zeng, Wanghan Xu, Hao Xiao, Shuhan Xue, Qiang Gao, Wanli Ouyang, Pheng Ann Heng, Zhenfei Yin, Yingcheng Wu, Ling Yang
bullets: Addresses costly feedback and unreliable world-model predictions as policies evolve.
Selects actions and learning data using JEPA-Anything-based predictive world models.
Adapts world models conditionally and retains updated policy–model pairs only after component and compatibility checks.
Reports gains in code repair, GUI task completion, laboratory planning, reaction optimization, and immune-science workflow development.
Scope includes multiple computational and scientific domains; the abstract does not specify broader limitations.],
papers.selection_reason: Uses predictive world models for recursive self-improvement and retains updated policy-model pairs.
papers.title: RSI-Anything: Unlocking Recursive Self-Improvement with World Models
papers.tldr: RSI-Anything uses predictive world models and validated policy updates to enable recursive self-improvement across diverse tasks with limited external feedback.

papers.abstract: We present HorizonNav, a video diffusion-based framework for anticipatory robot navigation that transforms a single RGB image and a text prompt into a geometrically aligned representation of plausible surrounding 3D space. Given the initial observation and a textual description of the reconstruction objective, a vision-language model, guided by designed instructions, interprets the scene and constructs structured prompts for a video diffusion model. The resulting video sequence provides plausible future observations of the environment, which are subsequently processed using monocular ORB-SLAM3 for camera pose estimation and Video Depth Anything for dense depth prediction. Our central contribution is a geometry-guided depth alignment stage that combines the estimated camera poses with triangulated visual landmarks to constrain dense depth predictions across multiple views. This alignment improves the geometric consistency of the reconstructed 3D environment, addressing inconsistencies that temporal coherence of the generated video alone cannot resolve. The experimental evaluation of navigation in imagined 3D environment shows that across a 19-scene horizon study, planning-feasible scenes increase from 13/19 at P20 to 15/19 at P81, while successful RRT trials increase from 62/90 to 75/90. In a separate corridor study, 6 of 25 evaluable generated-camera trajectories violate the reconstructed collision constraints; RRT planner recovers feasible alternatives in 5 of those 6 cases. A larger archive contains 58 usable reconstructions from 67 attempted cases, of which 36 support a downstream plan and 22 do not, exposing reconstruction and free-space failure modes rather than hiding them without lidar. Across 15 corridor reconstructions, the mean reconstruction error is approximately 0.30 m at matched structural landmarks.
authors: Hajira Amjad, Valerii Serpiva, Viacheslav Liubimov, Didar Seyidov, Dzmitry Tsetserukou
bullets: Generates plausible future views from one RGB observation plus a textual reconstruction objective.
Uses a vision-language model to guide prompts for video diffusion, then applies ORB-SLAM3 and Video Depth Anything.
Aligns dense depth with camera poses and triangulated landmarks to improve multi-view geometric consistency.
In a 19-scene horizon study, planning-feasible scenes rose from 13/19 to 15/19, and successful RRT trials from 62/90 to 75/90.
The approach remains subject to reconstruction and free-space failures; matched-landmark error was approximately 0.30 m across 15 corridor reconstructions.
papers.selection_reason: Video diffusion world model for anticipatory robot navigation with geometry-guided depth alignment.
papers.title: HorizonNav: Geometry-Guided Video Diffusion for Anticipatory 3D Robot Navigation
papers.tldr: HorizonNav uses text-guided video diffusion and geometry-based depth alignment to imagine and reconstruct navigable 3D surroundings from a single RGB image.

papers.abstract: World-action models (WAMs) predict a robot's actions together with the observations those actions will produce. However, the strongest models rely on video diffusion transformers that are far too computationally expensive for resource-constrained edge devices. We present SmolWAM, a latent WAM that we derive from the 2B-parameter Cosmos Policy by keeping its pretrained trunk and rebuilding its inference interface: single-frame visual latents, cached text features that preserve the trunk's attention sinks, 12 of 28 transformer blocks, and 1,008 tokens from which actions and future visual latents are read out in one rectified-flow step. Trained in 3.6 GPU-hours, SmolWAM succeeds in 95.5% of 400 LIBERO episodes at 57 ms and 2.3 TFLOP per 16-action chunk with 2.4 GiB of GPU memory, 11x faster than its teacher with 18.5x fewer FLOPs and 3.2x less memory, and its world head still forecasts scene motion.
authors: Timi Owolabi, Hikmah Olawore, Frances Adelakun, Ayotomiwa Oyewumi
bullets: Targets the high computational cost of video-diffusion world-action models on resource-constrained edge devices.
Rebuilds a pretrained 2B-parameter model’s inference interface using visual latents, cached text features, 12 transformer blocks, and a single rectified-flow step.
Achieves 95.5% success across 400 LIBERO episodes with 57 ms inference latency and 2.4 GiB of GPU memory.
Runs 11× faster than its teacher while using 18.5× fewer FLOPs and 3.2× less memory.
Its world head retains the ability to forecast scene motion.
papers.selection_reason: Efficient latent world-action model for robotic manipulation; fits VLA, manipulation, interactive world modeling, and edge-device efficiency.
papers.title: SmolWAM: A Latent World-Action Model for Robotic Manipulation on Edge Devices
papers.tldr: SmolWAM compresses a large world-action model into an edge-friendly latent model that rapidly predicts robot actions and future scene observations.

papers.abstract: Action-conditioned world models offer a promising foundation for generalist robotic intelligence by predicting the consequences of actions. However, existing robotic datasets provide limited coverage of the diverse interaction dynamics required for generalizable world modeling.
