Together, these results show that world models can serve as active coaches, turning imagined failures into targeted supervision for modular policy improvement. Project Page: https://robocoach-ai.github.io/
authors: Jiajun Liu, Yifan Chen, Yichao Liu, Jiayi Zhang, Ruoqu Chen, Shaoxuan Xie, Guocai Yao, Mengdi Xu, Sen Cui, Changshui Zhang
bullets: Addresses the high cost of improving long-horizon task compositions through additional end-to-end demonstrations.
Uses the RIDI loop: execute modular skill experts, simulate outcomes in COACHWORLD, diagnose the first failed subtask, and update targeted experts.
A progress judge aggregates failures to choose which subtask demonstrations to acquire and which expert adapters to update.
Imagined and real success correlate strongly across 22 task-policy pairs (rho = 0.840).

With 150 additional subtask demonstrations, success improves from 13.3% to 75.0% on Franka and from 40.0% to 83.8% on AgileX; transfer remains limited on held-out compositions (35.0% average success).
papers.selection_reason: World-model-guided coaching for compositional robot manipulation with action-conditioned world model.
papers.title: RoboCoach: World Models as Active Coaches for Compositional Robot Skills
papers.tldr: RoboCoach uses a world model to imagine failures, identify weak subtasks, and request targeted demonstrations that improve compositional robot skills efficiently.

papers.abstract: Embodied agents must determine where to act, anticipate the resulting scene changes, and interpret observed outcomes to guide subsequent actions. This requires connecting 4D interaction understanding, which explains how past actions changed the scene, with spatially grounded planning, which determines how and where to act toward a goal and anticipates the resulting scene changes. We introduce ChronoGraph, a functional 4D scene graph that links actions on affordance parts to semantic and geometric state changes. By representing observed and anticipated transitions in the same form, it provides a shared basis for understanding and planning. We construct ChronoGraphBench through an automatic data engine that converts human-interaction videos and simulated robot trajectories into graph-annotated questions for training and evaluating Vision-Language Models (VLMs) on both tasks. Using these annotations, we train ChronoGraphVLM by adapting pretrained VLMs in two stages. Graph-as-Chain-of-Thought supervised fine-tuning teaches the models to reconstruct observed transitions and predict future ones as graph traces before answering. Subsequent joint 4D graph reinforcement learning directly rewards graph properties and answer correctness. Experiments across model scales show improvements over the corresponding pretrained baselines and zero-shot transfer to VLM4D. Real-world demonstrations further show that graph-based planning and affordance grounding support mobile manipulation through existing robot skills without additional fine-tuning.
authors: Chenyangguang Zhang, Malgorzata Gwiazda, Guanlong Jiao, Yuanchen Ju, Federico Tombari, Koushil Sreenath, Marc Pollefeys, Sunghwan Hong
bullets: Links actions on affordance parts to semantic and geometric scene changes in a shared graph representation.
Introduces ChronoGraphBench, an automatically generated benchmark from human-interaction videos and simulated robot trajectories.
Trains ChronoGraphVLM with graph-based chain-of-thought supervision followed by joint 4D graph reinforcement learning.
Reports improvements over corresponding pretrained baselines across model scales and zero-shot transfer to VLM4D.
Real-world demonstrations show mobile manipulation using existing robot skills without additional fine-tuning.
papers.selection_reason: Functional 4D scene graphs learned from human videos enable interaction understanding and action-conditioned planning for embodied agents.
papers.title: ChronoGraph: Functional 4D Scene Graphs with Vision-Language Models for Interaction Understanding and Grounded Planning
papers.tldr: ChronoGraph unifies 4D interaction understanding and grounded planning through functional scene graphs that represent observed and anticipated state changes for VLMs.

papers.abstract: Although conventional world models - auto-regressive or diffusion models based on transformers or convolutional networks - may learn surface statistics of world dynamics, can they learn the exact world dynamics from its observed history? Leveraging cellular automata as a simple testbed, we find the answer to be no in many cases. Conventional architectures predict most pixels correctly yet rarely complete a rollout: a CNN predicts 96.3% of cells but completes 18.9% of rollouts; a joint diffusion model completes none. We trace the gap to three failure modes of these world models - namely, they fail to exactly capture spatial locality, temporal locality or temporal stability. Simple changes repair each: (1) for spatial locality, two-dimensional rotary positions lift a transformer from 39.1% to 100% on the Game of Life; (2) for temporal locality, handing each token its cell's previous-frame neighbourhood lifts the same transformer from 25.8% to 99.9% on unseen rules; (3) for temporal stability, causal freezing lifts the same diffusion weights from 42.2% to 99.9%. None of the three changes touches the architectural backbone; each only modifies the information flow within it. We also compare joint and ordered sampling on billiards and, in an exploratory study, on a simulated Burgers equation.
bullets: CNNs and diffusion models can achieve high per-cell accuracy yet rarely complete an entire rollout.
The study identifies three failure modes: inaccurate spatial locality, insufficient temporal context, and unstable temporal predictions.
Two-dimensional rotary positions restore spatial reasoning, while previous-frame neighbourhoods provide temporal locality.
Causal freezing improves temporal stability without changing the diffusion model’s backbone.
The fixes achieve near-perfect rollout completion in the reported Game of Life and unseen-rule experiments; scope is also explored on billiards and Burgers dynamics.
papers.selection_reason: Diagnoses why conventional world models fail to exactly capture dynamics on cellular automata and repairs this through information-flow changes.
papers.title: Why Do Conventional World Models Fail to Learn Cellular Automata?
papers.tldr: Conventional world models often match most pixels but fail to reproduce exact cellular-automaton dynamics because they miss spatial locality, temporal locality, or temporal stability.

papers.abstract: In interactive scenarios, an autonomous driving system is required to generate ego actions under the influence of other agents' behaviors. Existing World Action Models (WAMs) typically model other agents as components of the world model rather than as decision-makers that fundamentally shape the action of the ego agent, which impairs their performance in dense interaction scenarios. We introduce Reciprocal World Action Models (ReWAM), a game-theoretic world action modeling framework that captures the reciprocal influence between the ego agent and other agents by representing them as conditional responders whose actions are mutually influenced. We instantiate this framework with a Level-$k$ response hierarchy, where role-specific ego and other action DiTs exchange compact strategy tokens through cross-agent attention while remaining grounded in a shared representation of the future driving world. To learn the response policy of the ego agent from demonstrations, we formulate expert actions as samples from the best response distribution and jointly optimize the entire hierarchy using conditional flow matching. Our framework is evaluated on the NAVSIM dataset and achieves state-of-the-art performance compared to baselines. The improvement is particularly significant in interactive scenarios, validating that modeling reciprocal responses provides a more effective foundation for interaction-aware world action generation.
authors: Benshan Ma, Pei Liu, Ruiguo Zhong, Lang Zhang, Mingyue Feng, Yaonong Wang, Jun Ma
bullets: Addresses the weakness of existing World Action Models in dense, interactive driving scenarios.
Uses a game-theoretic framework with a Level-k response hierarchy for reciprocal agent behavior.
Role-specific action diffusion transformers exchange strategy tokens via cross-agent attention within a shared future-world representation.
Learns ego response policies from demonstrations by treating expert actions as best-response samples and jointly optimizing the hierarchy with conditional flow matching.
Achieves state-of-the-art performance on NAVSIM, with especially notable gains in interactive scenarios.
papers.selection_reason: Game-theoretic world action modeling that captures reciprocal influence between ego and other agents for interactive driving.
papers.title: ReWAM: Reciprocal World Action Models for Interactive Autonomous Driving
papers.tldr: ReWAM improves interactive autonomous driving by modeling the ego vehicle and other agents as mutually influencing decision-makers.

papers.abstract: World models offer a promising way to help robots understand how the physical world evolves and plan complex behaviours through imagination. Yet existing studies mainly demonstrate what these models can accomplish, leaving unclear when their predictions remain useful for planning and where they fail. We study this question using action-conditioned predictors built on five frozen self-supervised visual backbones: V-JEPA 2, V-JEPA 2.1, VideoMAEv2, VideoPrism, and DINOv2. We use frozen backbones to test representations intended to transfer across environments. We evaluate these models on diverse Meta-World manipulation tasks and real-robot interactions from BridgeData V2. We find that a world model guides action selection reliably only when the goal lies within, or slightly beyond, the trajectory it imagines during planning. With five-step rollouts, the length the predictor was trained on, the world model ranks actions reliably only for targets five to ten control steps ahead, whereas task goals lie 16 to 53 steps away. Neither an 81-fold larger predictor nor longer-rollout training extends this range; the encoder affects both range and closed-loop success, with V-JEPA 2.1 performing most consistently. More fundamentally, the limit persists under perfect prediction: using the real simulator, success falls from 92% to 41% as the target moves from five to twenty steps ahead of a five-step rollout. Planning therefore requires either longer imagined trajectories or closer subgoals. For distant goals, pure imagination succeeds in 23% of episodes, planning with feedback (MPC) raises success to 30%, imagining as far as the goal to 47%, and nearby expert subgoals to 76%. Used within its plannable range, a world model can also improve a vision-language-action (VLA) policy: choosing among eight actions the VLA proposes raises its success from 65% to 77% across 16 different tasks.
authors: Ali Alrasheed, Basim Azam, Naveed Akhtar
bullets: The study tests action-conditioned predictors using five frozen visual backbones on Meta-World and real-robot BridgeData V2 tasks.
With five-step imagined rollouts, models rank actions reliably only 5–10 control steps ahead, while goals are typically 16–53 steps away.
This planning-range limit persists with larger predictors, longer-rollout training, and even perfect simulator predictions.
For distant goals, success improves from 23% with pure imagination to 30% with MPC, 47% with goal-length rollouts, and 76% with nearby expert subgoals.
Within its effective range, world-model action selection improves a VLA policy’s success from 65% to 77%; V-JEPA 2.1 performs most consistently.
papers.selection_reason: Analyzes action-conditioned latent world models for planning and VLA improvement; fits interactive world models and embodied planning.
papers.title: The Planning Limits of Latent World Models
papers.tldr: Latent world models reliably guide robot planning only over short horizons, so distant goals require longer rollouts, feedback, or closer subgoals.

papers.abstract: World Models are appearing as the next major frontier in computer vision. However, their robustness is currently largely unexplored. We identify the phenomenon of hallucination in latent World Models: given a state and an action, the predicted next latent can decode to a scene that never occurs. Because the prediction is statistically ordinary and is fed back autoregressively by the model, the error is both silent and compounding. We study whether such latent hallucination can be detected, localised, and corrected at inference time, on a frozen self-supervised world model in the absence of ground-truth error labels. We introduce Masked Empirical-Bayes Neural Denoising (MEND), a single conditional score network trained by denoising score matching on real transitions, whose score field serves three roles: its magnitude detects hallucination, its per-token field localises it to specific image patches, and it defines an inference-time correction direction. On two navigation environments MEND detects hallucination with an AUROC of up to 0.80 without using actions, exceeding a single-Gaussian density baseline while also localising the error (per-token AUPRC up to 0.87) and correcting it, all from one score field. Our correction reliably reduces single-step latent error and improves predictions. We identify that a part of the error is tangent to the data manifold, hence, we focus on detection and localisation while highlighting promises of the correction.
authors: Ali J Alrasheed, Aryan Yazdan Parast, Basim Azam, James Bailey, Naveed Akhtar
bullets: Latent hallucinations can produce plausible-looking but impossible future scenes and compound through autoregressive feedback.
MEND is trained on real transitions with denoising score matching and requires no ground-truth hallucination labels or actions at detection time.
Score magnitude detects hallucinations, token-level scores localise affected image patches, and the score direction enables inference-time correction.
On two navigation environments, MEND reaches up to 0.80 AUROC for detection and 0.87 per-token AUPRC for localisation.
Correction reduces single-step latent error, but tangent-to-manifold errors limit its reliability; the paper emphasises detection and localisation.
papers.selection_reason: Addresses robustness in World Models by introducing a method to detect, localize, and correct latent hallucinations in a frozen self-supervised model.
papers.title: MEND: Label-Free Detection, Localisation, and Correction of Latent Hallucination in World Models
papers.tldr: MEND uses one denoising score field to detect, localise, and partially correct hallucinations in frozen latent world models without error labels.

papers.abstract: High-precision locomotion combines motion-command tracking with precise regulation of task-relevant physical states, enabling robots to interact reliably with their surroundings during motion. Joint end-to-end optimization can leave precision objectives insufficiently optimized, while reactive residual control adjusts actions only after deviations become observable. We present \textbf{LocoWM}, a world-model-guided preactive residual adaptation framework for high-precision locomotion. A base policy provides command-following locomotion, while an action-conditioned world model predicts a sequence of future physical states from proprioceptive history and the proposed base action. A residual adapter conditions on this predicted sequence to generate additive action corrections that compensate for anticipated deviations. Two-stage training first learns locomotion and action-conditioned dynamics, then freezes both modules while training the adapter, separating locomotion acquisition from precision adaptation. Experiments spanning terrain leveling, acceleration compensation, and push recovery demonstrate improved control precision and disturbance robustness over end-to-end and reactive residual baselines. Demos and code are available at: https://zhaozijie2022.github.io/LocoWM
authors: Zijie Zhao, Shengqian Chen, Xiaoxu Wang, Han Jiang, Yuanheng Zhu, Dongbin Zhao
bullets: Targets precise task-state regulation alongside motion-command tracking.
A base locomotion policy is paired with an action-conditioned world model that predicts future physical states.
A residual adapter uses these predictions to generate anticipatory action corrections.
Two-stage training separates locomotion learning from precision adaptation.
Experiments on terrain leveling, acceleration compensation, and push recovery show improved precision and disturbance robustness over end-to-end and reactive residual baselines.
papers.selection_reason: Presents a world-model-guided residual adaptation framework for high-precision locomotion, predicting future states to correct actions.
papers.title: LocoWM: High-Precision Locomotion through World-Model-Guided Residual Adaptation
papers.tldr: LocoWM improves high-precision robot locomotion by using a world model to predict future deviations and proactively adapt actions.

papers.abstract: Does memory-dependent control need nonlinear recurrent dynamics? We study simulated air-hockey defence under temporary loss of puck tracking. A DreamerV3 teacher outperforms a memoryless policy under tracking loss, while resetting the teacher's recurrent state sharply reduces performance, which demonstrates that the task requires memory. We distil this teacher into compact recurrent policies with a 64 dimensional state, with a combination of a diagonal linear recurrence and an optional rank-$k$ nonlinear innovation while retaining nonlinear observation encoders and action heads. Across five matched seeds, the purely linear recurrent model ($k=0$) matches both the GRU baseline and the teacher throughout the tested range of tracking loss. Increasing nonlinear innovation rank providing no measured benefits. This result is obtained on a fresh test split, which will be only opened after all models and analyses are frozen. The linear model requires fewer recurrent parameters and less computation than GRU, but performs comparably. These results suggest that, for this memory dependent control task, nonlinear representation learning around a simple linear memory mechanism can be sufficient, and that nonlinear recurrent dynamics are not necessarily required. These conclusions are limited to the simulated task, teacher, state dimension, and blackout horizon considered here, and to policies whose observation encoder and action head remain nonlinear.
bullets: The task requires memory: resetting the teacher’s recurrent state sharply reduces performance during tracking loss.
A DreamerV3 teacher was distilled into policies with 64-dimensional memory using diagonal linear recurrence, optionally augmented by rank-k nonlinear innovations.
The purely linear model (k=0) matched the GRU baseline and teacher across the tested tracking-loss range over five matched seeds.
Higher-rank nonlinear innovations provided no measured benefit, while the linear model used fewer recurrent parameters and less computation than GRU.
Findings are limited to the simulated task, teacher, state size, blackout horizon, and models with nonlinear observation encoders and action heads.
papers.selection_reason: Distils a world-model policy into compact recurrent policies for robot control, relevant to robot learning and latent action models.
papers.title: Linear Recurrent Memory Suffices to Distil a World-Model Policy for Robot Air Hockey
papers.tldr: A compact linear recurrent memory can match GRU and DreamerV3 performance for simulated air-hockey defence under temporary puck-tracking loss.

papers.abstract: Learning to complete tasks in unfamiliar environments with unknown rules remains a key challenge for LLM agents. Current LLM agents often record their discoveries in prose, which may not provide a compact, explicit account of how the environment works. Inspired by how scientists organize observations into testable, predictive theories, we introduce Schema, an agent harness that organizes learning and action through interactive program induction. The LLM agent decides what to investigate and how to act, expressing its evolving understanding of the environment as executable programs. The harness consists of a persistent program workspace and a small set of interfaces for checking these programs against the interaction history, planning within them, and executing plans under step-by-step verification. Schema raises ARC-AGI-3 RHAE from 58.7% to 99.2% with the same base model, solves 100% of the public DiG-bench games, and reaches the median performance of the top-50 human players on MazeBench. Extensive analysis shows the effectiveness of Schema in unknown mechanism discovery, and ablations confirm the contribution of each component.
authors: Guanning Zeng, Jiani Wang, Wenjie Ma, Shaofeng Yin, Chenyang Wang, Shichen Liu, Angjoo Kanazawa, Wode Ni, Xiuyu Li, Andrea Zanette, Haiwen Feng
bullets: Targets the challenge of completing tasks when environment rules are initially unknown.
Uses interactive program induction: the agent chooses investigations and actions while refining executable programs.
Provides a persistent program workspace plus interfaces for checking programs, planning, and step-by-step verified execution.
Reports strong performance across ARC-AGI-3 RHAE, DiG-bench, and MazeBench, including 99.2% on ARC-AGI-3 RHAE.
Ablations support the effectiveness of Schema’s components for discovering unknown mechanisms.
papers.selection_reason: Agentic program induction discovers and predicts environment dynamics, matching world-model learning with executable interaction-aware programs.
papers.title: Schema: Discovering Unknown Environments via Agentic Program Induction
papers.tldr: Schema helps LLM agents discover and use unknown environment rules by representing their evolving understanding as executable, testable programs.

papers.abstract: Physical reasoning from video requires inferring latent physical properties and dynamics beyond direct observation. Direct VLM inference remains unreliable on complex physical tasks without explicit modeling and validation, while predefined tool pipelines rely on task- and domain-specific priors that limit generalization across materials, dynamics, and reasoning tasks. We introduce Asking the World (ATW), a generalist agent that constructs and interrogates task-relevant executable worlds through two adaptive stages: World Modeling calibrates a world from video, while World Probing queries, simulates, and intervenes on it to obtain question-relevant evidence. Rather than prescribing the operations in either stage, ATW determines how to model and probe according to the scene and question. We develop PolyWorld Engine, a lightweight and highly programmable Warp-based multiphysics simulator for constructing and probing worlds with rigid bodies, soft bodies, cloth, ropes, fluids, and their coupled interactions. CEM-based system identification recovers task-relevant dynamics during World Modeling. The resulting world becomes an active workspace for question-directed physical experiments rather than a predetermined downstream tool. We evaluate ATW on CLEVRER, ContPhy, and three real-world scenarios. Using Gemini-3-Flash as its base VLM, ATW achieves 80.82% overall per-question accuracy on CLEVRER, improving direct Gemini-3-Flash by 46.50 points, GPT-5.5 by 13.58 points, and PhysMind by 8.27 points. On ContPhy, it reaches 70.56% overall accuracy, surpassing Gemini-3-Flash by 28.10 points and GPT-5.5 by 3.53 points. Across the three real-world scenarios, ATW achieves 71.67% accuracy, 28.33 points above GPT-5.5. These results establish agentic world modeling and probing as an effective, execution-grounded approach to generalist physical reasoning.
authors: Shenxiang Zeng, Chen Yang, Peiyao Chen, Guohui Zhang, Jiansheng Fan, Chen Wang
bullets: Addresses the limits of direct VLM inference and rigid, task-specific tool pipelines for complex physical reasoning.
Uses two adaptive stages: World Modeling calibrates task-relevant dynamics, while World Probing queries, simulates, and intervenes to gather evidence.
Introduces PolyWorld Engine, a programmable multiphysics simulator supporting rigid and soft bodies, cloth, ropes, fluids, and coupled interactions.
Evaluated on CLEVRER, ContPhy, and three real-world scenarios, achieving 80.82%, 70.56%, and 71.67% accuracy, respectively.
The approach is execution-grounded and designed to generalize across materials, dynamics, and reasoning tasks.
papers.selection_reason: Agentic physical reasoning by constructing, calibrating, and probing executable worlds from video is a strong world-modeling contribution.
papers.title: Asking the World: Generalist Physical Reasoning through Agentic World Modeling and Probing
papers.tldr: Asking the World improves video-based physical reasoning by adaptively building and interrogating executable simulations tailored to each scene and question.

papers.abstract: Equipping VLM agents with world modeling capabilities has shown strong potential for complex reasoning and long-horizon planning, while reducing the dependence of policy learning on costly real-world interactions. Existing methods mainly rely on prospective simulation to predict the consequences of candidate actions. However, this forward-only paradigm focuses on what will happen next and provides limited constraints for verifying whether an action is causally consistent with the observed state transition, which can lead to plausible-looking but physically incoherent behaviors. In this paper, we challenge the view of world modeling as only prospective prediction and introduce Retrospective World Modeling, a new agent learning paradigm that enables agents to reason backward by estimating the retrospective attribution distribution $P(\hat{a}{t}|s_t, s{t+1})$ for the action that most likely caused a given transition. Based on this capability, we formulate the Self-Consistency Reward (SCR), an intrinsic signal that measures the probabilistic consistency between the policy action and the retrospective explanation. Integrating SCR into reinforcement learning provides dense transition-level feedback and steers agents toward behaviors that are both task-effective and physically grounded. Extensive experiments across diverse agentic tasks show that our method substantially improves policy robustness and generalization over prospective-only world modeling baselines.
authors: Yongjiang Liu, Jie Zhang, Haoyue Zhang, Jingcai Guo, Deze Zeng, Song Guo
bullets: Prospective-only world models can produce plausible-looking but physically incoherent behaviors because they lack causal consistency checks.
The method estimates which action most likely caused a transition from the observed state pair, $P(\hat{a}_t\mid s_t,s_{t+1})$.
A Self-Consistency Reward measures agreement between the policy’s action and its retrospective explanation.
Adding this intrinsic reward to reinforcement learning provides dense transition-level feedback for physically grounded behavior.
Experiments across diverse agentic tasks report improved robustness and generalization over prospective-only world-modeling baselines.
papers.selection_reason: Retrospective world modeling with self-consistency reward for VLM agents, fitting interactive world models and vision-language-action learning.
papers.title: Beyond Prediction: Steering VLM Agents with Retrospective World Modeling
papers.tldr: Retrospective World Modeling improves VLM agent robustness by checking whether chosen actions plausibly caused observed state transitions, not just predicting future outcomes.

papers.abstract: Interactive video generation (IVG) models have achieved remarkable progress in producing controllable visual content guided by user-defined actions, yet their security vulnerabilities remain largely unexplored. In this paper, we present the first systematic study of backdoor attacks against the interactivity of IVG models. Based on this attack surface, we propose BadAction, which leverages action-guided triggers to achieve the attack. Specifically, BadAction implants predefined motion patterns into the action sequences of backdoor samples and associates them with a static target video. Once triggered, the backdoored model generates frozen future frames that no longer respond to subsequent user actions, while preserving normal behavior on benign action sequences. In addition, we explore a stealthier attack in which multimodal triggers jointly poison action, text, and image inputs. Experiments show that BadAction achieves average attack success rates of 91.0% with action-only triggers and 80.4% with multimodal triggers. Moreover, extensive defense evaluations show that BadAction successfully bypasses existing backdoor detection methods, revealing a critical security gap in the interactive video generation pipeline. Project page: https://wsad55.github.io/badaction01/.
authors: Zhihang Wu, Zhongqi Wang, Jie Zhang, Fengming Gu, Shiguang Shan, Xilin Chen
bullets: Studies backdoor attacks targeting the interactivity of interactive video generation models.
Embeds predefined motion patterns in action sequences and maps them to a static target video.
Triggered models produce frozen future frames while retaining normal behavior on benign inputs.
Extends the attack with stealthier joint action, text, and image triggers.
Reports 91.0% average attack success for action-only triggers and 80.4% for multimodal triggers, while bypassing evaluated detection defenses.
papers.selection_reason: Backdoor attacks on action-guided interactive video generation directly concern interactive world models and video generation.
papers.title: BadAction: Backdoor Attacks on Interactive Video Generation via Action-Guided Triggers
papers.tldr: BadAction exposes a backdoor vulnerability in interactive video generation models by using action-based triggers to make future frames freeze and ignore subsequent user actions.

papers.abstract: World-action models (WAMs) leverage pretrained video models to improve generalization in robot control by jointly predicting future visual states and actions. This capability comes at a substantial inference cost, as dense future-frame tokens are repeatedly processed during denoising. Prior methods address this by token pruning that prioritizes visual fidelity to reduce denoising costs in video diffusion models. However, these methods do not use action relevance to determine which future-frame tokens to retain during joint denoising in WAMs. In this paper, we propose Sparse-WAM, a training-free framework for action-guided sparse imagination that selectively processes future-frame tokens to accelerate WAM inference. We observe substantial overlap in the spatial distribution of attention from action tokens to future-frame tokens (action-to-future attention) between consecutive denoising steps, despite continued updates to the future representations. Motivated by this, we develop Action-Guided Token Selection to retain frame-specific action-relevant regions together with cross-frame context. However, a naive implementation can incur attention-scoring and token-packing overhead that offsets the computational savings from pruning. We therefore introduce Pilot, an efficient engine that reduces sparse inference overhead through lightweight scoring and cross-step reuse of token selections. On LIBERO with FastWAM-Joint and RoboLab-120 with Cosmos 3 Edge, Sparse-WAM achieves inference speedups of approximately $2.0\times$ and $1.8\times$, respectively, over dense eager inference on an NVIDIA RTX 4090, while largely preserving task performance.
authors: Xinling Xie, Haodong Wang, Jiazhi Mi, Zhiming Liu, Zicong Hong, Xiaoyi Pang, Qianli Liu, Yangjia Hu, Ying Chen, Zhengyang Yan, Song Guo
bullets: WAMs jointly predict future visual states and actions but are costly because dense future-frame tokens are repeatedly processed.
Sparse-WAM is a training-free, action-guided token-pruning framework for sparse imagination.
Action-Guided Token Selection uses action-to-future attention to retain relevant spatial regions and cross-frame context.
Pilot lowers pruning overhead through lightweight scoring and reuse of token selections across denoising steps.
On LIBERO and RoboLab-120, it achieves approximately 2.0× and 1.8× inference speedups, respectively, over dense eager inference.
papers.selection_reason: Action-guided token pruning accelerates world-action model inference.
papers.title: Sparse-WAM: Accelerating World Action Models via Action-Guided Sparse Imagination
papers.tldr: Sparse-WAM accelerates world-action model inference by retaining action-relevant future-frame tokens, achieving roughly 1.8–2.0× speedups while largely preserving task performance.

papers.abstract: World models aim to learn representations of real-world environments and predict their future evolution. Recent object-centric world models have made expressive progress by representing visual scenes as sets of object-level latent states, but object-object relations are often captured only implicitly, which limits explicit relational and temporal structure modeling and object-centric dynamic memory modeling. To address such challenges, we propose World-As-Graph (WAG), a graph-based object-centric world model that introduces relational inductive bias into JEPA-style predictive representation learning. The proposed WAG contains two main modules: (1) Relation-aware structure induction, which constructs time-varying latent graphs from object-centric slots and designs relation-aware object masking policies to guide relational object representation learning in latent space; (2) Object-centric memory transition, which maintains and updates object-level dynamic states by combining relational information from neighboring objects with historical memory, enabling effective autoregressive future prediction. Extensive experiments on both visual reasoning and robotic manipulation tasks could demonstrate the superior performance of our proposed WAG.
authors: Yaqi Yang, Shuo Huang, Yujin Huang, Fucai Ke, Jiatong Han, Xin Zheng
bullets: Addresses the limited explicit modeling of object-object relations and temporal dynamics in object-centric world models.
Uses JEPA-style predictive representation learning with a relational inductive bias.
Induces latent graphs and relation-aware masking policies from object-centric slots.
Updates object-level memory by combining neighboring-object relations with historical states for autoregressive prediction.
Evaluated on visual reasoning and robotic manipulation tasks, with the abstract reporting superior performance.
papers.selection_reason: Object-centric graph world model with relational inductive bias and memory for autoregressive future prediction.
papers.title: World-as-Graph: Relational World Modeling Through Latent Space Graphs
papers.tldr: WAG models environments as time-varying graphs over object-centric latent states to improve relational understanding and future prediction.

papers.abstract: Long-term precipitation nowcasting requires modeling radar-echo evolution while preserving localized high-intensity structures. Recent radar-specific studies motivate location-aware prediction and separating echo displacement from intensity change. However existing encoders learn historical representations mainly from final forecast errors. We propose PrecipJEPA, which couples a structured forecasting path with an auxiliary path that enriches its encoder from observed radar history. In the forecasting path, an online encoder first converts the observations into spatiotemporal tokens. The Task-Driven Future-State Predictor (TFP) combines these tokens with a recent-dynamics summary and spatiotemporal queries to construct future radar states. The Parallel Motion-Source Renderer (PMSR) decodes these states into motion and source-sink fields that transform the latest observation into future frames. During joint training, the History-Masked JEPA (H-JEPA) operates on the auxiliary path to predict masked historical features from visible context, directly supervising the same online encoder from the observed sequence. Experiments on SEVIR and MeteoNet show that PrecipJEPA improves highest-threshold CSI by 118.6% and 35.1%, respectively, over the strongest baselines, while maintaining the highest mean CSI throughout the 3-hour forecast.
authors: Yufeng Zhu, Dan Niu, Qiliang Wu, Weiwei Huang, Yixiao Liang, Yongchao Feng, Chunlei Shi
bullets: Addresses the challenge of forecasting evolving radar echoes while preserving localized, high-intensity precipitation.
Uses a Task-Driven Future-State Predictor to construct future radar states from spatiotemporal tokens, recent dynamics, and queries.
Uses a Parallel Motion-Source Renderer to decode states into motion and source-sink fields that transform the latest observation.
Adds History-Masked JEPA training to supervise the shared encoder using masked prediction over observed radar history.
On SEVIR and MeteoNet, improves highest-threshold CSI by 118.6% and 35.1% over the strongest baselines and maintains the highest mean CSI over 3 hours.
papers.selection_reason: JEPA-regularized future-state prediction for precipitation nowcasting, directly aligned with video world models.
papers.title: PrecipJEPA: JEPA-Regularized Future-State Prediction with Motion-Source Rendering for Precipitation Nowcasting
papers.tldr: PrecipJEPA improves long-term precipitation nowcasting by combining future-state prediction, motion/source rendering, and masked historical representation learning.

papers.abstract: Any-dimensional machine learning models, such as graph neural networks (GNNs), can be naturally trained and evaluated on inputs of different sizes and dimensions. Inspired by the GNN transferability literature, we show mathematical conditions under which a partial differential equation (PDE) learning-based solver can be trained in small dimensions and directly applied to solve a higher dimensional PDE in a zero-shot fashion. These conditions are based on symmetries in both the partial differential equation and the initial data. When the equations satisfy the symmetries but the data does not, which is the case for many PDEs arising from physics, we show that our theory gives a principled way of warm-starting low-dimensional PDE solvers for higher dimensional PDEs. We apply this method on the heat equation, Burgers' equation, and the compressible Navier--Stokes equations, improving the performance in both zero-shot and typical training regimes on high dimensional data. For example, we train a surrogate model on 2D Navier--Stokes data and achieve better results on 3D test data than a baseline surrogate model trained on 3D data, while only using 12$\%$ of the flops and 20$\%$ of the total data size.
authors: Wilson G. Gregory, George A. Kevrekidis, Ben Blum-Smith, Soledad Villar
bullets: Derives conditions under which any-dimensional models such as GNNs transfer PDE solvers across dimensions in a zero-shot setting.
Uses symmetries of the PDE and initial data; when only the equation has the symmetry, the method provides a principled warm start.
Demonstrates the approach on the heat equation, Burgers’ equation, and compressible Navier–Stokes equations.
For Navier–Stokes, a model trained on 2D data outperforms a baseline trained on 3D data while using 12% of the FLOPs and 20% of the data.
Scope: transfer relies on suitable PDE symmetries, while real-world initial data may not share them.
papers.selection_reason: Any-dimensional ML for PDE solving offers a transferable approach to learning environment dynamics in world models.
papers.title: Warm-starting PDE solvers with any-dimensional machine learning
papers.tldr: A symmetry-based transfer method lets PDE solvers trained in low dimensions warm-start or solve higher-dimensional problems, improving efficiency and performance.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon video generation requires models to effectively leverage an increasingly long generation history. As the generated history grows, retaining all previous content becomes increasingly expensive and redundant, making effective historical selection essential. Existing approaches often determine historical relevance based on the current content. However, information relevant to the present is not necessarily useful for future generation, while seemingly less relevant history may become important later. Our key insight is that historical information should be selected according to its relevance to future information needs. Capturing these needs does not require generating the full future; instead, a compact representation of what becomes important next is sufficient to guide historical selection. Building on this insight, we propose FrameMorrow, a prospective frame selector that predicts a small set of prospective tokens representing future information needs and uses them to identify relevant information from history. FrameMorrow selects explicit historical frames rather than model-specific internal states, enabling plug-and-play integration across diverse generators, including closed-source models, with little additional inference cost. We evaluate FrameMorrow across five benchmarks and 11 generative models spanning long-video generation, interactive generation, and action-conditioned world models. Extensive experiments demonstrate consistent improvements in long-range consistency, visual quality, and action alignment across diverse generation settings.
authors: Bo Yin, Xiaobin Hu, Jiaqi Zhao, Shuicheng Yan
bullets: Long generation histories become costly and redundant, making effective historical-frame selection important.
The method predicts compact prospective tokens that represent what future generation will need next.
These tokens guide selection of explicit historical frames rather than model-specific internal states.
The plug-and-play selector supports diverse, including closed-source, generators with little additional inference cost.
Experiments across five benchmarks and 11 models show improved long-range consistency, visual quality, and action alignment.
papers.selection_reason: Future-guided frame selection for long-horizon video generation and action-conditioned world models fits both video generation and world-model prediction.
papers.title: FrameMorrow: Future-guided Frame Selection with Prospective Tokens for Long-Horizon Video Generation
papers.tldr: FrameMorrow improves long-horizon video generation by selecting past frames according to predicted future information needs.

papers.abstract: Model-based offline reinforcement learning (MBORL) improves sample efficiency through model-generated trajectories. However, accumulative model error can drive imagined trajectories outside the offline data distribution, leading to unrealistic synthetic data and unstable policy optimization. Many existing methods primarily control rollouts using transition-level uncertainty. We propose \emph{in-distribution imagination} (IDI), a rollout control framework that estimates trajectory support in a learned representation space and adaptively truncates rollouts that leave the offline trajectory manifold. Combined with trajectory-regularized RL, an extension of entropy-regularized RL, IDI consistently improves performance in limited-data settings. Experiments show that trajectory support predicts rollout failure substantially better than transition-level uncertainty, highlighting the importance of trajectory-level rollout control in MBORL.
bullets: Addresses unrealistic synthetic data and unstable policy learning caused by cumulative model error.
Estimates trajectory support in a learned representation space to detect out-of-distribution rollouts.
Adaptively truncates imagined trajectories that depart from the offline trajectory manifold.
Combines rollout control with trajectory-regularized reinforcement learning.
Experiments show trajectory support predicts rollout failure better than transition-level uncertainty, especially in limited-data settings.
papers.selection_reason: Model-based offline RL with trajectory-level rollout control; directly relevant to action-conditioned world models.
papers.title: In-Distribution Imagination for Model-Based Offline Reinforcement Learning
papers.tldr: IDI improves offline model-based RL by stopping imagined rollouts when they leave the offline data’s trajectory manifold.

papers.abstract: Recent probabilistic weather forecasters train stochastic predictors with the continuous ranked probability score (CRPS) to generate each ensemble member in a single forward pass. These models learn the predictive distribution from the forecast context alone, which becomes difficult at longer forecast horizons where uncertainty is high. To learn the predictive distribution more effectively, we introduce auxiliary conditional denoising tasks that predict the same future state from the context and its corrupted version, which provides partial future information that can reduce prediction ambiguity. Building on distributional diffusion models, we learn the conditional distributions of these tasks with a single stochastic predictor by minimizing a proper scoring rule across noise levels. At inference, the predictor can still generate each ensemble member in a single forward pass at the fully corrupted endpoint. Standard CRPS training is recovered as the endpoint-only special case of our formulation, so our framework extends existing CRPS-based forecasters with only additional conditioning inputs. Controlled experiments show that the auxiliary tasks improve one-step forecasting across architectures, with larger gains at longer forecast horizons. The gains extend to high-dimensional global weather forecasting under both training from scratch and fine-tuning, along with improved calibration and potential benefits for generalization under distribution shift.
authors: Joonhyeong Park, Giung Nam, Hyungi Lee, Kyunghyun Cho, Byoungwoo Park, Juho Lee
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of learning highly uncertain predictive distributions at longer forecast horizons.
Uses auxiliary tasks that predict the future from context plus corrupted future information to reduce ambiguity during training.
Trains one stochastic predictor with a proper scoring rule across diffusion noise levels; standard CRPS is the endpoint-only special case.
Improves one-step forecasting across architectures, with larger gains at longer horizons, and extends to high-dimensional global forecasting.
Also reports improved calibration and potential robustness to distribution shift; gains are shown in controlled experiments and both scratch training and fine-tuning.
papers.selection_reason: Probabilistic diffusion-based forecasting of future environmental states; relevant to predictive world models.
papers.title: Proper Scoring Rule-based Diffusion for Probabilistic Weather Forecasting
papers.tldr: A diffusion-based proper-scoring-rule framework improves probabilistic weather forecasts by training with auxiliary partially informed denoising tasks while preserving single-pass ensemble generation.

papers.abstract: Learning partial differential equation (PDE) dynamics across varying domains is central to predictive modelling and data-driven discovery of governing equations. However, geometric variation alters both field representation and the governing differential operators, confounding geometric effects with intrinsic physical properties in the observed dynamics. This work identifies geometry-physics confounding as a unified failure mechanism for PDE learning across varying domains. In forward operator learning, this confounding increases the burden of inferring geometry-dependent operator changes from finite data, reducing data efficiency and generalisation. In equation discovery, omitting geometry-induced operators misspecifies the candidate library, leading to biased parameters, missed governing terms and spurious terms. We propose a de-confounding framework that makes the known geometry-to-operator transformation explicit. Geometry-induced coefficient fields improve prediction and data efficiency across five operator-learning benchmarks, while geometry-complete candidate libraries recover the generating equations and reduce held-out PDE residuals by more than two orders of magnitude in both evolving-domain systems. By separating known geometric action from intrinsic physics, the proposed framework supports more reliable and data-efficient PDE learning across scientific and engineering problems with varying geometries.
authors: Yinghao Cheng, Gengxiang Chen, Xu Liu, Qinglu Meng, Yixin Jing, Xiangguo Tang, Wenping Mou, Lihui Wang, Yingguang Li
bullets: Varying geometry changes both field representations and differential operators, obscuring intrinsic physical effects.
In operator learning, this confounding increases the data needed to infer geometry-dependent operator changes and harms generalization.
In equation discovery, incomplete candidate libraries can produce biased parameters, missed terms, and spurious terms.
The proposed framework explicitly represents known geometry-to-operator transformations through coefficient fields and geometry-complete libraries.
Across five operator-learning benchmarks and two evolving-domain systems, it improves data efficiency and reduces held-out PDE residuals by more than two orders of magnitude.
papers.selection_reason: Learned PDE dynamics across varying domains; de-confounding geometry from physics is transferable to predictive world models.
papers.title: Geometry-physics confounding impairs PDE learning across varying domains
papers.tldr: Geometry–physics confounding can undermine PDE learning on varying domains, while explicitly modeling geometry-induced operator changes improves prediction, equation recovery, and data efficiency.

papers.abstract: World models, game simulators, and long-take video creation require coherent scene evolution and sustained dynamics over extended durations. Autoregressive (AR) video diffusion provides a natural framework for long-horizon generation, yet extended rollouts often become near-static or lose visual quality. We hypothesize that these failures reflect the limited guidance provided by short-video supervision on how ongoing scene dynamics develops over longer durations. This motivates us to introduce LongTake, a two-stage training pipeline built around Long-Horizon Teacher Forcing (TF) on curated real long videos. Long-Horizon TF trains the AR model to predict later frames conditioned on long ground-truth video prefixes, extending direct supervision beyond the short training horizon. This supervision is designed to help the model sustain dynamics and preserve visual quality during long-horizon generation. Our central finding is that this training stage strengthens direct initialization for distribution matching distillation (DMD) under student self-rollout, without the intermediate few-step distillation stage used in standard pipelines. Under the same five-second DMD training setup, our initialization yields substantially higher dynamic degree than short horizon TF initialization on 30-second rollouts at comparable aesthetic quality, and surpasses the evaluated baselines in both measures. Hybrid DMD further reuses this teacher to extend supervision to later frames of the self-rollout while retaining bidirectional joint supervision over the initial window. On long-horizon self-rollouts, LongTake lies on the Pareto front of dynamic degree and aesthetic quality, and Hybrid DMD attains the highest dynamic degree among evaluated methods at both 30s and 60s.
authors: Byoungwoo Park, Jaemoo Choi, Juho Lee, Yongxin Chen
bullets: Addresses near-static scenes and quality degradation in long-horizon autoregressive video rollouts.
Uses Long-Horizon Teacher Forcing on curated real long videos to supervise predictions from extended ground-truth prefixes.
Provides stronger initialization for Distribution Matching Distillation without the usual intermediate few-step distillation stage.
Hybrid DMD extends supervision to later self-rolled-out frames while preserving joint supervision on the initial window.
Achieves the best reported dynamic degree at 30s and 60s, while maintaining competitive aesthetic quality among evaluated methods.
papers.selection_reason: Long-horizon autoregressive video diffusion with sustained dynamics directly targets video generation and world-model-style long-horizon prediction.
papers.title: LongTake: Learning to Sustain Dynamics in Long-Horizon Video Generation
papers.tldr: LongTake trains autoregressive video diffusion models with long-horizon supervision to sustain dynamic, high-quality generation over 30–60 seconds.

papers.abstract: Text- and image-conditioned world generators can create visually rich 3D environments, yet these worlds often remain silent or rely on soundtracks synthesized solely from text or rendered video. Although such audio can convey what should be heard, it lacks an explicit representation of where sound sources are located and how their perceived sound should vary with listener movement. We introduce Audible World Models, a training-free framework that incorporates sound into the generated world state. Starting from a text prompt, our system constructs a panoramic 3D proxy, separates it into semantic layers, identifies sound-producing foreground objects and ambient background regions, and synthesizes dry audio for each sound label. It then anchors these sources to reconstructed geometry and renders listener-dependent spatial audio using geometric acoustic propagation. By explicitly linking semantics, geometry, and sound propagation, the framework maintains persistent source locations while adapting the rendered audio to changes in listener viewpoint and motion. Experiments across 80 generated scenes demonstrate substantial gains in spatial consistency over text-, video-, and panorama-conditioned baselines, while preserving competitive semantic alignment. VLM-based assessments and human evaluations further indicate that our soundtracks are preferred for their audio-visual consistency, spatial plausibility, and motion-dependent behavior.
authors: Duowen Chen, Jinjin He, Gouthaman KV, Sandeep Bangalore Venkatesh, Bo Zhu
bullets: Addresses the lack of explicit sound-source location and motion-dependent audio in existing generated 3D environments.
Uses a training-free pipeline that builds a panoramic 3D proxy, separates semantic layers, and identifies foreground sound sources and ambient regions.
Synthesizes dry audio for sound labels, anchors sources to reconstructed geometry, and renders spatial audio as the listener moves.
Across 80 generated scenes, improves spatial consistency over text-, video-, and panorama-conditioned baselines while retaining competitive semantic alignment.
Human and VLM evaluations favor the results for audio-visual consistency, spatial plausibility, and motion-dependent behavior.
papers.selection_reason: Integrates spatially aware sound generation into 3D world models, linking semantics, geometry, and acoustic propagation. Relevant to world models and 3D generation.
papers.title: Audible World Models: Spatially Aware Sound Generation for 3D Worlds
papers.tldr: Audible World Models adds persistent, listener-dependent spatial sound to text-generated 3D worlds by linking semantic objects, reconstructed geometry, and acoustic propagation.

papers.abstract: Stochastic differential equations (SDEs) can be studied via It\^{o} calculus and rough path theory. For stochastic optimal control, these two frameworks give distinct Pontryagin Maximum Principle (PMP) optimality conditions with forward-backward SDEs (FBSDEs) or rough differential equations. We show that the adjoint equations of the It\^{o} and rough PMPs are connected via the conditional expectation $p_t^{\text{It\^{o}}}=\mathbb{E}[p_t^{\text{rough}} \mid \mathcal{F}_t]$, where $\mathcal{F}_t$ represents information available at time $t$. First, we derive a rough stochastic PMP for problems with adapted controls that does not use FBSDEs. Its proof extends the rough stochastic PMP over deterministic controls by considering stochastic needle variations. Second, we derive a unified PMP connecting the It\^{o} and rough PMPs, using It\^{o}-Stratonovich conversion formulas and duality identities between the forward tangent and backward adjoint SDEs. As a first application, we rederive the adjoint matching method for fine-tuning generative models. As a second application, we propose an indirect shooting method for a class of feedback problems. Overall, these results give a new conditional bridge connecting two popular frameworks for stochastic optimal control.
bullets: Derives a rough stochastic PMP for adapted controls without relying on forward-backward SDEs.
Establishes the relation p_t^Itô = E[p_t^rough | F_t] between Itô and rough adjoint equations.
Uses Itô–Stratonovich conversion and forward–backward duality to formulate a unified PMP.
Applies the framework to generative-model fine-tuning and an indirect shooting method for feedback control.
Provides a conditional bridge between two stochastic-control formalisms; the scope is the class of problems covered by the stated PMP assumptions.
papers.selection_reason: Connects stochastic optimal control theory (rough path and It	extsuperscript{o} frameworks) to generative models and feedback problems. This provides a theoretical bridge between control theory and generative AI, relevant to interactive world models.
papers.title: Unified Optimality Conditions for Stochastic Optimal Control in the Rough Path and It\^o Frameworks
papers.tldr: The paper unifies Pontryagin optimality conditions across Itô and rough-path stochastic control by linking their adjoint processes through conditional expectation.

papers.abstract: Local pedestrian-vehicle forecasting spans heterogeneous physical scales: pedestrians combine root locomotion with articulated motion, whereas vehicles are rigid bodies described by kinematic state and oriented extent. Existing road-agent forecasters typically omit pedestrian articulation, while pose forecasters leave vehicle futures outside the learned rollout. We introduce PV-WM, a history-only world model over structured post-perception tracks. It recurrently advances pedestrian root motion, 15-joint articulation, and learned vehicle states within a synchronized heterogeneous state. The generated pedestrian and vehicle chunks supply the next recurrent boundary; vehicle boxes are reconstructed from predicted center and heading with observed extent, and P-V geometry is recomputed after every transition. Relative to a matched one-shot complete-state predictor, recurrent execution reduces Root ADE by 12.7% and MPJPE by 14.8%. Feedback interventions show that later predictions depend on the content, temporal order, and pedestrian identity of generated articulation. Across 824 aligned Waymo contexts, with 797 providing valid future vehicle support, PV-WM reduces Root ADE by 5.2%, MPJPE by 7.6%, P-V distance error by 11.9%, and oriented-box closest-approach error by 5.8% relative to a validation-selected Modular Specialist. The single-network model uses 57.1% fewer parameters, 96.5% lower average FLOPs per local scene, and 25.5% lower measured p95 latency. PV-WM unifies this heterogeneous future state while preserving type-specific pedestrian and vehicle dynamics.
bullets: Addresses the gap between pedestrian pose forecasting and vehicle-inclusive road-agent prediction.
Recurrently predicts pedestrian root motion, 15-joint articulation, and vehicle kinematic states in a synchronized heterogeneous state.
Recomputes pedestrian–vehicle geometry after each transition and feeds generated motion back into subsequent predictions.
On 824 aligned Waymo contexts, it improves root, pose, distance, and closest-approach errors over a validation-selected modular specialist.
Uses 57.1% fewer parameters, 96.5% fewer average FLOPs, and 25.5% lower measured p95 latency than the specialist.
papers.selection_reason: Learned world model for heterogeneous pedestrian-vehicle dynamics directly fits world-model prediction of environment dynamics.
papers.title: PV-WM: A Heterogeneous Micro-Macro World Model for Articulated Pedestrian-Vehicle Co-Rollout
papers.tldr: PV-WM is a recurrent world model that jointly rolls out articulated pedestrians and vehicles, improving motion and interaction forecasting while using substantially less computation than a modular specialist.

papers.abstract: World-action models jointly learn robot policies and predict future observations, making the representation space an interface between control and prediction. We study the design of this space through controlled comparisons, finding that neither reconstruction fidelity nor pre-trained perceptual features alone ensure effective policy learning. These findings motivate ReWAM, a representation-centric world-action model built on pre-trained DINO features. Feature Calibration and a Temporal Representation Bottleneck organize these features into compact world states suited to dynamics modeling. Action-Grounded Representation Shaping routes only action-loss gradients to the bottleneck, thereby letting the policy shape what the representation encodes while the world model learns how it evolves. Without generative video pre-training, ReWAM achieves 93.6% success on RoboTwin 2.0. On RoboDojo, it achieves an average score of 12.29 and a success rate of 8.28% using approximately 600 hours of embodied pre-training data.
authors: Haoyi Jiang, Liu Liu, Xinjiang Wang, Zhihao Sun, Zequn Chen, Sen Wang, Xinjie Wang, Xia Chen, Jingfeng Yao, Weiheng Zhao, Shanglin Yuan, Zhizhong Su, Wei Sui, Wenyu Liu, Xinggang Wang
bullets: Reconstruction quality and pre-trained perceptual features alone do not guarantee effective policy learning.
ReWAM uses DINO features with Feature Calibration and a Temporal Representation Bottleneck to form compact world states.
Action-Grounded Representation Shaping lets policy gradients determine what the representation encodes while the world model learns its dynamics.
Without generative video pre-training, ReWAM reports 93.6% success on RoboTwin 2.0 and an average score of 12.29 with an 8.28% success rate on RoboDojo.
Evaluation is limited to the reported RoboTwin 2.0 and RoboDojo settings and approximately 600 hours of embodied pre-training data for RoboDojo.
papers.selection_reason: Representation-centric world-action model for robot policies and future-observation prediction.
papers.title: Rethinking Representations for World-Action Modeling
papers.tldr: ReWAM improves robot world-action modeling by shaping compact, action-relevant representations from pre-trained visual features.

papers.abstract: We introduce FracGen, a fracture-aware video generation model that produces plausible, controllable fracture dynamics from a single image of an intact object, conditioned on physics signals. To train FracGen, we build FracSim, a fracture-aware simulation framework that augments material point method (MPM) simulation with a continuum damage model, producing paired fracture videos and dense, pixel-aligned physical fields at no additional cost beyond standard rendering. FracGen leverages these maps in two ways: it is trained to jointly predict them alongside RGB video, encouraging the model to capture physical state rather than surface appearance; and it is supervised with physics-informed losses that encourage consistency among the predicted maps. As a result, FracGen captures distinct material-specific fracture behavior without expensive test-time simulation or per-scene tuning, while offering fine-grained control over where an object tears, how fast the crack propagates, and how much deformation precedes failure. We further introduce a benchmark for evaluating the physical plausibility of generated fracture video, and show through extensive experiments that FracGen outperforms existing video generation baselines in both physical and visual fidelity. Results are best viewed in our project website: https://fracgen.github.io/.
authors: Trong-Tung Nguyen, Jiahan Zhang, Anand Bhattad
bullets: Addresses the challenge of modeling material-specific fracture dynamics without costly test-time simulation or scene-specific tuning.
Introduces FracSim, an MPM-based fracture simulation framework that produces paired videos and dense physical fields.
Trains a video generator to jointly predict RGB frames and physical maps, with losses enforcing consistency among those maps.
Enables control over tear location, crack-propagation speed, and deformation before failure.
Experiments and a new benchmark show improved physical and visual fidelity over existing video-generation baselines.
papers.selection_reason: Physics-informed video generation of fracture dynamics with joint prediction of physical fields.
papers.title: FracGen: Learning How Objects Stretch and Tear with Physics-Informed Video Generation
papers.tldr: FracGen generates controllable, physically plausible object-stretching and tearing videos from a single intact-object image using physics-informed learning.

papers.abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE), popularized by large language models, is a promising paradigm for scaling visual generative models. However, conventional token-wise MoE routes tokens independently within a homogeneous expert pool and regularizes expert usage toward uniformity, making it poorly matched to video data that is spatiotemporally redundant and semantically long-tailed. We show that existing visual MoEs fall into a uniformity trap: semantically under-organized routing, compounded by uniform expert-usage regularization, scatters coherent patches across disparate experts, causing routing fragmentation and structural distortion. To address this, we propose SplitMoE, a split-role sparse architecture that breaks the shackles of uniformity. To accommodate the inherent semantic imbalance, we explicitly bifurcate the expert pool into semantic experts and generic experts, with semantic experts capturing high-level semantic abstraction and generic experts preserving residual visual information and flexible generative capacity. Leveraging prototype-guided routing and pull-push regularization, SplitMoE enables tokens to cluster naturally by semantic attributes rather than arbitrary balancing constraints. Extensive results show that under an equivalent activated-parameter budget, SplitMoE outperforms traditional load-balanced MoEs in convergence speed, routing coherence, and video generation quality across standard benchmarks. By revealing an emergent coarse-to-fine denoising logic, SplitMoE provides the community with a modality-aware scaling path, serving as a critical reference for building large-scale video world models.
authors: Yu Xu, Yuxin Zhang, Xiao Yang, Haotian Yang, Yizhi Wang, Xinwei Huang, Minxuan Lin, Angtian Wang, Chongyang Ma, Fan Tang
bullets: Conventional token-wise MoE routing scatters coherent video patches because it assumes homogeneous experts and uniform usage.
SplitMoE divides experts into semantic experts for high-level concepts and generic experts for residual visual details.
Prototype-guided routing and pull-push regularization encourage clustering by semantic attributes instead of forced load balance.
At an equivalent activated-parameter budget, it improves convergence speed, routing coherence, and video generation quality across standard benchmarks.
The method reveals a coarse-to-fine denoising pattern and offers a modality-aware scaling direction for video world models.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces SplitMoE, a novel architecture for scaling video diffusion models by addressing the uniformity trap, directly relevant to video generation and world model research.
papers.title: Breaking the Uniformity Trap: Scaling Video Diffusion Model via SplitMoE
papers.tldr: SplitMoE scales video diffusion models by separating semantic and generic experts, enabling more coherent routing and better generation than uniformly load-balanced MoEs.

papers.abstract: World simulation is inherently multisensory, demanding synchronized visual and acoustic dynamics in real time. Yet prevailing interactive world models remain strictly silent, focusing exclusively on visual rendering and control while overlooking the acoustic dimension. We present HelixWorld, a real-time interactive audio-visual world model where visual scenes and camera-grounded spatial stereo sound co-evolve natively under user interaction. We curate a high-fidelity spatial audio-visual dataset with true stereo acoustics and metric camera poses, upon which we pre-train a bidirectional teacher conditioned on 6-DoF camera trajectories and user actions. To enable low-latency causal interaction, we distill the teacher into a few-step streaming student via an online trajectory distillation loss, sustaining drift-free joint audio-visual rollouts at 24 FPS on a single GPU. Furthermore, we formalize spatial-acoustic consistency and introduce HelixBench to evaluate whether synthesized sound fields faithfully track dynamic viewpoint motion. Extensive experiments demonstrate that HelixWorld matches state-of-the-art silent world models in visual fidelity and responsiveness, while significantly surpassing existing baselines in camera-aligned spatial-acoustic immersion.
authors: Lei Ke, Jiahao Pan, Zeyue Tian, Jiaming Wang, Haoyuan Huang, Kam Man Wu, Pengjun Fang, Hongyu Liu, Chenyang Qi, Lin Wang, Ruibin Yuan, Weijia Chen, Fangneng Zhan, Qifeng Chen, Wei Xue, Yike Guo
bullets: Addresses the lack of acoustic dynamics in predominantly visual interactive world models.
Pre-trains a bidirectional teacher on spatial audio-visual data with 6-DoF camera trajectories and user actions.
Distills the teacher into a few-step streaming student for low-latency, drift-free joint rollouts at 24 FPS on a single GPU.
Introduces spatial-acoustic consistency and HelixBench to assess whether sound fields track camera motion.
Matches state-of-the-art silent models in visual fidelity and responsiveness while outperforming baselines in camera-aligned spatial-audio immersion.
papers.selection_reason: Real-time interactive audio-visual world model with user-action-conditioned spatial audio-visual rollouts.
papers.title: HelixWorld: A Real-time Interactive Audio-Visual World Model
papers.tldr: HelixWorld is a real-time interactive world model that jointly generates viewpoint-consistent visuals and spatial stereo audio as users navigate.

papers.abstract: Verifying a vision-based neural feedback system requires a model of the observations its controller acts upon. Such a model must capture the variation the sensor produces, while remaining tractable for closed-loop analysis. Generative adversarial networks (GANs) have served as perception surrogates, but they are large, reproduce complex scenes poorly, and are hard to verify. We explore stochastic world models as a richer class of perception surrogates. We train a world model with physically grounded latents, built from operations that standard verifiers bound. It reproduces held-out frames more faithfully than GAN surrogates with up to 130 times as many parameters. To verify these surrogates, we develop a procedure that combines falsification, adaptive refinement, symbolic, and backward analyses. On an emergency braking benchmark with a GAN surrogate, our procedure resolves the entire state space, 38% of which the state-of-the-art verifier left unresolved. On the RGB version of the benchmark, where no verification results have previously been reported, our procedure resolves over 80% of the state space with a world model surrogate.
authors: I. Samuel Akinwande, Mykel J. Kochenderfer, Clark Barrett
bullets: GAN perception surrogates are large, reproduce complex scenes poorly, and are hard to verify.
The paper trains stochastic world models using operations standard verifiers can bound.
The world model reproduces held-out frames more faithfully than GAN surrogates with up to 130× more parameters.
A new verification procedure combines falsification, adaptive refinement, symbolic, and backward analyses.
On an emergency braking benchmark, it resolves the entire state space, where the state-of-the-art verifier left 38% unresolved; on the RGB version, it resolves over 80% of the state space.
papers.selection_reason: Stochastic world models as perception surrogates predict environment frames for verification, fitting video world models.
papers.title: Stochastic World Models for Verifying Vision-Based Neural Feedback Systems
papers.tldr: Stochastic world models with physically grounded latents serve as more faithful and verifiable perception surrogates than GANs for verifying vision-based neural feedback systems.

papers.abstract: Behavior Foundation Models (BFMs) give humanoids a promptable policy over a latent behavior space, enabling one single vector to represent a motion to imitate, a pose to reach, or a reward to maximize. Forward-Backward representations successfully produce such spaces, but at the cost of hundreds of GPU-hours for a single robot. Moreover, when the training process is repeated for a second robot, it produces a second space unrelated to the first, resulting in embodiment-specific latents that do not unify or transfer. We address these problems with CrossBFM, treating the latent space as the transferable asset for various embodiments. As retargeting provides frame-level cross-embodiment correspondence, we propose a unified encoder architecture with no robot-specific parameters for distilling the behavior space to address all training embodiments simultaneously in less than a GPU-hour. Following this encoder, latent-conditioned trackers turn the distilled latent into whole-body control in a conventional PPO training manner in just 10 more GPU-hours. On three distilled humanoids, all three prompting modes transfer: motion tracking with latent-conditioned policy losing only $0.025$ rad to its joint-conditioned counterpart, smooth goal reaching between poses with no falls, and reward optimization for all $41$ reward prompts. Our experiments further reveal that 1) regressing the encoder on a quarter of the motion corpus costs only $5\%$ of tracking performance and 2) training the encoder on a subset of robots and evaluating on an unseen one recovers up to $89\%$ of the tracking performance of seen robots, demonstrating cross-embodiment generalization to morphologically similar robots. We also verify the pipeline on real robots across all three prompting modes and with flow-based generated latents. Project website: https://dotandung.github.io/crossbfm/
authors: Tan-Dzung Do, Tuan Dat Phuong, Nico Bohlinger, Cuc T. Trinh, Siwei Ju, Vien Anh Ngo, Jan Peters, Xinchao Wang, An T. Le
bullets: Addresses the high cost and embodiment-specific latent spaces of prior behavior foundation models.
Uses retargeting correspondences and a unified encoder with no robot-specific parameters to distill behaviors across robots in under an hour.
Trains latent-conditioned trackers with conventional PPO to convert shared latents into whole-body control.
Transfers motion tracking, pose reaching, and reward optimization across three humanoids, including all 41 reward prompts.
Shows robustness to reduced motion data and unseen, morphologically similar robots, and validates the pipeline on real robots.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes CrossBFM to distill a shared latent behavior space across different humanoid embodiments, enabling cross-embodiment generalization for motion tracking, goal reaching, and reward optimization.
papers.title: CrossBFM: Distilling a Shared Latent Behavior Space Across Humanoid Embodiments
papers.tldr: CrossBFM distills a shared, transferable behavior latent space across humanoid embodiments, enabling efficient cross-robot prompting and control.

papers.abstract: Interactive panoramic video generation aims to synthesize immersive 360\textdegree{} videos that remain visually coherent while following user-specified camera trajectories during exploration. However, progress is limited by a coupled data-and-model gap: existing panoramic video datasets are often short, weakly annotated, or lack camera trajectories, while existing camera-controlled video generation models are designed for perspective videos and do not directly support panoramic geometry. In this paper, we introduce MUGEN and Wan360 to address these limitations. MUGEN is a large-scale real-world panoramic video dataset tailored to interactive 360-degree world exploration, comprising over 1,300 hours of at least 4K panoramic videos with rich semantic and geometric annotations. Built on MUGEN, we further present Wan360, a camera-controllable interactive panoramic video generation model. Panoramic videos are commonly represented by EquiRectangular Projection (ERP), which unfolds a spherical 360-degree view into a rectangular frame with cyclic longitude seams and pole distortions. To this end, Wan360 introduces three parameter-free ERP-aware components: periodic longitude RoPE for seam-consistent positional encoding, ERP-aware padding for reducing boundary artifacts, and random roll yaw for consistent learning. For camera control, Wan360 uses a panoramic Pl\"ucker embedding that represents camera motion with ERP rays rather than perspective pinhole rays. Experiments show that MUGEN serves as a data foundation for panoramic world exploration, and that Wan360 enables high-quality, temporally coherent, camera-controllable 360-degree video generation.
authors: Jiaming Tan, Zhen Li, Shuwei Shi, Minggui Teng, Siqi Yang, Yuwei Wu, Bo Zheng, Chuanhao Li, Kaipeng Zhang
bullets: Addresses the lack of large, richly annotated panoramic video data and models that support camera control under panoramic geometry.
MUGEN provides over 1,300 hours of at least 4K real-world panoramic videos with semantic and geometric annotations.
Wan360 introduces ERP-aware components for seam consistency, reduced boundary artifacts, and robust panoramic learning.
A panoramic Plücker embedding represents camera motion using ERP rays instead of perspective pinhole rays.
Experiments demonstrate high-quality, temporally coherent, camera-controllable panoramic video generation.
papers.selection_reason: Camera-controllable 360-degree video generation for interactive world exploration; fits video generation and interactive world models.
papers.title: MUGEN: Interactive Panoramic World Exploration via Camera Control
papers.tldr: MUGEN and Wan360 enable high-quality, temporally coherent 360° video generation guided by user camera trajectories.

papers.abstract: Real-world robot learning is constrained by the cost of collecting experience and evaluating candidate behaviors. Video generation models offer a scalable foundation for visual simulators that predict action outcomes before physical execution. Yet they often favor visual plausibility over accurate action following and coherent robot--object dynamics, while action-conditioned simulators depend on scarce, embodiment-specific data that are difficult to share across incompatible control spaces. We introduce WorldLine, an action-driven visual simulator that decouples transferable dynamics learning from heterogeneous action grounding. WorldLine learns manipulation dynamics from more than 10,000 hours of action-free robot videos and grounds them using over 2,000 hours of action trajectories across more than ten embodiments.
